The London office, the empty boxes and the £1bn tax loophole

From the outside, the seven-storey building at 2 America Square looks like any other office block in the heart of London’s financial district. Located about half a mile from Tower Bridge, one might expect it to be a hive of commercial activity, teeming with employees holding important meetings. However, much of the property is home not to staff vying for their next bonus, but to stacks of nondescript black boxes arranged in neat lines. The building, leased by a Virgin Islands-based company called 48th Street Holdings Ltd, has found itself at the centre of a court case that has finally signalled the end of a tax avoidance scheme believed to have cost local authorities more than £1bn. For almost two decades, companies in England have been exploiting a legal loophole to avoid paying business rates on unoccupied commercial buildings. The controversial practice dates back to 2008, when the last Labour government changed business rates rules. This meant occupiers of vacant buildings no longer qualified for a 50% discount on the levy.

citation.title: The London office, the empty boxes and the £1bn tax loophole

text:
The London office, the empty boxes and the £1bn tax loophole

However, they were entitled to claim a three-month rate holiday at the end of each tenancy – and the “box shifting” scheme was born. With commercial property owners facing higher bills, a lucrative “rate mitigation” industry emerged. Historically, this typically involved boxes being moved into the empty space at the end of the three months and back out after just six weeks. The building then became unoccupied again and the clock was reset, allowing the owner to claim another three-month rate-free period. This cycle continued, designed to cut the rates owed by up to 67%, until a new long-term tenant could be found. It has been costing one London council an estimated £35m a year since the pandemic, when the number of claims for empty property relief doubled. However, last month a landmark ruling by three court of appeal judges looks to have sounded the death knell for box shifting. They ruled that the scheme “cannot amount to beneficial occupation”.

citation.title: The London office, the empty boxes and the £1bn tax loophole

text:
The London office, the empty boxes and the £1bn tax loophole

Interactive The case was brought by the City of London Corporation against 48th Street Holding Ltd and a second company, Principled Offsite Logistics Ltd (POLL), which provides “rate mitigation” services. 48th Street paid £27.6m for a lease on the office block in 2019 before it brought in POLL to save £111,475.30 in rates across a series of three-month periods in 2022 and 2023. POLL describes itself as “the largest and most reliable” provider of “empty business rates mitigation” in the UK and is jointly owned by a Labour councillor from North Hertfordshire. It claimed by 2021 to have already saved its clients “£500m” in rates and that “every council in the UK now totally recognises Principled as being robust in every way”. That bold claim followed a significant high court win in 2018, when POLL defeated a challenge from Trafford council. The judge in that case accepted that “the purpose of the occupation is not to store goods; it is, so to speak, to plant the occupier’s flag” and that “the motive … is rates avoidance for the landlord”, but added “the morality of that is neither here nor there”.

When the case against POLL and 48th Street came before the high court last year, Charles Bagot KC, sitting as a deputy high court judge, also ruled against the City of London. “I agree with POLL that if legislation produces clear tramlines and someone organises themselves to fall within them, then it is not for the court to get involved in moral judgments,” he said. “If the government does not like the position, it can amend it.” He concluded that “the RMS [rate mitigation scheme] is effective”. However, last month the court of appeal overturned that decision, with Lady Justice Falk ruling: “In my judgment, ‘occupation’ for, in effect, the sake of it, and which has no use, value or benefit other than rate saving, does not amount to occupation for the purpose of the statutory scheme.” A City of London Corporation spokesperson said: “We welcome the court of appeal’s decision, which represents a significant victory for local authorities across England. “This landmark ruling closes one of the most widely used tax avoidance schemes in the country and helps safeguard revenues that support essential public services.

UK households will take £2,400 financial hit from Iran war, analysis shows

UK households will have suffered a £2,400 financial hit, on average, from the Iran war by the end of 2027, new analysis shows. The Centre for Economics and Business Research (CEBR) has calculated that the jump in inflation since the conflict began, and weaker wage growth, will knock £1,100 off the real income of the average UK household in 2026, and by a further £1,300 in 2027. This adds up to a total of £70.4bn that will be wiped off UK households’ real disposable incomes by the Middle East conflict, according to the CEBR, an economic consultancy. Related: New UK cost of living crisis looms with soaring energy bills forecast to lift inflation The economic shock from the closure of the Strait of Hormuz hits UK households through two channels. “The first is direct: higher energy costs feed straight into bills and into the price of almost everything else, so each pound of pay buys less,” explained the CEBR senior economist, Liam Daly.

Is the government really on an ‘out-of-control’ spending splurge? It’s complicated

“Will the prime minister acknowledge reality … and admit Labor’s out-of-control spending is forcing families and small businesses to pay more for everything?” That was the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, kicking off parliamentary question time on Wednesday. The line of attack was no surprise. Official data earlier that day showed inflation jumped to 4.3% in the year to September, from 4% the month before. Rapid petrol and diesel price increases drove that high headline figure. But, even removing the impact of soaring fuel prices, underlying inflation ticked higher to 3.7% by the quarterly measure. Both measures are way above the Reserve Bank’s 2.5% target – and a fifth interest rate hike on Tuesday looks like a done deal. Frustrated Australians are increasingly inclined to believe Taylor’s argument. So how much has government spending been rising? Should we blame climbing public expenditure for the cost of living crisis? And what should the government do about it? Is the government spending more? The simple answer is: yes.

The first is defence, amid pressure on governments around the world to respond to an increasingly fraught geopolitical reality. The second is the national disability insurance scheme (NDIS). text:
‘We’re doomed anyway’: young people disheartened about the future are splashing out on the present

An Tran treats herself to experiences like concerts and movie tickets. The 21-year-old Sydney law student, who is working towards paying her tuition fees, says many of her friends spend their spare money on matcha, Labubu toys and trending makeup items. Tran, who moved from Vietnam two years ago, says she appreciates what she has in Australia but can understand why young people like her are concerned about the future. “We feel like we’re doomed anyway so why should we save?” she says. Related: Albanese concedes savings needed as he faces internal Labor pressure on cost-of-living crisis Young people feeling disheartened about the economy are choosing to spend their money in the present – regularly buying “little treats” such as takeaway coffees or even “doomspending” if it feels like there’s no point saving for the future. “If we believe in the future, we are much more likely to be able to defer gratification in the pursuit of it,” says brand strategist Eugene Healey.

citation.title: ‘We’re doomed anyway’: young people disheartened about the future are splashing out on the present

text:
‘We’re doomed anyway’: young people disheartened about the future are splashing out on the present

Healey says “little treat” culture – a pattern of consumer behaviour where people, especially younger people, buy “affordable, everyday luxuries” like matcha or lunch – has come about because traditional milestones feel out of reach. The rationale works like this: buying an $8 matcha five days a week for 48 weeks works out to $1,920 a year. Even if you saved that money, the median house price in Australia’s capital cities combined is now $1.1m and the median unit price $738,778, according to Cotality research published this month. Saving $40 a week and not getting to have a matcha during the work day may not seem worth it if even a 10% deposit feels out of reach and future job security is uncertain – especially amid the disruption to white collar industries caused by AI. The average homebuyer nationally needs to save more than eight years for a deposit, and more than nine years in Sydney. A recent report from realestate.com.au found that a typical household earning $125,000 a year could only afford 12% of the homes for sale across the country – also a historical low with the previous low watermark being 14% in 2008. Australians on lower incomes are virtually shut out of the market. The analysis showed that a household earning $76,000 could afford just 2% of homes on the market. Meanwhile, workers’ wages have barely kept up with inflation since cost of living exploded from 2022, making it harder to save. Healey says the social contract, where working hard and saving for the future ensured you would get ahead, has broken down. “Not only are you paying into the system with superannuation, but there is no guarantee now that if you do well in school, get a relatively good job [and] accrue university debt, that you’re going to be able to enjoy … even a fraction of the prosperity that previous generations took for granted,” he says.

Healey says doomspending is “perhaps a more advanced version or symptom of the same underlying feeling”. Cambridge dictionary, which began tracking the word last year, defines doomspending as spending money that you cannot afford in order to make yourself feel better, which people sometimes engage in when they feel anxious and uncertain about the future. “It’s not merely just, ‘Oh, things are a little expensive here and there [and] the major things are expensive, I deserve a little treat,’” Healey says. “It’s a quite significant paradigm shift [to]: ‘I don’t believe in what the future is going to look like any more … It’s much more rational for me to spend that money in the present and to enjoy what I have in front of me.’” Related: Electricity, insurance and eggs: see how life in Australia has got more expensive Terry Rawnsley, a senior economist at KPMG, says it is a “perfectly rational decision” to spend money on things that make you happy now, when the alternative – buying a home in the future – is unattainable.

Boots owner ‘closing in on sale to Canada’s Weston family for $9bn’

The private equity owner of high street pharmacy Boots is reportedly closing in on a deal to sell the business to the Canadian branch of the billionaire Weston family for $9bn (£7bn). Sycamore Partners, which bought the wider Walgreens Boots Alliance for $23.7bn in 2025, is said to be in advanced talks with the Westons, with the Financial Times reporting that a deal could be completed as soon as next week. If successful, it would mark the return of the Canadian branch of the Weston family to the UK high street, having previously owned Selfridges. Related: Greggs announces plans to shut four UK factories that could cost 740 jobs The family later sold the department store chain for £4bn in 2022. The Westons are widely known throughout Canada for owning the grocery store Loblaws and the pharmacy chain Shoppers Drug Mart. The UK branch of the family, which operates its businesses through a separate investment vehicle, is known for holding a majority stake in Primark through the parent company Associated British Foods.

Britain in talks with European allies over release of emergency diesel stockpiles amid Trump pressure

Britain is in talks with European allies over releasing emergency diesel stockpiles after Donald Trump threatened to cut off US supplies of the fuel. Ministers held calls with counterparts from the European Commission (EC), Germany, France, Italy and Ireland on Thursday to discuss whether to draw down reserves after the Trump administration told Germany and France to release their stockpiles to help ease soaring global energy prices or face a US export ban. The warning marks an escalation of pressure on Europe as Trump considers a potential wider ban to help lower domestic fuel prices before the US midterm elections in November. Trump said Washington could ask its European allies to release strategic diesel reserves. “We may do that. They have some diesel,” Trump told reporters on a midterm elections campaign trip to Texas, shortly after the Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, urged Europe to “immediately” release its reserves.

Crude oil exports from strait of Hormuz largely return to pre-war levels

Exports of crude from the strait of Hormuz have largely returned to levels seen before the outbreak of the Iran war, as oil producers and the shipping industry have found alternative ways of transporting crucial fuel out of the Middle East. Pipeline exports and ship-to-ship transfers are among the methods being used, according to analysts tracking the situation, while the US military continues to escort some vessels. However, flows of refined products such as diesel remain constrained, pushing prices higher. At least 16.5m barrels per day (bpd) left the region in September, according to figures from the global trade intelligence firm Kpler, equalling the pre-war average, excluding Iran. The figure is 10.5m bpd higher than the monthly average for March, during the first weeks of the Iran war. Interactive Since the conflict began on 28 February with US and Israeli strikes on Iran, Tehran has sought to exert its authority on the strait of Hormuz and has at times even declared the strategic waterway closed.

citation.title: Crude oil exports from strait of Hormuz largely return to pre-war levels

text:
Crude oil exports from strait of Hormuz largely return to pre-war levels

However, Iran’s control appears to have declined in recent weeks, as oil exporters have found workarounds to address the disruption. About 40% of the region’s crude is now transported without transiting the strait, compared with just 17% before the war, through Saudi and Emirati pipelines, according to Kpler analysis. Saudi Arabia was able to restart operations on its east-west pipeline in late September, after it was damaged during drone attacks, allowing exports from resume from the Red Sea port of Yanbu. In a sign of the other adaptations, the majority of crude transported through the strait of Hormuz is carried on a shuttle fleet mostly comprising very large crude carriers, sailing with their satellite transponders turned off. The cargo is moved on to different tankers in open water, usually off the coast of Oman or Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates. More than 70% of the crude that passed through the strait in August changed tankers, whereas before the war almost no Gulf crude changed ships in the Gulf of Oman.

However, the recovery in exports from the region remains unbalanced, and supplies of refined products remain constrained. This poses a problem for businesses and households that depend on refined products such as diesel to run their cars, vans and lorries. The average diesel price in the UK hit an all-time high of 199.18p a litre on Monday, with many motorists already reporting prices above £2 on some forecourts. “Diesel carries the sharpest risk,” said Kpler analysts, who found that less than 20% of pre-war levels of refined products shipped through Hormuz were being transported. They recorded a seven-day average of 677,000 bpd of refined products as of Monday, compared with 3.6m before the conflict. Even as oil exports from the region have increased, the level of threat to ships operating around the strait of Hormuz has not disappeared. “New routes emerge, cargos are rerouted, risk is priced in and absorbed. The danger is assuming that resilience equals security. It doesn’t,” said Richard Meade, the editor in chief of shipping publication Lloyd’s List.

Should cockpits stay locked from the inside? Flydubai stabbing raises flight security questions

Cockpit security on planes will come under renewed scrutiny after passengers and one wounded pilot joined forces to prevent flydubai flight FZ 1073 from crashing. With more than 170 people, mostly Israeli, on board the jet heading from Dubai to Tel Aviv, some have spoken of averting “Israel’s 9/11”. However, the changes made to plane design after the terrorist hijackings in the US a quarter of a century ago, locking cockpit doors from the inside, have divided expert opinion. Wednesday’s events, during which one pilot stabbed another and apparently tried to crash the plane, again raises the question of where the biggest threat lies. Related: Motive behind flydubai cockpit stabbing unknown as international investigation opens “We have as an industry lost more lives on commercial aircraft as a result of aircraft-assisted suicide since 9/11 than we have due to terrorism,” says Philip Baum, an international aviation security expert.

“And in most of those cases, it was because we had created a fortress that could not be broken into by the good guys who were outside the flight deck to neutralise the rogue individuals – usually pilots inside the cockpit.” On the flydubai flight, despite being stabbed, the captain Smit Machchhar managed to resist his attacker, the unnamed Omani co-pilot. Crucially, Machchhar was also able to ensure help reached him from the cabin by making sure the doors could be breached. Two pilots are normally required on deck under safety rules – primarily discussed for if one gets sick, rather than goes rogue. Since 9/11, commercial aircraft have also had locked doors in place where the pilot effectively holds the key. The configuration of locks can vary and while crew have access codes for emergencies, the pilot can normally override attempts to gain access – a system designed with hijackers in mind.

The crash of Germanwings flight 4U9525 in 2015 was, perhaps until this week, the most incontrovertible demonstration of the danger it posed: the captain locked out by a suicidal co-pilot who deliberately crashed the plane in the Alps, killing 150 people. It had been preceded by a smaller and less reported Mozambique Airlines plane crash in 2013, killing 33, that was judged by investigators to have been suicide by pilot, with the co-pilot apparently locked out. Questions also remain over the role of pilot intent in major disasters whose causes have yet to be proved – not least the mystery of Malaysia Airilnes flight MH370, as well as the Air India crash in Ahmedabad in 2025, or China Eastern in 2022. Without malign intent, doors can be opened in incidents of “pilot incapacitation”, such as heart attacks. A Lufthansa plane flew for 10 minutes over Spain in 2024 with no one at the controls when the captain went to the bathroom and was locked out of the cabin after the co-pilot blacked out.

But preserving security begins well before the cockpit doors: “The primary method is to ensure that the people that you are employing have gone through extensive background checks, gone through medicals, psychological appraisals – and that that process doesn’t stop once employment commences.” With the motives of the Omani co-pilot in the latest attack still as yet unknown, Israel is introducing measures to do greater background screening of pilots, while flydubai has cancelled further Tel Aviv flights and British ministers have said they will “be looking at” the safety of flights to Israel. US borrowing costs hit 24-year high as global bond sell-off intensifies

The global bond sell-off intensified on Thursday, driving 10-year US government borrowing costs to their highest level in 24 years in a frantic day’s trading. The threat of a renewed round of inflation from the persistently high cost of oil has spooked investors on both sides of the Atlantic, with central banks expected to raise interest rates in the coming months to prevent price increases from becoming embedded. The sell-off drove the yield, or interest rate, on 10-year US Treasuries to 5.34% – the highest level since 2002. In the UK, where surging borrowing costs are increasing the pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, before his first budget later this month, the yield on 30-year bonds hit 6% for the first time since 1998, before easing slightly later in the day. Yields on five- and 10-year UK bonds were also up. Related: Good news in US inflation report boosts chances Fed won’t hike rates Stock market investors sold heavily too, knocking almost 1.7% off the FTSE 100 in London – its worst daily fall since May.

US bonds weakened despite inflation data on Wednesday coming in lower than forecast, which was expected to calm investors’ nerves about the prospect of further increases in the cost of borrowing by the US Federal Reserve. Travelodge guests are still at risk, finds review launched after sexual assault

An independent review into Travelodge after a serious sexual assault has found that guests are still at risk, with room intrusions reported at nearly one in 10 of its hotels this summer. The damning findings were published in a 70-page report on Thursday, which was commissioned earlier this year after a man was convicted of a serious sexual assault against a Travelodge guest in Maidenhead in 2022. The perpetrator was handed a copy of the victim’s room key, having falsely claimed to be her boyfriend, and sexually assaulted her in her hotel bed. The victim – referred to as “Lily” in the report – was later offered what she described as an “insulting” £30 refund. The incident prompted further reports of security failings at the hotel chain, eventually leading to the resignation of Joanna Boydell as chief executive in August.

UK airlines to be banned from charging parents to sit with children

Airlines will be blocked from charging parents extra to sit with their children on planes, according to government plans. The new rule would require airlines to seat passengers aged under 14 next to their parents or an accompanying adult free of charge. Passengers will also no longer need to pay to tweak the name on their flight booking if they need to correct a mistake. It is understood that ministers will try to introduce the changes before the start of next year’s summer holidays. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said the rule changes are part of a crackdown on the “little charges that add up” when families plan their holidays. MPs are in the process of debating a new set of rules for travel companies, as the civil aviation (consumer protection and regulatory reform) bill makes its way through parliament. The proposed law will give ministers flexible power to set out passenger rights and the duties of airlines and airports.

Bosses of three firms that supply trains to UK railways made £3.5m last year

The chief executives of three firms that rent out trains to Britain’s railways were paid a combined £3.5m last year as they passed on almost £400m to shareholders in dividends. Rail unions accused the rolling stock companies (Roscos) of raking in profits at passengers’ expense. The figures emerged in accounts published this week after ministers announced a new rolling stock strategy for Britain’s railways. The government is considering direct ownership of trains through the public body Great British Railways rather than leasing them from the private sector. The latest figures show Porterbrook Holdings paid £80m in dividends and increased the pay of its chief executive, Mary Grant, by more than 10% to £1.44m. Eversholt Rail paid out £200m in 2025 shortly before it was sold by CK Hutchison to Beacon Rail, with its departing CEO, Mary Kenny, paid £1.33m. Angel Trains paid £111m in dividends and a relatively modest £700,000 to its boss, Malcolm Brown. Their pay far outstrips the highest salaries elsewhere on the railway, including the bosses of Network Rail and HS2.

G7 to release up to 100m barrels of emergency oil and diesel reserves

Leaders of G7 nations are to release up to 100m barrels of their emergency diesel and crude oil stockpiles after Donald Trump threatened to cut off supplies of US diesel. The French President, Emmanuel Macron, said ministers from some of world’s largest economies had agreed to release stocks from their strategic oil reserves after crisis talks on Friday. Macron convened the leaders’ video call to discuss the global surge in diesel prices, and Trump’s threat to cut off US diesel exports unless Europe tapped their own stockpiles to help cool global markets. Under proposals reportedly drawn up by Macron, the current G7 chair, members will release 50m barrels of diesel and 50m of crude oil into the global market to ease prices. The agreement suggests European countries will avoid being cut off from vital supplies of US diesel after coming under pressure from the White House in recent days to release their emergency supplies or face a US diesel export ban.

He added that the G7 members and partners would front-load a substantial diesel release within the first 20 days and that ministers would discuss the “possibility of additional diesel releases as necessary” in the coming days. “We have all committed together to releasing these strategic reserves in the proportions I mentioned, with a focus on diesel, and we are all committed to ensuring there are no export bans, and President Trump, in particular, was very clear on this point,” Macron said. text:
John Maynard Keynes: the cultured economist who governments turn to in a crisis

The sound of guns from the advancing German armies could be heard clearly by John Maynard Keynes as his train trundled across northern France in the spring of 1918. The evidence of the struggle on the western front was everywhere but Keynes, then a Treasury official, was not heading to Paris on war business; he was off to buy some art. Keynes made the risky trip to attend an auction of the studio of Edgar Degas, who had died the previous year. The man who would become the foremost economist of the 20th century returned to London with some impressionist treasures for the National Gallery, having successfully petitioned the chancellor of the exchequer to spend £20,000 at the sale. This story reveals much about Keynes. His skill in lobbying officialdom for funds at a time when the country was involved in a costly war. His love of art, which culminated in him being instrumental in setting up the Arts Council. His conviction that economics mattered less than the good things in life. All of which makes the title of James Graham’s new play about Keynes, The Standard of Living, wholly appropriate.

citation.title: John Maynard Keynes: the cultured economist who governments turn to in a crisis

text:
John Maynard Keynes: the cultured economist who governments turn to in a crisis

Keynes pored over statistics but was much more than a number cruncher. He had firm views about why the economy was malfunctioning in the 1920s and 1930s, but was just as interested in discussing philosophy with Bertrand Russell and Ludwig Wittgenstein. He believed a growing economy should provide the opportunity for more leisure time rather than the accumulation of monetary wealth. He revolutionised economics without having a revolutionary bone in his body. Born into a well-off academic family, Keynes went to Eton before studying maths at Cambridge. His circle of friends after university was the Bloomsbury Group, painters and writers who included Virginia Woolf, and two of his lovers, Lytton Strachey and Duncan Grant. This was a group that prided itself on being unconventional, on not accepting the status quo. Bloomsbury helped satisfy Keynes’s cultural needs but also helped shape his economic thinking. He did not see growth as an end in itself but rather as a means to live the good life or – as he put it – to live like the “lilies in the field”.

citation.title: John Maynard Keynes: the cultured economist who governments turn to in a crisis

text:
John Maynard Keynes: the cultured economist who governments turn to in a crisis

In Economic Possibilities for Our Grandchildren he foresaw a time when the economic problem had been solved, when the working week would be considerably shorter and “when the accumulation of wealth was no longer of high social importance”. His willingness to challenge the orthodoxy was demonstrated in an early book, The Economic Consequences of the Peace, which correctly predicted that the punitive terms imposed by the treaty of Versailles in 1919 would result in a humiliated Germany remaining bitter and vengeful. To the surprise of his Bloomsbury friends, Keynes later fell in love with a Russian ballet dancer, Lydia Lopokova, and the couple married in 1925 when he was 42. While forthright and confident when expressing his opinions, Keynes was self-conscious about his appearance, considering himself repulsive. Others agreed. Virginia Woolf once described him as like “a gorged seal, double chin, ledge of red lip, little eyes, sensual, brutal, unimaginative”. One of the central themes of the play is the battle of ideas between Keynes and the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek.

citation.title: John Maynard Keynes: the cultured economist who governments turn to in a crisis

text:
John Maynard Keynes: the cultured economist who governments turn to in a crisis

The latter believed that left to their own devices, free markets provided the best economic outcomes and that over the long term crises would be resolved without the need for state intervention. Keynes took the opposite view, summed up by perhaps his most famous quote: “In the long run we are all dead. Economists set themselves too easy, too useless a task if in tempestuous seasons they can only tell us that when the storm is long past the ocean is flat again.” By this he meant that the economy had no natural tendency towards full employment. Rather, high unemployment could last indefinitely unless the government was prepared to step in and stimulate demand. This argument formed the centrepiece of his most famous book, The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money. The General Theory, as it is commonly known, challenged conventional economic thinking and had a profound influence on policymakers in the decades after the second world war, when it was seen as the responsibility of governments to manage demand to secure full employment.

citation.title: John Maynard Keynes: the cultured economist who governments turn to in a crisis

text:
John Maynard Keynes: the cultured economist who governments turn to in a crisis

Keynes saw the many flaws in the capitalist system but was no Marxist. As an unashamed elitist, he saw it as his mission to save capitalism from itself, if only because he saw it as the best way to safeguard civilised values. “He is contemptuous of common men, especially when gathered together in herds,” the social reformer Beatrice Webb once observed. “He dislikes the human herd and has no desire to enlist the human herd on his side.” Unsurprisingly, the hard left have their suspicions about Keynes. As his biographer Robert Skidelsky wrote: “Marxists have long argued that Keynes’s ideas were taken up because they served the interests of the bourgeoisie in the 1930s and were dropped when they started to endanger capitalist profits in the 1970s.” It is certainly true that Keynes and his ideas fell out of fashion by the mid-1970s, a period when western economies were afflicted by rising inflation and weak growth at the same time.

citation.title: John Maynard Keynes: the cultured economist who governments turn to in a crisis

text:
John Maynard Keynes: the cultured economist who governments turn to in a crisis

Postwar Keynesian economists were baffled by the appearance of high inflation and high unemployment at the same time, and the new right – spearheaded politically by Margaret Thatcher and Ronald Reagan – emerged victorious from this era of “stagflation”. Inspired by Hayek’s ideas, it set about dismantling the postwar settlement based on full employment, state ownership, strong trade unions and generous welfare spending. Related: Can a ballerina do a stomp? Natalia Osipova on making her fearsome, foul-mouthed acting debut The 2008 global financial crisis saw the new right model come to grief. A belief that markets could never be wrong meant the dangers of excessive speculation were ignored and ultimately left the global banking system teetering on the point of collapse. For the first time since the 1930s there was a real risk of a full-scale depression and in those circumstances policymakers dusted down their copies of The General Theory in the search for a response. Keynes would have sensed a financial crisis was coming. He speculated on the financial markets, not always successfully.

citation.title: John Maynard Keynes: the cultured economist who governments turn to in a crisis

text:
John Maynard Keynes: the cultured economist who governments turn to in a crisis

In 1920, he created what would be today called a heavily leveraged hedge fund using money provided by his Bloomsbury friends – taking bets on currency movements – only to see his syndicate’s capital wiped out when the pound unexpectedly fell. Even so, he was aware of the risks. “Speculators may do no harm as bubbles on a steady stream of enterprise,” he said. “But the position is serious when enterprise becomes the bubble on a whirlpool of speculation. When the capital development of a country becomes the byproduct of the activities of a casino, the job is likely to be ill done.” Today, Keynes and Hayek are still revered by their followers on the political left and right respectively. US added just 29,000 jobs in September in sharp drop from last month’s gains

US employers added just 29,000 jobs in September, a sharp drop from last month’s gains, and unemployment rose slightly to 4.2%, a sign of a cooling labor market in the final jobs report before the midterm election. The numbers were under half of economists’ expectations of just under 70,000 new jobs. Most job gains were concentrated in the healthcare industry, which added 17,000 new jobs, while the information, financial and professional industries saw losses, according to the latest data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics. Earlier jobs figures were also revised down: Initial reports from July and August altogether dropped by 60,000. The labor market contracted by 10,000 jobs in July after revisions, while August saw 133,000 jobs added. Growth in average hourly earnings slumped to 3%, the lowest rate in over five years. The unemployment rate has remained relatively steady since last year, when it hit 4.5% in November. US jobless claims also inched lower for the fourth week in a row, the labor department said on Thursday.

US lawmakers have urged Starbucks to close newly opened outlets in China’s Xinjiang, saying it was a “morally bankrupt decision” to operate in a region where Beijing has been accused of widespread human rights abuses against Muslim minorities. Tesco has become the first supermarket to introduce paid “safe leave” for victims of domestic abuse, giving staff dedicated time to access support, secure their safety and take steps to move on with their lives. The UK’s largest private-sector employer is offering up to three days of paid leave which can be taken flexibly for activities such as attending court hearings, arranging emergency accommodation, changing locks, securing childcare or separating finances. Managers across the business, which employs 300,000 people, have also been trained to spot the signs of domestic abuse, support those affected and flag them to specialist services. Under the new policy, which was developed in partnership with the shopworkers’ union Usdaw, Tesco will not ask those suffering abuse to provide formal evidence to gain access to the special leave.

Utilities are public services – and should not be run as businesses

Will Hutton and Andy Haldane advocate “turning [utilities] into public-benefit companies with a primary, constitutional objective of delivering high-quality services, with profitability subordinate to that broader aim” (Andy Burnham talks about ‘public control’ of the utilities but it’s a minefield. Utilities should not be run as businesses but as essential public services. They do not function in isolation, and business models are unsuited to their functioning in the public interest. They have social and environmental as well as economic responsibilities that have to be met. For 20 years, prior to the advent of the Scottish parliament, local government functioned well in Scotland within a framework of regions and districts. The regions had powers and responsibilities for the wide range of functions that had to be coordinated and operated strategically at the regional level. They included water and sewerage.

Andy Burnham said he wanted to “rewire” the economy. Then he seemed to slam on the brakes, kicking most reforms into the 2030s. Local government reorganisation is on hold, along with an overhaul of the much-maligned water industry. Social care and significant welfare reform are matters to be resolved by the next government. A delay is understandable when the issues are knotty and plans on the left to replace the word “rewire” with “renationalise”, stir up accusations of taking Britain back to the 1970s. And yet delay is unnecessary when the knowledge is available now to get on with the kind of changes that rebuild public trust in time for a 2029 election. There are oblique ways of achieving success, and the measure of success should be customer satisfaction. Without this aim, the hopes of reform are lost. BT has been accused of “bullying” customers by temporarily cutting off their broadband to pressure them to upgrade to a digital landline, as providers race to switch households over before the January deadline. Telecoms companies have so far migrated 16-17m lines from the old copper network to digital voice over internet protocol (VoiP), which uses a broadband connection instead, in the biggest technological upgrade since the early 00s, when analogue TV was switched off. More than 80% of the previously unresponsive customers are understood to have subsequently taken the steps needed to switch over. “Throughout this transformation BT has been raising awareness of the switchover, supported by local events, advertising campaigns and partners – as well as direct communications to our customers,” said a BT spokesperson. “A small minority of customers are yet to move and haven’t responded to repeated communications about the change. The temporary broadband pause we have introduced for this small minority is intended to help prevent a complete loss of service when the old, analogue network is retired.

“In the final months of the programme, it’s critical that customers take action when contacted about the switchover – failing to do so could result in the loss of their services when the outdated network retires.” Campaigners are concerned that the 1.3 million households still on copper lines include vulnerable individuals, such as elderly people with only a landline and no internet and those in rural areas with patchy, or no, broadband and variable mobile coverage who worry about being able to call emergency services if there is a power cut. There are also around 2 million users of telecare services, most commonly personal pendant alarms or buttons that have traditionally relied on copper landlines, which are unaffected if the internet goes down. In December, Virgin Media was fined £23.8m for leaving thousands of customers, typically older and disabled people, without access to their alarms as it was transitioning customers in 2023.

The issue of vulnerable customers resulted in a pause of non-voluntary migrations to digital landlines, and ultimately resulted in the industry moving the copper landline retirement date from December last year to the end of this coming January. text:
UK urged to act as Polymarket takes bets on whether HSBC and Lloyds will fail

UK authorities are being urged to intervene after it emerged that the online prediction market Polymarket has been taking thousands of dollars worth of bets over whether HSBC and Lloyds will fail. Polymarket – the US-owned company which holds bets on anything from football matches, to the existence of aliens, to when a bomb drops on a city – has allowed users to take $77,507 (£58,530) worth of positions on whether the world’s biggest banks will go under by the end of this year. That includes lenders ranging from JP Morgan to BNP Paribas, as well as two of the largest on UK high streets: HSBC and Lloyds Banking Group. Related: Will prediction market ‘catch fire’ in UK, replicating US boom? While residents from UK, US, Canada and EU are banned from betting on Polymarket’s offshore platform, it leaves punters from across roughly 150 countries in a position to monetarily benefit from events that would create huge financial instability and threaten the health of entire economies.

citation.title: UK urged to act as Polymarket takes bets on whether HSBC and Lloyds will fail

text:
UK urged to act as Polymarket takes bets on whether HSBC and Lloyds will fail

In a sign that authorities are taking the issue seriously, the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) told the Guardian it had been speaking to international regulators about prediction markets, as part of efforts to protect “market integrity”. There are growing concerns over insider trading and market manipulation on Polymarket by bad actors hoping to win big on online bets. That raises the stakes for the banking industry, which has already been told to prepare for the risk of social media-fuelled bank runs, where customers withdraw cash at speed. Silicon Valley Bank and Credit Suisse collapsed in 2023 after big stock sell-offs and bank runs, both of which were accelerated by a frenzy of speculation on platforms such as X and WhatsApp. The Treasury committee member and Liberal Democrat MP Bobby Dean said UK authorities should intervene. “Polymarket has a poor reputation for stopping insider trading or bad actors placing bets on their platform, so it’s easy to see how it could be exploited to try to aggravate real shifts in market sentiment,” he said.

“If the bank-related activity grows on the platform and then a particular market was to escalate rapidly, it could even trigger bank runs,” Dean added. “I would urge our regulators to get in contact with their counterparts in the US to raise concerns. We should not turn a blind eye to the risks because they are relatively small today, we’ve all seen how quickly things can move in this sector.” Polymarket bosses said they did not see a problem with the bets themselves, arguing they were democratising markets that were previously restricted to elite traders and institutions. The company’s chief legal officer, Neal Kumar, said: “The information in these markets is already public. Banks, hedge funds and credit professionals have had access to credit default swap markets for years. You shouldn’t need to work at an institution like that to have access to information on a topic of this importance like bank failures.

“Polymarket simplifies the question, providing a much larger audience with information, and markets serve as a powerful source of information and combating disinformation.” However, academics have warned these platforms are creating a serious moral hazard, giving market participants “an incentive to engage in corrupt, illegal, or dangerous actions in order to rig the outcome of the contract”. Meanwhile, the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) used its twice-yearly risk report last month to warn that “a growing number of incidents illustrates that prediction markets are rife with inside trading”. “Market manipulation and insider trading risks reach new levels in the context of prediction markets, particularly on DLT-based [distributed ledger technology] platforms such as Polymarket, which operate with limited identity verification and where the platform itself may not know who is behind a given wager.” Polymarket’s offshore platform is built on a blockchain. Accounts are linked to crypto wallets that can be publicly traced but are difficult to link back to an individual.

While Polymarket is headquartered in the US, its markets are international and its users are anonymous. text:
A cargo ship, 20 crew, and a huge stash of cocaine: the seafarer imprisoned for smuggling – on no evidence

In the early hours of 6 October 2023, Elena Albokhari was woken by a text message from her husband. Ali Albokhari, 42, a Finnish-Syrian with dark hair and cherubic features, was chief mate on a cargo ship named the Phoenician M and had been at sea since June. The 180-metre bulk carrier had docked at Ereğli in the Turkish Black Sea a few days earlier and Ali was due to return home to Helsinki soon, but instead of feeling excitement, Elena was growing increasingly worried about his welfare. She’d had a similar feeling of unease a month earlier, when the ship had arrived at Barranquilla, Colombia. Ali had called in a panic to report that drugs had been found; Armada Nacional officers had marched onboard and uncovered holdalls stuffed with 137kg cocaine. Labels on the packages – the crest of Turkish football club Kayserispor – hinted at their destination: Turkey was the next port of call. “I never want to work as a seaman again,” Ali told Elena. “We are having big problems.” For two days, the ship was held at the port.

citation.title: A cargo ship, 20 crew, and a huge stash of cocaine: the seafarer imprisoned for smuggling – on no evidence

text:
A cargo ship, 20 crew, and a huge stash of cocaine: the seafarer imprisoned for smuggling – on no evidence

Elena, 39, a tour guide from Russia, was so anxious, she could barely sleep. Then she received a photo from Ali of the crew happily drinking beer in a restaurant – the drugs had been removed and, after a meeting with the harbourmaster, the ship cleared to depart. “So will you go on working as a seaman?” Elena asked. “Yeah,” Ali said. “Sometimes it happens … so it’s OK.” Yet when the Phoenician M arrived at Ereğli on 2 October, loaded with coal, it was targeted by Turkish narcotics officers. The ship’s captain, Marko Bekavac, 63, a steely Croatian with three decades’ experience as a seafarer, had already informed the ship’s management company about the incident in Colombia, and when Turkish authorities boarded, he immediately declared that drugs had previously been found on the ship. Despite this, officers delivered a statement: should anything be found onboard, he would be accountable. The 20 crew members, including citizens of Russia, Ukraine, Poland and the Philippines, were ordered to remain in the ship’s mess room as the police continued to investigate.

Nothing was found in an initial search but days later, as the coal was unloaded, suspicious bags were reportedly found buried in the cargo hold. They were packed with more cocaine. The captain and other crew were escorted from the ship. Ali, who was second in command, remained onboard as unloading continued. He had managed to keep hold of his phone and was sending Elena updates. These had done little to allay her fears. Now, in the middle of the night, a text message confirmed the worst: “They are going to arrest us.” * * * Unless we are related to a seafarer, or live near a major port, most of us don’t encounter the people who work in shipping. Yet without them our lives would grind to a halt. Oceanic trade routes are the thread that weaves the world together. Merchant shipping – often described as the “lifeblood of the global economy” – is responsible for the movement of 90% of trade; every year, 11bn tonnes of goods, from coffee to fuel to fashion, are transported by ship.

citation.title: A cargo ship, 20 crew, and a huge stash of cocaine: the seafarer imprisoned for smuggling – on no evidence

A cargo ship, 20 crew, and a huge stash of cocaine: the seafarer imprisoned for smuggling – on no evidence

The scale of the maritime infrastructure is staggering, but the 2.57 million seafarers who operate within it remain largely invisible, as do many of the challenges they face. Elena never thought of Ali’s work as inherently risky, and the life of a merchant seaman can seem mundane. Cargo ships travel at around 15 knots (17mph). A boat like the Phoenician M can take more than two weeks to traverse the Atlantic. The routine involves inspections, maintenance checks, paperwork and long stretches at sea. But seafarers have become vulnerable to rapidly shifting conflicts – from the Russian invasion of Ukraine to the battle around the strait of Hormuz – as well as poor regulatory oversight, abandonment by shipowners and abuse by port authorities. Seafarers’ rights are frequently neglected and they are too easily scapegoated for events outside their control.

citation.title: A cargo ship, 20 crew, and a huge stash of cocaine: the seafarer imprisoned for smuggling – on no evidence

text:
A cargo ship, 20 crew, and a huge stash of cocaine: the seafarer imprisoned for smuggling – on no evidence

When an incident occurs, it is often far easier for authorities to pursue crew members than the shipping companies that employ them, who have an incentive to let the blame fall on individuals, and the P&I (protection and indemnity) clubs that insure them are there to serve the company, not individual crew members. The very nature of the job means voyaging to far-flung destinations, so if things do go wrong, seafarers can be forced to navigate unfamiliar judicial systems, with discretionary legal support, and face long periods of detention in a foreign country. Data on the scale of the problem is limited, but one 2018 survey by Nautilus International, the maritime professionals’ union, found that 90% of seafarers feared criminalisation above anything else. A recent survey by InterManager, the ship management association, has compiled 118 known cases over the past three decades, with a peak of 23 cases in 2023. Senior officers are most at risk; in 63% of cases, the captain was imprisoned.

citation.title: A cargo ship, 20 crew, and a huge stash of cocaine: the seafarer imprisoned for smuggling – on no evidence

text:
A cargo ship, 20 crew, and a huge stash of cocaine: the seafarer imprisoned for smuggling – on no evidence

Cases of seafarer criminalisation range from fuel smuggling allegations to collisions, but of particular concern is the global drug trade. Much like any other commodity, the vast majority of cocaine is transported by sea. Ports in Colombia are key export hubs. Cargo ships are up to 400 metres long and usually have just a couple of dozen crew; it’s not hard to find a place to hide something on them. In 2019, Capt Andrzej Lasota, a Polish seafarer, spent two years in prison in Mexico after 240kg of cocaine – planted on the ship at Barranquilla – was uncovered during unloading at Altamira. He was charged with “negligence” for failing to be aware of the drugs buried under coal in the cargo hold. The case was widely condemned, and resonates with that of the Phoenician M. Ali is now the only crew member who remains imprisoned, three years after his arrest. The International Maritime Organization has said the case “demonstrates how vulnerable seafarers are when they fall victim to organised international crime”.

The International Transport Workers’ Federation (ITF), a union that represents seafarers, described it as a “gross abuse” of human rights. * * * As a seafarer’s wife, Elena was used to spending time apart from her husband. But now Ali – whom she would speak to by phone or message almost daily – was no longer contactable, she felt truly alone. When she called the German crewing agency, Team Ship, desperate for answers, it was still unaware of the incident. A number she had for the company responsible for the crew and the ship, Iskenderun Ship Management, a Turkish operator, went unanswered. She waited for a call from some sort of official body, explaining what was going on, but none came. Elena frantically tried to make contact with anyone who might know what had happened. After she posted on online chat groups for seafarers, she was messaged by the wife of a crew member who had not been among those taken by the police. Only after calling him was she able to piece together what was happening.

Ali, along with Bekavac and eight other crew members, had been arrested on suspicion of drug smuggling. Another week or so passed. Elena had another call with the crewing agency, which said lawyers would be provided by Iskenderun at no cost. “Don’t worry, they are in the police station, they are being questioned, then they will be released,” Elena recalls an agent telling her. “You just need to wait.” So she waited. But instead, the men were detained and charged. During those first days, Elena says, the crew had no legal representation. When shipping incidents occur, a lawyer is usually appointed by a local P&I club “correspondent”, an independent adviser who can act on behalf of the shipowner and the club. When a lawyer was appointed, the crew said they were encouraged to accept the charges and sign what they described as arrest warrants, written in Turkish. “So we did,” one told Human Rights at Sea, an NGO.

“We were detained.” UK P&I, the club that provided insurance for the Phoenician M, said all appointments in this case, “including legal representation and the P&I correspondent”, were made by the shipowner, not them. They added that while they were not bound to do so, they provided support for the crew’s “significant” defence costs. I remember when he received the call about the job. He was so happy Days turned to weeks, then months. The men were moved from a local detention centre to a maximum security prison. Ali was one of many now isolated from their families, terrified about what would happen next. “Every day I was crying inside of that cell,” one Filipino crew member told me, adding that for a long time he didn’t know why he was being held. As for Elena, six months passed before she was finally able to speak with her husband. He put on a brave face, telling her he was OK, but asked her to send money: “If nobody sends you money in prison, you can’t buy food, you can’t buy anything.” Elena sent money and clothes, and waited for the men to stand trial.

Another six months passed. Finally, on 16 September 2024, following a number of hearings at Karadeniz Ereğli high criminal court, a verdict was due. Elena was sure Ali would be released. While he sat in the courtroom, she spent the day at home, anxiously awaiting the outcome. Then she received a brief message from the Finnish embassy. “I’m so sorry ... ” it said. While the eight other crew members had been acquitted, Ali and Bekavac had been found guilty on the basis of “command responsibility” and sentenced to 30 years’ imprisonment. Elena was stunned. Eventually she replied, “What should I do now?” * * * Ali and Elena’s home is a one-bedroom flat in a modern housing estate not far from Helsinki’s airport. When I visit in September, Elena, true to her profession as a tour guide, has laid out a spread of local treats: pancakes, blueberry juice, grilled cheese with cloudberry jam. Ali’s suitcase, which she was able to retrieve after his sentence, is still slumped near the balcony door. She tries to remain optimistic for his return. Every week, she buys fresh flowers.

On the wall above it she has pinned a banner: “Welcome Home”. If the maritime industry is emblematic of the power of globalisation, Ali and Elena’s relationship is a story of what it means to live on its faultlines. Ali was born in Damascus, Syria. His mother raised him and his three siblings, together with his stepfather, who ran a shoe business. When Ali reached college age, his options for further education were limited – as were the countries he could travel to – so his family decided he should attend the maritime university in St Petersburg, Russia, which was the most affordable option. He graduated in 2011, just as Syria descended into civil war, meaning he could neither remain in Russia nor safely return home. He applied for asylum in Finland and was accepted, continuing his studies at the Novia University in Turku. In 2017, Ali was granted full citizenship. Elena was born in Moscow. Her mother was a language teacher, her father an electrician. As she got older, she, too, was eager to build a life beyond her homeland and spent time as a student in Spain.

She met Ali on a dating app in 2021. At the time, Elena, who had been working as a Spanish-language interpreter and tour guide in Russia, was hoping to continue her studies in Finland. If she managed to get accepted to a Finnish-language programme, the education would be free, and she was eager to practise with native speakers. When Ali struck up a conversation, she was intrigued by this Middle Eastern man who spoke her native Russian. He was at sea at the time, but they began speaking regularly over phone and video call. When Elena travelled to Finland to take her Finnish-language test, he met her at the airport. She passed her test and they married in January 2022. A month later, Russia invaded Ukraine. They had all these plans, Elena says, but Ali struggled to find a job. For the past decade he had primarily worked on Russian ships; now Russia was at war and he struggled to find work with Finnish companies, which Elena believes was due to his Syrian heritage.

Ali eventually secured a nine-month contract with a Russian shipping company, and Elena returned to Moscow to visit her mother. She was able to meet him briefly, when his ship stopped at Murmansk, but when Ali returned to Finland at the end of his contract, Elena became stranded in Russia for a further three months while she awaited the paperwork needed to leave. It was December 2022 when they finally reunited in Helsinki. For the first year of their marriage, they were like ships in the night. It took months for Ali to secure his next contract: not just a job but a promotion, too. “I remember when he received the call,” Elena says. “He was so happy.” In May 2023 he was packing his bags, preparing to head to London to join the existing crew as they finished their rotation. The ship he was heading for was the Clipper Palma. In June, under the new management of Iskenderun, it was renamed: the Phoenician M. Looking back, there were things about the job that seemed a bit off to Elena. Ali, who was appointed as the ship’s security officer, described the vessel as very old.

He was also critical of the attitude of Iskenderun. When the crew made requests they would be unresponsive; some of these requests would prove critical to the case. When Bekavac noted Barranquilla was on the list of destinations, he requested additional security personnel, as well as cameras and locks for doors and hatches, due to the high risk of interference from drug cartels. Iskenderun did not respond. Elena says the lawyer appointed to Ali by Iskenderun visited him in prison rarely and did not seem to be prioritising his interests. “They were saying, ‘Don’t say a single word about the company … otherwise he will spend a long time there.’” Since Ali was sentenced, Elena has been lobbying for his release while trying to keep her own life afloat. When he was arrested, she was still a relative newcomer to Finland, with no support network and no job, as she was still studying. Sanctions on Russia meant their credit cards did not work: “I was left without money, without help.” Elena was dismayed by the lack of support from the Finnish government.

While its consular service has visited Ali in prison a number of times since late 2024, statements on the case have been scarce, and it is notably absent from Finnish media. One reason may be that Finland and Turkey have not had the easiest relations in recent years. Ankara put up resistance to Finland’s application to join Nato in 2022; since then it has made a growing number of extradition requests for political dissidents, which Finland has largely rejected. For Elena, the apparent indifference to Ali’s plight has been underlined by Bekavac’s experience. The Croatian prime minister and foreign minister spoke out against the verdict, and his then wife, Katja, received support to arrange prison visits without delay. When Elena went to Ankara, she attended the Palace of Justice with her lawyer and without consular assistance. It took all day to navigate the bureaucracy of the building and, after submitting documents and photos, she had to wait a further two weeks before a prison visit was approved.

Katja, Elena says, was able to meet the captain without a barrier between them, but when she finally made it through the prison gates, after the humiliation of a strip-­search, she had to speak with Ali through a glass pane. “Psychologically, it was very difficult,” she says. During that first meeting, Elena was shocked by how much he had changed. “I have never seen my husband sad,” she says. “He’s always laughing, singing, dancing, but this time I didn’t recognise him. He was very thin, depressed and with grey hair.” The hardest thing was to contain her emotions: “When I’m alone here I can cry, I can tell my friends everything is very bad … but I can’t say such things to him. I have to support him.” She told him they had a new lawyer. That his mother was well. That they would be waiting for him. That they’d fight for him. After 40 minutes, their time was up. As Elena continued to battle for diplomatic support, travelling to Turkey to visit Ali every month, she became aware the Croatian authorities were working behind the scenes.

In August 2025, Ali watched from his cell as Bekavac was collected from the prison by a Croatian diplomat and flown home. In Croatia, there has been speculation that his release was negotiated as part of a prisoner swap with Mustafa Yiğit Zeren, a Turkish billionaire and close friend of President Erdoğan who was wanted by the Russians over alleged embezzlement of €600m. “Everything I know about the case seems to indicate that it makes no sense that he’s still in custody,” Tanner says. Elena says she spends all her spare time investigating the case herself, poring over the details as she grows increasingly suspicious of the motivations of all the parties involved. She pulls out a black folder of documents relating to Ali’s employment records. She also shows me her diary, a white book with a gold heart on the cover filled with neat handwriting. Its pages are full of memories, but from October 2023 they are blank. * * * As the case of Phoenician M has lingered on, it has drawn attention to the protections afforded to seafarers and the need for these to be reaffirmed. There are numerous international agreements designed to protect their rights, such as the International Labour Organisation Guidelines on Fair Treatment of Seafarers and the Maritime Labour Convention – often described as the “seafarers’ bill of rights” – but in practice they are at the beck and call of whichever jurisdiction they happen to sail into.

“It’s aspirational, but not very concrete,” is how James Turner KC, who specialises in shipping law, summarises it to me. Maritime organisations have also expressed growing concern at the extent to which supply chains are being exploited by organised crime. In 2019, MSC, the world’s largest ocean carrier, came under intense scrutiny after 20 tonnes of cocaine with a value of $1bn was discovered by US authorities on the MSC Gayane at Philadelphia. Large cocaine shipments were also found on three other MSC ships that year. An investigation by Bloomberg alleged the company had been infiltrated by members of a Balkan cartel. Eight Gayane crew members pleaded guilty of involvement in the drug-smuggling operation. Criminal actors clearly do exist in the industry, but innocent seafarers are also being caught in the net. Keith Svendsen, an executive at Danish group Maersk, told the Financial Times shipping companies were now dealing with “some of the most dangerous people in the world” and cited crew members coerced into helping smuggling gangs.

Fabrizio Barcellona, a coordinator at the ITF, says the issue is not with countries taking a strong stance against drug trafficking, but that seafarers are being scapegoated. “It’s not good enough just to put them in jail without clear evidence,” he says. Over the past decade, Turkey has become a significant hub for the importation of cocaine to Europe, and there is growing pressure to address the issue. Erdoğan’s government has been accused of allowing organised crime to proliferate, and high-ranking political figures have been accused of involvement in drug trafficking. Imdat Öner, a former Turkish diplomat turned public policy analyst, told me that instead of effectively pursuing organised crime networks, the authorities are focusing on low-volume trafficking of the sort found on the Phoenician M. “It allows the government, the police, to save face internationally,” he says.

David Hammond, a former military seafarer, qualified barrister and founder of Human Rights at Sea, has published a review of Ali’s case which calls it a “grave miscarriage of justice” and questions the prosecution’s integrity and motivations. Court papers state that the investigation was triggered by intelligence from Kayseri province police narcotics department, and the conviction based on evidence gathered following the seizure. But according to Hammond, Turkish police failed to request documentation relating to the Colombian incident, key witnesses were not interviewed, and no forensic evidence linking crew members to the drugs was presented. It is unclear why, of 20 crew onboard, only 10 were arrested. The prosecution seems to have rested solely on the rank and responsibilities of the crew. text:
Burnham’s plans for social care and its workers are admirable but changes must come quickly

As one of many hundreds of thousands of people in the UK with a parent with Alzheimer’s, the passage in Andy Burnham’s speech about social care moved me to tears. My mother had not even been diagnosed when I watched Theresa May announce her 2017 general election manifesto in a hall in Halifax – with care funding at its heart. Almost a decade of political neglect later, and Mum has now been in a care home for three years, with the funding coming overwhelmingly from our family’s own resources. Related: How will Burnham’s national care service work – and how will it be funded? So it was arresting to hear Burnham speak with clarity about his belief that personal care should be a question of “social insurance” – sharing the risk across families. In practice, personal care makes up a minority of the total cost of residential social care. Much of it is the “bed and board” that Burnham’s changes won’t pay for: the cooking, cleaning and upkeep.

citation.title: Burnham’s plans for social care and its workers are admirable but changes must come quickly

text:
Burnham’s plans for social care and its workers are admirable but changes must come quickly

But a sense that the burden is somewhat shared would be a significant step forward, as would Burnham’s apparent determination to put care workers at the centre of the plan – and to expend political capital in doing so. Addressing care workers directly, he said: “I see you. I thank you. And I am sorry that my profession has let down yours for so long.” It’s a long-held view of Burnham’s. I recall speaking alongside him at a fringe event about jobs and skills at Labour’s 2024 party conference, at which we both underscored the fact that we didn’t feel the carers who supported our respective parents were “low-skilled”. Yet the national care service, with its promised closer alignment with the NHS, will feel a very long time coming for families making their agonising way down the road to diagnosis and beyond. The next parliament seems too long to wait. As Stuart Hoddinott of the Institute for Government said after Burnham’s speech, the prime minister should “have the courage of his convictions” and stand it up sooner.

citation.title: Burnham’s plans for social care and its workers are admirable but changes must come quickly

text:
Burnham’s plans for social care and its workers are admirable but changes must come quickly

Even as a skeleton body, it could get on with setting standards and coordinating care better with the NHS, and could become involved in the negotiations on a fair pay agreement in the sector. That’s Labour’s ambitious attempt to introduce collective bargaining, including pay and progression, across a fragmented and poorly paid industry. Whatever the fledgling negotiating body agrees is due to come into force in April 2028. So far, Labour – under Keir Starmer – has set aside £500m to fund any uplift in pay. Joe Dromey, the general secretary of the Fabian Society, which has made social care a campaigning issue in recent years, suggests that may not be enough. “The first priority should be fixing the workforce crisis. We must give care workers the pay rise they deserve, through a more ambitious fair pay agreement,” he says. Tweaking the triple lock beyond 2030 is a sensible policy, and tying it to social care feels like good politics from Burnham – but it won’t put any money into an overstretched sector now, let alone into the pockets of those care workers.

citation.title: Burnham’s plans for social care and its workers are admirable but changes must come quickly

text:
Burnham’s plans for social care and its workers are admirable but changes must come quickly

As Hoddinott says, making progress between now and the next general election “would give Burnham a strong story to tell” – and make it less likely his changes would be swept away if Labour loses. While it seems to have been memory-holed by the political class, Boris Johnson was prepared to bust a Conservative manifesto promise in 2021 and introduce a £12bn-a-year “health and care levy” to “fix social care”. That was arguably a greater expenditure of political capital than rewriting the triple lock, and it was meant to take effect within months. In the event, of course, Johnson torched his entire stock of political capital by partying in lockdown, and took the policy down with him. But with Louise Casey expected to report next summer on how a national care service could be built and paid for, spending perhaps another two years after that in a “national conversation” will seem a very long slog for affected families.

citation.title: Burnham’s plans for social care and its workers are admirable but changes must come quickly

Frankly, having reported on that 2017 campaign, when May’s plans were quickly dubbed a “dementia tax” (there already is one, for goodness sake), Burnham’s hopes of achieving political consensus are high-minded but almost certainly hopeless. There are only a certain number of ways of raising the additional money that will be needed There is also a risk – voiced to me in Liverpool by one Labour MP – that extending the discussion about the right way to fund social care right through to the next election crowds out other arguments they may need to make. After all, there are only a certain number of ways of raising the additional money that will be needed, over and above the triple-lock tweak, and they are well rehearsed. There’s a national insurance rise à la Johnson, perhaps applied only to older workers; or a levy on all estates (a “death tax”, as it was called by the Tories when Burnham last advocated it, 15 years ago).

citation.title: Burnham’s plans for social care and its workers are admirable but changes must come quickly

Or there is the politically tougher but perhaps more honest approach that acknowledges general taxation will have to rise because of the growing needs of an ageing society – funding a more generous social care settlement as part of a wider shoring up of the public sector. It is admirable and refreshing that Burnham wants to build the political case for causes he believes in – and social care is more than ripe for that approach. But enough families like mine have struggled their way unsupported and forgotten through a system that fails them. Once he has a plan, he should just crack on with it – and that includes raising the money needed to make it work. Listen to Heather talk about navigating the care system in Tuesday’s Today in Focus podcast.

Chalmers says global economic turmoil will drive budget cuts, but Australia should avoid recession

Jim Chalmers has warned of “very substantial and intensifying” economic pressures on the horizon but insists he’s not planning for a recession, as he prepares to find new ways to cut the budget ahead of its mid-year update. The treasurer on Sunday called on critics of government spending to name the services that should be cut, as he points the finger at the private sector for driving up inflation in Australia amid the protracted conflict in the Middle East. Chalmers said the US-led eight-month war against Iran, which has severely curtailed global oil supplies from the region, has been “disastrous” for cost-of-living pressures. Related: The interest rate rise is the wrong medicine and an even worse alibi | Yanis Varoufakis He also said there was “very substantial and intensifying pressure” on the federal budget. “No serious observer of what’s going on right now would conclude anything other than [that],” he told ABC’s Insiders.

“The longer this thing drags out, the bigger the impact on the global economy and on the Australian economy, whether it’s … on inflation or downward pressure on growth. “We’re not anticipating [a recession] here in Australia, but certainly it is weighing on global growth, and we’re not immune from that.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Inflation has jumped to 4% in the year to August, from 3.5%, while the Reserve Bank lifted its key interest rate to 4.6%, the highest figure since 2011. Chalmers said the government was working on finding further savings to the budget in the mid-year economic and fiscal outlook, due in December, after cuts of $44.9bn over four years were identified in the May budget. The treasurer said cuts to government spending weren’t the only factor driving up inflation in the economy, and cutting larger sums would impact essential services. “If people don’t want us to strengthen Medicare, for example, or cut income taxes, or provide cost-of-living relief in other ways, then they should nominate where that should be cut,” he said on Sunday.

Costa’s coffee shops return to profit with iced drinks and matcha on the menu

Costa’s main coffee shop arm has returned to an operating profit after revamping its high street outlets and broadening its menu with iced drinks, matcha and fresher pastries. The chain, which has 2,700 outlets in the UK and Ireland out of 4,000 globally, and employs about 20,000 people, also opened a net 50 new outlets in the UK last year – its first net increase in several years. It plans a further 50 new UK outlets this year, including more drive-throughs and high street outlets. Demand from younger consumers for decaffeinated coffee and other options is driving sales growth amid concerns about drinking caffeine in the afternoon, while there is heavy competition on classic coffees from companies such as Greggs, Gail’s, Caffè Nero and numerous smaller operators. Costa says it is now the largest seller of matcha via cafes in the UK. The Costa Ltd arm made an operating profit of £20m in the year to 31 December 2025 after losses of £13.5m in 2024 and £5.8m the year before, according to accounts filed at Companies House. Revenues rose 5% to almost £1.3bn compared with 1% growth in 2024.

citation.title: Costa’s coffee shops return to profit with iced drinks and matcha on the menu

text:
Costa’s coffee shops return to profit with iced drinks and matcha on the menu

Philippe Schaillee, the chief executive of Costa, said the chain had experienced the strongest growth in visits in a decade. Sipping a Velvetino, a low-calorie iced coffee popular with younger drinkers, Schaillee said: “The coffee shop is increasingly a destination for morning and afternoon. People not only want caffeine but iced herbal teas and those drinks that people will drink in the afternoon and evening.” Showing off Costa’s new headquarters in St Albans, Hertfordshire, which will have space for 300 workers when it opens in January, he said it “really signals our confidence in the business”. Costa plans to remodel about 250 stores a year after updating more than 1,200 of 1,700 company-owned outlets. That includes adding more digital self-order kiosks, which are already in 200 UK outlets. The group is also selling more Podio office coffee machines, which launched in May and are intended to be “a barista in your office”. Schaillee said Costa was already the UK’s third biggest brand in home coffee machines, and said the potential there was “limitless”.

Costa’s coffee shops return to profit with iced drinks and matcha on the menu

Costa’s campaign to flag its strong performance comes after its owner, Coca-Cola, in February officially confirmed it had abandoned plans to sell the chain after bids failed to meet its expectations. Coca-Cola had high hopes for Britain’s largest coffee chain when it bought it for £3.9bn in 2018 from Whitbread, the owner of Premier Inn hotels. However, since then the chain has struggled in the face of rising costs, particularly the increase in coffee bean prices, and competition on UK high streets. Schaillee said coffee production – and potentially prices – remained high and could be affected by the El Niño global climate phenomenon, which is affecting coffee and cocoa growers in Latin and South America. “We need to be prepared for that,” he said.
