Jason Williams, head of division at the SFO, said: “We argued for a different outcome but respect the court’s decision in relation to Christian Bittar. The SFO remains committed to tackling the most complex fraud, bribery and corruption.” Ben Rose of law firm Hickman and Rose, who represented Bittar, said it was a “scandal that the SFO has consistently failed to uphold its duty to ensure that these trials are fair”. Peter Johnson, the ninth former trader who was convicted of rate rigging, also intends to appeal against his conviction. He pleaded guilty to conspiring to manipulate Libor in 2014. Ellen Gallagher, a partner at Vardags, who represents Johnson, said: “Peter’s fight to clear his name continues. “As the court made clear today, he has taken the first steps towards that appeal by filing provisional grounds.”

text:
Insurance model is no substitute for the NHS

In Dining across the divide (4 October), the young participant, Ted, is quoted as expressing his “desire to abolish the NHS and replace it with a social insurance model. This would still have provision for free treatment at the point of need, but people would pay through insurance systems, and they would choose the level of cover they’ve got. Those models deliver far better outcomes for patients.” As a retired insurance underwriter, I must disagree profoundly with Ted’s assertion. Let’s concentrate on business fundamentals. Insurance comes in two “flavours”: first, events that become likelier as time goes on – eg, life assurance. The older you get, the more likely you are to die and the more premium is needed to cover the risk; and second, events whose likelihood stays essentially the same over time, eg home insurance – the likelihood of a house burning down is much the same for everyone and the cost is spread evenly between policyholders. Clearly, medical insurance is flavour one. Premiums need to rise with age.

citation.title: Insurance model is no substitute for the NHS

text:
Insurance model is no substitute for the NHS

To reduce premiums and keep customers, insurance companies apply ever-increasing “excesses” and “co-pays” and can refuse to cover pre-existing conditions. The more you need medical insurance, the more expensive and difficult it is to get. There is also the business case. When you buy an insurance policy, premiums are calculated to include the cost of claims (about 60%); administration (about 10%); sales (about 20%); shareholder profits (about 15%); less investment returns (about 5%). In contrast, an NHS-style system does not require either sales costs or shareholder profits. Of course, there would be no investment return – but nevertheless, it is still about 30% cheaper to operate than an insured healthcare system. Like most sound business ideas, it’s simple arithmetic. Susan Jones Biggin Hill, London • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

Shein outsells British rival Asos as UK revenue hits £2.58bn

Shein, the online fast-fashion retailer founded in China, increased sales in the UK by just over a quarter last year, overtaking its British rival Asos. The company, whose global parent group listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange valued at just over $26bn (£19.6bn) last month, increased sales at its UK division by 26% to £2.58bn, according to accounts filed at Companies House. Pre-tax profits rose 18% to £45.2m even as the number of people employed by the group in the UK, mostly in sales and marketing, rose to 113 from 91 a year before. The company paid £11.2m in current tax – understood to be mainly corporation tax – up from £9.6m a year before. Shein said sales had been helped by a marketing partnership with the Wireless and Creamfields music festivals, a pop-up shop on London’s Oxford Street and Christmas gift events in Edinburgh, Manchester and Liverpool as well as London. Asos’s sales were £2.47bn in the year to 31 August 2025 – although this figure includes revenues outside the UK, unlike Shein UK’s comparable statistic.

citation.title: Shein outsells British rival Asos as UK revenue hits £2.58bn

text:
Shein outsells British rival Asos as UK revenue hits £2.58bn

Shein’s strong trading figures are likely to increase pressure on the government to bring forward action to change the “de minimis” rule that has underpinned the rise of the fast-growing online specialists Shein and Temu. Fears about China’s retailers and manufacturers dumping goods in the UK have grown since the US last year revoked its own de minimis exception for Chinese-made goods, crimping Shein’s expansion there. The retailer’s model is based on shipping orders of cheap clothes from Chinese factories to homes so that each order is low enough in value to avoid import duties. Under the US exemption, which was scrapped last year, parcels with a value of less than $800 (£600) shipped to individuals had been spared from import tax. The EU is also phasing out its exemption on customs duties for low-value parcels. It began in July by replacing the €150 de minimis relief with a flat €3 customs duty. The former UK chancellor Rachel Reeves said she would get rid of the UK’s rule, which allows overseas sellers to send goods valued at £135 or less direct to British shoppers without paying any customs duty, by 2028.

citation.title: Shein outsells British rival Asos as UK revenue hits £2.58bn

text:

However, major retail bosses have said the government should move sooner. Investors’ concerns about global government regulatory changes meant Shein’s value was far lower when it listed on the stock market than had been expected several years ago. It reached a valuation of $100bn in an April 2022 fundraising round, making it the third most valuable startup in the world, and then considered a £50bn ($66bn) float on the London Stock Exchange in 2024 before eventually launching in Hong Kong. Shein, founded by the entrepreneur Chris Xu, runs most of its operations from China but sells all its goods outside the country. It moved its headquarters to Singapore at the start of 2022 and has recently begun manufacturing in other countries including Turkey and Brazil. After forced labour concerns were raised, Shein said it had tightened its supplier policies, enforced through regular audits, with any child or forced labour violations becoming grounds for immediate termination of contract.

Trump establishes committee to investigate Fed governor Lisa Cook

Donald Trump announced on Friday that he is establishing a committee to investigate Lisa Cook, the US Federal Reserve governor, over allegations that she committed mortgage fraud, renewing his efforts to oust her despite a June supreme court ruling that her earlier firing was unconstitutional. Trump said a committee will consult with justice department officials to decide whether there is “cause” for her removal. The White House will hold an in-person hearing on 5 November to consider the allegations against Cook, which will be closed to the public but transcribed and published. Cook will be able to submit a written statement to present her own evidence and will be subject to examination from White House and her own legal counsel. “As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law,” Trump said in a statement posted to the White House’s website. Her legal team has maintained that the White House is “cherrypicking” facts and any claims of fraud are based on unrelated clerical errors.

citation.title: Trump establishes committee to investigate Fed governor Lisa Cook

text:
Trump establishes committee to investigate Fed governor Lisa Cook

In response to the announcement, Cook’s lawyers said that they had “grave doubts” that the White House hearing would be “a legitimate one that would conform to the law”. “But if it is anything close to objective,” they continued, “the conclusion will be that Governor Cook did not commit mortgage fraud, leaving no cause to remove her from the Federal Reserve Board.” They added that Cook “welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her”. Cook was appointed by Joe Biden in 2022 to a 14-year term, becoming the Fed’s first Black governor. Before her tenure at the central bank, she taught at Harvard University and Stanford University and served on Barack Obama’s council of economic advisers. Cook’s battle with the White House began in August 2025 when she was abruptly fired after Trump said she committed mortgage fraud by listing two properties in Georgia and Michigan as her primary residence and failing to report rental income on her Atlanta property.

citation.title: Trump establishes committee to investigate Fed governor Lisa Cook

text:
Trump establishes committee to investigate Fed governor Lisa Cook

Cook immediately sued the Trump administration, and the supreme court reinstated her after a 5-4 ruling that she could stay on as governor while fighting the fraud allegations. In June, the court ruled that Trump’s firing was unconstitutional because he did not follow proper procedure and give Cook an opportunity to dispute the allegations before she was fired. Cook was fired just as Trump was launching unprecedented attacks on the Fed’s chair, then Jerome Powell, in his blustering push to get the central bank to lower interest rates. Trump also launched a justice department investigation into Powell, which was dropped in April. Congress created the Fed to be an independent and non-partisan institution. Economists widely agree that a central bank unswayed by politics is essential for the stability of a country’s economy. Kevin Warsh, Powell’s successor, has repeatedly faced questions over how he will maintain the Fed’s independence. Before Trump picked him to lead the world’s most powerful central bank, he had echoed the president’s calls for cutting rates.

But because of elevated inflation brought on by the war in the Middle East, the bank ultimately voted to raise rates in its last meeting, which drew the ire of the White House just more than a month before the crucial midterm elections.

Virgin unveils its future cross-Channel train as it gears up to take on Eurostar

Flash interiors, fancy food and maybe even a bar: Virgin has unveiled a mock-up of its future cross-Channel train, with a pledge to create “something genuinely new”. The group is planning to launch rail services from London to the continent in 2030, with Eurostar facing competition for the first time since the opening of the Channel tunnel. Virgin has ordered 12 high-speed trains from the manufacturer Alstom, matching Eurostar’s for speed at up to 190mph (300km/h) but aiming to outshine the incumbent on design and customer experience. While Virgin’s last stab at reimagining UK train travel may have peaked with the talking toilet seat on its intercity services in 2013, it has said the future trains will draw inspiration from its airline, cruise and hotel arms. Although details are being kept under wraps, it said it would draw on Virgin Atlantic’s airport lounges, or Clubhouses, for “pre-departure and onboard social spaces” with “more flexibility to work, relax or socialise in style”. Food will be influenced by its cruise line menu and the design by its Virgin Hotels brand.

‘Our town is making jeans again’: meet the firm reviving jobs and skills in Wales

Worn on the streets of London’s Soho, San Francisco or Sydney, every pair of high-end jeans made by Hiut Denim comes from the rather unlikely location of a small coastal town in west Wales. Cardigan, with a population of just 4,200, has a proud history of denim production and was once home to Britain’s largest jeans factory, even if the town’s name recalls a different garment entirely. When jeans manufacturing in Wales was moved abroad at the start of the century, hundreds of local people lost their jobs and were forced to find work elsewhere. Hiut Denim was founded by David and Clare Hieatt in Cardigan in 2011. The couple, both originally from Wales, previously ran the ethical fashion brand Howies. They set up Hiut – the brand name blends their surname with the word utility – with the goal of reviving denim-making skills in the town and training up the next generation of skilled craftspeople. Elin Evans was one of those “grand masters”, as they are known in the company, with a lifetime’s experience of making jeans.

citation.title: ‘Our town is making jeans again’: meet the firm reviving jobs and skills in Wales

text:
‘Our town is making jeans again’: meet the firm reviving jobs and skills in Wales

Now 59, Evans is Hiut’s factory manager and has been in the trade since 1983, when she was 16. “I’ve done a full loop, because this is where I started,” she says, from her seat behind a sewing machine on the factory floor. Deftly handling the indigo fabric, she moves individual pieces through the machine and a pair of jeans begins to take shape. In its heyday, the Dewhirst factory in Cardigan where Evans once worked employed about 400 people, representing about 10% of the town’s population, and cranked out 35,000 pairs of jeans each week for Marks & Spencer. When Dewhirst decided to outsource production to Morocco, Evans was given the opportunity to move to Tangier. But the founding of Hiut led to her returning home to Wales and to a sewing machine. “I hoped it was like riding a bike,” she says, “but you never forget and the rest is history”. As Hiut took off, the company moved into what was once part of the Dewhirst factory, taking Evans back to the place she began her career.

citation.title: ‘Our town is making jeans again’: meet the firm reviving jobs and skills in Wales

text:
‘Our town is making jeans again’: meet the firm reviving jobs and skills in Wales

A slogan painted on the factory wall proclaims “Our town is making jeans again” and Welsh flag bunting flutters above the sewing machines, in celebration of the annual cultural festival, held this year in early August just a miles south of Cardigan. Evans and the other grand masters who joined Hiut have spent decades cutting pieces of fabric, creating pockets and stitching denim. The brand’s production levels are far removed from the mass manufacturing which previously took place in Cardigan – Hiut employs 20 people, who make 120 pairs a week. The company insists its product is no ordinary wardrobe staple. Each pair is made by hand from 17 pieces of fabric, with a “made in Wales” label inside the waistband and another label signed by the member of staff who stitched the jeans. Hiut also offers lifetime repairs. “The majority of the time, you know the name of the person that’s bought your jeans. You know your customer and the customer gets to know us as well,” says Evans.

“We’re very proud of what we’re doing and the quality is top notch.” Indeed, online fashion reviews praise Hiut’s attention to detail, such as neat seams and how all of the rivets featuring the brand’s name or owl logo are added by hand to ensure they face the same way. Such premium jeans come with a suitably premium price tag – about 10 times higher than the cost of a high-street pair – starting at £245 for men’s and women’s slim-fit styles, made from organic cotton from Turkey, and rising to £350 for pairs made from premium Japanese selvedge. Hiut customers includes TV personalities Ant and Dec and the brand got a big boost when the Duchess of Sussex wore a pair during her first official visit to Wales in 2018, resulting in a three-month backlog of orders. Despite such endorsements, the company hit financial difficulties in the wake of the Covid pandemic, when the founders approached some of their top customers to ask if they wanted to invest in the company. One of these was the German von Loeper family.

They initially became minority shareholders in late 2024, before taking over the company in September 2025. Johann von Loeper, 26, became the company’s chief executive, leaving a career in finance in London to move to Cardigan. He says his father, Philipp, was a loyal customer first, which prompted the family-owned investment group to take a stake in a firm beyond its usual investments in life sciences or agricultural companies. “We don’t do anything in retail or fashion really, this is more of a passion project,” von Loeper says. “My father sort of became obsessed with the product … I think he bought more than 30 pairs.” The family has committed to keeping the manufacturing in Cardigan, although von Loeper adds that the factory’s west Wales location creates logistical challenges when moving finished garments or bringing in photographers and models for photoshoots.

He adds: “The thing that attracted all of us to Hiut was the purpose of making jeans again, and not just for the sake of making jeans, but to have the jobs, to have to craft, to have skills remain here.” Some high-profile visitors have tried out the craft. A framed photo and letter from Kensington palace hangs on the factory wall, commemorating the March visit of Catherine, the Princess of Wales, where she had a go on a sewing machine. Walking past huge rolls of fabric from some of the most prestigious denim mills in the world – in Japan, Italy and Turkey – von Loeper says he faced a big decision shortly after taking over running the company. A key Japanese denim supplier warned Hiut and other long-term customers that operational pressures meant it was about to close its order books until 2027. “We bought £100,000 worth of selvedge in my first few weeks here because I said ‘let’s get it now before we run out’ and that was one of the better things I did,” he says.

When the von Loeper family took over, they said Hiut was “losing a lot of money every month”, but they believed that with investment and a new strategy, the brand could become profitable again. The new owners soon got to work updating the entire jeans collection, and are hoping to take on more staff so they can increase production. Von Loeper is aware that Evans and other grand masters are fast approaching retirement age and believes the company has a “five-year window” to hire and adequately train new employees. Developing nations face triple shock from energy crisis, El Niño and borrowing costs, UN warns

Developing countries face a triple shock from the energy crisis, El Niño and surging borrowing costs and need urgent support from the international community, the UN’s development arm has warned. Speaking before the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok this week, the UNDP’s administrator, Alexander De Croo, called for “solidarity and global action”. “Developing countries, their hands and legs are being pulled in different directions: it’s truly hard for them,” he said. Before the meetings, the UNDP published a report, No Time to Recover, which lays out the risks of what it calls the “compounding crises” of energy, climate and debt. Oil prices have been driven back above $100 a barrel in recent weeks since hostilities resumed in the Middle East. The report says that since the Iran war broke out earlier this year, up to 130 million of the world’s poorest people have been shielded from the full impact of high prices by emergency government measures.

citation.title: Developing nations face triple shock from energy crisis, El Niño and borrowing costs, UN warns

text:
Developing nations face triple shock from energy crisis, El Niño and borrowing costs, UN warns

But it warns many of them are now at risk, as governments run out of the resources needed to keep cushioning their populations against soaring costs. “What we see now is that countries are pivoting their policy and letting the price hikes flow through. They’re pivoting the policy because they have no choice, because their fiscal space is completely eaten up,” De Croo said. “We are witnessing a perfect storm that could throw tens if not hundreds of millions of people back into poverty.” Meanwhile, the worst El Niño climate pattern in perhaps 1,000 years is expected to cause widespread crop failures and increase the risk of extreme weather events, while at the same time the global bond sell-off is driving up government borrowing costs. De Croo said: “The cost today for bond financing for developing countries, it’s 9%. That is really, really high.” He added that the situation was expected to deteriorate between now and the spring.

citation.title: Developing nations face triple shock from energy crisis, El Niño and borrowing costs, UN warns

text:
Developing nations face triple shock from energy crisis, El Niño and borrowing costs, UN warns

“For each of the three things that we mentioned – fuel prices, El Niño and the bond markets – unfortunately for each of those at the moment, we don’t see any light at the end of the tunnel.” His warning chimes with the findings of separate research published on Sunday by the campaign group Debt Justice, underlining the social impact of high debt servicing costs. It shows that low-income countries classified by the IMF as either in, or at risk of, debt distress have cut their education budgets by an average of 8% since 2019, and wider public spending by 2%. Heidi Chow, the executive director of Debt Justice, said: “High levels of debt are having a devastating impact on people’s access to healthcare and education.” Debt Justice is calling for the outright cancellation of some of the most burdensome debts, and overhaul of the IMF-administered common framework for debt restructuring.

citation.title: Developing nations face triple shock from energy crisis, El Niño and borrowing costs, UN warns

text:
Developing nations face triple shock from energy crisis, El Niño and borrowing costs, UN warns

Chow said: “We urgently need debt cancellation – especially from the highest interest lenders like banks, hedge funds and oil traders.” De Croo said the UNDP did not oppose efforts to secure debt relief for some of the hardest-hit countries – but argued it would take many months to negotiate, and instead called for more urgent action. “We urge the international community – multilateral lenders, donors, and partners – to step up access to affordable finance so countries can sustain support for their most vulnerable households,” De Croo said. He praised the IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva’s recent call for spending restraint in developed countries, in the hope of taming bond yields. But he said: “We also need to have a coordinated policy for developing countries. And that coordinated policy for developing countries cannot just be, ‘you are at the end of the line and we’ll see what happens’.” He declined to say what the specific response should be, but stressed that it should create “time and space” for developing countries to carry out much-needed changes.

During the Covid crisis, G20 nations implemented a temporary standstill on debt repayments for developing countries. De Croo also pointed to liquidity measures available to central banks, such as the currency swap lines implemented by the US Federal Reserve during recent financial crises, to prevent markets seizing up. “What would help is a certain level of liquidity,” he said.

‘Halloweenmas’: how the spooky one-nighter turned into a month-long spectacular

The tree is up, the wreath is hanging on the front door and you’ve just opened your advent calendar. All told, it’s beginning to feel a lot like … Halloween. If it sounds like the stuff of nightmares then that’s the point: Britons are increasingly decorating their homes with ghoulish versions of Christmas traditions. Think of it as Halloweenmas. “What was traditionally a single-night celebration has turned into a month-long event mirroring many of Christmas’s traditions, but without the same level of expectation,” said Charlotte Broadbent, the UK general manager for the online wholesale platform Faire. Analysis of thousands of sales transactions on the platform revealed a huge rise in the number of Halloweenmas products available – up more than 500% in the past four years, from 425 in 2021 to 2,632 in 2025. The biggest areas of growth are trees, wreaths and ornaments. According to the budget retailer Wilko, Halloween trees are one of the biggest decorating trends of 2026. It said sales of artificial trees were 200% higher in September than a year ago.

Labour has got the message – it’s developing nations suffering most from bond market turmoil

From Washington to Paris, London to Tokyo, policymakers in every large economy have been counting the costs of bond market turmoil in recent weeks. But the brunt of the pain is being borne by heavily indebted developing countries that have little hope of influencing the whims of global investors, but pay the price regardless. Markets have responded to the war in the Middle East, and a spendthrift White House, by dumping government bonds – driving up borrowing costs just about everywhere. Finance ministers and central bankers gathering in Bangkok this week for the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank may be loth to point the finger at Donald Trump’s regime, but all are at least in part hostage to the US president’s war plans. That has made what was already a perilous situation even worse – just as the world is battling an energy crisis, and as developing countries urgently need to invest in adapting to the climate emergency.

text:
Labour has got the message – it’s developing nations suffering most from bond market turmoil

Even before the latest market gyrations, experts calculated that debt servicing costs absorbed 45% of government revenues in the global south, and 70% in low-income countries. That crowds out desperately needed spending on public services and investing for the future. Related: The next global economic emergency? Deepening debt in the developing world There have been growing demands for reform of the framework for international debt in recent years, including from African Union heads of state, and under the G20 chairs of Brazil and South Africa. The G20 – the forum in which Gordon Brown coordinated a global fiscal stimulus package in the depths of the financial crisis in spring 2009 – is meant to be an important body for discussing international economic issues. With a much wider membership than the G7, it has coordinated previous efforts on debt, including establishing the IMF-administered Common Framework, to which struggling countries can apply, and suspending repayments for hard-hit borrowers during the Covid crisis.

However, this year’s chair has been Trump’s US, which has placed much more emphasis on other aspects of the G20’s remit, including promoting global economic growth – somewhat ironically, given the main obstacle to achieving it is the war on Iran. Next year, the presidency falls to the UK, and Labour has made clear it will have different priorities. These will include seeking a global agreement on AI regulation, which seems a faint hope but is clearly worth pursuing. The UK also intends to put unsustainable debt on the agenda. The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, who will be in Bangkok, told Labour conference delegates last month: “Friends, I promise this. We will use our G20 presidency next year to meet our responsibilities and mobilise the world, building on the great achievements on debt and development of the last Labour government.” He was referring to 2005, when Brown and Tony Blair rode the vociferous Make Poverty History movement to the Gleneagles G8 summit and beyond, securing significant debt relief for more than 30 countries.

As the development minister, Kirsty McNeill, herself a veteran of that campaign, said recently, the circumstances now are very different, for two reasons. First, she said, “we’re now dealing with private creditors – the debt isn’t held by us. So that is quite a big shift.” And second, she suggested it was harder now to delineate a group of countries clearly deserving of support. “There isn’t this really clear demarcation between the very poor world and the very rich world that was true when I was starting out, and it was just a much starker and therefore more readily told story because the antagonists and the protagonists were just much clearer,” she told an event at the Labour conference. One ambitious plan drawn up by the thinktank Development Finance International (DFI) and shared with the government would involve 27 of the most heavily burdened countries being given a 10-year “holiday” during which their debt service costs would be slashed to below 10% of their revenues. Implemented by cutting interest rates and extending loan terms rather than writing off debt altogether, the $13bn-a-year cost would fall primarily on private creditors – which might have to be coaxed, cajoled, perhaps even legislated into taking part, as in previous debt relief initiatives. The “hope initiative” also envisages potential relief for another six small island developing states that do not meet the threshold on the basis of their debt burden but are regularly battered by natural disasters. US’s Reagan-era economic promises return as Trump’s AI-fueled growth fantasy

Back through political history to the age of Ronald Reagan, Republicans have repeatedly promised the US public that tax cuts would pay for themselves, firing up economic growth and filling the government’s coffers. The promise never really panned out. From the Gipper’s day on, the Republicans’ tax cuts inevitably increased the budget deficit. Despite its failure, though, the promise is back, coated in a fine new layer of artificial intelligence pixie dust. It will fail again. The treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, is relying on an AI-laced economy when he promises to deliver annual economic growth of 3% – a rate that, except for the rebound from the Covid pandemic, has been achieved only twice this century. Dreams of AI inflect Donald Trump’s fantasy that “we’re growing at a faster rate than we’ve ever grown before,” which will allow the government to “take care of the 40 trillion” in federal debt “over a period of time”. Financial markets, however, are not buying.

citation.title: US’s Reagan-era economic promises return as Trump’s AI-fueled growth fantasy

text:
US’s Reagan-era economic promises return as Trump’s AI-fueled growth fantasy

Last week, the yield on the 10-year treasury bond surged to its highest in almost a quarter century, more than a full percentage point higher than when Trump launched his misbegotten war against Iran. Interactive The war’s inflationary impact is the most immediate cause of rising bond yields. It already persuaded the Fed to raise short-term interest rates. But the treasury market is also being walloped by the US’s unbalanced finances. There is no realistic path for economic growth to generate the tax revenues needed to fix the US’s enormous and growing budget deficit. Investors are demanding more to cover the growing funding gap. Borrowing is likely to become more expensive still. Foreign central banks, which once reliably bought treasuries to build up foreign reserves and manage their exchange rates, have cut back on their exposure to US government debt. The treasury now relies largely on private investors seeking to turn a profit.

citation.title: US’s Reagan-era economic promises return as Trump’s AI-fueled growth fantasy

text:
US’s Reagan-era economic promises return as Trump’s AI-fueled growth fantasy

It finds itself competing for their money with the very AI superscalers on which it is pinning its future hopes, which are borrowing hand over fist to fund the buildout of datacenters to train their agents. Indeed, the US’s finances find themselves in a bit of a negative spiral, as rising bond yields put additional pressure on the budget. Interest payments on the federal debt alone are consuming 3.3% of GDP, up from an average of 2.1% over the preceding 50 years. And Trump’s fiscal management – his One Big Beautiful Bill Act is estimated to add $4.7tn to the federal debt through 2035 – is not making the budget math easier. The deficit already hit 6% of GDP – twice the size Bessent once promised. The Congressional Budget Office projected it will close in on 7% of GDP by 2033. And that was before Trump promised a $5,000 “dividend” to every US adult if the GOP kept control of Congress in the midterms. There is no realistic amount of growth that can fill the fiscal hole that Trump keeps digging. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFPB) sketched out a few scenarios.

citation.title: US’s Reagan-era economic promises return as Trump’s AI-fueled growth fantasy

text:
US’s Reagan-era economic promises return as Trump’s AI-fueled growth fantasy

Assuming the temporary tax cuts in Trump’s 2025 law are made permanent by a future Congress – an assumption that fits the historical pattern – and that the government does not recover the revenue lost when the supreme court struck down its national security tariffs, achieving a budget deficit of 3% of GDP by 2036 would require annual growth of 4.4% over the next decade. Achieving a balanced budget by then would require the economy to expand 7.2% per year. It is not impossible for AI to deliver this kind of growth. Some economists are willing to contemplate scenarios in which artificial intelligence boosts economic growth to 15% per year, by taking over much of the cognitive work usually performed by humans. But these scenarios do not appear likely. According to the CFRB, stabilizing the federal debt would require average growth in total factor productivity – a measure of how efficiently economic inputs are converted into goods and services – to hit 2.5% per year over the next decade. The US has only hit that once since 1959.

citation.title: US’s Reagan-era economic promises return as Trump’s AI-fueled growth fantasy

text:
US’s Reagan-era economic promises return as Trump’s AI-fueled growth fantasy

And that is despite massive productivity gains over the period from electrification, the completion of the federal highway system, the telecommunications revolution and the first wave of IT and automation. Even if AI supercharged the economy, its impact on the government’s finances would be muted, for it would massively shift the fruits of growth from labor to capital, and the tax rate on capital today is only about half the tax rate on labor. Moreover, such a shift in the distribution of economic spoils would probably call for massive government spending to sustain the livelihoods of the many workers left behind. What can we expect from the AI-pixie dust? At the moment people seem particularly worried about AI agents slipping their enclosures and killing us all. But even short of that, it is not a given that their impact will be inevitably positive for the economy, not to say the government’s finances necessarily provide the money for the federal government to right its finances. For one, their massive debt-fuelled investments are pushing interest rates higher, complicating government financing.

citation.title: US’s Reagan-era economic promises return as Trump’s AI-fueled growth fantasy

text:
US’s Reagan-era economic promises return as Trump’s AI-fueled growth fantasy

Their future promise, moreover, also comes with momentous risk. The Stanford economist Hanno Lustig estimates that for the owners of datacenters to break even on their massive investments in AI – estimated to reach $1.43tn this year – their revenue would have to grow by 45% on average every year for the next seven years. By 2032, it would amount to roughly 9.2% of GDP. A similar analysis by Jared Bernstein, former chair of Joe Biden’s Council of Economic Advisers, and Stanford economist Ryan Cummings, concluded that the nation’s six superscalers – Google, Meta, Microsoft, Oracle, SpaceX and Amazon – would need additional revenues of $13.1tn to $18.7tn over the next 10 years just to pay for their massive investments in AI. That is roughly the same as their total revenues over the last 10 years. It’s hard to forecast precisely what would happen to financial markets were these targets to be missed. But it’s safe to say that it might complicate the task of trimming the budget deficit and financing the US’s vast public debt. Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics.

Volkswagen boss backs EU plan to bolster domestic European industry

The boss of Volkswagen has backed EU proposals to boost its domestic industry, arguing European carmakers need to be able to “compete under comparable conditions” with Chinese rivals. Oliver Blume said “Made in Europe” rules from the EU “must reward real value creation in Europe”, speaking in Paris before the motor show this week. The rules are aimed at countering the rapid rise of Chinese brands in Europe in the automotive sector and other important manufacturing industries. Lower-priced Chinese manufacturers have prompted a crisis in several industries. Volkswagen is among the most-affected European companies. Germany’s biggest carmaker has launched a brutal plan to cut as many as 100,000 jobs. Blume said it was the “largest transformation programme in its history”. Related: Alarm bells sound in Brussels as EU sales of Chinese hybrid cars rocket The proposals for the Made in Europe rules, formally known as the Industrial Accelerator Act, would limit subsidies and public procurement to products with a large proportion of their materials and manufacturing coming from within the EU.

Blume listed a litany of challenges facing European carmakers, saying: “Europe is under enormous competitive pressure.” These included: high energy costs; lower demand as consumers struggle with high inflation; the need to be quicker to develop cars; and intense competition from China. It protects technological independence.” Volkswagen is exhibiting at the Paris show for the first time in 20 years. IFS: budget will be ‘work of fiction’ without clear plan to cover UK’s £35bn spending pressures

John Healey has been warned by Britain’s leading tax and spending experts that his budget risks being a “work of fiction” unless he sets out plans to cover £35bn in spending pressures. As the war in the Middle East rattles the public finances, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the damage from higher inflation meant the chancellor would need to either top up funds for his current government spending plans or impose deep real-terms cuts by the end of the decade. Against a febrile backdrop in the bond market, the thinktank warned Healey that failure to address the issue at his 28 October budget risked leaving the impression that Labour was setting unrealistic spending plans. Helen Miller, the director of the IFS, said: “Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the budget a work of fiction.” Related: ‘Costing billions’: is the pensions triple lock a lifeline or simply unaffordable?

citation.title: IFS: budget will be ‘work of fiction’ without clear plan to cover UK’s £35bn spending pressures

IFS: budget will be ‘work of fiction’ without clear plan to cover UK’s £35bn spending pressures

Her comment echoes a criticism levelled at Jeremy Hunt, the former Conservative chancellor, who before the 2024 general election was accused by the then head of the Office for Budget Responsibility of setting unrealistic spending plans. Publishing its influential “green budget” report, which analyses the public finances before Healey’s speech to the Commons, it called on the chancellor to avoid announcing a “steady as she goes” budget that delayed decisions until next year’s spending review. “If John Healey sets out spending envelopes for public services that he would not be willing to live within, his plan for meeting the fiscal rules will not be credible,” it said. Last week, the governor of the Bank of England, Andrew Bailey, said fiscal policy “must be credible and be seen as such by financial markets”. The following day, the Times quoted a government source as saying: “Andrew Bailey needs to focus on doing his job.” Miller said the Treasury adopting an assumption that “everything can be kicked forward” to next year’s spending review risked undermining the chancellor’s credibility.

“We would be better served by a chancellor who hopes for the best, but plans for the worst, rather than sets out plans that either say, ‘I hope it’ll be fine and some money will come in’, or ‘I’ll get a plan in a year’s time’.” Attention before the budget has largely focused on the hit to the chancellor’s headroom against Labour’s main fiscal rule to balance day-to-day public spending with revenues in 2029-30. With the war in the Middle East fuelling a dramatic sell-off in the market for government debt, higher borrowing costs are expected to erase a significant chunk of the £24bn buffer left by the former chancellor Rachel Reeves at the spring statement. Leading economists have predicted the market moves since the start of the war in February could wipe out about half of the headroom, adding to nerves in the Treasury over the risk of a market backlash. The IFS said that although the surge in debt interest costs could add £10bn to borrowing in 2029-30, the exchequer would benefit from higher inflation boosting tax revenue – meaning Healey could see headroom cut by only £4bn.

However, it warned against focusing on this buffer because the inflation shock rippling from the Middle East would also dramatically hit the government’s plan for funding public services. Higher inflation squeezes public spending power, forcing the government to choose between accepting real-term cuts and finding efficiency savings or topping up departmental budgets either by raising taxes or allowing an increase in borrowing. “It would be a choice to tolerate chunky cuts to the quantity or quality of some public services – cuts that would be larger if defence spending was increased within existing totals.” She said Healey would not need to make detailed plans for the next spending review period at the budget but merely set out overall spending envelopes that he would be prepared to live within. Time to tell US raider Saba Capital to get lost – again

Here we go again: another episode in the Saba saga, the story of a New York hedge fund causing havoc in the UK investment trust sector by taking big stakes in funds and then demanding change, often in only vague terms. The best that can be said about Saba Capital (and it’s not much) is that its belligerent boss, Boaz Weinstein, has disturbed the complacency that used to infect corners of the UK investment trust world, meaning companies that invest in other companies. It is now harder for a board to do nothing if the share price sits at a wide discount to the value of the underlying assets for long periods. Too often, though, Saba’s assaults look self-interested, short-termist or damaging for UK investors. The attack on Baillie Gifford US Growth Trust, a FTSE 250 constituent usually known by its USA ticker, is all three. Related: Nobel prize for economics awarded to two Americans, Hall and Woodford, for work on New Keynesian models – business live Regular shareholders in USA have roundly told Saba to get lost twice in the past 18 months but they will have to do so again if they value what they own, which they should.

The US raider, sitting on a near-30% stake, wants to install three of its nominees on the board via a vote at next week’s annual meeting. On a long view, USA’s performance has been excellent: an annualised return of 16.7% since launch in 2018, beating the S&P 500 over the period and within the top 10% of all UK investment companies. The only reason an opening, of a sort, has appeared for Saba is because the 16.7%-a-year returns haven’t happened in a straight line. The pop in AI valuations in late-2022 means USA’s five-year statistics are less impressive. But volatility is what investors accept when they buy into a strategy of backing high-growth US companies for the long-term. The portfolio is stuffed with stakes in big names in the AI world – Anthropic, Databricks, OpenAI, SpaceX and Stripe – that were acquired when the companies were smaller and sometimes still privately owned. A little bit of biodiversity in the UK investment landscape will be lost if USA falls under Saba’s control. What would a Saba-dominated board do?

Stellantis and Renault back UK to get EU car industry protection

Stellantis and Renault have backed the UK car industry for inclusion in proposed rules to protect EU industry, but urged the British government to consider limiting imports of Chinese cars. Emanuele Cappellano, who leads Stellantis’s European brands including Fiat, Citroën, Opel and Vauxhall, and François Provost, the chief executive of France’s Renault, said the UK should effectively be counted as one of the EU’s 27 member states for the purposes of the proposed “Made in Europe” legislation. The new rules aim to ensure EU subsidies and government procurement benefits Europe’s industry, rather than helping manufacturers from other countries. Europe’s car industry is under enormous pressure as it copes with lower demand than before the coronavirus pandemic, while also investing tens of billions of euros in shifting production to electric vehicles (EVs). The EU confirmed on Monday it would limit the number of hybrid electric vehicles imported from China to 350,000 cars a year. text:
Threat of AI share crash puts world financial stability at risk, says IMF

The threat of an AI share price crash rippling out across global markets is putting world financial stability at risk, the International Monetary fund has warned. In its twice-yearly Global Financial Stability Report, the IMF highlighted the sky-high valuations for AI companies along with their increasing debt pile as one reason that risks in the system are “elevated”. “The consequences of an AI correction could be global,” it warned. Aside from the US, Asian markets would be most exposed, and the UK and euro area potentially more insulated – though investors with US holdings would be hit. Athanasios Vamvakidis, the deputy director of the IMF’s monetary and capital department, launching the report, said: “The exposure of the rest of the world to US assets, particularly AI, is the highest it has ever been. So this is supporting the global economy through wealth effects today; but if we get a market correction it could have broad implications.” An AI crash was one of three “salient risks” to stability identified by the IMF, alongside rising government borrowing costs and the threat of a big cyber-attack.

It called this trio of factors “plausible near-term catalysts for a sharp tightening of financial conditions and market turmoil”. The IMF’s analysis underlined the interconnected nature of big AI companies, and the high levels of borrowing being undertaken to fund investment in the sector. “Weaker or less durable investment and profitability in AI could trigger a correction in AI-related asset prices, exacerbated by rising leverage, concentrated exposures, and circular financing arrangements,” it said. Such a reassessment would then “sharply reduce investment, trigger equity market corrections, and tighten financial conditions, with global spillovers”. The “magnificent seven” big tech stocks – Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla – account for more than 35% of the S&P 500 share index in the US, up from 12% a decade ago, and their total market capitalisation has increased by more than 50% in the past two years.

The hyperscalers are the companies building the underlying infrastructure for the AI rollout, including many vast datacentres. They include Amazon Web Services, Google, Meta and Oracle. Shares in semiconductor companies fell on Tuesday after the boss of Broadcom compared many AI investors to “casino” gamblers. Reports that the Chinese memory chip maker CXMT was making good progress on a new chip architecture also hit South Korean tech companies. The IMF also highlighted the growing leverage, or borrowing, that underpins the current boom and could amplify the effects of a crash. In particular, it identified soaring debts contracted by the companies themselves; hedge fund investment in the sector; and retail investors borrowing to speculate in AI stocks.

Bedbug infestation forces Qantas to ground plane in Rome

Qantas has been forced to ground a plane in Rome after bedbugs were discovered on the aircraft on its way from Perth. The parasitic insects were found in the front of the economy section of the Boeing 787 Dreamliner as it made its way from Perth to Rome for the QF5 flight on 9 October, a source with knowledge of the incident confirmed on Tuesday. Bedbugs are small, difficult-to-eradicate insects that feed on the blood of some mammals, including humans. As first reported by the SMH, the aircraft had to be taken out of service for cleaning after its arrival in the Italian capital, resulting in the cancellation of the Qantas Rome to Perth service on 10 October. Related: When bedbugs move into your home: ‘It drives you mad’ A Qantas spokesperson said the flight was cancelled to allow its engineers and maintenance teams to carry out a deep clean of the aircraft after “an issue identified on a small number of economy seats”. They said the airline wanted to “sincerely apologise” to customers for the disruption.

Affected passengers were given accommodation and rebooked on alternative flights within 48 hours of their original departure, Qantas said. The airline said its aircraft cabins were cleaned regularly and to an extremely high standard and treated with disinfectant every 50 days as a standard precautionary cleaning measure. Prof Michelle Power, a parasitologist at Macquarie University, said the bedbugs had “more than likely” been brought on to the plane in someone’s luggage or on a passenger’s clothes and then escaped into the cabin. “They’re associated with travel. People may go to a hotel that’s infested and because they like dark spaces and are attracted to the smell of human clothes, they make their way into someone’s luggage.” “They’re a flightless insect, without planes,” she said. Power said bedbugs were not dangerous, even though their bites could be itchy and irritating, but they were very difficult to get rid of and could hide in bedsheets and crevices for a long time without needing to feed.

IMF warns global economy ‘could soon test the limits of resilience’

The global economy “could soon test the limits of resilience”, as emergency oil stocks run low and government budgets become overstretched, the International Monetary Fund has warned. In its twice-yearly World Economic Outlook, the IMF said global growth had withstood the Middle East conflict better than feared over the past six months. It said the rerouting of oil supplies away from the strait of Hormuz, and the release of strategic energy stocks, had helped to contain the impact on oil prices from the US-Iran war. Related: IMF chief urges governments to tighten belts as global debt levels soar However, it warned that emergency stocks are now depleted, and high debt levels and deficits in many countries could leave governments with little capacity to protect consumers from any future jump in prices. “Without shoring up supply capacity and replenishing policy buffers, the global economy could soon test the limits of resilience,” it said.

A new messaging and payment “super app” marketed at British students uses servers owned by a Chinese company that has been put on a US military blacklist for its alleged affiliation to the People’s Liberation Army. ZyMix, which is being pushed on university campuses as the UK’s first super app designed “for gen Z”, combining chat, payments and community features, has a contract with a German-based subsidiary of Tencent Holdings, a Chinese conglomerate in Shenzhen. Tencent Holdings was added in January 2026 to the US Department of Defense’s (DoD) list of Chinese military companies, which is formally known as the section 1260H list. The citation on the DoD list says that the company, which is a gaming and social media conglomerate, is indirectly affiliated to the Chinese People’s Liberation Army. The blacklist is part of a US attempt to counteract what it regards as Beijing’s efforts to increase its military power by using technology from Chinese firms, universities and research programmes.

UK high street bosses urge chancellor to cut cost of employing young people

Some of the UK’s biggest retailers and hospitality businesses, including Tesco, Costa Coffee and the Co-op, have met John Healey to urge him to cut the cost of employing young people in his first budget. At the No 11 event on Tuesday morning, the chancellor heard from sector leaders – including the boss of Marks & Spencer, Stuart Machin, and Sainsbury’s chief executive, Simon Roberts – about the impact of the rise in employers’ national insurance contributions (Nics). Businesses want a partial reversal of the surprise move by Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, who lowered the earnings threshold at which they start to pay Nics from £9,100 to £5,000 a year. They argue the change contributed to the plunge in the number of high street jobs for young people and part-time workers and a rise in youth unemployment. They want the Nics threshold raised to £6,000, arguing this would help create jobs and ease inflation pressures on high streets. Retail and hospitality firms also hope Healey will ease the burden of business rates, and one source close to the meeting said they were optimistic on both fronts.

Fewer Britons plan to ringfence money for holidays abroad next year, says travel industry

The UK’s cost of living squeeze means fewer people plan to ringfence money for holidays abroad next year, the travel industry has warned. Despite war, wildfires and EES border checks, the numbers of Britons taking holidays climbed back to pre-pandemic levels this year – but rising costs may mean the numbers have peaked, according to an annual travel industry report on Tuesday. Numbers taking holidays at home and abroad continued to rise, although late bookings and shorter city breaks have been an increasing feature of holidays through 2026. Related: Bedbug infestation forces Qantas to ground plane in Rome Confidence in travel dropped slightly year on year but rebounded as fears over jet fuel shortages and flight disruption faded since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran in February, according to research from the industry body Abta. Overall, 88% of Brits took a holiday this year, matching the 2019 pre-pandemic peak, with a new high of 74% in the UK and 62% abroad.

UK shoppers seek deals as grocery price inflation rises again

Grocery price inflation in the UK has picked up further, prompting shoppers to turn to special offers to keep their bills down – while the price of chocolates has fallen in the run-up to Halloween. Supermarket prices were 2.5% higher than last year in the four weeks to 4 October, up from 2.3% last month, according to data from the retail analysts Worldpanel by Numerator. Spending on promotions over the last month was more than £250m higher than a year ago, with many shoppers using special offers to keep their grocery bills in check or to make pricier items and larger packs more affordable, Worldpanel said. Fraser McKevitt, the head of retail and consumer insight at Worldpanel, said: “With the autumn budget fast approaching [on 28 October], the cost of living continues to weigh heavily on the minds of shoppers. And the cost of filling up a car is only adding to the pressure on household budgets. “More than half tell us they’re very or extremely worried about petrol prices, and almost one in three say it’s already taking a real toll on their finances.

About 1.2 million households bought a pumpkin over the latest four weeks, up 10% year on year, while more than 250,000 households treated themselves to a pumpkin spice coffee. Bank of England and IMF bosses warn of cyber threat to trust in financial system

The heads of the Bank of England and the International Monetary Fund have issued a stark warning that rising cyber-attacks risk undermining trust in the financial system. Speaking on a panel about online fraud at the IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok, the governor of the Bank of England, Andrew Bailey, pointed to alarming headlines about self-replicating AI agents hijacking personal devices, and the French supermarket hack that heated fridges up to 50C. “If you try to say what’s at the heart of this debate about AI – for me, it’s about trust in technology and it’s about human control to achieve that trust in technology,” he said. Related: Global financial system is failing developing countries, says Ed Miliband Pointing to the key importance of technology in underpinning today’s financial system, he added: “If we don’t have trust in money, we don’t operate as a society.” Echoing his concerns, the IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, said the toll of cyber-fraud was now so great that people could decide to opt out of the formal financial system altogether.

text:
US inflation rose to 3.7% in September in blow to Republicans before midterms

Republicans are entering the midterm elections with the highest rate of inflation since the spring, according to a government report released on Wednesday. US price increases reached an annual rate of 3.7% in September, according to the latest data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, up from 3.4% in August. This final inflation report before the pivotal midterm elections comes amid polls showing widespread dissatisfaction with the Trump administration over the cost of living. Price increases are the highest they have been since the annual inflation rate reached a three-year peak of 4.2% in May. Gasoline accounted for over half of overall price increases, up 34% from last year. Fuel oil, which is used to heat homes, increased by 74% from last year, a worrying sign for households heading into the winter. Air travel, which many Americans rely on during the holidays, also increased by 22.4%. Overall, consumer prices went up 0.6% from August. Core inflation, which strips out volatile energy and food prices, also ticked up by 0.3% in September to 2.6% annually.

Average gas prices remain over a dollar per gallon more than last year, according to data from AAA. Meanwhile diesel, which powers domestic supply chains, reached a record high last month. September’s inflation rate is the highest it has been before a midterm election, with the exception of the pandemic, since 1990. Much of the anger is expected to be directed at Republicans, who control Congress and the White House. A tax crackdown on online marketplaces such as Amazon and eBay that could raise up to £1bn more for the Treasury is reportedly being drawn up for John Healey’s first budget. Under the proposed change, websites would be made responsible for collecting VAT at source for retailers on their platform who have an annual turnover of more than £90,000, no matter where they are based. The RBA keeps hiking interest rates – but are the rate rises actually working?

Interest rates have risen to 15-year highs and are pushing up mortgage default risks – but household spending is still growing. Economists say the surprising result shows this year’s four rate hikes have not yet fully hit the economy and may be less effective at fighting inflation than they used to be. If true, that could mean more interest rate rises are on the way. So are interest rate hikes working? What is the RBA trying to achieve by increasing interest rates? The Reserve Bank has increased its key cash rate to cut household spending and discourage businesses and workers from seeking higher prices and wages. It aims to bring inflation back under 3%. Related: Australian consumer confidence plunges to worst level since 1990s after RBA rate rise Financial institutions now face higher funding costs and have responded by lifting the rates they charge for home loans, business loans or bonds for big companies. But eight months on from the year’s first rate rise in February, spending is not going backwards.

The RBA keeps hiking interest rates – but are the rate rises actually working?

The slide in house prices is a sign that interest rates and higher borrowing costs are directly restricting economic activity, according to David Bassanese, the chief economist at BetaShares. House price slides are also an indirect channel for hikes to slow spending as homeowners tend to cut back when falls in home values make them less wealthy than they had been. RBA research suggests a 10% fall in housing prices – which is expected by mid-2027 – will cut consumption by 1.5%. Bassanese says consumer spending does not appear to have slowed yet by as much as past RBA models would imply. “We’re probably not seeing a major effect yet, but in theory, it should be starting to happen,” he said. The “wealth effect” of interest rates is typically slower-moving than the cashflow effect. But most homeowners are also wealthier than they were two years ago, with the median national price back to where it was in September. What about exchange rates? The Reserve Bank says the most important effect of interest rate rises is through the exchange rate.

Higher interest rates tend to push up demand to invest in Australia, lifting the Australian dollar, making imports cheaper. Related: Forget the inflation blame game – politicians should let the RBA get on with its job | Saul Eslake But the dollar has been fairly stable against other currencies because foreign central banks like the US Federal Reserve are also lifting their own interest rates. The Australian dollar rose from 65 US cents in November 2025 to 72 in May 2026, after the first three RBA rate rises but has fallen to 69 US cents. It has followed a similar path compared to an index of Australia’s trade partners, including China, Japan, Europe and South Korea. “We’re raising rates, but so is everybody else,” Bassanese says. “Our currency is not especially strong, although it has lifted somewhat over the past year.” How does higher unemployment stop inflation? Interest rate rises aim to push up unemployment but the hikes have had little effect this year. More jobseekers make it easier for businesses to find workers without lifting wages.

Higher wages would be passed on as higher prices for customers, so more unemployment tends to mean less inflation. But the jobs market has been surprisingly strong. Health and care sectors have rapidly hired thanks to bigger demand and government subsidies while productivity is going backwards, forcing businesses to hire more workers to keep up production. The RBA governor, Michele Bullock, has said she wants to see a small increase in jobless rates so there is less pressure from wages on prices, drawing criticism from unions. Unemployment increasing from 4.6% to 5% would represent an extra 60,000 people out of work if the workforce stayed the same size. But Bullock said after September’s rate hike that she does not expect job losses, instead hoping job creation will slow and more people will look to join the workforce, leaving jobseekers searching for longer periods. Markets expect only one more rate rise and not until May 2027. But the Deutsche Bank strategist Lachlan Dynan warns rate rises’ weaker effects add to the risk of another hike.

‘From liabilities to goldmines’: refineries eye record profits from diesel shortage

Days after Donald Trump announced a deal to import Russian diesel into the US in an effort to lower soaring pump prices, the world’s energy watchdog has warned that the global fuel shortage will drag into 2027. Trump’s temporary sanctions reprieve was criticised for offering “too little, too late” to temper the sky high pump prices triggered by the shutdown of war-damaged refineries in the Middle East and Russia – once the world’s second-largest diesel exporter behind the US. The International Energy Agency said on Wednesday that the shortage would stretch into the new year despite plans to ease trade sanctions or release emergency stockpiles, in a blow to the global economy. Related: Trump’s deal with Putin will have little impact on US diesel prices, experts say “Record diesel prices are already having broad economic consequences by raising the cost of goods and impacting real incomes, economic activity, and inflation,” the IEA added. Yet amid this gathering economic gloom some of the western refineries that turn crude oil into fuels are preparing to have their day.

The global shortage that has led to high prices on UK forecourts is poised to hand them record profits. “I prefer the world of disruption to the peaceful world,” the boss of the French energy company TotalEnergies, Patrick Pouyanné, mused last week. He said the energy crisis ignited by almost eight months of war in the Middle East had provided “plenty of opportunities if you’re able to capture them”. For Pouyanné, the key to reaping the benefits of a global fuel crisis lies in owning a string of refineries across Europe that stand ready to cash in by selling diesel into a starved market. Diesel accounts for 10% of the world’s energy consumption, and is known as a “workhorse” fuel for its role powering the equipment vital for sectors ranging from agriculture, mining and manufacturing to shipping and logistics. But by last month supplies into the global market had fallen by about 1m barrels a day from their 2025 level, owing to a combination of damage to refineries in the Gulf and Russia, and export restrictions from China. The soaring costs for businesses and consumers have economists worried.

They are already piling pressure on areas of the global economy from US farmers in the midwest corn belt to local bus operators in England. Many fear a broader impact, as fuel prices raise the cost of food, goods and transport across the economy. However, for some of the companies that turn crude into diesel this is a very lucrative crisis. Refinery ‘goldmines’ “We’re doing really well by being integrated,” Pouyanné explained. “Integration means your refineries in Europe, which you thought were liabilities, are suddenly becoming goldmines.” These goldmines helped TotalEnergies to its strongest quarterly profits in three years this summer, after income from its refining and chemicals business more than quadrupled to $1.8bn (£1.35bn) between April and June. TotalEnergies is far from alone in its good fortune. The biggest windfalls are likely to come from refiners in the US, where exports of fuel products have climbed by more than 50% in the past year from about 1.25m barrels a day to an all-time high of 1.9m barrels a day over the summer, effectively offsetting the losses from Gulf refineries.

Ukrainian soldier led team of divers sent to blow up Nord Stream gas pipelines, court hears

A Ukrainian soldier led a team of divers that, acting on the order of state authorities, laid explosives on the bed of the Baltic Sea to blow up the Nord Stream gas pipelines, a court has heard. On the opening day of his trial in the German city of Hamburg, Serhii Kuznetsov, who was a special forces officer with the Ukrainian military at the time of the pipeline attacks in 2022, was accused by prosecutors of being an accomplice to war crimes by attacking civilian infrastructure, causing an explosion, damaging property and disrupting public services. He appeared in court on Wednesday dressed in a grey suit, white shirt and black tie and flanked by his lawyers. Kuznetsov saluted as he entered the courtroom. He and his legal team listened in silence for 10 minutes as the federal prosecutor general read out the indictment, which was simultaneously translated into Ukrainian. Kuznetsov, 50, is alleged to have prepared and carried out the detonation of at least four incendiary devices of up to 27kg in weight at a depth of about 80 metres in the Baltic Sea close to the Danish island of Bornholm.

citation.title: Ukrainian soldier led team of divers sent to blow up Nord Stream gas pipelines, court hears

text:
Ukrainian soldier led team of divers sent to blow up Nord Stream gas pipelines, court hears

He is believed to have had six accomplices – four deep-sea divers, an explosives expert and a ship’s captain – who are alleged to have used a rented yacht and timer-controlled explosives. Kuznetsov and his country deny any involvement in the attacks. Kuznetsov’s lawyers argued that the trial should not be taking place at all, telling the court that the defendant, who they said had been held almost entirely in solitary confinement for 11 months, was being treated “like a pawn on a chessboard”. They stressed his inability to defend himself in the conventional manner due to his role as an army officer, which they said forbade him from speaking. It meant he was having to defend himself “with his hands tied”. They also disputed the accusation that the attack was sabotage of civilian infrastructure, saying the pipelines were “a weapon in the hand of the Russians”. The explosions took place on 26 September 2022, badly damaging the pipelines which had been constructed to carry Russian natural gas between Vyborg in western Russia and Lubmin, near Greifswald in northern Germany.

citation.title: Ukrainian soldier led team of divers sent to blow up Nord Stream gas pipelines, court hears

text:
Ukrainian soldier led team of divers sent to blow up Nord Stream gas pipelines, court hears

The blasts caused the Nord Stream 1 pipelines – Russia’s main gas supply route to Germany before Moscow cut the supplies in August 2022 – to burst. They also damaged Nord Stream 2, which was ready to carry gas but was never put into operation after Germany suspended its authorisation process just before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The attacks happened as European countries were seeking to transition away from Russian energy supplies in response to the Kremlin’s aggression. They exposed the dependence of Europe – and in particular Germany – on Russian gas as well as highlighting the murkiness of underground operations during wartime. Security observers initially blamed Moscow for the attack. Russia has denied involvement, in turn blaming the US, which has denied it just as forcefully.

In July, German state prosecutors accused Ukrainian “state authorities” of ordering the attack, arguing: “The aim was to permanently halt gas supplies via the pipelines and prevent Russia from using the revenue from natural gas trade to finance its war effort.” The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has denied his country was involved. Kuznetsov was arrested in August 2025 on a family holiday in Italy, with Italian police reporting that he surrendered without resistance. He had been travelling on a false passport. He was extradited to Germany last November after legal efforts to prevent this failed. Another suspect, Volodymyr Zhuravlyov, an air conditioner installer and hobby diver, was arrested on a European warrant in northern Croatia in August. He is fighting his extradition to Germany, having applied for asylum in Croatia. He denies any role in the sabotage.

Related: The Nord Stream riddle: echoes of mistrust ripple through Europe Aware of how potentially incendiary the trial could be, with Ukraine in effect in the dock for a crime committed against its ally – and one of its staunchest wartime supporters – the German government has declined to comment on the proceedings. On Wednesday, a group of protesters gathered outside the court holding Ukrainian flags and placards. One of them, a Ukrainian man in exile in Germany, said: “It’s a scandal that a Ukrainian is being accused of a war crime here today, when Russia is constantly committing war crimes in Ukraine.” The far-right populist, pro-Kremlin Alternative für Deutschland party, which is soaring in the polls, has seized on the Nord Stream plot to boost its argument that German aid for Ukraine must cease and the pipeline be reinstated so that cheap supplies of gas can help counter the cost of living crisis.

The pro-Ukraine protesters who turned out on Wednesday were just a few feet away from a group of supporters of the far-left BSW party, which echoes the AfD’s stance on Russia and would also like to see the pipelines reinstated. They were holding placards demanding a parliamentary inquiry to investigate any political motives behind the Nord Stream attack. Nord Stream was already a controversial subject before the attack. English and Welsh water firms could be forced to return £107m via lower bills

Thames Water, Yorkshire Water and other providers could be forced to cut tens of millions of pounds from household bills after the regulator said they had missed performance targets. Customer bills at Yorkshire Water could fall by £27 on average, while those at Thames could decrease by £7, according to estimates by Ofwat, the regulator of the privatised industry in England and Wales. The water industry has faced growing criticism in recent years amid rising bills, scrutiny over sewage pollution, high levels of debt and underinvestment in ageing infrastructure. As water customers cannot switch away from their provider if it underperforms, Ofwat instead has an “outcome delivery incentive” (ODI) system of automatic payments or penalties based on agreed targets. Yorkshire and Thames will have to return £75.1m and £45.8m, respectively, after missing targets in 2025-26, Ofwat said. The payments will add to the financial pressures on the companies, although Thames has been allowed to delay some of the penalties by a year.

The other companies that must return money to customers include: Dŵr Cymru (or Welsh Water), at £16.7m; South West Water, at £16m; and United Utilities in north-west England, at £13.4m. However, some companies will receive a reward payment because they met their targets – covered by higher bills. Severn Trent, which serves the Midlands, south-west England and parts of Wales, and Northumbrian Water are in line to receive an extra £41.8m and £35.9m respectively, Ofwat said. Northumbrian customers’ bills could rise by an average of £21, the regulator said. Severn Trent customers could pay £8 more per year. Overall, the industry is expected to cut its bills by a net £240m for failures during 2025-26. Of this, £107m is expected to be returned to customers via lower bills in 2027-28.

Cost of balancing Great Britain’s power grid reaches nearly £50m a day

The cost of balancing Great Britain’s power grid has soared to near-record highs of almost £50m a day after windfarms were turned off because of bottlenecks in transmitting power around the country. The grid operator paid £47.9m on Wednesday to turn windfarms off in areas with an oversupply of electricity and turn gas plants on in areas where supplies were tight. The costs, which are levied on to household energy bills, included a £1.6m payment for one half-hour period, and were some of the highest recorded since the early months of the Ukraine crisis in 2022. Related: Energy bills in Great Britain forecast to jump by £276 a year from January They add to the increasing costs of balancing the grid, which reached a total of £505m in September alone, the highest monthly cost recorded, and are expected to reach £3.2bn over the next year. The costs underline the growing concerns over the pace of Great Britain’s £150bn power networks upgrade, which is failing to keep up with new renewable energy projects being connected to the grid.

citation.title: Cost of balancing Great Britain’s power grid reaches nearly £50m a day

text:
Cost of balancing Great Britain’s power grid reaches nearly £50m a day

Overall, windfarms and hydropower plants with about 9 gigawatts of capacity were paid to not generate on Wednesday, according to the consultancy LCP Delta, enough to power more than 8m typical households. Instead, the grid operator was forced to pay for a string of gas and biomass plants to fire up and bought more electricity imports from Europe via high-voltage subsea power cables. The record costs have come to light days after the National Energy System Operator (Neso) was forced to call for “last resort” emergency assistance from its counterpart in France, which agreed to send last-minute power supplies to the UK on Monday and Friday last week. “The system overall wasn’t tight in terms of power supplies,” said Shivam Malhotra, the head of power trading at LCP Delta. “It’s the age-old story of a lack of infrastructure to transport power to where it’s needed, leading to lots of windfarms being turned off.” Related: What is Burnham’s GB Grid plan and could it bring down energy bills?

It’s quite surprising for this time of year,” Malhotra said. During the summer Neso faced severe grid challenges when a high-pressure heat dome led to a drop in renewable energy output and surging electricity demand to power air conditioning and refrigerators. Neso was forced to bring in independent investigators to look into whistleblower claims that its staff were involved in a cover-up of a near-blackout during record high temperatures in late June. The accusations, which were raised in parliament last week by the shadow energy secretary, Claire Coutinho, included claims that senior bosses at Neso were “risking blackouts to protect Neso’s reputation”.

Lisa Nandy ‘minded to intervene’ in Sky’s £1.6bn purchase of ITV

The culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, has said she is “minded to intervene” in Sky’s £1.6bn purchase of ITV, in a move that paves the way for deeper scrutiny of a deal that would create the UK’s biggest commercial broadcaster. Sky announced over the summer that it had reached a deal to buy ITV’s broadcasting and streaming arm, representing a big shift in the ownership of Britain’s public service media. Sky, which is owned by the US giant Comcast, sees the purchase as a chance to create a “UK-focused national streaming champion” that can survive in a media world dominated by Netflix, YouTube and Amazon Prime Video. Nandy said she was issuing her decision in relation to a series of “public interest considerations”. They included the need for free expression of opinion in news media, a “sufficient plurality of views” and a “sufficient plurality of persons with control of the media enterprises”. She said she also had to safeguard the availability of “a wide range of broadcasting, on-demand programmes or both, which … is of high quality and calculated to appeal to a wide variety of tastes and interests”.

citation.title: Lisa Nandy ‘minded to intervene’ in Sky’s £1.6bn purchase of ITV
