HelloFresh workers claim physical abuse and denied bathroom breaks in class-action suit

Workers at a HelloFresh facility in Newark, New Jersey, have claimed in court documents that they were verbally and physically abused and denied regular bathroom breaks, with one former worker telling the Guardian he experienced incontinence issues as a result. The newly proposed amended complaint comes in a class-action lawsuit first filed in August 2024 against the food prep service giant and staffing agencies. A New Jersey state court judge is expected to review the amended complaint in a hearing scheduled for 23 October. In the civil lawsuit, workers allege HelloFresh and temp staff managers took ID badges from temp workers that are required to be able to leave the facility, repeatedly threatened to call ICE and immigration authorities on workers, subjected workers to physical and verbal abuse, sexually harassed Hispanic female employees, and discriminated against the temp workforce that consisted primarily of Hispanic workers in violation of New Jersey’s anti-discrimination laws. A spokesperson for HelloFresh denied all allegations in the lawsuit.

“Upon learning of these allegations, which date from 2023 and years prior, we conducted a thorough internal investigation and found these claims to be entirely without merit. We vehemently denied these allegations when this lawsuit was filed over two years ago, and we continue to vehemently deny them today,” the spokesperson said in an email. In a reply to the lawsuit filed by HelloFresh in April 2025, the subscription-based meal kit delivery service denied the allegations in the lawsuit. Action Staffing, On Target Staffing and ProStaff Workforce Solutions did not respond to multiple requests for comment but have moved to dismiss the lawsuit. The lawsuit alleges HelloFresh assigned its Hispanic workers “the hardest work”, and that supervisors consistently made racist, abusive remarks to workers and berated them for speaking Spanish rather than English. Profit warnings from UK-listed firms at highest level in two years as Iran war drives up costs

The number of profit warnings from UK-listed companies has risen to the highest level in two years, as the war in the Middle East triggers a surge in costs for businesses before the budget. With less than a fortnight before John Healey’s tax and spending statement to the Commons, the consultants EY-Parthenon said companies quoted on the London stock market had issued 65 warnings in the three months to the end of September. As the war in the Middle East rattles the global economy, business leaders are pressing the chancellor for a package of emergency support to soften the impact from soaring fuel costs and energy bills. Healey has pledged to use his 28 October budget to give households and businesses “breathing space”. However, he has also warned that the government has limited resources to intervene as the conflict pushes the cost of borrowing to the highest level in decades, adding to the pressure on the public finances.

citation.title: Profit warnings from UK-listed firms at highest level in two years as Iran war drives up costs

It emerged on Sunday that Healey is preparing to announce measures to help thousands of high street shops, cafes, pubs and hairdressers with rising costs by using the budget to cut business rates for small companies. In a development that would honour a promise made by Andy Burnham in his Makerfield byelection campaign before entering Downing Street, the planned change, first reported by the Sunday Times, would result in the threshold at which small firms start paying business rates rising from £12,000 to £18,000. According to the EY-Parthenon analysis, housebuilders have already issued more warnings this year than during the 2008 financial crisis. Separate figures released on Monday from the property platform Rightmove show house prices have fallen by 0.1% over the past 12 months. Across all listed companies’ profit warnings, the most cited principal factor was policy change and geopolitical uncertainty, with rising costs also playing a large part.

Rising costs were the leading factor for 35% of the warnings issued, while 38% specifically cited the impact of the conflict in the Middle East. UK government promises disabled air passengers better safeguards

Disabled passengers will have better safeguards when flying, the government has pledged, including protection from damaged wheelchairs and support from trained staff. A report from an industry-led accessibility group said there was “much more to be done” but progress was being made, a year after a review led by Tanni Grey-Thompson demanded action to improve air travel in response to numerous incidents in which passengers had been left stranded without assistance. The Department for Transport said airports had added more staff training and a new standardised system has been set up to prepare airlines for handling mobility aids, after more than 1,000 wheelchairs were damaged in transit in 2024, equivalent to more than 80 a month. Is this the beginning of the end of the AI stock market boom?

The world is holding its breath as it waits to find out whether this year’s estimated $US1tn investment in artificial intelligence is resting on a castle made of sand. Last week, the Nasdaq 100 – an index of the 100 biggest non-financial stocks on the American tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange – dropped by 5.5%, triggering the usual angst that the AI boom is about to go bust. The recent rot may have started with the failure of Firmus, an Australian datacentre company, to list on the ASX. Related: AI firm Anthropic to commit 5% of shares to fund for ‘public good’ The multi-billion dollar initial public offering was, at one stage, on track to make Firmus worth more than Telstra – even before having delivered on its promised earnings. That proved to be a fever dream of its founders and a wake-up call to investors in Australia and around the world to reconsider the potential value of similar businesses. Interactive If this is the beginning of the end of the AI boom, it is only the very beginning, and tech stocks bounced back in Wall Street trade on Monday night.

Gerard Minack, of Minack Advisors, said his view was that investors were fundamentally overestimating the returns that AI providers will be able to deliver. “While I am becoming more confident that returns on AI investment will disappoint, I have no confidence calling the precise top of the AI market,” Minack said. Despite the recent wobbles, the Nasdaq 100 is still worth nearly three times more than at the start of 2023. On the S&P 500, meanwhile, tech titans Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla now account for 35% of the American sharemarket index, up from 12% a decade ago. The total market capitalisation of the so called “magnificent seven” companies has increased by more than 50% in the past two years. Raisah Rasid, a Singapore-based global market strategist at JP Morgan Asset Management, said what she was seeing in the recent sell-off was “a valuation reset, rather than the market questioning the efficacy of AI itself”. “This is still a long-term, structural transformation trend,” Rasid said. “This is very different from the dotcom bubble.” Rasid sees two potentially more meaningful threats.

First, that an open source AI model, potentially from China, could undermine the economics of AI and the hundreds of billions of dollars of investment – a concern shared by Minack. The second, said Rasid, is the risk that popular opposition gains a critical mass: for example, anger about datacentre developments or that AI will do more harm to workers and society than good. It doesn’t mean the whole thing is a disaster; there’s a reassessment under way.” The recent market action may also be evidence that investors are becoming more mindful of the risks associated with tech companies’ growing reliance on debt. New Bradford railway station will ‘transform travel across the north’

A new railway station will be built in Bradford to “transform how people travel across the north”, the government has announced. The station will be at the heart of the Northern Powerhouse Rail (NPR) scheme, built on the current Bradford Interchange site but allowing through trains between Leeds and Manchester. With the promise of more frequent and faster services, it is expected to support new homes and jobs for the West Yorkshire city, located alongside its Southern Gateway regeneration project and connecting to the proposed tram to Leeds. Approval of the station, which is expected to be built by the mid-2030s, has been regarded by northern leaders as a critical sign of political commitment to improving rail links across the north, after long delays in delivering pledged upgrades. The Department for Transport said that NPR would allow a “turn-up-and-go railway” for passengers from Bradford, with sufficiently frequent trains running across the north for people not to need to check timetables.

The mayor of West Yorkshire, Tracy Brabin, said: “Bradford has so much untapped potential, and faster, more frequent trains to Leeds and Manchester, and the transformation of the city centre will help to finally unleash it.” Henri Murison, the chief executive of the Northern Powerhouse Partnership, said the decision to build a new station at Bradford Interchange represented “a long-term commitment to the city and the wider north”. European air fares could rise by as much as 20% in 2027, Ryanair boss predicts

Ryanair’s chief executive has predicted a record increase in European air fares next year, as airlines grapple with fuel bills pushed higher by the Middle East conflict. Many carriers are not hedged against rising jet fuel costs, Michael O’Leary said, which he predicted would lead to airline bankruptcies and takeovers. He forecast these pressures would result in the price of plane tickets rising by as much as 20%. “You’re going to see air fares rise next year in Europe, I think by 10, 15, maybe 20%. You’re going to see ⁠the biggest increase in air fares, I would say, in history in Europe for the next 12 ​months,” O’Leary told a news conference ‌in Brussels. Jet fuel prices have soared in recent months, as the war on Iran has choked off fuel supplies. Jet fuel accounts for a large portion of carriers’ costs. The airlines body IATA previously predicted jet fuel prices would be 70% higher across 2026 – estimated to average $152 (£114) a barrel for the year, compared with $90 in 2025 – slashing airlines’ profits.

citation.title: European air fares could rise by as much as 20% in 2027, Ryanair boss predicts

Ryanair and many other European airlines had hedged their jet fuel requirements for 2026, O’Leary said, adding that Ryanair was 80% hedged at $67 a barrel at the time the Iran conflict began in late February. However, the boss of Europe’s largest airline said most European carriers, including Ryanair, do not have significant hedging in place from April 2027 onwards to protect them if oil prices remain high. “We’re 85% unhedged next year, and most of the other European airlines are in a similar position,” O’Leary said. Ryanair’s hedging contract for 2027 covered 15% of its fuel costs at $85 a barrel, he added, whereas spot rates are currently hovering at about double that level. EasyJet reported a £105m annual rise in fuel costs in July, adding it had hedged 62% of its fuel requirements for the first half of 2027 and 37% for the second half of the year. The airline announced in October it was cutting 700,000 seats from its winter schedule in an attempt to save fuel.

Billionaire Mukesh Ambani launches India’s biggest-ever IPO

India’s second-richest man, Mukesh Ambani, is launching what could be the country’s biggest-ever initial public offering (IPO), despite a stock market downturn. Mumbai-based Jio Platforms, a telecoms company backed by Meta Platforms and Google, is hoping to raise up to 302bn rupees (£2.4bn) and is targeting a 10.3tn rupees valuation when it floats on the stock market from Wednesday. Set up a decade ago as a subsidiary of Ambani’s conglomerate Reliance Industries, and led by Akash Ambani, the oldest son of patriarch Mukesh, Jio offers low-cost broadband to millions of Indians. Related: Indian billionaire’s payments firm plots biggest London flotation in years Jio secured 212 anchor investors on Monday before its blockbuster IPO. They include some of the world’s largest fund managers, such as: BlackRock; Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund; the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority; Fidelity Investments; Schroders; JP Morgan Asset Management; Franklin Templeton; Invesco; and Prudential. On Wednesday, shares will be offered to retail investors, and the IPO is set to close on Friday.

The family-owned conglomerate has been encouraging its 400,000-plus employees to buy shares, offering them a discount of 54 rupees a share. At the top end of the price range, Jio would be worth 10.3tn rupees, which would make it India’s fourth-largest company, behind its parent Reliance Industries, Bharti Airtel and HDFC Bank. It would be more than twice as much as the 4.9tn-rupee valuation in 2020, when Meta and Google invested in the company. However, the top valuation is far below initial expectations of more than £110bn when the telecoms group posted a draft prospectus in the summer. It comes amid a broader stock market slowdown in India, with the blue chip Nifty 5o index down more than 12% this year. Jio launched its telecoms services in September 2016. NatWest has ordered 13,000 staff to increase their in-office days from two days a month to two days a week, angering its staff union. The banking group, which serves customers under the Royal Bank of Scotland, NatWest, Ulster Bank and Coutts brands, will require all of its nearly 40,000 UK staff to follow a strict two days a week office schedule from February 2027, abolishing a remote-first policy for thousands of employees. Unite said it was a “kick in the teeth” for the 13,000 employees who attend the office only two days a month, and accounted for some of NatWest’s lowest-paid workers, including staff involved in technology, security, data analytics and human resources. The union said the change would pile additional financial pressure on staff already struggling with rising living costs, while undermining flexible arrangements for those with caring responsibilities or disabilities. Many had also structured their lives around flexible working agreements that were expanded during the Covid pandemic, it said.

Surprise drop in UK unemployment to 4.7% as John Healey’s first budget looms

Unemployment in the UK has fallen unexpectedly in the final snapshot of the jobs market before John Healey’s first budget next week. The jobless rate fell to 4.7% in the three months to August, from 4.9%, according to the Office for National Statistics. City economists had forecast a rise to 5%. In a further boost to the chancellor, the figures also showed that the number of payrolled employees rose by 13,000 between August and September, to 30.3 million. However, a slump in the number of job vacancies illustrated what some economists said was an economy moving sideways. After hitting a peak of 1.3m in the period after the pandemic, vacancies fell by 21,000 to 691,000 in the three months to September, the lowest since 2021 during the Covid pandemic. Related: Neet rates higher in England’s smaller cities and towns than in biggest cities Ben Harrison, director of the Work Foundation thinktank at Lancaster University, said the fall in unemployment “should not make the government complacent ahead of next week’s budget”.

What does the UK’s approval of the Jackdaw gasfield mean?

About four years and six energy secretaries after it was given the green light, the Jackdaw gasfield has been given consent to begin production 150 miles east of Aberdeen. So what does this long-awaited decision mean for the Labour party, household bills, the economy and the climate crisis? Does this break a Labour manifesto promise? No, because although the party vowed to “not issue new licences to explore new fields” in the hydrocarbon-rich basin, it made clear it would honour licences granted before it came to power. These fields include Jackdaw, which was granted a licence in 2022, and the larger Rosebank oilfield west of Shetland, which was approved the following year. Oil and gas licences give broad permission to explore an area for fossil fuels but consent is still needed to extract them. Although Jackdaw and Rosebank had both, they were blocked from starting production after a legal challenge by campaigners at Greenpeace and Uplift early last year. That ruling compelled the companies behind the project to resubmit their applications with extra information on the climate impact of the fuels produced.

What does the UK’s approval of the Jackdaw gasfield mean?

Jackdaw is owned and operated by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Norway’s state oil company, Equinor. Adura also hopes to develop Rosebank in conjunction with Ithaca Energy. A decision on Rosebank’s new application for consent is expected later this year. Will the Jackdaw decision lower energy bills? Probably not. Household bills are based on the price of gas in the UK wholesale market, which is determined by international prices that have soared amid disruptions to global supplies. These have included the loss of Russian flows to Europe and disruption to Gulf exports to buyers around the world – shocks far too big for the relatively small output from Jackdaw to outweigh. The Tories have claimed drilling could still help to lower bills under their plans to use tax revenues to cut VAT on gas and electricity bills for three years. However, this does not mean energy costs are fundamentally lower – or sustainable.

Meanwhile, Labour has cut VAT from electricity bills from this month until next March and ministers are understood to be planning to offer billions in energy bill support for low-income households at next week’s budget. What about the UK’s carbon emissions? Gas from Jackdaw could release between 23.6m and 35.8m tonnes of CO2 equivalent over its 11-year operational lifespan, but the carbon impact of new North Sea fields is “not clear cut”. That’s the view of the Committee on Climate Change (CCC), which advises the government on meeting its legally binding climate targets. There are two sorts of emission to consider: first, the “scope 1 and 2” kind, created from getting fossil fuels out of the ground and transporting them to users. These are relatively low in the British North Sea and make up about 3% of the UK’s total. In fact, the CCC has said there might be “emissions advantages” to the switch because scope 1 and 2 emissions from UK gas are by some estimates four times lower than from US and Gulf fossil gas imports. The second, far bigger impact is from the “scope 3” emissions created from burning the fossil fuel.

Although Jackdaw’s gas would release CO2 when used in homes, businesses, factories and power plants, there is no evidence it would lead to higher overall gas consumption. As Andy Burnham, the prime minister, said in July: “The question isn’t whether Britain will still be using oil and gas, the question is where does it come from?” A better way to reduce UK emissions would be to replace gas boilers and fossil fuel vehicles with electric alternatives powered by low-carbon sources. What about the impact on global emissions? Here, too, the answer is unclear. Some academics have suggested that more UK oil and gas would push up fossil fuel production globally unless output fell elsewhere. In 2024, the CCC said new fossil fuel developments would have a “minimal impact on UK carbon budgets” but if others followed the UK’s lead in increasing production, the cumulative impact could lead to “an oversupply that would pose a risk” to international targets. It urged the UK government to “reassess whether further exploration for new sources of fossil fuels” was aligned with its global climate obligations.

text:
French borrowing costs hit 24-year high as civil unrest and budget fears spook markets

France’s borrowing costs have climbed above 5% for the first time in 24 years as political concerns and the government’s failure to agree a much-delayed budget spook the financial markets. With some civic buildings still smouldering from recent riots, a fresh bout of selling pushed up the yield – or interest rate – on bonds issued by the second largest economy in the eurozone. The yield on the benchmark 10-year bond – known as obligation assimilables du Trésor (Oat), issued by the French Treasury – rose more than 8 basis points to 5% in morning trading, before easing to 4.99%. The French government has yet to pass its budget for next year, while the country has been rocked by increasingly violent street protests in recent weeks. Protests that began in September with students calling for extra funds to deal with mould- and rat-infested schools, a lack of teachers and large class sizes evolved into wider demonstrations about the rising cost of living. Initially calm protests have often been met with aggressive police tactics, sparking riots in many towns and cities.

Stores such as Louis Vuitton have been hit by looting, while protesters set fire to the town hall in Limoges. No single party has had overall control of parliament since the French president, Emmanuel Macron, called a snap election in 2024. The parliamentary gridlock has blocked his plans to increase the pension age from 62 to 64 and a series of measures designed to reduce or redirect state spending. France’s budget deficit was 5.1% of gross domestic product in 2025, while its debt pile stood at 115.6% of GDP. Forecasts for the deficit and debt show both increasing in the current financial year without remedial action. International lenders have become increasingly reticent about lending to Paris, accusing the government of becoming “fiscally incontinent”. Some have withdrawn from lending to France, notably Japanese fund managers, and those that remain have demanded a higher price for their loans, especially longer-period loans.

text:
Double blow to Healey as inflation rises to 3.5% and monthly deficit hits £24bn

Inflation surged to 3.5% last month while the government deficit was a worse-than-forecast £24.5bn, in a double dose of bad news for John Healey before next week’s budget. The Office for National Statistics said annual inflation rose from 3.1% in August, overshooting City forecasts of a rise in the consumer prices index (CPI) to 3.4%, as a result of the surging cost of fuel. Oil and gas prices have soared since the end of February, when the US and Israel launched their war on Iran, throttling the flow of fuel through the strait of Hormuz. Rising inflation has also contributed to higher government borrowing costs – the key factor behind the deterioration in the public finances since the spring statement in March. Official figures showed the government paid £10.9bn in debt interest last month: the highest September figure since records began, and only the eighth time the monthly number has been above £10bn. Payments on some government bonds rise in line with inflation. The ONS said higher inflation had added £4bn to debt interest costs in September alone.

Total government debt is estimated to have hit £3tn for the first time – although as a share of the size of the economy it has fallen to 94%, from 95% a year ago. In the financial year so far, public sector net borrowing was £97.8bn, the ONS said – £4.4bn lower than last year, but still £6bn higher than the independent Office for Budget Responsibility had expected. The twin pieces of bad news underline the fact that consumers are facing a renewed cost of living squeeze, just as Healey is also under increased financial pressure. The ONS said a rise in the cost of motor fuels was the single largest factor pushing up inflation in September. The average price of petrol rose by 8.2p a litre from August compared with a fall of 0.2p in the same period last year. Diesel, which is often refined in the Middle East, rose by 10.7p a litre last month compared with a fall of 0.4p a litre in September 2025. Air fares, which are heavily affected by the price of fuel, dropped in September by much less than usual after the traditional summer peak.

How might Andy Burnham tackle Thames Water debacle?

Andy Burnham has told officials to rip up their plans for how to fix Thames Water and present him with more radical options for what to do with the stricken company. Here are some ideas the prime minister is being urged to consider. Emergency legislation Burnham must introduce emergency legislation immediately to protect the supply of water for the public, said Richard Murphy, tax accountant and the brains behind Corbynomics. A new state-owned company, with a management team in waiting and all the necessary steps ready to take over the existing company’s systems, has to be put in place now. “A prime minister who cannot deliver water to maybe a quarter of the UK’s population would not be someone to be trusted with anything else. Andy Burnham has no choice but to address this matter, now,” said Murphy. The 1971 nationalisation of the Rolls-Royce aeronautical engineering company, to protect the national interest after it collapsed into receivership, could be used as a blue print. A similar national emergency exists now to protect the supply of water, Murphy said.

Murphy said that, in essence, Thames Water was financially insolvent, with real doubt about whether it could survive into 2027. Use Emergency legislation should ensure that the nationalisation is of the assets and undertakings of Thames Water, and not of the company itself. All financial liabilities of Thames Water would be left for the old company to settle. The government should not acquire them. The new company needed to be structured within days, said Murphy. “There is no time to wait.” Public control – probably via the courts Burnham must be prepared to go to court to take Thames Water back into public control, said Ewan McGaughey, professor of law at King’s College London. Moody’s has estimated a one-off cost of £14.5bn in 2019 to bring water into public ownership. But privatisation, said McGaughey, would cost up to £22bn extra for bill payers from 2025 to 2030, or £176 a household a year, in returns on capital to shareholders and banks, as set by Ofwat’s price review.

The higher the repair bills, the less that creditors or shareholders deserve under UK law, international law and our investment treaties, he said. He advises Burnham to prepare to go to court – creditors will probably sue – but they have no reasonable prospect of success. McGaughey says privatised water and the regulators have failed so badly that England pays among the highest bills in Europe, while nearly every river is illegally polluted, taps run dry and a trillion litres of water is leaked each year. Jim Chalmers has revealed December’s midyear budget update will project weaker growth and higher unemployment, as economists warn of a difficult six months ahead for the Australian economy. Two days after a senior Reserve Bank official foreshadowed the potential for another interest rate rise in under two weeks’ time, the treasurer in a speech on Friday morning will say “higher inflation is putting people under pressure, tighter monetary policy is weighing on domestic activity, and we can see that in the softening of the labour market”. “Treasury is in the process of revising all the numbers for the midyear update,” Chalmers will say, according to speech extracts seen by Guardian Australia.

Oil prices jump to five-month high as attacks threaten global supply

Oil prices jumped to a five-month high on Thursday after ​attacks in Saudi Arabia and hits to tankers in the strait of Hormuz threatened further disruptions to the world’s crude supply. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, rose by 3% to hit $112 a barrel for first time since 18 May. Yemeni Houthis, who are aligned with Iran, hit several targets in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, with two people killed and eight more wounded in a civilian airport in Dammam, and two people killed in a drone attack on a Saudi oilfield. Elsewhere the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said four vessels involved in “illegal” oil transfers in the northern ​Gulf were hit and caught fire after being tracked by its forces on Wednesday. It said three more vessels collided with mines west of the strait of Hormuz, and warned the US that continued provocations could lead to a wider response against its regional bases.

Concern is growing that conflict in the region could escalate further, almost eight months after Tehran’s effective block on the strait of Hormuz triggered what many feared would bring the greatest energy supply disruption in the history of the market. In the first weeks after the US-Israeli attacks on Iran, oil surged past $100 a barrel and market observers predicted prices of up to $150 a barrel as flows through Hormuz came to a halt. Oil peaked at $126 a barrel in April during the conflict and fell back below $100 in late May and then to lows of $71 at the start of July amid hopes of a ceasefire in the region. The price began to climb again after the memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran fell apart and fresh hostilities broke out in the Gulf.

Sainsbury’s expects challenging run-up to Christmas as households feel squeeze

Sainsbury’s has warned of a “pretty challenging” market in the run-up to Christmas as households are “finding it tough” and food producers face rising costs. Simon Roberts, the chief executive of the UK’s second biggest supermarket, called on the government not to “further aggravate” pressure on costs for business in this month’s budget. He said it was “important this government does not repeat what we have seen in previous budgets” in raising business rates and employers’ national insurance contributions. “That’s been really hard,” he said. After Sainsbury’s and other industry leaders met government ministers last week, Roberts said he believed “this government is really listening to business” especially on helping to create more jobs for young people. Roberts added that food inflation was not “anything like” some of the high levels forecast earlier in the year but suggested high energy and fertiliser costs could push up food prices next year. Roberts said that in a more unsettled global environment the UK needed to “improve food resilience and grow and produce more at home”.

He called on the government to increase tax breaks that support investment in technology – including irrigation and reservoirs – on farms, as the climate crisis is expected to lead to more hotter, drier summers such as this year’s. Shares in Sainsbury’s fell by about 3% on Thursday as the retailer revealed slower than expected sales growth of 2.6% in the six months to 12 September, with growth almost halving to 1.9% in the second quarter from 3% in the first. Strong online grocery sales – up 9% – and a 6% rise in sales of the retailer’s premium own-label Taste the Difference range helped with growth. Roberts said sales had slowed as shoppers had kept a tight rein on the number of items they bought because of a “focus on the cost of living” and had reduced spending on clothing and “big-ticket” items, such as furniture, at Argos. Sales at the catalogue shop were down 1.8% and Sainsbury’s general merchandise and clothing sales were down 3.4% in the half.

text:
Race to rearm: Telford gun hall brings tank barrel production back to the UK

For the last 20 years, Britain was unable to put a barrel on its tanks without buying from abroad. Relying on foreign allies seemed like a reasonable choice during years of relative security (for wealthy countries at least) after the end of the cold war. But Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has changed the calculation – and prompted a scramble to rearm among European countries, including the UK. Evidence of that scramble was on display on Thursday in Shropshire, where the UK defence secretary, Wes Streeting, opened a factory hastily constructed by Germany’s Rheinmetall to make barrels for artillery and British tanks. Such was the urgency that Rheinmetall’s chief executive, Armin Papperger, said the company had started investment “off the back of a handshake” before Christmas last year with Gen Sir Roly Walker, who leads the British army as chief of the general staff, without waiting for a formal contract. Eight months later, production of the first barrels at the factory in Telford has started.

citation.title: Race to rearm: Telford gun hall brings tank barrel production back to the UK

text:
Race to rearm: Telford gun hall brings tank barrel production back to the UK

Papperger said he was in talks to produce more ammunition in the UK as well, with a decision due in the next six to eight months. Streeting said: “It is not enough to simply out-innovate those who would wish us harm – though we must. We must also out-produce them too. Because advantage increasingly belongs to those who can manufacture at scale and field the capability fastest.” The factory takes a 3.2 tonne, 8-metre cylinder of specialised steel alloy and drills a hole through it to make the barrel shape. The surfaces are then honed to remove imperfections, before another turning tool adds spiral rifling to add to artillery accuracy. A specialised machine – one of only two in the world – increases the pressure inside the barrel to about 15,000 times the air at sea level to harden it for the explosive power needed to propel shells as far as 30km (18 miles). The Ukraine war will go down in history as the moment when militaries woke up to the brutal new reality of drone warfare. But for all the focus on uncrewed weapons, Walker said they cannot rival more traditional armaments for sheer firepower.

citation.title: Race to rearm: Telford gun hall brings tank barrel production back to the UK

text:
Race to rearm: Telford gun hall brings tank barrel production back to the UK

“In Ukraine, we know that both sides fire tens of thousands of rounds of artillery ammunition every day, and that generates a weight of fire and levels of lethality across the battlefield that drones alone cannot replicate,” said Walker, in a speech at the factory opening. He said it had been “sad” when the UK was unable to continue centuries of artillery manufacture that had lasted through the Napoleonic wars, two world wars and the cold war. Much of that work was carried out at the Royal Arsenal in Woolwich, which opened in the 17th century (and whose workers set up a football club that moved to north London in 1913). Yet production ceased in 1967, with the work scattered first around the country and then in some cases moving abroad. The new Telford gun hall will bring that capability back to the UK, albeit starting with production for guns for German-made, self-propelled, remote-control howitzers that take Nato-standard 155mm ammunition. However, in the future it will also be able to make slightly smaller tank barrels that use 120mm rounds.

citation.title: Race to rearm: Telford gun hall brings tank barrel production back to the UK

text:

These include the Challenger 3 tank, which is now going through final testing, and a British version of the remote-control howitzer planned for after May 2028. The factory will be able to make 245 barrels a year, plus 50 breeches – the part at the base of the barrel – although Papperger said annual capacity could theoretically be expanded to as much as 1,000 within four or five years, but only if the orders came in. Exports may also be on the agenda. Papperger added that Nato allies could manage with smaller output than Russia and its client states because of their higher quality. A Russian barrel will be able to fire about 500 times before breaking, while the products from Telford should survive as many as 4,000 shots, he said. Related: Royal Navy lacks resources to counter Russian threat in high north, MPs warn The Telford investment followed an agreement in 2024 between Keir Starmer, then prime minister, and his German counterpart, Olaf Scholz. It was part of a wide-ranging pact for the two largest military spenders in Europe to work together more closely.

Rheinmetall employs about 685 people in Telford, although only 35 will work in the gun hall, rising to 100 when it is at full capacity – hardly enough to kickstart the “reindustrialisation” of Britain desired by Andy Burnham. The bulk of the workers in Telford make the Challenger and Boxer armoured vehicles in a joint venture with Britain’s key arms maker, BAE Systems. Rheinmetall has been among the biggest beneficiaries of the massive increase in European spending on defence and in supplying arms to Ukraine. US intelligence services in 2024 reportedly foiled a Russian plot to assassinate Papperger in apparent retaliation against the company’s production of weapons for Kyiv. The German company’s market value has risen from about €4.2bn (£3.5bn) in the days before Russia’s invasion to €47bn on Wednesday, though it has dropped back from a peak of nearly double that last year.

Rheinmetall and other European defence companies, including BAE Systems and the British jet engine maker Rolls-Royce, have benefited particularly from European governments eager to reduce reliance on the US arms industry at a time when the White House has shown itself willing to divert supplies to its own militaries ahead of allies. Papperger said more governments were saying they wanted control over their weapons production. That could help to mollify Donald Trump, the US president, who has shown himself willing to undermine previously firm alliances. “To be a strong partner, you need strong armies,” said Papperger. “But on the other side, you need a strong industry. UK to relax post-2008 rules that hold City bosses accountable for wrongdoing

The UK is watering down rules introduced in the aftermath of the financial crisis that were designed to hold City bosses accountable for wrongdoing. The plans, put forward by the financial industry’s two top regulators, the Bank of England and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), include a reduction in reporting for “lower-level misconduct” and would also free 140,000 managers from extra checks. The proposals were announced as regulators hosted a dinner for City executives at the Mansion House in central London. They are meant to“significantly” reduce the number of roles that will be required to undergo enhanced checks and would require only the most senior executives – such as chief executives and chief financial officers – to be forced to prove they are “fit and proper” each year, and before taking new jobs. This will free about 140,000 staff from having to illustrate they are operating with “integrity” and following regulators’ conduct rules. It would be a watering down of measures that came into force in the mid-2010s, in response to widespread public anger over the 2008 banking crash.

text:
UK to relax post-2008 rules that hold City bosses accountable for wrongdoing

Related: Cyprus police investigate financial and tax affairs of ex-Chelsea owner Roman Abramovich The senior managers regime was meant to address the fact that few bank bosses were held to account for actions that contributed to the ensuing financial crisis. While the regime originally covered banks, it was later expanded to cover all financial services companies including asset managers and hedge funds. It is the latest set of City rules to have been scaled back since the government gave regulators a new objective: ensuring UK firms are competitive on the world stage. Those efforts have already helped lift the cap on banker bonuses, which were previously limited to two times a banker’s salary. The new changes will also lead to the loosening of rules around how often firms report bad behaviour by lower level staff. It means they will no longer have to report first warnings or “lower-level misconduct of limited relevance” to regulator’s targets, such as if staff are showing up late or dropping calls.

Instead, they only want to hear about “serious misconduct” and cases where staff are given final warnings or fired. Any initial cases of misconduct will still have to be flagged for top brass, including chief executive and chief financial officers. The Bank of England and FCA said that this would not mean bosses would get away with bad behaviour. Waitrose opens first new supermarket in eight years in north London

As part of a £1bn investment plan, Waitrose has chosen Cricklewood in north London as the location for its first supermarket in eight years. The upmarket grocer will open the store on Thursday and another supermarket in Hale Barns, Greater Manchester, next month. It also plans four smaller stores next year, including a supermarket in Oakham, Rutland, and three convenience stores in Bedminster (Bristol), Chalk Farm (London) and Springstead Village (Cambridge). In 2024, Waitrose, which has more than 300 supermarkets, said it planned to open up to four large supermarkets and 100 convenience stores over five years and would also refurbish a number of outlets introducing meat, fish and sushi counters, on-site bakeries and fine wine sections. The company has since ditched these specific targets and said it wants to focus on finding the right locations for new outlets.

After a difficult period, when sales were hit by IT problems which led to gaps on shelves, Waitrose is holding market share, according to the latest figures from market analysts Worldpanel by Numerator. However, the chain is coming under pressure from Marks & Spencer, which now has a higher share of the grocery market, under some measures, after opening a number of new food-led outlets. Sales at Waitrose rose 4% in the six months to 1 August. However, its underlying operating profit slid by £7m to £103m as it invested in keeping prices down and improving its loyalty scheme. text:
Some of Europe’s highest energy costs expected in Britain this winter

Great Britain is expected to pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe this winter as its reliance on imports to ensure a steady supply is forecast to deepen. Energy system operators have said the country will have enough gas and electricity to meet demand over the coldest months – in part because of paying higher market prices than neighbouring markets to secure imports. The official winter energy forecasts were published days after Europe’s gas market benchmark climbed to its highest level since December 2022 when Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine sent prices rocketing. National Gas, which runs Great Britain’s gas networks, set out its forecasts after striking an 11th-hour deal with the owner of a major Belgian pipeline to keep gas flowing into the country this winter by reversing a planned capacity cut. The energy regulator, Ofgem, approved the deal – which will add around 10p a month to the average gas bill. Without the intervention there was a danger of gas running out in the event of a worst-case scenario where an important part of the country’s gas networks failed as temperatures plummeted.

citation.title: Some of Europe’s highest energy costs expected in Britain this winter

text:
Some of Europe’s highest energy costs expected in Britain this winter

In addition to gas imports by pipelines, Great Britain is expected to increase imports of seaborne liquified natural gas (LNG) cargoes by about 5% from last winter, according to National Gas forecasts, at a time when market prices are three times higher than they were before the Middle East crisis severely disrupted Gulf supplies. Its winter outlook report suggested that prices could remain elevated if UK gas buyers need to compete more fiercely with countries in Europe for LNG cargoes amid low gas storage levels across the continent. Europe ended August on course to enter the cooler months with gas stores at their lowest level in 13 years owing to the slowdown in gas exports from Qatar, one of Europe’s biggest suppliers, and the increase in gas consumption over the summer to power refrigeration and cooling during the record heatwaves caused by the global climate crisis. The UK has some of the smallest gas stores in Europe after decades of relying on homegrown production from the North Sea.

Some of Europe’s highest energy costs expected in Britain this winter

UK production was forecast to fall by 6% this year compared with last winter, but the government’s controversial decision to approve the new Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea earlier this week, which was not fully accounted for in the winter forecasts, is expected to offer a modest boost to supplies when it starts up next month. Great Britain is also forecast to be a net importer of electricity over the colder months, according to the National Energy System Operator (Neso) separate outlook report. That is also likely to come at a higher cost owing to tighter European power supplies compared with last winter. The summer heatwaves reduced river levels across Europe, in a blow to French nuclear output and Norway’s hydroelectric reserves, which have remained below the 10-year minimum since late July. The UK paid a record £4bn on power imports over the year ending in August, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics this week, of which half was spent on electricity imported from France.

It has also made near-record payments over the past year to fire up gas plants while wind and solar farms have been paid to turn off due to bottlenecks in the grid. Even though Great Britain will use gas power plants less overall this winter compared with previous winters thanks to rising renewable energy levels, the need for gas to play a role during power supply crunches could be 7% higher than previously assumed. National Gas lifted its gas power demand forecasts for the most extreme electricity supply scenarios – when demand is unusually high and renewable output slumps – after noting over successive winters that gas plants have remained in high use when dark, still winter days lead to high electricity demand and lower renewable energy levels. Glenn Bryn-Jacobsen, a director at National Gas, said: “While supply diversity and flexibility remain sources of resilience, taken together these trends in demand and supply have resulted in tighter supply margins during periods of high demand and system stress.”

text:
Jim Chalmers faces a world of hard choices where the solution to one problem makes the other worse

Jim Chalmers in a speech last week offered the scant encouragement that the economy would be “a bit better” in a year’s time. Fast forward to Friday morning, and the treasurer revealed that his officials were busy downgrading their forecasts ahead of December’s mid-year budget update to show slower growth and higher unemployment. In other words, things are getting worse, not better. Related: Economy set to worsen, with higher unemployment and weaker growth on the way, Jim Chalmers reveals Overnight, a broadening Middle East conflict pushed the global benchmark oil price to US$113, and within sight of its April high of nearly US$120. Motorists are paying 60 cents more for a litre of petrol prices than they were before the US and Israel attacked Iran. That’s an extra $36 to fill up a 60-litre tank. Do that once a week and a family’s monthly fuel bill is $144 higher than in February. The New York Times overnight reported that the US and Israel have drawn up plans to restart attacks on Iran after the upcoming American midterm elections.

Westpac analysts have sketched out an “escalation” scenario for the Middle East conflict where oil climbs towards US$150, echoing warnings from the International Monetary Fund earlier this month. That worst-case scenario would have huge implications for inflation and interest rates, even as we brace for a potential fifth interest rate hike on 3 November. • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here Meanwhile, the one bright spot that has helped paper over many of the cracks in the global economy – the huge spending associated with artificial intelligence – has hit some serious wobbles. Investors are worried about the huge surge in debt among companies racing to build the infrastructure for an AI future – the trigger for another steep sell-off on Wall Street overnight. Community opposition to the massive datacentre build-out could stall the headlong rush towards an AI future. That is likely a good thing in the longer term, but in the short term is another stress to add to the wall of worries.

Rising chatter of a new tech stock bubble is naturally accompanied by talk of an imminent bust. With all this going on, no wonder that the treasurer can only offer the thinnest of gruel for Australians hungry for any evidence of an end to years of disruption, and of wages that can’t keep up with high and rising prices. High inflation, low growth and rising unemployment is a central banker’s “nightmare”, as the Reserve Bank’s Andrew Hauser has said. It’s also a nightmare for a federal treasurer who is increasingly unpopular and desperate for a win in the court of public opinion. “The pressures on people right now are very substantial and obviously that keeps me awake at night,” Chalmers told Politico. “And there’s a number of reasons for that, some of them are outside our control, and some of them we have some influence over. You know, providing some cost-of-living help, managing the budget in a responsible way,” he said.

“Those are the things that we can do, but in lots of ways we’re hostage as well to decisions taken in DC or Tehran or in Eastern Europe about two wars which are pushing up inflation around the world and weighing on growth around the world.” The high level of government spending is not helping the inflation fight, by any means – something the opposition is keen to point out at every opportunity. Related: Odds of fifth interest rate hike this year shorten as RBA deputy warns inflation outlook ‘worsening’ Productivity growth is, if not dead, then resting, and shows no signs of springing back to its perch. That means more inflation at lower rates of growth as the economy hits its speed limits sooner. But Chalmers is right when he says there’s a lot that is out of the government’s control. His options to alleviate voter discontent are limited, which is why he frequently falls back on platitudes and lines to the effect of “you think we have it bad? You should see other economies.” Sure, the government can lower petrol prices through another temporary cut to the fuel excise.

But the billions of dollars that pumps into motorists’ pockets makes it harder for the RBA to bring inflation back under control. Labor could go the other way and announce plans for big spending cuts in the December mid-year economic and fiscal outlook. That would help the central bank’s job, but would drag on an already weak economy and push unemployment higher – would they win any plaudits for that? This is Hauser’s “world of hard choices” – a world where the solution to one problem makes the other worse. UK government to make unprecedented intervention in setting of water bills

Ministers will make an unprecedented intervention in water bills and how companies prioritise investment, directing bosses to bring down costs and stop leaks and sewage overflows. Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, has told suppliers in England and Wales she plans to intervene in the next price review – conducted by the water regulator, Ofwat. Sources at the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said Andy Burnham’s 10-year plan, which will follow next week’s budget, would hand the government more robust powers to keep bills affordable and direct local investment. But sources close to Eagle said there also needed to be immediate action as companies began to make decisions before the next price-setting process, expected to conclude in 2029. There has never been government intervention in the five-year review process. It is run by Ofwat, which analyses companies’ business plans and determines how much can be charged to customers in their bills to fund investment and running costs.

It also called for far better communication and decision-making power handed to local communities and leaders. The first priority must be affordable bills, the letter says, adding: “Affordability means a laser focus on value for money for customers.” The letter says the public is clear about what the objectives for the industry should be. “They want clean rivers. text:
Oil price rises above $117 a barrel amid fears US will renew strikes on Iran

Oil has hit its highest level in more than six months as fears of fresh escalation in the Middle East conflict grip the energy markets. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, rose by about 3.5% on Friday to pass $117 a barrel at one point – its highest level since April. The jump came after Tehran said it would attack oil facilities, undersea cables, datacentres and AI facilities in the Gulf region if a new US-Israeli offensive was launched against Iran. Richard Hunter, of the broker Interactive Investor, said: “Widespread reports that the US is considering renewed military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections rather than pursuing a diplomatic route was enough for the price to pop, after what many had considered would be a brief conflict is now in its eighth month.” The oil price later eased back slight to sit about 2.7% up at just over $116 a barrel. Brent crude had traded at about $72 a barrel back in February, before the Iran war began, but soared to touch $126 a barrel by the end of April.

text:
Retail sales in Great Britain fall as struggling households cut back

Retail sales in Great Britain fell more steeply than expected last month, the latest negative economic update before the chancellor, John Healey, announces his budget next week. The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said the volume of goods sold fell 0.4% month on month in September, much steeper than economists’ consensus expectations of a 0.1% fall. The decrease, which was fuelled in part by poor online sales of autumn and winter wear because of an unseasonably warm September, comes as figures show consumer confidence in the UK has fallen at the fastest rate since the Covid pandemic. While retail sales dropped across almost all sectors of the industry, the volume of motor fuel sold soared 2.2% month on month despite prices at the pump hitting record highs, returning to levels last seen before the start of the conflict in the Middle East. In value terms, the 6.1% increase in fuel sales was the biggest month-on-month increase since 10.9% was recorded in March, the month immediately after the start of the US-Iran conflict.

And this fall in consumer confidence is also the kind of thing that makes the prime minister less likely to call an early election soon.” Non-store retailing, predominantly online sales, fell 2.2% month on month, the biggest percentage fall across the retail sector. Textile, clothing and footwear stores recorded a 0.9% fall, household goods retailers were hit by a 0.5% sales slump, while supermarkets dipped 0.4%, partly because of poor sales of clothing ranges due to the weather.

text:
UK consumer confidence falls at fastest rate since Brexit vote as cost of living bites

Consumer confidence in the UK has fallen at the fastest rate outside the Covid pandemic since the 2016 Brexit vote as the escalating economic damage from the war in the Middle East hits Britain. With less than a week before John Healey’s first budget, the latest barometer from the data company GfK indicated confidence plunged by 11 percentage points in October to -24 amid pressure on consumers from the rising cost of living. Highlighting the challenge for Andy Burnham and his chancellor before the statement on Wednesday, GfK said its consumer confidence index last fell by this much in a single month in July 2016, following the shock leave result in the EU referendum. The index – which has been closely tracked by the government and the Bank of England for early warning signs from the economy since the early 1970s – recorded its largest ever fall, of 25 points, in March 2020 just after the start of the first UK lockdown.

Boom in weight-loss drugs could lead to fall in beer sales, Heineken warns UK pubs

Heineken has warned British bars and pubs that the boom in popularity of weight-loss drugs could lead to a fall in sales of beer and cider. The world’s second-largest brewer sent a presentation to British hospitality customers earlier this month that said the use of GLP-1 medication – such as Ozempic and Wegovy – could reduce the desire to drink alcohol. This in turn could result in “fullness and fewer serves” of pints in pubs and bars, it added. The document, revealed by Reuters, said the GLP-1 era could lead to the tradition of the multi-pint drinking session becoming a less frequent occurrence. The Netherlands-headquartered company offered advice including promoting half pints, low- and zero-alcohol options and pairing drinks with small plates of food, or risk declines in customer visits and spending. “We see some changes in consumption behaviour among (GLP-1) users and will continue to monitor how these behaviours evolve in 2027,” said a Heineken spokesperson. “Consumer behaviour is evolving in response to a range of broader trends.

text:
More than third of post offices in TG Jones stores to shut by early 2027

Towns and even city centres face being left as “postal deserts” after it emerged that more than a third of post offices within the troubled TG Jones chain are closing. So far this year 36 branches within the high street chain formerly known as WH Smith have closed and a further 34 are set to close by early 2027, according to Post Office records analysed by the Guardian. TG Jones was bought and renamed by Modella last year. Before the private equity group’s restructure won approval from creditors in July, the chain operated 180 post offices and it had been feared that as many as 60 could be closed under the shake-up. Up to 150 of the 450 stores acquired by Modella are expected to shut, about 65 of which have already closed and at least another 46 are to cease operating early next year. This total of 110 announced closures include the 70 containing post offices. The larger-than-expected wave of TG Jones branch closures follows an announcement in the summer that 52 post offices will close within Morrisons Daily convenience stores this year, some of which are close to the TG Jones sites.

Telford’s last one is due to close in January. The majority of these lost sites replaced former crown post offices, the now almost entirely closed network of more than 100 directly operated large branches, which offered a full suite of services such as identity and passport checks, driving licence and banking operations. Some regions such as Essex, the West Midlands, Wales, Suffolk and Hertfordshire have been particularly hard hit. Six post offices in TG Jones stores in Essex are going, with Clacton-on-Sea and Brentwood shutting in January after the closure of ones in Basildon, Southend-on-Sea, Harlow and East Ham. text:
Bust companies revived in ‘phoenix’ deals more likely to fail again, study finds

Insolvent businesses reacquired by their previous management in “pre-pack” administrations are much more likely to fail again and tend to repay far less to creditors, research for the Guardian suggests. The study is the latest to raise questions about the practice of “phoenixism” – accounting’s controversial art of liquidating companies to allow directors to return with a new entity, free of debts. The process tends to involve pre-pack administrations, where a supposed corporate rescue is agreed before commencing insolvency proceedings. These orchestrated deals often leave unsecured creditors nursing large losses. HM Revenue and Customs estimates that phoenixisms cost taxpayers hundreds of millions of pounds a year. Cases have included owners extracting millions of pounds in dividends and loans from businesses they subsequently arrange to buy back from administrators. The study was commissioned by the Guardian from Turnstone Intelligence, which used AI agents to read official documents relating to more than 1,700 administrations during 2019.

citation.title: Bust companies revived in ‘phoenix’ deals more likely to fail again, study finds

text:
Bust companies revived in ‘phoenix’ deals more likely to fail again, study finds

The research company noted much poorer outcomes when a business’s assets were reacquired by “connected parties”, such as former directors and shareholders. It found that 44% of pre-packs had resulted in a second insolvency by July 2026 when assets were bought by a connected party. Just 26% of pre-packs produced a subsequent insolvency when the acquirer was unconnected to the failed company. Ben Sims, managing director of Turnstone Intelligence, said: “I was surprised how big the gap remains. These results support what many in the industry have long suspected and will feed the continuing debate as to whether saving these businesses is worth the impact on taxpayers and creditors.” The data showed that connected parties appeared far more likely to be permitted to defer payments in pre-packs. A total of 198 out of 303 connected-party administrations – 65% – allowed former owners and directors to reacquire the assets via future instalments. For unconnected pre-packs, 28% of buyers used deferred payments.

citation.title: Bust companies revived in ‘phoenix’ deals more likely to fail again, study finds

text:
Bust companies revived in ‘phoenix’ deals more likely to fail again, study finds

Unsecured creditors, who typically include HMRC, received a return in only 23% of pre-packs involving a connected party deferring payments, with those deals paying out just 1.58p in the pound. When the buyer was unconnected, 36% of pre-pack administrations resulted in repayments to those creditors, at a rate of 7.86p in the pound. “What was interesting to us was the sheer scale of losses,” Sims said. “You would hope these deals would provide better outcomes to creditors, but we see them getting almost nothing. Of course, the biggest loser is often the taxpayer.” The findings appear to closely mirror results from two well-known reports in the field: research by the University of Wolverhampton for the government in 2014 (Graham review) and a European Union-funded 2018 study. Both pointed to poorer outcomes in connected pre-pack administrations. Those issues were compounded when the assets were reacquired by connected parties through deferred payments.

citation.title: Bust companies revived in ‘phoenix’ deals more likely to fail again, study finds

text:
Bust companies revived in ‘phoenix’ deals more likely to fail again, study finds

Riz Mokal, an honorary law professor at University College London who co-authored the EU study, said: “These are striking findings and are consistent with our earlier work. They reinforce a wider concern that connected-party pre-packs can allow non-viable ‘zombie’ businesses to shed their unsecured liabilities and continue trading, harming not only their creditors, including HMRC, but also competitors that continue to pay their way.” The methodology used by the latest researchers was broadly consistent with the earlier, EU-funded study. They used AI agents to read filings submitted over the past seven years for administrations commenced in England and Wales in 2019 – which Turnstone said was “long enough for creditor returns to settle and buyer failures to show”. The sweep of insolvency filings identified 544 pre-pack sales in 1,738 administrations during 2019, with the study’s numbers checked by other computer models and verified by humans.

Phoenixism is legal and its defenders say the practice can deliver better returns for creditors, with experienced directors sometimes better-placed than newcomers to salvage a failed company. R3, an insolvency industry body, said the research looked only at cases that predated 2021 rules that “increased scrutiny of connected-party pre-pack sales and introduced additional safeguards and transparency requirements”. These included requiring independent evaluators to clear sales to connected parties. Caroline Sumner, chief executive of R3, said: “A connected-party pre-pack administration sale is a legitimate and regulated insolvency process overseen by licensed insolvency practitioners and subject to extensive professional and statutory requirements. The duties of an administrator in a pre-pack administration sale are to achieve the best outcome for creditors of the company overall. “It’s important to distinguish between phoenix activity and connected-party pre-pack administrations.

text:
Cutting ‘red tape’ is nothing but a red herring – and arguably counterproductive

Before becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham pledged to “end 40 years of neoliberalism”. But as he prepares for his first budget on Wednesday, his government is yet to let go of one of its most tedious cliches: red tape. In the run-up to the chancellor John Healey’s high-stakes Commons address, the government issued a press release last week promising his plans would include measures to “slash the red tape choking firms”. Named after the tape once used to tie up government bills, and popularised by the historian Thomas Carlyle, the phrase is straight from the neoliberal playbook and has long outlived its usefulness. Getting the interfering state out of the way of the wealth creators was a trope of Thatcher and Reaganite economics, and on this side of the pond it has been repeated ad nauseam by every government since. Thatcher unleashed the City with her “big bang” deregulation drive, and her successor John Major was enthusiastic about “hacking back the jungle of red tape”.

citation.title: Cutting ‘red tape’ is nothing but a red herring – and arguably counterproductive

text:
Cutting ‘red tape’ is nothing but a red herring – and arguably counterproductive

It was the man he appointed for the job – Michael Heseltine – who coined what has become the most hackneyed description of this particular approach: the “bonfire of red tape”. With Labour back in power, Gordon Brown celebrated a light-tough regulatory regime for the UK’s hard-driving financial sector – until the Treasury had to bail out the banks after the 2008 financial crisis. Boris Johnson wanted to unfetter Britain’s businesses from “Brussels bureaucracy” and waffled on during the Brexit campaign about bendy bananas. Yet, after Brexit, business groups said their members would rather comply with longstanding EU standards in many areas than adopt an entirely new UK regime. And bananas are no more or less bendy than before. Rachel Reeves had a more unpleasantly graphic way of making a similar point, referring to regulation as a “boot on the neck” of British business. There is nothing wrong with ensuring the interaction between business and the state is smooth. But even during the early years of neoliberalism, the free market good, regulation bad dichotomy was always unhelpful, for several reasons.

citation.title: Cutting ‘red tape’ is nothing but a red herring – and arguably counterproductive

text:
Cutting ‘red tape’ is nothing but a red herring – and arguably counterproductive

First, good regulation – a robust competition regime, for example – is essential to make markets work well. And even most enthusiasts for a laissez-faire approach would acknowledge the need for some basic quality standards – for food and medicines, for example. When it comes to the labour market, Labour has unashamedly adopted a pro-regulation stance. Its Employment Rights Act is the most significant increase in workers’ rights in a generation – but it inevitably, and deliberately, increases the rules firms must follow. That is to the benefit, ministers rightly argue, of low-paid employees trapped in insecure work. But a bonfire of red tape it is not. Labour posing as a champion of deregulation will seem unconvincing, given that context. Second, and ironically, the march of neoliberalism itself is a reason regulation has mushroomed in recent decades. As the Labour MP Yuan Yang argued in a recent lecture for the journal Renewal, as the state retreated from providing important services, watchdog institutions to oversee the private sector became necessary.

citation.title: Cutting ‘red tape’ is nothing but a red herring – and arguably counterproductive

text:
Cutting ‘red tape’ is nothing but a red herring – and arguably counterproductive

As she put it: “The neoliberal illusion, that privatisation liberated markets from state interference, obscures the reality that the state already significantly controls our privatised utilities, but through a maze of arm’s length regulatory agencies which operate outside democratic influence.” For the water sector, privatised in 1989, these include Ofwat, which sets bills (with the Competition and Markets Authority acting as an appeals body in the event of a dispute); the Drinking Water Inspectorate; the Environment Agency; and the Consumer Council for Water. Yet, as Yang points out, none are responsible for drawing up a coherent plan for the sector as a whole. “Everyone knows how this story ends: with our rivers polluted and our water infrastructure dangerously lacking.” Hacking away at the regulatory thicket fails to deal with the structural features of the economy that make the rules necessary in the first place. Mat Lawrence, the director of the thinktank Common Wealth and author of The Productive State, a policy paper influential among those close to Burnham, calls this “the regulatory state”.

“It is all down to attention to detail and everything we do is based around that.” Gary Billingham is demonstrating how the 28 pieces which make up an Ettinger wallet are cut from leather using a hydraulic press by the small team at one of Walsall’s last remaining leather goods factories. Billingham has been at the factory near Birmingham since the 1980s, when “there were three pages in the Yellow Pages” business directory listing leather factories in the West Midlands town. “They were everywhere. Interest rates unlikely to reach 4.75% by next summer, say City economists

Financial markets are wrong to predict the Bank of England will raise UK interest rates by a full percentage point or more by next summer, City economists believe. According to market-implied interest rate expectations, the Bank is likely to raise interest rates at least four times over the next year, lifting the bank rate from 3.75% today to 4.75% by the end of July, and possibly to 5% – meaning five rises – by December 2027. But a number of City experts believe such a sharp tightening cycle is unlikely, given there is little sign that the rise in energy costs is pushing up other prices sharply. “If you look at the swaps market, and you look at what’s priced in for the Bank of England, you’ve got four rate hikes and then no cuts ever. And I think you’d be hard-pressed to find anybody that really agrees with that,” said James Smith, a developed markets economist at the Dutch bank ING. “By next spring, I think they [the Bank] could be sounding the all clear, and by the end of next year they could be cutting rates again,” Smith told a briefing in the City last week.

citation.title: Interest rates unlikely to reach 4.75% by next summer, say City economists

text:
Interest rates unlikely to reach 4.75% by next summer, say City economists

Market-implied interest rates are calculated from the prices of a range of financial instruments, including derivatives such as “swaps”, to establish where traders think interest rates will be in future. Economists cite several reasons why market-implied interest rates expectations are high. One is that these expectations have been closely correlated with oil prices since the Iran war began. The higher oil prices have risen, the more rate increases have been priced in. An investor could be right that interest rates won’t rise as far as markets think, but if oil prices keep increasing in the meantime, they would face mark-to-market losses and potentially margin calls. “It can get pretty painful, so a lot of traders are quite reluctant to take this risk until there’s greater certainty about energy supply and the extent of inflation this winter,” said Smith. Many traders got burnt at the start of the current Middle East crisis, when most were positioned for further rate cuts this year, he said.

Sanjay Raja, the chief UK economist at Deutsche Bank, also doubts that the Bank will raise rates as fast as the market pricing suggests. “I do not believe that any mainstream forecaster thinks the Bank of England will hike to 5% by the end of next year with the information set we have today,” Raja said. “It’s not to say it won’t happen. But based on current projections, it seems less likely.” He has calculated that a lot of the forecast interest rate rises is actually “baked-in risk premia” – where investors require an extra return to protect them from uncertainty or instability. “Once we strip that out, we have estimated that there is only really ~50bps [half a percentage point] of hikes pencilled in,” he said. Deutsche Bank’s base case is for the Bank of England to take the bank rate to 4.25% by next February and then hold rates there until the end of 2027. The Bank of England is widely expected to raise interest rates to 4% at its next meeting, on 5 November, after UK inflation rose further above its target in September to 3.5%.

The boss whose twice-bust business appears to be back despite £3m debts

For three decades, the recruitment industry treated Andrew Woosnam well. Having learned his trade during the 1990s, he graduated to create his own firm at the turn of the millennium – which allowed him to bank millions of pounds in salary, dividends and loans and to buy assets including a grand house in Berkshire once owned by the comedians Dawn French and Lenny Henry. But life has become much tougher of late for Woosnam, whose recruitment business has twice entered insolvency proceedings since September last year. His three-hectare (six-acre) property – which cost £2.2m in 2013 – is now being eyed by insolvency professionals chasing him on behalf of creditors owed more than £3m by his bust companies, including more than £1m due to the UK taxpayer. This all represents a stark change in how Woosnam’s Premier Group Recruitment appeared just a few years ago, when it was trumpeting its status as an award-winning business.

citation.title: The boss whose twice-bust business appears to be back despite £3m debts

text:
The boss whose twice-bust business appears to be back despite £3m debts

Woosnam owned 99% of the shares in the company, which went into administration in September 2025 owing £2.9m, including £647,000 to HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC), who had begun enforcement proceedings against it. The recruiter’s assets were acquired three days later by a new company, called PGGBR Ltd, also owned by Woosnam, who made an initial £10,000 payment and promised administrators he would transfer a further £600,000 via monthly £25,000 instalments over the subsequent two years. Adding up the future promised payments meant Woosnam theoretically trumped the £321,000 of cash offered by a competing bidder for Premier’s assets, although his detractors might argue that this arrangement had all the hallmarks of a structure that has been criticised as being highly risky for creditors: pre-pack administrations. These can allow a connected party to buy back a business on a deferred consideration, and have been cited in a series of studies that appear to show they tend to result in worse outcomes. So it transpired in the Woosnam case.

The payments he had promised from his phoenixed business failed to materialise, while the new company ran up a further £400,000 debt to HMRC, according to the latest Companies House filings. The Guardian approached one of the Premier Group joint administrators based at KRE Corporate Recovery but he did not return phone calls asking about the case. Woosnam had received a £1.2m director’s loan from the defunct Premier Group and had taken dividends out of the company totalling almost £2m since 2022. He also appears to have received a further £200,000 via a director’s loan from PGGBR before the new phoenix company was placed into liquidation last month. If that sounds terminal, there is a possibility you may have underestimated Woosnam, whose twice-bust business now appears to have resurfaced for a third time.

Retail leads the way on paternity leave as government urged to improve offer

“Being able to take six weeks’ paid paternity leave, flexibly, made a huge difference to me and my family, giving me the time to support my partner and settle into being a new parent,” said Marks & Spencer employee Joe Erskine. The food and clothing retailer increased its paternity leave offering from two to six weeks at full pay in 2024, meaning Erskine benefited from the new policy when his second child was born 17 months ago. M&S and Tesco are among the retailers leading the way in offering enhanced paternity leave to their staff, new research has shown, highlighting the widening gap between the more family-friendly policies offered to new fathers working in the retail sector compared with those in construction, manufacturing and agriculture. Both companies offer six weeks at full pay to employees, far outstripping the statutory two-week minimum paternity leave offer and making them among the most generous of UK blue-chip companies listed on the FTSE 100, according to figures compiled by campaign group The Dad Shift and Ian Dinwiddy of Inspiring Dads.

Drive reindustrialisation from No 10 North or risk failure, MPs tell Burnham

Andy Burnham’s pledge to reindustrialise Britain is doomed to fail unless it is driven decisively from his new No 10 North outpost in Manchester, a group of more than 90 backbench Labour MPs have said. The PM has suggested that rebuilding the UK’s industrial capacity will be central to meeting his pledge to bring “good growth in every postcode”. John Healey, who will deliver his first budget as chancellor on Wednesday, used his speech at Labour’s conference last month to promise a “new age of industrialisation”. Related: France drops opposition to UK being included in ‘Made in Europe’ legislation However, in a briefing paper seen by the Guardian, the backbenchers warn that decades of deindustrialisation and deregulation mean the government no longer has the detailed understanding of industry needed to make such a plan work. “The state has lost capacity and has acquired a worrying set of behaviours which will inhibit reindustrialisation. The state has become less knowledgable about the state of the economy and our businesses, unable to comprehensively plan and slow to make decisions,” the paper says.
