The MPs are calling on Burnham to pass a new Reindustrialisation Act, to set clear targets for creating jobs by rebuilding the country’s manufacturing capacity, and to ensure ministers are held to account against them. “If we do not plan for reindustrialisation, we cannot achieve it,” the group argues. The briefing paper urges the PM to give the job of overseeing reindustrialisation to the first secretary of state, Louise Haigh, and base it at No 10 North, the Manchester outpost he established in July, which has already taken on some responsibility for growth policy. And the paper argues that the National Wealth Fund – the arm’s length body that invests in promising businesses – should be transformed into a Reindustrialisation Development Corporation, whose primary job is to provide capital for rebuilding UK industry.

text:
European gas prices soar to four-year high over winter supply fears

European gas prices have jumped to levels not seen since 2022 as fears continue to grow around the continent’s supply this winter and the conflict in the Middle East. Wholesale gas prices hit €97 (£81) a megawatt-hour on Monday, as temperatures across Europe fell and traders priced in stronger demand for heating. The UK’s month ahead contract also rose by 4% to 240p a therm, its highest level since December 2022 when prices were rocketing after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The jump in gas prices comes as fears grow that there could be further supply disruptions in the Middle East, amid reports the US and Israel have drawn up plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the US midterm elections. Those reports helped send the oil price as high as $117 a barrel on Friday. The international Brent crude benchmark retreated about 2% on Monday but remains at nearly $115 a barrel.

citation.title: European gas prices soar to four-year high over winter supply fears

text:
European gas prices soar to four-year high over winter supply fears

Europe is also facing a shortage of stored gas reserves as it heads into winter with stores at their lowest level in more than a decade owing to a slowdown in exports from Qatar and an increase in consumption in the summer to power refrigeration and cooling. European storage is now about 75% full, against a seasonal average closer to 80%. Britain’s energy regulators have said the country is expected to pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe this winter amid a reliance on imports to ensure a steady supply. The UK has some of the smallest gas stores in Europe after decades of relying on homegrown production from the North Sea. The UK paid a record £4bn on power imports over the year ending in August, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics, of which half was spent on electricity imported from France. It has also made near-record payments over the past year to fire up gas plants while wind and solar farms have been paid to turn off because of bottlenecks in the grid.

text:
Almost a quarter of European airline pilots fly when too fatigued to work

Three in four European airline pilots have taken microsleeps in the cockpit, while almost a quarter routinely fly despite being too fatigued to work, according to a report. The findings, based on a survey of almost 7,200 captains and first officers by the European Cockpit Association (ECA), include pilots reporting insufficient rest, pressure to extend working hours and fears of being penalised for declaring themselves unfit to fly. Almost a quarter (24%) of pilots admitted they usually continue flying rather than report themselves unfit due to fatigue, while another 16.8% said they call in sick instead. In aviation, fatigue can result from long duty hours, insufficient rest, irregular schedules and flying across time zones, which disrupt the body’s natural sleep cycle. It is a significant safety concern because it can impair pilots’ judgment, slow their reactions, reduce alertness and impair responses to unexpected situations. Under European aviation safety regulations, airlines are required to have systems in place to identify, monitor and manage crew fatigue.

citation.title: Almost a quarter of European airline pilots fly when too fatigued to work

text:
Almost a quarter of European airline pilots fly when too fatigued to work

The survey, conducted in August, found that three-quarters of respondents had experienced at least one microsleep – a brief, involuntary episode of sleep – while operating an aircraft in the previous four weeks. Pilots working for airlines based in Ireland and Malta reported the highest levels of microsleeps. More than a third said they were not getting enough rest to prevent fatigue from building up over time. Despite the prevalence of exhaustion, only one in three pilots said they usually reported themselves unfit for duty when fatigued. Half admitted they had operated a flight in the three months before the survey when they should have declared themselves too fatigued to fly. Almost half of the respondents said they feared negative consequences from management if they reported themselves unfit because of fatigue, while just 11.9% trusted their airline’s fatigue reporting system. Ian Holder, the managing director of the aviation safety consultancy Baines Simmons, said the results showed persistent differences in how airlines and national authorities manage fatigue.

“This survey captures how European pilots experience fatigue risk management in practice,” he said. He stressed that the findings represented pilots’ first-hand experiences rather than a direct measurement of aviation safety outcomes, but said the consistency of the results over three years highlighted areas requiring attention. Holder pointed to Finland and the Netherlands as evidence that stronger fatigue reporting cultures were achievable. Pilots working for airlines based in Ireland and Malta were among the most likely to fear management reprisals and the least likely to trust the reporting systems. The proportion of pilots who said they would fly when fatigued was higher in Spain, Ireland and France. Two in five of the pilots working for airlines based in Spain and a third of those working for Ireland- and France-based airlines said they usually fly when fatigued. text:
The regime change we need for Thames Water

Andy Burnham’s instruction to officials to look at all options for Thames Water and not feel constrained (Burnham urges officials to come up with more radical options for Thames Water, 19 October) is welcome, but the options will fail unless they answer the right question. Thames Water is not ill-regulated. It is extractively regulated. For 30 years the rules have allowed dividends paid from borrowing, debt loaded on to customers and sewage discharged into rivers as the cheaper alternative to investment. The creditors now asking for a further £2.4bn are not an aberration; they are the system working as designed. Nationalisation changes who owns the shares. It does not change the rules. A publicly owned Thames under the present regime would inherit the same debt and the same incentive to defer repair; within a decade “public control” would mean ill-regulation by another name. The Cunliffe review’s single water regulator closes one gap. It leaves the larger one: water is still regulated apart from the air, land and soil it moves through, though sewage in a river is a land, soil and water problem at once.

citation.title: The regime change we need for Thames Water

text:
The regime change we need for Thames Water

The prime minister’s 10-year plan needs a single environmental regulator, with a duty of candour, for air, water, land and soil, with three plain service duties: the service is delivered to standard, the money raised is spent on the service, and the charge is fair to the household that pays it. That, not ownership alone, is what a well-regulated industry looks like. Terry Barker Honorary professor of environmental sciences, University of East Anglia • Your report that Andy Burnham has instructed his team to explore radical solutions to the Thames Water crisis is welcome. But one solution already exists: the special administration regime (SAR), which could bring the company under temporary public control to stabilise and restructure it in the public interest. The forthcoming clean water bill may revisit legislation enabling greater public ownership, but reform must not delay action under existing powers. The Water Industry Act 1991 provides for special administration where statutory conditions are met. Thames Water’s financial instability, service failures and environmental record provide compelling grounds.

citation.title: The regime change we need for Thames Water

text:
The regime change we need for Thames Water

We at River Action urge the government and Ofwat to petition the high court to place Thames Water into an SAR. A creditor deal will not address the causes of its decline. An SAR offers restructuring that prioritises customers, communities and the environment over creditors. The government should also commission an independent feasibility study of alternative ownership, governance and financing models, including public, mutual and not-for-profit options. No new legislation is needed: the powers and grounds to intervene in Thames Water already exist. Water is an essential public service. Its future must be secured in the public interest. James Wallace CEO, River Action • If Thames Water is effectively bankrupt, I can’t see why shareholders should get compensation. Broke is broke. Rather than old-style nationalisation, I would turn it into a social enterprise and put it under the control of its engineers. There would be no shares, no dividends, and all profits would be reinvested in infrastructure, such as pipes and new reservoirs. Philip Clayton London • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today?

text:
Visa and Mastercard threatened with potential £5bn UK lawsuit over fees

Visa and Mastercard are being threatened with a potential £5bn lawsuit for allegedly stifling competition and charging UK businesses excessive fees. The law firms Harcus Parker and Hausfeld have lodged an application at the Competition Appeal Tribunal in hopes of pursuing a group claim that would compensate companies who, they claim, have been overcharged on customer card payments since October 2020. The claim will centre on multilateral interchange fees, which are set by Visa and Mastercard and then paid by businesses through their banks every time a customer pays by card. The argument is that the lack of competition has left businesses at their mercy – and paying higher fees on debit, credit and prepaid cards – as a result. The case will hope to claw back fees charged over the past six years, as well as interest on those losses. Sources close to the claim estimate that it could be worth about £5bn, based on the number of businesses allegedly overcharged between 2020 and 2026.

citation.title: Visa and Mastercard threatened with potential £5bn UK lawsuit over fees

text:
Visa and Mastercard threatened with potential £5bn UK lawsuit over fees

A spokesperson for Mastercard defended the interchange fees, saying the potential group claim was “speculative” and part of a “growing trend of opportunistic funder-backed litigation”. The case is being funded by Bench Walk Advisors, a London-headquartered firm that launched in 2017 and makes money from backing lawsuits. It is being led by Stephen Allen, a British businessman and former travel sector executive who has been pursuing Visa and Mastercard through a number of group legal actions since 2021. If the application is successful, an estimated 1m UK-based businesses, organisations and charities with less than £100m in revenues will be automatically included for compensation, unless they opt out. Their claims could be worth several thousands of pounds each. Larger businesses would have to actively opt in to be included in the claim, and could be due tens of millions over the claim period. However, it could take years for the case to reach a conclusion.

citation.title: Visa and Mastercard threatened with potential £5bn UK lawsuit over fees

text:
Visa and Mastercard threatened with potential £5bn UK lawsuit over fees

Visa and Mastercard last year agreed to pay a combined $167.5m to settle a class action lawsuit in the US which accused the two companies of conspiring to keep ATM access fees artificially high. That lawsuit was originally filed in 2011. Commenting on the latest group claim application, a Mastercard spokesperson said: “We strongly disagree with the basis of this claim. Interchange plays a vital role in supporting the UK payments ecosystem, and ensures people and businesses can pay and get paid quickly and securely. “This speculative claim does nothing to support UK businesses or consumers and instead reflects the growing trend of opportunistic funder-backed litigation. It is exactly the type of claim the UK government’s recently announced proposed opt-out class action reforms [put out for consultation this summer] are directed at preventing.” A Visa spokesperson said: “Visa continues to believe that interchange is a critical component to maintaining a secure digital payments ecosystem that benefits all parties, including consumers, merchants and banks.”

HSBC says ‘no pressure’ to move HQ out of UK despite prospect of higher bank taxes

A top executive at HSBC has tried to quash speculation that the bank could move its headquarters out of the UK over tax increases expected to be announced in Wednesday’s budget. HSBC’s chief financial officer, Pam Kaur, said there was “no pressure”, particularly from shareholders in its cornerstone Hong Kong market, to shift out of London despite lobbyists warning higher tax bills could drive big banks’ business abroad. HSBC on Tuesday revealed a 32% rise in third-quarter profits to $9.6bn (£7.2bn), alongside plans to give $2.7bn to shareholders through dividends and buybacks. Lobby groups have for months warned that banks could shift business and jobs to rival hubs if threatened with higher bills, with the JP Morgan chief executive, Jamie Dimon, saying he could even scrap plans for a new £3bn London headquarters if Britain became “hostile” to banks. A handful of wealthy businesspeople have already said they are leaving the UK, with some criticising Labour’s tax policies.

So that question is just not on the table,” Kaur said. HSBC has a strong shareholder base in east Asia, where it makes the bulk of its profits, and has twice been pushed to shift or split its operations in reaction to UK policies. That includes in 2015, when growing regulatory burdens and a new bank levy led HSBC to consider shifting its headquarters out of London to Hong Kong. The Conservative government later scaled back the levy to cover only UK-based assets, in a boon to HSBC.

Number of UK businesses in financial distress ‘at two-decade high’

The number of UK businesses in financial distress has hit its highest level in more than two decades, as pressure grows on the chancellor to provide more support to the private sector in Wednesday’s budget. There were 738,144 businesses in “significant” financial distress in the third quarter of this year, up 1.6% compared with the same period last year, according to BTG. That is the highest level since the administrator’s closely watched “red flag” report began in 2004. The UK’s support services, construction and real estate sectors were among the most vulnerable, with the highest numbers of businesses in significant distress – at 118,695, 108,340 and 99,908 respectively. The hospitality industry was hardest hit this year, with a 5% rise in the number of bars and restaurants in distress to 18,866. Struggling food and drug retailers rose by more than 7% to 19,269, according to BTG, which is one of the UK’s biggest insolvency practitioners and changed its name from Begbies Traynor in February.

citation.title: Number of UK businesses in financial distress ‘at two-decade high’

text:
Number of UK businesses in financial distress ‘at two-decade high’

The growing strain on UK companies comes as the chancellor, John Healey, prepares to give his first budget on Wednesday, against an increasingly volatile backdrop as the war in the Middle East disrupts the global economy, putting pressure on public finances and reigniting the cost of living crisis. The chancellor has vowed to use the budget to provide households and businesses with more “breathing space”. Mark Fry, the chief executive of BTG, said British businesses were “battling a combination of rising employment costs, inflationary pressures, higher energy prices and elevated borrowing costs. “Crucially, these pressures are not only affecting small businesses’ ability to operate, but also larger businesses’ ability to compete on a global stage,” he said. A freedom of information request by BTG also found that British businesses still owed £27.3bn in arrears to HMRC in VAT, corporation tax and PAYE at the end of August. About £24bn has been recovered since arrears reached a peak of £51.3bn during the Covid pandemic, compared with a pre-pandemic total of £11.4bn.

“With £27.3bn owed to HMRC, high levels of recovery activity and record financial distress across the economy, many companies are approaching this budget from a position of financial weakness rather than strength,” Fry said. “We hear from businesses that structural hurdles, weight of red tape, employment legislation and the tax burden alongside high interest and energy costs will need to be tackled if this is to be a budget for business.” Last week the prime minister, Andy Burnham, promised that his government would “slash red tape” for businesses, with plans to make compliance guidance clearer, simplify the UK’s corporate reporting requirements and extend import tariff suspensions on products favoured by businesses.

text:
The chaos in France is a ‘warning signal’ for Australia’s public spending and rising costs

The explosion of discontent that led to major protests and violence in France and across Europe is a “warning signal” that Australia could follow the same path without an “honest conversation” about the budget, economists say. Hundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday to protest against school underfunding, as complaints of insufficient teacher numbers and dilapidated infrastructure mingled with broader discontent about cost-of-living pressures. Here, and across the developed world, people are struggling to cope with the affordability crisis as households grapple with high and rising prices. The scale of the challenges in individual countries may be of a different order of magnitude but the grievances are common. Luke Hartigan, a senior economics lecturer at the University of Sydney, said it was clear there was no single factor behind the discontent in France but soaring energy costs were having a major impact. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here Fuel prices are up 36% this year in France, or three times the increase in Australia.

The US-Israel war on Iran has sent European gas prices soaring as the northern hemisphere approaches winter. Related: Jim Chalmers faces a world of hard choices where the solution to one problem makes the other worse More fundamental, however, is that France’s finances are buckling under its generous welfare state. France’s high public debt, stagnant economy and universal social security benefits have created a “binary” situation, Hartigan said, where citizens’ demands for better services and cost-of-living help are clashing with the country’s increasingly dire fiscal position. France has not balanced its budget since 1974. Meanwhile, total public debt as a share of the economy has swelled to nearly 120%, according to the International Monetary Fund. UK shop price inflation ‘highest since 2024’ as retailers struggle to limit price rises

Shop price inflation has risen to the highest level in two and a half years, according to the British Retail Consortium, which warned that “the dam is starting to break” when it comes to retailers trying to limit price rises for customers. The lobby group said shop price inflation was 2.1% year on year in October, a sharp rise compared with 1.4% in September, and an indication that retailers were beginning to pass on the rising costs of energy and food ingredients since the Middle East conflict broke out. It said food inflation, which has remained low during the past year, increased this month to 2.9% year on year – against a 2.5% rise in September – putting further pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, before his first budget on Wednesday. Non-food inflation, which includes items such as clothing and footwear, more than doubled in October, from 0.8% to 1.7% year on year. The price of Brent crude oil reached $117 a barrel in recent days, well above the $70 average in the months before the US and Israel attacked Iran in February.

Gas prices have also risen sharply, pushing the UK consumer prices index to 3.5% last month. Until this month, retailers had largely absorbed the higher costs of raw materials, mainly in response to weak demand from customers. In surveys, consumer confidence has declined sharply since the summer, when it became clearer the conflict in the Middle East was unlikely to end swiftly. Bank of England officials are expected to raise interest rates next week from 3.75% to 4%. Business secretary writes to Poundland owner as administration fears build

The business secretary’s team has written to the owner of Poundland amid fears that the cut-price retailer could collapse into administration, threatening to overshadow John Healey’s budget. Sources said that Gordon Brothers, the US investment firm that bought the 600-store Poundland chain for £1 last summer, looks set to appoint administrators to the struggling retailer. Jonathan Reynolds has written to Gordon Brothers to establish the latest situation at the company, which employs 12,000 staff. The company rejected the only bid to take on the group – which includes the 50-store Dealz chain in Ireland – as a solvent company in its entirety, from Northern Ireland’s Martin Property Group, earlier this week. It is understood Gordon Brothers is poised to file a notice of intention to appoint the advisory firm AlixPartners as administrator, potentially as early as Wednesday. This legal measure would protect Poundland from the demands of creditors for 10 days while a solution to its problems is sought.

text:
Fed holds interest rates steady in last decision before midterms

The US Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged on Wednesday during its last board meeting before the midterm elections, keeping rates at one of the highest pre-election levels seen in over 20 years. Two out of 12 board members voted against the pause, preferring to raise rates by a quarter point this meeting, the Fed board said in a statement. Last month, Fed officials raised rates for the first time since 2023, citing rising inflation, bringing rates to a range of 3.75% to 4%. Inflation has hovered for years above the Fed’s target rate of 2%, and for most of this year, the annualized inflation rate has remained above 3%. Though inflation rose higher in September, going from 3.4% in August to 3.7%, the pause signals the central bank is taking a wait-and-see approach ahead of the midterms next week. During a press conference on Wednesday afternoon, the Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, told reporters that the upcoming election played no role in deliberations. “Politics played no role in the decision,” he said.

GSK shares dive as weaker vaccine sales unnerve investors

Shares in GSK slid on Wednesday despite the UK drugmaker reporting better than expected financial results, as investors were unnerved by weaker sales of its respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and shingles vaccines and recently launched medications. Britain’s second-biggest pharmaceutical company reported a 19% decline in pre-tax profit to £1.9bn in the July to September quarter and £318m of restructuring charges, with more to come. Core operating profit and core earnings per share rose 5% and 1% respectively, however, beating analysts’ expectations. Shares dived as much as 7% at one point on Wednesday, and despite later paring back such losses to a 3.8% drop, it was the second-biggest faller on the FTSE 100 index of blue-chip businesses. Luke Miels, who took over from Emma Walmsley as GSK’s chief executive in January, has announced a number of acquisitions, including a £7.9bn US cancer specialist and a major cost-saving programme in July to speed up drug development.

British households face a “grim picture” for living standards as the war in the Middle East drags down growth and triggers a fresh cost of living crisis, the government’s independent forecaster has said. The government’s plan to fund a multibillion-pound nuclear plant at the Sizewell site in Suffolk represents a “terrible deal” for the UK taxpayer over the rest of the century, according to the government’s spending watchdog. North Korea is likely culprit behind $6.3bn crypto hack, ‘largest heist in history’

The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange has been hit by a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack described as the biggest heist in history, with experts identifying North Korea as the likely culprit. Binance said it would cover all customer losses as it froze $3bn of the affected assets. Analysts said the exchange had been subjected to an unprecedented attack with “never-seen-before” laundering patterns as the hackers made off with assets worth billions of dollars. Researchers said the theft was the biggest ever, dwarfing a $1.5bn crypto raid last year and the $1bn taken from Iraq’s central bank by Saddam Hussein in 2003. “This is almost certainly the largest theft of any kind in history,” said Tom Robinson, chief scientist at crypto consultancy Elliptic. Experts attributed the attack, which happened late on Thursday, to North Korean state-backed hackers. North Korea has a history of crypto hacking and was behind the theft of about $1.5bn in virtual assets from a Dubai-based cryptocurrency exchange last year, according to the FBI, in the previous record crypto heist.

Economists polled by Reuters had forecast GDP advancing at a 3.2% pace. Estimates ranged from ⁠a 1% growth rate to a 4.2% pace. Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, has summoned water industry bosses to Whitehall after the environment watchdog said their companies continue to pump effluent into Britain’s waterways at “unacceptable” rates. “People are sick of excuses,” Dame Angela said, after the Environment Agency rated eight of the nine water companies in England as “poor” or “requiring improvement”. The shop workers’ union Usdaw has urged Poundland’s owners to reconsider a decision to prepare the budget chain for administration, putting up to 12,000 jobs at risk. Gordon Brothers filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators to Poundland at the high court on Thursday, with the advisory firm AlixPartners lined up to run the process. The legal measure protects Poundland from the demands of creditors for 10 days while a solution to its problems is sought. Gordon Brothers previously rejected a management-backed rescue bid for the discount chain, which operates 600 stores, including Dealz outlets in Ireland. It bought the struggling chain for a nominal £1 from its previous owner, the European retail group Pepco, in June 2025. Only one bidder, Martin Property Group, a Northern Irish family-owned company, was interested in buying the entire chain and working with the existing management, led by Barry Williams, the chief executive.

The owner of Toblerone is taking legal action against a tiny British vegan chocolate brand that it claims has been copying the Swiss chocolate bar’s famous chunky shape. How big a deal is the $6.3bn Binance crypto heist, who did it, and are investments safe?

The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange has been hit by a $6.3bn heist that, according to experts, is likely to be the work of North Korea. This is not the first time a crypto market has been targeted by hackers, and the rogue state has a track record of this type of theft. Here we answer some key questions about what’s happened: Just how big a deal is this? It could be the biggest heist of any kind in history, according to Elliptic, a consultancy specialising in crypto-related crime. The incident, which took place late on Thursday, is more than four times bigger than the previous largest crypto hack, the $1.5bn one targeting the Bybit exchange last year. Elliptic says there does not appear to be anything comparable in the pre-crypto era. “This incident is almost certainly the single largest known theft of any kind,” says Tom Robinson, the consultancy’s chief scientist. “Before Bybit, that record was held by Saddam Hussein, who took $1bn from the central bank of Iraq in Baghdad on the eve of the 2003 Iraq war.

The Binance theft is more than six times larger.” So what exactly is cryptocurrency? This digital asset operates online, outside the traditional financial system. There is no physical version of the most popular form of crypto – bitcoin – or its peers, such as Ethereum, Ripple and Dogecoin. A cryptocurrency such as bitcoin runs on a combination of encryption, which is the sort of technology that keeps your WhatsApp messages safe, and peer-to-peer networks that allow computers to connect without a central server (think of the music-sharing sites like Napster at the turn of the century). In short, the owner of a bitcoin (or part of a bitcoin; you can buy them in fractions) has access to a private key – like a long password – which is needed to access the funds. These transactions are all stored and displayed on a publicly available ledger, like a school register, known as a blockchain. You typically store your private keys in a “crypto wallet”. There are varying estimates for how many cryptocurrencies there are but Coingecko, which monitors the market, claims there are more than 22,000 coins.

The entire market is worth about $2.7tn, so it is not a surprise that hackers and rogue states looking for funds are interested in a corner of the global finance industry that has so much money, is largely unregulated and is vulnerable to digital thieves. And what is a cryptoexchange? A cryptoexchange is where you buy, sell and trade digital assets such as bitcoin. They host your crypto wallets, which are typically “cold”, meaning they are not connected online and can be kept safer from hackers. A smaller amount sits in “hot” wallets which are linked to the internet so they can be used for quick withdrawals, making them of greater interest to hackers. Binance is the world’s largest of these exchanges in terms of the number of trades it carries out every day – at a value of about $95bn daily. How was Binance hacked? It does not appear that private keys were hacked. Instead, a Binance engineer’s laptop was infiltrated, which in turn allowed the attackers to drain “hot” wallets. Binance later added that there were “additional points of breach” in its systems as well as the laptop.

“Hackers rarely crack the cryptographic keys themselves,” says Robinson. “They instead target people with access to those wallets. Binance says the attack involved a compromised engineer’s laptop, along with other points of breach. This gave the attacker a way into Binance’s internal systems. From there, they made Binance’s own systems sign transactions that sent the funds to the attacker.” More than $2.5bn of the $6.3bn was taken in one transaction alone. “Crypto exchanges are safer than they used to be, but not immune to attacks such as this,” says Robinson. “This hack shows that even the biggest exchange can be breached through one employee’s laptop. What matters most for customers is whether the exchange can cover the loss. Binance says it will repay everyone from its own funds.” How do the hackers get hold of their haul? They will have to “cash out” the crypto and turn it into legitimate money, known as fiat currency. Chainalysis, a crypto research firm, has said the attackers used “never seen before” laundering patterns to exfiltrate the affected assets.

Phil Larratt, a senior director at the consultancy, says the thieves will now try to convert the crypto into fiat money in a process that “takes weeks and months, if not years”. “The process is patient and sophisticated,” he says. Laundering methods used by crypto hackers include visiting less scrupulous exchanges, using swapping services that exchange one type of crypto asset for another, and accessing brokers who will convert crypto to cash in exchange for a cut of the proceeds. Do we know who did it? This attack has been attributed to a North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor, a name assigned to it by the US government. The communist state, short of cash and hamstrung by sanctions, has a strong track record of crypto hacking. TraderTraitor emerged from Lazarus, a group working from North Korea’s Reconnaissance General Bureau, a military intelligence agency. Last year TraderTraitor was blamed for the $1.5bn theft from the Dubai-based Bybit. Elliptic and two other crypto analysis firms have attributed the attack to North Korea.

Elliptic said some of the funds taken from Binance have already been traced to wallet addresses used in a cryptoexchange hack last month that is also thought to have been carried out by operatives from the rogue state. Rafe Pilling, the senior director of threat intelligence at the cybersecurity firm Sophos, says North Korea had previously hacked conventional financial targets such as the Bangladesh Central Bank and even cash machines. And as a result you have groups like TraderTraitor that are specialising in attacking crypto firms and getting away with huge payments.” Are my crypto investments safe? Any guarantees will be coming from Binance itself, rather than any regulatory or government-backed safety nets. The exchange said in a post on X that it would “cover all losses” and “user funds are safe”.

It also said it had frozen about half the funds targeted in the hack, stopping the thieves from making off with that tranche of cryptocurrency. ExxonMobil and Chevron top estimates for Q3 as Americans feel gas price pain

ExxonMobil and Chevron reported better than expected quarterly results on Friday as the oil majors benefited from higher prices and record production. The boon for oil companies has simultaneously been a major pain point for consumers, who say the higher cost of living, especially gas prices, will affect how they vote in the upcoming midterm elections that will determine control of Congress. Gas prices for consumers are an average $4.20 a gallon, according to AAA, nearly $1.20 a gallon higher than a year ago. In a recent Harris poll for the Guardian, 36% of voters said the rising cost of living is the single most important issue this election. Besides the disruption caused by the wars in Iran and Ukraine that have driven up the cost of fuel, Exxon is also seeing strong production in its fields in Guyana and the Permian Basin in the south-west. Chevron said its results include one month of production in Venezuela where it is making a big investment. Utilization at Exxon’s US Gulf coast refineries was at 100%, and Gulf coast diesel production was at the second-highest on record.

Regular gasoline is up about 38% in the past year as well. Darren Woods, ExxonMobil chair and CEO, said investments such as the expansion of its Beaumont refinery in Texas have contributed to an increase in its distillate production by approximately 40% since 2019. For the third quarter, net income more than doubled to $3.72 per share. On an adjusted basis, profit totaled $4.23 per share, easily topping the average analyst estimate of $4.12 per share. Revenue during the three months ended in September rose 33% to $113.16bn, also beating estimates. The company, based in Spring, Texas, also raised its quarterly dividend to $1.07 and set a $20bn stock buyback plan. Houston-based Chevron said on Friday it earned $9.9bn, or $5.06 per share, during the third quarter, as revenue surged 36% to $67.8bn. Its results handily topped estimates.

Chevron, the second-largest US oil company, has had a presence in Venezuela since 1923. Last month it announced it will invest $7bn over the next five years in Venezuela. It said on Friday that following an accounting-related change during the quarter, it was now including those results. In pre-market trading, Exxon shares rose 1.9%. The stock is up 64% in the past 12 months. Chevron shares rose 1.1%. At a recent rally in Georgia on 24 October, Donald Trump told the crowd – despite, he noted, warnings from his advisers not to – that higher gas prices had ultimately been a blessing for all Americans. “Our country is making hundreds of billions of dollars because of what’s happened in the Middle East, because they’re coming to Texas and they’re coming to Oklahoma and they’re coming to Louisiana and they’re taking that oil,” Trump said. Trump said that “fake headlines” would claim that he “is talking about all the money they’re making while people are suffering at the pump”. “But I said, ‘I don’t give a damn, I’m gonna say it: we’re making a frickin’ fortune,’” he said.

Poundland in peril: how rampant inflation and price wars left £1 stores exposed

‘It was a very successful and simple proposition,” laments one former Poundland boss. With every product in the shop sold at £1, and the price in its name, its proposition to shoppers was the clearest of any UK high street chain. Now the UK’s first and biggest nationwide single-price retailer could disappear amid heavy competition and inflation that has eaten into its ability to offer bargains. Its potential collapse has brought distress for its up to 12,000 staff in the run-up to Christmas, and as shoppers head to the chain for Halloween costumes and treats. Meanwhile, its low-profile owners are facing questions from the prime minister over their behaviour in the week his government’s budget attempted to offer support to the high street. Poundland’s future hangs in the balance – and not for the first time – after the 36-year-old retailer filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators at the high court on Thursday, with the advisory firm AlixPartners lined up to run the process.

The legal measure protects Poundland, which operates 600 stores, including Dealz outlets in Ireland, from the demands of creditors for 10 days while a solution to its problems is sought. However, the prospect of it avoiding mass store closures and job losses diminishes by the day as suppliers hold back on deliveries, hurting its ability to trade. The chain’s potential demise comes after Gordon Brothers, the American restructuring specialist which bought Poundland for a nominal £1 from its previous owner in June last year, rejected a management-backed rescue bid for the whole chain by Martin Property Group. While the Northern Irish firm is still in talks about taking on Poundland, it is understood its offer amounts to about £15m. That would pay off only half the £30m shareholder loan, the majority of which was taken on by Gordon Brothers when it bought the company. The deal would also include taking on a further, asset-backed loan worth about £90m, it is understood.

This deal has been rejected by Gordon Brothers despite Pepco, Poundland’s former owner, which holds the other £7.5m of the debt, being prepared to wait for repayment in the hope of saving the business, as first reported by Sky News. One source who knows Poundland well said that Gordon Brothers had already taken about £10m in fees and interest out of the chain in the last year and that wanting another £30m was “egregious”. Gordon Brothers did not respond to a request for comment and has not confirmed this figure. Gordon Brothers said earlier this week that options for the whole and parts of the business “are being thoroughly and objectively evaluated, with a view to minimising uncertainty for Poundland’s people and all relevant stakeholders”. Sources close to the process said Gordon Brothers was unwilling to accept the Martin deal as the latest offer includes only about £7.5m up front and the rest over the next two years, leaving uncertainty for creditors, staff and suppliers.

One source said Gordon Brothers had sought bidders for the whole of Poundland but “the market had spoken” and only one little-known financial bidder with no history of running a large retail chain in the UK had come forward who might only go on to break up Poundland itself. Instead, the restructuring specialist is understood to believe that suppliers and staff would be safer with the “trusted established retail operators” who have already put forward firm offers for parcels of outlets that amount to about half of Poundland’s stores, which could be converted to their formats. If there was a potential owner to avoid this that hasn’t been accepted, then the business secretary and I want to know why that is the case.” For now, Gordon Brothers appears more keen on a break-up after losing faith in the likelihood of Poundland finding a route to long-term profitability amid tough times on the high street and heavy competition.

In the past, Poundland removed products if it could not sell them profitably for a pound, but its choices have become more limited. High inflation – triggered first by Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and then the Middle East conflict – has exposed a business model which always appeared to have a shelf life. In most supermarkets a two-litre bottle of milk costs over £2, a pack of KitKats is at least £1.50 and a tin of Heinz baked beans is about £1.40, according to the price comparison site Trolley. Cutting the size of Poundland has, meanwhile, reduced its scale, making it harder to get good deals from suppliers to protect margins. Poundland has also admitted that it made mistakes in recent years, including putting its Pepco clothing ranges into stores, which proved unpopular with UK shoppers.

Those with more to spare have more options in their supermarket shop, where they are increasingly locked in by loyalty-card-linked discounts. Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg

Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area. In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa, meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare). Soon, they were taking water for their panning and processing from the organisation’s two 25,000-litre water tanks, which are filled irregularly by the city government for the 100 or so rescued and injured animals on site. “We’ve asked them really nicely and haven’t ever refused them water to drink … But, for the first time ever, we closed the gate at 12 [midday], because we literally had about two buckets of water left,” Bailey said in mid-October. Police told her that the scale of the illegal mining was too big for them to do anything about, she said at the time.

citation.title: Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg

text:
Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg

About a week later, officers sheared away the grass that had partly hidden the zama zamas. But within a few days a smaller group had returned, although Bailey said they were now taking Claw’s water only for drinking. South Africa’s police regularly trumpet their success in tackling illegal mining. On 19 October, they said they had arrested 71 suspected zama zamas across the country in the previous week. However, researchers put the number of illegal miners in the tens of thousands. In 2019, Marcena Hunter, a researcher at the Global Initiative against Transnational Organised Crime, estimated that a tenth of South Africa’s gold production, worth about $1bn, was being exported illegally. Police operations have also led to tragedy. In 2025, 93 bodies were pulled from a mine shaft in Stilfontein, after officers blocked food and water from being delivered underground.

citation.title: Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg

text:
Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg

Meanwhile, there is no end in sight to the dynamics driving illegal mining, including the high price of gold, poverty, unemployment, corrupt politicians and police profiting, and the failure of mining companies to fulfil their legal obligation to seal mining shafts when they cease operating. South Africa’s modern history is tied to mining. In 1884, gold was found on a farm, sparking a gold rush that led to the creation of Johannesburg. Gold production peaked in the 1970s, but South Africa was the world’s largest producer, a title it held for more than a century, until 2007. In 2009, Morris Viljoen, a geology professor at the University of the Witwatersrand, estimated that the reef that gave the university its name had produced more than a third of the gold ever mined globally. Claw is housed in the old offices of the Durban Deep mine, which shut at the turn of the century, having once lent its name to an Elton John song. The city government claims there is still 40,000 tonnes of gold underground in the region. But, with the remainder lying ever deeper, the costs of recovering it have risen.

citation.title: Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg

text:
Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg

Mining companies are supposed to seal up old mine shafts and rehabilitate the environment around them. However, in 2025 there were “6,100 derelict and ownerless mines and 1,170 unsafe mine openings”, the mining minister, Gwede Mantashe, said in response to a parliamentary question. Zama zamas have stepped into those voids left in the earth. While there is no comprehensive data on them, experts agree that a majority are from neighbouring countries, principally Lesotho, Mozambique and Zimbabwe. The skyline south of Johannesburg is punctuated by the pale yellow ridges of mine dumps. Increasingly, the ground is also caving open. For politicians seeking votes in local elections on 4 November, the culprit is clear: illegal miners. In May, Kenny Kunene, the Johannesburg council member responsible for transport, took journalists on a tour of sinkholes that he claimed were the fault of zama zamas, including a section of Wemmer Pan Road that had completely collapsed. The road was once the main artery linking the city’s central business district to the south-eastern suburbs.

citation.title: Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg

text:
Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg

In one section it has completely disappeared, now raw earth pitted with the holes where illegal miners have been digging. However, when it comes to sinkholes, experts say zama zamas are being scapegoated. Rosalind Morris, an anthropology professor at Columbia University, who has worked extensively with illegal miners, noted that the porous dolomitic rock to Johannesburg’s south and west becomes unstable when water is removed. “The biggest culprit of sinkholes in South Africa is formal industrial mining, which dewaters at a scale of hundreds of millions of gallons of water removed from underground every day,” she said. “There are areas where there is a lot of residual gold, which are being very intensely mined by zama zamas, and some of that definitely causes structural collapse, there’s no doubt about it. But the idea that this was invented or caused for the first time by zama zamas is completely fallacious.” Zama zamas are also frequently blamed for violence in mining areas, including a September mass shooting in Wedela township, west of Johannesburg.

Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg

However, David van Wyk, the lead researcher at Bench Marks Foundation, said culpability laid with the often-feuding gangs that controlled access to the shafts. “The guys working in the mine are actually super-exploited cheap labour … The guys with the guns are the guys who take the gold,” he said. “They don’t go underground.” In Khutsong, about 50 miles (80km) west of Johannesburg, illegal miners, local and foreign, kept the township afloat, said Vusi Cele, the youth secretary for the local branch of Mining Affected Communities United in Action, a campaign group that advocates for “artisanal miners” to be granted mining licences. “Without those rents, it’s a ghost town,” he said. While Cele, 33, currently hustles above ground selling mobile phone covers and screen protectors, he said he too would mine if he could get a licence. “On the surface there’s peanuts,” he said. “Underground there’s money.”

UK house prices grow at slowest pace in two years as mortgage rates rise

UK house prices grew by an annual rate of just 0.5% in October, the slowest pace in more than two years, as higher mortgage rates put off potential buyers. The average price for a property in the UK stood at £273,566 in October, flat on the previous month and down from 0.8% in the year to September, according to the lender Nationwide. The slowdown in the market comes as buyers face higher borrowing costs. This month the average cost of a five-year fixed-rate mortgage hit the 6% barrier for the first time in three years. Related: What you need to know about Your First Home scheme for first-time buyers The average stood at 5.99% on Thursday, according to the financial information provider Moneyfacts, while the average two-year rate was not far behind at 5.97%. There has been no change in the Bank of England base rate since last December but volatility in the bond market has driven up the swap rates that influence the pricing of fixed-rate mortgages.

Property prices are likely to fall further, he said. “Surveyors report that new buyer inquiries remain weak. “Consumer sentiment dipped noticeably in October, with households becoming less confident about the outlook for the general economy as well as their own financial situation in the year ahead.” Tom Bill, the head of UK residential research at Knight Frank, added that the impact of rising mortgage costs “eclipses any support measure announced in this week’s budget”. This week the chancellor, John Healey, confirmed the government’s new £4.7bn Your First Home scheme, which is designed to give a helping hand to first-time buyers who do not have access to the “bank of mum and dad”.

Avanti West Coast paid out £20m in ‘delay repay’ passenger refunds this summer

Avanti West Coast paid out more than £20m to passengers in just three months this summer in refunds for disrupted journeys on Britain’s main intercity rail network. The intercity operator paid out almost as much in a four-week period to 25 July – £9.3m – as its annual profits for each of the past two years. It repaid a further £12.2m in the subsequent eight weeks. The “delay repay” compensation bill for slow-running or cancelled services has been spiralling upwards across the railway network in recent years, according to official figures, with Avanti the biggest payer – although never before at this scale. Most train operators are yet to publish this year’s payouts. According to the most recent published financial figures from the Department for Transport (DfT), covering all operators, the total passenger compensation for delays rose to £150m across the railway in 2024-25, up 8% compared with the previous year, of which about 27% was Avanti’s payouts (£40.5m).

citation.title: Avanti West Coast paid out £20m in ‘delay repay’ passenger refunds this summer

text:
Avanti West Coast paid out £20m in ‘delay repay’ passenger refunds this summer

Fare inflation and efforts to make passengers aware of their rights have contributed to the industry’s soaring bill, as well as the delays themselves. Compensation has become increasingly automated and some operators now proactively repay passengers who have been delayed. Under the contracts that replaced the franchising system since the pandemic, train operators’ income comes from fees paid by the DfT instead of depending on fare revenue, with the taxpayer instead taking any profit or loss from ticketing income or refunds. Avanti, which is due to be taken into public ownership next year as part of Great British Railways, paid out more than £50m in 2025-26, and is expected to pay out more than £70m this financial year. As heatwaves hit the railway, fewer than half of Avanti trains ran on time in July with passengers delayed by an average 19 minutes, according to figures from the Office of Rail and Road. Its peak payout period also covered the incursion of a large herd of cows on the tracks for several hours one Tuesday.

text:
Britain’s housing crisis won’t be fixed without a new tax landscape

John Healey’s critics on the right and left accused him of dodging the big questions in his first budget. The chancellor failed to announce reforms that might tackle some of Britain’s chronic problems, they say. Healey’s scatter-gun budget, as the Resolution Foundation called it, was more about politics than economics, and unapologetically so. Housing was one area of policy that took up a considerable chunk of his speech. And yet the measures amounted to very little, if a test of his policy changes was to ask how different will the UK be at the next election. Or, as that date is only two and a half years away, 10 years from now. Housing is more than a single element of a complex economy. It is both its driving force and a disease eating its way through the body, from the inside out. More than 80% of global investment is in property and the vast majority of that is in residential. Countries that once had a more communitarian approach, such as France and Germany, with a highly regulated mix of social, private rented and home ownership, have succumbed to building wealth through property.

citation.title: Britain’s housing crisis won’t be fixed without a new tax landscape

text:
Britain’s housing crisis won’t be fixed without a new tax landscape

It doesn’t seem to matter that Japan was ruined in the 1990s by a vicious property price crash. And China is still suffering domestically after Beijing allowed a property Ponzi scheme to develop that enriched the already super-wealthy and left tens of millions of middle-income earners in negative equity. Nowhere is the situation worse than in the UK, where property prices have cooled somewhat, but remain at levels that deny younger generations the chance to find a home at a reasonable price and some financial security. UK property has also become the method by which Gen Xers pay for social care for their parents and release housing deposits for their offspring. Then there is the debilitating leasehold/freehold split that is both a source of angry disputes and stymies investment in solar panels and insulation (who should pay?). The lack of regulation and ill-thought-out subsidies affecting new private housing means developers are incentivised to enter an arm-twisting contest with local authorities.

citation.title: Britain’s housing crisis won’t be fixed without a new tax landscape

text:
Britain’s housing crisis won’t be fixed without a new tax landscape

Without robust planning guidelines, developers champion building on flood plains or erecting tower blocks that are later dubbed ovens for their lack of ventilation in hot summers. And all the while the tax system is working to make the situation worse. The Oxford academic John Muellbauer has spent almost 40 years researching the UK’s housing system. He calls it “one of the most dysfunctional in the world”. In an academic article published in September by the British Academy, he says: “Many of the UK’s current economic and social problems, including its housing affordability crisis, can be traced to decades of land and housing policy failures. The role of land markets is strongly dependent on institutions, including land use regulation, financial regulation and property taxation.” The Treasury and Angela Rayner’s Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government have considered proposals from Muellbauer and others that remodel council tax, turning it into a fairer annual levy on households and using the reform to abolish stamp duty on transactions, which has calcified the housing market.

citation.title: Britain’s housing crisis won’t be fixed without a new tax landscape

text:
Britain’s housing crisis won’t be fixed without a new tax landscape

Rachel Reeves’s mansion tax is a good start. It is only a start though, because the former chancellor was persuaded to keep the council tax banding system when she should have applied a percentage to the 150,000-odd homes valued above £2m that will be captured by the new policy. There was the potential for a database of homes valued above £2m to be the beginning of a revaluation process, carrying on until all homes were logged. With a percentage tax of, say, 0.5%, applied to all homes, a £150,000 property would pay an annual tax rate of £750 while a £3m home would pay £15,000. Of course, the real problem is not the £3m homeowner for whom policymakers will have little sympathy – it’s the professionals occupying £1.5m homes in London, the south-east and affluent suburbs around other big cities, who will see council tax rates more than double to £7,500. The professional classes will be the worst affected in the short term.

citation.title: Britain’s housing crisis won’t be fixed without a new tax landscape

text:
Britain’s housing crisis won’t be fixed without a new tax landscape

Yet there will only be progress when this powerful lobby group of owner-occupiers – working and retired – are prepared to accept the trade-off with stamp duty, which would disappear for those who sell. There are plenty of people in government who understand the need to resolve housing market issues in a more fundamental fashion. The Treasury minister Torsten Bell is one. His book, Great Britain?: How We Get Our Future Back, talks about “our housing omnishambles”. However, they have had little influence on policy in this area so far. In his first budget Healey revamped a much-discredited help-to-buy scheme for new-build homes, which will only boost prices and line the pockets of developers. He also gave some more money towards council housebuilding, slapped an extra tax on landlords (that will probably push up rents) and promised to tackle homelessness. Healey and Andy Burnham put all their revolutionary zeal into a long, and possibly tortuous, process of devolution from London to the regions to kickstart growth.

citation.title: Britain’s housing crisis won’t be fixed without a new tax landscape

text:
Britain’s housing crisis won’t be fixed without a new tax landscape

However, it is tax incentives that are causing the problems, not whether policy decisions are made locally or centrally. Bad policy decisions can be made locally just as much as centrally. What makes the difference is a permanently reformed tax landscape that discourages treating housing as a store of wealth, allows people to move home cheaply – especially older homeowners who want to downsize – and supports the building of more truly affordable homes to buy and rent.

Railway engineering work over Christmas will cause 10 days of disruption

Passengers travelling on some of Great Britain’s busiest railway lines at Christmas have been warned of significant disruption from 10 days of engineering works. Work will close London’s Paddington station – affecting intercity trains to the west of England and Wales until January – as well as Birmingham New Street, the UK’s busiest station outside the capital, for five days over the holiday period. Passengers travelling between London, north-east England and Scotland will have to negotiate the part closure of the east coast mainline on Christmas Eve. Direct trains from the capital to parts of Essex and Norfolk will also be cut for much of the festive period. Network Rail said most routes would still stay open and that the Christmas period, when train services generally stop for 25 and 26 December, remained the best time to conduct essential works. Engineers hope to use the quieter festive days to carry out about £152m of works to improve reliability and capacity. The biggest engineering work is expected on the lines leading into London Paddington, including replacing a junction near Slough.

Boss of City regulator accused of threatening consumer group over £9.1bn car loan scheme

The boss of the UK’s financial regulator is accused of threatening a consumer group with “adverse consequences” if it blocked a £9.1bn compensation scheme meant to settle the motor finance scandal. Legal documents reviewed by the Guardian said the alleged comments by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) chief executive, Nikhil Rathi, amounted to “an inappropriate intervention by a public official”. The threat is said to have taken place during a Microsoft Teams call with the directors of Consumer Voice (CV) on 27 April, hours before the deadline to file legal challenges against the FCA’s proposed redress scheme for those missold car loans. Rathi warned that the City regulator would be “unable to collaborate” with Consumer Voice if it took legal action, “suggesting adverse consequences for CV’s future engagement with the FCA and adverse press briefings against it”, the filings said. “The implication was clear: the FCA’s willingness to engage constructively with CV was contingent on CV not challenging the scheme, and would give way to hostility if it did,” the documents claimed.

text:

Up until that point, the FCA had treated Consumer Voice as a “trusted expert consumer body”, the filings said. But once the group decided to challenge the scheme, “the FCA changed its position … now the FCA seeks to denigrate CV’s activities and motives in bringing this application”. Rathi also allegedly claimed that their potential legal challenge was the “biggest risk to the scheme” and that plans to get money to millions of victims by this Christmas would fail if directors followed through with their plans. The filings say it was not disclosed that three specialist lenders were also planning to challenge the scheme, only that the FCA had been “engaging with the banks”, who, over the previous weekend, decided not to challenge the payout plan. The episode marks a fresh controversy in the long-running saga surrounding mis-sold UK car loans, which prompted a contentious intervention by former chancellor Rachel Reeves last year, following intense lobbying by big banks.

Lenders have been arguing that a large compensation bill would risk spooking investors and causing long-lasting economic damage to the UK. Dry weather sewage discharges soar as water companies face scrutiny

The number of suspected illegal discharges of raw sewage into rivers and seas by water companies during dry weather increased significantly during the first five months of 2026. Related: ‘Tiny bit of rain and the sewage comes’: Brighton swimmers vent fury at sea pollution Dumping raw sewage into waterways during dry spells via overflows amounts to pollution. It is considered a breach of the permits given to water companies and is illegal. Discharging during dry weather increases the toxicity of the sewage pollution entering waterways. Rivers have less flow and volume, and there is no rainwater to dilute the sewage pollution entering the waterway. Last year, in what regulators said was tougher action on sewage pollution, water companies in England were for the first time required to report to the Environment Agency the number of times they discharged raw sewage from combined sewer overflows during dry weather. A dry day spill is flagged when an overflow operates despite little to no rainfall that day and the previous day. In 2025, water companies in England and Wales reported 8,576 dry spill pollution discharges.

citation.title: Dry weather sewage discharges soar as water companies face scrutiny

text:
Dry weather sewage discharges soar as water companies face scrutiny

But according to freedom of information requests submitted by Environment Agency whistleblower Robert Forrester, the pollution is getting worse, not better, despite the regulator’s promise of tougher action. Between January and May this year alone, water companies discharged raw sewage into rivers and seas during dry weather 7,280 times. The data is comparable as it is based on the same instruction and taken from the same data recording system. The water industry said the figures were as yet unverified and it was too early to describe them as dry spills. Forrester, an Environment Agency officer for more than 20 years, revealed failures by the agency to take on water companies’ illegal practices before leaving his job. “Dry day spills will almost always be deliberate and illegal, otherwise there would be non-stop raw sewage spilling from pipes,” said Forrester.

text:
Dry weather sewage discharges soar as water companies face scrutiny

Related: South West Water has worst environmental record in England, analysis shows “The huge increase in a much drier year appears to show that water companies have quotas of sewage to dump and will do whatever the weather, and whatever the risk to the public and the environment. Making money is the primary focus.” He said the regulator was no deterrent to the actions of the water companies. “This level of criminality shows that water companies do not believe they, or the government, will ever do anything meaningful to stop them.” Combined sewer overflows are an emergency system designed to be used in extreme weather to relieve pressure in the sewage system. But decades of underinvestment by the privatised water industry have led to the outflows being used regularly to discharge sewage. In the first five months of 2026, South West Water, which operates across Devon, Cornwall and parts of Dorset and Somerset, discharged raw sewage on dry days 1,299 times. This compares with 2,451 times during the whole of 2025.

Water companies are facing outrage across the country for discharging raw sewage via storm outflows in August following the first moderate spell of rain after more than six weeks of drought. Public mapped data revealed water companies including Southern Water and South West Water discharging raw sewage from storm overflows within hours of the first significant rain. In the south-west, after weeks of drought, the company’s own data suggested it discharged sewage into rivers and the sea for a combined total of almost 300 hours in the third week of August. Ed Tyldesley, a Liberal Democrat county councillor in north Devon, said the company’s own figures showed 664 separate spills across 184 sites despite just 16.5mm of rain across the south-west, according to data collated by WaterWatch. “They are using a storm system when there are no storms. It is unbelievable. The worrying thing is that this all seems to be getting worse,” he said.

London Stock Exchange to lose three more firms after takeover offers

Three more London-listed companies are set to be taken over as the value of deals removing firms from the capital’s under-pressure stock market so far this year passes $100bn (£74bn). On Tuesday, Bodycote, the FTSE 250 industrials group that has been listed on the London Stock Exchange since 1972, agreed a £1.84bn takeover by the US private equity group Veritas. The Macclesfield-based company, which offers services including heat treatment for manufacturing, metal joining and protective metallic coatings, had been the subject of a bidding war involving the rival European buyout group CVC. Shares in Bodycote soared 4.5%, making it the second biggest riser in the FTSE 250, after CVC indicated that it might make a counteroffer. “CVC is considering its position and a further announcement will be made when appropriate,” the company said. “Bodycote shareholders are strongly advised to take no action in response to the Veritas offer in the meantime.” Veritas said Bodycote’s prospects would be better served by being taken out of public markets.

Price rises gather pace in UK shops amid higher energy costs

The pace of price rises in UK shops rose to its highest level in two years in August, a trade body index shows, with higher energy costs pushing up the price of food and AI chip demand making technology more expensive. In-store inflation stepped up to 1.5% year on year in August, up from 0.9% in July, led by prices for tinned and packaged food which increased by 2.5% against 1.1% in the prior month, according to data from the research company NIQ for the British Retail Consortium. Inflation for fresh produce remained high at 3%, amid pressure on growers from the hot dry summer plus hefty fuel and energy costs. However, that marked a slight easing off from the 3.1% recorded in July, Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the consortium, said: “The impact of higher energy, input and commodity costs is beginning to filter through into prices, particularly for ambient foods which are typically imported and processed. “In non-food, electrical prices rose amid the ongoing AI boom, which is forcing up the price of memory chips and storage.

Meanwhile, retailers kept clothing prices low to offer value for families getting ready for the new school year. “The months ahead look challenging for households, with rising bills putting further pressure on budgets.” Mike Watkins, head of retailer insight at NIQ, said he expected price competition between retailers to intensify in the autumn months as businesses competed to attract families concerned about potentially higher energy bills. However, Dickinson said companies were facing “persistently high operating costs” that limited their ability to absorb price rises. She added: “If the government is serious about supporting growth while keeping the cost of living in check, it must address the cost of doing business, including by tackling the growing burden of business rates, packaging and employment taxes.” The evidence of higher shop prices comes after the boss of Asda said he was seeing inflation on some fresh food begin to rise after a hot dry summer that affected crop yields. text:
From milk to sausage rolls: how vending machines could help tackle UK ‘food deserts’

Fizzy drinks, packets of crisps and bars of chocolate: for decades, vending machines were known as a place to grab a quick snack. Now one family of farmers is trying to change that by bringing vending machines offering fresh milk and local produce – including scotch eggs, sausage rolls and brownies – to villages and other rural locations. Mark James, 70, and his sons Sam, 39, and Jacob, 36, first trialled vending machines as a way of selling their milk directly to consumers, giving themselves more control over the price they receive. “For the first time ever, we’re price makers rather than price takers,” Mark says. “If we weren’t doing [the vending machine business], we’d have to think about giving up milk.” Just under a third (30%) of the 4,500 litres of milk produced each day by the family’s herd of 130 dairy cows at Bodenham in Herefordshire is sold at their 17 Whole Moo World vending machines, located across Herefordshire and the neighbouring counties of Gloucestershire, Worcestershire and Shropshire. The remaining 70% is sold to a local milk processor.

citation.title: From milk to sausage rolls: how vending machines could help tackle UK ‘food deserts’

text:
From milk to sausage rolls: how vending machines could help tackle UK ‘food deserts’

When Whole Moo World took off, Jacob and Sam branched out into retailing cakes, sandwiches and other treats made by small local producers from vending machines. Their business, Tuckshop, now has 22 sites, mostly alongside the milk machines, and also allows them to sell empty glass bottles for milk. Jacob says farmers are “waking up” to the advantages of selling directly to consumers, even if they do not have a suitable location or the funds needed to build their own farm shop. UK long-term borrowing costs could halve chancellor’s budget headroom

The chancellor’s headroom against Labour’s fiscal rules could be almost halved at his first budget if the current global bond sell-off persists into the autumn, economists say. The UK’s long-term borrowing costs jumped to their highest level since early 1998 on Tuesday as investors dumped government bonds, betting on higher inflation. The yield – in effect the interest rate – on 30-year UK government bonds, known as gilts, hit 5.89% at one point as London markets caught up with a sell-off that swept Japan and the US on Monday, a bank holiday in the UK. Ten-year gilt yields were around 5.25%, their highest level since the 2008 global financial crisis. Higher yields progressively increase the cost of financing the government’s debt. If sustained, these would pass through to the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR)’s forecasts for John Healey’s 28 October budget. Deutsche Bank’s chief UK economist, Sanjay Raja, said that based on Tuesday’s yields, Healey’s headroom against the current budget rule would fall from £26bn at Rachel Reeves’s spring forecast to £13.8bn before covering any additional spending plans.

BP seeks to end years of boardroom turmoil with appointment of new chair

BP has appointed a new chair after a months-long search triggered by the controversial ousting of Albert Manifold, seeking to draw a line under years of boardroom turmoil at the UK oil and gas company. Ian Tyler, who has served as the interim chair and has sat on the BP board as a non-executive director since April 2025, will assume the role on a permanent basis immediately. His appointment comes after Manifold’s shock removal in late May after only eight months in the role, with BP citing “serious concerns” about his tenure. Amanda Blanc, BP’s senior independent director who led the search for a new chair and also runs the insurer Aviva as chief executive, announced on Wednesday she would stand down at next year’s annual meeting. She was criticised after Manifold’s short tenure as chair, because she had led the process that led to his appointment to replace Helge Lund. When Manifold left, Blanc said he had helped drive BP’s transformation but there had been “governance oversight and conduct issues” which the board deemed unacceptable. Reports claimed senior colleagues had felt belittled by Manifold.
