All the biggies of water companies’ performance – pollution, leaks and supply interruptions – got a mention as items in need of improvement. The plan is merely to reduce regulatory penalties by 50% in the current period. Haslett’s hope is that, come 2030, Pennon will be closer to earning a few rewards via Ofwat’s incentive mechanism. The point is that none of this will feel like a case of “shareholders never losing” if you’re unfortunate enough to own Pennon’s shares. Anybody who bought at virtually any point in the past five years has lost a packet. The price was £13.30 in July 2021. Now it is 361p, down 20% on Wednesday with the rights issue to a 22-year low. For good measure, the dividend is being cut by 30% on a per-share basis to reflect the new equity issuance. Reality has arrived at Pennon. Burnham might reflect that private investors can have their uses: the capital has to come from somewhere and shareholders can sometimes be forced to swallow some financial medicine. One could take the view that those investors deserve something even sourer, such as outright nationalisation.

Keir Starmer’s water bill, based on Sir Jon Cunliffe’s 2025 review of the water sector and including a stronger regulator, would have been published about now. Instead, we’ll get Burnham’s “strengthened” version some time next spring, according to the Westminster whisper. Given that it could take 12 months to become law, that will be four years for the Labour government to reform the water sector. That is shockingly slow. As Pennon’s fundraising demonstrates, even the current rickety system is moving faster.

citation.title: Burnham, take note: water shareholders have their uses – they can be squeezed for cash

text:
The UK energy secretary is flirting with a bad idea for bills – the ‘rising block tariff’

‘My mark of failure or success is whether I can get bills down or not. That’s the only thing I’m in this job to do.” So said Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, recently, bracing for the hike in energy bills that looks inevitable in January. Industry projections suggest £400-ish on an annual basis is on the way, with “stubbornly high” levels for the rest of decade even if wholesale gas prices cool down. So, yes, one can understand why “affordability” is Fahnbulleh’s “top priority”. And, as this newspaper reported last week, there is likely to be an intervention in that direction in chancellor John Healey’s budget this month: £1bn of extra support for poorer households this winter. But the chat in energy-land is about what comes after that – and what Fahnbulleh’s other remarks about covering the costs of the energy system in a “fairer” way seem to be hinting at.

citation.title: The UK energy secretary is flirting with a bad idea for bills – the ‘rising block tariff’

text:
The UK energy secretary is flirting with a bad idea for bills – the ‘rising block tariff’

Related: Ministers preparing to slash heat pump subsidies to fund defence spending Will the government finally get round to designing a co-called “social tariff” for energy – a way to get financial support to the most needy on a more targeted basis than the clunky warm homes discount, the mechanism Healey will be obliged to use? Will Healey, after chopping VAT from electricity for six months, do so permanently and then shift more green levies and other “hidden taxes” of energy transition into general taxation? And is Fahnbulleh also contemplating something very different? Welcome to the idea of the “rising block tariff” (RBT), the unwieldy name for the proposal to give every household an initial block, or allowance, of cheaper gas and electricity to cover “essential” use and then make subsequent blocks more expensive. In other words, heavier energy consumers would pay higher rates for their extra units. Fahnbulleh has got officials in her department to explore an RBT model. And, note, the New Economics Foundation, the thinktank she used to lead, is a proponent.

citation.title: The UK energy secretary is flirting with a bad idea for bills – the ‘rising block tariff’

text:
The UK energy secretary is flirting with a bad idea for bills – the ‘rising block tariff’

The Joseph Rowntree Foundation is another backer: in its version, the government could fund an RBT with, say, £5bn of public money, allowing bills to fall for most households – but, critically, the biggest savings would flow to light users, who tend to be low-income households. “An RBT would produce greater reductions in bills lower down the income distribution,” it says. What’s not to like? Plenty. There are at least three reasons why an RBT has few fans elsewhere, not even among charities and thinktanks that focus on fuel poverty. First, Citizens Advice regards low energy use as a poor proxy for low income in practice. Traditional electric heaters, with high electricity usage, “are more common in social or private rented homes, where people can’t change their heating system”, it argues. Quite: a progressive-sounding policy could end up being nothing of the sort, especially if second-home owners, by spreading their usage, are winners.

citation.title: The UK energy secretary is flirting with a bad idea for bills – the ‘rising block tariff’

text:
The UK energy secretary is flirting with a bad idea for bills – the ‘rising block tariff’

If the reply is that an incomes overlay could address tricky cases in both directions, why not just do the data modelling work to design a proper social tariff in the first place? Second, a rigid RBT would be an awkward fit with a renewables-heavy system where the most interesting innovations are “flex” tariffs to exploit very windy or sunny hours when wholesale power prices are dirt cheap. There is a danger of baffling consumers by making them mix their blocks with their flexes. Third, a core aim of the energy transition is to drive take-up of electric vehicles, heat pumps and so on. That becomes harder if the message to consumers is that “the more electricity you use, the more you’ll be charged per unit”. Lobby group Electrify Britain calls block tariffs “hugely counterproductive” for electrification: “You can’t ask families to go electric and then pursue a policy that would charge them more for doing so.” That feels the killer point: an RBT model cuts across too many other goals.

citation.title: The UK energy secretary is flirting with a bad idea for bills – the ‘rising block tariff’

text:
The UK energy secretary is flirting with a bad idea for bills – the ‘rising block tariff’

Fahnbulleh should keep things simple: go for a serious social tariff or discount scheme that effectively identifies “vulnerable” energy users. That idea has enjoyed wide support for years. Block tariffs are too complicated and fiddly to administer.

text:
The water torture goes on at Thames. Sector-wide reform isn’t moving much faster

It is strange now to recall that Thames Water had a prominent slot on what was known as “Sue’s shit list” – the internal Labour dossier, compiled by Keir Starmer’s first chief of staff, Sue Gray, of potential crises that could erupt at short notice and force the incoming administration to make some big decisions quickly. That was July 2024. Here we are – more than two years later – and the Thames script has barely advanced. We’re still waiting to see if the financial crisis at the over-indebted, under-performing water company will be resolved by a creditor-led recapitalisation, special administration or something else. Now Thames is seeking another £2.4bn slug of funding from creditors to stay afloat for another year and survive yet more back and forth between ministers, regulators and those same lenders. The new mystery element in the talks is what the prime minister, Andy Burnham, actually means by “greater public control”. Still, Thames was an outlier – albeit a biggie – one might say.

citation.title: The water torture goes on at Thames. Sector-wide reform isn’t moving much faster

text:
The water torture goes on at Thames. Sector-wide reform isn’t moving much faster

At least the government in 2024 cracked on with the job of deciding how to overhaul the wider water sector in England and Wales. Indeed it did: Sir Jon Cunliffe, a former deputy governor of the Bank of England, was commissioned to review what was needed and his detailed report landed in summer last year. The centrepiece was the abolition of Ofwat, the regulator. Steve Reed, the environment secretary at the time, embraced Cunliffe’s proposals and declared the “the biggest overhaul of water regulation in a generation” via a new water bill. Game on? Not exactly. The bill, which should have arrived this autumn, was delayed by the change of PM. Burnham has promised a “strengthened” version, which presumably will include the “public control” elements. In the meantime, Ofwat is still in place, and nobody knows which bits of the Environment Agency will be absorbed into the new super-regulator, or what the new body’s formal status will be. Will it, for example, be as formally independent as Ofwat, or will it be under a tighter ministerial leash? Credit rating agencies have noticed the uncertainty.

citation.title: The water torture goes on at Thames. Sector-wide reform isn’t moving much faster

text:
The water torture goes on at Thames. Sector-wide reform isn’t moving much faster

In dry language, Moody’s on Thursday issued a report noting that regulatory changes “appears to have stalled”, that “political scrutiny is heightened and may cause further delay” and the “potential increase in business risk will require stronger financial ratios to maintain credit quality”. Moody’s, note, did not downgrade its assessment of the “stability and predictability” of UK water regulation, as it did in late-2024. But it did tiptoe up to the line: one of its slides at Thursday’s conference warned: “Our score could fall further.” Why does Moody’s opinion matter? Simply because rating agencies influence the price at which companies can borrow, which can itself affect the financing costs passed on to customers in bills. The government should take the hint and decide what it actually wants from water reform. Emma Hardy, the water minister, at least indicated to the same conference that a formal transition plan to the regulator is coming soon. But that’s not the same as an actual water bill, which would reveal if the rest of the Cunliffe changes have survived.

citation.title: The water torture goes on at Thames. Sector-wide reform isn’t moving much faster

text:
The water torture goes on at Thames. Sector-wide reform isn’t moving much faster

It is, of course, entirely fair for an incoming PM to review what he wants from a bill. But the “public control” bit, if that’s delaying everything, needs to be nailed down sharpish. Is it simply the Cunliffe-compliant idea of greater powers of influence for mayors and local authorities? Or bigger changes to match the summer rhetoric? It’s impossible to tell – but it’s all taking far too long. And make a decision one way or another on Thames. Half a parliament to address a supposedly urgent 2024 problem is extreme water torture.

text:
A modest increase in bank taxes is not the end of the world for lenders

Everyone is familiar with the banks’ plea: raising taxes on them amounts to taxing the nation’s growth. If you increase how much banks pay, goes the argument, less interest will be paid on deposits and loans will cost slightly more, meaning we’ll all be worse off eventually. In terms of economic theory, it’s coherent, it should be said: in an ideal world, a chancellor would strive to lower costs of capital at every opportunity. In the real world, however, John Healey faces multiple competing demands, even from within a business lobby that extends well beyond the banks. As this newspaper revealed last week, the chancellor is likely to increase bank taxes in his budget next week. In the current climate of trying to “stay the course” on the fiscal rules by finding some money from somewhere, tapping the banks is a reasonable policy. Or, at least, better than most alternatives. First, today’s conditions for banks are plainly gentle: defaults are historically low and interest rates are high. Banks’ returns on tangible equity – a better guide to how they are doing than pure profitability – are heading towards 20%.

citation.title: A modest increase in bank taxes is not the end of the world for lenders

text:
A modest increase in bank taxes is not the end of the world for lenders

Most non-financial firms would love such a number. Provided Healey doesn’t go overboard, the flow of capital is not going to be seriously undermined when the starting point for banks’ returns is so good. Second, all the indications suggest Healey will indeed opt only for tweaks. If the mechanism is the surcharge that banks pay on top of corporation tax at 25%, then an increase to 8%, from 3%, would amount to £2bn-ish extra from across the sector. He may not even go that far. Analysts at UBS calculate that a doubling of the surcharge to 6% would reduce UK banks’ profits only by about 2% on average, with a roughly 3%-4% impact for the domestic-focused banks, meaning NatWest and Lloyds. That cannot be called a violent change in the operating climate, or a devastating blow for the shareholders or the equity-incentivised executives. Dividends or share buybacks may be trimmed a bit, but the share prices for both banks are up by a fifth in the past year. Third, we’ll have to wait to see whether any move by Healey is part of a wider financial services package that could include bank-pleasing elements.

citation.title: A modest increase in bank taxes is not the end of the world for lenders

text:
A modest increase in bank taxes is not the end of the world for lenders

There’s always scope for another hack at the thicket of regulations, for instance. Or help on capital buffers. And, if Healey is really as pro-growth as he claims, he’d consider this column’s perennial pre-budget suggestion to scrap or cut stamp duty on shares – a move that would seriously improve UK companies’ cost of capital (see Tax Policy Associates’ paper) and do wonders for banks’ wealth-management divisions. The point is that a small turn on the surcharge dial is better than other ways of extracting the odd billion or two for the banks. A windfall tax would be too arbitrary. Changing the way banks’ deposits are remunerated at the Bank of England would look like interference in the central bank’s independence. The surcharge is a well-understood mechanism. None of which, one suspects, will stop the howls of complaints from banks, or halt the grumbles about the loss of competitiveness versus other financial centres. But an extra £2bn, or less, from the financial services sector simply doesn’t sound like a gamechanger if Healey acts as expected.

citation.title: A modest increase in bank taxes is not the end of the world for lenders

text:
A modest increase in bank taxes is not the end of the world for lenders

Even JP Morgan’s Jamie Dimon, who likes to play politics at budget-time with his proposed new London headquarters, might reflect that some other European capitals – Paris, say – don’t look like a bed of roses.

text:
Jackdaw approval is a step towards a grownup North Sea policy

Andy Burnham hit the nail on the (well)head in his first fortnight as prime minister when he said: “The question isn’t whether Britain will still be using oil and gas, the question is, where does it come from?” It was a nod towards several awkward energy facts. First, oil and gas provided 75% of the UK’s energy in 2025, government data shows. Second, even with the rollout of domestic renewables for generating electricity, about 43% of overall energy was imported last year. Third, all credible paths to net zero emissions by 2050 involve using a lot of oil and gas on the way because we’re still in the foothills of electrification. Fewer than 2% of UK households have heat pumps, according to the lobby group Electrify Britain. While sales of EVs are accelerating, nearly 95% of vehicles on the road run on petrol and diesel. Meanwhile, hydrogen and biomethane have barely taken off as alternatives to gas for those industrial processes that require higher temperatures than electricity can achieve – tricky for a government pursuing “reindustrialisation”.

citation.title: Jackdaw approval is a step towards a grownup North Sea policy

text:
Jackdaw approval is a step towards a grownup North Sea policy

Fourth – and this one must alarm Downing Street – the global energy market has simply become less reliable. The strait of Hormuz can close overnight. The US president can threaten to ban diesel exports. Russian ships prowl the North Sea. Even the nice Norwegians, with an eye on their own energy consumers, scrapped a planned electricity cable to Scotland in 2023. It is no longer a world of always-available “just in time” supply. Thinking has shifted to “just in case” scenario-planning. And a truly scary scenario would be disruption to the 725-mile Langeled pipeline that is the primary route for gas supplies from Norway, 40% of the UK’s consumption last year. The pipeline is a security vulnerability if ever there was one (if you doubt it, watch Sky News’ recent report). Now we have the start of an answer to Burnham’s “where should it come from?” question. The Jackdaw gasfield, 150 miles east of Aberdeen, has finally been approved to produce in time for winter. About time, too. All the arguments from pragmatism were in the field’s favour.

citation.title: Jackdaw approval is a step towards a grownup North Sea policy

text:
Jackdaw approval is a step towards a grownup North Sea policy

As this column has said in the past, less North Sea gas would inevitably mean more imported liquefied natural gas, with the extra carbon emissions created by chilling the fuel to -160C for shipment and then “regasifying” it at the other end. Such cargos were 20% of UK gas imports last year, mostly from the US. It already feels absurd that the 24m UK households with a gas boiler burn any gas at all from the shale fields of Texas and Pennsylvania. Why increase the exposure if lower-polluting supplies are available off Aberdeen? More UK North Sea gas production won’t lower the price for consumers much, if at all. But that was never the argument. It was always about tax receipts, jobs, the national balance of payments, relative emissions and the security that comes with having domestic volumes piped straight into the national gas network. Jackdaw is not a gamechanger – it will be 6% of UK North Sea gas production at peak – but it’s definitely worth having while the UK is still using gas, which will be at least as long as the field’s 11-year life.

citation.title: Jackdaw approval is a step towards a grownup North Sea policy

text:
Jackdaw approval is a step towards a grownup North Sea policy

The next question is whether other “tie-back” gasfields in already-explored areas, such as Tornado, west of Shetland, will follow. The line in the government’s announcement about “asking the regulator to consider urgent cases that could benefit from similar measures now” suggests so. Rosebank, also near Shetland, is a trickier political proposition because it’s mostly oil, which is more polluting, and will be producing for longer. But the arguments aren’t wholly different. The common elements are still jobs, investment, taxes and the government’s ability to impose higher environmental standards during the production stage. Meanwhile, the “it’s all exported” objection to Rosebank misses the fact that the UK oil industry operates within a European network. If the UK had more than four refineries (compared with nine at the turn of the century), a chunk of Rosebank’s output might be processed at home. As it is, some – perhaps the majority – will come back to the UK as petrol, diesel and jet fuel once it’s been refined in Rotterdam or elsewhere in north-west Europe.

citation.title: Jackdaw approval is a step towards a grownup North Sea policy

text:
Jackdaw approval is a step towards a grownup North Sea policy

Take a step back and the North Sea debate is really about how much oil and gas it is sensible for the UK to produce itself on the way to net zero. On the current trajectory, only about a third of consumption will come from domestic sources on a net basis. Even offshore lobbyists reckon a boost to North Sea production would only get the ratio up to about a half, albeit the figure would obviously increase if consumption of fossil fuels can be made to fall faster. Nobody is talking about the UK becoming a net exporter again. Related: UK approves Jackdaw gasfield in North Sea Commitment to net zero by 2050 was intact, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, insisted. We wait to see what the new “energy wealth fund”, which will reinvest oil and gas revenues into renewable and low-carbon projects, means in practice. But the financial logic is sound: recycle the receipts from the old system to quicken the transition. Electrification, enabling consumers to make use of lower-carbon energy, is still the main story.

citation.title: Jackdaw approval is a step towards a grownup North Sea policy

text:
Jackdaw approval is a step towards a grownup North Sea policy

The bizarreness in the government’s previous approach was that, even as it proclaimed the virtues of “clean homegrown energy” such as wind, solar and nuclear, it pursued an approach that maximised imports when it came to oil and gas. Many, including the general secretary of the GMB union, Gary Smith, pointed out the flaw: it was hard for the UK to claim real climate leadership if it was simply off-shoring emissions. In a small way, Jackdaw addresses the UK’s extreme reliance on imports. It is a step towards a joined-up commonsense approach to energy security. The real transition test remains the pace at which the UK stops using fossil fuels.

citation.title: Jackdaw approval is a step towards a grownup North Sea policy

text:
Britain’s gas security needs reinforcement. Last-minute deals with Belgium are not a proper fix

After the overdue approval of the Jackdaw field in the North Sea, here comes a reminder that Britain still imports almost 60% of its gas and the stuff has to come from somewhere. We’re now doing a deal with Belgium to ensure enough supply can flow through a connecting pipeline this winter should a “low-probability but high-impact stress event”, to quote the regulatory mouthful, occur. To be fair, the arrangement to maintain capacity from Belgium is a belt-and-braces measure. The imagined events do sound genuinely stressful and may never happen. A critical piece of infrastructure, such as the two import terminals in Milford Haven to bring in liquefied natural gas (LNG) into Britain, would have to be out of action during a prolonged cold snap in which demand is very high. Equally, though, the “high-impact” bit matters: we’re talking about having enough supplies to run gas-fired power stations at full pelt if necessary to keep the lights on. You don’t take chances.

citation.title: Britain’s gas security needs reinforcement. Last-minute deals with Belgium are not a proper fix

text:
Britain’s gas security needs reinforcement. Last-minute deals with Belgium are not a proper fix

In short, 10p a month will be added to bills to cover the cost of paying Interconnector Limited, the Belgian owner of the pipeline, to maintain the compressors needed to shove big volumes of gas to Britain in a hurry if required. Without the arrangement, the company had already warned it would cut capacity, in part because the big pipe was not used much in practice last year. The first conclusion – the comforting one – is that the deal sounds like decent value for money. As insurance policies go, £1.19 a household a year is not much. The second, however, is that risks to Britain’s gas security are plainly mounting. The Ofgem document describing the Belgian deal says it was “the only currently available intervention identified that both addresses the immediate security of supply position for winter 2026/27 and provides continuing security of supply benefits over the following four years”. It was Belgium, plus any future deal on the Dutch pipeline, or nothing. Nor is the Belgian shuffle a cure-all.

citation.title: Britain’s gas security needs reinforcement. Last-minute deals with Belgium are not a proper fix

text:
Britain’s gas security needs reinforcement. Last-minute deals with Belgium are not a proper fix

“The agreement does not remove the need for further measures led by government that are likely to be required to support security of supply and wider gas system resilience over the medium and longer term,” says Ofgem. The government should take that line as a heavy hint to get a move on. Do we need more gas storage, more LNG terminals, or both? And post-Jackdaw, what’s a realistic appraisal of how much will be sourced from the North Sea? It is now almost a year since an alarming report from the National Energy System Operator (Neso) warned of an “emerging risk to gas supply security” in 2030. The government promised to “do whatever it takes” to avert a crunch but one cannot say it has actually done much. An interim response to the Neso report came in August but no timetable was given for choosing what kit or arrangements were needed and by when. The final response isn’t due until next year. Read the “winter outlook” report from National Gas, published on Friday, and a few points stand out. Yes, it’s good news that, with the help of the Belgian deal, this winter’s outlook is positive.

citation.title: Britain’s gas security needs reinforcement. Last-minute deals with Belgium are not a proper fix

text:
Britain’s gas security needs reinforcement. Last-minute deals with Belgium are not a proper fix

But the company also says that, even as annual consumption drifts down slightly, the peaks for demand remain as high as ever, driven by the role of gas-fired power generation when renewables output is low. Like Ofgem, National Gas says “continued progress on government plans to reform security of supply arrangements will be vital to address enduring challenges in the years ahead”. It is becoming a theme. The obvious answer is more gas storage to address Britain’s skimpy current levels. That could mean Centrica’s Rough facility in North Sea (currently due to close next spring), the Bains development led by dCarbonX off the north-west coast of England (which may happen anyway), more on-shore salt caverns or any combination. Or, perhaps, German-style forward-buying deals on LNG. But something has to happen soon. None of this infrastructure gets built quickly and that 2030 potential crunch is getting closer. Certainly, the government cannot agonise for as long as it did over Jackdaw. Eleventh-hour deals with Belgium are not a permanent fix for Britain’s gas security headache.

citation.title: Britain’s gas security needs reinforcement. Last-minute deals with Belgium are not a proper fix

text:
The chancellor’s pet PuFins have an important role – but they need more scrutiny

Two winners in the budget are known already. They are the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank, state-funded investment bodies that have rapidly become central to the government’s growth strategy. The former chancellor Rachel Reeves handed extra slugs of capital to both and now John Healey is going further. The NWF will get another £15.4bn over the next half decade, on top of its existing £27.8bn, and there’ll be another £5bn for the BBB, which already has £25.6bn. Expect a fanfare about “over 100,000 jobs across the country to be created” via the extra capital for these so-called PuFins. The term means public financial institutions. They invest in private sector assets, either directly or through third-party funds, with the aim of making a profit for the taxpayer – or, at least, earning a return that matches or beats the government’s cost of borrowing. Cue, also, another round of debate about whether Healey is engaged in fancy financial footwork to get around the constraints of his fiscal rules.

citation.title: The chancellor’s pet PuFins have an important role – but they need more scrutiny

text:
The chancellor’s pet PuFins have an important role – but they need more scrutiny

Reeves rewrote those rules in her first budget in 2024 to allow the value of financial assets – such the NWF and BBB’s loans and stakes in companies – to be netted off against the public debt. To fans, the principle makes sense. As long as the PuFins’ assets maintain their value and cover the interest on the government’s extra borrowing (a critical condition), it’s a way to boost investment. More critical projects can be built sooner, and possibly more cheaply; more companies may prosper to the eventual benefit of the public purse. Critics, such as the right-leaning Centre for Policy Studies in a report last week, see a “financial wheeze” that disguises the true level of government borrowing and stores up trouble, as the Blair-era private finance initiative did. The thinktank called for the wings of the PuFins to be clipped. Healey, it is safe to assume, will ignore that advice. The PuFins fall squarely within his theory for growth – the idea of “crowding in” private investment and spreading money around the regions. In Healey’s support, one can say state-backed co-investment vehicles are not new.

citation.title: The chancellor’s pet PuFins have an important role – but they need more scrutiny

text:
The chancellor’s pet PuFins have an important role – but they need more scrutiny

Governments of all hues have used them. George Osborne even launched a Green Investment Bank. And the NWF, despite its misleading name (it’s not a Norway-style wealth fund), to some degree merely replaces infrastructure lending that might have been done by the European Investment Bank in pre-Brexit days. As for the BBB, its focus on “scale-up” capital for young, fast-growing companies is designed to address a gap that has been a source of grumbles for decades. Both institutions are useful. There are questions, however, about potential overuse. Are the NWF and BBB sticking in all cases to their core role of “additionality”, the idea that PuFins should bring something extra to the party? They are not meant to be substitutes for private capital. They must crowd in rather than crowd out. The line can appear blurry at times. This column has questioned the £25m that BBB invested in Kraken Technologies, the software firm being spun out of Octopus Energy. How was that a case of “helping smaller businesses get the finance they need”?

citation.title: The chancellor’s pet PuFins have an important role – but they need more scrutiny

text:
The chancellor’s pet PuFins have an important role – but they need more scrutiny

Kraken was valued at a thumping £6.45bn, so wasn’t a small firm; and £25m was a rounding error within a wider $1bn fundraising. Similarly, the Centre for Policy Studies surely has a point when it wonders why the NWF lent to Scottish Power, “an investment-grade company with an investment-grade Spanish parent” on projects to upgrade to the electricity grid. The NWF’s ability to make long-dated loans probably helped the financing, but regulated utilities are supposed to be big enough to stand on their own feet. Weren’t there better targets for the NWF’s loans? To be fair, the websites of both the NWF and BBB are stuffed with case studies that fit the government’s priorities uncontroversially. For example, the latter’s follow-on £100m investment in Oxford Quantum Circuits, a quantum computing firm, was big and on-message. And, so far at least, the promise of gilt-like returns is intact, or not disproved. The BBB cites a “3.9% five-year adjusted return” but says the number would be higher if one was counting only its commercial activities.

citation.title: The chancellor’s pet PuFins have an important role – but they need more scrutiny

text:
The chancellor’s pet PuFins have an important role – but they need more scrutiny

In the case of NWF, it’s too soon to tell: last year’s return on equity was -2.6% but a gilt-like number was only ever promised in 2030-31. The requirement to co-invest with hard-nosed private investors is probably helpful. But there’s still the issue of being additional. “Assessing additionality is not a precise science, but rather an exercise in judgment,” concedes the NWF in its impact framework. An Office for Budget Responsibility-style body to scrutinise those judgments is starting to look essential. As the allocations from the Treasury increase, there is a risk that the definition of “additional” gets stretched. At the moment, the PuFins are only ultimately answerable to their sole shareholders, the Treasury (NWF) and the business secretary (BBB).

citation.title: The chancellor’s pet PuFins have an important role – but they need more scrutiny

text:
The chancellor’s pet PuFins have an important role – but they need more scrutiny

The Institute for Fiscal Studies, in its pre-budget assessment, said: “If the government follows the spirit of the guidelines, and aims to construct a portfolio of investments that align with government priorities and generate a profit, the cases where investment can occur through PuFins may turn out to be relatively limited.” That sounds like good advice. For the time being, there’s a fair argument there is room for more. The Resolution Foundation argues that, notwithstanding the extra £5.8bn from Reeves, the NWF’s capacity has “barely kept pace with inflation”. But policing the PuFins, and ensuring they stick to their “additionality” brief, is surely equally important. There will be problems if they behave like gannets. • This article was amended on 28 October 2026. The sole shareholder of the British Business Bank is the business secretary, not the Treasury as an earlier version said.

text:
Hold your nose: a £1.25bn subsidy for rich Rolls-Royce’s new engine had to happen

It wasn’t a “nothing” budget for engine-maker Rolls-Royce. The company was handed £1.25bn from public coffers to part-fund the development of a next-generation engine for single-aisle commercial planes. The chancellor buried this giveaway in two short sentences in the stodgy middle of his speech, presumably because it would look too much like a case of corporate welfare just after he had grumbled about the £14bn extra we’ll be paying in debt interest this year. Related: Give us all a share of Rolls-Royce’s profits And it’s not as if Rolls is on its uppers. The pride of Derby is the UK’s most radically improved major company of the past few years. It sits in fifth spot in the FTSE 100 index, sporting a market value of £105bn, and has enough spare cash to spend up to £9bn on share buy-backs this year. But there had been an air of inevitability about this subsidy ever since the company’s chief executive, Tufan Erginbilgiç, talked earlier this year about how he would “appreciate” financial support from the government in developing the UltraFan engine. Appreciate?

What he meant is that other governments would cough up if the UK didn’t. That, unfortunately, is how life works in the global aerospace business. Subsidies are a down payment on the jobs and factories that can follow. Germany, reeling from the woes of its carmakers, would love to have a bigger slice of the hi-tech UltraFan action (and has a role in the gearboxes anyway). The US aerospace industry is a study in how generous defence contracts subsidise civil operations. Healey couldn’t ignore those facts of aerospace life. Related: Budget 2026: key points at a glance What’s more, one can see how the possible long-term return on the £1.25bn could turn out very well. “The single biggest opportunity in aerospace over the next 50 years is to secure a UK engine position on next generation narrow body programmes,” said the government’s strategy document for advanced manufacturing. Aircraft engines are high-value products. About 80% would be exported, doing wonders for the national balance of payments. Projections of “tens of thousands of highly skilled jobs” eventually are credible.

text:
Private equity keeps picking off London-listed firms – and Westminster barely notices

The UK is in the business of “reindustrialising”, says the prime minister. If we are, an increasing portion of the activity will be under foreign ownership. Tuesday brought yet another overseas private equity swoop on a FTSE 250 industrial firm. This time it’s the Macclesfield-based Bodycote, which describes itself as “the world’s largest service provider of heat treatment and specialist metallurgical technologies” – think, for example, processes and coatings to toughen jet engine blades. The buyer is the US buyout firm Veritas for £1.65bn or 940p a share, or £1.85bn including debt. Unless, that is, the rival bidder, CVC, a European private equity firm, comes back for another bite, which the market clearly thinks is a possibility because Bodycote’s shares closed at 955p. The shame is that one cannot call 940p a stunning price. The valuation “does not appear particularly generous on a take-out basis”, said an analyst at the investment bank RBC, noting that it’s only 25% above the pre-bid level and the implied earnings valuation is merely in line with Bodycote’s 10-year average.

citation.title: Private equity keeps picking off London-listed firms – and Westminster barely notices

text:
Private equity keeps picking off London-listed firms – and Westminster barely notices

Indeed, nine-tenths of the “reasons for recommendation” section of Bodycote’s announcement sounded like an argument for doing the opposite. The passage started by saying how well the medium-term “optimise, perform, grow” strategy adopted in late 2024 was going. The plan was designed to find efficiencies and shift towards the expanding aerospace and defence sectors in pursuit of enviable financial metrics, including 20%-plus operating margins and a return on capital employed of 15 to 20% through the cycle. Good progress has been made, say the directors. On the way, there has been enough spare cash for £120m of share buy-backs while maintaining a 38-year record of growing or maintaining the dividend. And the board is “confident in the ongoing execution” of the strategy, with “the majority of remaining improvements under Bodycote’s control”.

citation.title: Private equity keeps picking off London-listed firms – and Westminster barely notices

text:
Private equity keeps picking off London-listed firms – and Westminster barely notices

It was only in the last sentence that the company also said it was “mindful of increasing structural challenges in certain automotive and industrial markets together with macroeconomic uncertainties which create meaningful risk to delivery of Bodycote’s medium term financial targets”. In other words, everything is going splendidly apart from a couple of risks – the sectoral one that the strategy is addressing, and the vague “macroeconomic uncertainty” that is a normal state of affairs for most companies. As a reason for accepting a bid at a mere 25% premium, it’s not terribly convincing. In Bodycote’s defence, one might say the takeover price could yet improve if CVC, which said it was considering its position, comes back. More depressingly, one suspects Bodycote simply lives in that unloved sub-£5bn capitalisation part of the stock market that suffers from lack of attention and lack of regular inward capital flows. It is harder to fight for independence if the unspoken market pressure is to accept a bid for the sake of certainty.

citation.title: Private equity keeps picking off London-listed firms – and Westminster barely notices

text:
Private equity keeps picking off London-listed firms – and Westminster barely notices

The mini-tragedy in this case is that there was a wake-up call of sorts for investors when Apollo, yet another US private equity outfit, expressed an interest in bidding at 885p in the spring before walking away. The net result, though, is that Bodycote’s 54 years of London stock market life will come to an end one way or another. The company joins a long list of departees this year, which on Tuesday alone also took in telecoms company Gamma Communications for £1.1bn and the Scottish energy firm Capricorn for £292m. Bodycote can still prosper under private equity ownership, of course. But a leading UK-based global specialist in its field, with 130 sites across 22 countries and 4,000 employees, is yet another bad one for the London market to lose. The remedies for this rate of exodus have been trawled over in this column many times – and none are easy.

text:
Burnham beware, the bond markets will demand proper answers in the budget

It’s too soon to say the bond markets have turned on Andy Burnham. Tuesday’s spike in gilt yields, taking the UK’s 30-year borrowing costs to their highest level since 1998, was part of an international sell-off of government debt. The main contributors are well known. The Iran war, by increasing the cost of energy, has overturned the comforting start-of-the-year thesis of falling global inflation and interest rates. A plunging Japanese yen has kicked away another assumed source of financial stability. The US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, hasn’t calmed nerves with his solo, and so far futile, attempt to bring down US yields. Meanwhile, the early stage of the AI revolution is an exercise in issuing squillions of debt before long-term returns on capital can possibly be assessed meaningfully. From the point of view of the mythical bond vigilante, in these circumstances it’s only logical to demand a higher return to lend to profligate governments with high debt ratios, which is most of them.

citation.title: Burnham beware, the bond markets will demand proper answers in the budget

text:
Burnham beware, the bond markets will demand proper answers in the budget

In a narrow sense, then, UK gilts were just moving with the market at a moment of rising financial risks in all directions. It’s just that the UK was already uncomfortably placed at the cold edge of the pack with the highest borrowing rates in the G7, a status largely reflecting a dismal 20-year record in keeping a lid on inflation and, especially now, a dependency on energy imports that stood at 43% in 2025. It is also true, unfortunately, that six weeks into the job Burnham and the chancellor, John Healey, have said nothing to make bond investors rethink the UK’s status. Investors have heard the dutiful commitment to Rachel Reeves’s fiscal rules, but Burnham’s Commons speech on Tuesday carried little sense of urgency about the UK’s financial predicament, or appreciation of how 10-year gilt yields at 5.2% will cause damage if sustained for long. More “public control” of utilities – the theme Burnham constantly returns to – may be desirable and play well on the backbenches.

citation.title: Burnham beware, the bond markets will demand proper answers in the budget

text:
Burnham beware, the bond markets will demand proper answers in the budget

But, even when the ambiguous meaning is made clearer, how does it translate into, say, substantially lower costs of building infrastructure? Should it really be a top economic priority? “Markets are sceptical that ‘devolution’ and ‘control’ are levers for lower government-led inflation,” said the Panmure Liberum economist Simon French. “Burnham/Healey’s unenviable task is to prove they are the right levers. If they fail then a very painful period of financial repression/demand side-led disinflation will be necessary.” There is an uncomfortable sense that the bond market expects next month’s budget to be a bigger event than Burnham and Healey will produce. The tone of Burnham’s Commons speech was “the last thing investors wanted to hear”, said the former Goldman Sachs economist Jim O’Neill – quite a verdict from a friendly critic who was being lined up for a role in government until recently. But one can see his point. He told the BBC that high government borrowing costs would force Labour to get real about dealing with the triple lock on the state pension and “excessive” welfare spending.

citation.title: Burnham beware, the bond markets will demand proper answers in the budget

text:
Burnham beware, the bond markets will demand proper answers in the budget

There has been little rolling of the pitch, as they say in Westminster, in either of those directions to date. It may be, of course, that impressions are mistaken and that next month’s promised 10-year economic plan turns out to be a big exercise in addressing energy costs, defence spending, social care, housing shortages and all the other main challenges. But it is also easy to imagine an alternative script in which hard decisions are deferred and the UK-specific action in the bond market turns uglier – especially if, say, disruption to global energy markets looks likely to last the winter. Labour has spent 2026 defenestrating one leader and anointing another. It needs something to show for it. Burnham speaks of giving businesses and consumers breathing space from the cost of living pressures. That task is easier when the government itself is getting some breathing space from the bond markets. Whatever the chosen mix of spending cuts and tax rises, the budget needs details.

text:
Jonathan Reynolds is right, Jaguar Land Rover doesn’t warrant use of public money

A default reaction to news of job losses in the UK car industry is to ask what the government is going to do about it. So, well done business secretary Jonathan Reynolds for giving the correct response to the question of whether public money will be used to support Jaguar Land Rover, which on Monday confirmed 4,000 job cuts over two years. His answer was no. It is the right stance because JLR’s cost-cutting cannot be compared to a Volkswagen-like existential corporate crisis. In common with most European carmakers, JLR has had a rotten 12 months thanks to Donald Trump’s tariffs, luxury taxes in China, inflation in the cost of raw materials and, in its case, a big cyber-attack. Yet the company continues to talk bullishly about double-digit growth around the next corner as it prepares to launch five new models. Here, for example, was the big-picture outlook assessment in May’s full-year results: “Looking ahead, JLR remains resilient and well placed to address the geopolitical, inflationary and regulatory challenges the industry faces.

citation.title: Jonathan Reynolds is right, Jaguar Land Rover doesn’t warrant use of public money

text:
Jonathan Reynolds is right, Jaguar Land Rover doesn’t warrant use of public money

Investment spend is planned to remain at £18bn over the five-year period from FY24 [full year 2024]. Monday’s job losses were characterised as a major – but not exceptional – programme to keep a lid on costs by finding £1.7bn worth of annual savings. Instead of breaking even, cash-wise, when it has sold 350,000 units, JLR wants to get back to 300,000, which was the level in 2024. That seems a reasonable ambition in a trickier market, especially after a period of heavy investment. As Reynolds said, car manufacturers have always flexed the size of their workforce at different points in the business and product cycle. Note, too, that the 4,000 job losses – out of 44,000 people globally and 34,000 in the UK – will be heavily skewed towards what JLR calls “salaried and management” roles, or white-collar workers in old lingo. In other words, there will be relatively little impact on factory workers who are paid hourly. An outsider may wonder if JLR isn’t simply overpopulated with managers.

citation.title: Jonathan Reynolds is right, Jaguar Land Rover doesn’t warrant use of public money

text:
Jonathan Reynolds is right, Jaguar Land Rover doesn’t warrant use of public money

Either way, the appropriate role of government is the normal one of assisting with retraining and re-employment and so on. One assumes action on that front will follow after talks with unions on Tuesday. State financial assistance might be a different matter if we were talking about new battery factories or other big capital programmes, or schemes to take the edge off the UK’s horrendous industrial electricity costs. But the job cuts, as JLR presents them, are simply about staying competitive – and there’s no reason for government to interfere in that process. The big corporate test ahead is chasing the US “luxury” market (and a starting price of £154,070 for the new electric Range Rover means the vehicle definitely qualifies as a luxury item) and avoiding what the chief financial officer calls “the killing fields of mass automotive”, a reasonable shorthand for Volkswagen’s predicament under competition from China. The next couple of years will be critical for JLR. By the same token, one cannot call the job losses a blow to Andy Burnham’s ambitions for “reindustrialising” the country.

text:
Jonathan Reynolds is right, Jaguar Land Rover doesn’t warrant use of public money

They’re unwelcome, obviously, but were signalled in May and are part of a specific corporate story. Indeed, the wider reindustrialisation challenge is working out what the prime minister means. On that score, Reynolds’s early contributions on his return to his old job have been less impressive. His descriptions of reindustrialisation have fallen into mushy “backing the industries of the future” generalities. Work to do on that score – but the position on JLR is correct.

text:
Yes, cut red tape. But shareholder votes on boardroom pay are not ‘pointless admin’

The government, like every other one in living memory, is on a mission to reduce red tape for business. The former chancellor Rachel Reeves promised “a blitz on bureaucracy” and “pointless admin” and here comes the business department with a 12-week consultation on “modernising corporate reporting to support long-term economic growth”. Never mind that cutting energy costs for business would, by an order of magnitude, do more to support growth than any bonfire of red tape ever will. The consultation is still worthwhile: clearing out accumulated clutter, exploring digital options and clarifying reporting “exemptions and exclusions” for small- and medium-sized companies could free up a bit of time for doing more business. But two ideas in this burden-lifting exercise are terrible because they involve an unacceptable loss of transparency. One is the idea of dropping annual shareholder votes on companies’ remuneration reports.

citation.title: Yes, cut red tape. But shareholder votes on boardroom pay are not ‘pointless admin’

text:
Yes, cut red tape. But shareholder votes on boardroom pay are not ‘pointless admin’

The supposed justification is that, since a binding vote on a company’s overall remuneration policy would still be required on a three-yearly cycle, there is no point in having an annual advisory-only poll on how the policy has been implemented. Such a weaselly idea could only have come from those FTSE 100 companies that resent scrutiny of their directors’ mega-bucks pay packages. Too bad: annual votes are a modest (and mostly ineffectual anyway) check on runaway boardroom rewards. Obliging the non-executives on the remuneration committee to justify their decisions to the outside world, in the knowledge the owners will vote, is a bare minimum requirement for retaining a bit of accountability in the system. If the chief executive has to squirm when, say, 30% of shareholders rebel, so be it. By rights, any reform ought to be in the other direction: it would be better to make the annual poll binding. The government’s other bad proposal is to encourage the trend among quoted companies towards online-only annual shareholder meetings.

citation.title: Yes, cut red tape. But shareholder votes on boardroom pay are not ‘pointless admin’

text:
Yes, cut red tape. But shareholder votes on boardroom pay are not ‘pointless admin’

It’s true that many such meetings struggle to attract attendances in double figures, so the desire to turn the thing into a glorified Teams call is vaguely understandable. But a well-established principle is at stake: even small investors in a listed company should have the right, once a year, to buttonhole the bosses and ask a question in the flesh. The best solution in a digital age is hybrid meetings – let the shareholders decide if they wish to turn up or dial in. It is hardly an onerous requirement on the company to make a meeting room available. Again, one suspects the dead-hand of corporate affairs departments at work: with honourable exceptions, they don’t like the hassle of dealing with retail investors or campaign groups. Sorry, but that’s life. One other piece of advice for the department: yes, it’s true that annual reports have grown monstrous in size – running to “98,000 words, longer than JRR Tolkien’s The Hobbit” on average, it complains. And, yes, burdensome reporting requirements explain part of the growth.

citation.title: Yes, cut red tape. But shareholder votes on boardroom pay are not ‘pointless admin’

text:
Yes, cut red tape. But shareholder votes on boardroom pay are not ‘pointless admin’

But it’s also true that companies don’t help themselves by padding out their productions with acres of irrelevant corporate babble. If, as the consultation says, annual reports are “a document primarily intended for investors and creditors”, make them easy to use. Part of the corporate instinct to write at Tolkien-like length stems, one suspects, is from fear of being accused of leaving anything out. The result, too often, is unreadable guff that doesn’t offer a concise account of the directors’ view of how the company is run and the risks and opportunities it faces. By all means, reform some of the reporting burdens – there are probably plenty to go at. But don’t undermine the transparency offered by annual votes on pay and annual meetings. And don’t allow companies to use “regulatory requirements” as an excuse for boilerplate communication.

text:
The ‘great grid upgrade’ is off track – ministers should spell out the risks for bills

It’s an open secret in the energy industry that “the great grid upgrade” – the £70bn programme to rewire the nation’s electricity transmission network to enable clean power by 2030 – is running over budget and behind schedule, and may end up costing consumers and businesses more in their bills than advertised. How far behind? How much more? It is impossible to get straight answers from the bodies overseeing the massive spending programme, which may continue at an even greater scale into the 2030s. The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (Desnz), its in-house body, the National Energy System Operator (Neso), and Ofgem, the supposedly independent regulator, publish acres of information on narrow matters, but none provides a clear big-picture assessment: how is the grid upgrade really going? Thank goodness, then, for Friday’s National Audit Office (NAO) report. The watchdog has unearthed a few hard statistics and demanded far greater official transparency. Prime minister Andy Burnham, in cost-of-living mode, should take note: trouble is brewing.

citation.title: The ‘great grid upgrade’ is off track – ministers should spell out the risks for bills

text:
The ‘great grid upgrade’ is off track – ministers should spell out the risks for bills

Of the 88 grid upgrade projects originally identified, 12 have already been completed (good news) and 12 have been subsumed into newer work (fair enough). But of the 56 deemed “essential” for meeting the government’s target of clean power by 2030, the NAO says 50 are “forecast to be delivered after their optimal date”. Of those, only 22 are forecast to be less than a year late; the rest are further behind schedule, with one put at between six and seven years behind. The “optimal” date, in this context, is the date required not only to fulfil the 2030 clean power deadline but also to keep a lid on the maddening “constraint costs” – payments to Scottish windfarms to turn off when the grid can’t handle their output, plus payments to southern gas-fired generators or interconnecters to France to start supplying electricity. On one windy day alone this week, such constraint payments reached £29m. The tally for the whole of 2026 is virtually guaranteed to top £2bn.

citation.title: The ‘great grid upgrade’ is off track – ministers should spell out the risks for bills

text:
The ‘great grid upgrade’ is off track – ministers should spell out the risks for bills

The big worry is that the upper end of Neso’s forecast for 2030 – a colossal £7.8bn, all going on bills – might be realised if the delays worsen. Related: Onshore windfarm applications hit 10-year high in England Therein lies the reason why a grid upgrade is needed in the first place: the transmission network suffered from a lack of investment, even before the switch to renewables started. The transition makes the work more urgent. But what is also revealed is a state failure, going back decades, to expand the grid to keep pace with additional generating capacity. The suspicion now is that the same mistake is being repeated. Many construction delays can be explained, it should be said. The NAO report cites standard stuff such as acquiring land rights, obtaining planning consents and legal challenges. But then there are procurement headaches caused by the need to wait for project‑specific signoff from Ofgem. There is also global competition for equipment as other countries expand their electricity networks.

citation.title: The ‘great grid upgrade’ is off track – ministers should spell out the risks for bills

text:
The ‘great grid upgrade’ is off track – ministers should spell out the risks for bills

According to the report, the government estimates that some kit has risen up to five times in price from 2022 levels, with delivery times becoming extended. In short, the whole thing is taking longer and costing more. But nailing down what it implies for that original £70bn figure, and thus bills, remains impossible. Nobody, it seems, is willing to put the numbers together. This passage from the NAO report is damning: “Publicly available information gives a partial and inconsistent view of progress towards upgrading the grid. Coverage is incomplete and key delivery risk metrics are missing. As a result, the available datasets cannot be reconciled with each other or the data we received from Ofgem, Neso and Desnz, and they do not give a clear view of overall portfolio delivery status.” The watchdog calls for Ofgem and Neso “to deliver critical projects on time and provide transparent reporting so parliament and the public can hold them to account”.

citation.title: The ‘great grid upgrade’ is off track – ministers should spell out the risks for bills

text:
The ‘great grid upgrade’ is off track – ministers should spell out the risks for bills

Related: More than half of clean energy schemes needed for Labour’s 2030 target offered grid connection On-time delivery may already be out of reach, but the demand for greater transparency is spot-on. Ofgem should publish medium-term forecasts for electricity bills, as this column has regularly argued, because the “network costs” element – what we’re talking about in this context – is capable of being forecast. Or it should take up the excellent idea from EDF, one of the big generators and retail suppliers, for “a live, publicly accessible tracker” to “radically increase transparency on cost and ongoing construction progress” and allow a strategic review. The political danger for the government is that, sometime around 2028, the delays and cost inflation will become impossible to ignore. Even some pro-renewables enthusiasts, who fully back the government’s stance that the upgrade is the only way to bring down electricity bills eventually, warn of a backlash if £70bn becomes a much larger number. Ministers should do themselves a favour: be open.

text:
Does Airtel Money mark the end of London’s listing drought? Not yet

A win is a win, but we should probably contain our excitement about the biggest flotation in London for five years. Airtel Money, a payments processor that operates in 13 African countries and should be worth between £6bn and £7bn, is a welcome addition to the stock market but it would be a stretch to say the event marks a definitive change in the weather to end the listings drought. Why? Because, in a sense, Airtel Money is already here. It is a 78%-owned subsidiary of Airtel Africa, an established FTSE 100 firm with a market value of £11.3bn ultimately controlled by Bharti Enterprises under the Indian billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal, also known for his 25% stake in BT. Related: London Stock Exchange to lose three more firms after takeover offers That means this was a home fixture for London in the competition with other venues. The Airtel/Bharti collective still had a look at the Middle East, the US and the rest of Europe, we’re told, but London will have started as a heavy favourite.

citation.title: Does Airtel Money mark the end of London’s listing drought? Not yet

text:
Does Airtel Money mark the end of London’s listing drought? Not yet

It is simply easier to spin off a subsidiary on a market where the parent is already known – and, indeed, a market where Airtel Africa was a top-performing Footsie stock last year. Ian Ferrao, the chief executive of Airtel Money, still made all the right noises to please exchange officials. London got the nod on account of its deep capital pools plus investors’ enthusiasm for fintech firms and their general understanding of African companies, he said. All true, but it’s also the case that it would have been simply odd to list Airtel Money on a different market to Airtel Africa. The latter is likely to remain the largest shareholder for years yet, and the two businesses are closely linked operationally. Airtel Money has grown out of Airtel Africa’s telecoms business, and one of its key growth opportunities is to persuade even more of the telephony customers to join the payments service. There are 75 million potential recruits to go at, on top of the established 53 million monthly active users, so there is a decent story to tell.

text:
Does Airtel Money mark the end of London’s listing drought? Not yet

It is one reason why the listing should go well, assuming the wider stock market environment remains calm. Airtel Money is capital-lite, converts a chunky proportion of its earnings into cash, carries the buzzy fintech vibe and is growing at about 20% a year. The cash-generative qualities mean no new equity is being raised, so it is really an opportunity for existing shareholders – including minority owners including TPG, ​Mastercard, the Qatar Investment Authority and Chimetech Holding – to cash in a few chips. As long as they don’t get greedy on price, it looks a relatively easy pitch for the promoters. For London, the listings game is really about winning a few high-profile names where the competition from overseas markets is tougher. The biggie remains Norway’s Visma, one of Europe’s biggest software companies. A listing was delayed earlier this year because of the so-called “Claude crash” – the sell-off in data-related sectors deemed to be under threat from AI tools – but private equity-backed Visma remains a top target given its valuation a year ago was put at almost €20bn (£17.2bn).

text:
Vistry is the laggard in a housebuilding sector full of cracks

The entire housebuilding sector is in a funk, grumbling about energy prices, the cost of labour, regulation, planning delays, taxes and more, but few have messed up a bad hand quite like Vistry. Three years ago this mashup of the Bovis, Linden and Countryside brands aspired to build 20,000 houses a year, and made itself the darling of the incoming Labour government by betting big on “affordable mixed-tenure housing” in partnership with councils, housing associations and institutional landlords. The City, too, fell for former executive chair Greg Fitzgerald’s promise that a “capital light” approach of pre-selling homes via a partnership model would yield oodles of cash. The share price doubled to almost £14 between October 2023 and August 2024. Fitzgerald departed in May after too many profit warnings and now, with the shares down to the bare foundations of 262p, it’s time for new chief executive Adam Daniels’ review of what happened. Short version: the logic of the partnership stuff wasn’t so silly, but the execution was horrible, especially in the south of England.

citation.title: Vistry is the laggard in a housebuilding sector full of cracks

text:
Vistry is the laggard in a housebuilding sector full of cracks

“The pace of change meant that the operating model, controls and culture did not scale consistently with the group’s volumes [of construction],” he said, a polite summary of a growth strategy gone awry. For good measure, a proportion of the land bank would not be acquired “under the investment approval criteria that will be applied in the future”, which read as a confession that Vistry simply overpaid for plots. The good news, of a sort, for shareholders is that the damage to the balance is not deemed so severe that fresh equity is required. Daniels’ prescription for recovery, however, is a long exercise in getting smaller and living with shrunken ambitions. The aim is to build 12,000 houses a year, rather than the 20,000-plus imagined by Fitzgerald. A greater proportion of those homes will be in the north of England. As for return on capital employed – a critical metric for housebuilders – the old idea was 40%. That’s been cut to 30%, and only by 2031.

citation.title: Vistry is the laggard in a housebuilding sector full of cracks

text:
Vistry is the laggard in a housebuilding sector full of cracks

It all sounds perfectly reasonable: keep things simple, fix the balance sheet by eating into the land bank, and concentrate on the parts of the country where market prices (which still matter for a mixed-tenure model) are holding up better. In Vistry’s favour is the fact that, for all its financial troubles, it’s still in the government’s good books. Burnham’s electricity grid idea is interesting – but it’s not ‘public control’

Did share prices shudder as Andy Burnham unveiled Great British Grid (GBG) as a public sector challenger to the trio of private sector firms that own and operate the electricity grid? Not exactly. National Grid and SSE, the two listed in London, were down by about 0.5%, in line with the wider market. That mild reaction looks correct. For all the talk of greater public control over the electricity grid, the prime minister is not threatening to nationalise anything or take control of any existing assets. As the detail of the energy department’s announcement made clear: “Great British Grid will complement, rather than replace, the existing institutions responsible for Britain’s energy system and the role of existing network operators remains unchanged.” Instead, GBG’s main role will be to put together competing bids for future transmission projects.

So, for example, rather than National Grid automatically getting the gig to build cables and pylons to bring offshore wind power from East Anglia to London, in future it could have to beat an offer from a consortium including GBG, probably in partnership with private sector construction firms and financiers. That prospect, however, is unlikely to alarm incumbent boardrooms because, to put it mildly, GBG will not arrive with terrifying sums of state money to blow everybody out of the water. GBG, said Burnham, will be “a branch” of Great British Energy (GBE) and, initially at least, will have to access its funding pot. That funding was £8.3bn for this parliament – and a chunk has already been raided to back small modular nuclear reactors. There is probably about £4bn left. If GBG gets half, we’re talking about £2bn of capital. For context, the grid upgrade in the 2026-31 cycle adds up to an investment programme of about £70bn, with much more to follow in the 2030s. Is GBG worth doing at all, then? Well, yes, it is.

Italy to place all 27 of its major cities on highest heat alert

Italy is to place all of its 27 major cities, from Trieste in the north to Palermo in the south, under the highest heat alert as the fourth heatwave to hit the country this summer intensifies. A red alert means there is a higher chance of an emergency owing to the health risk posed by prolonged extreme temperatures to the entire population. Twenty-five cities were on red alert on Wednesday, with two more to be added on Thursday, the health ministry said. It is the first time this year that all 27 cities monitored by the health ministry’s heat surveillance system have been placed on maximum alert. Related: Europe’s rivers are running dry, and the knock-on effects are disastrous | Yiannis Baboulias The cities on red alert are: Turin, Bolzano, Milan, Genoa, Venice, Verona, Trieste, Bologna, Florence, Perugia, Rome, Naples, Ancona, Pescara, Bari, Campobasso, Reggio Calabria, Palermo and Cagliari as well as Catania, Messina, Brescia, Viterbo, Latina, Rieti, Frosinone and Civitavecchia.

Australia’s new environmental protection agency approves coal project, angering climate groups

Australia’s new national agency for environmental protection has approved its first coal project, allowing a Queensland open-cut mine to keep digging until 2055 while clearing threatened woodland and koala habitat. The confirmation of the extension of the Saraji mine, which digs and exports coal for steel making, comes after the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, denied this week there was tension over Australia’s fossil fuel exports during talks with Pacific leaders. Flooding around the city of Malda in the Indian state of West Bengal since Thursday has had a devastating effect. The erosion formed a cliff edge on some of the beaches, along with exposing old asphalt, pipes and even pieces of an old pier. The flooding caused by the swell damaged homes and vehicles, as well as flooding streets, leaving behind a layer of sand.

Jumping beans: UK shoppers turn to legumes to save cash and improve diet

British shoppers are munching more beans, lentils, tofu and tempeh – while cutting back on real and plant-based fake meat – to save money and improve their diet. The amount of beans, pulses and soya bean derivatives sold in the UK increased by 7.3% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period last year, led by a rise in cheap dried lentils, an analysis has found. That was led by a 23% surge for cheap dried lentils, according to data from the market research firm NielsenIQ evaluated by the climate advocacy group Madre Brava. Shoppers turned to more upmarket legumes, including organic and jarred varieties, with sales of canned and jarred butter beans up by 30.3%. When he first arrived in his new home in a small village in the Italian Alps in March 2022, 15-year-old Denys* says he felt homesick and confused. He had been put on an overnight bus and relocated along with more than 100 other children from his orphanage in Berdiansk, in eastern Ukraine, which was one of the first areas to be invaded by Russian troops. “Ukraine was all I knew,” says Denys. “I had never left it my whole life.” But after he began going to school, making friends and integrating into Italian life, Denys says he no longer wanted to go back home. “I started to realise there was a different way of life I could be living,” he says. “One that didn’t involve airstrikes and poverty, and that could give me better opportunities for my future.” Thousands of Ukrainian social orphans – children given up to the state or taken away from parents considered unable to care for them – were evacuated overseas after Russia’s invasion in 2022. ‘In this new car, I feel patronised’: which driver assistance systems actually improve safety?

This new car I’m test-driving boasts all the latest bells and whistles – or, rather, beeps and bings. Peer sideways for too long checking traffic and the car emits an irritating sound. Should I take a hand off the wheel to scratch an ear, I’m admonished with a strident beep. When the car determines it’s too near a white line, it tugs the wheel against my hands and brakes as a car slows ahead. Its haptic “buttons” feel like fingers pressing back – as if an invisible presence has its hands and feet on the controls: a ghost in the machine I’m inside. Related: My rookie era: In my 30s, I went for my driver’s licence test – and failed four times Heading back to the caryard, a cryptic tone sounds. From the back seat, salesman Anthony says it’s the over-speed warning. We’re still on the 40km/h service road but the car “saw” the yard’s 5km/h speed-limit sign. Anthony advises disabling it on startup. “Most people leave it on, though,” he says. “Saves you getting done for speeding.” But Anthony has turned off the car’s fatigue-warning feature.

citation.title: ‘In this new car, I feel patronised’: which driver assistance systems actually improve safety?

text:
‘In this new car, I feel patronised’: which driver assistance systems actually improve safety?

The car doesn’t “know” me yet, so won’t detect if I’m tired anyway. “It doesn’t like sunglasses, either,” he says. I’ve read about some systems that are so crudely calibrated they’ll insistently demand you take a break by confusing energetic driving on a twisting mountain road with drunkenness or debility. Others declare you unfit to drive if you’ve had a cold or a rough night. You’ve already seen yourself in the bathroom mirror. Who needs a robot to rub it in? I last faced this kind of surveillance and intervention 50 years ago, seated beside a human driving instructor with dual controls overriding my own. I’m an experienced motorist but in this new car I feel patronised. Between the white lines, human. In this robot-on-wheels I’m no longer autonomous. And isn’t that supposed to be the inherent promise of the automobile? It used to be. But with freedom came much higher risk. Fifty years ago, cars were certainly more dangerous.

citation.title: ‘In this new car, I feel patronised’: which driver assistance systems actually improve safety?

text:
‘In this new car, I feel patronised’: which driver assistance systems actually improve safety?

Few 1970s cars had secondary safety features such as crumple zones, fewer still had primary (or active) safety aids such as lane-departure warning and autonomous braking. As driver, you were more or less in control of the car. There was no e-nanny on board to mitigate distraction or errancy. The result was an Australian road death-rate in 1975 of 26.6 deaths per 100,000 people. Today’s more crowded, complex and chaotic road network is paradoxically much safer, with an equivalent fatality rate in 2026 of 4.7. Mounting evidence suggests advanced driver-assistance systems (Adas) are one reason for this improvement. Monash University’s Accident Research Centre has identified distraction and drowsiness contributing to about 40% of crashes resulting in hospital visits in Victoria. Associate Prof Michael Fitzharris estimates that the introduction of Adas, including autonomous emergency braking (AEB), to Victoria’s passenger and light commercial fleet could prevent 40,000 serious traffic injuries over 30 years.

citation.title: ‘In this new car, I feel patronised’: which driver assistance systems actually improve safety?

text:
‘In this new car, I feel patronised’: which driver assistance systems actually improve safety?

“The findings make a compelling case for the rapid adoption of driver monitoring technology,” Fitzharris says. The federal government’s response has been to mandate lane-keeping assist technology and AEB on all passenger vehicles imported into Australia from 1 March 2029. (Ludicrously, the largest US monster utes are exempt.) But research and customer feedback have also identified problems with existing driver-assistance systems, including autonomous braking. I had cause to be sceptical about AEB in 2022 after renting a new four-wheel drive in central Australia. I was passing a slow vehicle turning right when my car suddenly braked hard on a bend, skidding in gravel towards a deep culvert. A moment later it computed there had been no danger anyway and released control back to me. I’d been briefly overruled by a machine, and could have been killed. After stopping to deactivate the active cruise control, I, the human, was back in charge.

text:
‘In this new car, I feel patronised’: which driver assistance systems actually improve safety?

The Australasian New Car Assessment Program (Ancap) has identified deficiencies with Adas, and in March announced new design protocols for driver-interface technology for the next three years. In cooperation with the European New Car Assessment Programme, Ancap will now penalise vehicles with intrusive, confusing or poorly calibrated safety systems. Ancap will also recommend the return of physical buttons or fixed areas on screens for key controls: horn, indicators, hazard lights, wipers and headlights. These changes acknowledge the danger of searching through complex screen menus while driving, and the absurdity of tech meant to reduce driver distraction but actually increasing it. Acknowledging criticism surrounding increasingly intrusive driver assistance technologies, Ancap’s chief executive, Carla Hoorweg, says the organisation’s updated guidance states that well-designed driver monitoring systems should support motorists, “not irritate them”.

text:

“Driver monitoring systems must demonstrate genuine capability to detect distraction and fatigue, and speed assistance systems must demonstrate both accuracy and meaningful driver engagement,” Hoorweg says. Such measures should encourage the evolution of today’s relatively crude interface platforms into sophisticated systems, including AI assistants more adept at relating to our species, and produce more self-driving, and potentially safer, cars. But could this advancing safety tech also create more bad drivers? Automotive engineers go to great lengths to isolate occupants from the road by reducing a vehicle’s NVH (noise, vibration and harshness). Most drivers value such designed detachment, along with electronic driver aids – particularly as commuting times increase and cars are increasingly used as mobile offices, infotainment platforms or salons (I recently saw a driver stopped at lights shaving his lathered head).

Related: Top album releases linked to rise in fatal crashes as ‘distracted’ drivers access music But tech that caters to these social changes can, in effect, discourage active, attentive driving and accommodate or even abet distraction. Doubts also persist about whether cosseted motorists will retain the skill levels of their unassisted peers. In a 2026 study, using a sample of 60 Australian drivers, researchers at the University of Delft concluded that use of Adas leads to the degradation of manual driving skills, with drivers showing increased risk-taking and decreased cognitive and physical engagement. The study also found that warning systems triggered varied adaptations, including dependence, warning fatigue and risk compensation, as drivers relied more on the car to drive for them. Acknowledging this potential, learner-driver Wil’s father disables his car’s Adas when teaching his son to drive. Wil, 29, says his father is concerned that relying too heavily on tech, at least initially, could result in his son becoming complacent.
