Wil is proud of being able to drive without Adas, and to be developing the awareness skills required to see the crucial “big picture” himself. Other new drivers, like 27-year-old Stephanie and her sister, prefer to leave their cars’ aids on. The siblings both learned to drive with Adas activated. Stephanie says lane-keeping assist helps her determine her car’s exterior dimensions and position it accurately. Another beginner driver, Sawyer, says she likes her car’s electronic aids: “Because they make me feel safe.” A clear generational divide is emerging as younger generations embrace the spread of digital culture – in this case, to the road – more readily than older drivers (like me). While accepting the raw safety statistics, I remain sceptical about the rise of robot cars. Who, after all, should we trust behind the wheel? Anonymous organic entities – our own species – or invisible electronic minders? Though driver-assistance features, including active autonomous braking, can still be deactivated in many cars, it’s telling that one brand calls its manual setting “classic cruise”.

Soon it may be “legacy cruise”, and only if a “no thanks” option remains at all. So I won’t be buying a new car yet. My decade-old vehicle has only two electronic aids, which I always leave on: tyre-pressure alert and blind-spot-monitoring (a boon for this old neck). For any future purchase, I’ll favour a car with minimal electronic intrusion, that allows disabling or at least muting, and with individual settings for multiple drivers that don’t need reconfiguring at each startup. Until then, I remain autonomously yours, a human at the wheel. And yes, you can trust me. I promise not to shave my head while driving.

From ticket booking fees to shrinkflation, six other ways Burnham could cut cost of living

Andy Burnham has announced he will ban fake discounts and make it easier to cancel unwanted subscriptions in an effort to improve life for UK consumers. In the long run, these so-called “everyday fixes” may not make as much difference to your wealth as increasing mandatory contributions on pensions or capping rents, but they will get rid of some day-to-day frustrations. Here are six other things he could fix while he is in the mood: Ban booking fees on tickets Buying a ticket for an event such as a gig or show doesn’t come with as many hidden costs as previously, thanks to consumer protection laws introduced last year. But the fact the fees are clearer does not make them all more palatable. In the days when you could choose to go to a box office, or between having your tickets posted or emailed, there may have been a justification for some of the add-ons to cover different costs for the promoter, but when there’s no choice, it sticks in the throat. Retailers do not charge “transaction” or “order processing fees”, so why can they still be slapped on tickets?

citation.title: From ticket booking fees to shrinkflation, six other ways Burnham could cut cost of living

text:
From ticket booking fees to shrinkflation, six other ways Burnham could cut cost of living

Stop direct debit hikes when your energy bill is in credit You pay your bill by direct debit and have been careful with your usage, so at the end of the winter, you are in credit – and then your provider tells you it wants to put up your monthly cost by £50. Of course, a rising price cap might mean you need to increase what you pay, but if you have already got a cushion, why should you hand over more? According to the regulator Ofgem, providers held a total of £3.2bn of customers’ money in the year to March, with the average household £135 in credit. Yet some households on fixed tariffs with large balances are still told that their supplier wants to increase their direct debit. Yes, you can refuse, but the onus is on you as a customer to make the effort. Providers could be banned from raising direct debits by more than the price change, or when customers have built up a surplus that covers a set percentage of their bills.

citation.title: From ticket booking fees to shrinkflation, six other ways Burnham could cut cost of living

text:
From ticket booking fees to shrinkflation, six other ways Burnham could cut cost of living

Cut sneaky shrinkflation We all know prices have been going up and sometimes a smaller pack for the same price is more welcome than having to shell out more, but when the cuts are sneaky, that’s bad for consumers. In France and Austria, there are rules designed to make it more obvious to shoppers when they are getting less product for the same – or sometimes even more – money. Demanding a simple “new pack size” message on products would at least alert people to the change and mean they are making informed decisions about what they are buying. Force companies to put a phone number on their homepage You’ve got a problem with a company and you want to get it sorted – and then you realise you cannot find a number for it anywhere. There are communications companies that have no “contact us” link anywhere to be seen, and energy companies that send you all round the houses looking for a way to get in touch. One of the recurring themes of Guardian Money readers’ problems is the struggle to find someone to help when something goes wrong.

citation.title: From ticket booking fees to shrinkflation, six other ways Burnham could cut cost of living

text:
From ticket booking fees to shrinkflation, six other ways Burnham could cut cost of living

Clearly, once you have published a phone number, you need staff at the other end answering the phone and offering some joined-up thinking, so this is only the start of the solution – but at least customers would not feel like companies were trying to hide from them. Bring forward plans to improve parking Fines for charging an electric car, debt notices that should never have been sent, fees when you have tried to pay and the app has let you down … Guardian Money has heard from readers encountering all of these things and more when simply entering a car park. The government has promised to sort it out: a code of practice was drawn up several years ago but was not introduced, and a new consultation on it ended last September. Meanwhile plans for a nationwide app that would bring together all of the different parking company apps, making it easier to pay while out and about, were watered down. Bringing forward and enforcing the planned code, so that drivers are not receiving bills for parking crimes they did not commit, would leave a welcome gap in the Guardian Money postbag.

From ticket booking fees to shrinkflation, six other ways Burnham could cut cost of living

Make insurers give you the best deal upfront A lot has been done to improve the experience of renewing your insurance policies. Insurers are supposed to offer existing customers as good a deal as they do new ones, and your renewal letter tells you how much you paid last year so that you can see if the cost has gone up. And yet the annual dance continues: if you don’t call your insurer and query an increase, shop around or threaten to leave, you will probably end up paying more than you need to. It is a system that still penalises those who stay put.

Tory tax break for banks has cost UK public purse £6bn, says TUC

Tax cuts for big banks have deprived the UK government of £6bn in revenues, according to campaigners, who are calling on the chancellor, John Healey, to increase taxes and force lenders to pay their “fair share” in the budget. Calculations by the Trades Union Congress (TUC), which represents unions with more than 5.3 million members across England and Wales, shows that the public purse is billions of pounds worse off as a result of tax cuts introduced under the Tory chancellor Jeremy Hunt in 2023. The then government agreed to slash the bank surcharge – an additional levy on lenders’ profits – from 8% to 3% that year. The move was meant to offset a rise in corporation tax from 19% to 25%, after the industry argued higher taxes would put them at a competitive disadvantage compared with other big financial centres such as New York. However, the cuts came just as lenders started reaping handsome earnings, thanks to rising interest rates. The UK’s four largest lenders – HSBC, NatWest, Barclays, Lloyds Banking Group – have now generated £200bn in pre-tax profits over the past five years.

citation.title: Tory tax break for banks has cost UK public purse £6bn, says TUC

text:
Tory tax break for banks has cost UK public purse £6bn, says TUC

The TUC says the 2023 cuts ultimately robbed the UK purse of tax revenues. Its analysis of HMRC corporate tax receipts shows the UK public lost out £2.3bn in 2023-24, a further £1.7bn in 2024-25, and £2bn in 2025-26 – totalling £6bn over three years. With banks pocketing record profits, the TUC said the surcharge should now be increased beyond its pre-2023 level at the 28 October budget. That could raise up to £60bn, which could be used to cover rising household bills as part of prime minister Andy Burnham’s drive to tackle the cost of living. “The Tories’ tax break for banks has cost the UK public purse £6bn and counting. It’s time to end it and to make sure banks pay their fair share,” the TUC’s general secretary, Paul Nowak, said. “At a time when families are struggling with soaring energy costs, taxing banks’ booming profits to cut bills is just plain common sense. There is a mountain of evidence to suggest that banks can afford to pay more tax – not least the record £25bn bonus pool they paid out last year.

text:
Labour is still searching for an energy fix for a new world

Amid the myriad of small measures, virtually everything in John Healey’s budget came back to the cost of energy. The higher energy prices that have resulted from the Iran war have pushed up inflation, are eating into households’ incomes, are a drag on businesses – and are the main reason why the forecast for GDP growth next year was cut from 1.6% to just 1%. And energy was the focus of Healey’s sole surprise in his consumer-facing policies – the £100 payment to 20m households in A-D council tax bands to help with fuel bills this winter. It will be funded, in effect, by tapping the banks for a few quid for 15 months via the bank surcharge. But the chancellor will know that £100 won’t look generous when the bills land. Gas prices are still rising, and leading supplier EDF’s latest prediction is that the regulator’s price cap will be hiked by £466 in January, pushing the annual rate for an average household to £2,189. When Labour took office in July 2024, talking naively about taking £300 off bills over the life of the parliament, the cap was £1,568. No surprise, then, that the messaging on energy is shifting.

citation.title: Labour is still searching for an energy fix for a new world

text:
Labour is still searching for an energy fix for a new world

Here is the passage in Healey’s speech that hinted at big changes ahead: “Today I’m setting a new course on energy: to get UK energy costs down in line with Europe. From this point, our Labour government’s priority is first and foremost cheaper energy, with clean power key to achieving this.” Interactive Thank goodness for the reset towards affordability. It is long overdue. The biggest impediment to economic growth, including the prime minister’s longed-for “reindustrialisation”, is the cost of energy in the UK. There is little Healey can do about international gas prices, but he can do “deep reform of our energy system”, as he put it. So what’s the plan? That, unfortunately, is where the “new course” turned blurry. Take the promise to introduce “a new cost control framework to drive down all aspects of energy bills”. The ambition is laudable, because energy bills have become littered with levies and charges – everything from socialising unpaid consumer energy debt to funding Sizewell C – that should more naturally be funded from general taxation. It’s about time the Treasury took an interest in such hidden taxes.

citation.title: Labour is still searching for an energy fix for a new world

text:
Labour is still searching for an energy fix for a new world

But the costs don’t disappear just because they are placed within a new framework. The tough question is how much a chancellor is willing to fund from Treasury coffers in the interest of lower upfront bills for consumers and business. It is not a small question, because wide-ranging definitions of levies can produce figures as high as £15bn. It’s good that Healey is demanding no new levies (unless they bring down bills), but that’s not the same as hacking into the existing thicket. Funding for green hydrogen projects is being taken on by the Treasury, which is a start. But come back in next year’s spending review, it seems, to discover the size of Healey’s scythe. More urgency is needed. There was a bit more clarity on the electricity generation side. “This government will only buy and build new projects when they lower bills and when they can connect to the grid,” said Healey. That reads as a strong hint that offshore wind commissions will be slowed until prices fall (which probably requires a fall in borrowing costs for developers) and the upgrade of the grid is more advanced.

citation.title: Labour is still searching for an energy fix for a new world

text:
Labour is still searching for an energy fix for a new world

Very sensible: sequencing matters, as the alarming costs of “wasted wind” demonstrate regularly. But Healey’s ambition to “break the grip of international gas prices” by switching older renewables projects on to lower fixed-price contracts is not new. Ed Miliband, when energy secretary, said the same. The test is how hard ministers are willing to twist the arms of renewables owners, who are very attached to arrangements that give them jackpot revenues when gas prices are high. The basic tension remains: for consumers to win, somebody has to be paid less than they were expecting. So, yes, one can applaud the change of tone and direction. A reset in energy policy to prioritise affordability was bound to arrive eventually. The drive to clean power also had to be a drive to cheap power. But one cannot yet say the new approach is joined-up. Policies to drive the electrification of homes and transport were not turbo-charged, which they need to be to reduce long-term dependency on gas and oil. And “deep reforms” to the electricity market are, to put it gently, a work in progress. More urgency needed.

‘I reside in Monaco’: billionaire said to have quit UK over potential wealth tax had already left

When the Sunday Times broke the news that David Reuben, one of the richest men in the UK, had apparently fled to the tax haven of Monaco, there was much pearl clutching. Reuben had moved from his Holland Park house in London to live full-time in the principality. Labour’s tax regime was blamed and there were said to be fears there would be a cascading effect across the economy, with wealth draining from the UK. text:
Why Andy Burnham’s devolution pledge will be tricky to deliver

On the road to Downing Street, Andy Burnham promised to transfer power from Westminster to every postcode in the country. After his first two weeks in office, the size and complexity of this project are becoming clearer. With a date set for the autumn budget, the work of filling in the detail that will underpin his devolution plans begins – starting with his proposal to hand England’s regional mayors a share of income tax to support local economic development. Despite its history as a patchwork of nations, the UK is among the most fiscally centralised countries in the developed world. The Centre for Cities estimates as little as 5% of tax revenue currently stays with mayors and local authorities. The rest goes straight to Whitehall and is allocated by central government. By contrast, 14% of tax stays local in France, and 22% in Japan. For years British devolution has been a messy patchwork in which Westminster has largely clung on to its position as ringmaster; just ask the parties pushing for independence in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. But the system in England is the messiest of the lot.

citation.title: Why Andy Burnham’s devolution pledge will be tricky to deliver

text:
Why Andy Burnham’s devolution pledge will be tricky to deliver

Successive governments have followed a piecemeal approach. Under the Conservatives, the creation of dozens of ringfenced funding pots fostered a begging-bowl culture. They were also no match for the billions of pounds in central government grant funding cut under austerity. Burnham allowing mayors to retain a share of locally generated tax revenues is, therefore, a good idea in principle. Many economists say the idea – first announced by Rachel Reeves earlier this year – would help to tackle Britain’s deep regional inequalities. In practice, the Institute for Fiscal Studies estimates that between 6% and 9% of local income tax revenues would be sufficient to fully replace the so-called integrated settlements, or central government grants, the mayoral authorities currently receive. But it will take time to introduce the plan and there are wrinkles to iron-out – not least how to avoid weaker local economies falling behind. The danger is the current fastest-growing mayoral authorities are typically the country’s wealthiest.

If the winners get to keep a rising share of income tax, the laggards would risk a self-fulfilling cycle of weak growth; limited scope for investment, and yet weaker growth. The reforms will also take a long time to bear fruit for a prime minister in a hurry. It will be 2028 before the income tax plan comes into full effect. Dozens of new mayoralties are also still in the process of being created – with a deadline of the end of that year to give people in places including Essex, Stoke-on-Trent and Warrington similar powers to the trailblazing mayoralties of London and Manchester. Last month the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development gave devolution a ringing endorsement. But it also warned that the starting point in Britain makes it challenging. First and foremost will be the challenge of repairing the damage caused by the Tory austerity years. English local government is a shadow of its pre-2010 self. Most places lack the staff and expertise to use their new money and powers well, at a time when many are struggling to do the basics such as collecting bins or filling potholes. Across England’s town halls, the workforce has plunged since 2009 from 2.2 million to about 1.1 million. While Greater Manchester and the West Midlands have established sophisticated analytical, policy and delivery teams – enabling them to make better use of the devolved powers – the OECD says many authorities have a shortage of resources and have limited technical expertise. The risk of making bad spending decisions is high. The shenanigans in Tees Valley, Birmingham, and the multibillion-pound debts amassed in Woking, Warrington and Thurrock are a serious red flag. Devolution plans strengthen case for written UK constitution, says Burnham

Andy Burnham has said his programme of devolution strengthens the case for a written constitution for the UK, a move that would fundamentally alter the workings of the state that have developed over centuries. The prime minister has long believed the UK’s “antiquated” political system needs a dramatic overhaul if opportunity is to be shared equally across the country. The UK is one of only a few major democracies without a written constitution, a document that codifies how a nation is governed within a set of fundamental rules. In a potentially historic shift, Burnham said this weekend that his government’s programme of decentralisation – which includes giving regional leaders much greater control over their finances – strengthens the argument for a codified arrangement. “It will increase the case for a constitution because Britain is changing through this, England is certainly changing through this,” he said. Burnham said the UK needed to devise a codified model of devolution that works for Wales, Scotland, Northern Ireland and the English regions.

The Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, whose summer has been dominated by the Guardian’s disclosure of a £5m undeclared gift and his connections with a fraudster, emerged on Monday to claim that his party would launch the “largest military operation in the English Channel since world war two” to prevent small boat crossings. Pointing to unrest at the Spain-Morocco border, he said the Royal Navy would be sent to the Channel to intercept all dinghies carrying asylum seekers should his party win power at the next general election. Politics Weekly Under so-called Operation Fortress, migrants would be detained and given food and water before being returned “under escort” on naval vessels to France or Belgium. But sceptics have questioned whether the plans would work. What would the Royal Navy be asked to do? Reform’s policy document indicates that navy offshore patrol vessels (OPVs), instead of the Border Force’s fleet of five cutters and six patrol ships, would “close on and shadow” dinghies in the Channel.

Three OPVs, each nearly 80 metres (262ft) long, are deployed around the UK, though they are due to be decommissioned in 2028 and may be sold to Uruguay. One, HMS Tyne, is currently shadowing a Russian frigate, the Neustrashimy, in the North Sea with a French corvette. An alternative, said Tom Sharpe, a former navy commander, would be to deploy a frigate, though he said it would be “an incredible waste of a military asset, to do a Border Force or ferrying job with a specialist warship”. What does the Royal Navy think? A master of any ship is taught they have a duty “to render assistance” to any person in danger of being lost at sea, and to proceed “with all possible speed” to those in distress, as spelled out in article 98 of the UN convention on the law on the sea, the foundation of maritime law. Though each incident will be different, Reform envisages that Royal Marines on inflatables would approach what are often packed dinghies to pick up those onboard – though refugees and migrants may not be compliant as they are likely to fear arrest.

Rupert Lowe’s ‘olive branch’ to Farage piles more pressure on Reform leader

Even by the standards of their rivalry, the speed at which Rupert Lowe’s olive branch to Nigel Farage morphed into fresh recriminations between the two was swift. It began with a softly lit 12-minute video posted on Sunday by the Restore Britain leader, looking straight to camera and referring to “Nigel” as he suggested his party could be willing to cast aside its differences with Reform UK and work together. Despite being suspended by Reform in March 2025, and going on to start his own party to chip away at Farage’s vote, Lowe said the two men should put “personalities and our past disagreements aside for the good of the country”. But Farage did not appear to be tempted. Speaking at a press conference on Monday, he in effect accused Lowe of bad faith, wondering aloud about the circumstances of the “offer” and accusing him of “screaming” and “threatening” colleagues when he was in the party ranks. By midday, Lowe had accused Farage of lying when he said he had been in touch with the Restore leader. But Lowe posted a screenshot of a curt “will call later” message from Farage on social media.

Whatever the truth, the exchanges are a reminder of how Restore has emerged as a very real obstacle in Farage’s road to Downing Street. Lowe’s offer to work together came after Restore finished fourth in the Greater Manchester mayoral election, ahead of the Liberal Democrats and Tories – a relatively impressive feat for an electoral startup only months old. The party also finished third in the Makerfield byelection, the strongest Westminster electoral performance since at least 2010 by a party that has not only endorsed explicitly far-right positions but welcomed far-right activists into its ranks. Many of its policy positions – a referendum on the death penalty, bans on halal and kosher slaughter and a deportation policy informed by an ethnonationalist view of British identity – make any deal with Restore almost impossible for Reform if the latter is going to broaden its base. That’s even aside from Lowe’s other demand: that the former Tory ministers in Reform’s ranks – such as Robert Jenrick – are denied a place in any Reform government.

Karen Newman, vice-president of the Board of Deputies of British Jews, told HuffPost: “It beggars belief that any party would select as a candidate a multiply convicted felon and the founder of a far-right group called National British Resistance.” “We have contacted the Conservative party to set out our concerns and call on them to rescind his selection and review their vetting processes.” Bonehill-Paine re-emerged in recent years as the creator of the Crewkerne Gazette, a satirical online account, and has a conviction for assaulting a police officer and burglary of a police station. He was convicted in 2014 of malicious communications over an anti-Islam hoax that led to death threats against the owners of a pub in Leicester. He was jailed in 2015 for more than three years after posting antisemitic material online ahead of a planned neo-Nazi rally. In 2016, he was found guilty of racially aggravated harassment of Berger, who is Jewish. The abuse directed at her was cited by the Jewish Labour Movement, which described Bonehill-Paine’s selection by the Tories as “appalling”.

text:
Labour members ‘have tougher view on welfare than you might think’, poll suggests

Andy Burnham has inherited a Labour membership that is sceptical about increased welfare spending, supportive of higher defence spending, and ranks the climate crisis as one of the country’s biggest challenges, according to new polling. The survey of 788 members between the end of June and the end of July shows them ranking health (43%), the economy (42%), cost of living (39%) and climate change (29%) as Britain’s most important issues, ahead of welfare benefits (7%) and immigration (6%). Related: Why we should support welfare spending Despite the internal rows within the parliamentary Labour party (PLP) on welfare spending and general public pushback, 47% of members surveyed by ThinkLabour believe the government is spending too much on welfare, compared with 21% who believe it does not spend enough. When asked whether they would prefer the government to fund its current welfare bill differently, 52% said taxes should be raised. Additionally, 70% of Labour members said only high earners should be taxed while 24% supported higher taxes on everyone to fund the current bill.

citation.title: Labour members ‘have tougher view on welfare than you might think’, poll suggests

text:
Labour members ‘have tougher view on welfare than you might think’, poll suggests

The survey reveals members overwhelmingly backed more spending on social care, with 73% saying the government should spend more on this through higher taxes, either on higher earners alone or through general taxation. It found 68% of members wanted Britain to spend more on defence, and among the supporters for higher defence spending, 61% backed paying for this through higher taxes. Three-quarters of Labour’s members said they had backed Keir Starmer in the 2020 party leadership contest. The survey did not ask members about Burnham’s leadership. However, a poll conducted just before Starmer’s disastrous local elections performance revealed Burnham had a net favourability of 72% among members at that time, suggesting he would be likely to win any leadership contest he could have fought in. Burnham won the leadership unopposed within the PLP so a vote from party members was not required. The data is likely to be watched by those in government and it is understood these findings have been shared with senior strategists in Downing Street.

ThinkLabour, formerly known as Labour Together, has become increasingly linked to Burnham’s premiership. The former CEO Alison Phillips recently left the thinktank to become the prime minister’s deputy chief of staff, alongside the former director of devolution JP Spencer, who is now working in No 10 North. Ed Owen, a former Labour adviser during the Blair administration, is the interim CEO. Christabel Cooper, ThinkLabour’s interim director of political strategy, said: “Labour members have a tougher view on welfare than you might think. They will be aware that welfare is something the Labour government has to get right if it is going to win a second term. And they also understand the importance of defence in a deeply uncertain world. “That’s why it’s important to understand what members actually say rather than just rely on assumptions about what they might think.” The survey, led by Cooper, comes after the organisation released a report titled Who is Labour For?

text:
Prisoner early release scheme gives Burnham his first taste of unpopularity

If Andy Burnham wanted to demonstrate he was the anti-Keir Starmer, the first fortnight could not have gone better. Instead of painting a gloomy picture of tough times and an economic black hole that would only improve with sacrifices such as cutting winter fuel allowance, Burnham’s first week was a blitz of small wins including cutting bus fares. But the new prime minister can only control so much. And like Starmer, within his first days in office he found himself facing immediate decisions where every call will make you unpopular. And – like Starmer – blaming your predecessor counts for nothing with an angry public. On Monday, the first day of the prime minister’s planned holiday with his family, the call had to be made on the early release of prisoners to stop the prison system becoming overwhelmed. Burnham excluded those convicted of rape, serious child sexual offences and grooming from the scheme. But some killers – including two who were convicted of the manslaughter of PC Andrew Harper – will be eligible.

citation.title: Prisoner early release scheme gives Burnham his first taste of unpopularity

text:
Prisoner early release scheme gives Burnham his first taste of unpopularity

In an article for the Telegraph, where frustration seeped from every syllable, Burnham admitted he had not wanted to take that decision and had hoped to find a way to stop even more convicts from being released early, some just a third into their sentences. “The truth is I wanted to go even further … I have pushed to the very limits of what is possible to do,” he said. Unlike the situation that Starmer and the then justice secretary, Shabana Mahmood, faced, this was not quite the emergency early release that was needed in 2024 because prison capacity was at crisis level. Interactive The government cannot in this case escape that this was the culmination of months of planning and legislation. This was the designed effect of the Sentencing Act, which was due to come into effect in September, a more managed way to avert the same issue. But whichever way you look at it, releasing killers, abusers and sex offenders early will always have a high human cost.

citation.title: Prisoner early release scheme gives Burnham his first taste of unpopularity

text:
Prisoner early release scheme gives Burnham his first taste of unpopularity

Ministers who were in Starmer’s first cabinet still talk with fury about the situation they inherited from the Conservatives in the summer of 2024, when just a handful of prison places were available in some regions before police would have had to stop making arrests. Mahmood in particular was scarred by the experience of the summer riots following the Southport murders, when prison capacity threatened the state’s ability to arrest the brawlers. But the careful planning of this managed early release – while the state builds more prison capacity – met the reality of the human impact over the summer as letters began to land from victims and families, including Harper’s widow, about the early release of perpetrators. Interactive Burnham paused the scheme when he entered office as criticism mounted – but he could not avoid the decision for ever. Even with the exclusion of sex offenders, he will please few with the choice to proceed and is likely to have to revisit the issue in the coming months if prisons start to reach crisis capacity again.

citation.title: Prisoner early release scheme gives Burnham his first taste of unpopularity

text:
Prisoner early release scheme gives Burnham his first taste of unpopularity

In his article, Burnham made clear the impossible choice he had faced, one which might give him more sympathy for his deposed predecessor. “I know I can look people in the eye and say to them there is nothing more I could have asked for without risking the prison system collapsing within months,” he wrote. There will be more of those big calls coming down the tracks where decisions will probably please no one and potentially inflame the parliamentary party – the immigration bill, welfare, Send changes, the war with Iran, the Palestine Action ban, North Sea oil and gas. The true test of enduring popularity will be how he navigates those hardest days rather than the sugar rush of his first fortnight.

citation.title: Prisoner early release scheme gives Burnham his first taste of unpopularity

Andy Burnham reveals wife’s reaction to third Labour leadership bid

Andy Burnham has revealed his wife’s dismayed reaction when he told her he wanted to make another attempt at becoming Labour leader. Burnham said that his wife, Marie-France van Heel, had been surprised by his decision to run, having lost contests in 2010 and 2015 to Ed Miliband and Jeremy Corbyn respectively. “She was like: ‘Not again; they’ve told you twice they don’t want you,’” Burnham told Elizabeth Day on the How to Fail podcast. “She took some persuading to be honest, because I guess she didn’t want to see me go through it all again and then end up the wrong side at the end of it, but she gives me good advice,” he added. Burnham recalled being an MP in his early 30s and thinking he had done well in interviews, only to find a text message from his wife that said, in capital letters: “ANSWER THE F***ING QUESTION.” “That’s the kind of feedback I’ve had from her,” Burnham said.

“She’s quite forthright, she’s Dutch and they don’t hold back, they’re pretty plain speaking and I’ve been on the receiving end of a lot of that over the years.” Burnham said his failed leadership bids made him “a much better politician” in the end and that losing in 2015, standing to be the mayor of Greater Manchester and challenging himself “really strengthened” him. Last week, Burnham promised to work collaboratively with other parties to find a lasting solution to social care. He told Day: “I feel that my generation of politicians is guilty of a shameful dereliction of duty, political cowardice of the worst kind in saying that this issue is too difficult and we’re not going to touch it. “In fact, social care has gone backwards and doesn’t that just say something how politics has really fallen?

It has to be radical, we’d have never created the NHS if we weren’t radical as a country at times.” The prime minister said there was a need for radicalism in politics now “given where we are”, adding that neoliberalism and trickle-down economics had not been kind to a lot of places across Britain, particularly former industrial hubs. “Sometimes in politics you have to say: ‘I’m going to break out of the consensus and start talking about those things in a different way’, and it’s what I’ve started to do,” he added.

Kemi Badenoch gives former neo-Nazi advisory role after he withdraws as Tory candidate

A former neo-Nazi activist who was convicted of harassing a Jewish MP has withdrawn as a Conservative election candidate after Kemi Badenoch offered him a role as an adviser to the party. Joshua Bonehill-Paine said on Wednesday that he had withdrawn from next year’s local elections, and that the Conservative leader had instead asked him to become an adviser to the party’s culture and integration commission, where he will specifically focus on how young men become radicalised. Badenoch, who has come under pressure in the last 48 hours from individuals and organisations including the Board of Deputies of British Jews, said she was “sad” that Bonehill-Paine felt he “won’t be given the space to explain his position and represent his community”. However, the handing of a plum job to him was immediately condemned by others including Luciana Berger, a Labour member of the House of Lords who was the target of a campaign of abuse by Bonehill-Paine when she was an MP.

“The decision to welcome this individual as an adviser to the Leader of the Opposition is no better than allowing him to stand as a council candidate,” she said on X. “It is a privileged and influential national role. As a victim of this man’s heinous crimes this appointment is an insult.” Both the Board of Deputies and the Jewish Leadership Council (JLC) had turned down the Tory party’s offer of a meeting with the former neo-Nazi, who previously described himself as a “nationalist, fascist, theorist and supporter of white rights” and re-emerged in recent years as the creator of the Crewkerne Gazette, a satirical online account. text:
If English devolution is to be a success, it must be done right

Devolution has become the flavour of the month (The Guardian view on England’s centralised state: Andy Burnham must unbundle it, 31 July). The case is well argued and the need for such reform fits neatly into the situation we find in the Tees Valley – chronic underinvestment, lack of economic growth, depopulation, and so on. But the Tees Valley has had a devolved authority for 10 years and the benefits of devolution have not landed. The Tees Valley authority was issued a best value notice in April 2025, though there’s nothing to show for it. The new-age proponents of devolution, by ignoring how Tees Valley became its basket case, are missing something vital. Devolution is discussed in economic terms in relation to the regions, and as political upheaval in relation to Westminster and the Treasury. What’s missing is acknowledgment of the political upheaval that it brings to the regions, and it is the weakness of that that the Tees Valley exemplifies. The mayor is the sole elected person in the authority. Leaders of local councils form the authority cabinet but do so in addition to their day jobs. Does the public know?

citation.title: If English devolution is to be a success, it must be done right

text:
If English devolution is to be a success, it must be done right

No, because the only combined authority news in the local press comes from the authority’s own press releases. It’s not hard to find people on Teesside who believe that there’s been a jobs bonanza here. But the problem of political weakness within the authority remains. Devolution cannot succeed until this problem is addressed. Scott Hunter Editor, Tees Valley Monitor • Andy Burnham is right to argue that England’s regions cannot deliver meaningful growth while power remains concentrated in Whitehall. Yet his intervention points to a deeper constitutional problem. England is being offered a form of devolution that remains inferior to the statutory settlements enjoyed by Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. While those nations have defined legislative frameworks setting out their powers and responsibilities, England’s regions remain dependent on piecemeal deals negotiated with central government. Burnham’s admiration for Germany’s postwar Grundgesetz (Basic Law) is therefore well placed.

citation.title: If English devolution is to be a success, it must be done right

text:
If English devolution is to be a success, it must be done right

The law not only defines the relationship between federal and state governments but also commits the federation to equivalent living conditions across the country. It offers constitutional clarity, stability and fairness. England has no comparable settlement. Instead, its uncodified constitutional arrangements allow power to remain concentrated in Westminster, leaving regional government dependent on the centre for permission, funding and direction. If England is serious about rebalancing its economy, constitutional reform cannot stop at creating metro mayors or devolving selected powers. It requires a coherent constitutional settlement that places England’s regions on a secure and equal footing, replacing ad hoc devolution with a durable framework that disperses power by right rather than by ministerial discretion. John Hall Alliance for Yorkshire • If devolution is to mean anything real at all, then actual power must be devolved, which would mean it sometimes being used for purposes some would not approve of.

citation.title: If English devolution is to be a success, it must be done right

text:
If English devolution is to be a success, it must be done right

Your editorial was arguing for devolution only for your approved purposes (transport, skills and industry, not tax giveaways). Devolution for me but not for thee? Richard Dowling Leighton Buzzard, Bedfordshire • Regarding the article (Devolution plans strengthen case for written UK constitution, says Burnham, 2 August), we should note that the argument about inequality doesn’t hold when we regard countries with inequality just as great as ours (if not worse), which have written constitutions, such as the United States and South Africa. Regional devolution, or a written constitution, are not panaceas, because any system can only work as well as the humans operating it. If we are to have a written constitution, it might be well to make it as brief as possible, concentrating on principles rather than specific rules, so as to preserve the ability of the government to act nimbly when required, especially in crises. One possible useful ingredient might be a rotating “citizens’ jury” within the Lords for handling complex or difficult issues, with the usual peers serving as expert consultors.

Badenoch defends decision to allow man jailed for antisemitism to stand as councillor

Kemi Badenoch has defended her party’s decision to allow a former neo-Nazi who was jailed for subjecting a prominent Labour politician to antisemitic abuse to stand as a councillor. Badenoch said her party was not giving Joshua Bonehill-Paine, who is standing for election in Somerset, a “national platform”. “This man is showing that he’s more than contrite, he’s actually working training Prevent officers, speaking in universities and schools,” Badenoch told BBC’s Radio 4 Today programme. “I am extremely worried about antisemitism and what I feel is that if we can’t have the people who have previously been radicalised, who understand what went wrong and are part of the fight against antisemitism now, if we’re saying: ‘No, no, no, you’re untouchable,’ then how can we pretend that we believe in rehabilitation? “I’m someone who’s quite sceptical about rehabilitation and I see this man as somebody who has been rehabilitated.” Luciana Berger, who was targeted by Bonehill-Paine in a campaign of antisemitic abusein 2016, said he fell short of the bar for standing for public office.

text:
Catholic or not, many of us share Andy Burnham’s beliefs

Julian Coman’s article about Andy Burnham resonated with me, as I share his belief in compassion, social responsibility and concern for those who are struggling (Like Burnham, I was an altar boy. His Catholic upbringing is shaping the way he governs, 1 August). Where I differ is in the suggestion that these values are rooted primarily in Catholicism. I grew up in inner-city Manchester during the Thatcher years, in a low socioeconomic working-class community facing unemployment, poverty and drug misuse. My parents were not religious, but they instilled in me a humanist outlook based on empathy, fairness and our shared responsibilities to one another. The same values were reinforced at my primary school. In a diverse inner-city neighbourhood, children from different backgrounds learned side by side. Looking back, religion barely featured in our day-to-day lives at school. Faith was generally considered a private matter. What united us was a simple understanding that everyone deserved respect, fairness and kindness.

citation.title: Catholic or not, many of us share Andy Burnham’s beliefs

text:
Catholic or not, many of us share Andy Burnham’s beliefs

We learned to see one another not as representatives of different beliefs, but as fellow human beings with a shared stake in our community and society. It was an inclusive environment that left me comfortable and confident in Britain as a diverse society. Through our families, teachers and local community, we came to appreciate the secular institutions that bound us together: the NHS, social housing and the welfare state. Children whose families had lived here for generations learned alongside those whose families had arrived more recently, but there was a shared understanding that these institutions represented something valuable, something to be respected, strengthened and improved. Civic responsibility, inclusivity and social justice were not religious lessons; they were human lessons. Those values shaped me, too, but they came from a secular humanist upbringing, my community, and Britain’s civic institutions. The compassion that Coman admires in Burnham may well have been strengthened by his Catholic upbringing, but compassion, solidarity and social responsibility are not the preserve of any one faith or worldview.

citation.title: Catholic or not, many of us share Andy Burnham’s beliefs

text:
Catholic or not, many of us share Andy Burnham’s beliefs

If there is a moral tradition worth celebrating, it’s the broader human one: the belief that we flourish not alone, but through our obligations to one another, regardless of faith. Lorna Peters Manchester • Julian Coman’s article was encouraging. The faith communities I know are all deeply involved in politics, justice, homelessness work and much more. At a recent local Labour party meeting, there were two Methodists (I was one), several Catholics and a couple of Quakers. Coman mentions the Methodist worldview that Margaret Thatcher inherited from her father. But Mrs Thatcher didn’t know her Methodist roots. Our founder, John Wesley, said: “The gospel of Christ knows of no religion, but social; no holiness but social holiness.” So when she said “there is no such thing as society”, she was denying her Methodist roots. Much worse, though, was that she was wrong and set in train the rise of individualism. Rev Richard Parkes Newcastle-under-Lyme, Staffordshire • Julian Coman has it pretty much spot-on. “The problem with Christianity is that no one has ever really tried it,” as my wise mother, Peggy Brown, always said.

citation.title: Catholic or not, many of us share Andy Burnham’s beliefs

Catholic or not, many of us share Andy Burnham’s beliefs

While I continue to disappoint myself in that regard, perhaps Andy Burnham will succeed in being the first to preserve integrity and hope in the fire of political separatism and selfishness. John Brown Hartford, Cheshire • Andy Burnham is Britain’s first lifelong Roman Catholic prime minister. Tony Blair converted to Catholicism when he left office and Boris Johnson, though baptised a Catholic as a baby, converted to Anglicanism at a later stage in his life. For hundreds of years – after the Protestant Reformation in the 16th century, until the Repeal of the Penal Laws in the early 19th century – Roman Catholics in Britain were stripped of economic, political and religious power. They could not hold civil or military office. They could not get educated, vote or practice a profession. Until 2013, a British royal could not marry a Catholic and, in fact, the monarch today still cannot be a Catholic. But now, in 2026, we have a Catholic prime minister, who has said his Catholic upbringing means a lot to him.

If this upbringing is shaping the way he is governing, we might see a focus on the common good and the influence of the social teachings of the Catholic church, including the need to put the poor and vulnerable first, the dignity of the human person, the dignity of work, the worker and the rights of workers, the call to the family and community, the work towards peace and solidarity in the world, and the care for the stewardship of God’s creation. Let us wish Andy Burnham luck in his endeavour to create a just and equitable society. Julia O’Shea Kilcummin, County Kerry, Ireland • The final letter above was amended on 9 August 2026. Questioning Lowe, the MP for Great Yarmouth, over his claims that “white Britons will become a minority by 2063”, the presenter, Nick Robinson, noted that the forecast Lowe referred to defined a “white Briton” as someone whose parents were both born in the UK. With the king’s late father, Prince Philip, having been born on the Greek island of Corfu, Robinson asked Lowe: “Are you aware that, by the definitions used in that particular report, King Charles is not a white Briton? Kemi Badenoch’s weird week: defence of ex-neo-Nazi raises questions over Tory direction

There was a moment in the middle of this week when a news alert raised eyebrows among the politically committed. It read: “Kemi Badenoch: Former neo-Nazi candidate would just be sorting out bins.” It was a collection of words that might prompt palpitations in the most sanguine of communications professionals, followed by panicked advice that retreat was necessary. But as a deeply weird week for the Conservative party came to a close on Friday, its leader appeared adamant she would hold the line. With Badenoch accused of aping Reform UK on policy and purging centrists from her party in recent weeks, her decision to stand by a man who was jailed after creating sexualised images of a Jewish MP and calling her a “rodent” has prompted concerns about the leader of the opposition’s political antennae and the Tories’ wider strategy. On Monday it emerged that Joshua Bonehill-Paine, a former neo-Nazi activist convicted of the sexist and antisemitic harassment of the Labour peer Luciana Berger, had been selected as a Conservative candidate for a local election in Somerset.

Nicola Sturgeon ‘has not spoken to’ estranged husband, Peter Murrell, since he was jailed

Nicola Surgeon has said she will not visit her estranged husband, Peter Murrell, in prison, has stopped speaking to him and views herself as a “mug” for worrying about his wellbeing and mental health earlier this year. During a podcast recording at the Edinburgh festival fringe, Scotland’s former first minister said Murrell had lied to her until the day he pleaded guilty to embezzling more than £400,000 from the Scottish National party. He was imprisoned for five years in June, and Sturgeon revealed she had not spoken to him since then. She told the broadcaster Iain Dale she had only discovered Murrell was due to plead guilty a week before he appeared in court. She later found out he had been negotiating his plea for months. “[That] hit me like a tonne of bricks,” she said. “He was still lying to me right up until the day he pled guilty.” She added: “He was very isolated over that period, he very rarely left the house, he wasn’t communicative, I was a bit worried about his wellbeing and his mental health.

Andy Burnham to tour Britain in effort to reconnect government with public

Andy Burnham is to undertake a national tour this coming week as he aims to improve the government’s connection with the British public during his premiership. The prime minister is expected to announce a set of policies that will help people financially as many struggle with the cost of living, as well as indicate his intent to improve high streets across the country. Burnham has previously given the public “breathing space” since succeeding Keir Starmer in the role last month, but is said to be in “listening mode” as he tours Britain and pushes his “10-year plan to bring back hope”. Related: Burnham urged to tackle cost of living crisis by pressuring Trump to end Iran war While an official itinerary has yet to be released by Downing Street, the prime minister is expected to visit areas where Labour has lost support in the last decade, as well as areas hit by declining industry. Port Talbot in south Wales, which is home to the largest steelworks in the UK, is likely to be one of the stops given the closure of its final blast furnace in 2024.

Home Office tells Italian man his right to stay in UK after Brexit was ‘error’

A 33-year-old Italian engineer who has been in London since 2018 has been plunged into a battle with the Home Office after officials told him they made a mistake allowing him to stay in the UK after Brexit. Fabio, who initially came to London to finish his doctorate and who has built a successful career working on energy and climate change, says he is shocked by the development as he has not broken any rules since Brexit. He was given settled status under the EU settlement scheme, permanent residency given to qualifying EU citizens after five years in the UK. The Home Office has now told him this was “in error” – and his wife, who he has been with since arriving in the UK, now has no right to remain as a qualifying family member of someone with settled status. While officials told him he could remain in the UK as they would not be removing his settled status, despite their claim to have made a mistake, the consequence of their error is that his wife now has no right to be in the country with him. “It was quite devastating for both of us. We have been here for a long time.

Pilot pulls off Count Binface stunt for Clacton byelection

A pilot has traced the shape of a bin with their flight path near Clacton before Count Binface challenges Nigel Farage in a byelection on Thursday. The light aircraft spent around half an hour between 2,100ft and 4,150ft above the sea near the Essex coastal town zigzagging to mark out the shape of a bin, according to data from Flightradar24. The plane took off from Earls Colne airfield near Colchester at 2.48pm on Saturday and landed at 4.13pm. The aircraft is in private ownership, according to Flightradar24, and the pilot’s identity is unknown. Voters will go to the polls in Clacton in a byelection triggered by the resignation of Farage, the Reform UK leader. Count Binface, a self-proclaimed space warrior who wears a bin-shaped helmet, is Farage’s main rival. There are also three candidates from the Official Monster Raving Loony party and numerous independents. All the main Westminster parties are boycotting the byelection, which they have dismissed as a stunt. A survey by Survation on behalf of Mandate Research suggests Farage will win 73% of the vote while Count Binface could get 20%.

We are a big part of those discussions and those dilemmas.” Falconer said he would use his role – now at cabinet level – to boost the UK’s participation in solving Europe-wide challenges outside the EU. “We are part of Europe and we feel the threats to Europe, whether it’s in eastern Europe from Russia invading Ukraine, or even wildfires and that shared sense of challenge in dealing with that.”

text:
Why we should support welfare spending

The finding that 47% of Labour party members surveyed believe the government is spending too much on social security is depressing (Labour members ‘have tougher view on welfare than you might think’, poll suggests, 4 August). But perhaps it’s not surprising given the relentless false “out of control” political and media narrative, when in fact spending on non-pensioner social security has remained at about 5% of GDP for the past decade. Social security was one of the main victims of austerity, leaving benefits too low to meet basic needs – hence the increased reliance on food banks. If members had been presented with the evidence from academics, thinktanks and charities showing that improving social security represents the most effective way of tackling child poverty, I suspect they may have been more supportive of spending in this area. The Institute for Government has suggested that it should be seen as preventive spending, reducing the demand on acute services. I trust that the “senior strategists in Downing Street” with whom the survey findings were shared won’t take the wrong lessons from them.

The Labour peer Luciana Berger has urged Kemi Badenoch to “listen to victims” and reverse her decision to give a national advisory role to a former neo-Nazi. Joshua Bonehill-Paine was jailed in 2015 for more than three years after posting antisemitic material online before a planned neo-Nazi rally. In 2016, he was found guilty of racially aggravated harassment for abuse directed at Berger, an MP at the time. He was also the founder and leader of the National British Resistance, a far-right group. Berger said she was still affected by his crimes more than nine years later, and questioned what safeguarding checks Badenoch and the Conservative party had carried out in relation to his appointment to the party’s culture and integration commission. Berger, who is Jewish, asked whether Bonehill-Paine’s new role could bring him to Westminster. She wrote on X: “Can I expect to come face to face with him on the parliamentary estate?” Badenoch’s spokesperson said Bonehill-Paine would not have a parliamentary pass and would not be on the estate.

Mother of Briton fatally shot by father in Texas urges Miliband to press US for new inquiry

The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, is being urged to push US authorities to reopen an investigation into a man who shot dead his 23-year-old British daughter while she was visiting him in Texas. Lucy Harrison, from Warrington in Cheshire, was fatally shot on 10 January 2025, the day before she was due to fly home to the UK. Her father, Kris Harrison, who admitted holding the pistol at the time, has never been arrested. A Texas grand jury decided not to prosecute the telecoms executive, originally from Liverpool, last year after what Lucy’s family described as an “inadequate” police investigation. Earlier this year, the senior coroner for Cheshire ruled that Lucy had been unlawfully killed and that Harrison’s actions amounted to gross negligence manslaughter. Lucy’s mother, Jane Coates, on Monday wrote to Miliband urging him to press the US authorities to reopen the investigation into her former husband, in light of the coroner’s findings.

Gun owners over the age of 21 are not required to obtain training or a licence in Texas, one of the most firearms-friendly US states. Treasury ‘materially contributed’ to suicide of personal assistant, coroner finds

The Treasury “materially contributed” to the death of Chloe Moffat, a 26-year-old personal assistant who took her own life after facing disciplinary proceedings, a coroner has found. Anna Crawford also found there was a risk of future deaths within the civil service from flawed handling of disciplinary proceedings. She said she would send a prevention of future deaths report to the head of the civil service, the Treasury, and the Advisory, Conciliation and Arbitration Service (Acas). Moffat had worked at the Treasury as a personal assistant for almost three years. She “loved her job” and had an “exemplary employment record”, the coroner heard during the three-day hearing. However, she was driven to “distress” by an informal meeting about an anonymous complaint at work. It alleged she had informally shared information about colleagues which she had been privy to during her job. Moffat had denied the allegation.

citation.title: Treasury ‘materially contributed’ to suicide of personal assistant, coroner finds

text:
Treasury ‘materially contributed’ to suicide of personal assistant, coroner finds

During the disciplinary process, the Surrey coroners court heard, she was not reassured that her job was safe even though she was unlikely to be dismissed, and she was not allowed to have a third party of her choice in the meeting. She had her job responsibilities temporarily changed and her access to the diary of her manager removed. This was despite the meeting being described as “informal”. The process left her “devastated” and convinced she had lost her job. The morning after the meeting, Moffat killed herself. The coroner found Moffat “appeared well and happy” before the meeting on 19 May last year and that there were no previous concerns about her mental health. She said: “I am satisfied that the shock and distress of the allegations and thinking she was going to lose her job contributed to her state of mind.” The Treasury’s human resources policy, which is in line with Acas guidelines, says that serious misconduct allegations have to be dealt with formally.

citation.title: Treasury ‘materially contributed’ to suicide of personal assistant, coroner finds

text:
Treasury ‘materially contributed’ to suicide of personal assistant, coroner finds

This is so the person involved is “not deprived of their rights”, such as having a third party present during meetings, being given five days’ notice and being informed of the likely outcome if the allegations are found to be true, the coroner said. She found that because decisions had already been made to limit Moffat’s role and responsibilities, the allegations “needed a formal process”. Crawford said: “I find the meeting was not in accordance with [Treasury] policy”, which “makes no provision” for such informal meetings. “The reason for this seems abundantly clear,” she added. “It is necessary to put safeguards in place, including informing about the likely penalty and the right to be accompanied.” The head of global issues at the Treasury, who was running the investigation into Moffat, said during the coroner’s hearing that she did not give Moffat prior notice of the meeting because “she did not want Chloe to worry about it”.

She had also told the court that when Moffat asked in tears whether she would lose her job, she had replied that she could not predict the outcome of any potential investigation. Earlier in the hearing, when asked if she would have done anything differently, Moffat’s line manager told the court: “No, I think we did all we could at the time with the information and advice we were given.” But the coroner found: “By handling the matter in the way they did, Chloe was denied safeguards. “The concern that she would lose her job did materially contribute to her state of mind and the decision to take her own life,” Crawford said. She found the Treasury played a part in Moffat’s death by not informing her that the likely outcome would be a written warning and not dismissal. Crawford was issuing a prevention of future deaths notice because the Treasury claimed these informal meetings were “standard practice”. “That is a matter of concern,” she said.

At a time when she needed support, reassurance and fair treatment, she was left frightened, isolated and convinced that her career and reputation had been destroyed.” Anne Moffat suggested the family may take further action: “We will continue to honour her memory and seek the changes needed to ensure that no other family suffers a similar loss.” A Treasury spokesperson said: “We continue to mourn Chloe’s passing as a colleague and friend. Terry Lewis obituary

Terry Lewis, the former Labour MP for Worsley, Greater Manchester, who has died aged 90, spent 22 years in the House of Commons. During this time he chalked up a remarkable record as a dissident from his party’s frontbench policy on a wide range of leftwing touchstone issues. It was his personal misfortune to be elected in 1983, when the influence of the left within Labour was about to be curbed, consigning him to a parliamentary career spent largely in opposition to his own leadership. His was a familiar figure on the backbenches of the Commons chamber, sitting in a trio with his fellow members of the so-called “awkward squad”, Dennis Skinner and Bob Cryer, harassing the government frontbench when the Conservatives were in office, while also plotting the next moves in support of his own campaigns, many of which did not concur with the party line. Lewis’s name always featured in lists of Labour’s most rebellious MPs. In the parliament from 1992 until 1997, he voted on 49 occasions against the advice of his party’s whips and, after Tony Blair then became prime minister, he held the record for a time as the top rebel.

citation.title: Terry Lewis obituary

text:
Terry Lewis obituary

He left Westminster in 2005, expressing his disappointment at the Labour government’s lack of commitment to socialist policies and five years later announced his resignation from the party, publicly tearing up his membership card of the organisation, which he claimed had “lost its soul”. He did not write a letter of resignation from Labour, claiming that in order to do so he would have had to write a short novel. However, he rejoined when his old friend Jeremy Corbyn became leader in 2015. Lewis’s politics were formed by the leftwing political and trade union culture of the postwar years in which he grew up in urban Manchester and from which he never deviated. A devoted Manchester United supporter, he was a hugely popular MP in the constituency – he called everyone “kid” and was himself sometimes known affectionately as “El Tel” – and this was largely because of his unwavering stance on the causes he espoused. He enjoyed his reputation as a Salford legend and when he retired he sent local friends and contacts a postcard of a solitary horseman in a desert landscape.

citation.title: Terry Lewis obituary

text:
Terry Lewis obituary

It was captioned “Into the Sunset” and printed on the reverse it read: “Still searching for the socialist alternative.” Terry was the son of Mary (nee Redfern) and Andrew Lewis, and was born in Ordsall, within a mile of Salford docks, where his father was employed as a dockworker. He was educated locally at Our Lady of Mount Carmel Roman Catholic primary and secondary schools in Salford and his constituency was an inner-city safe Labour seat, comprising parts of Salford. He won the seat when it was first established in 1983, standing against John Roper of the newly created Social Democratic party. Roper had been the former Labour MP in the area, for the seat of Farnworth – which had been absorbed into the Worsley constituency – and Lewis took more than 40% of the vote, beating him into third place behind the Conservative candidate. After further boundary changes in 1997, Lewis increased his share of the vote to 62.2%. He lived in Kearsley, north-west of Manchester, working as a power station charge engineer from 1960 to 1982 and, for the last year before his election to Westminster, as a personnel officer.

citation.title: Terry Lewis obituary

text:
Terry Lewis obituary

His first political experience came as a member of the Kearsley urban district council, to which he was elected in 1971, a year after joining the Labour party. Local government reorganisation in 1974 saw Kearsley absorbed by Bolton council, of which Lewis was a member (1976-84), serving as deputy leader for five years from 1978 and chair of the education committee in 1982-83. He was a founder member of the Bolton branch of CND. One of Lewis’s first votes, within a month of his election to the Commons, was in opposition to the defence estimates, but he was not a pacifist. He had done national service in the Royal Army Medical Corps (1954-56), yet boasted that he refused to sing the national anthem. He later opposed prevention of terrorism legislation, the Gulf war and the Iraq war. He was a bitter opponent of the Maastricht treaty legislation establishing the European Union. He regarded himself as a member of what he termed the “practical left” and opposed his party on benefit reductions, means-testing incapacity benefits and the abolition of student grants.

citation.title: Terry Lewis obituary

text:
Terry Lewis obituary

One long-running campaign he pursued, against British Telecom, was perhaps a precedent for the current debate about the impact of the internet. Lewis spent three years from 1986 vigorously lobbying BT to ban chat lines, warning of the danger of children becoming addicted to pornography. He was also ahead of his time in fighting to restrict smoking in public and to oblige tobacco companies to print health warnings on their packaging. Lewis suffered from poor health in his last parliament and announced his resignation before the 2005 election. In 1958, he married Audrey Clarke. She predeceased him, and one of their two sons, Andrew, died in 1975, aged 10. Lewis is survived by their elder son, David. • Terence Lewis, politician, born 29 December 1935; died 20 July 2026

text:
Will Andy Burnham’s everyday fixes be enough to get the public on his side?

It was last year that Martin Lewis, the money-saving guru, advised the government to find “100 small things that piss people off” and set about sorting them out. That approach has been adopted almost immediately by Andy Burnham since entering office, as he began his programme of “everyday fixes” to tackle problems that can be dealt with through minor policy tweaks. Labour strategists say the philosophy behind this is to show that Burnham notices the frustrations of people’s lives, and that he will be decisive about improving these issues. This started with scrapping VAT on electricity bills and capping bus fares. His latest policy assault is on garish signs on the high street and everything from excessive vape and betting shops to subscriptions that auto-renew without warning. It is applying to politics the “broken window” theory of crime that suggests clamping down on small-scale antisocial behaviour such as littering can help discourage more serious crime.

citation.title: Will Andy Burnham’s everyday fixes be enough to get the public on his side?

text:
Will Andy Burnham’s everyday fixes be enough to get the public on his side?

As much as anything, Burnham’s moves against rip-off Britain should be a warning to companies that the government is paying attention to their behaviour towards voters, as he mulls over how far to go with a programme of increasing public control over essential services. The intention is a long way from Keir Starmer’s promise to be a government that treads more lightly on people’s lives, as the new prime minister has taken a bet that voters want leaders who are active about everyday frustrations as well as embarking on major structural reform. Related: From ticket booking fees to shrinkflation, six other ways Burnham could cut cost of living Burnham’s instinct to show the public that he is prepared to act on their behalf is a sound one, according to Peter Kellner, the pollster and former chair of YouGov, who has written recently about the difficulty of winning round “ungrateful voters”. “Probably the best any government can do in the short run – short of some educational programme about where our taxes go – is gain the perception that they as politicians are on the voters’ sides.

citation.title: Will Andy Burnham’s everyday fixes be enough to get the public on his side?

text:
Will Andy Burnham’s everyday fixes be enough to get the public on his side?

This is the key to the Burnham bounce. Plainly the amounts of money involved on bus fares and VAT and so on are small in the great order of things. “But they are part of a story about where Burnham stands in relation to the responsibility of the government to look after people. How long this lasts I don’t know because we have yet to see what’s in the budget. And if at the end of the day they announce tax rises, then that changes. But if I were his communications adviser, this is what I would have advised him to do.” He said Tony Blair and Margaret Thatcher successfully told the stories of their premierships in their first five to six years, and that Burnham needs to do something similar in terms of building a narrative. “What we have yet to see is Burnham joining the dots of what he’s done so far. And it’s got to be something clearer than Starmer saying life is difficult and we are doing the best we can and we want to make Britain fairer and more prosperous,” Kellner says.

citation.title: Will Andy Burnham’s everyday fixes be enough to get the public on his side?

text:
Will Andy Burnham’s everyday fixes be enough to get the public on his side?

However, there is also a risk for Burnham that hailing small changes as achievements will veer into the dreaded territory of consumer gimmicks that American strategist David Axelrod warned against. The former Obama adviser, who was drafted in to help Ed Miliband’s 2015 campaign, memorably branded Labour’s approach on the cost of living in that election as: “Vote Labour and win a microwave”. In other words, it was a consumer retail offer of short-term bargains without an overarching big and inspiring message to pull it all together. Another cautionary tale can be found in the fate of the Joe Biden and Kamala Harris administration. Together they targeted price gouging and unfair consumer practices. But while the overall economy began to improve under Biden, voters never give the US government credit for small changes like holding down medicine bills and expanded child tax credits because they were unhappy about the lasting effects of food and housing costs inflation that had an effect globally.

citation.title: Will Andy Burnham’s everyday fixes be enough to get the public on his side?

text:
Will Andy Burnham’s everyday fixes be enough to get the public on his side?

It will be a test for Burnham how far he can reap the rewards of dealing with consumer frustrations at a time when he has little room for bigger giveaways to help with the cost of living while the economy is barely growing. Burnham must also guard against a third possible peril: the potential for mockery if the issues seem too inconsequential for a prime minister to be bothering with – in the vein of John Major’s “cones hotline” for people to report nuisance roadworks. The new prime minister, however, seems aware of these pitfalls. He is openly flagging the policies as small wins – while promising bigger structural change to take place in the longer term on social care and public ownership of utilities. Labour was also ready to paint Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, as out of touch when she tried to ridicule the cost of living policies by saying: “Is that it? The problems go way beyond bus fares and VAT on bills.” Polling so far seems to suggest that voters are tentatively impressed and moving back towards Labour at a time when both Reform UK and the Greens are sliding.

However, the latest data from Ipsos Mori says seven in 10 remain dissatisfied with the way the government is running the country. While they make think Burnham is outperforming the other parties and a substantial number feel he is on their side compared with other leaders, voters are still going to take some convincing that the new prime minister really will be able to change their lives for the better.

text:
Politicians among mourners at funeral service for Ann Widdecombe

About 100 family, friends and colleagues of Ann Widdecombe have attended a funeral service for the former Conservative minister, who was killed in her home in Devon last month. Politicians and broadcasters were among the mourners at Buckfast Abbey in Buckfastleigh, a Catholic abbey in Devon where Widdecombe regularly worshipped and which she described as her “safe haven”. A 90-minute requiem mass – where prayers are offered for the soul of the dead – was held for the former MP and Reform UK spokesperson. Before the service, police officers and sniffer dogs could be seen searching the grounds. Widdecombe died on 8 July, aged 78, after she was hit over the head with a hammer 21 times at her home in Haytor. Joshua Kerry, 28, of Rotherham, South Yorkshire, was charged with her murder on 20 July. It is understood that Reform leader, Nigel Farage, did not attend the funeral because he did not wish to be a distraction. He is expected to attend a public memorial planned for later this year.

Politicians among mourners at funeral service for Ann Widdecombe

Those slated to attend included the shadow chancellor, Mel Stride, the former Conservative justice minister Crispin Blunt and the broadcaster Iain Dale. The private mass featured a homily from the Rt Rev David Charlesworth, the abbot of Buckfast. He said: “In the midst of the shock, clamour and sometimes unwarranted comment surrounding her death, our response is to pray for the repose of her soul, to give thanks for her fortitude, and offer Holy Mass in this abbey church, which Ann called her safe haven.” An earlier statement from the abbey said: “Ann was a woman of profound faith, a faith which found expression in the public forum of politics. Ann was unafraid to express her unwavering convictions, formed through her Roman Catholic faith. She had a sharp intellect and was a dedicated public servant.” The order of service showed tributes would be paid by the Rev Roger Widdecombe, Widdecombe’s nephew, and Christian Sweeting, a close friend. Donations made in her memory will be divided between the Leprosy Mission and Abound, supporting the projects of the Christian Endeavour Hostel in India.

Nigel Farage has been standing in British elections since 1994, when he narrowly beat Screaming Lord Sutch of the Monster Raving Loony party into fourth place in a Commons byelection. He was elected five times to the European parliament before achieving his goal of abolishing his seat. Finally, after 30 years of trying, he was elected to the Commons as member for Clacton in 2024. He resigned that hard-won seat in July after a parliamentary inquiry was launched into a £5m gift he accepted from a Thailand-based businessman shortly before the general election, but is standing again in the resulting byelection on Thursday. The other major parties are not putting up candidates, so the chief contenders, according to the limited polling, are Farage and Count Binface. Riding high in the polls in 2015, Farage was so confident of winning Thanet South in that year’s general election that he pledged to resign as leader of Ukip if he did not take the seat. This led Al Murray, a comedian whose main persona is the Pub Landlord, a straight-talking conservative patriot, to stand against Farage.

text:
Polls close in Clacton byelection where Nigel Farage faces slew of fringe candidates

Polls have closed in Clacton, where thousands of residents in the Essex seat voted in a ballot featuring Nigel Farage and a range of novelty and fringe candidates led by Count Binface. The Reform UK leader resigned as the MP for Clacton at the start of July and forced a byelection in an attempt to address complaints over a deepening scandal about gifts he received. He is expected to face a formal investigation by the parliamentary standards watchdog, which was opened in May after the Guardian revealed he had received a £5m personal gift from Christopher Harborne, a Thailand-based crypto billionaire, in April 2024. Farage has denied the gift amounted to an inducement to run for office, insisting it was personal in nature. He has given a series of explanations for the gift, including that it was for his security and a reward for Brexit.
