The inquiry will look into allegations Farage was financially supported by the crypto gambler and convicted fraudster George Cottrell, a close friend, after the Sunday Times reported that Cottrell’s support included security and social media staff who worked on Farage’s online content in the year before he was elected. Reform UK claimed that was a “baseless and contrived story” and that no parliamentary rules had been broken. The inquiry, which was suspended on 8 July after Farage’s decision to force a byelection, could restart as soon as Friday if he is re-elected. If parliament imposes sanctions for failing to declare the gifts, he may be removed from the House of Commons and face a second byelection. All of the main parties have boycotted the byelection, announcing they would not stand candidates for a “media circus” and a “vanity project”. Instead, Count Binface, the self-declared “entirely independent space warrior” created by the comedian Jon Harvey, stepped into the void.

A record number of candidates are seeking election, presenting voters with the longest ballot paper in British electoral history. Among the 34 candidates on the ballot paper are independents, the actor and rightwing political activist Laurence Fox and three figures from the Monster Raving Loony party: Howling Laud Hope, Baron Von Thunderclap and Nick the Incredible Flying Brick. As well as the town of Clacton-on-Sea, the constituency comprises rural villages, farmland and several seaside towns and villages including Frinton, Walton-on-the-Naze and Jaywick, which last year was named the most deprived neighbourhood in England for the fourth consecutive time since 2010. The three polls that Jaywick topped before 2025 were published in 2010, 2015 and 2019. According to figures from the Office for National Statistics, the population of Clacton is older than the average in England. A third of working-age people are economically inactive, compared with fewer than one in five in the east of England. Of Clacton residents who voted in the 2016 Brexit referendum, 70% favoured leave.

After standing in multiple British elections since 1994, Farage was elected to the Commons as the member for Clacton in 2024. He won the seat with a majority of 8,400, taking 46.2% of the vote. The Conservatives came second and Labour third. The previous record for the largest number of candidates in a constituency election was held by the Haltemprice and Howden byelection in East Yorkshire in July 2008, which featured 26 candidates. It took place after Tory David Davis resigned his seat and stood again as a protest over the issue of civil liberties. The result may be seen as a benchmark to measure Farage’s relative success in this byelection. Davis won 72% of the vote in the election – which Labour and the Liberal Democrats did not contest – up from 47.5% at the 2005 general election, with a majority of 15,355. Farage’s critics argue that his standing as a contender to be the next prime minister has taken a serious hit as a result of the byelection, with much of the Reform leader’s time and energy spent in the Essex constituency.

text:
Nigel Farage set for decisive but arguably empty victory in Clacton

Voting has closed in one of the UK’s more unusual and least tense byelections, with Nigel Farage set for a decisive if arguably empty victory against dozens of independent, fringe, extreme or otherwise oddball opponents. The Reform UK leader sought re-election to his Clacton seat in early July in an attempt to regain the political initiative following weeks of scrutiny over gifts he received and other aspects of his financial affairs. He framed the byelection as a chance for local voters to show their disdain for mainstream politics in a “people versus the establishment” contest, but was caught out after all the other main parties declined to stand candidates. Farage, 62, was instead left competing against a vast if decidedly niche field of 33 other hopefuls, including 20 independents, several representatives from tiny parties and no fewer than three candidates from the Official Monster Raving Loony party.

While Reform will necessarily style the result as a clear endorsement of Farage’s record in the Essex seat, and of his tactic in calling the byelection, opponents will seize on any signs of a lower-than-expected majority or a slim turnout. Farage is being investigated by the parliamentary standards watchdog over allegations he failed to declare gifts and donations, including a £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne, first revealed by the Guardian. The process was paused when he resigned as an MP, but will resume once he is re-elected. Reform council leader, 20, defends record one year on: ‘The establishment will throw anyone under the bus’

George Finch, who made history last year after he was elected as leader of Warwickshire county council at the age of 19, is no stranger to criticism. His year at the helm of a minority Reform administration has been dominated by a string of controversies, including three code of conduct investigations and a no-confidence call – which he survived by just one vote. The latest controversy concerns a dispute over the region’s libraries. In June, Finch claimed he had received “a number” of complaints from people that the county’s libraries had been “promoting contested gender ideology”, prompting Warwickshire Pride to issue a statement, and the launch of the latest misconduct investigation. However, on Tuesday, the Labour MP Rachel Taylor accused Finch of attempting to “manufacture outrage”, citing data obtained via a freedom of information request that showed zero complaints had been made about books inappropriate for children in Warwickshire libraries since at least March 2024.

In response, Finch said he had “personally spoken” to people who had raised concerns and accused the Labour MP of a “desperate attempt” to “manufacture a political argument”. It is just one of several public spats that has come to define Finch’s polarising leadership. He told the Guardian he was being targeted because of his attempts to challenge the status quo at the council. Finch, 20, said the fact he was able to secure the top role at a second local authority, having been elected as leader of Nuneaton and Bedworth borough council in May this year, was further proof he still had the support of local people. “The establishment will happily throw anyone under the bus to protect themselves. When an animal is dying, it becomes its most ferocious. That is why they’re throwing code of conduct complaints at me. That’s why they produce these vote of no confidences, because they don’t like change,” he said.

Yvette Cooper says Labour ‘did not do government very well’ under Starmer

Yvette Cooper admits Labour has “not done government very well” in the last couple of years, and accused Keir Starmer’s No 10 of sidelining her during the launch of a key immigration policy when she was home secretary. Speaking on the Political Currency podcast with the former Conservative chancellor George Osborne, Cooper highlighted some of the difficulties ministers faced with Starmer’s leadership, which she summarised as “bring me solutions, not problems”. She said she had found a more collegiate style under Andy Burnham, and argued in favour of trying to form a national consensus around social care and reintroducing Sure Start-style children’s centres for young families under his leadership. Contrasting the new prime minister with Starmer, the health secretary said there had been “a style of leading the government that maybe doesn’t necessarily work in politics” under the last administration. As an example, she was critical of how she was in effect excluded from launching the immigration white paper in May 2025 while home secretary.

At the launch, which was fronted by Starmer, he spoke of introducing policies to deal with the risk that Britain could become an “island of strangers”, which Cooper later had to defend. Actually, we did a lot of the work on it in the Home Office, and a whole set of plans to bring legal migration back under control, a whole set of reforms around illegal migration and so on. “But then No 10 wanted Keir to announce it on his own and to front that up, and so I didn’t see what was going to be said or what the announcement was … that was the way that No 10 operated. “It was like, well, you can sit in the front row of the launch, but actually the prime minister is going to launch it.” She added: “I think Keir’s style of leadership was ‘bring me solutions, not problems’. text:
‘Let’s see what he can do’: will Burnham bring voters back in Labour heartlands?

Labour marked its worst performance in more than 50 years when voters went to the polls in Barnsley in May, but 100 days on from those seismic local elections, the political landscape has shifted drastically. Could the South Yorkshire town, where Reform UK reaped the benefits of dissatisfaction with Labour, prove to be a test case for whether the governing party has turned the tide? Labour had run Barnsley’s council since its inception in 1974, but was left with just 11 councillors after Reform triumphed with 42 seats. “I knew that it would be the most challenging set of elections that we’ve ever faced in Barnsley’s history,” said the councillor James Higginbottom, the new Labour group opposition leader. “What I didn’t necessarily expect was the scale of the Reform victory.” Catastrophic results in places such as Barnsley were a catalyst for Keir Starmer’s resignation. He has been replaced as prime minister by the former mayor of Greater Manchester Andy Burnham, who won the Labour leadership uncontested after a landslide byelection victory.

The parliamentary standards investigation has now resumed. Labour is now ahead in the polls for the first time since March 2025, with a YouGov poll on Monday giving Labour a two-point lead, at 24 points to Reform’s 22. Many in Barnsley used their vote in May to punish Starmer’s government, and while almost everyone the Guardian spoke to there this week said it was too early to judge the Reform council on their record, the new national political picture appears to be enticing at least some back to Labour. text:
Belt and braces PM: what wearing suit braces says about Burnham

The sartorial evolution of Andy Burnham reached another milestone this week when the prime minister appeared at a photocall in Derbyshire wearing a pair of braces under his suit. Navy, slimline and button-on rather than clipped, they were barely visible while he posed for a photo in Ilkeston. It was only when he unbuttoned his suit jacket to embrace members of the public that they were on view. Burnham’s £595 navy suit was made by Oliver Brown, a traditional tailor with shops in London and Chester, and is the same style worn in his official portrait. Called the Eaton suit, it is made from a 100% merino wool cloth woven by Alfred Brown in Yorkshire, and is made to measure. A spokesperson for the tailor said that while the suit was definitely theirs, the braces were not. If the trousers didn’t fit, wearing a belt would have been out of the question as they don’t have belt loops.

And yet, says Chloe Chapin, a fashion historian and author of the forthcoming book Suitable: The Sartorial Revolution and the Fashioning of Modern Men, “the trousers do have side fasteners, so he doesn’t really need braces at all, at least functionally”. A political insider who has worked on Burnham’s campaigns for the last two years told the Guardian: “Andy is not the teleprompter type of politician. This stuff is simply what he wears.” The former Greater Manchester mayor and his team think about his clothing and context, though, and it certainly isn’t an afterthought. “His clothes are trying to strike a balance between professional and capable politician – but also let people know that he’s different to other politicians,” the source says. As the first TikTok PM, no one understands this better than Burnham. “The optics are not divorced from the reality.” Braces originated in France in the 1700s as strips of fabric that were buttoned to a waistband. They quickly spread across Europe, like many French trends, though it wasn’t until 1820 that Albert Thurston started making the leather versions we know today.

Futile Clacton byelection has done Farage no favours

Dawn had long broken in the Essex town of Clacton-on-Sea when the results for the byelection came in. After a gruelling count, an atmosphere of deep exhaustion had settled over the room. Even the man with a dustbin on his head looked weary. As it was declared that Nigel Farage had won, as expected, there was no cheering in the room, which had been boycotted by the Reform UK leader and his supporters; instead there was only an overwhelming sense of futility. Farage forced the byelection at the start of July in an attempt take control of a narrative tide that had turned against him. After the Guardian revealed he had received a £5m personal gift from Christopher Harborne, a Thailand-based crypto billionaire, in April 2024, he had been dogged by questions about his financial backing. Other revelations followed and questions mounted. The parliamentary standards watchdog announced it was opening a formal investigation into gifts received by Farage, and his regular long press conferences abruptly stopped. When he did a very limited number of interviews, Farage, normally performatively affable, was testy and defensive.

He resigned as the MP for the Clacton constituency at the start of July, saying the “people of Clacton should be the judges of my actions”, and billing the fight as a “people versus the establishment” byelection. The establishment, however, chose not to play. All of the major parties declined to field candidates and take part in what they called a “media circus” and “vanity project”. Instead, Count Binface, the self-declared “entirely independent space warrior” created by the comedian Jon Harvey, stepped into the void. It felt, at times, less like an election campaign and more of a showcase for British humour, the ultimate distillation of the concept of a summer “silly season” of news. The sort the Americans used to run in the 1950s and 60s, that have long since been banned. From the first day Andy Burnham came into office, climate scientists, campaigners and some of the ordinary people surviving through this summer of extreme heat began to wonder when he would start to talk about the climate crisis. Up until this week, many held back from criticism. After all, he had only been in power for a couple weeks; it felt far too early to start to judge and call him out on it. But as we watched the footage of terrified horses galloping over cindering heathland in the New Forest while yet another wildfire took hold, it no longer felt too soon to wonder. Now people are asking aloud: why is Burnham ignoring what is in front of his face – the devastating impact of climate breakdown on the country and its citizens? “As the prime minister tours every region of the UK, it will be hard to miss the impacts of this extraordinary summer: wildfires, drought, parched farmland and people struggling to work in extreme heat,” said Emma Howard Boyd, the former head of the Environment Agency who is now a professor in practice at the Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change and the Environment.

text:
Post-Brexit rights for British citizens are being undermined in Sweden

Back in October 2020, the UK immigration minister stood up in parliament to reassure campaigners concerned about EU citizens who weren’t aware they had to ask the Home Office to stay in the country after Brexit. Using an example of a child in foster care who might not know they were an EU citizen until they applied for their first job, the Conservative Kevin Foster said the UK would take “a generous approach as to what reasonable grounds [for failing to apply] were”. In other words, the UK/EU Brexit agreement was designed to protect those who had exercised lawful freedom of movement, and they couldn’t just be chucked out of their host state because the UK had decided to leave the EU. The Home Office is not perfect, and is regularly criticised by campaigners for missteps over the implementation of the EU citizens chapter in the EU-UK withdrawal agreement. But “reasonable grounds” have been outlined in parliament, providing legal arguments to challengers.

Angela Rayner moves to protect pubs from being turned into houses or offices

All pubs will get protection from being turned into housing or offices under a shake-up of planning laws in England to be presented by Angela Rayner this week. Rayner is making the move because of concerns about the rate of pub closures in England, with Andy Burnham already having announced a cut in business rates for the hospitality sector. Cabinet ministers’ mobile numbers found online after Burnham targeted

At least three UK cabinet ministers have had their personal mobile phone numbers published online, amid mounting concern over the security of senior politicians after Andy Burnham was targeted by an impersonation scam. The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, the justice secretary, Alex Norris, and the Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, had their numbers available online with their names. A reference containing Streeting’s number has since been removed, a source told the Guardian, noting he does all his government business on his official government phone. Officials are understood to be working to take down the others. The leak, first revealed by Politico, come after Burnham exchanged messages with someone posing as Donald Trump’s chief of staff, Susie Wiles. The prime minister was in contact with an unknown individual pretending to be Wiles before concerns were raised about the incident. No messages of significance were sent and the suspicious activity was quickly reported to the appropriate authorities, it is understood.

Burnham to scrap restrictions on disabled people’s bus passes in England

Disabled people across England will be able to use their free bus passes at any time of day from next April, as Andy Burnham expands a policy he introduced as mayor of Greater Manchester. The prime minister has said the current weekday restrictions on when disabled people can use their bus passes will be removed from 1 April 2027. Their passes are valid only between 9.30am and 11pm on weekdays, although some councils pay to allow people free travel outside those hours. The change means disabled bus pass holders will be able to travel free on local bus services where the pass applies at any time of day or night. The charity Mencap welcomed the measures, noting that disabled people often struggle with the cost of living as well as the cost of their disability. Burnham is putting up £60m in funding for the change, with £40m coming from the Department for Work and Pensions and £20m from the Department for Transport. Government sources said the funding has no set end date and was not a one-off payment.

Hundreds of thousands of children would be tipped into poverty and destitution under plans unveiled by Reform UK to slash £50bn a year from the UK benefits bill, campaigners have warned. The warnings came after Reform published plans to drastically reduce disability payments, ban non-UK citizens from claiming benefits and introduce compulsory 20 hours a week unpaid workfare for thousands of long-term unemployed people. An overhaul of the sick pay system would require employers to cover an employee’s benefit payments for the first two years of their illness, the plans propose, while the two-child benefit limit scrapped by Labour last year would be reintroduced. Meanwhile, a leaked government analysis seen by the Guardian showed that cuts to disability benefits would be so steep that even those with terminal illness, blindness or profound learning disabilities would stand to lose as much as £10,000 a year.

Loosening of planning rules in England to allow more new homes near stations

Thousands more homes could be built within 10 minutes of transport hubs, including on green belt sites, under a loosening of planning policy announced by Angela Rayner on Monday. The housing secretary will set out changes to national planning guidance for England that will include an order for councils to have a “default yes” approach to housing developments that are within a reasonable walking distance of well-connected train and tram stations. If a proposed development is on green belt land, then the government’s “golden rules” state that they must have higher levels of affordable housing, new or improved green spaces, and be supported by the right infrastructure. The approach was put out to consultation under Rayner’s predecessor, Steve Reed, but the guidance will be confirmed as part of the new national planning policy framework (NPPF) this week. Rayner is billing the changes as part of the biggest rewrite of planning rules in more than a decade as the government moves towards its target of 1.5m new homes being built by the end of this parliament.

The decent way for countries to engage with the Taliban

You report concerns over increased diplomatic contact with Afghanistan and the Taliban (15 August). If nations wish to establish contact with the country and improve human rights, especially for women, may I suggest that they only use women to negotiate and to staff diplomatic bases. They might also insist on only dealing with women. If the Taliban desire legitimacy let them have it on decent terms. We are hoping it becomes common parlance. text:
Burnham declares almost £350,000 in donations in months before becoming PM

Donors to Andy Burnham gave almost £350,000 over the months before he became Labour leader and prime minister, with major contributors including his former adviser Sacha Lord as well as billionaires David Sainsbury and Gary Lubner. The new MPs’ register of interests also shows Burnham declaring hospitality and trips worth more than £12,000 – many of them relating to Greater Manchester in his former role as mayor but also including £1,500 of Glastonbury tickets in 2025, where he was speaking, and £500 of tickets to Ladies Day at Aintree this year. The register is the first in which Burnham has recorded his financial interests as an MP since he became prime minister. It also shows he recently set up a company called Office of Andy Burnham, which leaders often do to manage their financial affairs after leaving office, and that he owns a property in London with his wife, which is rented out.

Other cabinet ministers to make new declarations include Louise Haigh, the chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, who accepted £11,000 from Sainsbury to pay for legal advice and £7,500 of legal services from Bindmans law firm. A source close to Haigh said: “The donations related to legal services provided during the declaration period in relation to misrepresentation in the media.” Haigh is believed to have taken legal advice around media coverage about her conviction for fraud in relation to a missing phone in 2024. She resigned as transport secretary when it became public last November but has since been brought back to run Burnham’s leadership campaign and as one of the most senior members of his cabinet. Burnham’s donations, which began in March this year, include £20,000 from trade unions including Unison, the CWU and Fire Brigades Union. But the biggest financial supporter was Sainsbury, a billionaire and long-term Labour donor who gave more than £160,000, including paying for staff working on policy.

Lord, who was Burnham’s unpaid night-time economy adviser in Manchester, resigned from the role in January 2025 after the Arts Council England said that his company misled them in applying for a £400,000 Covid support grant, though Lord denies any wrongdoing. text:
Civil service chief got record £500,000 payout after Starmer dismissal

The former head of the civil service Chris Wormald received a record payout, in the region of £500,000, when he was forced out of the top job in Whitehall by Keir Starmer, it has emerged. The unprecedented payment was made after Wormald served just 14 months in the role of cabinet secretary before being replaced by Antonia Romeo. There had been speculation about the scale of the payout, first reported by the FT, after Cat Little, the permanent secretary of the Cabinet Office, had to request a ministerial direction from Starmer in February to override value-for-money concerns before she could approve it. In her letter to the prime minister at the time, she wrote: “In respect of value for money, I have consulted civil service HR and legal advisers and have had due regard to managing public money and the consideration of Sir Chris Wormald’s employment rights in the circumstances. The proposed award is greater than what Sir Chris Wormald would be contractually entitled to.

citation.title: Civil service chief got record £500,000 payout after Starmer dismissal

text:
Civil service chief got record £500,000 payout after Starmer dismissal

“However, I am informed that a settlement of this level is necessary given that this is a departure from a high profile, unique role that has been agreed at very short notice. Given the complexity of the legal position and the information to be considered at this time, it is not possible for me to conclude to the level required whether the proposed settlement amount represents value for money or not. “However, you as prime minister can take into account wider considerations, in particular the public interest in bringing this matter to a conclusion and the prevention of distraction from the effective operation of government.” The previous highest settlement was given to Tom Scholar, who was forced out as permanent secretary of the Treasury by Liz Truss as one of her first acts during her brief tenure as prime minister. He was given £457,000, including severance pay and compensation in lieu of notice and leave. Wormald is to become a crossbench peer after he was nominated by Starmer on leaving office.

Labour urges Gambling Commission to investigate firms linked to Reform UK donors

The Gambling Commission has been urged to investigate claims that companies linked to Reform UK donors and allies of Nigel Farage have been operating without a licence. The Labour party’s chair, Bridget Phillipson, has written to the watchdog asking it to look into Tether.bet, a Montenegro-based gambling company, and Fispay, a UK company owned by Reform’s data protection officer, Mowbray Jackson. It comes after the Sunday Times reported that both companies had been operating without a licence. Crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne’s £5m gift to Farage is already under scrutiny by the parliamentary commissioner for standards. George Cottrell, a convicted fraudster and long-term ally of Farage, is linked to Tether.bet, which issued a closure notice on its website on 12 August. It is against the law to provide gambling facilities without a licence in the UK under the Gambling Act 2005.

Jackson told the Sunday Times his company “exclusively” brokered private jet travel and it had never provided facilities for gambling, while Cottrell said he was a customer of Tether.bet and he has “never solicited clients for any betting company”. In her letter, Phillipson wrote: “In light of these allegations, I would urge the commission to investigate: Whether Tether.bet, and its operators, provided or advertised remote gambling facilities to consumers in UK without the required licence Whether Fispay Ltd, or any other UK company, provided or supported gambling facilities or services to consumers in the UK without the required licence.” Phillipson, also an equalities minister, added: “These are the latest allegations in a mountain of unanswered questions concerning Reform’s donors and finances. “Nigel Farage cannot dodge them for ever. He needs to stop making excuses and come clean with the public.” The Sunday Times published an investigation into links between Reform funders and Tether.bet.

Any suggestion that he was involved in unlawful gambling activity is wholly false.” Harborne and IFX’s representatives told the Sunday Times he had never had any role in the running and operations of IFX and that it “operates in accordance with applicable regulations and legislation across the markets it supports”. text:
Lord Horam obituary

Just about every parliament in modern times has thrown up MPs who change parties, but there have been very few such as John Horam, Lord Horam, who represented three parties in the Commons and furthermore served as a government minister for two of them. Horam, who has died aged 87, never reached cabinet rank but was a junior minister in James Callaghan’s Labour administration in the late 1970s and, after a peregrination with the Social Democratic party in the 80s, subsequently served in the Conservative government of John Major in the 90s. Winston Churchill, who entered parliament in the early 1900s as a Conservative, switched to the Liberals and then, 20 years later, became a Tory again, said: “Anyone can rat but it takes a certain amount of ingenuity to re-rat.” Horam deployed a different Churchillian phrase: “It is better to change your mind than be wrong all the time.” However, it did not stop him being greeted by the Labour leftwinger Dennis Skinner as a “dirty double-rat” when Horam rose to speak in his latest incarnation.

citation.title: Lord Horam obituary

text:
Lord Horam obituary

Horam was born in Preston, Lancashire, the son of Catherine (nee Harkness), who ran a dress shop and a newsagent’s at various times, and Sydney Horam, a fitter with Leyland motors. He was educated at the fee-paying Silcoates school in Wakefield, where he became head boy, and studied economics at St Catharine’s College, Cambridge, before joining the marketing department of Rowntree’s chocolate factory in York, where he played a small part in developing the After Eight mint in the early 1960s. He subsequently worked as a journalist for the Financial Times and the Economist before founding the Commodities Research Unit (now the CRU Group) in London, with a colleague, Robert Perlman, supplying data to mining companies. Horam had joined Labour at the age of 15 after hearing a speech by Hugh Gaitskell, who would become the party leader in 1955, though if there was a common strand in his politics it was as an economic free marketeer and opponent of incomes policy on the party’s rightwing. As a young MP, elected first for Gateshead West in 1970, he was actually a Tribunite anti-Common Market candidate, positions that he would change with time.

citation.title: Lord Horam obituary

text:
Lord Horam obituary

While he was later in favour of the European Union, he became a supporter of capital punishment, and an opponent of divorce law reform and lowering the homosexual age of consent. In a reshuffle in 1976, Callaghan appointed Horam a junior minister in the Department for Transport, serving under Bill Rodgers, who would become one of the leaders of the breakaway SDP. There he began piloting legislation through the Commons to make seatbelts compulsory (a measure lost in the calling of the 1979 general election that brought Margaret Thatcher to power) and presided over the widening of a stretch of the M1. After the election defeat, Horam, like others on the right of the party, grew increasingly disenchanted with Labour’s leftward drift and, while he served in Denis Healey’s shadow Treasury team, he left the frontbench after Michael Foot became leader. He was the first MP to join the Gang of Four’s Council for Social Democracy in January 1981 and was one of the first 13 to join the SDP two months later. His constituency was abolished in a parliamentary reorganisation and when he fought Newcastle Central in the 1983 election came only third.

citation.title: Lord Horam obituary

text:
Lord Horam obituary

By the mid-80s, Horam was continuing his political journey. The SDP, he declared, was becoming increasingly like a mark 2 Labour party: higher spending, higher taxation and an incomes policy, “a botched job – Labour without the loonies”. The Tories beckoned and, after discreet talks with Thatcher and Norman Tebbit, the party chairman, in March 1987, drawn by their “sensible and realistic economic strategy which was showing signs of success”, Horam announced he was joining them. David Owen, the SDP leader, said he was sad but relaxed about the defection. Although it was too late to find a seat for that year’s general election, Horam was back in 1992 as MP for the Conservative suburban London constituency of Orpington. In 1995, Major appointed him junior minister for public services and science, and eight months later moved him to the Department of Health. Still contrary, he had spoken out against the imposition of VAT on fuel and joined early Tory opponents of the euro.

citation.title: Lord Horam obituary

text:
Lord Horam obituary

The Tories’ defeat in 1997 ended his ministerial career and he subsequently served as chairman of the Commons’ environmental audit committee, as a member of the foreign affairs select committee and on the backbenchers’ 1922 Committee. He retired from the Commons at the 2010 general election and was given a peerage three years later. Horam was married twice, in 1977 to Iris Crawley and, after their divorce, in 1987 to Judith Jackson, a former Guardian and Sunday Times motoring correspondent. She survives him, together with her two sons, Lincoln and Fraser, from an earlier relationship. • John Horam, Lord Horam, politician, born 7 March 1939; died 24 July 2026

text:
Poverty and weariness in Nigel Farage’s Clacton

I live in the Clacton constituency, in one of the surrounding villages, some distance from the town, and I agree with Sarah Elizabeth Cox’s characterisation of the town (Farage has turned Clacton into a human zoo. Here’s the truth about what’s happening here, 12 August). When I go to Clacton to take my kids to the beach or to the cinema, there is a sudden shift in the character of the area. The deprivation radiates in some streets. It is painful to see the residents so keenly in need of a decent MP to offer genuine support for a town with so many problems being exploited by Nigel Farage. I have worked my way through a number of podcasts and news articles during this byelection and the 2024 general election campaigns. Those cherrypicked vox pops and even the broader and more balanced reporting speak of poverty and weariness in the Clacton population. Is it any wonder that a charismatic man offering a simple answer to complex problems is held on to so tightly? Vanessa Scanlan Great Bentley, Essex • So Nigel Farage couldn’t attend his election results because of security concerns – despite the £5m he was given for his security.

Blimey, Clacton must be dangerous. Leila Roberts Ripon, North Yorkshire • The Clacton byelection’s rash of joke candidates has been pretty much passed off by every media outlet as just another example of the “British sense of humour”, originating more or less from the frivolous establishment of the Official Monster Raving Loony Party in 1982. However, I am sufficiently old enough to recall that amid the laughter, anxious voices warned then that this could also fuel a debasement of the serious importance of politics and government in the UK. A case can be made that the far right’s rise in the UK has been partly fuelled by the way that politics has been reduced to a joke by such allegedly harmless shenanigans, which in fact implicitly or openly rely on reducing mainstream politics to the status of uniformly useless – “they are all the same”. text:
Things get even more tricky for Dicky Tice, the Reform deputy with lots of cash but zero self-awareness

These are the doggiest of dog days. Times when hours turn into days and almost nothing happens in between. Days of precious R&R, when only a few politicians venture out, and then only to fend off accusations they are doing next to nothing and prove they are still alive. Much like the rest of us. The silliest days of the silly season. Days that are made for men like Richard Tice. There are some politicians who have the gift of sounding as if they know what they are talking about. There are those who you suspect are bullshitting but still give the benefit of the doubt. Then there are the ones you only have to look at to know they are completely clueless in every way. Never within the same postcode as plausibility. A walking miracle because somehow they have managed to persuade their party association and constituency voters that what they really need is someone who is visibly dim and incompetent. August gives us space to celebrate these men and women. None more so than Dicky. The apex male of stupidity. The idiot’s idiot. It’s not clear if there has ever been much point to Dicky.

Things get even more tricky for Dicky Tice, the Reform deputy with lots of cash but zero self-awareness

Other than to encourage other halfwits that they can make half a name for themselves in public life providing they are blessed with plenty of cash and a total absence of self-awareness. Dicky likes to moan about diversity, equality and inclusion policies while remaining totally oblivious to the fact that were life to be a genuine meritocracy, he wouldn’t even make it to the starting line. But that’s not to say Dicky doesn’t have his uses. A man with no idea of his own limitations could be just what Nigel Farage was looking for. The perfect beta supplicant who could be relied upon to do whatever he was told. Just as long as the instructions were crystal clear. There were no complaints from Dicky when just before the 2024 general election, Nige decided he was going to be Reform party leader after all. Dicky knew his place. He smiled like the Mr Congeniality he hoped to be. Life was going quite well up until the Guardian revealed the £5m gift to Nige from Thai crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne.

Then the Sunday Times got in on the act with its reporting that if Farage became leader, Reform would repay or write off loans it received from Tice’s company in a deal presented by Farage and convicted fraudster George Cottrell. Things really began to fall apart. The last few months haven’t been kind either to Reform or Dicky. One misstep after another. The party has been sliding in the polls, has called a byelection in Clacton which achieved little more than delaying an investigation by the parliamentary watchdog and handing 9,500 votes to a man with a bin on his head. As for Nige, he’s chosen to keep a much lower profile ever since he failed to come up with a plausible explanation for why he needed so much money. Reform have needed someone to step up and fill the vacuum left by Nige and the only one who has been consistently available has been Tice. Their combative home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf has been sidelined, Lee Anderson has kept a low profile and the others don’t really count. Nige had high hopes for Robert Jenrick but Reform’s ratings plummet every time Honest Bob makes an appearance. Which may be why Dicky was sent out with Honest Bob on Monday to try and dilute the animosity. Only it didn’t quite work out as Dicky rather stole Jenrick’s thunder. Because what people took away from Reform’s press conference wasn’t that Dicky would quite like benefits claimants to clean the high streets, it was that Dicky was thoroughly enjoying the extreme hot weather. You could either get all doom and gloom about it. Or you could pretend it wasn’t really an issue, that attempts to combat it were a complete waste of time and try to make the most of it. text:
Swedish MP intervenes in ‘damaging’ Brexit row over elderly Britons ordered to leave

The deportation and removal of British citizens from Sweden over Brexit residency rights is damaging relations with the UK amid efforts to improve links with London, a Swedish MP has said. Håkan Svenneling, representative for Värmland, where a 78-year-old British widow, Joyce Thomas, has been given four weeks to leave Sweden after 21 years of residency, has written to the migration minister, Johan Forssell, asking what he “intends to do to stop the deportations”. Sevenneling, who is an opposition MP for the left, is to meet Thomas on Wednesday, exactly a week after she was told her appeal had failed over the removal order. Thomas told the Guardian: “I am in shock. I feel sick. An individual’s life is at stake at my age. It is hell. I have done nothing wrong.” The retired nurse moved to Sweden with her financier husband, to be closer to one of their sons and their grandchildren, when she was 57.

citation.title: Swedish MP intervenes in ‘damaging’ Brexit row over elderly Britons ordered to leave

text:
Swedish MP intervenes in ‘damaging’ Brexit row over elderly Britons ordered to leave

Her husband, who died of cancer in 2023, did all the administrative work in the household, but both Thomas and her friends have said repeatedly they checked if they had to complete any forms to remain in the country after Brexit, and were told they did not. Thomas made a late application to remain in Sweden in 2023, just weeks after they returned from the UK, but missing the deadline of 31 December 2021. She and her friends testify that her husband checked whether Brexit was going to affect their residency and they were told they did not need to do anything. Thomas, who is self sufficient and is not drawing benefit from the Swedish state, has spoken of the “hell” she is now in with the threat of imminent removal, separating her from her family, strong network of friends, and her husband’s grave. Svenneling says in his letter to Forssell that Britons lawfully in Sweden before the UK’s exit from the EU would see their “existing residency rights continue to apply” under the withdrawal agreement (W/A).

“It was not intended to result in elderly people who had lived in Sweden for decades losing their rights to remain because of a missed deadline or deficiencies in their application [to stay],” he said. Svenneling’s written parliamentary question adds to growing pressure on the prime minister, Ulf Kristersson’s, centre-right minority coalition to address increasing concerns over the way Sweden is implementing the EU-UK withdrawal agreement, an international, legally binding, treaty. “The United Kingdom has long been an important partner for Sweden in a wide range of areas. It is clear that the deportations now taking place are damaging bilateral relations between Sweden and the United Kingdom,” Svenneling said. He raised the case of Thomas, but also of another elderly Briton, Horace (George) Mason, 74, who has dementia and Parkinson’s and is in full-time care. Thomas moved to Sweden 25 years ago to be closer to his son Carl and his grandchildren. He, too, was given four weeks to leave.

His family tried a second legal route for him to remain in Sweden, arguing he had rights, under the European conventionon human rights, to stay close to family on whom he relied. text:
Can Andy Burnham rewire the ‘Treasury brain’ to boost growth?

Andy Burnham is far from the first prime minister to dream of taming the power of the mighty Treasury. Boris Johnson all but forced the resignation of Sajid Javid by handpicking his team; Margaret Thatcher favoured her economic adviser Alan Walters over Nigel Lawson, prompting the latter’s furious resignation; and Tony Blair and Gordon Brown’s power struggle was the stuff of Whitehall legend. Burnham’s approach harks further back still to Labour prime minister Harold Wilson’s Department for Economic Affairs (DEA), a short-lived attempt to bring long-term thinking to British economic policymaking. Related: Rising inflation underlines scale of Andy Burnham’s cost of living challenge The PM made the historical analogy as he gave fresh details this week of his plan to take control of growth policy from the Treasury and hand it to a new No 10 department in Manchester.

citation.title: Can Andy Burnham rewire the ‘Treasury brain’ to boost growth?

text:
Can Andy Burnham rewire the ‘Treasury brain’ to boost growth?

The DEA was responsible for drawing up a national plan for the economy, which began with the timeless exhortation: “We must pay our way in the world and produce more wealth inside this country.” The baleful influence of the Treasury, with its stranglehold over the public finances, has long been lamented by leftwingers, who accuse it of short-term thinking and ingrained, institutional caution. “The dual job of growth and control of the public finances sometimes clouds the growth mission,” Burnham told the Times. “Having No 10 leading on that growth mission means you’ve got maximum power to unlock the blockages where they exist in the Whitehall system.” Some of the most criticised decisions of Keir Starmer’s tenure were seen by many Labour MPs as resulting from this “Treasury brain” – from slashing winter fuel allowance to caving in to City lobbying on a bank windfall tax. Burnham hopes the new prime minister’s department, overseen by his powerful cabinet ally Louise Haigh, will open the space for some fresh thinking. “The new No 10 North innovation is more significant than people realise,” he said.

citation.title: Can Andy Burnham rewire the ‘Treasury brain’ to boost growth?

text:
Can Andy Burnham rewire the ‘Treasury brain’ to boost growth?

Burnham’s route to growth runs through devolution One of the few detailed policy publications the new cabinet has so far produced was on radical plans for devolution. The PM hopes handing additional powers to metro mayors will help bring together growth policies now scattered across Whitehall. Ruth Curtice, director of the Resolution Foundation thinktank and a former longtime Treasury official, says coordinating across these different policy areas – housing, education, planning and so on – could be the most effective use of the new Manchester-based unit. “No one department has all of the levers – the Treasury don’t own all of the levers,” she says. “I would see it as a positive thing that this No 10 says, ‘Given what a priority this is, we’re going to put more force behind it.’” Former Brown adviser Michael Jacobs, emeritus professor of political economy at the University of Sheffield, draws a comparison with the Office for Climate Change, which helped to coordinate policy across government.

citation.title: Can Andy Burnham rewire the ‘Treasury brain’ to boost growth?

text:
Can Andy Burnham rewire the ‘Treasury brain’ to boost growth?

Related: Andy Burnham calls on wider society to help end rough sleeping by Christmas “The really interesting version of this to me would be a new growth unit, drawing on and made up of officials from all the relevant departments.” Sanjay Raja, chief UK economist at Deutsche Bank, points out that Burnham’s pick for chancellor, John Healey, was instrumental in the creation of regional development agencies, way back in the Blair-Brown era. These were meant to bring a regional dimension to growth and industrial policy – but were scrapped by the 2010 Conservative-Lib Dem coalition. George Osborne went on to create and empower city region mayors as the focus for devolution. Given the pair’s joint interest in devolution, Raja argues that far from clipping Healey’s wings, “this is one of the more merged tag teams in No 10 and No 11 that we have seen”. Treasury power is inescapable Yet not everyone is convinced that it makes sense to create a policy counterweight to the Treasury.

citation.title: Can Andy Burnham rewire the ‘Treasury brain’ to boost growth?

text:
Can Andy Burnham rewire the ‘Treasury brain’ to boost growth?

Former Conservative chief secretary to the Treasury David Gauke says the Treasury’s control over tax and spend, which it will maintain under the shake-up, means it is inevitably powerful. “The Treasury is always going to be the most important department.” Indeed, he suspects stripping growth out of the Treasury’s remit would just exaggerate its tendency to fixate on penny-pinching. He also questions whether No 10 North can work: “You’re going to have this office, which will get at best a day a week of face-time with the PM, and little access to other ministers – and it will be trying to push the government in a more pro-growth direction.” A Treasury source stresses that, as the initial government announcement said, No 10 North will focus on “local growth”, and in particular devolution – rather than taking over economic strategy from No 11. The Treasury has “lent” a small number of staff to the new unit, while its second permanent secretary, Beth Russell, who was instrumental in the creation of the Treasury’s own northern outpost, the Darlington Economic Campus, has been working closely with the Manchester team.

citation.title: Can Andy Burnham rewire the ‘Treasury brain’ to boost growth?

text:
Can Andy Burnham rewire the ‘Treasury brain’ to boost growth?

More civil servants are being transferred from other departments, including housing and local government, and former Times journalist Sam Lister has been appointed as No 10 North’s director. However, Whitehall veterans point to the new department’s relatively modest resources thus far. Jonathan Portes, a former senior government economist and now professor at King’s College London, says the most important question, as Burnham’s new arrangements bed in, will be how the inevitable policy clashes will be resolved. “What happens when No 10 wants to do something, and Treasury says no – or says, ‘yes, we’ll pay lip service to this but don’t expect any spending to go along with it’?” he says. “That has been the historic response of the Treasury when No 10 has got more powerful.” Hannah Peaker, deputy chief executive of the New Economics Foundation thinktank, says the priority should be ensuring economic decision-makers – including the Treasury and No 10, but also the Bank of England and the Office for Budget Responsibility – work better together.

citation.title: Can Andy Burnham rewire the ‘Treasury brain’ to boost growth?

text:
Can Andy Burnham rewire the ‘Treasury brain’ to boost growth?

“While a more devolved approach could help accelerate regional growth, the most important remedy is better coordination between economic institutions so that they are all pulling in the same direction.” Will No 10 North open the space for more radicalism? In an article for the progressive Renewal journal earlier this year, Haigh complained of the Treasury that, “faced with the dual mandate of maintaining fiscal control and supporting economic growth, the institution defaults toward caution, prioritising near-term debt dynamics over longer-term economic outcomes”. In the run-up to Burnham’s bid for power, he appeared to suggest large-scale renationalisation of public utilities and radical tax reform would be on his agenda – alongside the long-promised shake-up of social care. But some of these ambitious and potentially costly plans are likely to come into sharp conflict with the institutional caution Haigh identified.

citation.title: Can Andy Burnham rewire the ‘Treasury brain’ to boost growth?

text:
Can Andy Burnham rewire the ‘Treasury brain’ to boost growth?

With a critical budget fast approaching, the new cabinet – north and south – faces a string of decisions on tax and spend; and other key choices loom, including on how to shape the future of the beleaguered privatised water industry. In the run-up to the last two Labour budgets, debate was dominated by the immediate challenges for fiscal policy, often played out noisily in public against a backdrop of febrile government bond markets. Burnham clearly hopes to shape a different debate, both inside and outside government, but the historic precedent he highlighted, in the Wilson era, underlines the difficulties of reining in the Treasury. Wilson’s temperamental secretary of state for economic affairs, George Brown, moved on after two years, by which time the national plan had been blown way off course. His role was then downgraded so it was no longer a cabinet position and, by 1969, the experiment with a separate Department for Economic Affairs was over – and its powers had been sucked back into the Treasury.

Labour ‘could lose up to 50 seats’ to Greens if new drilling in North Sea approved

Labour could lose dozens of seats to the Green party if the government allows new drilling in the North Sea, according to internal research shared with the Guardian. Green party analysis suggests up to 50 Labour MPs, including Andy Burnham’s key ally Louise Haigh, could lose their seats at the next election if the government fails to make urgent climate action a priority or allows new drilling for oil and gas in the North Sea. The research found that voters in these key Labour v Green seats want bold action to tackle the climate crisis, which has contributed to record heatwaves, devastating wildfires and crippling droughts this summer in the UK – and say Labour MPs will pay the price if the demands are not met. Rachel Millward, a deputy leader of the Green party, said: “If Labour won’t be swayed by the science or the moral imperative to leave all fossil fuels in the ground, perhaps they will listen to the polling.

Last month, Burnham – who has been tight lipped about the climate crisis since tacking office – said he would be “pragmatic” about oil and gas and that decisions on new drilling would be made “in due course”. “The question isn’t whether Britain will still be using oil and gas, the question is where does it come from,” he said. Many Labour MPs are increasingly worried about how support for expanded drilling will play with an electorate alarmed by the worst drought since 1976, record heatwaves, wildfires, and climate-related food inflation and potential supply shortages.

Reform politicians are such a joke, they deserve a slot on the Edinburgh fringe

You would need to have a heart of stone not to fall about laughing. There was a time not so long ago when Reform could give a passable impression of a vaguely functional political party. One that knew its audience and had learned how to get its message across through the media. Admittedly this was largely because the party was a one-man band with all its MPs accepting that they owed their entire existence to Nige. They were satellites to his sun. Nigel Farage was Reform, and Reform was Nige. In recent months, though, things have been falling apart and Reform now resembles an anarchic end-of-the-pier clown show. And chaos has seldom been this entertaining. The fun started when Nige had an uncharacteristic fit of humility and tried to pretend he was only a first among equals with the grandiose announcement of a “shadow cabinet” of four people. Largely because that’s about as many serious politicians as he had at his disposal. The trouble with this was the country took one look at Robert Jenrick, Suella Braverman, Richard Tice and Zia Yusuf and thought it must be a joke. Was that really it?

The idea of any of them in charge of a government department was genuinely terrifying. And Zia can’t even get elected as an MP. It’s doubtful any Reform constituency association wants anything to do with him. He’s a man whom people dislike on sight – it saves time that way – and who appeared to have been admitted to the Reform elite only because he had a lot of money that he was prepared to give to the party. That was just the start, though. Then came the money troubles. The £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne that Nige has never satisfactorily managed to explain. Other than as the going rate for a lifestyle most of his Clacton constituents could only dream of. There were also the financial transactions that originated from Posh George and his mum that were deemed worthy of investigation for money laundering. Hardly the stuff of the man of the people. As for Nige’s decision to call a diversionary byelection, that too has backfired spectacularly. Beating a man with a bin on his head was hardly sticking it to the establishment.

Montgomerie was about as loyal to Reform as someone who defected from the Tories a while ago could be. Which is to say, he was as close to being a loyalist as you can get. He actually believes in what the party is doing, rather than using it for career advancement. Though, for a bright man, Tim has been extraordinarily dim. When Nige says he wants to test his ideas, what he actually has in mind is a few emails from Tim telling him how marvellous he is. What has Burnham promised since he became PM, and when will it happen?

Andy Burnham has floated a number of policies, ideas and ambitions for his government since becoming prime minister, from shifting power out of Westminster, bringing services under public control and addressing the rising cost of living. But many of his promises are not actually firm commitments, so what has he pledged, how much will it cost and when should the public expect change? Cutting VAT from household electricity bills On his second day as prime minister, Burnham promised to scrap VAT on household electricity bills from October. He announced the immediate tax cut to help ease cost-of-living pressures. The government said the move would reduce the average household’s electricity bill by £45, though the actual saving could depend on how much each household used. Burnham said it would be funded by ending Keir Starmer’s digital ID scheme, which would have cost the government £1.8bn over three years.

citation.title: What has Burnham promised since he became PM, and when will it happen?

text:
What has Burnham promised since he became PM, and when will it happen?

Darren Jones, the former chief secretary to Starmer when he was PM, claimed the money for the digital ID scheme was still unfunded, however, and said Burnham would have to set out how he would pay for his new policies at the budget. £2 bus fares Single bus fares across England will be capped at £2 from January, down £1 from the current maximum, which reverses the increase Starmer and the former chancellor Rachel Reeves put in place in 2024. The cap will last until the end of 2027 and excludes London. It is expected to cost £454m, and ministers have said money has been allocated for devolved governments to make similar moves. About £400m will come from switching investment in international climate finance to loans, and the rest from savings in the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero’s budget. Experts have raised concerns that Burnham’s decision to use the aid budget to pay for cheaper bus fares in England will leave the world’s most vulnerable people at risk, especially those facing the most severe impacts of the climate crisis.

What has Burnham promised since he became PM, and when will it happen?

End rough sleeping in England by Christmas Burnham has made tackling homelessness a central policy for his government. Although he did not say he would completely end rough sleeping by Christmas, he said everyone sleeping rough would be offered a route off the streets. “We’re putting £442m behind a national drive to get everyone in for Christmas,” Burnham wrote in the Guardian, of which £102m will pay for medical care and addiction support, while £340m from existing housing budgets over the next three years will be used to get more people into accommodation and settled housing. The prime minister said he had not set a target for how much rough sleeping would fall, but instead said real progress must have been made by Christmas, because officials acknowledge they are not able to force people into accommodation they don’t want. Free 24-hour bus travel for disabled people Disabled people in England will be able to use their bus passes at any time of the day, seven days a week, from April 2027.

Burnham changed the entitlement from its current form – between 9.30am to 11pm on weekdays – so that disabled peoplewon’t lose out on free travel if they need to leave earlier for work or appointments. The government committed £60m to pay for the change, and has delayed the implementation of the policy until next spring so local authorities have time to change their current arrangements and the government has time to amend legislation. West Midlands bus network under public control Burnham has backed moves for the West Midlands Combined Authority to bring its bus network under public control, announcing an extra £11.5m over three years of new funding to help it manage the change. The money will pay for legal advice, staff and IT systems as the network changes hands. Burnham said about 4,800 jobs would be protected, and 750 buses a day would be kept running during the transition. The cost of the deal is still being ironed out, but the government is separately giving the authority more than £2bn over five years for zero-emission buses.

Racism and sexism have become normalised in Britain, says equalities minister

Racism and sexism have become normalised in Britain, the equalities minister has said, as she warned that young men were being sucked into violent misogyny by the “cesspit” of social media. Bridget Phillipson said she was increasingly worried about how commonplace misogyny and racism had become, fuelled by online interactions and statements by politicians she said would not have been acceptable a few years ago. She accused senior MPs from Reform and the Conservatives of having made racist statements in recent years, and accused the police of not taking violence against women and girls seriously enough. Speaking to the Guardian’s Politics Weekly podcast, she said: “I worry that we are at kind of a ground zero in terms of attitudes around violence against women and girls. Things that not very long ago felt totally unacceptable are becoming normal.

I think we’re seeing that in terms of attitudes towards women, and I think we see that in terms of attitudes around racism.” She accused the shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, and Reform’s economic spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, of having made racist statements in recent years. Earlier this year, Timothy called Muslims praying in Trafalgar Square an “act of domination”, while Jenrick came under fire in October after the Guardian revealed he had complained he “didn’t see another white face” on a trip to an area of Birmingham. “We’ve had pretty despicable things that the likes of Robert Jenrick have said in the past on his visit to Birmingham,” she said. “We had Nick Timothy, who said some appalling things about Muslim prayer. “Apparently I’m calling him names when I say that’s racist. Reform’s new economic adviser has called for end of pensioners’ triple lock

Reform UK’s new economic adviser has previously called the pensions triple lock unsustainable, advocated privatising the NHS and welcomed migration as a poverty alleviation tool, the Guardian can reveal. Robert Jenrick, Reform’s economic spokesperson, has appointed Mitchell Palmer, a rightwing economist at the free-market Adam Smith Institute, as one of his key aides. Palmer’s background is as a champion of economic liberalism, in many cases putting him to the right of Reform’s existing policy platform. His appointment comes amid tensions within the party between those who want to lean into its tax-cutting agenda and those who worry that steep cuts to welfare and other government spending will alienate voters. Palmer has previously called for the abolition of the triple lock, arguing it is an expensive and unsustainable way to protect pensioners.

Keir Starmer’s former chief of staff has lifted the lid on how “unbearable” it was working in No 10, revealing she feared her conversations were being recorded by colleagues seeking to leak her remarks to the media. Sue Gray, who was the most powerful adviser in Downing Street before her resignation in 2024, was highly critical of the working environment under Starmer, saying she was “disappointed” that he did not act on her concerns about staff briefing journalists against her. In an interview with the Political Currency podcast, shared with the Guardian, she gave her first major analysis of the extreme tensions in the early days of Starmer’s operation, providing an insight into the culture of what has been called a “boys’ club” operating with Downing Street. In the weeks before Gray quit, Starmer was accused of having lost control of his senior team after a series of acrimonious leaks to the media about his chief of staff’s pay being higher than that of the prime minister and her apparently difficult relationships with senior colleagues.

Burnham to dispatch 100 Whitehall officials to help regional mayors

Andy Burnham is to send more than 100 Whitehall officials to bolster the teams of regional mayors, after convening leaders from across England from his base at No 10 North to discuss how to spread growth. The government described the meeting as a “situation room” to bring local and regional leaders into national decision-making. After the call led by Burnham, the government said five to 10 civil servants would be sent to every mayoral authority for secondments of less than a year during a pilot programme in 18 mayoralties. Mayors requested the extra capacity at the first meeting of Burnham’s National Economic Council at the end of last month. There will also be a new civil service fast stream pilot in Yorkshire and Humber, and an expansion of the future leaders scheme, which trains high performers in the civil service, to mayoral and local authority officials. Burnham said his No 10 North office was “bringing together mayors from different political parties to work on these challenges, because people deserve problem-solving rather than point-scoring”.

Deselected candidate claims Lib Dems’ religious discrimination cost him £790,000

How much is a career in politics worth? The Liberal Democrats, despite admitting claims of religious discrimination, say about £22,800. A former Lib Dem candidate claims £790,000. It is a question before the Central London county court after David Campanale argued that discrimination against his Christianity cost him his political career in a civil case against the party. Campanale, a former BBC journalist, was selected in 2021 as the party’s candidate for Sutton and Cheam, but was removed in August 2023. The Liberal Democrats have admitted claims of direct and indirect discrimination on grounds of religion or belief under the Equality Act and their failure to deal with complaints Campanale made about his treatment, leaving the amount of damages to be determined by the court. Campanale’s schedule of loss, seen by the Guardian, puts his claim at £788,740.75, including interest. It seeks compensation for injury to feelings, aggravated damages, past and future earnings, the loss of an MP’s pension, counselling costs and the “loss of a chance”, or “loss of political capital”.

UK reports unexpected deficit of £1.8bn as John Healey prepares for first budget

The UK government ran a larger-than-expected £1.8bn deficit in July, underlining the challenges facing the chancellor, John Healey, as he draws up his first budget. City economists had expected a shortfall of zero for July, a month when Treasury receipts tend to be swollen by self-assessment income tax payments. At £17.1bn, the self-assessment tax paid in July was £1.7bn higher than the same month last year. But the Office for National Statistics said the government still ran the £1.8bn deficit, as “spending growth outpaced receipts”. In the first four months of this financial year the cumulative deficit was £56.7bn – lower than last year but still £2.3bn ahead of the figure forecast by the Office for Budget Responsibility. Healey will deliver his budget on 28 October. The public finances are expected to be gloomier than forecast at Rachel Reeves’s spring statement in March, when the Iran war had only just begun.

Moves in global bond markets in recent days have pushed up the yield – in effect the interest rate – on government bonds, creating a fresh headache for the chancellor. Martin Beck, chief economist at the consultancy WPI Strategy, said: “Ten-year gilt yields are above 5%, reflecting energy-related inflation concerns, and these will gradually feed through into a larger debt-interest bill as existing debt is refinanced. At the same time, the government faces pressure to loosen inherited spending plans, meet unfunded defence commitments and deliver on its own ambitions for housing, infrastructure and public services.” The UK’s large debt pile means small moves in interest rates can be costly over time. Andy Burnham says he wants to bring men’s World Cup back to UK in 2042

Andy Burnham has said he wants to bring the men’s World Cup to the UK in 2042, returning the tournament to Britain for the first time in almost eight decades. During informal discussions at No 10 North in Manchester on Friday, the prime minister told regional mayors he was keen for the tournament to be played in the British Isles. The World Cup took place in England in 1966, when the home side beat West Germany 4-2 in the final after extra time – the only time the country has either hosted or won the contest. Burnham, a keen football fan who has a season ticket at Everton, said earlier this month that it was “insane” only one World Cup had been held anywhere in the UK. Related: England’s 1966 World Cup heroes were fun, humble and unlike today’s stars It is understood an application to stage the competition could also involve other home nations, none of which have hosted any World Cup games. In recent years, joint bids between countries for major football tournaments have become more common.

Alongside the Republic of Ireland, England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland will host the men’s European championships in 2028. Work has not yet begun on any official bid for the 2042 event but it is understood Downing Street would support the FA should it choose to pursue it. Sources say Burnham has “broad aspirations” and “a general ambition” to bring more major footballing events to the UK. England made a doomed bid to host the 2018 World Cup, which was awarded to Russia amid allegations of corruption. In 2014, while serving in the shadow cabinet, Burnham said he was uncomfortable that the tournament was still allowed to take place in Russia after its annexation of Crimea. ‘We fear lessons will not be learned’: Chloe Moffat’s parents on their fight to hold Treasury to account

When a coroner ruled this month that the Treasury “materially contributed” to Chloe Moffat’s death, her parents breathed out in bittersweet relief. For a year, David and Anne Moffat had been forced to become detectives in the worst case any parent could have to solve: why their daughter took her own life. Chloe, 26, went to her job as a personal assistant at the Treasury on a Monday last May “happy as Larry” after a weekend she’d told her friends was a “10 out of 10”. She was planning a holiday with her sister, Alice, and arranging for friends to come for a dinner party the next weekend. She was, according to her father, living “the best life”. That afternoon, however, she was sent to a surprise disciplinary meeting with her manager and her manager’s manager, which the coroner found left her distressed and convinced she was going to lose her job. The following morning, Chloe was dead. Anne, 64, who is retired and used to work as the head of care at a children’s hospice, said: “When she first did it, we had to question Chloe.

citation.title: ‘We fear lessons will not be learned’: Chloe Moffat’s parents on their fight to hold Treasury to account

text:
‘We fear lessons will not be learned’: Chloe Moffat’s parents on their fight to hold Treasury to account

We had to question what might have driven Chloe to this.” She paused, and David added: “Criminality? Fraud? All sorts of things. Because why would somebody take their own life if they were the person that we expected?” Anne interjected: “Are they on drugs? Are they in debt? Everything. And so we searched and questioned our own daughter.” None of this was the case. After trawling through emails, talking to Chloe’s friends and colleagues and holding the Treasury to account in a gruelling, multi-day coroner’s court hearing, they found out their daughter had been mistreated by her employer. “After our investigations, it was clear it was literally that one-to-one meeting,” Anne said. “Chloe never recovered. She walked out of that meeting absolutely destroyed and never recovered and went down a black hole.” Speaking from their house in the French Alps, which they bought to be near Alice, who lives there and recently had a daughter, the couple seem exhausted.

citation.title: ‘We fear lessons will not be learned’: Chloe Moffat’s parents on their fight to hold Treasury to account

text:
‘We fear lessons will not be learned’: Chloe Moffat’s parents on their fight to hold Treasury to account

If the Moffats had not fought their daughter’s case, it is likely the coroner would have explained Chloe’s death with one word: suicide. Instead, she made a narrative finding, explaining the circumstances that led up to the death and laying blame partly at the Treasury’s door. Since that finding two weeks ago, the Moffats have had no contact from the Treasury to offer condolences or an apology. “Now that the inquest has said that the coroner has found them responsible for Chloe’s death, we would have expected for them to have written to us,” David said. Chloe was described as cheerful, popular and funny, and a person who took her job seriously. “I think Chloe was always looking to serve,” David said. Anne added: “I didn’t realise, but people like Chloe, who are bright, confident perfectionists, when they’re given a piece of shocking news such as they might lose their job, can be very vulnerable.” The young woman was blindsided after being presented with anonymous complaints that she had shared confidential information at work, which she denied.

citation.title: ‘We fear lessons will not be learned’: Chloe Moffat’s parents on their fight to hold Treasury to account

text:
‘We fear lessons will not be learned’: Chloe Moffat’s parents on their fight to hold Treasury to account

She was not reassured that her job was safe even though she was unlikely to be dismissed, or offered a third party in the meeting to give her support or advice. “If Chloe had known that it shouldn’t have happened, if she’d known her rights, she could have walked in and said: ‘I’m not having this meeting’, and walked out. But of course she didn’t. She didn’t know that, she was a people pleaser,” David said. The coroner found Chloe was denied her rights at work, such as being told what the likely outcome of the disciplinary process would have been, which was a written warning, and that she could bring a supporter with her. Instead, she felt ambushed and was convinced she would lose the job she had worked so hard for. Anne said: “I don’t know about the original complaints about Chloe, if they were malicious or to bring her down a peg or two – she was a big personality in the office.” Her parents are considering suing the Treasury for wrongful death, particularly as they have had no response from the ministry since the finding.

text:
‘We fear lessons will not be learned’: Chloe Moffat’s parents on their fight to hold Treasury to account

“If that’s the only way we’re going to get recognition, it’s a possibility,” David said. The Treasury is obliged to give the coroner a response to the prevention of future deaths report she issued to the civil service. The coroner found there was a risk of further deaths at the Treasury because of how the department handled disciplinary cases. The department brought a team of lawyers to the inquest, who pushed for Chloe’s death to be recorded as an unexplained suicide. “We definitely want to be in touch with the Treasury because we do want Chloe remembered for the Chloe that she was,” Anne said. “And be that a bench in her name or whatever, but we want her to be remembered, but we do fear that she is going to be brushed under the carpet and lessons will not be learned.” Unusually for an inquest, the small, drab room in Surrey was full of young people in their early to mid-20s – Chloe’s friends and colleagues, who wept throughout. Those who attended from the Treasury were not given bereavement leave to attend the inquest into their friend’s death.

citation.title: ‘We fear lessons will not be learned’: Chloe Moffat’s parents on their fight to hold Treasury to account

text:
‘We fear lessons will not be learned’: Chloe Moffat’s parents on their fight to hold Treasury to account

“They didn’t get any time off from the Treasury or support for that horrible ordeal they had gone through,” Anne said. The couple said they hoped the Treasury acknowledged Chloe and issued a satisfactory response to the prevention of future deaths report, so this nightmarish chapter could be closed and they could begin to grieve. “We need to grieve. And I’m not sure that we have. I think the inquest has delayed that,” Anne said. David said: “The hole it’s left in our lives is just enormous. We’re only still coming to terms with that. Sometimes we don’t feel we can attend family events because we’ve got something missing. We are a tight-knit family, we’ve all holidayed together. But now we don’t have Chloe.” They said they hoped Chloe’s case could help prevent other parents from going through the same experience. And they wanted to remember their daughter as the grinning, popular, confident, adventurous woman she was. “We have got so many happy memories. So that’s what we have to be positive about,” Anne said. “I think: ‘At least she didn’t have cancer,’ you know, and suffer.

She was literally happy up until that meeting.” David said: “I think for sure we will continue to want to ensure that we spread the word of what we have learned from all this.” A Treasury spokesperson said: “Our deepest sympathies continue to be with Chloe’s family, and the department continues to mourn Chloe’s death. “We are taking all concerns extremely seriously and are considering the coroner’s findings carefully. We have introduced improvements to guidance, support and wellbeing arrangements but recognise we must continue to take action to prevent this happening again.” In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. Badenoch says Reform defectors ‘some of the most dishonest people I have met’

Kemi Badenoch has called defectors who left for Reform “some of the most dishonest people” she has ever met, as she ruled out allowing “drama queens” to return to the party. Speaking at the Edinburgh festival fringe, the Conservative party leader again ruled out any prospect of an election deal with Nigel Farage’s Reform UK, insisting there would be no coalition between the parties. “Reform has people who left the Conservative party, some of the most dishonest people I have ever met in my entire life,” Badenoch told event host Iain Dale on Saturday. Multiple current or former parliamentarians have joined Reform from the Conservatives, including the former home secretary Suella Braverman and the former shadow justice secretary Robert Jenrick. After being sacked by Badenoch for plotting against her, Jenrick called his former party “rotten” and “failed”. Hitting out at those such as Jenrick who defected, Badenoch said: “These are people who left us when we were at our lowest, many of them the people who caused the problems in the first place and then ran away and pretended they had nothing to do with it.
