Why should we have them back?” The Conservative leader said she doesn’t want “drama queens” in the party, adding that she’s not “entertaining” parliamentarians she has heard are having indirect approaches from previous defectors. Badenoch said Farage’s party “is all over the place” and suggested the party announces a policy and forgets it the following day. Before becoming prime minister last month, Andy Burnham ruled out the possibility of calling an early general election, with Labour having won a landslide majority in July 2024. Burnham to face pressure at Labour conference to recognise Israel’s actions in Gaza as genocide

Grassroots Labour groups are gearing up for a conference showdown with Andy Burnham over Gaza, as the party’s members seek to force the prime minister to recognise Israel’s actions as a genocide and impose a full arms embargo. Momentum, Labour & Palestine, the Campaign for Labour Party Democracy and Palestine Solidarity Campaign (PSC) plan to ramp up pressure on Burnham before his first Labour conference as prime minister next month. The groups are circulating a model motion for Labour members to submit to conference, demanding the government accepts the findings of a UN commission of inquiry that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza, and to impose “comprehensive sanctions”, including a full arms embargo. The motion also demands that ministers impose comprehensive sanctions and ban trade that “aids or assists” Israel’s military actions in Gaza or its unlawful presence in the occupied Palestinian territories, including trade with Israeli settlements. Burnham’s refusal to use the term genocide has caused frustration among many Labour MPs, not just those on the left of the party.

Several MPs told the Guardian they welcomed Burnham’s apology, but wanted him to go further and explicitly “acknowledge Israel’s actions in Gaza as a genocide”. Weeks before he became prime minister, Burnham told the Guardian: “We’ve got to do more to put pressure on the Israeli government … let’s be honest, the UK was too slow to call for a ceasefire. And we must now do more to strengthen our approach.” But he stopped short of describing what was happening on the ground in Gaza as a genocide, saying that while there was “increasing evidence” of war crimes, it was for the international courts to make that ruling. The UK government has signalled that further measures against Israel could be coming. Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, said ministers would set out a “comprehensive set of measures” after Israel moved ahead with its controversial E1 settlement plans in the occupied West Bank.

Sarah Burwin had pleaded on TikTok in July for Burnham not to work from the building in Manchester that day, which hosts the government’s northern headquarters and the city’s register office. text:
Lord Snape obituary

In his first speech at Westminster in March 1974, a month after being elected as the MP for the then newly created Midlands seat of West Bromwich East, Peter Snape, who has died aged 84, described his constituents as a “special brand” of people. They were, he said, forthright and honest, with a down-to-earth sense of humour – a portrayal which the ensuing 50 years of active membership of both houses of parliament would also prove to be an unwittingly precise description of Snape himself. Lord Snape, as he became in 2004, having stood down from the Commons at the preceding election in 2001, was someone who enhanced political life because he was clever and funny and sharp as a tack, but, much more importantly, because he spoke with the authentic voice of lived experience. He had worked on the railways and been a regular soldier in the army. He knew what he was talking about and he instinctively understood what mattered to the men and women on the streets of West Bromwich, or anywhere else in the industrialised landscape of urban Britain.

citation.title: Lord Snape obituary

text:
Lord Snape obituary

He was sometimes wrongly characterised as being on Labour’s rightwing, because he had no time for what he saw as the self-conscious showmanship and posturing of the party’s left (Tony Benn was a particular bugbear) which, in his view, would do little to improve the lives of working people. His was a rooted socialism, founded by a fundamental belief in fairness and equality. He was also a skilful political tactician, a natural for the Labour whips’ office, in which he served in the difficult days of the Wilson and Callaghan governments before 1979. On one occasion, he was profoundly shocked, when sitting on the government bench as the “duty whip” during a late-night debate, to be unexpectedly joined by the prime minister, James Callaghan, who asked him conversationally (and sotto voce) if he had ever thought of emigrating because “this country is finished”. Snape was still a relatively new and young MP and discreetly kept this exchange entirely private.

citation.title: Lord Snape obituary

text:
Lord Snape obituary

That he failed to become chief whip on the three occasions he stood in 1983, 1985 and 1990 for a post that was at that time elected by Labour MPs, was a personal disappointment and more a reflection on the internal politics of the parliamentary Labour party at the time than on his suitability for the office. He also stood unsuccessfully in 1988 for the role of deputy chief whip. Snape was 55 by the time Tony Blair took office in 1997 and was then apparently deemed not a good fit for the red-rose “new” Labour government, despite unwavering party loyalty. When he left the Commons – with what proved the correct expectation of a peerage – he was subsequently an exceedingly assiduous participant in Lords’ debates. Snape was “a proud son of Stockport”, in the words of the prime minister, Andy Burnham, who also said: “He was a good friend to me.” He was a lifelong supporter of Stockport County FC, of which he was a board member from 2010 until 2013. He was born in Stockport, the only child of Kathleen (nee Critchley) and Thomas Snape. His mother was a former laundry worker.

text:
Lord Snape obituary

His father was a railwayman, a carriage and wagon examiner, but did not meet his son until he returned from second world war service, bringing his boy a train set as a gift. In accordance with his mother’s faith, Peter was a pupil at Roman Catholic primary schools in Stockport, St Bede’s RC College, Manchester, and Dialstone secondary school in Bramhall, before leaving aged 15 to follow his father into the railways. He first became a trainee signalman, living in lodgings beside his signal box, Edgeley No 2, constructed in 1884 and still standing today, south of Stockport. When he failed to be given charge of the box after four years, he gave notice and joined the army four days later. He served with the Royal Engineers and then the Royal Corps of Transport from 1961 until 1967 before returning to the railways as a goods guard for three years and then in a clerical post. He was an active trade unionist in the National Union of Railwaymen, joined the Labour party and in 1971 was elected to Bredbury and Romiley urban district council (then a part of Stockport) where he served until elected to parliament.

text:
Lord Snape obituary

He was swiftly preferred as an MP, serving as a member of the Council of Europe and the Western European Union in 1975 before joining the whips’ office. He was a senior whip (1977-79), a junior defence spokesman (1979-82) and a home affairs spokesman for a year thereafter. Neil Kinnock then appointed Snape as a transport spokesman, where he remained as a useful and combative member of the frontbench throughout Kinnock’s years as leader, from 1983 until 1992. His streetwise political expertise was often called upon as a “minder” in parliamentary byelections and he travelled widely on parliamentary fact-finding missions. A natural raconteur, Snape could spin any incident into an anecdote. The former prime minister, John Major, recounts in his memoirs how, on a tour of the Middle East in 1982, an all-party group of MPs was caught in crossfire near Bethlehem and had to throw themselves underneath a vehicle. In this incident only Snape “entirely by chance, he claimed, found himself beside one of our attractive guides”.

When they met Yasser Arafat on the same trip, the Palestinian leader asked how he should address one of the Tory politicians, Richard Needham, who had explained that he was a half-Jewish, half-Irish earl. “Kneeling,” said Snape. “Kneeling.” Another much relished anecdote involved a disagreement with Sir Alf Sherman, an adviser to the Thatcher government and based at 10 Downing Street, who wrote to Snape demanding an apology for what he alleged was libel, defamation, impropriety and bias, and threatening legal action. Snape replied suggesting that “some ill-educated nutter has obviously stolen your notepaper”. He heard nothing more. He suffered a costly court case in 2009 when a newspaper attempted to entrap him as available for hire, purportedly as one of four peers prepared to support legislation in exchange for a fee. Snape was cleared by the privileges committee and successfully sued the Sunday Times, which paid a “substantial sum” towards his legal costs. He also engendered unfavourable publicity as a result of a share option he had acquired when an unpaid non-executive director of Travel West Midlands, a council-owned bus operator.

The company was then bought by National Express, giving Snape an estimated £70,000 profit on his shareholding. Snape married Winifred Grimshaw in 1963. The couple had two daughters and divorced in 1980. He subsequently married Janet Manley, a schoolteacher, in 2004; they separated and she died in 2024. In later years he found great happiness with Lynda Waltho (nee Abbott), the former MP for Stourbridge. text:
From welfare to prisons: the challenges for Burnham when MPs return to Commons

Andy Burnham has enjoyed a month-long honeymoon period since he became prime minister, winning public support with a series of popular but relatively low-cost announcements. They have included cutting VAT on electricity bills, reducing the cost of bus travel and reviewing business rates for small businesses. But as MPs prepare to return to the Commons in just over a week, the prime minister is about to face his first real challenge in office, as he makes a number of key decisions that could create enemies but define his premiership. The budget John Healey gives his first budget as chancellor on 28 October penned in by the same constraints that faced his predecessor, Rachel Reeves. Burnham and Healey have promised to stick to the fiscal rules set by Reeves, which means the government’s day-to-day budget must be forecast to be balanced in three years’ time. They have also promised not to raise income tax, national insurance or VAT, which gives the chancellor little room for manoeuvre if he wants to raise money for potentially expensive policies such as bringing utilities under public control.

citation.title: From welfare to prisons: the challenges for Burnham when MPs return to Commons

text:
From welfare to prisons: the challenges for Burnham when MPs return to Commons

Many Labour MPs want Healey to raise wealth or business taxes to help pay for the government’s promises, but Treasury officials say such a move will not raise large amounts of money. The economists Jim O’Neill and Andy Haldane, both of whom have advised Burnham in the past, have recently warned against raising taxes on the private sector. O’Neill said this weekend: “We need more genuine risk-taking and more entrepreneurs, and we need to boost these sort of green shoots of growth that are there.” Welfare spending Over the next few weeks, the prime minister will be presented with two significant reports into how the welfare system is working: one on disability benefits by the minister Stephen Timms, and another on youth employment by the former minister Alan Milburn. In his interim report, Timms said the current system of personal independence payments (Pip) was not working, but admitted that there would have to be some “challenging discussions” on how to fix it.

citation.title: From welfare to prisons: the challenges for Burnham when MPs return to Commons

text:
From welfare to prisons: the challenges for Burnham when MPs return to Commons

Keir Starmer’s attempts to cut £5bn from the Pip system backfired when Labour MPs rebelled en masse, forcing the government to drop the plans altogether, in what was arguably the beginning of the end of Starmer’s premiership. Charities are already gearing up to resist any attempt by Milburn and the government to cut benefits or place sanctions on young people who fail to find work. Migration Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, wants to make migrants wait longer before they are eligible for settled status, which allows them to claim benefits and access NHS services. Controversially among Labour MPs, she wants to apply these changes to people who are already in the country, alongside a series of other changes to the migration system, including forcibly deporting families who refuse to comply with removal orders. Mahmood has been consulting on some of her proposals, and has suggested that some people could be given shorter waiting times than others before qualifying for settled status.

text:
From welfare to prisons: the challenges for Burnham when MPs return to Commons

It will soon be up to Burnham whether to allow her proposals to remain largely intact or to demand exemptions for some workers such as those in the care system. Asked by the Sunday Times whether he had made a decision on that package, he replied: “Not yet, no.” Prisoner release Next month, 5,000 prisoners are due to be released early in an attempt to ease the pressure on overcrowded prisons in England and Wales. The plans have already been watered down after a public outcry prompted Burnham to exclude those convicted of rape, serious child sexual offences and grooming from the scheme. Britain will boost Ukraine’s capacity to make its own long-range missiles, Andy Burnham will announce on Monday, as he travels to Kyiv for the country’s independence day on his first foreign visit as prime minister. Burnham will arrive in the Ukrainian capital on Monday morning at a crucial time in the war, with Kyiv braced for another wave of Russian missile attacks and the country’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, facing his most direct domestic challenge. The UK prime minister will use the trip to announce that the UK government will allow the European defence company MBDA to declassify information about UK-made components of the Anglo-French Storm Shadow/Scalp missiles to help Ukraine build its own version. While the announcement will probably take years to have an impact on the war, it is likely to escalate tensions with Moscow at an already fraught moment in UK-Russian relations. Since moving into Downing Street in July, Andy Burnham – a foreign policy neophyte – has expressed strong support for Ukraine. But on Monday he saw the bitter human cost of the war up close for the first time, visiting Kyiv during his first international trip as prime minister. The occasion was the 35th anniversary of Ukraine’s independence. Volodymyr Zelenskyy gave awards to the families of fallen soldiers. Relatives wept, hugging Ukraine’s president. Photos of young men in their prime were shown on a giant screen. The setting was St Sophia cathedral in the old heart of the Ukrainian capital. Built in the 11th century, the building predates Moscow and is a symbol of Ukraine’s ancient statehood. Next to it were modern weapons used by Kyiv in its struggle against Russia, including quadcopter drones and unmanned land robots. In a speech in front of other western leaders, Burnham compared Ukraine’s fight to that waged by Britain during the darkest days of the second world war. “My nation kept the flame of European freedom alive in the 20th century, you hold that flame in the 21st,” he declared.

Photo of Disraeli among missing parliamentary works of art, FoI request finds

A photograph of Benjamin Disraeli, an engraved portrait of William Wilberforce and a cartoon of Barbara Castle have all been misplaced by the UK parliamentary authorities, a freedom of information (FoI) request has revealed. The Press Association has been given a list of more than 65 works of art that have been missing since 2024. They also include a photograph of Margaret Beckett, the UK’s first female foreign secretary and the first woman to lead Labour, and a satirical cartoon by Martin Rowson from the Conservative leadership battle of 1995. A parliamentary spokesperson said it was a working collection, which meant that objects moved around frequently. None of the works had been permanently written off, they said. The photograph of Disraeli, Queen Victoria’s favourite prime minister, was taken by John Jabez Edwin Mayall. Mayall was a prolific Victorian portrait photographer who captured the images of many of the era’s best-known figures.

Art UK, which catalogues Britain’s publicly owned art, lists 212 Mayall works in UK collections including portraits of Charles Dickens, Karl Marx, Isambard Kingdom Brunel, the soprano Anna Bishop, the scientist Michael Faraday and the explorer David Livingstone. Mayall also made a fortune photographing Victoria and the wider royal family with his carte de visite portraits feeding the 19th-century “cartomania” collecting craze. The misplaced Disraeli photograph is likely to be the same as one in other collections, including the Royal Collection, showing a tired, heavy-lidded Disraeli in his 60s. The missing print of Wilberforce, the most celebrated campaigner against the slave trade, was made by the printmaker William Holl and his brother Francis. The Rowson cartoon is from the 1995 Tory leadership campaign when John Major resigned as party leader, telling opponents to “put up or shut up”. It shows Major seeking to lance the literal “boil” of the contest, as his deputy Michael Heseltine and challenger-apparent Michael Portillo look on. Rowson said the issue of cartoons going missing was not uncommon.

Rupert Lowe, the leader of Restore Britain, is on course to earn as much from the social media platform X as he does from his salary as an MP, after surging income from posts that include demands for mass deportations. Lowe has earned £932 an hour for his posts on X, formerly Twitter, since the start of the year, according to his own declarations in the register of MPs’ financial interests, which detail how many hours he has spent on X for each payment he received from the platform. UK to use Ukraine battlefield data to train AI to protect sensitive sites

AI models trained on Ukrainian battlefield data will be used to stop protesters and foreign states targeting UK defence sites, railways and energy plants under a deal struck between London and Kyiv. Private companies will also be given access to the vast trove of data from Ukraine’s Avengers AI lab to help build new systems, the first agreement of its kind in the UK. The scheme will be piloted at a UK defence site, building a model to identify protesters or a hostile-state attack. It uses AI-optimised sensors in buried fibre-optic cables to detect different kinds of movement. The government has suggested the technology, if proven workable, could be used at airports, prisons, railways and energy infrastructure. The controversial proscription of the activist group Palestine Action was sparked after the group breached RAF Brize Norton on scooters last June, a highly embarrassing security lapse as a result of which the group was able to deface two military aircraft with spray paint before escaping the site without being detained.

Kemi Badenoch plotted with fellow Conservative cabinet ministers to remove Rishi Sunak as prime minister months before the general election, it has been claimed. Anthony Seldon, who has written political biographies of every prime minister since John Major, has alleged in a new book that Badenoch, who was business secretary at the time, phoned several other cabinet ministers to ask “if anyone was interested in changing the captain”. An ally of Badenoch, who is now the Conservative leader, described the claim as “total bollocks”. The book about Sunak’s time as prime minister, which is being serialised in the Independent, says Badenoch did not respect Sunak, who she believed had been rude to her. Citing a series of sources, it says she sought to oust Sunak in 2023, when he faced considerable internal pressure over migration policy. It quotes one Conservative MP, who the book says is now a member of Badenoch’s frontbench team, as saying she was “a menace who orchestrated trouble in the cabinet” under Sunak.

text:
Why do some Labour MPs want electoral reform and will it happen?

Andy Burnham is facing new pressure to act over electoral reform, with nearly 100 of his MPs backing a commission to decide on a route to replace the first-past-the-post voting system. Why is this an issue for Labour – and will anything happen? What is the official government view? Officially, no change. The 2024 Labour manifesto only discussed elections in terms of changes to ID rules and allowing 16- and 17-year-olds the vote. Before becoming prime minister, Burnham said he would not deviate from the manifesto. Unofficially, things are very different. Burnham is a longstanding supporter of electoral reform, which is also the view of his party. In 2022, the Labour conference voted overwhelmingly to support a proportional electoral system. A similar motion was only defeated the previous year after unions blocked it. It is also worth noting that voting varies. While Westminster elections are first past the post, elections to the Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish parliaments are proportional, while mayors are elected using supplementary vote, which gives a weight to second choices. Why is there renewed pressure?

citation.title: Why do some Labour MPs want electoral reform and will it happen?

text:
Why do some Labour MPs want electoral reform and will it happen?

Two main reasons. The first is that the makeup of Labour MPs changed notably with the 2024 election. Many longer-standing MPs had been sceptical about electoral reform, arguing it was the party’s role to compete in a winner-takes-all contest as one of the two parties of government, and that proportional representation would create unstable coalitions. In contrast, many new MPs, like the bulk of Labour members, support change. Also, politics is different. First past the post had something of a rationale when Labour and the Conservatives won the bulk of votes. But eroded party loyalties have created an atomised system in which five parties – Reform UK, Labour, the Conservatives, Liberal Democrats and Greens – are bunched in a tight group. Even in the 2024 election, Labour won nearly two-thirds of all Commons seats with just a third of votes. Interactive What are the MPs hoping to solve with electoral change?

citation.title: Why do some Labour MPs want electoral reform and will it happen?

text:
Why do some Labour MPs want electoral reform and will it happen?

There is a very direct vested interest for some Labour MPs: Reform has polled regularly at around or above 30%, and if replicated in a general election it could send Nigel Farage to No 10 with a huge majority but on limited public support. There is, however, more to it. Supporters of a proportional system note that first past the post means millions of people end up having to vote tactically, picking a least-disliked candidate who may realistically win, rather than the person or party they truly support, which can create disenchantment and cynicism. They also point out that while supporters of first past the post argue it brings stability, a country with its seventh prime minister in just over a decade is hardly a beacon for this virtue. How would results differ under a proportional system? There are many different potential systems, all of which would bring varying results.

citation.title: Why do some Labour MPs want electoral reform and will it happen?

text:
Why do some Labour MPs want electoral reform and will it happen?

But as a broad guide, if the 2024 election had been held under a completely proportional method, rather than a Labour landslide Keir Starmer would have needed the support of other parties – perhaps the Lib Dems and Greens – to have got anything done at all. There is also another factor – as electoral systems change, so does voting behaviour. One of the main blocks to support for smaller parties has been the belief among voters that they cannot win and are thus a wasted vote. Under a proportional method this could change. So is anything going to happen? In the short term, no. Even with the prospect of a Reform government, Burnham has categorically ruled out any change to the electoral system before the next election, as this was not part of the 2024 manifesto. What the Labour MPs hope to achieve is a plan that could form part of the next manifesto – a commitment that if the party was re-elected, it would change the voting system. If this involved a proportional system, it would most likely get the support of the Lib Dems, Greens, Scottish National party and Plaid Cymru, all of which back such a move.

With Nige still sulking, it was left to Honest Bob to unveil Reform UK’s latest ‘policies’

It’s turning out to be one of the longer sulks in Nigel Farage’s already sulk-filled career. Few politicians are better at having a strop and holding a grudge than Nige. At least on this side of the Atlantic. Donald Trump could give Farage a run for his money, but skin doesn’t come much thinner than Nige’s. He’s the soul of the Reform party as long as he’s the centre of attention and the yes-men and women – that’s everyone – around him are saying yes. But the moment reality challenges his narcissism, the mirror cracks. There was a time when you couldn’t keep Nige away from a TV camera or a gathering of reporters. It’s what he lived for. But ever since the Guardian revealed his £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne, Farage has gone all shy. Unable to bear the humiliation of being seen for the man he really is. The posh. The entitled. The venal. The grifter. Everything he has spent the last 25 years trying to persuade people he isn’t.

Jenrick described the leader of his former party as a fantasist. “It was obviously very, very embarrassing for Kemi Badenoch. Wes Streeting describes ‘unbelievable volume’ of homophobic abuse since becoming defence secretary

Wes Streeting has described receiving a mass of homophobic abuse since he was made defence secretary last month, while also saying his appointment had been welcomed by some in the Ministry of Defence (MoD) as a sign of change. Until 2000, gay men and lesbian women were banned from serving in the UK military, with about 200-plus personnel thrown out of the forces each year due to their sexuality – an estimate, as proper records were not kept. Streeting, who is the first out gay defence secretary, told the All Talk podcast hosted by Iain Dale: “I have experienced more online homophobia in the last three weeks than I have in my entire life. “Unbelievable volume – because people cannot cope with the idea that a gay person might lead the armed forces of the United Kingdom.” He went on: “And I have two things to say in response to that. One is, firstly, being the first openly gay defence secretary has been almost entirely unremarked upon in the media.

Andy Burnham recently supported an even lower donations cap than previously reported, according to correspondence seen by the Guardian, as the row over next week’s elections bill escalates. The prime minister wrote to a campaigner in May outlining his support for a £500,000 individual donations cap, which he said would “guard against the perception of any one party being unduly influenced or swayed by one person or organisation”. In a follow-up email seen by the Guardian, Burnham went on to say he believed the cap should gradually be reduced – a proposal now being put forward by the Labour MP Stella Creasy. Campaigners are accusing Burnham of a U-turn after the Guardian reported the prime minister had decided not to back the attempts by Creasy and others to introduce a donations cap in next week’s elections bill. In his first message to Shaun Bowler, who runs the website wakeupgb.co.uk, Burnham wrote: “I do think there should be a cap on political donations. This would guard against the perception of any one party being unduly influenced or swayed by one person or organisation.

text:
Unlike needy Keir, trash-talking Andy speaks a language Trump understands

It makes a pleasant change. Not so long ago, Keir Starmer was falling over himself in his efforts to keep things sweet with Donald Trump. Offering the US president a second state visit within minutes of meeting him. Everyone knows you should never put out on the first date: it only makes the other person think you’re a pushover. Sure enough, The Donald banked the marching bands and the Windsor silver service, made polite conversation for three days and then went back to trash-talking him. Yet still, Starmer just sat there and took it. As if one word of criticism would be too much. Wittering on about the “special relationship” as if Trump gave a moment’s thought to the UK before he did anything. The rest of us wouldn’t have put money on the US president even being able to locate Britain on a map. It was only latterly, when The Donald chose to bomb Iran, that the penny finally dropped for Keir. And even then he looked pained by the apparent betrayal, as he resisted the calls of Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage to join in the war.

Words that had been loudly cheered at the time by many in Britain who had had enough of all the toadying. After all, it wasn’t as if the Trump-whispering had made any difference. If anything, it had only added to his contempt for us. You’ll never get any thanks from a narcissist. Nor did Andy have any regrets now that he was prime minister and was likely to meet Trump in person for the first time at the UN general assembly in New York at the end of next month. Far from it. “Shit happens” was pretty much his precis of what had gone down. He wasn’t going to apologise to The Donald for what he had said. Not least because he had meant every word. This was the real world. Politicians say stuff. Trump had said all sorts of things about him, too. That he had been mayor of “some town”.

It’s a Monday in August and as England burns in dystopian heat, Gordon Brown and I are in his office at the top of his house in North Queensferry, overlooking the moody waters of the Firth of Forth. It’s hard to recall the top of my own sauna-like house in London as we stand here in the cool, wearing wool suits and necessary socks, my coat slung over the back of a chair. “I was watching Raith Rovers – the local football team – on Saturday,” Brown says, “and it was really cold. (I’ll hear him tell it three times today.) That’s not to say Fife has been untouched by the multiple heatwaves. They had a few sunny days. One hit 24C – “a shock”, Brown says, July temperatures typically being 15-17C. Cleverly avoids culture war issues in pitch to be next London mayor

James Cleverly has pledged to run a “classically Conservative” campaign to become the mayor of London, insisting that his victory in the capital would be a stepping stone for Kemi Badenoch to become prime minister. The former home and foreign secretary denied he had resigned from the shadow cabinet to run for mayor following a shift to the right under Badenoch’s leadership. However, in a series of interviews on Sunday he avoided speaking about culture war issues, which have been a focus for the Conservative leader. “I am going to put forward a classic Conservative case to be the mayor of London, and it’s about enterprise, it’s about opportunity,” Cleverly told Times Radio. “That is a classically Conservative vision, and it will run in parallel to and supportive of Kemi’s plans for the country as a whole.” If he wins his party’s nomination, Cleverly is expected to run a more moderate campaign than the last Tory candidate, Susan Hall.

She drew criticism for claiming there was a “problem with crime” in the black community and was forced to apologise for liking a tweet in 2020 that had a picture of Enoch Powell captioned: “It’s never too late to get London back.” Hall lost to Labour’s Sadiq Khan in 2024, who won with 43.8% of the vote. Cleverly, who lost the Conservative leadership race to Badenoch, is considered a more moderate voice in a party that has moved to the right as support for Nigel Farage’s rightwing Reform UK has grown. Giles Dilnot, the editor of Conservative Home, who has worked closely with Cleverly in the past, denied a rift and said he thought it unlikely the MP for Braintree was using his attempt to become mayor as a route to become the next Conservative leader. “There is not a hidden side order of ‘what’s next’ here,” he said. Asked if Cleverly was likely to seek to put distance between himself and the Tory leader to attract more centre-left voters in the capital, he pointed to Cleverly’s 2024 speech during the Conservative leadership contest in which he called for his party to be “more normal”.

More public control is the way to grow UK economy, Burnham to tell MPs

Andy Burnham will drive home his pledge to bring more essential services back into public control, telling MPs in the Commons on Tuesday that it will be the only way to improve growth across the country. Burnham will address the house for the first time in 16 years from the frontbench, and six weeks since he became prime minister, after spending the summer recess announcing a slew of policies that will now be put before MPs. He will use the statement to put public control of services at the heart of his priorities for the coming months, sources told the Guardian, saying he would make the case that it would unlock investment, jobs and growth. Burnham will say that the cost of everyday services to family budgets is holding back the economy and promise a plan to regain control of the costs. A No 10 source said: “Andy is optimistic about our country’s future. He has a clear plan for how we turn things round.

He is determined we make this the moment we bring back hope.” The prime minister will face an early test of his commitment to public control as he mulls legislation to make it easier to bring struggling utilities such as Thames Water under government ownership. The Guardian reported last week Burnham was considering laws to make it easier to put companies into insolvency proceedings and then take control of them afterwards. He will also face crunch decisions on possible changes to the immigration bill to exempt carers, as well as pressure from MPs to back moves towards electoral reform. A quasi-judicial decision on whether to allow more North Sea drilling is also expected soon: a highly divisive issue within the party. On Monday, the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, sacked her shadow chancellor Mel Stride and shadow foreign secretary Priti Patel, promoting Andrew Griffith in Stride’s place in the hope of making further inroads in attacking Burnham’s economic approach.

After a relatively cheery summer in which he announced a range of eye-catching cost of living policies, Andy Burnham may find his return to parliament this week to be a rude awakening. While the new prime minister has enjoyed some success in the polls, he is faced with many of the same problems that stymied Keir Starmer and has some difficult and unpopular choices to make. North Sea oil and gas Related: Rejoining the EU, Burnham’s donors and the bedroom tax: Politics Weekly answers your questions – podcast The Rosebank oilfield and the Jackdaw gasfield have been in limbo for a year after a court case ruled the consent given to drill by the previous Conservative government was unlawful. Now, it is in the hands of the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, to make the quasi-judicial decision to allow the drilling to start. Burnham has promised to take a “pragmatic” approach to North Sea oil and gas as the unions complain about job losses caused by Labour’s manifesto promise to end all oil and gas licences and the Iran crisis tightens supply of gas around the globe.

But this will not impact bills, as gas is sold on a global market. He is said to be less sure about allowing Rosebank, which the former energy secretary Ed Miliband, who is now foreign secretary, referred to as “climate vandalism”. He faces a revolt from left-of-centre Labour MPs and the Green party’s outspoken leader, Zack Polanski, will undoubtedly make hay out of the decision. It is also a difficult choice to make after a summer of record-breaking heat, exacerbated by climate breakdown. Face-to-face with Donald Trump Burnham is due to meet Donald Trump in September at the UN general assembly in New York City. It may be hard to break the ice; when he was mayor of Manchester, he previously referred to Trump as “poisonous” and said he would not be welcome in the city. The US president has disparagingly referred to Burnham as the “mayor of a town”. But the pair may get along.

But now he has reportedly dropped this cap altogether after being lobbied by the unions. The measure would have been a key tool in stopping Reform, which relies on a few wealthy donors. text:
Can Reform UK recover from its summer horribilis?

Senior Reform UK figures like to boast that the summer time – and parliament’s longest recess – is when the party makes hay. Supposedly, it is when Nigel Farage and co can muscle in on the news cycle with provocative statements and new policies, painting “establishment” opponents as workshy layabouts. Last year’s summer break came with an added opportunity, which the rightwing populist party eagerly grasped, in the form of protests against hotels housing asylum seekers. As Labour and the Tories tempered their language, Farage eagerly weighed in, warning of the prospect of “civil disobedience on a vast scale”. Yet as August comes to an end, and with Reform preparing for its annual conference in Birmingham later this week, the party might look back on summer 2026 as a damp squib, or worse.

citation.title: Can Reform UK recover from its summer horribilis?

text:
Can Reform UK recover from its summer horribilis?

While almost weekly Reform press conferences have taken place and new policies have been rolled out – Robert Jenrick has been particularly busy with promises to slash the benefits bill and scrap supposed “red tape” for businesses – there has been no repeat of last summer’s unrest in England, aside from disturbances in the Norfolk market town of Thetford. There have also been missteps of Reform’s own making, not least the hint of internal divisions related to the noisy pronouncements of its home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf. Farage was eventually forced to reprimand him for calling Ben Wallace, a former Conservative defence secretary and veteran, a “traitor”. Divisions also surfaced around the suspension of Tim Montgomerie, a high-profile activist who defected from the Conservatives. However, perhaps the biggest error was Farage’s decision to spark a byelection in Clacton in an attempt to neutralise the pressure he was under over questions about an undeclared £5m payment by the Reform megadonor Christopher Harborne. Farage himself scaled back press events amid scrutiny after the payment was first revealed by the Guardian.

Though he cruised to victory over his closest challenger – Count Binface – the need to get the vote out meant Farage was pinned down in a corner of Essex for six weeks, rather than being free to roam the UK at will and entice media coverage in a way his lieutenants fail to. Related: ‘Disgraceful’: what one election photo tells us about British politics in 2026 The prospect of a “people versus the establishment” battle which Farage so clearly craved did not materialise when other main parties ignored the contest, while a parliamentary standards investigation into the payment has once again started after it was only paused during the byelection. Opponents have taken note. “You could say that Reform are quite good at tactics but bad at strategy, and with Clacton he made a strategic mistake because it bound him to one part of the country for six weeks,” said Giles Dilnot, the editor of ConservativeHome and a former political adviser who covered Farage for years for the BBC. “He made that decision in anger and you never make good strategic decisions when you are angry.

Then he had to take a break because of the understandable toll the byelection and all that went before it this year would have taken.” Dilnot suggested two other issues that will have caused worries in Reform ranks. First, despite Reform consistently attacking the Tories, signs of a knockout blow do not seem to have materialised. Second, the centralised way in which Farage has always run his political projects may now be taking a toll. “Over the 15 years it’s always the case he is both the biggest asset and biggest weakness of any party he has led. Everything is centralised, he falls out with people and voters can also be very polarised,” said Dilnot. Recent polls have indicated that the surge in support for Reform has stalled, with the party failing to break out beyond core supporters and signs that Farage himself might even be a drag on its further growth. Conservative reshuffle: who’s who in Kemi Badenoch’s top team?

Kemi Badenoch has kicked off the return to parliament with a reshuffle of her top team in order to take on Andy Burnham and Reform UK. She has made sweeping changes to the shadow cabinet and ruthlessly axed her shadow chancellor. Here is a run-down of the new characters sitting across from Labour on the opposition frontbench. Andrew Griffith Griffith, the MP for Arundel and South Downs, replaces Mel Stride as shadow chancellor, a role he has reportedly long coveted. He is loyal to Badenoch and was one of her first backers for leader in 2024. Previously the chief financial officer and chief operating officer of Sky and the chair of Just Eat, he entered parliament as an ally of Boris Johnson after allowing the former prime minister to use his £9.5m townhouse as his leadership campaign HQ in 2019. He later became Johnson’s business adviser in government before running for election later that year. Griffith was a backer of Liz Truss for leader and as her treasury minister was partially responsible for the disastrous mini-budget which caused economic chaos.

Andrew Griffith and Tom Tugendhat join Badenoch’s top team in Tory reshuffle

Kemi Badenoch sacked her shadow chancellor, Mel Stride, and the shadow foreign secretary, Priti Patel, in a sweeping Conservative reshuffle on Monday, replacing Stride with Andrew Griffith, and Patel with Tom Tugendhat. Stride, who had been shadow chancellor since Badenoch became leader, was widely seen among Tories as failing to make an impression at a time when Labour had been under pressure over the economy. Griffith, who was previously a high-profile businessman, moves from the shadow business brief, where he will be replaced by Claire Coutinho, the former shadow energy secretary. A senior Conservative source described Griffith, the former chief operating officer of Sky and chair of Just Eat, as “a no-nonsense, pro-growth shadow chancellor with real business experience”. “Kemi is changing the way the Conservative party approaches economic policy and creating a new economic leadership team for the next phase, focused on growth, higher living standards and fiscal credibility,” the source said. Badenoch paid tribute to Stride but confirmed in a statement that he would return to the backbenches.

text:
Letter: Michael Meadowcroft obituary

The obituary of the Liberal politician Michael Meadowcroft – my father – noted the premature death of my daughter Esther in 2022. She lived with complex and multiple learning difficulties and intractable epilepsy. While there were seizure-free periods, much of her life was stolen by the rare disease GAMT. Sadly this was not diagnosed until she was 30. She died a fortnight later; our persistent requests to start treatment during this time proved fruitless. Society struggled to include Esther. She was loud in quiet places and would rarely sit down, even when everyone else around her did. Nonetheless, she brought out the best in people. Consistent with his values of liberty, equality and community, Michael observed after her death that “not all individuals conform to some universal template … human society has to accept every Esther as a full member of it”.

Head of Viktor Orbán’s favourite thinktank quits over unpaid wages

The head of Viktor Orbán’s favourite Brussels thinktank has quit, citing unpaid wages since the change of government in Hungary. The sociology professor Frank Furedi said he was resigning as the executive director of MCC Brussels with “immediate effect” on Monday over “persistent failure to provide the contractually agreed funds”. Related: ‘Attack on civil society’: why Viktor Orbán’s favourite thinktank is in crisis A spokesperson for MCC Brussels confirmed Furedi’s resignation and said no one working for the organisation in the EU capital had been paid in July or August. MCC Brussels launched in late 2022 with a self-styled mission to shake up political debate in the EU capital, although critics said it defended Orbán’s illiberal rule in Hungary while using a well-funded position to attack civil society groups. It was an ostensibly independent offshoot of the Mathias Corvinus Collegium Foundation in Budapest, a training ground for Orbán’s Fidesz party that was lavishly funded by his rightwing nationalist government.

Soon after his victory, Magyar promised to end state financing for MCC Budapest and to investigate a large transfer of state assets to the organisation, which he described as a crime. Furedi has previously dismissed Magyar’s claims of a criminal transfer of assets to MCC Budapest as “bullshit”, while MCC Brussels said it condemned corruption by all politicians. Burnham’s reopening of Brexit debate is ‘biggest boost in my career’, says Farage

Nigel Farage has claimed that Andy Burnham has given him “the biggest boost in my career” by reviving the Brexit debate, which the Reform UK leader said had reopened a “huge flank” to his party. The prime minister’s pledges to the Labour conference and admission on Wednesday that rejoining the EU was among options the government would look at had put “put me back into the debate”, he said. Looking tanned and relaxed before his party’s first major rally since its conference last month, Farage indicated to reporters that he was relishing a return to the playbook that he and others deployed during the 2016 referendum. Dismissing polls showing that as much as 59% of the public favoured rejoining the EU, Farage told the Guardian: “Of course they do, until you tell them it’ll cost 25bn quid a year, until you tell him it’ll mean joining Schengen [the area of Europe that has open borders], until he tells them it will mean actually having to recommit to joining the euro. “Remember that the leavers haven’t made their arguments since 2016. The ‘remoaners’ have made their arguments every single week.

Group encouraging people to join Green party to back ‘Zionism is racism’ agenda

An organisation pushing the Green party to equate Zionism with racism has encouraged people to join the party specifically to support that agenda, and has links to activists who say that pro-Israel “infiltrators” must be rooted out of the UK, the Guardian has learned. Some Green members are increasingly concerned that the party risks being manipulated by extremist outsiders over a motion to be voted on at the party’s annual conference this weekend, which states that “Zionism is racism”. Some Jewish members have said privately they fear it will be difficult for them to remain in the party if the policy passes. Zack Polanski, who leads the Green party in England and Wales, has come under pressure to take a definitive stance on the motion amid worries the controversy will harm the party in next week’s key Holborn and St Pancras byelection, where Polanski is seeking to win Keir Starmer’s former seat. Related: Tension and dissent: inside the Green party’s antisemitism struggle The motion came top of a members’ ballot of policy issues to be debated at the event in Brighton.

The controversy reflects a longstanding debate about the definition of Zionism, the political movement whose supporters see it as the necessary struggle for a Jewish homeland, and whose critics see it as a colonial project that has inevitably led to the dispossession of Palestinians. The term Zionist is, meanwhile, sometimes used as a synonym for Jew by antisemites. Efforts to push the policy have been led by Greens for Palestine (GfP), a group not formally affiliated with the party. In repeated social media posts over recent months, GfP has urged backers of the idea to sign up as Green members specifically to get the motion debated at the conference and then adopted. Labour figures uneasy about Healey’s ‘underpowered’ approach to budget

Senior Labour figures are privately voicing unease about John Healey’s approach to his crucial first budget this month, against the backdrop of volatile global markets and soaring energy costs. The chancellor’s work has been made significantly harder by the global bond sell-off, which continues to raise the cost of government borrowing, and ever increasing energy prices as Donald Trump continues the US war with Iran. The yield – in effect the interest rate – on 30-year UK government bonds hit 6% on Thursday for the first time since 1998. Barclays raised some of its mortgage rates for the second time in a week, underlining the impact of these market moves on UK borrowers. The chancellor’s party conference speech, which centred on the theme of reindustrialisation, was warmly received by Labour members in Liverpool. But government insiders and other Labour figures cast doubt over the lack of detail about policy on investment and growth or any pitch-rolling for possible tax rises.

One senior Labour insider said they believed the chancellor was risking a fresh market shock on 28 October if he was not willing to be clearer about his approach to taxation, headroom and spending. Market moves since the spring are expected to have wiped out at least half of the £24bn “headroom”, or buffer, Reeves had built up against Labour’s fiscal rules. Healey is believed to be minded to accept a slimmer margin, but he gave no indication of his likely approach in his speech, aside from repeatedly stressing the need for discipline. ‘Total class act’: Marie-France van Heel is poised to be a very different PM’s wife

Sarah Brown called Gordon her hero, Samantha Cameron insisted David was “incredibly funny”, while Akshata Murty said Rishi was her best friend. When Marie-France van Heel spoke about her husband, Andy Burnham, in a rare public interview a decade ago, she joked that she had noticed his “good looks … and monobrow”. The spousal humanising of a party leader is a well-worn political tool, but van Heel is likely to be a very different prime ministerial partner. The former senior marketing executive is poised to play a more significant role in promoting Britain than any other spouse in the last two decades, stepping up her political engagements after stepping back from her own corporate career. Van Heel has chosen a political adviser to help her navigate the role at home and promote the UK’s interests overseas, the Guardian understands. She has shifted her role at Be.EV, an electric vehicle-charging network based in Manchester, quitting her job as chief customer officer to give her schedule more flexibility, while remaining on the company’s board.

In July 2016, the Manchester City player Yaya Touré ambled into a small bar near Beijing’s Workers’ Stadium and offered a bemused smile as dozens of Chinese fans rushed towards him. Ministers are working up sweeping plans for welfare changes including scrapping a key disability benefit for under-25s and replacing it with a multibillion-pound package of support to get into work, the Guardian has learned. Whitehall sources said the package of changes under debate was much bigger than previously thought, as Andy Burnham’s government hopes to persuade more people on benefits back into work. Re your editorial on Andy Burnham’s conference speech (29 September), the outcome that all governments should seek is a real improvement to people’s lives, particularly for those with the least, and without storing up problems for future generations. Andy Burnham plans to pass legislation to scrap the state pension triple lock in this parliament, even though the guarantee will remain until 2030, the government has said. The prime minister used his conference speech to announce a change to the policy, which guarantees that the state pension rises by the highest of 2.5%, inflation or earnings growth. Burnham also promised to exempt lower-income pensioners from income tax during this parliament.

Reform UK-run council boycotts reporter after row over potholes

Rows over potholes and a viral story about a garden gate have led to Reform UK’s latest confrontation with local media, after one of its councils announced it would refuse to engage with a reporter behind the stories. Reform-run Derbyshire county council has been accused of setting a “dangerous precedent” after withdrawing all cooperation with Eddie Bisknell, a Derbyshire Live journalist who is publicly funded to cover local democracy. Stephen Reed, the Reform council’s deputy leader, said the reporter would now have to work “twice as hard” to do his job after confirming that Bisknell’s inquiries would be ignored. It comes after a neighbouring Reform council last year banned journalists from a major local newspaper. Nottinghamshire county council eventually ended its ban on the Nottingham Post and its website, Nottinghamshire Live, after being threatened with legal action. In the Derbyshire case, Reform said its decision had been made after a “prolonged period of concerns”, which culminated in a story about potholes.

Councillors had hoped to produce positive headlines with a press release stating that the number of potholes in the county had been slashed from 12,000 in April to less than 700 – a figure it described as the lowest recorded in over a year. However, an article by Bisknell, one of a group of local democracy reporters funded by the BBC, reported that questions had been raised about statistics used in the release. The block on engaging with Bisknell emerged as the council took issue with another story about how a fence panel had been cemented across a gap in a wall between an 81-year-old woman’s garden and a council car park. He denied an outright ban had been imposed, saying Bisknell was still able to write about the council and attend public council events – a right enshrined in law. However, he confirmed the council would ignore his requests for information. “I want to be very clear: non-engagement is not a ban,” he said.

Polanski says he does not need to win ‘50/50’ byelection to stay Green leader

Zack Polanski has said his authority as leader of the Green party of England and Wales does not depend on winning next week’s Holborn and St Pancras byelection, amid suggestions the party’s popularity may have peaked. Polanski, who is trying to take Keir Starmer’s former seat from Labour, described the contest as “probably 50/50 right now” and “really on a knife edge”. Asked in an interview with the Guardian how much his position as leader depended on victory, Polanski said: “It doesn’t depend on it whatsoever.” He said the election had ramifications for politics nationally but “not for my leadership”. “I’ll be completely honest, it won’t surprise you to know that I want to win the seat,” Polanski said. “I think the seat is winnable, and I think it’s probably 50/50 right now. It’s really, really on a knife edge.” Senior Green party figures privately fear a defeat in Holborn and St Pancras could severely damage Polanski’s leadership, amid concerns the party’s rapid rise in membership and polling has not translated into campaigning strength on the ground.

The Welsh first minister has formally called on Andy Burnham to deliver a “new deal” in his first address to a Plaid Cymru annual conference since taking office. Rhun ap Iorwerth told party members during a keynote speech in Llandudno on Friday that his government had a “clear mandate” for devolving more powers from Westminster. The first minister, who beat Labour to lead his nationalist party to a first victory in Senedd elections in May, said he had written to Burnham on Thursday to ask the prime minister for “a new deal to redress the historic unfairness of our fiscal and constitutional settlement and to put Wales on an equal footing with Scotland as a bare minimum”. After being greeted by delegates with a standing ovation, ap Iorwerth said: “A new deal – the first of its kind – whereby a Welsh first minister invites the UK government to genuinely treat Wales not as a region of England but as a nation in its own right.

Would a gambling tax rise in the budget really shut shops and cost jobs?

Gambling industry kingpins are fuming about reports that the chancellor, John Healey, is considering increasing taxes on high-street slot machines in his first budget. The influential Social Market Foundation thinktank, the most vocal advocate for a rise in machine games duty (MGD), from 20% to 40%, thinks the measure could raise between £275m and £460m annually, on top of the roughly £610m collected last year. Its proposal is likely to meet with sympathy from Andy Burnham, a vocal and repeated critic of slot machines, who has already moved to tighten licensing laws so that gambling firms find it harder to open up new shops. The billionaire owner of Betfred, Fred Done, is among industry bosses who say such a policy would force shop closures, cost jobs and ultimately fail in its objective, depriving the Treasury of taxes. But not every figure in the gambling world agrees. Stewart Kenny, the co-founder of Paddy Power who has become a critic of his erstwhile industry, accused Done of “scaremongering”. So who’s right? It’s complicated … What does the industry say?

citation.title: Would a gambling tax rise in the budget really shut shops and cost jobs?

text:
Would a gambling tax rise in the budget really shut shops and cost jobs?

Bookies might be best known for bets on horses or football but they make big money from slot machines. The Betting and Gaming Council, an industry lobby group, commissioned a report from the accounting firm EY that estimated a duty rise to 40% could close up to 1,470 betting shops (nearly a third of the total 5,617), resulting in 15,900 job losses and a net loss to the exchequer of about £120m. Horse racing, which receives a levy from bookies’ profits, would also take a hit. Done said he alone would be forced to close about 495 betting shops, nearly half of Betfred’s estate, with the loss of 2,475 jobs and £67m in taxes. Entain, the owner of Ladbrokes and Coral, has written to Burnham saying it would have to make job cuts across its nationwide estate of 2,300 shops, were the policy to go ahead. Casinos and bingo halls are in the firing line too. Rank Group, which owns Mecca Bingo and Grosvenor Casinos, cautioned that a third of its venues could close, affecting 2,000 staff. Are they crying wolf? When dealing with bookmakers, it is wise to be sceptical. Back in 2019, Betfred had about 1,620 shops.

While most of the policies it objected to have come to pass, the number of shops has decreased by only about 330. Some of that is down to a broader shift to the web that has led to soaring online gambling revenues. In one Betfred TV ad, Done encourages punters to “come and see me”. In your neighbourhood bookies? No, at Betfred.com. Meanwhile, the Done family has taken out tens of millions of pounds in dividends, including £50m in 2022 alone. Any other examples? The Chronicle of a Death Foretold. It must be weird to realise that you have in effect made yourself obsolete inside a year. Worse, that you have actively accelerated your demise. Even AI doesn’t work at that speed. But that’s precisely what it looks as if Zack Polanski has done. Maybe he should just look on the bright side. He’s managed eight Liz Trusses. Not to be sneezed at. Polanski is partly a victim of his own success. A cautionary tale of being careful what you wish for. Like Nigel Farage, the leader of the Green party was one of Keir Starmer’s fiercest critics. Andy Burnham and Wes Streeting excepted. Keir wasn’t radical enough. Did not care enough about Gaza. Was too dull. And under Zack’s leadership, voters swarmed from Labour to the Greens. The party climbed to a record high of 18% in the polls and won the Gorton and Denton byelection against the staggeringly dim Matt Goodwin. But then Keir was airbrushed out of history and Labour chose a prime minister that a lot of people in the country actually liked. Someone who could communicate.

Even if they weren’t in love with Andy, voters were willing to give him a chance. Ever since, the Greens have tanked. Now they are down to 11%. Zack’s net approval rating’s almost as bad as Nige’s. Not content with this, Zack has almost certainly fatally holed his credibility by standing in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, which he is very likely to lose. Shares in brand Polanski have never been lower. The Green party conference in Brighton could not have come at a worse time. Zack didn’t want it to go ahead because he wanted to concentrate on his byelection campaign. Senior members of the leadership were briefing that the whole conference was pointless. But the conference did go ahead, and on Friday lunchtime it began with the local MP, Siân Berry, and Gorton and Denton MP, Hannah Spencer, doing their best impressions of a Duracell bunny. High energy, hyperactive enthusiasm. Like Blue Peter presenters on amphetamines. Everything was great. Never better. “Come on, everybody,” said Siân.

“We think the best of everyone.” We’ll reserve judgment on that till Sunday when some of the more toxic issues are aired. Hannah was also rushing on her run. “We have forced the government to change course,” she said. Mmm. And that’s sort of the problem. Siân and Hannah were just the warm-up acts for the main event. And with the arrival of Polanski to give his leader’s speech, almost all the excitement was sucked out of the room. The packed hall became like a dead zone. The slogan on the back of the stage said “real hope” but all you could feel was desperation. The sense that the Greens had had a fleeting moment in the sun and the long nights were drawing in. It is customary for a leader’s speech to be punctuated with standing ovations. That’s the whole point of them. Even if the leader is talking pure bollocks. Zack got two. One for saying Palestine and the other for “green revolution”. In Brighton, everyone gets a standing ovation for saying Palestine and green revolution. It’s written in the city’s DNA. Zack looked down from the start.

Normally he’s an animated speaker, but today he just looked defeated. As if he was trying and failing to will himself to care. It was just too big an ask. And maybe you couldn’t blame him. His team had chosen this day to brief the media that if they could persuade 30% of Labour voters in Holborn and St Pancras to vote for Zack, he would lose by only four points. That’s a bit like walking into A&E and being told by the doctors they can give you a heart and lung transplant but you are going to die regardless. “What a year,” he began. Indeed. Though maybe he didn’t need to spell it out so clearly. From fringe party to something more mainstream and back again. All over in a heartbeat. Zack couldn’t disguise the look of regret in his eyes. From time to time his head bobbed up and down, as if trying to get his brain to agree with him, but his body language spoke of an inner despair. text:
‘He feels more relatable’: Burnham’s conference speech wins praise from drifting Labour voters

“He’s offering what no other politician has offered for a long, long time. He actually feels like he’s one of us,” was how Neil, a geography teacher, described Andy Burnham in our focus group on Thursday night. Neil wasn’t alone in his praise: this group of Labour 2024 voters – some of whom had drifted to Reform, the Tories and Greens during the Starmer era – provided the most positive reception for a politician since Boris Johnson at the height of his Covid-vaccine bounce. Talent manager Megan said: “He feels more relatable to people from a working–class background.” Simran, another teacher, added: “He’s obviously better than the others in the short timeframe that he’s been in his position.” Linda, who works in banking, went further, saying: “He actually sounds like a person that’s there, not just for himself, but for all of us, which none of the others prior to him came across that way.” That praise for Burnham stood in stark contrast to his predecessor Keir Starmer who was, as contracts manager Craig put it, “just a shambles from the moment they won the election up until he left”.

citation.title: ‘He feels more relatable’: Burnham’s conference speech wins praise from drifting Labour voters

text:
‘He feels more relatable’: Burnham’s conference speech wins praise from drifting Labour voters

None of the group felt it would have been better to keep the former PM in place. Labour’s conference also seemed to have cut through the noise of the attention economy. Most had picked up at least something from the prime minister’s speech and liked what they had heard. After seeing the clip where Burnham spoke emotionally about the death of his father, the group, in contrast to some online criticism, appreciated a politician willing to show his human side. But what about two of the substantive proposals in the speech? On Burnham’s pledge to revisit the UK’s relationship with the EU there was an overwhelming feeling Brexit had been a disaster.

Most in this group had voted to remain, but even those like Darren, a field manager at a utility company who had voted Leave, felt cheated: “The amount we got told we were putting into the EU, I thought we could stand on our own two feet … we got told quite a few things, and it didn’t quite happen.” Interestingly, for most of the group it was less the economic impact of Brexit that worried them but instead the sense of isolation in an increasingly dangerous world and a less reliable US. But, and here is the caveat, once it came to the specifics of what rejoining may involve the group were far more cautious. Many felt if Britain could rejoin on its old terms it would be a “no brainer”. But the participants now worried that Britain would end up with a worse deal as punishment. Neil said: “I voted remain, but we’ll get utterly shafted if we rejoin … what do they gain?” Others described feeling 50/50 and nervous about where we’d end up. If this group is anything to go by, Burnham’s biggest fight won’t be in the principle but the details.

What about Burnham’s other, more controversial, pledge that the triple lock would be reformed to pay for social care? The discussion here revealed two things. First the rise in wages is less salient to people than other bits of the lock; most of the group felt as if their wages had not kept up with inflation for a long time anyway, so pensioners would not really lose out. As Linda put it: “My salary has not been increasing that greatly.” Second, reforming care is a real priority. For Tariq, who works in the pharmaceutical industry, this was an example that “sometimes you need to take hard decisions”. But the mood definitely shifted when the group were played a clip from Unite leader, Sharon Graham, opposing the move. Suddenly some participants worried this was “taking off pensioners” while others asked “couldn’t the highest earners fund it instead”. And the group were even more negative when they read former Institute for Fiscal Studies chief Paul Johnson’s analysis that triple lock reform wouldn’t pay for a national care service in the near term and so taxes would have to rise.

None of the group were willing to pay more taxes, personally, for care. text:
Badenoch returns to Conservative conference much stronger than a year ago

A year ago, Tory MPs were braced for the prospect of yet another leadership battle to topple Kemi Badenoch as the party sunk to historic lows of 14-16% in the polls. At the time, the word “November” was uttered in hushed tones – this being the decisive month when rebels would be able to mount a challenge, Badenoch having served 12 months in office. But times appear to have changed and – against the odds – the Tories have undergone what has been termed a “Keminisation”, with the leader asserting her style and authority on the party, despite its wider poor performance in the polls. “Right now, Kemi is the only thing that’s holding them up,” says Luke Tryl, the director of the More in Common thinktank, which conducts focus groups and polling. “If they ditched her, I think they’d be certain for electoral oblivion.” Badenoch is running a party still discounted as toxic and incompetent by much of the electorate, but polling numbers and focus groups suggest some of them have recently begun to give her more of a hearing.

citation.title: Badenoch returns to Conservative conference much stronger than a year ago

Badenoch returns to Conservative conference much stronger than a year ago

The party has crept up from the teens to the low 20s – occasionally edging ahead of Reform UK for the first time in almost two years. “It’s not great for them, but it’s a lot better,” says Tryl. “The problem is the party brand. She is now in our approval ratings net neutral and has been net 1 or net 2. She was in the minus 30s and now only her and Burnham have positive approval. “Progressives don’t like her, but when you come to those who might conceivably be Tory voters there’s a lot of ‘like her, don’t like the party, she tells it like it is, wish she was in another party’. I do think the Kemi bounce is real. People talk about her having improved and they have seen her PMQs clips.” Data from the other pollsters backs up the idea that the public is more open to Badenoch than before. James Crouch, the head of policy and public affairs at Opinium, said Badenoch’s approval rating had been rising since May 2025, when she was at -27, to -3 in its latest poll.

Tories plan to extend cuts beyond £47bn previously pledged, leak reveals

The Conservatives are planning to make sweeping cuts beyond the £47bn announced last year if they win the next election, according to leaked comments by the shadow chancellor. Speaking last year when he was shadow business secretary, Andrew Griffith told Conservative members he and fellow shadow cabinet ministers had discussed making further cuts in “every part of government”. The comments, which have emerged on the eve of the Tory party conference in Birmingham, suggested that the Conservatives are planning to make cuts similar in scale to those made during the austerity years should they take power. Related: More than a fifth of UK’s ‘austerity children’ scarred by poverty, study says Last October, Griffith said: “There are decisions made and signed up to by everybody to deliver that £47bn. Last week at the shadow cabinet, we talked about [how] we will need to go further. “The rate at which the economy is deteriorating, as well as our ambition to cut more taxes, means that we will have to find further savings, and I’m up for that in my department.

text:
Tories would expand free childcare to high earners, Badenoch says

The Conservatives have unveiled a proposed £700m childcare giveaway for high earners ahead of their annual conference, saying they would end the “cliff edge” where free entitlement ends at salaries above £100,000. The plan, set out the day before the event begins in Birmingham, follows the earlier proposal by Kemi Badenoch’s party to abolish most stamp duty, another change to taxation that would disproportionately benefit wealthier people. Under the current system, put in place under Rishi Sunak’s government, families with young children in England are eligible for 30 hours a week of free childcare, but this cuts off if one parent earns more than £100,000, irrespective of another parent’s salary. Under the Conservative plans, this limit would be abolished, with all parents working 16 or more hours a week able to claim the childcare. The party says it would cost aabout £700m a year, which it says would be paid for by cutting jobs at organisations such as Arts Council England and the Environment Agency.

text:
Return of the nasty party? Badenoch walks tightrope with ‘punch down’ policies

The forthcoming Conservative conference will be, almost everyone in the party agrees, notably more upbeat and unified than last year. There is a similar consensus that Kemi Badenoch is doing well as party leader. That is, however, not the whole story. “The mood is better but the facts are still very poor,” one Conservative MP said. “We are still a distant third in the polls, and if there was an election tomorrow we would lose, and badly. That means the mood is overhyped.” This is the inescapable shadow over the Tory gathering in Birmingham, which begins on Sunday. Almost two years since Badenoch was elected leader, her party is still polling lower than it did in 2024, when it suffered a catastrophically poor election result. There is, of course, context behind her MPs’ patience, not least the fracturing of the political landscape and the rise of a new competitor on the right in Reform UK.

But while Badenoch’s future is secure for now, there is concern among some Tories that her dogged focus on winning back support from Nigel Farage’s party, with little on offer to more centrist voters, poses both political and reputational risks. “We need to be attracting as many voters who left us for the Lib Dems as Reform, and I don’t personally think we have got the balance right,” a shadow minister said. “There is an economic offering, but they don’t want us to be so intolerant on social issues. The way we are going, we risk being seen as the nasty party again.” The phrase “nasty party” was coined by Theresa May in 2002, when the then party chair warned activists against focusing on too narrow a voter base and targeting other parts of society with punitive policies. Even if Badenoch has learned to prioritise core policy and walk away from culture war arguments, it seems she has not fully absorbed May’s lessons about not punching down.

text:
For Kemi, being the Nasty party is not toxic but a badge of honour

It’s a thought. A bold one. Possibly a career-ending one. But a thought nonetheless. When Theresa May told the Tory conference in 2002 that under Iain Duncan Smith the Conservatives had become “the Nasty party”, many members took that to mean they had become undesirable. Within a few years, David Cameron had moved the Tories closer to the “hug a husky” centre and by 2010 he was prime minister. Kemi Badenoch takes a rather different view. For her, being the Nasty party is a badge of honour. An aspiration. People had had it far too good with austerity, Brexit, Covid and the Liz Truss mini-budget. The country needed a reality check; a return to old-fashioned unpleasantness. A taste of genuine hardship. People had got far too used to getting something for nothing. Especially the physically and mentally ill. What they needed was a short sharp shock of intense labour from 8am to 8pm. That would make them feel better. And anyone found skiving would be banged up for a short time in prison. Say 10 years. And take a bow, her cheerleader-in-chief. The man whose sycophancy consistently goes above and beyond the call of duty.

We’re talking, of course, of the shadow home secretary, Chris Philp. He had chosen to mark the beginning of Tory conference with an interview to the Sun in which he had identified himself as a one-man vigilante force. For the next four days, he had personally guaranteed that Birmingham would be a crime-free zone. The Philpster would be on guard night and day to arrest all shoplifters and to check up on people who hadn’t paid their TV licence. From now on he would be a superhero. BatTwat. For Kemi, the beginning of conference was marked with the traditional BBC interview with Laura Kuenssberg. One where she would try to be the cosiest version of herself. The nasty leader with the heart of gold. A woman who could say in all honesty that “this was hurting her more than it was hurting you” as she removed someone’s benefits. This was Kemi returning in triumph. A year ago, her position as leader had looked ropey. Now the Tories have had a long, hard look around and concluded there actually isn’t anyone better. “Is this a return to the nasty party?” asked Kuenssberg.

The Greens have formally adopted a policy that equates Zionism with racism and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state, a move opposed by the bulk of the party’s MPs and which is expected to face legal challenge. Zack Polanski, who heads the Greens in England and Wales and missed the vote at the party’s conference in Brighton to campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, has faced criticism for a perceived lack of leadership on a hugely divisive issue. There have also been concerns that the policy change was pushed largely by newcomers who have little interest in the rest of the party’s platform. Four of the party’s five MPs opposed the motion. Adrian Ramsay and Ellie Chowns said they were “deeply saddened” while Siân Berry and Carla Denyer said they would support any Jewish members who believed they were being targeted as a result of the policy change. The binding policy motion, passed by 1,022 votes to 813, says Zionism – the movement for a Jewish state – should be “treated as any other form of racism”.

Ministers explore how to stop regional leaders misusing planned new spending powers

Ministers are mulling over how to ensure that England’s regional leaders do not misuse their newfound spending muscle, as Whitehall prepares to devolve more revenue to local levels. Ideas under consideration include a new select committee in Westminster, enhanced reporting rules and a new audit body focused on local and regional government. The Guardian understands the idea has even been mooted of allowing spendthrift mayors to be recalled by the electorate, as can happen to rule-breaking MPs. Related: Welsh first minister calls on Burnham to deliver ‘new deal’ on devolution The government will publish a white paper on “rewiring the state” later this month, setting out detailed plans to hand over more income tax revenue to regional mayors. Rachel Reeves suggested the idea in her Mais lecture earlier this year, and it has been adopted by Andy Burnham’s government, which sees devolution as a big part of its growth policy. However, officials are concerned about how to ensure local leaders are fully accountable for what they do with the additional cash – including in between elections.
