text:
Nigel Farage questioned by standards commissioner over £5m gift

Nigel Farage has been interviewed by the standards commissioner for an investigation into whether he should have declared a £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne. The Reform UK leader spent about half an hour being questioned over the money, the Sunday Times reported. Farage maintains the gift was for his personal security. The interview conducted last month is a sign the process is nearing a conclusion, although Reform UK is not believed to have been informed that the report is finished. An MP under investigation is usually notified before the conclusion of the process. If the commissioner finds that there has been a serious breach of the rules, the matter is passed to the standards committee of MPs and lay members, which can ask for further evidence. The committee can recommend a sanction or override the report. If it suggests more than a 10-day suspension from the Commons – and parliament agrees – the Reform UK leader could find himself facing a recall petition and second byelection in his Clacton constituency.

The rules state that financial support related to an MP’s job needs to be registered if given in the 12 months before they enter parliament. The Conservatives will announce a bonfire of regulations including abolishing affordable homes and community funding rules as well as scrapping Natural England and the Environment Agency. Artist calls in lawyers after Tories use his Burnham portrait without consent

An artist is considering legal action after the Conservative party used his cartoon to mock Andy Burnham. Stanley Chow, a Manchester-based illustrator who works for the New Yorker magazine, created a cartoon of the prime minister for campaign material in the Makerfield byelection earlier in June. At the Conservative conference this weekend, party workers handed out water bottles to journalists with the slogan “bottler Burnham” above Chow’s cartoon. He told the Guardian that the Conservatives did not ask permission before using his image: “I am taking legal advice, I may take legal action. It is copyright infringement, they are stealing my artwork to use for their own purposes. “An institution like the Tory party – there is no excuse for them not to do their diligence, and find out the rules of copyright. It’s amazing how it got signed off – that really disappoints me.” Chow first realised the cartoon was being used while watching Sky News. The presenters held the water bottles up to the camera and laughed at the joke slogan. “I was more shocked really,” Chow said.

Conservatives propose £10bn ‘Britannia Shield’ inspired by Israel’s Iron Dome

The Conservatives will announce plans to build a £10bn British “Iron Dome” similar to Israel’s air and missile defence system, which the party will christen “Britannia Shield” in an announcement at conference on Tuesday. The shadow defence secretary, James Cartlidge, will say Britain needs to be ready to defend itself from potential aerial attacks and that new investment was needed in advanced radar and interceptor missiles. Claiming it was “one of Britain’s most significant military programmes since the cold war”, he will say it is one that was “totally necessary because of the threats we face”. Britain’s military has traditionally believed it does not need to purchase Iron Dome-style air defence systems given other spending priorities and the fact that the UK has not faced drone and missile strikes as has Israel or Ukraine. Military officials argue that the UK’s strategy is based around deterring any attack or a full-blown war with nuclear weapons and that any conflict that involved a direct threat to the British homeland would almost certainly involve Nato allies assisting.

At the Labour party conference in Liverpool last week, Andy Burnham floated the idea of electoral reform. This week in Birmingham, the Tories have come up with a plan of their own: voting with their feet. How to put this nicely? Let’s just say that the Conservative party conference is extremely civilised. No queues for the food concessions. No queues to get into any of the halls. In fact, the organisers are delighted that anyone has turned up at all. This doesn’t feel like a high-octane meeting of a party preparing for government. More like a home counties meeting of the Rotary Club. On current evidence, if there is a general election next year – as Kemi Badenoch is trying to convince us there will be – then the Tories won’t be active participants. More like vaguely disinterested observers. For these four days, Birmingham is a city where you can sit and watch the world pass you by. Zack Polanski may regret not using his influence when Greens needed him to act

Shortly after the Greens’ triumph in February’s Gorton and Denton byelection, with the party polling above 20%, Zack Polanski seemed as if he might be taking the party into a new era. Now, some members fear he has led them off an electoral cliff. It is not Polanski’s direct responsibility that the English and Welsh Greens are saddled with an official policy stating that Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, is a type of racism, and that Israel should be replaced by a Palestinian state. The party is a direct democracy, and the members decide. As leader, Polanski’s only direct power is one vote on a two dozen-strong executive committee. But as a figurehead and public face, he holds much informal sway. And it is here, his critics charge, he has repeatedly failed to act. There have been growing fears among some Greens that with a welcome influx of new activists, more than tripling the size of the party since Polanski took over, came some highly motived and militant campaigners, many of whom focused almost exclusively on Palestine.

Entryism can be a problem for lots of parties, but with its cumbersome internal discipline and member-governed policy platform, the Greens are particularly vulnerable. For all that direct democracy is a level playing field, in practice Green policy is decided by the small proportion of members motivated and solvent enough to attend a party conference in person, or who bother to register for online or proxy votes. As such, Sunday’s “Zionism is racism” motion was actively supported by precisely 1,022 members, or about 0.4% of the total. While some argue that directly member-led policymaking is difficult in such an expanded party, many Greens back the current system, saying it generally makes for more considered ideas. Similarly, the motion has support among some mainstream Greens, including some Jewish members, who insist it will not target anyone for holding Zionist views. Either way, Polanski could not have unilaterally changed the way the party is governed.

But critics in the party say he could have said something about the way that Greens for Palestine, who tabled the Zionism motion, encouraged non-members to sign up specifically to get the policy adopted. But it nonetheless did, leading to the adoption of a policy that has prompted condemnation from outside the party, and considerable anguish inside it, with four out of the five Green MPs opposing the idea despite their otherwise strong criticism of Israel. The vote obliterated coverage of just about every other aspect of what was the party’s biggest and most ambitious conference to date, and seems likely to dog the Greens for years, especially given the apparent likelihood of legal action under equality laws.

Loss of green space could be issue that decides Holborn and St Pancras byelection

When HS2 construction began around London’s Euston station in 2017 and people living nearby watched parks and playgrounds give way to diggers and rubble, they were promised that the lost green space would be replaced. “They have to give it all back,” said Dorothea Hackman. “But they are destroying it – so there’s nothing to give back.” As the dust from the political party conference season begins to settle, disappearing green spaces and housing developments have become central issues in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. On Thursday, Labour and the Green party will contest the seismic seat vacated by the former prime minster Keir Starmer. Planning documents show that the high-speed railway project and surrounding developments will permanently swallow 14,404 sq metres of green space and playgrounds from the constituency, with more closed off as work takes place. The work forms part of the Euston section of HS2. The government estimates that the full high-speed railway between London and Birmingham will open between May 2040 and December 2043.

The biggest park under threat is St James’s Gardens, an 18th-century burial ground designated as a site of importance for nature conservation. While HS2 Ltd originally committed to replacing the gardens by building a new park on a concrete deck above the railway tracks north of the station, government cost-cutting redesigns have dropped that replacement park from the scheme entirely. Responsibility for the surrounding site now sits between public planners and private developers. While HS2 was approved directly by parliament, the private developer Lendlease is drawing up plans for commercial space and homes across the site. Camden council is assessing Lendlease’s plan, with a decision expected next year. Alice Brown, a cofounder of Climate Emergency Camden, said it was vital that green space was retained for people to take a break from the bustle of the station. “Otherwise it’s just going to be the site of the massive office building.” For people living around Euston, the development of their neighbourhood encompasses more than just the parks.

Hackman is a governor at Netley primary school, a stone’s throw from Euston. She is worried about what the new buildings will mean for the area’s falling pupil numbers. “Camden’s policy of failing to provide family-size housing means that all our families with children are driven out of the borough,” she said. “It’s very difficult to see how the social-cleansing consequences of what they’re doing can be of any benefit to our community.” For some, the byelection will be a chance to shock Labour’s grip on the council and the constituency.

Senior Labour party figures said it was very unlikely their party would cooperate with the Greens in the future after they adopted a policy treating Zionism as a form of racism. One Labour minister said they could not foresee how the two parties could work together, while a government official said Labour should formally rule out a future coalition or other arrangement. There is also pressure within the Liberal Democrats for them to end existing arrangements with Zack Polanski’s party, with some senior Lib Dems calling on the party to end its coalition with the Greens in Southwark, south London. Green members from England and Wales voted at the party’s conference on Sunday to adopt a binding policy that says Zionism should be treated by the party as racism, and which calls for a single Palestinian state in place of Israel. After the vote, Bridget Phillipson, the Labour chair, called the move “shameful”, saying it highlighted how vital it had been for her party to tackle antisemitism under the leadership of Jeremy Corbyn.

Reform MP raises concerns about second homes – then buys one for £800,000

A Reform UK MP bought an £800,000 second home on a picturesque Welsh island two days after raising concerns in parliament about the impact of second homes on rural communities. Sarah Pochin completed the purchase of a Grade-II listed property on the southern coast of Anglesey (Ynys Môn). The MP for Runcorn and Helsby in Cheshire bought the property two days after she submitted a written question on 15 June to the housing minister Matthew Pennycook, according to the Will Hayward newsletter. Pochin asked Pennycook “what assessment he has made of the potential impact of second home ownership on housing availability in coastal and rural communities”. Pennycook replied: “Excessive concentrations of short-term lets and second homes impact on the availability and affordability of homes for local residents to buy and rent, as well as local services.” According to the Land Registry, the purchase was made jointly with Pochin’s husband, Jonathan. The couple, who have submitted plans at Anglesey county council for changes to the property, retain ownership of another home in Cheshire.

text:
Why a PR voting system is the best bet for Britain

It is common in the argument against proportional representation (PR) to reach for Italy as a cautionary tale, as Gian Lorenzo Spisso does in his letter (A proportional representation voting system could spell disaster for Labour, 30 September). The irony is that Italy does not actually have a proportional system: it has a mixed system. If we want to assess PR, we should look at countries that actually use it – Germany, Sweden, the Netherlands, Denmark – hardly synonymous with political instability. Also, small parties or weak local representation are not unique to PR. The tiny Democratic Unionist party held the balance of power at Westminster less than a decade ago under first past the post (FPTP), while the Scottish National party and Plaid Cymru wield influence disproportionate to their UK-wide vote because their support is geographically concentrated. Germany limits fragmentation with a minimum electoral threshold. And systems such as Germany’s combine PR with constituency MPs, while Ireland’s single transferable vote system retains a strong geographical link between voters and representatives.

citation.title: Why a PR voting system is the best bet for Britain

text:
Why a PR voting system is the best bet for Britain

Gian’s letter does raise a more interesting point: FPTP encourages major parties to contain competing tendencies within broad internal coalitions rather than allowing them to form separate parties. But is it preferable for those coalitions to be internal and opaque, forcing voters into tactical choices, rather than external and explicit, requiring parties to negotiate and find common ground? The fundamental problem with FPTP is that millions of votes have little bearing on parliament. If your preferred candidate has no realistic chance of winning, voting for them does not translate into representation. In 2024, Labour won 33.7% of votes cast but 63.2% of the seats. That distortion is not a minor technical flaw. Who wields power depends heavily on where votes are cast rather than who people vote for. This disconnect is precisely why Britain needs electoral reform. The question isn’t whether PR is perfect, but whether we can design a system in which parliament reflects the votes people actually cast. Other stable democracies do so. Britain can too.

citation.title: Why a PR voting system is the best bet for Britain

text:
Why a PR voting system is the best bet for Britain

Tom Walker London • Re Gian Lorenzo Spisso’s letter and Zoe Williams’ article (Electoral reform could be a gamble too far for Burnham, 30 September), there are several reasons for the UK to adopt a more proportional voting system of which the most important is the moral one: it’s fairer. In the last general election, the current system gave us a government that only about 20% of the electorate had voted for. No wonder the public has been hostile since the start of this administration: almost 80% of us didn’t vote for it. There are other, more pragmatic reasons, particularly for those of us on the centre/soft left: if we are anxious to avoid having an extreme party in power, we need to ditch first past the post – and fast. Reform UK may be lagging a little in the polls at the moment, but with £76m behind them, they may be able to mount a campaign of mis- and disinformation that could persuade 30% of the electorate to vote for them – and they might win. If we don’t want an extreme right (or left) party in power, we need a way to elect MPs that reflects that view. We need proportional representation.

citation.title: Why a PR voting system is the best bet for Britain

text:
Why a PR voting system is the best bet for Britain

Of course, not all PR systems are the same. Italy uses a mixed system similar to the one used in Scotland for elections to Holyrood. However, as a report published by Make Votes Matter on possible future electoral systems points out, the Italian system “tilts the playing field rather than levelling it”. Its results do not reflect the views of the Italian population accurately. The crucial effect of any proportional system that meets the criteria of the “good systems agreement” (which sets out the standards that a system should meet to be considered by the proposed national commission) is to encourage cross-party collaboration and cooperation. It undermines the tit-for-tat squabbling so typical of our House of Commons and reduces the policy flip-flop of right-left-right administrations that makes it so hard for businesses, and individuals, to plan long term. It is precisely that collaborative, creative approach to policy that would encourage the stability and prosperity our people are longing for.

Up and down the country there are huge numbers of voters like me whose entire lifetime has been spent thoroughly fed up with our unfair system. I am 79 now, and my vote has never elected an MP since I lived in an urban area private rental in my early 20s. As a middle-class, left-leaning voter living in mainly middle-class towns and suburbs, my vote has been wasted in a succession of places. Of course PR could elect a rightwing government; it could also lock the right wing out of power for a long time, and as a democratic socialist I would be happy to live with the prospect of a long-term progressive coalition. PR would also give the Greens the scale of representation in parliament that their increasing national support deserves. text:
Badenoch’s inheritance tax gambit makes no economic sense

Kemi Badenoch’s inheritance tax gambit is a Conservative classic. After all, it was George Osborne’s high-profile pledge to “take the family home out of inheritance tax” in 2007 that put Gordon Brown off calling a snap general election. In practice, Osborne’s plan involved a £1m threshold for inheritance tax – and given the global financial crisis had blown a hole in the public finances by the time the Conservative-Lib Dem coalition came to power in 2010, it never came to pass. But the promise was grabby enough to change the political conversation – and contributed to Brown’s fateful decision not to go to the polls early. So politically, Badenoch’s flagship policy may have merit. IHT, as policymakers call it, is notoriously unpopular. Families never likely to be liable nevertheless fret about their kids having to paying it, while a cacophony of highly paid tax advisers offer to help them avoid it. The furious response to Rachel Reeves’s reform of the inheritance tax regime for family businesses and farms, with tractors streaming down Whitehall, underlined how unpopular it is.

citation.title: Badenoch’s inheritance tax gambit makes no economic sense

text:
Badenoch’s inheritance tax gambit makes no economic sense

But whatever its political logic, the Tory plan makes little economic sense. First, it’s worth pausing to underline how very wealthy the beneficiaries of this new policy are likely to be. The latest data from HMRC shows that less than 5% of estates – the wealthiest 5%, that is – were liable for any inheritance tax at all in 2023/24. And under current rules, by combining their tax-free allowances, a married couple can already pass on a property worth up to £1m to their children or grandchildren, without them being liable to pay a penny in inheritance tax. Badenoch’s new, much more generous regime would permit a couple to pass on the entire family home, however valuable, without paying any tax on it at all; and for good measure an additional £1m in other assets. And the more valuable the property, the bigger the gain. Clearly, in a sluggish economy where resources are stretched, there’s a question about whether that is the best use of the £6bn of taxpayers’ money the policy is reckoned to cost – compared with, say, investing in infrastructure where there might be the prospect of a return.

text:
Badenoch’s inheritance tax gambit makes no economic sense

Total revenue from IHT is forecast to be about £9bn this year, rising to £15bn by 2030-31 – Badenoch’s plan would wipe out about half of that. Worse than that though, it will create perverse incentives for older homeowners to do exactly what the economy needs them not to do, and hang on in a valuable property, for fear the proceeds of downsizing would be grabbed by HMRC . The Tories claim they’ll also abolish stamp duty, helping to oil the wheels of the property market and encourage downsizing; but for the most valuable homes, the benefits of not paying 40% inheritance tax above the current threshold would be likely to more than overwhelm the boon of a tax-free move. And that would be likely to mean far fewer family-size homes coming on to the market in the places up-and-coming buyers most need them to be available. As Arun Advani, of the Centre for the Analysis of Taxation at the University of Warwick, points out, the biggest beneficiaries would be in areas where housing is expensive. He says: “‘Where housing is expensive’ mostly means ‘where lots of people want to live’, usually because there are good jobs.

Reducing housing sales here will make it harder for young working families trying to upsize. Tories delight as satirical tapestry pokes fun at ‘turncoat’ Robert Jenrick

As Kemi Badenoch basked in the applause of the Tory faithful at the close of her pivotal speech at Conservative party conference last year, one member of her shadow cabinet looked less than enthused. Robert Jenrick, bested by Badenoch in the leadership contest a year earlier, looked on, and – as one shadow cabinet member now recalls – had to be prodded by Lord Ashcroft to applaud. “If you’re plotting against someone, then you at least pretend to like them,” they say. “The thing about Robert is he’s not even a good machiavellian.” Jenrick left the party a matter of months later, swiftly – and publicly – ejected by an ice-cold Badenoch after she got wind that he was planning to defect to Reform. This week, as the Conservative ranks enjoy their annual knees-up in Birmingham, the now Reform UK economy spokesperson has been swiping from the sidelines, accusing his old party of “once again copying our policies”.

George Galloway contests London byelection without setting foot in UK

George Galloway has been elected seven times to parliament, but his attempt to succeed for an eighth this week, in the London seat formerly held by Keir Starmer, is undoubtedly his most curious effort yet. Since the byelection campaign began, the leader of the Workers party of Britain has yet to set foot in the UK, let alone the Holborn and St Pancras constituency, because he is in what he describes as “self-exile” after being questioned by counter-terrorism police at Gatwick airport a year ago. Prolific social media feeds show that the veteran leftwinger has spent the past few weeks on a speaking tour in South Africa, with his most recent public appearance on Saturday at a pro-Palestine rally in Cape Town, though posts in the last 24 hours suggest he is in Shanghai, China. Prior to that he was in Moscow, repeatedly making his hostility to Ukraine and Nato as explicit as his support for Palestine and opposition to apartheid.

Meanwhile, social media feeds show handfuls of Workers party activists campaigning in the constituency without their candidate, fighting a peripheral campaign in a byelection considered to be a battle between Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali and Zack Polanski, standing for the Greens. “Sincere gratitude to my campaigners who are performing miracles on the ground in my enforced absence. Even if she did imagine there was no racism in football in the 1970s and 80s. But this bit was all too short and the speech began to feel like it was dragging into eternity. We’d still be trying to stay awake well into the afternoon. Finally the reveal – the inheritance tax reduction that would be funded by as-yet-unspecified welfare cuts. There would be no inheritance tax on anyone leaving their home to their children.

With an extra million-quid freebie thrown in, in case you needed to do it up after your parents had let it get tatty. You could hear the cheers from the country’s stately homes echo around the hall. Here was a party that really got it. Which was prepared to do something about the cost of living for the mega-rich. Even as Kemi was speaking, millions of ordinary citizens were phoning their brokers to liquidate their stock market assets so they could upgrade their £1m homes to something far more palatial. The property market in mega-homes had just gone wild. The people’s earl, Charles Spencer, could breathe easy. Althorp was safe. Let them drink champagne. There was just time for Kemi to pay tribute to Jeffrey Archer – the Tories have a soft spot for a convicted conman who ruined several lives – and then came the extended standing ovations. text:
Plan to cut disability support will harm young people

Reports that the government is considering removing the universal credit health element for disabled people under 25 will be alarming for families (Key disability benefit for young people may be axed under major welfare changes, 1 October). For many, it raises serious concerns about how they will keep disabled young people supported and able to participate in everyday life. At Contact, we hear from families worried about universal credit and its impact on disabled family members. Some receiving the health element are studying, working part-time or volunteering; others have disabilities so significant that paid employment is impossible. We recently joined more than 40 charities urging ministers not to take financial support away from disabled young people. We share the government’s ambition for young people to work and thrive, but we do not believe removing financial security will create those opportunities. Ministers have said that those with the most severe disabilities will be protected. But worried families still don’t know what criteria would apply or how hard it would be to prove eligibility.

citation.title: Plan to cut disability support will harm young people

text:
Plan to cut disability support will harm young people

Crucially, receiving the health element of universal credit does not mean a young person is not in education, employment or training (Neet). Before making such a fundamental change, ministers must publish the evidence. How many young people receiving the health element are actually Neet? And among those who are, how many cannot participate because of their disability or health condition? Disabled young people need opportunity and security. One cannot safely be traded for the other. Anna Bird CEO, Contact • This proposal to cut support for disabled young people rather than provide equal access to welfare sends a message to them that they matter less to society. Far from improving their independence or opportunities for work, such cuts would harm their health and push more people into poverty. It is careless to assume that employment support could fill the gap. Disability does not discriminate based on age; nor should the welfare system. A wheelchair, specialist equipment, transport or social care still costs the same whether you are 20 or 60.

citation.title: Plan to cut disability support will harm young people

text:
Plan to cut disability support will harm young people

Young disabled people deserve a social security system that respects their human rights and dignity equally. text:
Reform clears its own officials of breaking party funding laws despite police investigation

Reform UK has cleared two of its senior officials of breaking laws that ban foreign donations, despite the matter remaining under police investigation. The party published a 27-page report of an internal inquiry finding that Dan Jukes, Nigel Farage’s press adviser, and James Orr, its head of policy, had not breached funding rules. Party sources said they intended to pursue legal action against the undercover reporting group Verbatim, whose footage led to the investigation and was broadcast by Channel 4 News. However, Labour said the report was a “whitewash” given it was undertaken by the party’s legal secretary, Adam Richardson, a barrister with a longstanding association with the party, and Tom Waterhouse, its general secretary. Labour also said it was not credible for the party to distance itself from the scandal by claiming Orr and Jukes, two of Farage’s top team, were just contractors. Police have been investigating potential offences under electoral law since the broadcast in early September, saying they would widen an existing special inquiry relating to donations made to Reform.

citation.title: Reform clears its own officials of breaking party funding laws despite police investigation

text:
Reform clears its own officials of breaking party funding laws despite police investigation

Jukes, 30, and Orr, 47, will remain suspended by the party while the police inquiry continues. Jukes and Orr were filmed talking about a scheme in which a US donor paid for three polls with favourable narratives for Reform, costing more than £30,000. Donations from overseas sources are not allowed under political funding laws. Jukes also discussed the idea of the US donor giving £500,000 to Reform through his UK-based son. The men they thought were father and son were undercover reporters. Farage later met the undercover reporters as would-be donors over lunch in Clacton, and did not object when the idea of the scheme was explained to him. He later said he had not been listening. In its internal report, Reform said it did not excuse the “foolish” way in which Jukes and Orr discussed donations with an overseas donor. But it said the party had not commissioned the £30,000 polling from the US donor, as Jukes was a contractor rather than a staff member.

citation.title: Reform clears its own officials of breaking party funding laws despite police investigation

text:
Reform clears its own officials of breaking party funding laws despite police investigation

Orr was recorded suggesting the US businessman could pay for opinion polling to help with the party’s campaigns, which would “technically be a donation in kind” but “the reality is we could easily get away with it”. However, the internal report found that because Reform did not make any payment for the polls or directly arrange for them to be carried out, “the payments made to JL Partners were therefore not donations to Reform UK within the meaning of the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000”. In relation to discussions about the £500,000, which was never handed over, the report said it found no evidence that Orr or Jukes knowingly entered into or acted in furtherance of an arrangement to facilitate an impermissible donation. The report said: “Nothing was agreed, no donations were made and no formal position was presented to the party’s finance team, and nothing was accepted.

citation.title: Reform clears its own officials of breaking party funding laws despite police investigation

text:
Reform clears its own officials of breaking party funding laws despite police investigation

The party’s procedures for checking the identity of a donor and the source of funds were never engaged, because nothing reached them.” Orr had also told the undercover reporter: “If there’s a non-trivial chance of you guys directly giving a … five or six-figure sum, then we could do a lunch with Nigel.” The report said “the words used were unwise” but concluded that “they were not a price”. It also dismissed an incident in which Jukes discussed other purported foreign donors who had given money through their children, which would be against the rules. Jukes insisted “he simply invented circumstances for the purposes of not derailing the conversation” and that it was “foolish, loose talk” without foundation. The investigation “found no basis for the suggestion that any supporter of the party has given in the way described”.

citation.title: Reform clears its own officials of breaking party funding laws despite police investigation

text:
Reform clears its own officials of breaking party funding laws despite police investigation

As a result of the episode, which overshadowed Reform’s conference in early September, the party said it would bring in rules that the party treasurer’s office must be informed in writing of proposed donations and that no meetings with proposed donors should take place until background checks had been carried out. But Labour’s chair, Bridget Phillipson, said “nothing in it exonerates Reform or Nigel Farage from the serious allegations that they still face”. She added: “The scandals and multiple police investigations aren’t going away. It’s time to stop the desperate deflection and cover-ups.” A Reform spokesperson said: “Following the allegations raised by Verbatim Investigations and Channel 4 on 3 September, Reform UK commissioned a comprehensive internal investigation. “The investigation examined all relevant evidence, including witness interviews, documentary records and electronic communications. “Having concluded the review, the investigation found no evidence that any laws were broken. Reform UK takes its obligations on governance and conduct extremely seriously.

Reform clears its own officials of breaking party funding laws despite police investigation

“We consider that the production company – Verbatim – acted unlawfully and will be taking the appropriate legal action in due course.” Jukes told the Telegraph, which first reported the findings of the internal investigation: “I welcome the finding of this investigation, which crucially has found I did not break the law, as I have maintained from the outset. “I am also considering all appropriate legal remedies in relation to any false and damaging statements made about me. “For now, I will continue to take a break from politics to pursue other opportunities.” A spokesperson for Verbatim said: “We note that this report is an internal one authored by Reform’s own barrister and general secretary, and that a police investigation remains ongoing. We are confident in our journalism, which speaks for itself.”

text:
Tories accused of prioritising rich voters as Badenoch lays out inheritance tax cut plan

Kemi Badenoch has announced that the Conservatives would abolish inheritance tax on family homes if elected, prompting criticism that she is prioritising cutting taxes for the rich. The Tory leader also said couples would be able to leave an additional tax-free sum of £1m to their families, as the party attempts to shore up its traditional base in southern England. The move would mean the number of families paying inheritance tax – currently less than 5% do so – would fall by more than a half, Badenoch said, with the £6bn cost to be paid for by cuts the party says it has identified, including to the welfare bill. Related: The Conservatives’ ‘better tomorrow’ only includes rich people “My ambition is to abolish inheritance tax altogether, as soon as we can afford it,” she told the Conservative party conference in Birmingham. “I believe the people who work hard and save should be rewarded for that effort.

citation.title: Tories accused of prioritising rich voters as Badenoch lays out inheritance tax cut plan

text:
Tories accused of prioritising rich voters as Badenoch lays out inheritance tax cut plan

So this is my guarantee: no stamp duty when you buy your home, no mansion tax when you live in your home, and no inheritance tax on your home when you pass it to your children or grandchildren.” The Tories’ policy plans announced this week – also including support with childcare for those earning more than £100,000 and repealing the mansion tax – have been firmly focused on affluent middle-class voters, many of whom deserted the party at the last election. They have been welcomed by Conservative MPs and activists, who are relieved that Badenoch appears to be trying to shore up the party’s core support despite her natural proclivity to lean into culture wars on the right. However, the inheritance tax plans are likely to raise fears about overheating the housing market, giving elderly homeowners an incentive to stay in large family homes rather than downsize. The move also prompted accusations the party was favouring the rich over struggling families.

In a statement, Tax Justice UK said: “Kemi Badenoch has just announced a massive inheritance tax giveaway to some of the wealthiest people in Britain. This is a reckless policy that will deprive public services of cash when they most need them.” Stuart Adam, a senior economist at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said: “The biggest beneficiaries would be those with the highest wealth and the most valuable homes. These will mostly be people living in London and the south-east.” Reform UK suggested Badenoch’s inheritance tax plans would affect only 2% of houses, the majority in London. Its finance spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, said: “The Tory party is looking after its own in Kensington, Reform is looking after the country.” Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair and minister for equalities, said: “The Tories haven’t changed.

Kemi Badenoch has shown that the Tories’ choice is to do nothing to help ordinary families struggling with the cost of social care, prioritising the wealthiest instead.” Despite the Tories appearing more united this week than they have done for years, Badenoch did acknowledge in her speech that the party, still polling lower than at the time of its catastrophic 2024 election defeat, faced a long path to recovery. She issued an appeal to Reform voters to back her. “We let them down and we want them to come back home. They deserve better than Reform politicians,” she said. “We have changed our party. There is still a lot of work to do. People are looking through the shop window. They like what they see, but let’s be honest, not enough of them are buying it. We need to fix that.” Senior Tories have been urging Badenoch to focus more on the economy, which they hope will help them to win back middle-class swing voters in their traditional heartlands, and to pivot away from culture wars and migration.

Badenoch added that economic growth would be the “central organising principle” of the next Conservative government, cutting red tape in areas such as planning, building a third runway at Heathrow and implementing a new energy policy, while also creating jobs. Most of her speech, however, was devoted to attacks on her opponents, with the Tories desperate to edge ahead of Reform in the polls and be seen once again as the main opposition party on the right. Badenoch rejected calls from within her own party to “unite the right” by striking a deal with Nigel Farage’s party – reflecting warnings from her closest allies that doing so would risk toxifying the Conservative brand irrevocably. She said: “A year ago, those politicians were measuring up the curtains for No 10. Now, some of them are measuring up the curtains for their prison cells. “The circus goes on and on, and it will never stop because this is who Reform politicians are. So, to those who say ‘unite the right’, we are not uniting with that.

People deserve better and we are going to give them better than that: character, conduct and standards matter.” Badenoch also drew a sharp dividing line with Reform on race, after Suella Braverman, the former Conservative home secretary who defected to Farage’s party, suggested that minority ethnic people could not be English. “I don’t want to explain to my son when we’re watching our brilliant England team play football that some people don’t think our black players are English,” she said. “I remember back in the day when Ian Wright and John Barnes were playing. Nobody was questioning whether they were English. We certainly didn’t have sitting MPs questioning whether they were English. “We must not let these people take us backwards. That is not the country we are. Reform MPs are openly questioning people’s identity. “I don’t know whether you’ve noticed, but I am black. I am British. I am proud of my country. I’m proud of our history, all that we have done, and all that we will do in the world.” Badenoch acknowledged that last year her leadership of the party had been under intense pressure.

But she added: “Let me tell you, I’m not someone who gets written off, and neither is the Conservative party. There is a reason our party is still here after 200 years. We have adapted to every single challenge and every single age, and we are doing it again.”

text:
‘People are scared of her, to be honest’: Kemi Badenoch remakes Tories in her image

Kemi Badenoch has long said that the Conservatives were “under new management”, but in a TV interview to mark the end of a party conference at which she has been front and centre of more or less everything, she took the analogy further. “Your viewers will know that sometimes you have a football team that’s disappointing,” the Tory leader told GB News. “There’s a new captain, there’s a new coach, there’s a new owner, effectively – which is all me.” These are bold words even for a politician known to possess an iron-clad self-confidence. But they are no exaggeration. Badenoch is not only outperforming her party in polling terms, she is busy remaking it in her own image. The broad ideological direction was already set, with Badenoch saying explicitly at the start of this year that centrist ideas were no longer wanted. Some more moderate figures remain in her shadow cabinet, but they are signed up to a right-leaning agenda, including opposition to net zero and a bonfire of human rights protections.

citation.title: ‘People are scared of her, to be honest’: Kemi Badenoch remakes Tories in her image

text:
‘People are scared of her, to be honest’: Kemi Badenoch remakes Tories in her image

Those around Badenoch say, however, that her control goes further, with policy decisions such as the move to grant free childcare to people with incomes above £100,000, announced on the eve of the conference, made simply because she believes they are the right thing to do. “With policies it’s not about chasing certain groups of voters,” one shadow cabinet minister said. “She focuses on what she thinks needs to be fixed, what she feels is wrong.” Talking her out of a policy decision, they said, was a tall order: “It’s not going to happen – it’s tablets of stone. She’s not going to change her mind. She knows what the policies have to be.” Many political parties are, to a greater or less extent, a cult based around the leader, but this is particularly the case for the 2026-period Conservatives, where MPs say Badenoch is talked about on the doorsteps with an admiration and respect not accorded to their party more widely. MPs recount how her name is raised unprompted. One said: “She’s brought up in a positive way.

‘People are scared of her, to be honest’: Kemi Badenoch remakes Tories in her image

Crucially, in a world where most people couldn’t name more than a handful of politicians, they know who she is.” This starring role was obvious throughout the Conservatives’ conference in Birmingham, not least Badenoch’s arrival, which saw her greeted by a flag-waving crowd of activists chanting: “Kemi, Kemi.” Inside the venue, Badenoch was the heroic centrepiece of the party’s “Birmingham tapestry”, shown in mocked-up 12th-century form doing everything from chastising Wes Streeting to sitting in the turret of a tank. Such veneration is not just wishful thinking by a party eager to move on from a revolving door of previous leaders. While last year’s conference was viewed as make-or-break for Badenoch, even with her party still bumping along at 20% or so in the polls her position is now seen as secure, with the Conservatives more unified than they have been for years.

citation.title: ‘People are scared of her, to be honest’: Kemi Badenoch remakes Tories in her image

‘People are scared of her, to be honest’: Kemi Badenoch remakes Tories in her image

This is in part the result of some serial malcontents leaving for Reform UK, especially Robert Jenrick, as well as the party’s diminished size in the Commons, which as one shadow cabinet minister notes, is too small for factions: “We could just about fill a corner table in Pizza Express.” There are still private doubts, including Badenoch’s instinct to lean into culture wars rather than focus on the economy, which those around her believe is the party’s strongest electoral card. Some party figures also wonder if Badenoch is thinking about election strategy at all with her very personal suite of policy choices, which in Birmingham mainly consisted of giving tax breaks to wealthier people. This was capped in her end-of-conference speech with the announcement that a Badenoch-led government would exempt people’s homes from inheritance tax, an idea which, given that the levy only begins on property worth more than £500,000, is a largely theoretical idea outside London and the south-east of England.

text:
‘People are scared of her, to be honest’: Kemi Badenoch remakes Tories in her image

While such policies could be appealing to prosperous home counties voters who defected to the Liberal Democrats in 2024, this does not seem to be the plan. During another TV interview, Badenoch chided her questioner for suggesting her tax cuts were aimed at bringing back such support. “I’m very sad that you’re looking at this in crude electoral terms,” she said. “That’s how we’ve all got into this problem where we keep thinking about winning elections rather than thinking about what works.” One former Tory strategist said there was a risk of incoherence: “I can’t understand what is being achieved with these announcements. Forget lots of the small ones, just use the money and do a big tax cut for middle earners.” There was, they added, little chance things would change: “People are scared of her, to be honest. I think a lot of her team don’t know how to say no to her.” However, much like football, politics is not a one-person game, and a star player or manager will only get you so far.

And while Badenoch was at pains to praise colleagues in her speech, it is fair to say that the rest of the shadow cabinet is lagging. Andrew Griffith, Badenoch’s new shadow chancellor, was feted by his boss for his private sector business expertise. But on Monday he gave a speech widely seen as one of the worst delivered to any conference in years. It is a matter of profile as well as ability. While Badenoch is recognised by 90% of voters, according to YouGov polling, only 22% say they know who Griffith is. A number of his colleagues are on similar ratings, with pollsters saying even these are likely to be inflated by people who don’t want to admit ignorance. The experienced Tom Tugendhat, now in the foreign affairs brief, does slightly better, on 46%. Laura Trott, the shadow education secretary, hits 50%, but this is because some people mistake her for the Olympic cyclist, now Laura Kenny, formerly of the same name. There was some unease in Birmingham about Badenoch blotting out everyone else.

“Isn’t there a danger we are becoming a one-woman party?” one activist asked a fringe of shadow cabinet members. Others disagree. “It’s a normal dynamic for an opposition party that is unpopular,” said Nick Timothy, the shadow justice secretary. “It needs a strong popular leader that can pull it up and we should thank our lucky stars that we have her.” Either way, most Conservatives now accept that, for now, it is up to Badenoch to chart the Conservatives’ course, whatever it involves. One ally said: “We win elections on the economy but there’s no point telling Kemi not to do anything.”

text:
French minister invites UK to ‘come all the way back’ to the EU

The French finance minister has invited the UK to “come all the way back” to the European Union after Andy Burnham raised the prospect of a new referendum to reverse Brexit. Roland Lescure was speaking after the prime minister used his Labour conference speech to pledge that the government would explore closer ties with the bloc at a summit later this year. He used subsequent interviews to spell out how wide-ranging his consideration of Britain’s future with Brussels could be because Brexit had caused “more harm than good”. Asked about Burnham’s comments, Lescure told the BBC: “British people decided, and that’s obviously their 100% right, and if they’re willing to come back, they will have to decide. But what I can tell them is: come back, anytime.” Lescure said he wanted Britain back in the union to face emerging global threats together. Burnham said last week that the government’s options included keeping the current arrangements in relation to the UK’s relationship with the EU, seeking a customs union, returning to the single market, or going “all the way” with full membership.

citation.title: French minister invites UK to ‘come all the way back’ to the EU

text:
French minister invites UK to ‘come all the way back’ to the EU

He said ministers would examine “what is doable” and the “pros and cons” of each option. The prime minister is travelling to Germany for talks with the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, whose government has been supportive of Burnham’s suggestion that the UK could explore closer links with the EU. Related: Could the UK really rejoin the EU? Burnham and Merz are expected to agree on a deal for closer security cooperation against cyber-attacks on European countries but the two will also discuss UK-EU relations. Lescure also responded to comments by Burnham that EU rules to help European manufacturers would damage the UK. British government sources warned days earlier that the “EU reset” summit would be delayed again unless the bloc agreed to discuss legislation that could lock British business out of parts of EU industry. “Come back, and you’ll be at the table, and we discuss all these things together,” Lescure said. Nigel Farage has claimed Burnham has given him “the biggest boost in my career” by reviving the Brexit debate, which the Reform UK leader said had reopened a “huge flank” to his party.

text:
Honouring Sylvia and Emmeline Pankhurst on stage and in political action

There was a proud Pankhurst in the audience in Leicester as Sylvia: A Musical Revolution began its national tour (Suffragette cities: blazing Sylvia Pankhurst musical hits the road – in pictures, 3 October). A blazing show indeed – and one that, 98 years after women gained the vote on equal terms with men, asks how much remains to be done, how to do it and how women can bridge their differences to advance their common cause. As Sylvia Pankhurst’s granddaughter and Emmeline Pankhurst’s great-granddaughter, I honour both women. Their political paths diverged. I seek to reconcile their legacies through Centenary Action, the cross-party coalition that I lead, in a shared cause: dismantling the barriers to women’s participation, selection and retention in politics. Also in the audience were Philippa, a relative of Emily Wilding Davison, and Peter, a relative of Alice Hawkins. The connections endure – and so does the activism. Remembering past sacrifices means protecting the rights won and building on those struggles as we approach the centenary of equal franchise in 2028.

text:
Polls close in Holborn and St Pancras byelection as Labour hopes to retain seat

Polls have closed in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, a contest seen as a test of whether Andy Burnham can unite Labour’s voters or whether Zack Polanski can peel off support from the party’s progressive flank. Labour is seeking to retain Keir Starmer’s former north London seat, where he won a majority of more than 11,000 votes in the 2024 general election. The byelection is seen as a measure of the political landscape under Burnham, almost three months into his premiership. It is a significant first electoral test for Burnham, who succeeded Starmer in July, as part of a wider battle for younger leftwing voters who became disillusioned with the party under Starmer’s leadership over issues such as housing, the climate crisis and the war in Gaza. Polanski has sought to run an energetic campaign involving thousands of activists, leaving the Green party conference early after his speech in an attempt to prove he and the Greens are a serious rival to Labour, despite the latest polling.

citation.title: Polls close in Holborn and St Pancras byelection as Labour hopes to retain seat

text:
Polls close in Holborn and St Pancras byelection as Labour hopes to retain seat

The Greens are hoping to reproduce their byelection victory in Gorton and Denton in February where they overturned a Labour majority. However, the political landscape has shifted since then. Shortly after their byelection win in Greater Manchester, YouGov polling put the Greens on 21%, a few points ahead of Labour. But the latest YouGov survey put the Greens 16 points behind Burnham’s Labour, which was on 27%. The poll came as Burnham proposed a more ambitious pitch to progressives at his first Labour conference as prime minister. Holborn and St Pancras has a large number of students, younger voters and renters, with almost half of residents aged between 18 and 34, while about 45% were born overseas. Polanski has argued that electing him would increase pressure on Labour to deliver more radical policies, including stronger rent controls, greater action on the climate crisis and public ownership of Thames Water. But the leader of the Greens has faced questions about his own authority and was accused of being unable to articulate his thoughts on motions that became policies at his party’s conference.

citation.title: Polls close in Holborn and St Pancras byelection as Labour hopes to retain seat

text:
Polls close in Holborn and St Pancras byelection as Labour hopes to retain seat

In an interview with the Guardian last Friday, Polanski described the contest as “probably 50/50” and that it was “really on a knife-edge” while also insisting his leadership did not depend on victory. Asked whether losing the byelection would undermine his position, Polanski said: “It doesn’t depend on it whatsoever.” Senior Green figures privately fear a defeat could severely damage his reputation amid concerns the party’s increase in members has not translated into an advantage in campaigning. Labour has fielded Sagal Abdi-Wali, the 42-year-old leader of Camden council who arrived in Britain as a child refugee after her family fled civil war in Somalia. text:
Voting opens in high-stakes Holborn and St Pancras byelection

Voting has opened in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, a contest seen as a key gauge of Andy Burnham’s ability to energise voters and whether Zack Polanski’s Greens can still peel off support from Labour’s left. Polanski, who leads the Greens in England and Wales, is standing for his party in the north London constituency, previously held by Keir Starmer before he stood down as an MP shortly after resigning as prime minister. The seat is, under normal circumstances, a Labour stronghold. Starmer won it with a majority of 11,500 at the 2024 general election despite strong challenges from the Greens and a leftwing independent candidate, who is not standing again and has endorsed Polanski. In 2019, Starmer won by nearly 28,000 votes. Related: Loss of green space could be issue that decides Holborn and St Pancras byelection Polanski has run a highly energetic campaign. He has mobilised a large numbers of supporters to knock on doors, mimicking February’s Gorton and Denton byelection where the Greens overcame an even bigger Labour majority to take the seat. However, the political landscape has changed.

Voting opens in high-stakes Holborn and St Pancras byelection

Shortly after Gorton and Denton, YouGov polling put the Greens briefly above Labour, on a peak of 21%. The most recent equivalent had Polanksi’s party on 11%, 16 points behind Labour. Burnham, who succeeded Starmer as prime minister in July, is seen as having revitalised Labour, and used his speech at the party’s annual conference last month to set out a more ambitious and left-leaning collection of policies. Polanski’s fortunes in contrast appear to have declined, especially since last weekend’s Green party conference where a vote by members to adopt a policy equating Zionism with racism and calling for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state prompted condemnation and splits in the party. Four out of the five Green MPs have condemned the policy, while councillors and others have distanced themselves from it or in some cases left the party. While policy is decided by Green members in direct votes, Polanski has been criticised for not saying whether or not he backed the motion and leaving the conference before the vote took place to resume campaigning. The stakes are also high for Burnham.

Holborn and St Pancras could be promising ground for the Greens, with a young and diverse population that includes many students. About 45% of constituents were born overseas and 48% are aged between 18 and 34. Labour has campaigned hard, fielding as its candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali, the 42-year-old leader of Camden council who arrived in London in the early 90s, speaking no English, after fleeing war in Somalia with her four brothers and her mother, who trained as a lawyer in Somalia. Winners Andy Burnham Even his fiercest critics would struggle to argue that Andy Burnham’s first conference as Labour party leader was anything but a success. There was the requisite rapture among the Labour faithful after his deeply-personal speech, delivered without a tie or a lectern and, at times, with tears in his eyes. But even figures on the right, such as the broadcaster Piers Morgan, described it as “one of the best, and most powerfully delivered, by a British politician in a very long time”. The prime minister’s policy offering packed a punch too. He put forward radical progressive policies on social care, promising to “rip the plaster off” and make changes to the pensions triple lock, electoral reform and Europe. A YouGov poll after the conference showed that it had boosted the “Burnham bounce”, with Labour opening up a five-point lead over Reform UK in the polls. The upcoming budget, and next year’s spending review, will sorely test whether he can keep that momentum going and make good on his promises.

Ed Davey faces growing revolt against leadership as senior Lib Dem MP quits

Ed Davey is facing a growing revolt against his leadership of the Liberal Democrats, after the resignation of a senior frontbench figure on Friday. Charlie Maynard, the Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson, has resigned in an attempt to unseat Davey after months of frustration over concerns that the party is failing to cut through with voters, the Guardian understands. Daisy Cooper, the party’s deputy leader, immediately backed Davey, saying he enjoyed the support of the “vast majority of MPs”, who wanted him to lead them into the next election and were “furious at this distraction”. “We Liberal Democrats are the last line of defence against a Reform UK government, and Ed is determined to lead a strong and united party into the next general election whenever it comes,” Cooper said. “As Ed said at conference, we are in the fight of our lives against the right who want to turn our country into their version of Trump’s America.” Maynard’s resignation, first reported by the Financial Times, came four days after Alison Bennett, the Lib Dem care and carers spokesperson, stood down from the frontbench.

text:
Holborn and St Pancras byelection loss will disappoint Greens – but there may also be relief

Parliamentary byelections can generate all sorts of emotional responses, often very strong ones. But for the main contenders in Holborn and St Pancras, the feeling this morning might be more prosaic: relief. For Labour, Sagal Abdi-Wali’s victory with just over 45% of the total vote was widely expected, but it allows the party to credibly claim Andy Burnham as a politician able to reach people in both Reform-leaning areas such as Makerfield and in Green-friendly inner cities. Retaining a constituency formerly held by your last leader, Keir Starmer, and which has been overwhelmingly Labour since it was created in 1983, is in normal political times not that notable an achievement, but these are not normal times. A low turnout of 38.7% and Abdi-Wali’s numerically modest 3,364 majority that resulted might not appear the greatest endorsement of the government, but it is also likely to have been in part due to the widespread assumption that Labour would win.

Labour is starting to win back voters on the left who became disillusioned under Keir Starmer’s leadership, the party’s deputy leader has claimed after it saw off Zack Polanski and the Greens to win the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. Nigel Farage’s rivals are gearing up for a byelection in Clacton in the months ahead, amid speculation that the standards inquiry into his £5m gift is nearing a conclusion. Conservative sources said the party was ready to fight in Farage’s seat, although senior figures in the shadow cabinet are divided about whether it would be winnable, given Farage’s victory in a byelection over the summer. Other parties, including the hard-right Restore Britain, are also expected to put up candidates in the seat this time, after boycotting the August poll. Westminster is poised for a battle over the future of Reform if the sanction from the standards inquiry is a heavy one. The process could theoretically take place before Christmas if a decision is imminent, but the timelines of previous cases suggest it is more likely to be next year – if a serious sanction is imposed. In the cases of Margaret Ferrier, the SNP MP who broke lockdown rules, and Peter Bone, the Tory MP found to have bullied staff, it took well over six months from the conclusion of the commissioner’s report for a byelection to take place.

As ever, Jonathan Freedland is on the money in his article (The Green party’s anti-Zionism motion is yet another attempt to tell Jews how we should think, 3 October). As a non-religious Jew-ish Londoner, I am appalled at the passing of the motion to declare Zionism as a form of racism, and I am seriously considering leaving the Green party as a result. While I condemn the Israeli government’s actions against the Palestinian people, and I am not a Zionist myself, Zionism as defined by the motion is only one political interpretation and completely ignores ancient religious and cultural definitions held by many Jews who also condemn the current Israeli government. I have worked with Palestinians and Israelis on the West Bank and in Jerusalem in the cause of peace and reconciliation, and firmly believe in equal rights for everyone in Israel and the occupied territories. That cause will be set back by this decision, which will give fuel to antisemites who hide their racism under an anti-Zionist guise.

A Green Party MP has said she wants to make sure her party is not “vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists” amid the continuing fallout from the “Zionism is racism” vote. The party faces a political maelstrom over its policy decision last week to treat Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, as any other form of racism, and to back a single Palestinian state over a two-state solution. The motion was passed at the annual party conference with just over 1,000 votes, approximately 0.4% of the total membership. Related: What is Zionism and why do some critics describe it as racist? Ellie Chowns, the party leader in the House of Commons, said the ability to pass such a “significant and damaging policy” in that way made it clear the party’s structures and policymaking processes were not working. “I don’t think that policy, ‘Zionism is racism’, represents the large majority of Green party members, nor of people in the country,” Chowns told BBC’s Radio 4 Today Programme on Saturday.

Burnham faces questions over push to scrap photo ID voting requirement

Andy Burnham is facing questions over plans to speed up sweeping changes to Britain’s electoral system amid speculation that some of his closest advisers are pressing for an early general election. Ministers reportedly want to at least halve the time available for peers to scrutinise legislation that would make it possible to vote without photographic identification, lower the voting age to 16 and tighten restrictions on political donations. According to the Sunday Telegraph, the government is seeking to reduce scrutiny of the representation of the people bill in the House of Lords from an anticipated 10 days to fewer than five, despite plans for further substantial amendments. The reports come days after Labour’s victory over the leader of the Green party of England and Wales, Zack Polanski, in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, as well as Burnham’s own recent win in Makerfield, which have fuelled discussion within the party about whether Burnham should call a general election in pursuit of a fresh mandate.

text:

The prime minister does not need to call an election before 2029 and has repeatedly ruled out an early poll. The new voting legislation, first introduced under the former prime minister Keir Starmer, would allow voters to use bank cards without photographs as proof of identity at polling stations, easing restrictions introduced by the Tories in 2022. The proposals follow longstanding concerns that the requirement to show photo ID when voting disproportionately affects young people, those on lower incomes and minority ethnic communities. Polling published by the Guardian after the last general election suggested 6.5% of minority ethnic voters surveyed had been turned away from a polling station at least once, compared with 2.5% of white voters. The Electoral Commission separately estimated that about 16,000 people who attempted to vote in person were unable to do so because they lacked the required ID, and did not return.

Burnham was among seven Labour mayors who criticised the restrictions in 2024, comparing them to voter suppression tactics used by Republicans in the US, and describing the changes as a “brazen assault on our democracy”. Although Labour opposed the introduction of compulsory photo ID for voting, Starmer’s government stopped short of abolishing the requirement after taking office, instead proposing to widen the forms of ID accepted at polling stations. However, the Electoral Commission has warned that accepting bank cards would make it harder for polling station staff to verify voters’ identities. The bill also forms part of the government’s efforts to tighten political funding rules amid growing concerns about foreign interference in British elections. The Guardian revealed that ministers were planning further restrictions on political donations that could retrospectively affect the £72m given to Reform UK by the crypto billionaires Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne.

Andy Burnham says it is clear Russia interfered in Brexit referendum

Andy Burnham has said it is clear Russia interfered in the Brexit referendum, after seeking answers on the Kremlin’s involvement in the 2016 vote when he entered Downing Street. Burnham said he had asked whether Moscow had attempted to influence the referendum and received a confirmation that it had. Speaking on the podcast The Rest is Politics, Burnham said: “I asked the question coming to Downing Street: well, was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia? I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was.” Related: We need to stop disinformation in UK political adverts. Here’s a chance to do so Burnham’s comments mark a significant departure from the position taken by past Conservative governments, which insisted there was no evidence of successful interference by Russia in the referendum vote. The prime minister did not disclose who had given him the assessment, what evidence it was based on or whether any interference had affected the result of the vote.

It said the government had not provided any post-referendum assessment of Russian attempts at interference, in contrast to the investigation undertaken in the US after the 2016 presidential election. ‘We need less point scoring’: What party conference season taught us about UK climate action

New homes could be built without solar panels, heat pumps and high-grade insulation, leading to higher household bills if the Conservative party wins the next general election. Kemi Badenoch made scrapping the future homes standard (FHS) one of the central planks of her bid to become the next prime minister at the Tory party conference this week. The announcement gained little attention compared to her inheritance tax bombshell, but it would have more far-reaching impacts on a greater number of people. The UK is in need of approximately 6m new homes and failing to equip them with efficient and low-carbon energy sources would doom households to higher bills for decades to come. Related: Tories overstate net zero cost by nearly £500bn in apparent spreadsheet error The Tories quoted estimates of £30,000 for new-build houses, but the real cost is likely to be much less.

citation.title: ‘We need less point scoring’: What party conference season taught us about UK climate action

text:

Installing heat pumps, solar panels, batteries and insulation costs about £5,000 to £8,000 at the point of building – a figure estimated in 2024 when energy prices were much lower – to save more than £1,300 a year on bills, a saving likely to be substantially higher now. To retrofit homes after building would cost more than £20,000. Jan Rosenow, a professor of climate and energy policy at the University of Oxford, said: “Every home constructed today that runs on fossil fuels is a liability for the occupants. It also results in investor uncertainty and disrupts the supply chain that has been gearing up for this. What we need is less political point scoring and more long-term clarity.” Housebuilders have been among the biggest donors to the Conservative party, though this has fallen off in recent years. And according to the UK Green Building Council (UKGBC), the construction industry is well prepared for the FHS and will have to implement the policy before the next general election, so scrapping it is of little benefit.

A Syrian plastic surgeon is facing deportation from the UK after the Home Office revoked his refugee status, declaring it is now safe for him and his family to return to their home country. Despite Foreign Office guidance advising against all travel to Syria because of the “volatile” security situation, the government has classified it as a safe place for refugees to return to. The firm, founded in 2020, is owned by Bruno Rodrigues, a lawyer. Its main public face was Philip van Scheltinga, a Harvard graduate. Burnham to host Zelenskyy at No 10 in show of ‘rock-solid’ support

Andy Burnham will host Volodymyr Zelenskyy at Downing Street on Wednesday as the UK seeks to further underline its support for the Ukrainian president, in contrast to his difficulties with Donald Trump. The UK prime minister said his message to Zelenskyy and his country would be: “We are with you for as long as it takes.” To coincide with the visit, the UK has said it will move more rapidly in providing Ukraine with British-made lightweight multi-role missiles (LMMs) to help protect it from attacks by a new generation of Russian jet-powered drones. In parallel, Burnham and his ministers will push for a full international maritime services ban on exports of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG). The pair have already met twice since Burnham took office in July, when Zelenskyy visited a naval base in Portsmouth in the same month and when Burnham travelled to Kyiv in August.

text:
Russia did try to interfere in Brexit referendum, head of MI5 confirms

Russia did try to interfere in the Brexit referendum through social media and television reports, the head of MI5 said on Tuesday, but he added that did not mean the Kremlin had any impact on the result. Ken McCallum endorsed comments by Andy Burnham, who raised the issue over the past two days, though he said continuing to debate it risked giving the Kremlin a needless propaganda victory. During an annual threat update, the head of Britain’s domestic intelligence agency said the Russian-owned English-language broadcasters RT and Sputnik “came in pretty strongly around the time of the referendum” with biased anti-migration and anti-EU reports. He said there had also been “a second line of interference attempted through [internet] trolls”: an unspecified number of fake social media accounts, operating largely on X, that had sought to influence the result. Neither tactic was particularly sophisticated or successful, the spy chief said. There was a big difference between “what may have been attempted and what actually resulted”.

Both interference attempts have been previously cited in studies released in the years after the Brexit vote. The digital campaign group 89up said RT and Sputnik had published 261 mostly misleading articles highlighting immigration and other anti-EU issues that achieved 134m potential page impressions. Other studies have reported on a “troll army” of state-linked Russian accounts tweeting about the referendum in the run-up to the vote, though estimates of numbers active have varied wildly from 54 to 150,000. Burnham had first returned to the issue on Sunday, during a podcast interview, though at first it was unclear whether the prime minister had been given new intelligence on a topic that had largely been considered forgotten. “I asked the question coming to Downing Street: ‘Was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia?’ And I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was,” said the prime minister, implying he had a discussion or briefing on the issue.

text:
The Conservatives’ ‘better tomorrow’ only includes rich people

Kemi Badenoch’s conference speech rehearsed the argument that Andy Burnham’s economic policies were warped by his “nostalgia” for the 1970s, unlike her own forward-looking programme for “a better tomorrow” (Tories accused of prioritising rich voters as Badenoch lays out inheritance tax cut plan, 7 October). She appears not to see that her preference for a lesser-regulated capitalist market economy, with lower public expenditure, taxes and national debt, coupled with “tough love” welfare policies, is itself harking back to arguments that have circulated for centuries. Admittedly, her position is not as extreme as the one espoused at the beginning of the 19th century by the leading political economist David Ricardo, who argued that Great Britain would be happy and prosperous if the “evil” of the national debt was extinguished completely, and the country embraced a system in which trade is left “perfectly free” and taxation reduced to a bare minimum. His own “tough love” proposal was to scrap the Poor Laws, as they encouraged overbreeding by the working class, thereby depressing market-determined wages.

Britain will benefit from much closer trading relations with the EU even if that means giving up its ability to negotiate free trade agreements, the Scotland secretary has said. Douglas Alexander helped negotiate deals with India and the US when he was a trade minister under Keir Starmer. But he has told the Guardian he thinks joint trading arrangements with the EU – whether under a customs union or full membership – would be a bigger economic prize, not least because the EU has now negotiated its own similar deal with India. When Starmer was prime minister, ministers would argue against rejoining the EU because it would mean having to abandon trade agreements with other countries. Cryptocurrency exchange founded by Reform donor Ben Delo sued for £20m

A cryptocurrency exchange founded by the billionaire Reform UK donor Ben Delo is being sued for £20m over claims that the company mis-sold financial products in the UK. Lewis Barber, who is a software engineer, alleges that BitMEX offered crypto derivative products to investors in the UK, despite not being regulated or approved to do so by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). The claim filed at the high court but not yet served on BitMEX contends that under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 such contracts are void and that consumers are entitled to restitution of any bitcoin lost on those trades. Barber claims that he lost bitcoin between 2018 and 2022 to the value of £20m through trading the derivatives offered by BitMEX, which amplified gains or losses for investors depending on the changing value of the cryptocurrency. Barber’s lawyers allege he may be one of thousands of non-professional investors in the UK who sustained heavy losses after being sold derivative products by BitMEX in breach of FCA rules and consumer protection laws.

text:
Global financial system is failing developing countries, says Ed Miliband

The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, will claim the global financial system is failing developing countries, as he calls for a “new deal” for governments struggling under the burden of debt. Promising to throw the UK’s diplomatic weight behind urgent reform, he will evoke the example of the Gleneagles summit under the last Labour government in 2005 – the culmination of the Make Poverty History campaign. “The global financial system and indeed the global order is failing to serve developing countries on debt, on resilience and on climate. This is not just against our values but against our national interest,” Miliband is expected to say. “In the interconnected world we live in, more than ever, the opportunities and challenges we confront are collective.” Speaking in Bangkok on Wednesday, he will call for the World Bank and other multilateral development banks (MDBs) to use the resources they have available to lighten the load for governments trapped by hefty borrowing costs. “We need action on developing country debt through the MDBs,” he is expected to say.

Global financial system is failing developing countries, says Ed Miliband

“Action that leverages the balance sheets of the international financial institutions to support these countries to repay over longer time horizons, and crucially, refinancing, with better rates, to give them precious fiscal space.” The foreign secretary will be in Bangkok to attend the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings. He opted to take up the UK’s seat on the bank’s board himself instead of leaving it to the development minister, Kirsty McNeill. Labour’s manifesto in 2024 promised to restore the UK’s international reputation on development issues – but Keir Starmer subsequently slashed the aid budget to pay for defence. Campaigners have long claimed the high interest rates paid by many developing countries mean the repayments crowd out vital public spending – including on tackling the climate emergency. In sub-Saharan Africa, more than three times as much is spent on debt servicing as on education.
