Fund defence spending from tax rise on middle earners, thinktank tells Healey

The chancellor, John Healey, must be prepared to raise taxes for middle earners if he wants to fund significantly higher defence spending, the Resolution Foundation thinktank has said. Healey resigned from Keir Starmer’s government in June, protesting against what he argued was the then prime minister’s failure to adequately fund defence. But in his new post in No 11 Downing Street, Healey has made clear that he will wait until next year’s spending review before presenting a plan to meet Labour’s pledge of devoting 3.5% of GDP to defence by 2035. Related: Defence spending is an insatiable beast. John Healey is right to tame it | John McTernan In a new report, entitled Thin End of the Wedge, economists at the Resolution Foundation suggest he will not be able to raise the £28bn a year it would take to meet that promise without asking average workers to pay more. They say that despite historically large tax rises since Labour came to power in 2024, amounting to £70bn a year, the “tax wedge” – taxes on earnings, minus benefits – remains low by international standards.

“Despite recent increases, the UK still taxes average earners less than most of our international peers,” says the foundation’s chief economist, James Smith. The analysis shows that tax rises under Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, resulted in a 2.4 percentage point jump in the tax wedge last year – the largest for any country in the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD). Yet at 32.4% for a single earner on average pay, it remains below the average for the OECD and the G7 major economies, they say. When the economists looked at countries with higher public spending, they found these tended to ask their average workers to contribute more – instead of relying on business or wealth taxes, for example. “No other OECD rich country has a bigger state and a lower burden on average workers, so any politician promising both is not being realistic,” Smith said.

Green party members back Zack Polanski to stand in London byelection

Zack Polanski moved a step closer in his quest to become an MP on Wednesday, with local Green party members supporting him to become the party’s candidate in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. The party leader in England and Wales started campaigning alongside his fellow Green, Hannah Spencer, the MP for Gorton and Denton, in the Holborn area on Tuesday, and is seriously considering putting himself forward as the party’s candidate in the seat vacated by Keir Starmer on Monday. Green party sources said local party members would have the final say on the selected candidate, but the Guardian understands local members are supportive of Polanski running, with no clear local activist with significant support expected to oppose him. It is understood nominations will open soon and candidates will be selected by the end of next week. Lorna Jane Russell, the leader of the Greens on the local Camden council, will not stand, having previously expressed a desire to focus on her role as the leader of the opposition at Camden Town Hall and her pregnancy.

Burnham to crack down on UK mega-donors influencing politics

Andy Burnham’s government has pledged to “tackle the issue of mega-donors in UK politics” as soon as possible, with dozens of Labour MPs demanding an immediate cap on donations before the next election. The government outlined plans for a taskforce that will look at dealing with the influence of donors giving multimillion-pound contributions and suggested ministers wanted to find a “solution” to the issue quickly. Burnham has previously backed the idea of an annual donations cap in correspondence with a campaigner but the Guardian revealed last week that he was not in favour of including it in the new representation of the people bill debated by MPs on Wednesday. Trade unions have been pushing back against the idea of a donation cap over fears that a rightwing government could take steps to stop large donations from their movement. But during the debate, a string of MPs, led by Labour’s Stella Creasy, made the case for a cap on donations to help restore trust in democracy and argued there were ways of bringing in limits that would not restrict union funding.

A Reform spokesperson said Geoghegan and Crick were refused accreditation because the party viewed them as minor figures. They declined to comment on why Isaac was not given accreditation. Sadiq Khan fined over untaxed car falsely registered in his name

Sadiq Khan’s office has revealed he was the victim of a scam that led to him being fined for failing to tax a car that did not belong to him. The London mayor was found guilty last month under a system of “conveyor-belt justice”, in which magistrates decide on hundreds of cases a day, sometimes spending less than a minute on each. City Hall officials say the 24-year-old Nissan Micra did not belong to Khan or Transport for London. The mayor has been the focus of protests by motorists angry at the expansion of the ultra-low emission zone in London. Some said they planned to register cars in Khan’s name to make him liable for the £12.50 daily charge. The prosecution was undertaken by the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency, which accused Khan of being the keeper of the vehicle when it was spotted as being untaxed on 24 January. In a move that paves the way for the conviction to be erased after a court hearing on Thursday, the DVLA said on Wednesday evening that the case had been withdrawn after a review and it was investigating the circumstances. “This is a scam, which is a crime,” said a spokesperson for Khan.

“It’s not the first time the mayor has been the victim of a scam involving people falsely stating that Sadiq is the owner of a vehicle. Such behaviour is illegal, and the DVLA are aware.” A magistrate, sitting in a private hearing of the single justice procedure in Herefordshire, convicted Khan in his absence and ordered that he pay a £220 fine, £85 in costs and settle the £35.84 bill for unpaid tax on the Micra. The Press Association alerted the DVLA to the criminal conviction on Tuesday and its officials confirmed they were reviewing the case and investigating the circumstances of the prosecution. The mayor faces the possibility of having to appear in court to try to overturn the conviction. Reform’s media presenter worked for Chinese state propaganda channel

Reform UK’s top media presenter has worked for a Chinese state propaganda channel within the past year, the Guardian can reveal. Ray Addison, who presents the political party’s in-house podcast and social media campaigns, fronted films about Xinjiang province – where the Chinese government is accused of committing genocide – for state media in September 2025. In the videos, entitled Raymond’s Xinjiang Stories, some of which praise Chinese infrastructure, Addison described himself as a CGTN correspondent. The series was made after Addison left GB News in 2024, where he had worked as a news presenter and reporter. Xinjiang province has attracted international attention because of alleged human rights abuses against the region’s Muslim Uyghur population by the Chinese state, including claims of forced labour, sterilisation, re-education and mass surveillance. Addison’s work for China contrasts with the hard line Reform has taken on Chinese issues ranging from industrial relations to suspected Chinese state espionage within Westminster.

Zack Polanski has announced his intention to fight for the Commons seat vacated by Keir Starmer, setting up a high-stakes byelection pitting the mass campaigning of his Greens against a resurgent Labour under Andy Burnham. Local Greens in Holborn and St Pancras still have to formally select their candidate under a process that will not be completed until next Friday. text:
Nicola Close obituary

My friend Nicola Close, who has died aged 75 of cancer, was a public health leader who made a major contribution to the field as chief executive of the Association of Directors of Public Health (ADPH). Starting as its sole employee in 2007, she built an influential organisation currently employing 19 people. This became especially evident during the Covid-19 pandemic, when directors of public health, whose role includes providing local leadership and implementing national guidance, were thrust into the spotlight. To support members to work more effectively, and strengthen communication between central government and local communities, Nicola helped break down barriers to data sharing, and secure regular meetings between directors of public health and UK chief medical officers. In 2025 she was made MBE for services to public health. Born in Poole, Dorset, to June (nee Orson) and Douglas Close, a firefighter, Nicola attended Monmouth school for girls before studying mathematics at Somerville College, Oxford. There she met and married a fellow student, John Gilbert, in 1972. Divorced in 1982, she married Roger Flatman two years later.

citation.title: Nicola Close obituary

text:
Nicola Close obituary

During the 1980s Nicola gained an MA in philosophy (logic) from Birmingham University. She then worked as a maths and computing teacher at Westbourne high school in Ipswich, while also gaining a computer programming qualification and working as a computer analyst. In 1985 she moved to Cambridgeshire, as a consultant educational research analyst, and an adult education tutor. In 1994 she was appointed regional health authority clinical audit coordinator for East Anglia. I first met Nicola during this time, when I was completing specialist training in public health. Evidence-based medicine was becoming increasingly important to health policy, and public health had a lead role in promoting these initiatives. Nicola was well set to apply her mathematical, computer and teaching skills to public health practice, and in 1997 she became education and development officer with the Anglia Clinical Effectiveness Team at the Institute of Public Health in Cambridge. In 2001, she became director of Alpha (Access to Learning for the Public Health Agenda), providing public health and clinical governance education across the NHS, local authorities and voluntary sector.

citation.title: Nicola Close obituary

text:
Nicola Close obituary

Nicola, who was also a council member of the UK Public Health Association, recognised that wider social, economic and environmental factors determine health and wellbeing and, alongside her professional and family life in Littleport, Cambridgeshire, became a governor of Soham village college in 2004, two years after the terrible murders of two girls by the school caretaker. She went on to serve as chair of governors from 2007 to 2009. In 2006, during my final year as president of ADPH, I approached Nicola to help organise our annual conference. Under her leadership, ADPH grew into a highly successful organisation for directors of public health, who Nicola always fiercely defended, often quietly and without seeking credit. Her marriage to Roger ended in divorce in 2010. She is survived by four children, George and Heather from her first marriage, and Luke and David from her second, seven grandchildren and a brother, Douglas.

Nigel Farage sought to shore up his damaged leadership on Friday as he attempted to distance himself from two of his most senior officials reported to the police for apparently plotting to evade the law on foreign donations. As the scandal engulfed Reform UK’s party conference in Birmingham, Farage was forced to suspend close aides Dan Jukes and head of policy James Orr after an undercover investigation by reporters from a group called Verbatim. He later acknowledged Jukes and Orr had made “human error” and were “not authorised” to act in the way they did when trying to orchestrate donations to benefit the party from a fake US businessman, who was not permitted to give money. The Met police are now assessing the evidence after a complaint that Farage, Orr and Jukes may have broken political funding laws, with sources suggesting a full investigation is highly likely to be launched. They all deny wrongdoing.

text:
What is the latest finance scandal facing Reform UK?

Nigel Farage is facing yet another finance scandal following an undercover investigation into how Reform UK is funded. The potential wrongdoing – denied by the party – appears serious enough to have been immediately referred to the police by Labour and the Liberal Democrats. Here are the main legal issues for Reform and what any investigation will have to consider. What are the key allegations against Reform? There are at a number of separate possible strands for the authorities to investigate: 1. That Reform’s Dan Jukes and James Orr orchestrated payments totalling £32,500 for political polling from a donor who aides believed to be based in the US and therefore was not permitted to give money (but who was actually an undercover reporter). The payments should also probably have been declared to the Electoral Commission as a benefit in kind. 2. That Nigel Farage knew about the scheme, and congratulated the fake donors, saying “Boom – it worked”. 3. That a senior aide suggested a proposed £500,000 donation from the impermissible US businessman could be made via a UK intermediary. 4.

text:

The same aide suggested that similar arrangements may previously have been used to channel money from foreign sources to Reform through declared UK donors who were family members. 5. That Nigel Farage tacitly condoned the proposed £500,000 arrangement, saying “thank you both” when it was explained. What are the potential breaches of the law? The actions of the Reform aides, the party’s registered treasurer and possibly Farage himself could fall foul of section 61 of the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000, which covers offences concerning arrangements intended to evade the restrictions on political donations. Labour believes section 61(1) applies where a person knowingly enters into, or does an act in furtherance of, an arrangement that facilitates or is likely to facilitate a donation to a registered party from a person other than a permissible donor. The commissioning of £30,000 of polling could apply to this, as well as the attempt to solicit the larger £500,000 donation.

Catastrophic dangers await Burnham’s push for English devolution

Devolution in England is going to be messy and slow, and brings with it huge risks that Andy Burnham ignores at his peril. The prime minister’s devolution push will be messy because Whitehall’s ingrained anxiety about handing over money and power will lead to piecemeal deals, starting with a deal for Cornwall that will lack the much-promised driving force of a newly minted mayor. And there is every prospect that it will be slow now that the reappointed housing secretary Angela Rayner’s reorganisation of local government, creating hundreds of unitary authorities where counties and districts once ruled, is mired in judicial reviews. Some councils have run up huge debts in the last decade and it’s not clear how these debts will be divided among the new entities. There are claims that plans to divide some existing county councils into three, four or even five unitary authorities is politically motivated and that Labour has become seduced by the prospect of retaining a presence in local government through gerrymandering.

Last week, Hertfordshire county council and Newcastle-under-Lyme borough council became the latest local authorities to send letters to Rayner, seeking clarity on how the government reached its decision in their areas. A week earlier, Lincolnshire county council did the same. Farther south, Essex county, which is to be divided into five unitary authorities, found that the recommendation of Whitehall officials for just three new authorities was overruled by Rayner. Supposedly, all this infighting will be resolved by Christmas and England will be ready for an entirely new map of local authorities by next May when fresh elections will be held. Surely these councils and combined authorities, many of which are also embryonic, will struggle to become public institutions with verve, drive, knowledge and experience, able to make good decisions in time for the next election in 2029. When devolution is the prime minister’s big idea, one that will energise Britain’s spirit of enterprise, how it works is going to be crucial.

Rayner’s plan is rooted in a belief that local government has failed to work properly and that structural reform is the answer, saving much more over the longer term than the estimated £2bn initial cost. It is a belief that has no basis in academic study. It would be a relief to all of those involved in local government and devolution to know that somewhere in the world there was data illustrating how this kind of structural change improves services, saves money and, as Burnham would have it, supercharges economic growth. Unfortunately there isn’t any such evidence. It is, to use a well-worn cliche, just re-arranging deckchairs. And it is not just because the same people will be taking up the same roles in new offices (and yes, there will need to be five head offices instead of one in Essex). But there is nothing inherently valuable about them.” What improves services are reforms to the way public officials work, and that means difficult discussions with trade unions. There needs to be a level of accountability that is absent in significant areas of the public sector. And it will be crucial to change how public organisations relate to each other, how they work together, breaking down old silos and protective practices. It involves giving more information to local people and including them in decision making going forward. Geoff Mulgan, a University College London professor and the former boss of the Nesta thinktank, says devolution must answer basic questions people should know, such as how private and public services are delivered and who determines the outcome, from broadband to banking. “Otherwise it will remain entirely legitimate for populist politicians to say that people have lost control and to claim that they are the answer,” he says. Until now, Andy Burnham has been a lucky prime minister. In office for just over six weeks, no major domestic crisis derailed his plans over the summer, Reform has been on the back foot, and he arrived back at Westminster with his personal approval ratings soaring and optimism undampened. In their early weeks in office, his team were able to point to some inherited green shoots: below-forecast inflation figures, sustained growth, signs that sluggish productivity could be starting to turn around. Let me kick off by letting a little daylight in on magic. If you’ve got a book out in September, you’re probably sending the publisher the final version of the introduction four months earlier. So I guess the moment I truly knew that Keir Starmer was finished was the moment, in the first days of May, when I typed the words “we’ve had three prime ministers since my last book”. At that point it became an absolute cast-iron cosmic inevitability that we would have had yet another prime minister by the time the book was out. Nailed on. It’s the equivalent of lighting a cigarette so the bus turns up immediately. So, four prime ministers in four years … Good times, possibly, for someone whose job involves writing about prime ministers. But not good times for Britain, or indeed for the seemingly endless series of outgoing premiers. Being British prime minister has become the biggest ejector-seat job since the noughties, when the US would announce they’d killed “the al-Qaida No 3” about twice a month.

As Reform members at the Birmingham venue applauded Tice, there was plenty of agreement with his views. “I enjoyed the heat this summer,” said Jeanette Bowden, of Bexley. “I don’t think people need telling to take care of themselves.” Her partner, James, added, without scientific backing: “Carbon dioxide was much higher in the past, it was 10 times higher than this during the ice ages. Sweden confirms 458 Britons deported or forcibly removed since Brexit

Sweden has confirmed 458 British citizens have been deported or forcibly removed by police since Brexit. It is the first time the scale of the deportations of citizens who failed to secure residency in Sweden post-Brexit has been made public and comes amid mounting criticism of a cruel and hardline approach to Britons who had chosen to make the country their home before Brexit. Some have been told to go after more than 25 years in the country and even vulnerable elderly people with dementia have been affected. Downside of Burnham’s devolution drive

Where are the city regions and “strategic authorities” in most of rural Devon, Surrey, Hertfordshire and much of Kent and Essex? If Andy Burnham goes ahead with the local government reorganisation (LGR) he inherited from Steve Reed, we will be faced with vast tracts of non-place authorities with names such as Devon Coast and Countryside and North West Essex, which do not make sense as strategic authorities. They are what remain when the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government has completed its long-term aspiration of reducing the number of English councils and councillors.

text:
Downside of Burnham’s devolution drive

We estimate that when this LGR is completed, 90% of councillors and 75% of councils across England could have disappeared, eliminating almost all authorities based on real places and communities. Germany, with its Basic Law, much admired by Mr Burnham, operates with about 11,000 municipalities in a tiered county-municipality structure, and retains municipalities based on real places. The equalisation elements of the Basic Law, which sparks the PM’s interest, have been achieved without the introduction of huge anonymous unitary councils across Germany. England already has the largest units of local government across Europe; nothing is to be gained from making them larger and more anonymous. Farage still Reform’s best hope as rivals struggle to match appeal to party faithful

Few British politicians unleash the kind of evangelical zeal among their party faithful as Nigel Farage. Despite being weighed down by weeks of scandal, last weekend’s Reform UK conference showed that – as far as the membership is concerned – the lustre has not come off their man. So it was notable that Farage felt compelled to reassure his disciples that he wasn’t going anywhere. “I’m only here because of the failure of our political class, and I am determined to lead Reform to victory at the next general election. That is my job,” he told them during his speech. While support within the party for Farage remains rock solid, the same cannot be said for the wider public. Dogged by financial controversy and with a parliamentary standards investigation hanging over him, as well as the police looking into Reform, it is unsurprising that his ratings have slumped. The steady drumbeat of speculation over his future has continued.

By 2029, the likely date for the next election, Farage would be 65 years old. That would make him the same age – he tells friends – as Winston Churchill in 1940, the oldest first-time prime minister to take office in the modern era. Another five years at the helm would put Farage well ahead by that measure. Yet four out of five Reform UK members say they would want Farage to continue as leader even if the party is not in government after the next election, according to a poll of 850 members by Lord Ashcroft in June. Just 13% said he should step down if they don’t win. There are those inside the party who don’t think Farage will stick around even until the next election. “There are all sorts of reasons why Nigel could throw in the towel before then,” one Reform official said, citing family, security and money.

Hundreds of masked and hooded anti-migrant activists descended on an English coastal town and city over the weekend, blocking traffic in and out of the port of Dover, and gathering in Portsmouth after it emerged a boatful of people had been rescued at sea and brought ashore there. Those pre-existing groups all defined themselves as “patriots” – qualifying as such, in their eyes, by hatred of people migrating to the UK from abroad – and came mainly from the south of England, though their number also included representatives from the north-west. Its leader is Daniel Thomas, better known as Danny Tommo, the right-hand-man of the far-right extremist, fraudster and violent criminal Stephen Yaxley-Lennon – who wants people to call him Tommy Robinson. Thomas, whose large social media following has been part of the group’s recruitment drive, has claimed to have “handpicked” his group of activists for “quality over quantity”, according to the campaign group Hope Not Hate (HNH), which has been monitoring Patriot Platform. Thomas has said he wants “discipline” over “the drinkers” and “the violence”. And HNH has described Patriot Platform as a group of men portraying itself as devoted to protecting British women and children, and to Christian values. In reality, the organisation has said, its ranks are home to a host of violent criminals. That includes Thomas, who has himself spent time in prison for his part in a kidnapping attempt. He was also part of a group of 10 extremists banned from France in January, with French authorities saying at the time: “Our rule of law is non-negotiable.

The group of black-clad men gathered in Dover on Saturday morning and moved to block the A20, which leads into and out of the port. Traffic was stopped, causing delays of up to 30 minutes and four miles of congestion, according to National Highways. The men chanted “stop the boats” and “England till I die”, while the words “blood is on your hands” were sprayed on the floor outside a facility used to process people arriving in the UK. Despite the group having made clear it was planning something, the timing and details seem to have come as a surprise to Kent police, which said it was a “spontaneous protest” at which it made no arrests. The local MP, Labour’s Mike Tapp, said police appeared to have had “little advance warning” and questioned whether intelligence had been missed. “I will be asking why,” he said. “A clearly coordinated protest is not ‘spontaneous’ as described by police.

We can and must do better.” The action in Portsmouth, at which Thomas and a host of black-clad and masked men were also seen, appeared to be more spontaneous – with the Patriot Platform leader imploring people on a live stream to travel to Portsmouth to join the protest. What is the group planning next? Before it even pulled off Saturday’s action, the group was already threatening more protests. Polanski faces Green rival in his pursuit of Keir Starmer’s old seat

Zack Polanski is facing unexpected opposition from his own party in his attempt to fight the Holborn and St Pancras byelection for the Greens, with a local councillor saying he is also seeking the nomination, and that the seat does not need “a politician you’ll only see on a leaflet”. The intervention by Hamza Chowdhury, a Green representative on Camden council in north London, came as the date for the byelection was confirmed for 8 October, after Keir Starmer’s formal resignation as an MP. This is also potentially problematic for the Greens, given the vote comes just a week after their conference, meaning the final weekend of campaigning takes place as many party activists will be gathered in Brighton. In a post on Instagram on Monday, Chowdhury said he had received nominations from six other Camden Green councillors, among them Lorna Russell, the group leader in Camden for the Green party, which is the official opposition to Labour. However, it is understood that this does not mean the councillors support Chowdhury rather than Polanski.

‘We can win here’: Zack Polanski presses the flesh in Holborn and St Pancras

Zack Polanski has said he will remain as Green party leader even if he loses the Holborn and St Pancras byelection in a high-stakes contest for the left of British politics. Speaking to the Guardian while door knocking in the north London constituency, Polanski calls the Greens underdogs in the race but says he is confident he could beat Labour, which won the seat with a majority of more than 11,000 at the 2024 general election. The seat has been vacated by Keir Starmer, who announced last Tuesday he was leaving parliament having resigned as prime minister in June. The Greens are confident about their chances, with party activists having already “knocked on thousands of doors”, according to Polanski, but the race comes as the party has fallen in the polls. There have been murmurs that it might have reached its peak in dying days of Starmer’s premiership, exemplified by the party’s seismic win in the Gorton and Denton byelection in February. Polanski is not yet formally the Green’s candidate for Holborn and St Pancras but local members are likely to select him.

Polanski joined volunteers in King’s Cross over the weekend to speak to local voters. It was his fourth visit to the constituency in a week. Should he win, Polanski says he will not move to the area but cycle from his flat in Hackney. “I can cycle to the constituency really quickly. In fact, the length of the constituency is just as fast for me to cycle,” he says. “I’d regularly be here, doing surgeries and representing people.” Some political commentators have said the seat is a difficult one for the Greens to win and that his run is a high-risk proposition. “I think it’s nonsense,” Polanski says.

text:
Black-clad mobs and the puzzle of two-tier justice

In Dover and Portsmouth at the weekend, mobs of masked vigilantes in balaclavas acted in an intimidating and racist manner (‘Army of Christian patriots’: how a black-clad vigilante group swarmed Portsmouth, 8 September). Critical infrastructure was blocked, with roads, boats and transport disrupted. Police officers were injured and vehicles damaged. Permission for the orchestrated demonstrations was not sought or granted. Arrests? None. Imagine if this had been a masked pro-Palestine protest or an unauthorised environmental action disturbing the flow of traffic, intimidating the public and injuring police officers. There would have been hundreds of arrests. So, we have an extraordinary example of “two-tier policing”, with the police service being tough on Palestine and climate protesters while going easy on anti-immigrant demonstrations. To be consistent, it’s time to call for extremist racist organisations such as Patriot Platform to be designated as “terrorists”.

citation.title: Black-clad mobs and the puzzle of two-tier justice

text:
Black-clad mobs and the puzzle of two-tier justice

Or, at the very least, for the government and police to use the many powers they have to take robust action against the participants of this kind of shocking whipping up of hatred that has already led to racist pogroms in many parts of the UK. Gideon Ben-Tovim University of Liverpool • Zoe Williams is right to expose the hollowness of the hard right’s claim to “protect … our women” (Why does the hard right have such a high tolerance for domestic abusers in their midst?, 7 September). Last year, I was one of a number of women in a group protesting against Tommy Robinson’s Unite the Kingdom march. As we waited for our train home, our group was attacked by some of his supporters. I was punched in the face. I am due to give evidence in the resulting court case. The contradiction is hard to miss. A movement that presents migrants and refugees as a threat to women can apparently tolerate intimidation and violence against women who stand in its way. There is another disturbing contrast.

Black-clad mobs and the puzzle of two-tier justice

I am due in court myself, charged under the Terrorism Act after sitting peacefully in Trafalgar Square holding a placard saying: “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.” Masked far-right protesters can march through our streets intimidating refugees, migrants and Muslims, while peaceful protesters face prosecution under terrorism legislation. If the phrase “two-tier justice” means anything, surely this deserves scrutiny. Name and address supplied • It’s right that to undercut support for racism (Editorial, 7 September), an end to 15-plus years of austerity must be called not just in theory but in practice. That means spending on public services and infrastructure, not cuts, and wages at least keeping pace with inflation. There is also an immediate task. The far-right mobilisations in Dover and Portsmouth represent an attempt to build a fascist street force fuelled by the words of Reform UK and Restore Britain. As we approach the 90th anniversary of the battle of Cable Street, the lesson remains clear. They must not pass. text:
Commons breathes sigh of relief as UK finally takes a moral stance on Israeli settlements

Nobody can say they weren’t warned. The Andy Burnham government might have looked like Continuity Keir with more positive vibes for the first six weeks or so, but on Tuesday a new line was drawn. When Burnham said he felt Labour had not done enough on Palestine and Gaza, he had meant it. His decision to impose trade sanctions on illegal settlements in the West Bank was to be his first break with the past. Some opponents chose to get their retaliation in early, before Ed Miliband had even stood up to make the announcement in the Commons on Tuesday. Mike Huckabee, the US ambassador, declared on Sunday that Ed was guilty of “hating Jews”. Which rather implied he thought Ed hated himself. Huckabee also wondered when we would get round to sanctioning Russia, China and North Korea. Er … We have, Mike. Try to keep up. The Israeli president, Isaac Herzog, insisted that “the UK would be on the wrong side of history” if the sanctions were imposed.

citation.title: Commons breathes sigh of relief as UK finally takes a moral stance on Israeli settlements

text:
Commons breathes sigh of relief as UK finally takes a moral stance on Israeli settlements

Presumably that means that doing nothing as Israeli settlers, with the explicit endorsement of the Israeli government, seize land, burn homes and kill children is the right side of history. It’s a strange world we live in. Itamar Ben-Gvir, the far-right security minister, went completely rogue. His take was that this made “Las Malvinas” Argentinian territory. As though it was the sanctions that were the nail in the coffin for the Falklands. Still, there was some consistency there. The Israel government has never placed much weight on the rights of the Palestinian people to self-determination. So why should they bother to make an exception for the Falkland islanders? Nor was all the oppo to be found abroad. Kemi Badenoch wrote a piece for the Jewish Chronicle in which she insisted that the government was desperate to win back Islamists and that Jews would no longer be safe in this country. Bizarrely, though, she made no effort to engage with what the Tories proposed to do about the Israeli settlements. Presumably nothing.

citation.title: Commons breathes sigh of relief as UK finally takes a moral stance on Israeli settlements

text:
Commons breathes sigh of relief as UK finally takes a moral stance on Israeli settlements

Just give another nod and a wink to Benjamin Netanyahu as yet more Palestinians are forced off their land. I mean, it’s not as if the diplomatic efforts until now have had much effect. By contrast, the Commons itself was an oasis of calm. Proof that just occasionally MPs are capable of behaving and arguing as adults. A proper debate with proper arguments, sincerely held. This could have been partly helped by fewer than 10 Tory backbenchers having bothered to turn up – we have to assume most of them don’t care much either way what goes on in the West Bank – but the Labour benches were all but full. For most of them, this was a statement that was long overdue. Though there was little triumphalism to be seen. More like relief. Burnham even showed up to lend support. Miliband started by addressing his own Jewishness. He had reason to be grateful to Israel for providing a home to some of his relatives and he condemned all forms of antisemitism. But there was a separation to be made between the Israelis and the Israeli government. This was about righting a wrong, not giving in to hatred.

text:
Commons breathes sigh of relief as UK finally takes a moral stance on Israeli settlements

And these sanctions would only apply to goods and services provided to or from the illegal settlements. This wasn’t a blanket ban on everything Israeli. It was about taking a moral stance. At no longer being a bystander while a foreign government broke the law. It was time to live our values and fight oppression and suffering. We were not powerless. It was the only way to maintain the dream of a two-state solution. Nor were we alone. France and Canada had also joined other countries in imposing sanctions. The tone of the debate was immeasurably improved by having Tom Tugendhat reply for the Tories. Had Priti Patel still been the shadow foreign secretary, it would almost certainly have become a lot more bitter. Although Tugendhat was clearly operating with one hand tied behind his back. It wasn’t immediately clear what Tom really thought about the sanctions, but he was under instructions from Kemi to say they were definitely a bad thing and they needed to be opposed. So that’s rather what he had to do. Tugendhat began with a long list of things with which he agreed in Miliband’s statement.

text:
Commons breathes sigh of relief as UK finally takes a moral stance on Israeli settlements

That the settlements were illegal, that crimes had been committed, that Hamas were a terrorist organisation and that a two-state solution was the only workable outcome. You felt that in another world, Tom might have left it at that. But he had a job to do so he came out with a few comebacks. The sanctions wouldn’t work, British security would be compromised and 25% of the UK would die because we would no longer receive Israeli pharmaceuticals. As with Kemi, Tom couldn’t quite square all this away with his default position of doing nothing. Tugendhat considers himself a man of action. Someone who would much rather be seen to be doing something. Now he was left to endorse the option of continuing to let Netanyahu get away with allegations of literal murder. As if all our allies automatically got a free pass. An annual allowance of dead children. Up to 100 and we promise to look the other way. Much of the rest of the statement was taken with Labour MPs offering their appreciation to a government that had listened to their concerns. Nor was it just the home crowd.

text:
Neither political donations nor special interest groups should dictate policy

George Monbiot condemns Andy Burnham for his alleged subservience to the interests of the wealthy (Andy Burnham has already made a mistake that will cost him his premiership: he lost his nerve over political donations, 2 September). If true, I agree. But the same could be said of any interest holding sway in our politics. Lobbying groups, activists, unions, thinktanks, people who obsess about this, that or the other. It is surely not OK for our democracy – at local or national level – to have its priorities dictated by those with the shrillest voices, as well as those with the deepest pockets. Speaking from Scotland, I think that our public realm is a case in point. It seems special interest groups are, to all intents and purposes, the main driver of government policy now. And all too often, said influence is framed by an ideological mission that does not necessarily align with that boring, broad swathe of folks who don’t follow politics closely, and don’t see government as a means to progress personal hobbyhorses or single-issue causes.

citation.title: Neither political donations nor special interest groups should dictate policy

text:
Neither political donations nor special interest groups should dictate policy

The latter are, in their own insidious way, as injurious to democracy as the whispers of the wealthy in the ears of politicians. So too is turning a blind eye to such undue influence because its aims chime with your own beliefs. Leaders of any party must endeavour to serve not some, but all – without fear or favour – including those who didn’t vote for them. Not easy. No guarantee of success. But abandoning that principle makes our politics all the poorer. Colin Montgomery Edinburgh • I was surprised to see George Monbiot paying feasance to that liberal shibboleth, “the general interest”. If a society is fractured by inequalities of class, race, gender, sexuality, etc, then there can be no “general interest” until these are overcome. Ensuring trade union influence over Labour policy through the continuation of union donations acts as leverage against policy being captured by the likes of Lord Alli and Lord Sainsbury.

Unite, for instance, already has a community membership for students, claimants and pensioners, and has organised days of action against benefit cuts and sanctions. Monbiot’s proposal would not strengthen the power of benefit claimants, it would simply weaken the power of trade unions. text:
Remilitarisation and support for Ukraine must not slacken, US tells Europe

The US undersecretary of defence, Elbridge Colby, told European countries they “must not slacken” in their remilitarisation and their backing for Ukraine in a virtual meeting aimed at securing 300 Patriot interceptors for Kyiv. The influential Pentagon official praised Ukraine’s recent “stout defence”, which he said proved that Europe was capable of leading the defence of its own continent from Russian aggression rather than relying on the US. “Support for Ukraine contributes to Europe’s security,” Colby said at the start of a 50-country virtual meeting of the Ukraine contact group, reflecting what appears to be a warmer tone from the US on Ukraine. It helped, he continued, “to rebuild Europe’s military strength and industrial capacity. But words are not enough. Real money and industrial capacity must be put to work. Again, I underline that this is happening, but we must not slacken.” Led by its president, Donald Trump, the US has been pushing for Europe to dramatically increase defence spending and pay to supply American weapons, such as Patriot interceptors, to Kyiv, via a scheme set up by Nato.

Remilitarisation and support for Ukraine must not slacken, US tells Europe

The UK announced it had committed £100m to boost Ukraine’s air defences over winter by buying a package of US military equipment that will include urgently needed Patriot missiles, before the meeting had started. Ukraine is currently unable to prevent Russian ballistic missile attacks because of a shortage of Patriot interceptors, leading to attacks that have killed civilians and destroyed food and logistics warehouses over the summer. Wes Streeting, the UK defence secretary, said that Ukraine had been “pretty clear” about what it needed: “Three hundred Patriot missiles from partner stocks, 500 air-to-air interceptors with counter-cruise missile capability, $2bn for drones,” and continued contributions to other schemes.

‘It’s like a death sentence’ says British widow facing deportation from Sweden

A 78-year-old British widow facing deportation over from Sweden over Brexit has said she feels she is facing a “death sentence” just hours before she was due to be removed from the country. “I just want this nightmare to go away before I die,” says Joyce Thomas. “It is dragging me down. I am really not the same person I was. This has taken years. I just feel sick,” she adds as she packs her bags. Thomas, a retired nurse, who has lived in Sweden for 22 years, was given four weeks to leave the country in August, separating her from her son, grandchildren, large network of friends, her church and her husband’s grave. Her husband, Gwynne, died in 2023 of cancer. It was on a trip back from the UK in 2022, when they visited their second son in Brighton, that they first learned they should have made a formal application to stay in Sweden after Brexit. Her subsequent application to stay in the country in 2023 missed the official deadline but she said her husband who looked after all the household administration, had previously been told there was nothing the couple needed to do after Brexit.

The financial scandal around Reform UK has deepened as police expanded their investigation into allegations of illegal foreign donations and the elections watchdog said it was considering regulatory steps. Police confirmed on Wednesday they would broaden their inquiries into Reform after Channel 4 News broadcast an undercover sting by a group called Verbatim, in which a reporter posed as a foreign donor seeking to fund Reform. The Electoral Commission also said on Wednesday that it was “considering all relevant information and regulatory steps” in parallel with the police inquiry. Two of Nigel Farage’s close advisers, Dan Jukes and James Orr, resigned last week after footage was broadcast showing them discussing ways to get around electoral law with a reporter posing as the son of a foreign businessman. The fake US-based donor also paid for more than £30,000 of polling intended to benefit Reform that was not publicly declared. In the footage, Jukes also appeared to suggest the impermissible US donor could contribute through his UK-based son as a way to get round election law banning foreign donations.

There was a time when placing Israel under strict trade sanctions would have been a politically risky thing for a British prime minister to do. Andy Burnham, however, considers it an electoral asset. As Kemi Badenoch attacked him over defence spending at prime minister’s questions on Wednesday, Burnham deliberately turned the topic to the trade ban on illegal settlements which he had announced on Tuesday. With the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, sitting to his left, the prime minister said: “In this difficult and dangerous world Britain has to stand for something, Britain has to show leadership, Britain has to stand for fairness against injustice. “Where people are being bullied out of their homes and intimidated, we will always stand with the underdog and take what action we can to support them. That, Mr Speaker, is leadership on the world stage: Britain being true to what it’s always been about. “That is what the British people expect of us and that is what this government will do.” Related: Labour shifts on Israel, but what difference will it make?

Burnham sees sanctions against Israeli settlements as an electoral asset

– podcast Under the new sanctions announced on Tuesday, goods produced in illegal settlements in occupied Palestine will be banned from being imported into the UK and those who help build or finance settlements will face sanctions. The measures drew a sharp response from the Israeli government, which announced the closure of the British consulate in East Jerusalem. Domestically, the opposition has been led by Badenoch, who has long been a staunch ally of Israel. In a piece in the Jewish Chronicle, the Conservative leader warned that the prime minister risked “fanning the flames of antisemitism here at home”. “For all Labour claim to have rooted out antisemitism internally, the degree of anti-Israel hatred means that Labour’s approach to many of these issues is Corbyn in all but name,” she added. Others in her party, however, have struck a less aggressive tone. On Tuesday, the shadow foreign secretary, Tom Tugendhat, said: “None of us here rejects the government’s stated aim that we must do everything we can to end the circle of violence and support the Abraham accords and the two-state solution.

“What we reject is performative politics, acting alone, that leaves our envoys irrelevant and our voice weaker.” Some senior Conservatives even backed the government. Edward Leigh, who as father of the house has held his seat longer than any other MP, told the Commons on Tuesday: “I am proud to say that I absolutely and fully support what he is doing today, because it is about standing up for freedom, for morality and for justice for all people in this world.” Related: I believe in a two-state solution in the Middle East. That’s why we’re taking action to keep that hope alive | Andy Burnham The government has reason to believe it is on strong electoral ground with this decision. A poll by YouGov earlier in the summer found 50% of British voters supported a ban on trade with West Bank settlements, while only 16% were opposed. While Labour, Liberal Democrat and Green voters were the strongest backers of such a move, even Conservative and Reform voters were in favour overall.

Labour officials hope the announcement may help them make up ground with progressive and Muslim voters who have moved away from the party since the 2024 election. Many say they remain angry about an interview given by Keir Starmer soon after the Gaza war began in which the then prime minister said he thought Israel had the right to withhold water and electricity from Palestinians. The disillusionment among Muslim voters was particularly important in the Green party’s victory in Gorton and Denton. Meanwhile Labour lost a large part of its broader progressive base during the local elections, in which the Greens took a number of councils and mayoralties in central London. Zack Polanski, the leader of the Greens in England and Wales, tweeted on Tuesday: “Ed Miliband’s statement on Israel is only a first step. We need to go further: a full ban on goods, services & investment.” Labour and the Greens are now again locked in battle, over the Holborn and St Pancras seat, which Starmer has vacated.

Senior UK rabbis come out in support of sanctions on Israeli settlements

Prominent British rabbis have backed Ed Miliband’s sanctions on Israeli settlements, warning that the time for inaction on settler violence must come to an end. The intervention comes after the UK’s chief rabbi, the spiritual leader of mainstream Orthodox Jews in the UK, Sir Ephraim Mirvis, described UK sanctions against illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories as a “dark day for British Jews” and warned they could embolden people who “use hatred as a weapon against Jews”. The sanctions were also condemned by the Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership council. Related: Miliband rejects chief rabbi’s claim that West Bank sanctions put UK Jews at risk But other senior rabbis, many from the progressive wing of the community, have come forward to stress the diversity of views within the British Jewish community, with some backing Miliband’s sanctions, while others warned that concern about the measures should not become an excuse for ignoring settler violence and expansion, and others calling for the government to go further.

Jonathan Wittenberg, a senior rabbi of Masorti Judaism, said he was in the Palestinian village of Umm al Khair while Miliband was delivering his speech, and had seen the results of settler violence “with my own eyes”. “What is taking place today in the West Bank is a Chillul HaShem, a violation of God’s name of the worst order. We cannot stay silent. This is terrible for Palestinian people who want to get on with their lives in peace. It is terrible for Israel,” he said. Wittenberg added: “We must speak out. We must do so out of deep concern for what is human and just, and for the sake of Israel and Judaism. We cannot turn away.” While he acknowledged that the British Jewish community did not have to agree with everything the British government chose to do, he said: “The time is for action.” Rabbi Alexandra Wright from the Liberal Jewish Synagogue in London, vice-chair of the British Friends of Rabbis for Human Rights, said while not everyone in the community would support the sanctions, action was needed as “the occupation and escalating violence are harming Palestinians and Israelis”.

text:
Polanski calls for report on ecosystem collapse to be published in full

Zack Polanski has challenged Andy Burnham’s government to publish an unredacted version of an explosive report by the UK’s spy chiefs that found the collapse of overseas ecosystems would have catastrophic consequences for the UK’s national security. The Green party leader in England said the prime minister should come clean about the scale and impact of the climate and nature crisis and called on the government to publish in full the report that warns the UK faces devastating security consequences. Speaking at the Wild Summit event in Bristol on Wednesday, Polanski asked the prime minister: “Will you tell the truth – and release the full unredacted report from the joint intelligence chiefs? Or will you keep hiding the truth from the public?” The Guardian revealed last year that the report paints a devastating picture of severe food shortages, price rises, migration, political destabilisation and possible war, resulting from the collapse of ecosystems, fuelled by the human-induced climate crisis and over-exploitation.

citation.title: Polanski calls for report on ecosystem collapse to be published in full

text:
Polanski calls for report on ecosystem collapse to be published in full

A redacted 14-page version, including some of the report’s findings, was published in January but the government has repeatedly refused to publish the full version, despite repeated freedom of information requests from journalists and calls from MPs. Polanski, who is expected to be the Green party candidate in the upcoming byelection in Holborn and St Pancras, argued that the extreme weather experienced by much of the UK this summer should be a wake-up call for ministers. “It was a bleak preview of what is to come if we continue to allow the greed of corporations to come above the survival of our natural world – and all that relies on it. This must mark a turning point. Where we say: no more loss, no more quieting of birdsong, no more steady trickling of sewage and poison into our waters.” The report by the joint intelligence committee and other government departments, revealed by the Guardian last October, shows that the UK will face catastrophic consequences from the collapse of key ecosystems in other countries.

citation.title: Polanski calls for report on ecosystem collapse to be published in full

text:
Polanski calls for report on ecosystem collapse to be published in full

These include the Amazon rainforest, which scientists fear is reaching a “tipping point” triggered by deforestation and rising temperatures, which would turn the ecosystem from a huge absorber of carbon dioxide into a net source of carbon. Food shortages would be almost certain to result from the decline of ecosystems overseas, the report found, as would a big increase in global migration, with the potential to fuel unrest. Among the most alarming findings was that armed conflict, which includes nuclear war, was also a potential consequence. The report was due to be published at an event last October, attended by King Charles, in the Natural History Museum. However, at the last minute the publication was pulled, at the behest of Downing Street. In an interview with the Guardian after his speech, Polanski said the Green party would introduce a nature, biodiversity and national security bill to make climate adaptation “fundamental to everything we do”.

The party would also seek to appoint a climate resilience minister whose principal job would be to address problems such as extreme heat, surface-water flooding and wildfires. Polanski reiterated a commitment to introduce a basic income for farmers to “ensure those producing the food we rely on are paid properly for their work”. “We know farmers have had wrecked harvest after wrecked harvest. Their crops are struggling and on top of that you’ve got supermarkets where the bosses are taking record bonuses while fleecing farmers,” he said. Simultaneously on Wednesday, in a letter to Burnham, a coalition of green groups has warned that national security, public health and economic growth are at risk without urgent action to restore nature. The UK has a legally binding target to restore 30% of nature by 2030. This target, which was set by more than 100 countries during Cop15 negotiations in Montreal in 2022, is considered the minimum restoration needed to halt and reverse the global decline in nature.

The UK is currently on track to miss this target, with a recent plan to reach this target in England condemned as “pathetic” and “completely insufficient”. “Your government has diplomatic and legal obligations to halt the decline of wildlife and protect 30% of the land and sea for nature by 2030 … On the current path the UK will miss those targets,” the groups warn the prime minister in the letter. The letter also highlights that two-thirds of the UK’s protected nature sites need “urgent repair”, with many of these sites neglected or damaged by intensive industry, pollution and the climate crisis. The groups warn this leaves communities and businesses exposed to flooding, drought, wildfires and pollution. This warning comes as new research finds that about £2bn a year needs to be invested in protected nature sites – up from roughly £1.1bn today – to restore them by 2042. The groups are calling for more funding, stronger laws and decisive enforcement to “stop the abuses that are hollowing out our natural world”.

text:
UK disabled people could swap Pip cash for ‘in kind’ support in benefit overhaul

Some disabled people could receive “in kind” support rather than just cash payments under a radical overhaul of the personal independence payment (Pip) proposed by official government advisers, the Guardian can reveal. The proposal, from an expert committee largely made up of disabled people, is one of a number of striking “emerging recommendations” likely to form the basis of the government’s Timms review of Pip, expected to be published in the next two months. Rather than automatically receive weekly cash payments, currently between £30.30 and £194.60 depending on need, some claimants could instead swap part of the cash award for specialist equipment and aids, services, or skills and training. Pip would remain non-means-tested, but while cash would remain “the foundation” of the award, the idea that claimants would be offered the choice of practical rather than just financial support marks a potentially radical departure in welfare policy.

citation.title: UK disabled people could swap Pip cash for ‘in kind’ support in benefit overhaul

text:
UK disabled people could swap Pip cash for ‘in kind’ support in benefit overhaul

The committee does not address the costs of Pip – currently about £23bn a year – and does not discuss potential cuts in spending, although it acknowledges its reforms must stay within current Pip spending projections of £41bn a year by 2029. Although political and media debate has focused on the affordability of increases in Pip spending, the committee has focused primarily on improving people’s experience of Pip and better supporting ill and disabled people to participate in every day life. Other recommendations include: • Introducing a fast-track process to allow new claimants with a terminal illness to claim Pip more speedily – and reducing the number of benefit reassessments for people with lifelong or degenerative conditions. • Reviewing strict and “unnecessarily stressful” rules that suspend an individual’s Pip award automatically after they have spent more than 28 consecutive days in hospital. • Improving the way Pip assesses fluctuating issues such as mental illness to adequately capture the impact of conditions that vary over time.

citation.title: UK disabled people could swap Pip cash for ‘in kind’ support in benefit overhaul

text:
UK disabled people could swap Pip cash for ‘in kind’ support in benefit overhaul

While Pip is vital to help disabled people meet the extra costs of disability, it should also support individuals to live independently and help give them choice, dignity and control over their lives, the committee says. Pip should be tailored more closely to individuals’ needs and requirements, offering a wider range of support to help them achieve “participation and opportunity across every day life” including work, care and volunteering, it adds. The 12-strong committee of expert advisers, the majority of whom have lived experience of disability or long-term health conditions, are at the heart of a review commissioned to redesign the Pip benefit after the disastrous collapse of Labour’s planned cuts to disability benefits last year. A backbench rebellion forced the government into a U-turn on £5bn of cuts in the summer of 2025, amid public opposition to plans that would have slashed household incomes and pushed hundreds of thousands of people with disabilities into poverty.

citation.title: UK disabled people could swap Pip cash for ‘in kind’ support in benefit overhaul

text:
UK disabled people could swap Pip cash for ‘in kind’ support in benefit overhaul

The subsequent review of Pip, co-chaired by the welfare minister, Sir Stephen Timms, published an interim report in July this year which concluded that Pip was unfit for purpose and too often left vulnerable claimants feeling dehumanised rather than supported. Pip, which is claimed by nearly 4 million people in England and Wales, is designed to help claimants with the extra costs of disability, such as energy, transport and food. It is not linked to employment status, and about a sixth of claimants are in work. The committee insists the emerging recommendations are not final but will be tested for fairness and workability in a series of workshops involving thousands of people with disabilities across the UK to be held over the next few weeks. There may be resistance among campaigners to introducing non-cash elements within Pip awards. However, recent polling of Pip recipients by the Good Growth Foundation thinktank found half supported the principle of swapping part of their cash payment for services such as skills and training, home adaptations or therapy.

citation.title: UK disabled people could swap Pip cash for ‘in kind’ support in benefit overhaul

text:
UK disabled people could swap Pip cash for ‘in kind’ support in benefit overhaul

The committee’s recommendations are likely to be closely scrutinised by a separate review of the youth jobs crisis by former Labour MP Alan Milburn, who has made it clear that some of the cash spent on benefits for young people should be redirected towards providing them with training and skills. A Department for Work and Pensions spokesperson said: “These are not the final recommendations. The review will report to the secretary of state this autumn and he will carefully consider the final proposals within it. “The Timms review interim report, co-produced with disabled people, made clear that Pip is no longer fit for purpose. “Our goal is to deliver a system that supports disabled people and those with long-term conditions to live independent lives, while remaining fair, sustainable and fit for the future.”

Which one of us has not dreamed of getting a personal email from Nigel Farage? So imagine the excitement that Reform supporters must have felt when a message from their leader dropped into their inboxes late on Wednesday night. And mine. Could he also be about to offer everyone in the country £5,000 in return for electing a Reform government? Sadly not. Even Honest Bob’s planned welfare cuts won’t cover that. Instead, Nige was treating us all to his reflections on his party conference that had just ended. The only drawback was that there appeared to be some gaps in his memory. Let’s be kind and assume he was pushed for space. So let’s help him fill in the blanks. Dear John. ‘Wow.’ That’s what I kept thinking as our conference closed. Good start, Nige. Because that’s what I was thinking too. It’s not every party conference that is completely derailed by an undercover investigation into allegations of illegal sources of party funding. And it came completely out of the blue.

‘Fundamentally unfair’: Burnham must overhaul migration reforms, says TUC general secretary

Andy Burnham must overhaul Shabana Mahmood’s migration reforms or risk overstretching social care and fuelling far-right sentiment, the TUC general secretary, Paul Nowak, has warned. Speaking ahead of the TUC’s annual congress in Brighton next week, Nowak welcomed the “sense of optimism” around Burnham’s fledgling government, but he urged the PM to act in a series of areas, including migration and the cost of living. Burnham reappointed Mahmood as home secretary when he became prime minister in July. Her department is consulting on proposals that would force more than 300,000 low-paid workers to wait 15 years for the legal right to remain in the UK. These include many carers who came to the UK to fill vacancies after the Covid pandemic, and were told they could apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years. “I think it is fundamentally unfair to change the rules when people came to this country with one set of expectations,” Nowak said. “I hope we can think again on that.” He added: “There are 111,000 staff vacancies in social care at the moment.

citation.title: ‘Fundamentally unfair’: Burnham must overhaul migration reforms, says TUC general secretary

text:
‘Fundamentally unfair’: Burnham must overhaul migration reforms, says TUC general secretary

I want us to train up as many Brits as possible to do those jobs. But I suspect in a growing economy with an ageing population, we are still going to need people to come and live and work in the UK and work in sectors like social care.” As well as criticising the backward-looking changes, Nowak also condemned the idea of applying a 10- or 15-year wait to many new arrivals, as the Home Office has proposed. “Both my granddads came to this country after the second world war – one came from Hong Kong, one came from Poland. Both raised their families here. The idea that you could be here for the next 10, 15 years and you’d still have no legal right to remain in the country … how the hell do you plan? Can you buy a house? What does that mean for your employment? Do you have kids? Do you send them to school? I mean, it cuts across any effort to integrate at all.” Labour politicians supportive of the changes see them partly as a way of assuaging public concerns about migration, and neutralising the appeal of populist parties, including Nigel Farage’s Reform UK.

But Nowak suggested that by significantly lengthening the time before people can consider themselves settled in the UK, the approach could ultimately fuel far-right sentiment. “I tell you where you end up: you end up with Reform claiming that a woman who was born in Somalia and has lived here for most of her life and worked hard and contributed to our society, somehow isn’t fit to hold elected office in this country.” Reform UK’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, was recently accused of “straightforward racism” by Labour after he suggested the party’s frontrunner to replace Keir Starmer in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, former child refugee Sagal Abdi-Wali, was not British. Nowak acknowledged that many TUC members will have backed Reform in recent local elections, but suggested the party’s appeal may be waning. “Our members are a broad cross section of the British public. Of course, large numbers of them voted Reform, like other people did.

But certainly the evidence that we’re getting fed back from unions is that just like the British public, the more they see of Nigel Farage, the less keen they are.” Nowak claimed there was a “direct line” from the rhetoric of Farage and his allies, to what he called the “proto-fascism” of the balaclava-clad vigilantes who blocked infrastructure in Dover and tried to stop migrants arriving in Portsmouth last weekend. text:
Highs and lows of Keir Starmer’s time in office

Zoe Williams may be right to describe Keir Starmer as a poor politician, but what did we expect (Farewell Keir Starmer, a terrible politician whom we desperately wanted to be something more, 2 September)? After 14 years of economic stagnation and a succession of career politicians as prime minister, we had a leader who previously had a proper job and career outside politics. Starmer’s legacy might be to demonstrate why we need to invest in a better cadre of skilled professional politicians. Those still pining for Starmer may remind us of achievements such as removing the two-child limit on universal benefit, more free school meals, Best Start family hubs, greater employment rights, increases in the minimum wage, renters’ rights, more GPs, lower waiting lists, the Hillsborough law, better relations with Europe etc. But they shouldn’t bother – no one was listening then, and they certainly aren’t now. The Foreign Office has its first female head after the appointment of Lindy Cameron, the high commissioner to India. Cameron’s new role as permanent undersecretary at the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office means she will replace Olly Robbins, who was sacked over the Peter Mandelson scandal. Her appointment comes at a time of wider change at the top of the civil service, as Cat Little, formerly leading the Cabinet Office, is moving to become permanent secretary of the Department for Business and Trade, and Tom Riordan, a former local government official, is taking the top job at the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. Reform UK has been given a record £36m donation by Ben Delo, a British cryptocurrency billionaire convicted in the US for failing to implement adequate anti-money laundering controls. The businessman, who has moved back to the UK from Hong Kong, is now the biggest UK political donor by far, dwarfing the £15m contribution to Reform UK from Thailand-based Christopher Harborne. The huge donation will be a boost for party leader Nigel Farage at a time when he is facing a police investigation into overseas funding for Reform, plus a standards inquiry into a £5m undeclared personal gift from Harborne. It had been thought Delo could be caught by the overseas cap requiring donors to have been resident in the UK for 12 months before giving more than £100,000 but Reform insisted earlier this month that they were confident Delo would not have to take back any cash. Delo was convicted in the US in 2022 for failing to implement adequate anti-money laundering controls in his trillion-dollar cryptocurrency business BitMEX, before being pardoned by Donald Trump. He has previously given Reform £8m since the start of the year.

Portsmouth experiences second weekend of anti-immigration protests

Two men and a teenage boy have been arrested in Portsmouth at a far-right protest against immigration. Far-right activists have gathered in Portsmouth for a second weekend after a small boat with 140 people seeking asylum on board was intercepted last Sunday while heading towards the city. They were greeted by counter-protesters as police warned they would not tolerate incitement of fear or violence. Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary had warned that protesters wearing face coverings could be arrested under powers in the Crime and Policing Act. A 33-year-old man from Portsmouth was also arrested on suspicion of obstructing a highway and a 16-year-old boy, also from Portsmouth, was arrested on suspicion of violent disorder in relation to scenes last Sunday.

text:
Donations of £72m make Reform’s prospects both rosier and riskier

All things being equal, pretty much any political strategist would welcome a £72m war chest; a sum higher than the combined spending of every major party at the 2024 general election. But all things are not equal, and with such a huge amount comes risk. Reform UK has been vocal in its arguments that two sudden £36m windfalls from billionaires Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne merely “levels the playing field” with the bigger parties when it comes to funding. In one sense, this carries some weight. Of the £65m-ish spent in 2024 by the Labour, Conservative, Liberal Democrat, Green and Reform parties, less than a 10th was used by Nigel Farage’s party. Labour’s fighting fund was more than five times bigger. But these are unprecedented sums, donated at an unlikely time – an election is almost three years away even if Reform is convinced that Andy Burnham could seek his own personal mandate as early as next May. Related: Number of UK anti-migrant vigilante groups surges in last 18 months The donations give Reform huge scope to expand its electoral machine.

citation.title: Donations of £72m make Reform’s prospects both rosier and riskier

text:
Donations of £72m make Reform’s prospects both rosier and riskier

They could fund the employment of a new staff member in every UK constituency until the election, though their impact is magnified by the fact that parties devote resources to a much smaller number of target seats. So, what is the downside? There are two. The first is that every time Farage presents Reform as the voice of ordinary Britons, his opponents can argue it is in reality the plaything of people who are wealthy and disconnected from everyday life to a degree almost unimaginable to most voters. Delo and Harborne are strikingly similar: cryptocurrency billionaires who are either based overseas – Harborne in Thailand, although he is electorally registered in the UK – or formerly so – Delo recently returned to the UK from Hong Kong. Opponents will also make much of the fact that Reform’s pledges to liberalise crypto rules in the UK appear likely to make both men even richer, though the party argues this was its stance before it attracted such donors.

citation.title: Donations of £72m make Reform’s prospects both rosier and riskier

text:
Donations of £72m make Reform’s prospects both rosier and riskier

The second, and arguably bigger, concern for Reform is the renewed focus this places on Farage’s own finances, and the perceived cloud of sleaze which has in recent months become more dense around him and the party. As well as donating large sums to Reform previously, Harborne also gave £5m to Farage, a gift that Farage failed to declare on entering parliament, and which is being investigated by the parliamentary standards watchdog as a potential breach of MPs’ rules. Farage only disclosed the gift when the Guardian revealed it in April, prompting not just the standards investigation and the slightly quixotic byelection he fought to supposedly clear his name, but a subsequent period when the Reform leader skipped his previous timetable of regular press conferences to avoid awkward questions. Things became even worse for Farage on the eve of Reform’s annual conference a week ago when undercover footage broadcast by Channel 4 News seemingly showed senior Reform officials trying to avoid electoral laws on foreign donations, with Farage himself apparently informed.

citation.title: Donations of £72m make Reform’s prospects both rosier and riskier

text:
Donations of £72m make Reform’s prospects both rosier and riskier

The party has denied any wrongdoing, but two key Farage aides – Dan Jukes, his de facto chief of staff, and James Orr, Reform’s head of policy – have been suspended, and police are investigating any potential wrongdoing. Optimistic Reform officials may argue privately that £72m could buy enough advertising to blitz any negative coverage, and it is notable how senior figures, such as the deputy leader, Richard Tice, insist the party is“at war” with traditional media. But it is more complex than that, especially under Westminster’s first-past-the-post electoral system. If a party hopes to win it must not only convince its base to turn out and vote, but not be so toxic so that other voters unite to stop it. Polls show increasing numbers of voters see Reform and its leader as not just undesirable but shifty, even dishonest, and they are willing to vote however is necessary to stop Farage entering No 10. Will another £72m in donations from extremely rich men make such perceptions worse? Very possibly. And is that something Reform could do without? Definitely.

text:
A painful truth about post-Brexit immigration

Your report (Wife of British man at risk of deportation from Sweden calls on Burnham to intervene, 3 September) highlights a painful truth about post-Brexit immigration: families are being treated as administrative burdens rather than human beings. However, this harsh treatment cuts both ways. I am a 71-year-old German-American citizen, married to my British husband for 38 years. We have only ever been apart for work. We bought property in the UK in 2023 so my husband could retire there. After retiring from my job in Germany, I applied for a UK family visa on 1 April 2026, expecting to settle down with him and my two adult sons within six weeks. The lawyer was rather optimistic. Five months later, and over £7,000 on costs, I am still waiting. My application remains “under consideration”. I have hired a lawyer, involved an MP, filed official complaints, and paid for priority services, yet the Home Office remains an impenetrable wall. While British media rightly highlights the harsh treatment of UK citizens abroad, the UK Home Office is quietly inflicting the exact same cruelty on older spouses from allied nations.

citation.title: A painful truth about post-Brexit immigration

At 71, my husband and I are losing precious time together to bureaucratic inertia. If we expect European countries to show humanity to British citizens, the UK must show the same decency to the families of its own people. Vera-Lynn Watson Birkenfeld, Germany
