Burnham must understand Wales is ‘not a region in England’, says first minister

Andy Burnham has to be serious about devolution and understand that Wales is a nation and “not a region in England”, according to the country’s first minister. Rhun ap Iorwerth, who is the first non-Labour leader of the Senedd since devolution, told the Guardian that while he was encouraged by initial discussions with the new UK prime minister, he was wary about Burnham being captured by a consensus Westminster view against relinquishing further powers. Separately in the interview, ap Iorwerth said his party, Plaid Cymru, would be willing to cooperate with Labour in the future to keep Reform UK out of power, as he would always want to block the “destructive politics” of Nigel Farage’s party. Ap Iorwerth became Wales’s first minister in May, days after he led Plaid Cymru to victory in Senedd elections, breaking a 100-year period of Labour dominance, which included Labour being the biggest party in every vote to the Welsh parliament since it was created in 1999.

citation.title: Burnham must understand Wales is ‘not a region in England’, says first minister

text:
Burnham must understand Wales is ‘not a region in England’, says first minister

He has pushed for more powers to be given to his government, particularly over policing and the justice system, where Wales is the only UK nation not to have control. Burnham’s background as Greater Manchester mayor was a positive, ap Iorwerth said: “He clearly understands the benefits of getting devolution right for Manchester. I’ve had really positive, constructive discussions with him. “He now needs to know what devolution means for Wales, and it’s very, very different. We’re a nation. We’re not a region of England. There are different needs. We will work closely with the UK government on what empowering communities means. But it’s a totally different model, and it’s really important that Andy Burnham doesn’t confuse the two.” Speaking in London after meetings with UK government officials, ap Iorwerth said, although Burnham had assured him he would “not bypass devolution”, he was concerned about institutional resistance to handing over police and justice powers.

Dover unrest exposes serious flaws in Britain’s handling of far-right extremism

To anybody watching the videos of a group of masked men, all wearing black, descending on the port of Dover last weekend, it was immediately obvious that something novel and disturbing was happening: a mass intimidation in uniform not seen in Britain since the 1930s. Yet to the police and the rest of the UK’s intelligence apparatus, the arrival of the men chanting “stop the boats” was a surprise, despite the fact that residents of a village 18 miles away tried to report that dozens of men were congregating there on the Friday, threatening to go to Dover and “attack Muslims”. Intelligence specialists describe the events in Dover and the day after in Portsmouth as protests, as if they are on a par with cardboard-carrying campaigners marching on an approved route. The same definition was used by Kent police and Sarah Jones, the policing minister, on Monday. “Protest activity,” she told MPs. Such semantics are important to the state, though they appear to misunderstand the recent events.

Leaders at Celtic summit to affirm right to seek independence from UK

The first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland are to affirm their countries’ right to seek independence from the UK at a summit that is likely to challenge Andy Burnham’s devolution agenda. The Plaid Cymru leader, Rhun ap Iorwerth, the Scottish National party leader, John Swinney, and the Sinn Féin vice-president, Michelle O’Neill, are expected to sign a memorandum of understanding at a landmark conference in Cardiff on Monday that will call on Westminster “to prepare, plan and facilitate constitutional change in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland”. The three are meeting in their capacity as party leaders, rather than as officials in their respective governments, alongside the Sinn Féin president and leader of the opposition in Ireland, Mary Lou McDonald. They will also discuss Europe, international cooperation, the economy and energy issues. Plaid Cymru’s victory in May’s Senedd elections ushered in a new era for the Celtic independence movements, with separatist parties in government in all three countries for the first time.

How could Reform UK spend its £72m of new billionaire donations?

Nigel Farage once said he could spend his £5m gift from Christopher Harborne on Ferraris if he wanted to, given its unconditional nature. With the new donations to his party from Harborne and his fellow crypto billionaire Ben Delo of £72m over the past weekend alone, Farage’s party now has nearly enough cash to buy a Reform UK branded Ferrari for a party organiser in each of Britain’s 632 constituencies (though that would certainly be a waste and a bit of a tax headache). But what the cash can buy first and foremost for Reform is manpower. Already the party is seeking to recruit more than 60 local organisers in key areas of the country. Though the donation is certainly enough to staff every constituency in England, Scotland and Wales with organisers, that would also be a massive waste of resources in seats Reform UK is never likely to win. Instead, experienced regional staff can build impeccable targeting data for the seats Reform UK needs to win a majority.

That requires door-to-door canvassing to identify switching voters and non-voters who might be persuaded to turn out. For most parties, those kinds of local resources are only really deployed far closer to an election. Beginning that level of organising and data collection this far out could give Reform UK a massive head start at the next election, though other parties have very valuable legacy data from previous elections of which Reform has much less available. Trade unions, MPs and donors urge Burnham to revisit party funding rules

Trade unions, MPs and donors have urged the government to look again at party funding rules, after Reform UK insisted £72m in donations from two crypto billionaires was within the law. Andy Burnham, a previous backer of caps on domestic donations, has so far declined to insert any curbs in the elections bill that would apply to UK-based donors. Labour MPs have voiced anger on internal WhatsApp groups that the government did not act last week when the elections bill was in the Commons to restrict domestic donations after two donors – Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo – gave Reform UK a total of £72m over the weekend. The bill returns to the House of Lords next week where peers told the Guardian they would ask the government to look again at the issue. The communities secretary, Angela Rayner, suggested on Sunday that the donations could be caught in a new bill which would apply retrospectively on donors from outside the UK. The development minister, Kirsty McNeill, has declared herself “a huge believer in aid”, as she reaffirmed Labour’s manifesto pledge to return to a target of 0.7% of national income spending. McNeill, a former adviser to Gordon Brown and senior executive at Save the Children, declined to give any timetable, repeating the formula that the government would work towards the target “when fiscal circumstances allow”. But she made a full-throated argument for the benefits of aid – as well as promising to build new “agile partnerships” to work on development challenges. “I’m a huge believer in aid; I’m a huge believer in the quality of British aid, and when you have more of it, you can have more impact. And I think it’s important that colleagues hear that underscored,” she said. Repeating the manifesto pledge that Labour made before the 2024 general election to return to 0.7% – instead slashing aid the next year – McNeill insisted that in the Burnham government, “everyone from the prime minister down is a believer in the spirit that animated that manifesto”.

text:
Why English devolution is fraught with difficulty

Your editorial on Andy Burnham’s devolution plans rightly argues that greater local power must be accompanied by greater scrutiny (The Guardian view on Burnham’s devolution plans: power must be accompanied by scrutiny, 6 September). I work as a bid manager in the third sector, applying for publicly procured contracts to deliver employment and support services. From that perspective, the increasing devolution of funding has real potential: decisions can be made closer to communities and, importantly, local organisations should have greater opportunities to deliver services. Yet my experience is of an increasingly complicated and inconsistent commissioning landscape. Different local and combined authorities take markedly different approaches. Some have strong procurement practices, engage constructively with providers and appear well equipped to manage devolved funding. Elsewhere, processes can be fragmented, difficult to navigate and considerably less transparent. It is beginning to feel like a postcode lottery. There is also a contradiction here.

citation.title: Why English devolution is fraught with difficulty

text:
Why English devolution is fraught with difficulty

One stated benefit of devolution is the ability to engage more local suppliers, including smaller voluntary and community organisations with deep roots in the places they serve. Yet these are often the organisations least able to navigate multiple procurement portals, differing requirements and commissioning approaches. Large national organisations can resource this complexity; small local charities often cannot. My concern is not with devolution itself. But transferring substantial sums of public money must be accompanied by investment in local commissioning expertise, procurement capacity and meaningful scrutiny. As more funding moves away from Whitehall, we should ask not simply where power sits, but whether every place has the capacity to exercise it well. Haile Reed Birmingham • In your editorial, you focus rightly on accountability, but overlook something more fundamental: whether local authorities currently have the capability and capacity to deliver devolution at all.

citation.title: Why English devolution is fraught with difficulty

text:
Why English devolution is fraught with difficulty

England is already midway through reorganising local government, with 185 councils being reshaped across 21 areas into new unitary authorities, alongside six new mayoral authorities. Disruption is inevitable. This is happening against a backdrop of serious financial strain. Eight councils have issued section 114 “bankruptcy” notices in the last six years, compared with almost none in the 18 years before that. In a 2024 survey, the Local Government Information Unit found 51% of councils thought it likely they would issue such a notice within five years. Layering new devolved responsibilities on to institutions that are simultaneously being dismantled and rebuilt, and in many cases barely solvent, risks devolving responsibility faster than those institutions can actually deliver it. Devolution may well be the right destination, but the sequencing matters. Alan Coppin Former Crown Representative, Cabinet Office • Lamenting the decline of local media, your editorial proposes “a tax on social media giants to fund local journalism”. Yes please.

“It couldn’t be more different from a couple of offshore billionaires trying to buy our democracy … We will never undermine the rights of working people to organise collectively and democratically.” Trade unions are set to issue a statement on Tuesday on political donations condemning attempts by Farage to compare wealthy individual donors with individual members who donate to Labour through their union, and urging the government to go further on political donations. The head of Britain’s union movement, Paul Nowak, said the government must act to “stop the super-rich corrupting our politics”. But union sources had said there were “significant differences” between general secretaries on how to proceed. Unite’s general secretary, Sharon Graham, on Sunday broke ranks and backed a limit on individual domestic donations. But others, including GMB chief Gary Smith, fear it would lead a future rightwing government to curb union donations. Government sources said that calls from opposition parties for any changes to domestic donations to apply to the unions too were “not under active consideration”.

However, the government is understood to be looking at spending limits for parties, which are currently restricted to the year before a general election, with tighter limits in the weeks running up to polling day. In a letter to the Electoral Commission in August, Rayner and Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, wrote: “We believe spending limits on parties and candidates are too high, and ought to be reduced.” The government has also set up a cross-government “task and finish” team to consider threats to UK democracy, including political finance, illegitimate influence, and broader threats to political equality. Philip Rycroft, who produced an independent report on tightening electoral law around overseas donations, said the Reform donations reopened broader questions about donations and spending caps. “The time has come when this does need a hard look. It would have been better if the government had started out before we had these huge donations coming down the track,” he said.

They include one to enable ministers to set a cap on all donations at a later date, and another to prevent spending limits being raised without Electoral Commission approval. text:
Andy Burnham cancels engagements as his father’s death is announced

Andy Burnham has cancelled his engagements for Monday and Tuesday after his father, Roy, died. Among other plans, the prime minister had been due to speak to the TUC conference in Brighton on Tuesday. Burnham’s father had Alzheimer’s and was in a care home. In an interview Burnham gave in July, he said his father’s condition meant he was unaware that his son was about to become prime minister. “That’s a sadness because he would be [proud],” Burnham told the Times. “But the way I look at it, it’s his achievement as well. A whole family achievement, although he doesn’t know it.” Burnham has talked about wanting to improve social care, in part because of his experiences with his father. In one of his first speeches as prime minister, Burnham said it was humbling to see the “skill and the care and the professionalism” of care workers like those looking after his father, and that they should be paid more.

Among those expressing their condolences was Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, who posted: “My thoughts are with Andy and his family at this terribly difficult and sad time.” In her own post on X, Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, offered her condolences to Burnham and his family, adding: “No matter how old you are, or how much you try to prepare, losing your father is a profoundly painful experience. “A part of your life that has always been there is suddenly gone forever and it can feel as though a part of you won’t ever be the same again.” At the start of the Commons session on Monday afternoon, Lindsay Hoyle, the speaker, said: “I am sure the whole house will want to send our best wishes to him and his family at this sad time.” In Head North, the 2024 book he co-wrote with Steve Rotheram, the Liverpool city region mayor, Burnham described what he said had been a happy upbringing with his father, his mother, Eileen, and his two brothers in Culcheth, near Warrington in Cheshire. Roy worked as a telephone engineer, while Eileen was a GP’s receptionist.

Top civil servant sacked by Starmer received record £860,000 payout

The former head of the civil service Chris Wormald received a record payout of almost £860,000 when he was forced out of the top job in Whitehall by Keir Starmer. Cabinet Office accounts have revealed that the former cabinet secretary, who was sacked earlier this year, was paid £859,496 upon departure. The figure is an unprecedented amount, which required civil servants to seek a special direction from ministers to approve it because it was “greater than what Sir Chris Wormald would be contractually entitled to”. Wormald has since been made a member of the House of Lords, after serving as cabinet secretary for just 14 months. He was replaced by Antonia Romeo earlier this year. It was revealed earlier this summer that the size of the payout to Wormald was so vast that Cat Little, the permanent secretary of the Cabinet Office, had to request a ministerial direction from Starmer in February to override value-for-money concerns before she could approve it.

In her letter to the prime minister at the time, Little wrote that she needed special permission to grant such a high award, saying “in respect of value for money, I have consulted civil service HR and legal advisers and have had due regard to managing public money and the consideration of Sir Chris Wormald’s employment rights in the circumstances. The proposed award is greater than what Sir Chris Wormald would be contractually entitled to.” Little said she had been informed a settlement of that level was “necessary given that this is a departure from a high-profile, unique role that has been agreed at very short notice”. She said the prime minister could take into account “the public interest in bringing this matter to a conclusion and the prevention of distraction from the effective operation of government”. text:
Rise in abuse of election candidates is ‘changing politics’ in England

Abuse and intimidation of election candidates is “a serious and growing concern”, the Electoral Commission has said, as a review of this year’s local and mayoral elections in England revealed a surge in threats to those who stood. More than half of the candidates for Labour or Reform UK reported abuse while those most likely to be targeted were women, people from minority ethnic backgrounds and those with disabilities. A report by the commission said candidates described being spat at and verbally and physically assaulted. It found that levels of abuse had reached the point where it was changing the behaviour of people standing in elections. “I had to take my husband out on the door this time, which was a first,” said one candidate, who was among a third of those who said they may not stand for election again because of harassment or intimidation. They added: “I felt quite independent previously, but there was so much anger from men of an older age at the door and some younger men, all disillusioned by politics and let down.

citation.title: Rise in abuse of election candidates is ‘changing politics’ in England

text:
Rise in abuse of election candidates is ‘changing politics’ in England

“I did understand that, but it was the anger and insults and close confrontation at times which was so aggressive. I feel I have to protect myself in public and not be on my own, for the first time in local politics, and will never put myself in any vulnerable places on my own again.” Female candidates were more likely to change their behaviour over such concerns. More than three-quarters (79%) said they avoided campaigning on their own at least once, compared with 46% of male candidates, while 57% avoided speaking on controversial topics, compared with 32% of men. Vijay Rangarajan, the chief executive of the Electoral Commission, said: “Our single biggest worry now is this rise in abuse and intimidation. It’s not directed at any one party and there seems to be a variety of causes.” He said there was an increasing trend towards the “othering” of political opponents, “literally, a dehumanisation” and a blurring of the boundaries of civility, in some cases driven by social media. “I think we’re going to see a kind of complete blurring of the online and offline worlds,” he said.

“We’ve seen people in the real world walk down the street filming someone to produce an online video. So this kind of real, complete interaction between online and offline is a real feature.” Rangarajan said he was struck by two particular cases. One was a disabled candidate who said they were threatened on the doorstep but “couldn’t run away” because of their disability. Another was a candidate who was targeted on social media and whose daughter called from school to say she had seen the online abuse and people were calling her parent a racist, fascist and Nazi. UK ministers urged to act after US flies out diplomat accused of possessing indecent images of children

British ministers face calls to act after US authorities secretly flew out of the UK a diplomat accused of possessing indecent images of children. US officials reportedly raided the diplomat’s London flat in August before taking him to an American airbase and flying him out of the country, without warning the Metropolitan police. American personnel have no powers of arrest in Britain, and there was no formal request for the man to be extradited. Related: How the US bypasses British courts to try its military over crimes in the UK UK ministers are understood to be in contact with the US embassy over the incident, which could further strain relations between London and Washington. Elements of the case echo that of an American fighter pilot, first reported in the Guardian, who avoided being tried under English law for strangling a woman in Cambridge while off-duty. Capt Jacob Wulfson was tried by court martial at a US airbase and jailed for six months after being convicted of strangulation. He was acquitted of charges of sexual assault and aggravated sexual contact.

In a letter to the justice secretary, Alex Norris, his Conservative counterpart, Nick Timothy, said he was concerned US actions represented “a cover-up” and that the diplomat may have committed offences in the UK. “If this is the case, the diplomat should face trial in an English court.” Timothy said the incident was part of a “concerning pattern” of US authorities prosecuting American service personnel accused of offences against British civilians while stationed in the UK. Citing the Wulfson case, he wrote: “These cases should have been investigated by the English police and prosecuted in our courts. I ask you to urgently explain what action you are taking to address this, and what will be done to ensure the accused diplomat faces a proper investigation in this country.” The diplomat’s case has also been likened to that of the US state department employee Anne Sacoolas, who caused the death of the teenager Harry Dunn in a car crash in 2019. Sacoolas was able to leave the country shortly after the fatal collision when the US asserted diplomatic immunity on her behalf.

New special envoy for Britons detained overseas warns of limits of role

The special envoy for British citizens detained overseas has spoken about the difficulties he faces in his new role, as families express concern over the position’s mandate in complex consular cases. In his first public engagement, Alistair Burt, the former Conservative Middle East minister, spoke candidly about the difficulties and limitations of the new appointment, made following years of mounting criticism of how the Foreign Office handled the cases of British citizens detained overseas. “I don’t make policy. I’m not a minister. I don’t have that authority. It will ultimately be the foreign secretary and the prime minister who will need to make the changes in policy or changes in approach if required,” Burt told an audience in Westminster, following his appointment on Monday evening. “The best thing I can do is not disguise from you the difficulties of the role,” added the former minister. Related: Foreign Office appoints first special envoy for Britons detained overseas Burt, who plans to meet the new foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, later this week, was tipped for the post more than a year ago.

citation.title: New special envoy for Britons detained overseas warns of limits of role

text:
New special envoy for Britons detained overseas warns of limits of role

Burt was candid about the complexities of detention cases and of his role to “kick the tyres” of the policies involved. Burt, whose new role is appointed by the Foreign Office but not paid for by it, said he has already started to meet families of those with complex cases, and said there was “much to be gained” from stronger international condemnation. There is a strong view that the US special presidential envoy for hostages has secured more success and clout inside the diplomatic system, and used more innovative techniques to negotiate the release of Americans. Burt said he plans to meet his US and Canadian counterparts in the coming weeks, and is open to discussing broader cooperation with European leaders. The Foreign Office describes the purpose of the role as being to advance the government’s commitment to British nationals in the “most difficult and complex detention cases overseas” at the direction of the foreign secretary. The role is intended to advocate within and represent government, and engage with families.

A documentary was played showing the ordeal her family went through to secure her release, as well as that of Anoosheh Ashoori, for whom a historic £400m debt was paid to Iran. “I recognised the payment of the debt and I let my foreign secretary know repeatedly,” said Burt of Nazanin’s case, adding, “I got that one right.” That wasn’t the case, he admitted, for Matthew Hedges, a British academic sitting beside him, who was accused of spying for the UK government in the United Arab Emirates and was arrested and tortured. “Other cases I didn’t handle as well as I would have liked,” said Burt. “I’m very grateful that Matthew has seen me since to talk about his experiences.” While welcoming the appointment, Zaghari-Ratcliffe also expressed a fear of quiet diplomacy turning into an “excuse” for government inaction.

Reform declines to say if £72m donors returned to UK within 12-month limit

Reform UK’s deputy leader has declined to say when two crypto billionaires who gave a combined £72m to the party returned to the UK, as the architect of a review into overseas donations said anyone here for less than 12 months would be subject to a limit on donations. Richard Tice said that while he was completely confident Reform had complied with all current and proposed laws on donations, he could not say when Ben Delo returned to the UK from Hong Kong, or how much time the Thailand-based Christopher Harborne spent in Britain. “I’m not their executive assistant responsible for their day-to-day diary,” Tice told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme when asked about the details of their UK residencies. He added: “Everything we’re doing is in accordance with the existing rules and the rules of the legislation that’s going through parliament as we speak.” The legislation referred to, the representation of the people bill, does not currently contain any overall cap on individual donations, after lobbying from Labour-backing trade unions. Related: How could Reform UK spend its £72m of new billionaire donations?

In response to the mega-donations by Harborne and Delo, trade unions, MPs and donors have urged the government to look again at the bill. But in the wake of a report on overseas influence on UK politics by Sir Philip Rycroft, a former senior civil servant, Britons living overseas will be limited to giving a maximum of £100,000. The bill, which goes further than some of Rycroft’s recommendations, sets out that the cap applies to anyone who was not UK-resident for electoral purposes for at least a year from March 2026, applying retrospectively once the bill becomes law. Speaking to Today, Rycroft said that while he could not comment on the circumstances of Delo or Harborne, the residency rules would apply. “What I do understand is that the way the law will work, it will implement my recommendation on a limit for Brits abroad, as it were. But there will also be rules on, if they return to the UK, how long they have to live in the UK before they can count as domestic donors. “And my understanding is that they will have to be living in the UK for at least a full calendar year.

Will the £72m of donations to Reform UK be allowed?

Reform UK announced over the weekend the two biggest single political donations in British history: £36m from the Thailand-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne and a further £36m from another crypto billionaire, Ben Delo. However, by Monday experts were questioning whether the donations would be legal, especially under the elections bill that the government is bringing through parliament and which will apply retrospectively. Are the donations allowable? Here are the key questions which must be answered. Are Delo and Harborne registered as UK-based voters? Under current law, anyone can donate to a political party as long as they are a British citizen who is registered to vote in the UK. However, under the Representation of the People Act donors who are registered as overseas voters will be subject to a cap of £100,000 a year. The £100,000 cap will also apply for at least a full calendar year – from January to December – after they return to the UK. So someone returning to the country in the summer would have to wait for about 18 months before they can donate more than £100,000.

Crucially for Harborne and Delo, this rule will apply retrospectively from 25 March. So the question for both will be, were they registered as UK-based voters before that date? If not they will not be allowed to donate more than £100,000 each in a single 12-month period, making these donations impermissible. Sources have told the Guardian that Delo has been registered as a UK-based voter for years, but that is less clear where Harborne is concerned. A report by Channel 4 News last month said its reporters had seen records suggesting he had only registered as a domestic voter in June, in which case he would be subject to the cap until January 2028, and his donation would not be legal. Reform has refused to say when exactly both men registered as resident in the UK. Should Delo and Harborne be classified as domestic voters? Even if both men are registered as UK-based voters, this status can be challenged. To get on to the electoral roll as a domestic voter, a person only has to write to the local authority and sign a declaration saying the address at which they are registering is their “permanent home address”.

John Healey in talks with Canada about UK joining new global defence bank

John Healey is in talks with the Canadian government about joining a new global defence bank intended to help allies rearm to counter mounting security threats, just weeks after Rachel Reeves rejected the move. The chancellor is understood to be actively considering a bid to join the proposed Canada-led defence, security and resilience bank (DSRB), which proponents say could help the UK fund defence projects at lower cost, before planned talks with his Canadian counterpart this week. When he was defence secretary, Healey was understood to have been a strong advocate for keeping UK observers present at Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney’s, defence bank talks, despite resistance from the Treasury, which wanted to shut off those international discussions. Reeves, his predecessor as chancellor, was concerned the bank would not address the UK’s defence procurement issues and was more focused on lending to smaller defence firms in nations with lower credit ratings. The UK has had a AA credit rating since 2016.

More than 130 legal experts, including 18 king’s counsel (KCs), have written to Andy Burnham saying that sanctions on Israeli settlements “fall far short” of Britain’s obligations under the international court of justice’s (ICJ’s) finding that the occupation is unlawful. The group’s front page invites those visiting to “join the movement” at the website address for Patriot Platform, the vigilante group set up by Daniel Thomas, a long-term associate of the far-right activist known as Tommy Robinson. Addison Lee founder owes £20.5m in tax after UK tribunal ruling

The founder of Addison Lee owes £20.5m in tax after a tribunal dismissed a claim that he should be treated as a nom-dom despite living in the UK since childhood. John Griffin had argued he should be treated as a nom-dom due to his connection to Ireland, saying: “I was and am besotted with Ireland, infatuated with Ireland. I believe that I have always been and am Irish.” HM Revenue and Customs challenged the domicile status on Griffin’s self-assessment tax returns from 2013 to 2020, which would have allowed the 84-year-old to not pay UK tax rates on foreign earnings kept outside the country. This week, a London tribunal ruled in the tax authority’s favour. Related: Billionaire Chris Rokos, who paid £330m in tax last year, to quit UK Griffin was born to Irish parents in 1942 and briefly lived there until he moved to London at the age of nine, according to tribunal documents. HMRC argued that England should be considered Griffin’s home, with the businessman raising a family in Hertfordshire and building his London-based taxi empire, having founded Addison Lee in 1975.

citation.title: Addison Lee founder owes £20.5m in tax after UK tribunal ruling

text:
Addison Lee founder owes £20.5m in tax after UK tribunal ruling

Tribunal judge Michaela Snelders and tribunal member Gill Hunter said: “We are satisfied that by 5 April 2013, Sir John had settled in England in every meaningful sense.” “England was where he had established his home, raised his family, built his business, accumulated his wealth and organised his personal, social and professional life. “Although he retained a powerful emotional attachment to Ireland and a genuine hope that he might one day spend more time there, those sentiments never crystallised into a sufficiently definite intention to make Ireland his permanent home.” The tax chamber tribunal was told Griffin spent eight nights in Ireland in 2015, one of the years he claimed to be domiciled there, which the chamber ruled was “inconsistent with someone seriously preparing for permanent relocation”. As part of his appeal against HMRC’s stance, Griffin had argued that his domicile should be the same as his father, Jack, who had come to England from Ireland in search of work in 1935. Under UK law, a child’s domicile is the same as their father’s if the parents were married at the time of their birth.

text:
Addison Lee founder owes £20.5m in tax after UK tribunal ruling

Legal counsel for HMRC, however, said Griffin’s domicile status under UK law would have changed when his father’s domicile of choice became England. They argued it had done so some time before Griffin reached adulthood at the age of 21 in 1963. The tribunal agreed with HMRC’s stance. The ruling caps off a long-running inquiry into Griffin’s tax affairs and reflects the period after he sold Addison Lee to private equity firm the Carlyle Group in 2013. The business was reported to be worth £300m at the time. Having Irish domicile would have potentially allowed Griffin to avoid being taxed on earnings made outside the UK, a legal benefit of being classified as a nom-dom. The tribunal’s ruling makes his worldwide income from the period subject to UK tax rules, with HMRC calculating that he owes an additional £20.5m covering the seven-year period. Nom-dom status was scrapped by the Labour UK government in April 2025, after a promise a year earlier by Rishi Sunak’s Conservative administration to do the same.

Greens urge Zack Polanski to take stance on proposed policy declaring ‘Zionism is racism’

The Greens are pushing Zack Polanski to take a stance on a potential party policy stating “Zionism is racism”, with some fearing it could alienate Jewish supporters if it was passed. Polanski, who leads the Greens in England and Wales, has not spoken publicly about the motion, which came top of a members’ vote of policy motions to be debated at the party conference in Brighton at the start of October, and is thus almost certain to feature. The Greens make party policy by member votes at conferences. If passed, the motion would equate Zionism – the movement for a Jewish state – with racism, would call for a single Palestinian state, and would risk members who supported Zionism being disciplined for racism. While Polanski is believed to have reservations about the motion, some in the party believe he is wary of speaking out publicly to avoid angering left-leaning members who have joined the Greens in large numbers under his leadership, a number of whom have strong views on Gaza and Israel.

On days like this, it’s not hard to be overwhelmed by existential futility. At the current rate of progress, the UK looks on course to wipe itself out far sooner than it would with any interference from AI. Everything feels hopeless. Years of minimal growth and a cost of living crisis. The tech bros and the bankers may be getting richer. The rest of us? Not so much. And there’s no end in sight. Andy Burnham may offer better vibes, but he is fighting a losing battle against global forces – wars, energy prices, borrowing costs – that he can’t control. You can feel the hope drain out of him as each day passes. Mr Congeniality is not quite so congenial as he once was. All the economic forecasts suggest things are going to get even worse in the next year. Even Labour allies are preparing the ground for a tough budget next month. The chancellor, John Healey, has been making it known that even he is surprised by just how bad things are. Can’t think why. The rest of us have known for a while, and he’s had the benefit of sitting at the Cabinet table with Rachel Reeves for the past two years.

Money in people’s pockets is the key to economic recovery

Neil Kinnock’s timely letter (9 September) reminds us that we are not alone in suffering high gilt yields and borrowing costs. We are still feeling the fallout from Covid, and it needs mentioning that our national debt is similar to America’s and much less than Japan’s, and it never gets mentioned that Italy routinely runs 100% of GDP debt. But as Kinnock observes, the policies of several Conservative governments (including Brexit) have made things worse, and the problem for us is not so much the actual debt but our direction of travel. The aforementioned will make the bond markets view us with a more jaundiced eye. It was predictable that Jamie Dimon would pop up at this point (JP Morgan boss meets Burnham and Healey to warn against bank tax rise, 10 September). He talks about potential lack of investment by the banks. What investment? We aren’t even a nation of shopkeepers any longer; we’re a nation of pizza deliverers. The economist JK Galbraith comes to mind here. He said that when push comes to shove, it’s the regular spendings of the working masses that keep the high street going.

‘A man threatened to shoot me’: the abuse pushing UK councillors out of politics

Heather Williams has been shouted at in the street, received death threats, threats of sexual violence, and had dog faeces left on her doorstep. At one point, she didn’t leave her home alone for more than three months. It was not how she expected her life to be when she first ran to be a Conservative district councillor in South Cambridgeshire nine years ago. “It is very intimidating. I’ve had people threatening to rape me in my sleep, a man once threatened to shoot me,” said Williams, now opposition group leader on the council. “You do question whether you’re doing the right thing, what impact it is having on your family. Even my daughter has security protocols now.” Williams has installed extra security measures in her home including cameras, panic alarms and an app on her phone so she can be tracked if needed. She is not the only one – a new survey from the Local Government Association (LGA) found that over a third (35%) of councillors have made modifications to their home for security reasons.

text:
Alan Shute obituary

My father, Alan Shute, who has died aged 92, was a tenacious and principled trade union negotiator who rose to become assistant general secretary of the National Union of Civil and Public Servants (NUCPS). He was involved in many high-profile negotiations, including representation of some of the sacked GCHQ workers in 1984, when the Thatcher government banned trade union membership for employees. Originally a customs officer, after several years of voluntary union work Alan was appointed as a full-time negotiator for the Society of Civil Servants trade union in 1969. Around the same time, he was the first member of the society to appear on television – in an episode of The Eamonn Andrews Show discussing purported benefit fraud – and was interviewed by the Guardian soon after about working conditions in DHSS offices.

citation.title: Alan Shute obituary

text:
Alan Shute obituary

Colleagues described him as knowledgable and thoughtful in his approach, with one saying: “He was straightforward and honest, which wasn’t always the case either among management or other union colleagues.” Born in Southampton, Hampshire, to William, a stevedore, and Winifred (nee Thorne), a cook who trained at the Navy, Army and Air Force Institutes, Alan grew up during the wartime blitz on the city – his family were forced to move several times due to the bombings, and his uncle was killed in a direct hit on the Supermarine aviation works. After Itchen grammar school, and national service in the RAF, Alan started working for customs and excise, first in Glasgow, then Coventry and finally at Heathrow, before leaving to work full time for his union. Made assistant general secretary of the NUCPS in 1975, he gained a reputation as a calm negotiator and persuasive speaker, and was a great raconteur. Alan was a staunch Labour party member all his life and, after retiring in 1990 to Grantown-on-Spey, Scotland, with his second wife, Anne Maclean, whom he married in 1982, chaired the Inverness, Nairn, Badenoch and Strathspey branch of the party for a number of years.

His campaigning expertise and advice were hugely appreciated by the branch, as well as his unwavering commitment – in May 2026 he was still out canvassing before the Scottish parliament election. Outside political life, Alan was a keen birdwatcher, and became involved as a trustee in the preservation of Grantown’s woodland areas. He was also a lifelong – and often disappointed – supporter of Southampton FC. His first marriage, to Wendy Comben, in 1956, ended in divorce. Anne died in 2024. He is survived by his two children from his first marriage, David and me.

Monday It’s funny, isn’t it, how many things we take for granted in life? How many things go wholly unmentioned, even wholly unconsidered in any even minutely conscious way – and yet, when they are suddenly kicked away you realise just how much of your internal organisation, your mental integrity, your structural soundness altogether, rested on these unexamined pillars. One of mine, it turns out, is the belief – no, surely more than that? The sure and certain knowledge, in my bones if never alas vouchsafed by my mere mortal eyes – that Bruce Springsteen does not wear pyjamas. This is fundamental, surely? The Boss sleeps naked. This is an eternal verity. But no. According to what I can only describe as reports, he is a loyal customer of the venerable sleepwear shop Schostal in Rome, which was opened in 1870 by two brothers from Vienna. There’s a photo of Bruce hugging the manager, Shirley Braine – to whom he apparently sends regular postcards – and everything. So. There you have it. The Boss sleeps in pyjamas. Acceptable province of 1950s boarding school boys, your worst boyfriend, and your dad.

Former Labour deputy leader Tom Watson joins Palantir

Another former government minister has been hired by a controversial US AI company, this time Palantir, which has appointed Andy Burnham’s former ministerial colleague Tom Watson. The Labour peer and former deputy leader will operate alongside Palantir’s UK and Europe chief executive, Louis Mosley, as the company attempts to fend off pressure on Burnham’s government to axe its £330m NHS contract. It is also fighting Sadiq Khan in court over the Labour London mayor’s block on a £50m contract to use its AI in Metropolitan police investigations. Palantir also wants to win more public sector work in the UK, where it already has an annual turnover of £427m. The company was co-founded by the Trump-supporting billionaire Peter Thiel and provides AI-powered software to the Israeli military and the White House’s ICE immigration crackdown, leading to a public and political backlash against its deepening involvement in British public services. Alex Karp, its chief executive, said: “This is just the latest chapter of Tom’s forty-year fight for better public services.

Is the tie dead? Fashion connoisseurs hope not as House of Lords relaxes rules

The House of Lords has long been derided as a stuffy relic of the past. But now its benches, usually filled with haughtily dressed men, could soon resemble something more akin to “dress-down Friday”. One of the nation’s most storied chambers of power has enacted a rule change: men are no longer required to wear a tie in the House of Lords. Instead, they should opt for “business attire”. Ties have long been a knotty item of neckwear. For some, they are a nuisance: too tight and they are uncomfortable, too loose and they look a bit shabby. For others, such as Stephen Fry, who professed his love for ties in a 256-page book, they can add a touch of undeniable class. Peter York, a writer and style commentator, is firmly on the traditional side of the debate, saying the dumbed-down dress code will “end in tears”. “Lords are not famous for being well-dressed at the best of times. If they can go without ties, they can also wear plimsolls and stuff like that. They will look silly,” said York, who owns hundreds of ties.

Reform donor Ben Delo loaned £350k to academic later found to have engaged in online bullying

Reform UK’s new mega-donor Ben Delo gave a £350,000 loan to a conservative writer fighting a legal case in which a judge later found she had engaged in online bullying and regrettable conduct with a “whiff of threat and antisemitism”. Nina Power and her friend, the writer Daniel DC Miller, brought the legal action for defamation against the performance artist Luke Turner, who they had accused of falsely calling them antisemitic. At the same time, Turner brought a counter-claim against the pair accusing them of harassment. Their libel action failed on the grounds that Turner’s online reach was not big enough to have caused harm to their reputations, while the harassment case also failed on the basis that their conduct was not unlawful. The loan from Delo to help fund Power’s case before the 2023 trial shines a light on the Reform supporter’s involvement in backing a landmark legal tussle over the boundaries of free speech.

In the case, Miller, who is Jewish, and Power denied promoting fascist or antisemitic views, and said they did not know Turner was Jewish. The judge found there was “no overt antisemitism” displayed by the pair. She said the “radio frequencies of macabre imagery and casualness around antisemitic tropes into which Mr Turner tuned do yield a discernible signal but not one strong enough to be recognised objectively as antisemitic hate speech or a resolved engagement with physical violence sufficient to render this conduct quasi-criminal”.

Polanski request to postpone Greens’ conference to focus on byelection refused by party

Zack Polanski requested that the Greens’ ruling executive committee postpone the party’s imminent annual conference so they could focus on the Holborn and St Pancras byelection but was refused. While party officials say the formal request came from staffers worried about diluting resources by staging a conference a week before Polanski tries to win Keir Starmer’s former Commons seat, the Guardian understands the party leader wanted this to happen. In the end, the executive committee of the Greens in England and Wales, which has about 25 voting members including Polanski, voted against the plan on Thursday. The party expects about 3,000 people to attend what would be its biggest gathering, beginning in Brighton on 2 October. Calling off the event at such short notice would have cost the party a significant sum given it has rented a conference venue, and risked annoying members who have taken time off work and booked travel and hotels. The byelection, in which Polanski hopes to challenge for a traditionally safe Labour seat, takes place on 8 October, just four days after the conference finishes.

Ed Davey takes aim at Reform and Elon Musk as Lib Dem conference begins

The Liberal Democrats’ leader, Sir Ed Davey, took aim at Nigel Farage and Elon Musk on the first day of his party’s annual conference, saying Lib Dems would not give up the fight to defeat “nasty populism” and Reform UK’s “£72m arsenal of hate and lies”. On stage at Brighton Centre, Davey called on the assembled delegates not to be deterred in the face of Reform’s hope “that the anger and the hatred and the lies will grind us down until eventually we just give up”. He also praised earlier speakers for showing “why we care and why we fight” and contrasted this with Reform, which, he said, “care about their own bank balance and they fight because two crypto billionaires gave them 72 million quid”. Davey, who entered conference season having to address frustrations over his leadership expressed by some Lib Dem MPs, also used the speech to recall his early political life as a student campaigning successfully for his university college to boycott Barclays, due to its investments in apartheid-era South Africa.

George Osborne ‘thought Peter Thiel’s Bayeux tapestry visit would be secret’

George Osborne has said he thought no one would find out about a private viewing of the Bayeux tapestry he organised for the tech billionaire Peter Thiel at the British Museum. The former chancellor, who is chair of the museum, told the Big Brue festival in Somerset that he had been on holiday when Thiel was shown the medieval artwork. Thiel, who supports Donald Trump, is the founder of PayPal and Palantir, a software company that builds data integration, analytics and artificial intelligence platforms for government agencies and large corporations. Related: Do the British Museum’s links with Palantir and BP bring it into disrepute? Palantir has a swathe of British public contracts, including, most controversially, a £330m deal with the NHS, which it has held since 2023. The company also works for the US, Israeli and UK militaries. Its use of AI-powered software to support military strikes in Gaza and Iran, US Ice immigration raids and its access to NHS data has stoked concern.

Lib Dems have ‘moral responsibility’ to block Reform, says Ed Davey as party gears up for snap election

The Liberal Democrats have begun work on a new manifesto in case of a possible snap election, as Ed Davey said he understood the frustrations of some of his MPs who fear that the party’s message is currently at risk of being lost. But Davey also urged his party not to panic at static polling numbers, arguing that with tactical voting and fragmented political loyalties, he fully expects the party to do even better at the next election than in 2024, when it won 72 seats, the highest total for a century. Speaking ahead of the party’s annual conference in Brighton, Davey warned that discipline and focus were vital, given what he described as their “moral responsibility” in blocking a Reform-led government, predicting that Kemi Badenoch would eventually seek an alliance with Nigel Farage’s party. A manifesto working group, led by the Cheadle MP Tom Morrison, has already been created, Davey said, meaning the party can be ready if Andy Burnham calls an election. “We don’t normally do it this early,” he said.

However, it is by no means a unanimous view, with others saying the pace has picked up since the appointment of the party’s new political director James Holt, a veteran of the coalition years who then spent nearly a decade working with the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.

Scottish Labour’s new leader backs Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gasfields

Scottish Labour’s new leader Michael Marra has backed the development of the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gasfields in the North Sea in one of his first acts after being elected, calling for a “more rational” approach to energy policy. On Saturday, the MSP for North East Scotland won a near two-thirds majority to lead the party in Holyrood, becoming Scottish Labour’s 11th leader. He replaces Anas Sarwar after his shock decision to resign in July to join Andy Burnham’s new government as a trade minister. Dundee-born Marra said he would urge the British prime minister to back both fossil fuel projects despite warnings over their environmental impact. Neither is covered by the ban on new licences for drilling in the North Sea because their applications were already in the system when the Labour government took power, and there is growing expectation that ministers will approve the Jackdaw gasfield in the coming weeks. “I want Rosebank and Jackdaw to be approved,” Marra told reporters shortly after his election. “It’s the biggest issue in my region in terms of people’s voting intention.

But the truth is Scotland didn’t think we would be much better,” he said. “Scots know what we are against. They can’t tell you what we are for. Reform UK activists squabble over Farage’s plan for £72m donations

For Nigel Farage, the £72m lavished last week on his party by the crypto billionaire donors Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne finally places Reform UK on a level playing field with its political rivals. The donations are the largest received by a UK political party since declarations became required in 2001 and led to warnings Farage was aiming to “buy” his way to power, with a row still raging over whether they are legal. Related: Donations of £72m make Reform’s prospects both rosier and riskier Yet among Reform’s grassroots, the fattening of party coffers comes with challenges of its own, with some activists less than impressed by Farage’s announcement that the money would be used to hire 400 campaign managers in target constituencies. “We need more activists to knock on doors NOT managers,” one posted on a Facebook group used by Reform activists, where the sentiment was not unusual. Another party member, and former candidate, told others he was “puzzled” by Farage’s announcement, adding that the campaign managers would need an army of volunteer doorknockers.

The party is advertising this week for more than 60 roles, including four branch network coordinators – described as “the backbone of the party” – in various English regions. Forty-seven full-time campaign managers were also being hired in cities, towns and regions across Britain. Other positions include a call centre manager, two “local byelection managers” and a “councillor welfare manager” to work with the party’s 2,300 councillors and whose tasks would include “managing conflict”. Asylum seekers who arrive on small boats across the Channel are “wealthy men” who do not deserve the help of the British state, according to the Reform UK MP Danny Kruger. The former Conservative, who defected last year, said the fact that some migrants were paying people smugglers thousands of pounds – often using their life savings or borrowed money – made them well off. The claim was immediately dismissed by charities who support refugees. Speaking at the Big Brue festival in Bruton, Somerset, Kruger said: “By the way, most of them [are] comparatively wealthy and fit young men who’ve crossed safe countries to begin the journey to the UK.” Asked by the event’s moderator, the editor of the Independent, Geordie Greig, how he knew these men were wealthy, Kruger said: “Because they’re paying thousands of pounds. They’re paying thousands of pounds to people smugglers to get here.

text:
UK politics increasingly funded by billionaires as mega-donations surge

British politics is increasingly being funded by individual billionaires with a wave of mega-donations having flooded into UK political parties over the past two parliaments. A total of £179m has been donated by wealthy individuals since 2019, research reveals. The figures from the IPPR thinktank show how big money is playing an ever more influential role in Westminster, with a particular rise in mega-donations of more than £1m. The research found that contributions from individual donors have accelerated since the Brexit party received £10m from the Thailand-based billionaire Christopher Harborne and the Liberal Democrats were given £8m by David Sainsbury, the supermarket tycoon, who has now returned to Labour. Between 2001, when donation records began, and 2018, the total donated by individuals giving more than £1m averaged £3.9m a year. But between 2019 and 2025, that figure rose to £13.1m a year, almost three-and-a-half times as much, and far outstripping what would be expected with inflation. The research found 72% of all £1m-plus donations from individuals since records began had come since 2019.

Guardian analysis found that in some years, such as 2023, almost £7 out of every £10 in reported private donations to political parties came from wealthy companies or individuals who gave more than £1m in a calendar year. The figures are likely to raise fresh concerns about the influence of a small groups of wealthy individuals, which have already been heightened since two crypto billionaires, Harborne and Ben Delo, said they had each given £36m to Reform UK this month. Reform UK has said it is trying to redress the balance as the other parties have taken millions in mega-donations in past years. The Conservatives’ biggest donors include Frank Hester, who gave more than £20m before the 2024 election, and Labour’s Gary Lubner, who has given more than £9m in total. The IPPR figures draw on Electoral Commission data since 2001 and Transparency International analysis, plus the two record donations of £36m each to Reform UK from Harborne and Delo. There is increasing concern among Reform UK’s rivals about the issue of donations of more than £1m, with some Labour MPs pushing for a cap of £100,000 or £500,000 a year.

Farage says he wants to ‘hijack’ Trump’s ICE czar to help secure UK border

Nigel Farage has said he wants to “hijack” Donald Trump’s hardline ICE adviser and bring him to the UK “to secure our borders”. Speaking at an event in the US, the Reform UK leader also called for Europe to take a “more sensible view” of the US president’s administration rather than seeing it as “villainous”. Farage complimented Tom Homan, Trump’s adviser on the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Speaking at the event where Homan was a guest, he said: “I’ve got terrible news for you. We’re hijacking Tom Homan and taking him back with us to secure our borders.” Homan is Trump’s key adviser on ICE, which is under scrutiny over its aggressive approach to immigration enforcement after a number of fatal shootings by its agents, including two people in July. Salgado Araujo and Durán Guerrero were the 29th and 30th people that immigration officers have opened fire on since Trump took office last year, according to The Trace, an outlet that tracks shootings in its gun violence data hub.

In Trump’s first term, he helped to design some of the administration’s most draconian measures – most notably family separation, a strategy reportedly deemed too severe by officials in the Obama White House, but which later became central to Trump’s “zero tolerance” policy. Kemi Badenoch has accused Andy Burnham of “fiddling while Europe is at risk of burning”, as she repeated her call for the prime minister to cut the welfare budget to fund increase spending on defence. She said the government had to “fund our defence properly” at a time when former military chiefs have raised questions about Britain’s preparedness for war. ‘Flip the table and rise up’: Lib Dems’ president in combative mood as party gathers in Brighton

Standing outside Toynbee Hall in the East End of London, Josh Babarinde doesn’t exactly look like a rabble-rouser. But despite the well-cut suit and disarmingly large smile, the president of the Liberal Democrats is, apparently, up for a fight. “There are big modern giants that are getting in the way of people’s ability to thrive, and it is the job of Liberal Democrats to address that,” says the 33-year-old. “How are we going to do that? Well, first of all, we’ve got to flip the table over and rise up.” Flipping over tables is not behaviour normally associated with Liberal Democrat members, about 5,000 of whom are in Brighton for its annual conference this weekend. But Babarinde, frequently described as a rising star in the party’s ranks, wants his comrades to channel the spirit of the great Liberal thinker William Beveridge, who finessed his radical ideas on social reform in the 141-year-old Whitechapel building. Beveridge decried the five evils of want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness.

The historic 2024 election result gave the party 71 MPs, yet it has been stuck at about 11% in polls for months. Lib Dems propose big tech levy to fund £250m online crime agency

The Liberal Democrats say they will tax big tech to finance a new online crime agency, as they try to address concerns that not enough voters know what the party stands for. The plan, to be announced at the party conference on Monday by the Lib Dems’ home affairs spokesperson, Max Wilkinson, would create a new Online Crime Agency focused on offences including child sexual abuse material, trafficking in drugs and weapons, and deepfake AI-generated pornographic images. The planned budget of £250m a year would be paid for by an “online crime levy” on large AI and technology companies. Wilkinson is to tell the conference it is “time they picked up the bill” for offences they had enabled. Ed Davey, the party leader, on Sunday set out a proposal to cut fuel duty by 10p a litre for a fixed three-month period, as well as reducing the bus fare cap from £3 to £1 and other transport-related cost of living policies.

Feeling ‘forced out’ by Badenoch? Lib Dems conference welcomes young Tory defectors

Climbing the party-branded stairs of the Brighton Centre with a Liberal Britain tote bag over his shoulder, Cody Butler looks quite at home at the Liberal Democrats’ annual jamboree. But asked how he is finding it, the 21-year-old replied: “Odd.” The former Tory activist resigned as chair of the One Nation Conservative Network and left his old party in July, arguing that centrists, remainers and members worried about the climate crisis and conservation were no longer welcome in the party. A week ago, he joined the Lib Dems. “There is no easy way to describe joining a new political party, because it’s like finding a new family,” he said. “I was brought up in a Conservative association. I was the local Tory boy. So it’s great, but odd.” Butler is one of several youthful former Tories who have publicly defected to Britain’s third party and are in the process of setting up a new group: the One Nation Liberals. It’s a growing group, with other potential defectors believed to be waiting to see if they can survive in Kemi Badenoch’s increasingly rightwing party.

text:
Catherine Webb obituary

My daughter Catherine Webb, who has died aged 47 from metastatic ovarian cancer, was a senior Treasury official during a turbulent period in British politics and latterly bursar of Emmanuel College, Cambridge, where she had taken her undergraduate degree. Having begun at the Treasury in 2000, Katie played a key role in helping ministers to deal with the 2008 financial crisis and Brexit before going on to become the Treasury’s director of operations, managing all the non-policy aspects of the department. Katie was our first daughter, born to Jane (nee Holly) and me, in Bebington, Wirral, and brought up in the mid-Cheshire village of Hartford; my wife was a probation officer and I was a social worker. Katie was educated at Hartford county primary school, Hartford high school and then Sir John Deane’s sixth form college in nearby Northwich, where she was noted for her sophisticated grasp of economics and politics. By then she was already a Labour party activist, and when she moved on to study economics at Emmanuel she continued her political activism in tandem with a vibrant social life. On graduating in 2000 Katie eschewed politics to join HM Treasury.

citation.title: Catherine Webb obituary

text:
Catherine Webb obituary

Initially working on labour markets, welfare policy and poverty analysis, she went on to play a central part in tackling the 2008 financial crisis, including on secondment to the Bank of England to work on the team trying to save the failing Northern Rock bank. From 2011 she was key to developing the UK’s economic relationship with China as economic and trade counsellor at the British embassy in Beijing. Katie came back to the UK in 2015, promoted to director level, and held a series of roles at the heart of the UK’s relationship with the EU. She was the only woman among the senior Brexit negotiators, and led teams at the Department for Exiting the European Union and in the Europe Unit at the Cabinet Office. She returned to the Treasury in 2019 as director of operations and member of the management board, leading the department’s response to the challenges of operating under Covid-19 rules and establishing the Darlington economic campus, the northern branch of the Treasury. She was made a Companion of the Order of the Bath in 2020.

Catherine Webb obituary

In 2023 she left the civil service to become bursar at Emmanuel, with the remit to review and restructure the non-academic functions of the college, a task she performed while earning the respect and affection of its fellows and staff. As a civil servant, Katie was valued for her qualities of kindness and empathy as well as her intellect and technical expertise. Wherever she went, she had a gift for making friends and holding them fast. She had a great rapport with children, and was a generous and thoughtful aunt, godmother and significant adult to the children of many friends. Adept at many crafts, including cooking, breadmaking, quilting and sashiko, she was also a keen traveller. She loved to walk and cycle, and was a particularly enthusiastic swimmer, gaining great enjoyment from her membership of the London branch of Out to Swim, an LBTGQ+ aquatic club, and of the South London Swimming Club based at Tooting Bec Lido. She accepted her diagnosis, without rancour or complaint, and when curative treatment failed, decided to prioritise quality over quantity of life. Katie is survived by Jane and me, her sister Elizabeth and nieces Alice and Emily.

Ed Davey is to call for a global nuclear-style non-proliferation treaty to halt the development of super-intelligent AI when he makes his keynote speech at the Liberal Democrat conference, accusing Andy Burnham of relying on Donald Trump and “tech bros” to solve the problem. Nigel Farage dismissed the loss of Reform UK’s leader in Wales last week as a “bump in the road” as the party unveiled a replacement. Lib Dems reject ‘discriminatory and unworkable’ EHRC guidance on transgender people

The Liberal Democrats have rejected official guidance by the equalities watchdog on how organisations should implement the supreme court ruling on transgender people, calling it “discriminatory and unworkable”. The motion, passed overwhelmingly at the party’s annual conference in Brighton, makes the Lib Dems the first of the big three parties in parliament to call for a new approach to implementing last year’s ruling that the legal definition of a woman is based on biological sex only. The Greens have previously done so. Formal guidance from the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC), put out in May, is intended to tell service providers and others how they must balance the rights of trans people with the requirement for some spaces to be single sex. It has attracted criticism for being a de facto bar on trans people being in many public spaces by setting out that single-sex toilets and changing rooms must exclude transgender men and women when gender-neutral facilities are not always available.

text:
Another day, another Reform Wales leader. Grumpy Nige seems to miss the old one

Twenty-five or so Reform members of the Senedd were lined up against a wall. Almost as if they were in a police identification parade. Reform’s need to find a new leader in Wales is becoming habit-forming. First, Nathan Gill was banged up for 10 and a half years on eight counts of taking £40K in bribes to make statements in support of Russia. Easily done. Who among us hasn’t been tempted by the Kremlin? And then last week, Dan Thomas chose to stand down after being arrested on suspicion of assault and coercive behaviour, leaving the Welsh leadership spot open once more. He denies the allegations. It’s almost as if there’s a pattern emerging. That the job of Reform leader in Wales is somehow cursed. Otherwise law-abiding men and women suddenly find themselves accused of all sorts of things. So much so that it’s now the job that no one really wants. Yet politics abhors a vacuum, and someone has to do the job. So it was a decidedly grumpy-looking Nigel Farage who turned up in Cardiff on Monday morning to pretend to be interested in announcing the next Reform Senedd leader.

citation.title: Another day, another Reform Wales leader. Grumpy Nige seems to miss the old one

text:
Another day, another Reform Wales leader. Grumpy Nige seems to miss the old one

Perhaps he reckoned he had better things to do. The event – if you can call a five-minute announcement that – was supposed to kick off at 11.45. Nige was booked on the 12.18 back to Paddington and had hoped to be in London for a late lunch. No champagne and oysters. There were no undercover reporters posing as Americans trying to make a potentially illegal donation this time. Instead, there was a 20-minute delay. Nige really was going through the motions. He was thrilled by the results in Wales at the May elections, he began. He didn’t sound thrilled. Though that could be because Reform has been shedding support in Wales – as elsewhere – ever since. They have lost seven points in the opinion polls over the course of the summer and are looking less and less likely to challenge Plaid Cymru. “Dan Thomas has been doing a brilliant job,” Nige continued. “I am sorry for his personal difficulties.” This was just weird. Almost as if he hadn’t even considered what Thomas had been alleged to have done. Yeah, Dan. Great bloke. Brilliant Reform leader. Always buys his round in the pub.

It’s just unfortunate that he’s been arrested on suspicion of assault and coercive control. But it’s no big deal. He’ll soon be sorted. Nige doubled down, calling the arrest a “bump in the road”. Not a word of sympathy or support for the person he is accused of having assaulted or subjected to coercive control. Besides, he was clear that Dan would come back soon. There would always be a welcome in the Reform valleys for Dan. We all need someone like Dan. After the Song for Dan, Nige made the briefest of introductions to the new leader. Best to skip over the bit where almost half the Reform members of the Senedd had preferred a different candidate. The party in Wales is a hotbed of backstabbing. Not literally, mind. The job was going to Helen Jenner, the former deputy leader and Nige’s old-time Ukip mucker. “I’ve known her for years and I trust her,” he said. Helen mumbled her thanks and said she would build on the good work done by others. It wasn’t clear if Dan would take over from her if he is cleared of the allegations, which he denies. It sounded like a possibility.

UK to give support to Saudi jets in attempt to counter Houthi fighters

The UK has agreed to provide defensive air support to Saudi Arabia to help counter Houthi fighters and restore stability in the Middle East while driving down the cost of living at home, Andy Burnham has said, ahead of his first meeting with Donald Trump. The prime minister said he had agreed to a request for air-to-air refuelling of Saudi jets to defend energy infrastructure against the Iran-backed rebels and help keep oil flowing from the Gulf to ease global economic turmoil. Burnham also revealed he will use his first meeting with Trump on Tuesday to urge the US president to de-escalate the conflict in Iran, warning that “dark clouds of global instability” are directly affecting people’s lives all over the world. The turmoil in the Middle East has pushed up global energy prices, putting the UK economy under intense inflationary pressure and increasing government borrowing costs to multi-year highs just weeks before a crucial first budget for the new government.

On the flight to the United Nations in New York, Burnham told reporters that an RAF Voyager would help refuel Saudi jets for several weeks, in his first military deployment since taking power, after the Houthis advanced to areas adjacent to the crucial Bab al-Mandab strait. The key Gulf ally has used the waterway as an alternative route for oil exports bypassing disruption in the ⁠strait of Hormuz. The RAF operational support is in addition to the UK Sky Sabre air defence system already operating. “We have received a request from Saudi Arabia for military support and … I agreed to that request for defensive air-to-air refuelling. On cost of living pressures and acting to secure the interests of Britain, the wider region … we need to keep those pathways open,” Burnham said. The prime minister also plans to press Trump to wind down US action in Iran, which has destabilised the region, blocked key supply chains and unleashed global economic volatility, including in the UK, where the government will struggle to drive down the cost of living as a result.

The global security backdrop to the summit is bleak: European leaders have warned that Russia could launch a drone or missile attack on Nato territory within months to test the strength of the alliance. Andy Burnham does not rule out Brexit reversal being in next Labour manifesto

Andy Burnham has opened the door to fighting the next election on the UK rejoining the EU, but said his immediate priority was continuing to rebuild bridges with European allies. The prime minister, who will hold his first meeting with the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, on Tuesday, did not rule out including reversing Brexit in Labour’s next manifesto – but suggested the country should focus on securing closer trading ties first. Ministers have expressed fears privately that the EU reset has lost significant momentum since Burnham became prime minister, and a summit on the issue is likely to be delayed again unless the bloc agrees to discuss legislation that could lock British business out of parts of EU industry. Burnham has said he will stick to Keir Starmer’s red lines this side of an election, but he is under pressure from Labour MPs who opposed Brexit to change tack, in part because of the potential boost to growth, even though his own seat of Makerfield voted to leave.

Asked by reporters on his flight to New York on Monday for the UN general assembly whether he could rule out a reversal of Brexit being in the next Labour manifesto, he said: “Our focus at the moment is on a UK/EU summit which we hope will take place later this year. “My immediate priority is to build on the good work that Keir did in rebuilding bridges. Because those bridges were broken in the early part of this decade. And Keir did a good job in re-establishing that relationship. “What we have got to do now is go to the next level in terms of reaching practical agreement that will further boost the British economy. And those issues are the substance of the summit alongside EU requests around youth mobility.” The prime minister admitted he had concerns about the bloc’s “made in Europe” legislation, which is designed to curb China’s increasing presence but could also affect British industry and supply chains. He said he would share those concerns “in a constructive spirit” with von der Leyen. “The other issues you discuss, they are for another day,” he said of rejoining the bloc.
