text:
Call it a win: boredom but no temper tantrums in Burnham’s first face-to-face with America’s King Baby

How do you deal with a problem like The Donald? The simple answer is that you don’t. You can’t. The normal rules of political engagement don’t apply. The US president is like a five-year-old child with the world as his set of toys: a King Baby. Nothing is ever constant or predictable. What’s agreed one day can be forgotten the next. Any deal can be interrupted with a temper tantrum at any time. Trying to second-guess Donald Trump is a fool’s errand. So the primary aim of Andy Burnham’s first face-to-face meeting with Trump was to get out alive with his – and the UK’s – self-respect intact. To take no incoming damage. And whatever he did, not to offer the president a third state visit. Keir Starmer never really lived that one down. Putting out on the first date only encourages the other person to think you’re a pushover. The hoped-for result was a pleasant and almost forgettable bilateral meeting at the United Nations general assembly in New York.

citation.title: Call it a win: boredom but no temper tantrums in Burnham’s first face-to-face with America’s King Baby

text:
Call it a win: boredom but no temper tantrums in Burnham’s first face-to-face with America’s King Baby

It was only scheduled to last 30 minutes, so more like speed dating – one step up from two world leaders shooting the breeze while getting to know each other. Where differences could be acknowledged without causing a major diplomatic incident. All of which falls pretty comfortably within Burnham’s skill set. Andy’s stock in trade is an easy-going self-confidence. He’s comfortable in his skin in a way that Keir never was. Or maybe the artifice is just better concealed. He understands that trash-talking is all in a day’s work for most politicians. In the past, he may have called Trump all sorts of things. Poisoned politics. Someone who would be unwelcome in Manchester. Well, that was then, this is now. Things change. Just like Trump. Now he would be welcoming the US president to the G20 in Manchester next year. Who would have guessed? And it all looked to have gone pretty much to plan. Maybe Trump also wanted this meeting to go well.

citation.title: Call it a win: boredom but no temper tantrums in Burnham’s first face-to-face with America’s King Baby

text:
Call it a win: boredom but no temper tantrums in Burnham’s first face-to-face with America’s King Baby

His poll ratings in the US are dire, the midterm elections look like trouble and The Donald needs all the friends he can get – even if he had just tried to lose a few more of them in his speech to the UN earlier. A speech that had been even wilder and madder than many of his previous ones. Still, at least he hadn’t threatened to invade a Nato country this time. And it’s always good to learn of countries you never knew existed. Anyone for “Kazakhistan”? Taking questions with Trump afterwards, Andy didn’t look quite as self-assured as usual – he seemed very much on edge – but who could blame him for that? This was his first time as prime minister at the UN and The Donald always has it in him to blow any meeting out of the water. It was Andy who went first, trying to remember what they had just talked about. It had all been a bit of a blur. That was it – they had talked about Iran. In his earlier speech, The Donald had suggested it was a toss-up whether he came to a deal with Iran or whether he annihilated it. On the whole, Andy was in favour of a deal. Quickly if possible.

The war was causing a massive hit to the cost of living. Burnham then bigged up the deal with Saudi Arabia. The one where we send one plane to refuel Saudi fighters that don’t need refuelling because their targets are only a few hundred miles away. Finally, he mentioned the Falklands. By now The Donald was looking a wee bit bored. Unsure where the Falklands are or why they had been talking about them. text:
Lib Dems torn over whether to be voters’ first choice or the route to block Reform

One of the more dramatic moments in a Liberal Democrat conference otherwise short of them came late on Sunday, when the party frontbencher Lisa Smart told the polling veteran John Curtice that, in effect, he no longer understood modern politics. Curtice had warned the Lib Dems they risked being left behind, with the lack of a coherent national message seeing them all but ignored outside a few electoral strongholds. Smart’s response? In the new era of five- or six-party politics, and mass tactical voting, this does not matter. It was a distillation of the largely underground debate which has dominated the gathering in Brighton and is likely to define the party’s future. It is a battle between, depending on the stance, strategy versus recklessness, or caution versus ambition – or, more bluntly, whether the Lib Dems want to be the first choice of voters, or their route to block a Reform UK government.

citation.title: Lib Dems torn over whether to be voters’ first choice or the route to block Reform

text:
Lib Dems torn over whether to be voters’ first choice or the route to block Reform

The current choice, as decided by Ed Davey and his leadership team and argued forcefully by Smart, is a continuation of the 2024 electoral approach in which the party set aside a fully national campaign to focus relentlessly on a series of target seats, many of them held by the Conservatives. It worked. As Smart argued – after Curtice pointed out that the Lib Dems had won 23% of the vote in the 2010 election – in 2024 such careful targeting helped them take 72 MPs on little more than 12% vote share, adding: “I know which one I prefer.” Party strategists are adamant that with voting patterns atomised, many seats at the next election are likely to be won on tiny margins, with the key factors being tactical voting and a ruthlessly efficient ground game, both Lib Dem specialities. Davey and his team say even in public that they can improve on the 2024 result, the best in a century for the party. In private, there is talk of perhaps 140 MPs, and being the balance of power in a hung parliament.

citation.title: Lib Dems torn over whether to be voters’ first choice or the route to block Reform

text:
Lib Dems torn over whether to be voters’ first choice or the route to block Reform

None of this is impossible, but – as Curtice said – it relies on a series of external factors to remain constant, including no noticeable dip in Reform’s fortunes or a boost for the Tories, given the way the strategy hinges on a split vote across the right. But what is more pressing for a number of Lib Dems is the way the tactic can feel like a slightly desperate attempt to appeal to, or at least not alienate, the voters on the right and left that the party needs to enlist. As such, the policy offering on show in Brighton – and there has been no lack of policy – has felt at times a bit disjointed, with economic offerings based on tax cuts and lower regulation balanced by calls to protect human rights. What is lacking, some fear, is a wider vision, or any boldness. “Things need to change,” Carl Cashman, the Lib Dem opposition leader on Liverpool city council, told delegates from the conference stage.

citation.title: Lib Dems torn over whether to be voters’ first choice or the route to block Reform

Lib Dems torn over whether to be voters’ first choice or the route to block Reform

“I’m a radical because I’m a liberal, and the fact that liberalism has become synonymous with the status quo – it irks me so much.” Julian Brazil, the Lib Dem leader of Devon county council, was more abrupt still, saying his party was “sleepwalking into irrelevance” under Davey’s leadership. There is, however, no sign at all of a challenge to Davey. Even the more malcontented MPs accept he will take the party into the next election, and in many cases they also accept that his careful approach has merits. Those around the Lib Dem leader say he is aware of the concerns, but feels a huge responsibility to ensure the party wins enough MPs to prevent a Reform government, something Davey sees as the defining mission of his political life. Some argue that the apparent conflict is largely artificial, and it is possible to embrace Davey’s approach to the next election while also trying to redefine liberalism for the longer term. There are, inevitably, still frustrations. “It’s like being stuck on a bumper car, just being buffeted by what the other parties do, with no real control,” one MP said.

Donald Trump praises ‘natural businessperson’ Andy Burnham after first meeting

Donald Trump has praised Andy Burnham as a “natural businessperson” and said the UK was “more up” than under Keir Starmer. But he berated the UK for its decision to give up the Chagos Islands. In their first face-to-face meeting, Trump gave a warm assessment of the relationship, saying he thought Burnham had a “lot of assets on his side” and would be a “great prime minister”, adding: “We talked about everything from Rolls-Royce to energy to immigration – we covered a lot.” At a joint press conference after their talks at the UN general assembly in New York, Burnham said he and the president had “established a good connection in our early discussions and we’ve taken that further today”. UK officials had been somewhat nervous about the meeting, as Trump had previously described Burnham as “extremely liberal” and called the former mayor of Greater Manchester as the “mayor of a town”. But the meeting appeared to have gone to plan for both sides, with Trump praising the UK, saying: “I think you’re up.

Ed Davey promises £17bn income tax cut if Lib Dems are elected

Ed Davey has unveiled a plan for a £17bn income tax cut in a speech aimed at shoring up the party’s support among former Conservative voters, but which risked disappointing some Liberal Democrat MPs who want a bolder vision for the party. Addressing the party’s annual conference in Brighton, the Lib Dem leader said the proposal, which would eventually increase the threshold for paying income tax to £15,000 and raise the level at which people pay the 40p higher rate by about £6,000, would be paid for entirely by increased growth. This growth, the Lib Dems argue, would be created through rejoining the EU’s single market and customs union. As making a deal with the EU would take time, the actual tax cuts would only happen in the final year of a parliament, potentially as late as 2034, costing £17bn. In the interim years, thresholds would be raised by inflation, thus keeping levels effectively stable. There would also be a smaller increase to the 45p additional rate of tax, currently payable above £125,000.

citation.title: Ed Davey promises £17bn income tax cut if Lib Dems are elected

text:
Ed Davey promises £17bn income tax cut if Lib Dems are elected

Setting out what he described as “trusting people to spend their own money, not telling them the state knows best”, Davey took aim at what he called “the post-Brexit stealth taxes” of frozen thresholds, notably on the higher 40p rate. “Thirty years ago, just 2 million people paid it. Now it’s 9 million,” he said. “A tax band designed for stockbrokers is now holding back teachers and nurses. That’s not fair. It’s not right.” The plans mark a distinct shift in the party’s fiscal approach. While it is eyecatching and could appeal to the many former Conservative voters who backed the Lib Dems in 2024, helping them take 60-plus Tory seats, it is likely to cause unease among some of the party’s MPs. A number of them have called privately for a more ambitious and comprehensive vision of what the party stands for, amid polling that shows most voters do not have much of a sense of this. Davey’s advisers, however, argue that the cost of living is the subject that most affects many voters, and that tax cuts – even up to eight years in the future – directly address this.

citation.title: Ed Davey promises £17bn income tax cut if Lib Dems are elected

text:
Ed Davey promises £17bn income tax cut if Lib Dems are elected

Other elements of the speech included previously-trailed new policies, including a proposal for a global nuclear-style non-proliferation treaty to halt the development of super-intelligent AI. The tax-cutting plan is predicated entirely on the EU allowing a swift deal on single market access, which could become even more difficult if rightwing populists take power in more EU states, and on this then increasing growth. The Lib Dems insist the numbers stand up, saying they are based on a report from an independent economics consultancy, which calculated that a deal with the EU could generate 0.5% growth in the first fiscal year alone. Reform UK has already pledged to increase the personal tax allowance to £15,000, paid for in part by significant cuts to social security. Davey noted this in the speech, saying: “Think about that. Reform say you can have a tax cut, but only if they get to punish disabled people at the same time. We say no.

We can cut taxes and support the most vulnerable people in our country.” Opening his speech with a warning that black-shirted, and balaclava-wearing far-right protesters who gathered in Dover and Portsmouth “would tear our country apart”, Davey compared groups such as Patriot Platform to Oswald Mosley’s fascists in the 1930s, the National Front in the 70s and to Nick Griffin and the BNP. “Each time, they tried to turn neighbour against neighbour, tried to pit community against community, tried to turn our streets into battlegrounds,” he said. “But we didn’t let them. The British people said no.” He said this time, far-right vigilantes were not acting in isolation, but were the most visible part of a far-right threat that was “extremely well funded” and promoted by figures such as Elon Musk and given credibility by “cynical politicians like Nigel Farage”. Davey slammed Farage as a cynical politician who was “not just willing, but eager to fan the flames of hatred and intolerance to make himself richer”. He said: “It is the worst of Trump’s America.

We must not let it become Farage’s Britain.” Pointing to the £72m donations Reform had received from two crypto billionaires, Davey added: “If there was any doubt before, there can’t be now. We are in the fight of our lives. And it is a fight we must win.”

OpenAI’s George Osborne says datacentre nimbys holding back Britain

Datacentre nimbys are holding Britain back, George Osborne has said in reaction to nationwide protests about the giant water- and energy-guzzling structures. The former Tory chancellor is now the head of AI for countries at OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT. His job is to represent the company to governments around the world and he also has a role in enabling the building of datacentres and other infrastructure. Related: Even George Osborne might be a nimby if an AI datacente was built next to his home Speaking at the Big Brue festival in Somerset on Sunday, Osborne said: “You try and build a datacentre in Britain … I spent my life when I was politician trying to get people to agree to have new roads and railway lines and airport runways, and communities go up in arms – it’s really hard to build a datacentre.” He said the UK would lose its “sovereignty” over tech to the US if it failed to allow datacentres to be built. He explained: “You can either choose to have these datacentres in Ohio and Georgia and Michigan, which is where they’re all being built … we don’t allow these things to be built.

citation.title: OpenAI’s George Osborne says datacentre nimbys holding back Britain

text:
OpenAI’s George Osborne says datacentre nimbys holding back Britain

They’re going to be built elsewhere, and you know that’s a loss of some sovereign control over the physical location where these things are.” There have been protests about datacentres across the UK, including in central London, Devon and outside Holyrood in Edinburgh. People have said they are a blight on the landscape, questioned whether they will bring jobs to the local area, and argued they will take investment and space that could be used for affordable housing. There are also concerns about the vast water and energy use. The government has classified AI datacentres as critical national infrastructure to get them built more quickly. But the Green party in England has called for a moratorium on building them. Osborne dismissed the concerns over datacentres as nimbyism. He said: “I think a lot of the to opposition datacentres is very much like ‘not in my back yard’.

There’s an enormous building boom going on in the United States of datacentres, even as the political opposition undoubtedly is growing.” Verity Harding, the head of the AI and geopolitics project at Cambridge University’s Bennett School for Public Policy, said people had wider concerns over these centres. She said: “The reason everyone hates datacentres has nothing to do with datacentres. It’s the only tangible thing to protest against … [people] just don’t like what’s happening and they don’t feel that anybody’s in control or thinking about the impact of it. “It’s exactly because the tech industry execs are talking in this ridiculous way … You know, you cannot go out on the one hand and say this [AI] might kill everybody one week and then the next week go and appear at a big sales conference saying that you should integrate it into your business.” Bosses of OpenAI and Anthropic, two of the largest AI companies, will be meeting world leaders at the UN general assembly in New York City this week amid debate over the prospect of dangerous, superintelligent AI and whether and how it should be regulated.

Osborne said: “The fact that corporate leaders are sitting down with the presidents and prime ministers of the world in the UN security council I would say actually shouldn’t be alarming. It’s actually reassuring that people are beginning to try and use the kind of institutions of the world to think about how we regulate this new technology.”

text:
Lib Dems quietly commission review into religious inclusion amid case brought by dropped candidate

The Liberal Democrats have quietly commissioned a review into the treatment of figures within their ranks who hold religious views, weeks after the Guardian revealed a religious discrimination claim against the party by the former candidate David Campanale. Campanale, a former BBC journalist, was selected in 2021 as the party’s candidate for Sutton and Cheam but was removed in August 2023. He has argued in a civil case against the party that discrimination against his Christianity cost him his political career. Richard Newby, the former Lib Dem leader in the House of Lords, has been appointed to chair the party’s inclusion and faith review, which will examine how the party treats candidates and members of different faith and those without. The inquiry, which has not been publicly announced, was set up in direct response to Campanale’s case, the Guardian understands, with figures at the top of the party understood to be keen to show they take the issue seriously.

citation.title: Lib Dems quietly commission review into religious inclusion amid case brought by dropped candidate

text:
Lib Dems quietly commission review into religious inclusion amid case brought by dropped candidate

The Guardian revealed last month that Campanale was seeking almost £790,000 in damages after the party admitted direct and indirect discrimination on the grounds of religion or belief, and failures in dealing with complaints about his treatment. The case prompted the former Lib Dem leader Tim Farron and former deputy leader Simon Hughes to call for an independent inquiry into Campanale’s treatment by the party, as well as an apology. The party cannot comment on court proceedings and will instead use Lord Newby’s review to seek to answer the general question of whether people of faith are being discriminated against, and to what extent any evidence shows this. Hughes told the Guardian he would pursue a separate investigation once Campanale’s case was resolved. “The Newby review is explicitly not about any past or present legal case and cannot be about David’s case, which is still before the courts and with one remaining possible internal party appeal,” he said.

citation.title: Lib Dems quietly commission review into religious inclusion amid case brought by dropped candidate

text:
Lib Dems quietly commission review into religious inclusion amid case brought by dropped candidate

“The review however is greatly to be welcomed and I believe it will allow the party to meet one of the two big objectives which David, [the] Lib Dem Christian Forum, I and others were seeking.” The Newby review was announced last week to party members via an email from the Lib Dem leader, Ed Davey, and president, Josh Babarinde, days before the start of the party’s conference in Brighton. It will examine whether candidate approval, selection and deselection processes are inclusive of different faiths, whether candidates receive adequate support, the operation of complaints and disciplinary processes, and training for local party officers. A Lib Dem source said: “This review offers no remorse, no apologies to members misled so badly nor contrition towards the victims of breaches including Campanale and other Christians who once formed a bedrock of activists among our party’s nonconformist tradition. All should have had an apology by now.

citation.title: Lib Dems quietly commission review into religious inclusion amid case brought by dropped candidate

text:
Lib Dems quietly commission review into religious inclusion amid case brought by dropped candidate

“As it stands, the review looks like a ploy to impress a court judge as the review of Campanale’s case is meant to be published right before damages are considered.” Another source said: “The review doesn’t recognise the pain [Campanale’s case] brought on members, and it has to be asked why key individuals refused to act when they received complaints or requests to investigate complaints around Campanale’s deselection.” Campanale submitted a schedule of loss that puts his claim at £788,740.75, including interest. It seeks compensation for injury to feelings, aggravated damages, past and future earnings, the loss of an MP’s pension, counselling costs and the “loss of a chance” or “loss of political capital”. In his claim, Campanale said that at a meeting in January 2022 he was questioned about his Christianity by about 30 people and asked whether he was enjoying his “martyrdom just like Jesus did”. Questions have emerged within the party about the remit of the review. A number of Lib Dem figures and activists have also privately criticised its lack of formal announcement.

Lib Dems quietly commission review into religious inclusion amid case brought by dropped candidate

One figure questioned whether Newby would have access to complaints and candidate selection material, and whether the review would extend beyond religious faith to other protected beliefs. There is a particular concern among some members about whether the review will examine the party’s treatment of people with gender-critical beliefs. In a motion passed at party conference on Monday, members rejected official guidance by the equalities watchdog on how organisations should implement the supreme court ruling on transgender people, calling it “discriminatory and unworkable”. The party’s conference fringe programme over the weekend included discussions about Christian nationalism and political use of religion. The Lib Dems previously said the party was “home to people of all faiths and none, including many Christians”, but have declined to comment.

British banks warned not to invest in planned Israeli settlement before UK trade ban begins

British banks and financial institutions are receiving written warnings from MPs that they should not invest in Israel’s E1 settlement project even though new UK laws banning trade with illegal settlements are unlikely to be in place for months. A letter was sent to banks on Tuesday by the all-party Britain-Palestine group of MPs saying the onus was now on banks to review their obligations not to cooperate with new settlements. The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, announced two weeks ago plans for a complete ban on trade with illegal settlements and new sanctions on those co-operating with building the settlements. But complex secondary legislation needed for the powers to come into force may take six to nine months to pass through parliament. The issue is urgent since the Israeli government is seeking bids for two tenders for the construction of as many as 3,400 houses, including more than 1,300 for which the tender closes on 25 October, two days before the elections.

citation.title: British banks warned not to invest in planned Israeli settlement before UK trade ban begins

text:
British banks warned not to invest in planned Israeli settlement before UK trade ban begins

Israel’s finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, said in 2025 that the E1 settlement “practically erases the two-state delusion” by splitting up territory that would be set aside for a Palestinian state. The settlement plan has long been delayed due to its uncontested political impact on the prospect of a two-state solution, still the main peace plan backed by the west and Gulf states. Finance, insurance and guarantees are required before construction starts. One of Miliband’s motives in acting earlier this month, before the Israeli elections, was not just to express his deep concern at the scale of settler violence in the West Bank but to deter UK finance from helping with the tenders or the construction. It has been alleged that he overrode some diplomatic advice in acting before the elections. Related: UK to adopt tougher stance on Israel with illegal settlements trade ban The all-party group said: “The immediate question is what commitments institutions were willing to make while the detailed rules are being developed, and how they would respond when restrictions take effect”.

citation.title: British banks warned not to invest in planned Israeli settlement before UK trade ban begins

British banks warned not to invest in planned Israeli settlement before UK trade ban begins

The letter, signed by two Labour MPs, Debbie Abrahams and Andy McDonald, states: “Commitments made now may be difficult to unwind when restrictions commence; the allocation of costs will depend on the contracts and applicable law. We ask boards to consider this interim risk before agreeing new or increased commitments.” The letter adds: “We ask you to place potential E1 and settlement-related exposure on the board’s agenda and on the risk register, and to reach a reasoned decision on whether the associated sanctions, legal and reputational risk sits within the institution’s stated risk appetite.” It is argued that postcodes provide the locality of a product’s origin, and nothing is being attempted that would stop trade in general with Israel. Abrahams said: “We are not asking to pre-empt the law. We are asking boards a question they should be able to answer today: what exposure are you prepared to carry while the sanctions regime is written and on what evidence?” The all-party group said it intended to publish replies to its letter by 10 October.

text:
Cut NHS red tape and boost productivity to prevent 20,000 early deaths a year in England, report urges

The NHS in England could prevent 20,000 deaths and save £33bn a year by cutting red tape and boosting productivity, a report says. Research by the Health Foundation found the health service has been held back for decades by excessive regulation, short-term planning and insufficient capability to deliver major change. But rewiring the NHS, the world’s largest single healthcare system, by harnessing new technology, empowering staff and increasing capital investment could save both lives and money, it found. There is “substantial scope to improve outcomes within the funding already available to the NHS”, which could result in up to four extra years of good health for people on average, the report said. In terms of where deaths could be prevented, focusing on diagnosing cancer earlier and finding people with high blood pressure or conditions such as diabetes quicker would be key, it added.

citation.title: Cut NHS red tape and boost productivity to prevent 20,000 early deaths a year in England, report urges

text:
Cut NHS red tape and boost productivity to prevent 20,000 early deaths a year in England, report urges

The report called for a series of changes, such as releasing the NHS from unnecessary regulation, reporting and compliance tasks, as well as launching a “test-and-learn” approach to scaling up things that could improve productivity, such as use of artificial intelligence. “Our analysis suggests that if the NHS in England achieved outcomes closer to the best-performing comparable health systems, without spending more each year, it could potentially result in 18,500–20,600 fewer deaths each year from treatable causes and 2.5 to 4.5 additional years that people spend in good health on average,” the report said. Increasing NHS productivity is “sometimes … seen as exhorting hard-working staff to work even harder, in a system already under considerable strain” but this view must be challenged, it added. “At its heart, productivity means achieving better health outcomes from the resources available.” The biggest issues affecting productivity included the “constant churn”, too many targets, and not enough focus on health outcomes.

citation.title: Cut NHS red tape and boost productivity to prevent 20,000 early deaths a year in England, report urges

text:
Cut NHS red tape and boost productivity to prevent 20,000 early deaths a year in England, report urges

Researchers also heard from staff how poor IT wasted clinical time, how limited estate and equipment constrained healthcare and how gaps in administrative support shifted additional work to clinicians. While AI offered opportunities, the “NHS has repeatedly struggled to take advantage of the potential”, the report said. Anita Charlesworth, report author and senior economic adviser at the Health Foundation, said: “This is mission critical for the NHS, which cannot simply keep doing more of the same. “The problem is not a lack of committed and talented people or an absence of ideas; it is that the NHS is not set up to deliver sustained productivity growth.

citation.title: Cut NHS red tape and boost productivity to prevent 20,000 early deaths a year in England, report urges

text:
Cut NHS red tape and boost productivity to prevent 20,000 early deaths a year in England, report urges

“Our research points to a fundamental redesign of the operating conditions – not another disruptive reorganisation, but a reset to make improving productivity a defining focus for the NHS over the next decade and beyond.” Sir Ciarán Devane, chief executive of the NHS Alliance, which represents and supports the health and care system in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, said he agreed more could be done to deliver further productivity gains but there were “big barriers” that would need to be addressed. “Lack of capital investment has been a long-running drag on NHS productivity. More must be done to turn the tide on years of neglect … We also agree that a more streamlined, supportive regulatory system which encourages local autonomy and innovation will be vital for future progress.”

Reform UK-led council ends support for Show Racism the Red Card

Anti-racism education in some schools will be scrapped after a city council now led by Reform UK ended its 30-year support for the charity Show Racism the Red Card. Announcing the decision last week, the Reform leader of Sunderland city council, Christopher Eynon, said it would no longer support “politically charged organisations with an agenda”. Gary Bennett, the former Sunderland AFC captain and the charity’s head coach, said he was “shocked and disappointed” that Nigel Farage’s party had withdrawn vital funding. The move prompted a furious backlash from opposition politicians including Labour’s Bridget Phillipson, who described it on Tuesday as “misguided, cruel and in no way backed by the people of Sunderland”. Bennett, who became only the second black player in Sunderland’s history when he joined the club in 1984, was a founding member of Show Racism the Red Card when it was established in 1996.

citation.title: Reform UK-led council ends support for Show Racism the Red Card

text:
Reform UK-led council ends support for Show Racism the Red Card

The former centre-back, who remains a cult hero on Wearside, said he was “surprised, shocked and disappointed” that Sunderland council – the first local authority to have supported it – was cutting its ties after 30 years. Bennett said it would immediately disrupt the charity’s ability to teach local children in schools and provide workshops in prisons and workplaces. He said: “We’re not a political charity – they’re trying to say we are but we’re not. Sunderland were the first council to come onboard to help fund us, that’s the annoying thing. For something like this to happen now, we just want to know the reasons why.” Bennett said the racist riots across many English cities including Sunderland in 2024 showed there was “still lots of work to be done”. While Britain had come a long way since the 1980s, he said, there remained issues to confront around attitudes towards asylum seekers and migrants. “You’ve got all different issues going on now. It keeps moving, it’s always something else which causes some form of racism,” he said. “It’s something that is challenging every single day and we’ve got to keep the fight.

There’s still lots of work to be done and we can’t just ignore it and think it’s going to go away because it’s not.” Eynon, whose party gained control of the council in May, said the authority was not “stepping back from its opposition to racism or discrimination” and that “racism has no place in Sunderland”. He took issue with Ged Grebby, the chief executive of Show Racism the Red Card, describing Reform as a “very dangerous organisation”. Grebby defended his right to express personal views and said the charity had support across the political spectrum. Separately, Reform UK has been accused of “vice signalling” after its councillors in Bradford proposed to pull out of the Local Authority of Sanctuary scheme, which is intended to show a city is a safe place for migrant communities.

The Reform group that runs the council said it would be putting forward a motion at the next meeting in October to end the status, which it said has meant the council had “led Refugee Week engagement and utilised local libraries to celebrate all new arrivals into Bradford”, adding that “public services should instead be prioritised for Bradford residents”. The Reform councillor Jayne Morgan said the move “may upset oversensitive political opponents” but was firmly in the public interest. In response, Imran Khan, the leader of Bradford’s Labour group, said: “Reform failed to deliver on various promises they made to Bradford residents this summer, so instead they fall back on their usual toxic recipe of hate, victimhood and division.” He said pulling out of the scheme would “do nothing to help a single person” in Bradford. “This is vice signalling from Reform and all it does is damage integration and promote division and resentment, which helps no one,” he said.

text:
Burnham navigates diplomatic rapids in first Trump meeting, but turbulent waters lie ahead

On the flight out to New York this week, one of Andy Burnham’s senior aides warned him that meeting Donald Trump would be the political equivalent of white water rafting. While there is a well-known playbook the US president deploys when he first meets other world leaders, he remains a deeply unpredictable figure and any dealings with him can leave you crashing into the rocks. Trump’s strategy involves personal flattery, transactional diplomacy and a public evaluation of his guest’s skills. Related: Trump’s threat to annihilate Iran to UN general assembly is stunning, even for him When Keir Starmer first met the president at the White House early last year, it was there in spades. Trump praised his “beautiful” accent, said that Britain was a “wonderful” place and claimed that he had driven a “hard bargain” on tariffs. On the flight home, the clearly relieved former prime minister gave journalists a Trump-style thumbs up, telling them he was “happy” before returning to the front of the plane. But in time, their relationship fell apart.

citation.title: Burnham navigates diplomatic rapids in first Trump meeting, but turbulent waters lie ahead

text:
Burnham navigates diplomatic rapids in first Trump meeting, but turbulent waters lie ahead

Just over 18 months later, it was an apprehensive Burnham’s turn to head down the diplomatic rapids at the UN general assembly. As the new prime minister faced the press after their talks, the president again deployed the playbook – describing Burnham as a “natural businessperson” who had “lots of assets on his side”, while predicting he would be a “great” leader. The British side, including foreign secretary Ed Miliband and national security adviser Jonathan Powell, could not hide their relief when Trump kept his policy differences with the UK muted – beyond inevitable criticism of what he described as the “terrible” Chagos deal. Even on the issue that fully ruptured Starmer’s relationship with Trump – his refusal to allow the US to use British airbases for attacks against Iran at the start of the war – the president held his punches. “Some countries could have stepped forward. But there aren’t too many countries, frankly, that could have handled that,” he said.

citation.title: Burnham navigates diplomatic rapids in first Trump meeting, but turbulent waters lie ahead

text:
Burnham navigates diplomatic rapids in first Trump meeting, but turbulent waters lie ahead

Afterwards, British officials – even those who have witnessed the Trump strategy in action before and knew it would not necessarily last – were delighted with how the talks had gone. “It was the top end of our expectations,” said one. “All the issues you guys had written about – the Falklands, a united Ireland, Chagos – all fine.” They admitted the West Bank settlement trade ban was the one area they had worried about most. But a summer of diplomacy got Trump on board, and to their relief, he deferred to Burnham on the question. “It was a bit of a curveball, but it was better than him criticising it,” another aide said. Burnham even managed to use the moment to steer the raft – briefly – into calmer waters, explaining his hopes of drawing an end to the political turbulence that has gripped Britain for more than a decade, and creating a more “positive story” for the country instead. “More than anything, we just needed them to connect, and start building a relationship that we can leverage when we need to,” a third government official said.

citation.title: Burnham navigates diplomatic rapids in first Trump meeting, but turbulent waters lie ahead

text:
Burnham navigates diplomatic rapids in first Trump meeting, but turbulent waters lie ahead

But just as Starmer found that with time, policy differences between the UK and US made the relationship more difficult to navigate, so his successor is likely to find the same. Burnham’s team is right to be cautious about the unsteadiness that Trump can inflict – his international actions causing ripples in the UK too. The prime minister may have survived the first set of diplomatic rapids, but there are more to navigate ahead.

Burnham stands by claim UK is ‘in hock’ to bond markets

Andy Burnham has said he still believes the UK is far too exposed to global shocks, defending comments last year when he said the UK should be less “in hock” to the bond markets. He said the comments had been deliberately misinterpreted by the former prime minister Keir Starmer and his advisers and said his aim was not more borrowing and spending but a far more resilient economy. Burnham’s comments in an interview with the New Statesmen last year made waves before the Labour conference because of the then Greater Manchester’s clear ambitions to replace Starmer as prime minister. In a fresh interview with the magazine on Wednesday, he said he had intended to highlight how vulnerable the UK was to global price fluctuations. Government borrowing has climbed again over the past months as energy prices have risen in response to continued deadlock on the Iran war. The UK government borrowed a higher than expected £18.3bn last month, putting further pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, as he prepares for next month’s budget. Burnham said he wanted to build an economy that was far less vulnerable.

citation.title: Burnham stands by claim UK is ‘in hock’ to bond markets

text:
Burnham stands by claim UK is ‘in hock’ to bond markets

“I mean, the point about the bond markets, it holds – in that what I was saying was the country has left itself over-exposed,” he said, telling the magazine he was arguing for a “much more streamlined, productive state”. He said criticism from Starmer and the then chancellor, Rachel Reeves, was unjustified. “They couldn’t understand why I was saying some of the things that I was saying … [They] didn’t know what to do with it, but they did what they always do, which is they pulled one line out of it and then framed that one line within their world, rather than the one that I was talking about.” Burnham also addressed criticism from the Conservatives after he said during an exchange at prime minister’s questions that national security “should not come at the expense of social security” – which opponents said showed he was not willing to cut the welfare budget to fund increased defence spending. “It oversimplifies the political discourse that we need to have, doesn’t it?” he said.

Burnham, who will address his first Labour conference as prime minister in Liverpool next Tuesday, said he would set out his political vision, which would be a break from the economic and political mainstream of the past 40 years. “It’s about control,” he said. “If you strip it back, and all the fluff and, you know, the verbiage, you can actually strip it back to one word, which is control.” He said that would be a business-friendly approach, rather than purely statist. “People aren’t going to come in and invest in a significant way where the place isn’t functional and it’s in major decline,” he said, saying it was the state’s job to “create the optimum conditions for private-sector investment”. “We’ve just got to get that belief back into Britain that, yeah, we know what we’re about, we know what we stand for, that is what we’ve always been, so we can do it again.” In attempts to calm jittery bond markets, Burnham has previously said his budget would “stick to the fiscal rules” on debt and borrowing set out under Reeves, “but at the same time we will help reduce cost of living pressure on our constituents”.

England’s mayors should face greater scrutiny as powers expand, thinktank says

England’s mayors should face much greater official scrutiny to avoid Andy Burnham’s devolution agenda being “derailed by one bad decision”, a thinktank has said. Ministers will set out plans next month to give regional leaders control over potentially billions of pounds of additional funding under a “transformational” shift of power outside Whitehall. From 2028, mayors will be able to keep a share of income tax generated in their areas – giving them greater scope to borrow for major infrastructure projects – as well as retain business rates from 2027 and raise further funds through a “tourist tax”. IPPR North, whose researchers have worked closely with Burnham’s government, welcomed the “bold and ambitious” plans as a step towards “reversing decades of damaging over-centralisation that has held the country back”. It called for mayors to be allowed to keep a 5% share of income tax, which would move an extra £3.8bn a year out of Whitehall and roughly double the funding under their control. However, the thinktank said increasingly powerful mayors should be subject to much tougher oversight.

Watermelons: the term used to describe the members of the Green party of England and Wales who are green on the outside and red on the inside. People in this faction are environmentalists but bleed socialist ideologies. Of the roughly 160,000 people who have flocked to the party since Zack Polanski became leader last year, most are thought to be in this camp, drawn to a political space on the left that they see as vacated by the Labour party. But the author of a new book – The Green Socialist: Zack Polanski and the Battle for Britain’s Future – says this flavour of Green is nothing new. “What you’ve got to understand is that the party has been watermelon for at least 10 years,” says Russell Warfield, a former party staffer who has worked on election campaigns, including Polanski’s. “There’s often this dichotomy presented that there’s this ‘real core’ Green party who are these ecologists who really just care about conservation of the environment, then there’s this new cohort of hard leftists,” Warfield says.

Thinktank linked to Reform UK calls for abolition of state pension

A thinktank linked to Reform UK has called for the abolition of the state pension and £75bn worth of sweeping tax cuts in a “radical” report likely to influence the party’s platform for the next election. The Centre for a Better Britain’s (CFABB) report – which also calls for weaker rules for UK banks and Trump-style investment accounts offering £1,000 to newborns – will be formally launched at a private event with City executives on Wednesday. The 183-page report, entitled “Boosting Britain”, proposes abolishing taxes typically levied on wealthy Britons, including capital gains tax and inheritance tax, which it says disrupts family businesses and encourages people to move their wealth out of the UK. The CFABB – founded and led by the former Reform chief operations officer Jonathan Brown – also calls for the elimination of stamp duty on property and shares, digital service tax and air passenger duty, and a drastic reduction in “internationally uncompetitive” corporation tax from 25% to 15% over eight years.

The report said it amounted to a “a programme of radical reform to Britain’s financial system and tax code, designed ultimately to raise productivity and living standards through better-paid jobs, higher retirement incomes, higher business investment, more businesses starting and scaling, and less time and money spent on unproductive activity”. The report stresses that any tax changes would have to be matched by cuts to public spending – to avoid a Liz Truss-style market meltdown – but stopped short of outlining how exactly to match all of those cuts with cost savings. However, the CFABB says some ways to cut spending could involve closing the coveted public pension plan to new teachers and civil servants, and eradicating the state pension. The Department for Work and Pensions forecasts the state pension will cost the public purse £146.1bn in 2025 to 2026.

People claiming universal credit (UC) would have their payments cut by a third if they have not paid enough national insurance, under a Conservative plan condemned by one charity as “a fast track to increased poverty”. Under the proposals, those who receive this “subsistence allowance” would have it paid into a dedicated debit card that would prevent from them buying alcohol or tobacco, based on an Australian system that was scrapped after trials found limited evidence it changed behaviour. While the proposals are billed by the Conservatives as a way to push people into work, the poverty charity Trussell said trimming incomes so that people struggled with rent and transport was likely to make it even harder for them to find and keep a job. UK to launch military squadron to protect satellites in space

A new military unit dedicated to defending satellites, protecting services people need on Earth and potentially supporting offensive operations is being launched by the UK. The No III Space Effects Squadron will be announced on Wednesday, with the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, warning that Britain needs to “keep pace in the new space race”. “Control of the waves was the essential ingredient in 19th-century deterrence,” he will tell the Space Power conference. “That is why Britain built the finest naval power in history. In the 20th century it was control of the skies, and so we built a world class air force to protect us. This century will depend on control of space.” The new Royal Air Force (RAF) squadron will protect satellites used to warn of incoming missile attacks, provide communications and help guide ships, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) said. It will bring together specialist personnel from across the armed forces to counter hostile activity in orbit and defend satellites the nation depends on every day.

It is intended to support offensive and defensive space operations and will expand over time as new capabilities enter service. It’s a domain of direct competition, where our military advantage can be won or lost.” The UK has formally ruled out destructive anti-satellite missile testing and the government said on Wednesday that it continues to work through the UN committee on the peaceful uses of outer space to promote norms, rules and principles of responsible space behaviours. From idealists to struggling sceptics: how Labour’s majority depends on five progressive voter types – in charts

A new MRP poll suggests Labour would remain the largest party if a general election were held now, but would fall well short of an overall majority as Reform surged into second place. Behind those headline figures, research from Survation and 38 Degrees casts new light on five distinct voter groups who are collectively defined as the “progressive majority”. These people share concerns about living costs and the NHS, but differ over immigration, the environment, political trust and the pace of change needed to address the UK’s policies. Related: Tactical voting at next election could push Reform into fourth place, poll finds To build a parliamentary majority, Labour must hold on to the groups that have remained relatively loyal, while winning back voters drifting towards the Greens, Reform or political disengagement. In short, they need enough of this “progressive majority” to stay within the fold. Labour strategists – including Keir Starmer’s former chief of staff Morgan McSweeney – have often been wary of a tactic that seeks only to unite the progressive bloc.

The five groups are described as: Rooted traditionalists: Older, economically left-leaning voters who are highly concerned about immigration and less interested in environmental issues. Many moved from the Conservatives to Labour but could shift again, including towards Reform. Cost of living pressures and NHS access provide the strongest common ground with other progressive voters. Open-hearted idealists: Affluent, highly educated and the most socially liberal, pro-immigration and politically engaged group. They lean strongly towards Labour, the Greens and Lib Dems and are particularly open to tactical voting. Bills, NHS access and progressive taxation matter most, while tougher immigration policies risk alienating them. Quiet persuadables: The youngest and least politically committed segment, often holding centrist or uncertain views. Their support is spread widely across the parties and they are the most likely to vote tactically. They are potentially winnable, but need a compelling reason to engage with politics.

Tactical voting at next election could push Reform into fourth place, poll finds

Progressive voters could push Reform UK into fourth place and put Labour within touching distance of a majority if tactical voting is widespread at the next election, a major poll has found. Andy Burnham is beginning to attract a significant number of left-leaning voters back to Labour, motivated by a desire to stop Nigel Farage, the results suggest. The poll of more than 8,000 voters, shared with the Guardian, suggests a widespread openness to voting tactically. It also shows the prime minister’s most successful electoral strategy would be to unite the centre and left bloc of voters, while the right remains split. It would be a marked contrast to the tactics of Keir Starmer’s Labour before the 2024 general election, when the party tried to attract more conservative older voters. Such a tactic would be likely to unsettle some in Labour, given the same strategy was deployed for Ed Miliband’s failed bid in 2015, albeit before Reform’s arrival as a major electoral force.

Tony Blair says Britain should work towards rejoining EU in next 10 years

Britain should work towards rejoining the EU in the next decade, Tony Blair has said, adding to growing pressure on Andy Burnham to abandon Labour’s reluctance to revisit the 2016 referendum. The former prime minister has urged Burnham to use his 10-year plan in November to put the country’s membership of the union back on the table, a decade after it voted to leave. In a paper entitled A Path to Rejoining a Reformed Europe, the Tony Blair Institute (TBI) calls for the UK to accept free movement of people and make a financial contribution as the price of entry. The intervention comes after Burnham declined to rule out promising to rejoin the EU in the next Labour manifesto, though it also threatens to reopen the deep rifts caused by the vote 10 years ago.

Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, has called the Brexit vote a “catastrophic mistake” and said the party should aim to rejoin the bloc, while Burnham himself told the Guardian last year: “I hope in my lifetime I see this country rejoin the European Union.” But Burnham has said he does not wish to pursue membership of the union in the near term. UK ‘losing up to £6.5bn a year in EU trade’ without post-Brexit product deal

The UK is losing out on annual exports to the EU that could be worth as much as £6.5bn without a deal with Brussels that allows manufacturers to jettison duplicate product testing. In the latest attempt to calculate the loss of trade with the EU after Brexit, the IPPR thinktank said many companies have given up selling goods to the EU or set up subsidiaries inside the trade bloc after successive governments failed to secure a mutual recognition agreement that would avoid the extra administration costs. The thinktank estimated that the absence of such a deal may have cost UK exporters between £3.7bn and £6.5bn each year in lost revenue since the UK’s post-Brexit trading arrangements came into force in 2021. It urged the government to reopen talks with the EU, saying that the loss of trade amounted to about 0.18% of annual national income, or about three times what the UK government expects to gain from its trade deal with Japan, Canada, Australia and Singapore, known as the CPTPP deal.

He said the move would bring the UK into alignment with its largest trading partner, boost exports and kickstart growth. ‘We will get stuff done’: Burnham seeks to banish ghosts of Starmerism at Labour conference

Andy Burnham was not even in the audience for the prime minister’s speech at the Labour party conference this time last year. As Keir Starmer made the case for continuity to his restive party, Burnham was spotted slipping out over the bridge towards Liverpool’s Albert Dock. The then Greater Manchester mayor had been vying for the spotlight throughout the party’s annual gathering, presenting the argument for change. But even he could not have envisaged the schism that would take place in the ensuing 12 months and would put him on the main stage as prime minister at this year’s conference, beginning in Merseyside on Sunday. At the time, Starmer retained a tentative grip on the party, while Burnham was mocked for leaving Liverpool with his tail between his legs, awkward and abashed, especially over his controversial comments about the government being too “in hock” to the bond markets. But below the surface, disquiet was starting to take shape in the party.

After he succeeded Starmer in the top job in July, Burnham has made “Hope again” his conference slogan, with No 10 strategists pitching this year’s event as a definitive break with the past. Burnham has been promising to defy the political and economic consensus of the last 40 years since he was elected as MP for Makerfield in a byelection that proved to be the final domino for Starmer’s faltering leadership, and he will use this conference to set out how he aims to do this. It will also attempt to break old habits in the Labour party’s way of doing business, which has often been hindered by pessimism, fear and factionalism. Ravinder Athwal, the economist who wrote Labour’s 2024 manifesto, is taking on a senior role as an adviser to John Healey, in a move likely to fuel speculation about an early general election. The chancellor is keen to strengthen his team before the critical budget on 28 October, as the economy is buffeted by high oil prices and rising government borrowing costs. Healey has poached Athwal to be his senior special adviser from the business advisory group Flint Global, previously run by Andy Burnham’s chief of staff, the former Blair-era cabinet minister James Purnell. Athwal, a Cambridge economics graduate, was closely associated with drawing up Labour’s manifesto, and devising Keir Starmer’s five “missions”, which were meant to shape Labour’s approach to government. He worked as a senior economic adviser in Starmer’s Downing Street team but left after a year to join Flint Global. No general election before 2029, Andy Burnham says

Andy Burnham has said he will not call a general election before 2029, after days of speculation that Labour’s revival in the polls could tempt him to call an early contest. The prime minister was repeatedly questioned on the prospect during a round of broadcast interviews to regional media on Friday. He initially said he was “not particularly” tempted by the idea of an early election, but later became firmer, saying he would “knock that dead” and he was “not going to do that” because he was focused on getting on with the job. Asked by ITV Calendar whether the next election would be in 2029, Burnham said: “Well, yes, that’s when the next election will be. All of this speculation on an early election – I can knock that dead. “You know, people want me, new in office, to be getting on with the job of delivering on the things that we’ve discussed, rather than putting self-serving politics before that, which was what I would be doing if I call an election.

‘He looked at me and said: “So you really are working class”’: Alan Johnson on the need for better paternity leave

Parliament was in recess when Tony Blair called Alan Johnson up to his flat above No 11. The former prime minister was relaxed, padding around in his socks, while his son Leo played with his toys. Johnson, then the education secretary, spoke about his own son from his second marriage, who was a similar age. “Tony said: ‘Oh you’re a father?’” recalled Johnson. “I said: ‘Tony, I had three kids by the age of 20!’ He looked at me and said: ‘So you really are working-class …’” It may be almost a quarter of a century since Johnson introduced paid paternity leave during his time as the trade and industry secretary, but working-class fathers are still being shortchanged, the former minister has told the Guardian. Johnson has added his name to a growing number of current and former MPs and senior Labour figures calling for six weeks of paternity leave paid at 90% of earnings, capped at £1,200 a week, with the offer extended to self-employed fathers, who are currently the only parents with no entitlement to paid leave.

Why Ed Miliband has embraced his ‘awkward dad’ image in viral TikTok video

It sparked delight among the diehard Milifans and a begrudging smile from those less keen on the foreign secretary, but a viral video of Ed Miliband has – possibly – confirmed his status as the internet’s awkward dad. About 1.5 million people have viewed an interaction between Miliband and the TikTok personality Feroz Khan on the streets of New York, during which the digital content creator asks Miliband a series of questions including his name, job and his top piece of advice. Following the same formula employed by Khan in every video, Miliband is stopped in a seemingly – though of course not at all – impromptu manner by the influencer who says: “You’re very well dressed, what do you do for a living?” When Miliband, in New York for the UN general assembly, explains that he is the foreign secretary (adding that he is the UK equivalent of Marco Rubio when Khan claims not to know what that is), the influencer asks: “What makes your work so special?” Miliband gushes that he is “trying to make the world a better place”. So far, so soft serve.

Andy Burnham announces new homes scheme for first-time buyers

A new help-to-buy scheme aimed at giving first-time buyers who cannot rely on the “bank of mum and dad” is to be introduced in a big policy announcement by Andy Burnham. The programme, called “Your first home”, is intended to help buyers in England who have a regular income but have been unable to save for a large deposit or don’t have financial support from their family. Under the scheme, first-time buyers will get a 20% equity loan to help them buy a new-build home, with an initial interest free period and a requirement of a minimum deposit of just 2.5%. Household income caps and a deposit cap will be introduced to exclude those on the biggest salaries and with big savings pots, with the scheme targeted at those who may struggle to buy a home on their own. Price caps will ensure people can only buy modest houses. In an interview with the Guardian on the eve of Labour’s party conference in Liverpool, the prime minister said: “Too many young people are struggling with housing, with many giving up hope on ever having a home to call their own.

Andy Burnham is riding high ahead of the Labour party conference after a successful first meeting with Donald Trump, and with his party faithful excited by their uplift in the polls. He plans to bring a message of hope and optimism to the autumn gathering in Liverpool, and will benefit from goodwill among members as he makes his first speech as leader on Tuesday. However, the real tests will start to land from October onwards, with a difficult economic landscape, the ongoing impact of the war in Iran and domestic challenges to navigate. Here is what Burnham has to look forward to after the conference is over. The budget This is the most difficult event on the horizon for Burnham, set for 28 October, as the global economic picture continues to look bad in the face of the Iran war pushing up energy prices and wider inflation. Burnham’s chancellor, John Healey, has little room for manoeuvre, with government debt interest payments rising and his headroom shrinking. Big decisions on spending are likely to be put off until a bigger fiscal event in the spring, in the hope that the economic picture improves before then.

Angela Rayner stands by attack on care worker visa reforms ahead of Labour conference

Angela Rayner has stood by her criticism of Home Office reforms that would make it harder for foreign care workers to claim permanent residence in the UK, describing them as “disruptive”. Last year, Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, announced that low paid migrants on jobs below graduate level would have to be in the country for 15 years before applying for settlement. Rayner previously attacked the plans as being “un-British”. The policy was devised under the previous prime minister, Keir Starmer, to ease voter concerns about net migration numbers. Andy Burnham, who succeeded Starmer in July, is understood to be uneasy about aspects of the proposals and is considering exempting workers who have already moved to the UK. More than 100 Labour MPs are opposed to the reforms, as are many trade unions. Hinting at a potential schism in the cabinet in the run-up to Burnham’s first Labour conference as leader, Rayner said the changes would unfairly penalise staff who had “moved their lives here to look after our loved ones”.

Loyalist parade in Northern Ireland given go-ahead as almost 30-year ban overturned

A controversial loyalist parade along a nationalist street in the Northern Ireland town of Portadown is set to go ahead for the first time in nearly 30 years, after an overnight court ruling cleared it to proceed. The Orange Order parade down the Garvaghy Roadis scheduled for 8am on Sunday morning, and follows a last-minute legal back-and-forth. Northern Ireland was blighted for three decades by conflict between largely Catholic, pro-Irish republicans and Protestant, pro-UK unionists, and the Garvaghy Road became a major flashpoint during the late 1990s. After a five-hour hearing at a special sitting of the high court on Saturday, Justice Patricia Smyth issued an order temporarily suspending the parade. Smyth had urged all sides to “step back from the abyss” and take responsible decisions for “the sake of everyone in Northern Ireland”. But at 11.30pm on Saturday, at a sitting of the court of appeals, Lady Chief Justice Siobhan Keegan said the high court judge who granted the injunction against the march had “unfortunately erred in law”.

A new application at the high court to stop the Protestant parade from passing through the Catholic area was also dismissed in the early hours of Sunday morning. The time-limited sitting beginning at 12.20am on Sunday was heard before Justice Michael Humphreys who acknowledged the “unusual if not unprecedented circumstances of the last-minute proceedings. Outlining his decision, Humphreys cited case law that as a public body the courts must respect its judgment and “their decisions will not be lightly interfered with”. “The picture painted here is of a public body which took evidence from the relevant sources, weighed up the key issues which were in play and arrived at a reasoned decision,” he said. “The jurisdiction to impugn (a) public body’s decision on that basis is necessarily limited to cases where no reasonable decision could arrive at that outcome and in my view in this case that threshold has not been met.” Interactive The march down Garvaghy Road had been banned for 28 years due to widespread sectarian violence in 1998 outside Drumcree church.

Andy Burnham has said he can deliver on his promise of radical change for the country despite severe economic headwinds, telling the Guardian: “There’s always things you can do; it’s just whether you’re prepared to do them.” The prime minister acknowledged public finances were “challenging” ahead of next month’s budget but said delivering fiscal stability would be “crucial”, because only then would the government be able to focus on fixing bigger problems. A series of global economic shocks, including the Iran conflict, has put the UK economy under intense inflationary pressure and pushed up borrowing costs, leaving the government limited room for manoeuvre. Burnham refreshes the parts others can’t reach on the Andy and Laura show

In recent weeks there has been much speculation in some parts of the media that Andy Burnham would call an early general election. Speculation that existed largely in the heads of those writing the stories, as even the most favourable polls suggest Labour would lose its huge majority and become the largest party in a coalition government. But to stop the chatter dominating his party conference, Burnham made it clear there would be no early election. His reward? Headlines in the rightwing press that he had bottled it. By not calling an election he had never planned to call. Sometimes you just can’t win. There again, you might call this a first-world problem for the prime minister. This time last year, Burnham had been hanging around the fringes of the conference as he and his allies attempted one of the most half-arsed coups in living memory. One that fizzled out almost before it had started and became the butt of many jokes among Keir Starmer’s inner circle. Andy looked to have blown himself up on the runway, leaving Keir safe for the duration of the parliament.

Fast forward a year and Burnham is in No 10, Reform UK’s lead in the polls has disappeared, and Labour is looking a lot more competitive than even the most rose-tinted party members could have reasonably expected in such a short period of time. Andy must be pinching himself. Unable to believe his luck. All that’s changed has been him. Energy prices are still sky high as a result of the war in Iran. The cost of living is still way too high. Nigel Farage and Kemi Badenoch might have been a problem for Keir but they aren’t for Andy. You might even call them assets. No wonder then that Burnham was looking relatively chipper as he kicked off conference with the traditional lengthy interview with the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg. Only relatively chipper, because you’d need to be a halfwit not to be a little wary. These interviews can go hideously wrong – Liz Truss’s at the Tory conference in 2022 is a collector’s item – and prime ministers generally regard them as exercises in damage limitation. To survive without generating the wrong kind of headlines is the dream. “You look like you’re loving the job,” observed Laura.

To end the drift and division of the decade since Brexit – he could have gone back another five years and included austerity. To do politics differently. To bring back hope. Only, where he speaks to people’s fears and grievance, Andy has a way of making you feel better about yourself. You may still struggle to pay your bills, you may still fight to get a hospital appointment, but somehow you can believe in better days ahead. The triumph of hope over experience.

‘Rip the plaster off’: Andy Burnham sets out vision for universal free social care

Andy Burnham has said that he is going to “rip the plaster off” to fix the broken social care system, as he set out a vision for a universal service that would be free at the point of use for everybody in England. The prime minister said the new NHS-style social care service would be funded by “everybody” but did not give further details of how his radical long-term plan would be paid for. Speaking to Laura Kuenssberg on the BBC as the Labour party conference began in Liverpool, Burnham ruled out implementing reforms before the next general election – currently due in 2029. He said Labour would put the proposals into its next general election manifesto so that voters could give their endorsement, in the hope of reducing the risk that political attacks would sink the policy. The prime minister acknowledged that there were risks in a nationwide reform, likely to be costly and complicated to implement. “Somebody needs to grasp the nettle. I will be the one to do that,” he said.

He told Kuenssberg: “I’m going to rip the plaster off, if I can put it that way, because someone has to do it.” Burnham declined to give details about how a new system would be funded, saying a review was continuing and promising more details in his conference speech on Tuesday. text:
‘Don’t squander it’: Can Labour hang on to the Burnham bounce?

Even Andy Burnham’s closest allies accept that deposing Keir Starmer to install their man as leader was a huge political gamble. But if the mood at the Labour party conference in Liverpool is anything to go by, it is one that – so far – has paid off. The contrast with last year, when Starmer retained his grip on the party and Burnham slunk away from Liverpool early, could not be more stark. Their relief at their turn of fortune is tempered only by the fiscal headwinds ahead. Cabinet ministers recount how at their political meeting two weeks ago, they were shown a series of charts showing the metrics behind the Burnham bounce. One in particular stood out to those in the room. Related: ‘Rip the plaster off’: Andy Burnham sets out vision for universal free social care It was a graph showing whether the public felt the government was heading in the right direction. Until the end of June, it had been on a downward trajectory as public frustration mounted over Starmer’s leadership.

citation.title: ‘Don’t squander it’: Can Labour hang on to the Burnham bounce?

text:
‘Don’t squander it’: Can Labour hang on to the Burnham bounce?

But once Starmer announced his intention to step down and Burnham took over in July, the line suddenly rebounded and, while still in negative territory, has been moving definitively upwards since. “We’ve got a second hearing with the public,” one cabinet minister said. “We can’t squander it.” This time last year, just 14 months after coming to power, several were privately despairing about Labour’s electoral prospects. But with an energetic new prime minister and after a difficult summer for Nigel Farage, they now believe that a second term is winnable. It is perhaps unsurprising, then, that speculation about a snap election escalated in the run-up to the conference, to the extent that Burnham felt compelled to “knock that dead” and confirm a 2029 date instead. Some of the prime minister’s closest advisers wanted him to rule out an early election from the off, pressing him to be explicit. “The polling isn’t good enough. We could end up being the biggest party but we could lose our majority,” one said.

Another said: “Elections have to be about a choice, not a referendum on an alternative plan.” But others inside No 10 felt he should go to the country while the polling was good, Farage was on the back foot, and before Burnham’s big plans for change ran headfirst into fiscal reality. “Right now the public is willing to give us the benefit of the doubt – that won’t last for ever,” one said. Related: Andy Burnham shows his emotional side – podcast For his part, Burnham claims he can deliver on his promise of radical change for the country despite the severe economic headwinds, by delivering tangible – albeit smaller – improvements in the short term while setting out a longer-term vision to transform things such as social care and youth unemployment at the same time. “There’s always things you can do, it’s just whether you’re prepared to do them,” he told the Guardian at the weekend. “I do think it is crucial to have stability and to show that there’s a willingness to face up to the reality of some of these difficult things.

But actually from that stability, the permission can come to make bigger change.” The slogan of his first conference as leader has been “hope again” – but with the bleak global economic landscape there is less hope around than there was when he walked into Downing Street two months ago. The first crucial test for Burnham will be next month’s budget, at which he said the government would be “highly prudent” with the public finances, amid concerns that Labour needs to reassure the markets. But if the budget is about intent, next summer’s spending review is about proof, and as such, that could prove to be a make-or-break moment for this prime minister. ‘We’ve done everything by the book’: EU citizens left in limbo after UK government strips post-Brexit residency status

The Home Office faces legal action over a policy to strip residency rights from EU citizens who were in the UK before Brexit on the grounds that it gave them the status “in error”. It comes as a Home Office minister revealed that the government has contacted 1,473 citizens with post-Brexit residency rights to tell them the original decision to grant them residency was made in error. The campaign group the3million, which is aware of at least 50 cases, has put the Home Office on notice that it is seeking a judicial review of the policy, which it enacted in late 2025 but has only recently come to light. “In many cases, the Home Office is actually wrong to say there was a mistake. So people whose status was properly granted are now fighting not to lose it – this is a clear breach of the withdrawal agreement,” it said in an appeal to supporters to fund their case. Some of those who received notice were told they were not entitled to pre-settled or settled status because they did not submit passports with their original application.

text:
Facing up to the threat that Reform poses to our democracy

John Harris writes: “Reform is apparently in deep trouble, yet also still in with a serious chance. How come?” (Don’t discount Reform because it’s had a bad year. In our angry, fragile democracy, anything can happen, 20 September). Because it is a cult, just as Maga is a cult. It is sustained by faith, not fact. It offers simple solutions to problems of such complexity that most of us are incapable of understanding them. Reform UK would not exist without Nigel Farage. All his other “parties” only existed because of him. Its self-designation as outside “the establishment” is one of the few truths to be relied on – in the sense that it’s beyond the pale. It is an ethics-free zone. Farage is the tool of the US hard right in the UK. All that’s missing is the Christian end-times nihilism, and not many would be surprised if that clawed its way to the surface soon. Harris maintains that the next general election will be driven by emotion – all choices are. Our biochemistry sees to that before our prefrontal cortex even engages. And the choice will be stark. It will be about “me” or “we”.

Facing up to the threat that Reform poses to our democracy

Do we each retreat to our own little “green zone” or do we hang on to that glimmer of hope and work together? I believe Andy Burnham is sincere in his desire to do politics differently, but I am disturbed that he has said nothing yet about the systemic change necessary for a new, people-focused politics. The founding of a commission to inform a citizens’ assembly on voting reform would be a clear indication that he means what he says. I live in hope. Lyn Dade Twickenham, London • The threat that a Reform-led government poses to the UK is summed up in John Harris’s use of the phrase “munificently funded barbarism”. The rise of Reform and its ruthless rhetoric has helped generate the growth of violent racist militia-styled groups on our streets, whose increasing presence not only intimidates whole communities but creates an atmosphere of lawlessness and insecurity. Simultaneously, billionaires suddenly see an opportunity to buy influence in the UK’s democracy – loudly denied – and elsewhere tax exiles such as Jim Ratcliffe seem empowered to rant about Britain’s decline from when it was the greatest empire in the world.

Barbarism, it seems, can attract both interest and vast sums of money from some of the wealthiest people in the world.
