Houses can be built on floodplains despite failing safety test, says high court

Houses can be built on floodplains even if they fail a crucial safety test, according to a high court judgment that will be of “immense interest” to developers across England and Wales. The ruling clears the way for a highly controversial development of 190 new homes on north Somerset’s floodplains, despite the site being in “flood zone 3a”, the highest level of flood risk before land is considered a functional floodplain. Ministers and experts are so disturbed by the decision that it was agreed at a flood resilience conference on Wednesday to campaign for a change in the law that would stop the ruling setting a national precedent. As a result, Tessa Munt, the chair of the flooding and flooded communities all-party parliamentary group (APPG), will now meet Matthew Pennycook, the housing and planning minister, to ask him to change the national planning policy framework (NPPF). “This is a dangerous and nationally significant exploitation of planning loopholes,” Munt said.

Changing UK benefits for young people a ‘moral crusade’, says minister

Labour MPs have a moral responsibility to accept significant changes to the welfare system to help get more young people into work, the work and pensions secretary has said. In a sign he is looking to overhaul the welfare state, Pat McFadden said it was time for Labour to “renew” the system first created by the Clement Attlee government and given a new deal by New Labour. The cabinet minister said there would be “decisions to make and responsibilities to take” after two reviews of the system are published this autumn – on young people by Alan Milburn, and on a key disability benefit by the Timms panel.

He said Labour must decide “how we have a new system focused on opportunity, how we move from asking what are you entitled to, to asking how do we change your life … It falls to us, the party which did so much to create it, the party that holds it dear, to embrace the change needed.” His speech is a sign that the government is preparing the ground again for changes to the welfare system after Keir Starmer’s government was forced to U-turn last year on a £5bn-a-year programme of disability benefit cuts in the face of a Labour backbench rebellion. The revolt was fuelled by outrage that the plans would push hundreds of thousands of disabled people into poverty. Andy Burnham, Starmer’s replacement as prime minister, has said he will not shy away from changing the system in a “Labour way” that helps people back into work, rather than putting a figure on trying to save money on the overall bill. However, many charities supporting disabled people are nervous about the prospect of an overhauled system, after so many cuts in the past.

After the Timms and Milburn reviews conclude, the government is expected to design a new system and assessment process for disability benefits that is likely to require new legislation. It will also focus particularly on how to support younger people into jobs and training, building on the current “jobs guarantee” that funds employment placements for under-25s for six months, with disabled young people given fast-track access. Officials have been looking to see whether elements of other countries’ benefit systems can be borrowed, such as the Netherlands, where youth hubs tackle unemployment, and Denmark, which restricts access to the country’s “disability pension” for the under-40s, who instead are given help with flexible jobs and training unless they permanently have no ability to work. A million young people are now out of work, employment and training in the UK, and there has been a sharp rise in numbers of young people claiming disability benefits, particularly since the pandemic.

Billions of pounds worth of green levies could be taken off bills, the energy secretary has said, as the government investigates funding green infrastructure through taxes instead. Miatta Fahnbulleh is looking at how green projects are funded, including varying levies between customers and funding them all through general taxation. Paying for schemes such as windfarms, solar panels and home insulation through taxation however would either mean cuts elsewhere or raising taxes. Israel does not have a legal right to act on its plan to close the British consulate in East Jerusalem, the former attorney general Dominic Grieve has advised the UK Foreign Office. text:
Jean Clark obituary

My friend and former colleague Jean Clark, who has died aged 92, was a successful teacher, lecturer and a key figure in Labour politics in Harlow, Essex. After moving to the town as a newly qualified English teacher in the 1950s, Jean became a great community activist, as a Labour party member, and as a member of Victory for Socialism, a leftwing pressure group within the party, which helped to get Stan Newens elected as Harlow’s Labour MP in 1964. Joining the International Socialists, she played a leading role in the Harlow Tenants’ Action group, which staged a rent strike in 1968 against Harlow Development Corporation’s rent rises and succeeded in getting them reduced. The following decade she returned to the Labour cause, and became secretary of the constituency party. In that role, she helped lead my campaign for election as Harlow’s MEP in 1994. She then became a longstanding Labour councillor in Harlow, serving until her retirement in 2023. Jean, as she was known all her life, was born Valerie Jean, in Exeter, to Ernest and Daisy Tucker, who owned a hardware shop.

citation.title: Jean Clark obituary

text:
Jean Clark obituary

She was brought up in the West Country, where she was a county-level tennis player in her youth. After qualifying as a teacher in Lyme Regis, Jean moved to the rapidly growing new town of Harlow, where she taught English at Brays Grove school. Jean married a fellow teacher, Brian Clark, in 1957. They divorced while still relatively young and he later became known as the writer of the play Whose Life Is It Anyway? In the 1960s Jean gained a degree in sociology at London School of Economics, then became a lecturer at Balls Park teacher training college in Hertford, which later became part of Hertfordshire University, from where Jean retired as a senior tutor. Jean was warmly regarded by her colleagues and had many friends. A lifelong Guardian reader, she would walk every morning to Harlow Town station to buy her copy of the paper. A special tribute to her was held by Harlow council.

John Healey cheered the Labour faithful with his first conference speech as chancellor, offering an upbeat vision of a reindustrialised Britain with fresh opportunities for young people, but he gave little sense of how he intends to pay for Andy Burnham’s radical plans. Healey’s budget next month is widely seen both inside and outside Labour as the moment when the prime minister’s radical rhetoric about ditching 40 years of neoliberal orthodoxy risks crashing into fiscal reality. With the global bond sell-off driving up government borrowing costs, and eye-watering energy prices likely to push up household bills in the new year, he did deliver some home truths to Labour members and cabinet colleagues. He deliberately and repeatedly highlighted his role in the last Labour government, as an aide to Gordon Brown, at one point recalling lending Brown a tie to deliver his conference speech, which Healey wore as he spoke in a neat nod to that era.

However, the chancellor cautioned: “The money New Labour had in the 90s is simply not there now.” “The worldwide economic shocks – conflicts, trade tensions – are felt hard at home,” he added. “Britain has it harder now.” Like Rachel Reeves before him, Healey sought to argue that fixing the public finances was a precondition for rebuilding the economy. “The rock of fiscal discipline. It underwrites every promise this government makes … we can’t succeed without it.” Attacking the Conservatives for driving the UK further into the red during their 14 years in power, he claimed that current levels of UK debt were “an assault on our common sense; they’re an affront to our values” – although Reeves deliberately redefined the government’s fiscal rules to allow more borrowing to fund long-term investment, which Healey presumably doesn’t resile from. Labour’s modest reheat of help to buy is worth a try

There may be three reasons why the Labour government has hesitated until now to reheat the Tories’ decade-long help-to-buy scheme. First, the inflationary risks of throwing subsidies at the housing market at a moment when wider inflation, driven by energy prices and the Iran war, is on the march. Second, the political awkwardness of turning to George Osborne’s playbook. Third, the spectre of Jeff Fairburn, the shameless former boss of Persimmon who bagged a £75m bonus in 2018 as help to buy turbo-charged the value of his share-based incentives. The government would look foolish if, in its desperation to meet its housebuilding targets (or just miss them by a smaller margin), it created more Fairburns. So is Your First Home – Labour’s incarnation – justified? On balance, it’s probably worth a punt. Something has to happen to try to shift the housebuilding sector out of its current funk. The way things are going, and the way mortgage rates are heading, Labour won’t merely miss its target of 1.5m new homes in England in this parliament, it will be short by a few hundreds of thousands.

Like it or not, the government needs the private firms to boost construction. At the moment, the prevailing narrative is grumbles over labour costs, raw material costs, tax, regulation and more. Share buy-backs are being preferred over new projects. A tweak on the “affordability” dial at least has the virtue of getting results. Or, at least, that was a top-line conclusion in the official independent report published by the housing department earlier this month on help to buy. The scheme represented “very high value for money”, it said, with a net present social value of £25.1bn, in 2025 money, over its 2013-2023 lifetime thanks to the increase in housing supply. As for the inflationary impact, the report put it at two percentage points – far lower than popularly believed. From the government’s point of view, those trade-offs will look attractive when there is little else to excite in the economic outlook for 2027. Being seen to do something for aspiring first-time buyers unable to get on to the housing ladder is rarely a bad political look. Just don’t expect miracles.

text:
Reality pays a visit to the Labour party conference, but it’s the ‘Hope Again’ that kills you

It could be just me, but I’m beginning to find that all this “hope” stuff is getting me down. Everywhere you go at the Labour party conference, you are being urged to “Hope Again”. It’s on the screens in the main hall and on banners in the exhibition area. It’s on T-shirts, balloons and coffee mugs. It’s all just a bit much. Overkill. You now bump into Labour MPs who are visibly collapsing under the strain of having to walk around with an optimistic perma-grin. And the conference is only into its second day. Come Wednesday they will all be on intravenous Valium. What does “Hope Again” even mean? Is it an instruction? Have we all been hoping in a highly unsatisfactory way so far? Are we being sent back to hope school to learn how to be more upbeat? In which case, I rather think these remedial classes in hoping will be wasted on me. I’ve always been a bit miserable. It feels a bit like someone going round and telling you “Smile. It may never happen.” Or to “Keep calm and carry on.” There are also distinct echoes of Samuel Beckett: Fail again. Fail better. Only in Liverpool it’s: Hope again.

text:

Hope better. You also can’t help feeling that all this talk of hope is wasted on John Healey. He is a man with a naturally low-energy vibe. Someone in touch with the darker, more depressing side of his own personality. A man after my own heart. As someone with the touch of Harry Potter’s Dementors, ready to suck the joy out of any occasion, he knows that anything that can go wrong almost certainly will go wrong. Anything good is merely a transitory, illusory state. Take Healey to the football and he will show you a bad time. His home team of Rotherham might go 2-0 up in the 88th minute and John will assure you they’ve peaked too soon – they are nailed on to lose 3-2. I speak from experience. I’ve done it myself. John, meet John. Luckily for me, no one is expecting me to be a ray of sunshine. That’s way above my pay grade. Unfortunately for Healey, optimism was precisely what he was required to deliver in his first speech as chancellor to a nearly full Labour conference hall. To be the fiscal embodiment of “Hope Again”. To give us all a reason to live just a little longer.

Only he just couldn’t do it. He was never going to be able to do it. When John sees a “Hope Again” banner, what he reads is “Despair Again”. Come the end of his half hour on stage, he had managed to convert most of the audience to his way of thinking. At lunchtime, the queues for the assisted dying helpline tailed back into the city centre. Not that Healey didn’t give it his best shot. He dropped the word hope into almost every sentence – or his minders had dropped it in for him – and every time, the lights seemed to get a bit dimmer. It was a battle of hope against hope. People had come willing him to succeed. To pull off one of the most astonishing personality transplants of the year. Within minutes, though, a pall of depression hung over the hall. We were all just waiting for it to end. Hardly anyone could be bothered to even clap. The only standing ovation came for the reintroduction of the £15m Union Learning Fund. To give this some perspective, £15m is just a bit more than what the London townhouse of the Tory shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, is worth. Not that it’s a bad idea.

It’s just not going to reboot the economy. And it’s hard to blame Healey. Maybe another more dynamic and charismatic chancellor could have shifted the mood in the hall with feelgood vibes. But as well as being a bit miserable, Healey is also a realist. He knows things are tough and likely to get tougher. No amount of energy price caps and £2 bus fares are going to make a major dent in a cost of living which is only heading in one direction. Nor is it his fault. He is not responsible for austerity, Brexit, the war in Iran and the cost of borrowing. But he is the current fall guy. The chancellor tasked with fixing the unfixable. Nandy labels Farage ‘master of conspiracy theory’ over Fairford claims

Nigel Farage has been described as a “master of the conspiracy theory” by the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, after he tried to link events at RAF Fairford to small boat crossings. The Reform UK leader was criticised over his reaction to the arrests of the men on Sunday, when he said he had been warning for months about “Iranian agents” coming into the UK across the Channel in small boats. “We deserve to be told the truth about the Fairford bomb plotters’ identities,” he added in his post on X on Sunday. On Monday he posted a video in which he claimed to have received intelligence that the Iranian regime was using the small boats “to get their operatives into Britain”. Less than an hour later, Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) said that the five suspects were all British nationals. The men – three residents of Westminster and two others from Camden and Willesden, all London boroughs – have since been released on bail while the police investigate “multiple lines of inquiry”.

Palestine has become electoral issue in UK for first time, says solidarity campaign chief

Palestine has become a domestic electoral issue in Britain for the first time, according to the incoming head of the country’s largest Palestinian solidarity organisation. Aimee Shalan, who will take over as director of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign (PSC) in November, joins the organisation as demonstrations against Israel’s war in Gaza have snowballed into what organisers describe as one of the most sustained protest movements in modern British history. She said public anger over Israel’s treatment of Palestinians and Britain’s response was increasingly being expressed not just through demonstrations but at elections, in workplaces and trade unions and through consumer campaigns. Speaking before a PSC protest at the Labour party conference, Shalan said: “We’re seeing for the first time in British history Palestine become a domestic issue, electorally, at the national level and at the local level.” The shift was visible at the 2024 general election and 2026 local elections, where pro-Palestinian candidates made major breakthroughs.

She pointed to the 70,000 Palestinians killed in Israel’s war in Gaza and the more than 1,300, including at least 300 children, killed since a ceasefire was signed last year. Andy Burnham expected to say he will push ahead with electoral reform plans

Andy Burnham is expected to announce that he will push ahead with plans for electoral reform in his first conference speech as Labour leader, in the latest sign that he intends to radically transform the UK’s political system. The prime minister, a longtime advocate of reform, will kick off a process that could eventually lead to ditching the first-past-the-post system in favour of proportional representation. Government sources told the Guardian that Burnham would set out his plans in “broad strokes” in the speech, underlining his commitment to drawing up proposals before the next general election. Along with social care changes and closer ties with the EU, the plans – which would represent the most significant shake-up of the electoral system since 1918 – would then be put in Labour’s manifesto to get public backing. text:
Conference laps up Andy unplugged as he offers chance to take road less travelled

You’ve got to hand it to Andy Burnham. He left nothing out on the pitch. It would have been so easy to play it safe. To deliver a traditional leader’s speech to a home crowd. One we’ve been seeing from leaders of all parties for more than 15 years. Something warm, a feelgood vibes word salad with the odd minor spending announcement thrown in. Hell, the Labour conference would have probably settled for it. They already had all the hope that they had come for. The hope that they were back in with a fighting chance of winning the next election. They wouldn’t have even dared think that three months ago. But Andy did it differently. Just as he had promised. He had said he was a different kind of politician and he duly made good on that. Hope came with honesty, he said. And honesty was what we got. Nothing was redacted. No coded hints. Come the end of his hour-long speech, no one could be in any doubt about what he thought. More than that, what he believed. Not so much a speech, more an article of faith. This was Andy unplugged. Unmediated. That most elusive of hybrids.

Conference laps up Andy unplugged as he offers chance to take road less travelled

The career politician who can still make the political personal and deliver it fearlessly. Keir Starmer could never have done this, even if he had wanted to. He was just too naturally cautious. A man one step removed from himself. Andy was running on pure emotion. Some things you can’t fake. At one point, just as he was about to talk about his dad, he choked up. Unable to speak. It became a moment of communion. Burnham was not going to die wondering. He knew he might be delivering one of the longest suicide notes in history, but he did it anyway. Because he couldn’t not do it. Better to go down remaining true to his principles than being slowly airbrushed out of history like the previous six prime ministers. Failures all. Andy was prepared to burn through all his political capital right there in Liverpool, right then. Not just for his own legacy but for a country he wanted to rebuild. It was the only way he could look himself in the mirror. Honour his parents. It goes without saying that Andy was received with a long series of near rapturous standing ovations throughout the speech.

Not that this was a speech where anything so grubby as actual numbers were spelled out. This was all big-picture stuff. A reimagined vision of the future. Where the country didn’t feel permanently broke and broken. “All together now,” Burnham began. That would be his rallying cry. And he put his money where his mouth was. So many politicians use their conference speeches to trash the other parties. Many of the cabinet have done just that this week. But Andy didn’t once namecheck his rivals or use them to score points. The closest he got was to say we would all have failed if we voted in a divisive party on a vote of less than 30%. He would rather work with opposition parties for the common good. Fat chance. text:
From Brexit to electoral reform: key takeaways from Andy Burnham’s conference speech

Andy Burnham’s first speech to a Labour conference as prime minister was not only quite long, at over an hour, but unusually dense with policy. Here are some of the things he set out: Ending the pensions triple lock One of Burnham’s most concrete promises was to end the triple lock as we know it. For the last 15 years, the state pension has increased by whichever is the highest out of earnings, inflation or 2.5%. From 2030, if Burnham is still prime minister, it will instead rise by the highest out of inflation or 2.5%, meaning that for the first time since 2011, pensions will be allowed to increase by less than earnings. There is a backstop however – in years where earnings are higher than inflation or 2.5%, the government will guarantee that the state pension will be at least 30% of average earnings. This change to the earnings element of the policy sounds technical, but officials say it could save about £15bn a year by 2040.

National care service Burnham repeated his promise to create a national care service, saying it would be a system to which everyone contributes and from which everyone can benefit, free at the point of use. Hope Again is the conference slogan. But what felt even more apt was Try Again. But the “people pleaser” prime minister said he was prepared to weather the worst political pain to change the country. text:
A proportional representation voting system could spell disaster for Labour

Reading that Andy Burnham wants to push electoral reform forward and move the UK towards proportional representation (Report, 29 September), I found myself shouting at the screen. I come from Italy, where I have seen proportional systems at work. They drive a wedge between MPs and their constituents. They reward tribalism (yes, even more than here). They leave large parts of the electorate hostage to the whims of tiny parties, and force parties into ragtag coalitions that produce unstable, ineffective governments. And for all that, people do not seem to feel any better represented. Related: Why a PR voting system is the best bet for Britain Having lived in the UK since 2014 and watched its parties with an outsider’s eyes, I still see first past the post as the lesser of two evils. Brexit exposed a complete lack of leadership in David Cameron’s Conservative party, and it was an act of unprecedented self-harm that we are all still paying for, quite literally. But it also showed that parties outside the big two can exert enough pressure to force the party in power to adapt and, alas, to listen to voters.

Andy Burnham’s social care plans could be much more radical

In the aftermath of Andy Burnham’s speech to the Labour conference, media discussions are focusing on how to define social care and estimate its cost (How will Burnham’s national care service work – and how will it be funded?, 29 September). Most arguments assume that any new system will look like the existing one, with services outsourced to large companies, using contracts without scope for innovation, with rigidly defined targets, often delivered using poorly rewarded, precariously employed migrant workers. The reality is that many of the services needed by elderly and incapacitated people – such as cleaning, meal preparation, transport to medical appointments, household repairs and personal services such as podiatry, hair care, physiotherapy, counselling or therapeutic massage – are also required by others and are already freely available in local markets. The trouble is that they are most often supplied by online platforms such as Uber, Deliveroo or Housekeep with no commercial incentive to address social need.

text:
Andy Burnham’s social care plans could be much more radical

One solution would be to set up local platforms that supply these services to anyone, regardless of age or disability. Children using social media at younger age appear to do worse in school tests

Children who open social media accounts at the start of secondary school appear to perform worse in tests than those who delay, with researchers suspecting that the constant checking for updates is a major distraction for many students. Pupils who opened their first social media account aged 11 to 12 scored lower in mathematics and reading tests than those who waited a few years, with scores at age 16 differing between the groups by the equivalent of about six months of learning, the study found. The work does not prove social media is to blame, but the researchers took account of many other factors that could skew the results, such as the students’ academic performance before they had social media, their family structure and parents’ education. “I think we now know there is a problem and that it’s a complex problem, to do with how these platforms are built,” said Dr Marco Gui, the first author on the study at the University of Milano-Bicocca in Italy.

citation.title: Children using social media at younger age appear to do worse in school tests

text:
Children using social media at younger age appear to do worse in school tests

“Our research shows that at least during pre-adolescence, these social media are problematic.” Gui and his colleagues analysed surveys on the social media habits of more than 5,000 Italian schoolchildren and their results in standardised maths, Italian and English exams. When tested at age 13 to 14, those who had opened their first social media account at 11 or 12 scored worse than those who waited until at least 14 years old. The score gap at age 15 to 16 remained the same for Italian and widened for maths. Writing in Nature Human Behaviour, the researchers say the difference in scores is roughly equivalent to the early adopters falling behind by six months of schooling. Put another way, the benefit to those who delayed social media was about half that achieved with intensive and costly tutoring. While a performance gap was evident for maths and Italian, there was no impact on English, which the students were learning as a foreign language, possibly because so much social media is in English, providing “incidental exposure and practice”, the researchers said.

The continuous need to check messages, to see if something is happening in the online world, why you are engaged in something in the physical world you have around you,” Gui said. “This means being less present in the physical space of the family or the house. Starwatch: Mercury to reach farthest point from the sun

This week offers one of the better opportunities of the year to catch a glimpse of the solar system’s innermost world. Trapped in its small orbit, Mercury never strays far from the sun, meaning it is usually lost to the light of dawn or dusk. On Sunday, however, the planet reached its greatest western elongation, meaning it appeared at its greatest apparent distance from the sun in the morning sky. The next few mornings offer one of the best opportunities this year for catching a glimpse of the planet as it steadily brightens, improving the contrast with the gathering dawn. An early start and an unobstructed view towards the east-north-east will be essential to making the sighting. The chart shows the view looking in this direction from London at 04.30 BST on Tuesday. If your line of sight is free from obstructions, the planet will become visible about a handspan above the horizon some time between 04.30 and 05.00. Binoculars can help, but exercise caution: sunrise on Tuesday from London occurs at 05.28, so stop using binoculars well before this time to protect your eyesight.

The unprecedented pictures show processes on the surface that are likely to explain the decades-long mystery of why the corona, the sun’s outer atmosphere, is millions of degrees hotter than its surface. “These are the highest spatial resolution images of the solar surface ever acquired,” said Dr Friedrich Wöger, a senior scientist at the US National Solar Observatory, which operates the telescope near the summit of the Haleakalā volcano, on the island of Maui. Previous observations with the telescope found the sun’s surface to be a patchwork of granular structures each about the size of France. Those images picked out details as small as 30km across, but the latest are right at the limit of the telescope’s capability.

text:
Unprecedented images may explain one of greatest mysteries of the sun

“My first reaction was: ‘Wow, how can we see such tiny, fine-scale structures on the sun?” said Dr David Kuridze, an astronomer on the team. “This is something we have never seen before in any solar observations.” In the latest images, the small whirlpool-like structures on the sun’s surface were identified as signatures of what scientists call Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities (KHIs). These form when fast-moving plasma slides past slower moving fluid, creating shear at the interface. This sets up small disturbances in the sun’s plasma that grow into spiralling vortices that look like breaking waves. Scientists have seen KHIs in lakes and oceans, and in cloud formations on Earth, and even in the atmospheres of Jupiter and Saturn, but have never confirmed their existence on the sun. The details of the findings are published in Nature. Explosive events on the sun, from solar flares and jets to coronal mass ejections, are powered by extreme, fluctuating magnetic fields in the star. The explosions can cause widespread disruption on Earth, taking out power grids, satellites, GPS positioning and global communications.

The magnetic fields are generated by the movement of hot, charged plasma in the sun, but the physics isn’t fully understood. Astronomers know that magnetic field lines can twist around each other like braided hair, creating tension that is suddenly released when the tangled lines break. What is less clear is what starts the process. The swirling vortices are now a key culprit, explaining why the field lines become braided in the first place, and perhaps why the sun’s corona is heated to a few million degrees while the surface is a mere 6,000C. “This could solve this biggest mystery of the last half a century for solar physics and astrophysics,” said Kuridze. “When you have this instability in the system, it is very easy to cascade the energy into smaller scales. E-scooters far more dangerous than motorbikes or cycles, analysis suggests

Electric scooter riders are three times more likely to suffer traumatic brain injuries than motorcyclists, according to an analysis of accidents in England and Wales – which found women were particularly at risk of serious harm. Brain injuries accounted for more than a third of adult injuries on e-scooters, but riders also sustained more internal organ and blood vessel damage than did motorcyclists or pedal cyclists, the study found. The government has backed trials of rental e-scooters in England since 2020, but an additional 1m or so e-scooters are privately owned in the UK. These cannot legally be used on public roads, paths or cycle lanes, but police forces across the country have confiscated thousands because their owners were breaking the law. The accident analysis reveals that women were involved in about a third more collisions than men – and were more than twice as likely to report severe injuries. Children were also at risk with, 16% of e-scooter injuries in under 18s.

Safety fears as scientists make first viruses designed by AI

Scientists have made the first viruses designed by artificial intelligence in a milestone that raises hopes for new medicines but also concerns over how to ensure the technology remains safe. The viruses are specific kinds known as bacteriophages, which only infect bacteria and are used around the world to treat patients with persistent infections. In lab tests, a cocktail of the AI-designed viruses killed E coli bugs that were resistant to natural bacteriophages. Dr Brian Hie, a chemical engineer at Stanford University in California, used genome language models, the genetic equivalent of the large language models behind AI chatbots, to design functioning genomes for bacteriophages. The viruses were then made in the laboratory and pitted against E coli in a dish. The ability to “rapidly design” genomes and tune them for specific bugs while overcoming resistance could “transform phage therapy” and “expand biotechnological toolkits”, the researchers wrote in the journal Science.

citation.title: Safety fears as scientists make first viruses designed by AI

text:
Safety fears as scientists make first viruses designed by AI

But beyond the potential benefits, the scientists said the work raised “important biosafety, biocontainment and biosecurity considerations” and urged others who were designing whole genomes to “consult both safety and security professionals throughout the project”. Related: Science funding and unnecessary fear In an accompanying article, Prof Tom Inglesby and Dr Mori Hanke at the Center for Health Security at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, reinforced the warning, writing: “Although this is promising for life sciences applications, it also raises urgent biosafety and biosecurity questions. The ability to compose viral genomes using generative AI now exists; the governance to safely steer it does not.” Hie and his colleagues used AI models called Evo1 and Evo2 to design the new viral genomes. The models were trained on genetic data from 2m bacteriophages. The genetic code for viruses that can infect plants, humans or other animals was intentionally excluded from the AI’s training to reduce the risk of it designing dangerous viruses.

text:
Safety fears as scientists make first viruses designed by AI

The AI generated thousands of potential genomes from which the researchers selected nearly 300 to make in the lab. These were dropped into bacteria, which read the genetic code and churned out the new bacteriophages. The process was not efficient: only 16 bacteriophages proved to be viable, but a cocktail of them swiftly overcame resistance in two different strains of E. coli. Bacteriophage genomes are tiny, but Inglesby and Hanke said the work nevertheless proved that generative AI could create functioning viral genomes. Whether the same approach could be applied to other viruses was unknown, but they said work on pathogens that could infect humans, animals or plants should not be pursued. “Such genomes might encode new pathogens that … cannot be contained by existing countermeasures,” they wrote. Tom Ellis, professor of synthetic genome engineering at Imperial College London, said the work was impressive, but revealed how hard it would be to make more complex genomes. “This is literally the smallest and easiest genome to make,” he said.

text:

An AI trained on the genetic code of dangerous bugs could be used to design more harmful viruses, Ellis said, but controlling access to genetic data and having restrictions on making genomes that look dangerous would help. “Governments are working hard to do this already,” he added. “But honestly,” he said, “the threat from full AI design and writing of a genome of a virus or bacteria is very overblown when we consider that just taking existing pathogens and making gain-of-function changes to their genomes is so much easier and much more likely to be a real pathogenic threat.” Dr Filippa Lentzos, a reader in science and international security at King’s College London, said the most important point to intervene at the moment was when DNA was being manufactured. “It’s important to see the bigger governance picture and not focus regulation solely on the AI model,” she said. “A layered approach makes more sense: safeguards around model development and access, responsible research review, synthesis screening, and established laboratory biosafety and biosecurity.”

‘Spectral lines’ and a giant plume: what science saw when the SpaceX rocket hit the moon

A telescope in Chile has captured evidence of the impact caused by part of a SpaceX rocket slamming into the moon while travelling at 8,690km/h (5,400mph). The European Southern Observatory’s (ESO) Very Large Telescope observed “spectral lines” – a colourful illustration of sodium and lithium gas – in the plume of lunar dust stirred up by the impact. The ESO telescope recorded these “chemical fingerprints” of the plume, which were visible for five to 10 minutes, the observatory said. The plume measured a few tens of kilometres in size, according to Carl Schmidt, an astronomer from Boston University’s Center for Space Physics. Benjamin Fernando of Los Alamos National Laboratory in New Mexico, said earlier the collision could provide valuable data for future seismic experiments, and assessing “hazards from artificial space debris impacts”. Nasa hopes to soon establish a sustained human presence on the Moon, making it critical to better understand space debris in lunar orbit.

Where in the UK will get the best view of the solar eclipse?

For the first time this century, people across the UK will be able to see an almost total solar eclipse in the evening sky on Wednesday. A solar eclipse occurs when the moon moves between the sun and the Earth, blocking the sun’s light either partly or fully. This year, people in the UK and Ireland will see 90-96% of the sun covered by the moon for the first time since 1999 – and it’s their last chance until 2081. Royal Museums Greenwich said: “This will be the most coverage seen from the UK and Ireland since the 1999 solar eclipse, which was total from most of Cornwall and Devon.” Across north-western Europe, people will see about 88-95% coverage, while spectators in parts of Greenland, Iceland and northern Spain will see a total eclipse for up to two minutes and 18 seconds in duration. In the UK, viewers in the west will see the most of the sun obscured: 95% in Plymouth, 93.2% in Cardiff and 93.1% in Belfast. Spectators in Manchester will see 91.9% and Londoners will catch 91.4%. Farther north and east people will see smaller proportions, with Edinburgh at 90.7%, Newcastle at 90.2%.

She recommended finding hills with clear views to the west, for example Parliament Hill, Alexandra Palace [see footnote] or Primrose Hill in London, or rooftop venues. Because the eclipse takes place in August, there’s a stronger chance of clear skies. Tom Morgan, a Met Office meteorologist, said it was too early to be confident, but “given the summer we’ve had a lot of the UK will have reasonable viewing conditions”. At present, there is a higher risk of thick cloud and rain in Scotland and Northern Ireland, while the clearest skies are likely to be towards the south and the east of the UK. “For many it’ll be quite a spectacular and rare event,” he said. I’m ready to hop on a train north, south, east or west to find some cloud-free skies,” she said. text:
Britain’s Jurassic gold rush: the fossil hunters chasing fortunes on Dorset’s beaches

Bent double at the waist, Martin Curtis combs a stretch of a Dorset beach with the concentration of a man searching for a lost cufflink or wedding ring. The search is meticulous – and with good reason. What he hopes to find could be far more valuable than an errant piece of jewellery. Curtis is searching instead for the telltale spiral of an ammonite, the star-shaped rod of a crinoid or rocks of a particular shape and colour that suggests there is something very special inside. He is hunting fossils. Along Charmouth beach and elsewhere on the Jurassic Coast, families with children, seasoned collectors and lone day-trippers peer intently at the ground in search of traces of creatures that lived 190m years ago. While some are here for fun, a growing number are here for business. That growing professional interest reflects the rising popularity and value of Jurassic fossils, creating a thriving marketplace that has made some collectors social media celebrities and others very wealthy.

text:
Britain’s Jurassic gold rush: the fossil hunters chasing fortunes on Dorset’s beaches

A Guardian investigation this week revealed that one of Britain’s most significant collections of Jurassic fossils was recently sold to a museum in Abu Dhabi for what is believed to be an eight-figure sum. Related: One of UK’s best fossil collections sold overseas in ‘loss to the nation’ The collection, amassed by the private fossil collector Chris Moore, included 318 specimens, some of which may represent species previously unknown to science. The sale was described by some experts as a loss for the nation. Yet while British museums lacked the funds to acquire Moore’s collection, wealthy institutions in the Gulf did not. For the fossil hunters combing Charmouth beach, it is another reason to scrutinise every promising item of unusual shape, colour and texture. Fossil hunting – and the industry that has grown around it – is not a modern pursuit.

Perhaps England’s best-known fossil hunter and dealer, Mary Anning, was born at nearby Lyme Regis in 1799 and made breathtaking discoveries along this coastline, including the first complete plesiosaur skeleton – a huge long-necked marine reptile that lived during the Jurassic period before becoming extinct alongside most dinosaurs 66m years ago. Anning has not been forgotten. Her name and image are everywhere, from information boards along the seafront to the colourful Charmouth Heritage Coast Centre overlooking the beach. Here, fossil collecting is largely encouraged. “On the rapidly eroding West Dorset coast, fossil collecting is essential if specimens, some of which may be of great scientific value, are to be saved from damage or destruction by the sea,” notes the West Dorset fossil collecting code of conduct. And just as Anning sold many of her discoveries, fossils are still bought and sold today. Downstairs is a shop where small ammonites can be picked up for a few pounds, while larger specimens, painstakingly prepared within their surrounding rock, sell for several hundred.

Provided hunters follow the code of conduct, ownership of fossils passes to the finder. “Professional collectors have the most time, are able to react quickly to events that uncover the fossils – ie: storms and landslides – and have a great deal of local knowledge. But they need to sell their finds in order to earn a living,” the code notes. It is easy to understand how fossil hunting becomes addictive. It is the size of a penny and, though it is probably worth very little, I feel as if I have won the lottery. As a professional guide and fossil hunter, Curtis knows these beaches intimately.

“I spent a lot of my childhood on the beach with my father, finding fossils a bit further down the coast that way in Kimmeridge,” he says. Curtis says TikTok and Instagram have transformed the activity in recent years. It is perhaps not surprising that rare finds or beautifully prepared specimens can command substantial sums. “As fossil hunters, [when] we come to the beach, we are collecting to try to earn money. “It’s always sad when things like that go abroad” said Curtis, adding that Moore had worked hard on his collection. “The key thing is it’s being enjoyed by someone,” he said. “It’s all well and good having a good collection, but it’s no good stuck in a box somewhere.” There is a striking irony here. ‘You’re hit with a slam of shadow’: Nasa’s air mission to capture rare eclipse data

After lunch on Wednesday, two Nasa aviators will climb into a research plane and take off from Keflavik airport on a western tip of Iceland. They will climb north towards Greenland and then bank to head south on a gently curving course 40 miles (64km) off the Icelandic coast. Their mission can be described as chasing an eclipse, but in reality the eclipse is chasing them. As the plane cruises at 50,000ft (15,000 metres), the shadow of the moon will race up from behind, crossing the ocean below at more than 2,000mph (3,200km/h). The pilot will aim to reach the point of greatest eclipse, when the largest fraction of the sun is obscured by the moon, at the moment the shadow catches up with them. For anyone standing directly beneath – or treading water, given the geography – the world will go dark for 2 minutes 18 seconds. But by flying at 460mph along the path of the eclipse, the pilot can extend totality to nearly 3 minutes. Which gives them more time to observe the blotted-out sun.

There are no clouds above you, and then all of a sudden, you’re hit with this slam of shadow.” “You feel the temperature drop off; you’ll notice that you need more light from your instruments, and it’s kind of a weird, eerie shadow that you’re surrounded by. It wraps around the view in the cockpit,” he added. Hidden in the nose cone of the WB-57 aircraft are four cameras. These will take dozens of pictures a second of the occluded sun in different wavelengths of light. The images should capture large, looping ribbons of plasma called prominences and magnetic explosions called nanoflares. Space-based cameras are above such concerns, but can send back only so much data. “As you can imagine, this is terabytes of information,” Caspi said. But other planes have been used for eclipse missions. In 1923, the US navy sent a fleet of biplanes to observe an eclipse, without much success.

Fifty years later, scientists persuaded the French to cut holes in the roof of a Concorde prototype; hurtling over the Sahara at Mach 2, they kept up with an eclipse shadow for 74 minutes. The more scientists learn about the sun, the better they should be able to grasp space weather, the barrage of energetic particles and radiation that are hazardous to astronauts, satellites and even power grids and communications on Earth. Caspi said: “Understanding space weather is critical for us as a technological species, and it starts with understanding the processes at the sun.” Eclipses are not all about science though. “What percentage of humanity has ever witnessed a total solar eclipse? text:
Glyn Morton obituary

My grandfather Glyn Morton, who has died aged 86, was an environmental microbiologist based for most of his career at the University of Lancashire, rising from senior lecturer to professor and then head of department. In 2007 he was appointed emeritus professor. He published more than 140 papers and supervised dozens of researchers. He was a chartered biologist, a fellow of the Royal Society of Biology, and a president of the International Biodeterioration Society (1985-87). He was also a performer in many amateur dramatic and operatic productions, for the most part at the Lowther Pavilion in Lytham. Glyn became especially acclaimed for his many turns as Tevye in Fiddler on the Roof. Being an in-character father to multiple casts of daughters reflected both Glyn’s home life and his kind, welcoming nature as a man to whom anyone could become family. Born in Hanley, Staffordshire, Glyn was the youngest of the six children of Alice (nee Davies) and Thomas Morton, a shoe shop manager. The family moved to Pwllheli, north-west Wales, when Glyn was young, and he attended the grammar school there.

citation.title: Glyn Morton obituary

text:
Glyn Morton obituary

Drama came quickly to him: a vicar recognised that he had a good voice from singing at church and had some contacts, and this led on to Glyn performing on the BBC’s Children’s Hour radio programme in the 1950s. However, Glyn soon discovered a different passion – for science. He studied biology, zoology and botany at Cardiff University, graduating in 1962 and later gaining a master’s, then a PhD at Aston University in 1975. He began working life as a biology teacher at a girls’ grammar school in Birmingham, then St Anne’s college, in Lytham St Anne’s. Then he joined Harris College in Preston, which became part of the University of Central Lancashire (UCLan, now the University of Lancashire). . He was also director of research in the department of forensic and investigative science at UCLan. Glyn settled in Freckleton, on the Fylde coast in Lancashire, with his wife, Carole (nee Naylor), a teacher whom he had married in 1964, and they raised three daughters, Janet, Sue and Ann. They also embraced a friend of the family, James, as an unofficial son, and James’s children, Dylan and Maisie, came to view them as grandparents.

text:
Glyn Morton obituary

To know Glyn was to engage in animated conversation, enjoy his tremendous sense of humour, and hear endless dazzling stories. As a Butlin’s redcoat in Pwllheli in the 1960s he met a pre-fame Ringo Starr, whose then band had a residency at the camp. Glyn studied the decay of Maya temples in Mexico while travelling with the International Biodeterioration Society. As a student he once got stuck on a construction crane – in a rented tux. His 2007 emeritus professorship lecture epitomised this life well lived: stories and science woven together, all delivered as if he had been performing in the West End. Carole died in 2009. Glyn is survived by his children and by three grandchildren, Ben, Jacob and Emily.

Roman shipwreck with 500 amphorae found off coast of Sicily

A 2,100-year-old Roman shipwreck carrying about 500 amphorae has been discovered 3 miles off the coast of Mazara del Vallo in Sicily. Italy’s Carabinieri cultural heritage protection squad investigated the wreck with the help of divers and underwater cameras after receiving a tip-off from fishers. The vessel was found at a depth of about 46 metres (151ft) and was carrying hundreds of amphorae – ancient two-handled ceramic jars with a narrow neck – thought to have been used mainly to transport wine. The wreck, measuring about 21 metres long and 6 metres wide, was described by Italy’s culture minister, Alessandro Giuli, as “one of the most important underwater archaeological discoveries of recent years”. Giuli said the wreck offered “precious fragments of our history” and provided further evidence of the trade routes and exchanges that made the Mediterranean “a crossroads of civilisations”. The divers Giacomo De Mola and Igor Bisulli described how they came across the wreck. “Visibility wasn’t the best … I got closer. And my heart stopped.

citation.title: Roman shipwreck with 500 amphorae found off coast of Sicily

text:
Roman shipwreck with 500 amphorae found off coast of Sicily

Below me was a vast expanse of amphorae,” De Mola said in an Instagram post accompanying video footage of the discovery. “This is, without a doubt, the most incredible discovery of my life,” he said. “It’s hard to describe what it feels like to be among the first humans, in nearly 20 centuries, to see that place again.” Most of the ship’s cargo consisted of Dressel 1A amphorae, widely used to transport wine and particularly valuable to archaeologists because they can help reconstruct the commercial networks that linked Italy with other parts of the Mediterranean between the second and first centuries BC. Over the coming months, Sicily’s superintendency of the sea is expected to carry out a new phase of scientific documentation and research at the site. Archaeologists will seek to establish more precisely the date of the wreck, the origin and intended destination of its cargo, and the condition of the surviving material, while also drawing up measures to protect what officials have described as a site of exceptional archaeological significance.

Roman shipwreck with 500 amphorae found off coast of Sicily

The discovery is the latest in a series of important Roman wrecks found in Italian waters. In 2021, another Roman vessel dating from the second century BC was discovered off the coast of Palermo. The wreck lay 92 metres beneath the sea near Isola delle Femmine and images taken by an underwater robot showed it carrying a large cargo of wine amphorae. Before that, an almost intact Roman vessel dating from the second century BC was discovered in 2013 off the coast of Liguria. The ship, carrying about 50 valuable amphorae, was located by police divers about a mile off Alassio at a depth of about 50 metres. In that case, police were alerted to the wreck during a year-long investigation into archaeological artefacts believed to have been looted and sold on the black market in northern Italy. Italian police recover hundreds of illegally removed ancient Roman amphorae each year, many of them found in the homes or warehouses of collectors and art dealers. The waters surrounding Sicily are regarded as one of the Mediterranean’s richest areas for underwater archaeology.

Rush to find solar eclipse glasses as UK high street stocks run short

A frantic rush is on across the UK to find the right kind of protective eyewear ahead of Wednesday’s partial solar eclipse. High street stores are running out of eclipse glasses and online shoppers who track down a pair are being told they may not reach them until the end of the week. In other words, in plenty of time for the next comparable UK eclipse – in 2081 – but no good at all for Wednesday’s show. The Royal Observatory Greenwich said it was aware of a shortage of glasses. A spokesperson said: “We have sold out of solar eclipse glasses, both online and in our shops, due to an unprecedented volume of orders.” Related: Where in the UK will get the best view of the solar eclipse? Ordinary sunglasses are not safe to use and over the last few weeks consumer experts have been recommending specialised glasses. But try to get, for example, a pack of Lunt solar eclipse glasses (£14.99) on Amazon and the dispiriting message “free delivery Thursday 13 August” pops up. The Robert Dyas store was offering Bresser eclipse glasses for £2.99, but there was an “out of stock” message on its website.

People flocking to Spain to view solar eclipse could spark more ‘devastating’ wildfires

Authorities in Spain have warned of an increased risk of fires when hundreds of thousands of people head to the hills and beaches to get a better view of Wednesday’s total solar eclipse. “The vegetation is extraordinarily dry and the smallest spark or carelessness could lead to devastating forest fires,” the environment minister, Sara Aagesen, said on a visit to Niebla in the south of the country, the site of Spain’s latest fire. Relentless heat and scarce rainfall have created ideal conditions for wildfires that have scarred swathes of Spain in recent weeks, including a huge blaze west of the capital, Madrid. Police estimate that about 1.5m additional car journeys will be made on Wednesday, and there are fears that the volume of traffic could block access for emergency vehicles if fires break out in rural areas. Parking on hard shoulders or close to dry vegetation has been banned, as have barbecues and fireworks. Spain is among the best locations in Europe to view the total solar eclipse. The finance ministry says it expects 460,000 overseas tourists to visit specifically to see the eclipse.

Starwatch: Deep partial solar eclipse in UK to precede the Perseids

The annual Perseid meteor shower reaches its peak this week on the night of 12-13 August, and this year comes with an added bonus. Earlier on 12 August, a deep partial solar eclipse will be visible across the UK. The partial solar eclipse begins shortly after 6pm BST and reaches its maximum at around 7.13pm. From much of the country, about 90% of the sun’s diameter will be obscured, making this the deepest solar eclipse visible here since 1999. The sun will be low in the western sky throughout the event, so choose a location with a clear horizon. Remember that it is never safe to look directly at the sun without certified eclipse glasses or a properly filtered telescope or binoculars. As dusk gives way to darkness, the moon and the sun slip from view below the horizon to leave a moonless night. This will provide ideal conditions for the Perseids. The shower is produced as Earth ploughs through a stream of dust left behind by Comet Swift–Tuttle. Each tiny grain strikes our atmosphere at about 60 kilometres per second, burning up in a brief flash that we see as a shooting star.

Europe’s total solar eclipse: the best place to see it and how to view it safely

On Wednesday evening, millions of Europeans will experience a celestial treat: a solar eclipse. A wide band of north and central Spain, plus a sliver of Portugal and parts of Greenland and Iceland will experience a rare total eclipse. The light of the setting sun will be virtually blocked out across much of western Europe, including the UK, France, Belgium, Switzerland and northern Italy. Here’s what you need to know: What is a solar eclipse? A solar eclipse occurs when the moon passes directly between the Earth and the sun, resulting in the moon casting a shadow on the Earth. Viewers see a total solar eclipse when the sun’s light is fully blocked by the moon – meaning they are in the umbra of the moon’s shadow – and a partial solar eclipse when only part of the light is blocked, meaning they are in the penumbra of the moon’s shadow. “The moon and sun have to line up precisely for the moon to fully cover the sun and for you to see a total eclipse,” said Dr Megan Argo, a reader in astrophysics at the University of Lancashire and the vice-president of the Society for Popular Astronomy.

“Because the orbit of the moon is slightly tilted, it doesn’t appear to cross the disc of the sun from our perspective each time it orbits the Earth.” Whether viewers see a total or partial eclipse – or no eclipse at all – depends upon their location on the Earth’s surface. “You have to be right in the middle of the shadow to see a total eclipse, and that is quite a narrow track on the Earth’s surface,” said Argo. Interactive How rare is Wednesday’s event? This total eclipse will be the first in mainland Europe in two decades. The last event of this kind visible from the UK occurred in 1999, when parts of Devon and Cornwall were in the path of totality. The next total solar eclipse visible in the UK is not due to occur until 2090. Related: Spanish mountain village braces for astrotourists lured by total solar eclipse While the country will only experience a partial solar eclipse on Wednesday, experts are enthusiastic, noting the next comparable event visible in the UK will be in 2081. “This is the best [solar] eclipse that we’ve had in the UK since 1999.

text:
‘Real mummy’s curse’: health warning over growing trade in mummified human remains

A growing global trade in mummified human remains has been described by academics as “a real mummy’s curse” that poses a serious health risk to its enthusiasts and the postal services they use. Research into the secretive buying and selling of centuries-old human body parts including hands, feet and heads found alarming risks from dormant microorganisms and the toxic materials used to preserve the remains. A peer-reviewed academic article, The Real Mummy’s Curse: Health Risks Associated With the Sale and Trade of Mummified Remains, published in the International Journal of Cultural Property and online by Cambridge University Press, paints what the academics behind it describe as a “bleak picture”. A “semi-clandestine, often illicit” trade has been amplified in recent years through the use of social media, personal websites, e-commerce platforms and auction houses, but those involved appear to have little awareness as to how the living are being “exposed to various risks”, it says.

citation.title: ‘Real mummy’s curse’: health warning over growing trade in mummified human remains

text:
‘Real mummy’s curse’: health warning over growing trade in mummified human remains

An examination of 128 online posts on Meta platforms, e-commerce sites, web stores and auction houses found numerous cases of mummified remains on sale that showed clear signs of biodeterioration. But sellers provided no safety guidance and often used the postal service to transport parts to buyers, it was found. “Isolated body parts, such as hands and feet, were most frequently identified, followed by whole mummified heads,” the paper’s authors write. “Over half of the sample, 51.6%, consisted of heads in varying states of completeness and preservation, including whole or partial mummified heads, skulls or crania with soft tissue and/or hair, and tsantsas, so-called shrunken heads produced by the Shuar people of northern Peru/eastern Ecuador.” Mummification practices, whether artificial or natural, involve complex chemical and physical processes intended to delay decomposition. A range of toxic materials and substances have been employed over time to preserve tissues, including heavy metals such as arsenic, mercury, and lead.

citation.title: ‘Real mummy’s curse’: health warning over growing trade in mummified human remains

text:
‘Real mummy’s curse’: health warning over growing trade in mummified human remains

Mummified remains can harbour a wide variety of dormant microorganisms despite centuries of desiccation. Dormant fungal spores can become airborne when moved or disturbed, which pose health risks to the living, the academics warn. Inhalation of aspergillus spores was blamed for the deaths of 10 out of 12 of the conservation scientists who opened the tomb of King Casimir IV of Kraków, in modern-day Poland, in the 1970s, the paper notes. It is believed that a severe form of aspergillosis from inhaling spores may have also contributed to the death of Lord Carnarvon, the chief financial backer of the exploration of Tutankhamun’s tomb in the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. Carnavon’s death in 1923 has been cited as proof of the myth that those who opened tombs would be cursed with bad luck, illness or death, otherwise known as the “mummy’s curse”. Kirsty Squires, a professor of human bioarchaeology at the University of Staffordshire, who worked with Dario Piombino-Mascali, Clara Urzì and Damien Huffer on the research, said traders appeared to have little awareness of the dangers.

She said: “In some of the comments, they do make note of a mummy smell – which can be attributed to the biodeterioration of remains- yet some of the images uploaded show mummified remains that are not in protective cases but are exposed to the surrounding air, for example, in the room of a domestic dwelling which could be really dangerous. “When we were putting this paper together, there were some images of heavily deteriorated remains that were just on a stand with no glass cover. It didn’t look like it was temperature controlled, the appropriate storage conditions required for human remains.” The study found that it was not just those trading in human remains who were in danger. The academics write: “Given that postal and courier companies are being used to transport mummified human remains, warehouse workers, drivers, transportation hub workers and customs officials are all at risk as they are unlikely to wear the necessary [personal protection equipment] when they are initially in contact with these consignments.”

text:
Astronomers discover a new kind of cosmic object – a black hole ‘star’

Astronomers claim to have discovered a new kind of cosmic object, a black hole “star”, which is the size of the entire solar system and glows with a brilliant red light. The international team made the breakthrough after focusing their attention on a mysterious red spot in images of the early universe captured by Nasa’s James Webb space telescope. The object was lurking in the constellation of Cetus, the Whale, billions of light years from Earth. It is thought to have formed 660m years after the big bang, astronomers’ leading theory as to how the universe began. Measurements of the exotic body found that while it resembles an immense star, it releases 100bn times more energy than any known star can produce. The energy output is far closer to that observed from black holes than stars. “We have found a new type of astrophysical object, a black hole star,” said Dr Rohan Naidu who performed the work at the Kavli Institute for Astrophysics and Space Research, part of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. He is now at the University of Hawaii.

citation.title: Astronomers discover a new kind of cosmic object – a black hole ‘star’

text:
Astronomers discover a new kind of cosmic object – a black hole ‘star’

It “shines with the energy typically associated with black holes, but at the same time bears signatures classically associated with stars”, he added. The scientists were using the James Webb space telescope to search for the most distant galaxies in the known universe. After succeeding with a galaxy named Mom-z14, which formed a mere 280m years after the big bang, they turned their attention to other cosmic objects. Writing in Nature, the astronomers describe how they focused on an extremely bright red spot known as MoM-BH*-1, the reddest object in the telescope’s image archive. “The way its light is almost entirely red, and abruptly disappears below a certain wavelength, is so dramatic that there is no comparison among any known class of objects,” Naidu said. Computer simulations showed that rather than being an enormous star powered by nuclear fusion, the object is a black hole so swaddled in shrouds of dense gas that it radiates like a star.

text:
Astronomers discover a new kind of cosmic object – a black hole ‘star’

If the astronomers are correct, it suggests that scores of other mysterious Little Red Dots, or LRDs, that appear in nearly every deep space image from the James Webb space telescope are also black hole stars. Naidu suspects that black hole stars play a major role in the evolution of galaxies. They might be the seeds of present-day supermassive black holes, such as the one at the centre of the Milky Way. “For decades we have anticipated something spectacular must be afoot in the very early universe. Black hole stars may be the ‘something spectacular’. They may be the nascent, swaddled phase that marks the beginning of almost every supermassive black hole’s journey,” he said. Supermassive black holes are found at the centres of almost all galaxies such as the Milky Way and are thought to shape the fate of those galaxies. “They may govern when stars are able to form and when they cease forming, setting the course for everything that follows from star formation: the birth of planets, the rise of life, the emergence of species that may one day piece together this entire history,” Naidu said.

‘A mouse can’t tell us what works’: UK scientists to grow miniature human organs for drug testing

Miniature human organs and other tissues are to be grown from NHS patients’ cells in a drive to improve medicine testing and reduce the number of animals used in drug development. Scientists will use the clumps of tissue to learn how diseases vary between patients, helping them identify which treatments are best for different people based on the particular pathology underlying their condition. The move marks a shift away from the traditional use of animals as models for human disease, towards what researchers believe will be more accurate and reliable tests based directly on human tissues. “It’s going to have a major impact on the numbers of animals used and the way we develop new drugs in the future,” said Matthias Zilbauer, a clinical professor of paediatric gastroenterology at the Cambridge Stem Cell Institute.

text:
‘A mouse can’t tell us what works’: UK scientists to grow miniature human organs for drug testing

“We’re not saying there won’t be any animal use in the near or foreseeable future, because there are still certain issues that cannot be tested in these new models, but the reduction is very real.” Researchers have been growing tiny clumps of human organs, known as organoids, for more than a decade. Tests show that pieces smaller than a millimetre can mirror key features of full-scale organs and tissues, including how they falter with disease and respond to drugs. Armed with organoids grown from diseased human tissues, scientists can investigate whether new drug candidates reverse pathological changes in all or a subset of patients, and quickly identify ineffective drugs early in the process. Historically, more than 90% of drugs that clear animal testing go on to fail in human trials, raising questions about the value of the tests. US and European medicines regulators now encourage other approaches if available. “A lot of human diseases either do not occur in animals or occur in a different way because they’re not human,” said Zilbauer.

“We want tests and models that can tell us which treatments work, and in what patients, and a mouse cannot tell us that.” The new work will be run from a research hub in Cambridge, funded with £20m from the Medical Research Council. Researchers there will work with scientists more widely to create a library of standardised, validated organoids. These will be made available to academics and the pharmaceutical industry to help them bring new drugs to the clinic. The move is part of a plan drawn up by Keir Starmer’s government to fast-track the reduction of animals in research. The strategy relies on “new approach methodologies” (Nams), such as organoids, organ-on-a-chip systems and artificial intelligence, to process data and model biological processes. Last year, there were 2.54m animal testing procedures in Britain, down 3.8% on 2024. Scientists hope to shed light on young universe by using far side of the moon

Little is known about what was happening shortly after the big bang, but now researchers are hoping to shed fresh light on the matter by harnessing the far side of the moon. Scientists plan to put a suitcase-sized satellite into orbit around the moon, using the data it collects as it passes the far side to search for a radio frequency signal emitted by neutral hydrogen atoms in the early universe. More specifically, the satellite, nicknamed CosmoCube, will be looking for what is known as the 21cm line. Crucially, the older the signal, the more its wavelength has been stretched, or redshifted, to longer wavelengths, providing a way for its strength to be tracked over time relative to the cosmic microwave background radiation. “The main thing we track by looking at this signal is what’s the physical temperature of the gas during the early universe,” said Prof Eloy de Lera Acedo, the lead author from the University of Cambridge’s Cavendish Laboratory.

With the 21cm signal acting a bit like a thermometer, the team are hoping to study events from the start of the so-called “dark ages”, about 380,000 years after the big bang, through the cosmic dawn, when the first stars and galaxies emerged, to the end of what is known as the epoch of reionization, approximately 1bn years after the big bang. “The temperature of the gas is affected by the things happening in the universe at the time,” said de Lera Acedo. In addition he noted the amplitude and shape of the 21cm signal was expected to be influenced by dark matter, offering a way for experts to investigate the nature of this mysterious component of the universe. Researchers have attempted to detect the 21cm line before but it is difficult to do using Earth-based instruments. Not only is the signal weak but human-made technology – from FM radios to plane communication – can cause interference. Writing in the journal Nature Astronomy, de Lera Acedo and his colleagues said other challenges included disturbances created by the Earth’s ionosphere.

While experts at the Edges (Experiment to Detect the Global EoR Signature) radio telescope in Australia claim to have found the 21cm line, questions have been raised over the results. The team behind the CosmoCube mission, which is expected to last two years, said taking observations from the far side of the moon should avoid many of the challenges faced by Earth-based instruments. “The total cost is estimated to be just under £50m and the launching date – we expect it to be about five years from now,” said de Lera Acedo, adding that CosmoCube had already been granted more than £2m of funding by the UK Space Agency. Phil Bull, a professor of cosmology at the Jodrell Bank Centre for Astrophysics who is not involved in the project, welcomed the mission. “The CosmoCube measurements will help us understand the major ingredients of our cosmic origins – the processes that led to the formation of the first stars and galaxies, and lit up the Universe after a period called the cosmic dark ages,” he said.

‘A tax on being thin’: only high earners make overall savings on food bills from weight-loss drugs

The high cost of weight-loss medication is a “regressive tax on being thin” because the outlay outweighs any saving on food costs for all but the highest earners. Someone needs to have discretionary income of nearly £100,000 a year to actually save money after covering the £1,200 annual cost of GLP-1 medication, according to an analysis by the consultancy Baringa. “Our analysis shows that GLP-1s risk becoming a driver of inequality,” said Paddy Winters, a partner at Baringa. “Only very high earners will benefit from savings to their groceries whilst taking the GLP-1 pill.” A regressive tax is one that takes a larger percentage from lower-wage earners’ income compared with those who are more wealthy. Most users buy the drugs with a private prescription. A GLP-1 user with £39,000 left over after tax and essentials will spend £481 less a year on food. But it is not until someone has £97,500 left to spend after tax and other outgoings that their grocery spend is reduced by £1,200, according to Baringa. The cost is an average for the pill form of the medication.

citation.title: ‘A tax on being thin’: only high earners make overall savings on food bills from weight-loss drugs

text:
‘A tax on being thin’: only high earners make overall savings on food bills from weight-loss drugs

For “everyone else” the annual cost of the drug outweighs any reduction in spending on groceries, Winters said. “On top of that, users are spending more on vitamin supplements and personal care products like hair care, to manage side effects. In effect, GLP-1s become a regressive tax on being thin.” “We’re already seeing early signs that some people cancel their prescription after a few months because the cost adds up – but the weight comes back once you stop,” he added. “So the pattern is likely to be start, stop, regain and return, and to fund that cycle, we may well see people turn to debt.” There are 14.3 million adults living with obesity in England, according to the King’s Fund. In a recent report, the charity said the government “needs to ensure that the people who benefit from [weight-loss medication] most are not priced out of accessing them, and that we don’t end up with wider health inequalities caused by obesity due to affordability and access”.

It is estimated that 5% of adults, or nearly 3 million people, in Britain are on weight-loss medication, while 9% have taken it at some point, according to separate research by accountancy firm PwC. It expects this number to rise to 13% by the end of next year. About 60% of GLP-1 users are women, according to PwC. Among current users 6% come from households with income of less than £20,000, whereas 20% are from the wealthiest, earning above £100,000. Block export of ‘national treasure’ UK fossils, says MP

An MP has called on ministers to change export controls so that significant fossils can be classed as national treasures after one of the UK’s best collections, unearthed on Dorset beaches, was sold overseas. Last week, a Guardian investigation revealed that an unparalleled collection of fossils from the UK’s Jurassic Coast, comprising hundreds of specimens including ichthyosaurs, had been sold to the Natural History Museum in Abu Dhabi for what one source described as an “eight-figure sum”. The fossils, which belonged to the Dorset-based private collector Chris Moore, were initially offered to the Natural History Museum (NHM) in London and Amgueddfa Cymru (Museum Wales), but neither institution had the funds to buy them. Senior figures at Lyme Regis Museum have called on ministers to change the way fossil discoveries are recorded and sold. They said they were not informed of the impending sale of Moore’s collection or given the opportunity to acquire it.

citation.title: Block export of ‘national treasure’ UK fossils, says MP

text:
Block export of ‘national treasure’ UK fossils, says MP

A letter from Bridget Houseago, the director of the museum, to Edward Morello, the Liberal Democrat MP for West Dorset, notes that the UK’s cultural goods export controls – intended to give the country an opportunity to retain objects of outstanding national importance – do not cover fossils and other items of natural history because they are not “made”. This means that “some important and rare fossils can be sold without an export licence,” the letter states. Lyme Regis Museum was aware of Moore’s collection and considered it among the best private collections from the Lower Lias of Dorset, containing several unique specimens. Although the museum understood indirectly that Moore might eventually want to sell some or all of the collection, or have it placed on public display, it was unaware that a sale of the collection was under way at the end of 2025.

Dr Jonathan Evans, the chair of trustees at Lyme Regis (Philpot) Museum trust, said: “The museum was not approached either by Chris Moore, by the NHM or National Museum Cardiff [part of Museum Wales] or by any other government entity to check whether we might be interested in acquiring some or all of the collection.” Related: Britain’s Jurassic gold rush: the fossil hunters chasing fortunes on Dorset’s beaches The earlier Guardian investigation revealed that the NHM in London and Amgueddfa Cymru were required to sign non-disclosure agreements. There is no suggestion the sale of the Moore collection to the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi broke any rules. Existing codes of conduct stress the importance of fossil collecting. The West Dorset fossil collecting code of conduct notes: “On the rapidly eroding West Dorset coast, fossil collecting is essential if specimens, some of which may be of great scientific value, are to be saved from damage or destruction by the sea.” But as fossil collectors get older, many more private collections are likely to need new homes.

Evans and Houseago want fossils of exceptional scientific or national significance to be covered by the Waverley criteria – three benchmarks used to determine whether an object is classed as a “national treasure”.
