Olga Soffer obituary

Olga Soffer, who has died aged 83, brought a revolutionary idea into the conversation about prehistoric ice age people: women mattered. Inspired when working on archaeological excavations in the former USSR, and by remains from a dig in Moravia, in the 1990s she presented a case for women as makers of textiles, baskets and nets, critical to survival in bleak northern conditions 30,000 years ago. Her achievement was the more remarkable for her career path. By then a professor of anthropology at the University of Illinois, she had obtained her three degrees over three decades, partly while also working as a cosmetics buyer and fashion promoter for a New York department store. Since the 20s, Soviet Russia, looking to historical materialism, generously funded large archaeological excavations. Unlike most of her colleagues in the west, Soffer, whose family had fled Tito’s Yugoslavia and settled in Brooklyn in 1955, could read the reports. In 1977 she began years of travel and research, supported by grants from the US government, the National Geographic Society and many others.

citation.title: Olga Soffer obituary

text:
Olga Soffer obituary

Among 30 sites she worked on, four stood out: Mezhyrich, Ukraine; Avdeevo, Russia; and Dolní Věstonice and Pavlov, Moravia (now in Czechia). At such places, people built tent-like houses with mammoth bones. At Mezhyrich, 160 kilometres south of Kyiv, male archaeologists credited the remains to heroic male hunters. To Soffer there were too many mammoths – one house was assembled from 95 jaws. She argued instead that the bones had been collected from natural death sites, while noting that archaeologists had overlooked remains of smaller animals. “Maybe they killed one mammoth every 10 years,” she commented, “and never stopped talking about it.” Already doubting the existence of male-dominated ice age communities, in 1990 she noticed marks in a few tiny clay fragments excavated decades before at Pavlov. She showed them to James Adovasio, an archaeologist at Mercyhurst College, Pennsylvania, who had been digging with her at Mezhyrich, and who knew about basketry and textiles. He recognised impressions of woven threads. They went on to identify 79 such marks among thousands of clay scraps, from Dolní Věstonice and Pavlov, with explosive implications.

citation.title: Olga Soffer obituary

text:
Olga Soffer obituary

Adovasio saw evidence, fortuitously imprinted in clay, for cordage, plaited basketry and woven textiles, made from plants, not animal sinews or hides. Soffer found indications of dress and headgear, previously overlooked in favour of attention to breasts and buttocks (characterised by Soffer as “paleoerotica”), on small female figurines, many of which were found at Avdeevo (carved from mammoth ivory and stone) and Dolní Věstonice (ceramic), similar to the Venuses of Willendorf, west of Vienna, and Kostenki, south of Voronezh, in Russia. Soffer later wrote that the head of the Willendorf figurine offered the clearest depiction of a fibre-based woven cap or hat, “rather than a hairdo, as posited by scholars”. With Adovasio and his colleague David Hyland, Soffer conjured a world featuring mats, wall hangings, blankets and bags, shawls, shirts, skirts and sashes. Knotted string suggested nets, used by women to hunt small animals. She compared Palaeolithic tailoring to “something from Donna Karan or Calvin Klein”. A figurine’s beaded string item was a “skirt … to die for”. “We’re not talking protection from the elements here,” she told the New York Times.

citation.title: Olga Soffer obituary

text:
Olga Soffer obituary

The sophistication of the weaving and cord-making prompted Adovasio to suggest a history that went back at least 40,000 years. Noting more recent practices, they believed the crafts would have been invented and executed by women. In 2007 Soffer and Adovasio co-authored, with the science writer Jake Page, The Invisible Sex: Uncovering the True Roles of Women in Prehistory, in which they addressed a perceived male bias. It was widely reported, but the public narrative of ice age life was led by Jean Auel, whose multi-million-selling Earth’s Children novel series was to end in 2011. Soffer was consulted on two titles (The Mammoth Hunters and The Plains of Passage), but the protagonist Ayla, a blond, blue-eyed modern human who challenges the patriarchal world of Neanderthals, nonetheless wears animal skins. Soffer’s wider message, that what survives from the ancient past is a tiny and often misleading representation of reality, has yet to be absorbed, even by many archaeologists. Olga was born in Nazi-occupied Belgrade.

citation.title: Olga Soffer obituary

text:
Olga Soffer obituary

As an infant she was taken with her maternal grandparents to a labour camp: she was treated favourably by the camp commander, she was told, due to her Aryan colouring and looks. Her parents, Galina (nee Girs) and Alexander Shabunin, came from Russian migrant families scattered after the 1917 Bolshevik revolution. In New York, reached via Yugoslavia and four years in a displaced persons camp in Italy, her father assembled window blinds and her mother worked as a seamstress, while Olga went to Thomas Jefferson high school in Brooklyn. After obtaining a BA in political science (1965) at Hunter College, City University of New York, she began working at Abraham & Straus, a Brooklyn-based department store chain, first as an assistant buyer for cosmetics, then special events coordinator for fashion. In the latter role she created a gourmet festival featuring the television chef James Beard, and hired a young Brooke Shields as a model. Bored with work, she took night courses in art history at Hunter, which led to an interest in archaeology and ethnography, and her eventual MA in anthropology there (1975).

citation.title: Olga Soffer obituary

text:
Olga Soffer obituary

In 1978, having gone part-time at the store, she became an adjunct instructor of anthropology at Hunter, moving to Lehman College, then the University of Wisconsin at Milwaukee. After a PhD on the archaeology of eastern Europe at the Graduate Center, City University of New York (1984), Soffer joined the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign as assistant professor of anthropology. She rose to professor, with stints as visiting archaeology professor at the Centre de Recherches Archéologiques, France (1992), and heading the department of Slavic languages and literature at Illinois (1993–98). She retired in 2008 as professor emerita. Her awards included an honorary doctorate from the Russian Academy of Sciences. Both her marriages, to Mark Soffer, a history teacher, in 1962, and Dmitry Bobyshev, a poet and professor of Russian literature, in 1979, ended in divorce. She is survived by her daughter from her first marriage, Alex, and two grandchildren, Jake and Mena. • Olga Soffer, archaeologist, born 9 September 1942; died 20 June 2026

Science or fiction? Shadowy ‘paper mills’ let you pay to be a published author – of fraudulent research

Dr Reese Richardson’s phone constantly buzzes with notifications. The scientific research integrity specialist has been tracking shadowy organisations known as “paper mills”, which turn a profit by offering fraudulent academic authorship of scientific papers, IP registrations and other scholarly outputs. For a fee, paper mills offer to list people as authors of scientific journal articles, often of falsified research that bypasses the peer review process. Richardson has joined dozens of groups across apps such as Telegram, WhatsApp and Facebook where a buffet of fraudulent and fabricated research is advertised to hundreds of members. “I can just look through my notifications and I can see that I’ve gotten, like, 20 WhatsApp messages from paper mills in the last 24 hours,” he says. Scientists are under constant pressure to publish new research papers which, in many parts of the world, remain the currency of academia. They beget more grant funding and accolades, and enhance academic profiles. But robust, high-quality science takes time, and papers can take years to get published.

citation.title: Science or fiction? Shadowy ‘paper mills’ let you pay to be a published author – of fraudulent research

text:
Science or fiction? Shadowy ‘paper mills’ let you pay to be a published author – of fraudulent research

Paper mills offer a fraudulent shortcut, using instant messaging and social media platforms to find prospective buyers looking for papers and patents to stack their CVs. According to an analysis Richardson conducted with Anna Abalkina and Spencer Hong, the median price to buy authorship is around US$800 (A$1,150). In a recent paper, which has not yet been peer reviewed, the trio of scientists led by Richardson, formerly at Northwestern University in the US, detailed more than 18,000 advertisements from seven paper mills across seven countries between 2020 and 2026. Related: Is the staggeringly profitable business of scientific publishing bad for science? “We wanted to get an idea, across a wide range of paper mills, countries, topics and product types how much these things actually go for,” he says. “What we put together is the largest ever dataset of paper mill advertisements.” They found many groups advertising authorship of scientific manuscripts across Telegram, Facebook and various websites for as little as US$30.

citation.title: Science or fiction? Shadowy ‘paper mills’ let you pay to be a published author – of fraudulent research

text:
Science or fiction? Shadowy ‘paper mills’ let you pay to be a published author – of fraudulent research

In the last 15 years, paper mill activity has exploded, with one estimate produced by Richardson in 2025 suggesting their products have been doubling approximately every 18 months. The journal articles produced by these paper mills typically bypass the accepted scientific editorial process of peer review, either because the journals do not institute those processes or because editors are themselves part of paper mill activities. Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best reads This amounts to an industrialised injection of falsified data, polluting the scientific ecosystem and compromising medical research, drug discovery and clinical trials. The scale is massive: in 2023, Hindawi, a now defunct journal brand owned by major publisher Wiley, retracted more than 8,000 articles. A further 3,000 retractions came by the end of 2024. Richardson says his research is a useful starting point for trying to grapple with how and where paper mills operate, and who they target. The advertisements are like fingerprints at a crime scene, potential evidence of malicious activity.

“You can get a lot of information from the advertisements,” he says. He has directly tracked some of these to fraudulent papers in the scientific literature. Designs and IP for sale Other advertisements relate to copyrights and design registrations, another area ripe for fraud, which may provide buyers with legitimate intellectual property rights. Richardson notes one of the reasons to do this is to bolster resumes in service of academic advancement. Richardson has previously identified exploitation of IP systems in the UK, finding thousands of design registrations. His new work identifies 12 instances where design registrations were advertised by a paper mill operating in India and catering to Indian academics. Richardson’s data shows these design registrations are being advertised as “Australian design patents”. The paper mills sell positions as “owners” of design registrations, charging between $95 and $150 per owner, for up to eight people to be registered on any given design. A design registration application through IP Australia costs $200 in total.

Guardian Australia identified cases where the registrations were listed as patents on CVs. “They’re using the services of the Australian government to defraud others,” Richardson says. Can you solve it? A new goat for puzzledom’s GOAT

Today’s puzzle is a new twist on The Monty Hall problem, arguably the greatest maths puzzle of all time. (According to Gemini, who trawled the internet for me, it is the most discussed and debated recreational maths puzzle of all time.) Here’s how it goes, for those who may be unaware of it. You are a contestant on the US game show Let’s Make a Deal. Monty Hall, the host, asks you to choose one of three doors. Behind one door is a car. Behind the other two are goats. To win the car, which is what you want, you must choose the correct door. You choose a door. Before your chosen door is opened, however, Monty Hall opens one of the other two doors that he knows has a goat behind it. He opens the door and it reveals a goat. He now offers you chance to switch your choice to the other door. Do you stick, or do you switch? The intuitive reaction is that it makes no difference. If there are two doors left, surely each door has a 50/50 chance of having the car? This reasoning is fallacious. If you stick with your original choice you have a 1/3 chance of winning the car, but if you switch you double your odds to 2/3. Switch!

He reveals a goat, which you can tell is the ordinary goat and not the secretly valuable one. The host offers to let you switch doors. Should you? Solution No, you should not! What is interesting here is that when you want to win the car it makes sense to switch, but when you don’t want to win the car it makes sense to stick! The easiest way to explain the answer is to look at frequencies. Suppose the game is played a large number of times, say 3,000 times. The expected number of games in which your initial choice is the (door with the) car is 1,000. Then the expected number of times the host opens the door with the ordinary goat is 500.

(Because the host cannot tell between goats, and we assume that the host choses a goat at random.) The expected number of games in which your initial choice is the (door with the) ordinary goat is 1,000. Then the expected number of times the host opens the door with the ordinary goat is 0. The expected number of games win which your initial choice is the (door with the) golden goat is 1,000. Then the expected number of times the host opens the door with the ordinary goat is 1000. So in 3,000 trials, the host will open the door with the ordinary goat 1500 times. If you stick you will win in 1000 trials, a win probability of 2/3, and if you switch you will win in 500 trials, a win probability of 1/3. It is better to stick. I hope you enjoyed this puzzle. Starwatch: Vega the bright star will light the way to the constellation of Lyra

We turn our attention this week to one of the sky’s smallest constellations. High overhead from the UK after darkness falls, Lyra, the lyre, is easy to find thanks to the brilliant white star of Vega. The chart shows the view facing south and looking up towards the zenith from London at 22:30 BST on 17 August. As the fifth-brightest star in the night sky, Vega forms one corner of the summer triangle, with Deneb in Cygnus, the Swan, and Altair in Aquila, the Eagle, marking the other two. Having located Vega, the rest of the constellation is easy to trace even though the stars are much fainter. One of the second-century astronomer Ptolemy’s original 48 constellations, Lyra has the distinction of being a star pattern that actually looks like the figure it is named after. It represents the harp played by the Greek poet Orpheus. In Greek mythology, Orpheus played such beautiful music that he could charm wild animals, move rocks and even influence the gods. Becoming one of the Argonauts, Orpheus’s music protected the rest of the crew from the beguiling call of the Sirens.

Astronomers detect fastest known star in Milky Way

Astronomers have detected the fastest known star in the Milky Way, hurtling around the supermassive black hole at the heart of the galaxy. The star, called S301, travels at about 25,000km (15,500 miles) per second, 100,000 times faster than a commercial plane. It is also the closest known star to the Milky Way’s central black hole, Sagittarius A*, approaching it around the distance of Saturn to the Sun. “What is special about this star is that it’s orbiting Sagittarius A* on a very tight orbit, taking just 8.7 years to complete it, and is approaching the black hole at a mere 12 times the distance of Earth to the sun. That is unprecedented,” said Felix Mang, a PhD student at the Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics (MPE) in Garching, Germany, and an author of the study published on the findings. The star’s extreme proximity to Sagittarius A* means that it could open a new window on to the black hole’s fundamental properties and the extreme environment surrounding it. Like many objects in the night sky, black holes are predicted to spin.

citation.title: Astronomers detect fastest known star in Milky Way

text:
Astronomers detect fastest known star in Milky Way

According to Einstein’s general theory of relativity, a spinning black hole drags spacetime along with it, warping the orbits of surrounding stars. This effect is only meaningful for objects orbiting fast-rotating black holes at close range. S301 appears to have the perfect combination of a highly eccentric (lopsided) and very tight orbit. “For the first time, we would actually be able to measure very directly the spin of a massive black hole, which would be a key test of Einstein’s theory,” said Dr Stefan Gillessen, a senior scientist at MPE and a co-author of the study, which is published in the journal Nature. Previously it had been assumed it would require measuring the motion of multiple stars for several decades to estimate the spin of Sagittarius A*. The scientists were able to trace S301’s orbit back to 2017 and, by tracking it through its next closest passage in 2031, hope to have enough data. “With this star we hope to measure, within the next 10 years, the spin of the black hole,” said Mang.

citation.title: Astronomers detect fastest known star in Milky Way

text:
Astronomers detect fastest known star in Milky Way

The observations were made using the European Southern Observatory’s Very Large Telescope Interferometer (ESO’s VLTI) at the Paranal Observatory in Chile, which combines the light from four 8-metre telescopes. Although the star is unusually close to the central black hole, it is not expected to cross its event horizon, the point beyond which objects can never escape. “Black holes are perceived as these cosmic vacuum cleaners engulfing everything they can get a handle on,” said Mang. “But it’s just a massive object. It’s not really much different from something orbiting the sun and it’s going to remain on this orbit.” Dr Ziri Younsi, an astrophysicist at University College London, who was not involved in the observations, said: “This is incredibly important as a discovery. It’s very exciting because this thing comes insanely close to Sagittarius A* and it’s travelling, at its peak, at about 8% of the speed of light, which is crazy.” Younsi said that using the orbit to provide a measurement of the black hole’s spin would be a gamechanger for understanding the evolution of the Milky Way.

citation.title: Astronomers detect fastest known star in Milky Way

SpaceX Starship the talk of remote Australian island as Elon Musk’s engineers sent to retrieve it

Engineers from Elon Musk’s SpaceX are on their way to a remote Australian island to retrieve part of a Starship that dived into the Indian Ocean. The spacecraft – now floating off the coast of Christmas Island – was launched in Texas on 24 July, in the 13th test of the technology. After reaching orbit and releasing 20 non-functioning satellites, the upper stage of the rocket re-entered the atmosphere, landing in the ocean. In recent weeks, the company has been working to retrieve the 52m long piece of spacecraft amid rough seas, before towing it to calmer waters for further study. “The SpaceX Recovery team successfully guided Starship to a location just off the coast of Christmas Island,” the company posted on social media. “A team of SpaceX engineers is on their way to conduct additional analysis on the vehicle in calmer waters before attempting to return it to Starbase.” David Watchorn, the chair of the Christmas Island Tourism Association, said most islanders woke on Tuesday to see what appeared to be three big ships.

“But when you looked a bit closer, what looked a ship was a black rocket,” he said. The arrival of the spacecraft had been the talk of the island since, he said. text:
John Hall obituary

In the late 1950s my friend and Guernsey neighbour John Hall, who has died aged 98, was part of an intrepid team of British test pilots. During the cold war they helped with the birth of the English Electric Lightning, the first – and last – entirely British-built supersonic jet fighter. For years the Lightning was the RAF’s main interceptor, with a phenomenal rate of climb. American fighter pilots envied its performance; they called it “the pocket rocket”. To achieve such power, the prototypes required rigorous testing from John and his pals, who pushed them to their limits. Once he took a Lightning up to 36,000ft for something called a “cold soak” – an endurance test in which he ended up flying for 90 minutes with the plane in a completely frozen state. His hands became almost useless in cold agony, while the controls began to stiffen and he could only work them with jerky movements. Unable to lower the undercarriage normally, he just about managed a landing, after which the ground crew prised his 6ft 2in frame out of the aircraft and, hardly able to walk, he was led to safety.

citation.title: John Hall obituary

text:
John Hall obituary

He was fortunate to survive that escapade, and just as lucky to come back from a “structural integrity test” during which he took a Lightning out to one of the RAF’s North Sea firing ranges, trying to discover if it was possible to simultaneously empty the magazines that fed its two 30mm Aden cannon before the recoil from such heavy calibre ammunition shook the aircraft apart. He expected the entire body to crack apart, but fortunately, after “a bloody great bang” and the flashing of all sorts of warning lights, it held together. John was born in East Bridgford, Nottinghamshire, close to the market town of Southwell, where he attended Southwell Minster grammar school. He was 10 when the second world war broke out, and like many of his contemporaries longed to fly Spitfires. At 18, after the war was over, he trained at RAF Cranwell and his dream was fulfilled when he joined a Spitfire squadron that saw active service in the Suez canal zone. In 1952 he returned to the UK as an instructor on Meteor jet bombers, and by the late 50s he was part of the English Electric Lightning test pilot team.

citation.title: John Hall obituary

text:
John Hall obituary

He then left the RAF to work directly for English Electric (later BAE), but continued to test jets for the RAF on a part-time basis until a final move to British Caledonian airlines, with whom he flew commercial transatlantic flights in Boeing 707s for 25 years until retirement. John’s first marriage, to Shelagh Stone, ended in divorce, and afterwards he moved with his second wife, Tessa (nee Maxwell), to Guernsey, where he especially enjoyed the local swimming. He is survived by Tessa, three sons, James, Patrick and Richard, from his first marriage, and another son, Maxwell, from his second.

text:
Plantwatch: Cities make a surprising refuge for threatened UK wildflowers

Wildflowers are having a rough time in the countryside, mostly from the onslaught of intensive farming with fertilisers, pesticides and herbicides and less grazing. On top of that, there are building developments, competition from invasive plant species and the climate crisis to contend with. The UK has lost 97% of its wildflower meadows over the last century and over half of the country’s native flowers have been in decline for 70 years. But there is a surprising refuge for wild plants – in urban areas. Cities are often stressful environments, but that can help wildflowers by keeping down competition from other plants such as grasses. In fact, wildflowers generally grow best in low‑fertility soils which allows them to become established. Cities also have a wonderful variety of specialised habitats and microclimates in nooks and crannies. Gaps in pavements and walls, roadsides, roundabouts, disused railways, the banks of rivers and streams and the soil under urban trees can all provide safe plant havens.

citation.title: Plantwatch: Cities make a surprising refuge for threatened UK wildflowers

text:
Plantwatch: Cities make a surprising refuge for threatened UK wildflowers

Even the most rundown and derelict sites left untouched by humans can be plant refuges, but some of the best environments are where councils deliberately don’t use herbicides and restrict mowing to encourage wild plants to become established.

Artemis II crew to receive top US space medal for historic lunar journey

The crew of the historic Artemis II lunar flyby mission have earned the US’s top space medal, officials have announced. Cmdr Reid Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, and mission specialists Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen are set to receive the Congressional Space Medal of Honor on 28 August, the US space agency Nasa said. Nasa’s website indicates that only 30 astronauts have gained the honor – among them Neil Armstrong, the first person to walk on the moon, and John Glenn, who was the first American to orbit Earth and then served four terms in the US Senate. Related: Trump hosts crew of historic Artemis mission: ‘I would have had no trouble making it’ Wiseman, Glover, Koch and Hansen were selected for the medal, despite its name, by Donald Trump after the Nasa administrator, Jared Isaacman, recommended them to the president. The Artemis II crew broke Apollo 13’s record for farthest distance traveled from Earth during their 10-day mission, which began on 1 April.

citation.title: Artemis II crew to receive top US space medal for historic lunar journey

text:
Artemis II crew to receive top US space medal for historic lunar journey

They reached 252,756 miles (406,771km) as they swung above the lunar surface, surpassing the 1970 record of 248,655 miles as part of US plans to again land on the moon – then eventually reach Mars. Furthermore, Hansen – who is from Canada – became the first non-US citizen to fly to the moon. “This was not easy,” Wiseman said to reporters after the Artemis II mission safely ended with a textbook splashdown in the Pacific Ocean. “Before you launch, it feels like it’s the greatest dream on Earth. And when you’re out there, you just want to get back to your families and your friends. It’s a special thing to be a human, and it’s a special thing to be on planet Earth.” The medal ceremony scheduled for Wiseman and his colleagues at the Johnson Space Center in Houston comes four months after Trump hosted the Artemis II crew at the White House.

Trump has sought to embrace the Artemis II crew’s achievements despite his administration’s proposal to cut Nasa’s budget by 23%, including a 46% reduction for space science initiatives, for the 2027 fiscal year beginning on 1 October. A House commerce, justice and science subcommittee led by Trump’s Republican party responded by advancing its own Nasa budget proposal that would maintain the science projects the president has been aiming to eliminate. text:
Is this why close encounters with intelligent aliens have so far eluded us?

When thinking about why we have not encountered intelligent aliens yet, as Adam Kirsch does (The long read, 11 August), it seems to me that one factor gets neglected: fossil fuels. Alien life could develop intelligence on myriad planets, but to develop advanced technology that would enable them to get off‑world, they need to go through an equivalent of the Industrial Revolution, and that needed first coal, then oil and gas. There could be many intelligent alien races out there, but on planets without an easily accessible fossil fuel equivalent, they’d never get past a 17th-century level of development. Even if we can eventually detect life on planets outside our solar system, we’d never know these civilisations existed, as their signature from afar would be indistinguishable from that of a planet with just plant-like life and a fire ecology. It is entirely probable, as a result, that almost all alien races, if they exist, are living in an eternal equivalent of Game of Thrones’s Westeros, not Iain M Banks’s Culture, doomed never to be detected from afar.

citation.title: Is this why close encounters with intelligent aliens have so far eluded us?

text:

The Kayapó people of Brazil, for example, tell of Bep Kororoti, a visitor who shared knowledge and helped their ancestors build a stable and sustainable society. It’s easy to imagine a similar conversation among distant observers today. A younger voice might look at our atomic weapons and shake its head, predicting that we’ll finish ourselves off. An older voice might reply that humans have a habit of rebuilding, and that societies like the Kayapó show we can live with balance when we choose. Their verdict might be to wait a while, and see whether we can keep our civilisation going, before attempting contact. Given our history, who could blame them? Starwatch: Lunar eclipse to reward early risers in UK and Europe

The early hours of Friday 28 August will reward very early risers in the UK, Europe and Africa with a fine lunar eclipse. Though not quite a total eclipse, it will transform the moon into a dramatic sight as dawn approaches. The partial eclipse begins at 3.33am BST, when the moon’s familiar full disc begins to disappear behind the shadow of the Earth. By the time the eclipse reaches its greatest extent, shortly after 5.10am, only a thin sliver of the moon will remain in direct sunlight. The rest is likely to glow a muted coppery red as sunlight bent into the Earth’s shadow and filtered through its atmosphere reaches the lunar surface. As the eclipse unfolds, the moon will be sinking, so find an observation site with an uninterrupted view towards the western horizon, and enjoy the view as the eclipse slips from view while the dawn gathers behind you in the east. Unlike a solar eclipse, a lunar eclipse is completely safe to watch with the naked eye. Binoculars will even reveal subtle shades of colour across the moon’s surface.

Dogs blink more often when they see owners blinking, study finds

Stare into a dog’s eyes and you may encounter a bemused expression. But researchers have found that dogs blink more often when they see their owners doing so, suggesting there may be more to the mutual gaze than meets the eye. Scientists have previously found that dogs turn on the puppy eyes when humans look at them, and that their brains can distinguish happy human faces from other expressions – even telling apart fearful faces from those that are angry or sad. But while previous work has suggested dogs and humans may synchronise their blinking, and dogs may blink more when interacting with their owners rather than a familiar trainer, questions have remained over whether human blinking affects how often dogs bat their eyelids.

citation.title: Dogs blink more often when they see owners blinking, study finds

text:
Dogs blink more often when they see owners blinking, study finds

Dr Chiara Canori, the first author of the new study, from the University of Parma, said: “What we wanted to do here was experimentally isolate the human blink and separate it from all the other things that normally happen during a real social interaction, which has never been done before.” Writing in the journal Royal Society Open Science, Canori and colleagues report how they analysed recordings of 35 dogs of different breeds as each was shown two types of video. Both videos lasted 40 seconds and showed three people, one at a time: the dog’s owner and two unfamiliar humans. In one video, the humans each blinked once every three seconds, and in the other video they looked straight ahead without blinking. The results reveal dogs blinked more often when the on-screen humans blinked than when they did not. Further analysis found dogs only increased their rate of blinking when they were shown their owners blinking compared with when they displayed a still gaze – with the effect not seen for strangers.

text:
Dogs blink more often when they see owners blinking, study finds

“This suggests that the social relevance of the partner matters,” said Canori, adding that the results were not explained by dogs looking at their owners for longer. The team found no evidence that the dogs synchronised their blinking with that of humans. Canori said the findings suggested blinking – an important mechanism for protecting the eye and keeping it moist – may have acquired a social relevance. “As of today, however, we cannot say that a dog deliberately blinks in order to convey a particular message,” she said. “It may provide subtle feedback about attention or engagement and perhaps help coordinate an interaction with another individual, particularly with a socially important partner.” Canori stressed that owners should not interpret an individual blink as having a specific, fixed meaning. “Our study does not show that every time a dog blinks it is deliberately ‘saying’ something,” she said. “What our work suggests is that this apparently simple and automatic behaviour can nevertheless be influenced by the social context.

Dogs appear sensitive to blinking in other individuals, and their own blinking can change depending on who they are interacting with.” Dr Laura Cuaya, of the University of Vienna, who was not involved in the work, welcomed the findings but noted that the study’s design revealed more about how dogs perceive human blinks than whether they use blinking as a communicative cue. “Still, this study shows how socially sensitive our dogs are to subtle cues, such as blinking, on our faces,” she said. “I would be very interested to see researchers measure in their next studies whether our blinking behaviour changes when we interact with our dogs in social contexts.”

text:
Shingles vaccine linked to lower risk of heart attack and stroke, study finds

The current shingles vaccine appears to significantly lower the risk of heart attack and stroke, according to scientists who say it could help prevent thousands of deaths each year. The research, based on records of 70,000 people in the US, found that those who had received Shingrix had a 12% lower risk of a cardiovascular diagnosis in the following three and a half years. If confirmed, this benefit would be comparable to taking a daily blood pressure-lowering medication, the scientists said. Dr Maxime Taquet, a clinical lecturer at the University of Oxford, who led the study, said: “If confirmed in clinical trials, vaccinating older adults against shingles could prevent hundreds of thousands of coronary heart diseases, strokes and cases of heart failure worldwide, making it one of the most impactful interventions we could offer to protect both the brain and the heart in later life. The effect might be enormous.” Shingles is a painful and serious condition caused by reactivation of the chickenpox virus, which remains dormant in the body after an earlier infection.

citation.title: Shingles vaccine linked to lower risk of heart attack and stroke, study finds

text:
Shingles vaccine linked to lower risk of heart attack and stroke, study finds

It can cause a rash and nerve pain that may persist for months or years after the rash clears, a complication known as post-herpetic neuralgia. The first vaccine against shingles, Zostavax, was made available in 2006 and was based on a weakened version of the chickenpox virus. This was succeeded by a more effective vaccine, Shingrix, which uses newer vaccine technology and which in the UK is being made available incrementally to people aged 65-79 in a phased rollout. Several previous studies have suggested that vaccinated people may have a lower risk of cardiovascular disease. However, these studies compared vaccinated and unvaccinated people, leaving the results open to distortion. The new study got around this by comparing the incidence of cardiovascular disease in people who were vaccinated before and after the rapid switch from Zostavax to Shingrix in the US in 2017. The researchers tracked health records of 70,000 adults aged 60 and over for seven years after vaccination, which involved an initial dose and a booster.

text:
Shingles vaccine linked to lower risk of heart attack and stroke, study finds

Shingrix was associated with a 12% reduction in cardiovascular events – including heart attacks, heart failure and stroke – in the first three and a half years after vaccination. By the end of the follow-up, the vaccine was associated with a 4% lower risk of cardiovascular diseases, according to the study in Nature Medicine. While this represents a small change in absolute risk, the overall impact could be substantial given that heart disease and stroke are leading causes of death. “If confirmed in a [randomised controlled trial], the effect of Shingrix would be equivalent to antihypertensives,” Taquet said. Several trials are under way that could provide more definitive evidence. The scientists are also investigating why the vaccine may help to protect cardiovascular health. One possibility is that shingles may increase the risk of heart and vascular diseases, and so the more effective vaccine reduces this risk. Alternatively, the vaccine could be having broader effects on the immune system that suppress inflammatory proteins.

Sand overextraction weakening riverbanks as concrete demand soars

A booming demand for concrete has resulted in sand and gravel being extracted from riverbeds faster than nature can replenish it. A study published in Reviews of Geophysics shows that the demand for sand and gravel has more than doubled in the last two decades, with overextraction leading to weaker riverbanks, lower groundwater levels, coastal salt intrusion and poorer water quality. In 2024, city-building and infrastructure projects around the world turned 28bn tonnes of sand and gravel into concrete. Researchers reviewed data on sand and gravel extraction going back to 1974 and have shown that since 2000 demand has more than doubled, with more than 80% of current demand coming from Asia, supporting urban development and road-building across China and India in particular. They found much of the material was being extracted from rivers across Asia and Africa. Data on extraction is scarce but where it does exist the researchers showed that extraction often exceeded natural sediment replacement severalfold.

Sand overextraction weakening riverbanks as concrete demand soars

The researchers suggest that satellite imaging and river mapping can be used to better manage sand and gravel mining, helping to minimise negative impacts. And demand can be reduced by using materials more efficiently, plus developing alternatives such as processed construction waste, recycled glass and treated bottom ash from waste incineration.

text:
How to spot a psychopath: ‘It’s like the difference between a domestic cat and a wild cat’

The classic checklist for psychopathy was developed in 1980 by Prof Robert Hare, who is still the recognised giant of the territory. The 20 traits, which ranged from pathological lying to a lack of empathy, were based entirely on prison populations. This worked because not only did Hare have the benefit of a large sample, with pronounced psychopathic behaviours, but he was able to compare interviews and self-reporting with data collected about the individuals – so inconsistencies could be identified. However, Hare knew this approach was limited. In 1976, he said that he simply didn’t know to what extent his results could be generalised to non-incarcerated psychopaths, including female ones. “Research into the socially successful psychopath is badly needed,” he concluded. It will be a gut-wrenching moment for the horticulturalists at Kew Gardens when some of the magnificent trees in the Palm House have to be felled. “There are some sad moments ahead,” said Palm House manager, Will Spoelstra, who knows all the plants inside the cathedral-like greenhouse. But moving some of the 1,000 plants – and sacrificing others – is crucial as the botanists and horticulturalists at the world’s biggest plant collection, based in south-west London, race against time to renovate the Victorian-era glasshouse. The ornate ironwork is rusted and the 16,000 panes of glass it is comprised of are warped and damaged, making it difficult to maintain the hot, humid conditions its rare plants need. Some plants grown within are critically endangered, and in some cases, Kew holds the only specimens. “It is an exciting project,” Spoelstra says, “but we are going to lose some really nice specimens.” The giant palm trees whose fronds grow right to the roof of the building are not exactly portable, so will have to be felled.

Near total lunar eclipse will be seen from North and South America Thursday night

A near total lunar eclipse will be visible across large swathes of North and South America on Thursday night with millions of people expected to be able to see one of nature’s marvels. Lunar eclipses occur when Earth moves between the sun and the moon and its shadow is cast on to the lunar surface. In Thursday night’s event 96% of the moon will be darkened by the Earth’s shadow at its peak moment. The eclipse will be one known as a “blood moon”, as the Earth’s shadow will appear to be reddish due to the way sunlight is scattered by the Earth’s atmosphere. It will mainly be visible in the Americas but also in a few parts of Europe and Africa. It will begin about 9.23pm EST, peaking around 10.33pm EST. Earlier this month, millions of people across Europe watched a more dramatic solar eclipse where the moon blocked out the sun, plunging parts of the continent into a daytime darkness.

text:
Surprising AI breakthroughs raise soul-searching questions for mathematicians

I share Kasra Rafi and Bruce Schneier’s impression that recent mathematical breakthroughs by AI consist in clever recombination of existing ideas, not development of truly novel theory (No, AI doesn’t mean the end of mathematics – at least not yet, 25 August). The question is: what happens to mathematics if this changes? Like many mathematicians, I have done much soul-searching in recent weeks, especially since a key problem in my own field of group theory (the existence of non-sofic groups) was solved this month by OpenAI’s Astra model. Astra’s proof consists largely in a slight twist on theorems by my colleagues Gabor Kun and Andreas Thom. That said, even a few months ago I would have found the idea that AI was capable of such a breakthrough incredible, so it seems foolhardy now to bet against AIs achieving superhuman capabilities in all areas of mathematical thought in the coming years. This forces the question: what is the purpose of mathematical research? Is it simply to prove new theorems (at which task future AIs may be far better than humans)?

citation.title: Surprising AI breakthroughs raise soul-searching questions for mathematicians

text:
Surprising AI breakthroughs raise soul-searching questions for mathematicians

The great American mathematician Bill Thurston thought not: in his 1994 essay On Proof and Progress in Mathematics, he wrote that mathematicians “discover ... that what they really want is usually not some collection of ‘answers’ – what they want is understanding”. In other words, mathematics consists in the ideas living in human brains, with new theorems serving as markers for our progress in understanding and sharing these ideas. This matters, because the development of AI will stimulate debate about the value of mathematics as practised by human beings. If AI can churn out research papers faster and cheaper than humans, then administrators within cash-strapped universities will surely be tempted to regard their mathematical researchers as superfluous. On Thurston’s view, this would be a mistake, because the value of those researchers’ work consists less in the papers they write than in their contributions to the preservation and furtherance of mathematical knowledge among people.

Protect fossils from hammer-wielding tourists

I write this while sitting on Charmouth beach in Dorset with my required reading of the Saturday Guardian, as I do regularly. Your editorial (The Guardian view on the export of fossils: they deserve national treasure status, 21 August) produced a hollow laugh as – this being the centre of fossil hunting on the Jurassic Coast – I am surrounded by armies of hammer-wielding tourists busy smashing the daylights out of any rock available around them. The vast majority have no idea which stone types are likely to bear fossils and don’t report any finds even if they are lucky. Others take carrier bags full of stones back to their cars. Related: Abundant common fossils don’t need to be protected Thus, we have no idea what fossils are being lost to the record every single day here, and so I completely support the suggestion of giving them legal protection. Of course, amateur collecting has a valuable place in unearthing important fossil finds, but only if they are shared and documented. The Charmouth Heritage Coast Centre valiantly tries to educate and inform visitors, but sadly these will inevitably be the minority.

Nasa space telescope launches after surviving Trump budget cuts

A $4.3bn space telescope that Donald Trump tried to kill has lifted off from Florida as Nasa embarks on the next stage of its quest to unlock the secrets of the universe. The Nancy Grace Roman space telescope survived two rounds of proposed White House budget cuts, and began a million-mile journey into deep space from a launchpad at the Kennedy Space Center on Sunday morning. . Sunday’s launch marked “an endpoint for the engineers, ⁠but it’s a starting point for the scientists,” Julie McEnery, the telescope’s senior project scientist, told reporters, including Reuters, at a post-launch news conference. “It feels like I’m on the edge of a precipice, and we’re just about to set a foot off into the unknown.” Searching chiefly for exoplanets and clues about planetary formation, it is set to join the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes in the annals of Nasa’s storied history of space exploration.

But as next-generation equipment almost 10 years in the making, the Roman telescope, named for the space agency’s first chief of astronomy, who died in 2018, is many times more powerful than Hubble and will work to enhance the output of its stablemates, both of which continue to operate. According to Nasa, its 300-megapixel infrared camera will give Roman the same sharpness and resolution as Hubble, but with a field of view at least 100 times larger. The agency says each image will capture a patch of sky about 1.5 times bigger than the apparent size of a full moon. Roman also contains a specialized instrument known as a coronagraph that blocks glare from stars and makes it easier to photograph planets around them in detail. Nasa said it expected the images would reveal “giant worlds that are older, colder, and in closer orbits than the hot, young super-Jupiters direct imaging has mainly revealed so far”.

It is not entirely a successor to Hubble and Webb, which were launched in 1990 and 2021, respectively, but was designed to support and advance their missions, while making discoveries of its own. Nasa said Roman’s large panoramas would “uncover interesting targets that Hubble could follow up on using infrared, visible, and ultraviolet light to offer a more comprehensive view”, while Webb “can then use its larger mirror and more powerful vision to deliver even more detailed, ultra-sharp observations”. Roman, meanwhile, can view regions around objects Hubble or Webb observe “to offer context”. Its imagery, which Nasa expects will first come in early 2027 after months of calibration and tests in the telescope’s final orbit, will be made immediately public, allowing the agency, professional researchers and amateur astronomers an unprecedented opportunity for analysis.

Children need a better education in sniffing aromas, a leading historian of smells has said, noting it may improve their wellbeing and help them understand the world around them. Dr Will Tullett, of the University of York, said pollution had been found to impair people’s olfactory abilities, while many objects and substances today – from margarines to car interiors and even our own homes – were stripped of their original smells and “reodourised” with synthetic scents. “There is an open question about what the proliferation of those kinds of synthetic scents in our daily lives does to our ability to discriminate between different smells,” he said. As a result, Tullett said, there was a need for olfactory education. “I would love a world where at primary and secondary school people are taught to engage their noses,” he said, adding that training could also be done at home. He said one approach would be to encourage people to smell more items. “The more we smell, the more we enlarge the vocabulary through which we can describe other things,” he said, noting that sommeliers took a similar approach.

Forbidden planet: was Pluto’s 2006 demotion a big mistake?

Twenty years ago, Pluto got demoted. After a vote by the International Astronomical Union (IAU) in August 2006, Pluto was relegated from major planet to dwarf planet status. Our solar system dropped from nine planets to eight. At the time, many scientists were unhappy with the decision. Two decades on, the debate is, if anything, even more polarised. “The definition of a planet they created, you can’t use it at all,” says Philip Metzger, the director of the Stephen W Hawking Centre for Microgravity Research and Education at the University of Central Florida. “It makes the definition of a planet completely non-useful in science.” Metzger is one of a number of scientists and lay people who consider Pluto’s demotion a big mistake. For some, Pluto’s downgraded status is the source of their affection for the ex-planet. “Pluto represents the underdog that so many people root for, the small kid on the block that is being picked on,” says Kevin Schindler, historian at the Lowell Observatory in Arizona, where Pluto was discovered in 1930. For others, the IAU’s decision, and the way it was taken, is central to the debate.

About two years ago, Henry, who is 6ft 3in, weighed 210lb, which meant he was only slightly overweight, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention body mass index. Still, the thirtysomething who lives in the Pacific north-west had hypertension, sleep apnea and body image issues, so he started taking the weight-loss drug Ozempic. While he dropped pounds, he experienced constipation, a common side-effect, so he wanted to try retatrutide, another peptide which not only targets GLP-1 but two other hormone receptors as well. He had read about it in the news and on Reddit forums. The problem is, the US Food and Drug Administration has not approved the drug, so Henry bought it online from sellers in China. Starwatch: Sagitta’s arrow shape makes it easy to see against a dark sky

We are on the hunt for another small, northern summer constellation this week: Sagitta, the arrow. Although it consists of just a handful of faint stars, Sagitta’s distinctive shape (it really does look like an arrow) makes it easy to identify against a dark sky. The chart shows the view looking up towards the zenith while facing south from London at 22.30 BST on Monday. Sagitta can be found about partway along the imaginary line connecting Vega and Altair, which make up the summer triangle with Deneb. Although it is the third-smallest constellation in the sky, Sagitta has been recognised since ancient times. The 2nd-century astronomer Ptolemy placed it on his list of 48 constellations published in The Almagest. There are a number of stories from Greek mythology that could be attributed to the arrow. It could be the one fired by Hercules to kill the eagle tormenting Prometheus, or it could be one of Cupid’s famous arrows. Observers in the southern hemisphere can also see Sagitta during August, although it appears lower in the northern sky than it does from the UK.

‘Hugely exciting’ finds on tiny Scottish island shed light on spread of Christianity

To the residents of the Scottish island of Lismore, population 190, history is never very far away. The tiny island near Oban in Argyll has no row of shops or even a pub – if islanders want to meet for a coffee, the only place to do so is in the lively Gaelic heritage centre that records the many centuries of community life on the island. This quiet place, documentary evidence records, was home to a monastic settlement in the sixth century AD, when missionaries from Ireland were first moving into northern Britain to spread Christianity. But apart from a few fragments of an early carved cross, there was almost nothing to see from this period of history. A group of local people from the island’s historical society were determined to look a bit harder, however. After scraping together funding from grants, donations and legacies of locals and a crowdfunding campaign, they commissioned a professional archaeologist, Dr Clare Ellis of Argyll Archaeology, to lead a group of islanders and other volunteers in an excavation on the site of a much later medieval cathedral.

What the islanders discovered were extensive burial grounds, decorated stonework and early buildings – all the features belonging to a major sixth-century monastery, comparable to the much better known site of Iona a little to the south-west. In addition, the excavations uncovered rare evidence of slightly later high-status craftworking, including huge numbers of crucibles which had been used to cast gold and silver. The finds have shown that rather than being a small island church in an overlooked backwater, the monastery of Lios Mór, founded by Saint Mo Luóc or Moluag, was a high-ranking site of international importance, experts say. Do humans really have a ‘lizard brain’ lurking beneath our rational minds?

Humans have a cognitive quirk for the number three. Think of the many stories that use it, from The Three Little Pigs to Goldilocks and the Three Bears and The Three Musketeers. Public information and political campaigns use it for impact and ease of recall (“Stop, look and listen”; “See it. Say it. Sorted”; “Reduce, reuse, recycle”). And then there are psychological or philosophical frameworks: Freud with his id, ego and superego; Plato’s three parts of the human soul; the Holy Trinity. Well, it turns out neuroscience isn’t immune from tri-mania. In 1959 Paul D MacLean set out a new way of thinking about the evolution and function of the brain, which he christened the “triune” – three-in-one – model. It quickly became one of best known and most enduring concepts in human biology. His idea was that a trio of distinct brains are layered inside our skulls, one on top of the other, all fighting to generate our feelings and thoughts. Deep inside, at the centre, lurks the primitive lizard brain, retained from an ancestor we share with reptiles.

This contains ancient regions responsible for survival, helping us to hunt and forage, and driving our sexual impulses so that we reproduce. A second layer sits wrapped around the first, the so-called mammalian brain. It contains the limbic system, deemed to be the seat of our emotions. It enabled mammals to play, care for and nurse their young and communicate in some crude way. The third and final layer, sheathing all of this and making humans in particular a cut above, is the “neomammalian” brain: the eminently rational cortex. This, it was proposed, provides us with our superior intellect, capacity for language and ability to reason. According to MacLean, it helped to keep in check our primitive, lizard-like impulses and rudimentary emotional reactions. The analogy – of an onion-like brain made up of different strata – is now considered deeply misleading by neurobiologists Human behaviour was thought to be a result of interactions between all three layers of the triune brain. Frayed tempers, impulsive acts and short termism were signs of the lizard brain winning out.

citation.title: Do humans really have a ‘lizard brain’ lurking beneath our rational minds?

text:
Do humans really have a ‘lizard brain’ lurking beneath our rational minds?

The notion of reptilian impulses “breaking through” proved so popular it found its way into the worlds of pop psychology, business and self-help, and has proved remarkably tenacious. A mini-industry of books, talks and training grew up around the idea that you could draw on the power of the neomammalian brain to keep basic, unhelpful or destructive emotions in check. The underpinning analogy – of an onion-like brain made up of different strata – is now considered deeply misleading by neurobiologists. It’s easy to grasp, sure, and tells a compelling story. But evolution just doesn’t bolt-on neatly divisible mental capacities in this way. MacLean conducted dissections of living creatures to try to prove his theory, but the results, and his interpretations of them, have since been largely discredited. For example, it’s now accepted that many reptiles do actually possess the “mammalian” limbic system, while all mammals exhibit “neomammalian” features previously thought to be unique to “higher” ones like us.

text:
Do humans really have a ‘lizard brain’ lurking beneath our rational minds?

Alongside these anatomical observations, there’s the behavioural data too, with many “lower” animals good at problem solving, responding and learning via emotion, and communicating in complex ways. As Guy Leschziner, consultant neurologist at London’s Guy’s and St Thomas’ hospital put it to me: “the concept of different parts of the brain having different functions is extremely well established. However, to portray humans as having different brain layers, for example a ‘lizard brain’ underlying basic physiological functions, is not borne out by evolutionary or physiological evidence. For a start, mammals and reptiles split early in evolutionary terms. Whilst it is true that more primitive functions in our brains evolved earlier in the course of life on Earth, this view of three separate brain systems driving our basic instincts, emotions and logic respectively does not stack up.” Lisa Feldman Barrett, professor of psychology at Northeastern University is another contemporary voice actively debunking the lizard brain myth.

text:
Do humans really have a ‘lizard brain’ lurking beneath our rational minds?

In her view, rather than operating as a battleground between ancient instinct, raw emotion and sophisticated logic, the brain is a dynamic, integrated system, whose aim is to keep us alive by predicting and budgeting our energy requirements. Neuroanatomically and behaviourally, if not yet in the popular consciousness, the idea that we all have a lizard brain has been thoroughly discredited. Yet despite the mounting evidence, and the success of more recent frameworks, the triune brain endures. Shockingly, it is still being widely taught in introductory psychology textbooks (as one journal article mischievously titled “Your Brain Is Not an Onion With a Tiny Reptile Inside” showed). The study also highlighted some of the pitfalls of allowing the hypothesis to go unchallenged, which include giving students a false sense of how evolution unfolds, and promoting the idea that human beings have a monopoly on “rational” actions such as deferring gratification – sacrificing a short-term reward for a longer-term gain. Related: Is culture alive? So, what is it about MacLean’s model that we just can’t seem to let go of?

text:
Do humans really have a ‘lizard brain’ lurking beneath our rational minds?

Well, as we’ve seen, people really do seem to love threes. But perhaps there’s more to it than that. The triune brain tells us an ego-stroking story about our place in the world: that we really are the pinnacle of evolution, standing apart from other species. It reaffirms heady ideas about our sovereignty over nature, and tells a reassuring story about our logical, orderly, almost computational abilities. We are storytelling creatures, of course, but this is a story that needs updating – to one about how much in common we have with other animals, and how simplistic assumptions about the way our minds work are almost never true. • Dr Hannah Critchlow is a neuroscientist and author of The 21st Century Brain (Torva). Starwatch: how to spot Saturn as it makes it closest approach to Earth this year

This week offers an excellent opportunity to track down Saturn. The giant planet, situated about 10 times further from the sun than the Earth, reached opposition on 4 October. In this configuration, Earth is passing almost directly between the planet and the sun. This makes opposition an excellent time to see a planet: the distant world rises as the sun sets, remains visible throughout the night and sets around sunrise. It is also at about its closest point to Earth for the year. Saturn is easily visible to the naked eye, looking like a moderately bright, creamy-white object. Unlike most stars, however, its light remains steady rather than noticeably twinkling. The chart shows the view looking east- south-east from London at 2100 BST on 5 October. By this time, Saturn is already well clear of the horizon and will continue climbing higher as the evening progresses. It lies beneath the Great Square of Pegasus, which provides a distinctive signpost to the planet. Saturn is currently shining at about magnitude +0.3. Once you have identified it, try returning to it on subsequent evenings.

Nobel prize in medicine 2026 awarded for research into mysteries of brain

The Nobel prize in physiology or medicine 2026 has been awarded to three scientists for their work investigating the mysteries of the brain. Karl Deisseroth of the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and Stanford University, Peter Hegemann of the Humboldt University of Berlin and Georg Nagel of the University of Würzburg have been awarded the prize “for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics”. The Nobel assembly at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, Sweden, announced the winners on Monday. They will each receive an equal share of a prize of 12m Swedish kronor (about £900,000). The 2026 award is the 117th time the prize has been given. Of the 235 laureates – including the latest winners – only 14 have been women and none have been awarded to black scientists. In a nutshell the trio’s research led to the development of a light-sensitive switch that can be used to control nerve cells in the living brain, switching them on or off.

citation.title: Nobel prize in medicine 2026 awarded for research into mysteries of brain

text:
Nobel prize in medicine 2026 awarded for research into mysteries of brain

Jonathan Levin, the president of Stanford University, said the subsequent discoveries by Deisseroth, along with those of his fellow laureates, have deepened understanding of neural circuits and how they shape feelings, behaviour, and more. “Their implications are profound, not only for understanding the human brain, but for opening possibilities into new treatments for neurological and psychiatric disorders,” he said. The work had its origins in research by Hegemann, who wanted to explore how a green alga called Chlamydomonas swam towards light. “He discovered that its eye spot contains a light-sensitive protein that converts light almost instantly into an electrical signal, allowing the alga to move,” said Abdel El Manira, a professor of neuroscience at the Karolinska Institute and member of the Nobel assembly. Nagel and Hegemann identified the proteins, called channelrhodopsins, and working with frog egg cells they revealed that when the proteins were exposed to blue light, they allowed charged particles – or ions – to flow into the cell, producing an electrical impulse.

citation.title: Nobel prize in medicine 2026 awarded for research into mysteries of brain

text:
Nobel prize in medicine 2026 awarded for research into mysteries of brain

Further work by the pair revealed that when the genetic instructions for one of the proteins were inserted into human or mouse kidney cells, those cells became light sensitive. Deisseroth took the discovery even further, using rats to demonstrate that by introducing the gene for a channelrhodopsin into nerve cells, it was possible to produce electrical signals in them using light. He and his colleagues later applied the approach to nerve cells in the motor cortex of the brains of mice, allowing them to use light – delivered by tiny optic fibres passed through their skull – to trigger movement in the rodent’s whiskers. Subsequent work in mice showed the approach could also be used to investigate which networks of nerve cells were involved in the formation of particular memories, including fear. While rooted in basic science, the team’s work has already had real-world implications, opening up a field of medicine known as optogenetic therapy.

citation.title: Nobel prize in medicine 2026 awarded for research into mysteries of brain

text:
Nobel prize in medicine 2026 awarded for research into mysteries of brain

In one trial it was used to partially restore the sight of a man who went blind as a result of retinitis pigmentosa, a condition that results in damage to light-sensitive cells in the retina. In that case, the genetic instructions for making a channelrhodopsin were delivered by means of a harmless virus into retinal ganglion cells in the man’s eyes. He was then kitted out with light-stimulating goggles that captured pictures of the world around him and converted them into single-wavelength images that were projected on to his retina using pulses of light. Prof Botond Roska, the director of the Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology Basel who co-led the study, welcomed the announcement of the Nobel laureates. “This is truly wonderful news. I hope this helps to boost all efforts on optogenetic vision restoration to bring back vision to blind patients,” he said.

citation.title: Nobel prize in medicine 2026 awarded for research into mysteries of brain

text:
Nobel prize in medicine 2026 awarded for research into mysteries of brain

Anna Wedell, a professor at Karolinska Institute and a member of the Nobel committee for physiology or medicine, said the laureates’ work had provided new possibilities to map which cells were responsible for which functions, and which cells communicated with each other, opening up a new understanding of the function of the brain. “We’ve had anatomical maps and correlations, but now we have a tool that can provide cause-and-effect relationships so we can get a functional map of the brain, exactly pinpoint which cells do what, which cells are responsible for creating behaviours or even emotions and memories in the brain,” she said. Wedell said that by studying animals to understand how a normal, healthy brain worked, it was then possible to explore what happened when thing went wrong – for example in the case of diseases such as dementia, epilepsy and addiction. “By understanding which cells are active in these diseases in the mouse, we can also understand where to look in the human,” she said.

Skull fractures suggest servants of Egypt’s ancient kings were sacrificed

Court officials and craftspeople serving early Egyptian kings may have been sacrificed when their ruler died, according to research that found fractures in several ancient skulls. The royal cemetery of Umm el-Qa’ab near Abydos features the tombs and enclosures of the First Dynasty rulers of Egypt, and dates as far back as 3,000BC. Not only royalty were buried at the site: surrounding these structures are graves thought to belong to people associated with the royal households – including ladies, seal-bearers, inspectors and artisans. Writing in the journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, Dr Roselyn Campbell, author of the study from Purdue University in the US, notes: “While Aha, the first ruler of the First Dynasty, seems to have only had a few subsidiary burials, his successors included hundreds of subsidiary graves around their tombs and enclosures.” The graves of the retainers were excavated in the 1920s by the English Egyptologist Flinders Petrie, who believed them to be an example of human sacrifice – a view some later experts agreed with.

citation.title: Skull fractures suggest servants of Egypt’s ancient kings were sacrificed

text:
Skull fractures suggest servants of Egypt’s ancient kings were sacrificed

But there was a snag: Petrie did not find any evidence of trauma on the remains. While he suggested the individuals may have been buried alive, others suggested the retainers died naturally and were later reburied at Abydos when their ruler died. Campbell re-examined the skulls of 46 retainers excavated from graves surrounding the funerary enclosures of three different royals – King Djer, King Djet, and Queen Merneith – from the Duckworth Collections at the University of Cambridge. “This question of whether or not retainer sacrifice was practised in Egypt has been debated for over a century,” Campbell told the Guardian, but she said this was the first study to look at trauma and cause of death while examining human remains from the tombs. Campbell reports that 18 of the skulls showed signs of potentially lethal trauma such as fractures and – in one case – a chopping injury to the eye. Campbell believs Petrie may have seen the skull fractures but did not realise they were injuries that occurred around the time of death, rather than arising as a result of later damage.

citation.title: Skull fractures suggest servants of Egypt’s ancient kings were sacrificed

text:
Skull fractures suggest servants of Egypt’s ancient kings were sacrificed

The fractures, she adds, are unlikely to have been caused by a mace – a weapon often depicted in ancient Egyptian art as being used by a victorious king to smite his enemies. Instead they are more likely to have been caused by flat, wide objects made of wood or antler. “For the crania without trauma, we cannot be certain they were sacrificed. It’s quite possible that some of the retainers were sacrificed, while others were not,” she said. “With such a small sample size of the original burial population, we simply can’t see the full extent of these funerary rituals, nor can we be sure that this sample is truly representative of all the retainers.” Campbell noted the number of subsidiary graves tapered off quickly and seems to have disappeared with the beginning of the Second Dynasty. Salima Ikram, a professor at the American University in Cairo, said while the idea of retainer sacrifice was not totally new, “this paper is one of the few times that rigorous current methodologies are being used to evaluate these remains”. She added: “The practice was short-lived, with people being replaced by statuettes.

Possibly some or all retainers felt that this was a boon and that they would enjoy an eternal life in the service of the god-king, though they might also have resented it, been terrified, and tried to escape this fate.” Dr Dawn McCormack, an Egyptologist at Samford University, Alabama, said similar sacrifices had occurred across different cultures and times, adding that not everyone at the Egyptian site may have been compliant. “If you really think about what those scenes would have looked like, it would have been very gruesome,” she said. While noting that the study only involved a small number of skulls from the burial site, “the idea that some of the people may have been violently killed, I think, is something that in reality we might expect”, she said. • This article was amended on 6 October 2026. An earlier version quoted Rose Campbell as saying this was the first study to examine human remains from the Umm el-Qa’ab tombs; to clarify, this is the first study to do so with the purpose of identifying trauma and cause of death.

Making scents: could AI help perfumers take pressure off endangered plants?

Many of the world’s most expensive perfumes begin with a wounded tree. When some Aquilaria trees are damaged, they produce a dark, fragrant resin that becomes agarwood, or oudh – an ingredient so valuable that wild trees have been illegally felled in its pursuit. The result has devastated wild Aquilaria populations. But what if perfumers could create the smell without cutting down the tree? With the help of AI, scientists are learning to predict how molecules that have never been made will smell, reconstructing scent-producing genes from flowers believed to be extinct. Others have collected microbes from clouds and used them as a starting point for new perfumes. Now scientists and biotechnology companies say advances could soon allow the fragrance industry to reproduce scents and compounds from endangered plants without repeatedly harvesting them.

citation.title: Making scents: could AI help perfumers take pressure off endangered plants?

text:
Making scents: could AI help perfumers take pressure off endangered plants?

“Being able to recreate the scent of an endangered plant would be a huge win for both the environment but also the brands,” said Alex Wiltschko, the founder of Osmo, a Google Brain spin-off that has raised $130m to develop artificial intelligence capable of predicting and recreating smells. Osmo has recreated the scent of a rare tree from a piece of bark “the size of a finger”, Wiltschko said. A spectrometer analysed the sample, its AI reconstructed the chemical formula and the scent was reproduced in its laboratory. BioHarvest Sciences says it has created a stable cell culture from an endangered south-east Asian fragrance plant, allowing its valuable compounds to be produced without cultivating or harvesting the original plant. The plant has not been named for commercial reasons but BioHarvest has announced an agreement anticipating production of 20 tonnes of the fragrance composition, with limited production potentially beginning next year. “The challenge is that human demand can be effectively unlimited while biological supply is not,” said BioHarvest’s chief executive, Zaki Rakib.

citation.title: Making scents: could AI help perfumers take pressure off endangered plants?

text:
Making scents: could AI help perfumers take pressure off endangered plants?

“We believe biotechnology can help close that gap, not by replacing nature but by allowing us to use what nature has given us without continually putting the source under pressure.” But conservationists and perfumers say such claims risk giving advances in fragrance technology an environmental gloss they have not yet earned. “Calling this conservation is greenwashing,” said Mandy Aftel, the pioneering natural perfumer, author and founder of the Aftel Archive of Curious Scents. “Making a synthetic version of an endangered plant’s smell doesn’t save the plant.” She said producing a substitute did not stop people buying the original – or address other causes of a species’ decline. Rhian Smith, of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, agreed. She pointed to the Aquilaria tree. AI could help design an alternative to oudh, she said, but wild-sourced material remained highly prized. “It doesn’t completely take the pressure off wild plant populations,” she said. There is also the question of motivation. Wiltschko admitted that conservation was not “an explicit priority” for Osmo’s work.

text:
Making scents: could AI help perfumers take pressure off endangered plants?

Synthetic perfume itself is nothing new: the industry has relied heavily on synthetic ingredients for more than a century, and machines have long been able to identify molecules in a scent. “What’s changed is what happens after the data comes off the machine,” Wiltschko said. “What’s new is prediction.” He claimed Osmo had trained its AI on more than 5m human responses to smells. “That means it can predict how combinations of molecules will be perceived,” he said. Elsewhere, AI is claimed to be changing the whole world in which perfumers work. Christina Agapakis is not a perfumer, but her work reconstructing genes from preserved flowers has produced fragrance compounds that perfumers can use to create new scents. Another perfumer, Future Society, has gone into the clouds, making two flights in a small plane to collect living microbes. Thirteen were identified, producing 57 scent molecules, which became the starting point for Cloud Reverie, a perfume launched this year.

text:
Making scents: could AI help perfumers take pressure off endangered plants?

Even AI has its limits: a flower’s scent can contain hundreds of molecules and change according to which part of the plant they come from and the conditions in which it grows. It is still not enough for the purists. “The smell we got was this ghostly fragment of what had been lost,” Agapakis said of her project. She could not recreate the living organism, or the soil, climate, season and ecology that produced its scent, she said. “What we have to remember is, ultimately, however powerful AI is, a smell is not simply a formula or dataset.”
