Nobel prize in physics goes to Francis Halzen for south pole work on neutrinos

The Nobel prize in physics 2026 has been awarded to a researcher who turned an enormous block of ice at the south pole into a detector for ghostly particles called neutrinos that reach Earth from outer space. Prof Francis Halzen, a Belgian particle physicist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, led work on the IceCube neutrino observatory, which made the first detection of high-energy extraterrestrial neutrinos in 2013, soon after it was switched on. To build the observatory, scientists, technicians and engineers embedded thousands of basketball-sized light detectors into a cubic kilometre of ice to detect faint flashes of light that can result when neutrinos from space crash into atomic nuclei. Announcing the prize on Tuesday, the Nobel committee said Halzen won “for decisive contributions to the IceCube neutrino observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin”. He receives a prize of 12m Swedish kronor (about £900,000). “It feels strange,” Halzen told a press briefing on winning the prize.

citation.title: Nobel prize in physics goes to Francis Halzen for south pole work on neutrinos

text:
Nobel prize in physics goes to Francis Halzen for south pole work on neutrinos

“I hope it reflects on the really courageous people who joined me in the beginning of this project when no really respectable, conservative physicist would have joined me, but many talented people did.” Neutrinos are mysterious particles that are as elusive as they are ubiquitous. They pass through almost everything they encounter, from people to planets. Every second, billions of neutrinos from the sun pass unnoticed through the body. But every now and then, a neutrino will interact with the nucleus of an atom in a collision that can be picked up by a sensitive detector. Halzen realised that brief flickers of light from neutrino collisions could be detected in clear, glacial ice and in 1988 put forward a plan to convert a chunk of the south pole into a neutrino observatory. The detector uses Earth to shield against the background noise of cosmic rays, and has downwards-facing light sensors to detect neutrinos passing through the planet from the northern hemisphere.

Apart from a hostile environment for the team, the site benefited from being far from sources of interference and the risk of vibrations from earthquakes. After the first detection of high-energy extraterrestrial neutrinos in 2013, scientists working on IceCube identified the first cosmic source of neutrinos 3.7bn light years away. The observatory has paved the way for a new kind of astronomy. Until now, researchers have learned about the cosmos from light, other electromagnetic radiation, and gravitational waves. Neutrinos are considered messengers from the cosmos and provide fresh clues as to how the universe evolved. Halzen, who received the news while travelling in Italy, said he was working on a new proposal and hoped that winning the prize would help in getting it approved. Dr Patrick Dunne at Imperial College London welcomed the prize. “For all of human history the only way we’ve been able to understand things outside our solar system is with light.

Detecting neutrinos from astrophysical sources opens up a new lens, so it isn’t overstating things to liken this to when Galileo first pointed a telescope at the stars,” he said. “Neutrinos are the most abundant massive particles and their ability to pass through matter much more easily than light makes them ideal for observing distant phenomena or the inside of extreme phenomena like those seen by IceCube,” he added. Other experiments to understand neutrinos include the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (Dune) in the US and the Hyper-Kamiokande detector in Japan. The observations of cosmic neutrinos have led some scientists to speculate that the ghostly particles could be used by alien civilisations to send messages across the universe. Asked what he made of the idea, Halzen said: “I don’t think I’ll go there. Jonathan the giant tortoise, 194, offers up insight into secrets of longevity

The ancient quest to extend human lifespan has received a boost after scientists analysed the genetic code of the world’s oldest living land animal, a giant tortoise called Jonathan. The tortoise, which lives in the grounds of Plantation House, the official residence of the governor of Saint Helena in the South Atlantic, is believed to be 194 years old, making him a contemporary of Queen Victoria and Charles Darwin. Analysis of the animal’s DNA revealed a host of genetic variants in most of the biological pathways for ageing that scientists have discovered. Together, they help organisms to survive by repairing damaged DNA, regulating their metabolism and fending off cancer. But more intriguing to the researchers were chemical patterns on Jonathan’s genes that appear to protect the healthy functioning of his mitochondria, the tiny battery-like structures that power biological cells. Ailing mitochondria have been strongly linked to ageing and age-related diseases.

citation.title: Jonathan the giant tortoise, 194, offers up insight into secrets of longevity

text:
Jonathan the giant tortoise, 194, offers up insight into secrets of longevity

“We’re still trying to work out how ageing occurs and Jonathan gives us a real window on to what happens over a long period of time,” said Stephen Clark, a senior researcher on the project at the non-profit Kallel Foundation. “His mitochondria must be especially stable and that’s an insight into longevity in general. It’s important that the mitochondria are kept as pristine as possible.” The insight came when the international team, led by Benjamin Vaisvil, looked at chemical tags that attach to DNA, creating patterns that change over time. The tags, known as methyl groups, typically silence the genes they latch on to. Writing in Science Advances, the researchers describe how they compared the methylation patterns on Jonathan’s genes with those from other giant tortoises. The patterns on many of his genes were similar to those of other old tortoises, but the patterns on genes linked to mitochondrial function matched those from much younger animals. It is unclear whether, or how much, the chemical patterning contributes to Jonathan’s impressive lifespan.

citation.title: Jonathan the giant tortoise, 194, offers up insight into secrets of longevity

text:
Jonathan the giant tortoise, 194, offers up insight into secrets of longevity

Clark said the team now needed to validate the finding. “How do we test this idea?” he said. “Is there a way that makes the mitochondria young, or can we replace the mitochondria and see if it extends longevity? That’s one of the next steps.” The former senior veterinary officer of Saint Helena, Joe Hollis, took over Jonathan’s care in 2009. He was not faring well at the time. Cataracts had left him blind, he had lost his sense of smell and his beak was soft and crumbly, making it hard to forage. Hollis began hand-feeding him and six months to a year later, the tortoise had regained weight and sported a hard, serrated beak. In April, Jonathan was caught up in a viral crypto death scam when a message from a fake X account posing as Hollis claimed the tortoise had died. The news spread around the world before the Guardian made contact with Nigel Phillips, the governor of Saint Helena, who interrupted his bedtime routine to check on Jonathan. He found him asleep under a tree but “very much alive”. Jonathan certainly appears to be enjoying life.

A few months ago, he was found mating with Emma, who shares his paddock. Margaret Hamilton, trailblazer whose software powered Apollo 11 moon landing, dies aged 90

Margaret Hamilton, the computer pioneer whose software powered the first moon landing, has died, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) announced on Wednesday. She was 90. In an era before titles such as software engineer and computer scientist became mainstream, Hamilton, who died on 30 September, learned to program under the tutelage of a renowned MIT meteorologist. She continued to perfect the craft in an MIT laboratory, writing software that could detect enemy aircraft. When the institute received a Nasa contract to develop the Apollo onboard flight software, she jumped at the opportunity. Related: Margaret Hamilton: ‘They worried that the men might rebel. They didn’t’ “I was attracted both by the sheer idea and the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired,” she told the Guardian in 2019. In 1969, minutes before the Apollo 11 spacecraft was set to make history by landing on the lunar surface, an onboard computer’s alarm rang, indicating an emergency.

citation.title: Margaret Hamilton, trailblazer whose software powered Apollo 11 moon landing, dies aged 90

text:
Margaret Hamilton, trailblazer whose software powered Apollo 11 moon landing, dies aged 90

Faced with a decision of whether to abort the mission, the spacecraft continued on. The software was working just as Hamilton and her team intended. “It quickly became clear the software was not only informing everyone that there was a hardware-related problem but was compensating for it – restarting and re-establishing the highest priority tasks. The error detection and recovery mechanisms had come to the rescue,” Hamilton said. Barack Obama referenced the incident when he presented her with the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016. “Our astronauts didn’t have much time, but thankfully they had Margaret Hamilton,” he said. Hamilton is survived by her daughter, a son-in-law, two grandsons and four great-grandchildren, according to MIT. Reflecting on the mission, in a 2009 interview with MIT News, Hamilton said: “Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers; no time to be beginners.”

Nobel prize in chemistry awarded for work on mirror-image molecules

The Nobel prize in chemistry 2026 has been awarded to two scientists for discoveries that showed how chemical reactions can produce an overwhelming excess of one of two mirror image forms of a molecule. Henri B Kagan at Paris-Sud University in France and Kensō Soai at Tokyo University of Science in Japan have been awarded the prize “for the discovery of nonlinear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis”. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winners in Stockholm, Sweden, on Wednesday. They will each receive an equal share of a prize of 12m Swedish kronor (about £900,000). Many molecules, including amino acids that form the building blocks of proteins, can exist in two forms that contain the same atoms, but are mirror images of one another, much like a person’s left and right hands. This property is known as chirality. However, the chemistry underpinning life is surprisingly “homochiral”, or same-handed. Proteins are built almost exclusively from L-amino acids, while the sugars that form the backbone of DNA and RNA have the opposite D- configuration.

text:
Nobel prize in chemistry awarded for work on mirror-image molecules

How this homochirality could have emerged when chemical reactions in the laboratory typically produce equal quantities of both forms had long puzzled scientists. The question also had practical consequences: “Although these molecules look very similar, they can behave very differently when they interact with other molecules,” said Prof Andre Cobb, an organic chemist at King’s College London. “This matters enormously for medicines because many of the molecules in our bodies, including proteins that drugs target, are themselves chiral. So the ‘left-handed’ and ‘right-handed’ versions of a drug can interact with the body in different ways which can lead to different or weakened drug effects.” The drug thalidomide provides a potent example. During the early 1960s, thousands of children were affected by birth defects after their mothers were prescribed it to combat morning sickness during pregnancy. Researchers subsequently found differences in the biological effects of the drug’s two mirror image forms.

text:
Nobel prize in chemistry awarded for work on mirror-image molecules

Manufacturers wanted a way of steering reactions towards particular forms of the molecules that they produced, and Kagan and Soai eventually provided a solution. It began in 1986, when Kagan discovered that a relatively small imbalance between left- and right-handed forms of a catalyst could create a greater excess of one of the mirror image products than the other. Soai took the idea further, developing a reaction in which the molecules produced themselves acted as catalysts for making more of themselves, a process known as autocatalysis. “You have to be aware, this is probably the coolest experiment in organic chemistry ever,” said Prof Peter Somfai, an organic chemist at Lund University and a member of the Nobel committee for chemistry. In 2003, Soai demonstrated a reaction that produced almost exclusively one mirror-image form, reproducing the kind of molecular one-handedness found in living organisms for the first time.

Nobel prize in chemistry awarded for work on mirror-image molecules

Speaking by telephone at Wednesday’s announcement, Soai, 76, said he was “very proud” of the experiment as it offered a potential explanation for how the molecular one-handedness of life could have arisen. He described hearing the news about the prize as “one of the most exciting days of my life”. Taken together, Kagan and Soai’s discoveries had “reshaped our understanding of molecular chirality, how it is created, amplified and transmitted”, Somfai said. These insights have since become embedded in the development of catalysts that steer chemical reactions towards producing a particular mirror image form across different industries. “It is in the backsides of our heads all the time,” said Somfai. “It might be difficult to say that this drug or that drug was developed using this. I would say all of them because we use this as a tool. We use this as an understanding of how to develop catalysts and how they function.”

text:
Ada Yonath obituary

For years, the crystallographer and biochemist Ada Yonath had to contend with the disdain and sometimes derision of many of her contemporaries after she set herself the challenge of mapping the molecular structure of the ribosome. Ribosomes are found in all living cells. Effectively they are tiny factories that synthesise proteins, complex molecules that are vital for building and repairing the tissues and organs of animals and plants. Many scientists believed hers was a fruitless endeavour because ribosomes are so small – sometimes only 20 nanometres in diameter – irregular in shape and lacking internal symmetry. James Watson, one of the Nobel prizewinning discoverers of the double-helix structure of DNA, had tried and failed. But Yonath, who has died aged 87, proved her doubters wrong, and was rewarded with the 2009 Nobel prize in chemistry, only the fourth woman to receive it, which she shared with the biologist Venkatraman Ramakrishnan and biochemist Thomas Steitz. “I was met with disbelief, even ridicule in the international scientific community,” she said later. “I was called a dreamer, a fantasist, even the village idiot.

citation.title: Ada Yonath obituary

text:
Ada Yonath obituary

But when I succeeded, it created an overwhelming internal joy and those who once called me crazy or stupid became supporters.” I was called a dreamer, a fantasist, even the village idiot. But when I succeeded, it created an overwhelming joy. It was in the late 1970s, while being laid up following a bicycle accident, and indulging in some “easier” reading, that Yonath, then a young scientist based at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovot, Israel, chanced upon the article that would lead to her eventual breakthrough. Reading about the biology of polar bears, she learned that the bears pack their ribosomes in an orderly way in their cells prior to hibernating. “These stay intact and functional for months. So, if polar bears knew how to do it, we could too,” she reasoned. Yonath surmised that if she could crystallise ribosomes, she would be able to study their internal structure using X-rays and electron microscopy. However, ribosomes are fragile. Unlike other cell parts, they have no outer protective membrane and are easily damaged.

citation.title: Ada Yonath obituary

text:
Ada Yonath obituary

Figuring that ribosomes of organisms that live in harsh conditions were likely to be hardier and more able to survive crystallisation, she attempted to crystallise the thermophile bacteria Geobacillus stearothermophilus, found in austere environments around thermal vents and in desert sands. It took more than 25,000 attempts, but in the mid-80s, Yonath succeeded. She then froze the bacteria at –185°C, to stabilise its internal structure and to protect it from the X-rays, a technique she was an early successful pioneer of, now known as cryo bio-crystallography. Finally, in 2001 and 2002, after almost two decades of research, Yonath’s team succeeded in mapping, in three dimensions, the bacteria’s ribosome. The significance of this discovery extended beyond pure science. Many antibiotics work by binding to sites on a bacterium’s ribosome, stopping it from reproducing. Previously, making antibiotics was a hit-and-miss process because often they would attack human ribosomes as well as those of the bacteria.

citation.title: Ada Yonath obituary

text:
Ada Yonath obituary

But, armed with knowledge of the structure of different ribosomes, scientists could now deduce where on a ribosome an antibiotic would bind and so make the necessary structural alterations to the drug. Yonath demonstrated how more than 20 antibiotics function, paving the way for new products, and also studied how antibiotic resistance might be overcome. The Nobel committee specifically noted this work in its citation, highlighting the “fundamental and medically important aspects of ribosome function” leading to “the development of novel antibiotic drugs in the ongoing medical struggle against ever emerging drug resistance among bacterial pathogens”. Born in Jerusalem, into an Orthodox Jewish family, Ada was the elder daughter of parents who had emigrated from Poland to what was then British-mandated Palestine in 1933. Her father, Hillel Lifshitz, a rabbi and grocer, died when she was 11. Her mother, Esther, then moved with her two daughters to Tel Aviv, where she became a clerk.

text:
Ada Yonath obituary

Despite her modest income, she recognised her daughter’s keen intellect and obtained her a place at the fee-paying Tichon Hadash high school, where Ada taught maths lessons in lieu of school fees. In 1959, after two years of mandatory military service, she returned to Jerusalem to take a degree in chemistry at the Hebrew University, graduating in 1962, then a master’s in biochemistry (1964). Four years later she received a PhD from the Weizmann Institute for studies into the structure of collagen using X-ray crystallography. She accepted postdoctoral positions in the US, at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Carnegie Mellon University, in Pittsburgh, before returning to the Weizmann Institute, where, in 1970, she began her research into ribosomes and where she remained for the rest of her career. Despite the scepticism of many of her peers, she did receive long-term support and funding from Heinz-Günter Wittman at the Max Planck Institute for Molecular Genetics in Berlin, frequently travelling to Germany to exchange data and compare notes.

text:
Ada Yonath obituary

In addition to her Nobel prize, Yonath received numerous awards, including the 2007 Wolf prize in chemistry, second only in importance to the Nobel, and was elected as a foreign member of the UK’s Royal Society. Outside her work, Yonath was politically outspoken and critical of the Israeli government. Most recently, she criticised Israeli judicial reforms as a “genuine peril to democracy” and to Israeli scientific enterprise. Also, one has to love, and not be afraid of, a challenge.” Her marriage to Moshe Yonath, a schoolteacher, ended in divorce. text:
Astronomers detect mysterious burst of energy from a galaxy far, far away

A long time ago in a galaxy far, far away, a mysterious flash of energy was released into the universe. Astronomers have now detected that flash – a burst of radio waves which travelled for more than 10bn years before reaching Earth – what they believe to be the most distant fast radio burst (FRB) ever recorded. FRBs are intense bursts of radio waves that can emit as much energy in milliseconds as the sun does in months or years. These mysterious pulses were first discovered in 2007 and have puzzled scientists ever since, with speculation from some that they could have an alien origin. In a new study published in Science, researchers have detected an FRB that originated when the universe was only about 3bn years old, meaning it has travelled through “approximately 80% of cosmic history”. Related: Astronomers detect fastest known star in Milky Way The burst, dubbed FRB 20240304B, is believed to be the farthest yet detected, more than double the previous distance record.

citation.title: Astronomers detect mysterious burst of energy from a galaxy far, far away

text:
Astronomers detect mysterious burst of energy from a galaxy far, far away

The scientists detected the burst using the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa and subsequently identified its host galaxy using Nasa’s James Webb space telescope (JWST). Dr Themiya Nanayakkara of the University of Sydney, one of the lead researchers on the paper, said when the burst was produced, “there was no Earth, there was no sun”. Data from the JWST indicated that the burst originated from a “young, very small galaxy which is forming stars at a very high speed, with not many metals around it”. There are several theories as to what the source of FRBs is, including that they originate from magnetars, neutron stars with a very powerful magnetic field. “Whatever the mechanism that causes this radio burst has to account for that fact that it can be produced in … very young galaxies with very low amount of metals,” Nanayakkara said. More than 10,000 FRBs have been detected since 2007. Some repeat continuously, Nanayakkara said, while “some of them repeat for a while and then stop … and then there are some FRBs that only go once and we never see again”.

citation.title: Astronomers detect mysterious burst of energy from a galaxy far, far away

text:
Astronomers detect mysterious burst of energy from a galaxy far, far away

Whether the new distant burst is a one-off flash or will yield recurrent signals remains to be seen. “[But] the fun thing about FRBs is that we don’t need to know what is causing them to do some of the science we are doing now,” Nanayakkara said. This particular burst “has been travelling for 80% of the age of the universe”, he said, adding that further detections of distant FRBs would enable scientists to map unseen matter in the distant universe. Prof Matthew Bailes of Swinburne University, one of the astrophysicists who first discovered FRBs, described the new paper as “a validation of how powerful the FRBs are for probing the universe”. Bailes described them as “a very fundamental way of counting how many atoms there are in the universe”. FRBs are affected by the particles they travel through, enabling scientists to quantify matter that cannot be seen through optical telescopes.

text:
Astronomers detect mysterious burst of energy from a galaxy far, far away

Dr Sara Webb, an astrophysicist also at Swinburne University who was not involved in the research, said: “You can use them essentially as a line-of-sight count for how much matter they had to go through [to get to Earth].” The discovery suggests that “FRBs might have been very common in the early universe”, she added.

text:
Skies across the UK illuminated by the northern lights

The northern lights illuminated the skies across the UK on Friday and Saturday evening. Sky-gazers as far south as Devon, Hampshire and Kent were treated to the dazzling natural phenomenon, also known as the aurora borealis. The Met Office said sightings could continue during clear skies until Tuesday. Such occurrences are mostly visible near the Arctic Circle and northern Scotland. The aurora borealis is a natural light display in Earth’s sky, driven by solar activity and geomagnetic storms interacting with the upper atmosphere. Sightings will remain possible until Tuesday across Scotland and similar geomagnetic longitudes during clear skies, the Met Office said. Aurora displays occur when charged particles collide with gases in the Earth’s atmosphere around the magnetic poles. As they collide, light is emitted at various wavelengths, creating colourful displays in the sky. According to the Met Office, the sun emits charged particles known as solar wind, which travel at bout 1m mph.

Oxygen produces green and, at higher altitudes, rare red auroras, while nitrogen creates blue and purple hues.” Last year, experts said 2026 will be a peak year for aurora-spotting, as the sun has been in a heightened state of activity as part of its 11-year natural cycle.

text:
Starwatch: Mars signposts the beautiful Beehive cluster

The red planet, Mars, sails through the beautiful cluster of stars known as the Beehive this week. Catalogued as Messier 44, the cluster lies in the constellation Cancer. It has been known since antiquity, when its hazy appearance earned it the Latin name Praesepe, meaning a manger or crib. Although it is one of the brightest star clusters in the night sky, it can be surprisingly difficult to locate because Cancer contains no bright stars to guide the eye towards it. Thankfully, this week Mars acts as the signpost. The chart shows the view looking east from London at 0200 BST on 13 October. Mars will appear as a moderately bright, distinctly red-looking object. Once you have Mars in your sights, look carefully around the planet. From a dark location, the Beehive will appear as a faint, misty patch very close to Mars. Light pollution will make the cluster much harder to see, and wherever you are observing, make sure you allow sufficient time for your eyes to adjust to the dark. This can take about 20 minutes, so resist the temptation to look at the bright screen of your phone.

Keith Thompson obituary

My former husband Keith Thompson, who has died aged 86, was an academic and horticulturist specialising in the area of optimum harvest, and the packing and storing of fruit and root crops. Working as a crop scientist for the government-run Tropical Products Institute from the 1960s to mid-80s, Keith worked on overseas assignments in many countries including Trinidad, Colombia, Nigeria, Ethiopia, Zambia, Turkey, Thailand and Yemen. He was on a field trip outside Aden in 1986 when the coup happened that sparked the South Yemen conflict. He and his local counterpart trekked to a coastal refinery compound, and Keith and other British nationals were collected by a diverted HMY Britannia, the royal yacht, to land at Djibouti and fly back to the UK. Keith’s souvenir was a Royal Navy sweater to keep him warm. Born in Halifax to Hilda (nee Smith), a mill worker, and Harold Thompson, a lathe-turner at Churchill Redmond metalworks, Keith attended Copley junior school. Aged 10 on holiday in Bridlington, his cousin accidentally hit him in the eye with a golf club, and he lost the sight in that eye.

text:
Keith Thompson obituary

Due to missed schooling, Keith failed his 11-plus and at 13 joined Halifax Technical College, leaving at 16 with no qualifications. Horticultural interests led him to enrol as an apprentice gardener for Halifax Public Parks and he gained Royal Horticultural Society qualifications. By 1960 he had added some GCEs and A-level botany and zoology, and gained a place at Wye College, a University of London establishment located in the Kent countryside, to study for a horticulture degree. I met Keith at a graduation party in Canterbury, and we married in 1965. Two years later, Keith gained his PhD from Leeds University, and a daughter, Katie. Recruited by the government’s Overseas Development Administration (ODA), which financed the Tropical Products Institute, Keith and the family set sail to Trinidad, where he lectured in crop science at the University of the West Indies, and our son, Miles, was born. Subsequent teaching and consultancy posts followed, in Jamaica, Khartoum, Seoul and Bogotá before returning to the UK and the Tropical Products Institute in 1980, settling in Bromley, Kent, while continuing overseas assignments.

text:
Stop making sense: focus on sounds to help learn a language, study suggests

If you want to get really good at French, Arabic or Hungarian, don’t start with rote learning vocabulary and grammar, focus on how they sound instead, research suggests. A new study of how humans learn modern languages has found that the brains of the most talented linguists hear foreign terms as random noise, not words. Normally, when people learn a language, they try to understand it through the sounds of their native tongue. The more different the foreign language’s sounds and pronunciation are from the native language, the harder the new language will probably be to learn. But the best linguists master even the trickiest pronunciation much more easily. ​To find out why, researchers at UCL and Tohoku University, Japan, compared the auditory precision of 67 Japanese learners of English by measuring their ability to detect slight changes in pitch, length and tone, in non-speech sounds. Using functional MRI scans, they measured participants’ brain activity as they tried to distinguish between English vowel sounds that do not occur in Japanese.

citation.title: Stop making sense: focus on sounds to help learn a language, study suggests

text:
Stop making sense: focus on sounds to help learn a language, study suggests

They found that those with higher auditory precision mastered the pronunciation of new languages faster and more accurately than other learners and relied less on the brain’s left sensorimotor system (involved in language processing) when processing foreign-language sounds. Instead, their brain activity patterns were similar to those that occur when the brain processes non-speech sounds. With less interference from pre-existing patterns of their native language, it was simpler for these learners to accurately process new sounds. In contrast, those with lower auditory precision relied more on the brain’s left sensorimotor network when listening to foreign-language sounds. They used the pronunciation patterns of their native language when processing unfamiliar sounds. The latest findings challenge stereotypes that Britons are less adept at languages. Prof Kazuya Saito-van Poeteren, the lead author and professor of second language education at UCL Institute of Education, said: “I do not think British people are biologically bad at languages.

The problem is more likely to be that many people receive too little meaningful exposure, combined with teaching methods that do not necessarily train the auditory skills needed to make the most of that limited exposure. “If you only hear and use the language for a small number of hours each week, having a good ear may make a much bigger difference. Learners with high auditory precision can make very effective use of relatively sparse input, whereas others may need much more exposure before unfamiliar sounds begin to become established,” he said. Chris Davies obituary

My brother, Chris Davies, who has died aged 61 of cancer, was an academic metallurgist whose research helped to bring about a better understanding of why metals behave the way they do – and therefore how to control their properties during manufacturing. Much of his research took place at Monash University in Australia, where he had moved from the UK in the early 1990s. In particular, his work on the behaviour of light metals and alloys fed into the development of lighter, stronger and more reliable materials used in the making of aircraft, vehicles and medical devices. Chris’s studies also helped to support advances in 3D printing by providing insights into how companies can produce high-performance metal components more efficiently, with less waste and lower energy consumption. Born in Cardiff, Chris was the son of Jack and his wife, Margaret (nee Powell), both teachers of English. He attended Cardiff high school and then gained a degree in engineering at Imperial College London, where he stayed on to do a PhD.

In 1992 he moved to Vancouver in Canada to do two years of postdoctoral research at the University of British Columbia, before joining Monash in Melbourne in 1994 and remaining there until his death, initially in a teaching role but thereafter specialising mainly in research. In addition, Chris held a number of leadership roles at Monash over the years, including as associate dean of research, deputy dean of external engagements and deputy dean of operations in the Faculty of Engineering. He was president of the Academic Board from 2016 to 2019, and in 2025 was named to the Monash Honour Roll, a mark of the esteem in which he was held for his integrity, humour and unwavering commitment. Beyond his life in academia Chris loved reading, enjoyed print making, painting and drawing and appreciated music of all genres. He was an avid sports fan, having played club hockey in his younger days, and was a member of the Cardiff Nomads Angling Club. He is survived by his second wife, Sam (nee Lipscombe), whom he married in 2011, a son, Calum, from his first marriage to Louise (nee Hehir), which ended in divorce, and his siblings, Graham and me.

text:
Cyril Hilsum obituary

Cyril Hilsum’s research into stable liquid crystals and the devices in which they could be used paved the way for the flat-panel television and computer screens that are now ubiquitous in homes, offices and public spaces. Hilsum, who has died aged 101, was leading a Ministry of Defence team at the Royal Radar Establishment (RRE) in Malvern, Worcestershire, in the late 1960s when Harold Wilson’s Labour government, looking to develop a new generation of miniature radar systems, tasked him with creating flat displays to replace the bulky cathode-ray-tube screens used for traditional radar set-ups. Realising the key to flat-screen technology was the emerging science of liquid crystals, Hilsum organised a meeting of liquid crystal researchers – and soon realised there was only one person in the room who really understood anything about them: George Gray, from Hull University. Gray was immediately offered a contract, and began working with Hilsum and Peter Raynes, an optoelectronics expert at the RRE, on fulfilling the government’s brief.

citation.title: Cyril Hilsum obituary

text:
Cyril Hilsum obituary

By 1972 the three of them had developed a mixture that was suitable for use in screens, made largely of cyanobiphenyls, compounds that remain stable even when heated or exposed to sunlight or ultraviolet light. This gave the resulting screens durability in real-world applications. Although originally designed to support the RRE’s nascent radar technology, the liquid crystal displays (or LCDs) that used the mixture soon found practical uses elsewhere. While the MoD retained the patents, Hilsum persuaded the chemicals company BDH to manufacture and sell the mixtures under licence, eventually netting the government more than £100m in royalties from their use in watches and calculators, and then later in laptops, tablets and phones. Hilsum was born in Stepney, east London, to Benjamin and Ada, who were street traders. A bright boy who had learned to read proficiently by the age of three and spent hours dismantling toys to see how they worked, he went to Raine’s Foundation school in Bethnal Green, after which, during the second world war, he won a scholarship to University College London, which had been evacuated to Bangor in north Wales.

citation.title: Cyril Hilsum obituary

text:
Cyril Hilsum obituary

He graduated with a degree in physics in 1945 and later a PhD, meeting fellow student Betty Cooper at UCL and marrying her in 1947. He and Betty, who became a teacher, were keen Labour party supporters, and after the war would attend Winston Churchill’s meetings in order to heckle him. After an initial spell working for the MoD in central London immediately after the war, he moved in 1947 to the Admiralty Research Laboratory in Teddington, where he met Alan Turing, who worked at the nearby National Physical Laboratory, and whom he once beat at chess. By 1950, aged 25, he was leading a team studying military uses for infrared light, based at the Services Electronics Research Laboratory in Baldock, Hertfordshire. Hilsum joined the RRE in 1964 to carry out research into gallium arsenide, a semiconductor material that handles high-frequencies, and on the development of radar, transistors and light-emitting diodes (LEDs). In fact his work on semiconductors was as significant as that on LCDs, and included helping to develop infrared lasers that now underpin fibre optic telecommunications.

citation.title: Cyril Hilsum obituary

text:
Cyril Hilsum obituary

He was also instrumental in developing the Gunn diode, a high-frequency oscillator that generates microwave signals used in motion detectors and proximity sensors, including police radar speed guns – sometimes to his disadvantage, given that he was a fast driver. In tandem, his work on developing miniature radar systems led to Claribel, a device for detecting the trajectory of a bullet, which was used to locate snipers in Northern Ireland during the Troubles. In 1974 Hilsum became the UK’s chief scientific officer, the highest rank for a scientist in the civil service and a position he held until in 1983 he accepted the role of chief scientist, and later research director, at the General Electrical Company’s Hirst Research Centre in Wembley, north-west London. Always a promoter of women in sciences, at GEC he insisted his department hire equal numbers of both sexes. Hilsum served as president of the Institute of Physics from 1988 to 1990, the year that he was appointed CBE. He retired from GEC in 1995.

citation.title: Cyril Hilsum obituary

text:
Cyril Hilsum obituary

A fellow of the Royal Society, he won the Faraday Medal and in 2007 the Royal Society’s Royal Medal “for his many outstanding contributions and for continuing to use his prodigious talents on behalf of industry, government and academe”. The British Liquid Crystal Society awards the Cyril Hilsum Medal annually for the best contribution to liquid crystal technology. In later years Hilsum built a laboratory in his house in Pinner, Middlesex, where, aged 97, he came up with his final invention – an ink containing sensors to conduct electricity – earning him the last of more than 70 patents. He ascribed his longevity to red wine and chocolate, and was a lifelong reader of the Guardian. Betty died in 1987, and one of their daughters, Karen, also predeceased him, in 1997. Hilsum founded the Karen Burt award at the Women’s Engineering Society. He is survived by their other daughter, Lindsey, international editor for Channel 4 News, and a grandson, Alexander. • Cyril Hilsum, physicist and inventor, born 17 May 1925; died 23 September 2026

text:
Neanderthal remains may be earliest human ancestor find killed by a spear

A smooth round hole in the shoulder blade of a Neanderthal who died more than 70,000 years ago may be the oldest evidence so far of a human ancestor being killed by a wooden spear. Archaeologists spotted the distinctive injury after excavating skeletal remains of the adult and other Neanderthals from under nearly 8 metres of rock and sediment in the Shanidar cave in Iraqi Kurdistan. At least five Neanderthals were buried at the same spot over several years, in a depression no larger than a fridge that ran behind a huge boulder near the entrance to the cave. Some of the bodies appear to have been laid on top of others that were still decomposing. “They’re coming back to the same spot to place bodies over a number of years or several decades and that’s really quite unusual in in the Neanderthal archaeological record,” said Dr Emma Pomeroy, a biological anthropologist at the University of Cambridge. “It suggests there’s some kind of meaningful behaviour in depositing the dead there.” Researchers found only partial remains of the injured Neanderthal, an adult aged about 45.

citation.title: Neanderthal remains may be earliest human ancestor find killed by a spear

text:
Neanderthal remains may be earliest human ancestor find killed by a spear

The left shoulder blade that bears the wound was found with seven teeth, several ribs and fragments, and a near complete right hand that was leaning against the boulder. Close inspection of the shoulder blade revealed three fractures spreading out from the 1.5cm-wide hole and fragments of bone that filled the wound. The shards were probably punched out of the thin bone when the spear hit, the scientists said. The circular shape of the hole and the pattern of bone damage strongly suggest a wound inflicted by a wooden spear striking the body from the front.But whether it was a hunting accident or an intentional attack – a brutal jab from a foe, perhaps – is impossible to know. Pomeroy said the position of the wound and the force needed to push the spear through the chest, where it would have punctured the lung and probably severed arteries before punching out of the shoulder blade, pointed to a “kill shot” directed at the heart. “I don’t think that’s something you do accidentally,” she said. The spear wound was almost certainly lethal, but the individual was in bad shape before the fatal blow.

citation.title: Neanderthal remains may be earliest human ancestor find killed by a spear

text:
Neanderthal remains may be earliest human ancestor find killed by a spear

Examination of the teeth revealed a lower incisor split vertically, leaving only half in place, its neighbours twisted inwards, according to details published in Scientific Reports. “You’d need quite a severe hit in the face to split a tooth like that and to rotate the others,” said Pomeroy. “They might well have needed help because they would have been in terrible pain.” The split tooth was caked in hardened plaque that would have taken at least a year to build up. Chris Hunt, the emeritus professor at Liverpool John Moores University who co-authored the paper, said Neanderthals at Shanidar were taking ibex as their main prey and could have used wooden spears shaped like modern javelins to kill the animals. Because plant material decomposes so easily, very few wooden objects survive from prehistory, but timber spears from about 200,000 years ago have been discovered in Germany, preserved in waterlogged ground. The pointed end of a rounded wooden spear discovered in Clacton-on-Sea in 1911 is the oldest known at over 400,000 years old.

citation.title: Neanderthal remains may be earliest human ancestor find killed by a spear

text:
Neanderthal remains may be earliest human ancestor find killed by a spear

Last week, scientists in Spain described hundreds of wooden imprints and artefacts that show Neanderthals embraced woodwork, making trays, plates, tripods, spears and other items. But proof of fatal skirmishes is harder to find in fossils: we may never know how the wounded Neanderthal at Shanidar died. “Conceivably it was a hunting accident,” Hunt said. “We can’t, however, rule out that purposeful interpersonal violence was involved.”

text:
Norman McCubbin obituary

My brother Norman McCubbin, who has died aged 77, was a scientist who worked at the forefront of experimental particle physics. A leading light in experiments that took place on the Large Hadron Collider, the world’s biggest and most powerful particle accelerator at the European Organization for Nuclear Research (Cern) in Switzerland, he spent the last five years of his working life as director of the particle physics department at the Rutherford Appleton Laboratory (RAL) in Oxfordshire, until his retirement in 2012. Afterwards he became a tutor to undergraduates at St Anne’s College, Oxford, and was still in that role at his death. Norman was born in Pinner, Middlesex, the first child of Hugh, an accountant, and his wife, Pat (nee Rosenberg). The family moved to Leicester, where his brothers, Richard and I, were born, and then in 1958 to Kenya for Hugh to take up a post as finance director of the Kenya Farmers’ Association . When Hugh joined the UN’s World Food Programme, the family moved to Lesotho and later, Taiwan, while Norman went to Repton school in Derbyshire as a boarder.

citation.title: Norman McCubbin obituary

text:
Norman McCubbin obituary

After moving on to New College, Oxford, he gained a first-class physics degree and took a PhD. Between 1973 and 1979 he was a postdoctoral research associate at the University of Lancaster and then at RAL, working with the laboratory on the first hadron collider at Cern to study the dynamics of proton-proton collisions. He then worked at Cern as a senior (then principal) scientific officer, where he concentrated on the collisions of heavy ions. From 1990 to 1999 Norman led RAL’s Zeus experiment in Hamburg, studying the structure of the proton, and from 1999 to 2003 he was computing coordinator for the Atlas experiment at the Large Hadron Collider. Later he became divisional head of RAL’s particle physics department while continuing with some of his work at Cern until, in 2007, he became the department’s director. In retirement as a stipendiary lecturer in physics at Oxford, he was a popular tutor, relishing the core subjects of thermodynamics, statistical mechanics, relativity and symmetries.

citation.title: Norman McCubbin obituary

text:
Norman McCubbin obituary

More prosaically, he relished answering questions, via video from New Zealand, from his ever-curious seven-year-old great-nephew Hugh, about issues such as gravity, centrifugal force and quantum entanglement. Despite his dedication to his work, family and friendship always came first for Norman. We all basked in his warmth, love, humour and kindness, as well as that illuminating intelligence he wore so lightly. He is survived by me and Richard, two nieces, two nephews, three great-nephews and a great-niece.

text:
How an accelerating Earth led experts to adopt the leap hour

After decades of discussion, quibbling and worrying about clocks in computer systems, the world’s official timekeepers have voted to replace what many viewed as a tiresome correction: the leap second. It’s time, they say, for the leap hour. Delegates from 69 countries cast their votes on Thursday at a conference in France of the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, which ensures the world sticks to the same standards of time, weight, distance and more. The decision to adopt the leap hour from next year aims to reduce the risk of computers and other technical systems tripping over as their software grapples with minutes lasting 61 seconds – and, worse, 59 seconds – instead of a round 60. “After 30 years of debate, the leap second is making way for the leap hour,” said Dr Setnam Shemar, principal scientist in the time and frequency department at the UK’s National Physical Laboratory (NPL).

citation.title: How an accelerating Earth led experts to adopt the leap hour

text:
How an accelerating Earth led experts to adopt the leap hour

“This will reduce the risks to the systems and national infrastructure that depend on accurate time while still preserving the fundamental link between our global time system and the rotation of the Earth.” The vote at Versailles means that coordinated universal time (UTC) can drift up to an hour from astronomical time before a leap hour is needed, but that is unlikely to happen for thousands of years. “We already have daylight saving where we change by an hour and no one gets bothered about that, apart from losing sleep or getting an extra hour’s sleep,” said Shemar, who sat on the international timekeeping expert committee that proposed the leap hour. The more familiar leap year was introduced more than 2,000 years ago to ensure that the calendar year did not fall out of step with the time that the Earth takes to circle the sun. Adding a day to the end of February every four or so years does the job, because Earth orbits the sun every 365 and a quarter days. Leap seconds are a much more modern invention.

citation.title: How an accelerating Earth led experts to adopt the leap hour

text:
How an accelerating Earth led experts to adopt the leap hour

In 1955, Louis Essen and Jack Parry at the NPL built the world’s first practical, high-precision caesium atomic clock. The device revolutionised timekeeping, and in 1967 the astronomical definition of a second, based on the rotation of the Earth, was abandoned. Ever since, the formal definition of one second has been 9,192,631,770 vibrations of the caesium atom. Atomic clocks are exceptionally stable and precise. Their timekeeping has become critical for modern computer systems, communications, satellites, trading systems and electricity grids. But the Earth’s rotation is far less reliable. Its spin is affected by the planet’s molten core, the shift of the oceans, global jet streams and other natural forces. Broadly, Earth’s rotation is slowing down: when an asteroid doomed the dinosaurs, a day lasted about 23 and a half hours. Because of this, officials have added 27 leap seconds since 1972 to ensure UTC is aligned with astronomical time. The strategy endured for more than 50 years until scientists spotted a fresh reason to fear technological mayhem.

citation.title: How an accelerating Earth led experts to adopt the leap hour

text:
How an accelerating Earth led experts to adopt the leap hour

In the past decade, Earth’s rotation has sped up, meaning officials might have needed to add the first negative leap second, equivalent to lopping a second off UTC. The 30% probability of a negative leap second in the next decade brought the Versailles vote forward. “Leap seconds can be tricky enough to deal with,” said Shemar. Telecommunications, electricity grids and navigation systems used high-accuracy timing, he explained, but software updates could apply leap seconds at the wrong time, knocking networks out of sync. “After the leap second applied in 2012, there were some computer systems whose operating systems couldn’t cope with 61 seconds in a minute. The servers froze, they seized up. Systems went offline. And those are the sorts of failures that can happen with positive leap seconds,” Shemar said. Among the crashed websites were Reddit and LinkedIn. Separately, Qantas flights were hit with delays. Negative leap seconds come with even greater risks. “There could be software out there that hasn’t been tested on negative leap seconds because we’ve never had to apply one before,” Shemar said.

citation.title: How an accelerating Earth led experts to adopt the leap hour

text:
How an accelerating Earth led experts to adopt the leap hour

To test all the computer systems that talk to one another around the world would cost companies a fortune. It was this concern that swung the vote. Historically, the UK has grumbled about canning leap seconds because of the link with Greenwich mean time. Russia has also opposed the move, citing concerns of the impact on its Glonass satellite navigation system. The IERS Earth Orientation Centre, in Paris, tracks changes in the Earth’s rotation and other movements that feed into UTC. The centre also issues notices when leap seconds must be added. Dr Christian Bizouard, the director of the centre, approved of the vote, but said it passed the decision to people far in the future. “It’s kind of a philosophical discussion, because if a leap hour happens, it won’t be for a very, very long time,” he said. “What we are doing is pushing back the decision.”

text:
Margaret Hamilton obituary

Apollo was a bold, innovative project. It tested the boundaries of technology and human achievement, and took people to the moon. However, one thing it failed to challenge was the prevailing hierarchy. Nearly everyone involved in Nasa’s space programme in the 1960s was male and white. If you weren’t, you needed to be exceptional at what you did. Margaret Hamilton, who has died aged 90, was one of those exceptional people. Without her input, sending spacecraft into lunar orbit, and putting Neil Armstrong and his successors on to the surface of the moon, might have been impossible. Hamilton directed the software engineering division at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) Instrumentation Laboratory, which had been charged with developing the computer systems for Apollo. The result of this work was the Apollo Guidance Computer (AGC). This provided the astronauts with a computer-linked keypad, similar in appearance to a calculator and known by the acronym DSKY – short for Display and Keyboard – which they used for navigating and controlling the direction and manoeuvrability of the spacecraft.

citation.title: Margaret Hamilton obituary

text:
Margaret Hamilton obituary

In the Gemini missions, which preceded Apollo, astronauts used joysticks to control the spacecraft. AGC removed that necessity, leading to a more precise flight path while freeing the crew for other tasks. It was the first computer in the world based on the silicon-integrated circuits that are now mass-produced and found in everyday electronic devices such as smartphones, televisions and laptops. One AGC controlled the command module, which remained in orbit around the moon, while a second controlled the lunar module (LM), which descended to the surface. The astronauts could briefly take manual control as the LM approached the landing site, but otherwise AGC flew the two spacecraft automatically. In July 1969, Apollo 11 became the first mission to put humans on the moon. As its LM, codenamed Eagle, began its descent, alarms went off inside the module. Mission control considered aborting but Hamilton, listening in from MIT, had run the simulations so many times that she realised what had happened: a radar switch had been inadvertently left active.

citation.title: Margaret Hamilton obituary

text:
Margaret Hamilton obituary

She had seen this during simulations when Armstrong’s companion Buzz Aldrin had made the same error during training, and had previously instructed two of Apollo 11’s mission controllers, Steve Bales and Jack Garman, that unless it happened repeatedly they need not abort. Via the flight controller, Gene Kranz, they reassured Armstrong the alarm could be ignored. Five minutes later Armstrong informed the world: “The Eagle has landed”. Hamilton told the Times in 2019 that the Eagle’s safe landing was “maybe the most exciting moment of my life,” coupled with the realisation of “the things we’d gone through to get there … everything came rushing through my mind”. She was born in Paoli, Indiana, the oldest of four children of Esther (nee Partington) and Kenneth Heafield, both teachers. Early in her life, the family moved to Michigan, where Margaret graduated from Hancock high school in 1954, going on to study mathematics at the University of Michigan and then at Earlham College, in Richmond, Indiana. She gained her BA in 1958, the year she married James Hamilton, a fellow student at Earlham.

citation.title: Margaret Hamilton obituary

text:
Margaret Hamilton obituary

The following year they moved to Boston, where James was to study law at Harvard and where their daughter, Lauren, was born. Hamilton found work in the meteorology department of MIT, where her first role was developing weather-prediction software, alongside Edward Lorenz, the mathematician and meteorologist and founder of modern chaos theory. Her talent immediately became apparent and she was assigned work on the US air-defence systems before, in 1965, responding to an advert from the Instrumentation Laboratory – also a department of MIT – seeking people to develop software to send humans to the moon. She was successful, becoming the first programmer for Apollo at MIT, and, of more significance, the first woman working on the project. Within three years she was made assistant director, and soon after became director of the team of about 100. Unsurprisingly, she was the target of sexism, some which would have led to disciplinary action today – but rarely from her fellow programmers. She told MIT News in 2009: “Dedication and commitment were a given. Mutual respect was across the board. Upper management gave us total freedom and trust.

citation.title: Margaret Hamilton obituary

text:
Margaret Hamilton obituary

We had to find a way, and we did … There was no choice but to be pioneers.” As well as her deep knowledge, her insistence on running and rerunning programs searching for glitches was invaluable. One day, Lauren was playing with the command module simulator when she accidentally activated a program called P01 while the simulator was in mid-flight. It crashed the system. Hamilton took note, and when, during the flight of Apollo 8 in 1968, P01 was activated accidentally, her knowledge meant the problem could be fixed mid-mission. Her meticulous approach ensured no software bugs were ever known to have been reported during any crewed Apollo mission. She also earned herself the epithet “the rope mother” because the core memory for Apollo’s onboard computers was woven from strands of copper interlaced through magnets. These had to be meticulously threaded by hand using professional seamstresses. The work was intricate, precise and double-checked by Hamilton at every stage.

citation.title: Margaret Hamilton obituary

text:
Margaret Hamilton obituary

She even coined the term “software engineering”, to draw a distinction between her work and more theoretical computer science, and to explain to non-specialists what her department’s duties entailed. Once Apollo had been wound down in the early 1970s, Hamilton continued to work at the instrumentation lab. She focused on the Skylab space station and space shuttle programmes, and set up two software companies of her own, Higher Order Software in 1976 and Hamilton Technologies in 1986. Andrew Meade McGee, curator of computing at the Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum in Washington DC, described her as “a seminal figure in the creation of modern, software-driven computing”. He said: “Her practices, drawn directly from working on the AGC, reshaped the computing industry and software education, and still have influence today. Over the years she has inspired many women into STEM careers.

citation.title: Margaret Hamilton obituary

text:
Margaret Hamilton obituary

Back then, she was often the only woman in the room during Apollo gatherings of systems analysts, but she proved female engineers could excel when given a foot in the door.” When Hamilton received the presidential medal of freedom from Barack Obama in 2016, he said: “She symbolises that generation of unsung women who helped send humankind into space.” Among many other accolades, she collected the Augusta Ada Lovelace award in 1986 from the Association for Women in Computing, and in 2003 Nasa’s exceptional space act award for scientific and technical contributions. In 2017, a Women of Nasa Lego set was produced, which featured mini figures of Hamilton, the astronauts Sally Ride and Mae Jemison, and the Nasa chief of astronomy Nancy Roman. Last year Hamilton received the Michael Collins trophy from the Air and Space Museum in Washington, which recognises past and present achievements involving the management or execution of a scientific or technological project related to space exploration. It was collected by her daughter, as Hamilton was too frail to travel.

citation.title: Margaret Hamilton obituary

text:
Margaret Hamilton obituary

Her first marriage ended in divorce in 1967 and two years later she married Dan Lickly, an aeronautical engineer, whom she met at MIT. They were divorced in 1973. Thereafter Hamilton lived with Ron Hackler, a former colleague. He died in 2025. Her daughter survives her. • Margaret Elaine Hamilton, computer scientist, born 17 August 1936; died 30 September 2026

text:
Warning signs could predict inflammatory bowel disease a decade before diagnosis

Patterns of antibodies in people’s blood could predict the onset of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) a decade before diagnosis, according to research that raises hopes for catching the condition early. Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis, the two main forms of IBD, are typically treated only after symptoms appear, when the gut has already been damaged. But scientists found that the immune system sends warning signals up to a decade before diagnosis, paving the way for potentially earlier detection and even prevention. “For too long we have only been able to treat inflammatory bowel disease once the damage is done, and for many people that is too late,” said Dr Arno Bourgonje at the University Medical Centre Groningen in the Netherlands and the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York. “What we have shown is that the disease begins years before symptoms appear, and the immune system leaves warning signs long before diagnosis,” Bourgonje added.

citation.title: Warning signs could predict inflammatory bowel disease a decade before diagnosis

text:
Warning signs could predict inflammatory bowel disease a decade before diagnosis

“This is not yet a test that can tell someone they will become ill, but it is an important step towards catching the disease earlier and, one day, preventing it.” At least 3.8 million people worldwide live with IBD, an immune condition that drives chronic inflammation of the digestive tract, causing pain, diarrhoea and fatigue. The exact cause is unknown, but a misfiring immune system, genetics and microbes living in the gut can all contribute. Treatment relies on anti-inflammatory and immune-suppressing drugs, but many patients do not respond, and a significant number go on to have surgery to remove damaged sections of bowel. Longstanding inflammation also raises the risk of bowel cancer. This has prompted scientists to look for the earlier signs of disease, in the hope of identifying people at risk before damage begins. Bourgonje and colleagues at Mount Sinai and the Medical University of Vienna ran tests on blood samples taken from US military personnel. They examined 2,000 samples from 500 people, 200 of whom later developed Crohn’s disease, and 200 who went on to develop ulcerative colitis.

citation.title: Warning signs could predict inflammatory bowel disease a decade before diagnosis

text:
Warning signs could predict inflammatory bowel disease a decade before diagnosis

The remaining 100 developed neither condition. The blood samples were screened for antibodies that the immune system might have churned out in response to hundreds of thousands of fragments of proteins from bacteria, viruses, food and even the body’s own tissues. In people who went on to develop Crohn’s disease, antibodies against Epstein-Barr virus, which causes glandular fever, were more common, and the differences were already visible a decade before diagnosis. The signal was strongest in those who later developed more severe, complicated disease, which can narrow the bowel or create abnormal channels. People who developed ulcerative colitis showed a different pattern, including antibodies against one of the body’s own proteins. The findings, published in the journal Gut and presented at the United European Gastroenterology meeting in Barcelona, need to be confirmed in other groups of people, and the results show a link rather than proving the infections cause IBD.

citation.title: Warning signs could predict inflammatory bowel disease a decade before diagnosis

text:
Warning signs could predict inflammatory bowel disease a decade before diagnosis

But the hope is that IBD could eventually follow the path of type 1 diabetes, where a blood test can identify people whose immune systems have begun attacking the pancreas before any symptoms appear, allowing treatment that delays the onset of disease. James Lindsay, a professor of gastroenterology at Barts Health, who was not involved in the research, said the study provided “important insights into the causes of Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis, potentially adding new tools to help identify those at risk of IBD”. But he cautioned that the techniques were “very much a research tool” and not yet ready for the clinic. Marianne Radcliffe, the chief executive of Crohn’s & Colitis UK, a national patient charity, said: “For people affected by Crohn’s and colitis, research like this is an important step forward. Every new insight helps build a clearer understanding of how these conditions develop, including the changes that may occur years before symptoms appear.”

text:
Starwatch: Catch the Orionid meteor shower streak across the night sky

The annual Orionid meteor shower reaches its peak this week, offering the chance to see fragments of the most famous comet of all streaking across the night sky. The Orionids occur every October as Earth passes through a stream of dust left behind by Halley’s comet. As these tiny particles plunge into Earth’s atmosphere at about 66 kilometres per second, they heat the surrounding air and produce the fleeting streaks of light that we call meteors. This year, the shower is expected to reach its peak during the night of 21–22 October. Under ideal conditions, observers may see between 10 and 20 Orionid meteors per hour. Unfortunately, conditions this year are not ideal because of the presence of a bright waxing gibbous Moon. This will drown out many of the fainter meteors. Nevertheless, conditions improve during the early hours of the morning. The moon sets at about 03:00 BST, leaving a few hours of darker sky before dawn, just as Orion is climbing high into the sky. Find a safe location with as wide a view of the heavens as possible and simply watch with the naked eye.

text:
Mayer Hillman obituary

In the late 1990s, the social scientist and author Mayer Hillman predicted that, in the future, our children and grandchildren would ask us what we did to prevent global climate catastrophe. Twenty years later Greta Thunberg, addressing the UN, thundered: “You are failing us. But the young people are starting to understand your betrayal. The eyes of all future generations are upon you.” Twenty-five years ago, Hillman also warned that public denial of the climate crisis would only begin to crack when people in the global north were personally affected – by the creation of millions of environmental refugees from uninhabitable parts of the world, for instance, or after their homes had been flooded several times over and they could no longer insure them. Hillman, who has died aged 94, not only anticipated social and environmental problems decades in advance of most other people, he also came up with solutions that seemed outlandish at the time but are now considered unremarkable. In 1984 he proposed energy audits and thermal ratings for buildings; in 2007 EPCs (energy performance certificates) were rolled out across England and Wales.

citation.title: Mayer Hillman obituary

text:
Mayer Hillman obituary

In the early 90s, he suggested that road intersections should be raised to pavement level to give priority to pedestrians, a now commonplace practice. Cycle lanes and 20mph speed limits – Hillman was advocating these more than 40 years ago. Increasingly, his energies were taken up with the climate crisis. His 2004 book, How We Can Save the Planet, described it as “the most serious environmental threat that the world has ever faced”. He dismissed individual gestures as futile, even though he had not flown for decades. In an analogy with the consensus around wartime rationing, he proposed carbon rationing as the only way to prevent serious damage, foreseeing a time when people would pity someone passing in a car – a sign of an emergency requiring them to use up a precious part of their annual carbon quota. Born in West Hampstead, north London, to Scottish Jewish parents, Mayer (known as Mickey by family and many friends), was the youngest of three boys. His father, David, an orthodox Jew who fled the pogroms in Lithuania to settle in Glasgow, was a portrait painter and stained-glass artist; his mother, Annie, a GP. At the outbreak of the second world war, Mickey and his brothers, Ellis and Harold, were evacuated to homes in Rickmansworth, Hertfordshire. His gentile hosts offered him meat and fish, which, coming from a kosher home, he politely declined; Hillman was vegetarian thereafter. All three boys would come home for the Sabbath, leaving school early on Fridays to take the train to Finchley Road station. On Sunday evenings, they returned to Rickmansworth. After two years, their father acceded to their request to come home on condition they stay on at the Rickmansworth school. So, until the end of the war, they did the same journey in reverse, getting up at 6.30am, making their own sandwiches, and walking to the station.

While there, in 1956, he co-designed for a competition a prototype for the first pedestrian-oriented new town in the UK. Mayer Hillman musing on children, road safely, transport and planning Several years later, he decided to switch professions: the catalyst was Colin Buchanan’s influential 1963 report Traffic in Towns, which, while it recognised the potential downsides of rapidly growing car ownership, nevertheless argued for reorganising cities to accommodate it. Hillman disagreed and embarked on a doctorate at Edinburgh University, examining the social and environmental aspects of personal mobility and making the case for reducing the need for motorised transport. By then, in 1964, he had married Heidi Krott, who had come to Britain from Vienna in 1939, aged two, in her refugee mother’s arms.

A research post at the thinktank Political and Economic Planning, later the Policy Studies Institute (PSI), where he stayed for the rest of his career, allowed him to develop his most innovative thinking. In a 1979 report, Walking Is Transport, co-written with Anne Whalley, Hillman deplored the omission in national transport data of journeys of less than a mile, most of them walking. Unusually for a male researcher of the time, he recognised that this rendered women’s chief mode of travel invisible (15 years later, walking was added to official research data). From the early 70s, Hillman was also studying children’s independent mobility. His co-authored report One False Move (1990), comparing 1971 survey results with 1990, revealed a dramatic drop in children’s independent travel: where previously 80% of seven- and eight-year-olds had gone to school unaccompanied, 20 years later only 9% were doing so, the rest accompanied on foot or driven there, mostly by their mothers (Hillman alert again to the implications for women, in exhaustion and their ability to work outside the home).

Bad apple effect: study shows how people are influenced by rule-breaking of others

From politicians taking bribes to bullying and harassment in City firms, leaders have been quick to label those who break the rules as the odd “bad apple”. But new research backs up the idiom that one bad apple can spoil the barrel. Researchers have found that when people go beyond the rule-breaking they see in others, general compliance can swiftly turn into widespread rule-breaking. Dr Lucas Molleman, from the University of Amsterdam and the first author of the research, said the goal was to explore how individuals make decisions about rule-breaking in a social context. “Many people think of themselves as making sort of autonomous decisions, especially in these individualist cultures that we are from, like Netherlands, the UK,” he said. “But in actual fact, in many, many cases we are very much influenced by what others are doing.” Writing in the journal Proceedings of the Royal Society B, Molleman and colleagues report how they recruited 750 people in the US to take part in an online experiment, with the participants approximately evenly split between Republicans and Democrats.

citation.title: Bad apple effect: study shows how people are influenced by rule-breaking of others

text:
Bad apple effect: study shows how people are influenced by rule-breaking of others

The researchers asked each participant to complete an online task in which they saw an animated “shooting star” moving across a row of 100 squares as its intensity varied. Participants were instructed to pick the square that lit up most intensely to receive a monetary reward. However, participants received greater rewards for selecting squares further to the right of the correct square, and smaller rewards for selecting squares further to the left. Participants were then shown whether another participant had followed the rules or broken them, the extent of any rule-breaking, and their political affiliation, and asked if they wished to update their choice. The process was repeated six times. The results revealed participants showed large degrees of rule-breaking even in their initial choices, with 23% of choices involving squares with the highest reward.

text:
Bad apple effect: study shows how people are influenced by rule-breaking of others

However, the choices of others mattered: seeing others following the rules slightly reduced an individual’s rule-breaking, while seeing others making small beneficial violations – choosing a square a third of the way to the right, beyond the correct square – slightly increased rule-breaking. Crucially, seeing others flagrantly flout the rules by selecting a square even further to the right led participants to greatly increase their own level of rule-breaking. In some cases they went beyond the violations they had observed. The team say the findings were stronger when a participant had the same political leanings as others – something Molleman said chimed with other research, suggesting people who are politically aligned are more influenced by each other. The researchers used computer simulations to explore how the behaviour they had observed in the experiments would play out in a large group. The results showed that a situation could quickly get out of hand.

“A minority of escalating individuals, exceeding the rule violations they observe, they might cause a whole collective to spin out of control,” Molleman said. However, he noted that about a third of participants consistently followed the rules even though it did not lead to the largest reward. Prof Stephen Reicher, of the University of St Andrews, in Scotland, who was not involved in the work, said the study had limitations, including that the experiment was abstract and there was no penalty for rule-breaking, meaning the relevance of the work to real-world examples remained unproven. Reicher also stressed that the results went against the concept of contagion, instead showing that whether we are influenced by others depends on who those others are. “This is important because it implies that, say, we don’t riot simply because we see others rioting,” he said. “In fact, many people who see rioting respond by helping clear up after riots.”

The humble one-celled alga that helped scientists win the Nobel prize

A tiny alga has helped show how memories, feelings and behaviour form in our brains, in research by three scientists awarded the Nobel prize for physiology or medicine this month. Chlamydomonas is a one-celled alga that swims towards light using a light-sensing protein called channelrhodopsin, remarkably similar to the rhodopsin in our eyes. When the channelrhodopsin detects light, electrically charged ions rush into the cell from outside, triggering an electrical signal incredibly fast that tells the alga to move with its hair-like motor. In the research, the gene for the Chlamydomonas channelrhodopsin was transferred into living animal brain cells and flashes of light were used to switch individual neurons on or off, helping pinpoint the exact circuits in the brain that control behaviour, feelings, memories, movements, waking and sleeping, and other bodily functions. It could even switch on how mice gather their young in a nest or groom them.

Do people become less creative as they get older? Research makes surprising discovery

Ask a five-year-old to paint a picture and they will almost instinctively reach for the brush, but ask an adult to do the same and they will often hesitate and shy away. Now researchers say they know why. While it is widely assumed children are more creative than adults, a new study challenges this notion, finding adults outperform preschoolers on creative tasks but generally feel less confident and more anxious doing them. Dr Mathias Benedek, the senior author of the study at the University of Graz in Austria, said: “Children are so intrinsically motivated and absorbed in play that we often mistake their engagement with greater creative ability.” Writing in the journal Plos One, the researchers asked 92 preschool children aged four to seven and 70 adults largely in their 20s to complete three tasks. The first involved coming up with as many creative uses for a tin as possible in three minutes; the second involved drawing anything they liked with no stated time limit; and the third involved drawing an imaginary animal within eight minutes.

citation.title: Do people become less creative as they get older? Research makes surprising discovery

text:
Do people become less creative as they get older? Research makes surprising discovery

The results were then rated by judges on originality, usefulness and overall creativity. Participants were also asked to rate how much they enjoyed each task, how motivated and confident they felt, and how anxious they were doing it. The judges deemed the work by adults to be more original, useful and creative than that of children, particularly when clear goals and time limits were set. Conversely, children reported feeling more confident, motivated and less anxious completing tasks. “Adults outperformed children, demonstrating higher creative potential, but they had far less confidence. We need to look at what makes adults so anxious about their original ideas being rejected,” Benedek said. He said children approached tasks with greater intrinsic motivation and enjoyed the process of play, “whereas adults place more focus on the goal or objective”, limiting their enjoyment. As a result, children experimented more freely and treated mistakes as part of the process whereas adults, wary of judgment, often dismissed unusual ideas before trying them.
