text:
Do people become less creative as they get older? Research makes surprising discovery

The study, conducted at the University of Graz in Austria in collaboration with UCLouvain in Belgium and Yale University, has limitations. Among them, the research is based on a snapshot comparison of just two age groups, making it hard to draw conclusions about the impact of ageing on creativity. Children are also more likely to pick extreme answers on rating scales and have obvious differences in cognition. Nonetheless, Benedek and his colleagues suggest that the idea of creativity fading as we grow into adulthood is a misconception. “Adults don’t lose their creativity, instead they lose the confidence to use it,” Benedek said.

Orangutans prefer food associated with sounds of laughter, study suggests

Orangutans base their food choices on whether others appear to be having a good time, research suggests. Scientists studying captive orangutans have found that when the great apes heard the sound of their peers laughing before they searched a bowl for a tasty treat, they valued the reward more highly. Erica Cartmill, a professor of anthropology and cognitive science at Indiana University and senior author of the work, said the study is part of a larger project exploring whether animals feel joy and what the implications of those emotions are in areas such as cognition and learning. “One of our big motivations … is building on human research that shows that emotion has important effects on rational thought – and that they aren’t two separate things; they really influence one another,” she said. “We wanted to extend that to animals – in this case to orangutans.” Writing in the journal Biology Letters, Cartmill and her colleagues report how they worked with six orangutans based at two zoological institutions. The researchers first trained the orangutans to search through bowls to find food treats.

They then presented each orangutan with two bowls. One contained a tasty morsel buried under a harmless substance such as moss or sawdust, while the other contained a different type of material but no treat. Crucially, just before the researchers presented the bowls to the orangutans, they played a recording. This was either the sound of orangutans playing and laughing or environmental sounds such as wind, with the choice of soundtrack depending on which of two substances was used to cover the food that day. On the fifth day the team presented the orangutans with two bowls, but this time each contained a treat buried beneath one of the two food-covering substances. They then asked the orangutans to pick a bowl. The results from multiple trials revealed that, overall, the apes preferred to pick the bowl containing the substance associated with the sound of laughter, with four of the six orangutans showing a clear preference. Cartmill said the preference could be rooted in the sound of laughter putting the orangutans in a more positive emotional state when they learned to associate the substance with food.

text:
Plague risks in Russia and a dangerous delay on WHO pandemic agreement

Your editorial on the silence from Siberia after a worker died at a plague research institute there is right that the lack of information is the real worry (The Guardian view on plague in Russia: what is most worrying is the lack of information, 18 October). But the deeper failure is not Russian. It is that, six years after Covid, we still have no agreed system for sharing pathogens, or for sharing what is made from them. I spent three decades in Hong Kong, through bird flu, Sars and Covid, working on outbreak surveillance and sample-sharing between Hong Kong and the UK. It is also where this territorial argument began. In June 1894, two bacteriologists arrived to investigate the plague. Kitasato Shibasaburō was given lab space and immediate access to the bodies. Alexandre Yersin was refused access to the dead, and worked from a straw hut, having to appeal to the governor for his share of cadavers. Access to the material was allocated by favour, not by need. The organism carries the name of the man who was shut out: Yersinia pestis.

text:
Plague risks in Russia and a dangerous delay on WHO pandemic agreement

The pathogen access and benefit-sharing annexe to the World Health Organization pandemic agreement is the same argument in modern dress, and it has stalled on the same point. Poorer countries are asked to detect and share dangerous pathogens quickly. In return, they want a binding guarantee of what follows: 20% of real-time production of vaccines and treatments, half donated and half sold at cost. In article 13, the global supply chain and logistics network provides for a more equitable distribution of personal protective equipment. Richer countries prefer all that sharing to stay voluntary. The agreement cannot open for signature until this is settled, and it has now been deferred to 2027. All pandemics start with a rumour. The next pandemic is likely to be something we have never seen before, and whoever first holds the samples will not be us. If we cannot agree what they get in return, we should not be surprised when they are slow to hand them over.

It is the predictable product of rules that member states built without teeth. The International Health Regulations oblige governments to notify the WHO within 24 hours, yet provide no verification, no sanctions and no independent monitoring. States mark their own homework through annual self-assessments. The amendments in force since last September add an implementation committee that is, by design, consultative only. Member states, Britain included, chose this. They then starved the WHO of assessed funding, leaving it dependent on the goodwill of the governments it is meant to hold to account. Britain accepted the amended regulations in July 2025 and, with the United States gone, is among the WHO’s largest government funders. ‘It’s magic’: scientists rediscover how to make ancient Roman colour-changing glass

The Romans’ proficiency in the art of glass-making has produced some of the wonders of antiquity, but few of their creations better a 1,600-year-old masterpiece which sits in the British Museum. Depending on where a light source is positioned, the Lycurgus Cup changes colour, from jade green under normal lighting to ruby red when lit from behind – an astonishing feat of optical engineering that has confounded historians and glass-makers for centuries. Now scientists from the University of Sheffield have replicated its remarkable optical behaviour, using an ancient recipe derived from a fragment of the Roman “dichroic” (two-coloured) original. Dr Lisa Hollands, a technician at the university’s school of chemical, materials and biological engineering, said that replicating it has been “a labour of love” and “people have tried it before with limited success”. She added: “To me, it’s magic.” The fourth-century original bears a mythological frieze depicting the legend of King Lycurgus from the sixth book of Homer’s Iliad.

US military gives Elon Musk’s SpaceX access to sensitive tracking data

The US military has given Elon Musk’s SpaceX access to restricted space tracking data, raising a new round of questions about whether the Trump administration is attempting to hand over traffic control in Earth’s orbit to a controversial donor. The access also raises new national security questions, industry observers say. The move comes after Musk’s Doge in 2025 fired many of the federal government’s nascent space traffic control program’s staff, and the administration has twice attempted to financially gut the department, called the Traffic Coordination System for Space (Traccs). The moves were widely viewed in the industry as an attempt by Musk to privatize space traffic control. The defense department has now granted SpaceX access to its most precise data on potential collisions among satellites and other space objects, which will give Musk’s companies an advantage over competition that offers a similar service. SpaceX and the Space Force signed the new contract.

text:
Jean Phillips-Martinsson obituary

In 1984 Jean Phillips-Martinsson, a British woman living in Sweden, came across an article in the Lancet. It was about Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS), a rare genetic condition named after Andrea Prader and Heinrich Willi, two of the three Swiss paediatricians who discovered it in 1956. It was a lightbulb moment for Phillips-Martinsson, who had been in limbo for 14 years, wanting to know why her son, Anders, born in 1970, was floppy and unable to suck as a baby, and later had behavioural problems and was constantly hungry (hyperphagia). It turned out these are all key signs of PWS. Phillips-Martinsson contacted the article’s author, who was able to diagnose Anders. She said her first thought was, “Are we alone in Sweden?”, and through the endocrinologist Martin Ritzén she was put in touch with four other families with a PWS child.

They had all felt similarly isolated, and when they met for coffee on in April 1986 at Phillips-Martinsson’s house in Stockholm she said: “It was an extremely emotional situation for us all.” Phillips-Martinsson knew that a Swedish association would be too small to be effective – a global charity was essential She and the other parents wanted advice on PWS, which causes behavioural and mental health issues as well as constant hunger and weight gain. So that year she set up a Prader-Willi Syndrome Association in Sweden. But she knew it was too small to be effective: the condition is so rare (estimated to affect between one in 15,000 and in one in 25,000 people) that a global charity with a wider reach was essential. It helped that she had networking and research skills, and could speak several languages. With a background in PR and translating, over the next few years she poured her energies into researching PWS. She discovered fledgling PWS charities in other countries, including the Netherlands, the US and the UK, and in November 1986 attended the PWS-UK’s conference in Bristol.

In 1988 she was excited to hear from the American geneticist Dr Suzanne Cassidy. Thanks to a new technique called high-resolution analysis, geneticists knew that PWS resulted from an anomaly on chromosome 15. Research was taking place across the world, but it was not coordinated, and Cassidy wanted to bring researchers and doctors together in an international conference. Phillips-Martinsson and Cassidy met in 1989, forming an organising committee for a conference to be held in the Netherlands in 1991. During the next couple of years, a time she described as “being drowned in correspondence”, Phillips-Martinsson drummed up support from researchers, doctors and parents around the world, and secured sponsorship from the Swedish company Kabi Pharmacia, the World Health Organization and Nato. While much of the conference was devoted to scientific developments, Phillips-Martinsson championed the families, making sure one day of the conference focused on the concerns of parents and caregivers. The conference opened in May 1991 in the Netherlands, with 200 delegates from 22 countries.

They voted to form the International Prader-Willi Syndrome Organisation (IPWSO) with Phillips-Martinsson as its president. She served in this capacity until 1998 and remained its guiding force and honorary president to the end of her life. As president, Phillips-Martinsson networked extensively to bring more countries into the IPSWO fold, and supported the setup of national organisations in many countries in Europe and beyond. She travelled widely, speaking at PWS conferences in Europe, the US, Australia and New Zealand. On her watch, IPWSO began its programme of international conferences every three years. They put out regular newsletters, a vital mouthpiece for their community, and disseminated information about developments, such as clinical trials into growth hormones (now a standard treatment). To reduce global inequality, IPWSO lobbied for genetic testing, working to provide free diagnostic testing for people in underserved countries. IPWSO also created information resources on subjects such as diet, behaviour and education, and in 1992 established the first residential care facility for adults with PWS.

‘Maxxing’ is Dictionary.com’s word of the year: ‘It’s cooler than saying you’re doing more’

Maxxing is not a new concept. Dungeons and Dragons players have been “min-maxing” character stats for years; Will Smith was maxin’ and relaxin’ in the 90s; as far back as the 40s, the term was used in game theory. But in the past few years, as all facets of our lives are optimized, the suffix has become inescapable. We’re personalitymaxxing to charm our peers and sleepmaxxing to get the best possible rest; the Pentagon brags about “lethalitymaxxing”. People are proteinmaxxing their breakfast, tokenmaxxing their use of AI … cozymaxxing on a Friday night Steve Johnson The explosion in the word’s use has made it Dictionary.com’s word of the year for 2026. To choose each year’s word, Dictionary.com staffers investigate search trends, social media and the news, “and then we ask ourselves what’s telling the most compelling story of the year”, says Steve Johnson, director of lexicography for the Dictionary Media Group. “This year, maxxing stood out because it really connects to so many different parts of life.

Starwatch: Bright stars of Pegasus make this distinctive constellation easy to see

This week we will track down Pegasus, one of the most distinctive constellations in the autumn sky. Pegasus was one of the 48 constellations listed by Ptolemy in the second century. In Greek mythology, it represents the magnificent winged horse ridden by the hero Bellerophon. The easiest part of the constellation to recognise is the Great Square of Pegasus, a large pattern of four moderately bright stars. The chart shows the view looking high in the southern sky from London at 10pm on 26 October. Three of these stars, Markab, Scheat and Algenib, belong to Pegasus. The fourth, Alpheratz, is actually part of the neighbouring constellation Andromeda. Historically, Alpheratz was considered to belong to both constellations, but when the official boundaries of the 88 modern constellations were established, it ended up in Andromeda. The Great Square is the body of Pegasus. From Markab, follow a curving line of stars towards Enif (whose name means nose in Arabic) to trace the horse’s neck and head. Other lines of stars extending from the Square represent the horse’s front legs.

‘Ferritin face’: are social media claims about iron deficiency fact – or fiction?

TikTok is rife with influencers warning of “ferritin face”, a term they use to describe the pallor, dark circles, dry skin, and hair loss claimed to indicate low iron stores. But is this based on fact or fiction, and when is it time to head to the GP? What is ferritin? Iron is not made in the body, so typically we consume it in our diet. Ferritin is the protein responsible for storing iron in the body, particularly in the liver, and releasing it in a controlled manner. By measuring ferritin levels, which can be checked via blood tests, it is possible to get an snapshot of the body’s iron reserves, although experts warn such levels are not always a reliable guide. Blood ferritin levels of less than 30 micrograms/L indicate an iron deficiency, according to guidelines from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. However “a level below 50 might be a pointer of iron deficiency,” said Sue Pavord, professor of practice in medical haematology at Oxford University hospitals. Can low ferritin change a person’s appearance?

citation.title: ‘Ferritin face’: are social media claims about iron deficiency fact – or fiction?

text:
‘Ferritin face’: are social media claims about iron deficiency fact – or fiction?

The symptoms influencers describe, such as dark circles under the eyes, grey skin, cracked lips and hair loss, can be caused by a variety of factors, including genetics, stress and dehydration. But experts say low iron stores can have an effect. “Iron is needed for every single cell of the body. So if you are iron deficient, you will be very fatigued, have brain fog, your skin will look dull and saggy, you’ll look pale and tired,” said Pavord. “While we can’t diagnose iron deficiency from the face, it might be a suggestion that there is iron deficiency.” Prof Toby Richards of the University of East London and the Iron Clinic added such changes were particularly pronounced in people with very low iron stores. “They tend to be the really sick patients,” he said. Why might people have low ferritin? “Periods and pregnancies are the most common [causes],” said Pavord, but others include not getting enough iron – either from dietary choices or because of poor absorption, as can occur with coeliac disease.

Low ferritin levels can also arise as a result of blood loss linked to gastrointestinal problems, such as gastritis or polyps. “We also sometimes see it in athletes because of the high demand for iron on their bodies,” she added. What should people who are worried they might have low ferritin do ? Richards said those who are at high risk of low ferritin – such as people who have heavy periods, are pregnant or have had children, or are vegetarian or vegan – should ask for a blood test, adding that should include a full blood count, ferritin level check, and test for levels of B12 and folate. “This is a proper disease, and to put it into perspective, it’s the leading cause of disability in women of reproductive ability,” he said. Pavord also said those who are concerned about their ferritin levels should ask for a blood test, adding it was important to understand the cause of iron deficiency. “Older people suspecting iron deficiency would need a proper clinical assessment and investigations to look for a source of bleeding from the bowel,” she said.

How rising seas transformed dry land into Venice lagoon

Venice is famed for being a floating city, but research shows the land it sits on once lay many miles inland. Dramatic changes in sea level over 10,000 years have reshaped the northern Adriatic coastline, with much of the land that our ancestors roamed now lying beneath the waves. Samuele Ongaro, at the University of Southampton, and colleagues combined seismic data with sedimentary cores from the coastal basins of northern Italy, Slovenia and northern Croatia to model changes in sea level across the region and reconstruct past landscapes over the past 10,000 years. Their results, published in Quaternary Science Reviews, show that the present-day Venice lagoon was once dry land extending more than 30 miles from the coast, and that Trieste was previously an area of hills overlooking swamps and lagoons. Starting just over 10,000 years ago, sea level rose in fits and starts, sometimes by up to 25mm a year, forcing Mesolithic hunter-gatherer populations to shift their hunting and fishing activities as they adapted to a rapidly changing environment.

text:
Migrating seabirds face a surprising problem: jet lag

Seabirds returning from foraging trips can be thrown hundreds of miles off course by a form of jet lag that arises when their body clocks get out of sync with local time, researchers say. Tracking data from Manx shearwaters on the west coast of the UK revealed that when the birds returned home to their colonies after trips over the Atlantic, their rapid eastward flights disrupted their sense of time and navigation. The impact was limited on adult shearwaters because the birds were able to correct their bearings in flight. At most, the birds veered off course by about 15 degrees. After correcting their course, this added only an estimated 3 miles to a 600-mile journey. But less experienced birds were likely to have a tougher time, the study found, with first-time foragers at risk of flying off course by hundreds of miles. Most studies on birds’ biological clocks have been conducted under laboratory conditions but Dr Patrick Lewin, a behavioural and sensory ecologist at the University of Oxford, set out to investigate wild birds with the help of his colleagues.

citation.title: Migrating seabirds face a surprising problem: jet lag

text:
Migrating seabirds face a surprising problem: jet lag

Their analysis of 20 years of GPS tracking data revealed a clear effect when the Manx shearwaters flew east across lines of longitude as they returned home, leading their clocks to run up to an hour or so behind local time. “The bird’s internal clock can be subject to a jet lag phenomenon, manifesting as birds flying off course,” Lewin said. Like many animals, shearwaters use the sun as a compass. Because the sun moves across the sky as the Earth rotates, reading its position correctly relies on the birds adjusting their heading relative to the sun, using their body clock to keep track of the time of day. Sunset and sunrise keep the bird’s body clock in sync, helping them adjust to changes in local time. Writing in Science, Lewin said the mismatch between local time and the birds’ internal clocks could make them drift off course when the sun lay farther around the sky than expected. Surprisingly, the errors remained when birds followed the coastline, where landmarks could have guided them, further supporting the idea that the sun plays a central role in anchoring their sense of direction.

citation.title: Migrating seabirds face a surprising problem: jet lag

text:
Migrating seabirds face a surprising problem: jet lag

“For adult shearwaters, this lag has very limited impact on their overall journey, with errors adding a calculated 5km to a 1,000km journey,” Lewin said. “However, for first-time migrant birds, such orientation shifts due to sun compass errors could result in deviations of hundreds of kilometres as they lack a map sense to help reorient them when they lose their way.” Prof Richard Holland of Bangor University, who was not involved in the study, said it was a significant finding: “It seems to confirm in wild animals what more controlled experimental studies have shown: reliance on the sun compass for animals that move during the day, even when it is not accurate.” Manx shearwaters spend most of their lives far out at sea. They cover enormous distances but return each year to islands off the west coast of the UK to breed in burrows. “It’s not clear from the study what the consequences of these errors are, since the birds return to their colony and the errors are small,” Holland said.

“Nonetheless, it highlights the importance of understanding the role of biological rhythms across multiple contexts in animal behaviour, as more and more we are starting to realise just how important these are for numerous biological functions.”

Elfi Evans obituary

My father, Elfi Evans, who has died aged 90, was one of a rare breed of truly omnicompetent practising veterinary surgeons, as at ease treating cats and dogs as he was carrying out caesarean sections on horses and cattle, in his native Carmarthenshire. Ever industrious, Elfi also ran a smallholding at the family home, where he reared sheep, grew vegetables and developed a number of environmental projects with the help of the Welsh government’s Tir Gofal (Care of the Land) scheme to support the natural biodiversity of the region. The third of five sons, Elfi was born in Bancycapel, Carmarthenshire, to Margaret (nee Williams) and William Evans, and grew up on the family farm there, becoming used to hard work from a very early age. Speaking exclusively Welsh at home, his first experience of English came about during the second world war, from the exchanges he and his brothers had with the Italian and German prisoners of war working on the farm, and American soldiers stationed nearby. At the age of 15, against his father’s wishes, Elfi stayed on at Queen Elizabeth grammar school in Carmarthen.

citation.title: Elfi Evans obituary

text:
Elfi Evans obituary

He had ambitions to study engineering but, persuaded by his father that a veterinary degree was the better option, he started a BVSc at Liverpool University, travelling the eight-hour journey between his home and Liverpool on his Lambretta scooter at the start and end of each term. After graduating in 1960 and working for a period as a vet in Chwilog, north Wales, he returned to Carmarthen to set up his own practice, The Ark, assisted by his wife, Ann (nee Cadwaladr), whom he had met at Liverpool at combined medic and vet physiology lectures and married in 1962. By the 70s Elfi’s veterinary practice had developed into a three-partner operation, responding to increasing demands from the farming community across Carmarthenshire – as well as the rise in ownership of cats, dogs and more exotic animals, including an elephant, Valli, kept by the Skanda Vale religious community. In the early 80s he moved the practice to larger premises and started to specialise in diseases of sheep.

citation.title: Elfi Evans obituary

text:
Elfi Evans obituary

Elfi retired from the practice in January 2001, but it was short-lived as his knowledge and skills were urgently required throughout that year with the outbreak of the foot-and-mouth crisis across the UK. He and Ann had taken on and transformed the run-down smallholding near the village of Nantycaws in the late 80s. There, Elfi created ponds to attract and support wildlife and planted native species of trees within traditional orchard environments. The non-native fir trees, which he planted to provide shelter for the young saplings, were harvested over many years and given away as Christmas trees in return for donations, raising tens of thousands of pounds for the oncology department at Carmarthen hospital, where Elfi had been successfully treated for cancer in the early 90s. Elfi is survived by Ann, his three sons, Winston, Gavin and me, and eight grandchildren.

text:
Perfume bottle and child’s necklace among treasures found in Pompeii wardrobe

Fragments of personal objects, from makeup tools and a perfume bottle to coins and a child’s necklace, have been found tucked away in a wooden wardrobe sealed off for almost 2,000 years in the ruins of Pompeii. The artifacts provide an intimate glimpse of daily life in the ancient Roman city before it was devastated by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD79. The wardrobe was discovered in a room of a home on Via dell’Abbondanza, which was one of the most bustling streets in Pompeii. The items inside included tweezers, a small glass perfume bottle, an incense burner and a bronze lantern. But the most intriguing relic was a necklace featuring more than 20 small charms crafted from various materials and representing several deities, including depictions of the gods Bes and Mercury. The type of necklace, known as a crepundia, was traditionally worn by children. Its decorative charms rattled to help parents keep track of their children and could also help them be identified. “A crepundia had a very special function,” said Gabriel Zuchtriegel, the director of Pompeii archaeological park.

citation.title: Perfume bottle and child’s necklace among treasures found in Pompeii wardrobe

text:
Perfume bottle and child’s necklace among treasures found in Pompeii wardrobe

“It was a reminder of their parents who perhaps lived far away … it was very typical of this society of people, who were often displaced. Many people moved around in the Mediterranean area and tended to carry personal objects with them.” The wardrobe contained other items including 38 bronze coins, cooking pots and a wooden box with lead weights, suggesting that someone who lived in the home was a tradesperson. The fact that money and personal objects were left behind could point to the owners having to flee the eruption at short notice, Zuchtriegel said. Archaeologists also found the fragmented skeletons of two mice inside an amphora that had been kept in a storage area of the home. The home had previously been associated with a person called Cornelius Maximus owing to the discovery of inscriptions, which are no longer visible. Its ​facade was first excavated ​in 1912, but experts are only now delving into some of its rooms as part of a wider restoration project.

citation.title: Perfume bottle and child’s necklace among treasures found in Pompeii wardrobe

text:
Perfume bottle and child’s necklace among treasures found in Pompeii wardrobe

There are also excavations under way at the Villa of the Mysteries in a suburb of Pompeii, which also first came to light in the early 20th century. “It’s never been completely excavated, so we kind of want to finish the job,” said Zuchtriegel. “What’s interesting is that we’re not excavating in the part where the owners lived and where great frescoes are to be expected, but in the servants’ quarters. “So what we hope to find there is more insight into the daily life and economy of those who were somehow in the shadow of history. The majority of the inhabitants in the Villa of the Mysteries were actually servants.” Excavations at Pompeii regularly yield discoveries from the ruins of the ancient city. In 2025, a large and sophisticated thermal bath complex, which was thought to have been used by its owner to woo well-heeled guests, was found during excavations of a home on Via di Nola in Regio IX, a wealthy district of the city. A home containing a cramped bakery, where enslaved people were believed to have been imprisoned and made to produce bread, was found in the same district in 2023.

text:
From gold rush to cosmic questions: a South Dakota mine and the search for the secrets of the universe

For more than a century, the mining town of Lead, in the Black Hills of South Dakota, attracted workers with a taste for gold. Now, a flagship experiment being built in the old mine is drawing scientists in search of more intriguing riches: answers to the deepest mysteries of the universe. Construction of the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (Dune) in the former Homestake mine is due to start on Monday. Engineers will begin assembling four giant detectors inside caverns blasted from rock a mile underground. Once switched on, the detectors will quietly spark and flicker as ghostly particles called neutrinos hurtle through them. Some will arrive from the sun and distant supernovae, others in an intense beam sent through 800 miles (1,300km) of rock from a government laboratory near Chicago, Illinois. Observing the neutrinos could uncover entirely new science and shed light on cosmic spectacles, such as the death of stars and the birth of black holes.

citation.title: From gold rush to cosmic questions: a South Dakota mine and the search for the secrets of the universe

text:
From gold rush to cosmic questions: a South Dakota mine and the search for the secrets of the universe

Scientists are particularly hopeful of solving one of the most enduring puzzles in nature: why everything around us is made from matter and not its “evil twin”, antimatter. In other words, why we, and why anything, is here at all. Interactive “It’s a super exciting time to be working on this,” said Dr Kate Shaw, an experimental particle physicist on Dune from the University of Sussex. “Neutrinos do not make sense yet and they could open a door to new physics.” Neutrinos are the most abundant matter particles in the universe, outnumbered only by photons, the massless particles of light that illuminate the universe. They are produced in natural nuclear reactions, such as those that power the sun, in radioactive decay and in particle accelerators. Even by physicists’ standards, neutrinos are oddballs. The chargeless particles barely interact with other matter: about a trillion pass unnoticed through your body each second. Neutrinos come in three varieties, all with minuscule but different masses.

citation.title: From gold rush to cosmic questions: a South Dakota mine and the search for the secrets of the universe

text:
From gold rush to cosmic questions: a South Dakota mine and the search for the secrets of the universe

Weirdly, they change from one variety to another, a process called oscillation, as they travel. “It’s a very strange behaviour,” said Shaw. “It’s like me throwing you an apple and it turns into a banana.” Lead has a history with these peculiar particles. In the 1960s, the physicist Ray Davis followed miners down the shaft and built a detector from a 100,000-gallon tank filled with dry-cleaning fluid. Shielded so deep beneath the ground, the detector became the first to record neutrinos from the sun as they struck chlorine atoms in the fluid and turned them into argon. The mine closed in 2001 and transitioned, thanks to visionary forethought, into a dedicated subterranean laboratory, the Sanford Underground Research Facility (Surf). It is already home to the Lux-Zeplin (LZ) experiment which last month reported the first potential detection of dark matter. “We’ve gone from mining the Earth to helping scientists explore the universe,” said Robin Lucero, Lead’s city administrator, whose family has lived locally for generations.

citation.title: From gold rush to cosmic questions: a South Dakota mine and the search for the secrets of the universe

text:
From gold rush to cosmic questions: a South Dakota mine and the search for the secrets of the universe

“We’re incredibly proud and lucky that Dune is happening here, and Surf, which has other experiments like LZ. Having world-class science brings new opportunities, new people and new possibilities for our local businesses and especially our young people.” Unlike Davis’s apparatus, the Dune experiment is enormous. Made from more than 4,000 tonnes of steel, the detectors will stand up to five-storeys high and hold a combined 70,000 tonnes of liquid argon that must be chilled to -200C. Assembling the detectors should take nearly three years. Filling them with liquid argon, another year. “This is a heavy duty engineering operation,” and a partnership with the skilled local workforce, said Prof David Newbold, of the UK’s Science and Technology Facilities Council and a Dune spokesperson.

citation.title: From gold rush to cosmic questions: a South Dakota mine and the search for the secrets of the universe

text:
From gold rush to cosmic questions: a South Dakota mine and the search for the secrets of the universe

“It’s like building a ship underground.” The UK is the largest international partner in the US-led experiment and is making core detector components, critical computing to reconstruct events in the detectors, and the graphite target needed to generate neutrinos at Femilab, a particle physics facility in Illinois. Once operational, Dune will study an intense beam of neutrinos sent from Fermilab through 800 miles of the Earth’s crust and mantle. Most neutrinos will shoot straight through, but every so often one will strike an argon atom, creating a flicker of light and a pulse of electric charge. Analysing these will reveal intimate details about the mysterious particles. One big question surrounds the masses of different neutrinos. Which is lightest and which heaviest? The answer could reveal fundamental new forces of nature. And in an attempt to answer the matter v antimatter question, Dune will look for subtle differences between neutrinos and their antimatter twins, antineutrinos.

citation.title: From gold rush to cosmic questions: a South Dakota mine and the search for the secrets of the universe

text:
From gold rush to cosmic questions: a South Dakota mine and the search for the secrets of the universe

Beyond the beams of particles sent from Fermilab, Dune will also study neutrinos arriving from space, carrying with them fresh information on stellar explosions and the formation of black holes. Earlier this month, the Nobel prize for physics honoured the Belgian researcher Francis Halzen, who used a cubic kilometre of Antarctica to detect high-energy neutrinos from deep space. But detection is far from the end of the story. “This really is going to be a golden era,” Newbold said. “There’s a lot more of that to come.”

Full-blown adulthood: does it actually start at 50?

Name: 50 (and thriving). Age: You can work this one out. Appearance: Cool, calm and collected. Also, very tidy. Don’t you mean frazzled? Come on, wouldn’t you say you’re more together now than you were at 20, or even 30? Who says I’m not still in my 20s? Why are we comparing ages anyway? A new survey has found that 50 is the age at which Brits feel “most confident and in control of their lives”. And what source do we have to thank for this? British Gas commissioned the survey of 2,000 British adults. Getting the boiler serviced is one way to feel like a grownup, I suppose. The survey found that recycling, putting clothes away and knowing when bin day is were widely-agreed-upon indicators that someone had “got it together”. What’s wrong with a chairdrobe? It’s a perfectly workable system! It’s a pile of clothes, is what it is. Respondents also said that having a litter-free car, spare batteries to hand and washing up after a dinner party, instead of leaving it till the next day, were signs of adulthood. I knew I was right to buy that bulk pack of triple As.

It’s when you’ve got a spare CR2032 battery that you know you’re really nailing it. These do seem somewhat low or arbitrary bars for having your life together. Oh, so you want to hold people to owning a car, or buying a house, or becoming a parent? Not in this economy. True. But surely there are more meaningful markers of maturity than making your bed, or drinking two litres of water a day? As if you do either every day. Abundant common fossils don’t need to be protected

The vast majority of the fossils revealed on this rapidly eroding part of the Jurassic Coast hold very little scientific importance and are not in need of protection or recording (Letters, 28 August). Museums around the world have countless examples of the common fossils from these Lower Jurassic rocks, thanks to the efforts of fossil collectors, who since the pioneering palaeontologist Mary Anning (1799–1847) have saved fossils from the same process that reveals them, the action of the sea. The majority of these scientifically important fossils are saved from destruction after the winter storms, not during the peak tourist season in the summer. Allowing tourists to collect and take home their discoveries helps them foster a sense of curiosity and encourages an interest in the natural world, which is especially important for future generations. As in any busy tourist destination, there will always be ill-informed tourists.

Here at the Charmouth Heritage Coast Centre, our educational charity welcomes in excess of 100,000 visitors a year. It is free for all to enter and learn more about the past, present and future of our amazing coast through our award-winning displays of recent fossil finds. text:
Genetically modified pig kidney keeps man alive for record nine months

A genetically modified kidney from a pig called Wilma has kept a 66-year-old man with kidney failure alive for a record nine months and successfully acted as a “bridge” to a human transplant in a world first. Tim Andrews was seriously ill with end-stage kidney disease caused by type 2 diabetes and had only a 9% chance of receiving a human kidney within five years, against a more than 40% risk of dying or being removed from the waiting list. Kidney transplantation provides the best survival and quality of life for patients with end-stage kidney disease, but global demand for human organs far exceeds supply. Surgeons in the US successfully transplanted a kidney from Wilma, a Yucatan miniature pig, into Andrews, after genetically engineering it to be compatible with his immune system. The kidney kept Andrews free of dialysis for a record nine months, the longest period ever recorded, before it began failing and he received one from a dead human donor. It was also the first time a pig’s kidney had been used as a temporary “bridge” to a human transplant.

citation.title: Genetically modified pig kidney keeps man alive for record nine months

text:
Genetically modified pig kidney keeps man alive for record nine months

Details of the breakthrough, which offers hope to millions of people whose kidneys have failed, were published in the Lancet medical journal. Andrews, from New Hampshire, described the pig kidney transplant as a “miracle”, adding: “I was alive, and I hadn’t been in a long time.” He was able to cook, vacuum and take long walks with his dog, Cupcake, he said. Transplanting genetically engineered pig organs has long been proposed as a solution to the organ shortage. But the first pig kidney transplant into a living person, in 2024, ended after 52 days when the patient died from unrelated heart problems, and no previous studies had documented xenograft survival beyond two months, according to the Lancet. Before the transplant in January 2025, Wilma the pig had received 69 edits to her genome. Some of these were designed to dodge viruses that might pose a risk to humans, while others made the organ more compatible with humans, reducing the odds of immune rejection.

His case represents the longest dialysis-free survival following pig kidney xenotransplantation in a living human, and the world’s first transition to human kidney transplantation, the team said. “The organ shortage is the greatest crisis we have right now in transplantation,” said Dr Leonardo Riella, of the Center for Transplantation Sciences and the Division of Nephrology at Mass General Brigham. “We know that the best treatment option for patients with end-stage kidney disease who have developed renal failure is transplantation, but we simply don’t have enough human organs to transplant in a timely manner.

text:
Rich people more likely to steal children’s sweets, finds Ig Nobel prize-winning study

It’s that time of year again: a select group of scientists have been summoned to a ceremony to receive coveted prizes, be showered in paper planes, and leave with a 10tn dollar bill, albeit in the form of a phased-out note from Zimbabwe. It is, of course, the annual Ig Nobel awards. Not to be confused with the more prestigious and career-changing Nobel prizes that will be announced in Scandinavia next month, the satirical Ig Nobels are awarded for achievements that “first make people laugh and then make them think”. Milky Way at the dining table: Bath art show celebrates 18th-century brother and sister astronomers

From the garden of their Georgian townhouse in Bath in the late 18th century, a brother and sister made a series of extraordinary astronomical discoveries. A new art show in the house where the siblings – William and Caroline Herschel – worked and lived highlights their pioneering spirit and their domestic arrangements. The Irish artist Grace Weir, who created the exhibition in what is now the Herschel Museum of Astronomy, said she was deeply interested in the science that went on at the house, including the discovery of the planet Uranus, and fascinated that it took place in such a cosy environment. “It is a home,” Weir said. “Science does not take place in a vacuum. They would have had conversations about their discoveries across the dining table.” One of her artworks, On the Construction of Heavens, was inspired by William Herschel’s drawing of the Milky Way in 1785. Weir has had a copy of the drawing embroidered on to an antique linen tablecloth, which is laid over the family dining table.

citation.title: Milky Way at the dining table: Bath art show celebrates 18th-century brother and sister astronomers

text:
Milky Way at the dining table: Bath art show celebrates 18th-century brother and sister astronomers

“William and Caroline must have spoken about the shape of the Milky Way right here,” Weir said. “That would have been an unusual thing to talk about back then.” In the basement workshop, where William Herschel built his own telescopes, Weir has installed an LED digital counter that records the distance of Uranus from the Earth as it changes. A key element of the show is to make sure Caroline Herschel gets her share of the credit for the pair’s advances in science. William Herschel was a self-taught amateur astronomer who came to Bath from Germany in 1777. His sister followed, initially as a housekeeper. She quickly became his assistant, recording his findings, helping him with calculations, keeping his telescopes in order but then made discoveries of her own, finding eight comets and becoming the first woman in England to be paid as an astronomer. One of the most striking pieces Weir has created is a tribute to Caroline Herschel’s comet-spotting abilities.

Milky Way at the dining table: Bath art show celebrates 18th-century brother and sister astronomers

Called An Imperfect Account, it features a piece of meteorite and a piece of obsidian in the shape of one of Caroline’s worry beads. Weir said: “William had to persuade her mother to let her come to Bath. He recognised her intelligence and once she got here, they were incredibly collaborative. They drove each other along, they understood each other.” The pieces created by Weir are scattered around the house, meaning the visitor has to look for them. Weir said people were losing the art of observing closely. “The Herschels were masters of long looking, something we are losing by scrolling,” she said. Amy Frost, a senior curator at Bath Preservation Trust, said it was the first time in the museum’s history that contemporary site-specific artworks had been integrated. “It’s really exciting for us – it feels like a thread being created through time,” she said. The exhibition, called The As-Yet Unseen (a quote by William Herschel predicting the discovery of the planet Neptune), runs from 5 September until 3 January 2027.

My struggle, my burden, my shame was finally going to come to an end.” But as time went on it was hope, not weight, that fell away. “I was on [Ozempic] for nine months. And then I went on Wegovy for four months, then Contrave [an oral, non-GLP-1 medication], and then Mounjaro, and that was for a few months, and then nine months ago I started on Zepbound,” said Mercedes. “Nothing has worked.” A recently retired teacher in her 50s, Mercedes is among a small proportion of people for whom the powerful new weight-loss drugs, championed by celebrities for their transformative effects, do not work. Ozempic, a type 2 diabetes medication, and Wegovy, which is licensed for weight loss, both contain a drug called semaglutide that mimics a hormone that occurs naturally in our bodies: GLP-1.

Konstantinos Politis obituary

High above the Dead Sea’s south-eastern shore, pilgrims once climbed to a cave they believed had sheltered Lot after he fled the destruction of Sodom. For centuries the site survived in Christian memory alone, visited by occasional pilgrims such as St Stephen the Sabaite, until the Greek archaeologist Konstantinos Politis, who has died aged 67 following a series of strokes, began excavating in 1988. He uncovered a Byzantine basilica built over the mouth of the cave, its floors still adorned with mosaics laid in the sixth and seventh centuries CE. The discovery, at Deir ’Ain ’Abata, gave physical form to one of the Bible’s most vivid stories and set the course for a career spent excavating and protecting the archaeology of Jordan’s Dead Sea shore. Dino, as Politis was widely known, excavated the Sanctuary of Lot over seven seasons between 1988 and 1996. The site had been identified by an archaeological survey in 1986 as matching a sanctuary depicted on the famous sixth-century mosaic map at Madaba in Jordan, whose location had eluded archaeologists for more than a century.

citation.title: Konstantinos Politis obituary

text:
Konstantinos Politis obituary

In a disused cistern Dino found a communal burial of 32 people, all the adults among them male and many with degenerative disease, which led him to identify them as monks and to suggest that the monastery had also served as a hospice for the sick. Beneath the church his excavations revealed evidence of almost 5,000 years of human activity stretching back to the early bronze age. The church’s most recent mosaic was laid in 691 CE, more than half a century after the Muslim conquest. It names a local bishop, Christoforos, as well as a steward and a governor, and describes the sanctuary as a holy place. Evidently, Christians were not merely worshipping at the sanctuary under the new rulers but still embellishing their church, tangible evidence of the accommodation of Christian communities under early Umayyad rule. Dino spent nearly two further decades conserving and studying the site, culminating in a major publication in 2012. His work gained international media attention, and featured in documentaries including with National Geographic and the Discovery Channel.

citation.title: Konstantinos Politis obituary

text:
Konstantinos Politis obituary

In Greece, the national press dubbed him the “Greek Indiana Jones.” He was never content simply to excavate and move on. As early as 1996 he imagined a museum that would keep the discoveries in the landscape from which they came and, with the Jordanian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities, worked to make it a reality. The Museum at the Lowest Place on Earth opened to the public in 2012, 405m below sea level. He also helped establish a programme in the museum’s conservation laboratory, bringing international practitioners to train local staff in museological techniques, including object and mosaic conservation. His instinct to protect threatened archaeology was immediate. In 1996, while travelling to his excavations, Dino spotted bulldozers working in a field near Khirbat Qazone, scattering human remains across the ground. Looters had discovered an enormous Nabataean and Roman period cemetery. He intervened, later recovering one particularly well-preserved body, sometimes described as a “mummy” but in fact naturally desiccated by salt and heat, now held at Yarmouk University in Jordan.

He subsequently spent years salvaging and recording what remained of an estimated 5,000 graves, some containing rare preserved textiles, and among them a woman’s tombstone that read simply: “Afseni, the pretty girl”. From 1997 his attention widened to ancient Zoara at Ghawr as-Safi. Over the following decades he explored a landscape with a history stretching from prehistory to the Islamic periods, ultimately publishing the results in eight academic volumes. Among his discoveries was the largest known medieval sugar factory in Jordan and Palestine at Tawahin as-Sukkar. It reached its peak output during the Crusader and Mamluk periods between the 12th and 14th centuries, its mills, presses and furnaces revealing the industrial scale on which sugar was once produced beside the Dead Sea. Even this became a community project. Dino’s research demonstrated that indigo had once been grown in the valley before and alongside sugar. This evidence provided the impetus in 2013 for a Unesco project with the Safi Women’s Association to revive indigo cultivation, which had declined after synthetic dyes reached world markets in the early 20th century.

The women dyed textiles with the crop and sold them in the museum shop. With the museologist Georgios Papaioannou, Dino turned the story of sugar and indigo into exhibitions for Jordanian and international audiences. Supported by USAID and the American Center of Research in Amman, he also trained local community members in the management, protection and promotion of the Ghawr as-Safi archaeological sites. After Dino’s death, a local resident of Safi revealed that Dino had supported the village in another way, quietly paying for schoolbooks and schoolbags for children at the beginning of each school year. Born in Kozani, Greece, Dino was the son of Demetrios Politis, an officer in the Greek army, and Christine (nee Biller), a schoolteacher. He was educated in Greece, the US, Belgium and Britain, completing an MA at the Institute of Archaeology, University of London, in 1984 and a PhD in archaeology at the University of Ioannina in 2004.

Those already out and about at 5am this week will be rewarded with a beautiful waning crescent moon approaching Jupiter, while Mars watches on from a little further away. The chart shows the view looking east from London at 5am on Tuesday. The waning moon will be easily visible with about 10% of its visible surface illuminated. The brilliant beacon of Jupiter will be close by. The two are drawing together ahead of a conjunction later that day when the moon will pass less than a degree north of the giant planet. For comparison, the moon appears to be about half a degree wide in the sky. Unfortunately, the conjunction itself takes place at 7.11pm, after both objects have set from the UK. The following morning offers another opportunity, with the moon now on the other side of Jupiter. Mars adds to the scene. Look upwards and to the west and the red planet will be identifiable because of its colour. Mars lies in Gemini, while the moon and Jupiter are in neighbouring Cancer.

How meteorologists recreated weather that helped decide second world war

Dressed in a Royal Air Force uniform and sporting a trim moustache, Andrew Scott looks slightly queasy – as well he might. Behind him is a huge map of the Channel, and in front of him is Brendan Fraser, looming with a request: “I need a forecast,” he says. Starring in the film Pressure, based on a true story, Scott plays the meteorologist Gp Capt James Stagg – the man who must tell Gen Eisenhower – played by Fraser – whether conditions will be suitable for the D-day landings scheduled to take place on 5 June 1944. But a large storm is approaching the Normandy coast. The film, showing in cinemas in the UK and Ireland from 9 September, unites two topics that ceaselessly fascinate the British: the second world war – and weather. It is also a rare treat for meteorologists, who are not hugely represented on the big screen and are delighted to be portrayed as the heroes of a film. Dr Stephen Burt of the University of Reading, an adviser for the film, said the challenge Stagg and his colleagues faced was enormous. “To do a forecast beyond 24 hours was, in the 1940s, like trying to land a man on the moon,” he said.

citation.title: How meteorologists recreated weather that helped decide second world war

text:
How meteorologists recreated weather that helped decide second world war

Scientists had only recently started to use upper air data to predict the weather, he said, and largely relied on surface measurements of pressure, temperature, dew point, wind speed and direction, and experience-based intuition. One difficulty is that most of our weather comes in from the Atlantic. “Nowadays we have satellites and so on and we can see what’s coming, we have observations coming from the US,” he said. “But then there were … just a couple of ships, a couple of submarines maybe and some aircraft observations. And that’s it.” Crucially, the week before D-day was the hottest May week on record, Burt said – a high that was only broken this year. Then a huge storm blew up, with another close behind. Prof Ed Hawkins of the University of Reading, an expert in historical weather data collection and examination, including D-day, explains that there were three teams working on the D-day forecasts – although only two are depicted in the film – all feeding into Stagg. But they took different approaches and produced different forecasts.

text:
How meteorologists recreated weather that helped decide second world war

It was up to Stagg to reconcile the results and present a recommendation to Eisenhower that would, ultimately, affect 160,000 Allied troops. “Stagg was in a very difficult position. He left his very pregnant wife to come and do this very important task,” Hawkins said. The teams were split about the forecast for 5 June – with Stagg concluding the conditions would be too perilous. The landings were postponed. But by the evening of 4 June a consensus emerged: there appeared to be a small but suitable window on 6 June. The invasion was back on. “They managed to do the forecast, and the invasion, and get away with it,” said Burt. Burt and his colleagues agree that even modern systems based on artificial intelligence have struggled to accurately predict conditions for 6 June 1944 using data available from the time. “[I’d] still have been chewing my fingernails on morning of the sixth,” said Burt. Catherine Ross, a Met Office archivist, said film-makers used exact replicas of records from June 1944. “We were able to provide images of every single weather chart that was being produced at the time.

We had codes and examples of how the observations were sent in and all sorts of documentation,” she said. She notes that even before modern technology, allied forecasters were on the front foot in terms of access to data. They already had data from the UK and across the Atlantic. “But because of Bletchley Park they had broken the Enigma code, so they had access to all of the German weather observations as well,” Ross said. While the German forces may have been aware of the storms, they were not aware of a potential break in the weather. “Sometimes there’s no Atlantic on the [German] chart, which is where the weather was coming from in early June 1944,” she added. It is no spoiler that D-day was a success for the British, but the film sheds new light on the drama that unfolded behind the scenes. “It’s the most famous forecast ever made by the Met Office. Indonesian foragers may have sucked on mind-altering nuts 25,000 years ago, research finds

What may be the earliest known evidence for human drug taking has been traced to ancient Indonesian foragers who sucked on mind-altering nuts as long as 25,000 years ago. Analysis of two exceptionally rare skeletons from the Indonesian island of Sulawesi revealed dramatic tooth wear and traces of a psychoactive substance in the individuals’ remaining teeth, suggesting they routinely sucked on hard, abrasive betel nuts. Although little known in western societies, betel nuts are the world’s fourth most widely used psychoactive substance after alcohol, caffeine and nicotine, with an estimated tenth of the global population chewing the seeds. “We’ve found evidence for how this very common drug use habit, which is found throughout a lot of the Asia-Pacific region today, might have evolved,” said Prof Adam Brumm at Griffith University’s Australian Research Centre for Human Evolution in Brisbane. The work began when the team examined skeletal remains of two pre-agricultural foragers unearthed at two different sites on the island.

Is there any chance of getting a weather tsar in the model of Group Capt James Stagg, the wartime meteorologist, to adjudicate between weather forecasts (How meteorologists recreated weather that helped decide second world war, 8 September)? ‘Immature playground boasting’: Mathematicians uneasy at OpenAI’s latest scalp

It was a week that left mathematicians reeling. Hot on the heels of a flurry of cases of artificial intelligence furthering the field, OpenAI declared a major scalp: its latest AI model had cracked a Millennium Prize Problem, a puzzle with a $1m reward that had defied human brains for decades. The achievement bore little resemblance to how mathematical problems normally fall. A near-trillion dollar private company had unleashed 10,000 agents – AI systems that carry out tasks autonomously – on the problem. The bill was estimated at $15m. The trajectory towards AI capable of superhuman maths has long been clear, but to nail such a substantial problem so swiftly sent shock waves through the field. Mathematicians are asking what will be left for them if works in progress are hoovered up and claimed by others, and how they should train the next generation when even fiendish assignments can be solved at the press of a button. “I feel slightly shell-shocked,” said Prof Colva Roney-Dougal, the head of pure mathematics at the University of St Andrews.

Starwatch: A Venus-spotting challenge with a beautiful reward

This week’s Starwatch is a challenge but a beautiful reward awaits for anyone who succeeds. The question is: how early in the evening can we find Venus? On Monday, the bright planet has a close encounter with a young crescent moon. The moon will be just over three days old with about 14% of its visible surface illuminated. Unfortunately for UK observers, the two make their closest approach during daylight, passing within a moon’s width of one another around lunchtime. By the evening they will have separated a little, but they will still make an attractive pairing for observers with a particularly good view towards the south-west. The chart shows the view looking south-west from London at 6.30pm. The sun will still be above the horizon, so do not use any visual equipment and avoid looking directly at the sun with the naked eye. First look for the slender crescent moon, low in the south-western sky. Once you have found it, use it as your guide to Venus nearby. As the sun sinks lower, Venus should become progressively easier to see, although the moon and planet will be descending towards the horizon.

US confirms for first time it has deployed weapons in space

The US has deployed weapons in space, the US military has confirmed, in an extraordinary public announcement that analysts warn will accelerate a high-risk arms race with Russia and China in Earth’s orbit. The US secretary of the air force, Troy Meink, said Washington had active “on-orbit” weapons, meaning they had been deployed and were circling the globe. “Today, we continue to ensure we remain ready to meet the challenges of evolving threats wherever they exist,” Meink said on Monday at the annual Air, Space, Cyber conference. “This is why the United States now has, on-orbit, space-control weapons.” Meink said he would not go into the “specifics” of the weapons. However, a US Space Force spokesperson said space control could refer to “employing kinetic [combat] and non-kinetic means to affect adversary capabilities”. The statement added that “these capabilities can be employed for offensive and defensive purposes”. Responding to the US announcement, China’s foreign ministry said Washington was “preparing for war in outer space”, and warned against turning space “into a battlefield, as well as an arms race there”.

Scientists create mice with part-human brains

Researchers have created mice with half-human brains in an effort to understand and develop new treatments for disorders such as schizophrenia, epilepsy, cerebral palsy, intellectual disability and rare forms of dementia. The scientists transplanted lab-grown human brain cells into animals that were engineered to be born without a cortex or hippocampus. This made space for the human tissue to grow inside the rodents’ skulls. The procedure means scientists can now take cells from patients with brain disorders, turn them into brain tissue in the laboratory, and grow that tissue in living animals. The animals can then be studied to see how the disorder takes hold in human brain tissue, and how drugs might treat the conditions. “We’ve been trying really hard as a community to find therapeutic solutions for these conditions, but the reality is that in psychiatry and neurology we’ve been left behind [by] every single branch of medicine and we have fewer therapeutics than, again, every single branch of medicine,” said Sergiu Pașca, a professor of psychiatry who led the research at Stanford University.

While potentially transformative for brain medicine, organoids have sparked a wave of ethical concerns, not least around whether the clumps of tissue could become conscious or feel pain, and the welfare of animals implanted with organoids. Plantwatch: The insect-eating alpine plant that proves Darwin was right

In 1875, Charles Darwin predicted that Saxifraga candelabrum, a small alpine plant, could eat insects. Its leaves, petals and stems are smothered in tiny, sticky hairs and – just as the evolutionary biologist suspected – the sweet glue on the hairs can lure and trap midges before digesting them with an enzyme. The nitrogen from their remains is absorbed into the plant, which is essential for it to survive in the nutrient-poor soils of the Hengduan mountains in south-west China. The plant was also found to have genes related to those found in carnivorous plants. The study findings may point to other killer plants that trap insects with sticky hairs and feed off their remains. The leaves of the wild potatoes Solanum berthaultii and Solanum polyadenium are covered in sticky hairs and trap aphids and some other small pests, potentially opening the way to combine pest control with plant fertiliser. Other sticky-haired plants may follow a similar approach, according to a study in the Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society.

UK mathematician debunks myth around Parthenon’s optical illusions

A mathematician has uncovered what may be one of the longest-running myths in history after studying optical illusions and the Parthenon, the famed Greek temple that overlooks Athens. Scholars have marvelled at the building on the Acropolis hill for more than 2,000 years and heaped praise on its architects for their clever use of geometry. Its subtle curves are said to correct optical illusions that would have otherwise ruined the Parthenon’s clean lines. But after a detailed investigation, and a flurry of mathematical modelling, Prof Alain Goriely at the University of Oxford has reached an awkward conclusion. The optical illusions the curves are meant to fix are either nonsense or practically imperceptible. In short, the illusions are themselves an illusion. In his study, Goriely traces the myth back to the 1st-century Roman architect and engineer Vitruvius who wrote about the Parthenon 400 years after its construction. His account found its way into architectural books and became established fact. Today’s AI chatbots still churn out the tale.

citation.title: UK mathematician debunks myth around Parthenon’s optical illusions

text:
UK mathematician debunks myth around Parthenon’s optical illusions

“I do think it might be the oldest myth that we have,” Goriely said, “apart from religion.” A common claim that the mathematician challenges concerns the Parthenon’s base or stylobate. Measurements show the sides of the base are not horizontal but form a gentle arc that rises 6cm in the centre. According to Vitruvius, this corrects an illusion that would make the base appear to sag in the middle. The sagging effect has been attributed to two proposed tricks of the light. The first states that long horizontal lines simply seem to slump in the middle, but Goriely found no evidence for this. The second suggests that the Parthenon’s marble columns create the illusion. This is based on the Hering illusion where parallel lines on a 2D sheet can look bowed when other lines intersect them. But the Hering illusion is strongest when the intersecting lines are at acute angles. The columns at the Parthenon are too vertical to produce the illusion, and there is no proof it even works in 3D, Goriely said.

text:
UK mathematician debunks myth around Parthenon’s optical illusions

Another claim is that the bulges in the Parthenon’s columns – a curvature called entasis – corrects an optical illusion that would make them look too narrow in the middle. Again, Goriely found no evidence for the illusion. Moreover, the columns at the Parthenon bulge by a mere 18mm, which is barely perceptible at typical viewing distances. Goriely, who assesses and dismisses other supposed “optical corrections” in his paper concedes he “fell into a bit of a rabbit hole” pulling all the evidence together. He suspects the Parthenon’s architects had other reasons for the architectural features. The curve of the base may have prevented rain puddles forming and curved columns might simply have felt more organic and visually pleasing to the ancient Greeks, he writes in Royal Society Open Science. It is unclear why the myth has endured for so long, but Goriely suspects that the perception of ancient Greece as a supremely knowledgeable and ingenious civilisation is partly to blame. Unusually for an academic study, Goriely ends his paper by inviting readers to put it down and take a walk in a city.

Women with same health conditions as men ‘less likely to be offered active treatment’

Women with the same medical condition as men are less likely to be offered treatment such as surgery, a stent or a strong painkiller, research has found. A review of global research found that for several health problems, including cardiovascular conditions, kidney disease and Parkinson’s, women were less likely to receive the same treatment as men, revealing the extent to which women have significantly unequal care. Researchers at the University of St Andrews analysed 38 studies and found that in 33 of them women were less likely to be offered active treatment. Women with myocardial infarction, heart failure or an irregular heart beat were more likely to be given medication, whereas men were more likely to receive a coronary bypass, stent or other surgical treatment. Women were also less likely to be prescribed statins, according to the analysis, which was published in the journal Plos One.

And women were also less likely to be given opioids for pain management. For stroke and diabetes, however, there was no significant difference between the sexes in treatment. And women were more likely to be treated for dementia. The findings come amid growing concern about the gender health gap. In March, the then health secretary, Wes Streeting, said women were being let down by “medical misogyny”. The previous Conservative government appointed Lesley Regan as England’s first women’s health ambassador, to help tackle the gender gap. ‘Very messy eaters’: scientists solve the mystery of when black holes ‘burp’

Scientists have solved the mystery of when black holes “burp” – when the astronomical bodies launch jets after feeding on stars, blasting material enormous distances in space. Black holes are objects so densely compact that beyond a certain point their gravity is too strong for light and matter to escape. This boundary of no return is known as the event horizon – the point at which escaping would require something to travel faster than the speed of light. Despite their reputation as cosmic sinkholes, black holes are “actually very messy eaters”, said Dr Adelle Goodwin, an astrophysicist at Curtin University in Western Australia. Related: ‘Stranger than anything dreamed up by sci-fi’: will we ever understand black holes? “You have to get really, really close to a black hole to get to the event horizon,” Goodwin, also a Forrest Research Foundation fellow, said.

“Stars get destroyed further out than that.” Scientists know from rare observations of stars being torn apart by black holes – a process that involves a stretching effect known as “spaghettification” – that “only about half of the star that gets too close to the back hole will end up eventually being swallowed by that black hole”, Goodwin said. The other material is launched back into space in powerful jets and outflows, sometimes so large they “can influence the entire evolution of a galaxy”, she said. “You can think of it as a black hole burp.” But the timing of these burps had previously been mysterious to astrophysicists. “Sometimes it would happen a year after the black hole destroyed the star, sometimes it would happen three or five years after.” In new research published in the journal Nature Astronomy, Goodwin and co-author Dr Andrew Mummery from the Institute for Advanced Study believe they have found the answer, using radio telescopes to study 20 tidal disruption events – instances where stars are eaten by supermassive black holes.

The first occurs when the black hole is feeding at very high rates. The second occurs hundreds to thousands of days after the star is first torn apart, when the feeding rate drops to about 2% of the maximum rate at which a black hole can swallow material. She said the finding would enable scientists to precisely predict when such jets would be released, narrowing observation windows and freeing up precious telescope time.

Climate breakdown probably weakened the glacier that collapsed causing catastrophic floods and killing over a thousand people in Nepal and Tibet last month, the first scientific study of the disaster has found. Researchers identified unusually warm conditions before the glacier’s collapse, which sent an avalanche of 110m cubic metres (3.885bn cu ft) of snow and ice into the valley below. This triggered flash floods on an almost unprecedented scale, hitting communities downstream without warning. Tech billionaires trying to live for ever? That’s a waste of time, says physicist

Tech billionaires attempting to live for ever are, quite literally, wasting their time, a leading physicist has said. While some normal people are turning to unregulated peptide injections, cold plunges and supplements in an effort to defy ageing, the ultra-rich are aiming for immortality with even more drastic interventions: the tech chief executive Bryan Johnson has even tried injecting plasma from his 17-year-old son – although he later said he saw no benefit from it. Prof Jim Al-Khalili, who will be giving this year’s Royal Institution Christmas lectures on the topic of time, has said people expending their energy on trying to live for ever may be missing out on the here and now. “We have a finite interval of time in which we exist in the universe. And the more I study the nature of time, the more I think about it, the more I realise that I just want to make the most of the time that I have,” he said. “We’re [here for] a blink of an eye compared with the age of the universe.
