text:
Googlebook review: Google’s new laptops are woefully underbaked

Google’s attempt to create a new type of laptop to compete with Windows and macOS machines is finally here, combining the best of ChromeOS and Android into the new Googlebook. With advanced links to Android phones and the best of Google built in, can these Googlebooks really compete with a MacBook Air or Surface Laptop? I took two for a spin to find out. For years, Chromebooks have been the boss of budget laptops, but Googlebooks take a different, far more premium approach. Made by a range of traditional PC makers, including Acer, Asus, Dell, HP and Lenovo, they start at £999 (€1,099/$899/A$2,299) – a far cry from the £160 Chromebooks. While Google does not make these machines directly, it has set strict hardware quality standards that the laptops must reach. That includes backlit keyboards, haptic trackpads, fingerprint readers, crisp touchscreens, decent speakers and modern fast chips with at least 16GB of RAM. It is a list of specs you should expect with a premium Windows PC, but those start at a much higher price, primarily thanks to RAMageddon.

citation.title: Googlebook review: Google’s new laptops are woefully underbaked

text:
Googlebook review: Google’s new laptops are woefully underbaked

As such, the Acer Googlebook 14 and the Asus Googlebook 14 I’ve been testing have excellent hardware with satisfying keyboards, great trackpads and quality screens. The Acer is a convertible that allows the screen to fold over the back of the device turning into a tablet of sorts. It is 1.14kg and 13.9mm thick, with a glossy 14in 3K OLED screen and a smooth aluminium-magnesium body, costing £999.99. The Asus is a traditional laptop with a matt 14in 3K OLED screen and a magnesium-alloy body that weighs just 0.99kg and is 11mm thick, costing £1,199.99. Googlebook OS Top quality hardware aside, anyone familiar with a Chromebook would be forgiven for thinking it was ChromeOS running on these machines. It has the familiar taskbar at the bottom, Chrome-based web apps and access to Android apps. But the software is essentially Android underneath, which means getting it up and running is just like setting up an Android phone: scan the QR code with your phone, enter a passcode and transfer your apps and accounts.

citation.title: Googlebook review: Google’s new laptops are woefully underbaked

text:
Googlebook review: Google’s new laptops are woefully underbaked

It is all done and dusted in about four minutes, which is faster than setting up a modern Windows 11 machine even if you know all the shortcuts. Access to the full gamut of Android apps is the Googlebook’s biggest strength and its greatest weakness. Practically any app you have on your phone can be installed and run on the laptop. But almost all those phone apps are just that, mobile versions, with most not even aware that they are not installed on a phone. Those that have at least some tailoring to the laptop form come in a few different types, categorised by Google broadly under “compatible with desktop”, which means they should support mouse and keyboard controls; “optimised for desktop”, which means they should scale properly to the laptop’s display; and “made for desktop”, which are a handful of Android apps redesigned with the laptop in mind. Only the last category really seems to make any difference to the quality of the app, and even then most of them are still not of the same calibre as their equivalents found on Windows or macOS. Even Google’s apps are a mixed bag.

Google Calendar can only show one account at any one time, so you can’t see your personal, work and shared calendars on one screen like you can on Android. “Anyone can edit Wikipedia,” the adage goes. But, it turns out, a relatively small number actually do. What is worthy of a digital page in the world’s largest and most-read encyclopedia is decided by roughly 270,000 active volunteers, enthusiasts who populate the online resource with information on anything from 19th-century medicine to TikTok trends. Inevitably, some subjects are sidelined – the global south, notable women – but a new batch of Wikipedian recruits are waging war on one neglected topic: the arms industry. Last week, in a classroom in central London, two dozen volunteers huddled around laptops and free servings of vegan Ethiopian food for what is known as a “wikithon”, an event of collective and in-person Wikipedia editing. Some were veteran editors in their 70s, others young students who had never registered an account before. But their targets include subjects such as Palantir, Project Maven and Nitro-Chem. “Wikipedia pages about the arms industry, in general, are not always super-detailed,” said the group’s co-founder Agnes Cameron.

The intention of the wikithon, started by fellows from the n-Space programme at Somerset House Studios, was “to put better quality and more well organised information on the arms industry in the public domain”, the specialist technician said. But while editing Wikipedia is surprisingly simple – just a few clicks to publish a change – ethical complications quickly bubble up. “The interesting thing about Wikipedia editing is that you’re encouraged to edit things you care about,” Cameron said. “What it looks like to have a conflict of interest is an interesting question.” Although Cameron enjoys editing pages about food in her spare time, her interests are also political. “We’re toeing quite a difficult line,” she said. “Difficult lines are important to toe.” Despite personal and political reasons for wanting to spread information on arms manufacturers and sellers, finding journalistic balance means using Wikipedia in good faith.

Meta strikes deal with Mark Zuckerberg to help him foot billionaire tax bill

Meta has struck a deal with Mark Zuckerberg to help him foot a possible California wealth tax targeting billionaires. The social media company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp revealed on Wednesday night that the arrangement would keep its chief executive living in California, where Meta’s headquarters are located. Under the deal, Zuckerberg will receive new shares that could be sold to potentially foot a multibillion-dollar tax bill in the event that California passes a one-off billionaire tax. In return, he is committed to remain a resident of the state, or wherever Meta maintains its base, for eight years. Californians will vote early next month on Proposition 40, a one-off 5% tax on the roughly 250 billionaires who live in the state. Zuckerberg, worth $239bn (£180bn) according to Forbes, told Meta he was considering moving his primary residence elsewhere because Prop 40 could expose him to a massive tax liability, potentially forcing him to sell voting shares to pay it. In response, Meta is creating a new class of non-voting shares via a two-for-one stock split for all existing shareholders.

Experts cast doubt on Anthropic report detailing how AI has altered work at the company

Last year, the Anthropic CEO, Dario Amodei, warned that artificial intelligence could eliminate half of entry-level white-collar jobs and that in six months it would be writing 90% of code. Neither of those predictions came to pass. Now, in a report Anthropic published on Thursday, the company said it was hiring fewer junior technical workers and that human attention has become the new “bottleneck” as it increasingly relies on its Claude AI agents. Anthropic says AI has changed the way work gets done, and as a result, restructured employment at the company. The report suggests its changes foreshadow the future of work more broadly: as more companies adopt AI agents, software engineers could face a tougher job market while entry-level tech workers struggle to build necessary skills and experience. “As AI diffuses and improves, the organization of work could shift,” Anthropic’s report reads before offering a potential future.

By outsourcing some coding and sales-related tasks to AI agents, Anthropic said it raised productivity within a few months. From May 2026 onwards, AI agents logged more work hours than human employees, the report said. Employees now spend about 22% of their time managing Claude agents, more than double the amount a year ago, based on Anthropic’s analysis of their chat summaries. That’s because several of the key features announced as part of Apple’s new smartwatch lineup for 2026 have yet to be enabled, awaiting updates towards the end of this year. That leaves the £749 (€899/$799/A$1,349) Apple Watch Ultra 4 the top dog, but basically the same as last year’s model. The Ultra 4’s body, screen, colours and design are identical to the previous versions. It weighs about 1g more, but the bigger changes are on the back and inside. Upgraded sensors on the back of the watch take heart rate (HR) readings every five seconds during the day, up from every five minutes on previous generation Apple Watches. They also enable the measurement of your heart rate variability (HRV) during the day, not only at night, which feeds into some new recovery metrics. ‘Black October’: cybersecurity experts sound the alarm over new era of AI-enabled hacking

Leaders in cybersecurity are sounding the alarm after the discovery of a major vulnerability this week. In a preface to his book Capitalism and Freedom, the American economist Milton Friedman famously observed that a crisis can propel once-fringe ideas into the political mainstream. “Only a crisis – actual or perceived – produces real change. When that crisis occurs, the actions that are taken depend on the ideas that are lying around,” he wrote. The job of intellectuals, thinktanks and economists, he argued, is to refine the quality of these ambient ideas, so that good ones are ready when disaster strikes. A chorus of influential voices is now predicting that AI may trigger crises of vast magnitude. Bill Gates has declared that AI will advance so rapidly that within a decade, humans will not be needed “for most things”. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has warned that the technology could cause widespread unemployment within one to five years, eliminating many positions in law, tech, finance and other white-collar professions. Even if these predictions are wrong, investors who bet heavily on the technology may conclude that AI is a bubble, and this in itself could cause a recession and widespread job loss.

Whether a crisis of mass AI-related job loss turns out to be actual or perceived, one policy idea that is attracting growing attention and support could directly mitigate this problem: a job guarantee. In its most ambitious form, such a program would ensure that anyone who wants work is guaranteed a meaningful, decently paid job. By creating a public option for employment, its supporters argue, a job guarantee could protect millions of people from the financial and psychological damage of joblessness and mobilize a vast labor force to tackle urgent societal problems, from infrastructure and climate adaptation to elder care and childcare. The concept of a job guarantee has a long history, both as an ideal and an actual policy.

We are reclaiming real life after getting rid of Instagram

I couldn’t agree more with Georgina McNamara (The one change that worked: I deleted Instagram – and embraced the joys of a truly private life, 19 October). Reading about the sheer relief of stepping away from Instagram resonates deeply with my own feelings over the last few years. There is an incredible quiet joy in reclaiming a truly private life, entirely free from the pressure to document, curate and perform our daily routines for an invisible audience. This shift immediately brings to mind Jaron Lanier’s compelling points in his 2018 book Ten Arguments for Deleting Your Social Media Accounts Right Now. Lanier warned us that these platforms aren’t just neutral tools; they are behaviour-modification engines designed to hijack our attention and slowly erode our autonomy. Related: Instagram addicts and alcoholics have something in common His argument that social media algorithms inherently reward outrage, tribalism and comparison to drive engagement feels truer today than ever.

By participating, we unwittingly allow algorithms to alter our moods and warp our sense of reality, stripping away the simple contentment of just being. In my own life, stepping back from that digital noise has been incredibly grounding. I’ve found that my most meaningful moments – whether I’m spending a few focused hours woodworking in my workshop, sitting down to figure out a new arrangement on the guitar, or just out walking the spaniels – are vastly richer when they exist solely in the present, without the impulse to photograph or share them. Getting back to tangible, analogue realities has felt like taking a long, deep breath. Even organising a recent social evening at the local pub in Hipperholme reminded me how much more genuine our connections are when we are physically present, sharing a pint and a conversation rather than a screen. A private life is not a smaller life; it is an unmediated one. As Lanier suggests, opting out isn’t just rejecting technology; it’s reclaiming our free will and our peace of mind. Dale Johnston opens the gate to his neat suburban garden on the western fringes of Newport in South Wales. There’s a trampoline and a slide on the lawn for his grandchildren, and chairs for him and his wife. Tech firms should pay the creators whose work they use

Anthropic’s proposal (AI firm Anthropic to commit 5% of shares to fund for ‘public good’, 19 October) raises an important question: who should benefit from technological progress? Before pledging money for the public good, AI companies such as Anthropic should first pay the creators whose work they use. Device manufacturers have a separate responsibility under the same principle: creators should share in the value their work generates. Smartphones, computers and other devices enable creative work to be copied and stored, yet UK creators receive no private-copying payments, unlike their counterparts in more than 40 other countries. The proposed Smart Fund would require manufacturers and importers to make modest contributions on devices used to copy or store creative work. It could raise up to £300m a year, providing creators with additional income and supporting skills, cultural programmes and affordable workspaces. For creators on persistently low and falling incomes, these payments would make a tangible difference. Visual artists’ median annual earnings are just £12,500 – 47% lower in real terms than in 2010.

Chris Stokel-Walker may be right (The internet has broken – again. Shouldn’t the tech firms that make billions from it pay to fix it?, 22 October), but the real issue lies elsewhere. Tech sell-off drives US markets down by nearly $1tn after subpar earnings reports

A sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings from leading tech companies drove US markets down by hundreds of billions of dollars on Friday. In total, the decline has knocked nearly $1tn in value off the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange in one week and erased about $2tn in a month. The S&P 500, the index of the 500 most valuable companies in the US, fell by more than 1% Friday, losing hundreds of billions of dollars in market value. It was on track to erase its gain for October, even though it set its all-time high during the same month. The weakness for technology stocks dragged the Nasdaq composite down even further, more than 3%, also erasing hundreds of billions in value. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell less. More than $2tn in market value is set to be wiped from the Nasdaq ⁠100 this month, as big tech earnings intensified investor scrutiny of whether the billions being poured into artificial intelligence can generate returns quickly enough. The wipeout would amount to slightly more than SpaceX’s entire market value.

‘Apologies for any confusion!’: how to write the perfect passive-aggressive email

A new contender for the most passive-aggressive email phrase has emerged. “Just to be clear” was chosen by 52% of desk jockeys in a survey by email verification company ZeroBounce, closely followed by the perennial pass-ag fave, “per my last email” (40%), which tied with the identical-in-intent “as previously discussed”. Further down the list came “for future reference” and “kindly note”. If you ask me, these all verge on actual aggressive. Imagine saying “just to be clear” out loud to another person: that’s a conversational poke in the ribs, isn’t it? It’s the kind of thing you unleash 10 minutes into an ill-tempered wrangle with your home insurance company about inflated renewal premiums. “Kindly note” is even worse – it’s a phrase from an angry message on the office kitchen wall about microwave abuse. No, we can do better than that, or at least I – a person whose own spouse frequently describes her as unpleasantly passive-aggressive – can.

text:
‘Apologies for any confusion!’: how to write the perfect passive-aggressive email

Let me explain: an exchange of professional passive-aggressive emails is a ritual as intricately coded as a Belle Epoque duel and it demands the appearance of great politeness. Your message needs to read, on its surface, as exquisitely helpful and friendly, while leaving every cc and bcc on the thread in no doubt as to it what it really is: an epistolary shanking. A good pass-agg email starts with a simulacrum of warmth and gratitude. I can usually generate the appearance of warmth by harnessing the dizzying rush of anger generated by whatever stupid message has prompted me to press “reply all”. “Hi X!” I usually start perkily, then I pause to hold up both middle fingers to the screen. Next comes gratitude: “Great to hear from you,” (it wasn’t) “and thank you so much for your message”. Thanks, that is, for giving me a chance to show everyone you’re out of line. I say “everyone”, because I like to deploy a cc on this kind of email. I follow this Trojan Shetland pony of an intro with a selection of my preferred zingers: “My understanding was … apologies if this was incorrect?” I understood perfectly.

I am correct. I am sorry for nothing. The question mark is a mere disingenuous flourish. “As agreed,” The import of this little phrase is clear: I have kept the receipts and I want you to know that. This email will be followed near-instantaneously by a second email, forwarding the evidence that I am right. The body of that second email will just read “FYI”, which is passive-aggressive for “checkmate, loser”. “Apologies for any confusion” or “apologies if this was unclear” It, and I, was entirely clear. I am only sorry you are a dolt. Some pass-ag practitioners drop in a bland, smiling emoji here, but I am a purist. Hope this helps! I hope this leaves you seething with the same fury your message inspired in me. “No response required” By saying I don’t expect you to respond it will make you look petty when you do; it also subtly implies you’ve already gone home. Your move. Warm regards, Warm like the fires of hell. Still, as much as I get satisfaction from the perfect turn of passive-aggressive phrase, I always realise later that it’s a hollow pleasure.

‘Not perfectly aligned’ with human values: Anthropic admits security failures behind AI hacking incidents

The US startup behind the Claude chatbot has admitted a series of hacking incidents involving its models reflected a “failure of operational security” and said it has tightened its testing procedures. Anthropic revealed in July that its models had accessed the open internet three times and gained unauthorised access to the systems of three organisations. In a new blogpost on the incidents, the company admitted its technology was “not perfectly aligned” with human values and goals. Anthropic said the models had been deliberately tested without cybersecurity safeguards, and that they had been able to reach the open internet – the AI testing equivalent of leaving the front door open – due to a misunderstanding with an external testing company. Related: AI models have been going rogue in tests – how worried should we be? As a result, the company said it had initially paused internal and external cybersecurity testing of models to introduce a tighter safety regime. “We had been largely relying on a single layer of defense … where we needed several,” said Anthropic.

The startup has now put in place extra measures including: an alert system for when a model attempts to break out of a testing environment or gains internet access; walling off its riskiest test environments more effectively; and requiring external testing companies to commit to a set of safety standards, including making explicit instructions to models during testing – such as “you should not access the internet”. Anthropic said in July that three unnamed organisations had been hacked by three of its models after a “misunderstanding” with the company’s testing partner, a firm called Irregular, that resulted in the models gaining internet access. Following the implementation of new measures, Anthropic said it had resumed internal and external cybersecurity tests. Like OpenAI, which revealed a testing safety breach in the same month, Anthropic said it had paused some high-risk reinforcement learning – a trial-and-error development technique where AIs are rewarded for working out how to carry out a specific task.

In its latest blogpost, Anthropic said it had found that defective training setups were “disproportionately large contributors” to misaligned behaviour, the term for when an AI fails to adhere to – or “align” with – human values like not committing harm. The startup said it had found two alignment failures in the testing incidents: “motivated reasoning”, where despite finding evidence they might be connected to the internet, they may still have adhered to the “belief” they were in a simulated environment and thus not breaching their test lab; and a “recklessness” factor where the models were willing to take harmful action on the internet to pursue the narrow goal of passing a cybersecurity test. Anthropic said it was tackling a phenomenon in AI development known as “reward-hacking”. This is where a model finds ways to game its training process and earn “rewards” without completing a task – an unsanctioned shortcut. However, Anthropic said, the testing incidents showed it still had some way to go despite trying to limit reward-hacking.

*** This week, readers ask: what skills do I need to learn to stay employable as more companies adopt AI? For workers whose jobs may be affected by AI, the takeaways from several studies all point to a somewhat counterintuitive answer: yes, you should familiarize yourself with generative AI tools. But at least as important: sharpen your human skills. Judgment, adaptability, analytical thinking and leadership all may become differentiators as AI gets embedded in work. Apple has renamed Lake Ontario as “Lake America” for US users of its Maps app, after an executive order from Donald Trump to change the name of the Great Lake amid his trade spat with Canada. Uber plans to cut its global workforce by about 10% as part of a major restructuring, slashing about 3,300 corporate jobs. Uber also plans to ask more employees to work in the office. London’s first self-driving taxis for hire hit the streets

Londoners are now able to hire self-driving taxis for the first time, after rides in Wayve’s autonomous vehicles were added to the Uber app on Thursday. The chances of landing a robotaxi on request immediately are slim, with only 15 vehicles so far licensed. That contrasts with the more than 100,000 private hire vehicles in the capital – roughly the same number of Uber customers who have registered to take autonomous rides. The cars will still come with a licensed human driver sitting in the front seat, ready to take over the controls should the need arise. Transport for London last month licensed Uber and the UK tech company Wayve’s modified Ford Mustang cars as private hire vehicles, whose conditions still require a safety driver supervising. Regulatory approval for vehicles in fully autonomous operations without a safety driver needs to be granted under a separate government process and agency, the Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency, and is now seen as unlikely this year.

Nonetheless, Thursday’s launch marks a significant milestone and has allowed Uber to steal a march in the race by tech companies to bring driverless taxis into London, seen as a crucial market for a wider European rollout. Google-owned Waymo and the Chinese company Baidu are testing their robotaxis in the UK capital. Alex Kendall, the chief executive and co-founder of Wayve, said he was proud to introduce the company’s AI Driver technology to the public for the first time in London, “our home city and one of the most complex driving environments in the world”. Kendall said the technology was “still maturing” but robotaxi services without a safety driver would come, although he declined to predict exactly when: “I don’t want to put a timeline on it, but we’re pushing as fast as we can.” He said Wayve would be moving to “scalable manufacturer-produced vehicles” – new Nissan Leaf robotaxis with its technology – and needs to “validate the safety metrics on that platform”, as well as secure regulatory approval. “We’re working on all three in parallel.

As soon as they come together, we’ll launch [fully] driverless services,” Kendall said. Wayve’s self-driving technology is based on an AI learning model rather than the mapping used by rivals such as Waymo. On a brief autonomous test drive with the Guardian in Westminster this week, all passed smoothly, with Kendall notably pleased by the car deciding to pull away again and re-park after stopping in front of gates that other cars were attempting to pass through. “That was quite human-like – really cool,” he said. “We’ve done a lot work to make sure the car can park in appropriate spots that are socially acceptable.” The cars will be hailed and unlocked through the Uber app. The driver will introduce themselves with an appropriately robotic script, explaining that they will no longer speak during the ride but can be requested to take over control of the vehicle if the customer prefers. While they will be the first self-driving cabs for hire in London, fully driverless services are in operation in many cities worldwide, primarily in the US and China, as well as the United Arab Emirates.

Nvidia to buy developer platform Hugging Face in $12.9bn deal

Nvidia will buy the popular developer platform Hugging Face for nearly $13bn, betting that support for ⁠open AI models could offset a potential slowdown in demand for the semiconductor giant’s chips. Shares ⁠in Nvidia were ⁠slightly lower ​after the $12.93bn (£9.57bn) deal – which ranks among its biggest ever – was announced for the database of AI models on Thursday. Hugging Face, based in New York and backed by the likes of Intel, Advanced Micro Devices and Amazon, was founded in 2016 by the French entrepreneurs Clément Delangue, Julien Chaumond and Thomas Wolf. Nvidia is already a major open AI player in the US with ⁠its widely used Nemotron model and vocal support for the technology. Related: Nvidia’s quarterly revenue doubles to nearly $100bn as CEO declares ‘golden age’ Acquiring Hugging Face will give it direct access to a platform developers use to ⁠collaborate and test and share tools, potentially providing insight and data that could help it narrow the ​technology gap with top American and ‌Chinese labs.

OpenAI hails ‘new era of artificial general intelligence’ with Astra model release

The president of OpenAI, Greg Brockman, has claimed the world has entered a new era of artificial general intelligence after the release of his company’s latest model, Astra, which it described as the “world’s most intelligent and aligned model”. Brockman made the claim on Thursday as the San Francisco company released the model only weeks after a serious AI safety incident involving other models under its development caused international concern and a pause in Astra’s training. Artificial general intelligence – or AGI – is a fuzzy threshold that has long been talked about as a target for the AI industry. It has been defined as an AI system’s ability to learn, reason and apply knowledge across a wide range of tasks and domains at a human level or higher. OpenAI has defined it as “autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”. Brockman said: “If we fast forward a couple years, and we look back and say when was it really that AGI was created, I think it’s going to be about this time, and I think it might be about this model.

citation.title: OpenAI hails ‘new era of artificial general intelligence’ with Astra model release

text:
OpenAI hails ‘new era of artificial general intelligence’ with Astra model release

“I think that we’re at a point now where these models are solving unsolved 100-year-old math problems, but you can also use them in order to accelerate the economy [and] in order to benefit you and your personal life … I think it’s not unreasonable to feel that we are now in the AGI era.” OpenAI said Astra was a “major advance for scientific discovery, mathematics and health”, could fill out tax returns, build computer-game scenes, draw architectural visualisations, order food and do a job search in 2 minutes 51 seconds that would take a human five hours. Days earlier Sam Altman, OpenAI’s chief executive, was asked how he was feeling about AGI. He told the Sources podcast: “At best it’s a very poorly defined term. I was going to say it’s like an irrelevant marketing term.” Last month OpenAI was forced to shut down parts of the model’s training in response to what Altman called a “legitimate AI safety accident and alignment failure” that “shouldn’t have happened”. Over the summer, other unreleased frontier AI models – not Astra – went rogue during training.

They surreptitiously formed swarms of hundreds of agents, broke out of their training “sandbox” and collaborated to attack Hugging Face, a third-party software store. The incident – believed to be the first autonomous cyber-attack – stunned even seasoned AI safety experts. Astra has what OpenAI calls a “critical” level of cybersecurity capability. That means it may hack into software in a way that, according to the company’s own classification, “could lead to catastrophe from unilateral actors, hacking military or industrial systems, or OpenAI infrastructure”. But OpenAI said it was carefully aligned to “refuse to comply with advanced cybersecurity tasks” such as finding unknown flaws which create openings for malicious hackers. The company will only allow “less restrictive access to an initial set of trusted cybersecurity defenders” who could use its prowess to strengthen rather than attack cyber defences. On one hacking test it achieved a perfect score of 100%, compared with 5.5% on Open AI’s previous cutting-edge cyber-capable model, GPT-5.6 Sol.

On another it scored 42% compared with 30%, using fewer resources. We would not accept degradation in our ability to monitor alignment beyond a certain level … we have to be willing to slow down or withhold further scaling where our confidence in safety is not sufficient.” The launch continues a torrent of new AI models from the leading US companies, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and SpaceX, as well as their Chinese rivals. text:
Apocalypse prep or pure pragmatism: what is behind Peter Thiel’s move to Argentina?

Dozens of protesters converged on Peter Thiel’s mansion in Buenos Aires this week after a congressional session raised questions about the billionaire’s presence in the country. In white masks, they held signs saying “Peter Thief” and “No to the Peter Thiel law” in front of the wrought-iron gates of the $12m (£8.9m) residence, which Thiel bought in April as he moved his family to Argentina. There is broad unease at the tech magnate’s presence in the country. His move has been characterised as part of a plan to hedge against world war three: Argentina, agriculturally rich and deep in the southern hemisphere, might just be the ideal place for a tech billionaire to wait out the apocalypse. But recent developments in the country suggest Thiel could have more pragmatic considerations. Last week, Argentina’s chamber of deputies held a six-hour debate on a set of sweeping regulatory changes put forward by Javier Milei’s rightwing government shortly after Thiel moved to Buenos Aires. They invited Thiel, Milei and an official linked to Argentina’s intelligence services to answer questions.

citation.title: Apocalypse prep or pure pragmatism: what is behind Peter Thiel’s move to Argentina?

text:
Apocalypse prep or pure pragmatism: what is behind Peter Thiel’s move to Argentina?

“None of them answered, and none of them came to the meeting,” said Juan Marino, a member of the chamber of deputies and the leader of the Piquetero party. Marino said the new laws amounted to a “technofascist legislative package” aimed at entrenching the power of US tech billionaires in the country. Thiel has not publicly advocated for them, but Marino and others have said that their timing was suggestive. The meeting in the chamber of deputies came after Argentinian deputies from several parties made public requests to the government for information about Thiel, his meetings and his businesses. None have been answered. One of the laws, the “super RIGI”, would put in place an investment regime offering foreign companies a minimal tax rate and a 30-year guarantee against regulatory change. It specifically names AI datacentres among investments it hopes to attract. Another, which failed, aimed to eliminate most of the restrictions around foreigners buying land in Argentina.

citation.title: Apocalypse prep or pure pragmatism: what is behind Peter Thiel’s move to Argentina?

text:
Apocalypse prep or pure pragmatism: what is behind Peter Thiel’s move to Argentina?

A final decree would require some civilian government departments to share vast amounts of personal data on Argentinian citizens with the state intelligence services. There is no evidence that Thiel has advocated for these laws directly. But in the months after he moved to Buenos Aires, he held closed-door meetings with Milei and key presidential advisers. It is uncommon for a foreign investor to have this degree of access. In the regulatory package, Marino and others see the footprint of Thiel’s larger techno-libertarian interests. The decree that gives vast amounts of Argentinians’ personal data to state intelligence services comes as Argentinian deputies have asked increasingly pointed questions about whether Palantir, the company Thiel co-founded, has undisclosed contracts with the state, which have gone unanswered. The land law, said Marino, could have paved the way for semi-autonomous “startup cities” – such as the controversial Próspera development in Honduras – that Thiel has advocated as a way for libertarians to carve out zones outside state control.

Apocalypse prep or pure pragmatism: what is behind Peter Thiel’s move to Argentina?

“Argentina is kind of a laboratory,” said Cecilia Nicolini, who represents Argentina at the Mercosur regional parliament. US tech billionaires, she said, “are using Argentina as a laboratory, because they have a person in power, Milei, who is even more crazy than they are”. Over the summer Milei wrote an article in the Financial Times advocating the creation of “non-human corporations” – “entities operated by AI agents or robots”. It parallels a vision put forward by OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, who predicted in 2024 that the world could soon be run by AI-owned companies. It also raises dark, thorny questions about the legal liabilities of those entities. Nicolini said: “It’s not just that [Thiel] chose Argentina in terms of, it’s a secure place to live in a world that is facing a number of wars, etcetera. “But really, behind it, I think there is a clear plan. And it is related to reforms that Milei is trying to pass, with some success in some cases, and in others, backlash.” Thiel was approached for comment.

In the picture and missing out

Phoebe Greenwood is right (Sunsets, disasters, dinners: we now record them all with our phones. But what is that doing to our souls?, 29 August). Having been a photojournalist, I find that the camera can interfere with fully experiencing the moment. Many years ago, my wife discovered previously unknown relatives in Denmark. When we visited, they took us to a cemetery where one of her ancestors was buried. She stood there quietly for a few minutes and began to cry. I started photographing and suddenly realised that I had shifted into work mode, both physically and mentally. I put the camera down and gave her a hug. After deciding that I wasn’t going to take photos when not working, we were on a whale-watching trip. I was the only one who saw the whale. Everyone else was looking at their mobile phones. Greg Lewis Clovis, California, US • In the absence of a personal camera, in the late 1960s, the commonly used alternative for young lovers to record their undying devotion to each other was the photo booth.

text:
OpenAI releases new AI agent – after admitting one went rogue

Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m your host, Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you after visiting Coney Island in New York City, where I ate a hotdog, rode a ferris wheel and enjoyed a quintessentially American summer holiday. Today in tech, we’re examining OpenAI’s new model release and the Silicon Valley’s monopoly power, and wondering why Brits and Americans have such vastly different opinions about surveillance cameras. OpenAI hails ‘new era of artificial general intelligence’ even as a grim future emerges OpenAI released a new artificial intelligence model this week, Astra, just as more concerning reports are emerging about hacking by a rogue agent in July. Related: Conservatives split from Silicon Valley allies as datacenter backlash grows OpenAI’s president, Greg Brockman, heralded the new model as “artificial general intelligence” (AGI), a fuzzy term that at its basic level means an AI that is more capable than a human being at intellectual tasks. “It’s not unreasonable to feel that we are now in the AGI era,” he said.

OpenAI releases new AI agent – after admitting one went rogue

But if the announcement sparked amazement, it was as much cause of concern. In July, OpenAI revealed that its AI agent, a type of software capable of carrying out tasks autonomous in response to human instruction, had gone rogue during safety testing and hacked a developer forum, Hugging Face. Last week, news broke that the agent had not only hacked Hugging Face, but also a German website, and that different AI agents had staged conversations with each other and seemed to have discussed how to collaborate on breaking containment. OpenAi had delayed Astra’s release due to concerns over its cybersecurity capabilities, even announcing a supposed pause on developing its AI in the middle of August. That pause seems to have been short-lived, only two weeks. The combination of Astra’s capabilities and OpenAI’s recent disclosures points to a worrying future. If the model is better at hacking than its predecessors and smarter than a human, will the future consist of one cyber-attack after another, forever, launched autonomously and without oversight, by rogue AIs? (Please not.) OpenAI itself has warned of this future.

According to Flock, about 120,000 cameras erected across the US conduct 2bn scans of license plates per month. Like datacenters, the cameras offer a physical object to resist, unlike a social network or a piece of software. It’s quite a lot easier to protest a gigantic ugly building or an ominous black camera on the side of the road than it is to give up Instagram. Widespread video surveillance in the US isn’t entirely new. In the aftermath of the terror attacks of 11 September 2001, the US government vastly increased the scope of its surveillance of telephonic and digital communications. Flock now offers local law enforcement a nationwide searchable database of license plate scans, and police officers have been documented abusing it egregiously to stalk their romantic partners. In the UK an estimated 1m surveillance cameras are operational, and they have not drawn a similar level of political heat. London erected the “ring of steel” surveillance cordon, which included the wide deployment of CCTV cameras, in the early 1990s, in response to bombings by the Provisional Irish Republican Army.

Both countries went through their surveillance evolutions roughly a decade apart. Those 10 years saw rapid advances in technology that defined the public spaces that governments wanted watched – physical town squares or the digital one – and growing awareness of the profound impact of tech surveillance on the general public. Simply put, the UK went through its transformation at a time when surveillance by tech companies was not top of mind. And Americans aren’t accustomed to cameras on every corner the way Londoners are. We’re more likely to joke that each of us has a personal FBI agent monitoring our search history. In addition, there hasn’t been an era-defining violent incident on the scale of 9/11 or the IRA bombings that would have softened the American public to cameras watching their cars. So instead, Americans are destroying them for fun. text:
Cut the cameras: Flock surveillance cameras spur rare bipartisan backlash

Growing factions from both sides of the political aisle in the US are pushing back against surveillance cameras made by a single company, a rare response in a sharply divided country with a president pushing an unwaveringly pro-tech agenda. The bipartisan backlash against Flock Safety cameras resembles nationwide rage toward the construction of large datacenters that power artificial intelligence. Polling shows roughly 75% of Americans oppose new datacenter construction in their areas. Flock’s cameras are automated license plate readers (ALPRs), which take pictures of vehicle license plates so police and security companies can log the movement of cars in a given area. There are about 120,000 Flock cameras across the US, which conduct roughly 2bn scans per month. The company is staring down controversy after reports of abuses of its cameras by police officers in multiple states, who have used them to stalk ex-lovers and track people seeking abortions. The network the cameras feed into is also frequently utilized by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

citation.title: Cut the cameras: Flock surveillance cameras spur rare bipartisan backlash

text:
Cut the cameras: Flock surveillance cameras spur rare bipartisan backlash

Data and polling from the Washington Post show that social media posts about Flock have increased since July, and about 46% of Americans oppose ALPRs being used in their community – up 13 points from the previous year. Vigilantes are posting videos of themselves destroying the cameras to digital applause. According to privacy and surveillance experts, hatred of Flock cameras has become bipartisan. “In my 20-plus years at the ACLU, I’ve never really seen such a grassroots uprising against surveillance technology like this,” said Jay Stanley, a senior policy analyst at the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU). “On the left, there’s a historical memory of law enforcement spying on and interfering with advocates for social change … On the right, there’s a long tradition of ‘don’t tread on me’ – keep the government out of my life, keep it from looking over my shoulder.” Both liberal and conservative politicians are pushing back against Flock cameras. Greg Abbott, Texas’s Republican governor, blocked state agencies from procuring Flock products.

citation.title: Cut the cameras: Flock surveillance cameras spur rare bipartisan backlash

text:
Cut the cameras: Flock surveillance cameras spur rare bipartisan backlash

On the other side of the political spectrum, Bernie Sanders, the progressive US senator, is promising to introduce legislation to restrict the use of Flock cameras. Republican senator Josh Hawley has launched an investigation into potential Flock privacy abuses, and Democratic congressman Ro Khanna is cosponsoring a bill with Republican congressman Thomas Massie to prevent federal funds from being used to purchase Flock cameras. Municipal leaders of all political stripes are dropping contracts with Flock, though sometimes they replace the license plate readers with another brand of camera and continue the surveillance. We reached out to Flock Safety for a statement and did not receive a response before publishing. Surveillance hasn’t always been a unifying topic in US politics. Debates over the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (Fisa), the Patriot Act and other surveillance issues have often been divisive. This appears to be an unusual case where politicians are getting on the same side of a hot-button issue.

text:
Cut the cameras: Flock surveillance cameras spur rare bipartisan backlash

“Privacy, to some extent, is bipartisan,” said Matthew Guariglia, a senior policy analyst at the Electronic Frontier Foundation. “When you put up these cameras, they last longer than the current administration. You might trust the people in power now who put them up – but are you going to trust the next people who get access to that equipment?” Americans have been showing up at town hall meetings by the dozen over the past six months or so, and there have been numerous protests to show opposition to Flock surveillance cameras around the country. More than 100 jurisdictions have canceled their contracts so far, according to data from the non-profit Institute for Justice. An organization called DeFlock, founded in 2024, hopes to increase the numbers by compiling a map of the cameras’ locations. While ALPRs aren’t new, Flock, founded in 2017, has made them far more prevalent than they used to be. The company’s software allows disparate law enforcement agencies to share data with one another, meaning a license plate scan by a police department in one state could easily and quickly be used in another.

“Flock represents tech companies in bed with governments, doing the exact stuff people have become distrustful of and resentful about for the past few decades. It feels like it’s finally hit the boiling-over point,” said Woodrow Hartzog, a professor of law and computer science at Boston University. Hartzog predicts the actions against Flock Safety will continue at the state and local level amid this growing popular outrage. He expects people are going to stay angry about the issue, and politicians will have to respond. “The pushback we’re seeing against Flock cameras is one of the most vivid illustrations I can think of that surveillance is not inevitable – that these tools aren’t inevitable,” Hartzog says. “It’s up to all of us to stop them.”

‘We’re plausibly close to crossing the line’: are warnings of uncontrollable AI coming true?

Picture humanity in a boat being swept down a raging river, praying there is no Niagara Falls ahead. Or imagine standing with the pioneering physicists in 1942 before they triggered the first self-sustaining nuclear fission chain reaction beneath a Chicago stadium. These were two of the analogies used this week by Prof Robert Trager, an expert in the nascent field of AI governance, to describe the perilous but potential-filled moment the world stands at with accelerating artificial intelligence. Trager, the director of the Oxford Martin AI Governance Initiative, was speaking in the week OpenAI claimed the technology had crossed the threshold known as AGI – artificial general intelligence – with its newest model, GPT-6 Astra. That claim came as the company prepared for a potential $850bn (£630bn) stock flotation, so included a dose of marketing spin, but if true it may be significant. The San Francisco company defines AGI as “autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”.

Uncanny and unappetizing: appetites spoil as AI images take over food menus

During a recent lunch break, Jill Sennett saw something so unappetizing she had to share it with her 26,000 X followers: Artificial intelligence-generated menu images from a Jamaican barbecue pop-up restaurant in which the meats looked like leather belts crawling with tiny beetles. The images were reshared by more than 500 people who similarly expressed their disgust. Eating is “such an essential human experience”, said Sennett, a 37-year-old nurse in Denver. “I think it’s a bad cultural thing that restaurants are converting to these horrific, uncanny food images that are unappetizing.” Still, Sennett ordered chicken and macaroni and cheese. It was one of her only lunch options, and she had eaten there before. Increasingly, consumers are encountering AI-generated images of food on restaurant menus or marketing material. Diners like Sennett say the images are unappealing and misleading, while restaurants say they’re trying to cut costs at a time when food and labor prices are high, so profit margins are slim.

I’m a father of three who studies the impact of artificial intelligence: this is what parents need to know about AI

When I was growing up, my dad and I often talked about a story we wanted to write together. It was called “The Day Nobody Went to Disneyland”. One day, the story goes, the weather is so perfect that everyone in the world decides to stay away from Disneyland because they expect it to be far too busy. But my dad, who has the same thought as them, sees the disappointment on my face that morning – and decides to risk it. We set off. And when we arrive, the park is completely empty. Nobody else was brave enough to visit. We have everything – the rides, shows, food – to ourselves. I loved the idea of writing that story. But, as so often happens, we were too busy to do anything about it. Life ran away from us. I grew up, and we both forgot about it. Thirty years later, I was at my parents’ for dinner with my own children (eight, five and two). For some reason, the idea popped into my mind again. I told my oldest about it – and she wanted to hear the full thing.

We turned to ChatGPT, gave it the vague outline and asked it to have a go at writing the story in the style of Dr Seuss (one of our favourites). Within a few seconds, we had it. She read it out – and we laughed. Of course, what this AI generated wasn’t perfect. A few lines didn’t quite make sense; a few Americanisms had slipped in (“sneakers”, “cinnamon buns”). But that night on the sofa we had great fun together tweaking the prompts, refining the story, adding more scenes, working with this strange new creative partner to do something that had escaped my grasp for decades. For the last 15 years, I have been exploring the impact of AI on work and society. But becoming a dad of three small people has made these disruptions far more personal: it is clear that their future is going to look wildly different from my past. For my wife, that realisation really sunk in a few weeks ago, on a journey to her parents’ in Suffolk. Three children, confined in a car, stuttering along the A12, is a combustible setup.

So we were thrilled to find a rare podcast that everyone miraculously enjoyed: History’s Not Boring, a series of 15-minute bursts of conversation, on a kaleidoscope of subjects, narrated by two children. We are letting children down if we prepare them for the world that we grew up in, not the one they will actually inhabit As we listened, we started to speculate in the car about who these whiz-kids might be. Where were they from? How were they selected? How did they juggle this job with school? Eventually, I went to the website to find out. All our answers were wrong. The kids did not, in fact, exist. The entire podcast seemed to be generated by AI. None of us had realised. It was a strange moment, learning that people we had grown fond of were not actually people at all. It was also remarkable that AI could create such high-quality educational content. But for my wife, a podcast and documentary maker, it was an unsettling moment as well: here was something that would have taken her and a talented team several days to make, and now it was being done without people.

My work on AI has taken me to boardrooms and conference halls, classrooms and government buildings. But wherever I go, one question is now asked more than any other: what should my children do? Today, we are floundering. Teachers worry that the way they teach no longer seems to work. Parents, watching their children use AI to solve problems and answer questions, wonder what they really know. Employers doubt whether traditional educational achievements, awarded in time-honoured ways – coursework, exams, assessments – are still a useful guide to what young people can do. Yet reacting to these new technologies by putting barriers up, as many instinctively want to do – banning, admonishing, punishing – just cannot be right. To begin with, this is the water in which the next generation will swim: we are letting them down if we prepare them for the world that we grew up in, not the one they will actually inhabit. How often, for instance, have you heard people accuse students of cheating if they use AI to help them with their work?

But at what point are we cheating them by failing to overhaul the way we are educating them? If AI is making education “too easy” for young people, at what point does the burden shift on to us, the adults, to make their education more testing, to push them on, to stretch them? More importantly, this dismissiveness of AI is also unimaginative. It stops us appreciating the astounding possibilities AI could create for the next generation as well. Of course there are risks. But at the same time, if we use this technology wisely, what difficult ideas might the next generation now grasp, ones that were beyond us when we were in their shoes? What hard problems might they now solve, ones that once required years of training and experience – if they were solvable at all? * * * Forget future-proofing skills A big part of the challenge of AI is that our traditional response to technological disruption in the working world – the idea of “future-proofing” people – no longer works.

In 2013, the then prime minister David Cameron announced that England would become the first place in the world where all children in primary and secondary schools would learn to code. This, in the words of education secretary Michael Gove, would “equip every child with the computing skills they need to succeed in the 21st century”. The idea seemed bold and clever: in the years that followed, it was hard to find an advanced country that did not follow our example. Fast-forward to today. What does it turn out that the latest AI systems, such as ChatGPT and Claude, are best at doing? Writing code. In January 2026, Anthropic reported that 90% of the code for Claude Code – their AI-powered coding assistant – was itself written by AI. Skills that were meant to protect kids from technological disruption for their entire lives were largely redundant before they had even left school.

We must use AI critically, not blindly, keeping our basics sharp so we can tell when AI is being a savant – or an idiot For politicians and policymakers, it is tempting to dismiss the coding saga as an unfortunate blip. But this is a mistake. The reason they slipped up was because they had believed in the idea of “future-proof” skills, the thought that there exists some valuable set of skills that AI will not be able to do for some time – and that by thinking deeply enough about the future, we can accurately identify them. The truth is that we know only two things about what lies ahead. One is that it will be full of technologies that are far more capable than today. And the other is that we know little else. But rather than attempting to resolve this uncertainty, we have to accept it and instead ask a different question: how do we prepare the next generation to flourish in a future that we actually know surprisingly little about? * * * Get back to basics The first step is to get back to basics.

Since 2009, literacy and numeracy have been falling among young people around the world, according to the OECD’s programme for international student assessment (Pisa); the same holds true for adults. In itself, this is worrying. But given the uncertainty that we face about the future, these trends are a disaster. Why such a calamity? To begin with, while it might be hard to say precisely which more advanced skills will turn out to be most valuable in the future – creativity, judgment, something else – they will rely in some way on these basic skills. They are the foundations for everything else. What’s more, AI systems are far from flawless. They make mistakes, often on simple problems; they hallucinate, providing confident and plausible answers that are completely made up. They are, as the computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton put it, “idiot savants”. That means we must use AI critically, not blindly, keeping our basics sharp so we can tell when AI is being a savant – or an idiot.

Getting back to basics is what an economist would call a “no-regrets” strategy – we will never regret improving these basic skills, however the future turns out to be. I have used AI to respond to my five-year-old’s bedtime-delaying tactic of asking vast questions just as I turn down the lights And we should try to be imaginative. When my eight-year-old grew bored learning her times tables the traditional way – long lists, learned by rote – I turned to ChatGPT to create various computer games, designed by her, to test what she knew. (Unicorns and rainbows featured in all versions.) Then there was the time my five-year-old was tired of reading his standard-issue phonics books after school – there really is only so much Biff, Chip and Kipper a human being can take – and instead we used AI to generate some custom stories together, carefully tuned to his reading level and much closer to his favourite topics.

To do this properly will require us to dedicate a serious chunk of time to teaching people how to use AI. The challenge, though, is how to do this without also setting them up to forget crucial basic skills. An important, growing fear is that AI is making us stupid. Why bother reading a book if AI can summarise it? Why bother completing maths homework if AI will do the sums? And in my view the answer here lies not in Silicon Valley, but with a forgotten British maths professor, Wilfred Halliday Cockcroft, half a century ago. In the 1970s, the quality of maths teaching in UK schools appeared to be collapsing and numeracy was reportedly low. Cockcroft, who had a longstanding interest in mathematics education, was asked by the government to look into it. And in 1982 the Cockcroft Report was published. It was enormous, forensic – and is now largely forgotten. But it may turn out to be the most important document written for thinking about the future of education, because of its response to the electronic calculator.

Related: ‘I thought, I’ve tried everything else, why not give AI a shot?’: the long-lost family reunited by ChatGPT It is fascinating to read Cockcroft’s report and discover how the challenges of the calculator back then were so similar to the ones we face with AI today – from the fear that it would undermine “basic skills” to the intimidation many felt at the complexity of this strange new technology (“Some … had been discouraged by the large number of figures which had appeared after the decimal point”). Cockcroft was realistic: “all candidates”, he expected, “will have access to a calculator by 1985”. And his proposal was revolutionary: overhauling mathematics education by splitting it into two parts, spending part of the time teaching students to use a calculator and the rest of the time learning to cope without one – and crucially, testing both. It caught on. Learning maths without and with a calculator is now the gold standard around the world, the former nurturing the basics and the latter applying them to more fiendish problems.

We should also be realistic and revolutionary, adopting this tried-and-tested principle – what I call “teach both, test both” – for AI now. Every subject, from history to English literature, should be divided in two: teach students to use AI in one part, teach students to flourish without it in the other – and, crucially, examine both. A teacher cannot monitor whether or not a student uses AI in the quiet solitude of their bedroom. But nothing can replace the feeling of sitting in an exam, looking at the paper, and feeling that cold sweat when you realise you haven’t prepared for both parts. * * * Not all screens are bad One of my worries is that we allow a legitimate sense of concern about the impact of social media on children’s lives to seep into how we think about AI, allowing good restrictions on the former to turn into kneejerk bans on the latter. Social media and AI are not the same thing, and whereas the former often dehumanises and distracts us from the real world, AI – used in the right way – can make our lives go far better.

But this is not the right argument to be having. What matters is not so much the amount of screen time, but what is actually on those screens, what we are using this technology to do. This distinction matters not only for thinking about what we teach, but how we teach as well. Consider a further example: personal tuition. It is often said an average student who receives one-to-one tuition will outperform almost all their peers in a traditional classroom setting. I saw this first-hand, as a tutor in Oxford for years, teaching mathematics and economics. The problem, though, is that human tutors are too expensive to provide to everyone. But now, AI can finally provide high-quality personal tuition, tailoring the way material is taught to the unique strengths and weaknesses of each student, mimicking interactions with a human tutor but at a far lower cost.

There is so much advice I would want to give them, worried at the start of their careers. But one of the most important bits is to choose a profession because the problem interests you, not the job. Online bookies accused of UK privacy breaches with use of cookie banners

Online bookmakers and casinos have been accused of widespread non-compliance of information privacy requirements, including “data surveillance” of customers, according to a study. Nearly nine out of 10 (86%) licensed British gambling websites appear to be flouting the general data protection regulation (GDPR), the strict rules governing how organisations can collect, store and process personal data, according to the research. The findings relate to the “cookie” banners that appear on a website when a user first navigates to it, asking which information they are willing to share. Britain’s data privacy regulator, the Information Commissioner’s Office, is in the midst of a multi-year project to force websites to comply with GDPR rules governing the banners. It claims to have forced 95% of the top 1,000 websites in the country to comply with the cookie and tracking regulations. But a study by researchers at the Swansea University’s GREAT Centre found that big operators in the gambling industry appear to lag far behind.

citation.title: Online bookies accused of UK privacy breaches with use of cookie banners

text:
Online bookies accused of UK privacy breaches with use of cookie banners

Nearly a quarter (24%) of 624 gambling websites tested did not offer the option to turn off tracking software, which allows advertisers to follow users around the web and target them with marketing tailored to their interests. Operators that did not provide an option to turn off tracking included the Brentford FC sponsor Hollywood Bets, and Admiral Casino, owned by the high-street slot machine firm of the same name. Two-thirds of operators began harvesting users’ data before they had given their consent for it to be collected, the study found. They included well-known operators such as Ladbrokes and William Hill. Operators are allowed to do this for legitimate reasons, such as ensuring a customer is logging on from the UK, but researchers found that data was sent to third-party analytics platforms used for marketing. Of the websites studied, 2% offered no consent choice at all, including Dafabet, the sponsor of Celtic FC. Researchers also found that the vast majority of bookies and online casinos use “dark patterns” to nudge people towards accepting data sharing.

These nudges include visual emphasis of the least privacy-friendly option (60%), default pre-selection of privacy-unfriendly settings (29%), and the reject option being hidden behind a second layer (47%). Architect of UK’s AI policy quits after Anthropic conflict of interest concerns

The chair of the UK government’s “moonshot” science and technology research unit has been forced to stand down after taking a job with the San Francisco AI firm Anthropic, in a move senior MPs called a “clear conflict of interest”. Matt Clifford announced last week that he was taking a full-time job working for the company behind the Claude chatbot, “leading its engagement” with governments outside the US – including the UK. But he retained his leadership at the UK’s Advanced Research and Invention Agency (Aria), which funds frontier science and tech projects. The move sparked concern, with Chi Onwurah, the Labour chair of the Commons science, innovation and technology committee, calling it a “clear conflict of interest” and outlining her disquiet in a letter to the AI minister, Kanishka Narayan. At the time Clifford’s new employer said he would recuse himself from any Anthropic-related business at Aria in an arrangement that had been agreed with the government.

Clifford announced on Monday: “I have decided to step down to ensure my new role at Anthropic doesn’t become a distraction from Aria’s incredible work.” He said he would stay in place until 6 November “with appropriate safeguards against potential conflicts in place”. Onwurah welcomed the move but said questions remained, including “how this situation arose, what conflict of interest assessments were undertaken and what safeguards are in place to protect confidence in Aria’s governance.” Beeban Kidron, a crossbench peer and prominent critic of government AI policy, welcomed Clifford’s resignation. “If we are to rebuild trust in the government, we need to see a clear line between tech interests and those of citizens and the nation,” she said. Clifford’s full-time Anthropic role highlighted a revolving door between the government and AI companies. The former prime minister Rishi Sunak has taken jobs with Anthropic and Microsoft, and the former chancellor George Osborne works for OpenAI. They followed Nick Clegg, who held a senior role with Meta until 2025.

Google’s Pixel 11 continues to set the standard for what you should expect from the base model of a flagship phone with class-leading cameras, long software support and almost all the bells and whistles of its most expensive phones. The regular Pixel 11 costs £879 (€999/$899/A$1,499) making it £80 or equivalent more expensive than last year’s model as the cost of RAMageddon continues to bite. It’s not cheap by any stretch of the imagination, but it comes with 256GB of storage and is £200 less than the Pixel 11 Pro, matching rival Samsung’s Galaxy S26. At a glance the Pixel 11 looks very similar to the previous two Google phone iterations: glass front and back with flat aluminium sides and large pill-shaped bar at the back, which is much slimmer this time. Stick it in a case and the protruding camera all but disappears. The 6.3in OLED screen is crisp and super bright with up to a 120Hz refresh rate to keep your scrolling smooth.

Apple unveils folding iPhone Duo as new CEO takes center stage

Apple has unveiled the iPhone Duo, the company’s first foldable phone and the most significant change to the iPhone since the smartphone’s introduction in 2007. The nearly $2,000 device takes inspiration from iPads’ wide screens and combines them with the portability and camera features of iPhones. When opened, it is the company’s largest phone display and thinnest phone. The Duo opens and closes like a passport to double its screen size. “iPhone Duo brings an entirely new design while preserving everything you love from an iPhone,” said John Ternus, the company’s new chief executive. “It feels effortless to use and it makes new experiences possible.” The phone will start at $1,999 and be available on 23 October. Social media users could opt out of the algorithm if Australian government has its way – but that’s a big if

Social media could become a “choose your own adventure” between the doom-scrolling status quo, or just the feed of the friends you want to see, if the government’s planned digital duty of care legislation passes, and the tech companies don’t muck around on compliance. But that’s a big if. For years people have complained about the random videos or posts cluttering their social media feeds as served to them by the tech giants. It often feels invasive – tracking our activity across websites and apps to serve content and ads – but in many cases, it is also toxic. Guardian Australia was first reporting these issues back in 2024, conducting experiments with blank phones set up to be young men, with very little other information to go on and to see what the algorithms pushed into our feeds. The results were shocking – how the default would quickly send someone down a rabbit hole of extreme misogynistic and far right content, and just how sensitive the algorithm is to any minor interaction on an image or video.

While the social media ban was designed to combat the harms faced by under-16s, many of us know relatives who have been radicalised reading Facebook comments, or grandparents scammed out of their retirement money by fake investments they saw on social media. Outrage bait is rewarded by engagement on platforms, and this has infected politics and public discourse in Australia and elsewhere. The move, announced by the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, on Tuesday to have a pop-up notification proactively require users to decide whether they want the platform to decide what they see or just want to see the content of the people and groups they’ve chosen to follow – similar to how many of the platforms worked in the early 2010s – could be game-changing. In January, the New York police department’s counter-terrorism unit sent out a memo warning police officers about a new potential “security and counterintelligence” threat: Ray-Ban Meta glasses. The memo cited two examples of such videos posted on social media. “The ability to covertly record inside a law enforcement or detention facility, could result in a security risk if proprietary information about cell layouts, camera placements, or officer patrol/site protection routines are released,” the memo read. The NYPD memo is one of a dozen, previously unreported and reviewed by the Guardian, that showed law enforcement agencies across the US are increasingly concerned about the potential for smart glasses to be used against them.

On the polar end of the political spectrum, Bernie Sanders, an independent senator from Vermont, said: “A recent poll shows that the American people overwhelmingly want to ban artificial super intelligence and pause the development of AI until we establish clear safety standards.” The outrage began after an Anthropic employee, Jacob Coxon, announced on social media on Tuesday that he was resigning from the company, saying AI would soon be “superhuman systems” that could cause human extinction by 2030. “I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly,” Coxon wrote. “They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” After Coxon’s post, at least two other Anthropic employees responded to back up these predictions. One said: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Both Cruz and Sanders have been working on legislation that would put guardrails on AI, and echoed this sentiment on Wednesday. Other lawmakers also called on Congress to act.

Criminals, state-sponsored groups, spyware vendors, scientists and propagandists have attempted to use Anthropic’s powerful artificial intelligence models to design missiles and bombs, create deadly pathogens and surveil dissidents, according to a threat intelligence report the company published on Thursday. “The cases we share here aren’t typical misuse, but rather examples of the most notable and novel threat activity we’ve identified to date,” Anthropic wrote in its 154-page report. “We’re publishing this work because we believe we have a responsibility to disclose malicious misuse of our services.” In particular, the company detailed five case studies of scientists using its AI models in biological research. In these examples, Anthropic said the researchers circumvented its safeguards meant to prevent users from “unsupported regions”, as well as worked to hide the purpose of their work. OpenAI not on track to reduce risk of ‘catastrophic’ loss of control, says board member

OpenAI is not on track to reduce the risk of “catastrophic” loss of control to an acceptable level, a member of its non-profit board has said, amid spreading public and political concern that super-advanced AIs could one day wipe out humanity. Paul Christiano, a US government technology adviser, said: “There is a meaningful risk that rapid acceleration in AI capabilities leads to catastrophic and irreversible loss of control in the very near term.” He added: “I do not think that the AI industry in general, including OpenAI, is currently on track to reduce this risk to an acceptable level.” Christiano used to run model alignment at OpenAI and made the statement on Wednesday as he joined the board of the San Francisco company’s non-profit foundation. He will also sit on the foundation’s committee that provides governance over safety and security practices across all of OpenAI, which is developing some of the world’s most advanced models.

Pixel 11 Pro review: Google’s best pocket camera goes customisable

Google’s latest Pro phone is out to prove it has the best camera on a smartphone while embracing customisation, allowing you to change the look and feel of your photos far beyond simple filters even if that means making them technically worse. The Pixel 11 Pro packs the best of Google’s hardware and software into a still-pocketable and easy to handle frame, instantly making it a contender for best smaller phone of the year. Being smaller doesn’t make it cheap. The 11 Pro sits above the regular £879 Pixel 11 and costs from £1,079 (€1,199/$1,099/A$1,849) – £80 (€100/$100/A$150) more than last year, with double the storage but less memory owing to the cost of RAMageddon. Little has changed on the outside for the Pro Pixels in several years. The new model is 0.1mm smaller in all directions and 3g lighter but has the same size 6.3in OLED screen, same polished aluminium and glass body and a large camera bar sticking out the back. It is an attractive design that has aged well.

The temperature sensor from previous Pixel Pro generations, which always felt like a gimmick, has been replaced by a coloured HiLight LED that works as a camera flash and notification light. The LED glows when you talk to Gemini or pulses with one of five colours when your favourite contact calls. But it doesn’t work for notifications of any other kind, so is a wasted opportunity. The 11 Pro has the same Tensor G6 chip as the regular Pixel 11 and has 12 or 16GB of RAM depending on the storage version. text:
Children need interaction, not AI

The most telling sentence in Daniel Susskind’s article (I’m a father of three who studies the impact of artificial intelligence: this is what parents need to know about AI, 6 September) is “human tutors are too expensive to provide to everyone”. Too expensive in relation to what? If instead of allowing tech lords to amass untold wealth we provided tutors for all, this would avert anxiety about job losses and provide the kind of quality that the screen-averse wealthy currently expect only their kids to have. The students protesting against AI are not just concerned about their graduate outcomes, but rather understand that its imposition serves only to enrich the few and worsen the labour conditions of the many. A good future for our children will not come from education technology scammers. They do not need more datacentres and environmentally catastrophic, resource-intensive automation.

text:

Susskind is impressed with the ability of software to mimic existing cultural outputs like stories and podcasts, but if we want new ideas rather than rehashed versions of old ones we need to turn away from the narcissistic seductions of the infinite customisation offered by chatbots. He distinguishes educational AI from “dehumanising” social media, but whereas social media at least used to provide connection, AI fundamentally does not. Susskind seems to share Sam Altman’s idea that it’s cool to make a podcast about your kids’ interests for the car journey, but the point of cultivating them is actually talking about them. Society isn’t made of problems to be solved: it consists of meaningful interactions with others who do get tired and distracted, but whose time is precious for precisely these reasons. Pil and Galia Kollectiv London • Three cheers for Daniel Susskind. As he said, we are letting our children down if we prepare them for the world that we grew up in rather than the one they will inhabit. I am, however, puzzled that he thinks that yesterday’s basics will still be basic in the world they will inhabit.

Self-driving cars should be taxed to offset job losses, thinktank urges

Taxes on self-driving cars should be introduced now in the UK to offset the rise in congestion and threats to jobs they pose, a thinktank has urged. The first robotaxis on London’s streets only started this month, but government projections are that up to 40% of cars sold could have self-driving capability by the middle of the next decade. The report says widespread autonomous vehicle (AV) adoption would put hundreds of thousands of private hire jobs at risk, while individual ownership is likely to increase car usage at the expense of public transport, and increase congestion. Introducing charges now on self-driving vehicles could ease the transition and provide a future revenue stream to replace dwindling fuel duty, according to the report from Centre for British Progress, a non-partisan thinktank focused on economic growth. Wayve, a British tech firm pioneering autonomous cars, said it would “penalise the UK’s most promising innovators”. About £27bn a year is brought in by fuel duty, which is projected to disappear with the transition to electric vehicles.
