text:
How American political campaigns are using AI – and what they’re spending on the tools

New campaign finance disclosure data shines a light on which US political campaigns are using AI tools and how much they are spending on them. Candidates’, parties’ and committees’ spending reveals that AI is fast becoming an essential tool of politics. The candidates themselves are quiet about how they are using the technology in their own campaigns. It’s a sensitive issue that we have been tracking closely since we started writing our book, Rewiring Democracy, which examined how AI is beginning to influence politics. A September 2025 Pew survey of Americans found that more than 70% would think less of a candidate if they used AI to help write a speech. Itemized expenditure disclosure data from the US Federal Election Commission, dating back to 2020, reveals at least $17m in disclosed spending on AI technology vendors across 523 federal candidates and campaigns. Data from four states, California, Colorado, Massachusetts and Washington, provides a more localized picture going back to 2022.

citation.title: How American political campaigns are using AI – and what they’re spending on the tools

text:
How American political campaigns are using AI – and what they’re spending on the tools

Beginning with the AI behemoths, at least 80 federal campaigns and committees have reported spending with OpenAI since 2024. The total spending is not huge: only about $50,000 reported, skewing slightly more Republican than Democratic. The Republican National Committee is the largest overall buyer, with nearly $10,000 in reported expenses. Top individual users include the campaigns of Republicans Mike Lawler, John Kennedy and Bill Cassidy, as well as the California Democrats Ro Khanna and Ted Lieu. Most of these expenses are listed as office expenses, subscriptions to ChatGPT for staff, or research tools, rather than as specific political services. The company’s policies prohibit some political uses of their ChatGPT tool. OpenAI’s biggest competitor, Anthropic, has rapidly built a similar level of usage, but with a different split. At least 65 candidates or committees now report paying the Claude maker in 2026, up from essentially zero in previous years, with a nearly two-to-one Democrat-to-Republican ratio.

citation.title: How American political campaigns are using AI – and what they’re spending on the tools

text:
How American political campaigns are using AI – and what they’re spending on the tools

However, the largest individual user is the campaign of Tom Cotton, a Republican senator from Arkansas, who reported more than $4,000 in spend on Anthropic software in his June filing. Other major users are the Montana independent Senate candidate Seth Bodnar and Jason Knapp, who lost a Democratic House primary in Virginia, and the Democratic Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola. Candidates use either Claude or ChatGPT, rarely both, according to the disclosures. Only about 12% of campaigns or committees using either tool reported expenditures to both vendors. The Democratic lean of Anthropic usage may reflect the company’s alleged liberal skew and clashes with the Trump administration. In contrast, Elon Musk’s xAI caters to Republican interests and, accordingly, its meager usage comes almost entirely from the political right. Just seven federal and two state-level candidates or committees have reported paying xAI, a total of about $5,000, the majority of which was spent by the presidential campaign of RFK Jr in 2024, but also includes Republicans Dave McCormick and Thomas Massie.

citation.title: How American political campaigns are using AI – and what they’re spending on the tools

text:
How American political campaigns are using AI – and what they’re spending on the tools

More dollars go to the vendors specializing in political campaign applications of AI. For years, AmplifAI, which provides automated text messaging, essentially a new iteration on robocalling technology, was a dominant target of spending, soaking up $4.7m in campaign spending in the 2022 cycle alone. It was used heavily by Democratic candidates including Mark Kelly, Joe Biden, Bernie Sanders and Adam Schiff. Spending on AmplifAI, now owned by the troubled media conglomerate Triller, seems to have tapered off in the years since 2022. The new rising Democratic solution for AI-powered text messaging is Daisychain, which has so far garnered about $300,000 in reported candidate spend in the 2026 cycle – up from only about $50,000 reported in 2024. More than half of this year’s spending comes from the Senate campaign of Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. The closest equivalent on the Republican side has been Campaign Nucleus, associated with former Trump campaign manager Brad Parscale.

citation.title: How American political campaigns are using AI – and what they’re spending on the tools

text:
How American political campaigns are using AI – and what they’re spending on the tools

The AI-powered voter engagement tool has attracted six-figure spending from the Republican National Committee, multiple Pacs aligned with Donald Trump, and five-figure investments from Mike Johnson, Kari Lake and other candidates. It is displacing the legacy texting vendor Prompt.io, which has retained about $375,000 in 2026 spending to date, down from more than $500,000 in the 2022 cycle. But it continues to be used: the A More Affordable California Pac sponsored by Uber has single-handedly spent more than $1m on Prompt.io in 2026. The Republican Massachusetts gubernatorial nominee Michael Minogue has been a recurring customer, as has the failed Republican California gubernatorial candidate Ché Ahn and Republican-aligned Super Pac Neighbors for a Better Colorado. At the state level At the state level, the AI spending is smaller but growing fast. Across the four states studied, we found a total of at least $92,000 in spending confidently attributable to modern generative AI vendors since 2022. The spending is spread across at least 108 candidates and committees.

citation.title: How American political campaigns are using AI – and what they’re spending on the tools

text:
How American political campaigns are using AI – and what they’re spending on the tools

The growth has been explosive; there has already been about 10 times the amount of state-level AI spending reported in 2026 as there was in all of 2024. Much of the state spending mirrors federal patterns. Daisychain again has the highest overall spend, and OpenAI and Claude dominate among the general-purpose AI vendors. DonorAtlas – the AI-powered prospect research tool – sticks out for its usage in these states, sitting behind only Daisychain and OpenAI and buoyed up by nearly $4,000 in spending by the California Democratic party. Even though it has dominated so much media conversation, few candidates seem to be reporting spending on AI tools designed specifically to create synthetic audio and video, also known as “deepfakes”. We found just six federal candidates or committees reporting spending on the popular AI audio generator tool from ElevenLabs, with total spending of about $1,400 led by independent candidate for Colorado’s sixth congressional district Samir Witta.

citation.title: How American political campaigns are using AI – and what they’re spending on the tools

text:
How American political campaigns are using AI – and what they’re spending on the tools

The AI image generator service Midjourney has five reported federal campaign or committee users reporting about $1,600, led by Sholdon Daniels, the Republican primary runner-up in the Texas 30th district. Combined, those two firms had less than $100 in reported spend across the four states. However, recent data from the Wesleyan Media Project shows that at least 164 political ads in this cycle have included AI-generated media, supported by at least $80m in ad spending. What this illustrates is that candidate and committee disclosure reports are just the tip of the iceberg. They don’t cover spending on AI by political consultants, media firms and other vendors hired by the campaigns or by Pacs, or independent committees raising and spending money aimed at boosting candidates’ campaigns. Those entities aren’t required to disclose detailed expenditure reports, and are very likely where the bulk of campaign AI usage is happening.

citation.title: How American political campaigns are using AI – and what they’re spending on the tools

text:
How American political campaigns are using AI – and what they’re spending on the tools

Since a large fraction of all spending in the campaign cycle will happen in the final weeks leading to November, much remains to be seen about the totality of how campaigns will leverage AI and what impact its use will have on voters’ decisions. • This article was amended on 13 October 2026. An earlier version wrongly said that Prompt.io was a “Republican-serving texting vendor”. In fact, it is a non-partisan company.

Trial of live facial recognition in London stations leads to a false positive and no arrests

A six-month trial of live facial recognition (LFR) technology in London’s railway stations that cost more than £320,000 and almost 100 hours of police officers’ time led to one false match against a watchlist of suspects and no arrests. More than half a million faces were scanned between February and July this year in some of the capital’s busiest transport hubs during the British Transport Police (BTP) trial of the surveillance technology, which aimed to help catch offenders and people breaching court orders. A freedom of information document obtained by Liberty Investigates and shared with the Guardian shows that equipment hire and police staffing for the 18 deployments across the trial cost £320,786 and led to only one alert on a watchlist, which turned out to be an incorrect identification, also known as a false positive. Last month BTP announced it was extending the trial for a further four months and expanding the deployments to include London Underground stations.

text:

A fake image of a Georgia mayor kissing a person went viral. Can US voters trust everything they see?

An image of Bianca Motley Broom, the mayor of College Park, Georgia, kissing a man who was not her husband in a bar spread far and wide on Facebook. The fact that it was fake is spreading faster, now, but only after it had been seen by thousands of people. “I think this is a sad commentary about where we are in our democracy, and where we are in our political discourse,” Motley Broom said. “It also seeks to reinforce really tired stereotypes about women in leadership.” Six years ago, when Motley Broom first took office in the Atlanta suburb, a political enemy might have needed at least rudimentary skill with image-editing software to forge an image of a politician in a compromising position. Today, all that is required is a computer and a prompt for an AI image generator. The threat of deepfakes and misinformation driven by artificial intelligence has become a point of deep concern for legislators, advocates and the public.

A poll taken in mid-June by Rad Campaign, a digital marketing agency, and Women Who Tech, an advocacy organization for female entrepreneurs, showed that about 71% of respondents worry about AI-generated deepfakes and disinformation affecting elections, while two in three respondents said they were concerned about AI being used to sexualize women. “The findings show that Americans are more concerned about AI’s use in deepfakes, election disinformation, and the sexualization of women and children than its impact on jobs or the economy,” said Allyson Kapin, founder of the Rad Campaign and co-founder of Women Who Tech. The Trump administration has a penchant for deploying AI imagery. In January, the White House’s official account on the social media platform X posted a digitally altered image of Nekima Levy Armstrong, who had been arrested in connection with a demonstration that disrupted church services in St Paul, Minnesota. A picture of her calmly being escorted by a DHS agent was altered so that she appeared to be crying, and her skin had been darkened.

Fake images of Zohran Mamdami, New York’s mayor, also began circulating from a “parody” account on X in February, falsely depicting him and his mother in the company of the disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein. Using Google’s SynthID tool, Reuters debunked the images, but not before other accounts had recirculated them as authentic, fueling conspiracy theories. Despite significant apprehension around the potential economic consequences of AI, concern about deepfake images being used to sexualize women or children, or to influence elections, outstrips concern about AI affecting jobs by about three to one, Kapin said. “The public is deeply concerned,” she said. Fact from fiction Raphael Warnock, a Georgia Democratic senator, said in a video posted to Facebook that deepfake images had been circulating online falsely depicting him with health problems, with an armful of grandchildren he does not have – and with a full head of hair, which he said was funny, if problematic.

AI tool that copied actor’s ‘lustrous’ voice violated his rights, Tokyo court rules

A court in Japan has ruled that the human voice has legal protection after a landmark case involving a well-known actor and a TikTok account that he claimed had cloned his “lustrous” baritone voice in its AI-generated videos. Tokyo district court said on Wednesday that voices should enjoy the same protection as publicity rights, at the end of a closely watched legal action brought against TikTok by Kenjiro Tsuda – best known for voicing the character Kento Nanami in the anime Jujutsu Kaisen. But the court dismissed Tsuda’s request that the operator of TikTok remove the videos, noting that the user had deleted them soon after the suit was filed last November. “The unauthorised use of a performer’s voice … can be considered an infringement on publicity rights,” said the presiding judge, Aya Takahashi. The lawsuit is believed to be the first in Japan seeking to defend an individual’s vocal identity against AI-generated copies.

citation.title: AI tool that copied actor’s ‘lustrous’ voice violated his rights, Tokyo court rules

text:
AI tool that copied actor’s ‘lustrous’ voice violated his rights, Tokyo court rules

Japan’s voice actors, many of whom achieve star status through their “appearances” in anime, are increasingly worried that AI mimicry is threatening their livelihoods and the industry as a whole. An actor’s voice “is the result of years of rigorous training and apprenticeship”, Yuko Sasaki, executive director of the Japan Actors Union said ahead of the ruling. Tsuda, 55, claimed that the 188 TikTok videos uploaded on an anonymous account between July 2024 and September last year had been narrated by a “deep” and “lustrous” voice that could only be his. In response, the platform argued that the videos contained a “generic male voice” and that any perceived similarities to Tsuda’s voice were highly subjective. The verdict is the first in which a Japanese court has declared that the human voice is protected under publicity rights, a reference to the ability to control and profit from aspects of an individual’s identity, in Tsuda’s case his distinctive voice.

The protection applies “if the purpose of using the voice is exclusively to take advantage of its commercial appeal”, Takahashi said, describing a voice to be “as symbolic of one’s personality as portraits are”. The TikTok account, whose picture resembled Tsuda’s Jujutsu Kaisen character, combined images and AI-generated speech about urban legends, the occult and conspiracy theories. At one point, the account had more than 200,000 subscribers and, according to the legal complaint, the clips would have earned its owner between ¥500,000 (£2,395) and ¥75,000 in monthly revenue, the Kyodo news agency said. Related: We need ‘right to intervene’ in AI amid growing threat, says Bank of England boss Describing the content as “sordid”, Tsuda’s legal team claimed the account had only attracted attention because it had cloned the “attractive voice of a popular actor”. TikTok said in a statement it would “respect the court’s judgment while considering what steps to take after scrutinising [the ruling’s] details”.

We need ‘right to intervene’ in AI amid growing threat, says Bank of England boss

The governor of the Bank of England has called for the “right to intervene” in the AI industry amid growing fears that rogue models could take the financial system hostage. Andrew Bailey said the risks posed by frontier AI models – a number of which have gone rogue in recent months – were “real and increasingly significant”. Meanwhile, it was becoming harder for the public to have proper oversight of powerful AI models that were “functioning within a self-reinforcing loop”. That is putting financial stability at risk, with the new technology having increased the “scale and sophistication of cyber threats to the financial system”, he said. The governor warned it could threaten daily card payments, bank transactions, and stock and bond trading across financial markets. The comments came as the Bank’s financial policy committee (FPC) said the growing mountain of AI debt was increasing financial stability risks. The potential benefits of AI “are immense”, Bailey said but he added that authorities needed to be ready to step in.

citation.title: We need ‘right to intervene’ in AI amid growing threat, says Bank of England boss

text:
We need ‘right to intervene’ in AI amid growing threat, says Bank of England boss

In an opinion piece penned for the Bank of England’s Insight series, he said: “If we are to realise those benefits safely, we must answer one critical question. Should society retain the ability to intervene, to establish the boundaries within which these systems operate and to revise those boundaries as the technology evolves? To my mind, the answer is unequivocally yes.” But Bailey said authorities needed to figure out why they might be forced to step in. He said a “sensible starting point” would be rigorous testing of new AI models to understand how they behave and identify “credible points” where authorities could intervene. “In time, that understanding could be codified into a set of standards which will help to ensure consistency in approach across the financial system, and perhaps more broadly across the economy,” he said. However, the governor stopped short of calling for a regulatory clampdown, saying it was “not, in my view, the right place to start.

citation.title: We need ‘right to intervene’ in AI amid growing threat, says Bank of England boss

text:
We need ‘right to intervene’ in AI amid growing threat, says Bank of England boss

In the excitement surrounding AI development, there is a risk that we move too quickly to debates about regulatory architecture before establishing where the failure exists in the first place.” A growing number of lawmakers, AI researchers and even some AI companies have called for more government oversight of artificial intelligence in recent weeks. However, hopes for international cooperation faded after Donald Trump broadly rejected calls for more regulation of AI technology – most of which is being developed in the US – warning it could hurt efforts to compete with China and threaten economic growth. But Bailey said a set of standards could help safeguard the financial system from harmful AI, which may end up operating outside well-established “shared norms, obligations and responsibilities”. “Central banks have a responsibility to safeguard the stability of the system as a whole,” Bailey said. “We cannot stand aside and assume that technological progress will resolve these questions on its own.

citation.title: We need ‘right to intervene’ in AI amid growing threat, says Bank of England boss

text:
We need ‘right to intervene’ in AI amid growing threat, says Bank of England boss

The public interest requires that we engage with them now, before the risks become more difficult to contain.” Warning of the ballooning AI debt pile, the FPC said large players in the sector had taken on $450bn (£339bn) worth of debt between January and September this year, already overtaking the $333bn worth of gilts due to be issued by the UK government for the whole of 2026. That has tied investors – including hedge funds, asset managers and private credit firms – to the fortunes of AI companies at a time when those tech businesses have yet to turn a profit. “The rapid increase in artificial intelligence-related debt issuance broadens the exposure of capital markets to development in AI,” minutes of the recent FPC meeting on 25 September said. “The committee underscores the importance of timely and careful management of these intensifying, interconnected risks.”

More than 44,000 file legal objections to Palantir NHS platform handling their data

Tens of thousands of people have formally demanded NHS England blocks the Palantir-powered national medical data platform from handling their personal information. More than 44,000 people have filed legal objections to their health data being shared with, stored in or used by the nationwide Federated Data Platform (FDP) operated using the US company’s AI technology. The coordinated campaign utilises rights enshrined in data protection laws and means the NHS must stop using the data unless it can provide a “compelling reason” to continue. Hundreds of thousands of people have signed petitions demanding the government cancels its £330m deal with Palantir, and Andy Burnham will be required to make a decision to back or axe Palantir within months. Campaigners have voiced anger at Palantir’s work for the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, and two House of Commons select committees have called for Labour to exercise a break clause in the seven-year deal which comes into force in February 2027.

David Murray, a retired IBM systems engineer and one of those requesting the data block, said: “I am a believer in the NHS having really good data on their patients, but I want it to be something you can really trust to be used for the right purposes. I am not happy about Palantir’s involvement with the IDF in Gaza and ICE in America.” On Wednesday, the human rights group Amnesty International and patient campaign group, Just Treatment, parked a van styled like a shot-up Palestinian ambulance outside Palantir’s London HQ in a stunt that asked: “Why should a company linked to Israel’s destruction of Gaza’s healthcare system have any place in ours?” Protesters have also raised concerns, acknowledged by the NHS England chief executive, Jim Mackey, that the benefits to public health from the Palantir-powered platform may not be as significant as has been claimed. Palantir says the FDP, which is designed to connect sprawling health service data on topics ranging from surgery schedules to discharge planning, is helping to cut waiting lists and frees up beds.

Nandy says children’s social media ban only ‘staging post’ in online safety drive

Lisa Nandy has warned technology firms that the government’s online safety crackdown is not finished, saying that banning under-16s from social media platforms is only a “staging post”. Earlier this year the government announced that teenagers under the age of 16 would be banned from accessing “high-risk” social media apps, while safer platforms would be subjected to restrictions. The social media ban will come into effect by March, with further measures targeted at 16- and 17-year-olds – including restrictions on websites that allow infinite scrolling and algorithms promoting harmful content as well as tighter age-verification checks – to follow. Nandy has now vowed to go further. “We shouldn’t accept that this is the end,” the culture secretary said before her speech at the Labour party conference, which will be introduced by Georgia Harrison, a campaigner against image-based sexual abuse.

“This is a staging post to what must be a very active interventionist state, policing and regulating the online space so that people are safe.” She said the UK would be “pioneers of tech as a force for good” and would promote online spaces that were “genuinely safe, inclusive and empowering”. She praised the former prime minister Keir Starmer and the former technology secretary Liz Kendall for announcing the ban in June. But she felt there had been a “step change” in the government’s approach since Andy Burnham became prime minister in July and handed her the online safety brief. Comparing social media to real-world civic spaces, she said: “If we were in a situation where we were saying our town centres are now so unsafe that we’ve decided that every child is going to have to stay in their bedrooms, people would rightly be up in arms. “How have we got to a point where we’re saying these social media sites are so harmful and dangerous that we cannot conceive of any way of protecting our children except to remove them altogether?

Pete Hegseth appoints Elon Musk to US taskforce on future of warfare

Pete Hegseth announced on Wednesday that Elon Musk will co-lead a government project to study the future of warfare, marking the SpaceX CEO’s first return to government since he ran the chaotic, so-called “department of government efficiency”, or Doge. Musk will be joined by Palmer Luckey, CEO of the defense tech company Anduril, and Newt Gingrich, the former Republican speaker of the House. A defense department press release on the effort, called Project Meridian, described its goal as “identifying the capabilities required to achieve absolute technological dominance on the next-generation battlefield”. The project will run for 120 days and culminate in an unclassified public report of its recommendations. The defense department’s project brings Musk back into government work a little more than a year after his explosive tenure as leader of Doge, which gutted federal agencies while failing to achieve its stated cost-cutting goals. It is also a sign of how Musk has re-entered the good graces of the Trump administration after a dramatic falling out with the president last year.

The project intends to look at how the US military can utilize new technology and also carry out warfare in untested terrains including subterranean depths and on the moon, the defense department stated in its release. “We are witnessing rapid advances in artificial intelligence, autonomy, directed energy, robotics, biotechnology, among other critical high-tech areas. Combined, these new domains, new ways of fighting, and technological developments will profoundly alter the character of warfare,” Hegseth said in a memo. “To maintain global dominance, the United States must anticipate future operational environments and act decisively to develop the tools to dominate in them.” Musk and Luckey are far from independent arbiters of the future of warfare.

Regarding Adrian Chiles and his tracking apps (Location-tracking apps have turned me into a gibbering wreck – but I just can’t look away, 16 September), I have the reverse issue. I added a phone tracking app to my wife’s phone so that she can track me when I’m out and about on my own (it makes me feel safer on the mean streets of Islington). The problem arises when I call my wife to ask her if she knows where I am – she politely informs me that she doesn’t care, refuses to look at the tracking app, then hangs up! Perhaps she could give Adrian some coaching. Colin Dryland London • I recognise Margaret Squires’ frustration on clashing forecasts on various weather apps (Letters, 11 September). I must confess that I take a less scientific approach. I simply keep checking all the weather apps on my phone until one tells me what I want to hear. This means I often head out with an entirely unjustified confidence in the outlook. At this point, I’m less a weather‑watcher and more a curator of agreeable delusions.

Hotel prices in Europe jump before total solar eclipse

Hotel prices have surged in key European cities as hundreds of thousands of tourists flock to see the first total eclipse visible from the continent this century. Iceland’s capital, Reykjavík, has seen one of the biggest jumps in hotel room prices, being one of the few accessible locations to see the full eclipse before evening on Wednesday. Tourists there have been shelling out $793 (£587) on average to secure a room on Wednesday, a 98% jump compared with the same day last year, according to data from the travel and hospitality data group Lighthouse Intelligence. Spain is also steeling itself for an influx of tourists, as one of the best places on the European continent to view the total solar eclipse. The finance ministry said on Monday that it expected 460,000 overseas tourists to visit specifically to see the eclipse. The rate for a room in A Coruña in the north of Spain was up 135% compared with last year to $451 on average, while prices in Mallorca, where the eclipse is expected to be visible on the horizon at sunset, were up by 24% at about $448.

citation.title: Hotel prices in Europe jump before total solar eclipse

text:
Hotel prices in Europe jump before total solar eclipse

In Santiago de Compostela and Bilbao, hotel room prices have risen 34% and 67% respectively. Interactive Accommodation in small towns and villages in the eclipse’s path, as well as makeshift observatories set up by local enthusiasts, have been booked for months. There have been reports of US travellers taking part in house exchanges with people living in Spain’s Castilla y León, which is one of the best regions to view the eclipse. However, authorities in Spain are worried about an increased risk of fires, with police expecting 1.5m more car journeys than usual on Wednesday. They have warned that extraordinarily dry temperatures mean the smallest spark could lead to devastating forest fires, while traffic could end up blocking access for emergency vehicles if fires break out in rural areas. Authorities will undertake out a massive police operation and safety campaign, with plans to deploy 35,000 officers to help minimise risks.

citation.title: Hotel prices in Europe jump before total solar eclipse

Virginia Barcones, the secretary general for civil protection and emergencies at Spain’s interior ministry, said: “We’ve had an extremely tough summer in Spain, with yet another series of major forest fires. That’s why we must restrict any kind of activity that could generate a spark.” Parking on hard shoulders or close to dry vegetation has been banned in Spain, as have barbecues and fireworks. The València region has closed its natural parks and banned walking on rural footpaths. As of Monday evening, three large wildfires were burning in the provinces of Huelva, Segovia and Huesca. Fires have already scorched about 200,000 hectares this year – six times more than by the same date in 2025, according to the environment ministry. For those unable to make the journey, the US space agency Nasa has installed four high-powered telescopes in the small village of Villalibado in north-west Spain in order to livestream the eclipse to more than 10 million people. A partial solar eclipse will be visible across the UK on Wednesday, where it will reach its maximum coverage at 7.12pm in London.

text:
Passengers stranded in Cambodia after cruise halted due to high fuel costs

A luxury cruise ship that had embarked on a years-long voyage around the world was forced to suspend its operations and leave passengers stranded in Cambodia because of high fuel prices. The ship, known as the MV Odyssey, had been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, Cambodian officials told the Associated Press. The ship has a 650-passenger capacity. The Florida-based operator of Villa Vie Odyssey, the company that operates the cruise line, said it was working with passengers on organizing “temporary living arrangements”. The cruise ship had begun its journey in Belfast in October 2024 for what was described as a “continuous voyage around the world”. “Extraordinary increases in fuel costs have placed our current operating model under unsustainable financial pressure,” a statement on the company’s website said.

citation.title: Passengers stranded in Cambodia after cruise halted due to high fuel costs

text:
Passengers stranded in Cambodia after cruise halted due to high fuel costs

“We are working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and temporary living arrangements, and are supporting residents, crew, and employees as we evaluate restructuring and recapitalization alternatives over the next 60 days.” The ship is now docked at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, with a departure date still unclear. The price of fuel across the world has jumped since the start of the US war on Iran earlier this year. The ship’s operator said the monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia has risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800. The strait of Hormuz, which transports much of the world’s oil, has effectively been closed since 28 February, the beginning of the war. Oil prices climbed to above $117 a barrel this month. One resident on the ship, Randy Cassingham, wrote in a blogpost that he only discovered the cruise route’s cancellation after a company official posted a note on a message board for the ship on Monday morning. “It of course didn’t come from out of the blue: we’ve been well aware of problems,” Cassingham wrote.

citation.title: Passengers stranded in Cambodia after cruise halted due to high fuel costs

“It was a cascade of problems piling up on one another, from the business model to mistakes by management to the mentioned crisis in fuel cost and availability, and more.” Pamela Reckamp, a 59-year-old resident of the ship, told NBC News that company officials on the ship had held a meeting last month where they asked cabin owners to help them raise $1m so the ship could depart Ha Long Bay, Vietnam. “She said: ‘If we don’t get this money, we have about four days of the ship running,’” Reckamp said. “‘Then the lights will go off and the AC will go off.’” Carol Larson, 69, lived on the ship for 18 months along with her sister, Crystal Lavering, 72, she told the Associated Press. Larson, who is from California, expressed hopes that the journey could still be salvaged because she said the decision to live at sea had improved her health. Larson told the outlet that she bought her cabin for $120,000, paid in installments, with additional monthly maintenance fees under a program that offered her the option of living onboard the ship for up to 15 years.

Larson blamed Donald Trump for the problems facing the ship and the suspended journey, as the war on Iran caused fuel costs to rise significantly. text:
Streeting praises new series The Wargame for highlighting Britain’s defence needs

A docudrama depicting a Russian attack on a Britain led by an unlikely pairing of Michael Gove and Nicola Sturgeon has been praised by the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, for writing “my spending review submission”. The Wargame, due to be broadcast on Sky this month, features a string of former politicians advised by ex-securocrats, grappling with an unusually powerful Moscow, while highlighting limitations in the British military. It features Gove, who was a Conservative minister for more than a decade, as prime minister – a job he unsuccessfully ran for in 2016 – and Sturgeon, the former first minister and leader of the Scottish National party, as his deputy, in a mock Downing Street Cobra emergency situation room. Related: Russian warship carries out rare live-fire exercise 45 miles off UK coast Labour figures involved in the production include the former Scotland secretary Jim Murphy as foreign secretary, as well as Harriet Harman and the peer Ayesha Hazarika, who plays the role of director of communications in the embattled team.

citation.title: Streeting praises new series The Wargame for highlighting Britain’s defence needs

text:
Streeting praises new series The Wargame for highlighting Britain’s defence needs

After a preview screening at the National Gallery in central London, with many of the former politicians present, Streeting quipped: “On behalf of the association of UK defence secretaries, thank you for my spending review submission.” Though the war depicted was of “a low likelihood, albeit high impact”, Streeting said he anticipated the show would stimulate public debate on defence spending, currently planned to rise by about £30bn by 2035. Streeting said The Wargame would “play a role in making people think about where they would put defence in the order of priorities as voters”, though he added that wildfires, floods and other natural disasters should also prompt the public to think how they would be able to cope in a crisis. The scale of the cash increase, pushed for by the US president Donald Trump but signed up to by the UK and other Nato allies, is such that it would require taxes or borrowing to be raised, or substantial cuts from other government spending after the next election.

citation.title: Streeting praises new series The Wargame for highlighting Britain’s defence needs

text:
Streeting praises new series The Wargame for highlighting Britain’s defence needs

The five-part programme is a spin-off from a Sky News podcast presented by the journalist Deborah Haynes, who has helped to develop the television show. “We want our country to understand better what the threat is, what credible defence is”, she said. Producers said a series of incidents involving Russian sabotage in the UK and Europe had made the programme more relevant. During filming in mid-June, a Russian frigate south of the Isle of Wight unexpectedly fired warning shots near an approaching pleasure yacht in the Channel, terrifying a British couple onboard. Gove – who was a minister between 2010 and 2024 – said it had come as a surprise to him how limited Britain’s missile defence capability was during filming, an issue highlighted in the show. “For anyone watching, they will think: ‘WTF. How did we get into that situation?’” It was, he said, “quite sobering” for somebody who had been in government for as long as he had, though he had not been a defence minister.

A succession of cuts to defence spending made by Conservative and Labour governments from the end of the cold war until the early part of the decade have reduced defence investment and left the navy struggling to deploy warships and submarines. Since then, there has been a growing consensus across the centre of British politics for increased defence spending. Though Russia remains fully engaged in its war in Ukraine, Moscow retains the ability to conduct cyber, sabotage and disinformation operations in the UK. Sturgeon said the programme could help dispel “the optimism bias that this won’t happen”. Gove said: “I never thought I would say this, but I agree 100% with Nicola”. MPs ‘failing to learn lesson’ over freebies after accepting £400,000 of hospitality

MPs have been accused of failing to learn their lesson over freebies after taking almost £400,000 of hospitality to concerts, sport matches and other events this year, with Louise Haigh, Lucy Powell and Wes Streeting among those accepting tickets. Despite the outcry in 2024 over Keir Starmer accepting football tickets and gifts of clothing, MPs appear to have been declaring hospitality since the start of the year on a greater scale than previously seen. The most recent disclosures include £858 worth of tickets to a Harry Styles concert at Wembley from the PRS for Music industry group, which was accepted by Powell, the deputy leader and education secretary. And Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, accepted tickets to the Chelsea flower show from Lloyds Banking Group worth £1,839. Haigh also accepted a £1,314 ticket to the Ivor Novello awards, while Anneliese Midgley, the chief whip, enjoyed Brit Awards hospitality for two worth £3,432, hospitality at Cheltenham festival horse racing from the betting company Flutter worth £350, and tickets to the Grand National valued at £560.

All were backbench MPs while accepting the hospitality and have now been elevated to cabinet jobs under Andy Burnham. Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, accepted £1,480 of tickets to the men’s Wimbledon singles final while in her cabinet job, while Ellie Reeves, the attorney general, accepted a £1,314 ticket to the Ivors while solicitor general. Burnham declared hospitality worth about £6,000 this year – mostly relating to his former role as the mayor of Greater Manchester, such as £3,800 tickets to the Brit Awards in Manchester, but also £500 worth of tickets to Ladies’ Day at the Grand National in Aintree. The acceptance of free hospitality by MPs appeared to fall after mid-2024 when the spotlight fell on Starmer’s string of free tickets to watch Arsenal football games. In March 2025, Rachel Reeves, the then chancellor, said she would not accept free concert tickets again after she was criticised for using free tickets to take a family member to see Sabrina Carpenter at the O2 arena.

UK’s military needs to focus spending on domestic defence, not overseas missions – report

The UK’s military is too focused on global commitments at the expense of domestic defence, meaning the government’s planned increase in defence spending is likely to result in even greater waste, a thinktank report has warned. According to an analysis by researchers at the Transition Security Project, Britain has the most overseas-oriented military among European nations, with almost a quarter of the defence budget spent on commitments across five continents. Calling this a symptom of a “destructive, outdated foreign policy” centred on overseas missions that have often made the world less safe, the report says ministers should prioritise changing their approach rather than immediately increasing spending, with resources shifted from overseas commitments to domestic defence. Related: Profits boost for UK defence firms as governments increase spending The government is committed to spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035 and a defence investment plan (Dip) was unveiled in July at the tail end of Keir Starmer’s premiership.

citation.title: UK’s military needs to focus spending on domestic defence, not overseas missions – report

text:
UK’s military needs to focus spending on domestic defence, not overseas missions – report

Starmer’s defence secretary John Healey resigned over a refusal to commit to reaching 3% by 2030, but now that Healey is chancellor that target has been shelved for now. It would involve a doubling of the defence budget in nominal terms from £70bn in 2026 to £151bn in 2035, according to the Transition Security Project, a research centre that was spun out of Common Wealth, a thinktank with close links to Andy Burnham. Using figures from 2024-25, the study estimated that about 23% of the military budget for that year was spent on overseas commitments, costing just over £14bn, with the real figure likely to be higher. About £2.8bn was spent on deployments used to project force outside Europe, including bases in places such as Cyprus, Kenya and Oman and elsewhere as “strategic hubs” for projecting UK military power. The report says this makes the UK the most overseas-committed military among European Nato members, even if France has more personnel posted abroad. The Dip seems unlikely to reverse this, talking about continuing commitments on other continents.

citation.title: UK’s military needs to focus spending on domestic defence, not overseas missions – report

text:
UK’s military needs to focus spending on domestic defence, not overseas missions – report

The report questions whether more of the new money should be used for domestic defence, and whether the focus on overseas missions has made the UK safer. Since 2001, the study says, the UK has spent more than £51bn in modern terms on military interventions in Iraq, Afghanistan, Libya and elsewhere. “Britain’s decision to maintain a global network of military bases and force projection capabilities, combined with high levels of waste in the military procurement system, raise serious questions about how it is allocating public investment,” it says, urging the government to “review its military posture, prioritising defence over the global projection of military force”.

citation.title: UK’s military needs to focus spending on domestic defence, not overseas missions – report

text:
UK’s military needs to focus spending on domestic defence, not overseas missions – report

Kevin Cashman, a researcher at the Transition Security Project who co-authored the report, said: “Britain should not pour more money into a bloated military sector geared towards alignment with the United States while Washington starts wars around the world that drive up our bills.” Khem Rogaly, a co-director of the organisation and also a co-author, said: “The billions of pounds Britain wastes on global military deployments every year symbolise its destructive, outdated foreign policy. Britain should end its support for these attempts at global policing. Instead, it should focus its military resources on defence and its public investment on health, housing and the climate emergency.” There is an awareness among defence officials of the importance of avoiding waste, including the risk that an arbitrary focus on reaching a certain level of spending could exacerbate this. The intention is to focus instead on what is necessary – primarily on preparing the UK for a possible war in Europe.

UK to deploy fighter jets to protect Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks

RAF Typhoon fighters are to be used in efforts to protect Saudi Arabia from attack by Yemen’s Houthis, flying protective missions over the country’s cities and critical infrastructure as western allies increase their intervention in the escalating conflict. The operation – the most significant military mission signed off by Andy Burnham as prime minister – will involve RAF pilots attempting to shoot down Houthi missiles and drones, which attacked Saudi airports and oil facilities. The Ministry of Defence emphasised that the role of the fighters – whose number was not stated – would be limited. “These aircraft will operate in a defensive role and will not conduct offensive strikes against the Houthis,” it said. An offensive by the Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen that began in September has gradually escalated into a deadly regional conflict. This month the Houthis have attacked Saudi Arabia, the backer of Yemen’s officially recognised government.

citation.title: UK to deploy fighter jets to protect Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks

text:
UK to deploy fighter jets to protect Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks

Thirteen people were killed when a missile hit King Khalid international airport in Riyadh, the deadliest incident since September in a war that has claimed 19 lives in Saudi Arabia so far. Dozens more have been killed in Yemen by the surge in fighting. The death toll from Monday’s Houthi missile strike on a Yemeni government training camp has risen to 73, a brutal demonstration of the rebel group’s military effectiveness. Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said in a TV interview the UK had agreed to help Saudi Arabia to counter the “outrageous Houthi escalation that we’ve seen in recent weeks” and said the UK was “responding to protect civilians” from attack. HA Hellyer, a Middle East expert with the Royal United Services Institute thinktank, speculated that the UK could get drawn further into the conflict in the future, asking: “What does defensive mean?” He asked what the RAF would do if a Houthi attack happened on a Saudi ship in the Red Sea and the British were in a position to stop it. “The UK might say it was defensive but the Houthis would see it as offensive,” he said.

citation.title: UK to deploy fighter jets to protect Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks

UK to deploy fighter jets to protect Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks

Streeting, however, said that the fighter jets’ remit was narrow. “RAF Typhoons will fly defensive air missions to help protect Saudi airspace from drones and missiles,” he said. Military advisers said the UK would also provide an Atlas A400M transport aircraft capable of transporting heavy equipment, in addition to an existing commitment to supply air-to-air refuelling for Saudi fighter jets with an RAF Voyager. The refuelling mission has been extended by 90 days. The UK has long been a military ally of Saudi Arabia: BAE Systems has supplied it with 72 Typhoons in a deal originally worth £4.4bn. Riyadh has been considering buying another 48 in a negotiation that has dragged on for years. Though the UK only had a limited involvement in the US-Israel war against Iran, Typhoons from the RAF airbase in Akrotiri, Cyprus, and in Qatar, flew defensive missions in the spring and summer to shoot down missiles and drones launched by Iran and other proxies against Gulf states.

text:
Thousands of homes without power as Storm Austen hits south-west England

Thousands of homes are without power and schools were closed as the first named storm of the year hit UK shores. Storm Austen brought severe conditions to parts of the south-west, with a gust of 76mph recorded at St Mary’s airport on the Isles of Scilly on Friday morning. By 3pm, more than 31,000 homes in the south-west were without power, according to National Grid. Dozens of schools across Cornwall were forced to delay their opening, while others did not open at all. Flights were disrupted at airports in the south-west and on the Channel Islands, and passengers were being advised to check the status of their flight before travelling. Guernsey airport’s duty manager, Steve Ford, confirmed that normal service was not expected to resume before Saturday morning, with most of the fleet having been stranded on the UK mainland. The Dutch flag carrier, KLM, cancelled dozens of its scheduled flights for Friday and Saturday. Images showed part of Brighton’s West Pier falling into the sea after it was battered by wind and waves.

United Utilities fined nearly £1m after discharging raw sewage along Lancashire coast

United Utilities has been fined nearly £1m after illegally discharging raw sewage along the Lancashire coastline and polluting seaside holiday locations including Blackpool. The water company pleaded guilty to five environmental permit offences relating to a pollution incident along the Fylde coast in June 2023, and was ordered by Preston magistrates court on Tuesday to pay £964,225 in fines and costs. Sewage was released from pumping stations at Manchester Square, Anchorsholme and Chatsworth Avenue for more than 35 hours over several days in June 2023, affecting coastal communities in Blackpool, Lytham St Annes, Fleetwood and Cleveleys. The Environment Agency issued “no bathing” advice for all eight designated bathing waters along the affected coastline. United Utilities’ modelling showed that a sewage plume had reached seven bathing waters and significantly affected water quality. Communities and businesses along the coast were affected significantly by the contamination, according to the Environment Agency.

‘This quarter was otherworldly’: Palantir earnings surge past expectations

In a sea of companies reporting mixed financial results this quarter, Palantir stands out. Although Palantir was not immune to the AI jitters that caused industry-wide drops in share prices earlier this year, the AI and analytics company reported that its overall revenue grew 93% year over year to $1.94bn. That’s well over the $1.8bn Wall Street expected Palantir to bring in for the second quarter. The glowing financials sparked a 10% surge in share prices in the immediate aftermath. Despite growing opposition to Palantir’s work with various governments including the crucial role the company plays in the Trump administration’s immigration agenda, the company’s revenue from US government contracts grew 90% year over year to $809m. “This quarter was otherworldly: our US commercial revenue grew 149% year-over-year, our overall revenue grew 93% year-over-year,” Palantir’s CEO, Alex Karp, said.

Pomp over progress in Xi’s US summit with Trump is a win for China

If the Beijing meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in May was the “stalemate summit”, the second round of talks between the presidents of the US and China this week seemed to give up entirely on the idea of breakthroughs. Instead, it was described as a celebration of “diplotainment” rather than diplomacy, where pomp prevailed over progress and where one of the main outcomes was the news that two giant pandas would soon be sent from China to Atlanta zoo. Trump rolled out the red carpet for Xi’s arrival on Wednesday and broke with decades of precedent to meet the Chinese leader at Joint Base Andrews. Thus began a three-day state visit that involved a tour of Trump’s new helipad and the Marine One helicopter, and a 90-minute meeting that Trump described as “great” and that revealed, according to Trump, that Xi “has great interest in granite”. “The biggest takeaway is that Trump has been displaying an extraordinary degree of deference to Xi Jinping,” said Julian Gewirtz, who served as a senior China official in the Biden administration. But what of actual substance? Expectations going into the summit were low.

citation.title: Pomp over progress in Xi’s US summit with Trump is a win for China

text:
Pomp over progress in Xi’s US summit with Trump is a win for China

But the outcomes somehow still fell short. One of the biggest issues in the US-China relationship is trade. Last year, as Trump unveiled successive rounds of tariffs on Chinese goods, the White House accused China of unfair practices that it said contributed to the loss of 3.7m US jobs and inflated the trade deficit. The tariffs were supposed to suppress the volume of Chinese imports to the US and put pressure on China. To some degree, they worked. The US trade deficit with China in 2025 fell to $200bn, down from nearly $300bn in 2024. But experts have noted that some of this shortfall is made up for by Chinese goods being shipped to the US via third countries, a trend underlined by the fact that China’s trade surplus surpassed a record $1tn last year. Related: Trump swoons over strongman soulmate Xi – are you feeling jealous, Vladimir? With the US and China accounting for 43% of global GDP, their trade war has far-reaching implications for the world economy. So it was a relief not just to Beijing and to US consumers when the two countries agreed a temporary truce in Busan last year.

citation.title: Pomp over progress in Xi’s US summit with Trump is a win for China

text:
Pomp over progress in Xi’s US summit with Trump is a win for China

That truce is due to expire in November. China, where the economy is heavily reliant on exports, was reported to be pushing for the truce to be extended until the end of Trump’s term, in January 2029. On Thursday, it was revealed that Xi’s first state visit to the US in more than a decade had resulted in a mere two-month extension. That reflects “the lack of preparation for this summit beyond the pomp and circumstance”, said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society. William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said: “This summit largely achieved symbolism and ritualism over substance. That is very clear.” The short extension “reflects the level of fundamental differences that still exist between the two countries over a variety of issues”. China’s most powerful response to Trump’s tariffs was the decision to block the export of rare earths, critical minerals vital to US manufacturing and military supply chains. That seemed to skewer Trump’s leverage over China.

citation.title: Pomp over progress in Xi’s US summit with Trump is a win for China

text:
Pomp over progress in Xi’s US summit with Trump is a win for China

Gewirtz said: “Beijing’s retaliation … seems to have had a profound effect on [Trump] and his administration’s willingness to take risks vis-a-vis China.” Apart from the trade war agreement, the summit failed to achieve any meaningful progress on thorny issues in the US-China relationship such as artificial intelligence, Taiwan, the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and human rights. On Taiwan, which Beijing considers to be the most important issue in the relationship, Xi put pressure on Trump to weaken the US’s support for the self-governing island that China claims as its own. According to the Chinese readout of the Xi-Trump meeting, Xi told Trump he hoped “the US side will adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence”. For the US to state that it “opposes” Taiwanese independence would be a rhetorical shift from the current position of “does not support” such a claim, and would be a move welcomed by Beijing. Trump has not yet commented on whether he agreed to such a statement.

citation.title: Pomp over progress in Xi’s US summit with Trump is a win for China

text:
Pomp over progress in Xi’s US summit with Trump is a win for China

But it does seem he is no closer to approving a $14bn arms sale package for Taiwan, a sale that Beijing would like to see disappear completely. On Thursday, US Senate Democrats lambasted Trump for opting for “pageantry over purpose” and for failing to deliver agreements on “the economic and security issues that will shape America’s future”. Trump ignored recent warnings about the dangers posed by AI, writing on social media on Thursday: “I want ​to leave it exactly where it is,” adding: “That is China’s position also.” For China, the lack of big news from the visit is a win in itself. “The summit went excellently from the Chinese perspective,” Thomas said. Xi “got a huge amount of respect from the American president, the full state visit treatment [and] really great images beaming back to China of the Chinese and the American presidents interacting as peers on the global stage, without having to make any meaningful concessions or compromises.”

Tourist plane crashes during flight over Peru’s Nazca Lines, killing 13

Police in Peru report that 13 people, among them foreign tourists, have been killed in a plane crash in southern Peru, near the Nazca Lines. Local authorities in Nazca confirmed that 11 tourists and two pilots died when the Cessna Grand Caravan crashed in Pueblo Viejo, approximately 4 miles (6km) from the city of Nazca and roughly 12km from the Nazca Lines site. The passengers were identified as seven Italians, two Germans – believed to be a couple – and two Spanish people. The pilot and copilot were named as Americo Salazar Cuellar and Irenka Del Carpio respectively. The plane had departed the nearby city of Pisco at about 1pm local time (7pm BST) to fly over the Nazca Lines, but minutes later lost contact with the control tower and crashed at 1.20pm, police reported. The cause of the crash is as yet unknown, and the local authorities have launched an investigation. “We have information that 11 passengers and two crew members have died,” Police Major Jorge Andrade told reporters at the crash site. “Given the severity of the accident, there are no survivors.

citation.title: Tourist plane crashes during flight over Peru’s Nazca Lines, killing 13

text:
Tourist plane crashes during flight over Peru’s Nazca Lines, killing 13

We have recovered four bodies so far,” Andrade added. The Guardian has seen video footage which showed firefighters and police working amid the smouldering wreckage of the plane in the desert. Images appeared to show bodies on the sand. This deadly plane crash is far from the first at the Unesco world heritage site, which attracts hundreds of thousands of tourists every year. Several operators compete to offer overflights of the iconic lines which date to AD200-700, amid serious concerns about the safety and maintenance of the aircraft. In 2022, a small plane crash killed seven people, including two Chileans and three Dutch nationals. In October 2010, four British tourists and two Peruvian crew members were killed when a small plane operated by AirNasca crashed after flying over the lines. Earlier in the same year, three Chileans and four Peruvians died when a Cessna 206 crashed. In April 2008, five French tourists were killed in another crash, but the pilot survived.

“The investigation of the accident and the oversight of aviation operations are the responsibility of the competent authorities, who will determine the causes and assign liability in accordance with the law,” the municipality of Nazca said in a statement on Saturday. Peru’s tourism ministry expressed “deep sorrow over the tragic deaths of tourists and crew members” in a statement. The mysterious etchings in the desert, which include vast hummingbird, monkey and whale figures, are only fully visible from the air.

text:
‘A symbol of resistance’: the fight to save treehouse built on no man’s land next to Berlin Wall

Sometimes the currents of history converge in a single spot. In Berlin, one of the most intriguing of those places is a small traffic island with a lovingly tended garden and a ramshackle two-storey structure called the Treehouse at the Wall. In 1983, Osman Kalin, a Turkish “guest worker”, was looking in his corner of the city cleaved by the Berlin Wall for a patch of earth in which to plant his onions, garlic and cucumbers. Virtually on his doorstep in the Kreuzberg district was a slice of no man’s land next to the concrete barrier and barbed wire. Although it sat in West Berlin, cold war logic meant the lot officially belonged to the communist East. The east-west border cut a sharp angle near a curved street called Bethaniendamm. The wall was built to slice straight across the road, which left a triangle-shaped scrap of land on the wrong side. Neither side could use it and so nearby residents commandeered it as a dump – until Kalin came along.

citation.title: ‘A symbol of resistance’: the fight to save treehouse built on no man’s land next to Berlin Wall

text:
‘A symbol of resistance’: the fight to save treehouse built on no man’s land next to Berlin Wall

Perhaps it took an outsider such as Kalin to see the potential in the postage stamp of fertile soil beneath the orphaned furniture and discarded drug paraphernalia. And it required a certain audacity to build something abutting the wall patrolled by East German soldiers with shoot-to-kill orders. Over the decades, the “guerrilla garden” came to symbolise a rebel spirit in dark times, the ingenuity of immigrants who were often made to feel unwelcome, and the tragedy and absurdity of great-power confrontation in a city where citizens on both sides just wanted to breathe free. That’s a lot of mythology for one place to hold, and four decades of upheaval have left their mark. Now supporters of the Treehouse at the Wall fear it could be demolished by city authorities as a public safety hazard and are rallying to save it. Kalin, one of the first generation of so-called Gastarbeiter brought by West Germany to plug a labour shortage, was “a remarkable figure”, said Suat Özkan, the general secretary of Berlin’s largest Turkish community organisation.

citation.title: ‘A symbol of resistance’: the fight to save treehouse built on no man’s land next to Berlin Wall

text:
‘A symbol of resistance’: the fight to save treehouse built on no man’s land next to Berlin Wall

“Perhaps he wasn’t a master of language, perhaps he wasn’t the perfect architect, perhaps he wasn’t the perfect artist, but he created something artistic – something that became totally unique.” Kalin, who was born in 1925 in Anatolia, arrived in West Germany in the late 1960s as a manual labourer. Under the programme, about 14 million guest workers came to the country between 1955 and 1973. Despite the temporary nature of the scheme, many stayed on. Nearly 3 million people of Turkish origin now live in Germany, about 200,000 of them in Berlin. Kalin at first squatted the land with his flower and vegetable garden and a small improvised shed. Then, eventually, against the odds, he won permission from the East German authorities to stay, so long as whatever he built there would not be taller than the wall. In time he replaced the shed with the larger “treehouse”, which despite the name is not up in the branches but built around a mature trunk that was on the site.

citation.title: ‘A symbol of resistance’: the fight to save treehouse built on no man’s land next to Berlin Wall

text:
‘A symbol of resistance’: the fight to save treehouse built on no man’s land next to Berlin Wall

After the city reunited in 1990, Kalin faced eviction orders but found an unlikely ally in the neighbouring St Thomas church, which located 18th-century papers showing it was the rightful owner of the land and allowed him to stay. Since Kalin’s death as a local hero in 2018, his son Mehmet has tended to the property and his father’s legacy. “Right when two global political systems were facing off,” Özkan said, Osman Kalin carried out an “act of defiance against the GDR regime, against the system, to show that it is possible to stand up and carry out a kind of revolution”. He added: “It’s a symbol of resistance as well as a symbol against racism, discrimination and hostility.” Özkan said that more than six decades after West Germany established the guest worker programme, it was long past time for the reunited nation to pay tribute to its waves of immigrants. “We still haven’t managed to construct a central memorial,” he said, to the foreign labourers who helped build the postwar economic miracle.

citation.title: ‘A symbol of resistance’: the fight to save treehouse built on no man’s land next to Berlin Wall

text:
‘A symbol of resistance’: the fight to save treehouse built on no man’s land next to Berlin Wall

“This house should serve as a kind of memorial.” Stefan Zeppenfeld, a historian who published a book in 2021 about Turkish labourers in West Berlin during the cold war, said it took decades for Germany to acknowledge its transformation into a “country of immigration”. He noted that migrant labourers like Kalin were relegated to neighbourhoods close to the wall, such as Kreuzberg, that became prime real estate after the wall’s fall in 1989. Zeppenfeld said the treehouse crystallised many aspects of what made up Berlin and its people. “The history of German division or the iron curtain is still absolutely crucial and defining for Berlin, for Berlin’s sense of identity,” he said. “And I find it absolutely fascinating that this building is still standing – it’s one of the few tangible legacies where we can actually see agency by Turkish guest workers as a real part of the cityscape.” As a first step, Özkan is planning an open-air exhibition on the chain-link fence surrounding the structure, complete with archival pictures and Kalin’s extraordinary life story.

citation.title: ‘A symbol of resistance’: the fight to save treehouse built on no man’s land next to Berlin Wall

text:
‘A symbol of resistance’: the fight to save treehouse built on no man’s land next to Berlin Wall

The tension with city authorities ahead of a Berlin election in September is that supporters of the treehouse want to maintain its scruffy authenticity while safety and legal concerns have forced a conversation about its structural integrity. Outside, the wooden facade is made up of listing, mismatched planks. Tongue-in-cheek Nato and Soviet flags whip from erected poles while plum and apple trees mark the seasons. Inside, a jumble of black-and-white photographs and construction tools point to the Kalin family’s past and future in their garden idyll. A donated chandelier lends an unexpected touch of elegance. Florian Schmidt, a Kreuzberg district councillor, said his office was working closely with the Turkish community and Kalin’s son Mehmet, who has done extensive repairs on the house, to “grant the necessary permits” for it to remain.

citation.title: ‘A symbol of resistance’: the fight to save treehouse built on no man’s land next to Berlin Wall

text:
‘A symbol of resistance’: the fight to save treehouse built on no man’s land next to Berlin Wall

“Due to the unusual situation – the site being a no man’s land and the lack of planning permission – use of the treehouse was initially prohibited,” Schmidt said in an emailed statement, noting that Mehmet had been granted a temporary exemption to do work there. “Issues relating to ownership rights are also being clarified.” Adrian Sampson, of Alternative Berlin Tours, which spotlights the city’s subculture and street art, was leading a group of visitors past the treehouse on a hot July day as he explained Kalin’s legacy. “His story is about three things: resistance, community spirit and multiculture all together there. And that’s what Kreuzberg is about,” said Sampson, who is originally from Melbourne. Asked about speculation that the site’s days could be numbered, he said: “I think it’d be an absolute shame, like really a pity for the city, because it just makes a lot of people happy.”

First Australian mass mortality event suspected as deadly bird flu virus rapidly escalates among native birds

More than 80 dead and sick birds seen on rocks off the South Australian coast are suspected to be the first mass mortality event from the deadly H5N1 bird flu virus, only six weeks after the disease arrived in Australia. Authorities reported on Saturday that helicopter surveillance had revealed 49 dead greater crested terns on Baudin Rocks, near Robe, as well as 35 more sick terns. While some of the birds had been collected for testing, South Australia’s chief vet Skye Fruean said it was likely the first mass mortality event from the disease. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email South Australia also reported three suspected positive cases in other greater crested terns, including one inland at Monarto, suggesting the disease has begun moving away from the coast. The Monarto area is home to several poultry farms. Three silver gulls were also suspected positive, SA authorities said, adding to the first silver gull found a few days ago and confirmed positive by the CSIRO earlier on Saturday.

citation.title: First Australian mass mortality event suspected as deadly bird flu virus rapidly escalates among native birds

text:
First Australian mass mortality event suspected as deadly bird flu virus rapidly escalates among native birds

Kate Millar, the chief executive of conservation charity BirdLife Australia, called it a “very significant escalation of the bird flu situation in Australia, and a very bleak milestone”. “Sadly, we’re at the beginning of a long and challenging battle and birds and wildlife are going to need all the help they can get,” she said. Jack Gough, the chief executive of the Invasive Species Council, said it now appeared the disease was “starting to take off” and “mirroring the experience in South America of early detections, then rapid increases in numbers and spread leading to mass mortality events in wildlife.” “We are still at the very early stages of this devastating disease spreading, but the possible first mass mortality coming just days after the virus was declared not eradicable indicates how quickly this could escalate,” he said. Fruean said there was “nothing we can do” to stop the spread of the disease, but that surveillance was working.

citation.title: First Australian mass mortality event suspected as deadly bird flu virus rapidly escalates among native birds

text:
First Australian mass mortality event suspected as deadly bird flu virus rapidly escalates among native birds

The news came at the end of a significant week in the development of the disease when numbers jumped by 20 in just a few days to the current total of 53. Australia was the last continent to have the unwelcome arrival of a disease that has killed millions of birds and mammals around the world. Victoria this week confirmed its first cases of the virulent strain in a greater crested tern found in Portland, with the state joining Western Australia, South Australia, New South Wales and Queensland that have all recorded positive cases. On Saturday, Victorian authorities said samples from five crested terns had been sent to the CSIRO laboratory in Geelong, with preliminary testing suggesting more positive results. Five confirmed cases in birds at Seal Bay on Kangaroo Island also raised concerns for the welfare of the area’s Australian sea lions – an endangered species. Tens of thousands of seals have died worldwide from the disease.

text:
First Australian mass mortality event suspected as deadly bird flu virus rapidly escalates among native birds

But it has been the cases among silver gulls that has experts like Sean Dooley, the national affairs adviser at BirdLife Australia, concerned that the spread of the virus has now reached a critical new stage. “When people think of a seagull, they’re almost always thinking of the silver gull,” said Dooley. “They’re very common, and primarily they are coastal, but they do come inland and can turn up in Lake Eyre following floods,” said Dooley. Silver gulls are the second Australian native species to catch the disease, after dozens of detections in greater crested terns. But it is the silver gull’s behaviour and habits that have experts concerned because they scavenge from dead or dying animals, meaning they can easily pick up the disease from other sick birds. They also pick detritus from water bodies – lakes and flooded areas included – and these are known to be breeding grounds for the disease. “There is such a large population of silver gulls, and they move into other habitats. They could be the vector that takes bird flu inland,” says Dooley.

text:
First Australian mass mortality event suspected as deadly bird flu virus rapidly escalates among native birds

“They’re also really successful in urban areas and could bring the disease into those bird populations.” Because Australia has a high concentration of unique birds, the susceptibility of many native species isn’t known. But the fears are there is no reason to think they would manage any better than birds overseas. Birds that flock around water have tended to be the hardest hit. Examples include sandwich terns, black-headed gulls and northern gannets in Europe and, in Peru, pelicans. Dooley said the mood at BirdLife Australia this week had been one of “trying to suppress that sinking, gut-churning feeling”. The winter season for birdwatchers along the coast had been one of the best in 10 years, said Dooley, with rare petrels turning up in numbers along the east coast. “Now that has been heavily tinged because probably among those were birds carrying H5N1.” • This article was amended on 2 August 2026 to correct the spelling of Skye Fruean’s surname.

‘Just the tip of the iceberg’: how a Bali run club reignited tourist tensions on holiday island

When Annisa Rahmadani posted online about being rejected from a social running club in Bali, she expected a few sympathetic comments. Instead, her story went viral, prompted national politicians to weigh in, immigration authorities to intervene and ultimately, the club’s Dutch organisers barred from Indonesia. “I had no idea it would get that big,” said the 34-year-old university lecturer from the Indonesian city of Bandung. “But it seems it was just the tip of the iceberg.” The controversy centred on the expat-run Entourage running club. The group attracted a huge backlash after posts like Rahmadani’s circulated online and sparked allegations it was excluding Indonesians and accepting foreigners. Related: Who is ‘stealing’ Bali’s water? How tourism siphoned off a prized resource The club denies it excludes Indonesians and says the issue stemmed from its registration system incorrectly rejecting some Indonesian phone numbers. For many in Indonesia, the story hit a nerve, inflaming frustrations about an influx of wealthy foreigners and digital nomads on the island.

citation.title: ‘Just the tip of the iceberg’: how a Bali run club reignited tourist tensions on holiday island

text:
‘Just the tip of the iceberg’: how a Bali run club reignited tourist tensions on holiday island

It crystallised a feeling that parts of Bali are becoming socially and economically detached, places where locals says they increasingly feel like outsiders in their own home. “The patience of the locals had been tested for too long,” said Bali regional parliamentarian Niluh Djelantik. Bali has long been a popular tourist destination but since the pandemic, it has become a magnet for remote workers and digital nomads, drawn by the weather, surf, relatively low cost of living and relaxed visa requirements. Around tourism hubs such as Canggu and Uluwatu, co-working spaces, luxury gyms, paddle clubs and wellness retreats have overtaken warung food stalls and beach bars, alongside a growing foreign population choosing to stay for months or years. Despite an increase in jobs and income levels, the rapid transformation has brewed resentment among locals.

Infrastructure has struggled to keep pace, housing costs have soared and frustrations over cultural clashes – from topless scooter riders to foreigners disrespecting sacred sites – have angered the Balinese and the wider Indonesian population. “In Bahasa Indonesia we say, Seperti api dalam sekam (like a fire under the dry rice husk). It had been escalating, and the fire was always going to come out,” said Djelantik. Djelantik said not all foreigners were causing problems, but some ignored local culture, broke the rules or worked illegally. ‘Rife with discrimination’ Run clubs have become popular activities in Bali for locals and foreigners. The Entourage group had held a similar early morning “silent disco” event in May, with social media posts showing a crowd jogging through the streets with headphones. Rahmadani, a keen runner, had wanted to join their next early morning event in July with her British husband. He was immediately accepted while she was rejected.

The organisers later said they were targeting digital nomads and their registration system had incorrectly excluded some Indonesian phone numbers. Online, she found dozens of Indonesians reporting similar experiences, and screenshots of rejected applications quickly spread across social media. As criticism intensified, Entourage posted a statement denying it had intentionally discriminated against Indonesians. The run club said events were “open for everyone, including non-digital nomads”. The statement said Indonesians made up almost a quarter of participants and blamed an automated approval system for excluding some Indonesian numbers, adding it had paused events to review the processes. Entourage has been approached for comment. Immigration director-general Hendarsam Marantoko has since banned two Dutch nationals who were running the club from returning to Indonesia, described the club as “rife with discrimination against local residents”, and argued there “should not be a state within a state”.
