The far-right group has been doing this for years. Ben-Gvir has made series of visits to the site over the last three years, eroding norms and inflaming tensions. Jordanian officials have recently warned that it could be at risk of an “imminent” Israeli takeover. With national elections scheduled in October, and many eyes still firmly on Gaza (this weekend, Netanyahu rejected a US-backed 15 point plan for peace), the Israeli government appears to be racing to expand Israeli settlements and accelerate ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in the West Bank and East Jerusalem before its mandate expires. For this morning’s First Edition, I spoke to our senior international correspondent, Julian Borger, about the latest incursions, and how Israeli extremists are trying to create a new reality in Jerusalem.

Movie paradise? How Malta became a magnet for big film shoots

What links the Caribbean, ancient Rome, Enid Blyton’s Land of Spells, the south of France and the Bay of Pentos from Game of Thrones? They are all places that have been portrayed in recent and forthcoming films by a sunny archipelago in the Mediterranean Sea, no bigger in size than Sheffield. Malta has over the last decade risen to become one of the most popular places in Europe for American and British film-makers to set their works in, taking a lead in what has been described as an “arms race” to lure big movie productions with tax incentives. The EU’s smallest country has hosted more than 30 film and TV productions each year in each of the last three years, including a record 36 in 2023 and 2025. They include Jurassic World Rebirthand Gladiator II, this spring’s Blyton adaptation The Magic Faraway Tree and the new Jason Statham action thriller Mutiny, out at the end of this month.

The island is even starting to represent itself: the third season of Netflix’s detective drama Enola Holmes decamps from Victorian London to the then British-occupied island, and principal photography is due to start next year for TV auteur Stephen Poliakoff’s The Order, set on the eve of the 1565 siege of Malta by Ottoman forces. “For such a small European country, Malta is really punching above its weight,” said Adrian Wootton, the chief executive of the British Film Commission.

But in the past its film industry was essentially seasonal, said Johann Grech, Malta’s film commissioner. “Now, we have an industry that is working every day, all year round.” Its success is largely due to the broader global upheaval of how film-making is financed. Until the early 2000s, audiovisual productions in Europe were mostly funded by direct funding, such as film funds or selective grants. Over the last few decades, however, films are increasingly made possible by tax incentives, such as cash rebates that production companies are reimbursed after filming if they hire local crews or rent facilities.

Efforts to contain a “devastating” blaze in the New Forest will continue into a second night as firefighting crews race to protect the fragile heathland and rare species. The area hit by the blaze, which started after a van caught fire on the A31 near Ringwood on Sunday, is protected heathland that is home to a number of rare species, according to the New Forest national park authority. “Heathland is more rare than rainforest and takes decades to develop – the New Forest has the most extensive area of lowland heath remaining in Europe,” said Gillie Molland, the park authority’s lead ranger. “The loss of rare species and biodiversity is devastating and upsets the delicate ecological balance of the forest, as well as reducing grazing land available for commoners’ animals.” The blaze threatens rare species including all six UK native reptiles, Dartford warblers, nightjars and insects. Molland said recovery was possible, but it could take decades for some features of mature heathland to return. “Some rare heathland species may be lost or recover very slowly if local populations have been affected,” Molland said.

Native birds in captivity to be vaccinated against H5 bird flu as Australia prepares for more mass mortalities

Vaccinations against H5 bird flu will be rolled out for Australian native bird species in captivity as the deadly virus continues to spread across the country. The federal agriculture minister, Julie Collins, said on Tuesday that target native species in captivity would be prioritised with the first vaccinations to commence “in the coming days and weeks”. Collins said state governments would manage the program and announce the target species soon. “We’ve been very clear that we cannot stop the H5 bird flu from spreading among wild birds, but we can take action to protect the species most at risk,” the minister said. “Vaccination is now part of that response.” Related: Jean hoped bird flu wouldn’t come to Australia. Then it arrived – and she saw a tern ‘trembling and swaying’ Collins warned Australians they would continue to see “more spread and larger numbers – particularly of dead birds and mass mortalities around the country”.

The vaccination program would focus on captive species such as endangered birds that were part of conservation breeding programs in zoos and other facilities. The federal environment minister, Murray Watt, said it was difficult to vaccinate wild birds because a full course required two doses. But the commonwealth did plan to vaccinate wild birds where possible, he said. “It does take two vaccination doses to vaccinate birds, and it is difficult enough to catch wild birds once, let alone twice. [But] where it’s possible to vaccinate wild birds, we will do so.” Endangered birds in captivity include the orange-bellied parrot, regent honeyeater and Western Australia’s black cockatoos. Australia’s chief veterinary officer, Beth Cookson, said the vaccination rollout followed trials examining its safety and efficacy over the past 18 months. The government did not say which species or facilities had participated in the pilot program. “The trials and pilots that we’ve undertaken so far have provided us with some safety data across a range of different species,” Cookson said.

‘Every minute counts’ as rescuers race to find survivors after deadly Colombia earthquake

Colombian rescue workers are racing to find survivors after the country’s deadliest earthquake this century killed at least 240 people and left at least 3,000 missing. In Cali, one of the worst affected cities, firefighters said they had pulled a 35-year-old man from the wreckage of a collapsed building shortly before 4am on Tuesday – nearly 24 hours after the 7.4 magnitude quake rattled western Colombia. “We have found life under the debris … Every minute counts,” the fire department wrote on X alongside a video of a survivor being rescued from beneath a concrete beam. On Tuesday afternoon there was a sudden burst of applause after a 31-year-old woman named as Diana Troncoso was also rescued by firefighters after a 16-hour effort. “Getting out of there is a miracle,” her father, Álvaro Troncoso Torres, told journalists from local newspaper El País as he stood by the ruined building. Civilians reportedly pulled at least five survivors from a partly collapsed hotel, although elsewhere the bodies of some of the city’s 95 confirmed victims could be seen lying on the street under sheets.

Colombia’s president, Abelardo de la Espriella, was sworn into power in Cali only last Friday. On Monday night he was back in his country’s third-largest city, telling reporters that 5,000 homes had been destroyed and 188 people were missing in the surrounding department of Valle del Cauca. “We will get through this together,” Cali’s mayor, Alejandro Eder, told its 2.3 million citizens during a televised meeting with the new president. Eder said emergency responders had rescued 37 people from some of the 40 buildings that had completely collapsed in Cali. De la Espriella, who won power in June by vowing to launch a major crackdown on illegal armed groups, said more than 1,000 troops were being mobilised to avoid public disturbances amid reports of looting. The situation in Pereira, a city 130 miles to Cali’s north, appears similarly dramatic, with at least 53 people reportedly trapped in some of the 58 buildings that collapsed. Eleven people are missing, according to the local newspaper El Diario.

text:
France’s complex picture of collaborating with and combating Nazis

You editorial (The Guardian view on French cinema’s De Gaulle moment: present anxieties inform a new focus on the past, 5 August) informs us that some new French films covering the second world war are coming soon. Its focus suggested that most of these films will be of a “great men of history” kind. Whatever dilemmas faced leaders in this period, it was the grandparents and great-grandparents of the majority of cinemagoers who faced life-or-death choices and, in some cases, held the lives of their neighbours in their hands. From my research about members of my family and the areas where they were living, I’ve found local policemen arresting Jewish men and women (like my father’s uncles and aunt) and handing them over to the Nazis. These gendarmes were under the command of local administrators who were “honoured” to do the bidding of Nazi commandants. But then, if you scan the Resistance memorials (often in isolated rural places), you gather that some of the names on those memorials are of Jewish and, in one example I know of, a black member of the Resistance.

citation.title: France’s complex picture of collaborating with and combating Nazis

text:
France’s complex picture of collaborating with and combating Nazis

Even as the occupiers were facing defeat, Nazi generals were under instructions to massacre partisans, and some young French men joined the armed Milice, who worked with these occupiers to betray the Resistance. Sometimes, immediately after the war, reprisals against the Milice involved summary executions, while the local administrators who did the Nazis’ bidding may have been tried, found guilty and imprisoned but, soon after, walked free under state-ordered amnesties. This is a complex picture of grassroots, local choices, some being made in support of an illegitimate occupation, part of a Europe-wide genocide and rule by terror, and other choices being made to defy this. Michael Rosen London • French cinemagoers will be thinking about the threats to French democracy posed by the extreme right, but their interest in Charles de Gaulle runs much deeper. He symbolises resistance to all the forces outside the Hexagone which threaten its autonomy and identity.

citation.title: France’s complex picture of collaborating with and combating Nazis

text:
France’s complex picture of collaborating with and combating Nazis

To an extent inconceivable in the UK, the French have striven, since the second world war, to maintain freedom from outside interference – in the military sphere (weapons procurement and the nuclear deterrent), in the economic sphere (space exploration, Airbus, automobiles), in the cultural sphere (Paris and Notre Dame). This urge underlies the desire to maintain and defend the French language, a symbol of internal cohesion within French society and external distinction from the hostile world outside. None of these questions seem to concern people in the UK, but they should. Anthony Lodge Carnbee, Fife • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Flight paths and fridge magnets: how a fireball hunter tracked down New Zealand’s newest meteorite

Days after a massive fireball flashed through New Zealand’s skies last month, Steve Wyn-Harris spotted a small, black stone on the bare ground. The citizen astronomer was on the hunt for debris from the meteor that had flown over the North Island. He bagged the rock but wasn’t too confident, as he says most finds turn out to be “meteor-wrongs”. But when he held the thumb-sized rock next to a fridge magnet, to detect iron and nickel in meteorites, it clicked. Wyn-Harris did the test on a video call with other citizen scientists and geologists and after the click “we were all yelling”. “I went from doubting Thomas to a convert,” says Wyn-Harris. His discovery marks the 11th confirmed meteorite to be found in New Zealand. Meteorites are the leftover rock that hits the ground after the meteor has burned up entering Earth’s atmosphere. Finding the debris in New Zealand can be difficult, a consequence of the country’s sparsely populated, rugged terrain.

citation.title: Flight paths and fridge magnets: how a fireball hunter tracked down New Zealand’s newest meteorite

text:
Flight paths and fridge magnets: how a fireball hunter tracked down New Zealand’s newest meteorite

Wyn-Harris is the director of Fireballs Aotearoa, an alliance of astronomers, geologists and citizen scientists that now has a network of 200 cameras set up around the country designed to help document meteor showers and recover meteorites. On 28 July, the group and their cameras had tracked a meteor over the North Island, and people had rushed online to describe the dazzling display and a “huge boom”. Related: ‘Thought it was a plane on fire’: large meteor sightings stir delight in New Zealand Footage indicated there was an exciting possibility of many fragments from the meteor on the ground. After crunching data, including wind speed and flight path projections, the group zeroed in on an area where they calculated meteorites could be strewn. They kept the location a secret, worried a public appeal for help could trigger a “meteorite rush” – a martian meteorite found in Niger sold for more than $5m last year – though New Zealand law prohibits such sales.

citation.title: Flight paths and fridge magnets: how a fireball hunter tracked down New Zealand’s newest meteorite

text:
Flight paths and fridge magnets: how a fireball hunter tracked down New Zealand’s newest meteorite

Wyn-Harris says he found the meteorite near a riverbank while scouting farmland a day before he and the group were due to search the area. “I wasn’t so excited when I first spotted and bagged it because I’d only been looking around … for 40 minutes,” he says. But on the video call later that night a geologist looked at the rock and noted its crust had a meteorite quality. The next day, a team of 11 people carried out a wider search of the area. Two days after Wyn-Harris’s discovery, which weighed eight grams, Liam McGovern, a geology PhD student, found a second fragment, weighing 39 grams. Over 10 days, the search party discovered another four pieces, weighing 75g in total, including a fragment that had crashed on to the driveway of a house. Wyn-Harris says the meteor’s trajectory before it entered the atmosphere indicated it came from the asteroid belt, making it an “ordinary chondrite”. The name is “unfortunate, because they’re not ordinary,” he says. All four fragments will now be analysed further by Dr Marshall Palmer, a geologist who is part of Fireballs Aotearoa.

citation.title: Flight paths and fridge magnets: how a fireball hunter tracked down New Zealand’s newest meteorite

text:
Flight paths and fridge magnets: how a fireball hunter tracked down New Zealand’s newest meteorite

Palmer will give the meteorites an official name and, together, they will become New Zealand’s 11th documented meteorite. Prof James Scott, a geoscientist from Fireballs Aotearoa, says the pieces are “100%” meteorite, and he believes they likely share origins with New Zealand’s first meteorite discovered in 1863 nearby in Masterton. “Both likely come from the same parent body, which was an asteroid from near the start of the solar system. That blows my mind. We have two rocks, formed elsewhere in space from a smallish asteroid … that has been catastrophically destroyed, and yet they land within 10km of each other.”

text:
Nirmal Purja obituary

Nirmal Purja made his name in environments where life is reduced to its most elemental, and dangerous, terms. He believed, with an almost evangelical fervour, that “with relentless self-belief, anything is possible”. He spent his life testing the limits of that belief, first in military service and later on the world’s highest and most dangerous mountains. He has died aged 43 in an avalanche on Broad Peak, an 8,051-metre mountain in Pakistan. Purja was the most celebrated and controversial mountaineer of the past decade. His ambitious, no-holds-barred approach to high-altitude climbing brought a new emphasis to the world’s highest peaks, prioritising speed, visibility and multiple back-to-back ascents within a single season. His methods helped propel Himalayan mountaineering into the influencer age, reshaping the way people saw, and climbed, the world’s tallest mountains. He was also an astute self-promoter, frequently broadcasting his climbs and exploits from the high camps themselves. In a relatively short climbing career, Purja amassed a remarkable collection of records.

citation.title: Nirmal Purja obituary

text:
Nirmal Purja obituary

Among them were fastest ascents of multiple 8,000-metre peaks, the highest number of ascents of the world’s 8,000-metre mountains by a single climber (57), and the highest number of 8,000-metre ascents without supplemental oxygen (29). In 2021, he also achieved one of mountaineering’s most coveted feats: the first winter ascent of K2, the world’s second-tallest peak, alongside nine fellow Nepali climbers who sang the Nepali national anthem together as they reached the top. Purja was the only member of the summit team to climb K2 without supplemental oxygen. In 2018, Purja was appointed MBE after helping lead 13 fellow Gurkha soldiers to the summit of Everest, rescuing an ailing climber from high in the death zone, and breaking three world records for speed ascents on Everest and the nearby peaks of Lhotse and Makalu. Purja achieved global fame for his audacious 2019 project, titled Project Possible, where he summited all 14 8,000-metre peaks in a record six months and six days. The previous record had been nearly eight years.

citation.title: Nirmal Purja obituary

text:
Nirmal Purja obituary

The feat was immortalised in the hit Netflix documentary 14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible (2021) and his 2020 autobiography, Beyond Possible. The attention around his climbs brought his flamboyant, highly commercialised style of high-altitude mountaineering to a mainstream audience and propelled him into a rarefied circle of celebrity climbers that included Reinhold Messner, Sir Chris Bonington and Sir Edmund Hillary. Nirmal – also known as Nimsdai or Nims – was born in the remote village of Dana in Nepal’s Myagdi district. His father, Nanda Bahadur Purja, served as a Gurkha soldier in the Indian army, while his mother, Purna Kumari, cared for the household and the family farm. When Nims was four years old, his family moved to the Chitwan district in Nepal’s verdant southern plains, far from the mountains where he would eventually make his name. Nims was the youngest of four sons, followed by a younger sister. For many poor families in rural Nepal, service in the Gurkha regiments of foreign militaries offered a rare lifeline out of poverty.

citation.title: Nirmal Purja obituary

text:
Nirmal Purja obituary

Following in the footsteps of his three older brothers, Nims joined the 1st Battalion of the Royal Gurkha Rifles in 2003 after passing a gruelling exam that included running with heavy sandbags in a bamboo basket suspended from his forehead by a tumpline. Purja excelled at military service and was deployed in Afghanistan. After six years with the Royal Gurkha Rifles, he was accepted into the Royal Navy’s elite Special Boat Service (SBS) in 2009. The following year, he was wounded in action in an undisclosed location when a sniper’s bullet struck the butt of his rifle, sending shrapnel into his face and neck. During his service in the British military, Purja obtained British citizenship. He made his first forays into mountaineering while he was active with the SBS, climbing Ama Dablam (6,812 m) and Lobuche East (6,119 m) in Nepal. In 2014, he summited Dhaulagiri, his first 8,000-metre peak, in just 15 days. The experience convinced him that he possessed an unusual strength and resilience at altitude. After his celebrated Everest ascents, Purja decided to leave the SBS and pursue his 14 peaks project full time.

citation.title: Nirmal Purja obituary

text:
Nirmal Purja obituary

In his autobiography, he described the decision as “the latest in a long line of baffling career developments”. By the time Purja completed his 14 peaks record, he had progressed from paying client to company owner and guide. His expedition company, Elite Exped, quickly became a prominent player in the high-stakes Himalayan guiding industry. Purja leveraged his experience and growing fame to bring a new generation of aspiring mountaineers, many with little previous experience, to summits that would have been unthinkable for them only a few years earlier. He also launched a mountaineering gear brand, Nimsdai Store, and a skydiving outfit, Skydive Nimsdai. He invested in a helicopter charter company in Nepal, which provides basecamp services and high-altitude rescues using a jet-black Eurocopter B3e emblazoned with his personal logo in bold white lettering across the side. Purja also established the Nimsdai Foundation, with the mission of “giving back to the mountain communities of his homeland”. In May, Nims inaugurated a new porter shelter built by the foundation in the small trekking village of Lobuche, about five miles south of Everest base camp.

citation.title: Nirmal Purja obituary

text:
Nirmal Purja obituary

The project was intended to provide safe, comfortable lodging for the mountain workers who ferry supplies throughout the Everest region. In May 2024, the New York Times published an article in which two female climbers accused Purja of sexual assault. Through his lawyer, Purja “unequivocally denie[d] the allegations of wrongdoing,” calling the allegations “false and defamatory”. Others in the mountaineering industry alleged that Purja’s aggressive, self-promotional approach to climbing placed himself and his clients at undue risk, and that it ran counter to the more measured ethos traditionally associated with high-altitude mountaineering. Bonington, leader of the successful 1975 British first ascent of Everest’s south-west face, was quoted in the Times in 2019 as saying: “What he has done is quite extraordinary, but it isn’t mountaineering.” When describing his motivations for Project Possible, Purja wrote in his autobiography: “I loved the thought of ripping up the rule book.

text:
Nirmal Purja obituary

If I could show kids and adults alike what was humanly achievable, then my far-fetched ambitions might inspire others to think big and push themselves in ways that they previously considered unimaginable. I also liked that it would give the world a crazy story to remember.” The avalanche on Broad Peak that claimed Purja’s life also took the lives of nine other climbers and guides, several of whom were pursuing their own personal 14 peaks records. Purja himself was attempting his “hat-trick” project: becoming the first person in history to climb all 14 of the world’s 8,000-metre peaks three times, including twice without supplemental oxygen. Had he reached the summit of Broad Peak, only one mountain would have remained between him and a record that experts in the industry described as “nearly impossible” to surpass. Purja is survived by his wife, Suchi, whom he married in 2006, and their daughter, Himani. • Nirmal Purja, mountaineer, born 24 July 1983; died 30 July 2026

Russia frees ex-US marine four years after sentence disputed by his family

Russia has freed a former US marine who had been in jail since 2022, after Vladimir Putin granted the ailing American a pardon on humanitarian grounds. Robert Gilman, 32, an English teacher who briefly served in the US Marines, was travelling by train when he was arrested in the southern Russian city of Voronezh in January 2022 for allegedly kicking a police officer while drunk, according to Russian state media. He was later sentenced to four and a half years in prison, though his family has consistently denied the allegations against him. His father, Vladimir Gilman, who emigrated to Massachusetts from Russia, wrote in an October 2024 Boston Globe op-ed that his son had fallen ill when the incident occurred and had accidentally kicked the police officer. Concerns over Gilman’s health had grown sharply in recent weeks, and the White House and the state department had urged Moscow to release him so he could receive medical treatment in the US.

Jean hoped bird flu wouldn’t come to Australia. Then it arrived – and she saw a tern ‘trembling and swaying’

Bird enthusiast Jean Turner hoped avian flu would never arrive at her doorstep. At her home on Kangaroo Island in South Australia, bossy fairy wrens chirp at her from the deck, grey currawongs clumsily fall into her bird bath, and fluffy, hooded plover chicks emerge from speckled eggs in front of her binoculars. But online, images of Argentinian coastlines strewn with dead seal pups and researchers lining up rows of dead seabirds on Antarctic islands offered a warning of what could come. Related: ‘We expected it, but now it’s here’: on the frontline of Australia’s bird flu outbreak, people are distressed So when SA confirmed its first case of the deadly H5 bird flu strain, just over 200km away at Robe on the Limestone Coast, Turner was prepared to become a different kind of birder. “We had this fairytale belief that maybe we wouldn’t get it here,” she says.

text:

“But it’s here and now things are going to get harder and more confronting.” She is one of more than 120 volunteers who have signed up for the Bird Observers Network, which allows birders to contribute to the state’s bird flu response. default The partnership between the SA government, Conservation Council SA, Birds SA and Birdlife Australia trains volunteers to identify and report sick birds that may be showing signs associated with H5 bird flu. Since the network’s first session, Turner has already reported a sick greater crested tern, which was resting at the edge of a flock. While the other birds shuffled or flew around as she tried to get a better look, the sick animal did not respond. “It was standing on the jetty, trembling and swaying a bit,” Turner says. “It didn’t look well, it just looked really miserable.” Compared with the non-bird-obsessed general public, birders can offer greater detail when reporting potentially infected birds, says Steven Langley, the president of Birds SA.

Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email They can often recognise species more accurately, use their binoculars to observe possible abnormalities within a flock, and notice when birds they might see on their routine walks go missing. “We all just want to be able to do whatever we can to make a difference,” Langley says. “When you see these distressing images from overseas, you’re implanting them into your mind and on to the places and the birds that you have got a great deal of affection for.” Volunteers generally don’t receive further correspondence after they have made a submission but multiple crested terns found on Kangaroo Island have been tested and returned confirmed positive results for H5 bird flu since Turner’s report. The grim task of reporting dead wildlife is a familiar one to many SA birders after the toxic algal bloom which engulfed 20,000 sq km of coast, killing millions of sea creatures and becoming one of the worst marine mass mortalities in the world.

The first mass mortality event of the outbreak was detected last week among greater created terns at Baudin Rocks, just across the beach from Robe, where more than 80 dead and sick birds were spotted. Related: Penguins and dolphins among nearly 400 Australian species under threat from bird flu as ‘true extent of disaster’ revealed Langley says the impending disaster makes it even more important to take other actions to protect birds, including mitigating predator risks, reducing disturbance and providing and protecting more habitat. “When you lose a huge proportion of your breeding birds to bird flu, every single bird that survives is really, really valuable,” he says. “We need to be reducing disturbance to these birds.” For now, the SA government says it is continuing engagement with the community, the agricultural industry and the wildlife sector to bolster surveillance.

Syrian court sentences Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia for war crimes

A Syrian court has sentenced the country’s former president Bashar al-Assad and his brother Maher to death in absentia for crimes against humanity and war crimes during the 14-year civil war, in which about half a million people died. The two men fled to Moscow after being ousted by a lightning rebel offensive in December 2024 which toppled the dictatorial regime in just 11 days. The former president and his brother, who commanded the feared fourth division and was considered the regime’s top security official, oversaw a brutal crackdown in which government forces killed, arrested and tortured indiscriminately to crush protests that started in 2011. The court said Bashar al-Assad had been sentenced to death for crimes of “premeditated and intentional murder of more than one person and of children” as well as “torture, arbitrary arrest and crimes against humanity”. It said it would pursue international legal avenues to try to prosecute the two men, but Russian officials have previously declined requests to extradite its former Syrian allies.

citation.title: Syrian court sentences Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia for war crimes

text:
Syrian court sentences Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia for war crimes

The court also sentenced Atef Najib, Assad’s cousin and the former head of political security in Daraa, to death. Najib was responsible for the torture of a group of 15 young boys who had graffitied anti-Assad slogans on a wall in 2011 – an event that kicked off mass protests in the southern Syrian province, which then spread to the rest of the country. Najib’s trial was highly publicised, with pictures of him listening to proceedings while dressed in a prison uniform and held in a cage in court. The Syrian government has presented his trial as a landmark case in its pursuit of transitional justice, something experts say is key to healing divisions in the country. Syria has experienced explosions of violence in the post-Assad era. About 1,500 mostly Alawite civilians were killed in a wave of retaliatory killings in March 2025 after militants loyal to al-Assad attacked security forces. Al-Assad belonged to the Islamic Alawite sect – a minority group in Syria – and enjoyed strong support in the group’s coastal heartland during his rule.

citation.title: Syrian court sentences Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia for war crimes

text:
Syrian court sentences Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia for war crimes

In July 2025, more than 1,700 people were killed in massacres in the Druze-majority province of Suweida when local fighting evolved into sectarian killings. Low-level violence has continued in northern Syria until the present day, particularly targeting Alawite civilians. Syrian authorities have taken steps towards transitional justice, establishing committees and arresting Assad-era officials, in an effort to end intercommunal violence. Al-Assad became president in 2000 at the age of 34, inheriting power from his father, Hafez. He had trained as an ophthalmologist in London and was not initially supposed to be president, but became the heir after his brother, Basil, died in a car accident. Though styled as a young reformer who was supposed to allow some liberalisation in Syrian politics and its economy, his legacy was largely defined by his brutal response to the country’s revolution. Under his rule, Syria’s fearsome security apparatus was given a free hand to arrest, torture and kill civilians on an industrial scale.

At a temple in Thailand, parents mourn a 12-year-old mass shooting victim, and a father pleads for forgiveness

When the mother and father of the youngest victim of last week’s school mass shooting arrived at the temple north of Bangkok, teary-eyed parents came up to quietly offer condolences before the prayers began in front of the 12-year-old girl’s casket. Then, in a moment, the tone changed. A man arrived and dropped to his knees in supplication, sobbing and bowing his head in the traditional “wai” gesture before the couple who had lost their daughter, Naphat Chaimar. It was Nithi Yimruang, the father of the 14-year-old boy who had carried out the shooting, pleading for their forgiveness. Naphat’s father, Pongthon Chaimar, helped raise the man up by his arms, but his head remained hung in shame, even as Pongthon accepted the apology. The girl’s parents told Nithi they understood he too was going through a difficult time. His son, Patchat Yimruang, had shot his grandfather and grandmother dead before killing six people and injuring more than 30 at the prestigious Debsirin Nonthaburi school north-west of Bangkok. The teenager had then turned the gun on himself.

I’ve lost my child, as well as my parents. And seeing the little girl’s father being so kind and understanding toward me makes me feel even more guilty.” Related: Thailand school shooting toll rises to nine after 12-year-old dies, police say He still does not understand why his son did what he did, but he is left to reckon with the violence his own flesh and blood had committed. He leaves the temple of Wat Lat Pla Duk in Nonthaburi province before Monday’s funeral service begins. Grief, and a royal wreath The teenage boy had used his grandfather’s gun to carry out the attack. He had lived with his grandparents ever since his parents separated when he was two years old. But his father visited him every weekend, and took him to extra tutoring classes. “For me, he was number one. But he was a quiet, reserved child. He didn’t talk much and usually kept things to himself.

Toward the end, though, he became even quieter than before. “I used to ask him quite often how things were at school, and he would just say, ‘so-so’. I’d ask him how his classes were going, and he’d just say ‘so-so’. “But now, there’s no way for me to find out or ask him any more.” The shooting has resonated across the country, with the king and prime minister leading an outpouring of grief. The palace announced on Sunday the king had granted royal patronage for the victims, their family and relatives. The move means all the injured would be treated as patients under royal care, and royal sponsorship would be awarded for the funeral rites and cremations of those killed.

text:
Tuesday briefing: To drill or not to drill – Burnham’s first big climate test

Good morning. What a difference a new job can make. “To have a shot at staying within 1.5C global warming, we can’t have any new oil or gasfields … It’s irresponsible and shortsighted to be funding new #fossilfuels when we need to be getting to #NetZero.” This was the 2022 message from Miatta Fahnbulleh, now the secretary of state for energy security and net zero. It’s a testament to her remarkable rise that Fahnbulleh wasn’t even an MP when she posted it four years ago. Today, she is in the cabinet, facing (or is the face of, at least) one of the most challenging, and potentially controversial questions looming for the new government: to drill or not to drill, baby? Two sites are the focus of fierce debate. Yesterday, a public consultation on whether to greenlight extraction at one of them – Jackdaw – closed. Next Monday, it’ll be the same for the other, Rosebank. Andy Burnham has been silent about the climate crisis since taking office. As we enter yet another heatwave, what his government does next will be a defining signal of intent on the issue.

citation.title: Tuesday briefing: To drill or not to drill – Burnham’s first big climate test

But what would extraction actually mean, and how many options are open to Fahnbulleh? That’s the subject of today’s First Edition, after a roundup of this morning’s headlines. Five big stories Colombia | More than 100 people have died after a powerful earthquake struck western Colombia, collapsing and severely damaging scores of buildings in major cities including Cali and Pereira. UK weather | Almost three-quarters of England is now in drought, with four more regions officially declared, and as much of Europe braces for its fifth climate crisis-driven heatwave this summer. Crime | Police are investigating whether Joshua Kerry, the man charged with the murder of the former Reform UK and Conservative politician Ann Widdecombe, had any role in an attempted burglary last year at the then London home of Nigel Farage. China | More than a million people were moved to safety across eastern China by Sunday evening as powerful Typhoon Dolphin made landfall amid fears torrential rain would cause flooding and landslides.

Ukraine | Russia has banned voting against the war in September’s elections, after the supreme court upheld a suit brought by a small pro-Kremlin nationalist party, and stripped voters of their last option on the ballot: Yabloko, the country’s only remaining anti-war party. In depth: Two fields, one very big decision While often lumped together, Rosebank and Jackdaw are two separate sites, hundreds of miles apart. Rosebank is a proposed new oilfield 80 miles off the Shetland coast, containing 300 to 500m barrels of oil. It’s the UK’s last major undeveloped oil site. There is also gas at Rosebank, equating to roughly 1% of current demand. Jackdaw is a gasfield 150 miles east of Aberdeen. If operational, it could probably produce approximately 40,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day (bpd), which at peak is equivalent to 6% of the UK’s North Sea gas supply. Jackdaw could displace 2% of the UK’s imports of gas over its nine- to 12-year lifetime. Under UK law, all oil and gas under the ground or seabed is owned by the state. It’s our collective asset.

The government then dishes out licences for exploration and extraction of these fossil fuels to business. Often, these have complicated structures. Shell holds the licence to extract at Jackdaw. Rosebank is majority owned by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Equinor (mostly owned by the Norwegian state). A minority stake of Rosebank is owned by UK-based Ithaca Energy, a subsidiary of the Israeli energy conglomerate Delek Group. Delek operates in Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories. *** The case for drilling – and the holes in it Unsurprisingly, the PR from fossil fuel companies on Rosebank and Jackdaw is full of optimism. It will bring down bills! Energy security! Jobs! These are all claims that have been repeatedly debunked. The UK Energy Research Centre is scathing in its assessment: “Assertions that drilling the North Sea will provide energy resilience and affordability in the face of current fuel price shocks are a delusion.” Jackdaw would create only 27 direct full-time jobs, according to its owner.

citation.title: Tuesday briefing: To drill or not to drill – Burnham’s first big climate test

text:
Tuesday briefing: To drill or not to drill – Burnham’s first big climate test

Across both sites, there would be 880 jobs created during production, and 2,700 temporary construction roles. That’s no fix for structural decline. At least 70,000 jobs in the industry were lost in the decade to 2024, despite the Tories granting hundreds of licences. BP is now shutting down its North Sea operations. As our environment editor, Fiona Harvey tells me: “Whatever government does, jobs will decline. It’s unavoidable.” Because, the UK’s gas and oil is running out. Even if extraction is minimised, supplies are depleting: 90% has already been drained dry. Experts point to this as proof that new drilling won’t bolster long-term energy security. *** Who benefits from oil and gas? Drill or not, our household energy prices will unlikely be affected. Anything extracted wouldn’t be funnelled to UK residents at a knock-down rate: oil and gas are sold by private companies on international markets, which set the price. The scale of output from UK production is negligible in this global context.

citation.title: Tuesday briefing: To drill or not to drill – Burnham’s first big climate test

As we’ve seen, it takes one unreliable actor in charge of the world’s largest military to send global prices spiralling. Of course, there’s money to be made from tax – though these companies aren’t famed for coughing up when HMRC comes knocking. In 2024, Shell reported a negative UK tax figure of £12.5m while posting global post-tax profits of £18bn. In the same year, Equinor’s record was no better. Even if North Sea tax revenues were collected and somehow funnelled directly into energy bill subsidies, the impact would be limited. For context, after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Conservatives spent up to £80bn across two years shielding households and businesses from energy price hikes. Even by the oil and gas industry’s own estimates, the Rosebank and Jackdaw tax take would pale in comparison. And given the scale of tax subsidies available, campaigners suggest Rosebank could actually cost taxpayers money. That means underwriting the very businesses who help to cause the climate crisis we’re experiencing.

This, of course, would be exacerbated by any fossil fuels extracted by Jackdaw and Rosebank. Burning just Rosebank’s oil and gas would produce about 250m tonnes of CO2 over its lifetime. As Areeba Hamid, co-executive director of Greenpeace UK, put it to me: “Sections of the media just keep repeating myths and lies. We are expecting a fifth summer heatwave, wild fires are burning the country, oil and gas companies are posting billions in profits, while the rightwing press and fossil fuel companies are pushing for Rosebank and Jackdaw approval. It’s pure cognitive dissonance.” *** Over to Burnham Under the Conservatives, Rosebank and Jackdaw were approved, but a court ruled these permits unlawful after a legal challenge from Greenpeace and Uplift. New approval needed to be sought – the results of which are impending. Labour’s 2024 manifesto ruled out new licences for North Sea exploration, while stating existing ones would not be revoked. Insiders say a compromise might be struck, with only Jackdaw OK-ed.

Gas is needed for home heating and electricity generation, though in what should be diminishing quantities, and its extraction is less carbon intensive than oil. “Allowing it to go ahead is far less harmful than Rosebank,” Fiona tells me. And Jackdaw is a tieback, so can be connected to existing infrastructure. “It could therefore come online quicker.” Fahnbulleh is on holiday for the next couple of weeks. In the absence of answers, the briefing wars are in full swing. Reports that oil and gas execs are “near certain” that Rosebank and Jackdaw will get the go-ahead should be treated with caution, given their incentive to will this into fruition. Remember how Shabana Mahmood was definitely going to be Burnham’s chancellor? For all his flip-floppery, Starmer was generally steadfast in his climate commitments while PM, even if rightwing backlash tempered his ambitions. Burnham had a strong environmental track record as Manchester mayor. But he’s an unknown entity in Downing Street. Until last month, Ed Miliband held the energy brief, driving the last government’s decarbonisation agenda.

An experienced Westminster operator with decades of experience and press attacks, Miliband was resolute enough to stick with climate plans, however often he was heralded the “MOST DANGEROUS MAN IN BRITAIN”. Fahnbulleh looks like continuity. She has Miliband’s backing and before entering parliament, she held top jobs at left-leaning thinktanks, including as CEO of the New Economics Foundation (NEF), which expressed opposition to further fossil fuel extraction. But she’s a parliamentary newbie. How she’ll respond to power and significant external pressure remains uncertain. In an interview last weekend, she struck a vague but cautious note: “We’ve always been clear that oil and gas are part of the mix … We are doing the hard trade-offs to make sure that we are doing this transition in a way that still delivers affordability.” “It’s going to be tough,” Hamid says, “but Miatta has to stick to her position. Typhoon Dolphin hits Beijing as city braces for one-third of annual rainfall over 24 hours

Typhoon Dolphin hit China’s capital on Tuesday as the storm caused flooding in parts of Beijing’s Shunyi district. Rains are forecast to intensify overnight. Although the storm has been downgraded to a tropical depression, several districts in Beijing activated the highest level of emergency flood responses as the city braced for one-third of its annual rainfall, which is expected over the next 24 hours. Breakfast, lunch and natmad in Denmark – Scandinavian mealtimes explained

Confusion over the names of mealtimes (Letters, 2 August) also reigns in Scandinavia. Breakfast in Norway/Sweden is frokost/frukost, but morgenmad (morning food) in Denmark. Lunch in Norway/Sweden is lunsj/lunch, but frokost in Denmark. At least they can all agree on the main meal of the day, which is middag (midday/noon) but served in the early evening. If attending a wedding party or function in Denmark, don’t be surprised to be served natmad (night food) around midnight. It is used as a friendly indication that the event has come to an end, hence its colloquial name of skrub af mad (fuck-off food). Gary Calder Chandler’s Ford, Hampshire • On the Titanic, dinner for first- and second-class passengers was the meal served in the evening. For third-class passengers the meal called dinner was served in the middle of the day; later in the day they had tea and supper. Interestingly, there was no iceberg lettuce on the menus. Canadian airline WestJet agrees to settle flight attendants’ sexual harassment class action

The Canadian airline WestJet has agreed to pay C$4.5m (£2.4m) to settle a decade-long sexual harassment class action lawsuit levelled by its female flight attendants, who alleged the company failed to maintain a safe workplace. The suit followed allegations by Mandalena Lewis, a former flight attendant, that a pilot had sexually assaulted her and a colleague, but that WestJet kept the pilot flying, thereby putting other employees at risk. A British Columbia judge on Monday approved the terms of the settlement, which were finalised on 22 June after months of negotiation. The payment will be distributed among the 3,452 flight attendants in the class action after expenses are removed, including legal fees. WestJet agreed to hire a third-party to conduct a workplace inquiry that will examine the prevalence of harassment, the extent of underreporting and how reporting systems can be made more effective. The suit had called on WestJet to implement mandatory anti-harassment training for pilots, along with an admission of wrongdoing and an admission of a breach of employee contract.

Europe is the world’s fastest warming continent. What is to blame?

The whole world is getting hotter as carbon pollution from fossil fuel burning traps ever more heat, but Europe is heating up twice as fast as other continents. The consequences are increasingly deadly, with tens of thousands of heatwave deaths so far this summer. Why is Europe most affected by global heating? Land requires less heat than the vast and deep oceans to warm up, so all continents are warming more quickly than the seas. But Europe is particularly vulnerable for four reasons: changed weather patterns, its closeness to the Arctic, less snow and less air pollution. Temperatures in Europe have risen by 0.56C a decade since the mid-1990s, compared with 0.42C in North America, 0.36C in Africa and 0.27C in South America. How have Europe’s weather patterns changed? Shifts in how the atmosphere circulates over Europe have led to more frequent and more intense summer heatwaves.

Dr Samantha Burgess, from the EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service, said: “We see statistically significant changes in surface pressure patterns and other measures of circulation when we look at trends over the last 40 or more years, and on this timescale they are more likely associated with climate change than natural variability.” The association may be the result of a changing jet stream, a fast high-level wind that has a powerful influence on Europe’s weather and is itself affected by rising temperatures. Why is the Arctic important? The Arctic is the fastest warming region on the planet, despite having no land. This is because the white polar ice cap, which normally reflects the vast majority of sunlight back into space, is melting away fast.

Like the Arctic sea ice, this snow reflected sunlight and kept the continent cooler. But the climate crisis is shrinking snow-covered areas. In March 2025, Europe’s blanket of snow was about 1.3m square km below the 1991-2020 average, a 31% drop. Air pollution kills millions of people globally every year and so Europe’s record of cutting toxic air levels in recent decades is unequivocally a good thing. The German government has approved a draft law aimed at lifting many of the restraints on its spy agencies imposed during the postwar period as the country reels from two attacks in a month that have exposed serious security gaps. The controversial changes, which must still pass parliament, largely comply with a wishlist pulled together by the foreign and domestic intelligence services, which have long complained Germany lags behind its allies and enemies. “We are turning our intelligence services into genuine secret services,” the interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, told Bild newspaper, which called it a security “revolution” and “historic”. Israeli militants have besieged two Palestinian families in their homes since the weekend, aiming to take over their properties in the West Bank village of Qusra through a campaign of terror. A group of settlers and soldiers set up a tent outside the home of Yousef Hassan’s family on Sunday afternoon, trapping him inside with his wife and two young daughters. His mother, brother and sister, and three neighbours have also been blockaded inside, and their power and water have been cut off. The number of children involved in crashes on e-scooters has soared in recent years, with some as young as nine involved in collisions, research has found. Researchers carried out a review of injuries among the under-16s at three specialist paediatric trauma centres – Alder Hey in Liverpool, and Sheffield and Royal Manchester children’s hospitals – between January 2019 and December 2024. They found the average age of those involved in e-scooter collisions was 12, and almost 65% of those injured were male. The most common injuries were to the limbs, followed by head and facial injuries. Fewer than 2% of patients had been wearing a helmet. Half of the children injured were between 10 and 13 years old, with the youngest only nine. The three hospitals had recorded a total of 477 e-scooter injuries, with a significant increase in numbers since 2019. More than 80% of the injuries were sustained on private e-scooters, which can only be ridden legally on private land. The majority of the accidents had happened on public land, roads and parks.

New Zealand’s prime minister Christopher Luxon has survived a second leadership showdown in four months, just 87 days out from the country’s general election. In Venice, it’s not politics as usual as film-makers aim to recapture our attention

Europe is in an economic crisis that, unlike the eurozone downturn at the beginning of the millennium, cannot be measured in ratings downgrades and borrowing costs. For metrics, try engagement depth and consumer trust instead. The unedifying spectacle of the European Union’s falling out over the Ceuta crisis looks like the latest symptom of Europe’s shrinking attention economy. When more than 70,000 people crossed over from Morocco to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta at the start of the month, Rome hastily reintroduced air and sea border checks with Spain for one month; Madrid retaliated with spot-checks on travellers to Italy. Politicians were falling over themselves to match the wildfire speed of social media, for this was a geopolitical flashpoint that appears not just to have been engineered but also politically processed via short video clips online. The crossings were reportedly triggered by viral videos suggesting that Spain’s border with Morocco was opening, while their framing as an “assault” or “invasion” was amplified by accounts with links to the Russian military, as Aisha Down reported.

Wednesday briefing: Why the prison crisis is about much more than early release

Good morning. On his family holiday last week, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, was reported to be taking daily calls from Ministry of Justice officials about his government’s early release scheme. A furious public outcry has gathered pace since it emerged that the plan – brought in by his predecessor, Keir Starmer, to alleviate overcrowding in prisons across England and Wales – might include two of the killers of PC Andrew Harper and other serious sexual offenders, including grooming gang perpetrators. After several weeks of “system says no” briefings, which Harper’s mother Debbie Adlam has described as “a rollercoaster … really draining”, yesterday Burnham endeavoured to put a pin in it until September. Announcing that he had tasked the justice secretary, Alex Norris, with fast-tracking measures to free up prison space, the prime minister insisted he was “increasingly confident” that the early release scheme can be adapted to exclude the constable’s killers. He had previously intervened to exempt grooming gang members, rapists and those convicted of “serious” child sexual offences.

Zhu Rongji obituary

Zhu Rongji, who has died aged 97, was the fifth premier of the People’s Republic of China and one of its most effective administrators and economic reformers following its foundation in 1949. In 1991, Zhu was summoned to Beijing, in the footsteps of the then president and party secretary Jiang Zemin, and in the aftermath of the 1989 uprisings in Beijing and the collapse of the Soviet Union. As vice premier in the state council, and governor of the People’s Bank of China (1993-95), Zhu was put in charge of China’s economy at a time of immense turbulence, with many fearing that the country would once more turn inward as it had under Mao Zedong. Zhu implemented contentious and tough reforms to straighten out the highly inefficient state-owned sector, and to modernise China’s infrastructure. By the end of the decade, Zhu could rightly declare that the country had become “the factory of the world”, a status that in many ways it maintains. A straight-talking and forceful figure, he was famously harsh on corruption, once sacking a governor of Heilongjiang province on the spot for failing to meet growth targets.

citation.title: Zhu Rongji obituary

text:
Zhu Rongji obituary

This laid the foundation for his popularity within China generally, and the high regard with which he was held abroad. He seemed to come close to the ideal image of a Chinese leader possessed of moral dignity. Alone among high-level politicians of his period, he attempted to reach out to the population at large, and speak to them as an equal. Nor was he willing to stand on ceremony. As he stated in 1998: “I have prepared 100 coffins here – 99 for corrupt officials and one for myself,” according to the party newspaper People’s Daily. This gained him the nickname of “the Boss”. His most significant achievement as premier was to secure China’s entry to the World Trade Organization (WTO). What had begun in 1986 as negotiations over entry into the General Agreement on Tariffs and Taxes (Gatt), had spanned out over a decade, involving an epic series of agreements with both the EU, the US and dozens of other countries. In 1999, the deal with the US, which was the most contentious and important, was almost completed.

Zhu was on a visit to Washington, expecting to sign this off, but it was pulled by President Bill Clinton at the time because of domestic problems following the Monica Lewinsky scandal. Aiming some of his famous sharpness and temper at the Americans, Zhu reportedly told his officials that he was in awe of Washington’s incompetence and lack of foresight. The final deal was signed in 2001. It can be seen as a watershed moment in China’s attempts to modernise, and to internationalise its economy, with strong growth and a doubling of the Chinese economy over the next five years. Zhu retired after one term in power, in 2003, and was replaced by his protege, Wen Jiabao. For all the successes of his time in power, these did not come as easy gifts. In the 1990s, the state sector, which comprised most of the key enterprises, was riddled with debt, inefficiency and poor management. To address this, the whole social welfare and public sector framework had to be changed. Up to 60 million workers were laid off, some of them never employed again. Unrest was a striking feature of this period, with one commentator calling it a period of “ferment”.

Even WTO entry offered no panacea, with the agricultural and manufacturing sector going through painful adjustments. Zhu was an obstinate and hard-eyed man: he had to be, to deal with the issues he faced. Much of this toughness came from his early years. Born in Changsha, the capital of the central Hunan province – Mao’s home province, too – Zu was orphaned when young and brought up by two of his father’s brothers. He enjoyed a typically technocratic education, joined the Communist party in 1949, and graduated in electrical engineering from the elite Qinghua University in Beijing in 1951. His career through the 50s and into the 70s was rocky. He worked largely in the state development and planning commission (in charge of national implementation of the various five year plans), as an engineer, dealing with the typical duties of resource allocation in a command economy. But his criticism of what he saw as the inefficiency of Maoist policies during the infamous Hundred Flowers campaign of 1956-57, where intellectuals and officials were invited to offer their opinions on the party, led to his being branded a “rightist” and sent to the countryside to be a teacher.

His rehabilitation back into the central government in 1962 was short lived. Once branded with the stigma of being politically unreliable in Maoist China, suspects were never fully rehabilitated. In 1969, in the depths of the Cultural Revolution, which Mao started to wage war against what he called “bureaucratism and capitalist tendencies” in the CCP, Zhu was once more sent to one of what were euphemistically called “7 May schools” named after the central decree that had set thousands of them up across the country. In effect, they were mini-concentration camps. There he languished until 1975, when he was sent to Beijing for a third time to work at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, as an economist. A spell from 1979 to 1982 in the state economic commission, at the start of what has come to be known as the reform and opening up period, led to him being appointed as a vice minister. This marked his full transition from engineering to economics. It was as an economist that he was to have the greatest impact on China in the years ahead.

Zhu’s first step towards national and international prominence came in 1987, when he replaced Jiang Zemin as mayor of Shanghai. Shanghai was then at the dawn of its extraordinary growth, starting to build a foundation as the commercial centre of China, a position it had ironically enjoyed before the revolution, in the 20s and 30s. He was instrumental in making the city one of the special economic zones, in 1990, joining places such as Shenzhen, adjoining Hong Kong, and Xiamen, on the coast facing Taiwan. He also steered the city successfully through the trauma following the 4 June massacres in Tiananmen Square, Beijing, in 1989. Shanghai was largely to avoid the turbulence and recriminations that this event led to elsewhere. Zhu was frequently called the “Gorbachev of China”, though it was an epithet he disliked. Despite his suffering in the past, he remained resolutely committed to the Communist party and its continuation in power, and his economic reforms were targeted at ensuring that this happened.

He did not propose, or support, political reforms, and regarded Mikhail Gorbachev with something approaching contempt, for the way in which his policies had effectively led to the fall of the Soviet Communist party, and the break up of the USSR. Zhu’s fundamental objective, which he achieved, was to ensure that the PRC remained stable, and that it continued to deliver economic growth. He spent his retirement largely uninvolved in politics, appearing only from time to time at high-level party congresses, the last of which was in 2017. The last image of him appeared while he was in hospital in 2020. There is no record of what he made of the leadership of Xi Jinping, or of whether he shared the view that, after Mao and Deng Xiaoping, he was the person who had contributed most to China’s current economic success. He is survived by his wife, Lao An, a retired business executive, and a son and a daughter. • Zhu Rongji, politician and economist, born 23 October 1928; died 12 August 2026

At least 44 dead after overcrowded ferry capsizes on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe

At least 44 people have died after an overcrowded ferry capsized on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe, police said. The boat had a capacity of 90 people, but was carrying 114 adult passengers, five crew members and an unknown number of children, Zimbabwe’s civil protection unit (CPU) said earlier on Wednesday, citing ticket sales. A crew member told the national broadcaster ZBC that there were 153 people onboard when the ferry overturned on Tuesday after it hit large waves. A passenger told ZBC that the boat began taking on water about 30 minutes after it left the lakeshore town of Kariba, heading for islands and fishing camps. A specialised underwater team was flown to the area, the CPU said, as search and rescue continued on Wednesday. At the time, the CPU said the death toll was 15, with 27 known to be missing. Zimbabwe’s police updated the death toll on Wednesday afternoon in posts on X twice in the space of 32 minutes. In the first post, it said the death toll was 38, adding: “The bodies have been retrieved from the lake.” Then it said that 44 people were now known to have died.

He said: “A few moments later I get over 200 calls about [the ferry] sinking. A sad day indeed.” Lake Kariba is the world’s largest human-made lake by volume, stretching about 150 miles along Zimbabwe’s northern border with Zambia. It was created in the 1950s during British colonial rule, when the Zambezi River was dammed, displacing about 57,000 people. The Kariba dam supplies at least a third of both countries’ electricity. Potatoes ‘boil’ in the ground as record heatwave sweeps across swathes of Asia

In a potato field in Yanggu county, 80 miles (130km) north-east of Seoul, Lee Sang-hyuk dug into the soil and found nothing worth saving. A week earlier the crop, located in Gangwon province, had looked fine. Now the potatoes came up soft and collapsing, “like boiled potatoes”, spoiled by heat that had turned the ground into something closer to an oven. “It’s not just one or two fields like this. How can I even put it into words? It’s so upsetting,” he told local broadcaster SBS. His ruined harvest is one thread in a punishing summer across east Asia, as record heat swept through South Korea, Japan and Hong Kong in recent weeks. On 2 August, the south-eastern city of Yangsan recorded a temperature of 42.5C, the highest registered in South Korea since modern weather observations began in 1904. The heat has since been blamed for at least 31 deaths nationwide, according to the country’s disease control agency, while more than 900,000 livestock and 1.4 million farmed fish have died. Authorities issued a heat warning, urging people to “immediately stop all outdoor activities”.

DRC’s fast-growing Ebola outbreak spreads to sixth province

The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has spread to a sixth province, officials have said, a day after the head of the World Health Organization said the outbreak was on track to surpass the deadliest in history, which killed at least 11,000 people more than a decade ago. The current outbreak has killed more than 2,100 people out of more than 4,500 cases, according to the latest government figures released on Tuesday. At the same point in the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, the previous most deadly outbreak, 755 cases had been recorded, according to WHO data. Jean Kaseya, the director general of Africa CDC, said on Thursday that a death had been recorded in the previously unaffected Bas-Uele province. The man had travelled from Isiro, in Haut-Uele province, to Buta, the capital of Bas-Uele, where he died, Kaseya said. There are no approved vaccines or treatments for the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus that is responsible for the current outbreak. The death toll has been reached almost three times faster than in the 2014-16 outbreak.

An Italian businessman has admitted to masterminding a bomb attack at the home of Sigfrido Ranucci, a prominent investigative journalist, claiming it was intended to boost his security protection. Four other people allegedly commissioned by Lavitola were arrested in late June on suspicion of carrying out the attack. Cola said Lavitola had orchestrated the attack in order to boost Ranucci’s security detail amid threats to his life from the mafia. “He did it for Ranucci’s good, because he was a target of attacks,” he said.

Key Japan war shrine bans military cosplay ahead of second world war anniversary

Tokyo’s controversial Yasukuni shrine is banning military cosplay on its grounds, after the site become a focal point for displays by ultra-nationalist groups, often dressed in replica army uniforms or military-style dress. The clothing ban comes in the lead-up to the anniversary this weekend of the defeat of Japan in the second world war, also known as VJ Day, although the shrine has said the ban applies year round. The shrine honours 2.5 million Japanese soldiers and civilians who died in wars in the 19th and 20th centuries, but it has become a symbol of Japan’s militarism and wartime brutality, particularly in China and South Korea. Among those honoured are 14 men convicted by the Allies as class-A war criminals after the second world war.

Yasukuni initially issued the announcement forbidding the wearing of military attire last week, provoking a backlash from some who said it would stop serving members of Japan’s Self-Defense Forces from worshipping at the shrine. In response, Yasukuni issued an additional statement on Wednesday clarifying that serving personnel, and members of military forces from overseas, were exempt from the new rules. Past visits to the shrine by Japanese leaders and lawmakers have provoked angry responses from Beijing and Seoul. It was reported in domestic media on Thursday that prime minister Sanae Takaichi is not planning to visit the shrine on the anniversary of Japan’s defeat in the second world war this Saturday.

text:
‘Absolutely unacceptable’: Japan condemns visit by Vladimir Putin to disputed Kuril Islands

The Japanese government has reacted angrily to Vladimir Putin’s first visit to the disputed Kuril Islands, which are claimed by both Tokyo and Moscow. Japan’s foreign minister, Toshimitsu Motegi, summoned the Russian ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev, while the prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, called Putin’s actions “absolutely unacceptable”. Known in Japan as the Northern Territories and by Russia as the Southern Kurils, the islands were seized by the then Soviet Union in the closing stages of the second world war and have been a source of contention ever since. The Soviet Union declared war on Japan in August 1945 as Tokyo was about to surrender, and the dispute has prevented the two nations from signing a formal peace treaty. Takaichi told reporters in Tokyo that the islands, which are just off Hokkaido, were “both historically and under international law” a part of Japan and called the visit by the Russian leader “incompatible with Japan’s consistent position” on the territory.

Japanese television showed footage of Putin on the island of Etorofu, or Iturup in Russian, visiting a hospital, meeting residents and trying caviar at a processing plant, as well as comments condemning the visit by former Japanese residents who were deported when Russia took control of the islands. About 17,000 Japanese formerly lived on the islands, which today are occupied by about 20,000 Russian citizens. As well as its strategic significance, the island chain – consisting of Etorofu, Kunashiri, Shikotan and the Habomai islet group – provides access to rich fishing grounds and valuable mineral deposits. On Wednesday, Putin travelled to the nearby Russian island of Sakhalin, where he inspected navy drills and declared that the four disputed islands were recognised as Russian in international documents. Shinzo Abe, the late Japanese prime minister, had reached an entente with Putin over the territory, with visits by Japanese citizens to family graves resuming and talk of a future peace treaty.

I would like to point out that we are not threatening Japan. On the contrary, it has territorial claims against our country.” Though it is Putin’s first visit to the islands, Dmitry Medvedev went to Kunashiri in 2010 when he was president. Pentagon official and former Aukus sceptic says deal is ‘full steam ahead’, echoing Trump

Elbridge Colby, the third-highest-ranking official at the Pentagon and formerly an avowed Aukus sceptic, has mirrored his president’s language on the nuclear submarine deal, saying it is “full steam ahead”. Colby, a US under secretary of war, was the author of the Trump administration’s review of the Aukus deal, which would see the US sell three in-service Virginia-class submarines to Australia, before the development of Australia’s domestically built Aukus-class submarines. The original draft of Colby’s review was understood to be sceptical about the Aukus agreement’s prospects of success, but was rewritten – on some accounts twice – to more closely align with the president’s position that Aukus was “full steam ahead”. Related: A global threat for millennia: experts warn Australia’s nuclear submarine legacy will be weapons-usable uranium cache Colby told an Asia-Pacific press briefing on Thursday “we’re very pleased to say that Aukus is – as the president said – full steam ahead”.

Pillar one of the Australia-UK-US (Aukus) agreement involves Australia being given the technology to command its own fleet of conventionally armed, nuclear-powered submarines. text:
South Korean airport becomes busiest in world for global traffic amid Iran war

South Korea’s Incheon airport has become the world’s busiest airport for international passengers, in part owing to disruption in the Middle East caused by the Iran war. The airport, South Korea’s main gateway, about 30 miles (48km) west of Seoul, handled 38.39 million international passengers in the first half of 2026, according to preliminary figures compiled by the Airports Council International (ACI), the global trade body for airports. Heathrow in the UK was second, with 37.79 million, followed by Changi airport in Singapore with 34.53 million. It is the first time Incheon has topped the international passenger rankings since opening in 2001. The airport was 10th in the world in 2002, rising to fifth in 2018 and third in 2024 and 2025. Part of the increase was attributed to disruption caused by the US-Iran conflict, which weakened the role of Middle Eastern hubs such as Dubai and diverted some transfer traffic to alternative routes through east Asia, Incheon International Airport Corporation (IIAC) was quoted as saying by the Yonhap news agency.

citation.title: South Korean airport becomes busiest in world for global traffic amid Iran war

Related: Heathrow says need for expansion clear as it loses title of Europe’s busiest airport Incheon’s international passenger traffic was up 6.3% year on year overall, with rising numbers of foreign visitors also contributing to the increase. Foreigners accounted for 39.3% of Incheon’s passengers in the first half of the year, up from 35.2% for the whole of 2025. The proportion reached a record 44.4% in the second quarter, with IIAC attributing the increase largely to growing numbers of visitors from China and Japan, according to local media. Heathrow, in west London, recorded 40 million passengers in total in the first half of the year, including both domestic and international travellers, its busiest first half on record. Passenger traffic to Asia-Pacific rose 7.9%, while capacity to the Middle East reportedly fell 16.5% owing to the regional conflict. Earlier this week Istanbul overtook Heathrow as Europe’s busiest airport by total passenger numbers. Figures published on Tuesday showed 7.9 million passengers passed through Heathrow’s terminals in July, compared with Istanbul’s 8.15 million.

Incheon has also expanded its role as an international hub. It serves 101 airlines flying to 183 cities, including 158 international passenger destinations. A four-phase expansion completed in late 2024 increased the airport’s annual capacity to 106 million passengers. Kim Beom-ho, the acting president of IIAC, said the ranking reflected “the support of the government, the public’s encouragement and the hard work of everyone stationed at the airport”. South Korea also lays claim to the world’s busiest air route. The domestic corridor between Gimpo airport and Jeju island had 14.4 million seats scheduled in 2025, according to the aviation data provider OAG, more than any other route in the world.

text:
The west turns a blind eye to Xi Jinping’s repressive regime in China

In his article on China’s latest tool for suppression of minorities, the “ethnic unity” law, Simon Tisdall seems to take it as read that western governments will continue to pay lip service to notions of human rights in China while pursuing short-term economic goals, ultimately destructive to their own productivity (President Xi never wastes a good crisis. As Iran, Ukraine and Palestine distract the world, he tightens his grip, 8 August). This has been the pattern since June 1989, the Tiananmen Square massacre. His faint hope that the young urban Chinese might overturn Xi’s regime is a judgment on the failure of western governments to show any foresight, integrity, effective diplomacy, joined-up thinking or action. They rely on the self-sacrifice of individuals such as Jimmy Lai, Lobga Rangzen and countless – often to us nameless – individuals who put their lives on the line while we wring our hands and weep crocodile tears. Their response to this latest abuse of power seems to be limited to a change in their extradition policy to protect their own citizens.

citation.title: The west turns a blind eye to Xi Jinping’s repressive regime in China

text:
The west turns a blind eye to Xi Jinping’s repressive regime in China

They should understand by now that the law alone will not protect critics of Xi’s regime, wherever they are. Meaningful diplomacy on an international level is well overdue, but just as Europe has had to wean itself off dependence on the US for defence, so it will need to wean itself off China for trade. Jennifer Hubbard Burton-in-Kendal, Cumbria • Very striking is what Simon Tisdall’s article concedes and then ignores. It notes in passing an American administration displaying “disdain for international law and national sovereignty (as seen in Venezuela and Greenland)”, tariff wars against allies, and partners who now have to regard Washington as unreliable. Every charge laid against Beijing’s ambitions applies to conduct the article treats as merely regrettable background. Tisdall asks us to imagine a British prime minister banning the Welsh language from schools. It is an unfortunate choice. Britain did precisely that – the Welsh Not was an instrument of state policy, Gaelic was suppressed, and Irish self-determination was resisted by force for centuries.

The analogy does not illuminate China’s conduct so much as remind us that the moral vantage point being claimed is a recent acquisition. The repression in Xinjiang and Tibet is real and deserves condemnation. But condemnation is weakened, not strengthened, when it is deployed selectively as an instrument of strategic competition. Britain’s silence is not the “debilitating fatalism” Tisdall diagnoses; it is the ordinary conduct of a state that raises human rights with rivals and sets them aside with customers. Further, quoting a statement from a US admiral without criticism – from a rogue nation engaged in economic and political warfare against China – shows a bias I did not expect to find. Geoffrey Dixon Burston, Norfolk • Simon Tisdall writes “imagine what would happen if a British prime minister in London told the Scots they could not have their own parliament”. We don’t have to imagine – it happened in 1979. In the referendum that year, a majority of those voting said yes to a Scottish parliament.

Thursday briefing: What happens after an asylum hotel closes?

Good morning. This week, immigration minister Anna Turley announced, with minor fanfare, the government will stop using a further 13 hotels to house asylum seekers across the country. It brings the total shut this year to 44, in pursuit of Labour’s manifesto pledge, now reiterated by Andy Burnham, to cease hotel use completely by the end of this parliament. Doing so would remove what have become highly visible symbols of an increasingly toxic debate about migration. Less than 160 to go, according to the Home Office. There was a risk the announcement might be drowned out by howls of rightwing outrage after the prime minister dared suggest that middle-class areas also ought to house asylum seekers. “We cannot have a situation where it’s only the poorest communities in the country that receive all of the dispersal of refugees and asylum seekers,” Burnham said.

I spoke to specialist reporter Diane Taylor, who has followed shifts in immigration policy and the individuals who must live through them for decades. First, the headlines. The home office justification was public health – but I spoke to hotel residents back in 2020 who told me about cramped living conditions, limited access to food, drink and financial support, alongside spiralling mental distress. I still remember running through Glasgow city centre in June 2020 to reach the scene of a mass stabbing, and how my stomach dropped when I realised I was heading to a hotel housing asylum seekers.

When a hotel closes, asylum seekers are moved – often at short notice – to houses of multiple occupancy (HMOs), former military barracks or other, usually more basic, hotels.
