People may have been living in the same hotel for years, and the new accommodation may be several hundred miles away, forcing people to re-build their lives – language classes, legal support, friendships – from scratch. Two barracks – Wethersfield in Essex and Crowborough in East Sussex – are now full, with planning permission being sought to turn three more into accommodation for asylum seekers: RAF Linton-on-Ouse, RAF Barnham and Bicester Garrison. Residents in the Oxfordshire village of Piddington, close to Bicester, will – in an eccentric move – hold a referendum on seceding from the UK, in protest against plans to house more than a thousand male asylum seekers in the disused army barracks. The government estimates these new sites could eventually house about 3,750 people. According to the National Audit Office, barracks are not necessarily cheaper to fund than hotels, because of hefty set-up costs. As Zambians go to the polls on Thursday, the ghost of the current president’s predecessor hangs over the elections. The 78-year-old British widow threatened with removal from Sweden after 21 years has said she has been left feeling sick with worry after being told she had lost an appeal against deportation in a growing row over the country’s handling of Brexit. “I am in shock. I feel sick. An individual’s life is at stake at my age. It is hell. I have done nothing wrong. I don’t take anything from this country. I am self sufficient, I put money in this country, have no criminal record,” said Joyce Thomas from her home in Sweden on Thursday. Her plight, first revealed by the Guardian, has raised concerns in Brussels and in the UK about Sweden’s approach to the EU-UK withdrawal agreement, which was supposed to protect British nationals who lived in an EU member state before Brexit. Earlier this week another family told how their father, a dementia patient in full-time care, was also threatened with removal after 25 years in Sweden.

Canadian plasma clinics pause collections after deaths of two donors

A chain of private plasma donation clinics in Canada has said it is pausing collections after the deaths of two donors and a new government investigation into potential unsafe practices. Grifols, a Spanish healthcare company which runs 17 clinics in Canada and is the country’s only private clinic for plasma donation, said it informed Health Canada of its decision to temporarily pause collections on Wednesday. On the same day, the agency had issued a formal notice of non-compliance for failure to follow blood regulations, a senior official told the Globe and Mail newspaper. The two deaths occurred after plasma donations in October 2025 and January 2026, Health Canada said in March of this year. The donors, both of whom were in the province of Manitoba, went into “distress” while donating, people familiar with the cases said. Though Health Canada did not release the identities of the donors, friends said one was Rodiyat Alabede, 22, an international student and aspiring social worker who donated plasma in Winnipeg on 25 October.

text:
Canadian plasma clinics pause collections after deaths of two donors

Patient advocates reported at the end of May that there were concerns about whether Alabede had been properly screened. “They had staff taking plasma from donors who did not know how to extract plasma in a safe manner,” alleged Kat Lanteigne, a safe blood campaigner who represents Alabede’s family. “The [failures] were so egregious that … now we have more questions than answers,” she said in May. An autopsy showed Alabede died of cardiac arrest shortly after donating. Health Canada reported that it found “no link” between Alabede’s death and plasma donation. Patient advocates have called for a new inquest into her death, however, after alleging that “significant medical discrepancies” had been uncovered between her autopsy, which was completed two days after her death, and the medical summary drafted by Health Canada published on 27 March of this year. The Guardian has also seen Health Canada inspection reports from May that found deficiencies at Grifols clinics, including inadequate training for staff, failures in standard operating procedures, poor record-keeping and a failure by Grifols to remedy past issues.

Canadian plasma clinics pause collections after deaths of two donors

The Health Canada report also found that staff did not stop plasma collection when alarms went off, and described the company’s reporting as “incomplete” and “inaccurate”. Prior to the newly announced pause, donations were permitted at Grifols twice a week. The company paid donors up to C$100 (£55) for each donation. Plasma is a pale yellow, protein-rich liquid in blood that assists in moving red and white blood cells, along with platelets, through blood vessels, according to Canadian Blood Services, the non-profit that operates Canada’s national blood supply. Plasma also helps prevent excessive bleeding and is used to create medications for a variety of conditions including haemophilia, liver disease and various cancers. The plasma donation process differs from donating blood overall. A medical device called an apheresis machine draws the blood, separates it into individual parts, collects the components needed and then returns the remaining blood back into the body, according to Canadian Blood Services. The process takes about 90 minutes, whereas a general blood draw takes about 10.

In Canada, provinces and territories decide whether paid plasma clinics are permitted. British Columbia and Quebec do not allow the practice, for example, but Manitoba, where the deaths occurred, does not prohibit companies from paying donors for plasma. Grifols said it decided to pause collection “proactively and voluntarily” due to what it deemed “unfounded attention”. It said the pause would allow it to work with Health Canada and Canadian Blood Services. The company has denied the two deaths were connected to plasma donation. A spokesperson for that location said it was working closely with the company so that it could return to operations. “Canadians can be assured that this decision will have no impact on the safety and security of Canada’s blood and plasma supply,” Grifols said.

US firms that kept DEI policies despite ‘go woke, go broke’ threats thrived

Conservative backlash was supposed to put an end to the diversity, inclusion and equity (DEI) movement as companies were warned “go woke, go broke”. In January 2025, Donald Trump delivered a death knell, ending DEI within the federal government with executive orders and threatening to target companies that still supported it. Companies including Google, Goldman Sachs, McDonald’s and Walmart that had embraced DEI years earlier fell into line and announced an end to their policies. But new research published on Friday and shared exclusively with the Guardian found that companies that resisted the pressure and kept their DEI practices, including Costco, Apple and Delta Air Lines, performed just as well as their competitors who pulled back. For the research, Jacob Grumbach, an associate professor at at the University of California at Berkeley’s Goldman School of Public Policy, analyzed how S&P 500 companies fared after Trump’s January executive order.

He used what economists define as “abnormal returns” – the difference between how a stock was expected to perform versus how it actually performed – to isolate the impact of a company’s DEI decision. What he found was the firms that kept their DEI policies or voted down anti-DEI shareholder resolutions did just as well financially, even after Trump’s executive order, as firms that didn’t. In the days after the executive orders were signed, companies that kept their DEI policies actually performed better on the stock market than those that didn’t. Apple, for example, may have known it could maintain its DEI efforts in a way that Tractor Supply, another prominent company that pulled back its policies, could not. French court blocks Macron’s social media ban for under-15s

France’s top court has blocked a ban on social media access for under-15s, ruling that it infringed freedom of expression and privacy. The decision is a blow to President Emmanuel Macron as momentum builds around the world for Australian-style restrictions on children’s use of social media. A law approved by parliament in July would have barred under-15s from opening social media accounts from the beginning of September. Tech platforms would also have been required to close existing accounts within four months and use age-verification tools approved by ⁠France’s privacy regulator. However, the constitutional council found that while the law required users to provide proof ​of age, it failed to specify the “conditions and limits” ‌under which this should happen. It also found that the restrictions infringed freedom of expression and privacy. “The council holds that the contested provisions, on ‌the one hand, disproportionately infringe upon the freedom of expression and communication and, on the other, fail to provide the legal safeguards necessary to ensure the right to respect for private life,” it said.

Indonesia wildfires threaten orangutans rescued from animal traffickers

Orangutans rescued from wildlife traffickers face a new threat from the record number of fires that have broken out in Indonesia in recent weeks. Flames have come within metres of an animal rehabilitation centre in West Kalimantan as hot, dry and windy conditions have been amplified by a powerful El Niño and the human-driven climate crisis. In the first 13 days of August, Indonesia registered more than three times more forest fire hotspots than in the whole of the same month last year. This followed a record number of blazes between January and July. West Kalimantan has been at the epicentre. After 40 days without rain, there have been dozens of severe outbreaks of fire in the region. Flames threatened the Yiari orangutan rehabilitation centre this week. The fire moved rapidly from 1km away to within 100 metres of the perimeter within days, prompting staff to relocate the 60 resident orangutans to enclosures in the middle of the centre.

The centre’s director, Dr Karmele Llano Sánchez, said in her latest update that battling the fire had been relentless. “We were fighting it until 3am, but this morning it has reignited. The teams are working round the clock but they are exhausted.” The situation had reportedly stabilised as of Thursday evening, with all the animals safe, but the meteorological agency has said the hot, dry conditions are likely to continue and could lead to more outbreaks. Israeli military plans to transfer law enforcement in occupied West Bank to police

Israel’s defence minister wants to transfer law enforcement powers for Israelis in the occupied West Bank over to the police, a plan that Palestine’s vice-president described as a “flagrant violation of international law” and step towards full Israeli annexation. Israel Katz announced that he had ordered the military to draw up plans for the handover of responsibility for policing Israeli settlers amid domestic and international criticism of the army’s failure to tackle militants besieging three Palestinian families. The Palestinian vice-president, Hussein al-Sheikh, called for international intervention to enforce international law and stop a move that would “entrench the illegitimate annexation of Palestinian land”. Katz unveiled his plan as a settler siege in the Palestinian village of Qusra entered its sixth day. The Israeli army has proved unable or unwilling to remove the group of militants trying to drive out Palestinian residents through a campaign of terror.

Italian police recover paintings by Cézanne, Renoir and Matisse after heist

Italian police have recovered three paintings by the French masters Paul Cézanne, Pierre-Auguste Renoir and Henri Matisse that were stolen earlier this year from a private museum near the northern city of Parma, authorities have said. The raid took place overnight on 22-23 March at the Magnani Rocca Foundation, about 12 miles (19km) from Parma, after a series of high-profile thefts from other European museums. Police released footage showing two masked burglars entering through a window, grabbing the three paintings from the wall and immediately leaving the building, in an operation that took less than three minutes. The recovered works are Cézanne’s Still Life with Cherries, which authorities said was valued at about $7m (£5.2m), Renoir’s Fish, valued at $3.5m, and Matisse’s Odalisque on the Terrace, valued at $23,000. A statement from the Italian Carabinieri’s art recovery squad said the paintings were found during searches ordered by prosecutors, but gave no further details. The investigation is continuing.

‘Unprecedented’ rain kills five in Japan as thousands stranded at airport

At least five people have died in eastern Japan after “unprecedented” heavy rain that left nearly 7,000 stranded at Tokyo’s Narita airport and forced thousands to take refuge in government buildings. The torrential rains hit Chiba prefecture, east of Tokyo, on Thursday night, triggering landslide warnings and power outages. Evacuation orders were issued for more than 400,000 people in Chiba and other areas, and about 45,000 homes lost power, as 115mm of rain fell hourly, approximately the same amount usually recorded for the whole month of August. It was the first time the Japan Meteorological Agency has issued the highest level-5 warning for heavy rains and landslides for the prefecture. Two other people are reported to have died after being unable to escape from their cars during the flooding.

‘So much more respect for myself’: NZ ultrarunner Sophie Woods on smashing a 2,000km alpine run record

A couple of weeks into her record-breaking 2,000km run through Europe’s alps, Sophie Woods feared she might die. Woods and her photographer had just scaled a peak in Switzerland, when a severe thunderstorm engulfed them. “The lightning was going off around us ... there was nowhere to shelter in place [and] all the rocks around us were conductive,” Woods tells the Guardian, from her home in Andorra, nearly two weeks after she became the fastest person ever to run the Via Alpina, a rollercoaster network of alpine trails through eight countries. “I was slightly concerned that one of us was going to die,” she says. “I ran so fast to get out of that.” Related: ‘Maybe the suffering is the point’: what does it take to run 163km up and down a mountain? Woods set off from Muggia, near Trieste, in Italy on 4 July to run the mountainous Via Alpina trail winding through Italy, Slovenia, Austria, Germany, Liechtenstein, Switzerland, France, and Monaco with an ambitious goal: complete it in record time. It was an Odyssean feat.

Ontario free to axe Toronto bike lanes, region’s top court rules

The Ontario government is now free to rip out Toronto’s bike lanes on its busiest streets after the region’s top court ruled in favour of the province on Friday, overturning a lower court’s decision that decreed removal would violate constitutional rights. The win is significant for Ontario’s premier, Doug Ford, and his government, who have long railed against Toronto’s bike lanes, blaming the protected zones for the city’s traffic ills. In 2024, the Ford government passed legislation that would allow Ontario to axe Toronto’s lanes, despite the recent installation of the infrastructure by the municipality. But the effort to tear up the lanes covering 19km (12 miles) of road was paused after cycling advocacy organisations levelled a legal challenge against the province. Their challenge was supported in July 2025, when a superior court judge ruled removing the lanes was unconstitutional, as it would create a heightened risk of death or injury, in turn violating the right to life and security of the person. Those rights are protected under Canada’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

It helps pedestrians. It helps other drivers. It has a very strong traffic calming effect that we need in major cities,” he said. The court of appeal judges in their decision wrote that there is no charter right to bike lanes and the government is free to change legislation on the lanes if it wishes. They explained that courts cannot find legislation unconstitutional because experts predict the government’s policies will fail. “Neither the government nor the legislature is under any obligation to accept policy advice,” wrote Justice Huscroft in the decision. In reaction to the ruling, Toronto’s mayor, Olivia Chow, said she has been working with the province to negotiate a path forward “that keeps every road user safe”.

Nearly five years into the war, Russia is scrambling to find enough soldiers to replenish its ranks, as voluntary recruitment slows and its forces suffer heavy losses on the battlefield in Ukraine. With Putin showing no sign of abandoning his far-reaching territorial demands, even as Russia’s summer offensive stalls, the Kremlin faces a growing manpower headache. “The problem for the Kremlin is that it is getting much harder to find people willing to fight, even for crazy money,” said Aleksei Tabalov, a human rights activist and director of an organisation that helps Russian conscripts. I became very committed; I just wanted to serve my country and fight Taliban and destroy the terrorist groups.” He spent 12 years in the Afghan national army, most of those wearing the distinctive red badge of the special forces, “and we fought many hard battles”. Abbas served alongside Australian troops in southern Afghanistan, night-time missions by helicopter in late 2011, in the restive and mountainous Khas Uruzgan district. They promised they wouldn’t abandon us. But in the end, when they withdrew … we were left with our hands tied Abbas “There were many forces we served with: Germans in Kunduz, French in Kapisa, and especially we were with Americans. The Australian forces were in Uruzgan, and we went there. We took part in combat alongside them, especially in Khas Uruzgan, we … executed two missions with them by air.” Abbas said he and his comrades “were always on the frontline”. “We spent many days and nights with foreign forces.

I performed combat duties in [approximately] 20 provinces of Afghanistan.” He was wounded in a firefight in Laghman district, shot twice at close range. His bulletproof vest deflected the bullet that struck the left side of his chest, “but another hit my left arm, breaking the bone”. He was taken by US helicopter to Bagram hospital: “I still have a metal plate in my left arm.” Abbas remembers the camaraderie of his days serving alongside western troops with fondness: “We risked our lives to help each other on and off the battlefield and to rescue one another. They always called us brothers.” But he remembers too, the commitments that were made to him. “They promised they wouldn’t abandon us. But in the end, when they withdrew, they simply left us. And they did it in such a way that we were left with our hands tied, the entire army was disarmed. “Those who were high-ranking officials left, while the rest of us, sergeants like me, were left behind.

No one even asked about us.” When Kabul fell, Abbas was forced to burn most of his documents and destroy photographs: incriminating evidence in the eyes of the Taliban. A bare handful remain secretly in his possession: pictures on patrol with western forces, certificates of appreciation from foreign militaries commending his “outstanding commitment, dedication and support” to their operations. Life since the fall, with a wife and young son, has been precarious, often dangerous. His has been a shifting, uncertain existence in the shadows. As the Taliban swept northwards across Afghanistan, expanding and consolidating its control from the major cities to smaller, more distant villages, there were fewer and fewer places to hide. With his family, Abbas fled over Afghanistan’s arid, inhospitable border into Iran. There, with no legal rights, he is vulnerable to exploitation and extortion: landlords demand thousands of dollars for tiny apartments that have been condemned as unfit for habitation; he has been forced to take dangerous, illegal work for far less than a living wage.

When US bombs started raining down on Tehran, Abbas and his family fled once again for the mountainous countryside. “Our life in Iran is very difficult; refugees face a lot of problems. Especially for us former military personnel … we are still being threatened by Taliban groups even here. We also fear that we might be deported to Afghanistan.” Abbas said his family’s future depends on being able to find a safe country, far from the reach of the Taliban, and the American war which has blighted his Iranian exile. “I am waiting to see what will happen, but I am hopeful … I will build a better life for my family, a better future for my son.” Many in Afghanistan feel as Abbas does – betrayed by the foreign forces in whom they placed their trust. *** On the day of his second inauguration as US president, Donald Trump halted all Afghan refugee resettlement by executive order. The shutdown left more than 1,000 Afghan former interpreters and soldiers stranded in a US-run camp in Qatar, and hundreds of thousands more vetted applicants stuck in neighbouring countries like Pakistan.

“We also remain committed to assisting those who helped Australia’s mission in Afghanistan.” Until 2023, the Australian government ran a dedicated “locally engaged employee” (LEE) program for Afghans who worked for and with Australia “and are at risk of harm as a result of their work”. The program certified 2,059 Afghans – but only 1,208 of those have reached Australia, according to the latest government figures (along with 4,493 immediate family members). But hundreds of Afghans still living in hiding inside the country, or stranded in perilous situations elsewhere, say they were unable to apply before the LEE program closed, or had their applications rejected despite providing evidence of support for Australia, including fighting alongside Australian troops. A government review of the program found it was riven by “delays, double handling and confusion”, and it imposed an unreasonable administrative burden on those fleeing the Taliban seeking safety.

Abbas has family in Australia, and, having fought alongside Australian troops on their missions in Afghanistan, he applied for LEE protection from Australia. Missed out on tickets to see the Bayeux tapestry in London? A £1,000 hotel stay will get you in

Those hoping to snare a glimpse of the Bayeux tapestry when it comes to the British Museum this September faced nine-hour online queues, with the £33 tickets sold out within a day. But the monied guests of a five-star hotel in Covent Garden have not had to go to such arduous lengths to get a view of the nearly 1,000-year-old depiction of William the Conqueror’s victory over King Harold II of England at Hastings in 1066. Those staying at One Aldwych, where rooms cost more than £1,000 a night, are able to get tickets to the tapestry exhibition through a corporate partnership with the British Museum. Helena Dollimore, the MP for Hastings and Rye, said it was “outrageous” that those who could afford to pay for an expensive hotel room got free access to the exhibition while others had to scramble for tickets. Dollimore has been negotiating with the museum to get access for children of “1066 country”, which she represents, to see the exhibition free of charge.

Hotel guests are told they can select any date and time during their stay to be prioritised for tickets, and that there are “plenty of tickets”. However, there is a limit of one ticket per guest per stay. As well as a viewing of the tapestry, guests who book the Bayeux experience also get a themed cocktail and a full English breakfast. The hotel says on its website: “Just a short stroll through Covent Garden and Bloomsbury brings you to the British Museum, our official partner for this landmark season. Here, one of the most anticipated cultural events of our lifetime unfolds: the Bayeux tapestry on view, a loan from France in a historic, once-in-a-generation agreement.” Dollimore said: “It is outrageous that one of London’s most expensive hotels has been offered this access to the Bayeux tapestry. How can it be right that some are able to pay their way in while others have to scramble for a chance to see this piece of our heritage?” There has been huge interest in seeing the tapestry in the museum as it has arrived on English shores for the first time since it was made.

The first batch of tickets, which are sold out, were for slots between September and December. Two releases will follow in October and January for the remainder of the tapestry’s stay in Britain, which runs until July 2027. The British Museum said it had its biggest ever day of ticket sales when the first slots were released this summer, with bookings for the exhibition bringing in more than £2.5m. The tapestry has been on display at the Bayeux Tapestry Museum in Bayeux in Normandy since 1983 and will return there when the museum reopens after renovation. The French president, Emmanuel Macron, has faced a strong backlash for allowing the loan to go ahead, with critics saying he ignored expert advice that the artefact was too fragile to be transported to the UK. Bird flu has been evolving and migrating for 30 years. It is a far more deadly virus that has now arrived in Australia

In 1996, geese in poultry farms in the Guangdong province of southern China started to get sick with a virus causing “bleeding and neurological dysfunction” and then death. A strain of avian influenza had likely arrived as a relatively harmless virus in migrating wild birds but had morphed into something “highly pathogenic”, killing about 40% of infected geese. Now, after appearing and disappearing, evolving and mutating and traversing the planet – leaving millions of dead birds and mammals in its wake – a descendant of that same H5N1 virus is, 30 years later, killing wild birds in Australia. “Right from the beginning there was great concern about the emergence of this virus,” says Dr Frank Wong, a virologist and avian influenza expert at the CSIRO’s Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness. But why the concern? Many avian influenza viruses are known as “low pathogenicity” because they cause only mild symptoms, or none at all. High pathogenicity viruses cause serious illnesses and death.

Avian influenza viruses are also classified by the two types of proteins on their surface – hemagglutinin that has 16 sub-types and neuraminidase, which has nine. These are important because the proteins are what the virus uses to latch on to the cells of a host. The only versions of these avian viruses to have evolved into deadly strains are H5 and H7. Wong says until 1996 a H5 virus had never been seen before spilling into domestic geese to then become highly pathogenetic in domestic birds. “That was an immediate flag,” he says. In 2002, almost a million poultry birds in Hong Kong were culled after H5N1 detections. “All the ducks and geese were free ranging and in the 1990s we get these outbreaks of HPAI (highly pathogenic avian influenza).

This H5N1 Guangdong goose virus was isolated but they couldn’t control it,” says Prof Marcel Klaassen, a bird flu expert and ecologist at Deakin University who has been researching the H5N1 strain for 20 years. Related: Native birds in captivity to be vaccinated against H5 bird flu as Australia prepares for more mass mortalities “It circulated in Hong Kong and east Asia and it was not until 2005 that it was found in wildlife. By 2005, the virus has evolved into something that survives in some wild birds. “Something that does not kill a bird instantly gives the virus wings that takes it to Europe and Africa.” Wild ducks have been described as the “Trojan horses” of the H5N1 story. Waterfowl have evolved with the viruses and so can carry them around without being affected themselves. The virus re-emerged again in Europe in 2021 and the current lineage of concern has swept across the continent, through North and South America, to Antarctica and now Australia.

Since appearing in 1996, H5N1 viruses have infected more than 400 bird species and more than 100 mammal species, in particular seals and sea lions and also dairy cattle in the US. “Influenza viruses and how they impact different hosts is really a numbers game,” Wong says. “The more types of host animals that it is allowed to infect without there being some control, the more chances it has to pick up new traits. “It’s most successful trait is adaptability. So you want to give it as hard a time as you can to minimise its opportunity to become even more adapted to environments where you don’t want it.” Avian influenza viruses can evolve quickly because they are prone to errors when their genes are being continually copied. “Most mutations are not successful but, given the right environment and situation, some mutations might give an advantage,” Wong says. Farming poultry in dense populations for human consumption has helped new versions of the viruses to emerge.

“In a way, it’s like an incubator for highly pathogenic avian influenza that you don’t see in the wild environment,” Wong says. “In the wild it is not to the virus’s benefit to kill its host. But in a domestic chicken flock, if a virus mutates from low pathogenicity to high, it selects for that trait because the infection burns through that population.” Klaassen goes even further. “This is a man-made virus,” he says. “Did these viruses evolve in wildlife? No, they did not. “Low pathogenic viruses come in and, with high densities of birds and large numbers, you have an ideal environment for a virus to evolve. All of the high pathogenicity influenza viruses evolve in poultry.” Jump to mammals Since 1997, there have been about 500 human deaths from H5N1 – almost all of the cases recorded among people working in close quarters with infected poultry. Health authorities say the risk for humans is low, and there have been no recorded cases of human-to-human transmission of the virus. Related: When bird flu hit the UK, suffering seabirds died in their thousands.

Australia’s wild flocks will soon do the same But H5N1 has infected mammal species – in particular, pinnipeds like seals and sea lions that tend to share the same spaces as infected wild waterbirds. “At one beach we saw a line of dead elephant seals – a whole tideline of dead animals,” remembers Dr Rachael Gray, a veterinary scientist at the University of Sydney. Gray was monitoring for the disease in Antarctica in late 2023 – “essentially picking up poo” – when she witnessed the tide of death. “It was devastating,” she says. “In birds you see respiratory symptoms – nasal discharges. But what we are seeing more of are these neurological signs. In pinnipeds, they can’t walk properly. They have seizures and you see this clouding of their cornea. It is distressing to see. “When it sweeps through a colony, you are talking two to four days [of symptoms before death] in birds and a little longer for mammals.

“The virus has become well adapted at getting into mammal cells.” Tens of thousands of pinnipeds have died of the virus in South America and Antarctica, and Gray holds grave fears for what could be in store for Australia’s three resident pinnipeds – the New Zealand fur seal, the Australian fur seal and the endangered Australian sea lion. “On the first incursion, it will be awful,” she says. “Some might develop immunity, and hopefully that gets passed on to their offspring, but I don’t think we know enough yet [on how the virus response will evolve]. “The virus can survive for extended periods of time on different surfaces, particularly in cool conditions. That gives the virus a better chance to survive [in Australia] because it has arrived in our winter.” H5N1 arrived in Australia in migratory seabirds from the sub-Antarctic and genetic testing of the birds showed the virus was the same type that had killed thousands of elephant seals pups at Heard Island.

“Every year we got through without it we thought, ‘maybe Australia’s geographic isolation will help us’,” Gray says. “But that was a naive hope and now, maybe, I have naive hope that it won’t hit our sea lions and fur seals. History is telling me the opposite.”

Body found in Romania believed to be missing British hiker George Smyth

A body has been found in the search for an 18-year-old British man who went missing last year while hiking in Romania, UK police said. George Smyth, a geology student at the University of Bristol, went missing in November. On Saturday, Avon and Somerset police said a body found in the region of the country is believed to be that of Smyth. His family have been informed and are being supported by a family liaison officer, the force added. Smyth’s family said: “We are all devastated by George’s death. “He was the best of us and is deeply missed by his younger brothers, family and friends. “We want to thank Salvamont mountain rescue, who have worked tirelessly since November searching for George, despite very difficult and often dangerous conditions. “They are an amazing team, and have remained in constant communication, helping us greatly throughout this awful time.” Efforts will be made to return Smyth’s body to the UK once formal identification has taken place.

The family’s statement added: “We would also like to thank Avon and Somerset police and University of Bristol, who have gone above and beyond to try and find George, and to support us as a family. “Although this latest news is incredibly painful, the torture of waiting is finally over, so we can now focus on bringing George home and saying goodbye. “We would appreciate privacy while we continue to come to terms with this loss.” On Wednesday, mountain rescue teams said they had resumed their search in “previously indicated areas, under rock walls, in grates and in the hard-to-reach sectors” but without success. The student, from Newport in Shropshire, is believed to have left Poiana Brașov heading to Bran. He reached Țigănești, where he made an emergency call for help. At the time, rescuers said he was in a “very isolated and hard to access mountain area” and the weather conditions were extremely severe with strong winds, heavy snowfall and dense fog. The search and rescue operation also involved a canine unit, drones and helicopters being deployed.

‘He had magnetism’: Lula returns to site of political origins to launch fourth-term campaign

Day after day, tens of thousands of metalworkers would cram on to the football pitch in São Paulo’s industrial suburbs to demand higher wages and, perhaps unwittingly, transform the destiny of Brazil. “You weren’t just documenting a fact – you were documenting history,” said photographer Jesus Carlos, who immortalised the now legendary strikes of 1979 and 1980 with his 24mm lens. As Carlos snapped the sea of downtrodden but tenacious labourers, he remembers sensing the momentous nature of their challenge to Brazil’s military dictatorship, whose foot soldiers would surround the Vila Euclides stadium wielding truncheons and guns. “I was a photographer – but before being a photographer I was a leftie,” recalled the former Communist party activist, now 75. “So I was fully aware what all it meant … [and] that the whole situation would be really important for the future.” Carlos’s instincts were right.

text:
‘He had magnetism’: Lula returns to site of political origins to launch fourth-term campaign

The strikes in the industrial city of São Bernardo do Campo – a bold act of defiance against a regime that ruled with an iron fist – were subsequently credited with helping to pave the way for Brazil’s 1985 return to democracy and spawning one of the most influential and enduring politicians in modern Latin American history. For one of the key architects of those walkouts was Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a bushy-bearded, heavy-smoking 33-year-old union chief who became a household name in Brazil and a global icon as a result. The New York Times hailed him as “the continent’s leading working-class hero” and “a Brazilian equivalent of Poland’s Lech Walesa”, the activist who became the European country’s first democratically elected president after the fall of communism. In 1980, Lula helped found what became one of Latin America’s biggest leftwing political movements, the Workers’ party (PT), and in 2002, he was finally elected Brazil’s first working-class president after three unsuccessful attempts.

citation.title: ‘He had magnetism’: Lula returns to site of political origins to launch fourth-term campaign

text:
‘He had magnetism’: Lula returns to site of political origins to launch fourth-term campaign

The former lathe operator was re-elected in 2006 and won a historic third term in 2022, helping thwart an attempted coup led by his far-right opponent, the outgoing president Jair Bolsonaro. João de Deus Martinez, a metalworker who came to know Lula during the São Bernardo strikes, said his leadership potential had been obvious to those who saw him charm the throng in Vila Euclides. “There was no one who could beat him up there on the podium … He had this magnetism. People cried [when he spoke] – tears of hope,” recalled the scraggly haired 85-year-old whom Lula calls “Cabeludo” (Shaggy). Nearly 50 years after the São Bernardo strikes catapulted him to fame, Lula, now 80, is preparing to make an emotional return to Vila Euclides to launch the seventh – and final – presidential campaign of a storied life that began in rural poverty and took him to the highest job in the land. On Sunday, thousands of PT supporters are expected to fill the football ground in the city where Lula’s astonishing rise began to watch him fire the starting gun on October’s election.

citation.title: ‘He had magnetism’: Lula returns to site of political origins to launch fourth-term campaign

text:
‘He had magnetism’: Lula returns to site of political origins to launch fourth-term campaign

“Vila Euclides is more than a stadium. It’s a symbol of democracy. A cradle of change,” reads the invitation urging party activists to travel to “where it all began” to make their voices heard. Like 2022’s election, when Lula beat Bolsonaro by a whisker, this year’s contest is expected to be tight. Bolsonaro cannot run, after receiving a 27-year jail sentence for plotting to stop Lula taking power. His senator son, Flávio Bolsonaro, will stand in his place, with polls giving Lula a modest lead. “I don’t think it’s going to be a walkaway,” said Lula’s American biographer, John D French, who has charted the leftist’s trajectory since first visiting the ABC Paulista – the industrial region of which São Bernardo is part – in 1980. French called the factory strikes “a unique effervescence” of disgruntlement against worker exploitation and the “ignorant military men” who seized power in 1964 but suddenly found themselves on the back foot.

“Nobody knew what was going to happen, which is what made it dramatic, because there were a number of moments when it could have turned into a massacre,” recalled the academic, whose next book focuses on the reporters and photojournalists who chronicled the workers’ rebellion in the heartlands of Brazil’s automotive industry. Memories of that mobilisation, in which famous musicians, intellectuals, film-makers and politicians flocked to the region to champion the metalworkers and demand democracy, remain fresh to this day. “There was an awakening,” said Fernando Ferreira, 67, another photographer who covered the Vila Euclides assemblies. “Brazil is only what it is today because of the ABC.” Ademir Medici, a former newspaper editor who often interviewed Lula for the regional Diário do Grande ABC, said: “It was more exciting than a local derby between Corinthians and Palmeiras. It was thrilling. You thought: can this really be happening in my city? It gave you goose bumps.” Back then, Medici said the buzz around Lula was such that locals would boast of ties to the union boss, however tenuous.

“It was cool to go around saying: ‘I’m Lula’s friend! I know Lula! I used to play football with Lula!’” Lula’s newfound fame even earned him a flattering profile in the Brazilian edition of Playboy, in which the interviewer asked the union leader if he would consider posing nude. (Lula declined.) Related: Brazil’s Lula, 80, livestreams workouts before election against rival half his age But the ABC has changed dramatically since those heady days of people power, amid factory closures, sociodemographic shifts, union splits, public anger at PT corruption scandals, and a lurch to the right driven by social media and the evangelical church. Once known as the “red belt” – Brazil’s version of the Labour party’s “red wall” in the UK, or a smaller version of the US Democratic party’s “blue wall” – much of the region backed Bolsonaro when he won power in 2018. Today, only one of the seven cities in the ABC has a PT mayor. São Paulo state is governed by Tarcísio de Freitas, a close Bolsonaro ally who looks likely to be re-elected.

“If Lula turned up on Marechal Deodoro [São Bernardo’s main street] he’d be booed,” Medici claimed. Dalila Teles Veras, a PT-voting poet and cultural activist who also witnessed the strikes, lamented the rightward drift of an area so crucial to the history of Brazil’s left. “Today, the sons of those [1979] union leaders are grown men who subscribe to fascist ideas,” she said of their support for the Bolsonaros. “How do you switch sides just like that? text:
Concerns grow over increased global ties with Taliban in Afghanistan

The Taliban in Afghanistan have launched a diplomatic effort to end their isolation as major regional and international powers show a readiness to engage more closely with the repressive regime despite its systematic human rights abuses. Five years after the Taliban took power, an increasing number of countries are renewing ties or scaling up diplomatic contacts with the hardline Islamists, who seized power in Kabul in 2021 after 20 years of brutal insurgent warfare. Campaigners fear that the individual contacts by different countries risk undermining “coherent, consistent” demands for an improvement in human rights in return for any diplomatic concessions. Related: ‘When she turns eight they will take her’: rising number of Afghan girls being sold into child marriage The United Nations described a recent “cascade of [Taliban] edicts and laws” that have banned women from universities and most employment, denied teenage girls education and imposed strict dress codes. Minorities have been persecuted, while activists and journalists face repression.

Afghanistan has become a “graveyard for human rights,” the UN said in March. India, Qatar, China, Iran and several central Asian states all recently welcomed Taliban officials or opened new channels of communication. Russia, which recognised the Taliban government in Kabul just over a year ago, signed a military cooperation agreement last month. In June, the European Union held talks with Taliban officials in Brussels about returning failed asylum-seekers to Afghanistan. Individual European countries have also deepened their own contacts with Kabul. “There is no doubt there has been an evolution. The Islamic emirate is now in a confident position. They have realised they are indispensable for regional countries right now and even with Europe and the US they have identified how to engage,” said Shivam Shekhawat, at the Observer Research Foundation in Delhi.

Some western commentators have suggested more countries recognise the regime. Others want intensified “back channel” engagement. “We are not against any engagement … There is a need for engagement even if just for aid agencies to mitigate the ongoing humanitarian crisis but we are worried about the end goal of these contacts and the discussions that are taking place,” said Fereshta Abbasi, Afghanistan researcher at Human Rights Watch.

The European Commission downplayed its discussions in Brussels with a Taliban delegation, the first such formal encounter since 2021, as merely “technical” and focused on returns, but a Taliban spokesperson claimed it was a historic visit that was a step towards regularising consular relations with EU countries. The meeting prompted outrage. “You cannot condemn Taliban abuses in one breath and then announce talks on immigration in the next … The Taliban are telling their constituency back home that they are now accepted by the international community,” said Abbasi.

Powerful earthquake kills dozens in eastern Indonesia

A 7.7-magnitude earthquake that struck eastern Indonesia has killed at least 47 people, causing widespread panic and collapsing buildings and homes in a region prone to deadly seismic events. Rescuers have yet to reach Nagekeo, the area closest to the epicentre, because roads were blocked by landslides and communications disrupted. Authorities issued a tsunami warning, which has since been lifted, but there were at least 235 aftershocks, including one of magnitude 6.1. Indonesian authorities said monitoring showed no significant sea level changes that could indicate a tsunami. Tsunami waves of ⁠ 1.5 metres (3ft) were recorded in several areas. The Indonesian geophysics agency, BMKG, recorded the first quake at 4.58am on Saturday local time at a depth of 9 miles (15km) in the country’s Flores region. A second earthquake of magnitude 6.1 struck off northern Sumatra, Indonesia, hours after the initial quake, with no casualties yet reported. Rescuers around the port town of Maumere found 20 people dead, six severely injured and two trapped under the rubble, said Fathur Rahman, the head of the city’s rescue agency.

The death of an Irish teenager, electrocuted while taking a shower in a holiday home in Greece, has led to calls for tighter checks on appliances at tourist accommodation. Alex McKee, 17, is said to have died instantly when picking up the showerhead in a bathroom described as “outdoor and rudimentary” on Kimolos. “We are lucky there weren’t two deaths as a result of electrocution,” Agapitos Xanthis, a doctor on the island told Greek TV, recounting how the boy’s mother had described feeling a similar surge when she called him for help. “I told her to immediately turn off the mains.” McKee, from Cork, had been on the island barely three days when the tragedy occurred on 9 August. As the birthplace of his mother, Iphigenia, he and his family visited regularly, staying in the same stone house built more than 50 years ago. Israeli strikes on southern Lebanon kill 11 in worst toll since June truce

Eleven people have been killed, including three children, and 19 injured in two Israeli airstrikes on southern Lebanon, the worst toll since deals in June brought a lull in hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah. Israeli warplanes bombed a home on the outskirts of the village of Ansar, killing seven people and flattening the building early on Saturday morning. Rescue services were working at the site to try to find survivors and locate bodies. Another airstrike hours later on a home in the town of Deir al-Zahrani killed two, wounded nine and covered the streets in rubble and smoke. An Israeli drone also targeted a motorcycle in the nearby city of Nabatieh, but it was unclear if the driver was killed. Related: Israel deliberately starting wildfires in southern Lebanon, firefighters say The escalation came despite a June ceasefire in which most fighting between Israel and Hezbollah ended. Residents of southern Lebanon wondered if the attacks signalled further escalation to come or if it was safe to stay in their homes.

First Australian death of little penguin with H5 bird flu confirmed on Phillip Island

Australia’s first case of the deadly H5 bird flu in a little penguin has been confirmed on Victoria’s Phillip Island, only days after the state government announced it would begin vaccinating the species. Confirmation of the virus in the little penguin will spark a race to vaccinate thousands of birds, with the government announcing on Saturday it would begin the rollout on Monday. The government did not provide the exact location where the bird was found, but said it was not inside the island’s famous penguin parade area. A spokesperson confirmed the little penguin had died. There are about 40,000 little penguins on Phillip Island, making it the world’s biggest colony of the species and a major tourist attraction. Related: Bird flu has been evolving and migrating for 30 years. It is a far more deadly virus that has now arrived in Australia Environment advocates have been concerned about the potential for mass deaths of little penguins if the virus reached the island.

Zimbabwe boat accident death toll hits 68 as 22 more bodies recovered

Twenty-two more bodies have been recovered after a boat accident in Zimbabwe, taking the death toll to 68, police said on Saturday. The ferry capsized on Tuesday on Lake Kariba, on the border with Zambia. An investigation has suggested it was overloaded when it turned over during heavy winds. Eighteen children were among the people killed, Zimbabwe’s police said, in what is believed to be the country’s deadliest such disaster. Most of the passengers are believed to be villagers and fish traders who lived around the lake. Officials said the vessel was authorised to carry 90 people but was packed with 114 adults, five crew members and an unspecified number of children. Lt Col Joseph Muchechesi, commander of the boat regiment involved in the search operation, said: “So far today we have managed to take 22 bodies. We are confident that we will manage to retrieve all the bodies.” The civil protection unit said on Wednesday that 77 people had been rescued. Hundreds of people gathered at the district hospital in the lakeside town of Kariba to identify the bodies of their relatives and loved ones.

On Friday at 7pm, Thérèse Coffey was nine miles away from a nuclear power station when her phone made a loud, piercing and very worrying sound: it was a “severe” emergency alert. “Was expecting [a] much more specific alert, not a generic message on wildfires,” the former Conservative cabinet minister said on X. The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is now the deadliest in the country’s history, with at least 2,325 people dead, according to government data, surpassing the toll from the 2018-20 outbreak. The DRC’s public health institute said confirmed cases had risen to 4,945, including 101 detected in the previous 24 hours. The 2014-16 outbreak resulted in 28,616 cases and 11,325 deaths across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone, according to WHO data. More than 3,400 of the cases have been recorded in Ituri province, where the outbreak was first reported.

Monday briefing: What can Andy Burnham learn from Spain’s Pedro Sánchez?

Good morning. To international onlookers, Pedro Sánchez appears to have achieved the impossible. Where other European leftist and left-ish premiers have flopped and flailed, the Spanish PM has endured. Since June 2018, Sánchez has ruled from Madrid, implementing a raft of progressive policies. More recently, he has emerged as a leading, and often lone, left-wing European voice on the global stage, striking a defiant tone on everything from the Trump administration’s war in Iran (“the smokescreen of war to hide their failure”) to Israel’s actions in Gaza (“exterminating a defenceless people”). The fact that the international press has nicknamed him El Guapo (the handsome one) can’t hurt. At home, however, it’s a more complex story. Sánchez’s inner circle is in the midst of a damaging corruption scandal, and polling has his traditionally centre-left Spanish Socialist Workers’ party (PSOE) faltering. Meanwhile, recent scenes in Ceuta and apocalyptic wildfires throw up thorny policy challenges. European leaders have publicly turned on Sánchez – and this is with a general election looming next year.

A crude, low-tech animation about a cow and a skylark has become a sleeper hit at China’s box office, sitting alongside blockbusters such as The Odyssey and Spider-Man: Brand New Day in cinema revenue rankings. Niu Lai, which translates to The Cow is Coming, is an 86-minute budget animation about a newborn calf and a skylark whose relationship develops over the course of an abstract dream sequence. Released on 5 August, the film reportedly made just 7,700 yuan (£842) in its first 10 days of screenings, with fewer than 300 people nationwide buying a ticket. It did not have any promotional tour, pre-release publicity or even a trailer. But discussion online about how bad the film was turned it into a meme, which drove hordes of film fans to the cinema. It has now made more than 14.9m yuan, according to the movie tracking site Mao Yan, making it one of the top-performing films of the year.

Holy water: nuns fight Italian town’s plans to take away their beach club

A group of Italian nuns is fighting back against local council plans to take their beach club away from them – the latest flashpoint in the long-running debate about the monopoly of private concessions along Italy’s coastline. The dispute, described as “a holy war” by some local press, unfolded when a 50-metre stretch of sand at Bagni Gino Garrone, a beach resort in the Ligurian coastal town of Spotorno managed by nuns from the Suore di Carità di Santa Maria order, was designated for public bidding by authorities as they seek to comply with EU beach concession laws as well as regional regulations on free beach quotas. The nuns have been managing the resort since 1946 after being exempt from standard commercial rules because they were using the proceeds for charitable purposes, including funding an infant school they still run in Spotorno and a summer beach camp. For decades they have been renting out loungers and umbrellas, so operating much like thousands of other private beach concessions, the difference being – they claim – that the proceeds go to fund their charitable activities.

However, with the regulation governing beach use for social missions no longer existing, they were told by Spotorno’s mayor, Mattia Fiorini, that the concession would be reclassified as a “free equipped beach” and if they wanted to continue running it they would have to compete in a public tender. During a public debate on the topic, Sister Miranda, a nun in her 80s, challenged Fiorini. “It’s ours,” she was quoted as saying by the Turin edition of Corriere della Sera. “Why does the municipality want to take away our beach? If they do, we won’t even be able to keep the school running.” Operating it as a “free equipped beach”, meaning access is completely free and people can choose to pay a small sum to rent loungers and umbrellas if they wish, would be considerably less profitable, the nuns argued. Fiorini said if they wanted to continue managing the concession “they must participate in the tender, like everyone else”. The tender is due to be issued in the autumn.

After Hormuz, China looks to the promise – and peril – of the Arctic’s ‘ice silk road’

When Marco Rubio suggested that the world should look to new shipping lanes to bypass the logjammed strait of Hormuz, it’s unlikely he had the Arctic’s northern sea route in mind. And yet in recent months the promise of this 5,500km channel – cleaved through frozen seas by nuclear-powered icebreakers and illuminated by a sun that never dips below the Arctic horizon – has grown. Japan, Korea and India have all expressed interest in sending cargoes through the northern sea route (NSR), but it’s China that has established the first scheduled transit, with shipping company Sea Legend launching a regular service in recent days. The NSR, which cuts through the Arctic Circle along Russia’s northern coast, is only navigable during warmer months, but that window has widened due to shrinking summer sea ice. For some vessels, the route can more than halve the time it takes to get from China to Europe, but the benefits come with serious environmental and political risks that have the potential to outweigh the gains.

That direct journey from Ningbo-Zhoushan to Felixstowe in the UK takes as little as 18 days compared with more than 40 days via the Suez canal. Experts say the route is ideal for cargo that is sensitive to temperature, including electric vehicles, lithium batteries and solar products – among which China has become a dominant global exporter. As the only regular commercial cargo service on the route, Sea Legend will test whether Beijing’s longstanding Arctic ambitions can translate into a viable regular China-Europe trade route. The Chinese president, Xi Jinping, first publicly called for China and Russia to develop Arctic shipping routes and build a “polar Silk Road” in 2017. Russia, which controls much of the northern sea route, was initially wary of China’s growing presence in the Arctic. But after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Moscow has been left increasingly dependent on Beijing in the high north, giving China greater leverage and access.

Top album releases linked to rise in fatal crashes as ‘distracted’ drivers access music

The release of a new album by Taylor Swift might be a cause for celebration among her fans, but such events have also been linked to a more sombre phenomenon: an increase in fatal car crashes. The team behind a new study say it sheds light on the impact of distracted driving. “You can’t randomise people into using their phones, and drivers rarely volunteer what they were doing in the seconds before a crash,” said Dr Vishal Patel, first author of the study based at Harvard Medical School. “Album releases give you something closer to an experiment – a day when smartphone use jumps nationally for reasons that have nothing to do with road conditions, weather or who happens to be driving.” Writing in the journal Jama Network Open, Patel and colleagues report how they focused on the release of 10 major albums, launched between 2017 and 2022, selected for having the highest number of Spotify streams over a single day. These included Midnights, released by Taylor Swift on 21 October 2022; Scorpion, released by Drake on 29 June 2018; and Harry’s House, released by Harry Styles on 20 May 2022.

The team found streaming volume for the top 200 songs in the US was 43% higher on the date of major album releases compared with the days surrounding the releases – although such data does not reveal whether the music was being streamed in a car. “What it establishes is that these days are genuinely different in terms of national engagement with music, which is the premise the whole study rests on,” said Patel. The researchers used data from a population-based registry of fatal US motor vehicle crashes to look at the number of traffic fatalities on the dates these albums were released, as well as for the 10 days either side. After taking into account the day of the week upon which the album was released, as well as federal holidays, and time of year, the researchers found the number of US traffic fatalities showed a relative increase of 15.1% on the date of major album releases, compared with similar days either side. “This is equivalent to approximately 182 fatalities in the US attributable to the release days of the 10 included albums,” the team writes.

That’s several seconds of looking at a screen,” he said, adding unfamiliar music also demands more attention, while research has suggested listening to new, high-energy music measurably degrades driving performance. The researchers add the rise in traffic fatalities was greater among certain groups – such as younger drivers, male drivers, people who were driving alone, and people driving cars with a built-in infotainment platform. Bird flu has devastated wildlife around the world. What Australian birds are most at risk?

The deadly H5 bird flu that has devastated wildlife populations globally since 2021 is spreading across Australia. The federal government announced the first vaccination plans for captive native bird species last week and the Victorian government has moved to vaccinate wild little penguins after the first detections in terns on Phillip Island. On Saturday, the state government announced the death of a little penguin on the island, the first confirmed case of H5 bird flu in the species. But for those who don’t live in communities in southern Australia on the frontline of the highly pathogenic virus, the possibility that they will at some point see the severe consequences of H5 bird flu for native birds might not have registered. Related: First Australian death of little penguin with H5 bird flu confirmed on Phillip Island There is a level of uncertainty about how native species will be affected as they are exposed to the deadly strain for the first time.

Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Here are the birds experts are most concerned about – including some of Australia’s most common and loved species. Silver gull (seagull) The silver gull – or seagull – is in the “high risk” category of a government assessment of the potential effects of H5 bird flu on every Australian bird and mammal species. High risk means, where infections occur, the species faces potentially severe drops in population sizes or viability. When the first cases in seagulls were detected in South Australia in late July, it was viewed by experts as a new front for the spread of the virus. This is because gulls are highly mobile and found in high numbers all over the country, including wetlands, inland and cities. They gather in flocks and are scavengers – two things known to increase transmission. They are also a bird that many Australians interact with regularly.

Death and alleged torture of man in detention sparks protests in Syria

Syrians have protested over the death of a man who was arrested and allegedly beaten by security forces, sparking widespread anger at a practice thought to have ended with the fall of Bashar al-Assad. A crowd gathered in the city of Aleppo, demanding accountability for the security forces who are alleged to have carried out the torture, with participants holding signs and slogans such as: “Do not repeat the same oppression that we revolted against.” Protests were also planned to take place in front of Syria’s parliament in Damascus on Tuesday, as well. Mohammad Ghamira, a 29-year-old father of two and former volunteer in the White Helmets, had visited a police station in the coastal province of Latakia last week after an accusation of theft. Ghamira emerged from the station in a critical condition, and died in hospital on Sunday from “complications from cerebral and gastrointestinal haemorrhaging” that “resulted from a beating he sustained after being detained”, said Raed al-Saleh, the former head of the White Helmets and current Syrian minister of emergency and disaster management.

A picture of Ghamira pre-detention, smiling and healthy, next to another picture of him unconscious in a hospital bed with bruises on his body, went viral, sparking outrage in Syria. Ghamira’s parents told the police station chief prior to their son’s detention that he had haemophilia, a disease which makes it hard to stop bleeding once started, and asked them not to beat him. Even with the warning, Ghamira was beaten while in custody, Issam Ghamira, the man’s uncle, told Syrian state media. The Syrian interior ministry promised accountability for Ghamira, forming a committee to investigate his death and detaining seven members of the interior ministry for questioning. The interior minister, Anas Khattab, vowed a “fair punishment” after the conclusion of the investigation. “I confirm that any violation or abuse by the elements of the ministry of interior will be dealt with firmly within the laws and procedures followed and any violator will receive his fair punishment,” Khattab said in a post on X.

Despite the promises of accountability, Syrians were incensed by the allegations of torture, enraged that the practice continued even after the 14-year revolution aimed at stopping such brutality. Al-Assad’s regime used mass detention and torture on a systematic scale to control its population, accelerating its brutality when protests broke out against the government in 2011. The current government, made up mostly of former members of the Islamist rebel group Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), overthrew al-Assad in a lightning offensive in December 2024. It promised an end to the atrocities committed under the police state that al-Assad oversaw, dismantling the dense network of security agencies that oversaw the country.

Syrians for Truth and Justice documented 14 cases of individuals being tortured or dying in custody from June 2025 to June 2026, and said that “the change in political authority has not yet been accompanied by the effective dismantling of the structures and practices that enable torture”. If, before 19 July, few people in Italy beyond his family and friends knew who Abderrahim Fakir was, by the late afternoon of that day the final moments of his life were being watched across the country. Video footage widely shared online showed him being handcuffed and forcibly restrained by police on a street in Pilastro, a neighbourhood in the north-east of Bologna. Fakir, a 42-year-old small business owner born in Morocco but who had lived in Italy since he was a child, was pinned to the ground by two police officers as emergency health workers looked on. He repeatedly begged for help before his body stopped moving. Fakir was pronounced dead at the scene. The cause of death is still being established, although an initial postmortem indicated lung compression. Outrage over Fakir’s death spilled well beyond Pilastro, prompting protests in Bologna and Rome and fuelling a tense national debate over the far-right government’s approach to policing and immigration. The Kuril Islands: how a visit from Putin reignited a 150-year-old dispute between Japan and Russia

The diplomatic spat between Japan and Russia following Vladimir Putin’s visit to an archipelago of disputed islands north of Hokkaido continues to escalate, after Moscow summoned the Japanese ambassador on Tuesday. On Thursday Sanae Takaichi, Japan’s prime minister, called Putin’s actions “absolutely unacceptable” and Russia’s ambassador in Tokyo was immediately called in for a dressing down. Russia countered that it was Japan making unfounded claims on its territory. Why do the two nations care so much about this small group of islands – and why is this row boiling over now? Where are the islands and what is their history? Stretching about 1,200km from the tip of the Kamchatka peninsula in Russia to the north-eastern edge of Hokkaido in Japan, the Kurils are a volcanic archipelago of 56 islands. The southernmost island is less than 4km from Hokkaido. The disputed territory consists of just the four islands closest to Japan which were seized by the Soviet Union in the dying days of the second world war.

citation.title: The Kuril Islands: how a visit from Putin reignited a 150-year-old dispute between Japan and Russia

text:
The Kuril Islands: how a visit from Putin reignited a 150-year-old dispute between Japan and Russia

Known in Japanese as Hopporyodo, or the Northern Territories, in Russia they are simply referred to as part of the Kurils. Interactive Their history is complex and predates claims from the Japanese and the Russians: they were the indigenous home of the Ainu, whose lands spanned the Kurils, Sakhalin and Hokkaido. When Japan annexed Hokkaido in 1869, it took control of the four currently disputed isles, though it had already codified its sovereignty in an 1855 treaty with Russia. Another treaty, in 1875, gave Japan the whole Kuril chain in exchange for uncontested Russian control of Sakhalin, an island directly north of Japan. In the 1951 San Francisco peace treaty to resolve postwar territorial disputes, Japan renounced the Kurils, but maintained the four southernmost islands were part of its territory. The Soviet Union never signed the treaty. Why was Putin’s visit significant? Putin is only the second Russian leader to visit the islands, with Dmitry Medvedev visiting the islands four times between 2010 and 2015 as either prime minister or president.

citation.title: The Kuril Islands: how a visit from Putin reignited a 150-year-old dispute between Japan and Russia

text:
The Kuril Islands: how a visit from Putin reignited a 150-year-old dispute between Japan and Russia

But there is political symbolism in Putin – who has effectively held power since 2000 – setting foot on the islands for the first time, with Takaichi saying it would make it “more difficult to restore relations” between the countries. The late Japanese prime minister Shinzo Abe and the Russian president appeared to be edging towards rapprochement over the islands during the 2010s. But Russian deployment of anti-air missile systems in 2020 and a visit by the current prime minister in 2021 put paid to this. Japan has hardened its stance since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, imposing sanctions on Russia. Why are the islands important to Russia? The disputed territories give access to rich fishing grounds – Japan paid Russia for the right to fish there until agreement broke down in 2022 – and potentially valuable mineral deposits. But they also have strategic and symbolic importance. Russia has bolstered its military presence on the isles, which sit astride the line between the Sea of Okhotsk and the Pacific Ocean.

The Kuril Islands: how a visit from Putin reignited a 150-year-old dispute between Japan and Russia

Control of the islands gives Russia year-round access to the Pacific for its fleet based in Vladivostok, because the strait between the southern islands does not freeze in winter. What does it mean for Russia-Japan ties? Bilateral relations have taken a distinct downward turn in recent years. Moscow will have foreseen the almost inevitable reaction of Takaichi, a foreign policy hawk from the right of her party, to Putin’s visit to the islands. And the incident comes hot on the heels of revelations that an extensive Russian spy and military component procurement network was operating mostly unhindered in Japan. The Northern Territories issue has long been a cause célèbre for Japanese ultra-nationalist groups that protest aggressively outside the Russian embassy in Tokyo. While the Japanese government’s response will be more measured, Takaichi will be under pressure to continue taking a hard line against Moscow.

Lesley Urbach obituary

My friend Lesley Urbach, who has died suddenly aged 69, was passionate about human rights, and about education against racism and prejudice. In 2016 she helped to set up Generation 2 Generation, a pioneering Holocaust charity established to empower second and third generation Holocaust survivor descendants to present and preserve their family histories. As co-founder, associate director and trustee of G2G she shaped the organisation, not only mentoring speakers but delivering powerful presentations to schools and community groups, reaching tens of thousands of young people in the years since its inception. Lesley’s character and beliefs were shaped by the trauma experienced by her parents’ families. Born in Willesden, north-west London, she was one of four children born to Eva (nee Wohl) and Arnold Urbach, who had arrived separately in Britain in 1938 and 1939 respectively. Eva and her younger sister escaped Nazi Germany via the Kindertransport.

citation.title: Lesley Urbach obituary

text:
Lesley Urbach obituary

Eva got a job in an east London factory making military uniforms, and on her first day she met and subsequently married Arnold, a fellow Jewish refugee from Germany, who served in the British army and later worked as an interpreter during war crimes trials. Though Eva’s parents had attempted to flee to South America, they were murdered in Auschwitz along with more than 1 million others. They had sent their possessions on ahead in three trunks, which were eventually redirected back to the Urbachs when the war was over in 1947. Lesley and her elder brother Peter donated one of the trunks to the Imperial War Museum, where it is now part of the Holocaust Exhibition. Lesley went to the Jewish free school (now JFS) in north London, and studied history at University College London. She and I met in 1979, not long after graduation, at the University of London Library at Senate House, where we were both working as library assistants. We bonded over a Doris Lessing novel I was reading at the time and soon became friends. She was funny, warm and gregarious, and culturally voracious. She loved the theatre, and very much enjoyed music, especially jazz.

citation.title: Lesley Urbach obituary

text:
Lesley Urbach obituary

Lesley worked as an adviser for the National Careers Service for 25 years, first in Bristol and then in London, and after early retirement in about 2012 studied for an MA in Jewish history and culture at Southampton University. In 2015 she co-founded the Remembering Eleanor Rathbone Group, to promote awareness of Rathbone’s work as a campaigner for the rights of women and refugees. Through the JUMP programme, a befriending project for unaccompanied asylum-seeking children and young people managed by the Jewish Council for Racial Equality (now HIAS+JCORE), she befriended a young woman who came to Britain as a domestic slave, and between 2015 and 2020 she helped support Syrian refugees in Barnet. She was an active member of both the Beit Klal Yisrael community and the Finchley Progressive Synagogue, and worked for it to gain Synagogue of Sanctuary status earlier this year, of which she was extremely proud. A generous and inspiring godmother to many of her friends’ children, Lesley was colourful, exacting and charismatic, and a loyal, supportive friend.

Greek police believe a mechanical fault may have caused a helicopter to crash moments before it was due to land on the island of Sifnos, killing a British couple on honeymoon and the pilot. Andy Burnham says the UK will continue to “support Ukraine 100%” after Russia threatened consequences after strikes by British-made drones. The Russian embassy to the UK said on Monday that Britain had been deliberately escalating the Ukraine conflict and the deeper its involvement, “the higher the price it will pay”. Burnham, asked during a visit to Wolverhampton on Tuesday for his response to Moscow’s threat, said: “This is the UK doing what it has long said it would do, which is to support Ukraine 100% against this illegal war led by Vladimir Putin. “We are providing support so that Ukraine can defend itself, and that’s been the British position all the way through this conflict by previous prime ministers. It remains the case with me. We are not fair-weather friends. We will be there in Ukraine’s hour of need, and that won’t change.” The use of the drones made by UK companies is part of Ukraine’s “deep strike” campaign. However, it is not the first time Ukraine has deployed British-made equipment in Russia, having long used Storm Shadow missiles.

Phil Coughlin Houghton-le-Spring, Tyne and Wear • As Richard Tice encourages us to enjoy English sparkling wine instead of trying to mitigate the climate crisis (Report, 17 August), could this be Reform UK’s Marie Antoinette moment, considering the deaths, droughts, fires and water shortages affecting so many? Deirdre Burrell Mortimer, Berkshire • I can’t see “apranxiety” catching on – too ugly and too many syllables (Letters, 17 August). I’d suggest “climate fear” – blunter and shorter. Alec Murdoch Edinburgh • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

Philippine school shooter kills fellow student and himself in livestreamed attack

A student livestreamed himself shooting and killing another pupil in a classroom in the southern Philippines before taking his own ⁠life, ​the second school attack in the country in less than two months. The shooting took ⁠place at a school attached to Ateneo de Zamboanga University in the southern city of ⁠Zamboanga, a Catholic private institution in western Mindanao. Zamboanga city’s mayor, Khymer Adan Olaso, told the DZMM radio station that the ‌shooter “managed to enter carrying a high-powered firearm and a .45-calibre pistol”. Related: Philippines blocks GoreBox gaming app after school shooting kills three The interior secretary, Victor Remulla, confirmed the ninth-grade suspect had livestreamed the attack on social media. The shooter’s Facebook account has since been disabled. In the video, which was circulated by local media, the barrel of a gun is seen moving down a hallway before it is pointed into a classroom and fired. Children in school uniforms are seen screaming and rushing for an exit.

National police are now trying to “establish the motive behind the shooting, determine the ownership and source of the firearm used, and find out how it was brought inside the school campus”, the interior ministry said. Hours later, the Philippines’ customs department said it had ordered the “preventive suspension” of an agent who owned the guns “allegedly used by the student involved”. The customs deputy chief of staff, Noel Bendijo, told AFP that customs staff had acted on intelligence from their own officers in Zamboanga. “The information is that he was the father of [the alleged shooter] … As for the actual firearms used and how the kid was able to access them, all of those are still under investigation,” he said. “We’ve also spoken with the party involved. He understands but of course he’s also grieving because he also lost his child. That’s a nightmare for any parent.” Police when asked about the customs report said only that they were still investigating.

The Philippine president, Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr, said in an online post: “We grieve with the families and the entire [school] community over a tragedy that should never have happened. I have directed our law enforcement agencies to conduct a thorough investigation into this incident and to determine what more must be done to prevent another family, another school and another community from suffering the same grief.” In June at a public high school in Tacloban City, three students were killed and about 20 injured after two students opened fire on campus. In response, the government banned an online game, Gorebox, after it was discovered that at least one of the alleged shooters regularly played it, and reopened a senate inquiry on child safety in digital spaces. The department of education told a separate senate committee last month that more support was needed to prevent a “copycat phenomenon”, as more incidents of violence followed the shooting, including bomb threats, stabbing and the recovery of firearms and ammunition, local media reported.
