text:
What is behind Russia’s ‘consequences’ threat over UK sending drones to Ukraine?

Russia’s embassy in London has accused the UK of “deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis, while hypocritically professing a desire for peace” after it emerged over the weekend that Britain was supplying attack drones to Kyiv. What has the UK done – and what was Russia’s response? Ministry of Defence sources indicated that a report in the Sunday Times, that two drones made by British companies had been used by Ukraine’s military to attack targets inside Russia, was true, although only one, Nyan, made by BAE Systems, was named. The Russian embassy, seeking to maximise the impact of its remarks, added in a widely reported statement on Telegram: “London’s actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer”. Is the UK’s drone supply actually an escalation? Britain has been supplying weapons and providing financial support to Ukraine since before Russia’s full-scale invasion.

citation.title: What is behind Russia’s ‘consequences’ threat over UK sending drones to Ukraine?

text:
What is behind Russia’s ‘consequences’ threat over UK sending drones to Ukraine?

It has committed to providing £3bn a year in military aid until the end of the decade and to joining the EU’s €90bn loan scheme, which bankrolls Kyiv’s military effort, though many of the details of UK support are kept secret. The £100,000 Nyan drone is a medium-sized, jet-powered delta wing drone capable of delivering relatively small attacks at distances greater than 150 miles. However, while it looks hi-tech, it is not a munition that appears to be militarily significant. Britain has in the past supplied £1m-plus Storm Shadow missiles with a similar operating range that were used by Ukraine to launch attacks into Russia, but stocks have run short. Meanwhile, Ukraine has developed and manufactures its own Flamingo cruise missiles and longer range drones that it uses to attack Russia daily. So, why is Russia talking this up? It is as good an opportunity as any for the Kremlin to make a political point.

citation.title: What is behind Russia’s ‘consequences’ threat over UK sending drones to Ukraine?

text:
What is behind Russia’s ‘consequences’ threat over UK sending drones to Ukraine?

Western financial support is critical for Ukraine’s war effort and anything that might undermine public confidence in countries such as the UK is, from Moscow’s perspective, worth making, particularly in the summer when there is less domestic political news to crowd out the embassy’s remarks. Russia is also hurting economically from Ukraine’s sustained deep strike campaign that has targeted oil refineries and, more recently, ecommerce distribution warehouses on the outskirts of Moscow. Attacks are taking place on a near daily basis. It is the first time in the war that Ukraine has been able to hit targets in and around Moscow, more than 300 miles from its border, deploying a long-range capability that western leaders had refused to supply until Kyiv developed it for itself. It might be political, but are there signs of a wider escalation by Russia? Russia has been engaged in hostile behaviour towards the UK for years, including conducting two poisoning operations on British soil of defectors: Alexander Litvinenko in London in 2006, and Sergei Skripal and his daughter Yulia in Salisbury in 2018.

Russian hackers routinely target the UK, and regularly mount online disinformation campaigns. However, as the war in Ukraine remains almost deadlocked, and as Kyiv strikes closer and closer to home, Russia has become more reckless across Europe. It has conducted arson attacks using incendiary devices hidden in DHL parcels, including in the UK; flown 20 drones into Poland, and conducted an aerial harassment campaign across the continent. Moscow was almost certainly behind an attempt to attack Ukrainian cargo planes at Leipzig airport in Germany earlier this month with a small quadcopter drone armed with plastic explosive. It appears willing to spread the Ukraine war into Europe, including the UK. What else could an under-pressure Russia do to Britain? John Foreman, a former UK defence attache to Moscow, said he thought Russia was likely to engage in “more of the same” given its track record of hostility to the UK. “Russia is ‘relentlessly targeting’ the UK’s critical infrastructure, democratic processes, supply chains and public trust.

It has run sporadic campaigns of arson, sabotage, assassination and disinformation,” he said. “We know Russia is an aggressive, antagonistic and revisionist state. It has the intent to continue to target us unconventionally and will continue to do so.” An obvious concern is whether Russia’s brinkmanship spirals out of control; it will be for the UK and Nato to ensure that does not happen.

South Korea president calls for military independence in wake of Trump call to cut joint drills

South Korea’s president ⁠has renewed his push to regain independent control of the military from the US in the event of war and urged faster progress in acquiring nuclear-powered submarines after Donald Trump’s order to cut joint drills. On Sunday night, Trump instructed the Pentagon to “substantially reduce” this week’s joint military exercises with South Korea, saying the nuclear-armed North “has been unthreatening and respectful” and that the US president had a “very good relationship with Kim Jong-un”. Lee Jae Myung said on Tuesday that Seoul should ​proceed without disruption with ‌the planned transfer, during his term, of ‌wartime operational control, or Opcon, of South Korean forces from the US – a goal he and the government have long held.

citation.title: South Korea president calls for military independence in wake of Trump call to cut joint drills

text:
South Korea president calls for military independence in wake of Trump call to cut joint drills

Related: Trump’s move to gut South Korea alliance is ‘inane, haphazard decision’, lawmakers say “A strong alliance makes the foundation of security stronger, and strengthening our own capabilities increases our value and necessity as an ally,” Lee said in a cabinet meeting, describing the US-South Korea alliance and independent defence as ‌mutually reinforcing. The issue dates back to the Korean war, which ended in an armistice rather than a formal peace treaty in 1953, meaning the two Koreas remain technically at war. US troops have been stationed in South Korea ever since, and the country now hosts Camp Humphreys, the largest American military base outside the US. The two militaries train and operate together closely, including through large-scale annual exercises such as this week’s. Wartime Opcon, the authority to direct South Korean forces if fighting resumes, has rested with the US since the war began, exercised through the head of the allies’ Combined Forces Command, a position that has always been held by an American four-star general.

text:
South Korea president calls for military independence in wake of Trump call to cut joint drills

Seoul regained peacetime control of its own military in 1994, but the wartime authority has become a potent symbol of national sovereignty, and reclaiming it has been one of South Korea’s foremost security goals for more than two decades, repeatedly delayed under successive governments. This week’s now-curtailed drills were meant to help certify South Korea’s readiness to finally take it over, a process Lee has pushed to accelerate since taking office. Lee also called for faster progress on South Korea’s nuclear-powered submarine programme and on developing officers capable of integrated operations for future conflicts. The renewed push follows Trump’s call to make cuts to the planned 10 days of drills that started on Monday under the name Ulchi Freedom Shield, one of two main annual exercises held by South Korea and the US. They were expected to involve about 18,000 South Korean troops, alongside US forces and personnel from 11 of the 18 member states of the United Nations Command (UNC), the multinational body that oversees the 1953 armistice that halted hostilities of the Korean war.

During questioning in the Oval Office on Monday, Trump claimed North Korean leader Kim had responded to his order to the Pentagon but did not provide details. When asked what stage the conversations with Kim were at, Trump said “it’s very positive” but provided no further detail. Trump doubled down on his praise for Kim, saying their ties had reduced tensions. “You see, I’m actually making it much safer. Kim Jong-un has always treated me with great respect,” he said. “I understand him. He understands me.” Trump has previously suspended major US-South Korean military exercises in pursuit of diplomacy with Kim. After his first summit with the North Korean leader in 2018, that year’s Ulchi Freedom Guardian exercise was cancelled, while other drills were suspended or scaled back. The exercises were redesigned and resumed in modified form with changed names. The US president acted despite warnings from US and South Korean military officials that Kim’s regime is learning new battlefield tactics from sending North Korean troops to the Ukraine war.

South Korea city deluged by almost a metre of rain, triggering deadly landslide

Torrential downpours that pounded southern parts of South Korea since Saturday have killed one person and injured four others, officials have confirmed. Heavy rains have been recorded in South Gyeongsang province, including the city of Geoje, where an 800mm (31in) deluge over the weekend triggered a landslide, the interior and safety ministry said. The rain continued on Monday, bringing the cumulative rainfall total to 912mm by 6pm. Police and firefighters rescued three residents from an apartment building hit by the landslide, but one of them was found in cardiac arrest and was later pronounced dead at a hospital, according to Yonhap. Related: Torrential rain and flood kill nine in Japan amid wettest month in decades Two people were injured in Geoje and two others in nearby cities, the ministry said. Geoje received 805.7mm of rain from Saturday through to 8am on Monday, Yonhap reported, while the neighbouring city of Tongyeong received 671.9mm during the same period. Other parts of the province received between 240mm and 340mm of rain.

The heavy rains that have pummelled southern South Korea since Saturday have triggered warnings from authorities, forced about 390 people to evacuate and caused power outages at about 3,580 houses. The Korea Herald quoted weather officials on Tuesday as saying that South Gyeongsang province had received an entire summer’s rainfall in just two days, with record daily rainfall totals in the two cities of Geoje and Tongyeong. text:
Tuesday briefing: What the Simon Levy case tells us about the women the justice system keeps failing

Good morning. Last week, Simon Levy, a registered sex offender, was sentenced to a rare whole life tariff for the murders of Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo and Sheryl Wilkins. Both women, as well as others targeted by Levy, were vulnerable and involved in sex work. This was no coincidence: in the sentencing remarks, it was noted that Levy – who had a history of sexual offending dating back to 2018 – selected women who sold sex as his victims because he believed he could get away with it. In the end, he couldn’t. But why did Levy – like so many sexual predators before him – assume that he could harm women involved in prostitution with impunity? Amid the diligent and necessary coverage of the police and prosecution failings that left Levy free to kill and kill again, that question was overlooked. Victims and campaigners alike have raised concerns over the way the justice system treats the experiences of such women. I’d argue that, for decades, we have been overlooking violence against sex workers. That’s the subject of today’s newsletter – but first, the headlines.

In depth: The women who tell us where the danger is are being ignored A brief reflection on our media: this is the first instance I can recall in a case like this where victims were referred to as “women” first, and “sex workers” second in the majority of reporting. Coverage centred on the love in their lives, not the chaos: Carmenza’s excitement at becoming a grandmother, and Sheryl, a mother of four with “so many hopes and dreams”. And a third woman, named “ED” to protect her anonymity, who survived a brutal attack to give damning testimony: she was a classical pianist, trafficked from eastern Europe, who vowed in court “I will play music again and smile”. But here are the bald facts: women who sell sex face endemic levels of violence, and are often reluctant to report to the police because they don’t trust them to take their complaints seriously. National Ugly Mugs (NUM), a UK-wide charity working with sex workers, allows women to report violence, including anonymously, and sign up for alerts about clients to avoid.

citation.title: Tuesday briefing: What the Simon Levy case tells us about the women the justice system keeps failing

text:
Tuesday briefing: What the Simon Levy case tells us about the women the justice system keeps failing

The charity says that last year, they processed 1,047 reports of varying severities of violence, but only 8% of those women consented to sharing these incidents with the police. A year before that, in 2024, a snapshot survey of women involved in prostitution across Scotland found that 90% had experienced violence, including attempted murder, while a quarter had been sexually abused as children and a sixth sexually exploited before the age of 18. That study was published around the time that Iain Packer, another serial violent offender, was jailed for 36 years for the 2005 murder of Emma Caldwell and a catalogue of sexual violence against 22 other vulnerable women working in Glasgow. The case exposed chronic police failings, finding a dismissive attitude among the police towards women selling sex, and that they had normalised the violence sex workers encountered at the hands of the men paying them. Twenty years later, policing strategy has moved on significantly – overall guidance now follows a harm reduction model, and aims to prioritise the safety of women involved.

citation.title: Tuesday briefing: What the Simon Levy case tells us about the women the justice system keeps failing

text:
Tuesday briefing: What the Simon Levy case tells us about the women the justice system keeps failing

But the daily reality is that many women say this hasn’t filtered down to frontline policing and, while the focus is supposed to be on men buying sex, it’s women who are given cautions, fines, or arrested. *** What happened to the women who worked alongside Simon Levy’s victims? Sheryl Wilkins was murdered by Simon Levy in a Tottenham car park in August 2025, where he violently raped “ED” earlier that year. But women working alongside Wilkins had been complaining about police treatment for a year before her death, as local officers implemented ‘Clear, Hold, Build’: a national framework introduced in 2023 to tackle organised crime, which has since been used for lower-level antisocial behaviour, including begging, drug dealing and street-based sex work. ‘Closure zones’ were introduced to clear specific areas – including the same Tottenham car park – with women arrested and fined for breaching them. Police argue that the strategy was designed with safety in mind, including sign-posting women to better-lit areas.

citation.title: Tuesday briefing: What the Simon Levy case tells us about the women the justice system keeps failing

text:
Tuesday briefing: What the Simon Levy case tells us about the women the justice system keeps failing

Niki Adams, of the English Collective of Prostitutes (ECP), says that women were pushed into more isolated, unlit areas. “Women try to work in pairs, so they can indicate to somebody else when they’re getting into a man’s car.” The new strategy, Adams says, broke up that arrangement. This included Sheryl Wilkins, who had been displaced from her regular spot on Fore Street. “The other women that were working with her felt outraged and upset when she was killed, because they felt that it was a direct result of this policing”. More broadly, if women feel they are on the run from the police, it affects their ability to take regular clients. By law, while exchanging sexual services for money is legal, soliciting such work is illegal. “When you’re in that situation, with pressure to earn a certain amount of money for whatever reason, you’re more likely to go with people that you otherwise would have been wary of,” says Adams. Crucially, this deprives the police of vital intelligence.

citation.title: Tuesday briefing: What the Simon Levy case tells us about the women the justice system keeps failing

text:
Tuesday briefing: What the Simon Levy case tells us about the women the justice system keeps failing

“If you have a better relationship with the police, those smaller incidents get reported and a picture starts to build up if there’s a particular predator in the area,” says Adams. Since the murders of Valencia-Trujillo and Wilkins, the Met has sent specialist officers to the area with the express purpose of repairing mistrust, working alongside local charities to offer support with personal safety, housing and healthcare. *** Who is involved? Support agencies have been saying for some years that the group of women who sell sex is becoming increasingly diverse, as family budgets tighten during the cost of living crisis. While data is difficult to collect, estimates suggest a significant majority are mothers supporting dependent children. ECP and NUM report growing numbers of women seeking out their support services and, in a new development, some returning to prostitution having left it previously.

citation.title: Tuesday briefing: What the Simon Levy case tells us about the women the justice system keeps failing

Online adverts have changed how clients are sourced, with support groups saying the biggest threat to safety remains the fact that women risk arrest by working together indoors, pushing more of their work on to the streets. *** What would actually make women safer? Groups like ECP and NUM argue that decriminalising prostitution is the best way to protect women; others maintain that the focus must be on criminalising men who buy sex. It’s a debate that has polarised those who might otherwise be sisters in arms in the fight against violence against women and girls for decades. Belinda Brooks-Gordon, professor of forensic psychology at Birkbeck, has researched this territory and assessed the tides of policymaking for decades. She recalls writing to the national media with other academics in early 2006, in protest at the then Labour government’s plans to shelve managed tolerance zones in favour of a hardline approach to prostitution. “We were saying ‘this is really dangerous for women on the street’. They piloted a clampdown strategy in six cities, one of which was Ipswich.

Tuesday briefing: What the Simon Levy case tells us about the women the justice system keeps failing

And tragically, in the autumn of that year, five women were murdered there.” Brooks-Gordon is an adviser to the National Police Chiefs’ Council’s lead on sex work and trafficking, and bears witness to a hollowing out of funding, which has affected creative pilots and even surveillance of those on the sex offender register – which Levy was on – over the decades. “You’ve got a lot of energetic, well-meaning, and highly trained people wanting to do the best they can, and the resources they’re given are thinner and thinner,” she says. She recalls the Holbeck experiment set up in Leeds in 2014 and discontinued in 2021, which allowed street sex workers to operate freely in the area without fear of arrest between the hours of 8pm and 6am, but became the focus of ongoing protests by local residents for antisocial behaviour. “You have to address residents’ complaints, but where these managed zones operate they save lives – we know that from the Netherlands,” says Brooks-Gordon.

The Merseyside model, which has now been running for 20 years, treats violence against women selling sex as a hate crime and boasted a 67% success rate for rape convictions against sex workers after its first decade. But that work has not been adopted at national level. NUM is involved with an education programme for police forces about the benefits of community liaison roles. “A lot of really good work is being done on liaison,’ says chief executive Lynsey Walton, “but even if you have the best practice in place, it’s only in recent years that sex workers have been spoken to at all, so it’s very hard to retrospectively build that trust.” But doing so, as the Levy case brings home yet again, can be a matter for life and death. “How can our criminal justice system effectively identify and stop serial perpetrators if the people they target don’t feel sufficiently safe to engage with it?” says Walton.

‘Our task is to laugh at these enemies’: the Ukrainian unit posting drone videos of Russian soldiers’ last moments

To many observers they will appear dehumanising and offensive. To many Ukrainians, however, they are a brutal reminder of the fate that awaits Russian soldiers who take part in Vladimir Putin’s invasion, as well as a potent propaganda weapon. Over the past year and a half, videos of kamikaze drones chasing Russian service personnel to their deaths have become a distinctive genre on social media. They are the brainchild of Robert Brovdi, the head of Ukraine’s unmanned systems forces and founder of “Magyar’s Birds”, named after his call sign. Brovdi’s 414th aviation strike brigade has pioneered the use of battlefield video, much of it recorded by first-person-view drones. The death videos are known as yoblyks, a portmanteau that combines the root of the Ukrainian for “fuck” with an affectionate diminutive form. The closest English translation is probably “fuckling”.

text:
‘Our task is to laugh at these enemies’: the Ukrainian unit posting drone videos of Russian soldiers’ last moments

Early each morning, a military editor known by his call sign Catman sifts through battlefield clips recorded the previous day, selecting some for a two-minute compilation and adding pulsing or mystical music. A longer online reel is titled “Yoblyks of the Week”. Defending his work, Catman said the videos played an important role in demoralising ordinary Russians and revealing the true cost of the Kremlin’s unprovoked war. “My goal is to show Russians that if they mobilise in Ukraine they will be killed, that it’s a one-way ticket and death is waiting for them,” he said. He acknowledged that the clips were deliberately arranged to mock the victims, who are sometimes seen throwing sticks at the drones to try to knock them off course, or falling over as they run. Though the moment of death is not shown, the last frame is a closeup of a soldier’s face. “We have a phrase: laughter kills fear. Our main task is to laugh at these enemies and to depict them as helpless. This boosts the morale of our forces,” he said. “It’s impossible for me to feel sorry for them.

citation.title: ‘Our task is to laugh at these enemies’: the Ukrainian unit posting drone videos of Russian soldiers’ last moments

text:
‘Our task is to laugh at these enemies’: the Ukrainian unit posting drone videos of Russian soldiers’ last moments

It’s war, after all, not a movie.” Typically, the Russian soldiers are killed while walking or travelling by motorbike to the frontline. Some are unaware they are at risk from drones, Catman said, and appear to have been tricked by their commanders. “Their training is short. A lot die just two weeks after enlisting,” he said. He described most of the soldiers as “banal donkey men” ordered to carry provisions or fuel to exposed Russian positions. Others drag communication cables. Since February, when Elon Musk shut down his satellite internet service Starlink in Russia, officers in the rear have struggled to contact frontline units. Another member of Magyar’s Birds said there was compelling evidence the Russians were routinely misled about dangers. “You can see from the videos a lot of them are not even hiding,” he said. “They use their radio sets. A large number are fooled by the lie that everything will be OK, that they are going to their positions and are totally safe.” The brigade has an archive of about 3,600 videos.

text:
‘Our task is to laugh at these enemies’: the Ukrainian unit posting drone videos of Russian soldiers’ last moments

Only two feature women, both wearing combat uniform and carrying assault rifles. “There is no difference for me. They are all enemies,” Catman said. The videos play an important part in verifying Russian losses, which are running at more than 30,000 soldiers a month killed or injured, according to Kyiv. Brovdi said he had no qualms about publishing material that many in the west might find distasteful and morally dubious. “God forbid they should ever experience pain. Because those of us in Ukraine who have experienced real physical pain from war would never agree with that perspective,” he said. In daily posts, Brovdi uses language that some might find gratuitous, for instance describing Russians as “worms” pecked by “birds”. He said: “When the war started, everything changed. There was a desire to humiliate the enemy as much as possible, not with typical words but exotic ones. It was only natural that military technical folklore and coinages such as ‘yoblyk’ found their way into my speech. They existed before AI.” The videos have sparked several trolling subgenres.

Some Russian women post photos of themselves saying farewell to their husbands as they leave to take part in what Putin calls a “special military operation”. Ukrainians identify the men and subsequently reply with drone footage showing their deaths. According to Catman, the yoblyks have a wide audience, including inside Russia. “There is very little information there about soldiers who go missing. Some people search and take screenshots. Mothers or wives then post messages saying something bad has happened to their loved ones,” he said. Other videos show the killing of unarmed Ukrainian prisoners of war – a crime. The Russian internet includes AI-generated fakes that purport to show Ukrainian military personnel criticising their army leadership.

Anatolii Loza, a Ukrainian volunteer who was captured and imprisoned by Russia and recently swapped, said he saw nothing wrong with yoblyks. “International law doesn’t apply to killing combatants on the field of battle,” he said. “The Russians come to shoot our soldiers and civilians. They are wearing uniform. They deserve their fate.” Loza’s wife, Olena, said attitudes inside Ukraine hardened after spring 2022, when Russian forces killed hundreds of civilians in the cities of Bucha and Mariupol, leaving their bodies on the streets. Of yoblyks, she said: “I don’t find these videos informative. I’m already furious with Russia.” At the HQ of Magyar’s Birds, Catman said black humour was essential during wartime. “It’s important for our own people to say we are not just surviving. We need to show we are flourishing and hitting back hard against the enemy.” Betrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest, by Luke Harding, is published on 27 August by Guardian Faber. Ukraine’s dismissed defence minister calls for wartime presidential election

Ukraine’s recently dismissed former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov has called for a wartime presidential election in the most direct political challenge to Volodymyr Zelenskyy since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. The politician, whose abrupt sacking last month triggered a wave of protests, said that Ukraine had to “restore a full democratic process even amid a prolonged war” in a video address released online late on Tuesday evening. “Democracy cannot be held hostage by Russia. We are fighting precisely because we want to remain a free European state,” Fedorov said in his nine-minute speech. Though he did not mention Zelenskyy by name, Fedorov implied the current president presided over a poorly functioning state that was struggling to tackle corruption despite the national emergency. “People cannot endlessly live in a state where they do not understand why certain decisions are made. Why some reforms move forward while others are blocked,” Fedorov said, arguing that Ukraine could fight a war and hold a national poll.

“It is particularly dangerous when society develops the feeling that the main criterion for an appointment is not professionalism, results or the ability to transform the country, but personal loyalty to the system,” he said. Elections have been suspended in Ukraine since martial law was imposed at the start of the full-scale invasion by Russia. Zelenskyy’s five-year term ended in May 2024 but there has been little desire in Ukraine to hold a contest while war continues. The US president, Donald Trump, has previously demanded that Ukraine hold an election, though his once-fraught relationship with Zelenskyy has gradually improved over the past year as Kyiv has shown it can hold its own on the battlefield. Fedorov, 35, was Ukraine’s digital minister from 2019 until January, fronting the country’s wartime adoption of drones, before briefly serving in what was considered to be a successful stint as defence minister until July.

text:
Activist forced out of US after criticising Trump-aligned Colombian politician

In the week before Colombia’s presidential election, Beto Coral, a well-known activist living in the United States, travelled to Florida to persuade fellow Colombians not to vote for the far-right candidate Abelardo de la Espriella. Coral held banners outside polling stations in Miami warning that the millionaire lawyer, whose candidacy was endorsed by Donald Trump, would “help deport all of you”. The following morning the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, issued a memo to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) alleging that the activist had used his presence in the country “to conduct political activity” against a Colombian presidential candidate, and that DHS could take steps to “facilitate his departure”. Hours later, Coral was arrested. He said that, over the following 30 days in DHS detention, he was assaulted, deprived of food and water, and held in solitary confinement before securing his voluntary departure back to Colombia in mid-July, after more than 10 years living in the US.

Although other immigrants have previously been detained in the US over their political activism – most notably the Palestinian student Mahmoud Khalil for protesting against the war in Gaza – Coral’s case is being seen as the first involving remarks about a foreign election. “They detained me simply because I protested against a Trump-backed candidate,” said the 40-year-old activist, whose full name is Franklin Humberto Coral Garrido. Coral, who has no criminal record, alleges that his detention resulted from a request by De la Espriella, who went on to win the election and was sworn in earlier this month to replace the leftwing president Gustavo Petro, with whom Trump had repeatedly clashed. In early June the US deputy secretary of state, Christopher Landau, wrote on social media about Colombia’s election that those “tempted to undermine or manipulate the democratic process” were putting their visas at risk. “That’s why they call me El Quitavisas (the visa taker)”, he added.

The US state department and De la Espriella did not respond to requests for comment. Colombia’s new president already knew the activist from his years as a lawyer. Adviser to far-right Latin American leaders arrested for allegedly plotting to kill girlfriend

A senior adviser to many of Latin America’s new wave of far-right leaders has been arrested for allegedly masterminding the attempted murder of his girlfriend. The businessman and political consultant Fernando Cerimedo, 42, had been working as an adviser to the Bolivian president, Rodrigo Paz Pereira, and was one of the main strategists behind Javier Milei’s campaign in Argentina’s 2023 presidential election. He has previously been described as Maga’s man in Latin America – a reference to Donald Trump’s Make America Great Again movement – and is credited with helping secure the US president’s endorsement of the rightwing Nasry “Tito” Asfura, who won Honduras’s presidential election in December. On Tuesday morning, Cerimedo landed in Santa Cruz de la Sierra, in Bolivia, and was arrested before boarding another flight reportedly bound for Buenos Aires, Argentina. According to police, he was detained on suspicion of ordering a gun attack on Nadia Beller, a Bolivian lawyer who local media reported had been in a relationship with Cerimedo – who is married – since last year.

Beller told police she had been lured to the hotel after receiving anonymous messages promising to hand over evidence of alleged crimes committed by Bolivia’s leftwing former president Evo Morales, who is subject to two outstanding arrest warrants and remains sheltered in a coca-growing region. Beller said she believed the attack had been a trap orchestrated by Cerimedo. France’s ‘aid in dying’ law comes into effect after constitutional approval

Legislation granting incurably ill adults the right to assisted dying has been formally adopted in France after the text was approved by the country’s highest constitutional authority and published in the official journal. The law, known as a law on “end of life” or “aid in dying” rather than “assisted dying” or “euthanasia”, means France joins the small group of countries including the Netherlands, Belgium, Switzerland and Canada to have legalised the practice. Published on Wednesday after years of debate, it establishes a right to assisted dying for patients of legal age who are French nationals or long-term residents and suffering from conditions that are assessed as incurable and are causing unbearable pain. A doctor must verify the patient’s eligibility before a panel assesses whether the criteria have been met. Once approval has been granted, patients must wait at least two days before the procedure can take place and confirm their decision on the day.

citation.title: France’s ‘aid in dying’ law comes into effect after constitutional approval

text:
France’s ‘aid in dying’ law comes into effect after constitutional approval

The patient may withdraw consent at any time and must administer the lethal substance themselves unless they are physically unable to do so, in which case a healthcare worker can help. Until now France has allowed passive euthanasia – such as withholding artificial life support – and deep sedation before death, but people seeking active end-of-life options have been forced to travel to other countries where assisted dying is legal. Emmanuel Macron, who promised a right-to-die law in his 2022 re-election campaign, welcomed the news, which he said “concludes an exemplary democratic debate”, while the text’s author, a centrist MP, called it “a major step forward”. Macron’s office added that the law provided “an essential guarantee for our fellow citizens” and could now be implemented “in the certainty that it rests on fully established democratic, ethical and constitutional foundations”.

However, the Jérôme Lejeune Foundation, which provides lifetime care to people with genetic intellectual disabilities such as Down’s syndrome, expressed “outrage” and other campaigners said the law posed “an absolute danger to the most vulnerable”. All parliamentarians were given a free vote to express their personal convictions during the debate. Euthanasia is a controversial subject in France, which has a longstanding Catholic tradition, while the bill was also opposed by some health workers. The publication in the official journal follows several legal challenges, with critics arguing that the minimum two-day reflection period was too short and that entire healthcare institutions should be able to refuse on grounds of conscience. France’s constitutional council upheld the law in its entirety last Friday but ruled that certain provisions needed clarification, including the “conscience clause”, which will allow healthcare professionals to refuse to take part in the procedure.

That clause must also apply to private, typically faith-based healthcare facilities where assisted dying is “manifestly contrary” to their mission, it said, providing they were not the only establishments able to meet “local needs”.

text:
Germany’s firewall was meant to hold the far right at bay. It may have done the reverse

In just over two weeks’ time, Saxony-Anhalt – home to historic timber-framed houses, the dramatic Harz mountains and the birthplace of Martin Luther – will hold what could prove one of the most significant state elections in Germany’s postwar history. The vote, on 6 September, could see a far-right party whose local branch is officially classified by the country’s domestic intelligence service as “confirmed rightwing extremist” appoint a state premier and govern a state alone, for the first time. That could have big consequences for both Germany and Europe. With more state elections a fortnight later in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin, it could also end the consensus that, since the second world war, has kept the far right at bay in Germany. The far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has led most German national polls since April last year. It is comfortably ahead in eastern Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, and is even second in famously liberal Berlin.

citation.title: Germany’s firewall was meant to hold the far right at bay. It may have done the reverse

text:
Germany’s firewall was meant to hold the far right at bay. It may have done the reverse

In Saxony-Anhalt, the party – which dabbles in Nazi imagery, differentiates between “biological” and “passport” Germans, and whose rhetoric and policies are often way more extreme than many other EU far-right parties – is polling at up to 42%. Under Germany’s proportional representation threshold, which excludes parties that capture less than 5% of the vote, a score in the low-to-mid 40s could quite conceivably secure AfD an absolute majority in the Saxony-Anhalt parliament. As the Centre for Strategic and International Studies points out, that would have an immediate domestic impact. Germany’s 16 states exercise constitutional authority over education, policing, public broadcasting and regional civil administration. AfD’s proposed state-level measures include revising the school history curriculum to emphasise Germany’s “achievements” over its wartime crimes, defunding anti-racism initiatives, removing pride flags and rewriting the mandates of public TV and radio.

citation.title: Germany’s firewall was meant to hold the far right at bay. It may have done the reverse

text:
Germany’s firewall was meant to hold the far right at bay. It may have done the reverse

An AfD government could exploit state-level public recruitment criteria and make political appointments favouring ideologically aligned candidates, and, more broadly, create an intimidating environment where state employees prefer silence to conflict. At the federal level, winning a state government would also give the AfD seats in the Bundesrat upper house representing the states. That would not allow it to block legislation unilaterally, but it could table new policy initiatives and disrupt consensus. With no need to deliver actual results, it can promise voters whatever it likes (and it does). That, of course, has made it even more appealing. It doesn’t matter that crime is decreasing: most people, when asked, seem to think it’s on the rise. This is the finding of a study from King’s College London published earlier this week, which surveyed nearly 4,000 people in Britain. It found perceptions of crime far removed from reality and shaped more by feelings than by facts. Reform voters are most likely to believe that crime is a growing problem, and many of them think that most people convicted of homicide are ethnic minorities (they aren’t). This isn’t confined to one party, though: the public as a whole tends to wrongly assume most people convicted of homicide are from an ethnic minority when they are not, and to think crime is going up when it isn’t, according to the study. The boy behind the Baby Shark phenomenon: I used to hum it without even realising

“I just remember having fun dancing and playing on what felt like a huge set,” Geonroung Park says, recalling the day 10 years ago when he was filmed, aged seven, doing the hand movements to a children’s song about a family of sharks. That footage became Baby Shark Dance, now the most-watched video in YouTube’s history. It has racked up more than 17.2bn views and has held the platform’s global no 1 spot for 69 consecutive months. Despite becoming one of the most recognisable faces online, growing up as “the Baby Shark kid” was, Park says, mostly ordinary. Friends at school knew about the video and thought it was “cool”, but otherwise treated him much like everyone else. Related: Scared of Baby Shark? A short guide to the year’s most annoying song He remembers the song staying stuck in his head for a while after filming wrapped, catching himself humming it “without even realising it”. He found fame in a song, yet almost nobody has actually heard Park sing. The vocals belonged to another child performer. Now 17, Park is keen to change that.

More than 100 dead after goldmine collapses in Central African Republic

More than 100 people have died after an artisanal goldmine at a small village in western Central African Republic (CAR) caved in due to a landslide, local officials and aid workers said on Wednesday. The landslide happened on Tuesday afternoon in the village of Zamboye, about 50km (31 miles) from the town of Baboua and close to the border of Cameroon. Footage on social media appeared to show an avalanche of sand descend on a group of people, likely the miners, and cover them. A statement by a local public prosecutor said many others were trapped under the deluge. It did not mention the number of fatalities. However, Gervais Ganagoroh, a Red Cross volunteer involved in the relief effort, told the Associated Press news agency on Wednesday that more than 100 bodies had been recovered from the collapse and ⁠a senior official at a local mining association confirmed that number to Reuters. Related: ‘We’re hungry, there are no jobs’: a South African township’s desperate gold rush Local media in CAR reported that authorities had launched an investigation into the incident.

Rescuers are racing to retrieve the bodies of victims and find survivors among the miners, believed to be nationals of CAR and Cameroon. Authorities in Cameroon’s Eastern region said at least three of its citizens have been identified as victims in the incident. Bertrand Be Yangué, a member of the Zamboye youth council, said that “finding them alive would be a miracle.” He added: “We are saddened and heartbroken to see young men and women perish after coming to the mines to save their families from despair.” The toll is expected to rise as the rescue efforts continue, added Yangué.

Pakistan’s jailed former prime minister Imran Khan was briefly taken to a hospital in the country’s capital on supreme court orders after weeks of uproar about his deteriorating health. An 84-year-old woman has been discovered alive in the flattened remains of her home three days after a powerful earthquake hit eastern Indonesia, authorities have confirmed. The 7.7-magnitude quake struck off Indonesia’s Flores island on Saturday morning, killing at least 73 people, injuring more than 900 people and displacing nearly 60,000 others. A landslide triggered by the quake had blocked access to Nitunglea village where Paulina Pobi, 84, lived, leaving the elderly woman buried for three days under the collapsed bamboo walls of her home until Tuesday. Israel’s far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, has posted a gloating video of the construction of a gallows complex where Palestinians convicted of terror offences – but not Jewish extremists accused of similar crimes – will be hanged. Ben-Givr, who has previously attracted international sanctions and condemnation for his activities, said the new execution site would be equipped with viewing booths for families of victims to watch the hangings. He posted the video on social media of a visit he had made to the unidentified location, where he can be seen pointing at foundations being laid and boasting it was where “terrorists will be executed”. Photographs in the Israeli media showed a bulldozer and heavy construction work in a cordoned-off area, reportedly close to a prison. “I promised to worsen the conditions of terrorists in prisons – we kept it,” said Ben-Gvir in the video. “I promised to pass the Death Penalty for Terrorists law – we did.

The mayor of Como has set the wheels of controversy in motion for banning bikes in the walled historical centre of the lakeside city after being hit by one. Alessandro Rapinese’s ban, which comes into force in September, targets about 30 streets and means cyclists, whether on e-bikes or push bikes, will have to dismount and walk through those areas. Rapinese immediately came under fire, with resident groups and politicians from across the spectrum accusing him of waging a personal vendetta. Activists have started a petition calling for him to overturn the rule and cyclists are planning to ride their bikes through the specified streets in mid-September in protest. Defending his decision, Rapinese told Ansa: “I’ve been accused of adopting this measure because I was hit by an electric bike – certainly, that is true.

Mark Zuckerberg buys 440-acre Strancally castle estate in Ireland

It stretches the definition of pied-à-terre but Mark Zuckerberg now has a pad in Ireland: Strancally castle. The Meta chief executive and his wife, Priscilla Chan, have bought the gothic-style mansion and its 178-hectare (440-acre) estate in county Waterford to use as a base during visits to Ireland. “Mark and his family are excited to continue caring for this historic home and look forward to spending time in Ireland, where Meta maintains its international headquarters,” a spokesperson said on Thursday. The price paid in the off-market deal is not known but the Irish Times, which first reported the sale, estimated a value between €20m (£17m) and €30m: approximately 10% of the cost of his 387ft superyacht. The castle was built in 1830 for John Keily, a former Conservative MP, and designed on a lavish scale by the architects James and George Richard Pain, with a “brisk walk of four and a half minutes” needed to go from the dining room to the kitchen, according to the book The Houses of Ireland.

The South Australian premier, Peter Malinauskas, has declared a “significant escalation” in H5 bird flu in the state after the detection of three mass mortality events involving more than 1,000 greater crested terns. Malinauskas said the cause of the deaths was presumed to be H5 bird flu. State authorities were also investigating a suspected case in a little penguin found on Kangaroo Island, with the premier telling the state parliament the development was of “particular concern”. Separately, the Tasmanian government said it was investigating 28 little penguin deaths on King Island with testing under way to determine whether the birds died of H5 bird flu. text:
Thursday briefing: The million young people the UK is leaving behind

Good morning. Thousands of young people will be arriving at school in the next few hours to collect their GCSE results. Many will continue to sixth form, others will be heading to apprenticeships, and some will spend the next few years relentlessly pitching their CVs to AI bots. An estimated one million young people in the UK aged 16 to 24 are not in education, employment or training of any kind. These “Neets”, as they’re known, have preoccupied policymakers since the early 1990s. But their number is now higher than ever, an indication of economic inactivity, low growth and rising welfare costs that worry civil servants in Whitehall. Alan Milburn, formerly health secretary under Tony Blair’s government, is now conducting a high-profile review of Neets. His final report is expected later this year. The Neet issue exemplifies how an increasingly unhappy, isolated generation of young people are becoming detached from social institutions and losing faith in their own futures.

In depth: A generation falling through the cracks First, a brief note on language: nobody ever calls themselves a “Neet”. In May, Milburn published his interim report, which found that the UK has the second-highest rate of Neets in Europe, after Romania. An accompanying paper, Inside the Mind of a Young Neet, featured snippets from conversations with more than 400 young people who were out of work and education. Its authors heard from a 22-year-old who was competing in archery contests, a gardening fanatic who had taught themselves how to make raised beds, and an aspiring linguist who could read Latin and crochet flower baskets. These are skilled young people with huge potential and meaningful lives. The problem lies in a system that is failing them. Broadly, there are two explanations for why so many young people today aren’t in work or education. The first is the labour market.

Businesses have argued that rising national insurance contributions are deterring firms from hiring young workers, while others have speculated that AI is destroying entry-level jobs. The second, more troubling explanation, is the striking number of young people who are unwell or have poor mental health. The proportion of 18 to 24-year-olds with a long-term, limiting health condition has increased by 42% since 2019, while the number of 20 to 24-year-olds prescribed antidepressants increased by almost a third between 2015 and 2021. Britain now has the highest rate of anxiety and depressive disorders among 15 to 24-year-olds in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. “We often talk about the relationship between the labour market and poor health as being ‘bi-directional’,” Mon-Williams explains. People who are out of work are more likely to feel anxious or depressed, he says, while past experiences of anxiety or depression can become a barrier to entering the workforce. “Both come into play, which is why it’s so complex.” What emerges from these figures is a picture of generational misery.

Thursday briefing: The million young people the UK is leaving behind

As Mon-Williams puts it: “I really think we need to take a step back, take a good hard look at ourselves as a country, and ask : what on earth have we allowed to happen?” *** Why are young people so unhappy? There’s a tendency (particularly among ageing right-wing commentators who depend on young people paying taxes that fund the NHS and state pensions) to blame these rates of ill-health on a culture of over-diagnosis among self-indulgent “snowflakes”. The Born in Bradford study refutes this myth. Mon-Williams and other researchers have access to the health records of 13,500 young people born in 2007, from pregnancy through to the present day, as well as data about their mental health. Many participants suffering from mental ill health struggle to get any support. “The evidence shows that there’s a genuine mental health epidemic among that generation,” he says. “These are warning signs. Pity the country that doesn’t take them seriously.” Nor are Neets work-shy, or choosing to live off benefits rather than find a job. Most want to be in work or education.

Thursday briefing: The million young people the UK is leaving behind

About 314,000 of them are not receiving any benefits at all, and have effectively disappeared from the system. As Milburn put it in his interim report, caricatures of a generation uninterested in employment or using mental health as an excuse “are myths. Sometimes cruel ones.” Researchers have identified multiple reasons for growing rates of mental ill-health among young people, including financial precarity, housing insecurity, drastic cuts to youth clubs and youth workers, rising social media use and broken sleep (while compiling his interim report, a group of teenagers told Milburn they went to bed between midnight and three each night because they were scrolling on their phones). The disciplinary, top-button-obsessed culture of many academy schools can also contribute to these problems by excluding children with complex needs or neurodivergence, making it more likely they become a Neet later. “When you exclude a child, you’re consigning them to the probability of having a rubbish life,” Mon-Williams tells me. *** Has the pandemic made this worse?

The pandemic aggravated an ongoing mental health crisis, cutting many young people off from school and severing their friendships and social bonds. In his Born in Bradford data, Mon-Williams found a striking increase in the number of children who were absent from school after Covid. “Pre-pandemic, in Bradford, we had 3,000 children who were persistently absent,” he says. “Post-pandemic, that went up to 30,000. That’s a hugely worrying statistic.” Many young people missed out on opportunities to learn both academically and socially. “I lost the social aspect of connecting with people … maintaining eye contact, hand gestures and all sorts,” one young person told the Inside the Mind of a Neet researchers. For some, patterns cultivated in lockdown – long nights spent online, disrupted sleep patterns, minimal social contact and eroded routines – morphed into a semi-permanent stasis. *** What needs to change? Milburn’s interim findings acknowledges that there needs to be a “system reset”.

Donald Trump has announced a new campaign to isolate Iran’s economy, threatening “tremendous economic consequences” on any country that helps or does business with Tehran, a move that could set up a fresh confrontation with China if implemented. “Today, I am announcing the most crushing economic operation ever taken against any country!” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “Any country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran will itself face tremendous economic consequences.” His announcement however contained no detail on what actions would be taken or which countries could be affected, and comes as the war nears its six-month mark, with the president facing pressure over the cost of the conflict as the US midterm elections approach. A heavy Russian missile and drone bombardment has killed at least 16 people in and around Kyiv in one of the most intense aerial attacks on Ukraine’s capital since the start of the war. Vitali Klitschko, the city’s mayor, said homes, a school and a children’s medical centre were among the buildings damaged overnight in an attack that began at about midnight and was continuing into the early afternoon. The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said: “It was a massive attack – the Russians had been preparing for a long time, combining different types of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones, aiming to cause as much damage as possible to civilian infrastructure.” Explosions could be clearly heard from the city centre within minutes of the first warning at 11.51pm on Wednesday, earlier than the normal timing of Russian missile strikes. ‘Like a seagull in a stiff breeze’: what it’s like flying into Wellington, the world’s windiest city

It had been a smooth late-July flight from Auckland, until the plane started its descent into Wellington. Then the bumps and swaying began. “The more we went down, the rockier it got,” says Laura, a Wellington resident who wished to give her first name only. “There was one point where we must have got a horrible cross-wind and it felt like the plane was about to flip over. At that point, the entire flight screamed.” “I genuinely felt like I was about to die, which was pretty awful … and I had eaten a horrible burger before going on the plane – that all came back up.” The plane lurched back up into the sky. The pilot announced the weather was set to worsen and the plane returned to Auckland. Related: Flight paths and fridge magnets: how a fireball hunter tracked down New Zealand’s newest meteorite “We often call it a ‘Welly welcome’ when you get a bumpy landing, but this was a different level of scary, and obviously the pilots knew that because they didn’t land and didn’t try to do it again,” Laura says. Anyone who has frequently flown into New Zealand’s capital has a story to tell.

‘Like a seagull in a stiff breeze’: what it’s like flying into Wellington, the world’s windiest city

Wellington is the world’s windiest city, with an annual average wind speed of 29km/h. The city sits on the Cook Strait, a passage between New Zealand’s North and South Islands, making it prone to high winds that can compound around the airport, which is flanked by hills. This year’s “super” El Niño, a label assigned when sea surface temperatures climb by at least 2C, will be the strongest of the century, and that could intensify Wellington’s winds, as the city heads into spring – the windiest season. “There were some El Niños in the past where it’s ended up being very windy in Wellington … so we expect it to be windier and more westerly than normal,” says Dr Richard Turner, a research meteorologist at Earth Sciences. “I think those landings are probably going to be a little bit bumpy for the next few months.” ‘You think about your life a little bit as it comes down’ For many, the descent into Wellington can feel akin to sitting in a tiny boat as it’s thrown around on an angry sea. It is not uncommon to hear passengers gasping, praying or vomiting.

Without action wildfires in Europe will increase 39% even in best-case climate scenario, study finds

Wildfires are projected to burn 39% more of Europe by the end of the century even in the best-case scenario for stopping the planet from heating, a study has found, unless action is taken to manage them better. The increase in hot, dry and windy weather that leads to small fires turning into raging infernos is to engulf more of Europe as carbon pollution pushes temperatures higher. In the worst-case scenario the researchers modelled, which would see global heating reach 3.6C above preindustrial levels, the burnt area would almost triple. Improvements in fire management could moderate those increases by more than 70%, the study found, but not eradicate them entirely. “Investments into fire management could help to a certain limit, but if we go on a path of high emissions … we still see strong increases in burnt area,” said Maik Billing, an ecosystem researcher at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK) and lead author of the study.

Across the EU, this fire season is set to become the third-worst on record, behind 2025 and 2022, according to data published by the European Forest Fire Information Service on Thursday. More than 600,000 hectares have burned so far, with records broken for this time of year in Belgium, France and Slovakia. text:
Anxiety over war, wildfires and cyber-attacks leads to growth in cash stocks in EU

The number of banknotes in circulation in the EU is increasing despite widespread smartphone payments, new data shows, with wildfires ripping through parts of Europe fuelling demand for an emergency stash of cash. While cash plays second fiddle to contactless payments in many cities across Europe, the amount in circulation is actually going up, Philip Lane, the chief economist of the European Central Bank (ECB), said at the MacGill summer school conference in Ireland. The rise of cash has been linked to anxiety over wars and the impact of cyber-attacks on online and contactless payment systems, say experts. “The total stock of banknotes is continuing to grow. In transactions, it [the number of notes] is coming down, but in terms of the stock [it is increasing],” Lane said. Last year Marks & Spencer in the UK suffered a sustained cyber-attack which stopped the retailer taking online orders for weeks.

citation.title: Anxiety over war, wildfires and cyber-attacks leads to growth in cash stocks in EU

text:
Anxiety over war, wildfires and cyber-attacks leads to growth in cash stocks in EU

In 2025 EU residents were advised to stockpile enough food, water and essentials for 72 hours in case of an emergency such as this summer’s catastrophic wildfires in France and Spain, floods or storms as well as potential cyber-attacks or other hostile events. Households were encouraged to have a crisis pack including bottled water, a transistor radio, canned food and, critically, cash. ECB data, which has been tracking the number of bank notes in circulation since 2002, shows that their value has gone up from about €1tn in 2016 to €1.6tn in June 2026. More than 31bn notes are in circulation compared with 24bn just before the pandemic in 2019, with the €50 note the most popular in 2025 followed by the €100. European countries including Austria, Finland, Germany, Sweden and the Netherlands have already recommended that citizens keep between €70 and €100 per household, enough to pay for essentials for 72 hours should online and mobile apps go down.

Gun stash in German forest believed to be linked to Russia, say reports

Germany is seeking to extradite a suspect from Romania over the discovery of an underground stash of weapons in a forest near Berlin that German media reports have linked to Russian intelligence. Two weeks after German authorities found a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig airport, the interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, confirmed federal prosecutors had opened an investigation related to the secret cache of guns “on suspicion of preparing a serious act of violence that threatens national security”. “This case demonstrates that ‌we are operating under a high threat level,” he told reporters. As with the Leipzig incident, Dobrindt said he could not rule out the involvement of “foreign powers”. Earlier, local media had reported that German authorities had unearthed two handguns and ammunition about a year ago in a wooded area outside the German capital after agents of the domestic intelligence service received a tip.

Israeli settler attacks shift focus to West Bank areas under direct Palestinian rule

Violent Israeli settler attacks in the two areas of the occupied West Bank under direct Palestinian rule have almost doubled since 2025, as settlers pursue a self-proclaimed “great settlement revolution” in the very heart of the territory earmarked for a Palestinian state. According to a report by the Israeli human rights organisation Yesh Din, shared with the Guardian, data shows that almost two-thirds of incidents of settler violence so far in 2026 have taken place in the so-called Areas A and B – placed under Palestinian Authority governance in the 1995 Oslo accords. The report, The Next Frontier, Violence by Israeli Civilians in Areas A and B, describes the “rapid shift” in “violence and pressure exerted by the government, military and settlers on Palestinians … from Area C into Areas B and even A”. While all three designated administrative areas on the West Bank were intended under the Oslo peace deal to encompass the shape of a future Palestinian state, successive Israeli governments, driven by the settler movement, have pursued a long-term policy of undermining Palestinian claims.

text:
Mary John obituary

My mother-in-law, Mary John, who has died aged 85, was a developmental psychologist and an instrumental figure in the movements for equal rights for people with disabilities and for the rights of children. Mary found her vocation in the 1970s and 80s, as an academic specialising in disability in the social sciences faculty of the Open University, where she worked closely with Vic Finkelstein. During this time she also served on the US Committee on the Employment of the Handicapped under the Jimmy Carter administration, and helped to set up the European Commission’s Bureau for Action in Favour of Disabled People. In 1992, now at the University of Exeter, Mary hosted the first global conference on children’s rights to involve children themselves, and later edited the book series Children in Charge, which included her own title, Children’s Rights and Power: Charging Up for a New Century (2003). In 1996 she was given a European Woman of Achievement award, and in 1999, the OU awarded Mary an honorary doctorate for her lifetime’s work for disadvantaged people. Born in Wigan, Lancashire, Mary was the daughter of Elvira (nee Evans) and William John, a headteacher.

citation.title: Mary John obituary

text:
Mary John obituary

Aged seven, she was hospitalised with peritonitis and septicaemia, and put in an iron lung. As was medical orthodoxy at the time, her parents were not allowed to visit – but no one explained any of it to Mary. She later wrote she was “a child abandoned, bewildered, drugged, hallucinating and desperately solitary … This child faced the same problems that have beset children in many places, at many times – problems of recognition of her needs, of establishing identity, agency, of managing relationships wisely and richly, of exercising power and of finding a voice that is heard.” After Wigan county high school for girls, Mary studied psychology at the University of Nottingham, graduating in 1962. A Medical Research Council scholarship under Elizabeth and John Newson, who were revolutionising the study of parenting, followed, and in 1966 she completed her PhD on the social adjustment of children. Mary then lectured at Nottingham and Bristol universities, and for seven years at Exeter, before joining the OU in 1974. In 1990 she returned to Exeter as the first female professor of education.

citation.title: Mary John obituary

text:
Mary John obituary

She became dean of education and director of the Women’s Studies Centre in 1995, before being appointed deputy vice-chancellor the following year. After retirement in 1998, Mary continued to work as an author, editor and consultant. Outside work, Mary turned her hand to all kinds of creative endeavours: from a full-size papier-mache pony for her student union ball, to watercolours for friends, and an immaculate pair of curtains that still hang in our window. In 2008, she was learning calligraphy when a stroke left her with severe disabilities. Characteristically, she reflected on her situation from a societal and academic perspective. A marriage to John Croxen in 1964 ended in divorce in 1978. She is survived by her sons, Dan and Adam (my partner), four grandchildren, Cerys, Huw, Martha and Harry, and her sister, Heulwen. Her brother, Gareth, predeceased her.

Strangers in their own land: Mexicans deported from Trump’s America find refuge in ‘Little LA’

With its wide avenues lined with tall palm trees, its quaint cafes and old-school cantinas, as well as the mix of English and Spanish spoken on the street, the Tabacalera neighborhood in downtown Mexico City has a certain US feel – so much so that it is has become known as Little LA. The nickname is about more than appearances, however. In recent years, this corner of the metropolis has become a haven for many Mexicans deported from the US, particularly those who spent years or decades living across the border and for whom Mexico feels like a foreign country. In Little LA, they have found a more familiar place to belong. With the Trump administration embarking on a massive anti-immigrant crackdown, deportations to Mexico are expected to surge. Since taking office for the second time in January 2025, Trump has deported roughly 145,500 Mexican nationals. Christopher Gil Ortíz was one of them. He was on his way to work in Los Angeles in June this year when Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents stopped him, handcuffed him and threw him in detention.

citation.title: Strangers in their own land: Mexicans deported from Trump’s America find refuge in ‘Little LA’

text:
Strangers in their own land: Mexicans deported from Trump’s America find refuge in ‘Little LA’

After months of living in constant fear as an undocumented immigrant in Trump’s US, Ortíz said that when the detention finally happened he felt relieved. “At this point I was like, OK, that’s it, I’m going back,” he recalled. “It’s like they took a weight off my shoulders.” More than 30 years since he had left as a child, Ortíz was sent back to Mexico, leaving behind his wife and two young children. Dumped in the resort town of Tulum, he made his way to Cancún, only to have all his belongings stolen from his hotel room. Eventually, he ended up in Mexico City, where he had family. “I was nervous,” he said. “Even though I was born here, I have very vague memories of the city itself.” He was also facing the many challenges of being a deportee: getting his birth certificate, ID and finding a job. His sister sent him a TikTok post from an organization called New Comienzos (New Beginnings). Based in Little LA, it was set up to help returnees reintegrate. When he saw the post, Ortiz decided to check out Little LA for himself.

text:

“Seeing the palm trees, it kind of does make you feel like you’re in LA,” he said, adding that he was grateful to New Comienzos. “There’s a lot of people that are going through what I’m going through and I’m pretty sure there’s going to be more.” The New Comienzos founder and executive director, Israel Concha, said he was preparing for exactly that. “The atmosphere [in the US] right now is one of humanitarian crisis and panic. People no longer even want to take their children to school,” Concha said. “You’ll probably start seeing mass deportations in a few months.” Concha founded New Comienzos when he witnessed first-hand how little support the Mexican government was offering recent arrivals. In 2012, he was living in Texas with his pregnant wife and had started a successful private transport business. Python named Jodie Foster first snake to receive pioneering cancer treatment

A 15ft (4.5-metre) python is believed to be the first snake in the world to be given a pioneering, life-saving cancer treatment normally used on humans. The 50kg reticulated python, named Jodie Foster after the Hollywood star, has just turned 23 and lives at Chester zoo. Keepers first became concerned that she may be unwell when she began eating less and spending more time inactive in her habitat. She was diagnosed with a fibrosarcoma – a malignant tumour – in her jaw, which was removed with surgery but later returned and began to invade her jawbone. With her life at risk, she underwent electrochemotherapy. Now, months after the procedure, she is said to be eating normally and “back to her usual bright and feisty self”. Pythons can unhinge their jaws to swallow prey many times the size of their head, and in the months since her surgery zoo staff have observed that Jodie continues to strike, grip and swallow food without difficulty.

citation.title: Python named Jodie Foster first snake to receive pioneering cancer treatment

text:
Python named Jodie Foster first snake to receive pioneering cancer treatment

Ian Ashpole, a veterinary officer at the zoo, said: “When the tumour came back and started destroying part of her jawbone, we knew more surgery on its own probably wasn’t going to be enough. “We were facing the possibility of losing her as the tumour made it more and more difficult for her to eat, so we worked with cancer specialists to see whether we could adapt electrochemotherapy for a snake. As far as we’re aware, this is the first time it’s ever been used in one.” Jodie, whose name derives from when she first arrived and staff noticed her paperwork was marked “JF” – shorthand for “juvenile female” – is so big that no single operating table would have been able to accommodate her. Two were pushed together, making a platform the size of a double bed. She was anaesthetised in her own habitat and carefully carried to the zoo’s veterinary centre where she underwent the 90-minute procedure. Ashpole first removed the tumorous mass as well as part of Jodie’s diseased jawbone, before electrochemotherapy was administered to target any remaining cancerous cells.

text:
Python named Jodie Foster first snake to receive pioneering cancer treatment

Electrochemotherapy combines the cancer drug bleomycin with a series of carefully controlled electrical pulses delivered directly to the tumour site. The pulses temporarily make cancer cells more permeable, allowing the drug to enter more effectively. Jose Alvarez Picornell, of the University of Liverpool’s department of small animal clinical science, said: “Electrochemotherapy is an emerging treatment and this was the first time it had been used in a snake. The success of this treatment is a testament to the power of collaboration. By working closely with Ian, we were able to develop a plan that not only benefited Jodie Foster but will also contribute to the wider veterinary community.” A final check this week confirmed that Jodie remained free of any signs of the cancer returning. Picornell added: “We will be formally publishing details of the procedure so that veterinary colleagues around the world can learn from and build upon our approach.

This proliferation of alternative places to buy pre-loved fashion offers ease, often at a more competitive price point. Tiananmen Square vigil organisers in Hong Kong found guilty of ‘inciting subversion’

Two Hong Kong activists who organised annual vigils marking China’s deadly Tiananmen crackdown in 1989 have been found guilty of “incitement to subversion” in one of the most high-profile cases in Hong Kong since Beijing imposed its national security law in 2020. Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, and Chow Hang-tung, 41, “incited other persons to organise, plan, commit or participate in acts by unlawful means with a view to subverting the state power”, a press summary handed out to reporters said. The defendants each face a maximum penalty of 10 years in jail, with sentencing expected at a later date. Lee and Chow’s trial began in January and took place over 24 days. A third defendant, the 74-year-old former lawmaker Albert Ho, pleaded guilty in January. Chow, who represented herself, told the court in May that the law itself was on trial. A man who abandoned his seven-year-old son on Mount Fuji in Japan after the boy complained of feeling tired while on a family hike has been reprimanded by local police. A worker on Japan’s highest mountain discovered the child sitting alone on a bench near the sixth station of the Fujinomiya trail at an altitude of more than 2,000 metres (6,500 feet) on Thursday. After inviting the boy to take shelter at the station, the worker called the police, who took the child into protective custody. It emerged that he had told his father he was too tired to continue while they were hiking up the trail in the early hours of the morning. The man, who was from Japan’s fourth-largest city, Nagoya, gave his son some snacks and a soft drink. He then told him to wait for him before continuing his five-hour ascent to the summit with the child’s older brother, who had already gone on ahead. It would have taken him about eight hours to return, according to local reports. By the time police officers managed to contact the boy’s father, he had ascended to the eighth station, a three-hour hike from where he had left his son.

A 17-year-old girl has been killed after a teenager brandishing a sword attacked students at a school in Sweden, police have confirmed. Three other people were wounded in the incident during classes in the central town of Fagersta on Friday afternoon, including two boys aged 12 and 17 who sustained minor injuries. Swedish police are investigating whether the suspect was involved in online communities promoting school violence, a police source said. Detectives are investigating whether a TikTok account that posted a picture of a sword 20 minutes before the attack belonged to the person responsible, the source told Reuters. The image appeared to have been taken in a restroom at the school, according to the Dagens Nyheter newspaper.

text:
A bridge too far? Why link to Sicily is still a dream despite 2,000 years of plans

For more than 2,000 years, it has been an obsessive dream: a plan to link the Mediterranean Sea’s largest island to mainland Italy. It began with the Romans, who, according to Pliny the Elder, built a bridge of boats and barrels across the strait of Messina in 251BC to transport 140 war elephants captured from the Carthaginians. Centuries later, the fascist dictator Benito Mussolini embraced the same vision, followed by rightwing prime minister Silvio Berlusconi, who made the bridge a flagship project. Then, in 2022, after being appointed Italy’s infrastructure minister, Matteo Salvini revived the mythic ambition, claiming that the ferry crossings “cost people more in a year than it would cost to build the bridge”. Since then, however, there have been more promises than action. Salvini’s stated goal of breaking ground on the €13.5bn project in 2024 slipped to early 2025 and then early 2026. In February, with opponents openly mocking the repeated delays, the leader of the far-right Lega insisted construction would finally begin by this summer.

Former British and French diplomats urge action over Israel’s ‘erasure’ of Palestine

More than 100 French and British former diplomats have said Palestine is being erased in front of the world’s eyes and called for urgent action including trade and arms sales bans to press Israel to accept a Palestinian state. An unprecedented joint letter dispenses with diplomatic language by accusing Israel of ethnic cleansing and warning that the world no longer sees Israel as a genuine democracy. Arguing that Britain and France played a key role in the formation of the modern-day Middle East and noting that both countries took the step of recognising Palestine as a state in 2025, the diplomats contend that their countries now have a responsibility “to make common cause on the region’s fundamental fault line – equal rights for Israeli and Palestinians”. The letter, addressed to the French president, Emmanuel Macron, and the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, has been signed by 52 French former diplomats and 50 British former ambassadors, many of whom served in the Middle East, in senior posts in Egypt, Iran, Bahrain, Israel, Syria, Turkey, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Qatar.

The former boxing world champion Zolani “Last Born” Tete was shot dead outside his home in South Africa on Friday amid rampant violence in the country, which has one of the world’s highest murder rates. The 38-year-old athlete was arriving at his house in the Mdantsane township, Eastern Cape province, when two men in balaclavas got out of a car and shot him. He was declared dead at the scene. The killing of the boxer brought renewed attention to South Africa’s widespread violent crime. The country has recently had a decline in homicides, but remains one of the world’s murder capitals. An average of 58 people per day were murdered in South Africa in the first four months of 2026, according to government data. The UK recorded an average of 1.5 murders per day in 2025.
