The existence of the site was first reported on 14 August. Since then the institute has added a page headed funding, which states: “An earlier version of this page said the Institute operated without external funding, and that was true when it was written.” The site is one part of a broader effort, financed by tens of millions of dollars from the Israeli government and routed through third parties including the European advertising group Havas Media, to prime chatbots to make Israel’s arguments for it. A contract between Havas and another American firm working on the campaign commits it to the “deployment of websites and content to deliver GPT framing results on GPT conversations”. On 12 and 13 August alone it produced 73 reports, amounting to almost 354,000 words in two days. Nothing has been published since the first reports about the Hanover Institute. All but one of the 124 headlines on the website opens with a question resembling one that a user might type into a chatbot, including “Is Anti-Zionism Antisemitism?”, “Did Israel Expel Palestinians From Their Land?”, “Is Israel Carrying Out a Genocide in Gaza?” The reports are presented in a quasi-academic manner and are punctiliously sourced, with citations including the World Bank, UN agencies, the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics, Amnesty International and the text of the Genocide Convention.

text:
On scraps of land and under constant threat, Gaza farmers struggle to survive

As Gaza’s population of 2.1 million has been hemmed into an ever smaller slice of the territory, farmers are using every last remaining patch of unspoiled earth, no matter how tiny, in their struggle to survive. With severe shortages of water, fertiliser and pesticide, and with more than 80% of greenhouses ruined, it has taken inventiveness and determination to clear land of debris and coax new seedlings into life. Moreover, venturing out into the open to tend to plants can be deadly. Saqer Abu Rabee’s eldest son and brother were killed while at work growing food for their communities on their small agricultural plots in Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza. His son Yousef was 24 when he was killed by a drone-fired missile in October 2024. Abu Rabee was working in the fields 10 metres from his son when it happened. “The missile was aimed directly at him and I have no doubt that he was the intended target,” Abu Rabee said.

citation.title: On scraps of land and under constant threat, Gaza farmers struggle to survive

text:
On scraps of land and under constant threat, Gaza farmers struggle to survive

Yousef was well known locally as the driving force behind a collective first called We’ll Plant It and now simply Our Land, which brought together volunteers and encouraged farmers to go back to the land to restore agriculture in the area. “They decided to target him directly,” said Abu Rabee, who stressed his son had no political affiliations. “Before his death, we received daily threats from the Israeli army. They shelled our area every day three or four times while I was working alongside the labourers.” Abu Rabee’s brother Bilal was killed on 2 July after he went to retrieve some agricultural supplies from a destroyed building. His death came nine months into a partial ceasefire during which Israeli forces have killed more than 1,200 Palestinians. Abu Rabee is convinced farmers have become prime targets because of their role in sustaining Palestinian communities among Gaza’s ruins. The Israel Defense Forces deny targeting farmers or any civilians, saying they have only responded to imminent threats from Hamas since the October ceasefire.

citation.title: On scraps of land and under constant threat, Gaza farmers struggle to survive

text:
On scraps of land and under constant threat, Gaza farmers struggle to survive

Despite the risks, Abu Rabee, 48, is still at work every day cultivating a 1.4-hectare (3.4-acre) plot in Beit Lahiya that was an orchard of orange trees before the war. He said the orchard was bulldozed by the Israeli army. “We cleared it and rehabilitated it using only basic tools, manual labour and tremendous human effort. It took a great deal of time and hard work before it was ready for cultivation again,” he said. Out of that scrap of land, Abu Rabee says his family have produced hundreds of thousands of aubergine, tomato and pepper seedlings. They raise cash by growing their own aubergines to sell to wholesale traders, while most of the seedlings are distributed to other farmers or to individual households to plant in patches of earth around their homes and tents. He says the supply has transformed the local food market. Aubergines now cost less than two shekels a kilogram, compared with 40 shekels a few months ago. Peppers and mulukhiyah, a dark green leafy vegetable, are now selling at a tenth of their market price earlier this year.

citation.title: On scraps of land and under constant threat, Gaza farmers struggle to survive

text:
On scraps of land and under constant threat, Gaza farmers struggle to survive

“What has happened is that Beit Lahiya has regained a degree of self-sufficiency,” Abu Rabee said. “In my view, without Beit Lahiya, Gaza would face famine. Before the war, it was considered the food basket of Gaza Strip because of its fertile soil, fresh groundwater and light, productive land.” Increased aid and commercial deliveries under the ceasefire have brought Gaza back from the abyss of last year’s famine conditions, but according to UN agencies there are still 1.4 million people – 67% of Gaza’s population – facing crisis levels of acute food insecurity or worse. Much of the commercial inflows of food are of poor nutritional quality. The director general of the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), Qu Dongyu, has said the limited recovery will remain fragile without domestic food production. “Food security in Gaza cannot recover unless local food production starts again and farmers, herders, fishers and other producers can rebuild their livelihoods,” Qu said in July.

Most of Gaza’s prewar farmland is under Israeli military occupation, and the proportion has grown as the army has pushed the “yellow line” steadily forward over the course of the ceasefire. Goodbye to the Soviet Union – archive, 1991

Deputies stunned by plan for a la carte USSR By Jonathan Steele in Moscow 3 September 1991 The USSR’s supreme legislative body voted overwhelmingly yesterday to bury the existing union of 15 Soviet republics, allow the Baltic republics and any others that wish it to go free, and prepare for an economic confederation in its place. In a move which is no less dramatic than the suspension of the Soviet Communist party 10 days ago, the Congress of People’s Deputies adopted a new structure of power which gives radically new rights to the republics. They acted after hearing a report on the crisis meeting held in the Kremlin yesterday between President Gorbachev and the representatives of 11 republics. The Kazakh president, Nursultan Nazarbayev, read the report, which stunned deputies. Related: Dignified but bitter farewell to the Soviet Union – archive, December 1991 It turned the present system of Soviet power upside down by proposing three new bodies in place of the present parliament and union government.

citation.title: Goodbye to the Soviet Union – archive, 1991

text:
Goodbye to the Soviet Union – archive, 1991

There would be a state council, consisting of President Gorbachev and the leaders of the other republics which sign the union treaty, to handle foreign and domestic policy. An inter-republican economic council would manage the economy and bring in reforms. In place of the parliament would be a kind of senate consisting of 20 representatives from each republic. text:
‘So hacked off’: as election nears, New Zealanders despair at the main parties – and Opportunity knocks

For decades, Mattie Wall mainly voted for Labour, one of New Zealand’s two major political parties. A former diplomat and project manager, the South Island-based retiree felt that the party with working class origins aligned with what was important to her: a thriving country, and the environment. This year she is among the New Zealanders who are peeling away from the Labour and National parties – which swing in and out of power every few terms – to vote for an untested party that has never held a parliamentary seat. “In the past, I didn’t feel the frustration I do now with politics,” said Wall, 76. “I’m so hacked off with both parties, with all parties really. We’ve got Trump 2.0, AI’s sudden [surge], increasing climate change impact – what are we waiting for, revolution or societal collapse? Clinging to the old ways ain’t gonna cut it.” As New Zealand prepares for an election in November, Wall is among the roughly 5-8% of people according to recent polls who plan to vote for relative newcomers the Opportunity party.

Dr Aneeza Jalil, a hospital spokesperson, told the Dawn newspaper that 15 babies were on the ward at the time and that one baby was saved by a doctor. Women who had just given birth had to run down several flights of stairs and climb out of windows and down ladders to escape. The health minister, Mustafa Kamal, said many of the babies were in incubators or on oxygen, and that the oxygen canisters made the fire worse. Investigators said the fire was started by a faulty air conditioning unit, which exploded inside the nursery where newborn infants under intensive care were sleeping.

text:
‘A mockery’: how offshore tax havens are thwarting the UK’s transparency push

Since Britain’s offshore secrecy jurisdictions caved in to pressure from Westminster to embrace corporate transparency, finding out who owns a company in one of these island havens is, in theory at least, a piece of cake. Take the Cayman Islands. All you have to do is show that you have a “legitimate interest” in the data by proving that you are a researcher, journalist, member of a civil society group or a business person considering a transaction with the subject of your inquiry. Next, you must explain how the information will be used for “preventing, detecting, investigating, combating or prosecution money laundering or its predicate offences or terrorist financing”. There is a fee of at least $75 (£55) for each application. Until recently, this could only be done via the tricky method of an international wire transfer, although card payments are now available. Now, fill out a lengthy form outlining exactly what information you’re after, cross your fingers and wait. It isn’t exactly Companies House (for all its faults).

text:

Even when the form has been submitted, the subject of the inquiry can apply for a three-year “protection from disclosure” (at a cost of $1,000) to stop the information being sent on, on the basis that corporate transparency could expose them to harm. These applications are refused more often than not, a Cayman Islands spokesperson said, but justifications for exemption appear to be drawn quite widely. Reasons could include revealing any connections to “activity such as testing products on animals, which might lead to them being targeted by activists”, according to guidelines written by the Cayman Islands government. This is not an uncommon precaution. It is also available in the UK for a fee of £100. Transparency campaigners believe aspects of the system in the British Virgin Islands (BVI) are even worse. There, officials will inform the subject of any inquiry – perhaps a powerful oligarch or a narco-trafficker – of the name of any organisation asking the inconvenient questions, though not the names of individuals. Don’t expect a quick outcome either.

South African police arrest two Thai men for allegedly smuggling parrot eggs

South African police have arrested two Thai nationals in separate incidents for allegedly attempting to smuggle endangered parrot eggs out of the country as authorities try to stem the tide of wildlife trafficking. A 50-year-old Thai national was arrested at OR Tambo international airport in Johannesburg on 20 August, carrying 50 bird eggs in a homemade incubator in a hand-luggage bag, South Africa’s environment ministry said in a statement. The ministry said preliminary investigations indicated that the eggs were from parrot species listed under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (Cites), which regulates international trade in wild animals and plants to ensure species do not become extinct. It did not specify which species. Another Thai national, a 23-year-old, was arrested at the same airport on 16 July, allegedly trying to smuggle 418 parrot eggs in two homemade incubator bags. Thailand’s embassy in South Africa did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Good morning. When the Guardian asked Canadian readers whether they planned to boycott US products after dramatic escalations in the ongoing DC/Ottawa trade war, we received more than 2,000 responses within 12 hours. This inundation is perhaps evidence of the existential crisis many Canadians feel they now face, something often lost in the granular reporting of trade negotiations: this is about so much more than the price of lumber. Assailed by a US president who has repeatedly expressed a desire to consume Canada into a supersized 51st state, the country has felt perpetually on the brink of war – albeit an economic one – since Donald Trump’s early second-term tariff salvo in February 2025. This culminated in Canada’s finance minister announcing tit-for-tat tariffs on key American industries yesterday, further incensing the US president. Canadian PM Mark Carney has emerged as a leader whose refusal to be dominated by Trump is underpinned by an ambition to reorder global politics.

In depth: ‘If we’re not at the table, we’re on the menu’ The United States and Canada have enjoyed one of the strongest bilateral relationships in recent history. They share the longest unprotected border in the world, along with deep trading, security and cultural ties. But the second Trump presidency has brought about a fundamental breach in the shared values and understanding that once united the two nations. Trump has repeatedly threatened to annex Canada, as he yearns to access its critical minerals. Carney, a former Governor of the Bank of England, was sworn in as prime minister last year in the midst of Trump’s tariff wars, having never held elected public office before. He has since become the first western leader to openly acknowledge the hazard Trump poses to the global order. In a high-profile January speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, he urged “middle powers” like Canada to “act together, because if we’re not at the table, we’re on the menu.” Tariffs appear to have become a proxy for this political rupture.

text:
​W​hy are European leaders staying silent after our summer of climate shock?

The climate crisis means “we’re going to have to change everything – the way we live, the way we produce, the way we trade,” France’s veteran radical-left firebrand, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, told the summer congress of his France Insoumise party last weekend. The term “climate change”, said Mélenchon – the most likely rival to Marine Le Pen in next year’s presidential run-off, according to one poll this week – may sound “almost reassuring”, but its actual impact will feel like “landing on another planet whenever we leave home”. The speech is notable because despite the four heatwaves that have scorched Europe this summer, shattering temperature records, fanning unprecedented fires and causing thousands of excess deaths, few politicians want to talk about climate action. Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent, heating up twice as quickly as elsewhere. The consequences, as UN climate chief Simon Stiell puts it, are “reaching national emergency levels”.

citation.title: ​W​hy are European leaders staying silent after our summer of climate shock?

text:
​W​hy are European leaders staying silent after our summer of climate shock?

And yet major policy speeches by Europe’s political leaders addressing the climate crisis, making plain its causes, and laying out the changes that will be needed to live with it can be counted on the fingers of one hand. French voters have faced “silence from some politicians and inadequate pronouncements or demagoguery from others”, said Le Monde in a stark editorial, warning that “decision-makers on both the right and the left are losing credibility”. People want “a political message that translates into action, and sheds light on the future”, it said. The gap between “citizens’ heightened awareness of the crisis and the lack of commitment from their elected officials to address it” will trigger mounting frustration and anger. A mid-July Ipsos poll found environmental protection had jumped 12 points from June to become French voters’ fourth greatest concern, after what the pollster described as “a first real experience of what the hell of a significantly hotter world might look like”.

text:
​W​hy are European leaders staying silent after our summer of climate shock?

In the UK too, Labour party activists worry that despite the ever more visible impacts of the climate crisis, there has been no major political push from the government on the issue, even as voters become increasingly convinced of the need for action. And while Friedrich Merz said this week action was needed to “curb climate change and adapt to the consequences” (though not at a cost to German industry), he’s been accused all summer of ducking the issue for fear of boosting the climate-sceptic, far-right AfD. There are, of course, exceptions. Spain’s outspoken prime minister, Pedro Sánchez (pictured top), has long warned that “climate change kills”, and recently stressed: “It’s not enough to address the consequences; what we have to do is reduce its causes.” A French centre-left presidential contender, Raphäel Glucksmann, spoke this week of the need for an “ecological transformation” ending the use of fossil fuels, and pledged a 100-day “ecological revolution” if elected president (which looks extremely unlikely).

text:
​W​hy are European leaders staying silent after our summer of climate shock?

But the silence from most mainstream politicians is deafening, says Jean Jouzel, a veteran French climatologist. The political class in general, he says, “have simply not yet engaged with the reality of global heating. They have to tackle it head-on.” The root of the problem, Jouzel suggests, is that “politicians live in the short-term. Their horizon is avoiding any damage during their period in office. For me, a real political leader … has the courage to look to the medium and the long-term.” Short-termism, political polarisation and cost-of-living fears have, in effect, silenced leaders across Europe, as populist and far-right parties successfully frame green laws as an “ideological mantra” and the elite’s punishment for “ordinary working people”. The reasoning is clear: voters suffering high energy bills, food inflation and stagnating wages are unlikely to hail demands for real financial and lifestyle sacrifices in pursuit of an ill-defined climate gain. Carbon taxes and boiler restrictions carry electoral risk.

text:
​W​hy are European leaders staying silent after our summer of climate shock?

*** Local over global But that reluctance to address the real issue has shifted Europe’s climate debate away from long-term carbon reduction towards more localised adaptation – which, perhaps inevitably, has itself now become a battleground in the continent’s culture wars. Air conditioning is a prime example, now loudly touted on Europe’s right as a vital symbol of personal freedom and technological comfort, but widely decried by the left as environmentally irresponsible and symptomatic of long-term planning failures. “If I am elected president, I will put into place a massive air-conditioning plan,” Le Pen trumpeted this summer, arguing the technology had little or no impact on global heating: “When environmentalists don’t want something, they twist the studies.” The risk in all this is that by focusing on necessary but essentially reactive coping measures, leaders wind up reducing the existential challenges of global heating to debates over consumer choice and comfort that can fit into an electoral cycle. Meanwhile, vital long-term carbon reduction gets pushed further and further into the background.

As Dutch MEP, Gerben-Jan Gerbrandy, argues: “Nobody should feel guilty for wanting relief from extreme heat. Air conditioning saves lives.” However, he continues, neither should we “accept the cynical argument that the answer to rising temperatures is simply to install more air conditioning – while abandoning the very policies designed to tackle the causes of those rising temperatures”. Be that as it may, in the multiple European countries with national elections coming up over the next 18 months – including France, Italy and Spain – the climate emergency remains, for the time being at least, largely absent from the debate. Man on trial for Daphne Caruana Galizia murder claims he was framed

A businessman on trial for the murder of the journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia has spoken about the charges for the first time in court since his arrest seven years ago, telling the jury he was framed by police and had nothing to do with the killing. During four days of questioning by defence and the prosecution lawyers, Yorgen Fenech, 44, accused the most senior adviser to Malta’s prime minister of giving the go-ahead for the murder. Fenech’s defence lawyers have repeatedly sought to identify Keith Schembri, Malta’s most powerful unelected official in the years leading up to the killing in October 2017, as the mastermind and instigator. Fenech repeated those claims as he began giving testimony on Friday after unexpectedly waiving his right under Maltese law to refuse to give evidence at his own trial. Fenech claimed that Schembri, who was chief of staff to the then prime minister Joseph Muscat, repeatedly leaked sensitive details to him, including advance warnings of raids and arrests.

Strict production rules will be loosened for some of France’s most famous cheeses after drought and repeated heatwaves dried out grazing pastures, threatening the livelihoods of traditional dairy workers. Hiker reunited with backpack 60 years after he fell into a glacier in Austria

An 86-year-old mountaineer has been reunited with his backpack and climbing equipment after the kit emerged from a melting glacier in Austria – more than 60 years after he was forced to leave them there. Items including an ice axe, camera and a pipe dating from the 1950s or 1960s were discovered on the Sulztalferner glacier in Austria’s Tyrol region, at an altitude of 2,955 metres (9,700ft) above sea level, by a hiker in July. Austrian police began an investigation and through heavily frayed documents found in the backpack discovered the owner’s name and tracked him down. The man had fallen into the crevasse while crossing the glacier with friends in August 1963. The group was held together by a rope, so his friends were able to pull him free. Police said to reduce his weight he had removed his backpack and thrown it into the crevasse. They said the man, whom they did not publicly name, was too ill to collect the items himself, so they were returned to him via his son.

Known to his 8.7m TikTok followers as Dr Food, Georges Dib was a popular Lebanese food influencer who would hold giveaways, post behind-the-scenes tours of his food production facilities and wax philosophical about the ingredients of success. German health officials are seeking to reassure the public after two workers at the country’s biggest airport died of malaria. Mosquito traps have been set up at Frankfurt airport and a mosquito monitoring process is under way. A detailed investigation is being conducted to clarify how the workers contracted the disease. Since last month, six people are known to have caught malaria tropica – the most dangerous form of the disease – in connection with their work at the airport. Of the two that have died, one began getting sick at the start of July and the other in mid-August. The four other people who were infected have been treated in hospital and are now out of danger, according to Frankfurt’s public health department. Letters have been sent to all airport workers to raise awareness about symptoms and urge vigilance. Doctors are being asked to watch out for patients with unexplained fever who work in and around the airport.

Ratko Mladić obituary

After the Bosnian mountain town of Srebrenica fell to Serb troops in July 1995, its terrified Muslim residents were given assurances by the Serb commander of the conquering army, General Ratko Mladić, who has died aged 83. He told them: “Anyone who wants to leave will be transported, be they old or young. Don’t be afraid and don’t rush. Let the women and children go first.” In video footage of that day, the general can be seen patting the cheek of an eight-year-old Muslim boy and offering him chocolate. “Please don’t panic. Be careful not to lose any children. Don’t be afraid. Nobody will harm you.” By then, the Hague war crimes tribunal would later determine, Mladić had ordered the executions of all males of army age or deemed old enough to bear arms. More than 8,000 men and teenage boys were mown down in what would be the worst massacre Europe had witnessed for half a century.

text:
Ratko Mladić obituary

After many years on the run, in 2017 Mladić was convicted of genocide for the slaughter at Srebrenica, alongside convictions for war crimes and crimes against humanity for the many massacres over the preceding three years, as Mladić, his fellow generals, and the Bosnian Serb leadership sought to ethnically cleanse Bosnia of Muslims and Croats. At the time of his death, in a UN prison hospital in The Hague, Mladić, one of the most reviled mass killers in modern European history, was serving a life sentence. However, among nationalists in Serbia and the Serb half of Bosnia, the Republika Srpska, he is still portrayed as a hero – powerful evidence that the murderous ideology he embodied is still very much alive. Born in Božanovići, a village in the mountains of the southern Herzegovina region, Ratko was the son of Stana (nee Lalović) and Nedja Mladić. His parents were hiding out with a band of partisans fighting the Nazis and their local allies, the Croatian Ustaše. His given name means “warlike”, and his father was killed in battle before he was two years old.

text:
Ratko Mladić obituary

In socialist postwar Yugoslavia, ruled by the partisan leader Josip Broz Tito, the teenage Mladić served a short apprenticeship as a tinsmith, before finding his true calling in the Yugoslav National Army (JNA). He excelled at the military academy, graduated in 1965 and joined Tito’s communist party like any ambitious officer. In 1966 he married Bosiljka Jedić, had two children, Darko and Ana, and steadily rose through the JNA ranks to the level of brigade commander by the time federal Yugoslavia fell apart in 1991-92. The stocky, ruddy-faced soldier embodied all the contradictions of Yugoslavia. He mouthed the party’s mantra of “brotherhood and unity” among the country’s ethnicities, but remained a Serb chauvinist in his bones, with the desire for revenge, not just for the second world war, but for the Ottoman conquest more than five centuries earlier. After Tito’s death, the old socialist bromides began to lose their power. Slobodan Milošević, a wily smooth-talking ex-banker, took the helm in 1989 and soon realised that communism had run its course as the ideological rationale for the concentration of power.

text:
Ratko Mladić obituary

Serb nationalism on the other hand was resurgent, and Milošević deftly switched horses. Serb officers were put in charge of JNA outposts across Yugoslavia, and Mladić was dispatched to Kosovo with the task of suppressing majority ethnic Albanians, and then to Croatia in the summer of 1991, to fight against secessionist forces in that country’s war of independence. By then he was a colonel, with a growing reputation for ruthlessness in the field and the devastating use of artillery on enemy soldiers and civilians alike. So when Serb separatist leaders such as Radovan Karadzić in Bosnia were looking for a military commander to help them subjugate the republic and wrest control of Sarajevo, they called Mladić. The Republika Srpska army that he led was equipped and sponsored from Belgrade by Milošević, whose ultimate aim was to create a Greater Serbia in the wreckage of Yugoslavia. But how Mladić went about that was left up to him, and his ethnic bigotry and sadism was allowed to run rampant. In 1992, his forces took control of a horseshoe of territory in western and eastern Bosnia, slaughtering Muslims and Croats and setting up concentration camps.

text:
Ratko Mladić obituary

Of the estimated 100,000 dead from the Bosnian war, about 38,000 were civilians, and more than 80% of the civilian deaths were Bosniak (Bosnian Muslim), a statistic that owes a lot to the single-mindedness with which Mladić went about his task. Though ruthlessly effective in liquidating civilian populations, Mladić failed to overcome the improvised resistance put up by defenders of Sarajevo. Instead he oversaw a 47-month siege of the city (the longest siege of a capital in modern warfare), deploying mortars in the surrounding mountains and snipers in high-rise blocks in the suburbs, to pick off its citizens. “Pound them senseless!” he was heard to urge his men in one intercepted communication. Mladić’s true vision of Serb dominance relied on the destruction and uprooting of competing ethnicities. Unlike the foppish Karadzić, who relished the attention of US and European statesmen seeking to broker a peace deal, the general had no time for foreigners. An American official once asked him if he had ever been abroad. “I went to Geneva once. I didn’t like the beer,” the general replied.

text:
Ratko Mladić obituary

Almost single-handedly, Mladić killed off an effort to end the war in 1993 led by the US envoy Cyrus Vance and the former UK foreign secretary David Owen. Defying Karadzić, he convinced the Republika Srpska assembly to reject the Vance-Owen plan with a 45-minute display of nationalist bombast. He relished his brutal reputation, but it helped destroy his family. He had sought to ensure their safety by keeping them in Belgrade, but there Ana fell in love with a Serbian doctor, a human rights activist who was appalled at what was happening in Bosnia. He told her he would marry her only if she renounced her father. Trapped between romantic love and family loyalty, she took her father’s pistol from its display case one night in February 1994 and shot herself. Mladić refused to acknowledge any responsibility, preferring conspiracy theories and sinking into an ever darker view of the world and his place in it, as a Serb avenger for centuries-old Ottoman tyranny. When he led his troops into Srebrenica, a UN safe haven, he proclaimed the conquest was “a gift to the Serb people”.

“Finally, the time has come to take revenge on the Turks in this region,” Mladić declared to a camera held by one of his aides. He had convinced himself that he belonged among the pantheon of greats of military history, a student of Hannibal, Alexander the Great and Carl von Clausewitz, but his army crumpled rapidly when in 1995 western forces finally intervened on the side of Croatian and Bosnian forces in the wake of the Srebrenica genocide. Mladić escaped justice for more than 16 years. He was sheltered across the border in Serbia, where a special army unit was created to ensure he lived in comfort and secrecy at a succession of military bases. After the fall of Milošević in 2000, when Serbia embarked on what turned out to be a brief flirtation with liberalism and pro-western governments, Mladić’s protection fell away, forcing him to trust a constantly shrinking circle of loyalists, as he moved from one hideout to another, each more squalid than the one beforer. He was finally found in May 2011 by Serbian police in an outbuilding of a farm belonging to one of his cousins in the village of Lazarevo, near the border with Romania.

Ratko Mladić, the ‘Butcher of Bosnia’, dies in The Hague

Ratko Mladić, the infamous Serbian general who was serving a life sentence for genocide committed during the Bosnian war, has died in prison in The Hague. Mladić had been one of the main architects of the policy of ethnic cleansing during the Bosnian war. He was convicted of genocide for orchestrating the 1995 killing of at least 8,000 Muslims in the UN-designated “safe area” Srebrenica, the worst massacre in Europe since the second world war. Mladić, who was nicknamed the “Butcher of Bosnia”, had been in ill health after having a series of strokes. A UN international tribunal confirmed Mladić’s death, saying he had died in hospital in The Hague earlier in the day. “Mladić passed away today while hospitalised in The Hague,” the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals said in a statement, adding that judge Graciela Gatti Santana had ordered “a full inquiry into the circumstances” of his death.

The Nazis drove Bauhaus out of town. Now the far right is waging another war against the movement

The city of Dessau, where the Bauhaus design school flourished a century ago, catapulted Germany into the modern era and revolutionised global design. It is also where the Nazis drove the avant garde movement out of town and attempted to crush its utopian principles. A hundred years later, another high-stakes culture war over its legacy is looming. The EU’s biggest democracy will face one of the riskiest tests of the postwar period when Dessau’s home state of Saxony-Anhalt goes to the polls on 6 September. In what would be a first since Adolf Hitler’s time, a far-right party could win an absolute majority and take power in one of the 16 Länder. The Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) is running first in national polls and is poised to capture about 40% in Saxony-Anhalt. It has widened its double-digit lead among the state’s 1.8 million voters by homing in on the cost of living, fears around immigration, and the whipsaw effects of deindustrialisation and depopulation.

But the party’s programme also lays out a vision for Germany with Saxony-Anhalt as a foothold, in a plan oddly fixated on Bauhaus. “The state government is running an image campaign called ‘think modern’ that seeks to derive the identity of Saxony-Anhalt from Bauhaus,” reads one passage. The AfD said it is countering with “a ‘think German’ campaign” that promises a “new, patriotic cultural policy” and an end to funding for “anti-German art and culture”. *** Bauhaus’s blend of form and function in architecture, art and industrial design shaped everything from Ikea style for the masses to the user-friendly elegance of Apple products. It was also a buzzing hive of sexual liberation, new roles for women and international collaboration before the Nazis drove its “degenerates” into exile. In her modest, sleek-lined office at the Bauhaus Dessau Foundation, director Barbara Steiner said that much like a century ago, the AfD’s anti-Bauhaus crusade was a Trojan horse aiming for the heart of Germany’s open, liberal society.

text:
Thursday briefing: Will the government reform the system to bring down our energy bills?

Good morning. For too many people, this just doesn’t feel like breathing room. Andy Burnham entered Downing Street in July pledging to give consumers respite from the cost of living crisis. A day later he announced a VAT cut on domestic electricity from 5% to zero due later this year, saving the average household about £45 a year. But this pales against yesterday’s announcement that the energy price cap is rising another 4% from 1 October, the second jump in three months. The typical annual bill for household gas and electricity use will soon be a wallet-straining £1,723. Miatta Fahnbulleh, net zero secretary, worked valiantly during a media blitz yesterday to repeat early promises to help families out – the £2 cap on bus fares, action on free school meals – but the evidence is inarguable: British households are still paying more for power than many other European nations. For today’s First Edition, we ask: Why are Britain’s energy bills so high? And, what can be done to reduce them? But first the headlines.

In depth: ‘No single lever can be pulled to bring down prices without consequence’ A typical energy bill is made up of a standing charge, a fee to keep connected to the grid, and a unit rate for the amount of gas or electricity you consume. It also includes underlying charges to maintain and operate the energy network and government-mandated levies to fund social and environmental schemes. Britain has one of the most expensive energy markets in the world, driven in no small part by how the market price for our electricity is determined. According to our “marginal pricing” system, the price paid by suppliers for wholesale electricity at any give moment is dictated by the most expensive source of generation required to meet demand there and then. In the UK, this is regularly electricity from costly gas-fired power plants. Regardless of how much cheap wind or solar power we make, this highest common denominator still sets the price. Last year, 31% of the UK’s electricity was produced from burning natural gas, but it is estimated to have set electricity prices over 90% of the time.

Energy costs in the UK diverged from other European nations in around 2020, Doug Parr, chief scientist and policy director at Greenpeace tells me. That’s when Britain ended its reliance on coal in electricity production, which as recently as 2012 was responsible for 43% of UK supply. “Gas became the marginal cost setter, which meant we were much more exposed to the gas prices than other countries.” Subsequent wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have seen global gas prices soar, further hitting British bill-payers. Energy policy experts warn that, because successive governments have left our energy system to drift for years, no single lever can be pulled to bring down prices without consequence. That said, there are a number of short and longer-term reforms that current ministers should consider. *** Short term solutions Cut the levies – save £100 a year Energy bills don’t just pay for energy – over the years, additional subsidies have been quietly added, like funding the Warm Homes Discount Scheme, or paying for early renewables innovation.

By 2027, these levies will add over £100 a year to the average household energy bill, according to the climate thinktank E3G. Subsidies also add over 20% to an electricity bill for most businesses. Levy reform could reduce inflation by 0.3%, according to modelling by Nesta, though government departments would have to shoulder the funding shortfall. Deal with energy debt – save up to £70 a year Households struggling to pay inflated bills costs us all. By the end of this year, individuals will owe an estimated £7bn to their suppliers. That’s not just a problem for those in arrears: the cost of managing this debt crisis is passed on to every consumer, at between £50 and £70 a year. Immediate solutions include introducing a “social tariff” to provide cheaper energy for poor households; giving suppliers the income data they need to assess who is in fuel poverty; and tasking Ofgem with reviewing supplier debt collection practices. Once the rising debt has been curbed, a more radical option would be to write off the remaining amount.

Reactive pricing Suppliers could certainly make flexible tariffs, which incentivise people to use energy when it is cleanest and cheapest, available more rapidly. Octopus has a specific tariff for night storage heaters, for example, which it says can benefit the average householder by £128 per year. *** Longer term fixes Re-design the market – save up to £270 a year by 2030 The experts at E3G want to see major reform of market design, moving away from the current system where everybody picks up the highest price. “The government must put all electricity generators on to fixed price contracts,” says senior policy adviser Susie Elks, who argues this would also reverse the failures of privatisation where companies can make massive profits off electricity users as they have done during the past two energy crises. This approach is already used by 89 countries across the world and, according to the Common Wealth thinktank, would lower bills by an estimated £130 to £270 per household by 2030.

UK urged to help free British-Egyptian ‘arrested in Cairo over sister’s activism’

The UK Foreign Office has been asked to intervene to secure the release of a British-Egyptian woman who it is claimed has been arrested in Cairo because of her sister’s political activism. Eman el-Shazly, a 45-year-old based in Birmingham, was arrested on 16 August while visiting Egypt. Her lawyers say she has been detained in an attempt to silence her sister Mona, a relentless and harsh critic of the Egyptian government on her UK-based YouTube channel. Her two brothers have already spent three years in jail and, in May, were rearrested. They were previously held in pre-trial detention, facing charges of “promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation on social media, as well as broadcasting false news harmful to state security”. The UK Foreign Office has confirmed to the husband of Eman that she is being held in the Ramadan rehabilitation centre and her case has been given the same file number as that of her two brothers, Hassan and Eid.

A sanctioned shadow fleet tanker carries oil from Nato member Turkey to a Russian Baltic port. A deal is signed for Russian oil to be processed in Kazakhstan. In the space of a summer, Russia, once the world’s second-largest producer of crude oil, has been plunged into a desperate scramble to find sources of gasoline to plug the ever-growing holes in its refining capacity. Rescuers searching for survivors of deadly flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border have resumed their efforts after suspending operations when a debris dam burst its bank on Friday, increasing the risk of fresh flooding. Residents in Nepal’s Rasuwa district, on the border with Tibet, were seen rushing up hillsides ⁠on Friday to escape a possible surge in the river, ⁠according to witnesses. Fears of another flood came as authorities in Nepal and China said that at least 543 people had been killed in the disaster. More than 500 foreign citizens were among 826 people missing in Nepal, police and tourism ⁠officials said, including 177 from India, 90 from the US, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 25 from Canada. Chinese state media said at least 558 were missing on the Tibet side of the border, of whom at least 260 were foreign nationals. French far-right leader Jordan Bardella to address Reform UK party conference

The French far-right leader Jordan Bardella is to give a speech at Reform UK’s party conference in Birmingham next week as he attempts to boost international ties before Marine Le Pen’s bid for the French presidency next spring. Le Pen’s far-right, anti-immigration National Rally (RN) is high in the polls and she is predicted to reach the final round of the French presidential race in May. Related: Populism unites Le Pen and Farage. But she is a step closer to power Le Pen launched her presidential campaign this summer despite a Paris appeal court upholding her conviction for being at the centre of the embezzlement of more than €2.8m (£2.4m) in European parliament funds and funnelling the money into her party between 2004 and 2016. She has appealed against the ruling to France’s highest court. Le Pen, the RN’s parliamentary leader in the National Assembly and the party leader from 2011 to 2021, has said she will run for president on a joint ticket with Bardella as prime minister.

Friday briefing: ​Could Meta’s ​child‑​safety ​settlement ​open the ​door​ to global reform?

Good morning. It was supposed to be Meta’s big tobacco moment, but the tech company’s share price barely flinched on Wednesday – and fluttered upwards, even – after it settled a landmark lawsuit. The case was brought by 29 US states who accused the company of harming children with addictive and dangerous products. Against a rising tide of popular backlash, this legal action in the American courts pushed Meta to self-impose a level of regulation that Congress had repeatedly failed to, with a series of reforms now incoming to better protect children on Meta platforms. Some critics have argued the changes don’t go far enough. Around the globe, and sometimes out of the media glare, Meta is facing a tranche of lawsuits. For today’s First Edition, we look to some of these others battles to hold the tech leviathan to account, with the Guardian’s global technology reporter Aisha Down. But first the headlines.

In depth: ‘Our lives do not matter to them’ It looks to be a monumental moment. On Wednesday, Meta agreed to pay up to $18bn (£13.3bn) to a coalition of US states suing it over the harm Facebook and Instagram has caused young people. But more significantly, given the company’s trillion-dollar-plus valuation, Meta agreed to make changes to its platforms. The company is now framing this as a precedent for other social media companies to follow, calling on competitors like TikTok and YouTube to fall in line. The changes largely apply to under 18s and crucially will be turned on by default, marking a major shift from the previous opt-in system for parental controls and teen safety features. These include a two hour use limit per day, no access between midnight and 6am and no push notifications overnight or during school hours. Only parents will be able to disable these features.

While these new standards only apply in the US, optimists believe they could set new global minimum guardrails for social media safety. They mirror many of the limits the UK and Australian governments are already imposing, and on Thursday the UK government called on Meta to roll out the court-agreed protections to British children, as did the European Commission. King Harald V of Norway obituary

King Harald V of Norway, who has died aged 89, Europe’s oldest serving monarch, was the country’s third king since it regained independence in 1905 following the dissolution of its union with Sweden. Although he ceased to be head of the Lutheran state church in 2012 and subsequently lost his constitutional status as “holy” six years later, he did exhibit the Scandinavian moderation, stoicism and genial approachability that led a newspaper to name him Norway’s person of the year in 2017. The first Norwegian king to be born in the country since 1370, Harald was also related to both the Swedish and the British royal families. His parents were Crown Prince Olav, who was king as Olav V between 1957 and 1991, and his wife, Princess Märtha, a member of the Swedish royal dynasty. His grandparents were King Haakon VII, the first king of the independent country, who reigned for 52 years from 1905, and his wife, Queen Maud, daughter of Britain’s Edward VII. The family roots are Danish – from the Glücksburg dynasty – as were those of the Duke of Edinburgh and the former Greek royal family.

The mixed heritage made him sympathetic to refugees: “It is not easy to say where we come from. Home is where the heart is,” he said. He was Queen Elizabeth II’s second cousin and a knight of the garter. At the time of his birth, Harald was 16th in line to the British throne, though he had fallen in the rankings to around 80th in more recent years. Confusingly, he was not the fifth Harald to rule his country, but the sixth – the 10th-century Harald Bluetooth generally not being assigned a number in the list of Norwegian kings. The king never attracted a picturesque title as did some of his Viking predecessors – such as Bluetooth, Harald Fairhair and Harald Hardrada, who tried to seize the English throne a few weeks before the Norman invasion in 1066 and was killed at the battle of Stamford Bridge. Harald himself was only three at the time of the Nazi invasion of Norway in 1940, and he and his mother and two older sisters, Ragnhild and Astrid, initially fled to Sweden, which, trying to maintain its neutrality while accommodating the Germans’ attack on their neighbour, was reluctant to let them in.

A keen competitive yachtsman, he and his crews represented Norway at successive Olympics in Tokyo in 1964, Mexico City in 1968 and Munich in 1972, and won world championship medals through the 1980s and a European championship gold medal in 2005. If this was a conventional career, much less so was his determination to marry a commoner, Sonja Haraldsen, a shop assistant who was the daughter of an Oslo textile manufacturer, whom he had met at a sailing party in 1959. The friendship was kept secret for several years, partly because of Olav’s reluctance to have the heir to the throne marry someone who was not royal. In the end, Harald forced the issue by declaring to his father that if he was not allowed to marry her he would not marry anyone, thus bringing an end to the dynasty. The couple married in 1968. Harald was sworn in as king automatically following Olav’s death in January 1991. The Norwegian monarch’s duties are similar to those in Britain, with non-exercised executive power, and all official acts having to be endorsed by the governing council of state, equivalent to a British cabinet. The Norwegian parliament constitutionally debates whether to continue the monarchy every four years, and earlier this year, despite controversies concerning the royal family, voted in favour of its continuation by 141 to 26. The greatest crisis in the country’s modern history occurred on 22 July 2011 when the domestic terrorist Anders Behring Breivik murdered 77 people, mainly at a young socialists’ holiday camp on Utøya island. The king attracted public praise in the wake of the tragedy, when he met bereaved relatives and called for national solidarity and mutual support. He was seen to weep at the memorial service for the victims. Twenty-two Americans returning from a pilgrimage hosted by the Isha Foundation, were among 80 foundation members not yet located, founder and spiritual leader Sadhguru Vasudev said in a statement on Thursday. Please don’t rearrange our shoes when we turn up, paramedics in Japan urge

Etiquette, manners and consideration for others are integral pillars of Japanese society but there are times when they might go a step too far, according to one city’s emergency services. The fire department in the central city of Kanazawa has urged people not to tidy up the shoes that paramedic crews have taken off when entering a house, warning it could hinder their ability to get in or out quickly, particularly when carrying someone on a stretcher. In an Instagram video that has amassed more than half a million views since it was posted on 5 August, the firefighters demonstrate how paramedics leave their shoes positioned at entrances in precise spots so that three stretcher bearers can step straight into them without shaking the patient around, or risking dislodging their oxygen mask. It is customary for anyone entering a Japanese home to shed their footwear, and for homeowners to rearrange the shoes of guests or customers to face the doorway so that they can slip them on easily when they leave.

That policy is a 21st-century adaptation of the 19th-century Monroe doctrine by which President James Monroe sought to keep European powers out of the Americas. Trump’s version is about countering China’s growing footprint in the region and imposing US will through economic and military pressure.

The daughter of a woman missing in Nepal has told how she traced her mother’s location through a TikTok video posted hours before the devastating flash flood hit. The catastrophic flash floods that hit Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday, thundering down valleys and sweeping away entire villages, have killed at least 675 people, while more than 3,000 remain missing. Tulshi Patel’s mother, Hemangini Jitendra Patel, and her aunt, Hema Sunil Amin, set off on a pilgrimage in which they had planned to travel into Tibet, but the pair have not been contactable since the flash floods hit. text:
Was it a mistake for 99 Colombian guerrillas to lay down their arms?

In mid-June, 99 guerrilla fighters were flown by helicopter to a small settlement in a rural area of southern Colombia where they lined up and, one by one, handed their weapons to government officials: rifles, pistols, machine guns and grenade launchers. They also stripped off their heavy tactical vests, field packs and camouflage uniforms, which were each piled into a bonfire to mark the beginning of a new life away from an armed conflict that has claimed nearly half a million lives in the last six decades. That was precisely what the former president Gustavo Petro’s “total peace” plan had sought to achieve: negotiating with and disarming all of Colombia’s criminal groups, which are estimated to have nearly 30,000 members. But the group of just 99 people was the only one to disarm, and did so just three days before the presidential runoff, which was won by the far-right millionaire lawyer Abelardo de la Espriella, who had campaigned on a promise to end “total peace” and return to a full-on strategy of jailing or killing criminals.

citation.title: Was it a mistake for 99 Colombian guerrillas to lay down their arms?

text:
Was it a mistake for 99 Colombian guerrillas to lay down their arms?

Now, several weeks after the new president took office – and amid efforts to deal with the aftermath of the 7.4-magnitude earthquake, as his government has already begun the promised airstrikes against criminal groups – the 99 do not know what will happen to them. “We’re in limbo,” said Natalia Bríñez, 29, one of 13 women among the group staying in the temporary location zone, or ZUT by its Spanish initials, a government-controlled zone where, under surveillance and unable to leave, they were supposed to make the transition to civilian life over the following months. The former guerrillas are housed in beige brick buildings decorated with drawings they painted themselves, including doves of peace, with a communal dining hall where three meals a day are served. No weapons are allowed inside and soldiers guard the ZUT from a perimeter less than a mile away. One former combatant built a makeshift gym with weights made from metal pipes and tins filled with cement and sand, and there is an improvised football pitch, but most of them spend their days on their phones.

De la Espriella has repeatedly said his government will no longer negotiate peace agreements and has yet to announce what he intends to do regarding the people at the ZUT. The president has not responded to requests for comment. In theory, any arrest warrants against the group are suspended, and they remain under state protection until 25 December, when Petro’s decree establishing the ZUT expires. But De la Espriella could revoke the decree at any time. Armando Novoa, the former government official who led peace negotiations with the group, said “the worst-case scenario would be for the new government to close the ZUT, launch a military operation and try to capture or kill them. That would be a crime against humanity, because these people are unarmed.” Between 2 and 4 August, days before De la Espriella’s inauguration, Novoa led journalists including the Guardian through the ZUT. The Office of the High Commissioner for Peace, where he worked, has since been absorbed into the newly created National Security Commission – a move expected to result in more than 200 job losses – and Novoa has resigned.

For now, at least, the ZUT remains in operation and has a small library run by Bríñez, who has a phoenix tattoo on her left shoulder as a symbol of her rebirth away from the armed conflict. “The hardest thing for me has been being away from my children,” said Bríñez, who has a seven-year-old daughter and a 10-year-old son and speaks to them on video calls, but will only be able to see them in person once her “transition” is complete, a process that includes vocational training and psychosocial support. They were also supposed to receive financial support of about £425 a month, which had not yet been paid. In the meantime, some of them were planning to start a chicken-rearing business. The 99 made up a small part of a group of about 1,000 combatants called Commandos of the Frontier – most of whom remain armed – and are part of the National Coordinator of the Bolivarian Army (CNEB), a former dissident faction of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc) with about 2,500 members which controls the border with Ecuador.

The Petro administration said negotiations were also under way with other members of the CNEB, who published an open letter addressed to De la Espriella saying they were willing to continue talks with him. It is not known whether the president responded. The CNEB’s chief “peace negotiator”, Geovany Andrés Rojas, known as “Araña” (Spider), had been in custody since February under a US extradition request for drug trafficking, which Petro had delayed. Last Wednesday, De la Espriella ordered extradition. “It even surprised us that most of them simply called the group ‘the company’.” Petro repeatedly tried to negotiate peace agreements with larger groups. The armed factions took advantage of temporary ceasefires to continue expanding, a process that had already begun before he took office. They also clashed among themselves for control of territory and illicit economies, which many security experts say contributed to a rise in homicides, kidnappings and massacres. “Total peace” was an attempt to address what the landmark 2016 peace deal between the government and the Farc failed to resolve, as other armed groups and Farc dissidents remained active. Some security experts saw the agreement as rushed. “It was a somewhat irresponsible decision,” said Paula Tobo, a senior researcher at the thinktank Ideas for Peace Foundation, which published an extensive report on why Total Peace failed. Tobo said the 99 were now in a “legal limbo” because their protection rested on decrees that could be revoked and there is no legal framework for their transition to civilian life. In South Korea, it is illegal to travel to dangerous countries. Journalists say it’s making their work impossible

Shortly after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, freelance photographer Jang Jinyoung crossed from Poland into Lviv and travelled on to Kyiv, where he spent a fortnight documenting the war. South Korea’s foreign ministry had designated Ukraine off-limits days earlier, making unauthorised visits a criminal offence. He knew he was breaking the law but went anyway, as no Korean journalist had yet reported from inside the country. “Everything back home was being relayed through foreign outlets. I wanted to see it more directly for myself,” Jang told the Guardian. On his return he was placed under criminal investigation. After refusing to accept a summary fine, a court north-west of Seoul this month convicted him and fined him 5m won (US$3,600). Related: Russia and North Korea finalising first road crossing amid concerns it serves as Ukraine war supply route Many countries release travel advisories for their citizens, but South Korea is one of the few developed democracies that criminalises visits to blacklisted countries.

On Friday, the country’s maximum penalty for such an offence tripled – from a year in prison or a 10m-won (US$7,200) fine to three years or a 30m won (US$21,700) fine, at the court’s discretion. The government says the system is necessary to protect citizens’ lives and safety, but critics argue the restrictions go beyond what’s required, and those with a genuine need to travel, including journalists and aid workers, are being unfairly caught out by the law. The foreign ministry says it grants 5,000 to 6,000 exceptions a year, including about 50 to journalists. But permission is discretionary and decided case by case. In Jang’s case, the application process for Ukraine specifically had not opened when he departed for the country. His case has been condemned by domestic and international press groups, and he is appealing against his conviction and plans to challenge the law at the constitutional court. A Palestinian woman and an NBC News team are reported to have been attacked and injured by masked Israeli settlers in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on Saturday, amid worsening confrontations in the area. Benjamin Netanyahu said he condemned the violence committed “by a handful of rioters”. The attack occurred when four members of the news team were interviewing Aida Ahmed Abdullah and her family in the Palestinian town of Jalud, near Nablus. Abdullah told the outlet that they had been driven out of their home by settlers, and the team was walking down a hill toward the house. A car with Israeli license plates reversed up the hill toward them. At least four men with their faces covered leapt from the vehicle, hitting them with sticks and throwing rocks. “They jumped out, beat us, then jumped back in the car,” said NBC News correspondent Matt Bradley. Bradley was hit twice in the arm and treated at a nearby clinic. Abdullah, 51, was taken for medical care by the Red Crescent. Her injuries were not life-threatening. Three other members of the news team were also injured and treated.

Providers are seeing more patients in need of abortions later in pregnancy as abortion bans and restrictions proliferate in US states, all while access to insurance falls. Those bans and restrictions have also meant that later abortion care access has grown over the past decade in a handful of haven states and cities. Patients are showing up “later and sicker” in need of reproductive healthcare, said Diane Horvath, a co-founder of Partners in Abortion Care in Maryland. About 41 states have abortion bans or significant restrictions at some point in pregnancy. More than 20 million people have lost Medicaid coverage since 2023, while between 3 and 5 million people have lost or dropped their coverage through Affordable Care Act exchanges in recent months. “People are getting chucked off of Medicaid. The premiums are all going up,” Horvath said. Instead of seeking care early in pregnancy, she said: “They’re just not going in.

text:
Amin Mughal obituary

My friend Amin Mughal, who has died aged 91, was a Pakistani writer and critic living in exile in the UK, having been jailed for his political activities under the brutal regime of General Zia-ul-Haq. In London he worked as a journalist and commentator on BBC World Service Urdu, and was editor of Awāz, an Urdu daily published in London. He also wrote for the weekly Pakistani English-language magazine Viewpoint, based in Lahore, and the Daily Jang, published in Urdu and English in Lahore and London. His father, Mohammad Din, who served in the British Indian army in the first world war, ran a military hardware shop in Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh, central India, until the partition of the country in 1947. His mother, Fazal Bibi, was a homemaker and avid reader of newspapers. Following partition, the family settled in Kotli Loharan, in the Sialkot district of the Pakistani part of Punjab. There Amin was born, the youngest of five children, with a brother and three sisters. He went to the local high school and Murray college, then to Government College University Lahore for his BSc and a master’s in English.

citation.title: Amin Mughal obituary

text:
Amin Mughal obituary

In 1958, he was offered a lectureship at Government Islamia College in Lahore, where he taught English language and literature for 20 years. He was ousted from the college along with two communist colleagues, Manzoor Ahmed and Eric Cyprian, on charges of anti-Islamic activities, but the real issue for Amin was his trade union work – he had been secretary general of the West Pakistan College Teachers’ Association. The three of them founded Shah Husain college in 1970 and ran it until it was nationalised under Zulfikar Ali Bhutto two years later. Amin was also a member of the National Awami party, becoming its secretary general in 1970 and deputised for Mazhar Ali Khan (the father of Tariq Ali) on the editorial team of Viewpoint, which was launched in 1975. He was imprisoned many times and under Gen Zia was sent to the notorious torture cells of Lahore Fort. Arriving in London in 1984, Amin was in the forefront of the movement for the recognition of the Punjabi language in Pakistan.

text:
Amin Mughal obituary

For public debate, he wrote tracts in Punjabi on classical Sufi poets such as Shah Husain, Wāris Shāh, and Bulleh Shah, and also translated into English works of some contemporary Punjabi poets, including me. We met for the first time during a demonstration outside the Pakistan high commission, London, in 1985. I come from the other side of the India-Pakistan border and Amin and I shared our personal and political histories – everything except our denominations. He began working for the BBC and for Awāz in the 90s. For 20 years he did voluntary social service at his neighbourhood Royal Free hospital in Belsize Park. He also worked as a freelance translator and interpreter for the NHS and several local authorities in London. A voracious reader and a keen observer, Amin was one of the most ardent thinkers from Pakistan. He jokingly called himself a “Marxist Muslim and Buddhist”, and was a father figure to the leftwing Punjabi community throughout the UK. He is survived by 13 nephews and nieces.

Fifteen British nationals are reported to be missing in China as the search continues for survivors of the devastating flooding in Nepal and Tibet. Nepali and Chinese authorities confirmed an updated death toll of at least 810 on Sunday. More than 3,000 people are believed missing after flash floods triggered by a massive glacier collapse in the Himalayas on Wednesday engulfed Gyirong port on the Nepal-China border. Related: ‘The river has taken everything’: people return to remains of their homes in Nepal The 15 missing British people are among 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries missing in China, according to figures released by Chinese authorities, bringing the total of missing Britons between Tibet and Nepal to 48. The Tibet autonomous region’s government said the total missing there also included 104 Nepalis, 49 people from India, 33 from Latvia and 18 from the US. Thirty-three British people had already been declared missing on the Nepal side of the border.

Definitely no or maybe yes: what tipped the Icelandic referendum

It was always going to be a close contest. But on the night, the figures showed just how divided Iceland was on the issue of whether or not to restart negotiations with the European Union. After a nail-biting overnight count, the well-funded no campaign rejoiced on Sunday morning as the broadcaster RUV declared it the winner with about 52.8% of the vote. Given the size of Iceland’s population – barely 400,000 – the margins were tiny. Opponents had criticised the no campaign as fearmongering, its tactics compared by some to those deployed by Brexit activists in the UK’s 2016 referendum. Its depiction of fishing and farming, two issues inextricably tied to Icelandic national identity, as threatened by EU membership were central to its success. Results showed a big split between voters in the capital region and the rest of the largely rural country, where among some there is a sense that national identity is at risk of being forgotten.

But it was perhaps also the question on the ballot paper that, despite the allure of a closer relationship with Europe at a time of global volatility and an erratic US president threatening Iceland’s larger neighbour, Greenland, helped the no voters win the day. The question Icelanders were asked was “Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?”. A second referendum was to be held once a deal had been reached. Iceland, it is important to note, is already a member of the European Economic Area (EEA) and the Schengen passport-free travel area. Related: Sovereignty, farming and fishing: Iceland votes on its future with the EU This meant that a vote yes would have actually been a “yes, maybe”, whereas a no vote was always a clearer, more decisive move. At a yes campaign party at Reykjavík Art Museum in the Icelandic capital’s downtown area, at a point in the election night where yes seemed to have edged ahead, Þòrir Snoor, a yes supporter, said: “The no side has done a lot of fearmongering and done it very very well.” While he had a lot of peers who, like him, thought the euro could be the solution to the country’s high inflation and high interest rates, the 25-year-old admitted: “A lot of my friends have said they are scared of the European Union.” Wearing a blue EU cap, Snædis Inga Rúnarsdóttir, 30, agreed that the no campaign had been louder – and better funded. A headteacher in Nepal evacuated 900 children from a school moments before a deadly wall of water struck their town amid the devastating flash floods that have killed almost 800 people and left thousands missing. Rajendra Dawadi decided to halt classes and order children to higher ground after receiving warnings about the scale of the flooding heading their way. Dawadi, the headteacher at Tribhuvan Trishuli secondary school in Nuwakot, which has 1,600 pupils, said he had received four warnings from different people within minutes, including one from Betrawati, a town directly upstream. This prompted him to take immediate action. “I decided I shouldn’t delay any more,” he told the BBC. “Even if the flood was not coming, it was just a matter of a single day’s classes.” Dawadi said during the evacuation of the school he saw a hostel building about 100 metres from the river being engulfed by the torrent of flood water. “If we had made the decision 10 minutes later, all of us, including the students and me, would not be able to speak to you today,” he said.

Iceland rejects EU accession talks after divisive referendum campaign

Voters in Iceland have ⁠rejected ⁠a government proposal ​to reopen ⁠accession talks with ⁠the ​EU after a closely fought referendum campaign that divided the country against a backdrop of global volatility. After a long and anxious night for those on both sides of the debate, the no camp ended up with 52.8% of votes on Sunday morning and the yes camp with 47.2%. Voter turnout was high at 82.5%. The vote was held in the shadow of repeated threats by Donald Trump to invade or acquire neighbouring Greenland. Although Iceland is a Nato member, supporters of EU membership said European solidarity would provide greater protection if Trump ever made similar threats towards the smaller, Arctic island. At a press conference the prime minister, Kristrún Frostadóttir, said the campaign had “raised the debate in Iceland to a higher level” while acknowledging that there were aspects that “could have been done better”. Given how close the outcome was, she said, it was important to respect the views of yes voters.

Monday briefing: Nepal and Tibet’s floods are a warning for the future

Good morning. Over the weekend, rescue workers in Nepal and Tibet raced to find people who are still trapped in villages affected by catastrophic flash floods. As of this morning, the death toll stands at 903, and more than 4,000 people are missing. For those of you reading this in a place where life continues as usual, the scale of devastation is hard to fathom. In a matter of minutes, a torrent of mud and debris engulfed entire villages, snapped bridges and swept away people’s homes and families. Some survivors are marooned on top of buildings that rescue workers can’t reach. Others are trapped in tunnels beneath the ground. Many have no idea if their loved ones are still alive. The floods exemplify a wider threat. The delicate processes that have shaped our climate for centuries are unwinding at a terrifying pace. Scientists are still investigating the precise sequence of events that caused these floods, but as the planet heats up and glaciers melt, events like this will keep happening.

A lone Black woman’s defiance of Swedish neo-Nazis, 10 years on

The striking photograph showed a lone Black woman, her fist raised, standing in the path of hundreds of uniformed neo-Nazis on parade in 2016, and it made headlines across the globe. At the time, it was held up as a symbol of the resistance to the far right. But 10 years on, as Sweden gears up for elections in which the far right is expected to emerge as the second most-voted-for party, the woman in the photo sees it as a sign of the bewildering change that has gripped the Scandinavian country. “Ten years ago, people would say: ‘Oh we dislike the far right, the Sweden Democrats, we despise Nazis,’” said Tess Asplund, 52. “And now, they’ve become normalised. It’s like, what happened?” Related: Woman who defied 300 neo-Nazis at Swedish rally speaks of anger Her comments hint at the recent reshaping of Swedish politics, where the far right – once a pariah – has steadily marched into the halls of power. “I’m sad, afraid and ashamed of Swedish citizens,” said Asplund in an interview at a cafe in central Stockholm.

“It’s pure racism.” Ahead of a general election on 13 September, polls suggest that the centre-left opposition has a lead over the ruling rightwing coalition, meaning a change of government could be on the cards. But the Sweden Democrats, a party with neo-Nazi roots, is expected to garner the second-most votes in the country. In the 2022 elections, it also came second, paving the way for it to play a supporting role in a minority-run coalition. The party has long been dogged by accusations of harbouring violent racists and swastika-wearing Nazi sympathisers. It has used its leverage in government to consistently target migrants, including asylum seekers, as well as Muslims, ushering in ultra-restrictive migration policies and a discourse that routinely disparages the millions of people from around the world who have made Sweden their home and seek to contribute to it. Earlier this year, the Swedish prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, mused that if his four-party coalition won the upcoming election, the far right could enter government, in what was seen as a watershed moment for Swedish politics.

It was a sharp contrast to the Sweden that Asplund had stood up for on 1 May 2016. She and scores of others had travelled to the central Swedish city of Borlänge to rally against a planned march by the Nordic Resistance Movement, one of the country’s largest neo-Nazi groups. As she faced off against them, her act of defiance was caught on camera by the photographer David Lagerlöf of Expo, the anti-racism foundation in Stockholm. It soon went viral, with Swedish media likening it to another iconic image of resistance: a 1985 photo in which photographer Hans Runesson captured a woman taking aim at a skinhead with her handbag in the south-western city of Växjö. Media requests poured in from around the world. In Sweden, people began stopping Asplund on the streets, thanking her for her gesture, though she also grappled with a stream of online harassment and death threats on her home telephone line.

French high schools rush to put Macron’s phone ban into force

French high schools are rushing to put in place a ban on mobile phones this week as Emmanuel Macron pushes for children to spend less time in front of screens. Education unions warned that banning mobile phone use in lycées – where children are aged 15 to 18 – would be hard to implement quickly. Macron approved the high school phone ban this month after another measure he had hoped would be a key legacy, his proposed social media ban for under-15s, was knocked back as unconstitutional. The text of the social media ban is being rewritten in the hope it can be pushed it through before Macron leaves office in May. France has already banned children from using mobile phones in primary schools and in middle schools, or collèges, which are attended between the ages of 11 and 15. The government’s focus is now on banning mobile phone use among older teenagers at school from September, as it argues that too much screen time is harming children’s development.

The German government is imminently expected to announce who it believes was behind a suspected drone attack on a Ukrainian cargo plane earlier this month and to outline its response to the incident in coordination with its European and Nato partners. It won’t take much longer.” The government has so far declined to say officially who it thinks was behind the attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle airport on 4 August. There has been widespread speculation that it was coordinated by Moscow. A drone containing explosives was discovered near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft used to transport military supplies. Iran’s economy in crisis as US launches new sanctions campaign

For many Iranians, the new US sanctions campaign, called Operation Economic Outcast, seems superfluous given the grim economic situation in their country. Iranians are facing runaway food inflation, closed petrol stations and a seemingly never-ending depreciation of the nation’s currency caused by a lack of foreign exchange reserves. Vegetable oil in Iran in August cost 383% more than a year ago. The price of eggs rose by 294%, chicken by 177% and red meat by 148%. The cratering economy leaves the country’s political class on edge as they try to prevent economic conditions leading to social chaos. In truth, long before Donald Trump’s latest sanctions push, Iran’s economy had become a parallel battlefield in which the country’s economic commanders were struggling to maintain control. On 23 August, the US dollar reached roughly 2m rials on Iran’s open market, a new record. Three days later, Iran’s statistical centre announced that year-on-year inflation in August reached 84.4%; the rolling annual average rate was about 65%.

For British colonialists, the fertile and cool uplands of central Kenya were the “White Highlands”, to be reserved exclusively for European settlers. Local communities were forced from the land, which was turned into plantations for tea and other crops. In recent decades, descendants of the displaced have fought to reclaim their ancestral land, some of which is now occupied by multinational tea companies and other large corporations. The fight for restitution is the subject of Kikuyu Land, a documentary film directed by the Kenyan film-maker Bea Wangondu and her American counterpart Andrew H Brown that is being released in the UK on Friday. “Colonial structures didn’t just shape land and labour in Kenya.
