This could be told sadly in almost every part of the world.” In 1902, under Sir Charles Eliot, then commissioner of the East Africa Protectorate (present-day Kenya), a law was passed making vast tracts of fertile ancestral land “Crown land”, allowing the government to sell and lease land to white settlers to encourage their settlement and farming, ignoring African communal land ownership systems. Related: Kikuyu Land review – the colonial-era misery behind our morning cup of tea The policy attracted settlers and led to the violent displacement of local communities to marginalised, crowded and less-productive “native reserves”. In 1962, a year before independence, the colonial administration initiated a redistribution programme to transfer farms in the highlands from departing white settlers to landless Kenyans. The programme was aimed at purchasing land in the highlands from willing white settlers and reselling it to Kenyans on credit. By the time it ended in 1971, about 1.15m acres of land had been bought from 780 white farmers and sold to approximately 35,000 Kenyan families.

About three years ago I became interested in how Hitler’s National Socialist German Workers’ party (NSDAP) rose to prominence when Germany was still a democracy, because I hoped it could tell us something about the success of rightwing extremist movements today. From looking at historical sources, I realised that the Reichstag elections of 14 September 1930 were in many ways more important than what happened in 1932 and 1933. And I expected it to be an open-and-shut case. But the more I looked into it, the more I realised that most of the theories we have to explain the rise of the Nazis don’t make sense – the data tells a completely different, far darker story. How poor public transport policy is putting the brake on cities

Your analysis of slowing buses in global cities sets out the mechanism exactly, and the remedy follows from it (London buses in decline? Why public transport in global cities is slowing to a crawl – visualised, 23 September). Transport for London’s own calculation that a 10% fall in speed costs 6% of demand and Imperial College London’s finding of the same decline across 15 cities show what happens to buses as the traffic thickens around them. Retiming the lights will not reverse it, and London is already trying. The phrase to notice in the article is one used by TfL: signals will give more buses priority “where possible”. There lies the difficulty. On a route running a bus every two minutes, the signals are asked to intervene 30 times an hour in each direction, and the junction cannot recover between calls before the next bus arrives. Bristol city council’s engineers found precisely this when they reviewed their bus priority: in the most congested parts of the city, priority delivered no journey-time saving at all. This is a bigger brake on the economy than it looks.

text:
How poor public transport policy is putting the brake on cities

What holds a city back is the plain difficulty of getting across it to work, to customers, to the shops. A firm can recruit from a smaller area, a worker can reach fewer jobs, and a high street can be reached by fewer people. Much of the decline of the high street is a decline in how easily people can get to it. The cure is to carry the same people in fewer vehicles. One tram carries as many people as three or four buses, so it can be given priority junction after junction, and the crossing traffic still gets its turn. About 30 French cities have put trams through their centres since Nantes started in 1985, and they rebuilt those centres around them. Their central streets are visibly busier for it. Sheffield’s trams share a shopping street with cars and vans, and run to the same timetable in the peak as at midday. How poor public transport policy is putting the brake on cities

Buses have slowed down as dedicated bus lanes have been largely replaced by a poor choice of cycle lanes. London is an old city with narrow lanes and, with individual cycle transport given priority over mass public transport, it’s no wonder that buses have slowed and become erratic in service. One only needs to observe the utilisation of cycle lanes that are empty except during the peak hours of 7.30am-9am and 4pm-5pm on weekdays. That is a gross waste of valuable road space that could be used by buses. Having a dedicated bus lane instead of a cycle lane would speed up buses and make them more reliable. The bus lane could be shared by cycles and during peak times be dedicated to them, while being free for buses rest of the day. Sadly, politicians rarely look beyond elections, and fail to prioritise buses over bicycles. The authorities have wasted millions on cycle lanes while failing spectacularly to improve mass public transportation. Kyiv Independent editor: ‘Our readers want Russia to suffer but we can’t be propagandists’

Readers of Ukraine’s leading English news site “really want Russia to suffer” but that should not lead the title to downplay the military and political problems facing Kyiv, its editor-in-chief has said. Speaking to the Guardian before an event in London, Olga Rudenko said many of the Kyiv Independent’s most-read stories described Ukrainian deep strike attacks into Russia, potentially distorting its coverage. The Kyiv Independent, however, cannot afford to become propagandistic, she argued, and marginalise Russian military successes or reduce reporting on Ukrainian corruption because the subjects are not so well read. “We had a conversation in the newsroom when somebody raised that our website, in the mornings, is all about Ukrainian attacks on Russian Wildberries warehouses and so on,” Rudenko said.

The “core idea of the Kyiv Independent is that we’re not Ukrainian propaganda, we’re not affiliated with the government, we’re not Ukraine’s PR service,” the editor said. Rudenko said she had “no expectation” that the war would end any time soon, with Russia stepping up its bombing of Kyiv before winter and Ukrainian strikes denting its neighbour’s economy while diplomacy is stalled. It is a feeling that has hung over journalists at the site for some time. This year employees did not bother planning for a peacetime scenario in their annual strategy session. “It was the first time when this question wasn’t really arising,” Rudenko said.

New Google Maps images reveal massive scale of devastation in Gaza

An update to Google Maps has revealed the extent of devastation during the three-year Gaza war and the severity of the continuing humanitarian crisis faced by the territory’s 2.3 million inhabitants. The images were taken in June this year and show further destruction of homes, businesses, places of worship and infrastructure since a fragile ceasefire came into effect almost 12 months ago. They show huge tented camps lining much of the shoreline, often within a few metres of the sea. Gaza’s once busy main port, now badly damaged and empty of fishing boats, is surrounded by makeshift accommodation. Any available open space in Gaza City is packed with shacks, tents and huts. The images also show massive damage to northern towns such as Beit Hanoun, as well as the destruction of places of worship such as the Istiqlal mosque in Khan Younis. Major neighbourhoods in Gaza City such as Jabaliya and Shuja’iya, which were targeted in repeated Israeli offensives, are clearly now uninhabitable.

citation.title: New Google Maps images reveal massive scale of devastation in Gaza

text:
New Google Maps images reveal massive scale of devastation in Gaza

Swaths of rubble are visible in the south of Gaza, where a wide strip appears to have been cleared by Israeli forces along the border with Egypt. The town of Rafah appears to have been almost entirely reduced to rubble and Tel al-Sultan razed to the ground. More than 2.1 million displaced people are living in tents and temporary shelters in Gaza, where about 82% of structures – roughly 200,000 buildings – have been damaged, with about two-thirds of those destroyed, according to the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, Unrwa. A recent UN assessment estimated that the number of destroyed structures across Gaza had increased by 9% since the declaration of a ceasefire in October 2025. “The estimate of the total amount of rubble in Gaza is 61m tonnes. It is approximately 20 times the amount of rubble generated in all wars across the world over the last 18 years,” Jaco Cilliers, the UN Development Programme’s special representative in Palestine told the Guardian last month. The presence of human remains still buried under the rubble remains one of the most urgent humanitarian problems.

The German town where the right has banned new ‘stumbling stones’ for Nazi victims

The town hall of Heidenau, Germany has a freshly restored cream-coloured facade, tidy flower boxes on the windowsills and a charming shingled clocktower. At the entrance, closer inspection reveals a single brass plaque embedded in the pavement honouring the former mayor Paul Gröger, whom the Nazis hounded into killing himself. The plaque is one of 128,000 Stolpersteine (stumbling stones) across Europe, a donor-funded project keeping alive the memory of individual victims of the Nazi era. It is by some measure considered the world’s biggest grassroots memorial project, and has become an integral part of Germany’s “remembrance culture” for the atrocities committed under Adolf Hitler. But last week at the same town hall, the council of Heidenau voted to halt the laying of future stumbling stones. In a decision that drew a national outcry, the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party joined forces with the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) of Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, to help form the majority.

Thursday briefing: The long, long wait for a male contraceptive pill may soon be over

Good morning. Since the first vasectomy was performed in the 1890s (imagine being that volunteer), the male contraceptive armoury has barely advanced. The last reversible method was added to this repertoire centuries ago: while rubber condoms hit the mass market in the 1850s, earlier versions date back beyond ancient Egypt. This looks on the cusp of change. In a landmark announcement last week, the World Health Organization said it expects reversible male contraceptives to be available on the market within five to 10 years. But no major medical breakthrough has just been announced - the fundamentals of male hormonal contraceptives have been known for decades. So what is the science, how does it work and why has it taken so long to get here? That’s the subject of today’s First Edition. Before that, this morning’s headlines. In depth: The ‘agonisingly slow’ wait for male contraceptives It’s estimated that 70% of women in the UK have used the contraceptive pill at some point in their lives, having first been introduced here in 1961 (for married women only). The pace at which the pill proliferated is remarkable - the first trials of hormonal contraception for women began in the United States in the 1950s: by 1960 it was available, and within two years, 1.2 million American women were using it. Despite the pill’s wide uptake and high efficacy, the need for further effective methods of reversible contraception has remained consistent. Nearly half of all global pregnancies are unintended, with many resulting in unsafe abortions. An array of options have been developed for women to use - coils both hormonal and metal; implants, injections, patches, pills and vaginal rings. Men have condoms, and, well, coitus interruptus. Even with these limited options, about 30% of couples already rely on a male method. Male hormonal contraception targets sperm, which are constantly produced.

“This requires continuous, steady suppression, suppression all day, every day,” Richard Anderson tells me, “but it is proven to work”. Anderson is a professor of clinical reproductive science at Edinburgh University, and has spent decades in the field. It’s close to 50 years since the first hormonal contraceptives were tested on men, but their development has since been “agonisingly slow,” says Anderson. It’s not that scientific successes weren’t there. “While there have been refinements focused on optimal drug formulations, the fundamentals have remained the same.” *** How do male hormonal contraceptives work? While some research looks to target either sperm function or transport, most male contraceptive science today focuses on sperm production. A testosterone-based treatment can trick the brain into switching sperm creation off, while ensuring bodily hormones remain at a healthy level. In the late 1980s, proof-of-concept clinical trials were conducted by the WHO with weekly testosterone injections.

He was involved in a subsequent trial of 450 couples which confirmed hormonal suppression is “highly effective” in reducing sperm count. By the 1990s, the science was further fine-tuned. With the addition of progestin (a synthetic hormone also widely used in hormone replacement therapy), these male hormonal contraceptives became far more effective, with a success rate equivalent to female hormonal methods. The quantity of testosterone required also decreased with this new formulation, potentially improving long-term patient safety. More recently, the US National Institutes of Health funded a major international study of a testosterone/progestogen gel, with participants rubbing it into their shoulders daily. Trials have been conducted across North and South America, Africa and Europe (Anderson has overseen Edinburgh’s 40–couple cohort), with “surprisingly effective” early results and an “extremely low” pregnancy rate.

Ukraine persists with Russian oil refinery strikes in defiance of Trump

Ukraine is pressing on with strikes on Russian oil refineries, defying Donald Trump, who blames the attacks for exacerbating a global diesel shortage and pushing up fuel prices. Kyiv struck an oil facility in Russia’s southern Samara region overnight, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Thursday in a statement on social media. The Ukrainian president added that a Russian vessel in the Black Sea was hit, as well as a launch and storage site for attack drones in the Oryol region. Trump has urged Zelenskyy in a private phone call to halt attacks on Russian refineries and repeatedly suggested in public that Ukraine’s strikes are to blame for the squeeze on global fuel supplies. “Diesel is really hurt much more, not by the Middle East, but by what’s going on in Russia, because those diesel refineries are being knocked out at a pretty alarming rate,” Trump said on Wednesday.

He was one of the most passionate propagandists for Hugo Chávez’s Bolivarian revolution: a feisty leftist TV personality who spent more than two decades singing the movement’s praises on his state-funded show, The Razorblade. Mario Silva’s devotion was such that he often hosted his programme with Chávez’s portrait behind him and he had El Comandante’s curly signature tattooed on to his left wrist. Manes, an Israeli bank executive, immediately told a flight attendant seated nearby that something was wrong. When he did not react, she shouted at him: “Something is happening in there!” Seconds later, the man “simply went to the [cockpit] door and opened it”, Manes told Israel’s Channel 12 TV. Inside, the scene was the stuff of travellers’ nightmares: blood spattered over the cockpit walls and a brutal struggle in progress between the badly injured pilot and the co-pilot, who was armed with some kind of sharp weapon. There was no one at the controls of the Boeing 737. Manes shouted again: “He’s stabbing the pilot, he’s stabbing the pilot, come help!” Many of the details of what happened on flight FZ 1073 are still unclear, but what happened next is well documented by witness testimony and videos.

It remains unclear precisely how the commotion began, but debate over the issue exploded last week when a remark by Bolsonaro, whose movement includes many evangelical Christians, went viral online. In a recent broadcast, the former senator said one of his first acts as president would be to “decree that Brazil belongs to the Lord Jesus Christ”. Some Catholics took that as a sign that the Protestant politician planned to unseat Our Lady of Aparecida, although only the Vatican – which declared her Brazil’s patroness in 1930 – has the authority to do so. Those suspicions were reinforced by Bolsonaro’s reported links to JB Carvalho, an evangelical leader who has previously called for the patroness’s removal. In 2007, another Bolsonaro ally tried to introduce legislation to the same effect, although the bill was dropped. Bolsonaro has called claims he plans to unseat Our Lady of Aparecida “fake news”. He alleged the rumours were being spread by Lula supporters, as well as members of the Episcopal Conference of Brazil, a Catholic bishops’ organisation. The conference rejected the charge.

With the result expected to be even tighter than the last one – when Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro by less than 2% – even a small number of votes could mean the difference between victory and defeat. Lula has appeared on the campaign trail holding statuettes of the Virgin Mary while his wife, Janja da Silva, has worn a pendant honouring Our Lady of Aparecida. “As long as I’m president, no one will disrespect Our Lady of Aparecida. No one. People need to learn to respect all religions,” Lula told a rally in the Amazon. Lula’s vice-president and running mate, a devout Catholic called Geraldo Alckmin, published a video describing how he had received messages from Catholics “worried about the direction of the country and the terrible news that has been circulating”. Alckmin assured voters he and Lula would preserve and protect “religious traditions, so sacred to Brazilian families”.

text:
Friday briefing: How we covered the flydubai incident as it unfolded

Good morning. Shocking news of a cockpit stabbing. Graphic footage of bloodied crew members. Mid-air testimony from terrified passengers. This was the tenor of the heart-in-mouth reporting as the horrifying events unfolded onboard flight FZ 1073 to Tel Aviv: the early morning budget flight that plummeted 17,000ft in under two minutes before the courageous intervention of passengers and crew averted an apparent hijacking, potentially saving the lives of not just the 170+ passengers and crew on board, but many more. This morning, speculation and conflicting reports are continuing to emerge about this dramatic incident in the sky above the most geopolitically sensitive region in the world. So how does the Guardian report a swiftly developing story engulfed in misinformation, as accurately and responsibility as possible? I spoke to the reporters, bloggers and editors involved to find out. But first, this morning’s headlines.

In depth: ‘It was very, very tricky to untangle what was happening’ International leaders have rushed to praise Smit Machchhar, the captain of flight FZ 1073. Bleeding heavily from multiple stab wounds, he somehow managed to release his cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to gain entry and overpower his co-pilot turned assailant, an Omani national, who had attacked Machchhar in an apparent attempt to crash the plane. Other crew members were able to stabilise the flight and, just before 11am local time on Wednesday, the Boeing 737 Max made a safe emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. All 174 passengers on board escaped serious injury. Yesterday, as internationally coordinated investigations continued, the attacker’s motives remained unknown. Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox News it was “too early to say” if there was any Iranian involvement, while claiming the co-pilot had previously undergone radical Islamist indoctrination and was suicidal. Other senior Israeli figures have been more vehement, with ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, describing the incident as a “terror attack”.

India’s Cockroach movement launches new protests over changes to voter roll

India’s youth-led Cockroach movement kicked off more nationwide protests on Friday as thousands of people gathered in Mumbai, amid mounting concerns that millions of citizens are being unfairly stripped of their vote. The movement, which calls itself the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) and has massive support among the country’s gen Zs, returned to the streets to demand the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar. Kumar has become a highly contentious figure after a report in the Indian Express newspaper alleged irregularities and internal concerns about a process to revise and “purify” India’s electoral register, called the Special Intensive Revision (SIR). SIR, which was overseen by Kumar, has resulted in tens of millions of people being deleted from the electoral register. Large numbers are challenging their removal. Opposition politicians and civil society groups have alleged SIR is part of a widespread manipulation of India’s electoral system to benefit the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).

‘I was fighting for my life’: Indian pilot hailed as hero recalls flydubai cockpit attack

The Indian pilot who helped thwart an apparent attempt to crash a flydubai flight to Tel Aviv said his faith and his desire to save his passengers allowed him to make a “last push” to open the cockpit door as he fought for his life. Capt Smit Machchhar, who was recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, described to India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, how he helped save the plane and its more than 170 passengers. “I had suffered so many injuries that I had collapsed. At that time, I could feel that the aircraft was going down. I knew this was the last push,” Machchhar told Modi in a video call on Friday. “I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives.” His Omani co-pilot apparently stabbed him and set the plane on a steep descent, with the aircraft plummeting about 17,000 feet in the span of a minute. While still being attacked, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter, subdue the attacker and ultimately stabilise the plane.

‘I was fighting for my life’: Indian pilot hailed as hero recalls flydubai cockpit attack

The full circumstances of the attack are still under investigation, but a relief crew on the flight helped land the plane safely in Tabouk, north-west Saudi Arabia. Magnitude 4.8 earthquake hits Victoria with tremors felt across Melbourne

A magnitude 4.8 earthquake struck Victoria in the early hours of Saturday morning, shaking Melbourne and waking people across the whole region. Geoscience Australia said it detected an earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 4.8 at 2.01am near Leongatha, 130km south-east of Melbourne, with the tremors felt across the city’s eastern suburbs. Geoscience Australia said it had received thousands of reports from people who said they had felt the earthquake. Posting on Facebook, Brian Morley in Narre Warren said “felt it and woke me up”, while Theresa Stevens said: “Shook our house in Garfield.” Other posts indicated the quake had been felt in Preston, Heidelberg Heights, Venus Bay and many other parts of Melbourne. The quake was estimated to have struck at about 10km below the Earth’s surface. Victoria’s State Emergency Service said the earthquake was a “timely reminder” to remember the drill to follow during an earthquake and that was drop to the ground, take cover under a sturdy piece of furniture and protect your head and neck, and hold on until the shaking stops.

Spanish right wing votes down housing crisis plans as protest movement grows

Rightwing lawmakers in Spain have rejected emergency measures put forward to tackle the country’s housing crisis, pitting a fractured parliament against the widespread protest movement that has swelled in recent days. On Friday Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist-led coalition put forward two decrees that included a range of measures aimed at improving access to housing, from a ban on evictions until 2030 to the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room. As hundreds of protesters outside the parliament building in Madrid held up homemade signs bearing images of vultures, the conservative People’s party, the far-right Vox and the Catalan pro-independence party Junts voted against both decrees. The People’s party said it had voted in line with its belief that building, rather than regulating, was the best way to address the crisis. “Housing doesn’t become more affordable through decrees; it becomes more affordable by building ​more homes,” said the lawmaker Juan Bravo.

Tens of thousands of people heeded the call by housing campaigners to take to the streets, while encampments protesting against the housing crisis sprung up in cities across Spain. As dozens of school pupils sat on top of a pile of wheelie bins blocking a high school entrance in north-eastern Paris, Sophia, 17, was on the frontline of the barricade, when she would normally have been attending Spanish class. “We hope this grows into a massive youth protest movement,” said the final year baccalaureate student at Paris’s Lycée Voltaire, who did not want her real name published. She was on her second day of blocking the school entrance along with hundreds of others, ensuring all lessons were cancelled. “We just want to be listened to by the government. We’d rather stand here doing this than have to learn in poor conditions. It’s the only way to make ourselves heard.” “School is a right, not a privilege,” read a cardboard sign as Sophia listed the grievances of teenagers across France: a lack of state investment in education, overcrowded classes of up to 40 children in crumbling buildings, poor teacher pay, staff absences and an unequal system in which social background determined success.

Valeriya Tkachenko was dropping her son off at school in central Kyiv when the air raid alert sounded. Staff hurried the children and parents into the shelter, where the frightened lawyer spent the next two hours with her son. “I’m scared to death all day about what could happen to my son,” she said as she emerged from the shelter, already late for work. A day earlier, a Russian jet-powered drone had struck a school nearby. “And I can’t plan anything any more,” she said. “It’s not sustainable like this.” Across the city on Friday morning, Artem Marchenko, an IT worker, was forced to abandon his car and walk for 20 minutes across the Pivdennyi, or Southern, Bridge on his way to work after repeated Russian strikes damaged the crossing. He feared Russia would soon target Kyiv’s other bridges, paralysing movement across a city of about 3 million people, the two halves of which are divided by the Dnipro. On Saturday morning, Russia targeted a second major bridge connecting Kyiv, damaging the road surface on the Northern Bridge and temporarily halting traffic.

The Rev Ian Gregory obituary

There was a point in the 1980s when the Rev Ian Gregory, a former journalist and church minister, who has died aged 93, was himself making the news. In the time of Margaret Thatcher, the yuppy and union battles, Ian, my father-in-law, launched a campaign to bring back courtesy. Ever with an eye for a good headline, he called his campaign group the Polite Society. The landline in his Staffordshire house lit up with calls from newspapers and broadcasters around the world. The Los Angeles Times quoted Ian as saying that Britain had rebutted many enemies in the past 80 years, but “in 1986, the British people face national defeat at the hands of a sinister foe: our ignorant and ill-mannered selves”. During this heyday there was a warm seat for Ian on breakfast TV sofas, often side-by-side with pop stars – Rick Parfitt of Status Quo wore a Polite Society badge on his leather jacket for years after they met. Although the Polite Society may have had a conservative, nostalgic whiff about it, Ian was a radical in his Christian ministry.

citation.title: The Rev Ian Gregory obituary

text:
The Rev Ian Gregory obituary

Ordained in 1983, he was a much-loved minister at King Street Congregational church, Newcastle-under-Lyme, who was not afraid to question faith, and invited people to think rather than accept. He was one of few ministers who would marry divorced people. He blessed babies in pubs – because he believed in meeting people where they felt comfortable – and he held Christmas services for licensees. A pub chain asked him to train staff in the importance of courtesy, and this led to a hostelry in his home town being named after him: the Polite Vicar. Born in Bolton to Gabriel Gregory, a Congregational minister, and Lilian (nee Unsworth), a teacher, Ian went to Silcoates, Wakefield, a boarding school for the sons of Congregational ministers, then Peartree secondary school in Derby. In 1953 he went to Lancashire Independent College, a theological institution in Whalley Range, Manchester, where his father had also studied. Ian became a journalist after leaving college following a “scandal” when a bottle of ginger wine was found in his room there.

text:
The Rev Ian Gregory obituary

He said what made him a good journalist – getting things done by deadline and “being impatient with wafflers” – did not sit well with being a church minister, so the ministry had to wait. He knocked on the editor’s door of the Stockport Advertiser in 1954, was given a reporting job, and was told that all journalists wore a trilby hat. Ian took to it, and a trilby became a wardrobe staple. Ian was one of the first journalists to work at BBC Radio Derby when it launched in 1971; his combative interviews with the then Derbyshire county council leader, David Bookbinder, were well known. He retired in 2003. He continued questioning up to his death, reading theology and science books, and writing pamphlets from his garden shed office. Ian is survived by his wife, Trisha (nee Donaldson), whom he met in 1960 and married five years later, their children, Russell (my husband), Rachel and Jamie, four grandchildren and two great-grandchildren.

Bangkok at breaking point as floods turn streets into stagnant lakes

Bangkok is used to absorbing the sudden afternoon downpours that inundate the city during the rainy season. Even streets in many central high-rise districts can briefly turn into rivers, with rats and cockroaches racing out of sewers and taking temporary refuge on trees and buildings as the subterranean world is flushed out. But every city has a breaking point, and this year rain fell so fast and so hard that whole neighbourhoods of the Thai capital have been transformed, not into rivers, but stagnant lakes. In parts of the city, roughly 300mm of rain – the equivalent of half a year of average rainfall in London – fell in about two days. About 40 people died in flood-related incidents, according to the government. A number of the deaths were from drowning and several from accidental electrocution. Thousands of people stayed in more than 230 shelters across the city, authorities said. Suleemas Kurangkul, a 73-year-old resident of a block of flats whose ground floor stairs are still under water, said last weekend’s rain was not the usual evening storm but was constant, “like all day, all night”.

Shortly after his controversial speech to the United Nations general assembly in September, Donald Trump gathered a dozen like-minded Latin American leaders and boasted that rightwing candidates had won all seven presidential elections held in the region since he began his second term. “Everybody I’ve endorsed has won,” the US president said in New York to most of the leaders of the Shield of the Americas, an anti-drug cartel coalition of 15 countries governed by the right or far right. Those electoral victories – and the US takeover of Venezuela after capturing Nicolás Maduro – have left just six Latin American countries under leftwing governments: regional heavyweights Brazil and Mexico, small Uruguay and Guatemala, and the isolated regimes of Cuba and Nicaragua. ‘We swept a lot under the carpet’: Vichy regime film hits home in France of 2026

It is the story of how a lowly state administrator unthinkingly becomes a cog in the machine of an authoritarian regime, embracing the bureaucracy and logistics of sending people to their deaths – and it is drawing in audiences to French cinemas. The French film Notre Salut (Our Salvation), with its modern lighting, improvised scenes and anachronistic 1980s Europop soundtrack, is far from the standard historical costume drama about the second world war. But the award-winning film about the daily lives of ordinary people participating in the puppet Vichy regime that collaborated with the Nazis – and ensured the deportation of a quarter of France’s Jewish population to concentration camps – is poised to become a box office hit. The film, which has been given the English-language title A Man of His Time, had a strong cinema opening in France this week, particularly among young audiences, at a time when the country is soul-searching ahead of next spring’s presidential election.

Almost a third of voters said an in-out referendum would be needed first, while more than one in six felt that a general election mandate would be sufficient, and the same proportion thought parliament could make the decision. The overall findings will bolster the case of those inside Downing Street who want to promise at the next election that Labour would at least negotiate over re-entry, which the prime minister has said he wants to see “in his lifetime”.

Exactly 100 years ago the Guardian wrote about the opening of London’s first mosque, an impressive white building surrounded by immaculate flower gardens in the heart of south London suburbia. A report described the mosque, in its incongruous surroundings, as “a thing of beauty”. The journalists who attended the opening ceremony witnessed the mosque’s large black doors being opened with a silver key. About 600 eminent guests attended the grand opening. Ahead of centenary celebrations at the Fazl Mosque in Wandsworth, also known as London Mosque, there is lots of activity taking place. Putney Labour MP Fleur Anderson pops in and speaks about how well loved the mosque, which is home to members of the UK’s Ahmadiyya Muslim community, is in the area. “No street party is complete without the wonderful food provided by this mosque,” she says. According to Mahmood Rafiq of the Ahmadiyya Muslim Community UK, being part of the wider community is a key part of the mosque’s ethos.

Can anything politicians say at Sunday’s election stop young people from leaving Bosnia?

On a perfect October morning in Sarajevo, the motivation for young people to be leaving Bosnia and Herzegovina in droves is not immediately apparent. The country’s capital is basking in the autumn sunshine and the pavement cafes in the shadow of the Sacred Heart Cathedral are packed. People lingering over coffee and cigarettes mix peacefully with the Swedish football fans in town for their team’s Nations League match. But Sarajevo’s many charms have not been enough to keep young people in Bosnia. One local organisation that tracks emigration estimated that more than 600,000 people had left the country in the decade after the 2013 census, when the official population was 3.5 million. “If I weren’t optimistic, maybe I would also move out,” said Timur Vilić, a 28-year-old municipal councillor in Sarajevo, who is standing on Sunday for election to the cantonal government. He represents Our Party – a multi-ethnic, non-nationalist, liberal movement that he admits faces a struggle to appeal to voters in a country dominated by ethnonationalist parties.

On the edge of Piazza Navona, one of the grandest squares in central Rome, Barry and Linda, visitors from Texas in the US, stepped out of a golf cart. They planned to cross the square on foot, perhaps stopping to admire Lorenzo Bernini’s 17th-century Fountain of the Four Rivers, before being picked up by their driver at the opposite end. The couple had already done a walking tour on day one of their trip, and had been so exasperated by a stifling three-hour shuffle along a corridor towards the Sistine Chapel on day two that by the third day they wanted to give their tired feet a rest. “When I first heard you could do golf cart tours in Rome, I thought to myself: that sounds a little weird,” said Barry. “But then we decided to try it out.” He said the most enjoyable thing about the experience was “feeling the breeze”. Rome is a difficult city to navigate, noted Linda, especially its ancient narrow streets in the centre. “There are no sidewalks,” she said. “Our feet were hurting and we needed a break.” For visitors, golf cart tours offer respite from the heat, crowds and cobbles.

‘We want action’: Fijian climate activist sends message ahead of UN talks in Pacific

From her wooden veranda in Fiji’s remote Yasawa islands, climate activist Lavenia Naivalu remembers when the reefs were once so healthy, her grandfather would walk to the shoreline and return with fish. But life there has changed. “The reefs that the older generation of men spearfished in, no longer provide what they once did,” the 44-year-old says. “Young people … now must travel further out to sea to find fish for their families.” As she looks out at a white sandy beach, eaten away by rising sea levels, Naivalu recounts watching painfully as her three children “feel the brunt of changes in the climate. “I ask myself ‘what did they do wrong?’” The question is personal, but it’s also part of what drives her pursuit of climate justice for Pacific people, whose way of life is being threatened as the planet warms. At this year’s UN climate talks, known as Cop31, the region will be in the spotlight like never before.

What is Zionism and why do some critics describe it as racist?

Zack Polanski, the leader of the Green party, has said he is an anti-Zionist. As his party conference prepares to debate a motion that “Zionism is racism”, what precisely is Zionism and what is the history of the claim that it is racist? What is Zionism? Modern Zionism developed in the late 1800s out of several strands of thinking on the future of Jewish collective and cultural identity, emerging from a millennia-old religious yearning to return to Zion, which runs through Jewish holy texts. The term came, however, to be most associated with Theodor Herzl’s brand of political Zionism, the movement for Jewish self-determination and statehood in the context of rising European antisemitism. Although Zionism tends to be seen by critics as a monolithic political idea, its history has encompassed multiple, often contradictory, intellectual strands including the notion – proposed by the philosopher Martin Buber before the foundation of Israel – of a binational Arab-Jewish state in Palestine.

text:
What is Zionism and why do some critics describe it as racist?

Since the foundation of the state of Israel in 1948, the debate over Zionism inside the country has largely centred on liberal and rightwing, or “revisionist”, camps – the latter represented by Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party. Issues such as settlement, occupation and whether Israel should be defined as an ethno-nationalist Jewish state moved to the core of political contest. However, as Dov Waxman, a professor of Israel studies at the University of California, wrote in the Conversation last month, the issue is further complicated by the fact that, despite contested definitions, the idea of Zionism for many Jews represents something more amorphous: “Jewish liberation and sovereignty, a safe haven from persecution, a revival of the Hebrew language, and a renewed sense of collective pride, especially after the Holocaust.” What is the criticism of Zionism? One critique of Zionism – used as a shorthand for the state of Israel – is that it is a “colonial” project. Those critics, in parts of the left, in the wider Arab world and among some anti-Zionist Jews such as Polanski, would point to three pieces of evidence.

First, the violent displacement of Palestinians during the Nakba, or “catastrophe” for Palestinians, that accompanied the founding of the Jewish state. Second, they argue Israel has created an apartheid system of unequal rights in the occupied territories that denies Palestinian ambitions to statehood and their own self-determination and, third, that within Israel those of Palestinian origin are discriminated against. Before the establishment of Israel in 1948, Palestinians had a vibrant society across British Mandatory Palestine, but their connection to historical Palestine has often been dismissed or diminished by significant strands of Zionist thinking. At the heart of academic debate is how widespread the use by some early Zionists was of the notion of a “land without people” for a “people without land”, which critics have used as evidence that Zionism was a colonial enterprise at its very beginning.

text:
What is Zionism and why do some critics describe it as racist?

In contrast, Zionists point to the evidence of a historical presence of Jews in the Holy Land, as well as for many a promised biblical patrimony in a homeland from which Jews were displaced and that many hold up as a refuge in a hostile world. What is the history of the claim that ‘Zionism is racism’? The argument that Zionism is racism, while controversial, is not new. The phrase came to particular prominence during the cold war, when the UN passed resolution 3379 in 1975. The so-called “Zionism as racism” resolution compared “the racist regime in occupied Palestine” to apartheid South Africa. Sponsored’ by the Arab League and promoted by the Soviet Union, it passed with support from countries in the developing world but was later revoked in 1991 under pressure from the then US president, George HW Bush. Proponents of the argument say Zionism privileges the rights of Jews in Israel over non-Jews via a discriminatory system. Opponents of the framing describe it as antisemitic as it singles out Jews as a group to deny them alone the right to self-determination.

An employment tribunal two years ago found that the views of David Miller, a former professor of political sociology who was sacked by the University of Bristol in 2021, that “Zionism is and always has been a racist, violent, imperialist ideology premised on ethnic cleansing” amounted to a protected philosophical belief under the 2010 Equality Act, a case upheld on appeal.

Women given free cycling shorts to prevent upskirting on Oktoberfest amusement ride

Women have been given free cycling shorts to prevent upskirting on a famous amusement ride at the Oktoberfest in Munich, after an investigation revealed tens of thousands of voyeuristic videos circulating online. The Teufelsrad, or Devil’s Wheel, which rapidly spins around while people try to sit on it for as long as they can, is one of the beer festival’s oldest rides. But many of the videos discovered by German journalists focus on women whose traditional dirndl dresses have ridden up, often showing their underwear. The findings have revived concerns about upskirting – secretly filming or taking photos under someone’s skirt without consent, which has been illegal in Germany since 2020. It is punishable by a fine or up to two years in prison. But some women’s rights advocates have said the law is not enough to stop the abuse. According to the research by the Munich daily newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung, more than 32,000 videos linked to the Teufelsrad were found on Meta platforms alone, some of them with millions of views.

There are signs and police posters in German and English around the tent where the Teufelsrad is located that warn against filming under people’s skirts. Polls close in first round of Brazil’s high-stakes presidential election

The polls have closed in the first round of Brazil’s highly polarised and high-stakes presidential election that could change not only the direction of Latin America’s largest country but that of the entire region. The election pits the leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, against the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, an ally of Donald Trump and the son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup after his failed 2022 re-election attempt. Late on Sunday Bolsonaro was leading Lula in partial results. With results in from almost 65% of the country, Bolsonaro had 49.8% to Lula’s 42.25%, while several other candidates stood in the single digits. Lula and Bolsonaro have alternated as frontrunners in the final stretch, making the outcome unpredictable. In recent days both have focused on persuading undecided voters in hopes of reaching 50% plus one vote; if neither does, there will be a runoff on 25 October.

Egyptian journalist faces terrorism charges after entire newsroom detained

An Egyptian journalist has been charged with joining a terrorist group, days after an entire newsroom was detained in what rights groups have said is a crackdown on press freedoms. Last week, authorities arrested six journalists from the independent fact-checking and investigative platform Matsadaash – literally meaning “don’t believe” – accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and publishing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood. The outlet’s six journalists, Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal, were arrested by security forces over the course of two days. On Sunday, Egyptian authorities charged Ashraf with joining a terrorist group and spreading false news, according to a statement by the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, a NGO. The charges came after an interrogation that lasted from 10pm to 8am and focused exclusively on material published by Matsadaash, the rights group said. Ashraf was to be held for 15 days, pending investigation, while the whereabouts of the other five journalists were still unknown.

Abdelrahman Mansour, the co-founder of the platform, denied having any association with the Muslim Brotherhood, a transnational movement that was designated a terrorist organisation by Egypt in 2013 after the former president Mohamed Morsi, a senior Brotherhood figure, was ousted in a coup. Mansour called the arrests “one of the gravest attacks on journalism in Egypt’s modern history”. “My colleagues were doing what journalists should do: asking difficult questions, uncovering facts, and reporting on issues that affect people’s lives. They deserve recognition for their work. Instead, their homes were raided, and all six were taken away,” he said. “The government must answer this question: why have you arrested six journalists? ‘It’s glottophobia’: Brazilians in Portugal battle for linguistic recognition

Not long after she started studying to become a nurse in Portugal, Iracema Ferreira began bringing a dictionary to her classes as a retort to accusations she was speaking Brazilian, not Portuguese. “It was to show that those words are in the Portuguese language dictionary,” she said. A Brazilian speech therapist, Ferreira moved to Portugal in 2020 and later heard from several colleagues from her home country that the process of getting a licence to work in the European country was a dead end. The 45-year-old soon abandoned the idea of continuing the career she had practised for a decade and switched to nursing instead. The speech therapists’ struggle for recognition underlines what Brazilians say is a wider strand of prejudice still embedded into Portuguese society against the language variant of its former colony. “It’s glottophobia,” said Tanise Anhaia, president of the Brazilian Speech Therapists Association in Portugal (AFBP), using a term to mean linguistic discrimination.

Barely any Brazilians have been awarded a licence to practise as a speech therapist in Portugal since 2019, according to the AFBP, which was set up last year. One of the two exceptions is a woman whose lawyer argued his client’s rejection was “totally incomprehensible, illegal and unconstitutional” and got it overturned. For many Brazilians in Portugal the struggle will not come as a surprise. People from the Latin American giant make up by far the largest migrant group, numbering more than 480,000, according to the Portuguese migration agency, AIMA. (According to the Brazilian foreign ministry, the population is larger, at 628,000 in 2025.) However, as the size of the group increases, so do the reports of xenophobia. In 2022, the commission for equality and against racial discrimination reported that “Brazilian nationality” was the most common basis of discrimination in the complaints they received, forming 34% of all complaints. In 2023 Statistics Portugal reported that 55% of Brazilians said that they had suffered discrimination, the biggest proportion in terms of nationality.

Revealed: Government quietly dropped plan to prepare England for wildfires

The government quietly scrapped plans to prepare the countryside in England for wildfires, it has been revealed. This was despite new data showing fire crews do not have the proper protective gear to tackle them. This summer has been a potent reminder of the scale of the threat posed by the climate crisis, with the UK experiencing record-breaking wildfires after punishingly hot and dry weather turned large parts of the countryside into a tinderbox. In the third national climate adaptation programme, published in July 2023, the Conservative government, then headed by Rishi Sunak, said it would run a wildfire risk programme in England from 2023 to 2027 so land management would be adapted for the risk. However, it has now emerged the programme was never implemented, with the current government stating the commitment “was made by the previous government but was not brought into effect”.

Alistair Carmichael, a Scottish Liberal Democrat MP and the chair of the Commons environment food and rural affairs committee, said it was alarming that ministers had not prioritised work to adapt land for wildfire risk. “It begs further serious questions about whether this summer’s wildfires could have looked different with more resources on the ground,” he added.

text:
Knox Chitiyo obituary

My friend and former colleague Knox Chitiyo, who has died aged 65 of bowel cancer, was a Zimbabwean academic and later an important voice in Britain on his homeland and its future. He was regularly consulted by diplomats, business people, journalists, academics and activists. From 1992 to 2003 he was a senior lecturer in war studies and military history at the University of Zimbabwe, where he co-founded the Centre for Defence Studies, serving as its deputy director. He also taught on the joint command and staff course at Zimbabwe’s National Army Staff College and at the Gweru Military Academy, helping shape the strategic thinking of a generation of officers. As intellectual space in Zimbabwe tightened under Robert Mugabe, Knox moved to the UK in 2005. He joined the Royal United Services Institute, eventually becoming head of its Africa programme (2007-11), and developed an international reputation for his work on Zimbabwe, defence and security. In 2012 he became an associate fellow at Chatham House – a position he retained until his death.

citation.title: Knox Chitiyo obituary

text:
Knox Chitiyo obituary

Knox was born in Salisbury (now Harare) in Southern Rhodesia, then part of the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland, to Wynona (nee Chieza), a nurse, and McLeod Chitiyo, a pathologist. Growing up through the turbulent final decades of white minority rule in Southern Rhodesia, he attended a private, racially mixed secondary school, St George’s, which was run by Jesuits in Salisbury, an unusual experience that shaped his interest in race, identity and political change. After school he gained a general degree at the University of Zimbabwe, where he then built his academic career, completing a PhD and lecturing in history and war studies before simultaneously becoming deputy director of the university’s Centre for Defence Studies from 1995 and then leaving for Britain a decade later. Knox was particularly passionate about ensuring that Zimbabweans in the diaspora had a voice in policy debate in the UK. Beyond his role at Chatham House, he was president of the Britain Zimbabwe Society and served on the board of the Business Council for Africa, including as acting chair.

citation.title: Knox Chitiyo obituary

text:
Knox Chitiyo obituary

He was also a fellow of the Brenthurst Foundation, an thinktank on African economics and politics, and became a trustee of the Mines Advisory Group, a charity devoted to finding and destroying landmines in places affected by conflict. He brought warmth, humour and humanity to serious subjects, and moved easily between academics, soldiers, diplomats and politicians without losing either his independence or his kindness. In his spare time he wrote poetry and short stories and played the saxophone, including, he once told me, at Ronnie Scott’s in London. Knox is survived by his wife, Nhamburiko, a midwife, whom he married in 2002, and their son, Kyle, and his sister Cathy. • This article was amended on 6 October 2026 to correct some personal details.

Regarding your article (UK to open new refugee resettlement routes for Afghan women and Palestinians, 27 September), rather than focusing on whether or not Shabana Mahmood’s policy change will deter small boat arrivals (which it won’t), shouldn’t we be in uproar over her use of the language of “compassion” and “international obligations”? Up to 77m fish are slaughtered each year in the UK but there are no routine or mandatory inspections of fish slaughterhouses in England and Wales, it can be revealed. Concerns within government about the way fish are slaughtered date back decades but all of the official bodies responsible for animal welfare and food standards in England and Wales said they do not undertake regular inspections. When Animal Equality UK contacted the Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA), it referred the charity to the Fish Health Inspectorate (FHI). In response to a previous inquiry, the APHA had said it does not carry out mandatory inspections of fish slaughterhouses and suggested contacting the Food Standards Agency (FSA). Both the FSA and the FHI told Animal Equality UK that they did not carry out routine or mandatory inspections. Abigail Penny, the executive director of Animal Equality UK, said: “Fish are thinking, feeling beings, capable of pain. It is a disgrace that not a single government agency will take responsibility for checking on their welfare at slaughter.

Polish activists launch abortion pill locker to bypass near-total ban

They call it the “world’s first parcel locker for abortion pills”. Polish campaigners have launched a new means of distribution as part of their ongoing effort to skirt the country’s near-total ban on abortion. Painted pink and framed by zebra-striped curtains, the 22-compartment “AbortOmat” in Warsaw allows women to access the pills swiftly and anonymously using a six-digit code. The service was envisaged for those who cannot or do not want to wait days for mail delivery due to a missed miscarriage or health complications, or who worry about receiving the pills at home. “And why not?” said Kinga Jelinska, the director of the Women Help Women foundation and co-founder of the Abortion Dream Team, the two groups behind last week’s launch. “You can order underwear, cosmetics, mascara, whatever and receive it practically the same or next day,” she said.

In 2023, the protests were credited with helping to propel Donald Tusk, and his promises to overhaul the laws within 100 days, into power. Since then, political stagnation has set in, said Jelinska, citing comments made last year by Tusk in which the prime minister said there was “simply no majority” to change the laws to allow abortions until the 12th week of pregnancy. Tusk instead hinted that his government was intent on doing things differently, telling reporters that it would not prosecute those who helped to facilitate abortions. More than 400 schools in France to be closed on Monday as more protests planned

More than 400 schools in France will be closed or partly closed on Monday as authorities brace for another week of student protests. Lessons will be totally or partly suspended in 400 to 500 schools because security conditions “have not been fulfilled”, the education minister, Édouard Geffray, said on Sunday. The minister said 24 schools had been burnt or ransacked and 78 education staff members injured. text:
Exiled separatist leader is likely to return to a very different Catalonia

After years of legal wrangling, Spain’s constitutional court is expected to remove the last obstacle to the return of the former Catalan president Carles Puigdemont after nearly nine years in exile this week. Puigdemont fled in 2017 to avoid being jailed for his part in the failed and illegal independence push for which nine of his colleagues were imprisoned on sentences of up to 13 years, although all were released within three years. If on 6 October the court decides, as expected, that the charge of misuse of public funds is covered by the amnesty law passed by the Spanish parliament in 2024, Puigdemont should be free to return without fear of arrest. But will he come back like Lenin, leaping from the train in St Petersburg to galvanise the faltering revolution, or as yesterday’s man, the last of the Romanovs, bound for the dustbin of history? Whether he returns in triumph or, as he reportedly departed, in the boot of a car, Catalonia today is very different from the place he left nine years ago. Firstly, the political climate has changed beyond recognition.

text:
Exiled separatist leader is likely to return to a very different Catalonia

The fervour of mass demonstrations and constant conflict and provocation between Barcelona and Madrid has given way to a climate of cooperation. Since 2024, the region has been governed by the Socialists’ party of Catalonia (PSC), the first time since 1980 that a non-nationalist party has been in charge. Led by Salvador Illa, Spain’s health minister during the Covid epidemic, it has ushered in an era of entente with Madrid, where the Socialist Workers’ party, to which the PSC serves as a regional section, is also in the driving seat. Another change is that those young people who got fired up about independence are not only older now but face issues that are more pressing than sovereignty, principally jobs and housing. Wages are low, rents high and mortgages mostly out of reach. As a result, 82% of Catalonia’s 18- to 30-year-olds still live with their parents. On Friday Puigdemont’s Junts per Catalunya (Together for Catalonia) voted down the government’s progressive housing proposals, a move that won’t endear them to young Catalans, nor to their parents. The other big change since 2017 is demographic.

citation.title: Exiled separatist leader is likely to return to a very different Catalonia

text:
Exiled separatist leader is likely to return to a very different Catalonia

When Puigdemont went into exile, foreign nationals made up 13.8% of the population of Catalonia; the figure today is 18.7%. This shift is most marked in the capital, Barcelona, where 26.6% of residents are foreign nationals representing 181 nationalities. For nationalists, this raises the question: who is a Catalan? Jordi Pujol, the Catalan president from 1980 to 2003, insisted that a Catalan was anyone who lived and worked in Catalonia. Things are a little different now. Out of the disillusion of the independence movement has risen Aliança Catalana, a far-right nationalist party whose leader says “there isn’t room for everyone” in Catalonia. Specifically, there would be no room for Muslims, not even those born in Spain, which by implication would include, for example, the Barcelona and Spain football star Lamine Yamal. This has dragged Junts, traditionally the party of the Catalan bourgeoisie, to the right as those on the ethno-nationalist margins gravitate towards the unselfconsciously racist Aliança, whose positions on sovereignty are otherwise barely distinguishable from Junts’.

Over the past 25 years, Catalonia, and above all Barcelona, has gone from being a bicultural, bilingual Catalan-Spanish society to one that is multicultural and multilingual. Puigdemont’s pitch is based on identity and a historical sense of grievance at Spain’s perceived abuse of and disdain for Catalonia, a sentiment shared by many, perhaps most, Catalans. This ingrained sense of difference and grievance isn’t going away, but his vision may prove a harder sell than it was 10 years ago. As demography changes, so does identity. Immigrants now make up a quarter of the population, have their own identity issues and have no particular beef with Spain. As for independence, support never did reach 50%, and now hovers in the low 40s. Besides, as people migrate in search of a better or perhaps a more interesting life, it is becoming increasingly likely that the parents of those living in Catalonia will be from different countries, and their sense of national identity is multiple or simply not that important. Puigdemont’s lifelong dream is for Catalonia to take its place among the world’s independent nation states.

Flávio Bolsonaro poised to win Brazilian presidency after shock first-round victory

Flávio Bolsonaro is in pole position to win Brazil’s presidential election, after a far-right tsunami propelled him to a shock first-round victory over the incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, leaving progressive voters reeling. The 45-year-old rightwing candidate received 56.1m votes to Lula’s 53.8m – 47.03% to 45.16% – meaning the 80-year-old leftwinger has a mountain to climb if he is to bounce back in the second round on 25 October. Never, since the return of democracy to Brazil in 1985, has the first-round runner-up managed to turn the game around and win the second ballot. “Miracles are possible in politics. But I don’t see that happening,” the political scientist Miguel Lago said of Lula’s chances of snapping back. “I don’t see Flávio losing this election now.” Speaking outside the White House on Monday, Donald Trump told reporters: “Well, it’s a big victory: close but a very, very big victory. Amazing, actually.” Trump, who is a longtime ally of the Bolsonaro family, predicted the runoff would be “a very close election”.

Investigators believe the co-pilot who tried to take control of a plane from Dubai to Tel Aviv last week originally planned his attack for July but postponed the hijacking, possibly because a friend was among the crew, regional and Israeli officials have said. The evidence of prior planning suggests that Hamam al-Hammami, 29, may have specifically sought employment with an airline that flew to Israel in order to carry out the attack on last Wednesday’s flydubai ‌flight FZ1073, experts believe. Police and security agencies in at least six countries are scrambling to piece together the background of Hammami, an Omani national, and his intentions, as well as to establish if he acted entirely alone. Hammami allegedly used an emergency crash axe kept in the cockpit to launch a surprise attack on the pilot approximately two hours and 20 minutes after takeoff. The plane was carrying more than 180 passengers – almost all Israeli – and crew on a routine flight.

India’s supreme court demands answers over changes to voter roll

India’s supreme court has demanded accountability from the government and the election body over a controversial exercise that has led to the deletion of tens of millions of voters from the electoral roll and prompted mass protests. Demonstrations have erupted across the country in recent days as opposition parties, student groups and the youth-led Cockroach movement have demanded the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, the head of the Election Commission of India (ECI). They have accused Kumar of overseeing a direct attack on India’s democracy through an exercise to verify and “purify” the electoral roll in states across the country, which so far has led to 130 million names being removed. In Delhi, hundreds of people were detained as they tried to protest over the weekend. On Monday, the supreme court issued notices to Narendra Modi’s government, the ECI and Kumar to demand answers over concerns raised about the voter list revision, saying it expected all “to respond in a clear, transparent manner”.

The ECI has claimed the exercise is simply cleaning electoral rolls of duplicate, dead and ineligible names, as well as removing “illegal infiltrators”. However, large numbers of people in Delhi and states such as Bihar and West Bengal say they have been wrongly stripped of their vote and have struggled to get it back. Related: India’s Cockroach movement launches new protests over changes to voter roll There are accusations that revision of the electoral rolls particularly targets minorities such as Muslims, who are traditionally not voters of Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). The opposition alliance, led by the Congress party, have accused the ECI of being hand in glove with the government over alleged vote “chori” or cheating. Kumar was chosen to head the ECI by a panel headed by Modi. While the exercise, known as the special intensive revision (SIR), began last year, widespread outrage only recently erupted after a report in the Indian Express newspaper revealed multiple irregularities in the process, which were flagged in more than a dozen internal objections.

Another hearing in the cases will be held next week. The controversies over the ECI have once again driven India’s young people on to the streets in protest, amid rising frustration at the Modi government. The Cockroach Janta party (CJP), which led massive unrest over the summer that forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister, have once again mobilised and called for the resignation of Kumar. Iran’s oil minister resigns as country’s economic crisis worsens

Iran’s oil minister has resigned days after allegations that an intermediary trust selling Iranian oil abroad owed millions of dollars’ worth of export receipts to the state. Mohsen Paknejad’s departure comes as Iran grapples with a dire economic situation, including inflation running at 85%. An overall drop in oil receipts has led to a massive shortfall in foreign exchange earnings and one of the biggest drops in the value of the rial since the Iranian revolution in 1979. The Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, said he had accepted the resignation of Paknejad, who had given personal reasons for going. The rial is trading more than 10% lower than a month ago, largely due to the US naval blockade preventing Iran from selling oil, the mainstay of government receipts. Emergency government meetings over the weekend to combat the crisis have yielded little tangible progress, and there are growing reports that the professional middle class, notably teachers and nurses, are resigning in large numbers because their salaries are not keeping up with price rises.

Iran has been using informal networks known as “trustees” to bypass US sanctions and repatriate oil revenues. Imran Khan’s supporters have begun a march to Islamabad to demand his release from jail after efforts by the government to halt the protest failed. The march began in the former prime minister’s stronghold province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in north-west Pakistan on Sunday, according to leaders of his Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party. Concerns have grown over the health of the 74-year-old former Pakistan cricket captain who has been in prison since 2023. Party colleagues and family claim he is being held in solitary confinement and has been denied visits by his doctor or relatives despite having a serious eye condition and high blood pressure. The government had gone to extreme lengths to try to stop PTI holding the long march, including shutting down Islamabad and barricading the capital’s entrances with shipping containers and sandbags. Khan’s three sisters were among those detained last week on grounds of national security. Two rounds of negotiations between the government and PTI leaders took place over the weekend but broke down when Khan’s allies insisted that he be part of political talks.

Man caught with 300 tortoises and 77 parrots bound for Malta at Sicilian port

A Maltese man is facing animal cruelty charges after allegedly attempting to transport 300 tortoises and 77 parrots from Sicily to Malta. The animals were found packed into a car near the boarding area for a Malta-bound catamaran during an inspection at the Sicilian port of Pozzallo, the local unit of Italy’s financial police squad said on Monday. Police said they spotted the man “while he was transporting numerous animals” inside a car that lacked adequate space and temperature control. Subsequent checks by veterinarians found that 76 of the parrots belonged to species protected by the Washington convention, a global agreement signed in 1973 to protect endangered plants and animals from the risk of international trade. Police said the seizure was one of the most significant under the convention. The animals have been entrusted to a breeding facility, police added. The Maltese man faces charges of keeping animals in conditions that were incompatible with their nature and causing them severe suffering, along with breaching laws governing international trade in protected species.

Monday briefing: You asked, we answered – how will the US midterms go?

Good morning. Later today, Donald Trump will be in the state of Nebraska to rev up supporters as he kicks off a campaign blitz of rallies ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November. If his early speeches are anything to go by, cornhuskers can anticipate poll denial, accusations of veganism and an expletive ratio that my nine-year-old would love. And Nebraskans may love it, too: aside from one “blue dot” district in Omaha, Republicans argue their support is steady in the state that has easily backed Trump three times. This campaign is set against the president’s plummeting approval ratings, the unravelling of his Maga movement and an affordability crisis escalated by his unpopular war on Iran. But Trump supporters are also among the most motivated to vote, and Republicans have far deeper coffers to mobilise their base. I asked First Edition readers what you really want to know about the US midterms. Today, in a happy exercise in newsletter cross-pollination, I put your questions to our Washington editor Ankita Rao, who runs our US elections newsletter The Stakes. First, the headlines.

In depth: ‘We are prepared for anything’ You’d be forgiven, readers, if the state of US politics is perplexing you. On the one hand, there are voters who have little faith in the president’s war in the Middle East and are increasingly angry about his inability to make daily life more affordable at home. text:
‘The future is bright’: breeding programme brings world’s heaviest insect back from the brink

The population of New Zealand’s endemic wētāpunga – believed to be the world’s heaviest insect – is officially “increasing” thanks to a groundbreaking breeding programme that has overseen the release of 11,000 insects into the wild. “The future of wētāpunga is looking bright,” said Dr Chris Green, an honorary researcher at the department of conservation, who documented the success of the project for the New Zealand Journal of Zoology. Green co-authored a report released on 2 October that outlines the success of the breeding programme. “Eleven thousand individuals for release is extraordinary and outstanding.” A female wētāpunga can weigh as much as a mouse. Its body can grow up to 10cm long (nearly 4in) and its leg span can be as wide as 20cm. It is the largest of 70 wētā species and was once found across parts of the North Island before predation from introduced species and habitat loss contributed to their decline. By the 1990s, they were considered “endangered” and are now presumed extinct in the wild on New Zealand’s mainland.

citation.title: ‘The future is bright’: breeding programme brings world’s heaviest insect back from the brink

text:
‘The future is bright’: breeding programme brings world’s heaviest insect back from the brink

The insects reside primarily on a smattering of predator-free islands in Auckland’s Hauraki Gulf and off the coast of Northland. Related: A gentle giant: the shy wētāpunga is adept at living in the shadows But their fortune is starting to change. Over the past 15 years, tens of thousands of wētāpunga have been bred at Butterfly Creek, a wildlife facility, and Auckland zoo, enabling the release of wētāpunga across new predator-free islands and some mainland reserves north of Auckland. Butterfly Creek and Auckland zoo established husbandry techniques that, over time, have been scaled up to rear large numbers of wētāpunga in communal creches. The young wētāpunga – or nymphs – are fed a three-part diet of fresh foliage, fish flake protein and leaf litter. The protein is “critical” to the survival of the youngest nymphs, Green said. Once big enough to protect themselves, the insects are transferred to their new habitat. The efforts have led to 45 separate translocations to wild habitats, which is “a very high number in any recovery of a species”, Green said.

citation.title: ‘The future is bright’: breeding programme brings world’s heaviest insect back from the brink

text:
‘The future is bright’: breeding programme brings world’s heaviest insect back from the brink

Monitoring on two islands has shown wētāpunga have established self-sustaining populations, with fourth and fifth generations born there, in what Green said was a marker of success. As a result, the species’ conservation status has improved from “nationally endangered” to “nationally increasing”. “It’s so exciting, because we are unable to report that for so many of our other threatened species,” Green said. New Zealand is particularly vulnerable to species decline because of its high rates of endemism and problems with introduced pests. Green said the country was at the forefront of invertebrate recovery work and he was not aware of any other examples of breeding programmes working to this scale, or with such success. By documenting the project’s work, he hopes other institutions will feel encouraged to develop their own programmes. “That’s the extraordinary aspect of it – that we’ve been successful,” he said. “If other institutions can get into that sort of position, then there can be huge benefit for threatened species in New Zealand.” • This article was amended on 6 October 2026.

Norway plans temporary ban on smart glasses in some public places

Norway is planning a temporary ban on smart glasses in some public places, amid rising global concern at the spread of the AI-enabled recording devices. The Oslo government is planning a bill to prevent the use of the camera-enabled spectacles in parks, beaches, museums, shopping centres, schools, daycare centres, healthcare facilities, gyms and public events, although private use would still be allowed. There is already a growing patchwork of restrictions on the use of the glasses including in UK and US courtrooms and in pubs, cinemas and restaurants where owners have raised privacy fears. Torgeir Micaelsen, Norway’s minister of digital affairs, said he was “worried that ‌new, powerful technology is being introduced where people risk being ‌photographed, filmed or audio-recorded without knowing it”. “We do not want a society where people worry about being recorded without their knowledge, photographed or filmed in places and situations where they are accustomed to not being monitored,” he said. Norway’s Labour party, which heads a minority government, needs the support of other parties to pass the proposed ban.

It said it planned to submit a bill “as soon as possible”, while tasking an expert group with drawing up permanent regulations on the issue. It has sold at least 9m pairs of the Ray-Ban versions since the start of 2023. In the UK restaurateurs such as Jeremy King, who created the Wolseley and Delaunay restaurants, and pub chain Wetherspoons have already said they do not want customers using the devices. Cinemas said in August they had begun introducing policies to ban or restrict the use of smart glasses citing both privacy and film piracy concerns. Last week the governor of California, Gavin Newsom, vetoed legislation that would have penalised citizens for using smart glasses to record people without their permission in changing rooms, doctors’ offices and other spaces people generally consider private. Will Pedro Sánchez’s gamble to call snap general election in Spain pay off?

Spaniards will head to the polls on 29 November – months before schedule – after the country’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, announced a snap general election on Monday morning. The vote, which will be Spain’s fifth general election in 10 years, is likely to be dominated by growing anger over the housing crisis. Why has Sánchez called the snap general election? Although the next general election was due to be held sometime before the end of next summer, Sánchez has decided to gamble by bringing it forward in the hope that widespread anger over Spain’s housing crisis could work to his advantage and allow him to shore up his fragile mandate. The eviction last month of Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman who was removed from the home in Madrid where she had lived for 70 years, unleashed huge protests. Sánchez’s minority coalition government responded by putting together emergency measures that were put before congress at the end of last week.

text:
Will Pedro Sánchez’s gamble to call snap general election in Spain pay off?

Despite the evident strength of public feeling, the conservative People’s party (PP), the far-right Vox party and the rightwing, pro-independence Catalan party Junts voted down the measures, infuriating housing campaigners and many ordinary Spaniards. Sánchez, who has a well-deserved reputation for pragmatism, risk-taking and improvisation, has seen his chance. While his critics argue that his eight years in office should have given him time to address Spain’s housing problems, both the protests and the rightwing opposition to his emergency measures offer Sánchez the chance to leverage the issue for electoral ends. How are the polls looking? Not great for Sánchez’s Spanish Socialist Workers’ party (PSOE), which has been trailing the PP for months. Although the PP is firmly in the lead, it doesn’t appear to be on course for an absolute majority, meaning it would be forced to rely on the support of Vox to govern – possibly in a coalition. What would such a coalition mean for Spanish politics?
