Will Pedro Sánchez’s gamble to call snap general election in Spain pay off?

If Vox were to take office with the PP, it would be the first time that a far-right party has governed Spain since the country’s return to democracy after the death of Francisco Franco in 1975. The PP, which repudiated Vox in 2020, accusing them of being demagogues who practised a politics based on “fear, anger, resentment and revenge”, has since bitten its tongue and repeatedly entered into pragmatic regional coalitions with the far-right party. The price for Vox’s backing in those regions recently has been the adoption of the party’s hard line on immigration, including its “national priority” policy that insists Spanish-born people receive priority over those born abroad for housing and public services. It sounds like quite a gamble, then. Why is Sánchez prepared to risk the early election? The prime minister only just scraped his return to office in the last general election in July 2023 after he won the backing of Catalan pro-independence parties by promising a controversial amnesty law to those involved in the failed, illegal push for independence from Spain in 2017.

Sánchez’s minority coalition government with the smaller, leftwing Sumar alliance, has struggled to get legislation through a fraught congress and has not passed a budget since 2023. Nor do his problems end there. The government has also been fiercely criticised over its handling of the crisis in Spain’s north African enclave of Ceuta, which was sparked when about 70,000 people crossed into the territory from neighbouring Morocco in the space of 48 hours. Last, but by no means least, Sánchez’s administration, party and inner circle have been mired in corruption allegations over the past two years, which have proved acutely embarrassing for a prime minister who took office vowing to be a scourge of sleaze and graft.

text:
In both France and Spain, ruling parties must prove they can give young protesters hope

In Spain, tens of thousands of people in 50 cities have taken to the streets amid mounting fury over the country’s housing crisis, their feelings made plain on a banner at the burgeoning protest camp in Madrid’s Puerta del Sol plaza: “You can speculate on watches, jewels, crypto-bros and Ferraris. But not on our fucking homes.” In France, as high school pupils clash with police in often violent protests over long hours, missing teachers, crumbling classrooms and an opaque university admissions system, the angry slogans include: “More hours in class than for sleep”, “Fund study, not repression” and “I’d like to be worrying about my maths exam, not my future”. They may stem from different specific grievances, but the two waves of mainly youth-led protest exemplify a growing problem for western European governments: a generation of young people feeling increasingly denied the basic socioeconomic security that, by and large, their parents enjoyed.

citation.title: In both France and Spain, ruling parties must prove they can give young protesters hope

text:
In both France and Spain, ruling parties must prove they can give young protesters hope

The trigger in Spain, where rents have risen by 80% in a decade, was – perhaps ironically – the high-profile eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid after an investment fund increased her rent by 230%. For those spending more than half their income on housing (the monthly rental on a one-bedroom flat can cost an entire median salary), enough was enough. Rocketing rents, rampant property speculation, the boom in short-term tourist rentals and stagnant wages have combined to make an independent adult life increasingly unachievable for many young workers – and the state is seen not as a neutral mediator, but an active enabler of property speculation. In France, the protests began in the northern Paris suburbs but quickly spread nationwide, fuelled by young people’s anger at an underfunded education system that, the data shows, entrenches social inequality. Pupils routinely miss months of teaching owing to unfilled staff absences. Timetables run from 8am to 6pm – among the longest in Europe – in buildings with leaking roofs, cockroaches and collapsing ceilings.

citation.title: In both France and Spain, ruling parties must prove they can give young protesters hope

text:
In both France and Spain, ruling parties must prove they can give young protesters hope

In Paris last week, students on high school barricades saw budget cuts as a straightforward assault on their future. In their eyes, a system meant to promote social mobility now prevents it. Lacking parliamentary majorities and facing varying degrees of budgetary constraint, however, neither government has much room for manoeuvre. Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, on Monday called a snap general election after rightwing parties voted down his emergency housing legislation. In France, as student protests – and more than 5,000 arrests – forced the closure of up to 500 secondary schools on Monday, the centrist prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, has urged local authorities to prioritise filling long-term teacher absences and called urgent meetings to discuss repairing dilapidated school buildings. Taken together, the two crises highlight some core problems facing mainstream governments. First, young people in particular have come to see incremental measures – targeted tax credits, minor administrative reforms – as sticking plasters on altogether deeper socioeconomic wounds.

citation.title: In both France and Spain, ruling parties must prove they can give young protesters hope

text:
In both France and Spain, ruling parties must prove they can give young protesters hope

Second, facing mounting street pressure and opposition parties eager to exploit it, ruling coalitions – especially those that lack majorities – will struggle. And in France, heavy-handed policing risks alienating young voters from the mainstream even further. Meanwhile, radicalised opposition parties are actively weaponising the discontent. On the radical left, France’s Jean-Luc Mélenchon – backed by 47% of voters under 35 – has sided openly with the street, while in Spain, leftwing parties Podemos and Sumar have blamed the housing crisis squarely on out-of-control financial capitalism. At the same time, the populist far right is playing a law-and-order card, with Marine Le Pen’s National Rally (RN) in France seizing on footage of burning barricades to accuse centrist leaders of tolerating “unbridled violence” and Spain’s far-right Vox siding with the main conservative Partido Popular opposition to torpedo Sánchez’s emergency package, framing it as government overreach punishing landlords. Squeezed from both sides, mainstream governments face a spiralling challenge.

When an entire generation concludes that society’s existing frameworks guarantee them neither affordable homes nor functioning schools, political consent starts to evaporate and Europe’s establishment parties risk losing their legitimacy. Quebec poised to elect separatists to power for first time in more than a decade

Voters in Quebec are going to the polls in provincial elections which will probably result in victory for a party that has promised to hold a referendum on independence from Canada within the next two years. If polls are correct, the Parti Québécois (PQ) will form the government of the province of roughly nine million, the first time that the separatist movement will have gained power in the French-speaking region for more than a decade. A PQ victory in Monday’s election would also be likely to trigger a return to pitched battles over questions of language and identity between Quebec and the federal government. Long considered a declining force in Quebec politics, the PQ owes its resurgence to party leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon. The 49-year-old Oxford-educated lawyer and polyglot has positioned himself as a TikToking gen-X rebuttal to François Legault, Quebec’s long-serving Premier until he resigned early this year.

citation.title: Quebec poised to elect separatists to power for first time in more than a decade

text:
Quebec poised to elect separatists to power for first time in more than a decade

Analysts say that St-Pierre Plamondon’s electoral success is not because he is a separatist – the majority of voters do not support an independent Quebec – but because of his rightwing take on red-meat identity issues. He has blamed immigrants for Quebec’s overflowing schools, increased crime and skyrocketing housing prices, while promising to slash immigration levels and ban “conspicuous” religious symbols from the bodies of teachers and their students. He has derided his critics from the leftist Quebec Solidaire party as “woke”, and has taken to repeating the talking points of hard-right columnists. Many in the province agree with St-Pierre Plamondon’s rhetoric, even though it strays from PQ’s social democratic roots, according to radio host Patrick Lagacé. “Most Quebecers traditionally see themselves as being on the left. Yemen’s Saudi-backed government has announced the start of a new military operation to retake all territory held by the Houthis, even as the militant group made fresh gains on the ground, reportedly encircling a government-held city. The Houthis have increasingly targeted Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, and on Sunday said they had attacked oil infrastructure in the capital again.

Leaders of a Saudi-led coalition in Yemen claimed a broad air campaign involving 100 jet aircraft was under way on Monday against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels along the Red Sea coastline and farther north in the capital, Sana’a. The separatist Parti Québécois (PQ) won Quebec’s provincial election on Monday but fell short of enough seats to govern alone, returning to power with a promise to hold another referendum on independence from Canada. The European Commission wants to ensure there is no repeat Viktor Orbán among the next generation of EU member states, as it set out plans to prepare for the bloc’s enlargement into eastern Europe in the next few years. In an interview with the Guardian and other European newspapers, the EU commissioner for enlargement, Marta Kos, outlined proposals for special safeguards to protect the bloc from leaders who could flout democratic values and hold hostage decision making, a pattern of behaviour exemplified for many by the former Hungarian prime minister. “No more Viktor Orbán,” said Kos. “We have to have quicker mechanisms than only article 7 [a sanction that allows a member state’s voting rights to be suspended] if the newcomers would go against the rule of law, democracy or our values.” Under the plans Kos published on Tuesday, any new EU member state would face a 15-year probation period, during which they could be stripped of voting rights or EU funds for breaching basic democratic values or loyalty to the EU, the principle of sincere cooperation.

State parliament elects Germany’s first far-right speaker since second world war

Alternative für Deutschland has become Germany’s first far-right party to secure the position of speaker of a regional parliament since the second world war. Tobias Rausch, a former estate agent, was elected in the first round of voting on Tuesday in Saxony-Anhalt. He won 48 out of the 82 votes cast. Later in the day, Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, part of the AfD’s more extreme wing, was elected as Rausch’s deputy. The AfD, which is classed as “rightwing extremist” by the eastern state’s intelligence agency, won nearly 44% of votes in elections last month, dealing a hammer blow to Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, and his centre-right Christian Democrats (CDU). Rausch’s election to the role of president of the parliament – and its speaker – took place at the inaugural gathering of members in the state capital, Magdeburg. Twenty-nine voted against Rausch and five abstained. The AfD parliamentary group holds 39 seats, narrowly short of an absolute majority.

Germany arrests former intelligence chief over alleged spying

A former head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service has been arrested on suspicion of treason and spying on behalf of an overseas intelligence agency, in what prosecutors suspect could be the most egregious national security breach since the cold war. August Hanning, 80, was head of the federal intelligence service (BND) – which operates outside Germany to gather information across the fields of political, economic and military intelligence – between 1998 and 2005. He was arrested at his home in Nordwalde near Münster early on Tuesday. His former chief of staff, identified only as Manfred D, was arrested at the same time in Bavaria, on suspicion of “aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage”, according to a prosecutor’s statement. Media pictures showed Hanning, dressed in an open-necked white shirt, being taken from his redbrick house to a bullet-proof vehicle by masked officers.

citation.title: Germany arrests former intelligence chief over alleged spying

text:
Germany arrests former intelligence chief over alleged spying

Manfred D, who continued to work for Hanning’s successors at the BND after Hanning’s departure until the present day, is accused of using his role to gain access to classified information which he then handed to Hanning “in exchange for payment”, the prosecutors’ statement continued. “The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the federal intelligence service for internal purposes, particularly for executive intelligence briefings,” the statement said. Prosecutors believe that Hanning intended to resell the documents as part of a paid consulting role he had built up after leaving the BND, prosecutors added. To what extent and to whom he disseminated them remains part of an ongoing investigation. He is accused of using the information to “draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service”, prosecutors said. It was unclear if this information had reached its intended recipient, they added.

citation.title: Germany arrests former intelligence chief over alleged spying

text:
Germany arrests former intelligence chief over alleged spying

Over several years, Hanning is also believed to have passed on potentially sensitive political information, in part based on information passed to him by Manfred D, to a close contact representing a separate foreign intelligence service. Hanning and his legal team denied the allegations following his arrest. There was no immediate response from Manfred D. or his legal representatives. Several properties connected to both men were searched simultaneously on Tuesday, including in Berlin. Manfred D is due to appear before judges at the federal court of justice in Karlsruhe later on Tuesday, while Hanning is scheduled to appear on Wednesday. The allegations prompted shock in German political and intelligence circles, where memories resurfaced of historic espionage scandals. Hanning is thought to be the most prominent person to be accused of treason in Germany since Günter Guillaume, one of Willy Brandt’s personal aides, was exposed as a long-term Stasi agent in 1974. The “Guillaume affair” brought an abrupt end to Nobel peace prize-winning Brandt’s career, as he swiftly resigned as chancellor of West Germany.

Konstantin von Notz of the Greens, a prominent member of the same committee, urged the federal government to establish as soon as possible the “potential intelligence-related damage” that might have been done by Hanning’s alleged betrayal of Germany’s official secrets. “This is a truly outrageous and deeply disturbing story,” he told Der Spiegel. Suspicions over Hanning’s activities emerged as a result of an investigation into the kidnappings of the children from a prominent Hamburg business family, which is the focus of a major trial in the north German port city.

How dilapidated are French schools and how bad is inequality in the education system?

Hundreds of French high schools have been barricaded by teenagers and forced to close and hundreds of people have been injured amid clashes with police in the biggest youth protest movement in decades over the state of French lycées, where 15- to 18-year-olds are taught. School students say the education system is riven with inequality, that many buildings are in disrepair, class sizes are too big, and there are not enough teachers or funding. The French prime minister has promised to address what he called “legitimate” complaints, including on class sizes, long hours, dilapidated buildings and teacher provisions. So how bad are French high schools and what are the main problems? Is the French education system blighted by social inequality? Yes. A child born and schooled in a deprived neighbourhood in France has less chance of escaping their socioeconomic background than in most other developed nations, according to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.

citation.title: How dilapidated are French schools and how bad is inequality in the education system?

text:
How dilapidated are French schools and how bad is inequality in the education system?

Related: Schools blockaded as tens of thousands of protesters take to streets in France Éric Charbonnier, a French education analyst at the OECD, said there was a marked gap between the performance of the most advantaged and disadvantaged school students in France. “And often disadvantaged students are in disadvantaged schools,” he said. This has raised issues of the quality of learning being delivered and higher absenteeism of teachers. Teachers’ unions and sociologists have said children in France are often segregated by their background, postcode and income, with a direct impact on education outcomes. Are French high school buildings dilapidated and rat-infested with collapsing ceilings? Some are, namely in certain cities and low-income suburbs. Videos filmed by students and teachers have shown leaks, scurrying rats, holes in walls and ceilings, broken toilets and not enough chairs or tables, meaning teachers have to carry them from classroom to classroom. Some children said they had to learn in class while leaks were pouring into buckets, or move desks to avoid getting wet.

citation.title: How dilapidated are French schools and how bad is inequality in the education system?

text:
How dilapidated are French schools and how bad is inequality in the education system?

Many school classrooms experienced temperatures over 35C (95F) in the heatwaves of last May and June. Estimates in recent years have pointed to thousands of French schools at all levels, both primary and secondary, in need of repair. These include many 1960s school buildings. French regions are responsible for upkeep of high school buildings, but have asked for higher budgets from the government. A senate report has advised that billions need to be spent in the coming years to renovate and repair schools, as well as to address the impact of the climate crisis. Are class sizes bigger than other comparable countries? Yes, and often in urban areas. Charbonnier said: “There are an average of 29 students in French language lessons, compared with 26 across the OECD. However, this average masks substantial differences – particularly between large cities and rural areas.” Teachers and school students in Paris and its suburbs this week described many high school classes of 36 pupils or more, but in some rural areas it can be fewer.

citation.title: How dilapidated are French schools and how bad is inequality in the education system?

text:
How dilapidated are French schools and how bad is inequality in the education system?

Figures from the French education ministry show class sizes have increased in recent years. Are school days longer in France? Yes. “In terms of number of instructional hours, France really has more hours than most of the OECD countries,” Charbonnier said. This is true of primary and all levels of secondary education. Teaching is also squeezed into shorter periods, with 36 weeks of school per year, fewer weeks than the OECD average. High school pupils at barricades have complained of regularly having school days that run from 8am to 6pm, with many gaps during the day. Teachers said this was due to timetable challenges after changes to the baccalaureate that allowed for more individual choice of subject combinations. The French government has undertaken to review the length of school days. Are absent teachers not replaced, leaving pupils without key classes, even in exam years? Yes, sometimes. The education ministry has acknowledged that about 10% of teaching hours across the year are not delivered, for various reasons, and that it is urgent to fix this.

citation.title: How dilapidated are French schools and how bad is inequality in the education system?

text:
How dilapidated are French schools and how bad is inequality in the education system?

The education union SNES-FSU estimated that at least one teacher was lacking in more than half of all public middle schools and high schools at the start of the September school year. On the barricades, protesting students said there were more absent teachers not replaced in schools in low-income areas. In a question to parliament last year, the MP Bastien Lachaud, from the radical-left party La France Insoumise, asked if the government could confirm 2019 estimations by the parents’ organisation FCPE that school students in Seine-Saint-Denis outside Paris, one of the poorest areas in France, missed 20% of their teaching hours because absent teachers were not replaced – amounting to almost one whole year of missed schooling over a lifetime. In a response, the education ministry said it could not confirm that estimation but said an increasing number of absent teachers were being replaced. Unions said non-teaching staff could also be lacking, including school nurses and support staff for students with a disability. Does France spend less money on secondary education than its European neighbours?

citation.title: How dilapidated are French schools and how bad is inequality in the education system?

text:
How dilapidated are French schools and how bad is inequality in the education system?

No, France actually spends more than many other countries on high schools for children aged 15 and 18, but analysts question how the French government is spending its money and for what outcomes. For example, teachers’ middle and end-career salaries are comparatively low. Charbonnier said: “France’s expenditure on upper secondary education [lycées – or high schools] is 28% higher than the OECD average, while its spending on the first levels of education, including pre-primary and primary, is 11% below the OECD average.” He said the reason for France’s higher spend on high schools included its large provision of costly vocational programmes, which nevertheless often lack recognition even within France.

Israel’s ambassador to Australia says the third anniversary of 7 October is an opportunity for both countries to return to “traditional friendship” as hundreds gathered in Sydney’s east to mark the day. But, in the lead-up to commemorations on Wednesday marking Hamas’ terror attack, leaders of Australia’s Palestinian community say the federal government should do more to help the diaspora suffering since the war on Gaza. Hillel Newman spoke to the Australian Jewish community at Bondi Pavilion, saying it was moving seeing so many gathered in solidarity with Israel at 6.29am, the moment the massacre in Israel began three years ago. “I will never forget that hour in my entire lifetime … the trauma of that day will be with us for all eternity,” he told the crowd.

Israeli settlers beat press photographer as soldiers watch in West Bank

Armed Israeli settlers beat a photographer in the presence of Israeli soldiers, hospitalising him, as he covered worsening settler violence against olive farmers in the occupied West Bank. Jaafar Ashtiyeh, a 58-year-old veteran photographer for Agence France-Presse in Palestine, was assaulted by a group of settlers, who beat him with the butts of their rifles, despite him being marked as press. He was assaulted in view of about a dozen armed Israeli soldiers. Ashtiyeh suffered bruises to his head and torso and was taken to hospital, according to witnesses, his family and fellow journalists. Related: Israeli forces overwhelmed by violent settlers in ‘terrorist attack’ on Palestinian family His assault came amid a worsening wave of Israeli settler violence in the West Bank. Every year, settlers attack Palestinian farmers trying to harvest their olives – an economic lifeline for the beleaguered Palestinian economy – with few legal consequences. This harvest season has been particularly violent as the Israeli elections approach at the end of the month.

He was also hospitalised, with a gunshot to the foot, according to the Palestine Red Crescent Society. At least six other people then rushed towards the AFP journalists firing guns. Flávio’s surprise first-round election win highlights rapid rise of Brazil’s House of Bolsonaro

The weekend’s elections in Brazil not only put Jair Bolsonaro’s eldest son, Flávio Bolsonaro, in the lead in the presidential race, but also underscored how far the former president has come in building a political dynasty. As his far-right senator son heads into a runoff against the leftist incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a sweeping far-right victory in congressional races also secured seats for Jair Bolsonaro’s wife, two of his sons and one of his brothers. Few in the family have spent much time working outside politics since the patriarch led the way four decades ago, but the offices they now hold have had a significant upgrade. Former first lady Michelle Bolsonaro, 44, who divided her campaign with caring for her husband as he serves a sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup, ran for public office for the first time and was elected senator.

Kenya confirms first Ebola case as virus ‘surges’ in DR Congo province

Kenya has reported its first-ever Ebola death, the health minister announced on Tuesday, as the disease continues to spread rapidly through the north-east of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where the outbreak was announced in May. This is the 17th outbreak of the highly infectious, often deadly disease in the DRC. As of 2 October, 4,082 people had died out of 8,463 confirmed cases in the country since the emergence of the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, for which there is still no vaccine nor specific treatment. A Kenyan man who had been living in the DRC for seven years died after returning to Kenya, the Kenyan health minister Aden Duale told reporters. The man, who has not been named, had been treated in the DRC after falling ill about a month ago. He then travelled overland to the Ugandan capital, Kampala, before flying to Nairobi on 3 October. Kenya has previously never reported a case of Ebola, but neighbouring Uganda recorded 20 – almost all people who had travelled from the DRC – and two deaths, before being declared Ebola-free in August.

Fuel from South Korea being shipped to Russia as Ukraine war grinds on

Fuel is being shipped from South Korea to Russia via sanctioned tankers as Moscow scrambles for supplies amid the war in Ukraine, a move one expert said “undermines” Seoul’s public backing for Kyiv. Guardian analysis of port records and ship-tracking data found that in July and August over 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mostly diesel, was loaded at several South Korean ports on to seven tankers that made 14 voyages to Russia’s far east. Three of the vessels were under sanctions by the UK and EU, and one took on its cargo through a ship-to-ship transfer in South Korean waters – a method that can obscure where a cargo came from and lets ships avoid calling at port terminals. “It is shocking that EU-sanctioned tankers loaded fuel at South Korean ports and carried it to Russia”, said Isaac Levi, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Finnish thinktank.

But South Korea has long sought to balance its support for Ukraine with its desire to improve ties with Russia. Throughout the war, Seoul has ruled out sending weapons directly to Ukraine, in line with its practice of not supplying lethal arms to countries at war. Moscow has signalled an interest in restoring relations with South Korea, including trade ties. Outcry in Trinidad and Tobago after passing of police bill that could threaten press freedom

Journalists in Trinidad and Tobago have called for an urgent amendment to a sweeping new bill that increases police powers of search and seizure, which they argue threatens the country’s much-vaunted freedom of the press. The government says the special operations bill 2026, passed on 24 September, is designed to tackle alarmingly high crime and murder rates in the Caribbean nation. The country has spent more than a year in an almost perpetual state of emergency, with police empowered to bypass normal constitutional rights around arrest, detention, and search and seizure. But journalists in Trinidad and Tobago have called for explicit exemptions in the new legislation to prevent police from searching and seizing their notebooks, phones and laptops. In the past, journalists have been forced to challenge warrants empowering police to raid their homes and offices.

Although the country prides itself in honouring freedom of speech, ranking 19 out of 180 countries in the 2025 Reporters Without Borders press freedom index, this year it fell 13 places to 32, and journalists say they are deeply concerned about whether they can protect whistleblowers and vulnerable sources who share information on the understanding that they will be protected. The president of the Media Association of Trinidad and Tobago (MATT), Prior Beharry, said the organisation had called for clause 15 of the bill to be urgently amended “to explicitly shield our devices and materials … and confidential source information from standard police seizure”. Clause 15 prevents police from seizing “a tool of a lawful trade or business” or material protected by legal professional privilege. But MATT says journalism is not explicitly recognised as a protected trade, nor does the bill establish a procedure for handling confidential journalistic material discovered during searches.

Plague epidemic risk in Russia low after death of lab technician, WHO says

The World Health Organization has said the risk of an epidemic in Russia is low after the sudden death of a lab technician who worked at a plague research institute in Siberia. Darya Shipilova, who was 28, died last week, two days after falling ill. Russian media reports suggested she may have become infected after an accident at her workplace, where dangerous pathogens are kept and studied. Russian authorities have downplayed the incident and say Shipilova died of “pneumonia of an unknown aetiology”. Strict quarantine measures have been imposed at the research centre in the city of Irkutsk and in several neighbouring hospitals. Christian Lindmeier, a WHO spokesperson, said on Tuesday that there was no sign of a wider outbreak. “All ‌of the patients’ contacts have reportedly been identified and are being monitored for ‌illness, and none to date have shown ​symptoms of illness,” he said.

Riot police fire teargas as 250,000 take part in schools protests across France

Police have fired teargas at ⁠protesters as more than 250,000 pupils, teachers and parents demonstrated across France on the biggest day yet of a campaign for better high school conditions that has been marred by often violent clashes with police. Related: ‘This is state violence’: Paris students rage at politicians and heavy-handed policing The French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said at least 215 teenagers and 85 school staff had been injured since the protests began more than a fortnight ago, calling the figures “the heaviest ⁠toll in decades paid by the school system”. The country’s president, Emmanuel Macron, called key ministers to the Élysée Palace for talks on Tuesday night, French media reported. The interior ministry said 200,000 people had taken part in mainly peaceful marches in cities including Marseille, Nantes ⁠and Lyon on Tuesday, with 56,000 more joining the biggest demonstration in Paris. Organisers put the total at 450,000.

Trade unions and rights groups have accused the police of using unnecessary force against the young protesters in recent days, with Amnesty International saying French authorities should “put an end to the disproportionate police repression”. Japan PM leads outcry after US Marine arrested over alleged killing of woman on Okinawa

Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, has led public outcry over crimes committed by US servicemen after a marine suspected of killing a woman on Okinawa was arrested on Saturday. In a speech in parliament, Takaichi described the alleged crime as “heinous” and urged US military authorities to enforce discipline among American servicemen stationed on Okinawa, an island 1,000 miles south of Tokyo. Police said Devin Ballard, a 20-year-old lance corporal, had been arrested on suspicion of strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in Okinawan capital Naha early on Saturday. He is also suspected of stealing her wallet and backpack. Ballard denied the allegations, police said. If convicted, Ballard could face life in prison or the death penalty. The US military has paused all operations on the Japanese island for two days, following Ballard’s arrest. Lt. Gen. Benjamin Watson, commander of III Marine Expeditionary Force, said in a letter posted on social media that incidents allegedly involving service members “demand we pause for reflection”.

The US military will also impose a monthlong curfew from midnight to 5am starting Friday, the Kyodo news agency reported. The alleged crime has sparked an outcry on Okinawa, which hosts tens of thousands of American troops and dozens of bases. Crimes and accidents involving US troops on Okinawa have been a constant source of tension between Tokyo and Washington and the target of protests among local people. ‘All I want to do is cry’: trauma of 7 October survivors three years after the attacks

Keith Siegel spent many of his long hours in Hamas captivity in Gaza etching everything that happened after 7 October 2023 into his memory. For 484 days, he recited to himself every place he was held, the dates he was moved and every attack or humiliation he endured or witnessed. He aimed to store intelligence that could help Israeli forces free other hostages if he was released, to keep track of time as the days slid by and be able to tell his family what happened to him. Now his body is free, but he cannot loosen those memories. “I’m living a kind of dual life,” he said in an interview in Tel Aviv. “I’m here for some of the time, and I’m in Gaza some of time. It’s very challenging to convey in words what it was like.” Siegel and his wife, Aviva, were among 251 people taken captive to Gaza on the deadliest day in Israel’s history, when Hamas militants broke across the border to launch a wave of attacks on kibbutzim, border towns, military bases and music festivals.

The cemetery at Nir Oz contains two lines of fresh headstones, marking lives that all ended on that same date. A shared plot for a family of five – a mother, father and their three young children – has been made into a garden with space left for their still-living grandparents. Caretaker Shlomo Margalit, who will soon turn 89, points to the graves of three of his oldest friends, founding members of the kibbutz who came to Nir Oz from Haifa with him in the 1950s. “This is my life project, as well as my home,” Margalit said, explaining why he has come back to a place of such loss. Philipp Ruch believes that the impact of the 1929 Wall Street crash cannot explain the Nazi breakthrough at the 1930 Reichstag election, as the full effects of Black Thursday “didn’t fully arrive in Germany until July 1931” (‘Hitler was a lazy criminal who slept in until noon’: why most of what we think we know about the rise of the Nazis is wrong, 1 October). But unemployment more than doubled between 1928 and the 1930 election, and that fact alone might be thought sufficient to explain the change in Nazi fortunes. Not so, says Ruch, for “in regions where unemployment was high, the Nazi party performed relatively poorly. If anything, unemployment was a factor contributing to anti-fascist resilience.” This, however, marks a failure to appreciate how rising unemployment was seen by most Germans at the time.

In Big Girls Don’t Cry, the New Zealand coming-of-age film quietly devastating film festivals, there is a scene on a moonlit beach. It is a deeply relatable, deeply uncomfortable watch; reliving the teenage negotiation – or not – of consent feels unsettling and validating. “Yeah, an 18-year-old at the screening last night said, ‘I feel so seen and exposed,” director and writer Paloma Schneideman, 34, says. “I was like, whoa, that’s quite an astute way to think about it. One is cathartic and healing, and the other is quite confronting.” Schneideman says she wanted to tell a story about the place “between consent and non-consent, where it was just something we felt we had to do”. “It’s such a tricky space, and I don’t think we see it a lot.

Canada to indefinitely bar mental illness as sole reason for access to euthanasia

Canada’s federal government said on Wednesday it would advance legislation to prevent people whose sole health condition is mental illness from accessing euthanasia, an effort by the ruling Liberal party to address a clash in the country over who has access to physician-assisted death. Under the current rules, people whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness have been barred from accessing medical assistance in dying (Maid) to end their lives. But that ban – due to be lifted in March – has divided lawmakers over whether to permit this expansion of the Maid program. Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, the justice minister, Sean Fraser, said his government would indefinitely bar people whose sole condition is mental illness from accessing the program. He said that while there was no “perfect consensus” on this issue, upcoming legislation reflected the “correct” approach.

Canada to indefinitely bar mental illness as sole reason for access to euthanasia

Earlier this year, a government committee concluded the government should expand access to Maid and should “indefinitely exclude persons whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness from eligibility for medical assistance in dying”. That report also flagged the need for “increased and more equitable access” to mental health services. Canada’s Maid laws, drawn up after a 2015 supreme court decision, initially only permitted those who are terminally ill to be eligible for the procedure. But in 2019, a Quebec judge ruled that restricting access to those who had a “reasonably foreseeable death” was unconstitutional, forcing federal lawmakers to amend and expand the existing laws. In 2021, the law was updated so adults could receive an assisted death if two doctors confirmed an irremediable physical condition causing immense suffering that cannot be relieved. Given the uncertainty surrounding mental illness, lawmakers in 2021 initially put a temporary exclusion in place for people who suffer solely from a mental illness. They renewed that pause in 2023 and 2024.

The Liberal party’s legislation is also an effort to ward off a private member’s bill that would amend the section of the criminal code covering Maid so that “a mental disorder is not a grievous and irremediable medical condition”. Could the UK really rejoin the EU?

It was lobbed into the national conversation without fanfare or warning, almost a footnote in the UK prime minister’s first speech as leader to his governing Labour party’s annual conference last week. But Andy Burnham has kicked off a quiet U-turn on Brexit. By stating bluntly that the decision to leave Europe’s core political community had done “more harm than good”, Burnham broke a taboo in his own party, in effect, discarding his predecessor’s paralysing ‘red lines’ on Europe, and signalling he will not be bound by these constraints after the next British election. Over the coming six weeks Burnham will gauge public support before setting out options for the UK’s long term relationship with the UK’s largest market. Rejoining the 27-nation bloc will be one of them. Burnham is opening the door to Britain reversing Brexit. The famous red lines, or non-negotiables, enshrined by Keir Starmer in Labour’s 2024 election manifesto, were meant to reassure Brexit-supporting voters that under Labour there would be no return to a single market, customs union or the free movement of people.

text:
Could the UK really rejoin the EU?

But these pledges left Starmer with little room for manoeuvre with Europe, beyond warm words. The evidence that Brexit has stunted the British economy is not new. Estimates for the damage quitting the single market has already done range from 6% of 8% of GDP. What is new is a prime ministerial readiness to publicly acknowledge that harm and conclude that an ambitious new path is required. “This is the first time that a UK politician in power has been willing to stand up and say that Brexit is a failure that we must address or redress in some fundamental way,” Joël Reland, an analyst with the UK In a Changing Europe thinktank, told me. “Keir Starmer’s public message was that we will be sticking with Boris Johnson’s [2019] Brexit deal, but we’re going to improve it to make Brexit work. Burnham is saying Brexit doesn’t work and that we need a different form of deal. That has never been said before.” Burnham is not yet committing himself to fighting the next election on a particular course of action. Much will depend on the response he gets.

text:
Could the UK really rejoin the EU?

But all options – Lisa O’Carroll details them here – are on the table, from a customs union to re-joining the single market and becoming, like Norway, a rule-taker, to “going all the way”. But crucially, Burnham has already departed from the orthodoxy that makes questioning Brexit a heresy. Instead of shutting down the topic to limit his exposure to Eurosceptic attacks, the prime minister is meeting it head-on, Reland said. “Burnham could have done what every other leader before him has done since the 2016 referendum, and take a clear red-lines position against Brexit, but he didn’t. And I don’t see why you would do that unless you wanted to take on the political argument”. Why would Burnham choose this juncture and risk drawing down what Rafael Behr calls the Brexit curse? The economic rationale is the obvious one. “Burnham’s ten year domestic agenda promises radical reform of such things as the social care system, and somebody is going to have to pay for that,” argues Reland.

“One of the ways you can get economic growth is by rejoining your largest and closest trading partner.” The modest ‘re-set’ agenda launched by Starmer in May 2025 is stuck, bogged down in disputes, such as that over fees for EU students in the UK. A pencilled-in 20 November summit is still up in the air. Britain’s big impediment from outside the club is its lack of bargaining power. A cherrypicking attempt to coax the EU into a selective single market for goods only (without free movement of people) was firmly rebuffed by Brussels in May. And even if this reset were fully delivered, the government’s own figures estimate it would add at most, 0.3% to GDP by 2040. Labour meanwhile has lost votes to its left, particularly to the Greens, so a more progressive offer on Europe might be a gamble worth taking. New polling, as Pippa Crerar and Rowena Mason revealed at the weekend, shows that if Burnham’s preference is for rejoining the EU, almost half of the country already agrees. Gaby Hinsliff noted that among Burnham’s opponents the only one to react to the surprise move with “unfettered glee” was Nigel Farage.

Yet, she suggested, the Conservatives, also obsessed with economic growth, may not side with Farage given that most voters think Brexit has made them economically worse off. “It’s not in Tory long-term interests to strangle this at birth” wrote Hinsliff. *** A warm welcome? Events in Europe are also dictating the pace. “Welcome back!” was the French president Emmanuel Macron’s possibly tongue-in-cheek response to Burnham’s remarks. But it is a French-led project called “Made in Europe” that is both concentrating the PM’s mind and could ultimately undermine his ambition. Made in Europe is a highly protectionist idea for turning the EU into an industrial powerhouse, able to withstand competition from China. UK-made goods, if legally classified as non-European under the law, would be locked out, spelling trade devastation for the British car industry. Made in Europe is emerging as a symbol, Reland explained, of how geopolitics is driving the EU’s agenda, and widening its range of competencies to such areas as industrial policy, AI and tech sovereignty. “It is no longer just food and environment policy that is set at EU level but the big, strategic, hard security decisions too,” he said. Flávio Bolsonaro’s advance in Brazil’s election is grim jolt for climate campaigners

More fire, more ash, more crime, more death. And a globally important ecosystem driven ever more rapidly towards a point of no return. That is the prospect for the Amazon rainforest for at least the next four years if Flávio Bolsonaro holds on to the lead he established this week in the first round of Brazil’s presidential election. This appears to be of far more concern to the outside world than to voters in Latin America’s biggest, richest and most biodiverse nation. The far-right son of the former president and jailed coup-monger Jair Bolsonaro won 47% of the vote, putting him in pole position before the 25 October runoff with the incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who was backed by 44.2%. The result is an unnerving jolt to climate and nature campaigners. Taken out of context, this appears to be a vote against the forest. The current administration of Lula (as the veteran Brazilian president is best known) has reduced deforestation in the Amazon by almost 50%.

But that success secured little noticeable electoral traction for either Lula or pro-forest candidates in other polls held the same day. The former environment minister Marina Silva lost a bid for the Senate and Joenia Wapichana, a former head of Brazil’s Indigenous affairs agency, Funai, failed to win a seat in Congress. Out of 57 Indigenous candidates, only two won. Flávio Bolsonaro is the heir to the political legacy of his father, Jair Bolsonaro, a former army captain whose four years in power resulted in a 59.5% increase in Amazon deforestation, roughly equivalent to destroying 2bn trees. If he wins, Bolsonaro has promised to free his father, who was imprisoned for plotting a military coup and attempting to annihilate democracy in Brazil. He has said that his father could have any position he wants in his administration. Interactive Flávio Bolsonaro has shown that he will be just as willing as his father to dismantle protections for climate and nature and allow illegal miners, loggers and land grabbers to invade Indigenous territories.

As a lawmaker, he backed a 2019 bill to eliminate requirements for landowners in the Amazon to conserve a proportion of native vegetation. In his manifesto, he completely ignored the climate crisis. And he has courted support from some of the most predatory landowners in the rainforest. He is also part of a movement – Bolsonarism – that is geared towards maximising profits for extractive industries regardless of the environmental cost. Take its victorious candidate for the Amazonian state of Pará, Daniel Santos, who was fined $275,000 (£208,000) for deforestating 280 hectares (690 acres) of his land without authorisation and is now promising to waive such penalties. As a result of Sunday’s election, Bolsonarists now control seven of the nine states in the Brazilian Amazon, and could win an eighth in the runoffs. Bolsonarist influence in the legislature, which is dominated by agribusiness interests, is also growing. Flávio’s brother, Carlos, and stepmother, Michelle, were elected to the Senate, while an uncle and brother won seats in the lower house of deputies.

Even before the election, Congress had been pushing hard to weaken environmental protections. Now it will be almost impossible to stop, particularly given the current chaos in the supreme court, which has been a partial check on untrammelled expansion by miners, ranchers and monoculturalists. Against these forces, Lula would struggle to govern even if he wins the runoff. As a result, it is not just the Amazon that is in peril, but all of Brazil’s biomes, its traditional peoples and the stability of the global climate. The question now is why voters paid so little heed to these concerns. Environmentalists were often the target. Another factor is the expansion of US-style Pentecostalism, which is steadily supplanting Catholicism across Brazil, particularly in the Amazon. The political and environmental consequences of that religious shift can be seen by comparing the pro-nature treatise of the past two popes with the sermons of many evangelical preachers who encourage followers to seek wealth today as much as, if not more, than following moral creeds to ensure a good afterlife. Will Brazil be the next domino to fall to Trumpism and its bonfire approach to nature? The Bolsonaro family certainly hope so. Jair went so far as to salute the US flag. Flávio Bolsonaro, the far-right frontrunner to become Brazil’s next president, has vowed to “re-democratise” the South American country, increasing fears about a move into authoritarian rule if he wins power. Brazil was re-democratised in the 1980s after a brutal 21-year dictatorship that Flávio’s father, the disgraced ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, has long praised. Flávio, 45, beat Lula, 80, in Sunday’s presidential election first round and goes into the runoff on 25 October as favourite. On Tuesday, the rightwinger vowed to capitalise on the hugely increased far-right presence in congress after the election to change the constitution and “re-democratise this country”.

German court orders detention of former intelligence chief after spying arrest

A formal arrest warrant has been issued against Germany’s former top spy, with a judge ordering him to be held in pre-trial detention, a day after he was arrested on suspicion of treason and spying on behalf of an overseas intelligence agency. The 80-year-old market trader who became a Chilean music star

At a concert hall in the Chilean capital, Santiago, an 80-year-old man edges unsteadily down a steep staircase. With one hand he grips the metal bannister, in the other he carries a mug of hot water with a slice of lemon, as if heading to bed. But when the red stage curtain is pulled aside for him, Luis Gómez, or JM as he is universally known, transforms in an instant. He skips on to the stage to a roar from the crowd and launches into a bolero, punctuated by hip thrusts and shuffling two-steps. JM is the frontman of Los Crack del Puerto, and one of the last remaining voices of a golden generation. Born and raised in Valparaíso, Chile’s vibrant second city, JM’s late foray into music has taken him all around the country, as well as to Mexico, the UK, Argentina and France. But things could – and probably should – have worked out very differently. At 65, he was still hawking vegetables at the market he had worked at since the age of eight. This May, Los Crack del Puerto released their fourth record, Lo Mucho Que Nos Queda (So Much Yet to Come), as a cassette – to great acclaim.

“Singing has always been my release,” JM says in a wavering voice, in contrast to his confident onstage vocals. The father of two speaks with captivating enthusiasm about his life, often leaping to his feet to re-enact minor scenes. Scattered with bursts of song, most conversations return to his mostly tongue-in-cheek fear of his wife of 55 years, his penchant for sports clothing, or the market on Avenida Argentina in Valparaíso. JM was born in the O’Higgins neighbourhood of Valparaíso in 1945, the youngest of five children. He was three years old when his father died, and 10 when he lost his mother. For a time, he would sleep out on the street between parked cars, until his aunt and uncle took him in and laid down the law, insisting that he was home by 10pm each night. “JM” was a cheeky nickname bestowed upon him by the family – the initials of a childhood friend, Juan Muñoz, with whom they said he spent too much time. The moniker has long since replaced his full name. Valparaíso then, as it is now, was defined by its music.

As in many ports, cultures and ideas have long arrived in the city and been woven into its fabric; but the musical styles of its 20th-century heyday, from boleros to waltzes, tango to cueca, Chile’s official national dance, have barely changed in generations. “The same songs that were sung before are still the ones they sing now,” says JM decisively. Many now form Los Crack del Puerto’s repertoire. One of his cousins, Juan Navarro, known simply as Juanín, would bring friends home and play his guitar for them, and the younger JM would come sing along. The cousins remained lifelong friends while Juanín pursued a career in the police and JM sold vegetables at the market. “That’s still what I am – a market trader,” he says. Through middle age, the self-taught double act entertained crowds in Valparaíso’s bars – JM the entertaining foil to his more serious older cousin, who would perch on a stool to play his guitar, always in an immaculate pressed suit. “Sometimes Juanín would just invent chords,” says Los Crack del Puerto’s manager, Juan Nuñez.

“The rest of the band would stop and ask him what chord he’d just played, and he’d just shrug.” “JM was the entertainer, he can make anyone laugh,” Nuñez adds. But the dynamic worked. María del Carmen Abascal, symbol of Spain’s housing protests, dies aged 87

María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old whose eviction set off a nationwide wave of protests against Spain’s housing crisis, has died. News of her death came two weeks after Maricarmen, as she had come to be known across Spain, was evicted from the Madrid apartment where she had lived for more than seven decades. The pensioner, whose apartment had been purchased by an investment firm who sought to hike her rent by 230%, swiftly became a symbol of the many left behind by Spain’s surging housing market. Scenes of the eviction, which saw police use rounds of teargas as they carried out the order, made headlines across Spain. The shocking images – showing Abascal being forcibly removed from her home on a stretcher, flanked by protesters and police – swiftly crystallised into anger. About 10,000 people took to the streets of Madrid hours later, wielding signs such as “Shame” and “We’re all Maricarmen”. From Spain’s north to the south, people poured into plazas to protest the suffering wrought by rents that had soared 80% in the span of a decade while house prices had climbed 63%.

citation.title: María del Carmen Abascal, symbol of Spain’s housing protests, dies aged 87

text:
María del Carmen Abascal, symbol of Spain’s housing protests, dies aged 87

From the hospital where she was being treated for severe exhaustion, Abascal cheered on the fledgling movement. “I would like to be there with you all,” she said in a video shot from her hospital bed. “But I’m not that lucky. So from here, I ask you all for courage and to fight and defend what is yours.” As encampments began springing up across the country, the investment firm that bought Abascal’s home said she could return. The deal did little to quell the anger that had boiled over in the wake of the eviction. This week the wave of outrage led the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, to call a snap general election after rightwing and far-right parties voted down two emergency decrees his government had proposed to address the housing crisis. The Madrid tenants’ union said the solution had come too late for the octogenarian. “This was a completely preventable situation following an agonising ordeal,” it said in a statement announcing that Abascal had died in hospital, reportedly hours before she was due to sign a new lease with the investment firm that had evicted her.

text:

“The events triggered by the injustice of her eviction undoubtedly mark a turning point in the history of this country: massive demonstrations, encampments in the squares, an early election, and the call for a general strike,” it added. “The housing debate is at the center of it all, but the cost of getting to this point has been too high.” Sánchez offered his condolences to Abascal’s family and friends. “A hug also to everyone who’s feeling this loss today as their own,” he wrote on social media. “Rest in peace.” Spain’s health minister, Mónica García, said Abascal’s plight had “served to awaken awareness across all of Spain, lighting a fuse that cannot be put out”, and adding that her “dignity and courage” had shown the way. The Podemos MEP and former equalities minister Irene Montero was more blunt. “This isn’t a death; it’s a murder,” she wrote on social media. “Such bloody anger. Thank you for fighting, Maricarmen.” Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party (PP) – which voted against last week’s emergency housing measures – also offered his condolences.

“No campaigning, no political parties, no partisan ends, no more bricks in the wall,” he wrote on social media. “When a person dies there should be nothing but respect.” Her death came a day after Sánchez’s cabinet approved two new housing decrees intended to “maintain the spirit” of the two previous decrees that were voted down in parliament last week by the PP, the far-right Vox party and the rightwing Catalan pro-independence Junts party. The 21 measures include facilitating renting or buying a new home; extending eviction protections for vulnerable residents; regulating room rentals; imposing a new tax on seasonal rentals; prohibiting speculative real estate purchases; and granting tax breaks to property owners and tenants who pay on time. With the lower and upper houses of parliament dissolved following the calling of the snap election, the decrees will be voted on by the permanent council of congress, a special council that operates when parliament is not in session.

New Zealand greenhouse gas levels hit record highs threatening catastrophic glacier melts

New Zealand could be hit with more frequent and intense heatwaves and catastrophic glacier melts in the near future, as greenhouse gas levels hit record highs, a new report about the nation’s climate has revealed. Released on Wednesday, the Our Atmosphere and Climate 2026 report shows New Zealand is experiencing mounting climate pressures, which will have wide-reaching implications for the environment, native species and communities. “The signal is just becoming clearer … there are multiple indicators that are showing increased warming and the likelihood of climate change,” Dr Alison Collins, chief science adviser for the ministry for cities, environment, regions and transport (Mcert) told the Guardian. Related: World’s oceans absorbed record heat equal to 40 times annual global energy use New Zealand’s annual average temperature has risen by 1.36C since records began in 1909, and seven of the 10 warmest years on record occurred in the last decade, the report said.

citation.title: New Zealand greenhouse gas levels hit record highs threatening catastrophic glacier melts

text:
New Zealand greenhouse gas levels hit record highs threatening catastrophic glacier melts

“Whilst it sounds like a small amount … it is a significant baseline shift that’s having ramifications through nature, through our communities, and through businesses and industry,” Collins said. The report finds that as the climate heats, glaciers are shrinking. New Zealand has roughly 3000 glaciers, and they have shrunk in volume from 56 cubic kilometres in 1997 to 30 cubic kilometres in 2023, the report said. Modelling of glacier retreat shows a high risk of further decline on the horizon. Under the “low climate scenario” – which assumes low emissions – glaciers will very likely lose between 14 and 86% of their volume by 2100. Under the “high climate scenario”, that figure rises to between 69 and 100% of their volume. “We’re talking about substantial loss,” Collins said. Greenhouse gases have increased to record levels in New Zealand’s atmosphere, the report shows. There was a 30% increase in carbon dioxide since monitoring began in New Zealand in 1972. Methane levels had also slightly increased in 2025 to their highest concentration ever.

citation.title: New Zealand greenhouse gas levels hit record highs threatening catastrophic glacier melts

text:
New Zealand greenhouse gas levels hit record highs threatening catastrophic glacier melts

“That additional heat is showing up in rising temperatures, warming oceans, rising seas, shifting rainfall patterns and more intense extremes,” the report said. Among those extremes were heatwaves, which the report said were “very likely” to increase in frequency, length and intensity across the country. The number of days hitting more than 25C was also “very likely” to increase by 2050, which will expose people to heat-related health risks, including physical illness, disease and psychological distress. Marine heatwaves are also becoming more pronounced and affecting some native species, the report said. In 2025, the series revealed New Zealand’s oceans were warming 34% faster than the global average which has been linked to mass sea sponge bleaching, die-offs of southern bull kelp, large scale fish standings and penguin deaths. The three-yearly update from Mcert and Stats NZ collates statistics, data and research across five domains – air, atmosphere and climate, freshwater, land, and marine – to paint a picture of the state of New Zealand’s environment.

citation.title: New Zealand greenhouse gas levels hit record highs threatening catastrophic glacier melts

text:
New Zealand greenhouse gas levels hit record highs threatening catastrophic glacier melts

The report outlined a myriad of issues that will stem from continued warming, including damaging storms and cyclones that pose a risk to life, droughts affecting species and agricultural industries, sea level rise eroding infrastructure and housing and Māori communities having reduced access to culturally significant places. Severe storms, including Cyclone Gabrielle and the Auckland floods in 2023, have battered New Zealand in recent years, causing deaths, widespread devastation and billions of dollars in costs. New Zealand was built and developed around a relatively stable set of climate conditions and the report examines what happens when those conditions begin to change, Collins said. “Climate change is not just an environmental issue. It’s a human story. It’s an economic story.”

‘Neither war nor peace’: Palestinians in Gaza on existing amid disease, despair and ruins

Ahmed Ishtaiwi has six chairs. They are cheap and plastic and battered, but they are among the 43-year-old driver and mechanic’s most valuable possessions. Ishtaiwi lives in a tent near Deir al-Balah in central Gaza with his two daughters. Their former home is far to the north, in the now ruined town of Beit Lahiya, uninhabitable and impossible to reach. “When I sit on those chairs, I remember sitting in the garden at home, having breakfast and drinking tea. They remind me of my life there,” he said last week. Wednesday is the anniversary of the raid on 7 October 2023 by Hamas militants into southern Israel that killed 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and triggered a relentless Israeli military offensive that killed 73,000 Palestinians, mostly civilians, wounded many more and reduced swathes of Gaza to rubble. When Layan al-Jbour, a 15-year-old from the southern city of Khan Younis, tries to bring some order to the crowded makeshift shelter she shares with her parents, brothers and sisters in al-Mawasi, a strip of coastline at the southernmost end of Gaza, she recalls life before the war.

“When I tidy the tent, I remember our home and how I used to tidy it. I remember my room and how I used to make my bed. When I put a sheet over a table and arrange the bedding, the place looks like our old home,” al-Jbour said. Related: Former UN food agency official claims he was fired for highlighting hunger in Gaza “We hardly took anything with us from our home. We left everything behind, and the only thing I took was my schoolbag. It is the most precious thing I own now. It reminds me so much of my school days. I loved going to school and meeting my friends there.” Across Gaza, Palestinians describe daily routines full of challenges that nothing in their former lives prepared them for: shortages of water and of nourishing food, minimal healthcare, disease, unemployment, economic collapse and the continuing threat of death or injury. Despite a ceasefire a year ago, Israel’s airstrikes continue. Palestinians who have approached the “yellow line” that divides Gaza into zones controlled by the Israeli military and by Hamas have been shot dead.

In the last year, the overall death toll has risen by a further 1,400 people. Our local staff are telling us that this is just the next stage of the conflict.” Ramiz Alakbarov, the UN’s humanitarian coordinator for the Occupied Palestinian Territory, told the UN security council last month that despite the increase in supplies entering Gaza, the health situation remained critical, with “infectious diseases … widespread amid overcrowded displacement sites and inadequate water, sanitation and hygiene conditions”. If I go to my home I may die, and if I go to my farm, I may die too. This is not a life. Poland’s ‘solidarity’ push for EU energy resilience in face of Russian aggression

Two miles off the coast of Gdańsk, the white steel piles of Poland’s first offshore gas terminal rise from the slate-grey Baltic. Installed at a height eight metres above the waves, the floating cranes and construction vessels here are on the frontline of Europe’s push for energy security. Since the taps were turned off on Russian gas after Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine four years ago, Poland has turned to the global energy market for supplies. But while conditions are far from ideal as the Middle East war drives oil and gas prices to stratospheric levels, strengthening the diversity of the country’s energy mix remains a top priority for Poland, its Baltic neighbours, and the EU at large. Looking out to sea from the windswept beach backed by pine forest, Maciej Wawrzkowicz, the offshore project manager at the national gas company Gaz-System, and the construction manager Krzysztof Polatynski say the Baltic is not an easy place to build. Before work could start, Polish navy minesweepers were called in to torpedo unexploded mines and bombs from the second world war.

citation.title: Poland’s ‘solidarity’ push for EU energy resilience in face of Russian aggression

text:
Poland’s ‘solidarity’ push for EU energy resilience in face of Russian aggression

Construction is halted by storms, while the sea froze over last winter. But speed is important in this project of international significance. “Every quay that’s available right now in the area that has some prefabrication workshop space, a contractor is occupying them. And you are seeking for more. Gdańsk harbour is a significant construction place right now.” Poland used to import more than half of its gas from Russia but refused to pay in rubles in 2022 as the Kremlin became a pariah in the west over Putin’s war on Ukraine. A Norwegian pipeline under the Baltic and liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal at Świnoujście, close to the border with Germany, helped to keep most homes warm and the fires of industry burning. At Gdańsk the construction of the floating storage and regasification unit (FSRU) – a specialised marine vessel used to store and convert LNG – is planned to further bolster Poland’s booming economy. But it will also increase the country’s capacity beyond domestic needs – turning it into a hub for eastern Europe and its Baltic neighbours.

text:

Interactive Poland has LNG regasification capacity of 8.3bn cubic metres a year. Once the FRSU is operational in early 2028, that will add 6.1bn cubic metres a year of additional capacity. A second vessel at the Gdańsk FRSU is also planned for 2030 to lift total capacity to more than 20bn cubic metres a year. In an age of geopolitical challenges, the FSRU vessel also has a symbolic name: “Solidarity”, in a nod to its home port’s history, and Poland’s drive to strengthen EU ties in the face of Russian aggression. In the 1980s, as the Soviet Union crumbled, strikes at Lenin shipyard in Gdańsk over communist rule launched Poland’s Solidarność (Solidarity) movement. Led by Lech Wałęsa, it paved the way for independence and the transition to a free-market economy. Living standards have shot up since, from 40% of the EU average in the mid-1990s to 81% last year. Interactive Agnieszka Ozga, the director of the energy transition division, and her deputy, Paweł Sęk, say Poland has been working to diversify energy supplies for decades, with the 2014 annexation of Crimea by Russia accelerating the process.

But 2022 was a “gamechanger,” says Sęk. “After the war started, we knew what was going on and we knew many countries in our region would end up with no gas flows coming from Russia”. Since then the Gdańsk FSRU has grown in importance, says Ozga. “Not only for Poland. But also Slovakia; central and eastern Europe countries; the Baltic states. It is also very, very important for the European Commission: to end the isolation of the Baltic states, because they were fully dependent on inflows of gas from Russia.” However, there is also plenty of evidence in Gdańsk highlighting the energy challenges Poland must still confront. On the edges of the old town’s narrow cobbled streets, the red and white-banded chimney stacks of a Soviet-era coal-fired power plant belch out thick plumes of smoke. Tourist boats ferrying visitors to the Westerplatte peninsula – where the first shots of the second world war were fired – must also pass through the jet-black mountains of a coal dock. Coal accounts for more than half of electricity generation in Poland, significantly above the EU average.

The legacy of Soviet fossil-fuel infrastructure and centuries of domestic production in this resource-rich country mean it remains key for the economy. Interactive More than 80,000 people still work in coalmines, mainly in the south around the industrial city of Katowice – once called Stalinogród – as one of the few remaining coalmining regions still digging among EU countries fully committed to decarbonisation. However, cutting out coal in favour of LNG, renewables and nuclear power is seen as critical for Poland’s future sovereignty and prosperity. Relying on heavily polluting and costly fossil fuels, the country’s average wholesale electricity prices are the ninth highest in the EU – holding back growth in a country accustomed to powering ahead. As wages and living standards catch up to western European levels, Polish manufacturing is beginning to lose its competitive edge from cheap labour – a factor that had long attracted multinationals such as Volkswagen and Toyota to locate factories in the country. As a result, keeping down other production costs – such as energy – is growing in importance.

It will also require vast levels of public investment, at a time when the national debt is piling up and borrowing costs are rising. Separatists win in Quebec – but does that bring separation from Canada any closer?

The victory of the Parti Québécois in Monday’s election in Quebec might seem to bring its signature goal, of separating the French-speaking province from Canada, much closer – but Canadian unity may not be nearly as threatened as may first seem. The PQ’s victory was both impressive and disappointing. The party added 56 seats to its roster and more than doubled its vote share compared with the 2022 election, giving it its first taste of power in 14 years. Crucially, however, it was left five seats short of a majority, making its promise to hold a referendum after Donald Trump leaves office in 2028 nearly impossible. It also won with barely 28% of the popular vote, the lowest percentage for any government in Canada’s electoral history, according to the polling analyst Philippe Fournier. The vast majority of Quebecers voted for parties that want nothing to do with a referendum. It’s a reflection of the province’s 30-year aversion to another bruising debate about Quebec’s place in Canada – particularly in the wake of Trump’s tariffs and threats against the country.

text:
Separatists win in Quebec – but does that bring separation from Canada any closer?

The result not only puts another referendum in doubt, but a raft of other PQ initiatives too, including abolishing the monarchy and applying Quebec’s strict language laws to the province’s colleges. The new government will also face stiff opposition to its plans to reduce immigration levels, which have angered farmers and the business community. Meanwhile, the most popular politician in the province remains far and away the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, in large part because of his resistance to Trump. That has left the PQ leader, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, in an awkward situation for a separatist: he can’t be seen as a threat to Canadian unity. He essentially acknowledged this in his victory speech, pledging to be a “good-faith collaborator” with the rest of the country, and even addressing the crowd in English; then attempted to court the other side of the debate by announcing on Tuesday he would prevent the lieutenant governor, who represents the British crown, from swearing in his new government.

citation.title: Separatists win in Quebec – but does that bring separation from Canada any closer?

text:
Separatists win in Quebec – but does that bring separation from Canada any closer?

“Seventy per cent of Quebecers don’t want a referendum,” said John Parisella, who served as chief of staff to two Quebec premiers and the province’s delegate general in New York and Washington. “And every time they see Trump’s picture on the screen at night, it does nothing to improve a desire for separation. For a lot of Quebecers, the link with Canada is absolutely crucial, even if it isn’t necessarily emotional.” The vote, in fact, may have less to do with embracing separatism and more about punishing the current government. The election saw the total collapse of the governing Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ), which has been in power since 2018. An alliance of federalists and separatists (the party describes itself as nationalist), it didn’t win a single seat, and harvested just a third of its vote share compared to 2022. Its leader, Christine Fréchette, lost her own riding to the Parti Québécois, and on Tuesday afternoon she resigned.

citation.title: Separatists win in Quebec – but does that bring separation from Canada any closer?

text:
Separatists win in Quebec – but does that bring separation from Canada any closer?

In a province whose political discourse has focused on the federalist-separatist divide, the election also suggested a return to normalcy of sorts – with separatists returning to the PQ’s fold, while the federalist vote dispersed to the opposition Liberal party and the upstart Parti Conservateur du Québec (PCQ). The PCQ feasted on the CAQ’s support in the election, winning 19 ridings in the hinterland and in the Quebec City area, where leader Éric Duhaime won his seat for the first time. Founded in 2009, the populist party counts a prominent anti-vaxxer and a rage-bating anti-woke radio host as two of its winning candidates. The party was able to break through in part because of its promise to build an underground highway linking Quebec City to its suburbs across the St Lawrence, despite government reports saying the endeavor would cost as much as C$9.3bn (US$6.5bn) and do little to alleviate traffic. Montreal, meanwhile, went decidedly Liberal red, with leader Charles Milliard regaining seats on the island and in the traditionally English redoubt of the Eastern Townships.

citation.title: Separatists win in Quebec – but does that bring separation from Canada any closer?

text:
Separatists win in Quebec – but does that bring separation from Canada any closer?

The staunchly federalist Liberals, who are unaffiliated with Carney’s federal Liberals, will serve as Quebec’s official opposition. Governing with but a handful of seats in the province’s biggest metropolis will be challenging enough for the PQ; as history has shown, winning a referendum without it is somewhere near impossible. Canada faces another potential menace to its sovereignty in a little less than two weeks, when Alberta in the west holds a “referendum on a referendum” on secession. Happily for Carney, and unfortunately for Trump, polls suggest Albertans are as averse to dalliances with separation as their Quebecer brethren have now become to the east – no matter the party they just chose to govern.
