text:
Satellite images show attack jets at Chinese military facility in Laos

Satellite images show attack jets stationed at a new Chinese military facility in Laos, which opened last week and gives Beijing’s air force its first foothold in mainland south-east Asia. Images provided by the commercial satellite provider Vantor show eight light attack aircraft positioned at Ban Keun airport alongside what appear to be more than a dozen military vehicles lined up in rows. The planes’ shape matches that of the Chinese-made Hongdu JL-8 jet, a two-seat trainer that can be deployed in combat to carry bombs. Laos is reported to have four such aircraft, according to the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies. In a rare example of Beijing’s overseas military expansion, China opened what it said was a joint “support and training centre” at Ban Keun on 29 September. Interactive The airport, about ⁠30 miles (50km) north of Vientiane, the capital of Laos, has been significantly expanded over the past year. Satellite images taken months ago show farmland and dirt paths where there are now new buildings and a paved runway.

citation.title: Satellite images show attack jets at Chinese military facility in Laos

text:
Satellite images show attack jets at Chinese military facility in Laos

Aside from its island bases in the South China Sea, Beijing does not have a significant network of military outposts in other countries, and the Laos airbase would be its first facility in another country capable of handling fighter jets. The new satellite images, taken a day after the announcement and first reported by Reuters, show extensive construction work that appears to be focused on a future runway extension, which could make the airport capable of handling larger planes such as bombers. In its announcement last week, China’s defence ministry said the new centre would “help Laos strengthen the training of its air force pilots” and was not “directed against any third party”. Governments will be watching closely for signs of deployments or the installation of defence equipment that may serve wider military ambitions. After the announcement, the Singapore-based security analyst Collin Koh said it “may not be wrong to conclude this is the first full-fledged PLA [People’s Liberation Army] overseas base in south-east Asia”.

citation.title: Satellite images show attack jets at Chinese military facility in Laos

text:
Satellite images show attack jets at Chinese military facility in Laos

Over the past two decades, China has built up an extensive network of outposts on islands in the disputed South China Sea, including airbases with air defence installations. Otherwise, its navy’s sole overseas military base is a logistics base in Djibouti, on the coast of the Horn of Africa. The Laos agreement follows a similar programme established in Cambodia, at the Ream naval base on the Gulf of Thailand, although that facility has no runway. After years of speculation and denials, China announced in April last year that it had created the “joint logistics and training” facility in Cambodia. It said the centre would support the two militaries in “conducting regional counter-terrorism, disaster prevention and mitigation, humanitarian assistance, joint training and other operations”. US forces are believed to have used Ban Keun airport in Laos during covert military operations at the height of the Vietnam war in the 1960s and 1970s. Its development will be monitored by Vietnam, which maintains disputes with China over the South China Sea, and Thailand, which shares a border with Laos.

citation.title: Satellite images show attack jets at Chinese military facility in Laos

text:
Satellite images show attack jets at Chinese military facility in Laos

After the announcement last week, Thailand’s defence ministry spokesperson said Bangkok considered itself a close partner of both Laos and China and saw it as Vientiane’s sovereign right to decide whether to grant permission for a Chinese base. “Nevertheless, Thailand will continue to closely monitor developments and how the matter proceeds, particularly with regard to building mutual trust,” said R Adm Surasant Kongsiri. China’s government did not mention sending aircraft to Laos in its initial announcement, while the government of Laos has not commented on the project. The US-based Institute for the Study of War has described the Laos base as the “first PLA overseas military facility focused on air power”. In its assessment, the thinktank said the base was “not yet equipped to provide the PLA with the ability to execute major combat operations, unlike US military bases”. It said the base would give the Chinese military alternate routes to access to the South China Sea and strategic air routes. Reuters contributed to this report

‘The nurse used the torch on her phone to do the op’: hospitals stripped of resources in Ukraine’s occupied territories

Earlier this summer, the once bustling corridors of the district hospital in Hola Prystan, a city in the Russian-occupied Kherson region of Ukraine, were ominously quiet. At times, it was plunged into darkness during power cuts lasting hours. Much of the hospital’s medical equipment and supplies had been stolen and redirected to the military, and many experienced staff had gone. “They [the Russian forces] even took some of the furniture,” says Natalia Sergeevna, who spent more than two decades working as a nurse in the hospital before escaping to Ukrainian-held territory in July. In some ways, her hospital had been lucky, she says, with others in Russian-occupied territories repurposed for military use – as has been happening in regions bordering Ukraine – or simply closed down. Despite its bare-bones infrastructure and dark corridors, people still came to the hospital, says Sergeevna, often making difficult journeys across the mine-infested landscape of occupied Kherson.

In June, the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine said conditions in Oleshky and Hola Prystan, where Sergeevna worked, were becoming desperate, with thousands of people left without food, water and medicines. It said ambulances had stopped coming to people’s homes, with medical assistance only available for the most urgent cases and patients dying during attempted evacuations. Sergeevna says she had stayed in the hope of liberation, but by the summer things had become unbearable. “There is almost no available support to do any kind of surgeries; even basic procedures like removing polyps aren’t possible.

text:
The US has backed Libya’s Haftar clan. The UK should not make the same mistake

Patrick Wintour’s report (Libyan unity talks upended as warlord’s son linked to drone attacks on fuel facilities, 3 October) should not surprise anyone concerned with the attempts to end conflict and seek the unification of Libya. Saddam Haftar, like his father, Khalifa, has been backed by the US to support its aims and ambitions in Libya. There is no logic, if democratic elections are the goal, to be backing a member of the Haftar clan for any role in the future of Libya. The Libyan population want nothing more than peace, security and to use constructively the wealth that could be generated from their extensive natural resources for the improvement of their society. Instead, their resources are being dissipated in corruption and conflict, a state of affairs that benefits only the warmongers. As a result of representations received from Libya set out in a 9BR Chambers report, Libya: The Voice of the Tribes, the UK’s present and previous governments and successive ambassadors to Libya have been offered a role in brokering a peace and unification conference in this country.

citation.title: The US has backed Libya’s Haftar clan. The UK should not make the same mistake

text:
The US has backed Libya’s Haftar clan. The UK should not make the same mistake

All it required from the UK was to formally issue visas and invite the political leaders from east and west Libya, who would attend with the legitimate military commanders from both sides, rather than the bad actors. There has been no take-up by either Tory or Labour governments, with neither showing any confidence to do anything contrary to the policies of the US, which are doomed to failure. The benefits to the UK to be seen to be acting independently and in a role consistent with its status as a member of the UN security council would undermine the current perception of it being a declining power. It would also be an opportunity for the UK to assist in the reconstruction and development of an important economy with obvious benefits in its own search for trade. text:
Tropical Storm Isaias near Mexico is forecast to become a hurricane

Tropical Storm Isaias formed early on Wednesday in the warm waters off eastern Mexico and forecasters said it was expected to strengthen into the first hurricane of the belated Atlantic season, as early as Thursday, before hitting the US Gulf coast later in the week. Isaias succeeded Tropical Depression Nine as it strengthened overnight. It was located about 285 miles (460km) west of Progreso, Mexico, and about 580 miles south-west of where the Mississippi River spills into the Gulf of Mexico in Louisiana, according to the National Hurricane Center (NHC). The storm on Wednesday morning had maximum sustained winds of 40mph (65km/h) and was moving east to north-east at 8mph. default The first hurricane of the Atlantic season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905. Communities in the potential path of Isaias moved quickly to prepare for landfall, forecast as soon as Friday evening. Some Gulf oil wells paused production and an Alabama beach city canceled a weekend festival known to draw thousands of tourists. Florida’s governor declared a state of emergency for more than one-third of the state’s counties.

citation.title: Tropical Storm Isaias near Mexico is forecast to become a hurricane

text:
Tropical Storm Isaias near Mexico is forecast to become a hurricane

Isaias could become a major category 3 hurricane, with winds of 111mph (178 km/h) or stronger, before it strikes land, said Michael Brennan, director of the NHC. “We’re expecting multiple dangerous, life-threatening impacts along portions of the northern Gulf Coast beginning Friday and continuing into the weekend,” Brennan said in a video briefing Wednesday. It was not immediately known where the storm may make landfall on the US Gulf coast. The NHC issued a hurricane watch from Bay St Louis, Mississippi, to Indian Pass, Florida. The watch means hurricane conditions are possible within 48 hours. The hurricane center’s initial projections said the center of Isaias could come onshore somewhere between eastern Louisiana and the western Florida Panhandle. People in those areas were urged to prepare for the storm. “There is an increasing risk of dangerous wind and storm surge impacts along portions of the northern Gulf Coast,” the hurricane center, based in Miami, Florida, said.

“Residents from Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle should closely monitor the latest forecast updates and ensure they have their hurricane plan in place.” Forecasters added that there was “uncertainty in where the system makes the northeast turn and how fast it moves toward the coast”. The direction of the storm could see it make landfall where Alabama meets Florida early on Saturday, but the NHC reiterated that the exact path was uncertain. In Gulf Shores, Alabama, the storm threat caused organizers to cancel the National Shrimp Festival that had been scheduled for Thursday through the weekend. The event drew an estimated 325,000 people last year. The storm comes as the Atlantic hurricane season has been unusually quiet this year owing to a particularly strong El Niño, which disrupts storm formation over that ocean. Storm activity in the Pacific has been above average. ‘Palestinians will bear the cost’: UK consulate in East Jerusalem prepares to shut its doors

The UK consulate in East Jerusalem gave few signs it was at the centre of a geopolitical controversy this week, with little movement around the high-walled building save the fluttering of the union jack and the occasional car exiting the compound. The mission is to shut its doors on Thursday after Israel ordered its closure in response to a UK ban on trade with illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and sanctions on those who help build or finance them. The forced closure marked the lowest point in UK-Israeli relations for decades, with reports of the UK considering a retaliatory expulsion of 27 Israeli diplomats from London. It would be the Palestinians who pay the price for the consulate’s closing, warned Amjad Iraqi, the International Crisis Group’s senior analyst on Israel and Palestine. The UK consulate in East Jerusalem is separate from the UK embassy in Tel Aviv – which remains open – and provides services to Palestinians in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza, services they will now lose.

citation.title: ‘Palestinians will bear the cost’: UK consulate in East Jerusalem prepares to shut its doors

text:
‘Palestinians will bear the cost’: UK consulate in East Jerusalem prepares to shut its doors

“It’s quite telling that the Israeli government response was primarily about blocking the UK’s ability to support Palestinians, rather than the core of UK-Israeli relations themselves,” Iraqi said. “For [the Israeli] foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, the response is low-cost, in their minds it’s just Palestinians bearing the cost.” Related: UK threatens to expel Israeli diplomats over planned East Jerusalem consulate closure Israel has already curtailed the diplomatic activities of the Netherlands, Spain and Norway in the occupied West Bank. Palestinian residents of Sheikh Jarrah, the East Jerusalem neighbourhood that is home to the consulate, appeared resigned when asked about the impact the closure might have on their lives. “I mean, it was the British that were the basis of the issue, wasn’t it? They were the ones who signed the Balfour declaration?” said Abu Abdo, a 79-year-old former repairman and resident of Sheikh Jarrah, referring to a 1917 document by the British foreign secretary Arthur Balfour, which expressed support for a Jewish state in Palestine.

citation.title: ‘Palestinians will bear the cost’: UK consulate in East Jerusalem prepares to shut its doors

text:
‘Palestinians will bear the cost’: UK consulate in East Jerusalem prepares to shut its doors

It was a dramatic end for the consulate’s tenure in East Jerusalem, which since its move to the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood in 1967 has experienced its fair share of political upheaval. The UK government first bought the plot that would become its consulate in 1963, when East Jerusalem was still under Jordanian control. It was meant to be a direct liaison between the UK government and the Jordanian-administered West Bank and East Jerusalem. The compound took four years to build and was finally ready for the UK consul-general to move into by 1967. By the time the new consul-general moved into the premises, however, East Jerusalem was no longer under the control of the Jordanians. Just weeks before John Henry Lewen was to move into the building, the six-day war broke out and Israel captured East Jerusalem from the Jordanian forces. Lewen assumed his post at the consulate in a changed East Jerusalem under Israeli control. The consulate he oversaw occupied a unique position as the UK did not recognise Jerusalem as being under any single country’s control.

As the UK foreign secretary told parliament in June 1967: “Our consul-general in Jerusalem is subordinate neither to the ambassador in Tel Aviv nor to the ambassador in Amman, but directly to the Foreign Office.” Lewen’s tenure was marked by the political problems that plagued Jerusalem in the aftermath of the six-day war and the birth of Israel. In 1969, a bomb was placed under the window of a consul secretary, harming no one but damaging the compound. Years later, Palestinians would present their grievances to the British consulate in Sheikh Jarrah. In 2017, protesters demonstrated outside the consulate to mark the centenary of the Balfour declaration. Men placed flags in the consululate windows reading “Balfour is a crime”, while schoolgirls carried thousands of letters written by Palestinian students asking Britain to apologise for the declaration. This week, however, there was little sign of the political turmoil which the British consulate had waded through during its 60 years on the site.

Ukraine says Russia bombed apartment block as birthday gift for Putin

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia’s military of deliberately killing civilians and bombing residential buildings as a macabre gift for Vladimir Putin, who celebrates his 74th birthday on Wednesday. Ukraine’s president described Russia’s overnight drone and missiles strikes, which killed at least 24 people, as “despicable”. “The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively,” he said. Video showed a ballistic missile slamming into a five-storey apartment block in the town of Pryluky in the northern Chernihiv region. The concrete building collapsed, entombing those inside. Eighteen people died, including four children, officials said. Zelenskyy identified them as Oleksandr, Kyrylo, and Serhii, who was one year old, as well as eight-year-old Maksym. He said five children were among about 50 people who were injured. Rescuers continued to pick through the rubble, with several residents not yet accounted for, he added. “Today, on Putin’s birthday, the Russian army ‘presented’ him with the destruction of a residential block in Pryluky,” Zelenskyy wrote on social media.

Naval drone hits oil tanker off Russian resort city Sochi, triggering massive blaze

An oil tanker off Russia’s Black Sea coast was struck by a naval drone, triggering a huge fire and black smoke cloud that blanketed parts of the resort city of Sochi, Russia’s transport ministry has said. The transport ministry said a Liberian-flagged tanker had been attacked and that “crude oil is burning openly in the waters of the Black Sea”. “Firefighting efforts will begin once the fire’s intensity has subsided and rescue vessels can safely approach the tanker,” the ministry said. A crew of 23 – all Indian citizens – had been rescued, it added. Russia and Ukraine have targeted commercial shipping around the Black Sea since the conflict began, and Russia has recently attacked grain vessels carrying Ukrainian goods near the coast of Romania. There was no comment from Kyiv on the attack.

Good morning. There was a time when Bank of England interest rate announcements passed (most of us) by entirely unnoticed. He wasn’t alone: by the 1990s, central bank independence had become the global norm. The Bank is tasked with promoting monetary and financial stability. The government dictates a target inflation rate (now 2%), and the Bank sets interest rates it hopes will help achieve this. Now Bolotana, located in the Margine area of central Sardinia about 70 miles (110km) from the island’s original blue zone, has emerged as a new potential candidate, researchers say, generating centenarians every year in a trend driven by women. A study by professors at Sardinia’s University of Sassari and the University of Alabama at Birmingham in the US, published in the scientific journal Frontiers in Aging, found that 13.8% of women in the village who reach the age of 70 will live to 100 – placing it second in the world for female longevity after Hong Kong.

Growing up, Ayu would watch his parents put together hand made leather shoes on the ground floor of their three storey home in the Chinese city of Wenzhou. By the mid eighties, Chinese economists had a name for this type of bottom up economic growth story: the Wenzhou model. The deposed Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, have been indicted for alleged conspiracy to commit torture, according to Manhattan federal court papers unsealed on Thursday. The superseding indictment was unsealed shortly before Flores appeared at court in her ongoing push for pretrial release – which was denied by Judge Alvin Hellerstein. Maduro and Flores have been jailed in New York City since early January. They were captured by US special forces during a shocking predawn assault on Caracas and transported to New York to face “narcoterrorism”-related charges in a move that sparked widespread international outrage. Charging documents at the time alleged that Maduro spearheaded a “corrupt, illegitimate government that, for decades, has leveraged government power to protect and promote illegal activity, including drug trafficking”. Maduro and Flores have previously pleaded not guilty in the criminal case against them. CNN on Wednesday first reported that a new indictment was expected.

Maduro, Flores and other Venezuelan leaders “presided over a system of repression that relied on violence against political opposition, arbitrary detention, and the torture of detainees, including United States citizens”, the just-released charging document said. Maduro and Flores, the superseding indictment alleged, “sat atop that violent power structure”. They allegedly “developed and facilitated the systems which they and their co-conspirators used corruptly to amass immense wealth and power, rewarding allies with ill-gotten funds and terrorizing perceived opponents through persecution and violence”. Flores was integral to this effort, authorities claimed, saying she “helped develop this system of repression and ordered that individuals be tortured to protect her family members’ illegal activities”. The victims of their torture included US citizens “who were believed to pose a threat” to Maduro’s power.

Ethiopia launches drone attack against Eritrean troops who crossed into Tigray

Eritrean troops who crossed into Ethiopia’s Tigray region have come under drone attack from government forces, raising the risk that renewed internal conflict in Ethiopia could trigger an all-out regional war between the neighbouring countries. Military vehicles carrying soldiers drove across Eritrea’s southern border into Tigray on Wednesday, reaching the town of Adigrat 25 miles (40km) south, according to civilian witnesses, a militia commander and the conflict monitoring group Acled. Eritrean troops were then targeted by Ethiopian government drones on Wednesday evening and Thursday morning, Acled said. Eritrea has a historical enmity with the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which launched an offensive against the Ethiopian government on 23 September, but that previous hostility has been superseded by Eritrea’s desire to head off a perceived risk of Ethiopia invading it, in order to access the Red Sea. In the last two weeks, the TPLF and six other armed groups in Ethiopia have fought the government in Tigray and the neighbouring regions Amhara and Afar.

Former Labour MP cleared over role in fraudulent Covid-19 testing company

A former Labour MP and justice minister has been found not guilty of charges around his role in a fraudulent Covid-19 testing company. Shahid Malik, 58, was MP for Dewsbury between 2005 and 2010 and served as a minister in three departments in Gordon Brown’s government. Malik was one of five people charged with offences relating to RT Diagnostics, a company that prosecutors said was a “cash cow” set up to take advantage of the UK government’s expanding test-and-trace system in March 2021. On Thursday, Malik was found not guilty of fraudulent trading, causing a public nuisance and money laundering in a trial at Bradford crown court, which was, unusually, conducted without a jury. The trial began in October last year and jurors were sent out to start their deliberations in March. In April, they were discharged by Judge Smith after an allegation of jury tampering. Smith took the decision to continue the trial without the jury, and that he would decide on the verdicts.

The court heard that Malik started the business with the pharmacist and former Labour councillor Faisal Shoukat, 39, when the third national lockdown was ending in March 2021. Shoukat was found guilty of all three offences. Paul Moore, 57, who had a senior role in RT Diagnostics and was Malik’s office manager when he was an MP, was cleared of causing a public nuisance and of fraudulent trading. Lynn Connell, 64, a manager at the company, and Alexander Zarneh, 70, who was its clinical director, were also cleared of the same two offences. Prosecutors said RT Diagnostics, which made £6.67m in three weeks, was set up in “shoddy and inadequate premises” in Halifax and gave out false negative results to customers. The defence barrister, Jonathan Laidlaw KC, said Malik’s role in the business had been “very limited indeed” and he had acted as “a facilitator – putting the money up and making introductions”. Giving his closing speech to jurors in March, Laidlaw said Malik never went to the premises when it was in operation.

French ministers scramble to appease students after 10 days of protests

High school students have again blockaded schools and marched through cities across France, promising to continue their campaign against the poor state of the national education system in the 10th day of protests that have left hundreds injured. Large crowds took to the streets on Thursday for mainly peaceful demonstrations in cities including Lille, Rennes, Nantes, Lyon, Toulon and Marseille, while in Paris a large procession marched through the city centre to the Place de la Bastille. An estimated 25,000 students thronged the square in the east of the capital, with some climbing the monument at its centre, which commemorates France’s 1830 July revolution, while waving the tricolour flag and singing the Marseillaise. As the evening drew in, riot police fired teargas and crowd-dispersal rounds and carried out repeated baton charges to clear the protesters, some of whom hurled bottles, paving stones and other projectiles at the heavily armoured squads.

Italian opposition cries foul as Meloni’s electoral reform passed in secret ballot

A controversial overhaul to electoral law that critics say is aimed at boosting Giorgia Meloni’s chances of clinging on to power in elections next year has been given final approval by the Italian parliament. Meloni, the Italian prime minister, says the new system, which introduces a fully proportional model, including bonus seats for any coalition that wins the most votes, will bring about greater political stability, while opposition parties argue that it mainly serves the interests of those in power. The change was passed in a secret ballot in the lower house with 227 MPs voting in favour and 164 against. There were protests from opposition politicians who held up signs decrying the law as a “scam” and a “con” when the result was announced. Opposition parties have vowed to challenge the changes in the constitutional court, arguing that the bonus seat element, which would be granted to any coalition that reaches a vote threshold of 42% of the vote, distorts voter representation.

Millions on alert as Hurricane Isaias set to bring dangerous storm surge

Millions of people from Louisiana to Florida were under hurricane warnings on Thursday as Hurricane Isaias heads toward the US Gulf coast, with weather officials warning of dangerous storm surge, hurricane-force winds, heavy rainfall and flooding. Isaias intensified from a tropical storm into the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season on Wednesday night, and has prompted state of emergency declarations in Florida, Alabama and Georgia, as well as evacuation orders and school closures in several Florida counties as officials urge residents to prepare for its arrival. The National Weather Service (NWS) said on Thursday evening that Isaias, now a category 2 hurricane, had sustained winds of 100mph (160km/h). It is expected to make landfall in the northern Gulf coast late Friday or early Saturday. The NWS warned that Isaias was “expected to strengthen and be a strong hurricane when it approaches the northern Gulf coast on Friday” and that it was expected to bring a “life-threatening storm surge” along parts of the northern Gulf coast.

Storm surge warnings, issued when there is a “danger of life-threatening inundation from rising water moving inland from the coastline”, are already in effect from the mouth of the Mississippi River to the Suwanee River in Florida. Residents in the affected areas have been urged to follow advice from local officials and evacuate if instructed to do so. The NWS further warned that “preparations to protect life and property from storm surge and damaging winds in the warning area should be rushed to completion today”. default Hurricane warnings were in effect from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, to the Bay/Gulf county line in Florida, with the NWS warning that “damaging hurricane force-winds are expected over portions of the Florida Panhandle, southern Alabama, and southern Mississippi”. Residents were being urged to prepare for possible “long-duration power outages”. Tropical storm warnings were in effect from parts of Louisiana to west of Ocean Springs, Mississippi, and from east of the Bay/Gulf county line to Aucilla River in Florida.

Isaias was expected to bring heavy rain to the central Gulf coast and much of the south-east from Friday into the weekend, with 3-7in of rain expected from south-eastern Louisiana to the Florida Big Bend region. The NWS warned that localized rainfall totals of up to 15in were possible, and noted that flash and urban flooding was possible, along with isolated river flooding. Isolated tornadoes could also develop on Friday night in coastal areas of Alabama and the Florida Panhandle and far south-western Georgia, the NWS said, adding that “the tornado threat will continue Saturday for eastern Alabama, Georgia and northern Florida”. On Thursday afternoon, the Georgia governor, Brian Kemp, issued a state of emergency ahead of Isaias, for all 159 counties, enabling emergency management teams to “make necessary arrangements and position needed resources ahead of the storm’s impact”. “As we always do with weather events, we’re hoping for the best but preparing for the worst,” Kemp said.

Indonesia accused of ‘gross negligence’ in wildfires lawsuit as haze tests region

The Indonesian government has been accused of “gross negligence” in a class action lawsuit over its handling of wildfires that have cloaked large parts of South-east Asia in a toxic haze, shuttered schools and caused a spike in respiratory illnesses. The lawsuit, filed by indigenous and civil society groups in the Indonesian part of Borneo, named President Prabowo Subianto and the governor of West Kalimantan among 10 defendants. The case seeks comprehensive recovery and rehabilitation measures that would include covering the healthcare costs of residents. Related: ‘The physical toll is visceral’: How Indonesia’s fire haze affects millions - visual guide None of those named in the lawsuit attended the opening day of court in West Kalimantan’s provincial capital Pontianak on Wednesday, leading judges to adjourn the hearing until 21 October. “We feel sad and regretful about their absence … But on the other hand, we also understand that perhaps this haze condition caused them to be unable to land in Pontianak,” the plaintiffs’ lawyer, Glorio Sanen, told reporters.

citation.title: Indonesia accused of ‘gross negligence’ in wildfires lawsuit as haze tests region

text:
Indonesia accused of ‘gross negligence’ in wildfires lawsuit as haze tests region

Sanen said the case was “a step to address the problem” of wildfires that flare up annually in Indonesia, where they are often lit as a cheap way to clear land for oil palm planting. Indonesia, the world’s largest producer of palm oil, has been accused of not doing enough to stop the so-called “slash and burn” land clearances, although the government has vowed a crackdown and deployed the military to fight the fires. The blazes hit a crisis point this year due to an unusually intense El Niño weather phenomenon, which has created drier-than-usual conditions, sending a putrid smog to Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore, and even the Philippines. The transboundary haze has angered Indonesia’s neighbours. Schools in the Malaysian state of Johor, just north of Singapore, were to be closed on Thursday and Friday due to deteriorating air quality, local authorities said. The four plaintiffs in the West Kalimantan lawsuit, which was filed last month, include a chapter of Indigenous NGO AMAN and the local branch of Catholic ​Youth.

text:
Bullet and blast injuries … and a constant need for blood: inside South Sudan’s overwhelmed trauma wards

By 11am on a recent Thursday, Dr Slobodan Mirosavljev had already seen two critically wounded patients at Juba military hospital. The day was barely halfway through, but the surgeon couldn’t say how long he would be at the facility. A patient shot in the abdomen, head or chest could arrive without warning. A helicopter could bring several critically wounded people from another part of South Sudan. A mass casualty incident could fill the wards within hours. For Mirosavljev and his colleagues, uncertainty has become part of the job at the hospital, where the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) supports surgeries for weapon-wounded victims of renewed fighting between the military, known as the South Sudan People’s Defence Forces (SSPDF), and the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-In Opposition (SPLM-IO), which is loyal to former vice-president Riek Machar, and allied groups. The conflict has increased the demand for surgical care, overwhelming an already fragile and under-resourced health system in the world’s youngest country.

citation.title: Bullet and blast injuries … and a constant need for blood: inside South Sudan’s overwhelmed trauma wards

text:
Bullet and blast injuries … and a constant need for blood: inside South Sudan’s overwhelmed trauma wards

The fighting has intensified in the past year, particularly in Jonglei state, an opposition stronghold, amid a political crisis fuelled by the president, Salva Kiir, sidelining Machar. Machar and Kiir were members of the Sudan People’s Liberation Army, a guerrilla movement that fought for independence from Sudan, which it gained in 2011, with Kiir becoming president and Machar the first vice-president. South Sudan descended into a bloody civil war in 2013 after Kiir fired Machar and later accused him of planning a coup. Machar founded SPLM-IO, whose fight against the army in the ensuing civil war killed more than 400,000 people and displaced nearly half the country’s population. The fighting took place largely along ethnic lines, between Kiir’s majority Dinka community and Machar’s Nuer, the second largest ethnic group in the country. In 2018, Kiir and Machar signed a peace deal – ending the civil war, creating a unity government of the two parties and returning Machar to the vice-presidency.

citation.title: Bullet and blast injuries … and a constant need for blood: inside South Sudan’s overwhelmed trauma wards

text:
Bullet and blast injuries … and a constant need for blood: inside South Sudan’s overwhelmed trauma wards

But implementation of the agreement has barely got off the ground, as the two parties are constantly at odds over power sharing. The renewed conflict was triggered by a deadly attack by the White Army, a rebel group that was allied to Machar during the civil war, on a government garrison in Nasir county in Upper Nile state in March 2025. It resulted in Machar being charged with murder, treason, crimes against humanity and other serious crimes in connection with the attack, and Kiir suspending him from his post. The actions have inflamed tensions in the country, with Machar’s supporters saying the charges against him are politically motivated and observers saying they risk jeopardising the peace agreement and plunging the country, where elections are due in December, into full-scale civil war. Related: South Sudan risks return to full-blown civil war as violence escalates The events have also coincided with increased fighting between militias and government forces in parts of the country that has killed hundreds and displaced more than 200,000 people.

text:
Bullet and blast injuries … and a constant need for blood: inside South Sudan’s overwhelmed trauma wards

Last month, the UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan expressed concern that the renewed violence and political tensions continued to place civilians at risk. “Visit after visit, we continue to hear from people who bear the consequences of violence, displacement, insecurity and the failures of those with political and security responsibilities to prevent and address those harms,” said the commission’s chairperson, Yasmin Sooka. *** At Juba military hospital, patients, medical workers and visitors moved between wards as the rainy season settled over the country. The sounds of footsteps, hospital trolleys and hurried conversations mixed with the steady hum of ceiling fans and the smell of disinfectant. Some patients recovering from gunshot wounds sat along covered walkways. Others waited on crutches, while patients further along in their recovery carried out morning rehabilitation exercises. As the fighting intensifies, the facility must be prepared to receive weapon-wounded victims at any time.

text:

For the surgical teams, that means there is no such thing as a predictable workday. Mirosavljev said that before midday they had had their morning meeting, received reports from the night shift team, seen critical patients in the high dependency unit, and started operating. The Serbian surgeon has been working at the hospital since August 2025. He operates on some of the most seriously wounded patients and supervises surgical teams. His day usually starts before 8am with a briefing, followed by ward rounds, consultations, emergency admissions and operations. Surgeries end in the early evening on typical days, but can go late into the night when critically wounded patients arrive. Besides victims of political violence, the patients arriving at the hospital include those wounded in communal fighting and cattle-related conflict. In the first six months of this year, the ICRC evacuated 266 injured people from conflict areas and brought them to the facility. Most cases at the hospital are gunshot wounds, and others include stab wounds, broken bones and explosive injuries.

text:
Bullet and blast injuries … and a constant need for blood: inside South Sudan’s overwhelmed trauma wards

Mirosavljev estimated that one in 10 involve serious head injuries, including bullets entering the skull. For surgeons, the numbers translate into a daily struggle against blood loss, infection and damage to vital organs. Some patients require several operations. Every week, the medics receive at least two or three “very difficult” injuries from bullet or blast injuries to the chest and abdomen that need multiple surgeries, Mirosavljev said. For such patients, surgery is only the beginning. “They need a lot of blood; they need a lot of support,” he said. Blood is among the most critical resources in the trauma unit. The hospital may have about 15 units available, with capacity sometimes reaching 20. A single severely wounded patient can require half of that supply. Medical teams and hospital management work to find donors, sometimes relying on patients’ relatives and the national blood bank in Juba. But maintaining a reliable supply remains difficult. *** The consequences can be serious when several casualties arrive at once.

text:
Bullet and blast injuries … and a constant need for blood: inside South Sudan’s overwhelmed trauma wards

Rose Ochieng, the ICRC’s health coordinator in South Sudan, said the surgical department at Giada military hospital was operating at more than 160% of its bed capacity at the most recent peak this year. She said: “We are doing what we can to keep pace: adding overflow beds and recruiting more physiotherapy staff. But demand is growing faster than the capacity of trauma services. And it is civilians caught up in the fighting who are paying the price.” For emergency room nurse Mubarak Jamal, uncertainty begins every morning. Jamal is from Central Equatoria state and has been working at the hospital since 2024. At the outpatient department, there are a limited number of beds. On a normal day, he said, the department sees about 30 patients. Between seven and 10 may be people suffering weapon-related injuries. Normal days, however, can disappear quickly, Jamal said, recalling that they received more than 93 patients in one day in the last mass casualty situation.

His responsibility is to ensure the emergency department is prepared for whatever arrives overnight – restocking supplies, knowing who is working during the night, and how they will coordinate with the colleagues from the operating theatre and other departments. And survival is not the end of treatment. For physiotherapist Lotto Charles, the real measure of recovery is whether a patient can eventually return home and live independently. Charles, from Eastern Equatoria state, has worked at the hospital since 2016. His job includes rehabilitating the injured. Many of his patients are recovering from gunshot wounds. He lists others: “There are multiple fracture patients, patients with nerve injury, patients with lung collapse, and bedridden patients with extensive soft-tissue injuries who are not able to move.” His work can include casting broken limbs, managing patients on traction, and helping them regain muscle strength and movement. One day last month, he treated five patients. One needed to have a cast removed, modified and reapplied.

Another required exercises to restore knee movement. A bedridden patient was assisted out of bed for the first time. For Charles, the reward comes when a patient who arrived on a stretcher walks out of the hospital. “That really motivates me a lot – that at least I’m doing something to help the community,” he said. For Mirosavljev, that makes the difficult days worthwhile. “It’s a good feeling when you do the job, and people survive … and they walk out,” he said.

Israel’s downgrading of UK consulate aims to tighten its hold on Jerusalem

Israel’s attempt to close the British consulate general in Jerusalem was primarily designed to deter London from imposing sanctions on settlements in occupied Palestine. But it also served the current government’s ambitions to fully annex Jerusalem as a national capital, diplomatic and legal experts said. The UK mission to the city has an unusual diplomatic status, which dates back to before the founding of the state of Israel, rooted in a vision of Jerusalem as a neutral enclave under international control. Unlike other consulates general around the world, it is not a satellite of the British embassy in Tel Aviv. Instead its diplomats are part of an independent team, who report directly to London. Related: British consulate in East Jerusalem will stay open as UK mission, says Ed Miliband That is anathema to those in Israel who claim all of Jerusalem as their territory. Israeli forces occupied East Jerusalem in 1967, and the Knesset passed a law annexing the city in 1980, but that status has not been recognised by most of the world.

citation.title: Israel’s downgrading of UK consulate aims to tighten its hold on Jerusalem

text:
Israel’s downgrading of UK consulate aims to tighten its hold on Jerusalem

Gideon Sa’ar, the Israeli foreign minister, threatened to close the consulate general a month ago in an attempt to deter the UK government from proceeding with plans to bar trade with West Bank settlements and put sanctions on companies that provide them with services including financing. The UK threatened to respond with a mass expulsion of diplomats but the two countries appear to have backed away from a full-blown diplomatic spat as Israel prepares for national elections, due on 27 October. Britain will rebrand its consulate general ⁠as a UK “mission” and reduce the number of diplomats, but it will remain independent of Tel Aviv in a compromise one source described as a temporary “ceasefire”. If Israel gets a new leader in three weeks, negotiations on the status of the consulate and its staff could resume. Maintaining a foothold in Jerusalem and the independent status of UK diplomats was important, said Daniel Seidemann, an Israeli lawyer and expert in the geopolitics of Jerusalem who has advised western diplomats including a British foreign secretary.

“The arrangement that the UK arrived at with Israel was probably the optimal among a number of options that were even worse. So I’m not faulting anybody, but this is far from a victory,” he said. “The British presence in Jerusalem after almost a century and a half has been downgraded from one of the diplomatic mission to another office. And that is a stark qualitative change.” There are seven other consulates general in East Jerusalem, all opened before 1948, representing their nations’ interests in Jerusalem and occupied Palestine. Like the UK one, they are independent and report directly to their foreign ministries. They have long been a particular thorn in Israel’s side because of their unusual status, which reflects the designation of Jerusalem as “corpus separatum”, an independent body, under the UN’s 1947 partition plan for historic Palestine. Never implemented, it envisaged Jerusalem as a sort of Vatican-like independent enclave, under international administration.

That clashes with Israel’s claim on the city, and Sa’ar’s attack on the consulate should be seen in that context, and not purely as a response to sanctions. “This is part of the overall attempt to establish the primacy of a very specific Jewish-Israeli Jerusalem,” Seidemann said. “Any diplomatic presence in Jerusalem that does not pay fealty to the government of Israel and Israel’s sole sovereignty is targeted.” Other countries have missions based in Ramallah to manage relations with Palestinians, but these are technically subsidiary to Tel Aviv embassies. The US had a consulate general but closed it after Donald Trump recognised Jerusalem as the capital of Israel during his first presidency. The UK sanctions plan represents the most consequential attempt by one of Israel’s allies to halt settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank. Israeli banks are rattled by a proposal they fear could affect their business, Haaretz reported on Thursday.

An assessment by Israel’s Association of Banks laid out concerns that they could be affected, and they are refusing to say whether they will provide financial guarantees needed to underpin construction contracts for the E1 settlement in the West Bank. When Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, announced his plans, he said the timing was driven partly by the Israeli government’s decision to put out tenders for this project. Israel’s finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, has boasted that it will “bury” the possibility of a Palestinian state by severing parts of the occupied West Bank. Israel promotes film that mimics NAZA documentary

The Israeli government is promoting an online film project that mimics the style of NAZA, the award-winning documentary that details Israel’s mass killings of civilians in Gaza, in an attempt to counter the real film’s findings. The real documentary, directed by the Oscar-winning film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, and produced by the Guardian, is in cinemas and will be shown in more than 50 countries. The Israeli government has denounced the film and announced plans to strip Abraham and Szor of their citizenship, accusing them of treason. In recent days, Israeli embassies have been promoting a link to a hastily produced online film entitled NAZA: The Real Story. Mimicking some of the style of the real documentary, including the use of anonymised interviews shot on rooftops in Tel Aviv, it is hosted on a website called nazadocumentary.com. Ariel Averbuch, an Israeli attorney and army reservist who made the new documentary, described it as an “offensive move” intended to shift the world’s focus from allegations about the Israeli military’s killing of civilians.

citation.title: Israel promotes film that mimics NAZA documentary

text:
Israel promotes film that mimics NAZA documentary

The film claims that Israel has the “most moral army in the world”. Another film-maker listed on the website for NAZA: The Real Story is Roi Danino, a candidate for the rightwing Israel First party. The website domain was registered on 16 September, six days after NAZA’s premiere at the Venice international film festival, where it won the special jury prize after receiving the longest ovation in the festival’s history. Initially, the website falsely presented itself as a promotional page for NAZA itself, naming Abraham and Szor as the directors, and listing film festivals where the documentary was due to be screened. “Shot at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, the film reveals in detail the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of terrorists in Gaza,” it said, distorting the film’s official synopsis by removing the reference to the deaths of Palestinian civilians. That wording was removed from recent updates of the website, once the video for NAZA: The Real Story had been added to the page.

It now appears as a platform for the rival film, with a counter that implausibly suggests the short film has been watched more than 42m times. (The film’s official YouTube page is listed as having just 30,000 views.) According to a technical analysis, the discrepancy suggested the viewer counter could have been driven by requests made to the website, by humans or bots, rather than the number of people who actually watched the video. When asked about the source of the 42m claim, Averbuch said he did not know and referred the questions to his tech team. The Israeli military has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians in Gaza since the Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023, in a military campaign that a United Nations commission has described as genocide. The 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders in the original film NAZA detail how an AI-assisted apparatus of mass surveillance was activated during the Gaza war, revealing the systems that were used to target Hamas operatives in the knowledge large numbers of Palestinian civilians would also die.

The Israeli embassy to the US, which shared the new documentary on its social media, said the ministry of foreign affairs was not involved in producing the film, and that it had intended only to “amplify the message of its creators and expose wider audiences to arguments challenging and dismantling the blood libels and false allegations”. Related: NAZA film-makers say they spoke to more than 100 sources about Israeli actions in Gaza The Israeli government said on Thursday that it was awarding the film-makers with a certificate of appreciation “for their contribution to Israeli public diplomacy”, claiming the production had garnered tens of millions of views. A Guardian spokesperson said: “We are aware that the Israeli government has been promoting a film hosted on a website that initially – and falsely – claimed it was Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s documentary. “This was a brazen attempt to mislead audiences and distract from the urgent questions raised by NAZA.” As well as its global cinema releases, NAZA will be available free on the Guardian’s website from late November.

Related: NAZA: how and where to watch the Guardian’s acclaimed Gaza documentary Averbuch is the founder of an organisation that says it conducts “advocacy warfare”, including through the publication of scripts to help influencers criticise Abraham and Szor’s critically acclaimed previous film, No Other Land, which documents the destruction of the Palestinian village Masafer Yatta. The two Palestinian co-directors of No Other Land, Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal, have been harassed or detained by the Israeli military since the film won an Oscar in 2025. Israeli government officials have scrambled to discredit NAZA’s content, while far-right activists have threatened to hunt down the directors. The Israel Defense Forces’ chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, has said they will use “every tool at our disposal” against the film, while the military has issued a 10-page response to the film, which was based on interviews with more than 100 sources with knowledge of the military systems used in the war.

Within a week of NAZA’s premiere, Israel’s ministry of culture had announced a formal investigation into the documentary, calling for Abraham and Szor to be stripped of their citizenship. Demonstrators gathered outside the home of Szor’s parents, demanding that the she face the death penalty, and a mural depicting the film-makers through the sights of a gun appeared in the Israeli city of Ashdod. On Monday, the far-right Israeli activist Mordechai David announced he was fundraising in order to establish a team that would “chase” Abraham. “We’ll find him,” David said in a video posted to Instagram. Japan beer giants raided over suspicions they colluded to set the price of beverages

Japanese authorities have raided the country’s four biggest breweries over suspicions they colluded to set the price of beer and other beverages – a practice media reports said could have forced drinkers to pay over the odds. Officials from the Fair Trade Commission this week searched the offices of Asahi Breweries, Kirin Brewery, Suntory Beer and Sapporo Breweries – which together control more than 90% of the domestic market. The quartet are suspected of violating the anti-monopoly law. The commission’s secretary general, Hiroo Iwanari, confirmed an investigation had begun, but declined to give details. The companies said they would cooperate with authorities. July 2026 was worst on record for wildfires in England, data shows

This July was the worst on record for wildfires in England, provisional data shows, with England experiencing a clear upward trend in the total number of wildfires recorded. This summer has been a stark reminder of the vulnerability of the UK to climate breakdown, after punishingly hot and dry weather turned large parts of the countryside into a tinderbox. Provisional government data reveals 1,354 wildfires have been recorded so far this year, with 624 of these in July alone, making 2026 the second worst year on record. July’s wildfires included a devastating fire that burned close to the Sizewell B nuclear power station in Suffolk and destroyed vast areas of a protected nature reserve. The summer of 2026 was the UK’s hottest on record, according to provisional data from the Met Office, with 40 days of temperatures above 30C (86F) recorded, smashing the previous record of 34 days. Scientists have said the record heat of 2026 has only been possible due to the climate crisis driven by fossil-fuel burning.

Even before María del Carmen Abascal died on Wednesday night, a mere fortnight after her eviction from the Madrid flat where she had lived for most of her life, the frail 87-year-old woman had become the enduring face of Spain’s housing crisis. The route up the Widowmaker Arete, a 1,700ft wall in British Columbia, is deceptively described as “mostly easy slab climbing”, interspersed with “short steep sections that can include finger cracks” and “blocky face climbing”. It requires careful planning, and the right equipment. When 16-year-old Bryce Vincent Gowryluk found himself facing its sheer headwall last week, he had neither. He did, however, ask the AI chatbot Claude for directions. Last week, Gowryluk had to be rescued after those directions proved wildly incorrect, in the latest incident to raise questions about the growing reliance on digital maps for wilderness navigation. On Saturday morning, Gowryluk took a gondola up to the top of Grouse Mountain and, while ascending, asked Claude to plan a route to nearby Crown Mountain and back. After navigating scree and more than 2,000ft of elevation gain, the summit promises 360-degree panoramic views of Greater Vancouver, the Fraser valley and the Capilano watershed. Typically, the trek takes eight hours and hiking guides warn it is not for beginners.

As he climbed, Gowryluk soon realized the terrain was far too steep and that he was stuck at the base of a cliff. He phoned his mother, then called emergency services for help. Police notified North Shore Rescue, which sent a helicopter, but Gowryluk was too close to the rock face for the rotors, so two members of the rescue team were hoisted down to lift him up. He was flown to the rescue base near the Cleveland Dam. In their debrief the rescue crew said Gowryluk was “far off” his intended route. Thursday briefing: Why young people are taking to the streets across France

Good morning. In my experience, at any protest, the most memorable and encapsulating slogans are always the ones written by hand with marker pen on cardboard placards. “School is a right, not a privilege,” read one such sign held aloft by a student in Paris, where huge youth protests over the state of high school education have brought tens of thousands of young people and adults on to the streets, with further strikes planned today. “A state that gasses high school students is a weak state,” another sign said, referencing growing public anger at alleged police brutality towards young protesters. Tens of thousands of young people have also taken to Spanish streets in recent weeks to protest against the country’s deepening housing crisis. And outside the Labour conference in Liverpool last week, a crowd of jobless young people protested against what they saw as their bleak employment prospects.

In depth: Why have young people taken to the streets? The most significant youth movement to emerge across France in recent decades started on 17 September. Pupils returning to the Lycée Saint-Exupéry in Créteil, southwest of Paris, after the summer holidays, discovered they couldn’t continue their studies because of the extent of staff absences. The 15- to 18-year-olds blockaded their high school in protest. After negotiations with the education ministry, those staffing gaps were filled, but the impassioned complaints about crumbling buildings, overcrowded classrooms, and long school days – alongside a wider sense of inequality in the education system – resonated in the suburbs. “This movement grew from the ground up, from teenagers speaking to others outside their lycées. And over a couple of weeks, it has spread to hundreds of schools across France,” Angelique tells me.

There’s a tendency to mythologise youth protest, especially in France – my uncle Joss was in Paris in 1968, and I lapped up his tales of pulling up cobblestones with his bare hands to build barricades. But youth activism is often diminished. When I reported on the schoolchildren who protested against the war in Iraq in 2003, and those who took part in climate strikes more than a decade later, adults repeatedly questioned whether they were swayed by older provocateurs or just wanted an excuse to dodge school and indulge in petty vandalism. (In my experience: no, no and no.) So it is in France this past month. “This is very much a youth movement,” says Angelique, comparing it to similar protests in 2006 over an unpopular youth employment contract, which were organised by students’ unions. “High schoolers are organising themselves without a centralised system or even spokesperson. That’s historic, and it’s taken the government by surprise.” *** Who are the teenagers on the streets?

This week, the sociologist Fabien Truong, who has written widely on youth protest culture, praised the “maturity and coherence” of the protesters. He pointed to a “social media effect” whereby teenagers in wealthier areas were sharing videos of scurrying rats, gaping ceilings and leaking toilets in poorer schools. “It’s beautiful, this solidarity with students from more privileged backgrounds fighting for others and more equality.” This is precisely what Angelique has witnessed on the streets of Paris in recent days, where some of the most elite state schools have also been barricaded. They told me: ‘We’re told in France that state education is a great leveller, but that’s not the case. We are being taught our lessons, but we’re getting out on to the street because we can’t bear to know that other students in poorer areas are in buildings that are crumbling’.” *** What’s wrong with French schools? As Angelique sets out in this helpful explainer, the pupils’ grievances are backed up by evidence – and the prime minister himself has described them as “legitimate”. Thousands of French schools at all levels, both primary and secondary, are in need of repair. Class sizes are bigger on average, and school days are longer, than in other comparable countries, while about 10% of teaching hours across the year are not delivered because of absent teachers. And yet France’s expenditure on high schools is 28% higher than the OECD average. What’s going on? The high spend can be explained in various ways, Angelique tells me. France has a lot more high school buildings to maintain than other countries, and many more vocational courses that cost more to teach.

At the same time, more spending is desperately needed on staff. Teacher shortages are linked to very low pay progression through the profession, while there are severe difficulties in finding teachers to work in deprived areas. There’s also a shortfall in other crucial roles, including school nurses and support staff for pupils with disabilities. *** How have adults responded? Angelique tells me that what has defined how adults are responding to this burgeoning movement is the behaviour of politicians and police. Initially, the French government “had its head in the sand”, she says, distracted by public anger at rising fuel costs and a difficult budget process. “And when it suddenly woke up, the reaction was not a political one, it was a police crackdown.” Eighteen investigations into possible police brutality are already under way after injuries allegedly involving the use of police weapons, including a 15-year-old who lost his hand after contact with a stun grenade and a 14-year-old whose jaw was shattered after police allegedly beat him and fired a form of rubber-bullet launcher.

EU ‘pulling out all stops’ with minerals projects as it tries to avert China trade war

The EU is “pulling out all the stops” to fend off an imminent potential trade crisis with China, the industry commissioner, Stéphane Séjourné, has said, as the bloc announced its backing for a string of critical materials projects. Séjourné said on Friday that the EU would support 46 new strategic projects to accelerate supplies of critical raw materials by 2030 across the bloc. “We could face a crisis in the coming months,” he said. “We may face trade tensions that could also trigger a crisis in a number of sectors. We need to be prepared for that. And we’re getting ready right now.” The new projects include plants for supplies of lithium, gallium and rare earths needed for the auto, defence and renewable energy industries, with a funding cost of €21bn (£17.8bn). They were unveiled just as the EU works to avert a trade war with China, with the trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič, continuing talks on Friday in Beijing aimed at reducing China’s “unsustainable” £1bn-a-day trade surplus with the bloc.

The co-pilot who tried to seize control of a passenger jet flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv last week was planning to launch a suicide attack targeting the passenger terminal at Israel’s international airport, prosecutors in the United Arab Emirates said on Friday. Hammam al-Hammami attacked the plane’s Indian pilot with an emergency axe, but failed to prevent his badly injured colleague from opening the cockpit’s security door to allow passengers to overpower his assailant. Passengers then tried to control the aircraft, which was safely landed in Saudi Arabia by a flydubai pilot who was among about 180 passengers. Dr Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, attorney-general of the UAE, said on Friday that al-Hammami, who is in Emirati custody, had admitted he had tried to execute a “premeditated terrorist plot to … launch a suicide attack targeting the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion airport near Tel Aviv, with the aim of causing the greatest possible loss of life”.

Good morning. Labour has won the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, heading off a challenge from the Greens and confirming prime minster Andy Burnham’s ability to consolidate vibes into votes. Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali – who is currently leader of Camden council – won 12,292 votes while her closest rival and Green party leader, Zack Polanski, received 8,928 in a byelection that was called after former prime minister Keir Starmer resigned from his London seat last month. Running out of royals: why calls are growing to let Japan’s princess Aiko take the throne

Her face is splashed across magazine covers. Fans flock to online stores to snap up her outfits. At official engagements, huge crowds wait in the crushing heat to catch a glimpse of a woman revered for her ‘regal dignity, beauty and aura’. Princess Aiko, 24, is the most popular member of Japan’s imperial family, but according to law she will never be empress and, as the country runs out of royals, more and more Japanese people are asking why. Related: Japan’s second in line to emperor’s throne comes of age amid succession debate The debate has gathered momentum in the years since Aiko, the only child of Emperor Naruhito and Empress Masako, has transformed from a shy primary school pupil into a young woman at ease with public and media attention. Under a law established almost 140 years ago, women are forbidden from ascending to Japan’s Chrysanthemum throne. But the regulation defies public support for changes that would allow a woman to become empress regnant and avert a looming succession crisis.

text:
Running out of royals: why calls are growing to let Japan’s princess Aiko take the throne

The imperial family is facing the same demographic winds buffeting the rest of the country: three decades ago it had 30 members; now there are just 16, only five of them men. Japanese citizens support a change, irrespective of their political loyalties. In a poll conducted in April by the Mainichi Shimbun newspaper, 72% favoured the idea of a woman becoming emperor, while just 10% opposed it. Pressure to change the male-only succession law, passed in 1947 but based on legislation introduced during the Meiji era in 1889, is intensifying, forcing the conservative government of Sanae Takaichi to address the dearth of male heirs to the 1,500-year-old imperial throne. Just three men comprise the current line of succession – Emperor Naruhito’s younger brother, Crown Prince Akishino; his son, Prince Hisahito; and the emperor’s uncle, Prince Hitachi, who is 90. If Prince Hisahito, a 20-year-old university student, and the first male born into the imperial family for four decades, does not have a son, the line of succession will come to an end within a generation.

Previous governments have tried to solve the succession question by considering legislation that would finally bring gender equality to the rarefied corridors of the imperial palace in Tokyo. But pressure from conservative MPs – and Hisahito’s birth in 2006 – brought the debate to an abrupt end. Takaichi triggered anger this summer when her party and its conservative allies pushed through amendments that will safeguard the male-only succession for generations. The changes, which go into effect later this month, allow women to retain their royal status after marrying non-royals, and resurrects male-line descendants belonging to 11 “collateral branches” of the family that left the imperial fold after the end of the second world war. In theory, that means a distant male relative could be “adopted” into the heart of the family provided he is single and aged over 15. If he marries and his wife gives birth to a son, that child would then join the line of succession. The fate of Japan’s imperial family has attracted international attention.

Why a Chilean salt flat is a microcosm of the extractive frontiers of green capitalism

A high-altitude desert plateau traverses Argentina, Bolivia and Chile. I am on the Chilean side, sitting in a Jeep along with two other researchers. The afternoon air is thin and brisk but the sun is piercing – a combination I am familiar with from years of living and travelling in South America’s Andean range. The landscape is a study in contrasts and contours: broad basins suddenly cut off by sweeping curves; flat expanses sliced by near vertical ascents. The Licancabur volcano looms large above us. Vegetation and humidity levels change rapidly with the rising altitude, bringing cooler temperatures, wetter air and denser plant life. We are driving to the Salar de Atacama – the Atacama salt flats – the largest of several dozen salt flats in northern Chile, and the third largest in the world. The brilliant white flat lies in a high basin 7,500ft above sea level, enclosed by the even higher Andean mountains to the east and the Domeyko mountains to the west.

This striking landscape – the salt flat, the flamingos, and the neighbouring Indigenous communities – is under threat from a counterintuitive source: our efforts to save the planet from catastrophic climate change. Just beneath my feet is nearly one-quarter of the world’s lithium reserves, suspended in water saltier than the ocean. Lithium is essential to addressing the climate crisis. It is a key ingredient in the rechargeable batteries that play a starring role in eliminating carbon emissions from transportation and energy – the two highest emitting sectors. But extracting this lithium will come at escalating social and environmental costs. It is this dilemma that has brought me to the salt flat. When it does rain in the Atacama, it’s hard to overstate the intensity of the floods. The scientific term for closed basins like the Atacama is “endorheic” (etymologically, “inside” and “flow”), for water can flow down into the Atacama basin but it cannot leave – except by evaporation. And this is the key to Atacama’s extraordinary lithium brine. After deluges like the one I experienced, water pours down the surrounding mountains; during the long dry spells between storms, it trickles down ravines from the precious mountain springs. As it flows, the water leaches lithium from the volcanic rock, picks up wind-scoured lithium dust, and carries it down to the nucleus, or centre, of the salar. This pooled surface water can only escape through evaporation, and with every drop of water that evaporates, the concentration of lithium in the remaining brine increases.

citation.title: Why a Chilean salt flat is a microcosm of the extractive frontiers of green capitalism

text:
Why a Chilean salt flat is a microcosm of the extractive frontiers of green capitalism

Without the parched and sun-blasted Atacama’s extraordinarily high evaporation rate, lithium concentrations would not reach the “economical” levels prized by mining companies. Yet further lithium enrichment takes place out of sight. Remaining water gradually seeps into the ground, creating underground wells of lithium-rich brine. These wells are linked to complex hydrothermal systems. Then the heat of magma, especially near the Andes’ active fault lines, drives circulations of subsurface brine through fissures and porous geological strata, dissolving even more lithium out of the subsurface rock. The resulting brine deposits anywhere from four to 200 feet below the Atacama’s salty crust represent a potential bonanza to corporations. The Atacama’s singular coincidence of climatic, geological, geothermal and hydrological conditions makes it one of the least expensive places on Earth to mine lithium.

citation.title: Why a Chilean salt flat is a microcosm of the extractive frontiers of green capitalism

text:
Why a Chilean salt flat is a microcosm of the extractive frontiers of green capitalism

And at each step, the process of “mining water” is intimately related to the very environmental conditions that formed the valuable deposits in the first place: miners pump the underground brine to vast evaporation ponds on the surface, where natural evaporation concentrates the brine yet again, increasing its lithium levels 40-fold, from approximately 0.15% to a whopping 6%. One cycle of the process can take 10 to 24 months, depending on brine quality and weather conditions. But this relatively low-cost, low-tech and supposedly low-impact extractive process nonetheless imperils the species and communities that call the Atacama desert home. And it is a microcosm of a planetary phenomenon: the expanding extractive frontiers of green capitalism. Everywhere that mines are dug up to provide raw materials for the energy transition, global climate action comes into conflict with local environmental protection. Mining always transforms, in many ways irrevocably, the landscapes in which it occurs.

citation.title: Why a Chilean salt flat is a microcosm of the extractive frontiers of green capitalism

text:
Why a Chilean salt flat is a microcosm of the extractive frontiers of green capitalism

In remaking the earth in the image of extractive capital, physically and chemically separating what is deemed valuable from often toxic waste, mining evokes the image of terraforming so central to science fiction. But if terraforming is supposed to make a lifeless planet as verdant as Earth, mining, to the contrary, often leaves parts of Earth itself uninhabitable. While the environmental impacts of mining brine are less obvious to the naked eye than, say, mountaintop removal, extracting the lithium-rich liquid does in fact threaten a fragile, desert water system, along with the ecosystems and people that depend on it. The world’s oldest, driest desert may appear bereft of life. Ecologists call it a “polyextreme” environment, given its altitude and high direct solar radiation, its intense aridity, its huge diurnal temperature swings and its densely saline lakes. Those who study such polyextreme environments alternately describe them as low-diversity, with relatively simple webs of life, or astonishing in their biodiversity. It all depends on perspective.

citation.title: Why a Chilean salt flat is a microcosm of the extractive frontiers of green capitalism

text:
Why a Chilean salt flat is a microcosm of the extractive frontiers of green capitalism

Plants and animals have evolved to make do with less and saltier water and, above all, the abundant energy of relentless sun. Extremity stimulates nature’s creativity. Artemia, or brine shrimp, thrive in hypersaline lakes that would be intolerable to most species. These tiny creatures are a key node in the plateau’s food chain. The brine shrimp eat bacteria and phytoplankton (microscopic plants) and are, in turn, food for Chilean flamingos. The flamingos, too, have adapted to the saline lagoons, evolving a filter in their bills akin to the lamellar membranes of oysters or whales to strain the microscopic plants and animals from the brine. The flamingos are a barometer of wetland health. As the birds travel the salt flats in search of food and mates (attracted through a courtship ritual of synchronised dancing), they link together the saline lakes into a web of habitats. And as these habitats suffer, so do flamingo populations: all three of the Atacama salt flats’ endemic flamingo species are in decline.

citation.title: Why a Chilean salt flat is a microcosm of the extractive frontiers of green capitalism

text:
Why a Chilean salt flat is a microcosm of the extractive frontiers of green capitalism

The distinct drivers of this population loss reveal the compounding harms afflicting this fragile environment. Warmer average temperatures due to climate change evaporate surface water faster, reducing the blue-green algae essential to flamingo and Artemia diets. And the noise and traffic associated with mining operations appear to directly disrupt the flamingos’ breeding. Related: ‘The source of all life is here’: plan to mine lithium in Chilean salt flat sparks fears of water scarcity Researchers are struggling to predict the overall direction of the multiple processes changing the Atacama. Science can only play catchup, documenting the impacts long after the harm has occurred. Lithium extraction’s threat to the liquid supporting its ecosystem is a slow-motion disaster, with planetary causes and consequences. This fact raises existential questions for the planet’s zero-carbon future.

citation.title: Why a Chilean salt flat is a microcosm of the extractive frontiers of green capitalism

text:
Why a Chilean salt flat is a microcosm of the extractive frontiers of green capitalism

In the Atacama, global supply chains intersect with local food chains, webs of economic production undermine webs of life, and colonisation and postcolonial state-building erase ancient histories of continuous Indigenous settlement. And these unexpected entanglements are just the beginning of the story. In more ways than I could have imagined when I first stepped foot on the Atacama salt flat on that blustery day, this extractive frontier is a portal into our planetary future. The task of achieving a globally just energy transition is daunting. But it is possible. Achieving it requires understanding supply chains in reverse, starting from what we produce and consume and working backwards to their material inputs and, further still, to the relentless scramble for new extractive frontiers. Policies that promote alternatives to car use, reduce sprawl, encourage more compact batteries and require recycling would all reduce the scale of mining needed for carbon-free transportation.

citation.title: Why a Chilean salt flat is a microcosm of the extractive frontiers of green capitalism

text:
Why a Chilean salt flat is a microcosm of the extractive frontiers of green capitalism

We can start by demanding supply chains organised around justice for everyone they touch, rather than profits for just a few. Just as any workplace is simultaneously a site of exploitation and locus of worker power, and any mine is at once a setting for extraction and a potential scene of community resistance, the supply chains of green technologies are both a means of domination – of people and of nature – and fertile ground for making the world anew. This is an edited extract from Extraction: The Frontiers of Green Capitalism by Thea Riofrancos, published by Icon Books at £20 in the UK.
