Christian nationalism in Britain driven by people who seldom go to church, says report

Christian nationalism in Britain is being driven largely by people who rarely attend church and are more concerned with defending the country’s Christian heritage, according to research. The report, by the thinktank Theos, identified five different groups within the UK in a survey that looked at their attitudes to Christianity and Britishness. The group whose views most closely resembled Christian nationalism, termed “identity integrationists” by the researchers, accounted for 11% of respondents, making it the smallest of the five groups. Although 81% of this group identified as Christian, just 13% attended church weekly, only slightly above the 11% average across the population surveyed. Less than a third (31%) prayed weekly, while 47% expressed an interest in the Bible. The group was strongly hostile to immigration and Islam. Just 19% agreed that Christian values required welcoming and supporting asylum seekers, while 30% supported the equal treatment of religions in public life.

citation.title: Christian nationalism in Britain driven by people who seldom go to church, says report

text:
Christian nationalism in Britain driven by people who seldom go to church, says report

In contrast, another group in the survey with high levels of Christian affiliation, were considerably more religiously observant and less hostile to immigration and religious diversity. They comprised 13% of respondents. Among these “belief integrationists”, 31% attended church weekly, 46% prayed weekly and 62% expressed an interest in the Bible. Almost half (48%) agreed that Christian values required welcoming and supporting asylum seekers, while 63% supported the equal treatment of religions in public life. Although they are the group containing the highest proportion of practising Christians, only 18% of belief integrationists think that defending Britain’s Christian culture and heritage is important for being Christian, compared with 90% of the Christian nationalist group. At a time when crosses have been carried at Unite the Kingdom rallies and crowds have chanted “Christ is King” at protests, the research challenges the idea that the growing prominence of Christian nationalism in Britain reflects a revival of Christianity.

citation.title: Christian nationalism in Britain driven by people who seldom go to church, says report

text:
Christian nationalism in Britain driven by people who seldom go to church, says report

Instead, the findings suggest that Christianity is increasingly being invoked as a marker of British identity amid wider anxieties about immigration, Islam and cultural change. The results are based on a survey of 1,765 adults conducted in April 2026, which identified five distinct groups according to their attitudes towards Christianity and British national identity. More than half of Britons surveyed (55%) said they would be unhappy if their local church closed and became a mosque, including 37% who would be very unhappy. More than a third (37%) agreed with the conspiracy theory that the white population of Europe was being deliberately replaced by migrants from Muslim countries, sometimes known as the ‘great replacement’ theory. Nick Spencer, a senior fellow at Theos and one of the report’s authors, suggested that the difference between the two most highly affiliated Christian groups’ attitudes towards asylum seekers might partly reflect their religious practice and ethnic composition.

citation.title: Christian nationalism in Britain driven by people who seldom go to church, says report

text:
Christian nationalism in Britain driven by people who seldom go to church, says report

The more practising Christian group were the most ethnically diverse of the five groups, with 20% identifying as non-white, while identity integrationists were among the least diverse. Spencer added that there was also “a difference between Christianity as an idea and Christianity as an embodied practice”. “If it matters enough for you to haul yourself out of bed on a Sunday morning, to spend time with people who you don’t choose – you don’t choose who you’re sitting next to in the pew, you don’t choose who’s next to you in the communion rail – it becomes a bit more human and more humane.” Arun Arora, Church of England bishop of Kirkstall in Leeds, said the distinction between cultural Christianity and practising faith was central to understanding the findings. “What is it to be a disciple? It’s threefold: deny yourself, take up your cross, and follow me,” he said.

citation.title: Christian nationalism in Britain driven by people who seldom go to church, says report

text:
Christian nationalism in Britain driven by people who seldom go to church, says report

“And what I think’s interesting about the nationalists is that they want to take up the cross at marches, and display it, but there’s less of an interest in denying themselves and following Jesus.” He argued that the lessons for church leaders weren’t just to encourage church attendance, but to be out in the community. “If as the church we’re going to wait for people to come into the ark to be saved, to use Noah’s ark analogy, then we’re going to be waiting a while,” he said. “Whereas the responsibility for us is to bring that full gospel message of discipleship, of what that requires, the costly nature of discipleship, to be able to expound and articulate that, and the passionate love of God for his people, and his world, and not just those who carry certain passports.” The Rev Dr Helen Paynter, a theologian who has researched the far right’s use of Christianity, said the findings highlighted the responsibility of churches to welcome people across the political spectrum.

citation.title: Christian nationalism in Britain driven by people who seldom go to church, says report

text:
Christian nationalism in Britain driven by people who seldom go to church, says report

But, she added: “The church is and has been since its inception a multi-ethnic, multinational group, and may not rightly be equated with any nationality or ethnicity. In fact, the ‘average’ Christian in the world today is poor, female and black.” For Paynter, one of most important findings is the starkly different attitudes evidenced by those who are practising Christians, compared with those who claim the label. “The Christian faith is not just an identity that we can put on like a coat; it involves an encounter with transcendence which must be transformative of all our values.”

‘Cockroach’ party leaders say India is ‘at war with its citizens’ as protests enter second day

The leaders of India’s Cockroach movement accused the Narendra Modi government of declaring “war with its own citizens” and vowed to continue with their protest after being released from police detention, as anti-government unrest rocked Delhi for a second day. The three leaders of the youth-led Cockroach Janta party (CJP) were taken into custody on Saturday when thousands were detained by police as authorities went to extreme lengths to prevent young people taking to the streets to protest. By Sunday morning, a magistrate had ordered that the three CJP leaders, Abhijit Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, be released on the condition that they would not “breach peace” for a year. In a social media post soon after his release, Dipke, CJP’s founder, pointed his criticism directly at the prime minister. “Modi, as PM, is an embarrassment to India. Never has this country seen a bigger coward and bully,” he said.

citation.title: ‘Cockroach’ party leaders say India is ‘at war with its citizens’ as protests enter second day

text:
‘Cockroach’ party leaders say India is ‘at war with its citizens’ as protests enter second day

Saturday’s protest was called by the CJP alongside student groups and civil society leaders to demand the resignation of India’s election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of an “assault on democracy” by overseeing an exercise that has deleted 130 million names from India’s electoral roll. Related: ‘Cockroach’ leader among thousands detained in Delhi protest crackdown Kumar is accused of implementing the voter roll revision to help Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) entrench its power and to disenfranchise minority groups such as Muslims who are not traditionally part of the BJP’s voter base. Those who attempted to take part in Saturday’s demonstration were ruthlessly obstructed by a security crackdown, in which more than 25,000 police barricaded roads and the internet and public transport were shut down. More than 7,000 people were taken into police custody, many before they had even reached the protest site in the centre of the capital.

‘Cockroach’ party leaders say India is ‘at war with its citizens’ as protests enter second day

Despite the heavy-handed police response, it was still an unprecedented display of dissent against the powerful Modi government, which has been notoriously intolerant of any political opposition or criticism over its 12 years in power. Several senior opposition leaders were among those who tried to protest and were detained. By Sunday, the centre of Delhi still resembled a high-security fortress, with roads blocked by barricades and tens of thousands of police and paramilitary still deployed. Supreme court judges have ruled that the government must restore internet and reopen the capital’s metro stations. Small groups of students and Cockroach supporters, many freshly released from police detention, again attempted to demonstrate in Delhi and were detained. Among those taken into custody for a second time was the student leader Neha Bora, whose repeated defiance in the face of the police crackdown has made them a figurehead of the movement.

In a video they posted on social media after they were picked up by Delhi police, Bora showed a detention bus with metal grilles over its windows and four small “jail-like” compartments secured with latches. They said six to eight protesters were crammed into each of the compartments, leaving little room to breathe, and that male protesters were subjected to verbal abuse and physical violence. “So many troops, so much police presence, so much violence, abuses targeting mothers and sisters, caste-based slurs – why?” Bora said in the video. “Simply because you want to protect a thief, Gyanesh Kumar.” Marching alongside Bora was Surbi Yadav, 20, an undergraduate student at Delhi University, who said police detained her on Saturday morning. She accused police personnel of dragging her, injuring her arm and leg. “They treated us like animals. They pushed us into a bus and took us to a sports facility that had been turned into a detention centre,” Yadav said, while showing scars on her arms.

“The police kept misbehaving with us on the way and warned us against taking part in the protests.” Yadav was released on Saturday evening. By Sunday afternoon, she was back on the streets with other students, holding a placard. She vowed to return the following day and keep protesting until their demands were met. “We are not afraid any more. The government and the police will have to understand that,” she said. “They can use as much force as they want to silence us, but it will be futile. In fact, it will only backfire. Every day, more people are turning against this government because of the way it is treating protesters.” At a press conference on Sunday afternoon, the CJP leaders Das and Ranka condemned the police and government for turning Delhi into a “war-like situation” and reiterated their message of defiance that “this fight is on”. They added that it was no longer just about Kumar but also targeted at Modi and his home minister, Amit Shah. “The state is at war with its own citizens,” Das said.

“An atmosphere of fear has been created in country, it’s clearly being done to save one person. However, the BJP’s spokesperson, Gaurav Bhatia, said earlier that the voter roll revision was a legitimate exercise to remove dead and illegal voters and refuted any political interference. “These are baseless allegations being levelled by an irresponsible opposition,” Bhatia said. “The claim that democracy is being destroyed and that the constitution is being undermined has no basis and not an iota of evidence.” The weekend’s protests had drawn support from the leader of India’s opposition alliance, Rahul Gandhi, who has accused the Modi government of “vote chauri” or vote cheating through the voter roll revision. At least 139 dead including children after migrant boat capsizes off Djibouti

At least 139 people, including 15 children, have died after a boat carrying 305 migrants capsized off the coast of Djibouti, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said. Another 84 people are still missing after the incident, which, according to survivors, happened near Guhere, north of the fishing town of Obock, during the night of 8-9 October when the boat was travelling from Djibouti to Yemen. Eighty-two people, all Ethiopian nationals, survived the capsizing, the UN agency said. It described the incident as one of the deadliest boat disasters recorded on a migration corridor between the Horn of Africa and the Arab peninsula known as the eastern route. “This is a devastating loss of life. Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives,” said Alexandre Coissac, the IOM’s chief of mission in Djibouti. The organisation is providing healthcare, psychosocial, food and other assistance to 64 survivors at its Obock migrant response centre. The IOM is working with local authorities to provide emergency assistance.

citation.title: At least 139 dead including children after migrant boat capsizes off Djibouti

text:
At least 139 dead including children after migrant boat capsizes off Djibouti

Djiboutian authorities are continuing search and rescue operations, and local authorities are providing medical care to survivors and arranging burials for those who died. The eastern route is one of the busiest migration paths in the world. Hundreds of thousands of people a year, mostly Ethiopians and Somalis, use it to reach Gulf countries, mainly Saudi Arabia. Some have been forced out of their communities by conflict and natural disasters, and others move to seek work and other economic opportunities. The route accounts for most of the migratory movement from the Horn of Africa. The other main ones are the northern route to north Africa and Europe, and the southern route to southern Africa. The eastern route is also one of the most dangerous globally, with some people dying from walking long distances in searing heat and others from the capsizing of boats that smugglers have crammed them on to in the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.

citation.title: At least 139 dead including children after migrant boat capsizes off Djibouti

text:
At least 139 dead including children after migrant boat capsizes off Djibouti

Coissac said: “This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities.” In 2025, more than 900 people died or went missing along the route, according to the IOM’s missing migrants project, while the number undertaking the journey increased by 18%. In March, nine people died and 45 went missing after a migrant boat capsized. This week’s tragedy shows the movement is happening despite fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthi rebel group and Saudi-backed government forces for control of strategic heights on the Red Sea coast. The violence has forced more than 3,800 people to cross to Djibouti to seek protection, according to the country’s office for assistance to refugees and disaster victims (Onars).

text:
Did Trump get one thing right about Greenland?

One of Donald Trump’s more diabolical talents is his ability to land on the right things in the wrong way. Since his first term, Trump has been obsessed with the Arctic – Greenland in particular – something that has puzzled and enraged many, particularly in Europe. He first brought up the idea of buying the icy landmass from Denmark in 2019. Right after re-election, he began ramping up his rhetoric about acquiring it “one way or another”, threatening the Nato alliance and the foundations of post-second world war security. Trump got his way – thankfully without military force – in September, when the US and Denmark signed an agreement that allowed for many more US troops on the island, albeit without the sort of takeover that the president enjoys “joking” about. “The United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland,” Trump wrote on social media. “We will work with the people of Greenland in its development and construction.” Europeans could be forgiven for doubting that the US president would help any country in its development, let alone Greenland.

citation.title: Did Trump get one thing right about Greenland?

text:
Did Trump get one thing right about Greenland?

But the truth is that there is something in Trump’s obsession with a place that has more reindeer than people, and he isn’t the first to suggest the US should own it; President Andrew Johnson floated the idea in 1867. The fact is that since the cold war, Greenland has played a crucial role in North American security, with airfields close to the eastern seaboard, vast mineral resources and a location perfectly suited to tracking Arctic weather (something crucial to military movements). More recently, it has become a pawn in the US-China geopolitical struggle. As Jeff Landry, the US special envoy to Greenland wrote in early 2026, greater American presence there would “facilitate deployment of advanced missile defense systems” and “crowd out hostile Chinese and Russian influence”. While there are no explicit Chinese or Russian security threats on the island now, many in the administration fear that if Greenland becomes independent – as it has said it wants to be by 2033 – it will be more open to Chinese or Russian influence campaigns. Whether you agree with them or not, the region is certainly becoming a geostrategic hotspot.

citation.title: Did Trump get one thing right about Greenland?

text:
Did Trump get one thing right about Greenland?

Russia is upping energy transit there to avoid global choke points, and China declared itself a “near-Arctic state” in 2018. Security and military drills have been conducted by both countries close to US territorial waters near Alaska. All of this puts the US’s biggest adversaries squarely in its back yard, at a time when it’s unclear what the new, post-neoliberal world order will be, and how either Europe or Greenland will fit into it. Beyond geopolitics, there’s another reason for all the interest in the Arctic: climate change. When the seas at the top of the world were frozen solid, nobody cared much about what was happening there. But over the past few decades, global heating has opened the possibility of resource extraction (the Arctic seabed is filled with gas, oil and rare-earth minerals, most of which have yet to be mined or even claimed by individual nations). It has also made possible the passage by sea of energy supplies and goods – something that has been coveted by various powers for hundreds of years.

citation.title: Did Trump get one thing right about Greenland?

text:
Did Trump get one thing right about Greenland?

In August, a Chinese shipping company, Sea Legend, started a weekly trans-polar commercial route across the Arctic, through Russian territorial waters. It claims that the voyage will cut the usual 40-day journey time between Europe and Asia in half, something that seems pretty attractive given the Houthi threat in the Red Sea. Of course, to take advantage of new pathways in the Arctic, you need ships, icebreakers in particular. The US, which has very little capacity in this area, has recently started trying to make them jointly with Finland, a project that was endorsed by both Joe Biden and Trump. But the lack of icebreakers is symptomatic of a larger problem. In 1975, the US shipbuilding industry was ranked No 1 in terms of global capacity, with more than 70 commercial ships on order for production domestically. Just over 50 years later, the US now produces less than 1% of the world’s commercial vessels. China, meanwhile, has tripled its production relative to the US over the past two decades, producing more than 1,000 ocean-going vessels last year, versus the US’s 10.

citation.title: Did Trump get one thing right about Greenland?

text:
Did Trump get one thing right about Greenland?

The resulting asymmetry comes with commercial and military concerns for the US, but also for any country that depends on it for security. More than 90% of military equipment, supplies and fuel travels by sea. That goes to a larger point – conflict in the Arctic is happening against the backdrop of the end of the neoliberal era, which brought modern globalisation and great wealth, but also increased inequality and a sense that policymakers operating at a great height in the national interest were sometimes out of step with the economic reality of communities on the ground. The pendulum is now swinging back. In the US, Repubicans and Democrats alike are pushing industrial policy to restore industries such as shipbuilding and chip-making. While efforts are sometimes couched with xenophobic, anti-China rhetoric, the truth is that one country dominating any strategic industry isn’t in the interests of workers or nation states. It’s an issue that the EU, too, is now coming to terms with, as cheap Chinese electric cars, steel, lithium batteries and solar panels move from US markets to Europe.

citation.title: Did Trump get one thing right about Greenland?

text:
Did Trump get one thing right about Greenland?

Trump’s focus on Greenland may not be as misplaced as it seems at first glance, then. But there’s a glaring flaw in his approach. In a world that will be dominated by new spheres of influence, the US needs friends. Europe does, too. Shared supply chains, security agreements and trade pathways can all be used to mutual advantage. But it will take careful statecraft of the kind that this administration isn’t exactly known for. Trump’s limbic brain knows that Greenland, and the Arctic at large, is important. What he doesn’t seem to understand is how to put aside his own ego and ambitions to make sure that the US can secure its own hemispheric back yard in ways that don’t destroy its existing alliances. Here’s hoping the next administration does better: the US’s future will depend on it. • Rana Foroohar is a columnist and associate editor at the FT and the author of Sea Change: America’s New Great Game in the Arctic Circle (Swift). Further reading Chokepoints by Edward Fishman (Elliott & Thompson, £10.99) The Next World War by Peter Apps (Wildfire, £12.99) Unfrozen by Mia Bennett and Klaus Dodds (Yale, £20).

France’s other schools problem – the teens violently smashing up their old primaries: ‘They think it’s not worthy of respect – so they trash it’

Like most French primaries on Wednesdays, Marcel Pagnol school, in the eastern suburbs of Lyon, was shut on 19 June 2024. But at 6.30pm that evening, two boys turned up late for school – by two years. Former pupils there, the 13-year-olds struggled to break through the crispy lattice of the front-door window with a garden fork and a broom. Using a window-breaker, they finally created an opening large enough to force their way in without hurting themselves. What happened next is captured in a video the pair subsequently posted on Snapchat. Once inside they prowl the classrooms, corridors and canteen, slinging around scooters and smashing up computer equipment, setting off fire extinguishers and upending furniture. They help themselves to pouches of Capri‑Sun from the fridge: “I don’t give a fuck – I’m taking the lot.” The boy not filming sets small fires as they move through the building, squirting each one with a little jet of lighter fuel. “I love what’s happening here!” says his accomplice.

citation.title: France’s other schools problem – the teens violently smashing up their old primaries: ‘They think it’s not worthy of respect – so they trash it’

text:
France’s other schools problem – the teens violently smashing up their old primaries: ‘They think it’s not worthy of respect – so they trash it’

“I love fire.” But the exhilaration soon turns to panic. With a thick black canopy of smoke creeping along the ceiling of the main corridor, they realise it’s time to go: “Come on, come on, there’s smoke everywhere. Fuck, I can’t see a thing!” They’re soon scarpering into the surrounding streets in broad daylight, the cameraman sipping his Capri-Sun as a column of smoke rises from the school, and police cars converge on the site. It’s a pattern of carnivalesque destruction – like the mass burning of cars during urban riots – that seems distinctively French The Marcel Pagnol arson was perhaps the most serious incident of a phenomenon that has swept the whole of France in recent years: comprehensive trashings of school premises that go well beyond isolated acts of vandalism. There were at least 15 cases in 2025; a similar number in 2024.

More than half a century after he started sexually abusing children, and enjoyed prestige as Ireland’s Olympic swimming coach before fleeing to the United States, George Gibney has faced justice. The 78-year-old was sentenced to 15 and a half years in prison at the central criminal court in Dublin on Monday for abusing four young female athletes in the 1970s and 1980s. It was the culmination of a decades-long effort by victims, police, journalists and others to track down and extradite Gibney from the US. He was convicted in July of 39 counts of indecent assault and one count of attempted rape after a closely watched trial that detailed harrowing abuse. Judge Micheál P O’Higgin called Gibney a “manipulative predator” who had insinuated himself into the lives of children under his care. “It was predatory in nature and a gross breach of trust,” he said. “He used his coaching role to access and assault defenceless children under his care.” The judge said Gibney had once enjoyed a stellar reputation and that the sentence reflected the gravity of his offending.

Houthi attack on Riyadh airport forces swift rethink of Trump’s new strategy

The reckless missile attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh on Saturday did not just export the death and misery inside Yemen to Saudi Arabia, it also left Donald Trump forced to reconsider his diplomatic and political strategy designed to take him into the midterm elections next month. The US president’s plan had only been unveiled on Friday. He said it was the result of “a world problem” – spiralling diesel prices – which he blamed on Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s attacks on Russian oil refineries. He was going to keep the political temperature down on his war of choice in Iran and its spillover in Yemen until after the midterms. In pursuit of this strategy, he claimed the Iranian blockade in the strait of Hormuz was in effect broken, producing figures on daily oil barrel exports to assuage the markets. As a further insurance he also claimed it was impossible to negotiate with the Iranians since there was no single leadership in Tehran. Saudi Arabia, in conjunction with Turkey, and Pakistan, were largely to be left to sort out the Houthis along the Red Sea.

Thousands without power in Florida and Alabama as Isaias moves north

As what was left of Hurricane Isaias moved north on Sunday, bringing moderate to heavy rainfall across the central Appalachians and the mid-Atlantic region, nearly 396,000 customers across the Florida Panhandle and southern Alabama remained without power. Heavy rainfall associated with the storm could bring isolated flash flooding and strong wind gusts and remain a threat across the south-eastern US, especially near the southern Appalachians, according to the National Weather Service (NWS). That could bring scattered power outages and downed trees and power lines. Life-threatening surf and rip current conditions were expected to continue along the Gulf and south-eastern Atlantic coasts. According to the National Weather Service, parts of the Carolinas and Virginia, including Raleigh, Richmond and Washington DC were under threat of tornadoes on Sunday. Related: Four dead as Isaias weakens to post-tropical cyclone after striking Florida panhandle At least four deaths were linked to the storm, including two people killed when trees fell on to homes in Florida and Alabama.

This has been the first hurricane to make landfall in the continental US in two years, since Milton struck western Florida in October 2024. Physicians’ group calls for ban on raw milk – as it’s becoming increasingly popular in the US

As raw milk becomes increasingly popular among Americans, there have been several recent disease outbreaks tied to the product, alarming public health officials. Last week, the American Academy of Pediatrics called for a ban on sales of unpasteurized milk in the United States. More people have started drinking raw milk, doctors say, because of influencers who have touted its health benefits; Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, who until recently promoted it; and a lack of trust in government regulators. But there is no evidence for claims that it reduces lactose issues and can cure allergies and boost immunity, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and public health groups argue. And whereas raw milk producers say that pasteurization eliminates flavor and health benefits, public health officials say it keeps people safe.

US businesses started using pasteurization, a process in which milk is heated to destroy pathogens and bacteria, in the late 19th century. As more producers adopted the practice and regulators started requiring it, the country saw a dramatic decrease in the infant mortality rate. In 1987, the FDA banned the interstate sale and distribution of raw milk, but businesses were still allowed to sell it within their states, depending on their laws. During this century, more Americans started consuming raw milk and, over the last decade, many states have loosened their milk regulations. In 2024, raw milk sales increased by 17.6%, according to the market research firm Circana.

Riyadh airport hit again after deadly Houthi missile attack, Saudi authorities say

A projectile hit a passenger terminal at the airport in Riyadh on Sunday, the day after a deadly missile attack on the facility carried out by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebel group killed 13 people. An unidentified projectile hit terminal 4 at King Khalid international airport, starting a fire, killing one person and injuring 11, according to Saudi civil aviation authorities. Air defences also intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of the airport. It was the latest of several attacks on the airport in the past week. The escalating attacks threatened to draw more countries into the Yemen conflict and further widen the regional fallout of the US-Iran war, which has already spread to Lebanon and Iraq. In a post on X, the British embassy in Saudi Arabia advised against all but essential travel to the cities of Jeddah and Dammam and to avoid almost all airports.

‘Stab to the heart’: arrest of German ex-spymaster sparks calls for reform

The ex-spymaster August Hanning once criticised Germany’s own intelligence services as “vegetarians” among prowling carnivores, demanding broader powers to keep the country safe in a treacherous world. Often described as a “godfather” of Germany’s 21st-century security architecture, Hanning is now charged with treasonous espionage and handing state secrets to a foreign power in one of the most spectacular alleged intelligence breaches of the postwar period. If true, Hanning may have irreparably damaged Germany’s global security cooperation while exposing grievous internal vulnerabilities, in a tale ripped from a far-fetched political thriller. “This is an incident that has the potential to escalate into a genuine national scandal,” said Konstantin von Notz, a Bundestag member who sits on the parliamentary intelligence supervisory committee. Von Notz warned of a “devastating” loss of trust among partner countries “whose support we cannot do without in the current extremely tense security situation”.

Tuesday’s scenes from a small town in Germany staggered even seasoned spy watchers: masked commandos led Hanning from his estate in his birthplace, Nordwalde, to a black police van, his familiar bespectacled face framed by neatly combed white hair. His expression was calm and focused, his wrists without handcuffs. The detention of the 80-year-old, who ran the federal foreign intelligence service (BND) from 1998 to 2005, marked a first in a western democracy given his previous rank, according to experts. Federal prosecutors believe Hanning ran his former chief of staff, identified only as Manfred D, as a mole at the BND, paying him to spirit out nearly 2,000 documents, at least some of them classified, over 12 years. He then allegedly exploited the intelligence for clients of the private consulting firm he launched after retiring – a legal business model that drew fierce criticism over the course of a tumultuous week. Hanning is in pretrial detention and has, through his lawyers, denied passing on confidential documents to foreign powers. If convicted, he could face 10 years in prison.

Steve Jones obituary

My friend Steve Jones, who has died aged 77, had a working life devoted to humanitarian causes, with a particular focus on Bangladesh and India. In retirement he then dedicated a sizeable portion of his time to charity work, helping people with the lung disease pulmonary fibrosis get the help and treatment they needed. Steve was born in London to John and Lettie, who were both teachers and shared the surname Jones. After secondary school in Crawley, West Sussex, he studied geography at Bristol University, worked for a short time as an economist for a company that became part of British Airways and then embarked on further studies at Cambridge University, where he gained a certificate in anthropology and began a PhD. While there he became involved with Operation Omega, a group that smuggled humanitarian aid across the border from India to Bangladesh during its war with Pakistan in 1971. This led him to cut short his studies so that he could begin work as a consultant economist and project planner.

Over the years he worked on many projects, including for the University of New South Wales from 1984 to 1986 in the Solomon Islands on a smallholder project and a post-cyclone survey. In 1989 his work took him back to Bangladesh, where he was employed by the World Bank to develop a flood action plan. Fourteen years of his life, from 1992 to 2006, were then spent with the Department for International Development, working on ways to help tackle the social and economic problems related to rural poverty in India. He was also particularly proud of a cyclone recovery and reconstruction project he worked on in 2007 for the World Bank, which led to the building of cyclone shelters in Bangladesh. In 2006 he became a trustee and then chair of trustees of the Humanitarian Centre in Cambridge, which later became the Centre for Global Equality. Two years later he had to leave work after being diagnosed with pulmonary fibrosis, but eventually he was lucky enough to receive a lung transplant that prolonged his life considerably.

Man rescued from cave on Sardinia after being trapped by rockslide for 26 hours

A 31-year-old man has been pulled alive from a cave on the Italian island of Sardinia after being trapped roughly 10 metres below ground for 26 hours following a rockslide. In a huge and complex operation, rescuers worked non-stop after Luca Olmetto became trapped in the Gorroppeddu cave in the rugged Urzulei mountain range in central-eastern Sardinia on Sunday afternoon. He had been exploring the cave with his girlfriend, who was a few metres behind him and narrowly missed the collapse, which completely blocked the entrance to the cave. She managed to escape unharmed and immediately raised the alarm. Rescuers managed to reach Olmetto, who was conscious and responsive throughout the operation, by late Monday afternoon after manually removing rubble and earth blocking a narrow passage. They then proceeded with the delicate operation of removing the large amounts of debris that covered the caver before extracting him from the cavity. According to Rai News, Olmetto was brought to the surface just after 6pm CET and stabilised by medical staff before being airlifted to hospital.

Ariel Weil, the central Paris mayor, ​said the Marché des Enfants ‌Rouges had been “totally destroyed” in the blaze, which broke out soon after 3am. “The worst was avoided: the fire did not spread to the surrounding buildings,” he said. “But there is a lot of emotion. A lot of sadness.” The market was established in 1615 during the reign of Louis XIII and took its name from a nearby orphanage, the Hospice des Enfants Rouges – founded in 1536 by King Francis I and his sister Marguerite de Navarre – whose child residents were habitually dressed in red. The structure was listed as a historic monument in 1982 but narrowly escaped demolition shortly afterwards when Paris city hall, led by the then mayor, Jacques Chirac, approved radical redevelopment plans that would have replaced it with an underground car park, a council daycare facility and community centre.

A determined campaign by local residents and neighbourhood associations, backed by intellectuals, writers and artists including film-makers and photographers such as Bertrand Tavernier and Willy Ronis, who captured its traders on camera, gathered tens of thousands of signatures in protest and the plans were eventually abandoned in the mid-1990s. Rather than demolish the building, the city undertook a six-year, 13m-franc (about €3m, or £2.5m today) renovation project, restoring the market’s historic wood and ironwork frame and glass roof. Les Enfants Rouges reopened as a food court in 2000. While still hosting some traditional stalls including a greengrocer, butcher, cheesemonger and fishmonger, the 1,000 sq m market was mostly given over to more than a dozen stands offering French, Lebanese, Moroccan, Japanese and other street food at the counter or at casual chairs and tables.

French centre left must wage ‘existential battle’ to prevent far right winning presidency

The European lawmaker Raphaël Glucksmann has urged the French centre left to wage an “existential battle” to prevent Marine Le Pen’s far right winning the 2027 presidential election after he was chosen as the social democrat candidate for the presidency. “We’ve got to rid our hearts of the spirit of defeat,” Glucksmann, the founder of the small party Place Publique, said on Monday morning after his decisive win in a centre-left primary race held by the Socialist party. In his first interview since being designated a presidential candidate on Sunday night, Glucksmann told France Inter radio that the country was living in a “historic moment”, with the far right at the gates of power. He said the 2027 presidential election campaign would be brutal and “like no other we have ever experienced”. He said it would be unbearable to have a centre left “that doesn’t believe in victory”, adding that he could restore a “pride in social democracy”.

His candidacy marks the first time the Socialist party will not have its own presidential candidate since the party was founded in 1969. German minister quits after ‘indecent’ attacks intensify during bereavement

Germany’s labour minister and co-leader of the centre-left ⁠Social Democrats (SPD), Bärbel Bas, has quit both posts, citing the death of her stepdaughter and subsequent political attacks against her, in a stinging blow to the fragile coalition government. “After my stepdaughter’s death, I realised that I need time to come to terms with my grief,” Bas said in a statement posted on Facebook, without giving further ⁠details. Explaining her departure from frontline politics, Bas explicitly blamed public broadsides against her as she grappled with the family tragedy, “unfortunately also from among the ranks of the coalition partner [Friedrich Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU)]”. She said the attacks “continued to intensify during this difficult time for me personally”. Some CDU lawmakers had criticised Bas’s absences during a crunch phase of an economic reform drive seen as crucial to the teetering government’s survival, although it was widely known she had experienced a death in her immediate family.

I wish you and your family strength,” he wrote on X. Alice Weidel, co-leader of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland, also gave Bas her sympathies but said her angry words towards the CDU demonstrated that Merz’s coalition government “is at its end”.

She added: “We need a fresh start for Germany.” The AfD, Germany’s biggest opposition party, is leading national opinion polls at about 30% after a strong showing in September’s regional elections, which also resulted in gains for the hard left. Indian opposition figures lead march to police barricades around supreme court

Delhi police have again obstructed protests in India’s capital as thousands of people returned to the streets, led by opposition leaders, to demand the resignation of the election commissioner. After mass unrest in the capital over the weekend, when thousands were detained and harassed by police as they attempted to take part in a protest led by the gen Z Cockroach movement, on Monday the main opposition leaders led another procession through Delhi, this time to the supreme court. The leader of India’s opposition alliance, Rahul Gandhi, alongside other opposition figures and student groups, had declared their intention to march to the court and submit a petition calling for India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, to step down. Kumar has become a deeply controversial figure for his role in an exercise to verify and “purify” India’s electoral rolls, which has led to more than 130m names – more than the population of Japan – being deleted from voter lists since last year.

Opposition parties and civil society groups allege Kumar implemented this special intensive revision (SIR) to help entrench the power of Narendra Modi’s government and his Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). Muslim voters and other minorities who are traditionally not BJP voters have allegedly been disproportionately affected by the deletions. The election commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted ‌voters could re-enrol, while the BJP has accused its rivals of trying to undermine democracy by questioning legitimate electoral processes. Several metro stations were closed on Monday in central Delhi and police barricades prevented thousands of protesters getting within 600m of the supreme court, forcing them to turn back. Indonesia looks to mosque loudspeakers to double as earthquake warning systems

Scientists working on an early warning system in earthquake-prone Indonesia have taken the spiritual path to designing a network of alarms that will reach even the remotest communities: they hope to use mosques to save lives. A five-year trial is assessing whether the ubiquitous loudspeakers used to broadcast the call to prayer can double up as warning klaxons for earthquakes. “Every community has a mosque,” says project lead Dr Inoue Hiroshi, speaking to the Guardian from Indonesia. The pilot scheme was the brainchild of the Japanese disaster scientist, who says he came up with the idea nearly two decades ago while researching deadly quakes in Sumatra, Indonesia. Inoue, of the Disaster Prevention Research Institute at Kyoto University in Japan, is working with the Indonesian government to assess whether the country could implement an early warning system similar to Japan’s.

citation.title: Indonesia looks to mosque loudspeakers to double as earthquake warning systems

text:
Indonesia looks to mosque loudspeakers to double as earthquake warning systems

“I thought if Indonesia had the same service and people received the warning before the shaking came, then many people among those few hundred wouldn’t have died,” he says of a devastating 2009 quake in western Sumatra which killed at least 1,000 people. Indonesia’s disaster agency has to grapple with huge distances and hard-to-reach territories, but it has the benefit of an already established network of regularly serviced loudspeakers, something many other countries do not. With the largest population of Muslims worldwide, Indonesia has hundreds of thousands of mosques, which broadcast the call to pray five times a day. The pilot scheme has already hooked up several mosques to its seismic sensor network. For an earthquake early warning system to save lives, there are two critical factors – it needs a network of alarms, and they need to work. “The advantage of a mosque speaker is that they’re existing and well maintained,” says Inoue. “For any disaster infrastructure, maintenance is the big challenge … but the mosque speaker is maintained by the people”.

citation.title: Indonesia looks to mosque loudspeakers to double as earthquake warning systems

text:
Indonesia looks to mosque loudspeakers to double as earthquake warning systems

Many modern disaster preparedness strategies work using mobile phones, although those are vulnerable because earthquakes can disrupt communication infrastructure. The country has a tsunami early warning system dating back to 2008, but the earthquake initiative could be a “breakthrough”, says Andi Eka Sakya, senior researcher at the Indonesian government-affiliated National Research and Innovation Agency and the Indonesian head of the joint research team. While tsunamis affect coastal areas and can be predicted in minutes or even hours, earthquake waves move through the ground at incredible speeds, and Sakya says a village 50km from the epicentre could have only five to 10 seconds to respond. “It’s still a prototype, and they don’t issue warnings to the public yet,” he says. “The ultimate goal is actually to alert the people so that they can respond as early as possible.” The project, which runs until 2030, is also looking at installing alarm systems in school loudspeakers and using radio and television transmissions.

citation.title: Indonesia looks to mosque loudspeakers to double as earthquake warning systems

text:
Indonesia looks to mosque loudspeakers to double as earthquake warning systems

Indonesia and Japan both lie on the Pacific Ring of Fire and are frequently affected by earthquakes. Researchers are looking at how behaviours and survival strategies differ between Japan and Indonesia. In Japan, official disaster guidelines focus on the widely used “drop and cover” strategy – taking immediate shelter, for example, under a table and staying indoors. In contrast, low-rise homes in some developing countries like Indonesia are frequently built from unreinforced masonry that is highly vulnerable to collapsing, and so people have survived by escaping outside. In some cases, two-storey buildings in Indonesia have seen the first floor crushed and the second floor remain relatively intact. “The way people react is they quickly escape out of the room,” says Inoue. “They know how to survive.” Because standard international advice does not always suit fragile buildings, project researchers are conducting simulations and human experiments to establish guidelines grounded in science. “This is actually one of the main research topics,” says Inoue.

Indonesia looks to mosque loudspeakers to double as earthquake warning systems

Other countries in the Muslim world have looked at similar systems. When the United Arab Emirates government planned to start its Barakah nuclear power plant, an official on the project said mosque loudspeakers would be part of a broader network of alarms in the event of a radiation leak. A far more extensive mosque loudspeaker project is going on in Uzbekistan, where the Ministry of Emergency Situations announced a pilot project this year for devices to be installed in 272 mosques. The alarms would alert people to floods, mudflows, landslides and avalanches. “The selection of mosques is not incidental,” the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), which partnered in the initiative, said in a statement. “They are traditionally perceived as authoritative social institutions with significant influence on local communities.”

Lebanon’s only church-bell maker on keeping a 300-year family tradition alive

The story of Lebanon’s last remaining church-bell maker begins with a rifle. In the 18th century, Youssef Gabriel, a local metalworker, was secretly making and equipping Arab revolutionaries with rifles to assist their revolt against the Ottoman empire, which controlled Lebanon at the time. Then, one day, a Russian engineer came to the Lebanese town of Beit Chabab to make a church bell. Gabriel, intrigued, shadowed the man and picked up the process on sight. Or, another story goes, the Maronite patriarch at the time, frustrated by the Ottoman empire blocking the import of church bells to Mount Lebanon, tasked Gabriel with making a bell. After several attempts he succeeded and decided to give up making arms, converting his gunsmithery into Lebanon’s first church-bell foundry. Where the stories converge is that the village, impressed with Gabriel’s handywork, rechristened him Youssef Naffah – naffah meaning useful or successful in Arabic. Three centuries later, the Naffah family is still making church bells in Beit Chabab.

citation.title: Lebanon’s only church-bell maker on keeping a 300-year family tradition alive

text:
Lebanon’s only church-bell maker on keeping a 300-year family tradition alive

Once one of 10 bell foundries owned by the family, the workshop operated by the master bell-maker Naffah Naffah and his two sons is the last remaining production centre for church bells in Lebanon. It is also the sole source of church bells for much of the Middle East and even Lebanese diaspora communities in Europe, Australia and the US. Naffah, 57, said: “We have to pass it down to our kids, it’s been 300 years. I didn’t have any choice. My own father, he would come to the workshop when he could barely even walk.” The foundry sits under his home on the edge of a hill overlooking the red tiled roofs of Beit Chabab and the Lebanese coast that stretches beneath it. The picturesque town, in the Mount Lebanon range about a 30-minute drive from Beirut, offers an escape from the city’s chaos and a refuge from the violence of the country’s last two wars. The ceiling and walls of the foundry are blackened from decades of smoke that has belched from the furnace, and the floors are cluttered with bells in various stages of construction.

citation.title: Lebanon’s only church-bell maker on keeping a 300-year family tradition alive

text:
Lebanon’s only church-bell maker on keeping a 300-year family tradition alive

Outside are mounds of white clay mixed with goat hair, each layer drying before the next is applied. The final product forms the interior mould that the molten metal is poured around. Inside the workshop, modern tools mix with the ancient, a hydraulic press sitting next to a well-worn anvil placed on top of a tree stump. Each bell takes about two months to make. It takes about 40 days to make the interior mould and another month to create the outer mould, with crosses, decoration and the workshop’s signature imprinted on the white clay as it hardens. The third and final stage is the quickest: a foundry is heated using burning wood, and a mixture of copper and tin is placed inside to be melted down over 24 hours. When the metal is ready, it is poured over the bell mould, hardening within three minutes. The workshop produces about 25 bells a year, about 20 of which go to churches in Lebanon. The cost of the bell depends mostly on the size, with every 100kg (220lbs) costing $8,000 (£6,000). A medium-size bell that is ready in the foundry and weighs about a tonne costs about $80,000.

citation.title: Lebanon’s only church-bell maker on keeping a 300-year family tradition alive

text:
Lebanon’s only church-bell maker on keeping a 300-year family tradition alive

“I hate giving the bells away, it always makes me upset, like I’m giving away a child,” said Naffah. He pointed to a mould being worked on, imprints of crosses on its clay interior. “Look at this bell, it’s the work of my two hands. I’ve poured my heart and soul into it.” Each bell bears the names of those who worked on it. One bell ready to be installed has the name of Naffah, his son Charbel and the patron who commissioned it. Other bells in the shop for repairs – one from 1910, another from 1932 – bear the names of Naffah’s grandfathers. The family maps Lebanon by its churches, finding evidence of their ancestors up and down the small Mediterranean country. The earliest surviving bell that bears their name is in the town of Qalaat Sahyoun and was forged in 1725. The ringing of the bells is part of daily life in the villages that wind through Lebanon’s mountains and dot its sprawling coast; on a Sunday morning, the sound mingles with the chirping of the birds.

text:
Lebanon’s only church-bell maker on keeping a 300-year family tradition alive

During the Hezbollah-Israel war in Lebanon, which reignited in March, the Christian villages of south Lebanon were cut off from the rest of the country. Israel’s ground invasion, which bulldozed dozens of villages in south Lebanon, mostly spared the Christian villages, but it left them isolated. The church was a crucial source of comfort for the besieged Christians. It organised the distribution and transfer of aid in and out of towns and across frontlines when necessary. Naffah, Charbel and his other son Youssef are determined to preserve this Lebanese tradition and their place within it. Charbel will succeed his father as the master of the family workshop, and Youssef helps when he is not busy with his studies at medical school. Youssef said if Charbel ever decided he no longer wanted to make bells, he would leave medical school and take his place as master of the foundry. “We have six churches in the village [Beit Chabab]. If all of the bells played at the same time, I could distinguish between each one from their sound alone,” he said, surveying the village from the edge of the foundry.

“Traditions are important to us. We are living and breathing tradition here in this workshop.”

text:
Monday briefing: What will it take to turn around our struggling education system?

Good morning. I’m back, but don’t get too excited. I’ll just be making guest appearances here and there. Now, on to children, who – if the steady stream of warnings is anything to go by – are in serious trouble. There’s the pull of addictive screens, a sharp drop in children reading for pleasure, a global decline in academic performance, and a notable rise in youth mental health struggles. Together, these trends point to a wider crisis in learning. Much of the focus has been on phones and social media. A global study published last week found an association between increased screen exposure and lower academic achievement and poorer language development in children. In the UK, phones are already banned during the school day, and from spring of next year, under-16s will not be able to access major social media platforms such as TikTok, Snapchat and Instagram. But are we focusing on the wrong thing? Today, I speak to Jenny Anderson, award-winning journalist and author of The Disengaged Teen, about why so many young people are disengaging from learning, and what it might take to turn that around.

In depth: ‘We’re shuffling kids through a system that feels like prison’ There is a real and growing crisis in young people’s engagement with learning. According to recent research, fewer pupils now say they find school engaging. In 2020-21, 42% of students said they found what they learned interesting either “always/very often” or “quite often”. By 2023, that figure had fallen to just 28%. Nearly half of pupils do not take part in extracurricular activities, while severe absence – defined as missing more than 50% of school sessions – are on the rise in England. Pupils are also becoming less happy at school. The share of pupils who say they are happy at school dropped from 65% in 2020-2021 to 50% in 2023-2024. Perhaps most strikingly, survey data suggests pupils feel worse, physically and mentally, than they did during the Covid-19 pandemic. Jenny Anderson argues this points to something more complex than distraction from phones: a fundamental problem in how our schools are designed.

She identifies four modes in which students approach their education: • Passenger: Students who are coasting along and doing the bare minimum. This is about 50% of students. • Resister: Students who withdraw or act out. These are learners dubbed the “problem children”, but they are actually just children struggling with problems. • Achiever: Students who aim to get gold stars in everything without knowing why. They have the highest rate of mental health challenges of all the modes. • Explorer: Students who are curious, self-aware and driven. They have agency: the ability to set a goal, and the skills and will to go after it. While achievers may appear to represent the pinnacle of academic performance, Anderson argues that it’s actually the explorer mode. These dynamic modes aren’t fixed, Anderson argues.

Nobel Prize for economics awarded to Hall and Woodford for work on ‘smoothing’ crises

Two US economists have won the 2026 Nobel economics prize for their work developing models that help central bankers and finance ministers to stabilise their countries, avoiding long recessions and runaway inflation. Robert Hall of Stanford University, California, and Michael Woodford of Columbia University, New York, were recognised for developing the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”, giving policymakers better tools to smooth out the peaks and troughs of their economies. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said it was recognising the pair for generating “a paradigm shift in stabilisation policy”, awarding them the prize worth a combined $1.2m (£900,000). Related: Nobel prize for economics awarded to two Americans, Hall and Woodford, for work on New Keynesian models – business live “New Keynesian models, a result of their research, allow us to explain and quantify how stabilisation policy affects business cycles and are now used by central banks and finance ministries around the world,” the academy said.

citation.title: Nobel Prize for economics awarded to Hall and Woodford for work on ‘smoothing’ crises

text:
Nobel Prize for economics awarded to Hall and Woodford for work on ‘smoothing’ crises

These models improved on John Maynard Keynes’s stabilisation models, which struggled to handle the impact of the oil shock in the 1970s, when countries suffered high inflation, weak growth and high unemployment at the same time. Related: John Maynard Keynes: the cultured economist who governments turn to in a crisis Hall and Woodford demonstrated how traditional models could be reconstructed, based on how individual households and businesses collectively affect an economy through their actions. Hall’s work was based on forward-looking consumer behaviour rather than the more mechanical rules of thumb used by Keynes, which linked key variables such as inflation, unemployment and gross domestic product (GDP). Woodford built on this work to create the New Keynesian model, a full macroeconomic stabilisation framework that is the main tool for policymakers now. This model was used after the 2008 financial crisis by policymakers as they steered the global economy away from the risk of a second great depression.

“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world. With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” John Hassler, the chair of the committee for the economics prize, said. Hall and Woodford’s work also led to the development of forward guidance, where central bankers communicate where they expect interest rates to be in the future. That became an important tool after the 2008 financial crisis, and the Covid pandemic, when interest rates were cut to record lows. Forward guidance has had its critics, though – the current chair of the US Federal Reserve, Kevin Warsh, has argued it should only have a “limited and circumscribed” role in normal times, to avoid “creating ambiguity in the name of clarity”. And in 2014, the then Bank of England governor, Mark Carney, was labelled an “unreliable boyfriend” for dropping hints over interest rate rises that never came to pass. Woodford said he was “elated”.

Roman Abramovich aides falsified paperwork to disguise assets and dodge tax, records suggest

Aides of Roman Abramovich – including staff at the global accountancy firm Deloitte – falsified paperwork mapping the oligarch’s sprawling offshore business empire, records suggest, helping his businesses dodge tax and disguise assets. New analysis of leaked corporate records uncovers what appears to have been a long-running and carefully orchestrated strategy of backdating documents. The Russian billionaire’s closest aide, London-based Eugene Tenenbaum, appears to have been involved in the backdating and may also have given false evidence to the UK high court during a potentially costly lawsuit, the papers indicate. Abramovich’s personal and financial affairs are now restricted, owing to sanctions imposed by the UK and EU in response to Russia’s war on Ukraine. But the documents raise questions about how Abramovich was able to shield his financial affairs from the authorities for more than a decade, with the apparent assistance of apparatchiks and blue-chip advisers.

The findings are based on the Cyprus Confidential leak, more than 500,000 documents, first released to the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ) and analysed by organisations including the Guardian, the Bureau of Investigative Journalism and the BBC. The digital paper trail charts the reorganisation of billions of pounds that the former Chelsea FC owner obtained via the controversial acquisition of oilfields in the frozen wastes of Siberia, amid the break-up of the Soviet Union. From 1999 until at least 2013, a cadre of aides and accountants tasked with shifting the funds between offshore jurisdictions deployed tactics that experts say may have constituted fraud and tax evasion. This, it seems, involved backdating documents to create a convenient paper trail showing that agreements and transactions had taken place years earlier. Lawyers for Abramovich denied any wrongdoing and said he relied on the advice of his advisers and Deloitte Cyprus. Tenenbaum denied any wrongdoing and said he also relied on the specialist advice given by Deloitte Cyprus.

Heavy rainfall fuelled by a supersized El Niño weather pattern briefly forced Argentinian authorities to close tourist access to the famed Iguazu Falls, amid fears that rapidly rising water levels would cause the river to burst its banks. It later said the area would reopen to tourists on Tuesday, citing a “gradual decline” in the river’s flow. José María Hervás, the director of the Iguazu national park, said access was closed because “it just keeps raining” and the volume of water being released from dams upstream on the Iguazu River was not falling, reported the Buenos Aires Times. The Iguazu Falls, recognised by Unesco as one of the world’s largest and most impressive waterfalls, sits on the border of Argenina and Brazil and spans approximately 2,700 metres.

At least five people have died after Hurricane Simon and Tropical Storm Rachel pummelled Mexico’s Pacific coast, causing flooding that downed trees and electricity poles, blocked roads and inundated homes. Simon claimed the life of a 71-year-old man who died when a wall collapsed in Chilpancingo in the southern state of Guerrero, governor Evelyn Salgado said at a press conference. The Spanish lawyer Miriam González Durántez has launched a new liberal, centrist party, vowing to clean up politics and give voters an alternative to the dominant socialist and conservative parties as the country gears up for next month’s snap general election. González Durántez, an ex-EU adviser who is married to the former British deputy prime minister Nick Clegg, says her new party, Democracia21, will offer a modern, transparent kind of politics that “doesn’t feed on fear, insults or nostalgia”. Democracia21’s manifesto accuses both the ruling Spanish Socialist Workers’ party (PSOE) and the rightwing People’s party (PP) of squandering decades of government for short-term political ends. “In the meantime: housing became unaffordable, young people left, bureaucracy grew like a religion, and bickering took the place of governing,” it says.

Pope Leo has lung cancer, the Vatican said late on Tuesday. A same-sex couple are suing authorities in Slovakia for refusing to register their Austrian marriage, testing whether a landmark EU court ruling can turn recognition abroad into legal security at home. Their fight exposes a clash between European obligations and national restrictions – and what that means for LGBTQ+ people living under Robert Fico’s populist-nationalist government. Ivan Novotný, 31, and Metod Špaček, 51, married in Austria in 2020, but six years on, their marital status at home remains unrecognised. There is no same-sex marriage in Slovakia, a socially conservative, predominantly Catholic country; neither is there any form of civil partnership. But Novotný and Špaček, who are both lawyers and former diplomats, are not asking for that. They want the Slovakian authorities to recognise a marriage that was concluded legally in another EU country – something the bloc’s top court has said is mandatory for all EU members. “I’ve said this publicly several times, and [LGBTQ+] activists in Slovakia have criticised me for it: Metod and I are not discriminated against here.

How a scandal engulfing Brazil’s top court could return the Bolsonaros to power

Thundering to a crowd of thousands of far-right supporters in São Paulo on 7 September, Brazil’s Independence Day, the senator Flávio Bolsonaro focused less on his opponent in the presidential election, the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, than on someone who is not running at all. “Whoever votes for Lula is voting for Alexandre de Moraes,” Bolsonaro shouted, referring to the shaven-headed supreme court justice once described as “Voldemort” by Elon Musk. Although Lula did not appoint Moraes to the court, Bolsonaro’s supporters have linked the two men ever since the judge oversaw the case in which the senator’s father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, was sentenced to 27 years in prison for attempting a coup. Now, just days before the election runoff on 25 October, Moraes is once again at the centre of a presidential scandal – one that Lula believes may have helped Flávio Bolsonaro overtake him to emerge as the frontrunner. The justice once hailed as democracy’s “saviour” for containing Jair Bolsonaro may now have helped pave the way for the family’s return to power.

citation.title: How a scandal engulfing Brazil’s top court could return the Bolsonaros to power

text:
How a scandal engulfing Brazil’s top court could return the Bolsonaros to power

The scandal began with a police investigation, which found that Moraes’s wife’s law firm had a contract worth about £20m with Daniel Vorcaro, the banker accused of orchestrating Brazil’s largest banking fraud. Text messages also emerged suggesting a close relationship between Moraes and Vorcaro, though the judge denies the messages are authentic. Investigations subsequently revealed that at least four other justices had links to the disgraced banker, meaning half of the court’s 10 current justices have been drawn into the scandal. The crisis peaked last month with a ferocious exchange of insults between Moraes and another justice during a televised court session. A series of rulings followed in which the pair – as well as other judges aligned with each side – overruled one another, dominating public debate for weeks. Lula, the day after losing the first round, blamed his poor result in part on having to “carry on his back … the promiscuity” of the supreme court, in what many political observers saw as an attempt by the president to distance himself from the crisis.

text:
How a scandal engulfing Brazil’s top court could return the Bolsonaros to power

His campaign coordinator, Edinho Silva, said that, “in the eyes of society … [Lula] paid the price for that institutional damage”. Although analysts point to a range of reasons for the far right’s lead, from household debt to a simple preference for Flávio Bolsonaro, many agree that the supreme court crisis played a decisive role, particularly among indecisive voters who, with the electorate generally divided between two similarly sized left and right blocs, are the ones who ultimately decide the election. “These are people who thought that, just as they see congress, the country’s highest court had become corrupt, too. That deepened apathy among some who might otherwise have voted for Lula and fuelled the anti-system sentiment that feeds the far right,” said Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right and has spent recent months interviewing undecided voters. “We asked people about the court crisis, and they would say: ‘Everything is very confusing, but one thing we do know is that the big villain is Alexandre de Moraes,’” she said.

text:
How a scandal engulfing Brazil’s top court could return the Bolsonaros to power

“Precisely the judge who jailed Jair Bolsonaro now emerges, for these people, as the big corrupt figure and the main villain.” Conrado Hübner Mendes, a professor of constitutional law at the University of São Paulo and a leading scholar of the supreme court, said Moraes put himself in that position by “embracing the role of heroic protagonist”. The judge blocked some of Jair Bolsonaro’s moves during his government and drew the ire of far-right figures such as Musk and Donald Trump. The US went as far as to impose sanctions on him, in a move widely seen as an attempt to interfere in Jair’s trial. On Monday, Moraes authorised Flávio Bolsonaro to resume visiting his father after a 90-day ban imposed in July, when the senator read out a letter from his father that Moraes considered a breach of Jair Bolsonaro’s ban on using social media. Legal scholars and some on the Brazilian left, while acknowledging Moraes’s decisive role in the coup trial, have also criticised several of his other rulings as authoritarian.

How a scandal engulfing Brazil’s top court could return the Bolsonaros to power

“He took on a huge responsibility, and now he has thrown that away in the most mediocre way possible, with this alleged corruption case,” said Mendes. While acknowledging the contract between the law firm run by his wife, Viviane Barci de Moraes, and the disgraced banker – who is worth an extraordinarily large sum by Brazilian law firm standards – Moraes denied any wrongdoing. He said he had never ruled on any case involving Vorcaro and that there was therefore no conflict of interest. Vorcaro has been behind bars since he was arrested in November as he prepared to board a private jet from São Paulo to Malta. He is accused of leading a scheme through his Banco Master involving aggressive fundraising, unrealistic returns and falsified balance sheets that left an estimated £9bn hole, much of it involving public money and pensioners’ savings.

Text messages extracted from Vorcaro’s phone show that, two days before his arrest, the banker asked someone whom police later identified as Moraes: “Do you think … I need to get out [of the country]?” Moraes denies being the recipient and accuses a fellow justice, André Mendonça, appointed by Jair Bolsonaro, of using the police against him for electoral reasons, allegedly to benefit Flávio’s campaign. Mendonça is one of the four other justices suspected of having links to Vorcaro. An institute he created is said to have taken out an £800,000 loan from one of the banker’s associates, though he says it has already been repaid. In the other justices’ cases, investigators uncovered links ranging from a £64m contract to an alleged stake in a fund that received £5.2m from Vorcaro. All deny wrongdoing. No reports had linked Lula to the scandal until Friday, when Veja magazine reported that Vorcaro allegedly said he had paid £4.5m to finance a 2024 Oliver Stone documentary about the president.

The federal police and the public prosecutor’s office, however, said the banker had neither made the allegation nor provided evidence to support it in his testimony. Lula denied receiving money from the banker. Flávio Bolsonaro is being investigated over what happened to the £20m he was caught on tape asking Vorcaro to provide for a biopic about his father. One suspicion is that the money helped cover living and travel expenses for his brother, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, during his self-imposed exile in the US, where he lobbied the Trump administration against Lula. The senator said all the money went towards sponsoring the film, which still has no release date. Besides Flávio Bolsonaro’s lead, the far right’s sweeping victory ensured an even more conservative congress in 2027, including the senate majority needed to impeach supreme court justices – a demand among his father’s supporters since the former president was convicted. “With the scandal, the justices handed Bolsonarismo something it still didn’t have: an impeachable offence that could justify their removal,” said Mendes.

“A court that ignores conflicts of interest and immerses itself in relationships with political and economic power is a court that has already become corrupted.” Even if no justice is impeached, should Bolsonaro win, he could be entitled to fill four seats as justices retire during his term, leaving the court with at least six of its 11 members appointed by either him or his father. “We can expect a court completely servile to the government,” Mendes said, adding that the separation of powers would be at risk and that the justices themselves bear part of the responsibility. “The court ended up doing to itself the work an autocratic project needs – and brought itself down”.

Tuesday briefing: Could Burnham take Britain back towards the EU?

Good morning. After a holiday spent contracting nursery bugs from an 11-month-old, it’s good to return. Yesterday, Andy Burnham marked his first day back after party conference by calling for a closer relationship with the EU and drawing a line under a decade of “drift and division”. On Sunday, he said it was “clear” the Kremlin had been involved with the 2016 Brexit referendum vote. Both statements mark a break, rhetorically at least, from his predecessors. Conservative governments long insisted there was no evidence of Russian interference in the Brexit vote. Keir Starmer attempted to put the entire issue of Brexit behind him, treating it as a historic event rather than a cause of economic pain. But for all his words about a closer relationship with the EU, Burnham has kept the details pretty vague. Today’s newsletter, with the help of the Guardian’s Brussels correspondent Jennifer Rankin and our senior political correspondent Peter Walker, asks what his stance might actually amount to. That’s after the headlines.

In the years after it voted to leave the European Union, Britain became something of a laughing stock among EU member states. “It was like a box set TV drama. People in Brussels would be staying up to watch votes in the House of Commons,” Jennifer Rankin, who moved to Brussels to cover the EU for the Guardian in January 2016, tells me. Civil servants in Brussels grew to regard the UK as one might regard a belligerent and ungrateful elderly relative, an impression that reached its apotheosis when the former Northern Ireland secretary Brandon Lewis admitted that the UK’s Brexit arrangements for Northern Ireland would break international law (albeit in a “very specific and limited way”.) “From 2016 to 2020, the UK was seen as a model of how not to run your country,” Jennifer says. This impression softened after the passing of the Withdrawal Agreement Act in early 2020, and the Windsor framework deal, which amended the arrangements under the Northern Ireland protocol in 2023. “That was a turning point in drawing a line under the bad blood of the Brexit years,” Jennifer says.

Keir Starmer’s government then sought to cooperate with the EU on various issues such as security, food and fishing, but the “reset” he pledged to deliver was tightly circumscribed by his red lines: no rejoining the single market, no customs union, no freedom of movement. After his conference speech, Burnham suggested he might be open to reconsidering this when he suggested, somewhat cryptically, that the UK could go “all the way” (presumably towards full EU membership), and yesterday he called for a “longer-term discussion” about Britain’s relationship with the EU. But what might that actually mean? *** Could the UK rejoin the EU? Burnham has been “showing a lot of ankle” to remainers over the last few weeks, Peter Walker tells me. During his Labour conference speech, he promised to lay out “different options” for Britain’s long-term relationship with Europe, and acknowledged that Brexit had caused “more harm than good”. “It’s pretty clear that a decent majority of people would like to push a switch that meant Brexit had never happened,” Peter says.

Indeed, a YouGov poll in January 2025 found that just 11% of people thought Brexit had been more of a success than a failure. And as recently as last week, the Messina Group, a polling company, reported that half of voters say they would like to rejoin the EU. The economic consequences of Brexit are now well known, and research has estimated that, a decade after the referendum, UK GDP per head is between 6% and 8% lower than it would have been without Brexit. Yet reversing this decision would require another referendum, which would be politically fraught, reigniting a debate that splintered the country a decade ago, and reducing a highly complex and technical issue to a binary decision. It’s hard to imagine Burnham – or any politician, for that matter – wanting to fight the next election while pledging something so divisive. Notably, even the Liberal Democrats, the most pro-EU of the major parties, favour rejoining the single market and customs union but describe UK membership of the EU as a “long-term goal” rather than an immediate priority. *** What other options are on the table?
