text:
What is at stake in Serbia’s election? The key players, main issues and potential fallout

Serbia’s 6.5 million voters go to the polls on 25 October in a watershed parliamentary election characterised by civil unrest, a new political landscape, allegations of irregularities, an uncertain outcome and the potential of far-reaching consequences. Here is a brief guide to the key issues. What is the story and why does it matter? Two events frame this election. The first was the collapse of the Novi Sad railway station canopy in November 2024, which killed 16 people and uncovered massive government and institutional corruption, setting off two years of anti-government protests. The second was the hero’s funeral accorded to the Serbian general Ratko Mladić, the “Butcher of Bosnia”, who was convicted of orchestrating Europe’s worst massacre since the second world war but buried with military honours in Belgrade last month.

citation.title: What is at stake in Serbia’s election? The key players, main issues and potential fallout

text:
What is at stake in Serbia’s election? The key players, main issues and potential fallout

Amid international outrage but intense Serb nationalist pride, the increasingly authoritarian president, Aleksandar Vučić, who has dominated Serbia’s politics for 14 years, resigned to lead his ruling Serbian Progressive party (SNS) list in an attempt to become prime minister. Against him is the Student List, a grassroots, decentralised, student-led coalition that has evolved from a spontaneous protest movement after the Novi Sad disaster into a serious parliamentary challenger offering a clear alternative to the traditional parties. It matters because Serbia is an EU-candidate country that continues to balance ties with the west, Russia and China. Media bias, voter intimidation and electoral list irregularities mean any result could be contested, prompting mass protests and exacerbating regional instability. Who are the key players and parties? Vučić’s SNS anchors the “United Serbia” list. The party relies on control of the public purse, favourable media coverage and strong nationalist backing, but its campaign has been overshadowed by accusations of systemic voter manipulation.

citation.title: What is at stake in Serbia’s election? The key players, main issues and potential fallout

text:
What is at stake in Serbia’s election? The key players, main issues and potential fallout

The Student List eschews party hierarchies or a single figurehead, preferring locally respected academics and professionals, and operates through university networks. Its quickfire, humorous campaign has mobilised large numbers of disengaged voters. That means Serbia’s traditional opposition parties have been largely marginalised, with their collective support falling from 30% to 10-15%. Some parties have switched allegiance to the Student List. Others, such as European Serbia, may not clear the 3% electoral threshold. Meanwhile, Serbia’s rightwing, nationalist bloc is riven with disagreements and has been further weakened by the unexpected withdrawal of the We the Power of the People party over allegations of Russian influence. Some of the nationalist vote may switch to the SNS. What is the likely outcome and when will we know it?

citation.title: What is at stake in Serbia’s election? The key players, main issues and potential fallout

text:
What is at stake in Serbia’s election? The key players, main issues and potential fallout

Opinion polls are conflicting and not especially reliable, and there are significant concerns about electoral integrity, with allegations of state violence against opposition activists and government manipulation of voter registration lists and overseas voting arrangements. Over the past few months some polls have put SNS ahead, some the Student List, and others have forecast a neck-and-neck race. There is therefore a serious risk that whoever claims a 126-seat majority in the 250-strong parliament, the result will be contested. Analysts at the European Council on Foreign Relations suggest five main possible scenarios. The SNS could score a convincing victory, with the Student List entering parliament as a strong opposition; or a narrower, contested win, leading to street protests and legal challenges. The result could be inconclusive, with neither main coalition securing a majority. In that case, smaller traditional parties such as the Socialists could become kingmakers, or the election could be re-run.

citation.title: What is at stake in Serbia’s election? The key players, main issues and potential fallout

text:
What is at stake in Serbia’s election? The key players, main issues and potential fallout

The Student List could win a majority, but find the result contested by Vučić and the SNS, again leading to protests and possible violent repression; or it could secure a clear mandate allowing a peaceful transfer of power and setting Serbia on a very different course. Polling stations open on Sunday at 7am local time and close 8pm, with early independent and unofficial projections expected from about 9pm and preliminary official results from the electoral commission in the early hours of the morning. What might be the consequences? Within Serbia, the immediate fallout will depend on whether voters accept the result as legitimate. A victory for either side marred by obvious irregularities, or a disputed transition, could lead to civil unrest, violent clashes and institutional paralysis. Even if the Student List does win and manages a peaceful transfer of power, governing – as Péter Magyar is finding after defeating the illiberall Viktor Orbán in Hungary – will present major hurdles. Reforming 14 years of centralised SNS control will not be easy.

Internationally, the election will affect the EU: an irregular Vučić victory would force Brussels to decide whether to continue transactional diplomacy or freeze integration funds, while a Student win would require immediate financial aid and a clear path to accession. The Trump administration in the US sees commercial gains in Serbia and launched a “strategic dialogue” with Belgrade in mid-2026 on energy and technology. An SNS-led government would probably maintain Serbia’s awkward geopolitical balancing act. A Student-led administration, on the other hand, would offer a chance to shift the western Balkan country much more decisively into the European fold.

Shamonda virus detected in human for first time in France

A man in France has become the first human known to have contracted Shamonda virus, with investigations under way to explore whether it contributed to his death. Shamonda virus is a type of bunyavirus and is spread by bites from infected midges. According to the Austrian Agency for Health and Food Safety, in animals such as cattle, sheep and goats it can cause diarrhoea, lack of appetite and a decline in milk yield, “as well as abortions and congenital abnormalities in newborn calves, lambs and kids”. “In Switzerland and Germany, the presence of Shav [Shamonda virus] genetic material has also been reported in the brains of horses that died from neurological symptoms,” the agency said. The virus has previously been found in farm animals outside Europe, but was first detected in livestock on the continent in the summer. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said the patient in France was the first recognised human infection. It also noted that he had already been seriously ill and had a compromised immune system, meaning it was unclear whether the virus played a role in his death this month.

Shamonda virus detected in human for first time in France

“Investigations into whether the virus caused or contributed to the patient’s death and how the infection was acquired are ongoing,” the ECDC has said. Prof Tom Solomon, the director of the pandemic institute at the University of Liverpool, said the risk to the general public appeared to be very low. “Shamonda virus has been circulating in animals, particularly cattle, but also sheep, goats, horses and alpacas, for many years, yet this is the first recognised human infection,” he said. “This suggests that transmission to humans is extremely unusual.” But unknowns remain, he said: “We don’t know whether healthy people can become infected without developing symptoms, what symptoms the virus might normally cause, or how frequently it might cause serious disease. “French authorities believe the neurological complications in this patient were very likely linked to the infection, although investigations are continuing.

Thursday briefing: The crisis putting maternity units in England at risk of closure

Good morning. Over the summer, doctors in the emergency department at the North Devon district hospital in Barnstaple, one of the most remote in the UK, received a crash course on delivering a baby. Their training covered subjects nobody wants to hear about when they’re imminently expecting: shoulder dystocia, postpartum haemorrhage, and neonatal collapse. “I’m hoping that we won’t see such emergencies,” one doctor said. “It’s been an intense time.” That crash course was necessary because maternity services at the hospital have been indefinitely suspended due to staff shortages. Other remote hospitals across the country are expected to do the same, as NHS trusts struggle to recruit enough staff to safely deliver babies. Earlier this week, the Guardian reported that up to 20 maternity units in England could shut. The story sheds light on a maternity care crisis that has been rumbling on for years, and shows how childbirth has changed dramatically over the last decade.

Two units, the one in Barnstaple and another in Yeovil, Somerset, have already suspended maternity services because of staffing shortages, while a hospital in Newry, Northern Ireland, plans to permanently shut down its maternity services. One reason for these potential closures is that people are having fewer children. The Royal Free hospital in North London recently announced that it was permanently closing its maternity unit because the number of women having babies locally has fallen by almost 30% in the last seven years (four of the area’s primary schools have shuttered during the same period).

But the main concern for many units at smaller hospitals in rural and coastal areas is staffing. These are often areas without alternative provision nearby. At the same time, childbirth has changed. More women than ever are now getting C-sections or having births that require medical intervention from doctors, and smaller maternity units are also grappling with a widespread lack of obstetricians. “If you don’t have enough doctors, you can’t run a service safely, so more and more smaller hospitals are considering losing their maternity units altogether,” Denis says. *** Why are more women having C-sections? The rapid growth of caesareans, both planned and emergency, appears to be one of the primary reasons that some smaller hospitals are considering suspending maternity services.

The proportion of births performed by caesarean increased from 31% in 2019 to 45% in 2024, and last year was the first time in England that more babies were born via c-section than “natural” births (a term that many women find pretty grating because it implies there’s a hierarchy between births with medical intervention and those without). “England’s rate of caesareans is unusually high compared to similar European countries, and all of the experts I speak with think this is just going to keep going up and up,” Denis says. This dramatic rise in caesareans has several causes, including changes in clinical practice designed to reduce the risk to babies and (quite rightly) give women more choice over how they give birth, as well as an increase in pregnancies among women who are over the age of 35 (the average age of parents in England and Wales has been increasing steadily for the last 50 years). But this isn’t the whole story. Some women are also worried about the type of care they might receive during vaginal births.

Successive reviews portray a state of crisis, with burnt-out and exhausted midwives, a growing risk of serious injuries, and women of colour experiencing persistent racism and discrimination. A national review of maternity services in England from 2022 to 2024 by the Care Quality Commission warned that serious harm in maternity care risked becoming the norm. “There’s real concern among maternity doctors that women are reading endlessly negative headlines about the poor quality of NHS maternity care, which is leading them to ask for C-sections,” Denis says. As the rate of caesareans increases, trainee midwives are struggling to gain the experience of dealing with more complex births, potentially creating a cycle in which more women end up having caesareans. “Rather than building huge obstetric units and planning for a far higher caesarean rate, which is where we’re currently heading, the NHS should be investing in community-based and continuous midwifery care, alongside excellent obstetric care for women who need it,” Debbie Garrod, a midwife and antenatal educator, tells me.

*** How is the fear of medical negligence claims affecting childbirth? Another reason for this rising rate of caesareans is something known as “defensive practice”. This is when doctors, nurses and midwives make decisions to avoid blame or complaints, rather than because those decisions are necessarily in a patient’s best interests. The cost of settling all outstanding maternity-related claims in England was estimated at £37.5bn last year, nearly two-thirds of the NHS’s total £60bn clinical negligence liabilities bill. The US state department has ordered some diplomats and the families of US government employees to leave Saudi Arabia as the gulf kingdom faces a barrage of near-daily attacks, with at least three people killed at an airport and oilfield. Health officials across Africa are racing to determine how Nigeria’s first Ebola patient ⁠in more than a decade ⁠became infected, amid fears ​the outbreak could spread further after reaching a fourth African country. The Swiss foreign ministry said on Friday the patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, had not travelled to the Democratic Republic of ⁠Congo, where the outbreak was first detected in mid-May before spreading to Uganda, Kenya and now Nigeria. The woman was believed to have contracted Ebola while travelling with her husband in Uganda, the ministry added. The new information contradicts accounts from Uganda, which previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo, and will raise concerns about the ability of authorities to contain the outbreak, which is already the most geographically widespread in history. The Ugandan government reported Ebola cases in May and June before WHO declared it Ebola-free in August.

EU leaders to press Burnham to pay more towards Ukraine’s defence

EU leaders will press Andy Burnham at a summit in Brussels to contribute more to Ukraine’s defence effort in 2027. EU officials argue that the UK, Canada and Japan should do more to support Ukraine, but entreaties to these G7 countries for extra financial aid at recent international meetings have not been answered, Brussels says. The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, will call on the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, to contribute to Ukraine’s looming financial shortfall at an EU-Canada summit in Montreal next week. A similar request to the British prime minister will be made when he meets von der Leyen and the European Council president, António Costa, for a long-awaited EU-UK summit on 20 November in Brussels. It comes as the UK chancellor, John Healey, prepares for his first budget next week, weighing numerous calls for more spending against the rising cost of government borrowing and a darkening economic outlook. Healey said earlier this month he was “working on different ways we can step up support for Ukraine – military, diplomatic and economic”.

Foreign ministers at a summit of eight European and Middle Eastern countries have urged the US and Israel not to renews their attacks on Iran, warning a fresh outbreak of fighting would spread conflict and push oil prices even higher. The development of a new multinational “anti-war bloc” represents a challenge to the increasingly open plans by the US and Israel to relaunch strikes on Iran while talks on Tehran’s nuclear programme remain deadlocked. The Turkish foreign minister, Hakan Fidan, joint convener of the summit in Istanbul, said: “Military intervention in Iran is not any kind of solution. We agreed that a new military attack would spread the war and the conflict in the region. All the countries around the table do not want the war to spread even more, once again.” Ministers also demanded an end to the Houthi assaults on Saudi Arabia, and an immediate opening of the strait of Hormuz currently blockaded by Iranian ships and drones.

Puppy love: Finnish 24-hour newborn pup livestream is TV smash hit

A 24-hour Finnish TV show dedicated entirely to the live progress of a dog and her six newborn puppies is drawing millions of viewers. As well as a 24-hour webcam, Pentulive (Puppy Live) includes live evening chat sessions with the dogs’ breeder, a podcast and an instant notification service that updates followers on the puppies’ progress – from their birth to weigh-ins and first nail trims – for eight weeks. This is the sixth season of the hit show by the broadcaster Yle, and the latest contribution to the growing Nordic cultural phenomenon of “slow TV”. The trend started in Norway in 2009 with Bergensbanen, a seven-hour train journey broadcast on NRK, and was followed in Sweden by SVT’s Den stora älgvandringen (The Great Moose Migration), which features unnarrated glimpses of moose from the north of the country making their annual journey to summer grazing grounds. Pentulive has long attracted interest from outside Finland, but this year it is also being broadcast in Sweden (under the name Valparna live). Yle recently announced that it had also sold the format to a broadcaster in the Netherlands.

Good morning. As waves of youth-led protests swell across Europe, prompted by the cost of living, unaffordable housing and education standards, in Serbia the younger generation is taking on the apparatus of the state itself. In tight-run parliamentary elections this Sunday, the country’s most consequential political movement in decades, Student List, is challenging former Slobodan Milošević henchman Aleksandar Vučić and his 12-year domination of Serbian politics. Two years on from a singular national tragedy that galvanised public anger at state cover-ups and corruption, gen Z have channelled their energy and fury into a bold experiment in direct democracy, creating a genuinely leaderless, grassroots movement that is firing up disaffected voters across the country. I spoke to Julian Borger, our senior international correspondent, who has just returned from Belgrade, about their hopes of emulating the defeat of Vučić’s ally, Viktor Orbán, in neighbouring Hungary and the potential for a democratic domino through central Europe. Israel launches collective punishment campaign in Hebron after two soldiers killed

Israel has launched a campaign of collective punishment against Palestinians in Hebron after gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers and injured three near a checkpoint outside the city. Benjamin Netanyahu announced a siege on Hebron and neighbouring Halhul and said residents of the gunmen’s home neighbourhoods would all be forced out. He promised mass demolitions of homes. The first destruction began within hours of the attack, as ministers who had been on the campaign trail ahead of elections on Tuesday rushed to the site of the shooting. The far-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, posted a video of himself in front of a bulldozer as it tore down a Palestinian home near the site of the firefight. The destruction of a home built without permits aimed to “create deterrence and exact a price”, Smotrich said. There was no claim of a connection between the building’s owners and the attackers. Soon after the destruction began, Israel’s high court issued a temporary order to stop the demolitions.

Opposition deepfake video of Spanish PM’s wife sparks outrage before election

A political ad from Spain’s main opposition party that used a deepfake video of the prime minister’s wife has sparked outrage and set off a wider debate on AI, as the deeply polarised country gears up for general elections next month. Launched this week across the social media channels of the conservative People’s party (PP), the video used artificial intelligence to manipulate the likenesses of various people linked to Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party and appeared to show them admitting to acts such as soliciting prostitutes and taking kickbacks. An AI-generated version of Sánchez’s wife, Begoña Gómez, for example, speaks about receiving a university post thanks to her husband’s job, while a deepfake of the former Socialist president José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero speaks about hiding jewellery in a safe. Both lines are nods to ongoing investigations in which Gómez and Zapatero have denied any wrongdoing. The Socialist party was swift to respond to the video, which by Friday had racked up nearly 2m views.

text:
Paddy Donnelly obituary

My husband, Paddy Donnelly, who has died aged 70, was a South African who moved in the early 1980s to London. There he worked for the International Defence and Aid Fund for Southern Africa (IDAF), which funded the legal costs of people tried or imprisoned for anti-apartheid activity. In addition to its legal work, the IDAF had a large archive of photographs relating to apartheid, and Paddy ran that side of the operation, processing and distributing photos of ongoing state violence to media outlets, campaigning groups and many other organisations. He was an accomplished photographer himself, and many of his photos were held in the archive. He had begun by taking pictures of townships and displaced people’s camps, and when he came to the UK he photographed anti-apartheid political meetings as well as visiting or exiled South African singers, musicians and activists. Paddy was born in Germiston, south-east of Johannesburg, to parents of Irish descent: John, a bottle store manager, and Peggy (nee Sheridan), a yoga teacher.

text:
Paddy Donnelly obituary

After attending the Christian Brothers’ school in Boksburg, near Germiston, he did national service in the Defence Force, where he avoided any serious soldiering by becoming a photographer. Afterwards he studied journalism and music at Rhodes University, Eastern Cape, before moving on to teach photography at Mafikeng College (now Mahikeng City College) in North West province. In his early 20s, over a two-year period, his father, mother and sister Marge all died of cancer, and after their deaths he decided to emigrate to the British Isles, first to be a photographer in Dublin and then to London, where in 1983 he joined the IDAF. We met when I visited the IDAF to source some photos for the publications section of World University Service, where I worked, and after many years together we married in 2016. After four years at the IDAF, Paddy moved to the Catholic Agency for Overseas Development (Cafod) in London, where for more than a decade he was their media officer, also briefing photographers who were sent to record projects that the agency supported around the world.

During his time with Cafod he was invited to photograph Nelson Mandela on his July 1996 visit to London as president of South Africa. In 2006 Paddy returned to his homeland to join Africa Media Matrix, a training department for investigative journalists and documentary film-makers based at Rhodes University. He worked there until he retired in 2021, and then returned to the UK to live in York. There he sung in the Yorkshire Bach Choir, having previously been a member of the Barts and Highbury chamber choirs in London and the Byrdsongs choir in the Eastern Cape. He donated some of his photos and archival material to the Legacy Centre in London, a history and education hub located in the former offices of the African National Congress. Remembering a time when Afghan women had a voice and agency

Your article, with its account of forced marriage, illustrates how Afghanistan’s 22 million women and girls need to be freed from Taliban-imposed misogyny (‘I am still a child, it cannot be good to be married’: how drought forces Afghan families to sell girls as brides, 15 October). It was not ever thus. Under Russian suzerainty in 1965, four Afghan women were the first to be elected to the Wolesi Jirga, or lower house of parliament. In 1966, I watched two of them, bare‑headed and wearing western-style clothes, discussing a political topic with three of its male members and the future president Babrak Karmal. I also saw several post‑puberty girls not wearing the burqa. This, and reforms such as secondary education for girls, was supplemented by highly visible aid. The two-mile Salang tunnel through the Hindu Kush mountains, linking north and south Afghanistan by road for the first time, is a good example. The problem is: how can we restore such freedom without the use of force, which seldom works.

text:
Severe flooding in eastern Spain and UK hit by first named storm of winter

Storm Adam brought torrential rain to eastern Spain earlier this week. In Pego, Alicante, 632mm fell in 36 hours, with 430mm of this falling in just six hours, while the Valencian town of Oliva received 600mm in 24 hours. The severe flooding led 145 municipalities across Valencia and Alicante to impose a temporary lockdown on about 850,000 people on Monday. At least five people have died, 500 have been rescued and 2,100 evacuated. The storm also affected the Balearic Islands, with more than 130 incidents recorded in Ibiza including standing water at the airport causing some flights to be diverted or suspended. Although the worst of the storm has passed and conditions are improving across Valencia and Alicante, local disruption is expected to continue. The first named storm of the winter for the UK is tracking through the Channel. Two senior military observers say they watched a mysterious black triangular object flying at an extraordinarily high speed over a sensitive site in the western US earlier this year, in the latest tranche of reported UFO sightings released on Friday by the Trump administration. The unidentified object showed none of the characteristics of a conventional military aircraft, their report to the defense department said, and it vanished suddenly and silently within seconds, leaving no exhaust trail or other evidence of its existence. A deadline for a youth mobility scheme between the EU and the UK could be deferred by six months in a bid to ensure Andy Burnham has a successful “reset” summit on 20 November, diplomats have said. EU ambassadors in Brussels on Wednesday heard that the UK was still insisting on international tuition fees, quotas and an NHS surcharge for EU students. Sources say the UK also continues to push for a cap of about 50,000 a year on the numbers of EU citizens allowed in the country for work, travel or study under the mooted youth experience scheme (YES) visas. Some EU member states want the cap much higher, at between 100,000 and 500,000. Others want no cap at all. The UK is also insisting that any YES visa holders pay the £1,035 NHS surcharge to cover potential doctor or hospital visits, although it is understood that a 25% discount has been suggested.

Suspect arrested over fire at Hitler’s ‘Eagle’s Nest’ retreat in Bavaria

Police have arrested a 33-year-old German citizen after a fire ripped through Adolf Hitler’s former mountain retreat in Bavaria, leaving the historic Nazi meeting place – known as the Eagle’s Nest – largely destroyed. About 200 firefighters were deployed on Friday night to tackle the blaze at the Nazi dictator’s remote, purpose-built Kehlsteinhaus residence, a protected building on the peak of Obersalzberg in southern Germany. Flames rose high into the air as firefighters approached the scene to find the building “completely ablaze”, police said, adding that nobody was injured in the fire. Lisa Maier, a police spokesperson, said firefighters struggled to tackle the blaze due to its location at an altitude of 1,834 metres (6,000ft). The building, which was one of the few undamaged monuments of the Hitler era, was only accessible with “heavy breathing apparatus”, she said. Built by the Nazis and formally inaugurated by Hitler on his birthday in 1939, the Eagle’s Nest has been preserved as a monument to “the insanity of the regime”, according to its website.

A British woman has died in the Bahamas while trying to rescue her two sons after a current swept them away as they were snorkelling. The Royal Bahamas police force said it had launched an investigation after the death of a 36-year-old woman on Tuesday. The Foreign Office said it was in contact with the woman’s family and was providing support. Bimini is a small island group between the largest landmass in the Bahamas, Andros, and Miami in the US. It is the closest point in the Bahamas to the US mainland. The islands are best known for once being home to Ernest Hemingway and are also home to a world-leading shark research centre.

Hundreds of thousands march across France in protests over schools and policing

Hundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday in largely peaceful protests to support schoolchildren’s demands for more teachers and repairs to dilapidated buildings, as Emmanuel Macron faces a social and political crisis in his final months as president. The prosecutor’s office in the southern city of Nice said on Sunday that 59 people had been taken into police custody, including 11 suspected of belonging to extreme-right groups. They were alleged to have gathered with the intent of committing violence. Some were arrested in two vehicles with masks, gloves, gas sprays and truncheons, the prosecutor’s office said in a statement to public broadcaster FranceInfo. Local media in Nice had reported extreme-right groups coming to the city centre and targeting demonstrators on Saturday. In Paris, at least 110,000 people marched along the eastern edge of the city, according to government estimates.

They supported high schoolers but also complained of the high cost of living and the government’s heavy policing, saying riot police had been sent to target school protesters over the past month, instead of the government offering political solutions. The mood in Paris on Saturday afternoon was peaceful and lighthearted, with brass bands playing and children and grandchildren present. Some people carried banners critical of the government’s policing, saying: “Oppression breeds rebellion” and “The right to protest”. But at the end of the Paris demonstration, at Porte de Vincennes on the city’s eastern edge, different groups of masked men dressed in black emerged who had not appeared to have taken part in the peaceful march. Some groups of masked men threw glass bottles and stones at police, who responded with teargas, water cannon and stun grenades. A bin was set alight and fireworks were set off towards police. Riot police also charged a larger crowd of protesters at the end of the Paris march, using batons against them.

The government estimated that at least 400,000 people had marched across France. Trade unions estimated the number at double that. The interior ministry said there had been 1,314 arrests, 75 fires and 24 shops looted – less than last weekend. Laurent Nuñez, the interior minister, said that at various street marches across France there were what he called “high-risk groups” who “broke away from the main body and sought to commit acts of violence”. More than 70,000 police were on the streets of French cities, with shops boarded up and many museums closed.

Israeli soldiers raze neighbourhood in Hebron, driving families from homes

Israeli troops have levelled a neighbourhood in Hebron, driving out hundreds of families in collective punishment for a militant attack on an army checkpoint outside the West Bank city, local Palestinian authorities said. The Hebron municipality estimated that 35 hectares (86 acres) had been destroyed or marked for destruction and about 1,500 people had been evicted from their homes by Saturday afternoon in the district of Ein Deir Baha. The whole city of 250,000 people was sealed off by checkpoints on every point of entry. Videos sent by a Hebron resident showed a substantial area of devastation with every house over several blocks flattened in an urban area. One video showed soldiers marking Palestinian houses with a sprayed black cross, another showed a bulldozer tearing down a stone wall on a hillside and another showed a large residential building festooned with Israeli flags. People said the building was the home of a prominent Hebron family that had been commandeered as a temporary military headquarters.

Smotrich also called for “a comprehensive military campaign … exactly like in Gaza and Lebanon”. Ein Deir Baha, the focus of the demolitions, was alleged to be the home district of the two gunmen.

‘Bolso shows all signs of fascism’: the journalist who predicted Brazil’s future – and paid the ultimate price

“Bolso shows all signs of fascism, as do his supporters,” the murdered British journalist Dom Phillips told me before his death. “His sons are all more extreme if anything.” These words were written in 2018 by the Guardian contributor shortly before the election of the far-right former army captain Jair Bolsonaro as president of Brazil – a prospect that Dom viewed with dread. As he predicted back then, this would lead to more mortalities, more destruction of the Amazon rainforest and more danger for journalists. His own life and death were to prove the prescience of this foresight. Dom was killed four years ago alongside the Brazilian indigenous expert Bruno Pereira, but his views feel alarmingly relevant once more as Brazil braces for a presidential runoff this Sunday in which a member of the far-right Bolsonaro clan is once more a favourite to win – despite all the dangers that poses to the environment and those who seek to protect it.

Although the difference between them is within the margin of error and Lula appears to have gained momentum, the possibility of another Bolsonaro administration is likely to fill any friends of Dom and Bruno with alarm. Dom was no diehard political leftist. In an earlier election, he shocked me by expressing support for the centre-right challenger Aécio Neves because he felt the then Workers party administration had become too entangled in corruption. But while Dom eschewed ideology, he had clear ideas about the importance of sound, considerate government in the interests of people and the planet. He saw the Bolsonaro family as a menace to both. Looking back through our exchanges of WhatsApp messages, I am struck by the prescience of his observations.

Kim Jong-un crosses newly opened bridge into China

Kim Jong-un has visited China, inaugurating a bridge that connects the two countries and saying he hopes to expand cooperation with his neighbour. The North Korean leader arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong on Saturday after crossing the New Yalu River Bridge, according to South Korea’s unification ministry, which handles affairs related to North Korea, and China’s official Xinhua news agency. He met Wang Huning, a member of the standing committee of China’s Communist party. The pair toured a car factory, and promised to strengthen the bilateral relationship. Kim said his country “stands ready to work with China to carry forward their historical friendship and expand practical cooperation, thereby delivering tangible benefits to the peoples of both countries”, according to Xinhua. Wang then accompanied Kim to the bridge to send him off, Xinhua said. Related: North Korea has opened up bridges to Russia and China – in which direction will it go?

The visit appears to be timed to underscore the strength of Kim’s ties with Beijing ahead of the 25 October anniversary of China’s first major victory in the Korean war, which came days after Chinese troops crossed the Yalu River into North Korea in October 1950. Japan’s Kyodo news agency said on Saturday that traffic controls had been imposed around the bridge and near a museum about China’s role in the war, and that hotel bookings nearby had been restricted. Diplomatic sources told the agency the measures were linked to a visit by a senior North Korean official. The 3km bridge opened in mid-October, 12 years after China finished building it, after being held up by delays on the North Korean side. In early September, North Korea and Russia opened the first road bridge across their own short border, leaving Pyongyang newly linked by road to its main backers. The trip is Kim’s sixth visit to China and his first since September 2025, when he attended a military parade in Beijing alongside the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin. Xi visited Pyongyang in June, his first trip there in seven years.

‘We can’t let the far right take power again’: Lula voters in final push before Brazil runoff

Naiara Boroni, Nikolas Domingues and Jodersson Diego live in the same city and do not know one another, but said they had done the same thing in recent days: persuaded at least one person who had not voted for the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the first round to choose him in this Sunday’s runoff. In Boroni’s case, it was her grandmother who had not turned out; in Domingues’s, a cousin who had chosen a candidate who finished fourth. But Diego achieved what to many sounds almost impossible in such a polarised country: he said he had persuaded a woman who voted for the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro to switch sides. “She’s a student of mine and didn’t vote for Lula because of her evangelical church. I didn’t argue; I tried to explain that he wasn’t everything they said he was, and she said she had changed her mind,” said Diego, 33, a dance teacher from Belo Horizonte, the capital of the state of Minas Gerais.

Winning over voters who abstained or cast null votes, and flipping as many others as possible, is at the heart of Lula’s strategy as he tries to do what no presidential candidate has ever managed in Brazil: overturn a first-round defeat like the one he suffered to Bolsonaro on 5 October. Lula received 3.8 million fewer votes than in 2022, when he ran against the senator’s father, then president Jair Bolsonaro – who would go on to lose the runoff and try to stage a coup, which failed after the heads of two of the three armed forces refused to join him. Serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest, he chose his eldest son to stand in his place. Flávio Bolsonaro has said that, if elected, he will pardon his father and receive the presidential sash from him. The senator won 5 million more votes than his father and saw his party sweep elections for congress, state governments and state legislatures, which made him the clear favourite for many analysts.

In the three weeks of campaigning since then, however, polls have shown the gap steadily narrowing, and the two are now about even, with Bolsonaro still slightly ahead, but only by fractions of a percentage point. “The scenario is one of a very tight tie, but with Lula’s campaign performing markedly better in the runoff,” said political scientist Manoel Leonardo Santos, a professor at the Federal University of Minas Gerais. Of the 10 cities with the highest abstention rates, eight are in Minas Gerais, the country’s second-largest electorate after São Paulo and a historical bellwether in presidential elections. More than one million Lula supporters rally on eve of Brazilian election runoff

More than one million supporters of Brazil’s leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, have streamed on to Rio’s most famous beach for a giant protest they hope will propel him towards a historic election fightback against his far-right rival, Flávio Bolsonaro. Nearly 159m Brazilians will vote in the election’s runoff on Sunday, with the pair tied in the polls after Bolsonaro won the first round on 4 October by 47% to 45%. On Saturday, under a fierce sun, red-clad crowds packed the 2.5-mile Copacabana beach in an attempt to help Lula clinch a dramatic and unprecedented comeback. Never since the return of democracy to Brazil in the 1980s has the first-round loser managed to bounce back. Josias Silva, a 61-year-old truck driver, voiced confidence that his 80-year-old president, who was first elected in 2002, would win a fourth non-consecutive term. He carried a homemade sign to the carnival-like procession reading: “Lula re-elected.

We don’t want hatred. We don’t want guns. We want a country of love,” added Silva, celebrating the large number of people who came to witness one of the final presidential campaign rallies in Lula’s storied 50-year political career. “There’s never been a demonstration like this one. This is the biggest protest in the history of Brazil. And we are going to win tomorrow with more than 60% of the votes,” Silva claimed. text:
Modern life is stuck in a sea of sameness. The pursuit of beauty is a necessary antidote

By the time it’s 5pm on a Friday, the headache and dry eyes have well and truly settled in. Maybe it’s a long day in front of your four screens while funnelling white noise through a large pair of headphones to cancel out the calls of your co-workers. Or maybe it’s the almost chemical wash of white fluorescent lights that shine from the low ceiling in your open-plan office, or the feeling of enclosure as you look out the window on to the reflective walls of other towers. To lift your spirits, you decide to treat yourself to a weekend at a beachside Airbnb. But the town is not how you remember it as a kid. The farmland has been turned into identical housing estates broken up by highway-hugging shopping centres with the same Guzman, Woolies, Chemist Warehouse, Dan Murphy’s and Priceline as all the other shopping centres. They’re not the only things that are samey. The cars in the car park are mostly white or grey, and stepping out of them, people are in near-identical athleisure or shorts and T-shirts.

citation.title: Modern life is stuck in a sea of sameness. The pursuit of beauty is a necessary antidote

text:
Modern life is stuck in a sea of sameness. The pursuit of beauty is a necessary antidote

Related: Our lives and identities have moved online – and it’s driving us insane | Brigid Delaney The Airbnb is how it was depicted in the pictures (minimalist, fancy handwash in the bathroom, Anko soft furnishings) but there is something dispiriting about it. Just like the cars, the interior is grey and white, and it smells of surface cleaner. It’s a house devoid of colour, personality and character. The beach itself is still beautiful, but coming out of the ocean you can’t remember where you left your towel. Every inch of sand is taken up with the same stripy Cool Cabana tents, rendering the visual landscape hectic and disorientating, as if you’d hit your head and were seeing double. At the cafe (minimalist, blond wood, pot plants, $7 flat whites) you run into some people from school who you haven’t seen for ages. You can’t quite put your finger on it but they look different, weird almost. There’s something uncanny about their faces, with their foreheads smooth as a screen, their lips and cheeks plumped.

citation.title: Modern life is stuck in a sea of sameness. The pursuit of beauty is a necessary antidote

text:
Modern life is stuck in a sea of sameness. The pursuit of beauty is a necessary antidote

Looking around – with everyone wearing the same athleisure, staring into the same screens, drinking the same coffee, pouring it into the same-looking plastic faces – you wonder when did all this happen? Where did all the beauty go? *** It’s difficult to believe we are lucky enough to be born on a blue, watery planet that is covered in flowers. And that on this planet everyone is a completely unique individual, all 8.3 billion of us, with our own specific way of expressing ourselves, our unique faces and bodies, our idiosyncrasies, desires, aversions and tastes. Because right now we are stuck in a sea of sameness. Whether it’s the design of our offices, the interior of our houses (major paint brands like Dulux and Sherwin-Williams say grey is a top-searched and frequently used colour, with the Financial Times reporting that grey is chosen because it may result in better resale value) or the cars we drive. Modern life is becoming drabber, uglier, more uniform and a lot less pleasing to look at.

citation.title: Modern life is stuck in a sea of sameness. The pursuit of beauty is a necessary antidote

text:
Modern life is stuck in a sea of sameness. The pursuit of beauty is a necessary antidote

But there are signs of a resistance – with one of the most fascinating being discussions around the need for beauty. The left are reawakening to the fact that fighting for better material conditions for all people extends to what was previously thought of as a frivolous or optional extra. But beauty – and the elevation of beauty – is central to the project of flourishing. This is an ancient ideal, and its suppression by the powerful is equally old. Beauty is not slavishly following trends but working out what you like, what makes you happy – and going with that The Greeks had a concept that bound beauty, goodness and truth together as kalos kagathos, literally “beautiful and good”. In The Symposium, Socrates describes beauty as the thing that draws the soul upward towards truth, justice and the divine. Ugliness, in this framework, was not merely unpleasant, it was a form of moral disorder. Throughout history, there have been times when beauty has been elevated (the Renaissance) and suppressed (the factory districts in the Industrial Revolution).

citation.title: Modern life is stuck in a sea of sameness. The pursuit of beauty is a necessary antidote

text:
Modern life is stuck in a sea of sameness. The pursuit of beauty is a necessary antidote

And in times of suppression, movements have emerged such as the Arts and Crafts movement in the 1860s, aimed at restoring dignity to working people through the elevation of beautiful objects in their homes such as wallpaper, textiles and furniture. We are living in a time where originality and beauty have been suppressed, where everything has become so frictionless and optimised (such as the grey homes optimised for resale, not for living in) that concerted efforts must be made to turn back towards beauty and individuality, even if it has no explicit market value. The tipping point for me is the very devaluation of the role of human-made art, writing, music and design by the rise of machine-made art in the form of AI slop. I can live (I guess … ) with the grey houses and the bland homewares, but not with removing humans from the creation of writing, art and beauty in favour of AI. Suffragists, unionists and workers have long fought under the banner of bread and roses – that is, having basic biological needs met while also having access to the things that elevate the spirit and please the eye.

citation.title: Modern life is stuck in a sea of sameness. The pursuit of beauty is a necessary antidote

text:

Now the project has some new energy. You see it in Zohran Mamdani’s New York (he used the campaign slogan of “Roti and Roses”) where there was bread in the form of a promise of freezing rents, but roses too. Everything from the way his campaign posters, font and videos were designed – with an eye for pleasing human-made (in contrast with the Truth Social slop, such as Trump as Jesus ) – to policy decisions such as releasing 70,000 free Metropolitan Opera tickets, has at its core the importance of flourishing on all levels. Related: Critical thinking is one of the most important aspects of being human, according to Stoicism. So why are we handing it over to a machine? | Brigid Delaney Beauty can be something we vote for, but it is also something that right now we must fight for – whether we advocate for the natural world, or better-planned communities and housing. It is also something we co-create with the world. Beauty is not slavishly following trends but working out what you like, what makes you happy – and going with that. It could mean a maximalist apartment where the walls are pink.

citation.title: Modern life is stuck in a sea of sameness. The pursuit of beauty is a necessary antidote

text:
Modern life is stuck in a sea of sameness. The pursuit of beauty is a necessary antidote

Or it could be wearing colour when everyone else is in black. Or it could be nurturing pot plants in your office or helping with a community garden. Or maybe it’s creating your own art, or employing an artist or writer, rather than using AI. Beauty made by humans (and in the case of nature, protected and nurtured by humans) is not just pleasing to the eye and the spirit, but it is a form of protest. A pushback against dehumanisation of our current age. • Brigid Delaney is the author of five books, including The Seeker and the Sage

North Korea has opened up bridges to Russia and China – in which direction will it go?

For more than a decade, local Chinese residents pilloried it as nothing more than an empty bridge that led to a North Korean vegetable patch on the other side. Fast forward 12 years and dozens of trucks are now traversing the bridge linking China to North Korea, boosting trade for the reclusive regime. But it has also triggered concern that it could intensify a struggle for influence over the North between Beijing and the region’s other major power, Russia. Interactive The New Yalu River Bridge connects the north-eastern Chinese city of Dandong with Sinuiju in North Korea and has four lanes and stretches 3km (1.9 miles) across the Yalu river. It is expected to ease congestion on the ageing Friendship Bridge nearby. It opened on 15 October, about a month after another major crossing – this time between North Korea and Russia. The first road bridge across their short shared border, named the Yakov Novichenko Bridge, reportedly made Chinese officials uneasy, coming on top of signs from the North Korean leader Kim Jong-un that he is prioritising ties with Moscow.

citation.title: North Korea has opened up bridges to Russia and China – in which direction will it go?

text:
North Korea has opened up bridges to Russia and China – in which direction will it go?

Interactive “China’s interest in buttressing its influence in North Korea is certainly reinforced by the diversifying North Korea-Russia relationship — ties that China tolerates but watches closely as they add complexity to its relationship with its provocative neighbour,” says Carla Freeman, director of the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies’ Foreign Policy Institute. Since late 2024, the North Korean leader has sent ammunition and as many as 16,000 troops to support Vladimir Putin’s war in Ukraine, and has held two summits with the Russian president in the past three years. In 2024, the leaders signed a mutual defence pact that includes a clause requiring the countries to come to each other’s aid if attacked. In return for arms and combat soldiers, Pyongyang is getting hard currency, real-time battlefield experience for its troops, weapons technology and the opportunity to extend political and economic cooperation beyond its traditional ally China.

North Korea stands to benefit from increased trade but for China, the bridge could be of more geopolitical value than economic given how little trade China does with its neighbour compared with its other partners. However, the insular regime in Pyongyang is thought to be reluctant to increase its economic dependence on China, by far its biggest trading partner and aid donor, and may still resent Beijing’s previous support for UN sanctions targeting the North’s nuclear weapons programme. In the past two years, however, Russian and Chinese support for UN sanctions has collapsed. “The main restriction on trade with North Korea is not the infrastructure but international sanctions,” says Justin Hastings, a professor of international relations and comparative politics at Sydney University.

“However, because China’s enforcement of UN sanctions has become desultory and Russia has actively repudiated their enforcement, North Korea is in a position to benefit from increased trade and weapons help (at least from Russia).” The North’s “open” border with China contrasts dramatically with the one it shares with South Korea. Kim is trying to play the two against each other, but China and Russia are not rivals like the Soviet Union and China were in the 1970s.” Kim is more likely to turn to China improve his country’s struggling economy, while Beijing is eager to revive its role as the North’s biggest influence, according to Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul. “After expanding military cooperation with Russia … Kim Jong-un is leveraging his windfall from Moscow for additional gains from Beijing. ‘It’s part of our history’: can the menú del día survive Spain’s changing eating habits?

A little before lunchtime each working day across Spain, evidence of one of the lingering, if less notorious, legacies of the Franco dictatorship is carefully traced in chalk, marker pen and printer ink. Beckoning to hungry workers from blackboards, whiteboards and pieces of paper hastily taped to windows, the competitively priced menú del día, or daily set-price lunch, has been part of everyday Spanish life for more than half a century. But while 4m menús are still served each weekday, Spain is slowly losing its appetite for the familiar ritual. Back in 2009, the country’s best-known chef, Ferran Adrià, went so far as to pronounce it dead – a victim of changing eating habits, economic downturns and bistro-style restaurants trying to charge €20-€30 (£17-£25) for what should be a simple starter, a hearty main and a choice of pudding or coffee … with bread and a drink thrown in. Seventeen years later, however, the diagnosis seem a little premature.

citation.title: ‘It’s part of our history’: can the menú del día survive Spain’s changing eating habits?

text:
‘It’s part of our history’: can the menú del día survive Spain’s changing eating habits?

A new book by the Spanish food journalist Lakshmi Aguirre charts the history and evolution of the menú and argues that while the tradition is indeed in hot water, it hasn’t quite had its chips. Her book – Menú del Día: Everyday Scenes of a First Course, a Second Course and Pudding – begins with the unpalatable fact that it all began with a tourist menu dreamed up in the mid-1960s up by the Spanish dictator Francisco Franco’s information and tourism minister, Manuel Fraga. The regime was keen in the aftermath of the “years of hunger” that followed the Spanish civil war to show foreign visitors that food was plentiful, good and affordable. So it was that establishments serving food should offer “a starter of soup, a main course chosen from at least three options and based on egg, fish or meat and accompanied by a side dish, and a pudding based on fruit, something sweet, or cheese”.

citation.title: ‘It’s part of our history’: can the menú del día survive Spain’s changing eating habits?

text:
‘It’s part of our history’: can the menú del día survive Spain’s changing eating habits?

The price was set at between 50 and 250 pesetas and, to stop unscrupulous restaurant owners watering down the drinks, the law stipulated that the accompanying quarter-litre of vino had to be “reds and whites from Spain that are pure, clean, pleasant on the palate and with an alcohol content of not less than 12%”. In the early 1970s, the menú del día was rebaptised to make it look less like an attempt to woo – and sometimes gouge – tourists, but also to give ordinary Spaniards the idea that they, too, could indulge. It is now so ubiquitous that many in Spain have no idea of its genesis. “When I was working on the book and people asked me about the menú del día, I’d mention Manuel Fraga and lots of them would throw their hands up in shock,” Aguirre said. “Some people know, but the vast majority don’t. It says a lot about us Spaniards; we forget very quickly.” Researching the book, which includes personal reminiscences and a hefty selection of recipes, led Aguirre to consider the place of the menú in the popular consciousness.

citation.title: ‘It’s part of our history’: can the menú del día survive Spain’s changing eating habits?

text:
‘It’s part of our history’: can the menú del día survive Spain’s changing eating habits?

“It’s part of our history, yet it’s changed over the years, reflecting the evolution of Spanish society,” she said. “It originated from something as terrible as a dictatorship, and today it has become a deeply ingrained custom. We feel a sense of nostalgia as we realise it’s fading away.” The threats to the set lunch, whose average price today is €14.70, are many. Increasingly time-poor, many Spaniards now opt for a quick lunch, eating food from home at work or popping to a supermarket for a ready meal to microwave in a soulless canteen. Rising energy and food prices are making it harder for small, family-run restaurants to offer a rotating daily selection of starters and mains. All of which explains the rise of the “dish of the day”, which offers restaurants a cheaper alternative to the traditional choice of three or four mains, and the increasing diversity of some menús, which now feature Latin American staples as a reflection of Spain’s changing demographics.

citation.title: ‘It’s part of our history’: can the menú del día survive Spain’s changing eating habits?

text:
‘It’s part of our history’: can the menú del día survive Spain’s changing eating habits?

“The menú del día purists reject such options, but it has always been a reflection of the society that consumes it – and that’s exactly how it should be,” Aguirre said. “Spain today isn’t the same as it was in the 1980s, it is far more diverse and pluralistic, and as a result diners have changed as well. The menú del día exists for those who need it, for people who may come from many different backgrounds.” Aguirre’s menú of choice would be a simple but well-cooked vegetable stew followed by hake in green sauce or baby squid in ink, and then leche frita (fried custard) or rice pudding. But, as she points out in her book, the surroundings are almost as important as the cooking. Her benchmarks for a good menú del día spot include simple dishes, a regularly changing menu, chips that aren’t frozen, a chorus of regulars and “a chalkboard free of any trace of words such as avocado, burrata, tartare, truffle or sourdough bread”.

citation.title: ‘It’s part of our history’: can the menú del día survive Spain’s changing eating habits?

text:
‘It’s part of our history’: can the menú del día survive Spain’s changing eating habits?

That chalkboard should, by preference, be written “by someone who’s never heard of lettering”, and bonus points are awarded if the child of the owners is doing their homework on a table down the end. As it hobbles slowly towards what may be its demise, the menú del día has become something that transcends a filling and reasonably priced midday meal. “What’s being lost is a meeting point,” Aguirre said. “A centre of community gravity where families with limited financial means can afford to eat out, and where those who live alone can find some company during a meal, which remains a deeply social activity. “It’s a place where joys, sorrows and problems can be shared, or where you can simply enjoy a bit of breathing space, as well as a place for those who live far away or who don’t have the time to go home for lunch.” The true privilege of the menú, she added, lay “not just in being able to pay for a meal, but also in having the time to enjoy it”.

Storm Boelo to bring 80mph gusts and heavy rain to parts of UK

The UK is bracing for a second storm this weekend, as strong winds and heavy rain are expected to disrupt travel and cause further power cuts in the north. Storm Boelo, the second named storm of the season, is expected to bring heavy, frequent showers and winds potentially exceeding 80mph to northern parts of the UK. Thousands of homes in the south-west of England have already been left without power after Storm Austen hit the region on Friday. The Met Office has advised people to stay indoors as much as possible and said the storm will bring danger to life from flying debris and crashing waves. The forecaster has issued an amber alert, its second most severe weather warning, covering Scotland, the north of England down to Carlisle from 9pm Saturday to the same time on Sunday. Another amber warning is also in place for the north-east of Northern Ireland from 9pm Saturday to 10am Sunday. Related: How autumnal high pressure brings on the dark doldrums A large yellow warning for very wet and windy weather will cover the whole of the UK’s north from midday Saturday to 9pm on Sunday.

Violence, intimidation and fear: 10 years on from the ‘Jungle’, life in Calais migrant camps is harsher than ever

In the decade since the demolition of the “Jungle”, an area of Calais where thousands of asylum seekers set up makeshift shelters before embarking on Channel crossings to the UK, everything and nothing has changed. This week, in a woodland clearing not far from one of Calais’s busy main roads, several brightly coloured tents are pitched. A jacket hanging from a tree branch blows in the brisk autumnal breeze alongside a belt decorated with union flags. It is only October but the wind makes the temperature feel several degrees chillier. “I live in a tent,” says Adam*, at a nearby charity-run phone charging session. He is an electrical engineering student from Sudan who fled his country when the war started. “We have been evicted so many times. It is not worth having any possessions because the police take everything.

Nonetheless more than 200,000 asylum seekers have made the journey from Calais to the UK since the “Jungle” – one of the largest of its kind in Europe – ceased to exist. On the 10th anniversary of it being torn down, about 4,000 people remain in smaller camps in Calais, Dunkirk and Boulogne, waiting to cross the sea. The predominant nationalities hoping to reach the UK are almost the same as they were in 2016 – Eritreans, Sudanese, Somalis, Iranians and Afghans. Their resolve to reach the UK, where they believe they will be safe, has not weakened.

In 2016 almost nobody crossed the Channel in small boats. But from 2018 onwards, small boat crossings began to rise. A policy of “zero point de fixation” was introduced in France to prevent the establishment of another large encampment. As a result, small living sites in wooded areas – particularly in Calais – are evicted on average once every 48 hours, with asylum seekers having tents, clothing and other possessions destroyed or confiscated by police in the process. Most will set up a new camp nearby, often with donations of tents from charities.

In 1987, the Israeli human rights attorney Felicia Langer was paying a visit to the Neve Tirza women’s prison when a client named Siham shared some disturbing news: the prisoners held there had recently been sprayed with a chemical agent that left them writhing on the floor. Langer grabbed a tissue that had been exposed to the substance – a piece of evidence, perhaps, in a future legal case. Then, on impulse, she lifted it to her face and inhaled deeply. Her hope, she wrote later, was that doing so might enable a doctor to identify the toxin. This anecdote appears in Anti-Zionism: A Jewish History, by Benjamin Moser.

In it, the Pulitzer prize-winning author profiles a dozen Jews who actively opposed Zionism, before and after the establishment of Israel – from Aaron Samuel Tamares, a Polish rabbi who began inveighing against Jewish nationalism in the late 19th century; to British diplomat Edwin Montagu, who sought to derail the 1917 Balfour declaration promising a Jewish state in Palestine; to Israeli “new historian” Avi Shlaim – figures he sees as part of “a hidden tradition … of people who, though long dismissed and despised, were ultimately proven right”. Along the way, he seeks to dismantle the Zionist “fairytale,” as he puts it, piece by piece. Langer’s heedless act made her ill but failed to provide the evidence she’d hoped for. An Emirati diplomat who as UAE ambassador to the UN helped secure the delivery of humanitarian aid to Gaza has entered the race as a late contender to succeed António Guterres as the world body’s secretary general. Lana Nusseibeh, who is of Palestinian heritage, is widely noted for her advocacy of the Palestinian cause and the two-state solution and has won the endorsement of the state of Palestine. She is however facing criticism over the UAE’s contested role in arming the Rapid Support Forces in Sudan, a group that has been accused of genocide by two successive US administrations. Nusseibeh, 48, has been one of the leading UAE diplomats denying reports that the UAE supplied weapons to RSF leader Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo in defiance of a UN arms sales ban. A grouping of Latin American and Caribbean states, CELAC, has also sent a letter of objection to the security council, claiming her late entry came just as a consensus was emerging behind their region holding the UN top job.

The camp in the heart of Lisbon had been set up after thousands of people marched along one of the Portuguese capital’s main thoroughfares to rail against housing prices that have soared past average incomes in the country. Now I realise how devastating it is to lose your home.” At midday on Sunday, he was in a Hebron market shopping for a change of clothes for his grandchildren, uncertain how long the family’s exile would last. He had heard that the house was being used as a base by Israeli soldiers and looking up at the house, perched on the side of a steep hill, he could see some lights on but no sign of life. The Hebron municipality said that 370 families, nearly 2,000 people, had been displaced by the army sweep through Ein Deir Baha. In its official comments, the Israeli army had said that the displaced population had left voluntarily, that “civilians who wished to evacuate were permitted to temporarily leave the area”. Ahmaro was outraged at the suggestion that he had any choice about fleeing. “Never, never, never. Why should I leave my house?” he asked. Abdul Halim al-Tamimi tried to stay put when the military came at 1.30am. The 77-year-old was told his family had only 10 minutes to vacate their home.

“An intelligence officer told me if we didn’t go, they would displace us the same way they have done it in Gaza,” he said. “We stood there in front of the house, and we refused to leave until we were faced by three military vehicles and they forced us out.” By the time the Tamimi family left, it was 3am on Saturday morning. On Sunday morning their home was festooned with large Israeli flags and ringed with military vehicles. The army had turned the substantial villa into its headquarters. In its statement, the Israeli military claimed that 2,000 local people were from the Jaba’a clan, from which the gunmen were allegedly drawn, and which the army claimed was “associated with Hamas”. The claim drew consternation and derision from people in Ein Deir Baha. They numbered the extent of the Jaba’a clan at 150 at most, with no known reputation for radicalism. “We are from a completely different family. We are innocent people. We have nothing to do with the whole thing,” Tamimi said.

‘This is a symbol for Europe’: streets of Belgrade resound with joy after Vučić defeat

Standing on the streets of Belgrade, as passing cars honked excitedly and revellers high-fived police officers, Sara, 24, gestures to the streets around her to explain just how much things had changed for Serbia’s student-led movement. Moments earlier, the country’s longstanding leader, Aleksandar Vučić, had conceded defeat to the student movement, ushering in a seismic political shift in the Balkan country. It was a surreal reversal of fortunes for the hundreds of thousands of people who had spent nearly two years peacefully protesting against a ruling power that had become increasingly authoritarian. “It’s very strange that on the very streets where the police beat us, on the streets where we retreated countless times in the face of the gendarmerie, we are now standing here as the victors,” says Sara. The realisation saw people pour into streets across Serbia to mark the incredible trajectory.

citation.title: ‘This is a symbol for Europe’: streets of Belgrade resound with joy after Vučić defeat

text:
‘This is a symbol for Europe’: streets of Belgrade resound with joy after Vučić defeat

In Novi Sad – where the protests had begun in November 2024 following the deadly collapse of a train station roof – thousands gathered in celebration after Vučić conceded that the Students’ List movement had likely won between 135 and 140 seats in the ‌250-seat parliament, while his rightwing SNS party had 105, citing preliminary results. In Belgrade, tens of thousands of people flooded the city’s main boulevards, chanting euphorically, waving flags and setting off flares against an unrelenting backdrop of honking car horns. “Oh my gosh, I don’t know how to explain it,” says Tamara, 35. “I’m so happy and excited.” Sunday’s results would ultimately set Serbia on a path towards “freedom and hope for a better tomorrow,” she says. But she was under no illusions that it would come easily. “I know we have a tough period ahead of us, I do,” she says.

‘This is a symbol for Europe’: streets of Belgrade resound with joy after Vučić defeat

“But even so, it’s a huge relief and gives us energy to keep going.” The tremendous task of reversing the country’s drift towards authoritarianism and deeply entrenched corruption now falls to the list of 250 candidates, which includes more than 160 doctorates as well as a sprinkling of farmers, athletes and others. Adding to the challenge is the fact that the students’ policy platform downplayed some of the country’s more divisive issues: the question of future EU membership has been left to a referendum, and Kosovo is claimed as an integral part of Serbia. On Sunday, however, many were simply thrilled to celebrate the end of a government that had become known for routinely threatening its critics and chipping away at press freedoms. “The people have won! The people defeated a dictator! The people will lead Serbia!” Nebojsa Cosic told Reuters as people in the street linked arms to dance the traditional Serbian folk dance, Kolo.

‘This is a symbol for Europe’: streets of Belgrade resound with joy after Vučić defeat

The crowds were also swift to descend on the central park in Belgrade where Vučić’s loyalists had camped out for more than a year, joyfully tearing down the fences and tents that had blocked off access to the park. Duško Suvajac, 52, points to the broader implications as the elections kicked off 10 pivotal days of ballots across the globe in which the authoritarian right is facing off against pro-democracy forces. “This is a symbol for Europe and the world,” he says. “It’s a demonstration of how freedom can defeat evil.” As he spoke, those around him hugged, kissed, cried and screamed with joy. For many, it was a singular moment to reclaim the same streets where the student-led call for change had been met by police wielding batons and teargas and even a suspected sound cannon. “It’s simply the realisation of our dream,” says Sara. “We will remember this moment for the rest of our lives.”

Brazil: defeated Flávio Bolsonaro ordered to surrender passports

The far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro was banned from leaving Brazil and ordered to surrender his passports just hours after his dramatic loss in the presidential election to the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. The ruling was issued by Alexandre de Moraes, the same supreme court justice who oversaw the trial of the senator’s father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, for attempting a coup. Bolsonaro posted a video saying the decision was based on an interview his brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, gave last Friday urging his brother to leave Brazil if he lost the election. On Monday night, Bolsonaro’s party issued a statement acknowledging the election result, saying: “We recognise the presidential result proclaimed by the electoral court, but believe that the questions raised need to be properly clarified through a balanced and democratic political debate.” Bolsonaro, like his father four years ago, has still not conceded defeat to Lula.

citation.title: Brazil: defeated Flávio Bolsonaro ordered to surrender passports

text:
Brazil: defeated Flávio Bolsonaro ordered to surrender passports

Related: How the streets and social media drove Lula to a historic comeback in Brazil The court’s brief ruling regarding his passport only refers to a criminal case in which the federal police are investigating Flávio Bolsonaro over his possible involvement in a money-laundering scheme. The ruling orders him not to have any contact with his friend Willer Tomaz, a lawyer linked to betting companies that police suspect were being used to launder about £680m. It also cancelled all of Bolsonaro’s passports, including the diplomatic one he holds as a congressman, and ordered him to hand them over within 24 hours. Bolsonaro was the first to speak publicly about the matter, before Brazilian media were even aware of the judge’s decision. In a video posted on social media, he said he had just left a visit to his father, who is under house arrest in Brasília, when “Lula’s federal police were at his door and in the middle of the street, and I was served with an order to hand over my passports and I am also prohibited from leaving the country”.

He added that, although his brother – who is in self-imposed exile in the US – told a US podcast on Friday that he favoured the senator leaving Brazil if he lost the election, “I never said that”. When his Senate term ends early next year, Bolsonaro will be out of public office for the first time in 24 years, and therefore without the special immunity afforded to officeholders. He is under investigation in another criminal case, too, over what happened to the £20m he was captured on tape asking a disgraced banker accused of corruption to provide for a biopic about his father. The Folha de S Paulo newspaper reported that Flávio Bolsonaro had been persuaded to drop his plan to seek to annul the election, which he had announced after the result was declared on Sunday night. Bolsonaro had claimed that the two-hour extension of voting – intended to allow voters who had been unable to access the mandatory free public transport to cast their ballots – had harmed the election, despite the fact that his own campaign had also argued for an extension.

text:
France will lurch from crisis to crisis until it confronts its retirement timebomb

I’m writing in response to your editorial (The Guardian view on France’s protests: a polarised country is in a perilous political moment, 19 October). While the focus is on Emmanuel Macron, let us not forget the hierarchical structure of French administration, from mayors to MPs to senators to prefects and heads of region. All are part of the government, but few stood up to bring leaky school roofs and missing teachers to national consciousness. I deplore the senseless destruction of shops and state buildings. But I also deplore the fact that students had to protest to be heard. In the many administrative tiers of this highly hierarchical country, no one acted and inertia prevailed. Centrally, the government is financially challenged but refuses to acknowledge that having a huge deficit, an ageing population and a low retirement age are perhaps connected. Modest attempts to increase the retirement age also provoked violent protests. Financial tools for individual retirement remain complex and restricted. Thus, this sclerotic system presses on until the next crisis.

citation.title: France will lurch from crisis to crisis until it confronts its retirement timebomb

text:
France will lurch from crisis to crisis until it confronts its retirement timebomb

Neither side of the populist fringe offers a viable path forward. Marine Le Pen’s National Rally and Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s La France Insoumise actively avoid confronting the retirement timebomb, preferring politically expedient promises over fiscal reality. If a system treats retirement as a sacred cow even when the meaning of work is being redefined at lightning speed by AI, if it’s acceptable to have productivity grind to a halt in August because the wisdom of asking employees to all take four to five weeks off in the same month while we live in a 24/7 world is never questioned, and if that same system lets young people study by rote in leaky classrooms while offering its over-60s free social dinners, let us not be surprised if the pressure valve is showing signs of fatigue. My concern is how much steam will be let out at the next convulsion. Muriel E Cockcroft France • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.
