Japanese prosecutors charge US marine suspected of robbing and killing woman

Prosecutors in Japan have filed formal charges against a US marine suspected of murdering and robbing a woman while stationed on the country’s island of Okinawa, according to Japanese media. Devin Jacob Ballard, a 20-year-old lance corporal assigned to Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Okinawa, is charged with fatally strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in the city and stealing from her a backpack containing a wallet, the public broadcaster NHK reported. Ballard had initially been arrested in Yagi’s killing on 4 October, about a day after she was found dead in Naha, Okinawa’s capital. Prosecutors indicted him in the case on Sunday, and he has reportedly denied the charges. Related: Japan PM leads outcry after US Marine arrested over alleged killing of woman on Okinawa NHK and other Japanese media outlets had previously reported that Ballard was arrested after surveillance camera footage from near the scene of Yagi’s killing showed a man entering a room with a woman and later leaving the scene with her belongings.

citation.title: Japanese prosecutors charge US marine suspected of robbing and killing woman

text:
Japanese prosecutors charge US marine suspected of robbing and killing woman

Ballard evidently matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage, was confronted and agreed to accompany investigators voluntarily to a local police station, Japanese media reported. While being questioned by police, Ballard denied having a hand in Yagi’s killing, saying, “I don’t know anything about it,” NHK reported. But during subsequent questioning Ballard was alleged to have “made statements that partially hinted at his involvement”, the broadcaster reported. A statement reported by NHK and reported to Yagi’s family on Sunday expressed a hope that Ballard “will confront what he has done and make amends commensurate with what he has done”. “She lost her life at the young age of 39,” the statement from Yagi’s family added. “She … wanted to live much, much longer.” Yagi’s killing prompted protests in Okinawa and the Japanese capital of Tokyo, with political leaders publicly condemning her killing. It also triggered a curfew and alcohol ban for US military members stationed in Okinawa, where most of the 54,000 US troops in Japan are based.

Japanese prosecutors charge US marine suspected of robbing and killing woman

Crimes committed by US troops in Japan – including rape, assault, hit-and-run and drunk-driving – have long strained relations between the countries, which are close military allies. A Japanese court in June 2025 sentenced US marine Jamel Clayton, then 22, to seven years in prison after he was convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a woman in her 20s. In 2017, a former US marine and civilian military base worker named Kenneth Shinzato was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local Okinawa woman. US military forces in Japan that same year banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated US marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing a local driver, age 61. The Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper reported that about 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested since the US returned Okinawa to Japan after the second world war in 1972. There were 80 such arrests in 2024, constituting a 20-year high.

text:
How the streets and social media drove Lula to a historic comeback in Brazil

After the first round of the Brazilian presidential election three weeks ago, the leftist incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva reportedly told allies he could not understand how he finished second after a government he considered the best of his three terms. A mood of dismay swept Brazil’s left, and because 9 million voters for the other candidates, all of them on the right, were expected to mostly transfer to senator Flávio Bolsonaro, analysts widely saw the far-right senator’s victory as certain. Then, on the night after the election, students from the Fluminense Federal University took to the streets of Niterói, a city of 480,000 across Guanabara Bay from Rio de Janeiro, to protest against the return to power of a member of the Bolsonaro family, whose patriarch, former president Jair Bolsonaro, Flávio’s father, is under house arrest for attempting a coup.

citation.title: How the streets and social media drove Lula to a historic comeback in Brazil

text:
How the streets and social media drove Lula to a historic comeback in Brazil

Two days later, another student protest took over downtown Rio and, in the days that followed, similar ones spread across the country in organic demonstrations that analysts and Lula himself agree gave new life to his campaign and played a decisive role in his historic comeback in the runoff. Related: ‘Democracy always’: Lula vows no return to dictatorship in Brazil after election win “I want to thank the generosity of Brazil’s young people who took to the streets to defend democracy,” Lula said in his victory speech on Sunday night after defeating Bolsonaro. Political scientist Fábio Vasconcellos said Lula’s victory, in which for the first time in Brazil’s democratic history a second-placed candidate overturned a first-round defeat in the runoff, could be explained by a combination of the streets, social media and the machinery of government – in recent weeks, Lula approved a “package of benefits” at the limits of what electoral law allows, including increasing and bringing forward payments from the main cash-transfer programme for poor families.

citation.title: How the streets and social media drove Lula to a historic comeback in Brazil

text:
How the streets and social media drove Lula to a historic comeback in Brazil

“The streets and social media almost overlap,” said Vasconcellos, a researcher with the Representation and Democratic Legitimacy group at the Federal University of Paraná. Two days after the first round, congressman André Janones, a Lula ally, created a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army”, where Janones sent audio messages, videos – often beginning with shouts of “Guys, urgent!” – and dozens of daily instructions on how to make pro-Lula content perform well on social media. The channel had 60,000 followers by the end of its first day and, by election Sunday, more than 10 million, and Lula’s digital reach overtook Bolsonaro’s. In his victory speech, Lula called Janones “our general”, who had the role of “raising the morale of our troops every day”. The congressman’s relentless efforts, which included a 24-hour YouTube live stream on the eve of the vote, led to him being admitted to hospital last week – the only day the WhatsApp channel went silent.

citation.title: How the streets and social media drove Lula to a historic comeback in Brazil

text:
How the streets and social media drove Lula to a historic comeback in Brazil

Lula’s campaign also overhauled his online communications, and the incumbent, who turns 81 on Tuesday, began recording selfie videos despite not owning a mobile phone. On Sunday night, he said he had been given a phone and that “from now on I’m going to talk a lot to the Brazilian people, many times a day, directly”. With the streets and social media, “the mood of defeat was gradually replaced by hopes of a comeback over those three weeks,” said Vasconcellos. Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right, said Lula’s comeback also represented “a broad rejection of the Bolsonarista project for Brazil”. Related: Lula supporters celebrate shock election victory – in pictures She has been interviewing undecided voters since May and said “the fear voters had, workers had, of losing rights and also of a possible concentration of power in Bolsonaro’s hands was very clear”, which meant that even people who did not like Lula voted for him this time. Bolsonaro had won 56.1m votes in the first round and received 3.7 million more in the runoff. Lula, by contrast, went from 53.9m to 64.2m.

citation.title: How the streets and social media drove Lula to a historic comeback in Brazil

text:
How the streets and social media drove Lula to a historic comeback in Brazil

The more than 10m-vote increase came both from persuading voters to turn out after historically high abstention in the first round and from convincing voters from other candidates, including Bolsonaro. “Some undecided voters we interviewed said Bolsonaro was a playboy who sided with big business, while at the same time spontaneously saying that, if he won, there would be a dictatorship in which people would lose rights,” said Rocha. Bolsonaro was also embroiled in several controversies recently, including saying he would use the new, even more conservative congress to change the constitution and “re-democratise” Brazil, as well as the two federal police inquiries in which he is under investigation over alleged corruption and money laundering. Many analysts have also pointed to the weight of Lula himself. “If it were another candidate, Bolsonaro would already have won in the first round,” said political scientist Helcimara de Souza Telles. Marco Aurélio de Carvalho, Lula’s campaign manager, answered without hesitation when asked what explained the historic election fightback: “President Lula.

How the streets and social media drove Lula to a historic comeback in Brazil

We have a great statesman on our team. We have a star player. That’s what absolutely made the difference. I haven’t the slightest doubt about it.” The question already occupying the minds of Brazil’s left is what happens next, given that Lula has said this was his last election. “That is a very big challenge because, in the polling on this, Lula’s dominance is still very strong. There is no one in his party with the same leadership,” said Rocha. Vasconcellos believes Lula’s re-election campaign, “from what we saw on the streets, offered the Brazilian left an opportunity for renewal”. “Lula’s party can learn from what happened and find better ways to connect with young people and urban voters who feel their concerns are not being heard,” he added. text:
Lula wins historic fourth term as Brazilian president in defeat of far-right Flávio Bolsonaro

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the Brazilian president, has staged a dramatic election fightback, defeating his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, to claim a historic fourth term in power. With 100% of votes counted the 80-year-old leftist received 4.4m votes more than Bolsonaro, with a 51.79% share to his 45-year-old rival’s 48.21%. However, soon after Brazil’s electoral authority confirmed Lula’s victory, Bolsonaro refused to concede defeat and asked for the results to be annulled. Lula narrowly lost the first round of the election to Bolsonaro in early October, casting his political future into doubt and plunging progressive Brazilians into three weeks of despair. Never, since the return of democracy in the 1980s, had the first round runner-up won the second vote. But Lula did precisely that on Sunday, prompting joyous scenes on the streets of São Paulo, where he had been following events, and at the hotel where he was watching the count.

citation.title: Lula wins historic fourth term as Brazilian president in defeat of far-right Flávio Bolsonaro

text:
Lula wins historic fourth term as Brazilian president in defeat of far-right Flávio Bolsonaro

Addressing a packed crowd of ecstatic supporters in a São Paulo conference hall, Lula said: “We are going to change the way that this country is governed … This election was a defeat for denialism … I want to thank God and to thank you, Brazilian men and women of this country … it was democracy that made this happen.” Interactive After the result was confirmed, Alexandre Padilha, Lula’s health minister, said: “This is a huge victory for the Brazilian people who in the second round had the chance to think about what President Lula means for the environment, for the defense of our national health service and our education system and the Brazilian constitution. And the risks that the extreme right candidate entailed. “It’s a massive victory – not just for Brazil. It’s also an important signal to the rest of Latin America and to the world,” Padilha added. The 80-year-old appears to have made up much of the difference through what his allies had identified as his main opportunity: persuading his voters to turn out.

citation.title: Lula wins historic fourth term as Brazilian president in defeat of far-right Flávio Bolsonaro

text:
Lula wins historic fourth term as Brazilian president in defeat of far-right Flávio Bolsonaro

After a record abstention rate of 21.08% in the first round, which disproportionately affected Lula voters because they tend to live further from polling stations, the rate fell to 19.21%. Speaking during Lula’s victory speech, Bolsonaro said it was “impossible to concede the election result” and that his legal team would seek to have the election annulled. Following in the footsteps of his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, who four years ago also refused to acknowledge his defeat to Lula – before attempting a coup and being convicted for it – the senator cited a supreme court justice’s decision to extend voting hours as the alleged reason. His speech made no mention of the fact that his campaign had also asked the electoral court to extend voting hours, but he nevertheless said Justice Cristiano Zanin’s decision to extend voting by two hours to 7pm “was not normal, it was unacceptable” and amounted to “changing the rules of the game while the game was being played”.

For Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, the victory represents a sensational final chapter in a storied political career that began when he emerged as a union leader in São Paulo’s industrial suburbs in the late 1970s. After entering politics, the former factory worker who was born in rural poverty made three unsuccessful presidential bids, in 1989, 1994 and 1998, before finally becoming Brazil’s first elected working-class president in 2002. Lula stepped down after the maximum two consecutive terms allowed by the constitution but returned to power after winning the 2022 election against Bolsonaro’s father, then the incumbent president Jair Bolsonaro, who was subsequently jailed for plotting a coup. Lula’s win is bad news for Jair Bolsonaro who is serving a 27-year sentence for that botched power grab and was hoping to be freed and given a role in government had his son prevailed. It is also a blow for Donald Trump, the Bolsonaro clan’s most important international ally.

The US president had been hoping Bolsonaro would become the latest in a series of pro-Trump leaders to take power in Latin America, including Abelardo de la Espriella in Colombia, Daniel Noboa in Ecuador, José Antonio Kast in Chile and Javier Milei in Argentina. Confirmation of Lula’s victory was greeted with anger and bewilderment in Brasília, where Bolsonaro is living under house arrest and where his son watched the count. On Sunday night, political leaders applauded Lula. The Mexican president, Claudia Sheinbaum, said: “Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won. Congratulations, ⁠President Lula!”, while Paraguay’s president, Santiago Peña, said “I salute the ⁠Brazilian people for this great democratic journey.” Lula’s victory came after his supporters staged two massive shows of support on Saturday, with more than a million people flocking to Rio’s Copacabana beach and an even larger number marching on Paulista Avenue in São Paulo.

Netanyahu reportedly pressured military to attack Iran in run-up to election

Benjamin Netanyahu has resorted to increasingly alarmist rhetoric and reportedly put pressure on Israel’s military to take action against Iran as his far-right coalition narrowly trails in the polls ahead of Tuesday’s close-run elections. Related: What you need to know about the most consequential election in Israel’s history The Israeli prime minister posted an AI-generated image of a nuclear mushroom cloud destroying Tel Aviv, telling Israeli voters to choose him or risk nuclear annihilation. “Anyone who cares about their own physical existence, that of their family, and their loved ones should have a trembling hand before voting for [the opposition],” he wrote in a social media post about Iran’s nuclear programme. Israel’s Channel 12 news reported that the prime minister and the armed forces chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, clashed in recent days over a directive to the military which could “potentially spark an immediate conflagration with Iran at a very sensitive juncture”, by provoking a miscalculation by Iran.

citation.title: Netanyahu reportedly pressured military to attack Iran in run-up to election

text:
Netanyahu reportedly pressured military to attack Iran in run-up to election

Zamir is reported to have requested the directive, the details of which were not specified, to be presented to him in writing. Netanyahu denied the report, and the defence ministry later denied any intention to carry out military operations against Iran. On Monday however, CNN reported that Netanyahu had tried to convince Donald Trump to launch a renewed assault on Iran in recent weeks, renewing the war both men started in February. The report, confirming an earlier account in the Financial Times, said Trump had ruled out any such action until US congressional elections next week. ‘We built this land’: descendants of enslaved people are reclaiming their history across South Africa’s vineyards

At Groot Constantia, the oldest wine farm in South Africa, the 450,000 visitors who pass through its gates annually can admire the picturesque vineyards sloping towards a bay ringed by mountains or enjoy a glass of sweet Grand Constance, reputed to have been Napoleon’s favourite wine. Unusually among the region’s old vineyards, there is also a museum that includes the history of slavery, run by state body Iziko Museums. Panels display information about enslaved people – about 30 of whom lived on the estate at any given time from its founding in 1685 until slavery was abolished in 1834 by the British colonial government – detailing everything from their work to what they ate. Two plaques list the names of people forcibly taken from Mozambique, Madagascar, India, Sri Lanka and Indonesia. “Today we pay tribute and acknowledge the enormous contribution of these men, women and children in the success of Groot Constantia and also acknowledge their oppression and suffering under slavery and their resilience and courage,” the plaques read.

What you need to know about the most consequential election in Israel’s history

On Tuesday Israel held its first election since the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks, the deadliest day in the country’s history, which resulted in the deaths of about 1,200 people, the majority of them civilians. Since then Israel has pursued a war of annihilation in Gaza, launched two inconclusive wars with Iran, and intensified a campaign of state-backed ethnic cleansing in the occupied West Bank. Domestically the coalition formed by Benjamin Netanyahu has taken aim at democratic institutions, including the supreme court. Many Israelis have described this election as the most consequential in their country’s history. Who are the main players? The prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has led Israel for 19 out of the last 30 years, most recently at the head of a far-right coalition. He is seeking a new mandate with the endorsement of the US president, Donald Trump, and the fight is personal as well as political. He is on trial for corruption; losing power may mean a greater risk of jail time.

citation.title: What you need to know about the most consequential election in Israel’s history

text:
What you need to know about the most consequential election in Israel’s history

His main rival is Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the Israeli military and relative political newcomer, the son of Moroccan immigrants who rose to the heart of Israel’s establishment from humble beginnings. His son and two nephews were killed fighting in Gaza in 2024. He lacks Netanyahu’s charisma, but has embraced that as part of a campaign positioning him as the opposite of Israel’s current leader, down to the name of his new party – Yashar, or “Honesty”. What are the key issues for voters? Israel’s security is at the heart of the election, overshadowing even the soaring cost of living. Opponents of the current government point to the catastrophe of the 7 October attacks, the erosion of democratic institutions, rise of religious extremism and the cost of open-ended, multi-front wars. They have promised a state commission of inquiry into 7 October, and most have pledged to end draft exemption for ultra-Orthodox men, a source of deep resentment among families whose loved ones are serving or have been killed.

citation.title: What you need to know about the most consequential election in Israel’s history

text:
What you need to know about the most consequential election in Israel’s history

They are also concerned about international isolation, amid broadening sanctions over settlement expansion, and an accelerating brain drain among the elite. Netanyahu has tried to shift blame for 7 October on to Israel’s security establishment, and despite presiding over the deadliest day in Israel’s history, he claims to be the only leader with the experience and international contacts to keep the country safe. He recently posted an AI image of a nuclear bomb hitting Tel Aviv on social media, with the claim “anyone who cares about their physical existence” should pause before voting for the opposition. His far-right allies have called for the ethnic cleansing of Gaza and the occupied West Bank, and expansion of settlements. His ultra-Orthodox partners want to preserve a decades-old exemption from conscription and subsidies for religious study. What are the polls saying? Most pre-election polls showed Netanyahu’s Likud and his current coalition parters losing their majority. That fall in voter support has been fairly consistent for more than two years. They also showed a clear anti-Netanyahu majority.

citation.title: What you need to know about the most consequential election in Israel’s history

text:
What you need to know about the most consequential election in Israel’s history

However, those opposition seats were divided between the bloc of Jewish Israeli parties, led by Eisenkot’s Yashar, and parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel. The Jewish Israeli parties are unlikely to have a majority on their own, but have mostly ruled out going into coalition with Palestinians. Palestinian politicians have indicated they might support a minority government of the Jewish Israeli parties in order to unseat Netanyahu’s far-right coalition. How does the system work and when might we get results/a new government? The Knesset has 120 seats, with lawmakers voted in through a system of proportional representation. No single party has ever claimed a majority of 61 seats, so Israel has always been governed by coalitions. When the results are in, the president invites the party with the largest number of seats to try to agree a governing coalition. The first indication of actual voting counts usually emerges in the early hours of the morning.

citation.title: What you need to know about the most consequential election in Israel’s history

text:
What you need to know about the most consequential election in Israel’s history

Getting full results could take much longer, with the outcome potentially hanging on the electoral fortunes of two small parties, which need to win 3.25% of the overall vote to take up seats in the Knesset. If they cross it, they each get four seats, which would have a significant impact on coalition building options. The far-right Amcha Yisrael is led by the former general Ofer Winter, who has pledged to back Netanyahu for prime minister if he gets into the Knesset. The Reservists is a rightwing Zionist party focused on ensuring universal conscription whose leaders sit between the two blocs. They have ruled out joining any government supported by either the ultra-Orthodox – key Netanyahu allies – or Palestinian parties whose backing Eisenkot is likely to need. If it goes down to the wire, counting could take more than a day. How democratic is the vote – and who is being disenfranchised? About 15 million people live in areas under Israeli control.

text:
What you need to know about the most consequential election in Israel’s history

Just over 7 million Jewish Israelis and 1.7 million Palestinian citizens of Israel live within the country’s pre-1967 borders, known as the “green line”, and have full voting rights. In the occupied West Bank, more than 500,000 Israeli settlers can vote. They live among 3.1 million Palestinians who are subject to military rule and do not have the right to vote. In occupied East Jerusalem more than 230,000 Israelis with voting rights live among 350,000 Palestinians who cannot vote. Two million Palestinians in Gaza, who live under Israeli military occupation, according to the international court of justice, also have no vote.

Xi Jinping’s corruption crackdown in the spotlight as China prepares for meeting of top leaders

When Xi Jinping came to power in 2012, he pledged to stamp out corruption all through the ranks of the Communist party. More than a decade later, the pace of investigations has not slowed. Last year, China’s disciplinary authorities opened investigations into more than 1 million people, including more than 100 officials at or above ministerial or provincial level. As Chinese Communist party (CCP) officials kick off an important meeting this week, discipline – and party loyalty – is high on the agenda. For those who try to read the tea leaves of elite Chinese politics, concern about the apparent lack of discipline is dominating CCP discussions. The “fifth plenum” began on Monday and is set to focus on “major issues on advancing the party’s full and rigorous self-governance”, according to a Chinese state media. In party-speak, “governance” is a byword for discipline, loyalty and anti-corruption.

citation.title: Xi Jinping’s corruption crackdown in the spotlight as China prepares for meeting of top leaders

text:
Xi Jinping’s corruption crackdown in the spotlight as China prepares for meeting of top leaders

Related: Taiwan charges five men over plot to run over comedian for his Xi Jinping jokes As Xi continues to crack down on corruption, the fact that investigations nearly always result in a conviction begs the question over whether targets are truly guilty of corruption, or are they just political rivals to the people in charge. Kerry Brown, director of the Lau China Institute at King’s College London, explained that in Xi’s worldview, which is obsessed with discipline and loyalty, there may not be much difference between the two. “If you’re corrupt, you’re not politically loyal. If you’re politically loyal, you’re not corrupt,” Brown said. He added that in the CCP system, “corruption is not just material things”, but also “spiritual corruption”, which includes political disloyalty. Some analysts argue that the reason that the anti-graft drive is so enduring is because corruption is a feature rather than a bug of an authoritarian, top-down political system with a sprawling bureaucracy that governs 1.4 billion people.

citation.title: Xi Jinping’s corruption crackdown in the spotlight as China prepares for meeting of top leaders

text:
Xi Jinping’s corruption crackdown in the spotlight as China prepares for meeting of top leaders

Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, said: “Xi has made the party less corrupt and strengthened his control, but he knows that tougher punishment cannot fully resolve the problem of officials putting their own interests ahead of the party’s. “Xi’s answer is to keep tightening discipline, making anti-corruption a permanent method of governing with no obvious point at which he can declare the job done,” Thomas said. The job may be never ending, but the plenum is an opportunity to refocus the party’s energy on discipline. The fifth plenum is the fifth of seven gatherings that normally happen in every five-year cycle between CCP congresses. The plenums bring together more than 300 members of the CCP’s Central Committee, the most senior officials in the party hierarchy. The meeting is particularly significant because it is likely to be the last substantive meeting before next year’s 21st Party Congress, where a new Central Committee will be chosen, and where Xi is expected to be anointed for a fourth term as the head of the CCP.

citation.title: Xi Jinping’s corruption crackdown in the spotlight as China prepares for meeting of top leaders

text:
Xi Jinping’s corruption crackdown in the spotlight as China prepares for meeting of top leaders

Eliminating anyone who poses a risk to his authority or to the party’s credibility is a key priority for Xi. And potential threats are everywhere. Nearly 15 years after Xi took office, according to CCP proclamations and a host of recent investigations, the problem is still not stamped out. “It is a deeply ingrained part of [Xi’s] worldview,” said Brown. “Everyone else is corrupt”. In the past, Xi has warned that the party could “lose its ruling status and inevitably be eliminated by history” if it could not get its house in order. “This is by no means an exaggeration,” he said. The current focus on party governance comes amid a host of high-profile investigations against senior party and military leaders.

citation.title: Xi Jinping’s corruption crackdown in the spotlight as China prepares for meeting of top leaders

text:
Xi Jinping’s corruption crackdown in the spotlight as China prepares for meeting of top leaders

In January, Zhang Youxia, China’s top general and a man second only to Xi in the military hierarchy, was placed under investigation; he was expelled from party last month, having already been removed from the military’s top ruling body, the Central Military Commission (CMC) A host of other purges means that the CMC, which normally has seven members, has been reduced to just two: Xi and Zhang Shengmin, the CMC’s head of discipline. Other recent scalps include Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang, and Huang Qifan, the former mayor of Chongqing. Huang had long been known as the ultimate survivor in Chinese politics because of his connections to the scandals in the early 2010s in which Xi’s political rival, Bo Xilai, the former Party boss for Chongqing, was embroiled in the death of the British businessman Neil Heywood. Bo was ultimately convicted of bribery and embezzlement, for which he is serving a life sentence, but Huang survived. No longer.

Some China analysts have asked whether the recent purges, which have reached the highest echelons of the Party and military ranks, indicate instability in the regime. But Xi likely sees it differently. Corruption investigations demonstrate who is in charge. Plus, Brown added, they are “the most easy and natural tool by which to enforce unity and discipline”.

Bayeux tapestry becomes pop culture hit as young people more keen to see exhibition than top films

A 1,000-year-old embroidery may be an unusual candidate for a pop culture moment, but young people are seemingly more willing to shell out for tickets for the Bayeux tapestry than spend money on Hollywood blockbusters. In the first hour that the second round of tickets to view the tapestry were available last Wednesday, payments from Monzo cardholders to the British Museum reached £14,100 and were 48 times that of a normal Wednesday morning. More than half (55%) of those buyers were aged under 35. This was double the opening mornings for this year’s blockbuster films: the critically acclaimed The Odyssey, at £7,000, and the box office smash hit Spider-Man: Brand New Day, at £6,300, according to the bank’s spending data for its 16 million customers. Tickets for the Bayeux Tapestry, which is on display in England for the first time since it was taken to France in the 11th century, are significantly more expensive than the average cinema ticket, at £33 for standard adult peak tickets and £27 for off-peak.

citation.title: Bayeux tapestry becomes pop culture hit as young people more keen to see exhibition than top films

text:
Bayeux tapestry becomes pop culture hit as young people more keen to see exhibition than top films

However, adjusting for the more expensive entrance fee – as well as the limited availability of tickets compared with a blockbuster movie – highlights the huge appeal of the tapestry. Related: Bayeux tapestrymania has gripped Britain. But what does it say about our own age of war and upheaval? | Charlotte Higgins As a result, buyers spent five times more on average at the checkout than on Spider-Man’s opening morning, at £97 versus £19. By the time the Bayeux tickets had been on sale for two hours, Monzo customers had spent £30,500. Enthusiasm was such that many buyers were willing to travel from across the country for the once-in-a-lifetime event, with almost half of the buyers based outside London, and the furthest purchases coming from Glasgow. Thousands joined an online queue to secure tickets when they went on sale at 10am on Wednesday, with spots selling out within three hours – beating the first wave, which sold out in 24 hours. The frenzy has drawn comparisons with big pop cultural events such as Glastonbury festival and the Oasis reunion tour.

The British Museum said the response to the tapestry going on display last month had been “extraordinary”, leading it to make changes to address lengthy queues for ticket holders, including banning visitors from taking photos. The exhibition has received rave reviews for its meticulous display of the woven record of the Norman Conquest, which is treasured for its impressive technical prowess, skilful storytelling and historical value. The Guardian described it as “a stupefying, thrilling, horrifying masterpiece that shakes the earth”.

‘Zero-energy companionship’: bizarre hobby takes seed among China’s stressed young adults

Young adults in China looking for a cheaper, low-maintenance alternative to having children or pets have found an answer: raising bricks. Bricks may not be as cuddly as cats or as life-affirming as human offspring, but they also cost next to nothing. “No cats, no dating, I started raising a brick,” wrote one brick parent on social media. Raising “brick babies” is easier than caring for house plants, involving spraying them with water a few times a day then waiting for moss spores already present in the atmosphere to attach themselves and grow. One Chinese media article described the bricks as being “practically immortal”. “If you forget to water them, the moss goes dormant. If you remember to water them again, the greenery returns.” A hashtag related to the trend has attracted more than 5m views on the Chinese social media platform Weibo. Chinese commentators have linked the trend to young people looking for low-effort routes to finding meaning in life. One brick “parent” told Chinese media the hobby created “a sense of accomplishment no less than completing a long-term project”.

citation.title: ‘Zero-energy companionship’: bizarre hobby takes seed among China’s stressed young adults

text:
‘Zero-energy companionship’: bizarre hobby takes seed among China’s stressed young adults

One user on Xiaohongshu, an Instagram-like platform, also known as Rednote, posted a picture of their rusty-coloured brick, saying “no output required, no KPIs to hit, no need to beg it to bloom [and] no comparing its growth with others”. Another user wrote: “My friends asked if I’d lost my mind. I said no, I’m just starting to raise a brick. “A brick gives me a sense of certainty that feels way more grounded than a lot of relationships. Psychologists call this ‘zero-energy emotional companionship.’ It fulfils your need for company without demanding any obligation to give love in return.” Young people in China are increasingly shunning the traditional expectations of society, such as having children and working long hours in strenuous jobs, assuming they can find one in the first place. Nearly one in five 16- to 24-year-olds, excluding students, are unemployed, according to official statistics. Some estimates put the unemployment rate much higher. China’s birthrate is in decline and fell to a record low last year.

text:
‘Zero-energy companionship’: bizarre hobby takes seed among China’s stressed young adults

Faced with a sluggish job market after years of intensely competitive studying, many young people are choosing to shun the rat race and opt instead for “lying flat” – pursuing a low-effort, low-stress lifestyle; one well-suited to raising bricks. The trend has become so popular that Chinese media have started to warn about the health risks. Cultivating moss could lead to the spread of mould, with some “brick parents” reportedly complaining of itchy eyes and runny noses. Xuedong Li, a retired professor of moss from Beijing’s Capital Normal University, urged people to keep their bricks in an enclosed environment. “It is best to wear disposable gloves and a mask during handling to reduce spore inhalation and skin contact,” Li told Chinese media. ‘It’s the smell of freedom’: Belgrade cleans up after Student List triumph

Student List cleaned up at Serbia’s parliamentary elections. So it was only fitting that the morning after a night of raucous celebrations, the movement’s supporters were gathering, bin bags in hand, at Pioneers Park, opposite the national assembly building in Belgrade. For the previous 18 months, this small patch of greenery – with its established trees and playground – had been a no-go zone. A pro-government camp known as Ćaciland had taken over the space with convicted criminals living there in white tents, happy to attack journalists, or anyone else who came too close. Police stood by but did nothing to prevent the violence. On election night, it seemed that thuggery might be on the cards again. Half an hour before the polls closed, large numbers of masked, black-clad men started gathering in and around Pioneers Park. Their intimidating presence gave credence to pre-poll predictions that the governing Serbian Progressive party (SNS) would not hand over power without a struggle. What happened next took almost everyone by surprise.

citation.title: ‘It’s the smell of freedom’: Belgrade cleans up after Student List triumph

text:
‘It’s the smell of freedom’: Belgrade cleans up after Student List triumph

Shortly after the polls closed – and before any projections of the results had been published – Aleksandar Vučić told supporters at SNS headquarters that they had suffered a comprehensive defeat to the Student List. As cheers rang around the heart of Belgrade, he added that he did “not want unrest” or “anything like that on the streets”. The riot police stood aside and the barriers blocking access to the area around Pioneers Park were removed. The goon squad made a rapid exit – and Student List supporters joyfully ransacked Ćaciland, setting fire to some of the tents. But this is not a movement that likes to leave a mess. Over the two years of anti-corruption protests that led to the Student List’s victory, participants have always cleaned up after themselves. So the call went out for volunteers to restore Pioneers Park to something approaching its previous state. Hundreds of people answered the appeal and joined municipal workers to remove the remains of Ćaciland.

citation.title: ‘It’s the smell of freedom’: Belgrade cleans up after Student List triumph

text:
‘It’s the smell of freedom’: Belgrade cleans up after Student List triumph

Some dismantled the mangled white tents, while others painstakingly cleaned and disinfected the climbing frames, swings and slides in the children’s playground. Radomir Dalic painstakingly combed over the grass to remove cigarette butts and other rubbish. Apparently relishing his labours, he said he was overjoyed that the park was finally rid of “criminals with violent intentions towards us”. “Yesterday was a big victory, so today is the smell of freedom,” he added. “We are in garbage, but it’s the smell of freedom.” Tamara Tomic wore yellow rubber gloves for the occasion – and radiated similar pride in taking part. “Gathering here and cleaning this place just shows that we want to live nicely,” she said. “We want to enjoy the city, enjoy a normal life without violence and without anyone torturing us.” For now, nobody is asking too many questions about how the Student List will govern. In fact, Serbian voters have taken something of a leap into the unknown – because this is a movement that operates unlike a traditional political party. It has no hierarchy and no leader.

citation.title: ‘It’s the smell of freedom’: Belgrade cleans up after Student List triumph

text:
‘It’s the smell of freedom’: Belgrade cleans up after Student List triumph

Its candidates were chosen by a series of student assemblies, with nominations ranging from academics to athletes, economists to engineers. The Student List did publish an 11-point plan. Most of these points deal with anti-corruption measures – ironically, the pitch that secured victory in 2012 for Vučić and the SNS. Other commitments include judicial reform, media freedom, affordable housing and improved access to healthcare, with the promise of “a doctor in every village”. But beyond the domestic priorities – in essence, a clean-up for public institutions – little is clear. The Student List went into the elections without naming a candidate for prime minister, let alone a possible cabinet. Kurt Bassuener, co-founder of the Democratization Policy Council, said he was concerned about what that might mean when the euphoria of victory died down, and the serious business of forming a government began. The thinktank chief added: “I’m hoping that there is a dream scenario plan here – they have portfolios and people who have credibility in particular issue areas and they can hit the ground running.

citation.title: ‘It’s the smell of freedom’: Belgrade cleans up after Student List triumph

text:
‘It’s the smell of freedom’: Belgrade cleans up after Student List triumph

Because the danger of a broad coalition like this is that the fissures will show soon after victory.” Ilija Srdanović, the candidate ranked first on the Student List, has played down the potential for strife. A cardiologist at the university in Novi Sad, the city where a deadly roof collapse sparked the student protests, he has protested alongside the students since the early days. However, he was keen to emphasise that his ranking on the list did not mean he would become prime minister. “The student movement is fully democratic,” he said, adding that the aim was to buck Serbia’s history of “creating the cult of personality or leadership”. The 250 candidates on the Student List were “equal subjects in this struggle”, Srdanović insisted, with “numerous candidates who can be chosen for the prime minister position or any other position”. But his confidence does little to reassure those who have noticed that the broad spread of views held by Student List candidates could lead to trouble.

‘It’s the smell of freedom’: Belgrade cleans up after Student List triumph

Despite Vučić’s warnings that a Student List government would impose sanctions on Russia and recognise Kosovo’s unilateral declaration of independence, the movement’s foreign and regional policy remains opaque. “We have not seen seas of EU flags at demonstrations by students or the marches across Serbia,” said Michael Davenport, a former EU and UK ambassador to the country. “There are massive policy areas where there is no consensus among the Student List or those have been elected. The approach towards accession to the European Union is not clear, nor is the position with regard to regional issues like Bosnia and Herzegovina and, very particularly, Kosovo.” Many people are happy to leave these concerns for another day. Vučić and the SNS have fallen – and the cacophony of car horns continued throughout Monday as drivers passed the clean-up crew in Pioneers Park. One visible symbol of the old regime has been swept away. The Student List voters are hoping more will follow.

Chinese markets lose trillions as race for AI supremacy with US takes its toll

Trillions of dollars have been wiped from China’s stock markets in recent months amid increasing anxiety about the future of artificial intelligence, as Beijing races against the United States for dominance in the sector. The STAR 50 Index, which tracks technology and innovation companies on the Shanghai stock exchange, has plunged 40% since June. Other indexes of major companies dropped by about 20% over the same time period. The precipitous drop has wiped out $2.4tn from the Chinese stock market since May, according to Bloomberg. AI stocks account for over 40% of the stock market value in China and Hong Kong, according to Goldman Sachs, meaning that any dent in value will send shockwaves across the whole domestic market. Related: US bans use of China’s DeepSeek AI tools by government agencies The fall suggests that despite the government’s best efforts to boost China’s technology industries, particularly those which harness the power of AI, the domestic economy does not have the power to sustain a booming market.

citation.title: Chinese markets lose trillions as race for AI supremacy with US takes its toll

text:
Chinese markets lose trillions as race for AI supremacy with US takes its toll

The Chinese government has invested heavily into AI, including a 60bn yuan state-backed AI investment fund which started pumping money into domestic developers this month. But Chinese consumers have proved stubbornly reluctant to part with their cash in many parts of the economy – including technology – meaning that many tech companies struggle to turn a profit. The lack of profits is one of several reasons for the sell-off. Another is the threat of western countries, especially the US, extending bans on Chinese technology. “This year, the profit margin is not as good as expected. And the US is raising rates. And China’s domestic demand is so weak,” said Dan Wang, the China director for the Eurasia Group. She said that there was a “general anxiety” among technology companies about whether or not the state-backed model would work in the face of weak consumer demand. The US has banned humanoid robots from China, citing national security risks, and is thought to be considering a ban on Chinese components in data centres.

citation.title: Chinese markets lose trillions as race for AI supremacy with US takes its toll

Chinese markets lose trillions as race for AI supremacy with US takes its toll

China is heavily reliant on exports and restrictions in the US hurt its domestic companies, which struggle to sell enough products at home. As China races with the US to pull ahead in AI, Beijing has doubled down on robotics – also known as embodied AI – as the key to rolling out the technology across society. Robotics is also seen as the answer to China’s demographic problems, such as the ageing population and the shrinking workforce. But the demand for robotics is being driven by government agencies and research institutions, rather than everyday consumers, for whom the products are still too expensive and not yet practical for home use. Humanoid robotics and robotic dogs have been popular in the entertainment industry but are yet to be useful in home settings. Shares in Unitree, China’s leading robot-maker, have halved since they started trading in August. “It doesn’t look like embodied intelligence could turn into profits in the in the mass market,” said Wang.

Thin profit margins, rising rates in the US, and weak domestic demand were all contributing to a “general anxiety” among technology companies, she said. China’s government wants local investors to invest their money domestically. China has in recent months restricted overseas investment, with more regulations taking effect from 1 December, but these moves have not led to greater investment in the Chinese markets. The company is expected to bring in as much as $100bn. China has no such blockbuster IPOs on the horizon.

And despite pressure on policymakers to introduce stimulus measures to boost investment, none are expected to be announced during a politically sensitive period in China. This week the top officials in the Chinese Communist party are gathering for the fifth plenum, an important meeting that will lay the groundwork for next year’s 21st Party Congress. There is no appetite for risky or potentially destabilising policy measures before then, even if there is a chance they could boost the economy. Flávio Bolsonaro flees Brazil after presidential election loss, reports say

The far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro has reportedly fled Brazil and is on his way to the United States after losing Sunday’s presidential election to the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who called the act “shameful”. A report by the news website Metrópoles, citing people close to the politician’s family, said he was en route to the US. “The plane is in flight,” Metrópoles reported, without making clear where it had departed from. Bolsonaro allies told Metrópoles that he would land in Florida on Tuesday afternoon and planned to request political asylum. “The Donald Trump administration has been informed,” the website added. Argentina’s government confirmed that Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters had crossed the border into Argentina and boarded a private flight to Ecuador, at 11.30pm on Tuesday night. “They did so with valid travel documentation and without any legal impediment to entering the country,” Argentina’s National Directorate of Migration said on X.

Israel election too close to call as exit polls give Netanyahu bloc slightly fewer seats

Israel’s election appeared to have delivered no clear winner on Tuesday night after a historic turnout by voters for an election described by some as the most consequential in the country’s history, and marked by a record participation by Israeli Arab voters. Exit polls published on Tuesday evening suggested that the opposition bloc of parties led by the former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, Gadi Eisenkot, would win most seats in the Knesset by a slight margin, edging out Benjamin Netanyahu’s right and far-right coalition despite the prime minister’s Likud emerging as the largest party. The result is likely to set off weeks of jockeying over who can form a coalition government before a prime minister is declared or another round of elections is called, but represents a sharp electoral rebuke to Netanyahu. After a day in which Israelis streamed to polling stations across the country, exit polls suggested Netanyahu’s ability to command the loyalty of a large core of Likud party voters remained undimmed despite his rejection by large numbers of Israelis.

While Eisenkot could theoretically assemble a majority by forming a government with the Arab parties, he ruled that out before the election. The exit polls – if they prove accurate – suggest a struggle for either Likud or Eisenkot’s Yashar to find a road to a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. Likud’s projected showing, not for the first time, appears to have defied predictions in the run-up to the vote. Jacinda Ardern joins University of Sydney as lecturer and mentor

The former New Zealand prime minister Jacinda Ardern will lecture and mentor at the University of Sydney after moving to Australia earlier this year. Ardern begins this month and her work will focus on empathetic leadership, social cohesion and civic trust. The University of Sydney said Ardern would be based in its school of public health, exploring ways to address global health challenges and focusing on equity, inclusion and wellbeing. The former prime minister will host guest lectures and masterclasses and will engage in mentoring, but the university said it was not a full-time teaching role. “I’m delighted to be joining the University of Sydney,” Ardern said. “I’ve found myself especially focused on the question of leadership since leaving office – and how we can better support and encourage the kind of leadership needed to tackle our many global challenges.” Related: Jacinda Ardern and husband Clarke Gayford buy $5.3m home in Sydney’s northern beaches The University of Sydney vice-chancellor, Mark Scott, said he had long admired the courage and humanity Ardern brought to public life.

“Dame Jacinda led New Zealand through events of profound consequence and her leadership demonstrated that empathy and resolve do not compete with one another; each can strengthen the other,” he said. “For our students, the opportunity to learn from Dame Jacinda is exceptional. They will meet not only a former prime minister, but a thoughtful teacher with a great deal to share about public leadership and service.” In an ABC Conversations interview in July, Ardern said she believed people were seeking empathetic leadership despite many world leaders embodying a “dominant style” of leadership. “You see people voting for parties [that] are often on the fringes of the mainstream. When you dive into the research, the majority of those who are doing that are often not voting for the ideology – they’re just voting against the status quo because they don’t think it serves them any more. “So I think all the signs actually point to people wanting something different than what they’re getting now.” Ardern retired from politics in January 2023, after more than five years as prime minister and the leader of the Labour party.

text:
The life and death of Jaysley Beck: how her mother turned detective – and took on the military

When Leighann McCready phoned her 19-year-old daughter, Jaysley Beck, on 15 December 2021, she got no reply, but brushed away her worries. “Jays always, always answered her phone, but it was early, eight in the morning,” she says. Beck, an army soldier in the Royal Artillery, had been at a party the night before at her Wiltshire barracks. She was probably asleep. It was a busy time, the Christmas countdown. Soon, Beck was expected to be back home in Cumbria, where her parents – McCready and Anthony Beck – own a village pub. McCready had already bought matching Christmas pyjamas for Beck and her older sister Emilli to wear on the day. Beck had been preparing for the holidays, too. She had been Christmas shopping two days earlier, calling and consulting throughout the day with her mum, who was transferring the cash to cover it all. She’d bought presents for herself and her sister: a Gucci bag, a belt and a purse. For her dad, she’d bought tickets for a James Blunt concert for the two of them to attend together in February.

citation.title: The life and death of Jaysley Beck: how her mother turned detective – and took on the military

text:
The life and death of Jaysley Beck: how her mother turned detective – and took on the military

At the end of the spree, Beck had messaged her mum: “We’re two so lucky girls aren’t we, Mum? Thank you, thank you, thank you. I love you with all my heart!” Despite all this, as the hours passed that Tuesday in December, with still no word from Beck, McCready began to feel a deep foreboding. She knew that, in the preceding weeks, her daughter had been struggling through a strange and intense period of escalating harassment from her line manager. With this in mind, Emilli offered to call one of Beck’s friends at the barracks, who assured them that Beck was probably fast asleep. “He said he was five minutes away and he’d go and wake her,” says McCready. “That five minutes just seemed like forever. I continued ringing Jays’ phone – until somebody else answered it. The voice said: ‘Hello, can I ask who I’m speaking to?’ And I just knew. They didn’t even have to tell me.” Gunner Beck had taken her life, alone in her bedroom. Her suicide threw a spotlight on the British army and the treatment, safety and protection of female recruits.

citation.title: The life and death of Jaysley Beck: how her mother turned detective – and took on the military

text:
The life and death of Jaysley Beck: how her mother turned detective – and took on the military

For the last five years, ever since Beck’s death, McCready has fought for answers and accountability. She has found some, but believes there is still far more to uncover. At every step – the service inquiry, the inquest and a subsequent police investigation – McCready has been in the public eye, talking to the press, advocating for her daughter. Now, she features in a Stacey Dooley documentary, Death in the Barracks, which follows the family’s continued search for justice. She still can’t quite believe that any of it is real. “Grief is not what you see on TV, where you instantly fall to the floor and break down in tears,” says McCready, who has worked for 30 years in the care sector, much of it as an end-of-life nurse. “The moment I found out, I automatically went from being a mum, a partner, a daughter, to quite literally feeling as if I was putting my uniform on. It was about protecting a family and guiding them. No matter how many interviews I do or how many times I see Jays’ photo in the news, it doesn’t register. That isn’t my daughter – and this isn’t my life.

citation.title: The life and death of Jaysley Beck: how her mother turned detective – and took on the military

text:
The life and death of Jaysley Beck: how her mother turned detective – and took on the military

I call it my ‘invisible uniform’ and I have never taken it off.” Beck had joined the army at 16. “As a child, I used to call her my baby muck-magnet,” says McCready. “She was a cheeky little chops – pulling out her pigtails, collecting snails. She loved helping her dad with DIY. You always knew when Jays was around.” Aged 15, she’d returned from a school careers day intent on joining the army. McCready wasn’t keen. “I hadn’t expected that in a million years,” she says. “I thought it was a phase, but she was determined. She put her heart and soul into it. I remember her running round the village wearing backpacks weighted with bricks to build her strength up. She was only tiny – probably a size six in clothes.” After Beck’s initial military training, her family attended her passing in parade at Army Foundation College Harrogate. “It was magical,” says McCready. “I was a proud mum.” Beck settled happily into army life – but in her final six months, that changed.

citation.title: The life and death of Jaysley Beck: how her mother turned detective – and took on the military

text:
The life and death of Jaysley Beck: how her mother turned detective – and took on the military

In July 2021, at a training exercise, Beck was sexually assaulted by Michael Webber (then 39, married, and a battery sergeant major). She escaped, then spent the night hiding in her car. When Beck reported the incident to senior officers, she was advised not to be “a female troublemaker”, and was urged to think of Webber’s career, and his family. Eventually, after she reported it a second time, Webber was asked to write Beck a letter of apology. He was promoted shortly afterwards. This meant that, three months later, when her line manager, bombardier Ryan Mason, 32, began showing an obsessive interest in Beck, she had no faith in any complaints process, and nowhere to turn. McCready had known all this as it happened. “Jays told me everything,” she says. Her daughter had even shared Mason’s messages on a family WhatsApp – he sent more than 4,600 in two months. The family had tried to advise and support her, but they were hundreds of miles away, and military protocol was a strange, sealed world. “When she was assaulted by Michael Webber, she’d said: ‘Get off me, sir.’” says McCready.

citation.title: The life and death of Jaysley Beck: how her mother turned detective – and took on the military

text:
The life and death of Jaysley Beck: how her mother turned detective – and took on the military

“I remember my first reaction was: ‘How, Jays, did you call him “sir”?’ Some of it was over my head.” In the days after Beck’s death, as their home filled with military personnel, McCready became determined to bring all she knew to light. “Jays was not going to be another statistic. She was not another ‘sudden passing’,” she says. “I was not a ‘grieving mum’. You have to be stronger than that,” she continues. “I had to keep going for Jays and also for Emilli. What would she do if I broke? She’d crumble, she wouldn’t be far behind me.” Christmas was days away, so McCready asked Emilli how they should spend it. Should they even get a tree? “Emilli said: ‘Lets do the tree, and let’s still go to Auntie’s as planned for Christmas Day.’ So that’s what we did,” says McCready. “It didn’t feel right, but nothing would have felt right. I printed up a big picture of Jaysley and asked if I could put it in the tree so she’d be watching.” McCready didn’t touch any alcohol – in fact, she hasn’t had a drop since losing her daughter. “I don’t want alcohol to affect my emotions,” she says.

citation.title: The life and death of Jaysley Beck: how her mother turned detective – and took on the military

The life and death of Jaysley Beck: how her mother turned detective – and took on the military

She doesn’t watch TV either. “I don’t think it’s good for my mindset. I remember trying to settle down one night – I think it was [with] Gogglebox – and the first thing that was shown was a mortuary. I couldn’t turn it off quick enough.” Her “invisible uniform”, her years in end-of-life care, guided all her decisions in those first weeks. “I knew I needed to be kind to my mind, to bubble-wrap it and protect it,” she says. “I chose not to see Jays after her passing and I don’t regret it. I know from my work that it’s just a shell left behind, and do I want to see my daughter’s shell? Instead, I can close my eyes and she’s that happy little girl – she’s smiling, she’s singing, she’s running round the block with her backpack on. I didn’t deal with the coroner – I didn’t want to know details.” What she did want, instantly and urgently, was to visit Beck’s room in Larkhill garrison. She had to push for access. “I was told I was not allowed, so we had a meeting. I explained how much I needed this moment. I wanted to lie on my daughter’s bed.

I wanted to know the last bit of music she played – Jays loved music, we always shared songs and playlists. What was the last bit of laundry she put in her laundry basket? How do her clothes smell?” The family were finally allowed entry on 28 December, although they were initially informed that they had to be accompanied. “I said: ‘Absolutely not.’” McCready had another motive, too. “I needed to gather as much information to find out what happened,” she says. “I wanted the letter of apology from Michael Webber – I knew exactly where she’d filed it. I wanted her smart watch and her laptop. I got all of them. I did want her phone, too – but Wiltshire police had already taken that.” Months later, when the police had done nothing with the phone, McCready returned to Wiltshire to collect it, having argued successfully that she had paid for it – so it was in fact hers, not Beck’s. “Not only had I put my invisible uniform on, in my mind, I was also becoming a detective,” McCready says.

“I sat down with a roll of wallpaper and I did a timeline.” She also found a lawyer through the Centre for Military Justice. “We’ve been on this journey together and we’ve had to push for every single inquiry and investigation since.” There have been some answers. After the inquest, the coroner’s summing-up report found Mason’s “intolerable harassment” and “the daily barrage of messages, calls and face-to-face encounters” to have been a significant factor in Beck’s suicide. As her line manager, Beck found Mason possessive and manipulative, setting the rota so that they were always together. He said that he loved her, composed messages that ran to essays, called her at night and engaged in lengthy conversations, sometimes until 4am (when she had to be up at 6am). On 7 December 2021 – a week before Beck’s death – Mason and Beck had been staying in a hotel for a recruitment event when Beck left suddenly in the night, after calling a friend while in tears, who drove over and took her back to barracks.

text:
The life and death of Jaysley Beck: how her mother turned detective – and took on the military

At the inquest, giving evidence, Mason said that he did not know the reason for Beck’s sudden departure that night. (He left the army the day after the recruitment event.) The summing-up also found that the earlier mishandling of Beck’s sexual assault complaint against Webber had left her “with a feeling of injustice but, more importantly, [a loss of] faith in her ability to complain effectively”. After the inquest, Webber was charged with sexual assault and, last October, pleaded guilty. He was sentenced to six months. Other factors were identified as “significant” by the coroner, foremost Beck’s “turmoil” around her intimate relationships. In November 2021, she had separated from her long-term boyfriend – although the two remained friends. She’d then embarked on an affair with a married sergeant. She was a 19-year-old girl, says McCready, making some mistakes and finding her way – and none of this explains why her daughter, who had never reported any mental health problems, should so suddenly end her life.

text:
The life and death of Jaysley Beck: how her mother turned detective – and took on the military

“Truth be told, there are still so many unanswered questions,” says McCready, “but I’m trying not to let them into my head. It won’t change anything for Jays. Instead, I’m trying to focus on changing things for the next people.” She welcomes MoD plans to tackle “unacceptable behaviours” in the military, including a Violence Against Women and Girls taskforce and a tri-service team, covering the army, navy and RAF, which will take serious complaints out of the single chain of command. “It’s going in the right direction,” she says, “but it’s not enough. The reporting system has to be independent, separate from the army. I’m still contacted daily by soldiers, veterans and their families who have their own stories of rape, assault, bullying, harassment – and it’s not just females.” She hopes the Dooley documentary will encourage more to come forward, and she’s in the process of establishing a formal organisation, Jaysley’s Voice, to advocate on their behalf. Meanwhile, Christmas – that most difficult anniversary – is coming.

‘We want a full apology for slavery’: Commonwealth at a crossroads as king heads to the Caribbean

King Charles’s upcoming Caribbean tour could accelerate moves to remove him as head of state in several countries unless he does more to confront the monarchy’s historic links to slavery, campaigners have warned. The king will embark on a nine-day tour on Tuesday, visiting the Bahamas and Guyana before travelling to Antigua and Barbuda, and will attend the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm). Related: King Charles urged ‘as human brother’ to support reparations talks at Caribbean summit Patrick Vernon, a cultural historian and UK representative of the Global Jamaica Diaspora Council, said the stakes for this trip could not be higher for the future of the royal family’s standing in the region, warning: “I think it’s the biggest crossroads for the Commonwealth since its creation.” Charles is expected to deliver three significant speeches during the trip, but will follow government advice not to issue a formal apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade. The British government has also ruled out paying reparations.

Legacy of 7 October looms large as a divided Israel goes to the polls in record numbers

Election day in Israel began with a protest by some of the voters with most at stake. Bereaved families of those killed in the 7 October attacks held a minute of silence at 6.29am, the moment when Hamas launched its onslaught just over three years ago. They gathered in a Tel Aviv plaza that has become known as “hostages square” because it was the centre of demonstrations demanding the return of more than 200 captives from Gaza. Holding pictures of their loved ones, they stood in silence then called on voters to remember the losses and betrayals of that day when deciding on the next government. “Three years after the massacre, our loved ones will not be voting today. Go out and vote – remember them at the ballot box. This is what these elections are about,” the group said. They are not explicitly backing any political party, but one of their key demands is a state commission of inquiry into the attacks. Benjamin Netanyahu has resisted this and it has become a rallying point for the opposition parties trying to unseat him as prime minister.

Netanyahu’s strongest challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, started the day by visiting communities attacked on 7 October. “If someone in the government had a shred of responsibility, they would start the morning here,” said the former military chief and leader of the Yashar party. Standing in a cheering crowd, Eisenkot called on all Israelis to vote to get rid of “the worst government Israel has known”. He noted that victory wasn’t certain, adding that “we are on perhaps the most critical day since the founding of the state”. As the day wore on, it became clear that voter turnout was shattering all records and among those lining up at polling stations were tens of thousands of Israelis who live overseas. A bipartisan “Fly&Vote” initiative was set up to support those who wanted to return because electoral law only allows voting in person. While not everyone coming back was opposed to the government, anecdotal evidence suggested many were opposition supporters who held the view that Israel faced an existential choice. Monica Moria, 58, and her husband, Ron, flew in to Tel Aviv from Barcelona.

Melting glaciers in Dolomites reveal cache of first world war munitions

A significant cache of unexploded bombs from the first world war emerged this summer from rapidly retreating glaciers in the Dolomites, the Italian army has said. The devices, which included Italian artillery shells and French mortar bombs, were removed and defused by the army’s Julia Alpine brigade, according to a statement. The weapons originated from the white war, a battle between the Austro-Hungarian army and Italian troops across treacherous and bitterly cold terrain between 1915 and 1918. More than a century later, hikers reported several sightings of bombs during the summer, mostly in the area of Canal San Bovo in the Primiero Valley in eastern Trentino. The soldiers then conducted an extensive sweep there and across other high-altitude and glacier locations in the Trentino Alto Adige region of the Dolomites. They recovered and neutralised 250 explosives, including “18 Italian 75mm artillery shells and 37 Thevetot mortar shells – a French-made device that was also supplied to the Italian royal army during the first world war”, the Julia Alpine brigade.

citation.title: Melting glaciers in Dolomites reveal cache of first world war munitions

text:
Melting glaciers in Dolomites reveal cache of first world war munitions

It is not the first time that relics of the white war have emerged from melting glaciers, whose retreat has accelerated over more than decade. “It is very much a consequence of global heating,” said Stefano Morosini, a professor at the University of Bergamo and the coordinator of heritage projects at Stelvio national park, where some of the explosives were also found. “In recent years, at the end of each summer, these dangerous artefacts emerge and each year there is a higher number. They have been conserved by the ice for more than 100 years. Some had already exploded but many hadn’t, so now when they re-emerge, they are very, very dangerous.” The advice to hikers and mountaineers is to “never touch any type of explosive device you might find, regardless of where it is located” and to promptly report any discovery to police.

citation.title: Melting glaciers in Dolomites reveal cache of first world war munitions

text:
Melting glaciers in Dolomites reveal cache of first world war munitions

Fought mainly in the Dolomites of Trentino Alto-Adige and the Alps of the Lombardy region, the white war was a period of history frozen in time until the 1990s, when global heating started to reveal an assortment of perfectly preserved relics, including weapons, sledges, letters and diaries. Related: Melting ice reveals first world war relics in Italian Alps A wooden barracks that had been dug into a cave on the top of Mount Scorluzzo, a 3,095-metre (10,154ft) peak overlooking the Stelvio pass, reappeared in 2015 after the ice which had sealed it off for almost a century completely melted. The shelter had been hastily locked up when the first world war ended in November 1918, and the soldiers abandoned most of their belongings. Beds made of straw as well as clothes, lanterns, newspapers, postcards, coins, and tinned food were found well preserved inside. A white war museum to host the relics is scheduled to open in Bormio in June 2027. The white war is estimated to have claimed as many as 180,000 lives, although the majority of deaths were likely caused by avalanches, falling down mountains or hypothermia.

Dozens of corpses, some still in their uniforms, have emerged from the melting ice over the past 15 years. The relatives of an Italian soldier were able to bury him in 2017 after documents revealing his identity were found with his body on Presena glacier. Eleven people died when a huge mass of the Marmolada glacier broke off in 2022. “It is becoming more and more impossible to access the glaciers during the summer because of the very long heatwave at high altitude,” he said. “If you come to the area, you can see how fast the glaciers are retreating and how strong the impact of climate change is.” • This article was amended on 28 October 2026. Oleshky truce appears to hold as two European leaders have ‘frank’ call with Putin

A local ceasefire in a southern Ukrainian city under Russian occupation appeared to be holding on Tuesday, with both sides ceasing drone attacks ahead of an apparent evacuation of about 2,000 trapped and desperate civilians. The temporary truce began at 3am in Russian-controlled Oleshky. The city sits on the Dnipro River and is about 3 miles (5km) from Kherson, a larger city on the opposite bank. Ukrainian troops recaptured Kherson in autumn 2022. Interactive Witnesses reported that the deadly frontline across the river was quiet for the first time in four years. The pause in fighting is due to last until 11pm on Sunday, Ukrainian officials said, and represents a significant if limited moment of de-escalation. Finland’s president, Alexander Stubb, and Norway’s prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, held what they described as a “frank and substantive” phone call with Vladimir Putin about efforts to end the war in Ukraine. Støre indicated afterwards that big differences remained.

text:

The two Nordic leaders said the call – a rare instance of direct contact between Putin and western leaders – was linked to upcoming talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US, expected to take place in Abu Dhabi next month. The ceasefire in Oleshky appears to be an attempt by the Kremlin to curry favour with Donald Trump before the trilateral meeting and next week’s US midterm elections. The first lady, Melania Trump, requested the humanitarian mission, and in a post on X said it was brought forward by two days to allow the delivery of critical aid. Its geographical scope had been extended beyond Oleshky “within the Kherson region”, she added, to provide safe passage for convoys. Calls for a ceasefire were also issued by Pope Leo, the United Nations, EU officials and the Council of Europe. Between 1,500 and 2,000 people in the city have been living under a complete blockade by Russia. The last delivery of food to stores was in May, and many people are now starving and eating weeds.

The Ukrainian military has airdropped food using drones but locals say Russian security forces detain anyone who takes it. Some Oleshky residents have managed to escape, walking or cycling past bodies lying on the street and the burnt-out shells of vehicles. Ukrainian observers say the Kremlin is planning a major propaganda tour this week in which Kyiv is blamed for Oleshky’s destruction. Trump-supporting US media channels have been invited to witness the evacuation, in which buses will take residents to occupied Crimea and Russia. Ksenia Arkhipova, who fled the city in 2022 and now, as a volunteer, helps others leave, said some residents have told her they fear Russian officials may “filter out” evacuees with pro-Ukraine views.

text:
Olivia Chow elected as Toronto mayor for second term in victory for progressives

The mayor of Toronto, Olivia Chow, promised more rental housing, free school lunches and reduce fares for frequent transit riders after she was elected to a decisive second term as mayor in a wave of support for progressive councillors. The tightly fought election saw record turnout but Chow ultimately turned in a dominant 13-percentage-point win over her rival, Brad Bradford, receiving 54% of the vote compared with his 41%. Many had been expecting a far closer race, given weeks of polling that suggested a dead heat between the pair who presented differing visions for Canada’s largest city. Chow bet that voters would accept her policies to confront a mounting affordability crisis that has engulfed major cities around the world. On Monday night, she thanked her supporters and Bradford. “I know we share a love for Toronto and a belief in its future,” she told a jubilant crowd. “We can disagree on how we get there, or what it looks like, but I do not doubt we both want what is best for our city.” Chow, 69, has long been a fixture of the city’s politics.

She previously served as a school board trustee, city councillor and federal member of parliament. Her total of more than 532,000 votes nearly doubles what she received in 2023. Bradford, a former city councillor and urban planner, spent much of the campaign focusing on what he said was Chow’s failure to stem the rising cost of living and to address crime. He told residents crime was so bad in Toronto that he slept with a baseball bat next to his bed. While auto theft and high-value property crime have risen, most other categories – including homicides, firearms-related violence and assault – have all dropped significantly in recent years. Bradford said more police were needed, and pledged to cut taxes and city spending. In a city that has experienced antisemitic vandalism and shootings at Jewish schools, Bradford aimed to ally himself with Toronto’s Jewish community, and said that Chow’s decision not to attend a debate on antisemitism meant she wouldn’t be an effective voice to combat hate.
