For her part, Chow increased the size of the police department’s hate crimes unit and pushed a “bubble zone” bylaw that barred protest within 50 meters of places of worship, schools, childcare centers and other vulnerable institutions. In his concession speech, the 40-year-old took a conciliatory tone. “I want her to succeed. And my supporters and the nearly 400,000 people that cast a vote for us tonight, they want her to succeed too,” he said. “We all love this city. We know it can be better.” Bradford also acknowledged the daunting odds against his candidacy: no incumbent mayor who has sought re-election in Canada’s largest city has ever lost. Chow also benefited from her apparent ability to manage a fraught political relationship with the Ontario government and its premier, Doug Ford. When she was first elected in 2023, Ford said she would be an “unmitigated disaster” for the city. Pablo Escobar tried to bomb me in Bogotá. To stop the cartels infiltrating Europe, we should legalise cocaine

I congratulate the Guardian on this investigation (Latin American organised crime ‘may operate in 16 European countries’, 13 October). It has already prompted a strong call from the former Colombian vice-president Marta Lucía Ramírez for effective international cooperation to counter the transnational criminal threat. I have followed the “war on drugs” pretty closely since I was the British ambassador to Colombia in the heyday of Pablo Escobar, but I was still shocked to learn of the scale of the Latin American criminal presence in Europe, including supposedly political insurgents such as the Colombian ELN and various Farc dissident factions. The fivefold increase in the cocaine trade in the last decade has boosted organised crime on both sides of the Atlantic. It underlines dramatically the failure of the “war on drugs”. In 2001 you published an opinion piece by me saying that this war was unwinnable and that state supervision of legalised drugs would be preferable.

I argued that aggressive law enforcement had greatly damaged producer and transit countries without reducing the flow of drugs to consumer countries. Prohibition ensured that the incentive of high prices for cheaply produced drugs was simply too great. So it has remained. However, legalised cannabis regimes are now working in Canada, Uruguay and more than 20 US states, providing possible models for cocaine. The situation has been complicated by the development of extremely strong synthetic drugs, such as fentanyl. Of around 80,000 drug overdose deaths in the United States in 2024, 22,000 were cocaine users, while 48,000 had used fentanyl. It strikes me that the availability of such dangerous drugs would make the alternative of legally controlled and safer cocaine worth an experiment, on top of the reduction of violence and corruption that legalisation should bring.

Rise of Palestinian parties in Knesset will redraw Israel’s political landscape

The big gains made by Palestinian parties in Israel’s general election pose an urgent and fundamental challenge to the country’s mainstream opposition: either cooperate with Arab Israelis or hand Benjamin Netanyahu a roadmap to political survival. In the wake of Tuesday’s exit polls, the leader of the opposition bloc, Gadi Eisenkot, declared them a victory for “Israel’s Zionist national majority” but the real outcome looks as if it will be far more complex than that. The greatest change between the new Knesset and the old will be the dramatically increased representation of Palestinian parties, which are projected to win 17 to 18 seats, up from 10. That redraws the battle lines on Israel’s political landscape. Arab Israelis will not so easily be sidelined and ignored. Related: Coalition talks loom as Israel exit polls suggest Netanyahu and Eisenkot blocs tied The exit polls placed Eisenkot’s opposition bloc and Netanyahu’s governing coalition tied.

text:
Rise of Palestinian parties in Knesset will redraw Israel’s political landscape

Though the prime minister’s Likud party could still be the strongest single party, neither side has enough to get 61 seats in the 120-seat parliament for a majority. If confirmed by actual results, that would give Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, discretion over who he asks first to try to form a government. If one candidate cannot succeed in six weeks, the challenge is passed on to the next option. It could be an extremely long process, and all this time Netanyahu’s coalition would stay on in a caretaker role. Eisenkot could argue he has a chance of negotiating his way to a Knesset majority. To do so, however, he and his partners in the “change” bloc would be obliged to sit down to talk with the Palestinian groupings, the Joint List and Ra’am (an acronym for the United Arab List). They would probably find Ra’am and its leader, Mansour Abbas, easier to talk to. Abbas has already participated in a right-leaning government of Naftali Bennett, now a junior partner in the Eisenkot bloc.

Abbas has a Jewish Zionist deputy, he has shown willingness to make political compromises and stated emphatically on Tuesday that his priority is to “bring down Benjamin Netanyahu, [Bezalel] Smotrich, and [Itamar] Ben-Gvir in this election”. However, most estimates based on the exit polls show Ra’am as the smaller of the two Palestinian groupings, with seven projected seats in the new Knesset and it is not clear that would be enough, even if a pact was made with the consent of the other members of Eisenkot’s bloc, to produce a majority government. Negotiations with the Joint List, with 11 or more projected seats, would be tougher. Eisenkot has laid down four conditions: recognise Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, accept the values expressed in Israel’s declaration of independence, accept conscription for Palestinian Israeli citizens, who are exempt, and denounce Hamas as a terrorist organisation.

Sardinian restaurants ban families from using phones at the table

A group of restaurants in Sardinia are banning families from using smartphones and other devices at the table in a quest to encourage conversation. The initiative, called A tavola senza schermi or At the table without screens, is being spearheaded by Anna Cau, the children’s ombudsman for the Italian island. It is part of a campaign to curtail excessive screen use among children and inspire interaction during meals. Parents and their children will be required to put their phones away when dining at any of the 15 restaurants that have volunteered to participate in the scheme during a one-month pilot exercise beginning next week. Cau, a former juvenile magistrate, said: “The idea is not to rely solely on prohibitions or to place the burden of responsibility entirely on parents, but to ensure our broader environment supports parents in their role and helps minors integrate with others. “We need real-world settings that strengthen and accommodate the lives of both adults and children.

citation.title: Sardinian restaurants ban families from using phones at the table

text:
Sardinian restaurants ban families from using phones at the table

This initiative is a small step within a broader philosophy that guides my approach to this highly complex issue.” After families hand in their devices, restaurant staff will give them a “reunion kit” containing games and drawings. The kit, which has been designed by the Italian federation of paediatricians, is aimed at helping under-18s start conversations with their parents, such as sharing stories about their day. The kit includes a brochure outlining the risks of digital overexposure and tips on managing social media use at home. “The restaurants will offer an alternative activity in the form of a game which is intended to foster interaction,” said Cau. “Obviously, the games are structured with time limits within the context of a restaurant lunch or dinner.” Cau worked on the scheme with the Sardinian wing of Fipe-Confcommercio, an association uniting the catering, tourism and entertainment sectors. Emanuele Frongia, president of the federation on the island, said the 15 restaurants had readily agreed to participate. The plan is to expand the initiative on a voluntary basis.

Trump reopened an LGBTQ+ suicide hotline. But the department that runs it vows to ‘restore biological truth’

For nearly three years, counselors through the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline for LGBTQ+ individuals answered more than 1.5m calls, texts and online chats – until the Trump administration terminated it in July 2025. But now, more than a year later, the service is back online. The federal agency that oversees the lifeline, Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (Samhsa), shuttered the specialized national lifeline service known as the “press 3” option for financial reasons last year, though critics cited political motivations. After pressure from activists, LGBTQ+ organizations and politicians, Congress approved legislation to allocate more than $33m to services for queer youth, including to the specialized lifeline. While suicide prevention and LGBTQ+ rights groups celebrate the reinstatement, details about the rollout and how the counselors will be trained remain shrouded in secrecy.

Tuesday briefing: How a journalistic hunch revealed the scale of Britain’s problematic cocaine use

Good morning. How did Britain become a cocaine nation? Our series investigating how a drug once associated with affluence and exclusivity has become an everyday habit, in pubs, dinner parties, festivals and workplaces, has the answer. The series reveals that the surge in consumption in recent years has coincided with a 10% increase in related crimes, record deaths and domestic abuse. This is the kind of original reporting in which journalists put a hunch to the test: supporting their conclusions with a scrupulously analysed dataset and a revelatory source, uncovering some surprising new insights in the process. But how does that journalistic process work, from premise to publication? I spoke to north of England correspondent Robyn Vinter and data journalist Michael Goodier, the duo behind the investigation, to find out more. But first, the headlines. A review published in the aftermath of the disorder found that more than half of fans said they had seen cocaine use either inside Wembley stadium or on the way from the station. “I thought ‘God, that’s remarkable that people felt confident to take it so openly’,” Robyn tells me. Then came the anti-immigration riots of 2024: Robyn noticed that some of the perpetrators of violence were also facing cocaine-related charges. She later observed open cocaine use among marchers at Tommy Robinson’s Unite the Kingdom rally in London.

And when she covered Glastonbury for the Guardian last year, “people were taking coke in the crowd in front of everyone,” – par for the course at a music festival, you might think – but Robyn noticed a difference: “a few years ago people were a bit more careful about hiding it.” Robyn began to wonder whether cocaine use might be at an all time high – and, considering its well recorded effects as a drug that causes paranoid and impulsivity, she asked herself: what might the overall effect on society be from all this? *** From theory to numbers: ‘It was one of those journalistic hunches’ Those were the ideas that Robyn brought to Michael, who began to dig into the available data, first sending freedom of information requests to all 45 territorial police forces in the UK.

(Please don’t skip over this bit: as someone who has FOIed the 45 herself, and chased up, and chased again, I appreciate what a task that is.) Michael discovered that police forces across Britain had recorded a 10% rise in recorded crimes in which the class A drug was mentioned since 2019, while the Home Office estimates that cocaine use at sites across England has risen by 26% since 2021. The data also showed that the record-breaking rise in cocaine use was associated with crimes ranging from assault to dangerous driving, and Robyn had a particular theory she wanted to explore about domestic abuse: “It was one of those journalistic hunches: what’s it like to be in a relationship with somebody who is taking a lot of cocaine?” She contacted domestic violence specialists who explained that, while cocaine use doesn’t make a non-violent person violent, it can make an offender more likely to act on their impulse to do harm.

Again, Michael’s data work suggested Robyn’s suspicions were correct: Home Office figures show nearly six in 10 police drug tests carried out on people arrested on suspicion of domestic abuse tested positive for cocaine use between July 2025 and June this year. *** Parsing the data: ‘sewage doesn’t lie’ Assessing data on illegal drug use is tricky, Michael explains, because some people may not want to admit to taking drugs. Crime survey data – which asks individuals about their habits – suggests the number of people reporting cocaine use has fallen slightly since the pandemic. But that’s completely different to analysis of wastewater by Home Office scientists, which shows a significant rise in cocaine levels in sewage, up 26% between 2021 and 2025. “It’s always important to speak to experts in the field about which data they think is more representative,” Michael tells me. One such expert is Dr Josh Torrance, a specialist in drug markets, who thought the direction of travel shown in the wastewater analysis was broadly accurate. “Sewage doesn’t lie,” says Michael.

The plummeting price of cocaine – apparently the only consumer good exempt from the cost of living crisis – was evidently a factor in its growing use, but assessing this data presented another challenge. Torrance shared price data he had gathered from online drug dealers who ply their trade on Telegram channels and other forums. “Obviously that’s illegal behaviour, so we had to agree with him about which data he was willing to share, and what we were able to publish, to make sure we weren’t exposing any sources in the process.” *** ‘People thought I was a cop’ A running theme of the reporting is the way that cocaine use has become normalised, moving from being the drug of choice for the affluent to something snorted off the toilet cistern in the local pub. But its apparent omnipresence doesn’t make it any easier to talk about. Robyn struggled to find anyone willing to be interviewed about their cocaine use, past or present, without using a pseudonym. During her research, she headed to a music festival in the north of England.

Russian strikes on Kyiv killed one person and wounded eight, with mayor Vitali Klitschko saying medical facilities and an intensive care unit had been damaged in the late Monday attack. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a ballistic missile attack had struck the grounds of a university campus in the Ukrainian capital. “The missiles hit very crowded areas, and there is not a single military facility nearby. This was a strike directly on the city, on its infrastructure,” he said on social media. The strikes on Kyiv came hours before a truce in the ravaged Russian-occupied city of Oleshky was due to start, after months of reports that residents faced dire food, water and medicine shortages. The truce, aimed at allowing humanitarian aid into Oleshky, was to begin at 3am local time (0100 GMT). No end date for the truce has been provided. The city in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region has been caught in the crosshairs of fighting between the two sides since 2022, when it was seized by Russian forces.

A Russian strike has damaged a major bridge spanning the Dnipro River in Kyiv, Klitschko said on Tuesday, following reports of multiple ballistic missiles launched towards the Ukrainian capital. “A strike hit the Southern Bridge. Metro infrastructure on the bridge was also damaged,” the city’s mayor wrote on Telegram. City officials said train services across the bridge had been suspended. Ukraine’s military has begun using specialised aerial rescue drones to evacuate wounded soldiers from the battlefield, carrying two stranded troops to safety near the Russian border in the first such operations. The newly developed StarGate drone, a six-rotor aircraft fitted with an enclosed evacuation capsule, was used in two separate missions over the past week, the 475th Separate Assault Regiment, an elite unit, said on Monday. Developed by Ukrainian technology company SkyFall, the drone is intended to reduce rescue times from hours to minutes, reaching hard-to-access combat zones currently served by unmanned ground vehicles.

citation.title: Ukraine war briefing: Russia strikes Kyiv hours before truce begins in war-ravaged city Oleshky

US bans vehicles from China’s BYD at Japan military base, calling them ‘unacceptable’ risk

One of America’s biggest overseas military bases has banned vehicles made by the Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD over security concerns, the US military in Japan said on Tuesday. The ban, which went into effect this week at Kadena airbase on the southern Japanese island of Okinawa, has fueled speculation that similar measures could be taken at other US military facilities as part of Washington’s crackdown on Chinese technology it suspects of being used to collect sensitive information. “These vehicles present an unacceptable and unmitigable risk to our personnel and our mission,” Lieut Col Alli Stormer, a spokesperson for the US air force 18th Wing at Kadena, said in a statement. Related: ‘BYD effect’: electric vehicle boom becomes unexpected tool to combat inflation The restrictions apply to all BYD vehicles, including privately owned cars, taxis and delivery vehicles, reports said, adding that security personnel stationed at the base’s gates had been instructed to block BYD vehicles and instruct drivers to turn around.

citation.title: US bans vehicles from China’s BYD at Japan military base, calling them ‘unacceptable’ risk

text:
US bans vehicles from China’s BYD at Japan military base, calling them ‘unacceptable’ risk

Kadena, the biggest US air force base east Asia, would be directly involved in responding to a crisis involving China, Russia or North Korea. Its inventory includes the powerful Typhon missile system, which is said to be capable of firing Tomahawk missiles as far as 1,600km, putting parts of China and Russia within striking distance. Kadena also hosts fighter planes and aircraft used for mid-air refuelling, surveillance and reconnaissance, according to its website. The move comes amid concerns of potential information leaks via vehicle-mounted technologies such as cameras, sensors and GPS devices, South Korea’s Yonhap news agency said. American military officials have not identified a specific threat, but the ban is part of wider measures taken by the US and other western countries to restrict Chinese smart technology in vehicles, mobile phones and other devices they fear could be used to “spy” on their owners. In June the Pentagon added BYD to a list of 188 Chinese firms it believes have ties to the country’s military, drawing a protest from Beijing.

citation.title: US bans vehicles from China’s BYD at Japan military base, calling them ‘unacceptable’ risk

text:
US bans vehicles from China’s BYD at Japan military base, calling them ‘unacceptable’ risk

The blacklist also includes the automaker Nio, e-commerce firm Alibaba and internet company Baidu. The US defence department banned the sale and use of smartphones from Chinese companies Huawei and ZTE at military bases worldwide in 2018, again citing security concerns. China has imposed similar restrictions on US-made Tesla vehicles. In 2021, it barred them from some government compounds due to security concerns over ⁠cameras installed on the vehicles. Beijing removed that restriction in 2024 after Tesla won an endorsement from the country’s top auto industry association. BYD, which has not immediately responded publicly to the Kadena ban, overtook Tesla as the world’s biggest seller of battery-electric vehicles in 2025. It is now expanding overseas, including in the world’s fourth-biggest auto market, Japan, where in July it launched its Racco electric minicar in the hope that the small, cost-efficient vehicle would carve out a place in a market dominated by domestic brands. With Reuters

Second fatal train collision this year casts doubt over Spain’s high-speed rail network

Spain’s high-speed rail network, the most extensive in Europe and the second largest in the world after China, has long been a point of pride in the country. But Wednesday’s deadly crash – the second in nine months – has recast the spotlight on questions about safety. Officials said at least 68 people were killed on Wednesday morning after a high-speed train slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks, leading to the derailment of several carriages. The two trains were believed to be carrying 544 passengers. Speaking to reporters, Spain’s transport minister, Óscar Puente, traced the collision back to a security system that had stopped working at about 8.30am local time. The computer malfunction brought an estimated six trains to a halt along a 63km stretch of track. Soon after, the central command in Madrid instructed one of the trains involved in the crash to resume service at normal speeds, sending it colliding into a train that was still sitting stationary on the tracks, said Puente.

citation.title: Second fatal train collision this year casts doubt over Spain’s high-speed rail network

text:
Second fatal train collision this year casts doubt over Spain’s high-speed rail network

“It was the control centre – via its operators – that made the decision to resume operations, under circumstances that, from our point of view, are inexplicable,” he added. State-owned rail operator Renfe said in a statement that its train had been instructed to continue on its way and had crashed into ​the stationary Iryo train “for reasons we don’t know”. The accident follows a crash in January that killed 46 people and left dozens more injured near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía. Media on Wednesday were swift to point to the parallels between the two crashes: both involved the same train operators and took place on the line connecting Madrid to the southern region of Andalusia, which is the oldest on Spain’s high-speed network. The first crash sparked conversation over safety on the line, a debate that rail unions say has continued. Wednesday’s disaster came a day before a planned 24-hour work stoppage at Renfe by Spain’s largest train drivers union. “Our goal is to change the system and make it safer,” the union said earlier this month.

citation.title: Second fatal train collision this year casts doubt over Spain’s high-speed rail network

text:
Second fatal train collision this year casts doubt over Spain’s high-speed rail network

Their reasons for taking action ranged from the need for climate emergency protocols to ensuring channels of communication for workers to convey concerns. The union also called for guarantees that trains would be “reliable and safe”, adding: “We demand real and definitive technical solutions to the safety and reliability issues that have long plagued our rolling stock.” Interactive It has also called a rolling, six-day strike for drivers at the high-speed rail operator Ouigo. The January crash sparked a bout of political finger-pointing over whether Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party government had spent enough on railway maintenance in a country where travel by train accounts for about 57% of all transport. While the causes of the January crash remain under investigation, a preliminary report suggested that it could have been the result of defects in the track or in a weld between two sections of track. The report noted, however, that several other possibilities were also being investigated.

citation.title: Second fatal train collision this year casts doubt over Spain’s high-speed rail network

text:
Second fatal train collision this year casts doubt over Spain’s high-speed rail network

Train travel grew by 40% from 2019 to 2024, coinciding with a period in which the country opened up its rail network to private companies. In the first half of this year, 25 million passengers used a high-speed train in Spain. The government says it has increased spending on railway network maintenance by 54% since taking power in 2018. Spain spends more than any other country on its high-speed network, averaging about €1.5bn (£1.26bn) a year from 2018 to 2022, according to a Reuters analysis of EU data. More than 90% of Spain’s train network is equipped with the highest level of safety control systems in the EU. Much of the funding, however, has seemingly been directed at new infrastructure, with about 16% earmarked for maintenance, renewal and upgrades. Data from the European Commission suggests Spain’s maintenance investment in its 4,000km (2,500 miles) of high-speed lines has lagged behind countries such as Germany or Switzerland although some of this could be attributed to differences in the age of the rail lines and the cost of public works and materials.

citation.title: Second fatal train collision this year casts doubt over Spain’s high-speed rail network

text:
Second fatal train collision this year casts doubt over Spain’s high-speed rail network

Until this year, Spain had among the lowest accident rates in the EU, with just one or fewer fatalities per thousand kilometres of track, according to data from Eurostat, the statistics arm of the EU. On Wednesday, Spain’s prime minister said measures would be taken to rebuild trust in the country’s high-speed rail system. “Because it is simply unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year, as we have,” said Sánchez. The crash was Spain’s worst rail accident since 2013, when 80 people died after a train veered off a curved section of track outside the north-western city of Santiago de Compostela.

‘Don’t be stinky’: recruitment a ‘huge issue’ facing Aukus submarine program

Australia faces an uphill battle to recruit and train enough naval personnel to serve on submarines planned for the future fleet of nuclear-powered vessels under the controversial $368bn Aukus deal, a retired admiral has warned. As the Virginia-class submarine USS Colorado arrived at HMAS Stirling south of Perth on Tuesday for a month of routine maintenance and to help build Australian expertise, retired admiral Peter Briggs said more people needed to be enrolled in the navy’s submarine program. Related: We want you! ADF recruitment rates are growing, even as the odds of conflict rise. Why are people signing up? As part of a $368bn trilateral defence deal, Australia will acquire between three and five Virginia-class, nuclear-powered submarines from the United States to replace its six diesel-electric Collins-class vessels, which are becoming obsolete. The new submarines are much bigger and require up to 134 crew – more than double the number needed for the Collins class. The Royal Australian Navy says it has 230 personnel in various stage of the US nuclear-powered submarine training pipeline.

citation.title: ‘Don’t be stinky’: recruitment a ‘huge issue’ facing Aukus submarine program

text:
‘Don’t be stinky’: recruitment a ‘huge issue’ facing Aukus submarine program

“Of these, approximately 145 have completed US Naval nuclear power training and are now building experience training on US Navy SSNs [a hull classification for nuclear-powered submarines],” a navy spokesperson said. “By 2030, we expect to have 400 Royal Australian Navy officers and sailors trained and ready to serve.” But Briggs urged a more intensive recruitment plan to crew the bigger boats. “We have got to triple the size of the submarine arm and we’ve got to train them in nuclear skills,” he said. “You are heading toward needing a submarine arm of 3,000, that’s the hill you have to climb.” About 850 submariners are qualified to operate Collins-class vessels. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here The Virginia-class boats are intended to bridge the transition from the Collins-class fleet to the future SSN-Aukus submarine, an even bigger design being developed by Australia and the UK. “The personnel side is a huge issue but it’s not the only one,” Briggs said. Related: Hegseth calls US-built nuclear submarines the ‘apex predator’ of the seas. But are they right for Australia?

citation.title: ‘Don’t be stinky’: recruitment a ‘huge issue’ facing Aukus submarine program

text:
‘Don’t be stinky’: recruitment a ‘huge issue’ facing Aukus submarine program

The former submariner argued that maintaining two different submarine types would add complexity to training, logistics, maintenance and spare-parts arrangements. The Australian government did not respond to questions about recruitment targets and whether a workforce development program was on track. Recruitment is further complicated by the need for more than a dozen different trades, from radio and sonar operators to cooks and electricians. After spending the next month is Perth, the USS Colorado will return to the city’s waters again in late 2027 as part of the Submarine Rotational Force-West program, which is designed to help Australia build the skills and infrastructure to operate its own nuclear fleet. From 2027, the program will see up to four US and one UK nuclear-powered submarine rotate through HMAS Stirling. Paul Johnson, HMAS Stirling fleet base west commodore, said the USS Colorado maintenance period would be used to “practise and test our procedures across a range of nuclear-related operational scenarios”.

citation.title: ‘Don’t be stinky’: recruitment a ‘huge issue’ facing Aukus submarine program

text:
‘Don’t be stinky’: recruitment a ‘huge issue’ facing Aukus submarine program

Officials stressed that no radiological material would be transferred during the maintenance period and that nuclear-related exercises would be simulated. Late last year, Senate estimates heard that US submarines carrying nuclear weapons could rotate through Australian ports despite a non-proliferation commitment. The USS Colorado captain, Justin Reeves, said the US government would not “confirm or deny the presence of nuclear weapons on specific platforms”. Colorado was built in 2018 and arrived this week carrying conventional weapons, including four torpedoes and four “payload tubes” that can be used to house and launch weapons. It took two weeks to travel to Perth from Pearl Harbor in Hawaii with 160 men and no women aboard. A sign labelled “Berth Rules”, taped to the wall near the submarine’s entryway, listed “Don’t be stinky” as the crew’s top priority once they reach port. The demands of living and working in confined spaces for extended periods presents another recruitment challenge for officials.

citation.title: ‘Don’t be stinky’: recruitment a ‘huge issue’ facing Aukus submarine program

text:
‘Don’t be stinky’: recruitment a ‘huge issue’ facing Aukus submarine program

Sleeping arrangements can involve bunks stacked three high, while “hot racking” allows three sailors to share two beds by rotating their sleeping schedules around watch duties. In some circumstances, and when accommodation is limited, sailors may sleep in torpedo rooms. Reeves said the vessel is “built for combat, not for comfort”. Nuclear submarines don’t need to refuel, meaning their range is effectively infinite. “The limits of its endurance are really food and toilet paper, and that’s several months’ worth,” Reeves said. “Being nuclear-powered is a massive advantage.”

US ambassador suggests Trump could blame Canada if midterms don’t go his way

The US ambassador has suggested Canada could be blamed if Republicans perform poorly in next week’s midterm elections, the latest intervention from a controversial figure who has been accused of inflaming a bitter dispute that has angered and baffled residents of both countries. On Wednesday, CTV news reported that Pete Hoekstra told business leaders at a closed door meeting that if a number of swing races – including Maine and Michigan – go to the Democrats, it could make things harder for Canada because Donald Trump might try to blame the loss on it. “That’s an interesting way of framing it,” the prime minister, Mark Carney, told reporters when asked about the allegations. For months, Canada and the US have been locked in a bitter tariff war, with Ottawa retaliating against illegal US tariffs and targeting goods in states that rely heavily on trade with Canada. Carney said that Canada “will pursue” such a deal if it presents itself, but that Ottawa’s trade negotiators are “not in that position right now”.

citation.title: US ambassador suggests Trump could blame Canada if midterms don’t go his way

text:
US ambassador suggests Trump could blame Canada if midterms don’t go his way

Hoekstra is a deeply polarizing figure in Canada, particular for his response to Trump’s rhetoric about making Canada the 51st US state. Speaking to a Michigan radio station last year, he described the threats as a “sign of affection” and questioned why Canadians were offended by what he characterized as a “generous offer”. He had previously described Canada’s 2025 federal election as “anti-American”. This year a House of Commons petition signed by more than 225,000 Canadians called for his expulsion, suggesting his statements violated diplomatic protocols, including the prohibition on diplomats interfering in the internal affairs of a host country. More recently, Hoekstra has accused Canadian officials of interfering in US elections, pointing to Canadian politicians who have criticized the tariffs in US media, and the province of Ontario’s anti-tariff advertisement that ran on US television. “We see all of that. We are monitoring it. We are evaluating it.

And if some of it becomes election interference, America will respond to it,” Hoekstra, who comes from Michigan, recently told a Canadian podcast, adding that Canadians should “keep your nose out of American politics”. Canada’s industry minister, Mélanie Joly, who was a target of Hoekstra’s comments, told reporters in Ottawa that her country “would never do that” and said Canada would “never accept that also being done to us in Canada”. Carney, while in Turkey, told reporters there was “no merit” to the claims of interference and that he was “disappointed that their envoy sees that as his role, to make these suggestions”. Roland Paris, the director of the Graduate School of Public and International Affairs at the University of Ottawa and a foreign affairs adviser to the former Canadian prime minister Justin Trudeau, said the remarks were an “extraordinary thing” for a US ambassador to say about his host country and looked like an effort to “manufacture a pretext for the Trump administration’s own political difficulties”.

“The job of an ambassador is to represent the interests of his country, but it’s also to maintain channels of communication and build relationships and manage disagreements,” he said. “His comments have repeatedly aggravated tensions instead of helping to manage them. text:
Derrick Harriott obituary

Derrick Harriott, who has died aged 87 following a long illness, was an influential figure in Jamaican popular music. A singer-songwriter who began his career in 1958 leading the pioneering harmony group the Jiving Juniors, Harriott had an intrinsic feel for music and an ease with tackling diverse styles. His distinctive productions helped artists such as Keith and Tex, the Kingstonians and Junior Murvin to come to prominence in the late 1960s, and the Ethiopians, Big Youth and Scotty in the 70s. An early mentor to Dennis Brown, Harriott was also one of the first to collaborate with King Tubby, commissioning the experimental engineer to mix the captivating dub B-sides to singles such as Brown’s Concentration and the Crystalites’ Blacula in 1973. The youngest of six children, of whom a sister died in infancy, Harriott spent his formative years in a staunch Seventh-day Adventist household on Duke Street in downtown Kingston. His parents both worked at the nearby Excelsior College, where Harriott’s uncle, Wesley Arthur Powell, was headteacher, and after his mother emigrated to New York, Harriott’s father ran a small commercial school.

citation.title: Derrick Harriott obituary

text:
Derrick Harriott obituary

Music was an important part of daily life, since his father was a clarinettist, his uncle, Samuel Powell, a singer and his brother, Winston, a professional saxophonist. He discovered jazz balladeers such as Billy Eckstine and Nat King Cole, doo-wop harmony group the Ink Spots and local spiritual singer Jimmy Tucker through radio broadcasts, all of which influenced his approach to singing, as did Donnie Elbert’s forlorn ballad What Can I Do, which he heard on a local sound system. While attending Excelsior in 1957, Harriott entered a talent contest held by the journalist Vere Johns at the Palace theatre with a rendition of the Turbans’ When You Dance, and subsequently formed the duo Sang and Harriott with fellow Excelsior student Claude Sang Jr, whose brother, Herman, led a popular session band, the City Slickers. Sang and Harriott won a series of talent contests with original ballad You’re Mine, All Mine, and after Sang moved to New York to further his education, Harriott formed the Jiving Juniors with fellow Excelsior student Eugene Dwyer and Dwyer’s friend, Maurice Wynter, with Herman Sang joining on the piano.

citation.title: Derrick Harriott obituary

text:
Derrick Harriott obituary

In August 1959, Harriott joined his mother in New York but frequently returned to Jamaica to record and perform with the Jiving Juniors. The group’s Lollipop Girl was the breakthrough hit recorded for Duke Reid in 1960 and the spiritual Over the River was a big hit for Clement Dodd in 1961; recordings were also made for Chris Blackwell. Back in New York in 1962, Harriott formed a new Jiving Juniors with Claude Sang, Valmont Burke, and Winston Service of the Downbeats. Sessions with the Teacho Wiltshire Orchestra yielded the hit Sugar Dandy, which Harriott produced and issued on the newly formed Crystal label. Harriott then launched his solo career with his popular cover of What Can I Do, which, like Sugar Dandy, was delivered in a convincing falsetto, his ability to switch between tenor and the higher register giving Harriott an edge on his rivals. The wide range enabled Harriott to subsequently broaden his repertoire, his solo successes of the mid-60s including the mento John Tom, the soul ballad I’m Only Human and edgy rock-steady tearjerker Walk the Streets, as well as the Murvin-penned biblical allegory, Solomon.

citation.title: Derrick Harriott obituary

text:
Derrick Harriott obituary

But Harriott will always be best remembered for The Loser, a 1967 landmark recounting romantic missteps that was expertly arranged by bassist Boris Gardiner, the song framed by Joe Isaacs’ offbeat drum rolls and Lloyd Delprat’s choppy piano chords. Soon after, Harriott opened Derrick’s One Stop, a record shop on King Street in Kingston. Focusing more on record production, he scored with Rudy Mills’ John Jones, a tale of romantic betrayal that was popular with skinhead audiences in Britain, as was the Kingstonians’ Sufferer; Keith and Tex’s adaptation of the Temptations’ Don’t Look Back and the Spanishtonians’ Stop That Train were also successful, as was the Ethiopians’ Rastafari-themed No Baptism. Scotty’s Riddle I This was a chart topper in 1971 and his Draw Your Brakes appeared on the soundtrack of The Harder They Come; Big Youth’s Cool Breeze charted in 1973, just as Harriott moved his shop to larger premises at Twin Gates Plaza in the Half Way Tree business district.

citation.title: Derrick Harriott obituary

text:
Derrick Harriott obituary

During the 70s and 80s, Harriott’s greatest solo successes came through adaptations of soul, funk and disco: Psychedelic Train was partly inspired by the Temptations’ Psychedelic Shack and there were hit adaptations of the Chi-Lites’ weepy ballad Have You Seen Her?, Ronnie Jones’ funky disco foray Soul Sister and Don Covay’s jealousy track Checkin’ Out, as well as the sensual soul-influenced original Skin to Skin and a funky reggae adaptation of Dazz Band’s futuristic disco-funk track, Let It Whip. Although his output waned from the mid-80s, Harriott continued to perform to audiences internationally, his appearances at the Legends of Ska festival in Toronto in 2002 and at the London International Ska festival in 2015 among the most memorable. He was awarded the Order of Distinction in 2009 for his services to the Jamaican Music Industry and a Lifetime Achievement Award from the Jamaica Reggae Industry Association in 2019. Harriott is survived by his eight children, his sister, Loy Shegog, and numerous grandchildren and great-grandchildren. • Derrick Clifton Harriott, singer, songwriter and record producer, born 6 February 1939; died 24 October 2026

citation.title: Derrick Harriott obituary

Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr

Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country. Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt. According to Mada Masr, Attalah was released after the news outlet had paid a fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; £40,100), prompting statements of support from global human rights groups. “Lina Attalah was released after we paid the said fine,” said her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari. “In the process, we discovered that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to a year in prison, as well as a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds,” he told AFP. Attalah’s defence team had appealed that sentence, and a new court hearing was scheduled for 11 November, Azhari added.

citation.title: Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr

text:
Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr

Related: The news website that’s keeping press freedom alive in Egypt | Leslie T Chang Attalah founded Mada Masr in 2013, after coming to international prominence in 2011 during the Arab spring. An advocate for press freedom, she has been arrested on a number of occasions. Attalah’s detention, and the ordered closure of Mada Masr – which says it had applied for a licence to operate three years ago and had no reply from Egyptian authorities – follows the arrest of the entire six-person team at the independent factchecking platform Matsadaash, who were charged with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood. Attalah’s legal team suggested she had been, in effect, ambushed during a court appearance, with a judge appointing a defence lawyer for her before security personnel detained her in the courtroom. The crackdown “can only mean that Egypt’s security agencies are moving from years of harassing independent media to wiping them out completely”, said Hossam Bahgat, the head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), who attended the court hearing.

citation.title: Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr

text:
Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr

“This escalation validates our fears that the arrest and continued detention of the six Matsadaash journalists would signal a crackdown of unprecedented magnitude,” said Bahgat. “It risks fully eviscerating the narrow margin of press freedoms that have been carefully maintained in Egypt over the past decade, albeit amid great personal sacrifice – a margin that had allowed the continued operation of a handful of news outlets and human rights organisations despite frequent harassment, including through legal avenues.” According to EIPR, the recent moves against independent media follow an increasing frequency of statements from the Egyptian president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, since August claiming a conspiracy to destabilise the country. He has said he intended to remain in power until 2030 to protect Egypt from “traitors, criminals, and saboteurs”. Reporters Without Borders said the court’s decision was “outrageous” and “shameful”, urging authorities to release Attalah “at once”. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) also condemned the verdict.

citation.title: Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr

text:
Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr

Amnesty International said the verdict represented “a crushing blow to press freedom”. Egypt is among the top jailers of journalists globally, with 25 currently behind bars, according to the CPJ. Attalah’s lawyers took steps to challenge the ruling, with a hearing in a retrial of the case scheduled for 11 November. Underlining concerns over the crackdown, Pen International issued a statement with several dozen civil society organisations condemning the moves. “Though this is the sixth case brought against Mada Masr in six years, this is the first time that a case of this nature has been referred to trial,” the writers’ association said. “For years, Egyptian authorities have leveraged their repressive and restrictive tactics against independent media outlets to harass journalists, restrict their operations and chill freedom of expression. To escalate to the step of referral to trial must be read as a clear intent to entirely shutter the independent media space, and to permanently close what remains.”

EU backs away from offer to Canada to start ‘associate member’ talks

The EU has backed away from its offer to Canada to start talks on becoming an “associate member” after disagreements between member states just as an EU-Canada summit was set to begin in Montreal. A draft of a joint statement to be issued after the end of the summit, which runs Thursday and Friday, showed a watered-down version offering “an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself”. The issue was triggered after the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, surprised nearly everyone by announcing in last month’s state of the union address that the EU would consider “associate membership” for Canada. The declaration had been hailed as a landmark in EU history, offering a non-EU country such close ties to the bloc, which has not allowed any state membership since Croatia joined in 2013. It was also seen as a sign that the call by Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, at the Davos summit in January for “middle powers” to work together was paying off.

citation.title: EU backs away from offer to Canada to start ‘associate member’ talks

text:
EU backs away from offer to Canada to start ‘associate member’ talks

But instead of announcing a work programme on developing “associate membership”, the draft communique, seen by the Guardian, states the two sides would “work to define by the 2027 EU-Canada summit the concept of an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself, to reflect, through this even closer association, our common endeavour and cooperation towards our shared goals of prosperity, economic security and strategic autonomy”. Associate membership had been mooted, and rejected, previously for countries such as Ukraine. Von der Leyen’s declaration caught EU capitals by surprise and led to pushback politically and legally. Given “associate status” has no definition, diplomats wondered about such issues as whether Canada could join the European Council, legislative bodies or decision-making processes without a vote. In Serbia, a new type of democracy is taking hold, and Europe is watching closely

In April of last year, dozens of students set off from Serbia, intent on making it to Strasbourg, France on bicycles. The aim of the arduous, 13-day transcontinental journey was simple: to make their voices heard in Europe and beyond. In their home city of Novi Sad, students had been holding near-daily protests after a deadly roof collapse at the city’s main railway station. As their push for accountability and justice spread across the country, it was met with baton-wielding police, teargas and a political class that branded these young people as traitors. Their trek to Strasbourg was aimed at casting a spotlight on the deepening erosion of democratic values in their home country. “Serbia needs Europe’s support,” the students explained in an open letter to the French president, Emmanuel Macron, as they arrived in Strasbourg and met with MEPs and officials. “We are not riding toward Europe to flee Serbia. We are riding to bring it back.” On Sunday, their movement made headlines across the world as the students were catapulted from the streets of Serbia into the halls of power.

‘It all happened in a split second’: survivors recount details of deadly train crash in Spain

Josimar Medina woke a little before 9am on Wednesday to find himself airborne and hurtling through his carriage on the fast train from Madrid to Seville. “I remember flying through the air and looking for my girlfriend, who was also shooting through the air,” said Medina, a 31-year-old tourist from the northern Peruvian city of Chiclayo. Once he landed, he looked around and realised just how lucky he and his girlfriend, Vitoria Maia, had been. “I saw people with cuts, people covered in blood, people missing limbs, and I saw one person who had nothing left below the chest,” said Medina. “I saw people with their heads crushed and people with mutilated arms.” The Peruvian stood recounting the details of Wednesday’s deadly rail crash, in which at least 68 people were killed and dozens more were injured, wearing a light brown T-shirt stained with the blood of a young American man he had helped move to safety.

As it was, the couple climbed out of the train and helped the injured while they waited for medics and Guardia Civil officers to arrive at the scene of the crash, which took place amid vineyards and olive groves near the small town of Urda in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha, near the city of Toledo. Within hours of the crash, Urda had been transformed into a frantic emergency response centre, with a local sports centre pressed into service as a triage post for the walking wounded. Cars, vans and trucks from the emergency services in Castilla-La Mancha and neighbouring Madrid crowded the streets. Get out! Another train could hit!” said Fredrich. “We saw all the people were also getting off. Many of them had head injuries and were covered in blood. King Charles to discuss legacy of slavery with Commonwealth leaders at summit

King Charles has confirmed he will discuss the legacy of slavery at a summit with Commonwealth leaders as he begins his Caribbean tour. The king arrived in the Bahamas on Tuesday to a ceremonial welcome and attended a youth rally at Clifford Park, the site where the country officially gained its independence from British colonial rule in 1973. His arrival comes as a poll suggested strong support among young people and Labour voters in the UK for a dialogue on slavery reparations. The poll, conducted by More in Common last week and published by the reparatory justice movement Repair Campaign, found that 40% of Britons supported a meeting on reparatory justice, while 19% were undecided. But Repair Campaign elder and former St Vincent and the Grenadines prime minister Ralph Gonsalves pointed to disaggregated data showing that support was considerably higher among younger people, with 60% of those aged 18-24 and 51% of those aged 25-34 backing a meeting on reparatory justice.

citation.title: King Charles to discuss legacy of slavery with Commonwealth leaders at summit

text:
King Charles to discuss legacy of slavery with Commonwealth leaders at summit

The poll also suggested that a majority of all ages who voted Labour (58%) and Liberal Democrat (57%) in the last election favoured a meeting. The findings come as the UK faces intensifying pressure from Caribbean leaders to apologise for its role in slavery and agree to a structured dialogue on reparations. “The bulk of the young people under the age of 35 are saying we have to have that conversation. This should prompt him, like the Dutch prime minister, to give a full formal apology,” Gonsalves told the Guardian. He also urged King Charles to apologise and help establish mechanisms for a dialogue, adding that he was disappointed with the King’s maiden speech in the Bahamas, which he described as “falling far short of what he had said before”. Charles acknowledged the “appalling atrocity of slavery”, describing it as something “which forever stains our history, when he attended the ceremony marking Barbados’s historic transition to a republic in 2021.

text:
Racism needs to be understood as a global phenomenon – our humanity depends on it

Around the world, racism is fueling a new wave of global unrest. In recent weeks, demonstrations in France turned violent amid mounting frustrations over socioeconomic and racial inequities, led by a younger generation that has had enough. Earlier this month, the Green party of England and Wales’s decision to define Zionism as a form of racism sparked controversy and renewed public debate about what racism is and who gets to decide it. In September, electoral gains by Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party raised alarms in a nation with a dangerous history of racist, antisemitic fascism. And for the past year, the Trump administration has pushed ahead white supremacist agendas throughout the United States, highlighted by violent Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids targeting people by race, regardless of citizenship status. To understand each of these examples of racism in isolation would be a mistake. They are connected. Racism is not merely a series of random occurrences affecting certain people in certain places.

citation.title: Racism needs to be understood as a global phenomenon – our humanity depends on it

text:
Racism needs to be understood as a global phenomenon – our humanity depends on it

It is more than institutional discrimination in schools or workplaces or even systemic inequalities in healthcare and policing. Racism is an interconnected, global phenomenon, spreading throughout our human ecosystem and embedded in world order. This global racism, which I name and define in my new book Global Racism: A Challenge for the World, is dangerous – it underpins wars and threatens our very humanity. Global racism is an old story and an evergreen one. It is often powered by leaders who seek to divide humans through dehumanizing “us v them” narratives. In 1095, for example, Pope Urban II called upon Frankish nobles and common folk alike to take up arms against the Seljuk Turks, urging them in one account of his speech “to destroy that vile race from the lands of our friends”. Nearly nine centuries later and a continent away, the Hutu Ten Commandments, published in 1990 in a Rwandan newspaper, invoked ideologies of racial superiority that created the conditions in which the Rwandan genocide unfolded four years later.

citation.title: Racism needs to be understood as a global phenomenon – our humanity depends on it

text:
Racism needs to be understood as a global phenomenon – our humanity depends on it

The worst things we humans have ever done to one another – slavery, genocide, segregation, apartheid – have been justified and sustained by ideologies underlying global racism. When this racist fervor subsides, we realize that such acts have not only killed countless people but diminished our humanity. Today, evidence of racism’s global disruption is clear. According to the United Nations, racial discrimination is among the most common forms of discrimination worldwide, often intersecting with gender discrimination against women and girls. A Pew survey found that across 36 countries a median of 68% of adults consider racial or ethnic discrimination as a significant worldwide problem. The international community recognized the need to confront such challenges back in 1965 when nations created the first treaty banning racial discrimination, defined as certain acts of discrimination on the basis of race, color, descent, national or ethnic origin (but not nationality). A laudable first step, the treaty failed to define and ban racism, alongside racial discrimination.

citation.title: Racism needs to be understood as a global phenomenon – our humanity depends on it

text:
Racism needs to be understood as a global phenomenon – our humanity depends on it

Understanding global racism reveals why this gap matters. Racism can’t be eliminated by banning acts of racial discrimination, nation by nation, alone. Racism’s deeper roots are embedded not only in how humans and the institutions we create behave, but in what we believe. White supremacist movements, for example, teach followers to believe that being white makes someone inherently superior to everyone else. This ranking of humans by group based on a construct that has no basis in biology isn’t accidental. It is by design and always has been. Today, because of social media and new technology, global racism moves throughout our human ecosystem with rapid speed, making it possible anywhere and everywhere people are. Consider the racist, anti-immigrant riots that erupted last June across Northern Ireland after a knife attack in Belfast, where people violently targeted minority communities, setting fire to homes and vehicles. It exposed how far-right ideologies amplified online could help drive people to commit racist crimes.

citation.title: Racism needs to be understood as a global phenomenon – our humanity depends on it

text:
Racism needs to be understood as a global phenomenon – our humanity depends on it

Like a spark that turns into a raging wildfire, racism doesn’t go viral without hot, dry, windy conditions in the air that allow it. Launching an effective campaign to combat global racism starts with dismantling the ideological architecture that allows racism to thrive. Many governments, however, have been reluctant to do this, privileging free speech and ideas even when the unfettered exercise of those freedoms enables the spread of racial hatred. But protecting the right to express an idea, however objectionable, should not mean allowing racist beliefs to become systems of power. An idea, after all, is not the same as an ideology. The difference, according to Merriam-Webster, is between an idea as a “formulated thought or opinion” and an ideology as a “systematic body of concepts”. The goal isn’t to police an individual’s ideas; it is to stop national leaders who command military power and vast resources from spreading ideologies of racial superiority that threaten peace and security.

citation.title: Racism needs to be understood as a global phenomenon – our humanity depends on it

text:
Racism needs to be understood as a global phenomenon – our humanity depends on it

WEB Du Bois warned of precisely this danger in 1935 in an unpublished essay, A Pragmatic Program for a Dark Minority. He described a world in crisis, where leaders of nations amassed power built on platforms of racist ideologies that promised a bleak future for everyone. “All this,” he wrote, “must inevitably move toward an increase of race hate and war.” History proved him right. The Holocaust, the Rape of Nanjing, and US internment of Japanese Americans, among other horrors, were all built on ideologies of racial superiority. Du Bois understood something we still miss today: racism is not a national peculiarity but a global force, one that degrades those who wield it as surely as those who suffer under it – and that, left unchecked, threatens to plunge the world into chaos and war. Racism is, indeed, a global force, but so is our ability to overcome it. Recognizing global racism is the first step. For nations, this requires banning racism, alongside racial discrimination, under international law. For the rest of us, this means giving up the allure of ideologies of racial superiority.

citation.title: Racism needs to be understood as a global phenomenon – our humanity depends on it

text:
Racism needs to be understood as a global phenomenon – our humanity depends on it

Like all global challenges, real solutions will require collective action. We can start by demanding dignity from our leaders and from ourselves. Why should we try? Because the future of our human species depends upon us acting as one. Anna Spain Bradley is the author of Global Racism: A Challenge for the World and a professor of law at the UCLA School of Law

Soviet tanks crush resistance 5 November 1956 Before dawn yesterday Soviet armoured forces moved into Budapest and attacked “rebel” strongholds. At 8am the Soviet High Command in Hungary ordered Imre Nagy’s government to surrender by noon “or Budapest will be bombed”. Soviet armoured forces then went into action. Spain’s Sánchez declares three days of mourning after at least 68 killed in Toledo train crash

The Spanish prime minister has declared three days of mourning after at least 68 people were killed and dozens more injured in a collision between two high-speed trains that officials suggested was caused by an “inexplicable” error at the central command centre. The trains, one from Spain’s state-owned Renfe and the other from the private rail company Iryo, were travelling on Wednesday morning in the same direction on the line that stretches from the Spanish capital, Madrid, to the southern region of Andalusia. After the Iryo train came to a halt, the other slammed into its rear, knocking several carriages off the track near the town of Urda. The tragedy was the second major deadly high-speed train accident this year in Spain, rattling a country where the extensive rail network has long been a point of pride. “Today all of Spain is grieving,” the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said. In January, 46 people were killed and dozens more injured after two trains – again, one from Renfe and one from Iryo – collided on the same line near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía.

citation.title: Spain’s Sánchez declares three days of mourning after at least 68 killed in Toledo train crash

text:
Spain’s Sánchez declares three days of mourning after at least 68 killed in Toledo train crash

On Wednesday Sánchez said it was “unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed train accidents in the same year, as we have”. The causes of the accident were under investigation, he added. On Wednesday, prime minister Edi Rama’s government adopted legislative measures imposing fines of up to 500,000 leks (€5,500, US$6,130) for “anyone who chooses to remain in a crowd” that is carrying out acts of violence or looting in a public space, or “concealing their identity”. The average salary before tax in Albania is €930 (US$1,026) per month. Police were also given powers to temporarily restrict gatherings in certain areas, including near educational, healthcare and government institutions if there was a risk of violence. The measures also provide for sanctions against online incitement to violence and compensation for small businesses damaged during protests. The measures take immediate effect but must be approved by parliament within 45 days to remain in force. Rama said on Sunday that he was inspired by a French bill, passed by the parliament’s upper house on Wednesday, that would make protesters financially liable for damage caused during street demonstrations.

text:
Flávio Bolsonaro’s defeat is a major blow to Trump and his orange wave

For Donald Trump, Brazil’s presidential election was meant to represent the crest of the “orange wave” – a three-year surge of rightwing triumphs that has reshaped Latin American politics in the US president’s tangerine-hued image. The far-right candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, was supposed to claim the presidency on Sunday, bringing the region’s biggest democracy and economy into Trump’s orbit, after similar victories in Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Honduras, Ecuador and Peru – not to mention the capture of Venezuela’s government after the country was invaded in January. But Brazilian voters had other ideas, turning out in huge numbers to vote against the pro-Trump populist and return the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, to power. On Tuesday, as Lula celebrated his 81st birthday to the sound of samba in Brasília, Bolsonaro fled to Miami on a private jet. “This is a significant blow, indisputably, to Trump’s regional strategy,” Benjamin Gedan, the director of the Stimson Center’s Latin America programme, said of Bolsonaro’s defeat.

“[Trump] was perceived to be steamrolling over South America, having invaded Venezuela and seen close allies win elections in Argentina and Chile, in Bolivia and Colombia. That momentum had given the impression that he could determine political outcomes throughout Latin America – and he clearly enjoyed it,” added Gedan, a former White House South America adviser. “This is a region where he was really perceived to have a successful foreign policy, and this just flies in the face of that image.” The US setback was celebrated in China, whose rapidly growing influence in Latin America Trump has been trying to combat with his so-called “Donroe doctrine” of regional domination. “[Lula has] effectively thwarted Trump’s strategy for the region … Trump failed to bring Brazil, the largest nation in South America, under his sway,” Hu Xijin, a prominent Beijing propagandist, enthused on X. Trump has responded to his ally’s failure by halfheartedly querying the election, which Lula won by 4.3m votes. “I think the election was really strange … It’s so terrible to see,” he told reporters.

“But I wasn’t involved,” Trump added, despite a months-long campaign of economic and diplomatic pressure apparently designed to boost Bolsonaro. Despite Trump’s decision to offer shelter to Bolsonaro – who is facing several criminal investigations in Brazil – many observers suspect the US president is unlikely to pick a major fight with Lula over his rightwing ally’s plight. “One of Trump’s good qualities - and I mean this sincerely, even though it sounds ironic – is that he can smell a loser, and he wants to be around winners,” said Michael Paarlberg, a former Latin America adviser to Bernie Sanders. text:
Brazil’s victory for the planet and democracy: seven lessons from Lula’s win

Thank you, Brazil, for demonstrating how the far right can be trounced while protection for the Amazon is strengthened. In a world where nature and democracy appeared to be bleeding out in tandem, voters and forest defenders in this global south powerhouse have shown it is possible to staunch the flow. This should provide much needed inspiration and, more practically, a playbook for social and environmental movements in other countries facing elections, including the US, Spain and France. Related: Lula miraculously beat the Brazilian far right and Donald Trump. But have no doubt: the region is still in peril | Jordana Timmerman The astonishing comeback victory of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Sunday’s presidential runoff against his extreme right challenger Flavío Bolsonaro has brought oceans of rapturous supporters on to the streets, while also thrilling conservationists, climate activists and social justice campaigners across the world.

citation.title: Brazil’s victory for the planet and democracy: seven lessons from Lula’s win

text:
Brazil’s victory for the planet and democracy: seven lessons from Lula’s win

Coming just weeks after the Lula administration announced a record fall in Amazon and Cerrado destruction, they hope Brazil can now go on to achieve its target of zero deforestation by 2030 and continue to support a global transition away from fossil fuels. That would provide a huge boost to flagging global efforts to stabilise the climate and protect degraded ecosystems. It would also set a remarkable example of leadership by the global south. Big battles lie ahead. In the Amazon region itself, far-right members of Bolsonaro’s party have won the governorships of seven of the nine states and a large number of municipal mayorships. Brazil’s congress is now dominated by agribusiness and mining interests that have set the political agenda in recent years, and will push hard to allow more extractivist industries in indigenous lands, expand road-building, privatise rivers, weaken environmental protections and possibly attempt to impeach the president.

text:
Brazil’s victory for the planet and democracy: seven lessons from Lula’s win

In the regional sphere, Lula, alone among the leaders of main South American nations in not aligning with Donald Trump’s so-called Shield of the Americas, will face pressure from Washington to channel critical minerals and other natural resources to the US, rather than selling to China or Europe, or leaving them in the ground. And, on the planetary level, Brazil faces the threat of accelerating global heating, which is pushing the Amazon ever closer to the point of no return. So although Sunday’s result will hopefully provide a little breathing space for the Amazon and other crucially important biomes, the joy and hope that Brazil has gifted the world will quickly fade unless it inspires political change in other countries. In that sense, the biggest environmental impact of Lula’s victory may be the lessons it provides for campaigners elsewhere. Here are some initial takeaways: Related: Brazilian Amazon deforestation falls to lowest on record as pivotal vote looms 1 Politics matter.

There is no higher environmental priority than defeating the far right, which is a Trojan horse for extractivist – and often criminal – groups to capture states and erode protections for people, democracy and the environment. Just look at the 59.5% surge of Amazon deforestation under the 2019-2022 term of Jair Bolsonaro – the highest level of any four-year presidency in Brazil. Compare that with the 71.2% fall during the Lula administration. Over the past year, forest loss was 3,335 sq km, the lowest level since the start of satellite measurements in 1988. And Lula is not, by any means, an environmentalist. He has approved several destructive projects himself, but he is a people person who listens to the voice of social movements. 2 Don’t give up. Lula was largely written off by the markets and some polls after his first-round defeat. No first-round loser had ever previously come back to win the runoff. Lula was able to do so by securing an extra 10m votes over three weeks. The energy for this came from the streets and the forests. Social movements organised giant rallies in cities.

text:

In the Amazon, indigenous, riverine and quilombola groups travelled by hours – sometimes days – to reach polling stations by boats or buses. 3 Mobilise a campaign army. The first round of Lula’s campaign had been stodgy, old-fashioned and defensive – three traits that are also often applicable to environmental campaigns. This was transformed during the runoff, when federal deputy André Janones launched a “Lula’s Army” WhatsApp group that used humorous memes, live streams and algorithmic outreach to seize digital territory that had long been dominated by the right. By voting day, this army had 10m “soldiers”, about 8% of the electorate. Volunteers devoted hours posting stories and spreading messages across social media, speeding up the Lula campaign’s response time and emotional impact. Everyone was instructed not to share or respond to posts by the opposition camp. 4 Go on the offensive against US tech giants. Lula’s campaign accused Meta, which runs the Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram social media platforms, of political favouritism towards Bolsonaro in its algorithms and AI tools.

Meta denied bias but acknowledged technical failures. Brazil’s electoral court ordered corrective action. Among the most popular chants of Lula supporters was “Hey Meta, vai tomar no cu!” (Hey Meta, go take it up the arse!). Many on the left have blamed US social media platforms for spreading rightwing disinformation and fearmongering, causing recent electoral defeats in Colombia, Chile and Peru. Lula made clear that would not be allowed in Brazil: “We had to overcome foreign interference through digital platforms, which we will have to regulate. We cannot have a monstrously large corporation earning millions and billions paying no taxes to this country and trying to steer our election results.” 5 Reclaim the flag. Brazil’s green, yellow and blue national colours had been associated with Bolsonaro’s movement in previous elections. This time, Lula seized it back by posing in a national football team strip while his “army” launched a campaign called “The green and yellow is ours”.

Before voting day, millions of people across Brazil and the world – from Indigenous leaders in the Amazon to Hollywood celebrities and European football stars – flooded social networks with images of themselves in Brazil colours making an L (for Lula) sign with their thumb and little finger extended. 6 Increase social spending. Amazon protection may have galvanised conservationists, but the far greater motivations for many Lula voters were record low unemployment, robust wage growth, a 15% increase in “bolsa familia” poverty relief payments and a promise to raise the minimum wage. The importance of combining social justice with climate and nature action is widely recognised by Brazilian environmental groups. Without it, elections are lost and protests can erupt in the streets – as the world learned from France during the violent gilets jaunes (yellow vests) demonstrations of 2018. 7 Defend sovereignty, democracy and sustainability.

Lula and his army called out the interlinked threats posed by the Bolsonaro family’s fealty to Donald Trump (now doubly confirmed by Flávio’s post-election flight to the US), Bolsonaro’s desire to change the constitution and promise to open up exploration of the Amazon and other biomes. This reflects a global phenomenon. Now that seven of the planetary boundaries essential for the flourishing of life have been breached, more and more people are affected by business activities that make the situation worse by destabilising the climate, damaging ecosystems and polluting the air, soil and rivers. This makes it harder for extractive companies to secure a social mandate so they become more inclined to either break the law or support extreme politics that override democracy.

Now it needs others to follow.

Lake Ontario, the vast body of water that straddles the US-Canada border, has gone by many names over the centuries: Lac Saint-Louis, Lacus Ontarius, Skaniadorio, Cataraqui Lake. But one thing it will never be called, says the Canadian rock star Bryan Adams, is Lake America. In his new song Lake Ontario, Adams takes aim at the US president, Donald Trump, accusing him of “breaking the peace” between the people who live on the lake’s shores. Trump signed an executive order in August directing US federal agencies to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America”, echoing his earlier, widely mocked decision to rename the Gulf of Mexico “the Gulf of America”. Related: Neil Young files second lawsuit against Trump for unauthorised use of Rockin’ in the Free World at rallies The move further escalated a feud with Canada that has strained the longstanding alliance between the two countries. Trump’s decision has largely been met with derision in Canada, with some pointing out that the province of Ontario is named after the lake, not the other way around.

Outcry after Call of Duty maker uses real footage of deadly Seoul crowd crush in new video game

Bereaved families in South Korea have demanded that the makers of Call of Duty remove harrowing footage of the deadly 2022 Seoul crowd crush from the latest instalment of the video game. The clips, which are seconds-long, appear in the opening moments of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, and are used to represent a scenario of civilian casualties during a fictional North Korean invasion. One shows a scene of chaos with a figure performing CPR on a victim lying in the street. Another shows rows of bodies laid out in the road, and a victim being carried away on a stretcher. A total of 158 people were killed in a narrow alley in Seoul’s Itaewon nightlife district during the Halloween weekend in 2022. Two more have since been recognised as victims, having died from trauma caused by the disaster.

Related: ‘The audience gets to be in on it’: How narrative-led gameplay is Call of Duty’s greatest weapon They said people who had taken part in the rescue or witnessed the crush were still living with trauma, while hateful comments about the victims were spreading online in connection with the game’s premise.
