However, the spokesperson also highlighted that the European court of human rights issued an interim finding in May that obliged Polish authorities to “refrain from hindering the taking up and exercise of judicial duties” by judges who are still waiting to be sworn in. The confrontation sets the battle lines before next year’s parliamentary election, with polls pointing to a close race between Tusk’s broad coalition and the nationalist right. However, experts remain divided over whether the government’s procedural gambit at the court is lawful. Poland’s Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights said on Saturday the legal basis for the temporary suspension was “questionable”, warning it would “not contribute” to restoring the court. The foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, conceded that the events outside the court were “not elegant”, but insisted: “The alternative was to concede an unconstitutional transformation of Poland into a presidential republic.” Nawrocki held some cross-party political talks on Saturday, with no apparent breakthrough.

When the Australian human rights lawyer Eva Buzo emerged from the sea on to the shores of One Man Beach in Montego Bay on Sunday after her gruelling, nearly 11-hour-long swim, the thunderous pulse of welcome drums was drowned out by the chants of “free beach” from jubilant supporters. Here in Jamaica’s tourism capital, against a backdrop of jagged mountains and sunset-tinted clouds, Buzo – a celebrated marathon swimmer – said she was pleased to help support the important work of the Jamaica Beach Birthright Environmental Movement (Jabbem) and others fighting for free public access to Jamaica’s beaches. “People’s rights are more important these days than ever, and people keep on trying to encroach on our fundamental freedoms,” she said, calling the privatisation of beaches a colonial legacy. ‘The last fortress’: historic Athens cafe closes as countercultural area gentrifies

It has been the hangout of writers, artists, poets and politicians, doctors and lawyers, radicals and revolutionaries for as long as anyone can remember. And for 44 years, Christos Vanas, the proprietor of Mouria, has let them all in. Every day at 7am, the taciturn former waiter has been the first man to step inside the historic cafe in Exarchia, the heart of leftwing Athens. It is a ritual he has kept punctiliously, opening up the famous gathering place before he himself has had his first coffee. “Only Saturdays are different,” says his daughter Areti, drawing on a Karelia, the aromatic Greek cigarette that, like Mouria, has been around for more than a century. “By 5am, he is here serving tsipouro and other [alcoholic] spirits to warm up the stallholders of the street market outside.” But this weekend will be Vanas’s last. After a send-off expected to last into the small hours, the cafe’s large, iron-framed doors will shut forever on Sunday when patrons walk out of the mosaic-floored institution. It will be the closing act in a drama that began with the expiry of the premises’ lease last summer.

In New Zealand’s bellwether seat, what are locals thinking as a knife-edge poll looms?

It’s a hot spring day in the Auckland suburb of Onehunga, and the main strip is starting to hum with life. Builders slip into a bakery for a snack, retirees chat over coffee outside cafes and a shoeless man zips by on a scooter. There are few signs New Zealand’s general election is looming along this shopping strip but Onehunga and neighbouring suburbs that make up the electorate Maungakiekie, will be closely watched when New Zealand heads to the polls on 7 November. “The royal family enslaved us! Apologise now! Reparatory justice now!” King Charles and the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, will be greeted with messages as they travel through Antigua’s capital, St John’s, to attend meetings at the Commonwealth leaders’ summit next week. On billboards, placards and T-shirts, in letters and at a candlelight vigil for the thousands of Africans trafficked to Antigua and Barbuda during the transatlantic slave trade, the message from the Caribbean will be pervasive: slavery reparations is not an issue they “are going to be able to dodge”. James Knight of Citizens for Reparatory Justice, which is organising some of the demonstrations, said the king and UK government had made protest necessary.

Riot police deployed to Poland’s constitutional court after judge suspended

Riot police were locked in a tense standoff with protesters outside Poland’s constitutional court on Friday night after its top judge was suspended in the latest escalation in a decade-long dispute over the court’s legal status. The clashes followed a controversial decision by a group of government-appointed judges to suspend the court’s contested president, Bogdan Święczkowski, and his deputy, Bartłomiej Sochański, amid disagreements over the bench’s legitimacy. The move prompted a furious reaction from the rightwing opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, with its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, condemning what he claimed was an “assault” on the court. The court frequently ruled in favour of Polish legislation over EU law and the European Union accused Poland’s highest court of being too close to the nationalist political power of the time.

Josh was having a drink at Commander D, a popular gay bar in Taipei, on a Saturday afternoon when several police officers suddenly burst in. “Squat down and don’t move,” they shouted. The 28-year-old was among 51 customers to be rounded up and taken away for questioning over suspected breaches of public decency rules. “I didn’t expect something like this to still happen these days. The police operation was criticised by rights groups as heavy-handed, and has unsettled LGBTQ+ communities in Taiwan. On Saturday the island hosts one of the region’s largest Pride parades, and some say the police operation is emblematic of a persistent, wider stigma that risks jeopardising its global image as a LGBTQ-friendly destination.

Ukraine war briefing: Moscow’s Lavrov snubbed at G20 in Atlanta

The EU’s foreign policy chief has accused Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov of presenting “lies” in G20 meetings in Atlanta about the Ukrainian conflict and suggested Moscow was not ready for peace negotiations. “We were talking about the big geopolitical crisis, including Ukraine, and we were able to address Sergei Lavrov head-on with this,” Kaja Kallas told Agence France-Presse on the sidelines of a meeting on Friday. “Of course, he put forward a lot of lies, a lot of false narratives that we were also able to then rebuke.” Kallas said Russia did not appear ready to move ahead in peace talks. “Even if they would have said this in words, their deeds tell something else,” she said. “July, August, and September have been the deadliest months for civilians in Ukraine.” She added: “They should show with their deeds that they are ready to negotiate, but they are clearly, clearly not.” At the talks, which are focusing on global economic growth, energy security and trade, European officials pushed Russia to secure a ceasefire in the Black Sea, an important agriculture export corridor.

Plans for a traditional family photo of G20 ministers were called off after some European officials objected to appearing alongside Lavrov. Moscow has been shunned by most of the West since it invaded Ukraine, and Lavrov himself remains under international sanctions. The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said: “We do not engage in that way with the Russians and have not for a number of years.” German foreign minister Johann Wadephul said there would be no photo because “there is no normality with Russia”. US secretary of state Marco Rubio spoke briefly with Lavrov on the sidelines of the G20 meeting, with the Russian minister saying both sides had a “decent talk”. The traditional “family photo” to open the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting has been abruptly cancelled in the US after a host of nations – including Australia and the UK – refused to appear beside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, pulled the plug after several European officials, the UK and Australia made it known they would boycott or walk out of the snapshot that often kicks off such international gatherings. Rubio still opened the talks in Atlanta with an appeal for unity on the issues that threaten international security and trade. “We are in a critical moment,” Rubio told his colleagues. “We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises.” Related: ‘We hope he’ll accept’: US invites Putin to G20 summit at Trump golf club About one-third of countries at the talks made it known they would not appear beside any Russian representatives. European Union nations had made clear they would boycott any photo with the Russians.

British aid worker mistakenly identified as a survivor of Nepal-Tibet disaster

A British aid worker was mistakenly identified by Nepalese authorities as a rescued survivor after returning to Kathmandu on a humanitarian aid flight. Alastair Chambers, a 45-year-old former Gloucester councillor, said he flew to Nepal last week to distribute sleeping bags, food and essentials to communities cut off by collapsed bridges. After spending several days in a village near the Trishuli river in central Nepal, Chambers returned by helicopter to the capital, where he was greeted by police officers asking for his details. “I gave them my details, just abiding by the rules, and they obviously thought that I’d been rescued,” Chambers told the Press Association. Chambers appeared on a list of 119 names released by local authorities on Tuesday. An army spokesperson then told reporters at a press conference that a British national was among those rescued. “I was contacted by about 15 different journalists in the last few hours, just asking how I was and how I’m feeling after being rescued, and I had to say: ‘Well sorry, I haven’t been rescued,’” Chambers told PA.

text:
Edouard Balladur obituary

For many months before the 1995 French presidential election, Édouard Balladur, the incumbent prime minister, seemed certain of victory. Opinion polls consistently gave him a lead over his conservative rival Jacques Chirac, and the main leftwing candidate. But, as other politicians have discovered, polls can be misleading and voters change their minds. When the ballot papers were counted it was Chirac who won and succeeded François Mitterrand as president. The defeat of Balladur, who has died aged 97, was due partly to his lack of appeal to young voters, a consequence of his public image which, somewhat unfairly, was that of an aloof aristocrat. When he first became a minister, the satirical weekly newspaper Le Canard Enchaîné dubbed him “his courteous self-importance” and Le Monde’s cartoonist Plantu depicted him as a bewigged 18th-century nobleman being carried around in a sedan chair. His manner and style – three-piece English tailored suits, dislike (figuratively and literally) of getting his hands dirty and obvious distaste for close personal contact – did not play well in the context of a presidential contest.

citation.title: Edouard Balladur obituary

text:
Edouard Balladur obituary

There was nothing aristocratic in Balladur’s background, however, about which he maintained a certain mystery. He was born in Smyrna, now Izmir, in Turkey, the youngest of the six children of Pierre Balladur, the manager of a local branch of an Ottoman bank, and Émilie (nee Latour). His parents became naturalised French citizens in 1932 and the family moved to France when Édouard was six, settling in Marseille, where he went to school at the Lycée Thiers. Balladur began studies in law at Aix-Marseille University, then continued them at the Institute of Political Sciences (Sciences-Po) in Paris, living for a while in the Roman Catholic hostel where years earlier Mitterrand had resided. A bout of tuberculosis temporarily interrupted his studies; once cured he completed his military service in Algeria, which was then a French colony, two years before the war of independence, when tensions were high. On his return to Paris, he was accepted into the École Nationale d’Administration (ENA), then the nursery of France’s political, business and technocratic elite.

citation.title: Edouard Balladur obituary

text:
Edouard Balladur obituary

He began his career with the Conseil d’État and the former state broadcasting organisation ORTF but caught the eye of Georges Pompidou, Charles de Gaulle’s prime minister, and became his adviser in 1964. This gave him a ringside seat during the student riots and civil unrest of 1968, and the negotiations that eventually got the country back to work after a national strike. In 1969, Pompidou succeeded De Gaulle at the Élysée, and Balladur went with him, becoming secretary general of the presidency. After Pompidou’s death in 1974, a leading industrialist took Balladur under his wing, and he ran two subsidiaries of a major company, making useful contacts in business. For many years he enjoyed a plum sinecure as president of the company operating the Mont Blanc tunnel. In 1980, he returned to politics. Chirac, who had walked out of his job as President Valéry Giscard d’Estaing’s prime minister in 1976 to found the conservative RPR party and pursue his own presidential ambitions, sacked two of his closest advisers and invited Balladur to replace them.

text:
Edouard Balladur obituary

Chirac’s first presidential bid the following year failed (though it sank Giscard), but five years later the conservative right recaptured the Assemblée Nationale, and Chirac was appointed prime minister after negotiations with the socialist Mitterrand in which Balladur played a key role. In this, the first “cohabitation” (in which the president and the government are of different political families), Balladur was appointed minister of finance, economy and privatisation. He was a powerful minister, but was in office for only two years. In 1988, Chirac made a second presidential bid and lost again. The re-elected Mitterrand called a general election, and the Socialists were able to form a minority government. Balladur returned to the world of business, where he now cut a more substantial figure after his experience in government, and set about establishing networks of friends and contacts. It was clear that the Socialist-led government was heading for defeat in the 1993 general election. Chirac, as the leader of the right, was the obvious choice as prime minister after a conservative victory.

citation.title: Edouard Balladur obituary

text:
Edouard Balladur obituary

But he had been so bruised by his experience as prime minister under Mitterrand’s presidency during the first cohabitation that he was not eager to repeat the experience. Balladur emerged as the clear favourite for the role, acceptable to both Mitterrand and the right. It was evident at the time that Chirac saw Balladur as a proxy for himself. One of his closest allies even suggested Balladur might make weekly visits to Chirac in the Paris city hall, where he reigned as mayor, to brief him on government business. But Balladur established himself as his own man. The second cohabitation, unlike the first, was a courteous affair. The public took to the new prime minister, and seemed to appreciate the absence of confrontation between Mitterrand and Balladur. Balladur had never been one of the barons of Gaullism or Chirac’s version of neo-Gaullism, and his instincts appeared to favour Christian democracy on the German model more than the national populism of the likes of Charles Pasqua or Philippe Séguin.

There was no shortage of crises – over reform of immigration laws, a strike at Air France that saw clashes between workers and police, the minimum wage for young school leavers, funding for church schools and the plight of French fishermen. Abroad, there were some serious questions over France’s role in the genocide in Rwanda. But Balladur avoided taking on protesters, preferring discreet withdrawal when it appeared there was strong opposition. He was credited with a success in the talks on the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (Gatt) in 1993. It rapidly emerged that, far from being a surrogate for Chirac, Balladur was a man with views and, more importantly, ambitions of his own. Month after month, polls showed strong public support for him. Relations with Chirac and his allies deteriorated in spite of occasional public and unconvincing displays of unity. It is not clear when he decided to stand for the presidency, but he formally declared his intention in early 1995. Much of the centre-right and two significant RPR figures – Pasqua and the future president Nicolas Sarkozy – rallied to him.

text:
Edouard Balladur obituary

But Chirac had found an issue on which to campaign: the “social fracture” in French society. In the slightly improbable role of the outsider castigating the technocratic elites, Chirac struck a chord, particularly with the young. Balladur’s efforts to reach out to the people, including climbing on tables at public meetings, to much general derision, were less successful. His opinion-poll lead melted, and in the first round of voting Lionel Jospin, the socialist candidate, came top with 23% of the vote, followed by Chirac with a little under 21% and Balladur at 18.5%. Chirac won the run-off. The new president was not the man to forgive what he regarded as treason, and in the new government there was no place for Balladur, who, however, retained political ambitions. When it became clear that Jean Tiberi, Chirac’s successor as mayor of Paris, was tainted beyond political redemption by scandal, Balladur, after some hesitation, declared his candidacy. If he had hoped for help from Chirac, he was disappointed.

Tiberi and Balladur split the centre right vote, allowing Bertrand Delanoé to become in 2001 the first leftwing mayor of the city since the Paris Commune 130 years earlier. Balladur continued to serve as an MP until 2007. In later years, questions began to be asked about the financing of his 1995 presidential campaign. The allegations centred on the sale of submarines to Pakistan and possible bribes, commissions and kickbacks. In 2002, a bomb in Karachi killed 14 people, 11 of them French employees of the national shipbuilders. Al-Qaida was initially suspected, but later it was suggested that on taking office Chirac had stopped the payment of kickbacks to middlemen and the bombing had been an act of revenge or intimidation. There were reports that some of the money had found its way into Balladur’s campaign funds. Certainly, claims that the huge sums of cash in large-denomination notes paid into campaign accounts were the product of the sale of T-shirts did not convince everyone. Several members of his entourage were investigated and charged by magistrates looking into alleged misappropriation of public funds in what became known as the “Karachi affair”.

In 2017, Balladur himself was charged with funnelling kickbacks on state arms deals with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, alongside the former defence minister François Léotard. In 2021, the court of justice of the Republic ruled that there was no evidence that Balladur had personally ordered payments linked to the contract, nor sufficient proof to establish the origins of his campaign financing, and he was acquitted of all charges. Léotard was found guilty, and given a suspended prison sentence and a fine. Balladur’s wife, Marie-Josèphe (nee Delacour), whom he married in 1957, died last year. They had four sons, Pierre, Jerome, Henry and Romain. • Édouard Balladur, politician, born 2 May 1929; died 31 August 2026 • Stephen Jessel died in 2025

Germany blames Russia for drone attack at Leipzig airport

The German government has blamed Russia for the drone attack on Leipzig airport last month, calling it “dangerous behaviour” and part of a systematic and concerted effort by Moscow to “cause great damage” through a large number of hybrid attacks. The interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, and the foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, ended weeks of speculation and the government’s hesitancy to blame Russia, saying in a brisk 10-minute briefing in Berlin that all indications were the Russian state had provided the knowhow and equipment for the planned attack and “low-level agents” were recruited to carry it out. A drone loaded with explosives was discovered at Leipzig/Halle airport on 4 August near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane used to transport weapons to Ukraine. It failed to detonate but could have caused a catastrophe, authorities said. Russia will face a package of penalty measures, Wadephul said, adding that the German government saw “a need for appropriate and necessary action in this situation”. It would respond “to this hybrid attack in Leipzig with proportionate and measured, yet equally resolute, action”, he said.

text:
Iceland’s close ties with EU mean no vote is not a Brexit-style rejection

Iceland’s 52.8% to 47.2% vote against reopening EU accession talks is, undeniably, a blow for Brussels. But claiming it as a Brexit-style victory for “national sovereignty” or evidence of broad rejection of the EU misrepresents the reality of the island’s relationship with the bloc. For the EU, Iceland was a dream candidate: small, stable, prosperous and strategically located in an increasingly contested Arctic. Eager as it is to wield more geopolitical clout and revive flagging momentum around enlargement, a vote in favour would have given Brussels a very welcome boost. Instead, Iceland’s rejection handed Eurosceptics another stick with which to beat the bloc. France’s Marine Le Pen said the result showed the appeal of a Europe of “free, sovereign nations” rather than closer integration, while Reform UK’s Nigel Farage congratulated Icelanders on “voting to keep their independence”. But Iceland is a very special case. Its situation bears precious little relation to Brexit or even to a broader EU-critical movement.

citation.title: Iceland’s close ties with EU mean no vote is not a Brexit-style rejection

text:
Iceland’s close ties with EU mean no vote is not a Brexit-style rejection

Icelanders did not vote to isolate themselves from the EU, tear up any treaties or “take back control” – they voted to preserve a close, customised and largely successful relationship. Unlike accession candidates in the western Balkans or eastern Europe, Iceland does not need EU structural funds to build infrastructure or boost living standards. High per capita wealth generally insulates its population from the economic pressures that can make EU membership an attractive financial proposition. As part of the European Economic Area (EEA) and Schengen passport-free travel area, Iceland is already solidly within the European fold. It accepts free movement of goods, capital, services and people. Its markets – financial services, energy, transport – are EU-regulated and its social and environmental standards are those of the EU. That means it adopts roughly 75% of EU law and directives into domestic law and there is no question of changing that. Icelandic citizens already enjoy full EU single-market rights without full EU membership, and that, a narrow majority decided, was, on balance, good enough.

citation.title: Iceland’s close ties with EU mean no vote is not a Brexit-style rejection

text:
Iceland’s close ties with EU mean no vote is not a Brexit-style rejection

Although the official reaction in Brussels was muted, some acknowledged EU dismay. “The EU doesn’t inspire people any more,” said the Belgian Green MEP Saskia Bricmont. The centrist MEP Sandro Gozi, who represents France, called it “a warning Europe should take seriously”, adding that the bloc’s “power of attraction” should not be taken for granted. Opposition to full membership was focused heavily on the country’s fishing industry, which accounts for 15% of its GDP and 40% of export revenues and which the no campaign claimed would inevitably be threatened – as during the 1960s and 70s “cod wars” with the UK – were Iceland to join the EU’s common fisheries policy. The vote also revealed a stark divide between people in the capital, Reykjavík, who largely saw membership as an additional form of security for a geographically isolated country in the age of Trump and Putin, and those on the rest of the island, many of whom are fishers and farmers, who overwhelmingly voted against.

citation.title: Iceland’s close ties with EU mean no vote is not a Brexit-style rejection

text:
Iceland’s close ties with EU mean no vote is not a Brexit-style rejection

But if Iceland’s particular circumstances mean the “no” victory was not an ideological rejection of the EU and all it stands for, it nonetheless holds lessons for Brussels. The first is that existing EEA/EFTA states are harder to persuade to join the EU than countries outside the single market. Related: ‘Winter panic’: EU gas stores at their lowest level in 13 years For non-EEA nations, joining the EU offers transformative individual and economic benefits – unrestricted access to the world’s biggest trading bloc, freedom of movement, huge financial aid. For citizens of EEA states such as Iceland (and, for that matter, Norway), most of those already exist. When the status quo provides 80% of the benefits of membership and poses no threat (real or imagined) to emblematic national industries, the incremental gains of full accession become a hard sell. What should worry the EU more is that despite growing doubts about the US and Nato security umbrella, Icelanders were not won over by the bloc’s protection offer.

citation.title: Iceland’s close ties with EU mean no vote is not a Brexit-style rejection

text:
Iceland’s close ties with EU mean no vote is not a Brexit-style rejection

For all the talk of the bloc “stepping up” as a defensive force, its mutual defence clause, which provides for solidarity if a member state is attacked, did not convince. There is, clearly, work to be done there. But as the EU law professor Alberto Alemanno argues: “Iceland’s referendum result does not reject European integration … It shows that close integration short of membership can be stable, credible and politically attractive.”

Opponents of Madrid’s newly constructed Formula One circuit have accused the regional authorities of putting profit before people’s wellbeing after tests for the inaugural Spanish Grand Prix at the track later this month yielded noise levels that were many times the legal decibel limit. The regional government of Madrid and the city council are hoping that the 5.4km-long (3.3 miles) Madring circuit – which has been built in the north-east of the Spanish capital at a cost of €83m (£71m) – will attract visitors, boost the local economy and put the city firmly on the motor racing map. The Madring bills itself as “a perfectly connected circuit: just 20 minutes from the city centre”. But recent track tests using Formula Three cars have worried local people who are taking legal action over the construction of the circuit and the noise it is expected to generate. The Stop F1 Madrid platform, which was formed a year ago, said neighbours had recorded average noise levels of 102.7 decibels during the tests, with peaks of between 107.7 and 109.1 decibels. The maximum noise level permitted in residential areas is 55 decibels.

The population of the world’s heaviest parrot, the kākāpō, has surpassed 300 birds for the first time in 75 years, after a record breeding season triggered by the mass fruiting of a native New Zealand tree. Ninety chicks were officially added to the population of the critically endangered birds on 1 September, pushing the total to 325 – a record high since recovery efforts began. “The last time the population is thought to have exceeded 300 birds may have been as long as 75 years ago,” said Deidre Vercoe, the conservation department’s kākāpō recovery operations manager. “We had a four-year gap between breeding seasons, so it’s fantastic to finally see the population increase after all that time.” Related: ‘My lovely distraction’: live stream of kākāpō – world’s fattest parrot – and her chicks captivates New Zealand Kākāpō, the world’s only nocturnal and flightless parrot, were once abundant across New Zealand. But their population plummeted after the introduction of predators such as cats and stoats. By the 1900s, they were nearly extinct.

Singapore asks the $70,000 question: who wants to start a family?

With leafy cycle paths, rooftop water parks and child-friendly restaurants, Singapore’s east coast is one of the best places in the island city-state to raise a family. Finance worker Lee lives in an apartment here with his wife and two cats, but like an increasing number of Singaporeans they do not intend to have children. They worry about the challenges of bringing them up, and the disruption to their lives. He knows his parents want grandchildren: “They brought it up a couple of times when we were younger, but now they don’t bring it up any more.” Related: The tipping point: what happens when deaths outnumber births? The 34-year-old, who requested his last name only be used, says he and his wife feel the same. “We are happy with our lives right now, so adding a kid will kind of complicate that,” including giving up travel and not being able to go out to restaurants. A survey released this month by YouGov has found that many Singaporeans feel the same, with one in four saying they don’t plan to have children.

Grappling with a historically low birthrate, the city-state announced sweeping measures to encourage couples to have children, but it is unclear how successful those measures might be. The prime minister, Lawrence Wong, has said the government will provide almost S$70,000 (US$55,048; £40,647) in direct financial support for every child by the time they turn 17. The policy begins at birth with a S$10,000 baby grant, and two separate $5,000 grants for medical and educational expenses. Other provisions include S$2,000 in “child credits” from ages one to 16, lowering government-subsidised preschool fees to S$150 a month, and giving people more parental leave. “Singapore’s future will only be as strong as the families that build it,” Wong said. Singapore’s birthrate for women of reproductive age – known as the total fertility rate – is a record low of 0.87. Peekaboo island: the floating forest confounding nature watchers in western Canada

A thickly forested island appeared mysteriously on a western Canadian lake. Nearly 150 metres (500 feet) long and 75 metres (250 feet) wide, the land mass took local people and experts by surprise. It wasn’t on any maps or navigation charts. One boater approached and took a video of the island, capturing nearly 100 trees undulating in the chop of the lake. And then, within days, it disappeared. On Monday, the island made its second appearance – nearly 20 miles from its location earlier in August – in stunning aquatic displacement that has left residents wondering how an entire island can seem to simply vanish. The mystery has unfolded in the middle of Williston Lake, a long and narrow reservoir created after the W.A.C Bennett dam flooded the region in the early 1970s. At nearly 1,700 sq km (650 sqmiles) it is the largest body of freshwater in the westernmost province. Bob Gammer, a spokesperson for BC Hydro, the government-owned utility that operates the reservoir and dam, said the island was “quite something and rather unbelievable” when he first saw the images.

Tuesday briefing: Scotland has promised on violence against women – can it deliver?

Good morning. Violence against women and girls, in all its myriad forms – physical and mental, blatant and insidious – is a global challenge. It reaches back through millennia and, lately, it has been turbo-charged by technology, which offers abusers new ways to shame, harass and monitor victims. What would it take to eradicate it? Scotland’s first minister John Swinney wants to find out. Today, he will set out his programme for government (the Holyrood equivalent of the King’s speech), and Swinney surprised many when he pledged to put ending violence against women at the heart of his government’s ambitions for the coming year and beyond. But haven’t we been here before? Scotland has produced a raft of radical strategies, as well as legislation hailed as the international gold standard on domestic violence. So what hasn’t changed? For today’s newsletter, I spoke to equalities campaigner Talat Yaqoob, who co-chaired the Scottish government’s National Advisory Council on Women and Girls after four years until last month.

Bayeux tapestry loan symbolises ‘entente amicale’ between France and UK, says King Charles

The loan of the Bayeux tapestry was “the best possible symbol” of the “entente amicale” between France and the UK, King Charles said, as he visited the famous embroidered masterpiece at the British Museum in London. Though the tapestry recounts a conflict, “here it is today, nearly 1,000 years later, as a precious symbol of trust, at a time when trust seems sadly to be in short supply between nations,” he said. The “70 metres of memory and artistry” were a reminder “that our two nations have been bound together for almost a millennium”, added Charles, speaking at the new exhibition and accompanied by the French president, Emmanuel Macron, and UK prime minister, Andy Burnham.

British man deported from Sweden despite living there since childhood

A 34-year-old British man who has lived in Sweden since he was 10 has been deported in the latest of a series of Brexit-induced catastrophes for UK citizens in the country. John Sellers was told to leave despite living in Sweden for 24 years, having been educated in the country and newly married to his Swedish partner, Caroline. “It is time people know how people are being treated here, and it is time to show what Brexit has caused,” he said, as he described his near seven-year struggle to remain in the country. “Quite frankly, we have been holding our tongues too long. I am very well aware that different countries have different rules on immigration, but none of this would have happened were it not for Brexit,” he said. His parents moved to Sweden from Essex under the free movement rights that came with the UK’s membership of the EU because they liked the education system and thought it was a “good place to bring up children”. His father died when he was 16, and his mother moved back to England after he started a college course to become a teacher.

text:
New constitution in Guinea-Bissau will undermine democracy, opponents say

Guinea-Bissau voters have approved a new constitution, which critics say will undermine democracy, that significantly expands presidential powers ahead of elections due in December. According to provisional results, 70% of voters approved sweeping changes in the tiny west African state’s first constitutional amendment since revisions that ended the one-party socialist state more than three decades ago. The turnout for Sunday’s referendum was reportedly over 55%, amounting to an estimated 544,060 people. The new constitution will reduce the number of seats in parliament from 102 to 65 and cut electoral constituencies from 29 to 12. New provisions will require presidential candidates to have lived continuously in the country for at least five years before the vote, which is believed to target diaspora-based politicians with significant followings.

Since then it has had at least 10 coup attempts, half of which have been successful. The most recent came after last November’s disputed presidential elections. Both candidates declared themselves winners, citing electoral malpractice by the other’s camp. The military forcefully intervened, setting up a transitional ruling council headed by Gen Horta Inta-A Na Man, a former military chief of general staff. Na Man said: “What we want after this referendum is to allow whoever wins the elections to see out their mandate without hindrance.” Nelson Moreira, the second vice-president of the transitional council, said the outgoing constitution, which came into effect in 1993, had often been cited as “the cause of instability in Guinea”.

Gun found in French lake is analysed by 2012 Alps killings investigators

Experts are examining a gun found by tourists to determine whether it might have been used to kill a British family in the French Alps 14 years ago. In what remains an unsolved murder case, Saad al-Hilli, 50, his wife, Ikbal, 47, and her mother, Suhaila al-Allaf, 74, were shot dead on a road near Chevaline, a remote Alpine village near Lake Annecy, in eastern France, in September 2012. The couple’s two young daughters, then four and seven, survived but a passing cyclist, 45-year-old Sylvain Mollier, was also killed. The French prosecutor Marie-Céline Lawrysz confirmed that a pistol, thought to be a Luger, was uncovered on 20 August by two tourists swimming in Lake Annecy. The weapon is currently being analysed by ballistics experts in France in connection with the al-Hilli cold case. During the initial investigation, pieces from the butt of the weapon used in the killings, a vintage Luger P06-29 pistol, were found on the ground near the British-registered BMW estate car that the family had been driving at the time of the attack.

Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong pleads guilty in second national security case

Joshua Wong, one of Hong Kong’s most prominent pro-democracy activists, pleaded guilty on Wednesday to conspiring to seek foreign sanctions against Hong Kong and China, a national security charge that carries a maximum life sentence. Prosecutors have accused Wong, 29, of working with the exiled Hong Kong activist Nathan Law to urge foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades or other hostile measures against China. The court heard that Wong had visited foreign countries and met foreign politicians to lobby for sanctions against Hong Kong and China. The prosecution said he had continued to call for sanctions on Hong Kong and China after the implementation of the national security law and that he had posted meetings on his social media accounts. Wong has been continuously imprisoned since November 2020. He has spent nearly six years in detention and had been due to be released in January 2027. No eggs, no potatoes but ‘a lot of imagination’: how Spain cooked in war’s hunger years

Few dishes are simpler to prepare than Spain’s signature dish of tortilla de patatas, which – aside from disputes about onions – requires nothing more than two basic ingredients and a pinch of salt. But where to begin if you have neither eggs nor potatoes? That is the question the chef and food writer Berta Álvarez Acal sets out to answer in Recetas de Guerra (Wartime Recipes), a compilation of recipes covering the years of hunger after the end of the Spanish civil war in 1939. In the case of the tortilla de patatas, the absent eggs and potatoes were substituted by moistened bread and onion to try to simulate the texture of an omelette. “There was a formula using water, bicarbonate of soda and a bit of oil which simulated an egg perfectly and the potatoes are substituted by bread to make a tortilla that really is delicious,” Álvarez said. In the recipe for “fried squid without squid”, deep-fried onion rings masquerade as squid while the “wartime hake” is instead salt cod. As for the “wartime and postwar breakfast”, this consists of “coffee” made from a blend of barley, malt and chicory.

Álvarez did not just compile the recipes. “We recreated them and shared them with friends and family,” she said. “Some dishes, although they were prepared from scraps, surprised us as they were real gems, others were not so great.” The recipes in the book span the period from the founding of the second republic in 1931 to the phasing out of ration cards in 1952.

‘I want to live’: the disabled people unable to go abroad because of care funding refusal

Disabled people are being blocked from travelling abroad by NHS care boards and local councils that refuse to let them use their care funding outside the UK, the Guardian has learned. Campaigners warn of a “postcode lottery” in England where the right of a disabled person to travel overseas depends on where they live or the whim of local officials – even when there is no extra cost to the taxpayer. Disabled care users report having to abandon travel plans at the last minute, or go for years without a break, when authorities refuse to pay for their care abroad, even though they have agreed to meet all the travel expenses. The Guardian is aware of instances where individuals have had requests for care and support for overseas travel turned down by NHS officials – only to have the decision reversed when they threatened legal action. Lucy Robinson, 38, told the Guardian she had been prevented from attending international work events and going on a holiday because health officials in Oxfordshire had refused to allow her to use her care package abroad.

Japan halves speed limit to 30km/h on all narrow city streets

Drivers on residential roads in Japan have been forced to take their foot off the accelerator, after the speed limit was slashed from 60km/h (37mph) to 30km/h in an attempt to reduce deaths and injuries among pedestrians on narrow urban streets. The new limit, which went into effect on Tuesday, applies to residential roads with no centre line or maximum speed signs, media reports said. Narrow roads with no centre lines or pavements are a common sight in crowded Japanese cities, with data indicating that children and older people are at particular risk of being involved in a fatal or serious accident. They account for about 70% of the country’s general roads, the newspaper said. Authorities hopes the restrictions will address concerns that residential areas are not experiencing the same improvements in safety seen on larger roads.

Wednesday briefing: ​What’s behind the global backlash against datacentres?

Good morning. This summer, datacentres have become targets of resistance across the world. Ever since the arrival of ChatGPT, big tech has been lobbying for the creation of enormous new facilities. Many governments claim they’re essential in any country that wants to cash in on AI. Campaigners argue datacentres drain resources and exacerbate the climate crisis. The Scottish National Party has backed a moratorium on new developments; so has the Greens. The boom has been immense, and so has the backlash. Today’s newsletter explains why. At First Edition, we’re keen on pushing the boundaries of frontier technologies (no luddites here), so today we’re trying something new: we’ve produced a video to accompany this newsletter, and you can watch more on the Guardian’s Instagram page. Let us know what you think by replying to this email. How’s that for innovation? Before you do, here are the headlines.

In depth: ‘We’re in an extremely anti-democratic moment with AI’ In August I attended a meeting of campaigners and councillors in the east London borough of Tower Hamlets, where the government has recently approved plans for a 5,200 sq metre datacentre on the site of an old brewery off Brick Lane. The meeting, held on a sunny Monday evening, went on for three hours, in a stifling hall so packed that organisers had to create an overflow room. It’s a testament to how divisive the subject has become. The new east London datacentre won’t be anywhere near as large as the “hyperscale” datacentres that power AI, which are typically 10,000 square feet or more. Neither is it the first to be built in the area (there are already three similarly sized developments nearby). But attenders I spoke with shared the same concerns as other campaign groups globally. They worried about the amount of energy the building will consume (5.2MW, according to a local campaign group, which is enough to power 15,000 homes), about its use of water (projections for this haven’t been released), and about the noise and heat it could emit.

They have good reasons to be concerned. The IMF estimates that by 2030, datacentres will consume more energy than all but the world’s three largest state emitters (China, India and the United States). They are already driving up electricity prices: one analysis found that wholesale electricity prices rose 267% over five years in locations near datacentres in Virginia. And although the industry argues that technology in newer AI datacentres consume less water than older facilities, not even the Environment Agency knows how much water datacentres use. It’s one of many unknowns. Much of the anger here centres on how it’s been approved. Despite fierce opposition from local residents and Tower Hamlets council, which wants the site to be used for hundreds of homes, housing secretary Angela Rayner intervened, overruling the council to approve the application, citing its creation of 44 homes (only six of which will be socially rented) as a “significant” public benefit.

Globally, the number of “hyperscale” datacentres has nearly tripled since 2018. The UK had 52 datacentres in 2000, and today there are an estimated 520, roughly 48 of which are “hyperscale”, though it’s impossible to get exact figures, since nobody (not even the government) knows the total number that have been built. In the US, where local governments have signed NDAs with tech companies, information is shielded from scrutiny. In the EU, Microsoft and other American tech companies successfully lobbied to conceal the environmental impact of their developments.

Secrecy is power, particularly when your industry devours massive amounts of energy, much of it powered by fossil fuels. Because developers can wait years for an electricity grid connection, many are now opting to build their own gas-fired power plants instead. In the UK, more than 100 datacentres intend to burn gas to generate their electricity. It’s possible that some may do this permanently. These are reasons you might expect more scrutiny of these developments, not less. “We’re in an extremely anti-democratic moment with AI,” the Guardian’s tech correspondent Aisha Down tells me. The Starmer government tended to proselytise about the benefits of big tech. Since the start of this year, the government has allowed datacentres to opt into Nationally Significant Infrastructure Projects (NSIPS), where the secretary of state rather than local councils make planning decisions, enabling developers to bypass local scrutiny. Two of the first datacentres to opt into the NSIPs scheme are applying to build new private gas power stations to fire up their operations, which will together be responsible for more than 4.5m tonnes of carbon emissions. “Most people don’t want diesel generators running constantly near where they live,” Aisha says. “That sort of thing is upsetting to communities.” *** What are they good for? The question is whether we need the “hyperscale” variety. There has been lots of noise among policymakers about the UK being an “AI maker, not an AI taker” that can’t afford to be left behind in the AI “race” or lose its AI “sovereignty.” But nobody seems to agree on exactly how datacentres achieves these vague aims. Will they rejuvenate post-industrial areas with shiny new jobs? Probably not. Will they help the UK “shape the AI revolution”? It’s hard to see precisely how, when US tech companies building many of the datacentres on UK soil retain control over infrastructure, IP and profits. “People in the highest echelons of power seem to be making policy based on AI Fomo and vibes,” Aisha says. We’ll return to this vibes-based strategy and the risky financing of the AI boom in future newsletters. For now, it’s clear these fights reflect a feeling that datacentres are something done to communities, regardless of whether they consent. The Burnham government hopes to reignite people’s faith in democracy by giving them more control. The battle over datacentres will be a major test of that commitment.

text:
What’s really behind Trump’s deference to Putin?

Could Donald Trump be a Russian asset? The headline on a review in the Guardian of my new book Betrayal has provoked heated international debate. Written by the historian Lawrence Freedman, the piece generated thousands of comments from across Europe and beyond on social media. Many people responded with a single word: “Duh!” Trump’s relationship with Vladimir Putin is the biggest mystery in international politics. In 2017 I wrote a book called Collusion, which set out Moscow’s operation to support and cultivate Trump, going back decades. The US president, of course, denies links with Russia. But in his second term, his behaviour towards Putin has been as weird and perplexing as during his first. For example, at the Alaska summit last year the US president applauded his Russian counterpart, meeting him at Anchorage airport and rolling out a red carpet. Trump seemed uncharacteristically nervous, as he waited for Putin to emerge from his plane. At their joint press conference after talks, he allowed the Russian president to speak first. It was a bizarre act of deference. Why?

citation.title: What’s really behind Trump’s deference to Putin?

text:
What’s really behind Trump’s deference to Putin?

There are, I think, overlapping reasons for Trump’s submissive behaviour. I explore them in Betrayal, (which is published this week in Denmark by Politikens Forlag, with Italian, Finnish and Ukrainian language editions to follow.) As I mentioned in a Q&A with Guardian readers, one factor is ideological: Trump’s Maga supporters see Russia as an “anti-woke” kindred state. Putin leans into this idea, positioning himself as a defender of conservative values, under threat from a decadent and godless Europe. High-profile Trump supporters have travelled to Moscow. Erstwhile Maga cheerleader and former Fox News host Tucker Carlson even absurdly praised the Russian capital’s well-stocked supermarkets. Another explanation – advanced by Fiona Hill, the former White House adviser – is strongman envy. Trump would like Putin’s freedom of action, when it comes to making money and crushing opponents. It is evident the US president prefers the company of autocrats.

text:
What’s really behind Trump’s deference to Putin?

By contrast he frequently badmouths European democrats, among them the former British PM Keir Starmer (“no Churchill”), and Giorgia Meloni (“I felt sorry for her”.) A third theory is kompromat, a KGB term to describe potential compromising material. We know from declassified records that the Czechoslovakia secret police began spying on Trump in the 1970s, when he married a woman from behind the iron curtain. He visited Moscow in 1987, on a trip organised by a Soviet state agency, and subsequently made many visits to Russia including in 2013 for the Miss Universe beauty pageant. What exactly happened on these excursions is unclear. But I know from my own experience in Moscow – I was the Guardian’s bureau chief from 2007 to 2011 – that Russia’s intelligence agencies are adept at surveillance operations. Shortly after I arrived, the FSB broke into the apartment I shared with my wife and our two children. They left clues, busting open the window in my son’s bedroom, with a perilous drop to the courtyard below. The British embassy advised us our home was bugged.

text:
What’s really behind Trump’s deference to Putin?

Possibly, Putin’s ghost-like spies had installed video cameras too, we were told. Over the next four years we experienced on-off harassment from a shadowy and paranoid state. There were mysterious break-ins, veiled threats from foreign ministry officials, and a summons to visit Lefortovo, the FSB’s infamous pre-detention centre and gloomy prison. Undoubtedly, the KGB and FSB will have spied on Trump too, as well as on other high-profile foreign guests. A 2020 report by the US Senate intelligence committee alleged that the FSB has secret cameras inside the Ritz-Carlton hotel, where Trump stayed during his 2013 trip. There will be tapes. They may be innocuous. But Putin knows what they show, and Trump knows that Putin knows. *** Consequences remain the same Does this make Trump an asset? My conclusion is that the terminology doesn’t much matter. As the chess champion Garry Kasparov notes, if Trump were an asset, or an agent of influence, what exactly would he do differently? Since 2025 he has stopped direct US military aid to Kyiv, humiliated Volodymyr Zelenskyy in the Oval Office, and repeated Kremlin lies and disinformation.

text:
What’s really behind Trump’s deference to Putin?

The US president’s Russia-friendly actions have consequences. I have been visiting Kyiv for nearly two decades, and have spent much of the past five years reporting from Ukraine and the frontline. I was in the capital in February 2022 when Putin tried to seize it. Since then, the conflict has evolved. It is no longer fought with armoured vehicles and tanks, and has become instead a hi-tech aerial battle. Most nights, Russia bombards Kyiv with kamikaze drones and ballistic missiles. Ukraine, meanwhile, carries out its own long-range strikes. It has the world’s most innovative drone and counter-drone industry. But Kyiv badly lacks US-made Patriot interceptors – the only system capable of shooting down fast-moving ballistic missiles. Trump refuses to send Patriots or allow Kyiv to develop its own version under licence. And so civilians die – families, elderly couples, teenagers – entombed under the ruins of pulverised apartment blocks. At night you hear explosions, a moped-like growl from enemy drones, and booms from Ukrainian air defence. Asset or not, Trump is doing little to make this horror stop.

Care workers and others fleeing UK modern slavery win visa reprieve

Care workers, chefs and others in danger of losing their migration status under post-Brexit rules if they leave an exploitative employer will be helped by new visa changes, the Home Office says. Officials said if an employee was found to be a victim of modern slavery they would be allowed to work for any employer for the remainder of their visa. The migration status of people on skilled worker visas was tied to a sponsoring employer, under a scheme introduced to fill post-Brexit labour shortages by Boris Johnson’s Conservative government in 2021. It meant workers on that route, who have no recourse to public funds, risked having to leave the UK if they lost their job and could not quickly find a new sponsoring employer. Campaigners have been warning the rule was being exploited by rogue employers, who use workers’ precarious status in the UK to underpay them, force them to put in long hours, or to force them into zero-hour conditions.

text:
Climate injustices have been laid bare in the Nepal-Tibet flood disaster

The recent glacial collapse and catastrophic floods in Nepal and Tibet are not isolated tragedies (Report, 28 August). They reflect accelerating climate disruption that disproportionately affects the countries and people that are least responsible for global emissions. As climate change intensifies, glaciers around the world, including in the Himalayas, are melting at unprecedented rates, destabilising ecosystems and causing glacial collapse and ice-and-rock landslides, destroying settlements, villages and livelihoods in minutes. No one died when a Swiss glacier collapsed last year, owing to early-warning systems that were in place. But a lack of early-warning systems means that the disaster in Nepal and Tibet has led to hundreds of deaths and thousands missing. Events like these are not “natural disasters”. They are due to global warming and climate injustices, and also flawed development policies, including rampant property developments on vulnerable floodplains. They call for better disaster preparedness and investment in early-warning systems. Most importantly, they require global action.

EU’s ability to defend against invasion remains in doubt, finds official report

The EU’s ability to respond to a foreign invasion by 2030 remains in doubt due to a continuing reliance on the US and fragmented national defence systems, according to a report from its official auditor. The European court of auditors (ECA) said the EU was much better prepared than before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine of 2022, but achieving its goal of defence readiness by the end of the decade would be difficult. “Achieving defence preparedness in the EU by 2030 remains challenging,” said Marek Opioła, an ECA member who led the review of the EU’s defence policy published on Thursday. “There are still major difficulties such as fragmented national systems or industrial bottlenecks. We also still rely on the United States.” Speaking to the Guardian, he stressed the EU could “still make major progress” if it sharply increased defence spending and rapidly expanded ammunition production. Between 2020 and 2025, EU member states increased defence spending by 79%, a response to the Russian threat and a belated effort to meet Nato spending targets.

Gloria Steinem obituary

Gloria Steinem, who has died aged 92, was a writer, community organiser, political campaigner and a charismatic feminist activist who called herself “an entrepreneur of social change”. She spent much of her life on the road, often accompanied by equally committed fellow campaigners. Steinem loathed public speaking, but during two years travelling in India in her 20s, she moved from village to village, with “a sari, a cup and a comb” in a group countering religious intolerance. She said she learned then, as Gandhi taught, that a message was all the more powerful delivered “eye to eye”. Steinem, unlike some of her contemporaries, never recanted or modified her many causes, which included civil rights, violence against women, and the struggle for equality. She continued to argue that every economics course ought to start not with production but with reproduction, and an understanding of the patriarchal instinct to restrict a woman’s right to contraception and abortion. She was one of Donald Trump’s most outspoken critics throughout his rise to power.

More than 800 Indonesian students and teachers have fallen ill in separate incidents of food poisoning linked to President Prabowo Subianto’s free-meals program this week, with dozens hospitalised after they with struck with nausea, vomiting and stomach aches. The conclusion of the longest-running murder trial in Maltese history has left a country in turmoil, and a grieving family still searching for answers. At 7.30pm on Wednesday, gasps and cheers echoed around hall 22 of the courts of justice in Valletta, as a jury pronounced a businessman accused of ordering the murder of the investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia not guilty. Yorgen Fenech, 44, had been facing a life sentence if convicted. Now, after nearly seven years in and out of custody, he is free to return to a gilded life as the heir to one of Malta’s biggest fortunes. In her reporting, Caruana Galizia had taken aim at many powerful figures, including Fenech and the politicians he was close to. Her revelations, and the fallout from her violent death in a car bombing in October 2017, had ultimately led to the resignation of the prime minister, Joseph Muscat, and several members of his government. Within weeks, three hitmen accused of planting the bomb were arrested.

After Wednesday’s decision, the long search for whoever was responsible for hiring them must begin again. The party has been in power since 2013. Caruana Galizia’s family described the verdict as “justice denied”. The attorney general is considering whether to appeal for a retrial. The chances of success may be slim: both charges brought against Fenech were dismissed by an 8-1 majority. It had taken nine years, a relentless family campaign and a determined judge to bring Fenech before a jury. In the end, they took him at his word.

Serbians targeted with spyware in country’s ‘largest documented wave of surveillance’

At least 14 people from across Serbian civil society were targeted with advanced spyware earlier this year in what the digital rights group Share Foundation said was the largest documented ​wave of such infection in Serbia to date. The wave of spyware infections was discovered in August after Apple notified people in 110 ⁠countries that they had probably been victims ⁠of mercenary spyware. The Citizen Lab, which carries out forensic analyses of spyware attacks, released an analysis on Wednesday showing that at least one of the Serbians had been targeted with the NSO Group’s Pegasus spyware, which would have given the attacker “total access to the device”. Related: Spyware can easily fall into the wrong hands – investors should take note Share said those targeted included members of a Serbian student movement that has been a thorn in the side of the government of Aleksandar Vučić since 2024. Coalescing out of countrywide protests that followed the collapse of a train station that winter, it is one of the largest student movements in Europe.

Spain’s PM says no evidence ‘whatsoever’ Morocco behind Ceuta border breach

Spain has seen no evidence “whatsoever” that Morocco planned or facilitated a mass border breach into its north African territory of Ceuta, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has told parliament. The address on Thursday followed the emergence of a police report, commissioned by a judge and widely quoted in the media, claiming Moroccan border forces had actively aided about 70,000 people to cross the border in late July. “I ‌can assure you ‌that no institution – not the diplomatic service, nor the European Commission, ‌nor any international body – has provided the Spanish government with any solid evidence that Morocco planned or carried out the incident. None whatsoever,” Sánchez told parliament. Speaking the morning after about 50,000 people marched in Madrid to protest his handling of the Ceuta crisis, the socialist prime minister also denied the government had received any warning of the mass breach, saying no reports to authorities had anticipated “the scale or probability of what eventually happened”.

A leading Swedish opposition party has promised an urgent reprieve for British nationals facing deportation from the country over Brexit administrative issues. Niels Paarup-Petersen, the migration spokesperson for the Centre party, said it would introduce laws to end the suffering of people such as the 78-year-old British widow Joyce Thomas if, as polls project, it forms a new centre-left coalition after the general election in 10 days’ time. Thomas has been told to leave by next Wednesday after 21 years in Sweden. Paarup-Petersen said if his party got into power it would reopen the application process so British citizens threatened with deportation could reapply to stay in Sweden. He said: “We have seen many appalling cases, people who are in a vulnerable state who have every right to be here but are being denied that right because of a minor administrative problem. There has been no leeway whatsoever. “People are paying the price, but Sweden doesn’t win either.

The US and Venezuela: a century-old relationship drenched in oil

Written in the middle of the last century, the US Department of State memo conveys its message in a curt and undiplomatically honest tone: the glue that binds Washington to Caracas is, and is always likely to be, oil. “All US policies toward Venezuela are affected in greater or less degree by the objective of assuring an adequate supply of petroleum for the US,” the 1950 document reads. Decades later, little appears to have changed. After a brazen night-time kidnapping of the country’s leader earlier this year, Donald Trump announced last week that the US was taking majority control over about a fifth of Venezuela’s oil reserves. That deal, according to the White House, “secures our energy dominance for the next century”. How much it will benefit Venezuelans is yet to be seen. The country’s importance to the US has been proven time and time again over the past century. Home to what are now known to be the world’s largest known oil reserves, Venezuela kept allied planes, ship and tanks well fuelled during the second world war.

Interactive Washington and Caracas largely cooperated over the following decades, with US energy companies heavily involved in Venezuela’s oil industry, and profiting from it immensely. But relations took a nosedive in 1999, when Hugo Chávez became president. A self-professed socialist and anti-imperialist, Chávez made alliances, and often oil deals, with China, Iran and Russia. Venezuela switched 180 degrees to become a natural adversary of the US, alongside its ally Cuba. Relations deteriorated further when Chávez was briefly detained by his own military after a deadly crackdown on mass anti-government protests. The attempted overthrow lasted only two days and he was soon back in the presidential palace, accusing Washington of involvement in the failed coup. Chávez deepened Venezuela’s dependence on oil exports in the years that followed. In 2007, he stepped up his battle with Washington with a wave of nationalisation in which he seized oilfields, including those that US firms had operated. Caracas had nationalised the oil industry decades before, but had allowed US companies to profit from the extraction.

‘We continue to suffer’: victims of apartheid-era Sharpeville massacre demand compensation

The day dawned brightly on 21 March 1960, as residents of the South African township of Sharpeville gathered to protest against pass laws, which forced “Black, Indian and Coloured” South Africans to carry documents at all times specifying where they were allowed to be. Abraham Mofokeng joined the march, one of dozens organised nationwide by the Pan Africanist Congress (PAC), a breakaway group from the African National Congress (ANC). “The weather was very nice, the sun was out. You could not have suspected that the day would go so horribly,” said Mofokeng, who was then a 20-year-old factory worker. Mofokeng, now 86, was among the thousands gathered peacefully outside the police station in Sharpeville, which is about 40 miles south of Johannesburg in a heavily industrialised region known as the Vaal Triangle. The crowd was singing, he said, when officers opened fire without warning. At least 91 people were killed and 238 injured, in what became known as the Sharpeville massacre. As Mofokeng fled, a bullet grazed the inside of his right foot, ripping his shoe off.

A woman fell to the ground before him; he jumped over her and kept running. Only later, when he noticed blood running down his legs, did he realise he had been shot in the back, where a bullet remains lodged in his spine. Mofokeng is among three claimants suing the South African government, in a case filed on Thursday, for compensation for the massacre. If the case is successful, dozens more could file claims. The case is part of a wave of litigation demanding justice for apartheid-era crimes, amid widespread disillusionment with ANC-led governments that have failed to rectify South Africa’s huge racial inequality and poverty since the end of apartheid over three decades ago. In January 2025, 25 survivors and relatives of victims of apartheid state violence sued South Africa’s government for failing to prosecute cases referred to it by the post-apartheid Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC). That May, the president, Cyril Ramaphosa, announced a judicial inquiry into potential political interference, which is still ongoing.

Spokespeople for South Africa’s justice department did not respond to a request for comment on the Sharpeville compensation case. In the immediate aftermath of the Sharpeville massacre, police claimed protesters had been throwing rocks at them. “I don’t know how many we shot,” said Col J Pienaar, the local police commander, according to a story published by the Guardian the following day. “It all started when hordes of natives surrounded the police station. My car was struck with a stone. If they do these things they must learn their lesson the hard way.” In July 1961, in response to victims filing compensation claims, the white minority regime passed a law indemnifying the government and anyone acting under its authority for any actions taken “in good faith for the prevention or suppression of internal disorder, the maintenance or restoration of good order, public safety or essential services, or the preservation of life or property”. The law, which was made effective retrospectively from the date of the massacre, is still in force today.

The wife of a British man detained by police in Stockholm on Tuesday ahead of a threatened deportation has pleaded with Andy Burnham to get involved in the Brexit catastrophe unfolding for many British citizens in Sweden. Several people have been injured in a shootout in central Kyiv between two branches of Ukraine’s security services, in an incident Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as “disgraceful”. The shootout, which took place on Wednesday morning in a downtown area of the capital, was between officers from the domestic security service, the SBU, and the military intelligence directorate, the HUR. The SBU said in a statement on Thursday that the shootout “definitely shouldn’t have happened” and that it was assisting state investigators. The clash appears to have been sparked by the SBU’s recent arrest of a Russian man fighting for Ukraine under the supervision of the HUR. Local media reported that while the SBU was searching an apartment linked to the investigation, HUR officers arrived and shots were fired; three HUR officers were injured. The SBU said that, together with the HUR, it had foiled a Russian-backed terrorist plot targeting a Russian opposition leader who had recently arrived in Ukraine.

Deadly escalation in Black Sea attacks prompts fears of even higher food prices

A summer of hostilities in the Black Sea proved deadly for seafarers, as Russia and Ukraine attacked each other’s ships and port infrastructure, preventing vital grain exports and prompting concerns that the conflict will push global food prices even higher. More crew were killed in the Black Sea in July than during the entirety of the war before that month as the conflict has intensified, making the body of water the most dangerous in the world for commercial shipping. This is despite the conflict between the US and Iran, with vessels still being targeted in the strait of Hormuz, Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. As many as 23 people died in July as a result of attacks on 35 ships in the Black Sea, according to estimates from the Turkish seafarers’ union Türkiye Denizciler Sendikası. Attacks on vessels continued into August and escalation in the Ukraine war has prompted the head of the UN shipping agency, the International Maritime Organization, to condemn the “deterioration of maritime security around the globe”.

Russia first launched waves of attacks on port infrastructure and vessels anchored in Ukrainian Black Sea ports in the months after its invasion in 2022, preventing Kyiv from exporting grain. In July, Russia again struck Ukraine’s main grain export hubs of Odesa and Chornomorsk. However, the recent escalation in the Black Sea and neighbouring Sea of Azov – connected by the Kerch strait – has also resulted from Ukrainian retaliatory attacks. Drones have hit Russian vessels, including tankers Kyiv says belong to a shadow fleet of hundreds of ships used by Russia to evade sanctions on its oil exports. Ukraine has targeted ships and port buildings at the Russian Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, vital for oil and grain exports. In a grim illustration of the danger to vessels and their crew, an abandoned Russian-flagged cargo ship – with a burned-out command deck – recently ran aground on Turkey’s Black Sea coast as startled holidaymakers looked on.

Europe calls out Russia’s ‘hybrid war’ in public. But how can it make Putin pay?

Russia’s suspected sabotage campaign across Europe appears to be gathering pace again, confronting governments with a problem they have struggled to solve since the start of the war in Ukraine: how to impose a meaningful cost on Moscow for attacks that remain deliberately below the threshold of conventional war. Over the past month alone, an explosives-laden drone was discovered next to a Ukrainian cargo plane at Germany’s Leipzig airport, Poland has faced suspected acts of sabotage, and a string of unexplained explosions and fires have hit defence facilities supplying Ukraine across Europe. The attacks, aimed at sowing chaos and undermining support for Ukraine, vary widely in their ambition and sophistication, but share a common feature: they are often difficult to trace conclusively back to Moscow. That ambiguity is built into the way the operations are organised. Russian intelligence services have shifted away from relying primarily on professional operatives dispatched across Europe.

Instead, suspected saboteurs are increasingly recruited remotely, including through Telegram channels, and paid in cryptocurrency to carry out individual tasks – allowing the Russian intelligence officers directing them to remain safely at home. The pattern was evident in Denmark this week, where authorities warned that Moscow was recruiting Danish citizens to carry out sabotage against defence companies with ties to Ukraine. But the growing scale of the attacks, and the speed with which European governments are now prepared to point the finger at Moscow, suggest the mood may be changing. When an incendiary parcel burst into flames at DHL’s Leipzig hub in July 2024, it took about nine months before German investigators reported a concrete link to the GRU, Russia’s military intelligence agency. This time, Berlin moved far faster. Within days of the second incident at Leipzig airport, German officials publicly blamed Moscow – a sign both of growing confidence in identifying Russian operations and diminishing patience with what officials see as an increasingly brazen campaign of sabotage.

Yet while Berlin has become quicker to point the finger at Moscow, its punishment for now has followed a more cautious path. Germany’s response to the failed Leipzig drone attack appeared calibrated to keep tensions in check, underscoring the harder question of what Europe can actually do beyond sanctions and diplomatic expulsions without risking a direct military confrontation. Berlin announced the closure of a Russian cultural centre and a Russian consulate, prompting Moscow to shut down the already gutted Goethe-Institut – a measured retaliation rather than a real escalation. Europe’s room for retaliation is also constrained by the powers given to its intelligence agencies. Unlike the CIA, many European services are primarily tasked with collecting intelligence and have far less latitude to conduct covert operations abroad. That leaves governments with relatively few tools between diplomatic and economic punishment on one end of the spectrum and overt military action on the other.

Germany urges EU to cut Russians’ holiday visas after sabotage attacks

Germany is urging its European partners to introduce tighter limitations on Russian citizens entering the EU on tourist visas, after recent sabotage attacks which Berlin has blamed on Moscow. German authorities are investigating a Belarusian national, who also holds a Russian passport, over the alleged attempt to attack Leipzig airport using drones and explosives. The man is alleged to have entered the Schengen area on a tourist visa issued by the Italian embassy in Minsk, the capital of Belarus. Security sources said he did not appear to have ever travelled through Italy. Germany’s foreign ministry has complained that too many visas were being issued to Russians. “The number of visas issued for Russian nationals for holidays in the European Union is too high,” a spokesperson said. Sources close to the government say the sheer number of visas being issued to Russians goes against the spirit of sanctions related to the Ukraine war, and make it impossible to know who is entering the EU and for what purpose.

Figures show that Italy issued more Schengen visas than any other country in the bloc in 2025; between them, Italy, France and Spain received three-quarters of all visa applications from Russians, according to Euractiv. Italy issued more visas to Belarusians than any other EU country last year, and the number has risen sharply since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. According to European Commission statistics analysed by the Italian news website Linkiesta, Italy issued just 2,968 visas to Belarusian citizens in 2021, compared with 50,709 last year. A similar trend can be seen with Russia. Italian visas issued to Russian citizens rose from 63,894 in 2021 to more than 165,000 in 2025, almost tripling despite the war. Germany’s government this week announced measures to hit back at the Kremlin, after it said Russian intelligence was likely to have been behind the alleged Leipzig plot. These included closing the Russian consulate in Bonn, summoning the Russian ambassador to the foreign ministry, and tightening the monitoring of Russia’s shadow fleet of illegal vessels carrying oil in the Baltic Sea.
