text:
Much of Europe already levies a tourist tax – a nice little earner for Italian hotspots

A nightly tourist tax may be unfamiliar territory in the UK, but countries in continental Europe have been cashing in on these kinds of levies for decades. Tourists usually need to pay the tax on the day they check out of a hotel or holiday let, and are often surprised by an extra fee on top of their accommodation costs. Among the earliest introductions of a tourist tax was in Austria in 1842, specifically targeting those who stayed in spa and wellness retreats. Similar measures were later implemented in France, Italy, Germany and Switzerland as a way to prevent the inhabitants of towns hosting such high-end resorts from paying for costs incurred by wealthy visitors. Italy’s tourist tax structure has gone through various changes. During Benito Mussolini’s fascist regime, it was broadened to include any town or city classified as a tourist destination. The tax was then completely abolished for the World Cup in 1990 as Italy embraced more visitors, only to be brought back in nationally in 2011, with Rome becoming the first city to reintroduce the levy.

citation.title: Much of Europe already levies a tourist tax – a nice little earner for Italian hotspots

text:
Much of Europe already levies a tourist tax – a nice little earner for Italian hotspots

Depending on the destination, and sometimes the hotel type, the nightly fee typically ranges from between €1 (£0.86) and €10 per person, although guests of five-star hotels in Milan pay €12. Venice has also had an entrance fee in place since 2024, although that is only targeted at day-trippers. The overnight levy is a serious earner for popular Italian destinations. In 2024, Rome made €222.4m, followed by Milan (€109.3m), Florence (€82.9m) and Venice (€38.9m), according to data from Siope, the finance ministry’s tracker of public money flows. The revenues are supposed to be spent on local services, especially in towns and cities buckling under the pressure of overtourism, or on maintaining monuments. However, the reality is that cash-strapped municipalities use it for other expenses. “All municipalities want the fee because they need the money,” said Gianluca De Gaetano, the manager of the Rome unit for Federalberghi, the hotels’ association. Tourists mostly just absorb the payment, even if begrudgingly.

Fascism on the rise in the UK, Anglican bishop says

Fascism is on the rise in the UK, a Church of England bishop has warned, condemning the “twisted theology” of the self-described “Christian patriots” who demonstrated at ports on the south coast last weekend. The masked, black-clad, anti-migrant agitators – led by Daniel “Danny Tommo” Thomas, a former bodyguard of the far-right influencer Tommy Robinson – were heard chanting: “Christ is King.” Arun Arora, the bishop of Kirkstall in Leeds, said the incidents in Dover and Portsmouth were part of an increasingly worrying and disturbing rise in attempts “to tear the social fabric of our country” this year. Arora said the disorder that followed the “evil” killing of Henry Nowak in Southampton earlier this year, the subsequent racist firebombings in Belfast, anti-migration protests in Thetford, Norfolk, and a recent incident in Lancashire – in which the BBC reported that a six-year-old boy had a racial slur scrawled on his forehead – were “the first steps on the journey to open fascist nationalism that takes pride in conflict, hostility and division”.

Fascism on the rise in the UK, Anglican bishop says

Arora added: “The biggest threat to England’s fabric today is to be found in the tidal wave of nationalism that threatens to destroy the foundations of community, to devastate social cohesion and threaten any sense of unity within this United Kingdom. “What we have seen on our streets in Southampton, in Belfast, in Thetford, in Portsmouth, in Dover is the playing out of a new machtpolitik – the ideology that argues that might is right – that threatens not only those of us who are likely to be targeted or attacked but threatens our way of life as a country. “This goes beyond the racism that many of us grew up with in the 1970s. Rather it is a return to the 1930s, where those dressed in blackshirts gathered on the streets under the banner of fascism.” Arora said the church had to challenge the “sinful idolatory” and “twisted theology” of so-called Christian nationalists, saying they were using the cross of Christ as a fashion accessory, with no understanding of Jesus’s message of love. He added: “We need to be consistent and unequivocal in our theology that there is no national flag that sits atop the cross ….

Houthis seize key Yemeni port of Mocha in drive to take control of Red Sea coast

Houthi forces in Yemen are making a concerted drive to take over the country’s Red Sea coast fully, claiming control of the key port of Mocha in the most serious wave of fighting with the Saudi-backed government in years, bringing the Iran-aligned group closer to full control of a key shipping route. Seizure of the coast and some of the islands in the sea would be a strategic disaster for Saudi Arabia and the US, taking Iran and its proxies closer to full control of two choke points for western shipping on opposite sides of the Arabian peninsula: the Bab al-Mandab at the southern end of the Red Sea and the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf. Observers have said a reduction in hostilities – the most intense since the UN-sponsored ceasefire of April 2022 put an end to major military exchanges – now seems unlikely in what is seen as an attempt by the Houthis to open a second front in the Iran-US war, alongside the battle for control of Hormuz.

But in the past 48 hours the Houthis had major advances south, down Yemen’s west coast, taking them closer to the high ground overlooking the narrow Bab al-Mandab strait. The fighting has also raised questions about whether Saudi Arabia, which on Thursday launched as many as 40 airstrikes on Houthi targets, will activate the Mecca defence agreement and ask its co-signatories, Pakistan and Turkey, to send forces. Malta warned of corruption crisis after ‘utter disbelief’ over Daphne Caruana Galizia verdict

Malta is vulnerable to “repeated instances of high-level corruption” unless it strengthens the rule of law and protections for journalists, the Labour peer Shami Chakrabarti said at the opening of an inquiry into judicial failures following the death of Daphne Caruana Galizia. Chakrabarti, a member of the House of Lords and former director of the human rights group Liberty, has been named special rapporteur for a Council of Europe investigation into the fallout from the assassination of the anti-corruption journalist, who died in a car bombing in October 2017. Malta is in turmoil after the acquittal of a wealthy and politically influential businessman, Yorgen Fenech, of any involvement in Caruana Galizia’s murder. Fenech denies paying a middleman €150,000 to have her killed. At the inquiry’s first hearing, on Wednesday, Chakrabarti said the verdict had “staggered many throughout Maltese society and beyond. “It’s now almost nine years since the assassination that struck at the very heart of Maltese public life but a mastermind has not yet been held accountable,” she added.

The first witnesses on Wednesday were the journalist’s eldest son, Matthew Caruana Galizia, and her sister Corinne Vella, who questioned the verdict, which dismissed both charges against Fenech by an 8-1 majority. Related: Sabotage, leaks and political ties: the story of the Daphne Caruana Galizia murder trial Matthew Caruana Galizia told members of the council’s committee on legal affairs and human rights: “The Maltese public have seen all of the evidence against the accused, and the vast majority were convinced of his complicity in the murder. And this is why there is this atmosphere of utter disbelief at how the jury could have reached such a decision.” Malta’s state prosecutor is understood to be preparing an appeal, with the aim of securing a retrial. The Council of Europe, founded in 1949 after the second world war, created the European convention on human rights. It is led by an assembly drawn from members of the parliaments of its 46 member states.

The procedure, known as the rule of law conditionality mechanism, was first used in 2022, against Hungary. “If there is such huge problem in matter of rule of law and a function of the Maltese institutions, the EU should apply a similar procedure on increasing pressure for reform,” said Bulai. An ocean away from Nepal, Sonia spends her spare time piecing together clues about missing flood victims: ‘I wanted to be useful’

A chain of flowers tattooed from knee to foot, a gold nose ring worn on a left nostril, a primary school tie caked in mud: these are the images that linger in Sonia Patil’s mind as she tries to help Nepali flood victims find their loved ones. More than 1,300 have died and at least 5,500 have been reported missing since a glacial collapse sent a torrent of water, mud, ice and debris through riverside communities along the Nepal-Tibet border on 26 August. Families and friends of those reported missing have spent weeks searching through graphic photos of bodies, which were uploaded by Nepali police for the community to identify. Related: Who are the Australians missing in the Nepal floods? What we know so far Some show only partial corpses – disconnected torsos, limbs splayed at unnatural angles, decomposition eating away at extremities – while in others, the faces of flood victims are turned to the camera, their expressions frozen in their death masks.

citation.title: An ocean away from Nepal, Sonia spends her spare time piecing together clues about missing flood victims: ‘I wanted to be useful’

text:
An ocean away from Nepal, Sonia spends her spare time piecing together clues about missing flood victims: ‘I wanted to be useful’

Patil, a Melbourne-based chef, has no direct connection with Nepal or any of the people whose loved ones have been reported missing. But when she saw videos of their grief, she knew she could help share their burden. “It’s a very harrowing task for them,” she says. “If I had lost a family member, the prospect of coming across their body in that condition would be unbearable. “I knew I wanted to be useful, it’s the least I can do, even if it’s just being another pair of eyes.” Almost every day since the disaster, she arrives home at midnight after a 12-hour shift and spends another four to five hours on the Nepali police website, trawling through the hundreds of images of decomposing bodies and limbs. If any have distinctive features – such as clothes, tattoos and jewellery – she adds them to her list and posts it to Facebook groups filled with those looking for their loved ones. It can be a confronting and tedious process, Patil says.

text:
An ocean away from Nepal, Sonia spends her spare time piecing together clues about missing flood victims: ‘I wanted to be useful’

During the day, the Nepal police website slows or malfunctions under the weight of all the families looking for information, so she finds it easier to work at night. The listings, which grow by the day, may only show partial remains, and most only have one image per body – meaning she cannot see any other angles. Missing persons posters are also spread across multiple platforms, forcing Patil to search across the internet to crosscheck information. But no matter how hard it is, she says it is worse for those on the ground. “It’s very disturbing to know that I may be looking at a picture of a live person and somebody who is deceased at the same time, trying to compare them,” she says.

“I find it easier when I go in with the mindset that all the images on that website are all human: they have lived lives, they have stories, they have families looking for them.” Related: As Nepal’s morgues fill, Parkrit hopes her DNA can be used to find her mother Patil is part of a group which includes people from the US, Europe, New Zealand and other countries who work together to identify bodies. They generally look for matches for those who have reached out to them with photos of their missing friends and family. It is difficult to be 100% certain through visual identification alone, as many images of the bodies are unrecognisable. So when members think they have made a match, the group asks relatives to submit their DNA to labs in Nepal for official confirmation. If they believe they have made a match for someone who has not asked for their help, the group tries to report it to Nepali authorities.

Making a likely identification is bittersweet for everyone involved, Patil says, because while they are glad a family will get closure, “it’s not a great feeling to know that person is no longer here”. North Korea has built new uranium facility to expand nuclear arsenal, UN agency says

The embroidery tapestry tells the story of the events that culminated in the Battle of Hastings in 1066, when William the Conquerer defeated King Harold. 3. It was supposedly commissioned by Bishop Odo, William the Conquerer’s half-brother, for his newly built cathedral in Bayeux in 1077. He was prone to “self-aggrandisement” (in Lewis’s words), which is why he gave himself a starring role in the tapestry. 4. But it wasn’t made in Bayeux. Researchers think it was probably made in England, near Canterbury. 5. It’s embroidered on linen, with 10 colours of woollen thread likely dyed with woad, madder and indigo. 6. Its nine panels were embroidered separately, and then stitched together to form a continuous picture. 7. None of them are having a good time: one is weeping at her husband’s deathbed, another is fleeing a burning building and a third is being assaulted by a priest. 12. This third figure is Ælfgyva (meaning elf-gift), the only named woman in the tapestry. Scholars think that she could be Emma of Normandy, who was accused of having an affair with the Bishop of Winchester. 13. The rapid Houthi advance in Yemen: why it matters and what’s at stake

Violence has erupted again in Yemen, where a rapid advance by the Houthis in recent days is threatening another waterway critical to global shipping. More than 1,000 people have been killed or wounded, and tens of thousands displaced by the most significant fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces in years. Though the immediate catalyst for the fighting has been the US-Iran war, it stems from years of conflict in Yemen itself. Who are the warring parties in Yemen’s civil war and who are their backers? The two main parties fighting in Yemen’s civil war are the Yemeni government forces alongside their allies, and the Houthi movement. Yemen’s government controls the north-east of the country, and its southern port. The government is the internationally recognised authority in the country, but is chiefly backed by Saudi Arabia and a coalition of Arab countries which intervened on behalf of the government during Yemen’s civil war.

The government’s control of the country is contested by the Houthis, who hold the western part of the country, including its capital, Sana’a. The Shia group is broadly aligned with Iran and comprises part of the “axis of resistance”, a coalition of Iran-aligned armed groups in the Middle East, such as Hezbollah. But while the group is aligned ideologically with Iran, which supplies some arms shipments, the Houthis are considered an independent group with their own policies. A variety of smaller armed groups are also active in the country. What’s been happening in recent days? Last week the Houthis launched a wide-ranging offensive to take parts of the western coast of Yemen and gain a more strategic position over Bab al-Mandab. Fighting then broke out across multiple fronts in Yemen as the Saudi-backed government forces tried to reconsolidate their position, with clashes starting in al-Jawf, al-Baydaa, Taiz and Hodeidah.

Denise Davies had bought two tickets for her husband John’s birthday. As a taxi driver who also runs black cab heritage tours of London, he was looking forward to expanding his historical knowledge. At £33 a peak-time ticket, the exhibition’s cost has attracted some criticism – but Denise felt it was worth it. “I could go to Alton Towers and it would cost me an arm and a leg. This is something special. I would have paid whatever it was because we’re never going to see it again … it’s a tick on the bucket list, basically.” • This article was amended on 11 September 2026 to describe the tapestry as being stitched, not woven, by female embroiderers.

Wall Street Journal publisher convicted in Hong Kong of deterring reporter from union role

A Hong Kong court has convicted the publisher of the Wall Street Journal of deterring a reporter from taking up a trade union role, in a case that raised concerns about press freedom in the city. The newspaper dismissed Selina Cheng just weeks after she was appointed chair of the Hong Kong Journalist Association (HKJA) in 2024. She was told at the time her termination was officially due to restructuring.

citation.title: Wall Street Journal publisher convicted in Hong Kong of deterring reporter from union role

text:
Wall Street Journal publisher convicted in Hong Kong of deterring reporter from union role

Outside court on Thursday, Cheng said: “If reporters’ employment rights are not sufficiently safeguarded, or when their rights are violated and not enforced in law, then we can no longer work safely as reporters.” Principal magistrate David Cheung ruled that Dow Jones Publishing, the parent company of the Wall Street journal, was guilty of “preventing or deterring an employee from exercising trade union rights,” but acquitted it of “dismissing or discriminating against an employee because she exercised those rights.” Cheng, who covered China’s automobiles and energy sectors for the WSJ, said her editor had told her that employees should not be seen as advocating for press freedom in “places like Hong Kong”, saying it could be perceived as a conflict of interest. She alleged her employer had attempted to prevent her from taking up a role in the union.

text:
Wall Street Journal publisher convicted in Hong Kong of deterring reporter from union role

Related: ‘She’s not afraid of anyone’: the prison writings of one of Hong Kong’s last outspoken democracy activists She said the company told her that she needed to seek the firm’s approval for outside activities and requested her to leave her then-board position at the association. Cheng launched the private prosecution against Dow Jones Publishing after losing her job in July 2024, weeks after taking up the position as chair of the union. The company pleaded not guilty to both charges, which each carry a maximum fine of HK$100,000 (about $12,750). Sentencing is expected to be handed down at a later date. During the trial, the defence argued that Cheng was terminated because of redundancy and that the prosecution had not sufficiently proved that the firm’s management instructed Cheng’s supervisor. The defence also accused Cheng of acting in bad faith in a previous hearing. But magistrate David Cheung said that Cheng’s termination “was motivated by wrongful and unjustified application of their code of conduct” when it insisted Cheng needed to seek prior approval to stand as chair of HKJA.

text:
Wall Street Journal publisher convicted in Hong Kong of deterring reporter from union role

Cheung said he accepted Cheng’s explanation, describing the former WSJ reporter as “honest and reliable”, adding she was clearly motivated by “the wish to see justice”. Cheng’s termination alarmed journalists, who are already operating in an increasingly restricted media environment in the city, where foreign outlets have traditionally faced less pressure than local news outlets. “The WSJ set a very bad precedent by punishing an employee who was exercising her constitutionally protected rights in Hong Kong,” said Eric Lai, a senior fellow at the Georgetown Center for Asian Law. The WSJ maintained there was no link between Cheng’s role in the Hong Kong union and her termination. At the time of Cheng’s dismissal, it issued a statement saying: “The Wall Street Journal has been and continues to be a fierce and vocal advocate for press freedom in Hong Kong and around the world.” HKJA is the oldest journalist union in Hong Kong. It was established in 1968 and is registered as a trade union representing journalists and workers in news.

AfD’s new state MPs include ex-Stasi officer, former porn actor, neopagans and neo-Nazis

The Alternative für Deutschland is facing scrutiny over the suitability of some of its prospective new MPs – including a former Stasi officer and a former pornography actor – just days after its historic win in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt. Presented by the AfD’s lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, for a photocall in the state capital of Magdeburg on Thursday, some of the members-elect were revealed to have a range of questionable backgrounds, including criminal records, Stasi pasts and connections to far-right networks. German media has revealed that among the 39 parliamentarians who will represent constituencies across Saxony-Anhalt in the state parliament, is a man alleged to have participated in pornography films and falsified academic qualifications; a former officer for the East German secret police, the Stasi; and several members under criminal investigation for their involvement in neo-Nazi organisations.

Two MPs are facing investigations into allegations they sought to continue the activities of the banned rightwing extremist organisation Artgemeinschaft, a neopagan group that has embraced nationalist and antisemitic ideas. The younger of the two is also alleged to have violated the law in relation to weapons, according to the public prosecutor’s office. Both reject the allegations. The erstwhile pornography actor was convicted for stealing bedding in bulk from a hotel. A court confirmed he had been a pornography actor after he contested a local newspaper’s claims. He was expelled from a university after being found to have falsified his school leaving certificate, Die Zeit reported. The MP says he was readmitted after a legal challenge. An ex-Stasi officer, aged 78, who won a direct mandate in his constituency, has admitted to having worked for the ministry for state security in the communist GDR, focused on East German citizens who wanted to permanently emigrate. His role as an MP-elect has been criticised by campaign groups on behalf of victims of the former East German dictatorship.

Also, an investigation by the broadcaster ZDF revealed that some AfD ministers-elect who were also members of the previous parliamentary group, had ties to rightwing extremist groups. This included some having been members of the subsequently outlawed Homeland-Loyal German Youth group, HDJ. At one stage one of them had led the organisation, while an adviser to the AfD’s parliamentary group wrote a biography described as an “homage to national socialism”. Among the prospective MPs are a number with pro-Kremlin links, as well as some who visited members of the Maga movement in Washington. Russian president Vladimir Putin initially said he would not comment on the AfD victory, but speaking to reporters during a visit to India for the BRICS summit later blamed “western globalists”. “I think that everything happening in Europe right now is basically ‌the result of system errors by the so-called West … the western globalists in politics, security, and economics,” Putin said. The AfD has promised to curb migration and restore ties with Moscow.

Asked to respond to the questionable biographies, in particular of the two MPs under criminal investigation, Siegmund, a former fragrance salesman who was unanimously re-elected as the AfD’s parliamentary group leader on Thursday, referred to the men in jest as “the bad guys” and said “we will await the results of the investigations and then discuss them”. Tiananmen Square vigil organisers jailed for seven years in Hong Kong

Two pro-democracy activists who were put on trial for organising an annual Tiananmen Square massacre vigil in Hong Kong have been sentenced to seven years in jail, in one of the city’s most significant national security cases. Chow Hang-tung, 41 and Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, were found guilty in August of incitement to subversion. The court found they had “incited other persons to organise, plan, commit or participate in acts by unlawful means with a view to subverting the state power”. Chow and Lee were leaders of the Hong Kong Alliance, which for decades organised the city’s annual vigil in memory of those killed in the bloody crackdown on pro-democracy protesters in Beijing in 1989. Lee and Chow received prison terms of seven years, and seven years and three months respectively. Albert Ho, a 74-year-old former lawmaker who pleaded guilty in January, received a sentence of five years and two months.

citation.title: Tiananmen Square vigil organisers jailed for seven years in Hong Kong

text:
Tiananmen Square vigil organisers jailed for seven years in Hong Kong

Their case represented one of the last high-profile national security trials to be heard in Hong Kong, as the national security law imposed by Beijing in 2020 extinguishes what was once one of the world’s most widely watched pro-democracy struggles. The Alliance disbanded in 2021 following pressure created by the introduction of the national security law. Related: ‘She’s not afraid of anyone’: the prison writings of one of Hong Kong’s last outspoken democracy activists The case had centred on a slogan that was used for decades by the Alliance: “end one-party dictatorship”. The court ruled that the defendants “intended to cause others to lose confidence in the Chinese Communist party by stirring up hostility and causing division”. The defence said that the Alliance was simply exercising its right to freedom of speech. One supporter who attended the sentencing told the Guardian: “A demonstration that lasted for more than 35 years without any problem is suddenly being seen as subversion.” Chow, a UK educated barrister, represented herself in court.

citation.title: Tiananmen Square vigil organisers jailed for seven years in Hong Kong

text:
Tiananmen Square vigil organisers jailed for seven years in Hong Kong

She has been in detention since 2021 and while in prison has frequently written letters published on her social media. In August Chow wrote a note to the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, calling for Britain “to adopt a more robust stance in the face of the growing threat from a totalitarian and aggressive China”. The UK Foreign Office said it condemned the use of the national security law in convicting the two activists. Before sentencing, members of the public queued up for days to secure a seat in the court. Some in the queue had prepared food and umbrellas in preparation to stay overnight. Hong Kong and Macau were once the only places on Chinese soil where it was permitted to hold public vigils to mourn protesters who died on 4 June 1989 in Beijing. Hundreds, possibly thousands, were killed when the People’s Liberation Army put a bloody end to pro-democracy protests. For decades tens of thousands of people would gather in Hong Kong’s Victoria park to take part in a candlelit vigil. In 2020, Beijing’s sweeping national security law in effect banned public commemoration.

citation.title: Tiananmen Square vigil organisers jailed for seven years in Hong Kong

text:
Tiananmen Square vigil organisers jailed for seven years in Hong Kong

In recent years, activists who attempted to publicly mark the day said they were frequently followed, searched and detained by plainclothes police. Authorities said the national security law would only affect a small number of people and was needed to return order after a year of often violent anti-government protests in 2019. But critics say it has transformed the city. “It is still surreal to me,” Lee’s wife, Elizabeth Tang, told the Guardian. “Every time the Alliance had an activity, they would get the police permission for every one. “The vigils are what made Hong Kong different,” she said, recalling the public commemoration that are now banned. “It’s very unjust. Complete silence is really very scary.” The case has seen widespread condemnation from foreign governments and human rights groups who criticised the use of the national security law to convict peaceful protesters and ban the vigil.

Emma Bonino, radical Italian politician who stood up to Vatican, dies aged 78

Emma Bonino, the radical Italian politician who led campaigns to legalise abortion and divorce against the objections of the Vatican, has died aged 78. “Today we lose not only our leader but also one of the most clear-sighted, courageous and free figures in the political history of our country,” the small party she founded, More Europe, said on Facebook on Friday. Bonino served as a European commissioner and as foreign minister in Italy but was best known as a militant feminist dedicated to political and humanitarian causes. “Her life was a long struggle against everything that denies freedom: against clandestine abortion, world hunger, the stranglehold of party politics, female genital mutilation, punitive justice, genocide, and every form of authoritarianism,” her party said. A former member of Italy’s Radical party, Bonino commanded respect across the political sphere.

citation.title: Emma Bonino, radical Italian politician who stood up to Vatican, dies aged 78

text:
Emma Bonino, radical Italian politician who stood up to Vatican, dies aged 78

Italy’s far-right prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, paid tribute to her, saying that although their “backgrounds and perspectives differed, that never prevented me from acknowledging her significance and her role in our nation’s public life”. Even after the Radicals’ political star faded, Bonino remained a key political figure and human rights campaigner active in Italy for more than five decades. With her sharp wit and cutting insights, she appeared frequently on Italian TV. After a cancer diagnosis in 2015, she would appear in public wearing colourful headscarves. Bonino first got involved in Italian politics after she became pregnant aged 26 and had an abortion, even though it was illegal at that time. “I decided that never, never, never again should anyone have to suffer this humiliation,” she said. Related: Emma Bonino: Italy’s pro-Europe, pro-immigrant conscience She went on to hand herself in to the police, turning her private “offence” into a ⁠public act of defiance. The arrest ⁠made headlines, fuelling a campaign that eventually ​led to the legalisation of abortion in 1978.

Emma Bonino, radical Italian politician who stood up to Vatican, dies aged 78

It also launched Bonino into parliament with the Radical party, a small but relentless force for civil rights. During her 50-year political career, Bonino served as foreign minister, trade minister and EU affairs minister in Italian centre-left governments of the 2000s and 2010s. She remained an outspoken supporter of Europe and the rights of refugees and migrants. “You can look at the fights I have waged with this point of view: I support a democratic liberal order and believe in the centrality of the individual, his rights but also his responsibilities,” she told the Guardian in 2018. Over the years, Bonino cultivated a deep friendship with the late Pope Francis, despite their conflicting views on key ethical issues, including abortion and euthanasia. Bonino said that during their conversations Francis always encouraged her to bring forward her humanitarian battles, defending those most in need. When asked what battles she still needed to fight, Bonino would say: “Many, too many.

Human rights, world hunger, free scientific research … Ten lives won’t be enough.” Bonino is survived by her siblings, Domenica and Giovanni, and their children.

text:
Enjoy Łódź – but don’t omit its tragic past

I was shocked to read your travel article detailing the delights of Łódź without a single mention of the city’s past as the site of one of the largest ghettos during the second world war (A city break in Łódź, Poland’s capital of cinema and factories, 5 September). The article says: “I ask Anna how Łódź fared in the second world war. ‘It was not too badly damaged,’ she says. ‘Both the Germans and the Russians wanted the industry intact.’” I wonder how the surviving family members of the perhaps 200,000 people who died after being herded into the ghetto, often to work as slaves for the Nazi war effort, would feel about that. Łódź is indeed a wonderful city, and I have watched its transformation since I worked there in the late 1980s. Your article highlights the many great pleasures of the city today, as I too experienced on my most recent visit in July. But as so many have said in the past, if we ignore history, all too often we repeat it. Dr Richard Bradbury Exton, Devon • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

text:
How a month-long competitive food tour is rewriting the story of Rio’s favelas

Even at the age of nine, Maria Cristina de Sales knew exactly when to ask her mother’s colleagues at the slaughterhouse for a piece of the pig they were butchering: when they got close to the pork leg, her favourite part. When she grew up, Sales followed the path of many others from Brazil’s deprived north-east and moved south in search of better work opportunities. She arrived in Rio de Janeiro and, unable to afford a home in tourist-heavy south zone, moved to a favela further north. She crossed the city every day to work as a receptionist and secretary, but only really found her footing 15 years later when she and her husband opened a burger restaurant, inside the favela. “The doors that aren’t open to us in the rest of the city, we open for ourselves here,” said Sales, 39, inside her restaurant in Maré, a favela complex that emerged in the 1940s in a vast mangrove area, settled by workers who could not afford to live in – or had been evicted by the state from – the wealthier parts of the city.

citation.title: How a month-long competitive food tour is rewriting the story of Rio’s favelas

text:
How a month-long competitive food tour is rewriting the story of Rio’s favelas

What usually dominates the headlines about Maré, a complex of 16 favelas home to 140,000 people, are problems such as poverty, armed drug traffickers and bloody police operations, but Sales’s restaurant has joined an effort to change that perception. From 1 October, local bars and restaurants will take part in a month-long competitive food trail made up entirely of Maré establishments, hoping to attract visitors from across the city who are often afraid to visit a favela. “We face prejudice simply for saying that we live in a favela, but there are a lot of good things here,” she said. Were it not for the surrounding alleys so narrow that sometimes only one person can pass at a time, the tangled web of electrical wires crowding the utility poles and the occasional young man riding a motorcycle with a rifle, Sales’s restaurant could be anywhere else in the city – a family-friendly, air-conditioned burger joint. The superhero-themed decor was a request by Sales’s sons, and includes a life-size Spider-Man. Her entry for the food trail will be, of course, a pork leg, made into burger named Peppa Pig.

citation.title: How a month-long competitive food tour is rewriting the story of Rio’s favelas

text:
How a month-long competitive food tour is rewriting the story of Rio’s favelas

“It’s a reference to my story: a girl who came from the north-east, went through hell and is now here, proud and still fighting – just like many other people here in Maré,” she added. One sweet-and-slightly-spicy element of the dish – a pineapple jam with chilli and ginger – she learned to make at Casa das Mulheres da Maré, a centre set up by a local NGO, Redes da Maré, to support women and which organises the food trail, called Comida de Favela, or Favela Food. “When we improve the quality of life of a woman in Maré, we’re improving the whole community,” said Mariana Aleixo, 38, the centre’s coordinator, herself a chef who was born and raised in Maré and has worked in the kitchens of Rio’s luxury hotels, including the Copacabana Palace. The food trail is now in its fourth edition – the first was held in 2015 – and is one of four finalists in the Best Culinary Festival in Latin America category at the 2026 World Culinary Awards, which will announce the winners in October.

citation.title: How a month-long competitive food tour is rewriting the story of Rio’s favelas

text:
How a month-long competitive food tour is rewriting the story of Rio’s favelas

The 16 restaurants – selected from more than 150 applicants, most of them Black-owned – receive management and marketing training and, starting this year, guidance on how to support customers who report sexual harassment. The winners, chosen by customer vote, receive cash prizes. Reflecting the origins of many residents or their ancestors, many of the dishes feature other references to north-eastern cuisine, such as the “North-eastern Explosion”, a pizza topped with cassava cream, coalho cheese – similar to halloumi – and carne de sol, a lightly salted cured beef usually fried in a clarified butter similar to ghee. “Gastronomy is the biggest economic sector in the community,” said Aleixo, noting that of the roughly 3,200 businesses in the area, about 1,200 are restaurants and bars. Aleixo said she had approached sponsors of other food festivals across the city and had never succeeded in securing their support. “I believe it’s because of prejudice against favelas,” she said.

citation.title: How a month-long competitive food tour is rewriting the story of Rio’s favelas

text:
How a month-long competitive food tour is rewriting the story of Rio’s favelas

Although the aim is for visitors to experience the favela from a “perspective other than violence”, Aleixo acknowledges that some may witness something that the thousands of people who live there have to contend with: the occasional presence of armed drug traffickers. Police generally do not patrol favelas unless carrying out operations. The food trail has no connection to the criminals, who also do not interfere with its activities because they seem to understand that it benefits the community. “Some of the experiences we live through here are very violent, and we want the city to have access to that. Understanding that sense of indignation that residents often have is important so that people can build a different repertoire for thinking about public security in Rio,” she said. “Violence exists here just as it does in other parts of the city, but it does not define Maré entirely,” added Aleixo.

citation.title: How a month-long competitive food tour is rewriting the story of Rio’s favelas

text:
How a month-long competitive food tour is rewriting the story of Rio’s favelas

Despite the invitation to outsiders – Favela Food’s social media pages often advertise shuttle vans to bring visitors from other parts of the city and take them back again – another aim is to encourage the circulation of people and money between the complex’s own favelas. While Sales’s burger restaurant is in the Parque União favela, the snack bar run by Beatriz Santos Antônio, 39, is in the Nova Holanda favela, a 15-minute walk away. Born in another city in Rio de Janeiro state, Antônio arrived in Maré 16 years ago because she could not afford to live elsewhere. She and her children went through periods of hunger, but neighbours helped them, and she drew on cooking skills learned from her mother to start selling cassava fritters. Her entry for the food trail consists of four elliptical fritters, a classic Brazilian bar snack that Antônio has taken to new heights: crisp on the outside and moist inside, filled with either roast beef or prawns with cream cheese.

citation.title: How a month-long competitive food tour is rewriting the story of Rio’s favelas

text:
How a month-long competitive food tour is rewriting the story of Rio’s favelas

“I’ve come a long way,” said Antônio, smiling as she wiped away tears and made the final preparations for her first time taking part in Favela Food. “Today, these tears are no longer because of hunger. Today it’s a story of happiness and of being able to encourage other women to start their own businesses too. There is also a lot of happiness in the favela.”

citation.title: How a month-long competitive food tour is rewriting the story of Rio’s favelas

text:
Friday briefing: Would a wealth tax save our public services or be billionaire repellent?

Morning pals, and let’s join in a heartfelt ευχαριστώ (thank you) to hedge fund billionaire Chris Rokos for the estimated £330m he paid to the UK Treasury last year, and sadly won’t be contributing in future as he’s relocating to Greece. The publicity shy tycoon (and former Tory donor) has not made explicit his reasons for leaving the UK: so one can only speculate Rokos may be drawn by the noted health benefits of the Mediterranean diet, or the Greek government’s attractive €100,000 flat tax for overseas investors. Predictably, one man’s decision is now being framed by some as a dire warning to government to halt taxes on wealth in the UK. Conversely, campaigners are arguing ever more stridently for a specific wealth tax. With taxes already at their highest level since the second world war, could this be the goose to lay the cure-all golden egg and fix our crumbling public services? I spoke to our senior economics commentator, Aditya Chakrabortty, whose response might not be what you first expect it to be. And, yes, we get into goose-plucking too.

In depth: We need to think about what wealth actually means Taxes are at record highs; satisfaction with public services at rock bottom. It’s a dichotomy familiar to us all from our own private focus groups, be that the street WhatsApp community or the bowling club. Alongside this, wealth is rising exponentially while wages are not: from 2000 to 2025, for example, average weekly earning rose just over 100% while property prices went up by about 240%. According to the British Social Attitudes Survey, the segment of the public who say the government should further increase taxes to spend more on health, education and welfare is at its lowest level in over a decade, at 36%. Aditya offers me a quote from Jean-Baptiste Colbert, the minister of finances under King Louis XIV of France: “The art of taxation consists in so plucking the goose as to obtain the largest possible amount of feathers with the smallest possible amount of hissing.” “This has become harder to do as the tax burden has got higher,” Aditya tells me.

“And so wealth taxes have really emerged as an attractive option to people in government, and to campaigners, not just here, but around western Europe and in America too.” *** What is a wealth tax and how would it work? Most advocates, when they talk about a wealth tax, mean an annual tax on assets over a certain threshold. The Green party of England and Wales, for example, proposes an annual tax of 1% on assets above £10m and 2% on those above £1bn, estimating it could raise almost £15bn a year. The campaign group Patriotic Millionaires – a bunch of likable sorts including Gary Lineker, Brian Eno and Val McDermid – suggests a 2% annual tax on total net wealth exceeding £10m, projecting revenue of £24bn a year. Oxfam, which is campaigning alongside them, says this rate would affect 20,000 people – about 0.04% of the UK population – and highlights polling carried out this May by YouGov, which found 76% of the public support “this fair wealth tax”. Campaigners present this as a slam dunk – minimal hissing for maximum feather.

But dig into that polling a wee bit further and you’ll find the YouGov tracker poll, which instead indicates that Britons, over the past seven years, have a baseline preference for taxing income, rather than assets. It seems that, while the public are attracted to the concept of a wealth tax, they’re pretty selective about how wealth is defined. *** Why not start plucking? Critics of a wealth tax, in the right-of-centre thinktanks and the publications that report on them, argue that taxing the same wealth every year would penalise saving and investment; that a specific wealth tax would require expensive and unwieldy new administrative apparatus to value wealth; that focusing on the super-rich to raise revenue would make the UK a less attractive place for those people to work and invest. Aditya may not share their ideology, but he has his own reasons for being sceptical about current wealth tax campaigning, which he argues “offers apparently easy solutions, which will always affect someone else and never me”.

Crucially, he says, if you’re running the government, the money raised by an annual wealth tax doesn’t make much dent in your bills, relatively speaking. The highest estimate is less than a third of the £80bn the UK government is planning to spend on defence annually by the end of the decade. And, once a tax is in place, so the dodges begin. “The one thing that the wealthy have in droves are advisers to show you how to avoid taxes.” “It doesn’t mean you shouldn’t do it,” he adds, “just don’t oversell it as a magic bullet.” *** What’s this about a one-off wealth tax? So with that bubble burst, Aditya points us to what he considers the most substantial piece of work done on wealth taxes in the UK to date. A couple of academics and a tax barrister came together during Covid lockdown, when the rest of us were struggling with the recipe for banana bread, to form the independent Wealth Tax Commission. They propose a one-off wealth tax, arguing that its fairer because it targets people with the most ability to pay, is very difficult to avoid and wouldn’t distort behaviour because it’s one-time only.

Accounting for behavioural responses and admin costs, they estimate this would raise a total of £260bn at a rate of 5% over £500,000 per individual, payable at 1% per year over five years. To be clear: this would be paid by individuals whose total wealth after mortgages and other debts, and after splitting the value of shared assets such as a jointly owned family homes, exceeded the tax threshold, and only on the value of wealth above that threshold. For example, a wealth tax levied at 1% above £500,000 would require a couple to have net wealth of more than £1m before any wealth tax would be payable. This is where Aditya gets excited: “£260bn is more than we get from income tax in a year. It would be transformative – you could put it in a sovereign wealth fund and invest in renewables. Or you could put it directly into the NHS and schools.” It would, however, affect a very different tranche of the population – those de facto millionaires with property in desirable parts of Edinburgh or Manchester or London. And that’s where the hissing starts up again. *** Are there other ways to tax wealth?

We’ve heard it many times before over other proposed taxes on wealth: Rachel Reeves reversed her plans to end inheritance tax breaks for farmers after lobbyists drove tractors up to the doors of parliament and drowned out speeches with their horns. When Ed Miliband proposed a mansion tax on properties valued over £2m, to raise £1.2bn annually for the NHS, in his 2015 manifesto, he was eviscerated by the rightwing media, party critics and Myleene Klass, who confronted him in a TV debate, arguing the tax wouldn’t just touch the super-rich but would devastate “little grannies” who bought modest London homes that had simply skyrocketed in value over the decades. But times change, don’t they? And Reeves was able to avoid a similar backlash when she introduced a similar council tax surcharge on properties worth £2m or more at the last budget. The Institute for Fiscal Studies has argued consistently that, rather than introduce a new wealth tax, the government should sort out the mess of current capital and property taxes.

In May, Wes Streeting received a mixed reception when he proposed equalising capital gains with income tax, as part of his brief tilt at Labour leadership, describing it as a “wealth tax that works”. And of course, HMRC could get better at collecting tax from the super-rich: its own estimates suggest that at least £2.1bn extra could be raised from closing the wealthy tax gap. The trouble with getting more granular on wealth taxation, Aditya says, is that many of the groups affected – whether that’s farmers, lawyers or GPs in partnerships – are also very well-networked and good at making a noise about the specific unfairness of targeting them as opposed to others. Which takes us back to the more subtle point about burden-sharing and democracy that underlies his arguments: by focusing on the billionaires in the corner, we avoid looking at the millionaires in the mirror – and having an honest conversation about what wealth is and how sophisticated those who have it are at lobbying against further taxes on it.

Iran’s Houthi allies capture strategic island on vital oil shipping route

Yemen’s rampant Houthi forces have captured the strategic island of Perim in the Bab al-Mandab strait, expanding their control of the narrow waterway, one of the ​world’s vital shipping routes. The Iran-aligned Houthis took control of the volcanic island after forces allied to the UN-backed, Aden-based government left in the latest of a dramatic series of reverses along Yemen’s west coast in recent days, including the loss of the port city of Mocha on Thursday. Saudi Arabia, which supports and bankrolls the official Yemen government, mounted air raids on Houthi positions in Mocha on Friday. The Bab al-Mandab strait links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez canal. Perim island, also known as Mayun, divides the waterway in two, close to its narrowest point. The United Arab Emirates, a former Saudi ally in the anti-Houthi coalition, had been building an airbase on the island before ending its active involvement in the conflict in January. Interactive Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab to export its crude since Iran has been targeting vessels in the strait of Hormuz.

It said it had shut its East-West pipeline as “a precautionary measure”, blaming the attack on several drones that came from Iraq. In a statement carried by the state-run Saudi Press Agency, the kingdom said it would not respond to the attack to give the Iraqi government “an opportunity to take the necessary measures”. The pipeline, also known as the Petroline, runs for 1,201km (746 miles) from the Abqaiq oilfield in the kingdom’s east near Bahrain and Qatar, to the port city Yanbu at the Red Sea. Built in the 1980s, it has played an important role in Saudi Arabia’s ability to export oil after the disruption of the strait of Hormuz during the Iran war. Full Houthi control of shipping in the Bab al-Mandab strait, alongside Iranian control of the strait of Hormuz, would strengthen the chokeholds of anti-western forces over global energy shipments.

Ireland holds its breath as its leftwing president prepares to meet Trump

Catherine Connolly, Ireland’s president, once said she abhorred Donald Trump’s policies. In his sole previous comment on Connolly, the US president seemed to think she was a man. Now that they are about to meet, Ireland is holding its breath. Trump is to fly into Dublin on Saturday morning for a two-day visit centred on golf. But before making it to his beloved greens, protocol obliges him to meet a woman who has given every impression of loathing him. A courtesy call to Áras an Uachtaráin, the Irish president’s official residence and workplace in the city’s Phoenix Park, has left the government anxious and the media reaching for popcorn. “What could possibly go wrong?” headlines ask. Many in Ireland are rooting for Connolly to let rip at Trump for his policies and rhetoric on immigrants and the Middle East. Others hope she will stifle any criticisms to avoid provoking a visitor who could upend Ireland’s economy. The taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said he had no concerns “at all” about the encounter, but one senior official said the government was on tenterhooks.

‘World’s most profitable football business’: Abramovich’s frozen Chelsea cash earns £175m

Funds from Roman Abramovich’s sale of Chelsea FC have earned at least £175m in interest while locked in a UK bank account, new accounts show, leading one analyst to describe the company housing the frozen cash as “the most profitable football business in the world”. Accounts for Fordstam, the company through which the billionaire Russian oligarch owned Chelsea, show that the proceeds of the sale completed in May 2022 have risen from £2.3bn to nearly £2.5bn. Abramovich, who was hit with UK sanctions in 2022 over his ties to Vladimir Putin, has previously pledged to donate the money to victims of the war in Ukraine. However, the funds have yet to be released, amid an ongoing legal dispute with the British government about how the money should be used. The picture is further complicated by a separate criminal investigation by the Jersey authorities into the original source of the oil tycoon’s wealth.

Russia targets Kyiv petrol stations for first time with jet-powered drones

Petrol stations in Kyiv have been hit by jet-powered drones in a wave of targeted Russian attacks as the bombardment of Ukraine’s capital enters a new phase of intensity. At least two people were killed and 12 injured in strikes on two petrol stations on Friday morning, according to the city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko. The rush-hour strikes follow a similar attack on a petrol station on Thursday, the first of its kind in the capital. At the Ukrnafta petrol station in the Pochaina neighbourhood in northern Kyiv, bystanders said three people had been injured in Friday’s blast – the manager of a nearby car wash, his wife and the driver of a passing car. The blown-out vehicle was stranded by the side of the road, its windows shattered and seats spattered in blood. Witnesses said they had heard two explosions, and local authorities later said Russia had carried out a double-tap attack on the facility. “This is probably one of the most difficult periods of the war because life is just like on a rollercoaster,” said Anastasiia Demchenko, 30, who works at a delivery company opposite the petrol station.

He arrived with nothing other than the clothes he wore that morning. Hours later he was banged up in a detention centre close to a Stockholm airport to await deportation. But the migration agency rejected his application, and he and his wife have been fighting with the Swedish authorities ever since. In a message passed on by Lily, he said he was the only Briton in the detention centre, where he described being hemmed in by three lines of fences separated by a “no man’s land”. “I arrived here with nothing apart from the clothes I had on,” Charles said. “We were told the meeting … with the border police was to discuss my case. text:
They drive toward tornadoes. We went with them to see how their work could save lives

On a narrow road in southern Iowa, my phone shrieked. Tornado warning. Take shelter now in a basement or an interior room on the lowest floor of a sturdy building. Again, the alert sounded. Then again. As if shelter were a choice. I peered through a peephole of scratched glass, wedged into the lead storm-chasing truck with tornado researchers Josh Wurman and Karen Kosiba. On either side of us, only fields. No houses. No basements. No sturdy buildings. The dark belly of a storm dragged across a horizon gone an eerie green. For tornado chasers, it was a near perfect sky. My son Cheney, a photojournalist, was somewhere behind us in a rental car alongside two other research vehicles. The convoy was strung out across miles of highway. He had been tracking my location, but now I had lost cell service. I couldn’t reach him. I kept dialing. No answer. When a call finally went through, Cheney told me the wind was driving the rain so hard the road had disappeared. “I’m scared,” he said. Blinded, he had turned one way, then the other. Finally, he stopped.

citation.title: They drive toward tornadoes. We went with them to see how their work could save lives

text:
They drive toward tornadoes. We went with them to see how their work could save lives

Either direction, he feared, could put him in a tornado’s path. Cheney was no stranger to danger. He has covered Ukraine during wartime, spent a New Year’s Eve alone in a car reporting on Chicago homicides, and crisscrossed the country documenting violent weather, including the devastating 2021 tornado in Mayfield, Kentucky. I hadn’t heard him express fear since childhood. Then he said it again. “I’m scared. I don’t know what to do.” *** About 1,200 tornadoes strike the United States every year. Between 2020 and 2025, they killed roughly 410 people, injured nearly 3,800 and caused about $8.5bn in reported property damage. The tornado map is changing too. A 2024 study found 25% fewer moderate-or-stronger tornadoes in the western US and 12% more in the east, where mobile homes are more prevalent, basements to get to safety are scarcer, and twisters more likely to strike at night. Sometimes the change from ordinary to deadly takes only minutes. Several months earlier, physician Jason Persoff had told me about chasing near Joplin, Missouri, in May 2011.

text:
They drive toward tornadoes. We went with them to see how their work could save lives

A little after 5pm, he and his partner began looking for hotel rooms, figuring they were done for the day. “Suddenly, it was as if someone vomited on the radar,” Persoff remembered. “It was incredible.” A violent tornado seemed to emerge from the sky almost fully formed. Its sound lodged deep in Persoff’s body. “I felt irrational fear,” he said. “Like a primal warning.” They pulled over to help stranded truckers as police arrived. Persoff told one officer he was a physician. “I hope you don’t work at St John’s,” the officer told him. “That hospital’s been destroyed.” “That’s still one of the most terrifying things I’ve ever heard,” Persoff said. More than 150 people were killed in that tornado. Wurman, whose team I traveled with, is among the researchers trying to understand why some storms produce tornadoes while others do not, and what tornado winds do close to the ground – knowledge that could improve warnings and help engineers design buildings to withstand them. But the systems built to study and forecast tornadoes are under strain.

text:

In the first four months of 2025, the National Weather Service lost roughly 13% of its workforce – more than 560 employees – to firings, retirements, resignations and attrition. By the 2026 storm season, the agency was hiring again, but staffing gaps remained, and some stations were unable to maintain the twice-daily weather-balloon launches on which forecasters and researchers rely. Scientists I spoke with said they had lost confidence in forecast guidance. Chris Weiss of Texas Tech, who led a parallel chase team with the National Severe Storms Laboratory, was blunt: “I don’t remember when a suite of models has performed as poorly as this year.” Frustrated by the blurred, distant view from fixed-site radar, Wurman invented the Doppler on Wheels – mobile radar laboratories known as DOWs – three decades ago. Filling one with diesel costs about $1,000, and that is the inexpensive part: the greater investment lies in the trucks, trained graduate students and experienced crews that take years to build. But funding has become more uncertain.

They drive toward tornadoes. We went with them to see how their work could save lives

By the end of this field season, neither Wurman’s team nor Weiss’s could count on support for the next one. Cessily Skinner, whose family has lost two homes to tornadoes in west-central Georgia, closely monitors every approaching storm. Now the cuts give her another reason to fear: “As someone who lived through a storm with all the data in place,” she said, “it’s terrifying to think, ‘OK, so now we really are guessing.’” *** With Cheney still on the line, a team member plotted his location against the storm. The radar could see what he could not. A tornado we were tracking was east of him and moving east. Cheney should be safe, she said, as long as he stayed put and waited it out. I repeated this to him. As we spoke, the rain loosened. The sky lifted. The road reappeared. Cheney pressed the gas and began closing the distance between us. The second radar truck arrived first. Fifteen long minutes later, Cheney’s rental car came into view. Relief and disappointment arrived together. The convoy was whole again. But the day had yielded none of the data the scientists had come for.

Several tornadoes touched down across the region that afternoon. None crossed the roads where our instruments were waiting. The storms left behind a sky ribboned with dark clouds. Some team members stood outside the trucks and applauded its beauty, lifting their phones for photographs. Wurman and Kosiba were not among them. They were already studying the models, deciding where the team should spend the night to be best positioned for morning. *** Tornadoes offer enough spectacle to draw film-makers, thrill-seekers, and carloads of chasers with cameras. But scientists who chase for data need more than drama. They need geometry: an open horizon, a road in and a road out, a storm that forms where the instruments can reach it. Even when everything lines up, a mobile radar crew can spend weeks following one promising storm after another, only to watch each weaken and dissolve before the instruments capture the measurements they came for. Why do they keep doing it?

For data analyst Paul Robinson, the pull started with an image on television: Dorothy clutching Toto, calling for Auntie Em as a black twister writhed in the distance. “The Wizard of Oz is still my favorite movie tornado,” he said. “For me, it captures the feeling.” Growing up in West Virginia, he began keeping a notebook, recording the weather whenever it turned severe. But 31 May 1985, turned that interest into purpose. Everyone on this team seems to carry a storm they cannot forget. Robinson’s was not a single tornado but an outbreak: 43 twisters tearing across Ohio, Pennsylvania, New York and Ontario, killing 89 people. “That convinced me that maybe I could do some good by going into tornado research,” Robinson said. Research scientist Trevor White’s defining storm came later, on 24 May 2016, near Dodge City, Kansas. “Every chaser and their mother came out,” he recalled. “We were on it from the time it was a small cumulus cloud. I had never seen a storm that could effortlessly produce tornadoes.

I counted three on the ground at the same time.” In two hours, a dozen tornadoes formed beneath the supercell. It was nearly perfect in the way that mattered most: no one died, and the tornadoes remained mostly over open country. But even experienced researchers cannot always remain beyond a tornado’s reach. In 2013, veteran tornado researcher Tim Samaras was killed near El Reno, Oklahoma, along with his son Paul and colleague Carl Young. Samaras was Wurman’s friend. Wurman’s team was tracking the same tornado that day. Asked by a reporter whether the deaths made him reconsider his work, Wurman noted that covering extreme weather “isn’t dangerous statistically”. Samaras, he said, was among the most responsible chasers he knew. Wurman would not speculate about what had gone wrong but said his own team would review its procedures. Wurman and his colleagues then returned to the data, reconstructing the motion of the nearly impossible-to-see subvortex that had overtaken Samaras and his team. He pursues the sky at its most theatrical without surrendering to drama himself.

He would rather leave a question open than force an answer the data cannot support. “I wish this research were more of a eureka thing,” Wurman said, “but it’s not. We can’t do laboratory-type experiments. We can’t put 10,000 patients into a study. Meteorology is horrible that way. We’re trying to understand what’s special about the circumstances where tornadoes form and what it looks like when they do. But we can’t control the environment.” “Every time we’re in a disaster area, I carry with me the trauma of people who survive it,” White told me. “I don’t know if we can do anything to ease the impact of that experience, but I’ll never stop searching. The only thing worse than a human tragedy is a human tragedy where you can’t learn anything.” *** A mile outside Good Hope, Illinois, the deployment order came. Our truck slid to a halt on the shoulder of a two-lane road slick with rain. Robinson jumped out to unleash the radar dish. It began sweeping the sky, each rotation shuddering through the vehicle.

Back in the driver’s seat, he talked to himself – “c’mon, c’mon” – as he worked the controls to lower a stabilizing pad into the mud, trying to keep the vehicle’s right side from sinking. He kept the left wheels on the pavement, he told me later, in case we needed to move fast toward – or away from – a tornado. In the back, White balanced one keyboard on his lap and kept several others within reach. Four screens glowed in front of him. “Frustrating,” Robinson murmured. “We’re getting data, but I want to see it; I want to see the fury.” The horizon closed around us. From the front passenger seat, I watched a low shelf of black clouds over the cornfields, its ragged underside reaching down in unfinished gestures. The walkie-talkie crackled, then Wurman’s voice came through. “What do you see?” No one answered immediately. White and Robinson studied the screens and conferred quietly in technical shorthand. They were looking for a hook curling in the rain, a couplet tightening in the wind field, some sign that the atmosphere had made up its mind. The clouds kept darkening. The dish kept turning.

text:

The truck kept shuddering. Robinson waited through one scan, then another, watching new data appear on the screens over White’s shoulder. Finally he spoke, his voice tight. “It’s falling apart, isn’t it?” After a few more minutes, Wurman confirmed he saw the same. He called out a new waypoint and then we were speeding again down a country road, pursuing the uneasy hope at the center of this work: a storm dangerous enough to teach but merciful enough to spare. *** When things align, the value of a single intercept can endure for years. On 18 May 2013, the team captured data from an EF4 tornado near Rozel, Kansas. It remained on the ground for about 30 minutes, long enough for the researchers to hold position and gather unusually rich measurements. “That gave us a chance to dig in deep,” Kosiba said. “And that data is still being used by engineers today. That’s why you have to keep going out, even with the misses. We’re in it for the long haul.” A 2024 study co-authored by Wurman and Kosiba analyzed mobile-radar wind profiles from 36 tornadoes.

Those findings helped shape new national standards for designing buildings to withstand tornado winds, showing the potential impact of readings collected in the path of storms. This is the scale on which science advances: one measurement clarifying another, a dataset enduring long after the tornado itself disappears. Behind every chase is a life forced to accommodate the forecast. We had driven 2,000 miles in three days, from dawn until after dark, crossing and recrossing North Dakota, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Iowa and Illinois. Wurman’s team had gone weeks without the intercept they needed. Weiss’s team had endured an equally disappointing season. “We put in the same effort for fewer results,” Weiss told me. “We have lives and families, and we’re making a lot of sacrifices. So when it doesn’t work out, it eats at you.” White has a soft spot for hummingbirds. He keeps several feeders at home, and goes to great lengths to find someone to refill them when he’s gone. His absence is measured out in sugar water. He carries a small stuffed hummingbird on the road.

“I told my wife a week ago we’d be home tomorrow. Instead, we are still out here, and there’s no end in sight,” he said. “But there’s something fundamental about this research that draws me in. The best version of me is the version that does this work.” Before this trip, I had imagined storm chasing as a form of appetite, the desire to see the most violent thing the sky could make. I hadn’t understood its strange rhythm: tedious hours beneath empty skies, then sudden races down country roads, decisions pressed into seconds, and moments of stark fear. The work demands patience when nothing happens and clear judgment when everything happens at once. Inside the truck, it looked less like appetite and more like devotion: painstaking, deliberate, largely invisible. In a culture that rewards quick verdicts and emphatic claims, these scientists let the sky contradict them. They reverse direction and answer to evidence rather than personal conviction. That discipline feels radical. Years from now, the data they gather may become a stronger roof, an earlier warning, hospital walls that hold.

As a religious Jew, I am disappointed at the reaction of some of our communal leaders and bodies to the sanctions on trade with illegal Israeli settlements (UK accuses Israeli ‘terrorists’ of ethnic cleansing in West Bank with government backing, 8 September). While much of the British media may choose to platform one view as being representative of the Jewish reaction to these sanctions, I would point to organisations such as Yachad and Na’amod, which provide an alternative anti‑occupation narrative. Who are the 514 people accused of starting French wildfires and what motivates them?

One is a boy of 15, who threw a burning cigarette into a wood near Bordeaux. Another is a 36-year-old man who set a paper bag of rubbish on fire in bushes near Perpignan. A third is a 50-year-old woman accused of lighting 17 fires south of La Rochelle. According to the French interior ministry, since the start of a summer in which a record 115,000 hectares of forest, scrub and heathland have gone up in flames, 514 people – including 198 minors – have been arrested on suspicion of starting wildfires. Who are they, and what motivates them? Experts say arson is an under-studied field in France. It remains, according to Thierry Toutin, a criminology researcher with the national police, “a mysterious crime, often hard for people to understand”. Two hundred years ago, under Napoleon, deliberately starting a wildfire in France was a crime so grave it carried an automatic death penalty by guillotine. These days, sentences start at 10 years in jail and a €150,000 fine, rising to 15 years if protected forests or reserves burn, and life if someone is killed.

citation.title: Who are the 514 people accused of starting French wildfires and what motivates them?

text:
Who are the 514 people accused of starting French wildfires and what motivates them?

Arsonists have “many different profiles”, Toutin said in an essay for The Conversation. Several French departments have set up dedicated arson groups uniting police, forestry board experts and local services to help identify, find and prosecute them, he said, but still: “These are often crimes that are unsolved, or don’t lead to convictions, because the fire has destroyed the evidence.” France’s official statistics classify wildfires by their cause: natural, such as lightning; accidental (say, a vehicle fire or electrical fault); involuntary professional (sparks from a machine); involuntary individual (a cigarette or barbecue) – and voluntary. In practice, as a government PSA has repeated all summer on radio, TV and online, nine out of 10 fires are caused by human activity, with roughly two-thirds classed as involuntary (which, if negligence is proven, carries a jail term of one to five years). That means fully one-third of wildfires in France each year are set deliberately, with the intention of doing harm.

text:
Who are the 514 people accused of starting French wildfires and what motivates them?

In 2025, the last year for which full figures are available, deliberate acts of arson were the biggest single cause of forest fires in France, accounting for 29.4% of blazes. Interactive Among those convicted this summer are a 27-year-old man diagnosed with autism and schizophrenia who set fire to a letter to his late daughter in tinder-dry vegetation near Béziers. He was sentenced to four years of detention and treatment. Perpignan court last week sentenced a 51-year-old man to five years in prison for lighting four fires in July and August. In Les Sables d’Olonnes, a volunteer firefighter – reported to police by his superiors – was handed a three-year suspended sentence. In Lyon, a 29-year-old man with a police record for theft, trafficking and domestic violence was convicted of setting a fire that destroyed more than a hectare of land, took 71 firefighters to extinguish and forced the evacuation of 150 people.

text:

Those convicted of negligence include a motorist who lit a fire to alert emergency services after he broke down (six months, suspended) and two restaurant owners in the south-west who defied a red fire alert to light a charcoal grill and set off fireworks. An early analysis based on police reports and obtained by Le Figaro showed 97.5 % of arson suspects arrested this year have been men, aged on average 32.5, with 28.7% under 18. More than 95% were French citizens. Of a relatively small sample of 80 suspects, 37 were unemployed. Exactly what drove them to act is often much harder to establish. In principle, criminologists identify four main categories of motivation. Some arson attacks are carried out in the context of a conflict: a dispute with a neighbour; criminal rivalry between gangs; revenge against someone or something. Other arsonists may act for financial gain, such as a false insurance claim, or out of ideological or political conviction. The remainder display some kind of pathology, often psychological – including a small number of genuine pyromaniacs.

“Arsonists may be after money, or revenge, or be trying to cover up a crime. They may be under the influence of alcohol or other substances,” said Laurent Layet, a psychiatrist. “A pyromaniac’s sole objective is to set fire to something.” Pyromaniacs “have difficulty organising their personalities”, Layet told France Inter radio. “They are often impulsive, and they have trouble controlling their emotions. Often, they are quite isolated socially.” Classified as an impulse-control disorder, pyromania is characterised by “a fascination with fire, by a mounting tension before the act, and then a feeling of pleasure or relief immediately afterwards”, he said. But pyromaniacs are typically organised, aware of the consequences of their acts, and considered criminally responsible. They also represent barely 5% of the people who deliberately set fires. Another equally small group are firefighters – mostly volunteers, very rarely professionals – who deliberately set fires for the glory that comes from extinguishing them.

Over the years, France’s departmental fire services have set up filtering mechanisms to detect such personalities during the recruitment process, including psychological tests. They acknowledge that each year, some slip through the net. But the motivation of most people who deliberately light wildfires is rarely quite so clearcut. For many, it boils down to an ill-defined “act of defiance – to confront the system, and get pleasure from destroying other people’s property”, said Johanna Rozenblum, a clinical psychologist who works with the fire service. A strikingly large proportion of the arsonists she had dealt with had “marked antisocial profiles”, Rozenblum said. And in the case of minors, adolescent impulsiveness and frustration combine with “immaturity and internal revolt” to prevent them fully realising the devastating scale of the damage they risk doing.

Pressure builds in Spain to deny US extradition request for leftwing donor

Attorneys for James “Fergie” Chambers, the US citizen and wealthy donor to leftwing and humanitarian projects who is currently imprisoned in Madrid and sought in extradition, have submitted a brief ahead of a decisive government meeting on the case. Meanwhile, Chambers’ partner, the actor and activist Stella Schnabel, met last week with multiple members of the Spanish parliament to assert his innocence. The legal team’s arguments include that the US government has failed to identify specific acts of violence or damages personally attributable to Chambers and instead is seeking to criminalize acts linked to political protest. They also assert that at least one figure of US law underpinning the request – “conspiracy to commit riot” – has no equivalent in Spanish law, which would also help render the extradition invalid. Related: FBI raided Spanish vacation rental of wealthy leftwing funder James ‘Fergie’ Chambers after his arrest It is the first known case of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas.

text:
The far right’s rise is a wake-up call for Europe

Rafael Behr is right to warn that far-right parties, Maga ideology and Kremlin influence threaten Europe’s liberal democracies (European democracies are running out of time to turn away from the abyss, 9 September). But he overlooks the role of the liberal centre itself in creating the conditions for their rise. While Thatcher, Reagan and their successors weakened trade unions and workers’ bargaining power, subsequent centre-left governments largely accepted these changes rather than reversing them. Under the banner of the “third way”, they expanded labour market insecurity, embraced financialisation and allowed private interests to penetrate ever deeper into public services. Social and economic inequality soared. From the anti-globalisation movement and post-2008 anti-austerity protests to more recent pro-Palestinian mobilisations, the liberal centre has relied increasingly on policing, surveillance and legal restrictions to contain political opposition. Decades of economic insecurity, shrinking democratic participation and declining faith in established institutions have created fertile ground for the far right.

Benjamin Selwyn Professor of international relations and international development, University of Sussex • Jörg Lau rightly identifies the shattering of Germany’s postwar consensus in Saxony-Anhalt, but framing this as a sudden rupture obliterates decades of the political establishment’s structural rot (Friedrich Merz is now on borrowed time. But that’s not why the AfD’s triumph is seismic, theguardian.com, 8 September). Germany’s crisis began with suppressing authentic reckoning. In the immediate postwar era, former Nazi party members were allowed to dominate state institutions. This continued until the 1970s. Willy Brandt, the “Historikerstreit”, the countrywide discussion of the series Holocaust and Goldhagen’s book Hitler’s Willing Executioners were short glimmers of real change. Then the institutionalised remembrance culture emerged.
