It was top-down – a state-directed ritual to appease European partners that reinforced the German “nanny state” mentality. In eastern states like Saxony-Anhalt, this top-down moral framework was forced on a population thrust into the post-1989 market shock. Now, with an ageing demographic and economic stagnation straining the social safety net, this abandonment is coming due. The AfD feeds on these unhealed wounds, exploiting anger over stale ritualised politics and, once again, channelling economic angst into xenophobic nationalism. Merz is a product of decades of missed opportunities. But the AfD is not an alien shock to the system. Mainstream parties built the void the far right now occupies. Swedish election: centre-left parties lead by just a single seat with most votes counted

With most of the votes counted, Sweden’s national election remained too close to call on Sunday night, with left-wing parties holding a lead of just a single seat according to a partial tally by the election authority. Earlier in the night, exit polls suggested that the country was on course for a brand new left-leaning government. But as the votes were counted, it was apparent it could take days for the outcome to become clear. With 80% of votes counted, there was just one seat between the left and right blocs. The left-leaning opposition parties, led by Social Democrat Magdalena Andersson, had 175 and the rightwing parties, led by the Moderates prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, had 174. At 10:30pm local time, broadcaster SVT predicted there were only 20,000 votes between the blocs. The election authority said a preliminary vote count may not be ready until Thursday.

Africa’s richest man aiming to make $23bn from continent’s biggest-ever IPO

The fortune of Africa’s richest person could swell by two thirds to nearly $60bn (£44bn) after his refinery in Nigeria listed publicly in the continent’s biggest-ever initial public offering. If Monday’s flotation of Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals on the Nigerian exchange goes to plan, then Aliko Dangote will add a further $23bn (£17bn) to his $35bn net worth. Dangote, who has framed the offering as “an IPO for the people”, hopes it will draw in a broad mix of institutional and retail investors with a minimum subscription of just 10 shares at a cost of 5,250 naira (£2.94). The share purchases have a month to complete, with the process finishing on 13 October. The IPO has been marketed to young Nigerians in particular, through banking platforms and fintech ventures, as a way of building wealth and growing the economy. If completely subscribed, the refinery’s value is expected to rise to about 65.22tn naira (£36.5bn).

China dismisses AI ‘fearmongering’ as spy chief warns of threat to Communist party rule

China has dismissed what it said were “fearmongering” calls for the US to block Beijing’s AI industry, even as the top Chinese spy chief warned the evolving technology could threaten Communist party rule. The US tech entrepreneur and Anthropic chief executive, Dario Amodei, wrote an essay published over the weekend that called for a global slowdown in AI capabilities, but also said Washington should actively impede Beijing’s advancement in order to keep a technological edge. Warning that AI could give the Chinese Communist party a chance “to militarily dominate democracies”, Amodei said he believed “a Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the US and the world”. China’s ministry of foreign affairs responded to a question about Amodei’s essay by saying all parties should work together on AI. “Fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance, which serves no one’s interest,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a press conference on Monday.

He said that while “global pacing will require cooperation with China”, steps were needed to “keep democracies’ AI lead over autocracies as large as possible”. Other tech bosses, including the OpenAI CEO, Sam Altman, the Google DeepMind chair, Demis Hassabis, and the SpaceX chief, Elon Musk, have posted general support for Amodei’s lengthy essay, although not specifically on China. Nine EU countries further delay EES border checks

Nine EU countries, including France, are delaying the introduction of fingerprinting for non-EU citizens as they plead for more time to introduce the new border controls at busy airports in the bloc. The entry-exit system (EES), which was due to come into force in full on 6 September, has been delayed multiple times to avoid visitor congestion around large events, including the Olympics in 2024. Now nine countries, including the holiday hotspots France, Greece, Portugal and Italy, have told Brussels they need more time. Germany, Malta, the Netherlands, Switzerland and Belgium have also sought extra time. Spain, which had teething problems, is implementing the EES fully. Related: ‘Pretty shambolic’: new EU border checks cause stress for UK travellers The EES, which was first adopted by the EU in 2017, was officially launched last October and was due to become fully operational in April but early problems, particularly in Greece and Portugal, led to a further reprieve for member states.

citation.title: Nine EU countries further delay EES border checks

EU sources say the system is considered a success with about 200m registrations and 70,000 people stopped from entering the Schengen area, up from 43,700 in June. These include people without visas, those who have overstayed their 180-day allowance or Britons who have overstayed their 90-day allowance. Criminals using forged passports or ID documents have also been apprehended with fingerprint and facial image records exposing the use of different passports by individuals. The delays in those nine member states are not countrywide. Fingerprinting has started at the Eurostar terminal in Brussels and Antwerp port but not in all airports. Large airports, such as Frankfurt and Schiphol – two of Europe’s busiest international hubs, are also taking biometrics but small airports may not be fully up to speed. Sources say just 12 airports out of 1,500 border crossing points are still having issues. France has also not introduced checks in the Port of Dover where French police are in the unique position to do border controls in a non-EU country.

The far right’s march to power in Sweden has been halted, but its influence remains

Since the party was founded in 1988, the story of the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD) has been one of such continuous growth that a triumph in Sunday’s general election seemed inevitable. In 2022, the party capitalised on electoral gains – and the desperation of right-leaning parties to form a minority administration – and almost made its way into government. A supporting role in prime minister Ulf Kristersson’s Tidö coalition earned the party, which has neo-Nazi roots, huge influence and mainstream acceptance by the political establishment. This year’s election had been billed as final confirmation they were no longer pariahs but serious political heavyweights. Early in the campaign, Kristersson announced that, if his coalition were to win, the SD would take key ministerial positions. But Sunday’s results suggest the march of the far right into the heart of Sweden’s government has been halted – for now. Having fallen from Sweden’s second biggest party to third place and, with the right-leaning parties unlikely to be able to form a coalition, the SD appears to have lost its route into government.

citation.title: The far right’s march to power in Sweden has been halted, but its influence remains

text:
The far right’s march to power in Sweden has been halted, but its influence remains

“What we saw yesterday [Sunday] was a historic setback for the Sweden Democrats,” says Niclas Nilsson, a lecturer and researcher at the anti-racism foundation Expo. “The party has grown in every government election since 1988.” The SD’s leader, Jimmie Åkesson, appeared visibly shocked when he addressed supporters late on election night. He said it was obvious they had lost some percentage points, but claimed they were still “winners”. He appeared to suggest his decision to be a team player and support coalition partner the Liberals may have played a role in their loss of support. It is perhaps too soon to say why the party shed votes, said Nilsson, but some of its supporters may have gone to the Moderates, who had a good night. Another factor may have been that, after four years closely involved with the government, the SD is no longer able to claim it is an anti-establishment party. Turnout was about 80%, comparatively low for Sweden, which may also have played a role.

citation.title: The far right’s march to power in Sweden has been halted, but its influence remains

text:

default There is also the fact that much of what the SD stand for has now become part of the Swedish political norm: anti-immigration, harsh approaches to crime and punishment, an attitude to integration that puts the onus on people moving to Sweden to abandon their culture and religion to adapt to “Swedish” norms. Their influence has spread to the centre-left Social Democrats who – after losing the last election – shifted their crime, immigration and integration strategies to the right. If the Moderates end up joining a coalition government with the Social Democrats, then the SD will be the biggest party in opposition, meaning it will still have a prominent role on the national stage. But if the Social Democrats are able to form a government without the Moderates, then the SD will again be on the outside looking in, which could help steer national conversation, politics and societal norms away from the right. How it responds to this moment will be key – to the party’s survival and the tenor of Swedish politics.

Gulf states have postponed a critical meeting with Iran on the future of the strait of Hormuz owing to a lack of Arab consensus and growing Saudi Arabian anger with Tehran for helping the Houthis loosen Riyadh’s grip in Yemen. The stalemate over the vital waterway came as Houthi rebels launched a fresh barrage of missile and drone attacks on Saudi military targets. A Houthi military spokesperson claimed its forces had attacked the King Khalid airbase in Khamis Mushait, hitting fighter-jet hangars, radar systems, runways and landing strips, ammunition depots and additional targets. Last week, Tehran-backed militias in Iraq forced Saudi Arabia to close a critical east-west pipeline that had been acting as a means for Riyadh to export oil after Iran effectively closed the strait of Hormuz. The closure of the pipeline, the postponement of the Hormuz meeting, and the Houthis’ seizure last week of Yemen’s Red Sea coast – which gave the group control over another vital waterway, the Bab al-Mandab strait – combined to drive up oil prices above $108 a barrel on Monday.

Indonesian police are investigating the deaths of three Australians who died in Bali over the weekend, with initial reports suggesting a father killed his two young children before taking his own life. The man, 57, and his two children, seven and four, who are also Indonesian citizens, were discovered deceased in a bungalow in Kuta on Sunday morning. The witness then met the bungalow owner and both returned to perform a check before contacting the “neighbourhood head”, Kelian Lingkungan. Residents “knocked and pounded” on the door before it was forcibly opened, and the three bodies were located.

Robin Morgan obituary

The poet, novelist and political theorist Robin Morgan, who has died aged 85, was a key figure of second-wave feminism. From 1976, she was a contributing editor of the influential Ms magazine, founded by her friend and close collaborator Gloria Steinem, and served as its editor in chief from 1989 until 1994. In 1967, she co-founded the radical activist group New York Radical Women, and the following year, the Women’s International Terrorist Conspiracy from Hell (Witch), which used street theatre and other actions to protest against cultural sexism. In 1970, she edited the anthology Sisterhood Is Powerful, now considered a foundational text of second-wave feminism, and, with the royalties received, founded the Sisterhood Is Powerful Fund to support women’s organisations. In all, she published 22 books, including three landmark anthologies. Morgan was one of the first feminists of her generation to point out the misogyny within male leftist counterculture.

citation.title: Robin Morgan obituary

text:
Robin Morgan obituary

Her 1970 essay Goodbye to All That, published in Rat, a leftist newsletter, scorned both the so-called “sexual revolution” and the male radicals who expected women to type out their manifestos and share their beds while denying them political voice. She coined some of the feminist movement’s most effective and enduring slogans, including “Porn is the theory; rape is the practice”, a line that captured her lifelong opposition to pornography. On the anti-feminism backlash, which characterised the women’s movement as dangerous, she observed: “We are the women that men have warned us about.” She came up with the term “herstory”, for history written from a female perspective. It was a direct action with New York Radical Women that first put Morgan in the spotlight: in 1968, she helped organise a protest against the Miss America pageant in New Jersey during which women tossed bras, girdles and cleaning equipment into a “Freedom Trash Can” – although it was not set on fire, this gave rise to the derogatory put-down of feminists as “bra burners”.

text:
Robin Morgan obituary

Born in Lake Worth, Florida, Robin was the daughter of Faith Berkley, a shop assistant, and Mordechai Morgenstern, a gynaecologist. The couple were not married, and Faith had moved to Florida from New York to hide her pregnancy. Robin was 20 when she first met her father. Pushed by an aunt into child modelling, she was a performer from the age of five, with her own programme, The Little Robin Morgan Show, on the New York radio station WOR and a starring role on the popular TV show Mama between 1950 and 1956. In her teens she rebelled, leaving acting to become a writer, and at 16 began studying literature informally at Columbia University in New York. She joined a writing workshop, where she met the poet Kenneth Pitchford, a founder of the Gay Liberation Front. Married from 1962 until their divorce in 1990, they had a son, Blake, in 1969. As a former leftist revolutionary, when Morgan joined a newly formed women’s group in the 1960s, it was her intention to convert them to Marxism; instead, they converted her to radical feminism. She never lost her taste for coalition work, but her politics were now unambiguously her own.

In The Demon Lover: On the Sexuality of Terrorism (1989), she made connections between violence and misogyny by men on both left and right. “It is the common denominator of strutting machismo,” she wrote, “that links the random killings of the street terrorist with murderous state terrorism.” Her Fighting Words: A Toolkit for Combating the Religious Right (2006) took on Christian fundamentalism with equal force. Alongside Steinem and Jane Fonda, she was a co-founder of the Women’s Media Center in 2005. Its aim was to improve both representation and the positive participation of women and girls in the media. In 2008, she published Goodbye To All That #2 – an essay on the misogyny aimed at Hillary Clinton during her run to become the Democratic presidential candidate. Mass-forwarded by Clinton’s daughter, Chelsea, it went viral. “Me, I’m voting for Hillary,” Morgan wrote, “not because she’s a woman, but because I am.” In 2015, she organised a conference on the sexual exploitation of women in the sex industry, hosted by the Carter Center, Atlanta, the organisation founded by the former US president Jimmy Carter to promote human rights.

Robin Morgan obituary

As a result of her friendship with Carter, an indictment of pornography appeared on his website – a first for a former president. Carter was also the first male guest on Morgan’s weekly radio programme, WMC Live. I first met her in 1997 at a meeting in a Manhattan cafe, where Andrea Dworkin had gathered a group together to talk about how to call rapists to account through the criminal justice system. Softly spoken, she wore her feminist notoriety lightly. There was nothing egotistical about her; she once told me that her most important work was mentoring later generations of political activists. Close to her heart was the Sisterhood Is Global Institute, a feminist thinktank founded in 1984 with Simone de Beauvoir, which raises money for organisations improving the lives of women and girls globally.

text:
Robin Morgan obituary

The anti-pornography scholar and activist Gail Dines said that Morgan “saw porn as front and centre of radical feminist theory and politics … she talked about the disgrace of the third wave, and how missing porn as the material and ideological mouthpiece of patriarchy would destroy feminism.” Asked in a 2007 interview for the Humanist magazine what it meant to be a radical feminist, she replied: “It means daring to be uncompromising, daring to be angry.” Her poetry collection Dark Matter (2018) explored ageing, mortality and resilience. She was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease in 2010, and, according to her son, feared decline, not death. On the question of generational handover, she was unyielding. “It’s only natural for people to want to stay in charge of the movement they poured their life energies into,” she once said. “Get your own damned torch,” she told a young woman who intimated that it was time to pass hers on. “I’m still using mine.” She is survived by her son, Blake. • Robin Evonne Morgan, poet, writer and feminist activist, born 29 January 1941; died 5 September 2026

Sweden’s political parties launch coalition talks as both blocs try to secure power

Sweden’s political parties have launched coalition negotiations as the Social Democrats leader, Magdalena Andersson, started the long and difficult process of trying to form a new government. Full results from Sunday’s election are not expected until after overseas votes are counted on Wednesday, but with 95% of the votes counted, the Social Democrats and the centre-left bloc had a narrow but growing lead of 176 seats to the right-leaning parties’ 173. Related: The far right’s march to power in Sweden has been halted, but its influence remains After losing support for the first time since they were founded, the far-right Sweden Democrats, who were hoping to enter government for the first time, appear to be out of the picture. But many of its policy ideas – on immigration laws, integration and crime – have become mainstream, including in the centre-left. Both Andersson and the outgoing centre-right prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, of the Moderates have each said they want to explore possible coalition options to secure power.

Uganda reverses Invictus Games withdrawal after reassurance from King Charles

Uganda has U-turned on its decision to withdraw from the Duke of Sussex’s Invictus Games after the country’s military chief said he had been reassured by King Charles that there was “no problem” with its participation. Last week, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, the eldest son of the Ugandan president, Yoweri Museveni, made the surprise announcement the country would not participate in the games in a post on X. He said he was motivated by his respect for the king amid division over the “Harry-Meghan nonsense”. However, a post on Monday from the spokesperson of the Uganda People’s Defence Force (UPDF), Chris Magezi, announced that Kainerugaba had reinstated Uganda’s participation in the 2027 Invictus Games, which will be held in Birmingham. Magezi wrote that the shift was prompted by a telephone conversation between Kainerugaba and the principal private secretary to the king and queen, Clive Alderton. Alderton had “revealed that King Charles III was moved by Gen Kainerugaba’s sensitive consideration of the king’s opinion on the upcoming Invictus Games organised by Prince Harry, the Duke of Sussex”.

text:
Emma Bonino obituary

In 1974 the Italian feminist activist and later politician Emma Bonino, who has died aged 78, became pregnant. A doctor had told her that she was “sterile”. She attempted to get an abortion and found a doctor in Florence who was willing to help her – for a fee. Bonino felt humiliated and angry – all abortions were illegal in Italy at the time – and became involved with the Radical party, an organisation interested in civil and human rights, and the growing feminist movement. She and other militants set up a network of centres “for sterilisation and abortion” (CISA) across Italy that challenged the law by providing safe and free abortions. A magistrate in Florence issued an arrest warrant for her and others for the crime of “organising abortion”. In June 1975 she went to vote in regional elections in her home town of Bra, outside Turin. She asked the president of the polling station – who had once been her teacher – to have her arrested after voting. Outside the Carabinieri station, Bonino, smiling, held up her hands in the feminist “triangle” symbol. The crowd applauded. The photo made all the front pages.

Bonino said that she did not want any other woman to go through what she had. The press reported in 1976 that thousands of abortions had been arranged this way through the CISA networks – all of them classed as crimes. Bonino spent time in prison in the forbidding Le Murate complex in Florence. Along with the other militant prisoners, she asked not to be released. Her imprisonment was a powerful political weapon. She was then released and in 1976 elected to the chamber of deputies for the Radical party. For complicated political and legal reasons, the whole process with regard to Bonino dragged on for years, right into the 1990s. She was never actually sent to trial, although others were, and were cleared, after decades. At this time an extraordinary political movement emerged in Italy around civil and political rights and the growing feminist movement. The mechanism of the referendum had been inserted into the Italian constitution in 1948: a referendum to abrogate laws could be held if 500,000 signatures could be collected.

Bonino was one of the key leaders of this movement. Born in Bra, Emma was the daughter of Catterina (nee Barge) and Filippo Bonino, and grew up partly on a farm, something which she described later as “deeply boring”. The Panama canal plans to again cut maritime traffic due to worsening drought caused by the El Niño climate phenomenon, further choking up one of the world’s most important shipping lanes. The canal handles 5% of global maritime trade and about 40% of US container traffic; it is favoured by shippers because it usually reduces cost and transit times, especially for companies trading between China, Asia and the US. From October, an average of 29.5 vessels will be allowed to transit daily – down 18% from 36 in August, according to a draft plan submitted to Panama’s parliament. In September, officials cut daily transits from 36 to 32 because of the drought. Tuesday briefing: How to understand Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland’s joint call for change

Good morning. Back in May, the shape of British politics shifted dramatically. I’ll forgive you if you were too preoccupied refreshing Andrew Sparrow’s live blog for the latest speculation about Keir Starmer to notice, but since 7 May, centre-left nationalist parties that ultimately aspire to leave the UK have been in government for the first time simultaneously in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. This week sees the initial codification of that shift. In Cardiff yesterday, Plaid Cymru leader Rhun ap Iorwerth, Scottish National party leader John Swinney and Sinn Féin vice-president Michelle O’Neill (who shares power with the Democratic Unionist party) affirmed their countries’ right to seek independence from the UK. Along with the leader of the opposition in Ireland, Mary Lou McDonald, they signed a memorandum of understanding that called on Westminster “to prepare, plan and facilitate constitutional change in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland”. And they posed for a fair number of group photos too.

With each of the sister parties having a different timeline towards a referendum and its own domestic pressures, it’s tempting to dismiss this as spectacle over substance. However, these first ministers are not shouting into a vacuum. They are part of a cross-national conversation in which devolution is the defining project of the UK’s still newish prime minister. For today’s First Edition, I spoke to our Wales correspondent, Bethan McKernan, in Cardiff about why this agreement is more than a photocall, and checked in with colleagues in Scotland and Ireland for the view from there too. Islamist extremist violence in Africa’s Sahel region is set to reach historic highs after a series of sweeping offensives by groups linked to al-Qaida and Islamic State, according to new figures compiled by the conflict monitor Acled. As the US marks the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks launched by al-Qaida against targets in Washington and New York, the statistics underline the continued expansion of the veteran organisation in parts of Africa – in stark contrast with its relative weakness elsewhere. Compiled by Acled, which stands for Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, the statistics focus on the centre of Islamic militancy in three countries – Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger – which together comprise a huge and hotly contested zone at the heart of the strategic Sahel region. So far this year, 2,145 events have already been logged.

A building housing about 100 displaced Palestinian families has collapsed in Gaza City, killing at least 21 people in their sleep, including 11 children, forcing rescuers to dig through the rubble with their bare hands as they search for dozens of people believed to be trapped. A rescue team from Gaza’s civil defence said they had recovered the bodies of five children among the victims, while 25 injured people were taken to hospital. Medical sources said rescuers could hear the voices of people trapped beneath the rubble as they tried to reach them. The bombed-out multistorey building, which contained four apartments on each floor, had previously been hit by Israeli strikes during the war, leaving its structure badly weakened and at risk of collapse. When it gave way on Wednesday, it fell on to tents beside it housing displaced families, witnesses said. The collapse highlights the continuing danger facing tens of thousands of Palestinians living in an estimated 2,000 buildings damaged by Israeli airstrikes across Gaza.

Datacenter rush will create ‘tsunami’ of discarded electronics, report says

The ongoing campaign to build thousands of massive datacenters for AI will create a “tsunami” of discarded electronics, putting the world on a course to triple its annual generation of toxic e-waste in the next 25 years, a new report projects. The electronic trash AI generates in the next 25 years could fill enough shipping containers to encircle the globe six times, it said. Yet, says the report by the non-profit environmental group Basel Action Network (BAN), there is no plan to deal with that waste – which typically contains toxins like lead, mercury, cadmium and forever chemicals, as well as valuable metals that are challenging to reclaim. “Already electronic waste is the fastest-growing waste stream on the planet and only one-fifth is properly managed,” said Jim Puckett, co-founder of BAN, which works to see that toxic waste doesn’t end up getting dumped on the world’s poorer communities. Experts concur.

The discovery of the bodies of eight women around Johannesburg’s international airport, including five in the past week, has prompted an outpouring of fear, grief and anger over a lack of progress in tackling femicide. When Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo did not return after going for a run on 9 September, her eight-year-old daughter alerted relatives, who contacted police. The 38-year-old’s body was found on Saturday and identified by relatives on Monday. The news of her disappearance had gone viral. Police said in a statement on Saturday that four women’s bodies had been found since 15 July in Kempton Park, across the highway from OR Tambo international airport. All were half-naked and with visible bruising. On Monday and Tuesday, two more bodies were found in the town of Olifantsfontein about 15 miles north of Kempton Park. On Tuesday, police said another woman’s body had been found 25 miles to the south-east, naked and decomposed.

The acting police minister, Firoz Cachalia, said on Wednesday that another woman’s body found in Olifantsfontein on 7 September, was being added to the investigation. “In this country we are prey,” Sakane Mokoena posted on Instagram after confirmation of the death of her friend and fellow runner Moselakgomo. South Africa has one of the highest rates of femicide in the world. Women were killed at a rate of 12.2 per 100,000 people in 2022, nearly six times the global rate, according to the UN Office on Drugs and Crime. For years, women have called on the South African government to take gender-based violence seriously. After hundreds of women protested on the eve of the G20 summit in Johannesburg in November 2025, President Cyril Ramaphosa declared it a national crisis. However, the lack of a concrete plan or action has frustrated campaigners – and women keep being killed. The latest deaths are being investigated by specialist officers, who said on Saturday: “Women in and around Kempton Park are urged not to walk or run alone, particularly in isolated areas.

Is EU’s offer to Canada a blueprint for Britain – or a reminder it is out in the cold?

Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, has been advocating closer alignment with “middle powers” since January in the face of recklessness in Washington. But what should worry another middle power, the UK, is that it was Brussels that came up with Wednesday’s big reveal in Strasbourg. To a standing ovation at her State of the Union address, Ursula von der Leyen said she wanted to open the door to Canada becoming the EU’s first “associate member” in a push to forge new ⁠links among allies in “an openly hostile world”. The European Commission president’s deal could be seen as an “earthquake” offer said Joël Reland, of UK in a Changing Europe, though it remains “deliciously vague”. But it also sets Canada apart from the UK, which could, once upon a time, have had some sort of associate membership with the EU were it not for the drive for a clean-break Brexit. The last time associate membership of the EU was mooted was in relation to Ukraine as an off-the-books novel way of bringing Kyiv closer to the bloc without become a fully fledged member state.

Just moments earlier she spoke about the need for the EU to diversify urgently its supply of critical raw materials (CRM) and rare earths currently dominated by China, allowing it to follow Japan and stockpile said minerals needed for everything from the car to the defence industries. It is not a new subject – after all the EU has been grappling with China’s export surplus since 2023 and it introduced the Critical Raw Materials Act as far back as 2024. The prospect of an enhanced relationship with Ottawa is one that Keir Starmer might have dreamed of. Canada has something the EU desperately needs – rich supplies of CRM and rare earths – and the EU has something Canada urgently wants: new markets for products it can no longer sell into the US in the face of a trade war with Donald Trump.

EU moves closer to social media ban for under 13s

The EU will move forward with plans for an under 13s social media ban, the head of the European Commission has confirmed. Ursula von der Leyen said on Wednesday that social media apps were “depriving children of their childhood” and big tech platforms needed to prove the safety of their products. She promised a draft law for a total ban on social media for under 13s, while children aged 13-15 would be allowed “mini accounts” under parental supervision with time limits on apps. The commission will publish its social media plan on Thursday, which will have to be agreed by the European parliament and 27 EU member states if it is to become law. Von der Leyen also promised that the commission’s Digital Fairness Act, due to be submitted to the European parliament this year, would tackle features such as addictive design, which she said was “harming everyone”. Interactive Related: Social media bans go global: big tech faces a reckoning after Australia’s crackdown The commission president made the comments in Strasbourg as part of her annual state of the union address.

In a wide-ranging speech covering the EU’s place in a turbulent world and plans for continent-wide legislation, she also promised a European heatwave plan and committed to an emergency response mechanism to deal with sudden inflows of migrants in response to events in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in August. Von der Leyen also made an unprecedented invitation to Canada to become an “associate member” of the EU, and pledged to set out ideas for a European security council involving Canada, Norway, Ukraine and the UK. The former German defence minister said the EU needed its version of Nato’s article 4 – an “emergency security protocol” that means all member states would convene at the request of another in response to a hybrid attack. “Europe needs its own counter-hybrid playbook,” she said.

France gives guillotine the chop – archive, 1981

French abolish guillotine From Paul Webster in Paris 27 August 1981 The French cabinet yesterday agreed to end the death penalty as the first of a series of sweeping reforms over the next four months. President Mitterrand also called on the government to “amplify” what he called the positive actions of his first three months in office by ordering nearly 20 major projects to be carried out before Christmas. They range from the nationalisation programme to a reflationary, anti-unemployment budget for 1982. The programme outlined by Mr Mitterrand, who obviously feels the need to reassure a public worried by rising unemployment, increasing inflation and a threat to the franc, will be a crucial test of the government’s capabilities, and the decision to put the abolition of the death penalty at the top of the list of urgent reform should set a decisive tone – particularly as two-thirds of the French people favour the guillotine. The previous regime dithered over a decision on the death penalty for seven years, rejecting at least 10 attempts to raise the question in parliament where it has not been fully debated since 1911.

Until yesterday, France was the only country in Europe which had not abolished the death penalty. (This is an edited extract). Related: From the archive, 29 July 1976: Guillotine returns after two years France gives guillotine the chop By Paul Webster in Paris 19 September 1981 French deputies last night voted to condemn the guillotine and end capital punishment in the first parliamentary vote on the issue for 70 years. The vote was overwhelming – 363 to 117 – even though opinion polls showed that more than two-thirds of French people wanted to retain the death penalty. The guillotine was introduced 190 years ago as a humane instrument to replace torture and hanging for commoners. It was responsible for thousands of deaths, including more than 2,500 during the two years of terror in revolutionary Paris when Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette were executed. The last public execution was in 1939, and during the war the Vichy Government executed a woman for adultery. The 17 executions for murder in the last 20 years have been national controversies.

Students in Gaza ‘devastated’ after plan for them to study in Belgium fails

Students who are unable to leave Gaza and take up scholarships at Belgian universities have said they are devastated after Belgium’s government hit deadlock on a plan enabling them to leave the war-torn territory. Ahmed Abujami, a 28-year-old doctor in Gaza, said he was “deeply disappointed” after Belgium’s five-party coalition government last Friday failed to agree on an evacuation plan for 13 students and researchers in the territory. Abujami has a scholarship to do a one-year master’s degree in public health at the Institute of Tropical Medicine in Antwerp. He hopes to gain skills and experience to rebuild Gaza’s shattered health system. “I was devastated by the failure to reach an agreement on Friday,” he told the Guardian via a messaging app. “We have already lost so much because of the war and now we are facing the possibility of losing another academic year.” Like many of the 12 other students, he is unable to apply for a visa to Belgium, which can only be done in person in Jerusalem or Cairo, but is blocked from leaving the Gaza Strip.

Merz cancels UN visit after AfD election win puts his leadership on the ropes

Powerful German state leaders from Friedrich Merz’s party have rallied behind him as speculation builds that his days in office may be numbered. The chancellor’s hold on power has looked increasingly shaky since a bombshell regional election result earlier this month in which the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party routed his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party in Saxony-Anhalt. With two more states heading to the polls on Sunday where the AfD is expected to perform well, Merz cancelled a plan to speak at the UN general assembly in New York next week because “his presence is required in Berlin”, a government official said on condition of anonymity. The announcement triggered fresh rumours that the unpopular chancellor could be preparing his own exit or wanted to remain and fight off a potential coup. With Merz on the ropes after just 16 months in office, eight ⁠state premiers from the CDU issued a surprise joint statement backing him. ‘Made in Europe’ law threatens UK plans for reset with EU

The UK government’s EU reset summit will be delayed again unless the bloc agrees to discuss legislation that could lock British business out of parts of EU industry, government sources have said. The “Made in Europe” legislation – formally known as the Industrial Accelerator Act – is designed to curb China’s increasing presence in European industry, but was not on the reset plan agreed by the former prime minister Keir Starmer and the European Commission chief, Ursula von der Leyen, in London in May 2025. A follow-up summit was due to be held in July this year, but was cancelled after Starmer’s resignation. The government is now looking to change the roadmap, with one source saying that “Made in Europe should be on the agenda”. It is understood that Hamish Falconer, the new cabinet minister with responsibility for the reset, told the EU’s trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič, this was the UK’s new priority when the pair met last week.

Michelin-starred Seoul restaurant fined for serving dessert topped with ants

A South Korean court has fined the operator of one of Seoul’s most celebrated restaurants and its chief executive for serving a dessert topped with ants, an insect not approved for consumption under local food safety law. The operator of Evett, a two-Michelin-star restaurant in the affluent Gangnam district, was fined 10m won (£5,400) and its chief executive 15m won, Newsis reported. Prosecutors had sought a one-year prison term for the chief executive and a 20m won fine for the company. The judge at Seoul’s western district court, Lee Se-chang, said the offence was “by no means light”, citing the length of time the dishes had been sold for, the restaurant’s use of them to promote itself and tests that found heavy metals above permitted levels in the ants. He said he had taken into account that the defendants admitted the offence, that the chief executive had no previous criminal record under the food safety law, that the number of ants served appeared lower than prosecutors had calculated and that the restaurant no longer used ants.

Nato needs “more UK and more Europe” to deal with the most dangerous security environment faced by the west in a generation, the secretary general of the 32-country military alliance said this afternoon on a visit to the UK. People protecting nature and land set up self-defence units amid threat of murder

Nature and land defenders were murdered at the rate of one every three days last year, prompting many communities to set up self-defence units, according to the latest annual death toll by the independent watchdog Global Witness. Organised crime groups or professional killers were implicated in more than a third of the 124 killings of defenders in 2025 as narco-trafficking activities overlapped with intrusions into indigenous territories and environmental crime, such as illegal logging and wildcat gold mining. This was particularly true in Latin America, which accounted for 85% of last year’s deaths of people trying to protect forests, rivers and other ecosystems. Colombia had the highest toll with 39 killings, followed by Brazil with 26 and Honduras with 12. In Asia, the most dangerous country for defenders was the Philippines, with 12 killings – many during crackdowns by state security forces. Since Global Witness began compiling statistics in 2012, the overall global tally is now 2,375 deaths and disappearances – on a par with a small-scale war.

Former French culture minister goes on trial over corruption charges

Rachida Dati, a former French culture minister, has gone on trial in Paris on corruption charges linked to dealings with the Renault-Nissan carmaking group. Dati, 60, is accused of illegal lobbying when she accepted €900,000 (£770,000) in lawyer’s fees from a Netherlands-based subsidiary of Renault-Nissan while she was a member of the European parliament. The court will have to decide what the money was for. Dati’s legal team denied all corruption allegations, saying she worked “exclusively” as a lawyer for the Renault-Nissan subsidiary. French prosecutors argue that she was instead paid to lobby for the carmaking group, an activity that is banned for members of the European parliament. Prosecutors said there was a lack of evidence to show Dati had carried out legal work. Dati was placed under investigation in 2019 on suspicion of illegally lobbying for Renault-Nissan between October 2009 and February 2013, when she was an MEP. Dati is on trial with Carlos Ghosn, the disgraced former Renault-Nissan chief, who will be tried in absentia.

Singapore pays people to pick up a book in battle against doomscrolling

Singapore is paying its citizens to pick up a book for at least 15 minutes a day in an effort to fight the rise of doomscrolling. The affluent city-state hopes its gamification strategy, which launched this month, will improve concentration, critical thinking and the imagination of Singaporeans. Under the scheme, readers accrue points that can be redeemed for a few cents. People will have to log 50 daily reading sessions on a government website to earn S$1 (80c). A session of 15 minutes or more is rewarded with 20 virtual coins, with 1,000 coins needed for a dollar payment. One reading session is allowed daily. Sweden voted against more power for the far right – but are centrists listening?

Europe’s focus turned nervously to Sweden on Sunday, after an explosive election in Germany just a week earlier placed a far-right party, officially classed as “extremist”, on the brink of power in a German state for the first time since the Nazi era. A party with neo-Nazi roots has been pulling the government’s strings in Sweden for the last four years. Would the country’s general election put the far right formally in government? Or would enough Swedes opt for a gear change, having seen the Sweden Democrats’ hardline (some would say poisonous) agenda in action? Votes were still being counted on Wednesday but it was immediately clear that the far-right Sweden Democrats had suffered a setback; their first loss of support among voters since entering parliament for the first time 16 years ago. The party slipped from being the country’s second biggest party to its third. The centre-left Social Democrats appear poised for a return to power, although it could take months for their leader, Magdalena Andersson, to form a coalition.

And is there a message for mainstream leaders across Europe, many of whom seem fatalistic about a continent-wide far-right surge? France goes to the polls in April while governments in Italy, Spain and Poland, all face their electorates later next year. Benjamin Netanyahu said on Wednesday that he would seek new laws allowing Israel to strip citizenship from people who “smear” Israeli soldiers, escalating the campaign against the Oscar-winning film-makers behind the Gaza documentary NAZA, who have faced threats from senior government and military officials and groups of far-right Israelis gathering outside their families’ homes. Nato head: Britain must show ‘credible path’ of annual defence budget increases

Britain needs to show “a credible path” of annual increases in its defence budgets to meet a Nato target of spending nearly £30bn more on the military by the middle of the next decade, the head of the alliance said on Thursday. Mark Rutte, Nato’s secretary general, said that Britain could not wait until just before 2035 to lift defence spending to 3.5% of GDP, in an unusually pointed intervention a day after he met prime minister Andy Burnham. In an interview with the Press Association, he said: “And that is why you need a credible path towards that 3.5%, and yearly increments.” The alliance’s secretary general, a former Dutch prime minister, made similar remarks to the BBC, where he said that the UK understood that the target could not be met “in one go in 2034” and that it would have to be achieved gradually. Earlier on Thursday, Rutte met with Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, and Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary. He saw Burnham on Wednesday, at a business park in Didcot, and also met representatives from the defence industry.

Keir Starmer signed the UK up to a Nato-wide target of increasing defence spending to 3.5% of GDP in the summer of 2025, under pressure from the US president, Donald Trump. The figure has since been endorsed by Burnham and his chancellor, former defence secretary John Healey. Current spending plans, covering until 2028/9, show defence spending levelling off at 2.7%, nearly £30bn below the ultimate target, raising the question of how it would be achieved after the next general election. It is unclear if taxes or borrowing would have to rise, or other government spending cuts. Healey resigned as defence minister in June because Starmer would not commit to lifting defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030. At the time Healey said Labour needed to set “a clear path” to meet the Nato commitment, similar language to that used by Rutte in his interviews. But since then Healey and Burnham have avoided committing to the 3% by the end of the decade.

All smiles in Strasbourg but uncertainty clouds Canada’s EU membership plan

Mark Carney received a rapturous reception in the European parliament when he gave his speech on Thursday welcoming a proposal for Canada to become the EU’s first-ever associate member. Politicians queued to shake his hand and take selfies. One described the speech as a historic moment. “Europe has extended a hand, and Canada has taken it,” said the German Green MEP Terry Reintke, who borrowed a Canadian ice hockey shirt for the occasion. But the prospect of Canada’s associate membership is uncertain, not least because no one is sure what it means. “I’m not quite sure why she [von der Leyen] used that term because there’s simply no legal definition,” said one senior politician. “This has just raised lots of questions.

Sweden’s PM resigns after centre-left bloc wins slim majority in election

Sweden’s centre-right prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, has stood down, clearing the way for Magdalena Andersson, the Social Democrats leader, to attempt to form a government. In a victory speech on Thursday, Andersson said the Swedish people had “voted for a new direction for our country, voted for unity and against division”. She added: “The Swedish people have voted to take Sweden forward and I will realise the new direction that you have voted for.” Among the priorities she named were the climate crisis, schools, healthcare, elderly care and immigration policy. Andersson spoke as the preliminary count for Sunday’s election was finally completed, with 176 seats for the left-leaning opposition parties – a narrow three-seat majority over the right-leaning ruling Tidö coalition supported by the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD). There were 50,359 votes between the two blocs. default Earlier on Thursday, Andersson, who was Kristersson’s predecessor as prime minister, sent an invitation to the other left-leaning parties – Left, Centre and Green – for initial coalition talks.

Thursday briefing: Yemen’s war continues to threaten oil supplies– but what about its people?

Good morning. The lightning advance of Houthi militants along the west coast of Yemen over the past week has prompted fears of a spiralling conflict in the region and a new oil supply crisis. For families living in the Middle East’s poorest country, the most significant fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces in years is a crisis upon a catastrophe, with escalating civilian casualties and at least 100,000 displaced in recent days. Houthi fighters have captured strategic islands across a critical Red Sea trade route, the Bab al-Mandab strait, one of the most important shipping routes in the world – almost 15% of global sea trade passes through it. The strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s traded oil and gas transited in peacetime, has remained largely blocked since the US and Israel launched airstrikes in February, so the prospect of Iran and its allies exerting pressure on two maritime choke points has global implications. The price of crude oil has already begun to spike.

‘Harrowing reading’: what the inquiry into NZ fugitive father Tom Phillips revealed

A major public inquiry into the disappearance of fugitive father Tom Phillips, who hid in New Zealand’s wilderness for nearly four years with his three children, has found authorities played down the harms he inflicted on his children, and did not do enough to protect them. Taking his children, of whom he did not have legal custody, Phillips disappeared into the rugged North Island wilderness in 2021. That disappearance was preempted by an earlier, shorter stint where Phillips went bush with his son and two daughters, aged five, seven and eight at the time. Related: Hidden for nearly four years: how the saga of fugitive father Tom Phillips unfolded in New Zealand In August 2025, Phillips was shot dead by police in a shootout. Here are some key findings of the inquiry, which investigated agencies’ engagement with Phillips before and after he disappeared. Agencies overlooked harm Phillips was causing Over “significant periods”, police and Oranga Tamariki (OT), the ministry for children, “underplayed or overlooked” the harm Phillips was causing before and after he vanished, the inquiry found.

They were too slow to identify important information, and the search was launched too late. Police intentionally adopted “a low-key approach”, the inquiry said. “This strategy appears to have been predicated on the misconceived view that there were no concerns for the children’s welfare.” The inquiry found OT was dismissive of multiple concerns raised by the maternal family after Phillips’ first disappearance, telling the family court the children were “completely fine” and further OT involvement was perhaps not needed. Significant family concerns minimised Had OT taken into consideration the significant concerns of the children’s mother and two other sisters, they “may have prevented or made more difficult” his second disappearance, the inquiry found. The sisters, who had lived with their stepfather Phillips for some years, repeatedly raised concerns over his pattern of isolation and harm he caused.

The inquiry found OT failed to hear her concerns before Phillips disappeared the second time. She also notified police that Phillips stashed multiple firearms “all over the place” six months before he disappeared. Police questioned her credibility because of a “custody dispute in the background” and did not respond to her allegations. His alcohol consumption concerned them, and his home was “very dirty”. They formed the view he was controlling and difficult to live with. A person close to Phillips was concerned that, if cornered, he would turn “violent”. Trump threatens to stop trading with EU over ‘laughable’ membership offer to Canada

Donald Trump has threatened the EU with “serious tariffs” and a halt to trade after the bloc proposed making Canada its first ever associate member – an idea he derided as “laughable”. The US president said that if the EU moved forward with the plan, Washington could impose “very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe”. He added: “If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe.” Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, is due to address the European parliament on Thursday, a day after the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, invited his country to become the EU’s first “associate member”. Von der Leyen pitched closer cooperation on tech, defence and energy to Carney, telling the European parliament that, as democracies faced a “fracture in the international rules-based system”, Brussels and Ottawa needed to pull closer together. She said: “This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength.

Ukrainian drone forces have killed a Russian general who had just been made a Hero of Russia after false claims that Moscow’s forces had captured the Donetsk city of Kostiantynivka. Maj Gen Anton Grunis died in eastern Ukraine on Saturday. “General Grunis was ​eliminated on September 12,” said Ukrainian drone commander Robert Brovdi, adding that the general was the seventh Russian military commander killed by his drone forces. Another Russian commander, Apti Alaudinov, posted confirmation that Grunis had died. The battle for Kostiantynivka is gruelling for Ukraine but war analysts say it remains contested. ‘We live with a big burden’: survivor of abusive Spotlight priest hopes clergyman’s death brings closure

A survivor of childhood sexual abuse by a defrocked Boston Catholic priest who was portrayed admitting to molesting minors in the Oscar-winning Hollywood film Spotlight says he hopes the clergyman’s recent death in prison helps victims of his crimes and their families “keep pressing forward every single day”. “We live with a big burden in our hearts and on our backs,” Keith Townsend said on Wednesday while reflecting on the criminal charges which he successfully pursued against Ronald Paquin, who was imprisoned in 2019 and died in custody at age 83 on 11 September. “And my hope is that people can find closure and move on.” Those remarks by Townsend, 52, during a telephone interview were a notable reaction to the death of one of the key figures in the clergy sexual abuse and cover-up scandal with the Catholic archdiocese of Boston that – among other consequences – prompted the resignation of the institution’s archbishop, Bernard Law, at the end of 2002, as well as policy reforms across the US church.

He was stripped of his clerical status and imprisoned in Massachusetts for that abuse, which was first publicly exposed in a Pulitzer-winning series of investigative articles by the Boston Globe newspaper’s Spotlight team. Paquin was freed in 2015. And learning of that release motivated Townsend – once a St John altar server, too – to come forward and report being abused himself by Paquin while on camping trips to Kennebunkport, Maine, between 1985 and 1989. As Townsend put it, he was between the ages of eight and 13 when Paquin molested him. Townsend recalled Paquin plying him with drugs and alcohol during the abuse, eventually leading him to battles with substance abuse addiction and incarceration. A Maine grand jury indicted Paquin in 2017 on new charges of gross sexual misconduct in connection with Townsend and another individual.

Brazil’s Lula announces higher welfare payments and free weight-loss jabs ahead of election

Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has announced a 15% increase in the country’s main cash-transfer programme for poor families, as well as free weight-loss jabs, prompting criticism from opponents who say the moves are electorally motivated just two weeks before the presidential election. On 4 October, the leftwing incumbent will face the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who has been gaining ground in recent weeks. The rise in the monthly payment, from about £98 to £113, that he announced on Thursday is due to take effect on 19 October, just before the likely runoff vote on 25 October. The increase is expected to benefit between 15% and 20% of voters in what promises to be one of the closest ever presidential races in Latin America’s largest country. Lula said it was not really an increase, but an adjustment in line with inflation to “protect the purchasing power of the most vulnerable families”, but his opponents have criticised its timing so close to the election.

citation.title: Brazil’s Lula announces higher welfare payments and free weight-loss jabs ahead of election

Flávio Bolsonaro called it an “act of desperation” after polls showed him gaining ground – although the most recent survey, released on Thursday night, still showed Lula numerically ahead despite the technical tie. The senator added that Lula was trying to “buy the votes of the poor”. Created in 2003 during his first term as president, the programme, called Bolsa Família, was a flagship cash-transfer policy that helped lift millions of families out of poverty during his first two terms. Currently, families with an income of up to £32 per person are eligible, covering about 50 million people, or roughly 27 million of voting age. The programme has long been fiercely criticised by rightwing politicians, including by Jair Bolsonaro, although he kept it in place during his presidency. On the eve of the 2022 election, Bolsonaro announced a 50% increase in the monthly payment, prompting Lula’s campaign to file a case with the electoral court alleging abuse of political power and electoral use of the state machinery.

British woman who was kidnapped in Malawi rescued by police after shootout

A British woman kidnapped in Malawi last week has been rescued by police after a shootout in which four of her alleged abductors were killed. Nusrat Osman was abducted outside her home in the southern city of Blantyre on 11 September at about 12.30pm. Police had offered a reward of 30m Malawi kwacha (£12,950) for information leading to her rescue and the arrest of the perpetrators. Malawian police announced Osman’s rescue late on Thursday in a statement. “There was an exchange of fire between police and kidnappers, who were armed with [an] AK47 rifle and a Girsan Regard MC pistol. In the process, the criminals got shot and were taken to hospital where they succumbed to their injuries.” it read. A police officer, deputy inspector general Mlowoka Noel Kayira, was also shot during the operation. “He is currently receiving medical attention at the hospital and is in a stable condition,” police said. Osman, a 47-year-old auditor and mother of two, was safe and “not too shaken” after her ordeal, her brother Shobi Jiwa told the Sun, expressing his gratitude to Malawi’s police.

Jiwa reserved special thanks for Kayira. “He is the hero of our family. He’s the hero of the country,” he said. “He’s the hero of the world, actually, for putting his life at risk and taking a bullet into himself for my sister.” Kidnappings are rare in Malawi, which has experienced a rise in pickpocketing and house burglaries by often armed men in recent years amid unstable, crisis-ridden economic conditions. The landlocked southern African country is one of the world’s poorest nations, with a population of about 22 million and an average annual income of just $672, according to the World Bank. In 2024, a country report by the US state department’s diplomatic security service said: “Kidnappings are not a widespread concern in Malawi, and there have been no recent high-profile incidents involving westerners. “Historically, expatriates have not been significant targets for kidnappings in the country.

Disabled people need right to travel abroad, say UK MPs amid ‘ridiculous’ restrictions row

Disabled people must have a guaranteed right to travel abroad, MPs and peers have said, as further cases emerged of individuals barred from taking holidays as a result of “ridiculous” rules imposed by local NHS care boards and local councils. Leading figures have called on the government to bring in clear national guidelines to ensure people who require full-time personal assistants (PAs) are not prevented from using funding for their 24/7 support team for breaks and work trips. Wide variations in local rules governing foreign travel mean whether a disabled person can take their care team abroad can depend on where they live, the whim of local officials or whether they are prepared to mount a legal challenge. The call came as it emerged two men with the same health condition and care packages, living 40 miles from each other, are subject to different rules regarding overseas travel with their PA support team.

Drivers ignoring roadwork closures to skip queues ‘wilfully putting lives at risk’

Drivers ignoring roadwork closures to skip queues are putting lives at risk, National Highways has warned, after recording hundreds of incidents this year where cars were deliberately driven through cones or barriers. Flight chaos for hundreds of thousands was caused in ‘millisecond’ by software error

A software defect in part of the UK’s air traffic control system corrupted flight data “in the space of a millisecond”, leading to a six-hour outage and mass airline cancellations and delays across the UK last week, National Air Traffic Services has said. But ministers said the Nats report into the incident still left questions unanswered, saying they needed “to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos”. According to the report, the error first occurred at 10am and was notified to engineers who investigated – but the system appeared to be working again, until 12.30pm when a repeat occurred and a major incident was declared. text:
Friday briefing: After two months as PM, is Andy Burnham passing his own test?

Good morning. Remember the Makerfield test? When Andy Burnham was elected as an MP back in June, he reassured wary voters that the constituency was not a “stepping stone” (to be fair, it was a bit) but a “touchstone”. He meant that the policies his government devised would have to matter on the high streets of Ashton and Hindley Green. “A Makerfield test at the heart of British politics will make sure that the places Westminster has neglected will now get fairness,” he said. As the Commons breaks for the jamboree of high ideas, low gossip and crap karaoke that is party conference season, it’s a good moment to ask how Burnham’s early decisions as prime minister – he’s been at it under two months, right enough – meet that test and what it tells us about his government. I spoke to someone who, since that byelection, has immersed himself in the opinions of Makerfield voters, and those living in constituencies like it, Luke Tryl, UK director of the research agency More in Common. But first the headlines.

In depth: ‘The top thing for people in Makerfield was that life was a struggle’ “Who cares what Makerfield man or woman thinks? I’m a Holborn and St Pancras via Caerphilly gal myself,” you might be muttering into your overnight oats. But here’s why it matters: Makerfield, like dozens of similar post-industrial seats in the north of England, is the sort of seat Labour used to win so easily they could put up a ham sandwich as a candidate. Things have since changed. The area voted to leave by 65% in the Brexit referendum, and in the May council elections, Reform won all eight council wards in the constituency with about 50% of the vote. In his byelection dispatches from Makerfield, Luke Tryl found a pervasive sense of being left behind and forgotten – despite being “at the centre of the universe”, as one constituent put it, for one frantic month of campaigning.

text:
Friday briefing: After two months as PM, is Andy Burnham passing his own test?

According to the voters Tryl spoke to, the Makerfield test should consist of three elements: Burnham showing that he “gets it”; a record of delivery; and a national plan to address the issues that Makerfield residents share with people across the country. So how has Burnham fared on some of the early challenges he’s faced? Cost of living measures “The top thing we heard in Makerfield was a sense that too much of life was a struggle,” Tryl tells me. And More in Common’s polling has found that, so far, Burnham’s early cost of living measures are very popular across the country: 86% of Britons had heard about the bus fare cap, seven in 10 thought it reflected well on the government; about 8 in 10 had heard about the VAT cut on household electricity bills (amounting to an average of about £45 a year per household), and 67% said that it landed well. Voters in Makerfield-like areas are realistic, says Tryl: “They say: ‘£45 is not going to change my life’, but they see it as a statement of intent”.

citation.title: Friday briefing: After two months as PM, is Andy Burnham passing his own test?

text:
Friday briefing: After two months as PM, is Andy Burnham passing his own test?

People who are slightly more engaged with politics specifically mention the budget as a test point: earlier this week Burnham warned of “difficult choices” ahead. The cut-through of these measures to voters is striking: “Part of it is just the ubiquity of Andy Burnham,” says Tryl. Most recent More in Common polling shows people are more likely to have seen him on social media than any of the other party leaders. A fifth of Britons (22%) have seen “Cool Dad” Burnham on social media in the past week, compared to 20% for Reform leader Nigel Farage. I’m fascinated to see that for under-25s that rises to 35%, compared with 13% for Green leader Zack Polanski, who is often touted as catnip for younger voters. Immigration More in Common polling in June estimated that 62% of Makerfield residents consider immigration to be a top issue, making it one of the most concerned constituencies in the country about that issue. Here, Burnham gets a mixed review. The idea of taking in refugees through capped, controlled routes is popular in Makerfield, where voters worry over a lack of control.

That’s why Tryl argues that one policy that really does pass the Makerfield test is the community sponsorship scheme, part of Shabana Mahmood’s controversial asylum reforms. But while Burnham has won back Labour-Green switchers over the summer, he’s not been so successful with Labour to Reform defectors – and Tryl believes that’s because he has yet to move the dial on migration. Take, for example, the shift in people’s perceptions: 52% of Britons now cite concern that local women and girls would be at risk of sexual violence as the top reason why they’d oppose asylum accommodation in their area (previously, they were more likely to refer to pressure on services). In socially conservative areas such as Makerfield, voters feel this “much more strongly”. “I think this is an achilles heel”, says Tryl. Prisoner release It’s not just constituencies such as Makerfield where voters think the criminal justice system isn’t tough enough: across the country, nearly two-thirds of Britons think prison sentences are too lenient.

text:
Friday briefing: After two months as PM, is Andy Burnham passing his own test?

“The case of Andrew Harper outrages people across the board,” Tryl tells me, “but particularly in somewhere like Makerfield.” So Burnham played a bad hand well, by explaining the competing priorities to the public, and taking time to examine options before finding a partial solution. “Taking the public on that journey – especially in Makerfield where people are very distrustful of politicians – was important,” says Tryl. Climate Burnham, who is now facing intense pressure over whether to approve oil and gasfields in the North Sea, wrote in the Guardian yesterday that the UK must fully commit to reaching net zero by 2050. While Labour-Reform switchers in places like Makerfield are often deeply worried about climate change, there’s also concern that net zero policies will unfairly punish ordinary people. For many, the issue of climate change falls below more pressing daily concerns like the cost of living crisis. In this context, More in Common’s polling suggests the main test for Britain’s energy policies will be whether they can lower household bills.

So Burnham’s early failure to support a domestic cap on donations is unlikely to be a decisive factor when constituents in Makerfield next head to the ballot box. But for the recipient of those crypto-millions, the damage has been done: more than one in three voters now name Farage’s “sleaziness and corruption” as a barrier to them voting Reform. Rather than the party’s core voters, who seem unmoved by the continuing financial scandals, it is Labour-Reform switchers in seats such as Makerfield whose faith has been shaken. But Tryl cautions against over-stressing the issue. “At the next election, if the status quo on cost of living, core public services, andimmigration still feels pretty bad, I don’t think donations in themselves will be an issue” he says. Russians go to polls against backdrop of Ukraine war and Putin’s tightening grip

Russians are going to the polls to elect a new State Duma in a tightly controlled vote stripped of meaningful competition and with little doubt about the result. Vladimir Putin’s United Russia is expected to extend the grip on parliament it has held for 23 years, alongside a handful of nominal opposition parties that reliably vote with the Kremlin on the issues that matter. The three-day vote begins on Friday, with results expected after polls close on Sunday. For all the predictability of the outcome, the first Duma election since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 is taking place against the backdrop of a war that, once distant for many Russians, is increasingly intruding into everyday life. Swarms of Ukrainian drones have struck oil refineries, factories and logistics hubs across Russia over the summer, while polling has pointed to growing anxiety about the course of the fighting and what may still lie ahead. Against that backdrop, the Kremlin has tightened its grip further.

Over the past 18 months, tens of millions of Russians have been forced to install a new app on their phones – a violet-blue button designed for messaging and payments, called Max. Authorities have touted it as a patriotic alternative to Telegram and WhatsApp; Russian glitterati have promoted it in rap videos and comic routines. This summer, it became the country’s most-used messaging app. It is a product of VKontakte, the Russian social media company, which is deeply entangled with the Russian state. The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, reportedly owns an indirect stake in Max. Max is Russia’s version of a “super-app,” combining an ecosystem of services into a single platform. It is a container for a number of “mini-apps” that now facilitate everyday life in Russia – banking apps, a messaging service that aims to replace Telegram, and apps for essential government services. The best-known super-app in the world is WeChat, China’s everything platform which facilitates the state’s social controls.

These amount to a “backdoor” into its entire mini-app ecosystem on every user’s device, said Roya Ensafi, an associate professor of computer science at the University of Michigan. “We have studied Russia’s escalation of internet control for the past decade,” said Ensafi. “What Max provides is the cleverest and also the scariest tactic by authoritarian governments” to surveil their citizens. Sweden’s soul and worrying political shift

I am writing in response to Martin Gelin’s article (How Sweden lost its soul – and stopped being Sweden, 11 September). Gelin is right to lament how far Swedish politics has moved from the liberal internationalism of the Fredrik Reinfeldt era. Having grown up in Malmö, I have seen how border controls with Denmark affect an Öresund region whose everyday life has long depended on easy movement across the strait. Gelin is right to see this retreat from openness as consequential. But to say that Sweden has therefore “lost its soul” goes too far. Its political shift is neither uniquely Swedish nor evidence that the country has somehow ceased to be itself. Reinfeldt’s “open your hearts” Sweden faded in much the same European political moment as Angela Merkel’s “Wir schaffen das” Germany. Across the European mainland, mainstream parties have adopted more restrictive positions on migration. The cases involving British citizens that Gelin describes are troubling, but Britain’s departure from the EU is also part of the explanation for why Britons in Sweden now face immigration rules from which freedom of movement once spared them.

citation.title: Sweden’s soul and worrying political shift

text:
Sweden’s soul and worrying political shift

Sweden has changed. So has Britain. Neither exists in a vacuum. There is nothing wrong with romanticising an open, internationalist Sweden. As a young Swede studying at Cambridge, I am susceptible to that image myself. But defining one particular political settlement as Sweden’s “soul” risks turning nostalgia into national essentialism. Perhaps Jantelagen – the Scandinavian suspicion of thinking oneself exceptional – offers a more Swedish conclusion. We should not imagine that our political upheavals make us uniquely fallen. Sweden has changed, considerably and sometimes regrettably. It has not stopped being Sweden. Alvin Engström Cambridge • Martin Gelin’s analysis of how Sweden is losing its soul rings true – unfortunately. After living in Sweden for 33 years, I have never felt more like a foreigner than I do now. I am British (of Scottish origin) and moved to Sweden in 1993, at the age of 37, to live with my Swedish husband and our two children. I remember being so impressed by the social benefits, the access to good and affordable childcare and the job opportunities for women – precisely the ideals Martin describes. Over the past 10.

In recent years, I have repeatedly been asked whether I consider myself Swedish (I have dual nationality). At first, I didn’t think much of it, but over time, I began to find the question very irritating. On one occasion, an older Swedish woman said it didn’t matter if I didn’t feel Swedish, because “we see you as one of us anyway”. I am ashamed to admit that I snapped at her over the word “us”; I know she meant well, but it made me realise just how divisive the question was. The mere fact that it was being asked by nice, ordinary, polite people was playing right into the hands of the far right. I love my life in Sweden and have no plans to move, but the divisiveness has got under my skin and is hard to ignore. Jean Fridh Katrineholm, Sweden

Donald Trump announced on Friday that the US had struck an Arctic security pact with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland, after threatening for much of his second term to annex the semi-autonomous Danish territory by force. A bitter inquest is under way among Yemen’s anti-Houthi forces as to how what was being billed as a decisive assault on Sana’a, the Houthi-controlled capital, suddenly collapsed into a military rout. Denmark and Greenland say US military agreement will not compromise Arctic territory’s sovereignty

Denmark and Greenland have said any agreement with the US to develop a significant military presence in the strategic Arctic territory will not compromise Greenland’s sovereignty. In a statement on Saturday clarifying an announcement by Donald Trump that an agreement had been reached to give Washington “permanent control” ⁠over Greenland’s security, Denmark and the semi-autonomous territory ⁠expressed hope that a deal would end friction with the US over the issue. Greenland’s prime minister, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, said he was pleased with the proposed deal. “The agreement recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of our kingdom and ​the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination,” he said ​in a post. Related: US and Denmark reach security deal after Trump’s threats to take over Greenland “Next week could be a good week – for Greenland, ‌Denmark and the United States,” Denmark’s foreign minister, ‌Lars Lokke Rasmussen, said in a statement.

Denmark and Greenland say US military agreement will not compromise Arctic territory’s sovereignty

“A time of uncertainty will hopefully give way to a binding agreement that strengthens security ‌in the Arctic and the north Atlantic, and thereby our shared security within Nato Europe – while respecting the Danish kingdom’s red lines,” Rasmussen said. The US, Denmark and Greenland said late on Friday they had reached a deal to allow the US to develop a significant military presence on Greenland, while prohibiting US adversaries from building their ⁠own bases on the island. The deal is expected to be signed during the UN general assembly next week. Key details of the agreement have not been made public, including the degree of the US military presence in the self-governing Danish territory and whether any formal power over foreign policy and resources would be ceded to Washington. Trump said on social media that under the deal, “the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America”.
