But today eight patrols are moving along the river, by helicopter or boat – and every few hundred metres they encounter more evidence of illegal gold mining, operations that have laid waste to more than 500 hectares of the park’s rainforest in the last year, according to satellite mapping data from Amazon Conservation. In total, more than 140,000 hectares have been lost to mining in Madre de Dios – a shocking 97.5% of the total deforestation caused by mining in Peru’s Amazon rainforest, an area twice the size of the US state of California. Military crackdowns on illegal mining in the Amazon are not new in Peru. A play based on the trial of the men who drugged and raped Gisèle Pelicot will come to London for one night only this November – and promises to feature a star-studded cast. The four-hour production of The Pelicot Trial: Tribute to Gisèle Pelicot has been performed around the world, including in New York City and Avignon, the city in France where the trial took place. This autumn, it is coming to London County Hall, the home of Agatha Christie’s Witness for the Prosecution. “I saw it in French originally – all four hours of it. It was jaw-dropping, harrowing, really emotional,” said Nadia Fall, artistic director and co-chief executive of the Young Vic, which is putting on the performance. “It was the act of witnessing that really got me: it is long-form and testimonial in form.” Fall expects the show to sell out immediately. “Because it’s one night only, what we are able to do is ring our best actors, people you will know ‘off the telly’ as well,” Fall said. The full cast will be announced before tickets go on sale in the coming weeks. Fall added: “The ensemble rehearses together just once.

Jordan Bardella, the head of Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally (RN), has claimed a “total war” is being waged against his party as he faces a political storm after the publication of antisemitic comments he allegedly wrote as a young party member. Bardella, who is facing calls from political opponents to resign, said on Tuesday that the report by the investigative website Mediapart was false. To a standing ovation from his party’s lawmakers and senators at a meeting in parliament, he said the report was an attempt to damage his party as Le Pen tops the polls before the 2027 presidential election. “We are seeing the beginnings of a total war, an attempt to destabilise the presidential campaign,” Bardella said. He accused Mediapart of wanting “to kill my political career” and said he would take legal action for defamation. Le Pen, at Bardella’s side, said she had “absolute confidence” in him.

A large shark has become an unlikely tourist attraction after getting trapped in a narrow city canal in South Korea for more than a week. More than 600,000 people are estimated to have visited a waterfront park in the southern port city of Busan since the 3.5-metre shark – nicknamed Bukang-i after the name of Busan’s North Port – was first spotted in its waterway on 18 September. Experts believe it to be a bronze whaler shark that followed prey from the sea into the canal and could not find its way out. The coastguard in the city about 200 miles (325km) south-east of Seoul tried to drive it out on the day it appeared but suspended the operation six hours later, on the advice of scientists who warned that forcing the animal could harm it or make it aggressive. Saudi Arabia is being urged to reconcile with the United Arab Emirates over Yemen as the price Riyadh must pay to form a military alliance capable of driving the Houthis back. Relations between the UAE and Saudi Arabia in Yemen, where both had backed anti-Houthi forces, plummeted in January this year when a force with which the UAE had been aligned – the separatist Southern Transitional Council (STC) – was attacked and defeated by Saudi Arabia in a move intended to squash its attempt to recreate a separate southern state. The UAE subsequently in effect quit Yemen. But the unexpected success in mid September of the Iran-aligned Houthis’ drive to the narrow Bab al-Mandab strait against pro-government forces has transformed the geopolitics of the region again. The push south defeated the previously UAE-backed National Resistance Forces led by Tareq Saleh, whose front rapidly collapsed.

Spain announces plan to ease housing crisis amid outcry over eviction of 87-year-old

Spain’s Socialist Workers’ party-led coalition government has approved a range of measures aimed at easing the country’s housing crisis, including extending a ban on evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, after a public outcry over the eviction of an 87-year-old disabled woman from her Madrid apartment last week. Two decrees have been approved by cabinet but will need to be approved in Congress, where the coalition lacks a majority. The government has requested a special parliamentary session on Friday in the hope of getting the decrees passed as soon as possible. Although the fine print has yet be revealed, the main decree includes: extending restrictions on evictions of vulnerable tenants to 2030; regulating temporary lettings and lettings by room; a ban on so-called vulture funds buying property until 2028, plus a two-year extension on current rental agreements that are due to expire at the end of 2028. A separate agreement was reached on the automatic renovation of rental agreements.

Good morning. Vehicles suspected of carrying explosives zipping across Britain, entirely unbeknownst to authorities, is a disconcerting prospect. Initially, it seemed precisely this had occurred in Gloucestershire early on Sunday. Antarctic winter sea ice falls to third-lowest level on record as scientists warn of ‘now problem’

Antarctica’s winter sea ice has peaked at its third-lowest level on record, falling a million square kilometres – or almost 400,000 square miles – short of the long-term average, scientists have confirmed. Confirmation of the peak meant the four lowest years on record for the continent’s sea ice – a vital component of the planet’s climate and critical for marine life – had all occurred in the past four years. Satellites have been watching the continent’s sea ice since 1979, and this year data showed the sea ice peaked on 14 September at 17.59m square kilometres, about a million square kilometres short of the average maximum or an area roughly twice the size of Spain. Dr Walt Meier, a senior scientist at the National Snow and Ice Data Center at the University of Colorado, said the centre had held off in declaring the maximum because there was a “lot of potential variability” at this stage in the continent’s sea ice cycle. But the levels of sea ice had been falling since 14 September and he now thought “the maximum has been reached”.

citation.title: Antarctic winter sea ice falls to third-lowest level on record as scientists warn of ‘now problem’

text:
Antarctic winter sea ice falls to third-lowest level on record as scientists warn of ‘now problem’

Antarctica’s sea ice goes through an enormous annual swing, melting through summer to below 2m sq km in recent Februaries and then growing through winter reaching above 17m sq km in September. But recent years have seen records broken for low sea ice in both winter and summer, raising concerns that global heating could be driving the losses. “The past four winters have had the lowest sea ice maximum on record – that’s a very clear indication of a system that has changed,” said Dr Ariaan Purich, a Southern Ocean expert at Monash University in Melbourne. “This is not a one-off event any more. The sea ice is no longer covering the same extent of ocean that it used to. We are seeing low winter after low winter and that suggests the sea ice is behaving differently because we have warmed our climate. “This is not a future problem. It’s a now problem.” Interactive In June, the Antarctic peninsula saw a heatwave with temperatures 20C above normal while scientists pointed to a France-sized area of open ocean where ice should have been.

text:

In early August when sea ice should be steadily expanding, a large area of the Amundsen Sea to the south of the Pacific lost ice. Purich said changes in winds associated with the El Niño climate pattern in the tropical Pacific had likely played a role in reducing the sea ice in that region. Dr Phil Reid, who monitors Antarctic conditions at Australia’s Bureau of Meteorology, said El Niño tended to change the movement of storm systems around Antarctica leading some to be held in the same place, churning up the sea ice below. But he said even without an El Niño, “I think we would still be in a similar position … and that is a bit disconcerting”. “The atmosphere will play around a bit, but in the end thermodynamics wins. If the water is too warm, you won’t have as much sea ice.” Purich said as Antarctica now emerged from its “polar night”, sea ice reflects the sun’s energy during the day. But less sea ice meant the Southern Ocean could take up more heat.

Ice shelves slow down the advance of glaciers and the continent’s vast ice sheet that has the potential to push up global sea levels by many metres if it reaches the ocean. As well as providing habitats for algae and krill – critical elements of the continent’s food web – unstable sea ice has raised concerns for other species, including emperor penguins, that use the ice to breed and raise young. Dr Will Hobbs, Antarctic sea ice expert at the University of Tasmania, said since reaching its peak earlier this month, Antarctic sea ice had been dropping “faster than usual”. “We could be looking at another low summer and that’s when things get really worrying,” he said, pointing to concerns about impacts on ice shelves. “How sensitive is the global climate system to this loss of sea ice? We are still working to put numbers on that. But the system is changing faster than we are understanding it.”

Economic growth and democratic decline: the ‘cotton king’ who reshaped Benin

In recent years, a building boom has reshaped Benin’s largest city, Cotonou, and a shiny new coastal road has reduced journey times to Ouidah, the west African country’s spiritual and cultural capital. In the last decade, Benin’s annual GDP has grown from 3% to 6%, a regional high, and an industrial zone has been launched north-west of Cotonou to help industrialise the relatively small nation’s largely informal economy. “Benin is now looking like a paradise,” said Savossou Stanislas, a 40-year-old tyre repairer in the official capital, Porto-Novo. The rapid infrastructural development has been overseen by Patrice Talon, the president from 2016 till this May. For years, Benin was so content being in the shadow of Nigeria, a neighbour about eight times its size and with about 16 times its population, that Talon’s predecessor, Thomas Boni Yayi, once quipped during a visit to Abuja that “Benin is the 37th state of Nigeria”.

Talon, who also enjoys good relations with Nigeria and called on it to help quell an attempted coup d’etat in December, chose a different path: to engineer enough growth for Benin to be recognised in its own right. The Kagame model Widely believed to be Benin’s richest person, Talon, known as “the cotton king”, made his name in agriculture but diversified into banking and hospitality. Before becoming president, he had financed the campaigns of Yayi and Yayi’s predecessor, Mathieu Kérékou. Critics say his development agenda has come at a severe cost: once held up as a poster child for democratic transition in west Africa, Benin has also undergone democratic decline since Talon took power. In many respects, Talon modelled his governance style on the leader of another relatively small African country: Paul Kagame. The archetypal “benevolent strongman”, Rwanda’s de facto leader since 1994 has also combined repression with policies aimed at economic and social transformation. In time, the two men became allies and Talon even appointed two former Rwandan officials to head sensitive Beninese government agencies.

Benin has also sought the east African nation’s help in countering a growing insurgency along the border with Nigeria. By the end of Talon’s first term, strict new election laws and heavy registration fees had purged a lot of the opposition from parliament. In 2019, the government shut down the internet during a parliamentary election as people protested against the changes. The judiciary was co-opted to muzzle dissent, resulting in the targeting of several dozen former allies and dissidents, including the opposition leader Reckya Madougou, who is in prison on charges of “undermining the state”, and the journalist Hugues Comlan Sossoukpé. In April 2021, a month after Madougou’s arrest, Essowé Batamoussi, a judge at the court for the repression of economic offences and terrorism, resigned his post and fled to France to seek asylum. “There was no justice in her [Madougou’s] case,” Batamoussi said. “We received an empty file and a threat: if we did not put her in jail, we were in danger.” Last November, it became apparent how deeply Talon had control of every major aspect of life in Benin.

Within a month of parliament approving the amendment, mutineers led by a former commander of the national guard attempted a coup, citing Talon’s authoritarianism and inability to tackle rising insecurity. Only one opposition candidate was approved to stand in April’s presidential election, which was won by Talon’s hand-picked successor, Romuald Wadagni, with more than 94% of the vote. In August, Talon himself returned to centre stage as president of the senate. Morgan Assogba, a Cotonou-based geopolitical analyst, described Talon as a “gigantic political actor with a good understanding of how politics works in Benin”, who had reshaped the political arena to suit his economic development drive.

‘We’re afraid of dying’: Brazilian news site will not cover upcoming elections after threats

Four years ago, during Brazil’s last presidential election, the tyres were slashed on the pickup truck used for reporting by Tapajós de Fato, an independent journalism website in the Brazilian Amazon. Days later, a cat’s severed head was left next to the car park, alongside a note bearing the name of one of the site’s founders, Marcos Wesley Pedroso, and a warning that he would be next. Last July, security cameras outside Pedroso’s house showed cyclists circling the block, whistling and filming his car until, minutes later, another car crashed into it. “I believe they wanted me to come outside so they could ambush me,” said Pedroso. Police have not identified those responsible or established whether the cases are connected, but Pedroso sees them as part of a wider series of threats linked to Tapajós de Fato’s reporting on environmental and Indigenous rights violations, land disputes, and pesticide contamination in the Amazonian state of Pará.

French court jails six men for manslaughter over mass drowning in Channel

A Paris court has jailed six ⁠men for manslaughter over the deaths of at least 27 people in the worst mass drowning on record from a small-boat crossing in the Channel. Seven other men were ⁠found guilty of lesser smuggling charges with varying degrees of seriousness, including facilitating illegal immigration as part of ⁠an organised gang and criminal conspiracy. Five years on, another four people are still missing. The court heard that the sinking of an inflatable dinghy in November 2021 was caused by “individuals driven by greed, with utter disregard for human life”. Prosecutors said the convicted men helped launch a “substandard small boat, uncertified, unfit for navigation on the open sea, overcrowded and lacking appropriate lifejackets”. Emmanuel Daoud, a lawyer for one victim’s family, called the proceedings a “trial of greed, cynicism and inhumanity”. Twenty-seven people were confirmed dead when their inflatable dinghy sank in the early hours of 24 November 2021. Four people remain unaccounted for.

How Europe’s housing crisis is fuelling a new movement

It was billed as one of the largest real-estate events in Europe, attracting as many as 15,000 people ranging from investment firms to developers. But as the District trade show and summit got under way last week in Madrid, housing campaigners from 140 organisations across the globe turned up, intent on holding their own “counter-summit” to push back against the idea of housing as a financial asset. Many of the campaigners arrived in the Spanish capital as Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman who uses a wheelchair, was being evicted from the apartment where she had lived for seven decades. As anger over the eviction gave way to days of protests and an encampment in the heart of Madrid, the presence of campaigners from Italy to Ireland was a poignant reminder of the global dimension of the crisis. The eviction underscored how brutal access to housing had become for so many around the world, said Teresa Mamede, a housing campaigner from Lisbon who travelled to Madrid for the counter-summit.

How Europe’s housing crisis is fuelling a new movement

“Nobody among us is safe from having this happen to them.” The Guardian has long reported on the depth of the housing crisis across Europe. Within the EU, prices soared by 53% between 2010 and 2024, according to Eurostat, while rents increased 25% over the same period. Not all countries have been hit equally; while Vienna remains a bright spot for its ample stock of public housing that has tempered rental costs, Estonia has seen rents surge 208% in the same time period, while Ireland and Hungary have seen increases of more than 100%. Some of the soaring costs can be chalked up to the “ever-intensifying social experiment” playing out in Europe, research fellow Tim White noted last year, as officials see whether the machinations of finance capitalism can deliver on the fundamental need for housing. “The evidence now seems overwhelming: no.” Instead, vulnerable people and minorities have been disproportionately affected by the market’s shortcomings, while others warn that the crisis could drive voters into the arms of the far right.

“We cannot remain stuck in the rhetoric of defending democracy, inclusive societies and equal opportunities if people’s standard of living is getting worse,” Jaume Collboni, the mayor of Barcelona, told me last year. Samba the capybara is still at large. Along with her older sister, Tango, the intrepid rodent made her escape from Marwell zoo in Winchester in March. Tango all but gave herself up on day two; Samba broke for the marshy wetlands of the River Itchen. Word spread and within days the fugitive was an international social media star. But despite an intense search, the dense Hampshire countryside has afforded her a haven. Six months on, Samba remains elusive. Marwell’s staff still aren’t sure how the capybaras escaped, although they have their suspicions. Tango and Samba were born on Jimmy’s Farm and Wildlife Park in Suffolk in the summer of 2025. They arrived at Marwell zoo on Monday 16 March, to great excitement. “They were a little bit shy when they got here, as you would expect,” says Laura Read, the chief executive of Marwell Wildlife. “But they were fine.” They were immediately placed in a quarantined habitat, as is standard procedure for new arrivals. The plan was to keep them there for 30 days. The next day, the vet and zookeepers did their morning checks and everything was fine.

On the makeshift workbench in the cramped front room of a cottage near the frontlines of the Russia-Ukraine war, there are all the accoutrements of a drone workshop. The walls are lined with pliers and rolls of duct tape; the table is cluttered with screwdrivers and piles of wire. Propped up against the wall are two kamikaze drones. Only one item looks out of place in this Ukrainian village house: a pot of Chinese longjing tea, the leaves wilted from repeated top-ups. Good tea is one of the many things that Tim misses about his life in China. His parents post monthly supplies to Ukraine. “I think about all of it,” the 44-year-old said, of his home country. “It brings back memories and emotions.” Tim’s teapot at the drone workshop Tim, who asked to be referred to by his English name, is the lead volunteer in a Ukrainian military unit that this year launched an unusual project: to recruit soldiers from the country seen as Russia’s biggest backer, China. Many Ukrainian military units have their own brands and public presences as they compete with each other for funding and new recruits.

One of the pilots of a plane flying from the United Arab Emirates to Israel stabbed his fellow pilot and appeared to try to crash the aircraft, the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has said, as Israeli officials said they were investigating whether the incident was an attempted terror attack on Israelis. Eyewitnesses reported chaos onboard the flydubai flight, as the attacker tried to barricade himself and the wounded pilot in the cockpit, and then attempted to disable the controls, forcing the plane to descend 17,000 feet in just two minutes. Passenger Yaniv Hayoun later recounted how he and other passengers heard screaming and felt pressure as the plane dived before forcing their way into the cockpit and finding the attacker at the instrument panel. “I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and dragged him out first,” Hayoun said during a meeting with Netanyahu after the plane had landed safely and the passengers were flown to Israel.

An independent commission set up by the Swedish state has called on the country’s government to apologise for the “harm and injustice inflicted upon the Sami people” and to start a national process for “redress and reconciliation”. Tokyo succumbs to ‘rain fatigue’ after a record 35 consecutive days of showers

Residents of Tokyo awoke to a familiar sound on Wednesday: raindrops splashing against windows and balcony floors. The Japanese capital has seen a record 35 consecutive days of rain that experts blame on a combination of climate change and El Niño, which has created a prolonged front of high pressure in the Pacific Ocean. The record rainfall has triggered a sharp rise in the price of vegetables, cast a shadow over tourism and left millions of Tokyoites wondering if they will see sunshine again. Central Tokyo has been drenched by 629mm (24.8 inches) of rain between the start of September through to Monday this week, nearly three times the normal level, according to the agency. It experienced just 45.8 hours of sunshine over the same period, the second lowest on record, the Mainichi Shimbun said, while on 14 days the sun did not appear at all.

What we know so far about alleged stabbing of pilot by co-pilot on flight to Israel

One of the pilots of a plane flying from the UAE to Israel stabbed his co-pilot and appeared to try to crash the plane, the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said, as Israeli officials said they were investigating whether the incident was an attempted terror attack on Israelis. Here is what we know so far: A commercial plane travelling from Dubai in the United Arab Emirates to Israel was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, after an apparent brawl between its pilots prompted distress signals that briefly raised fears of an attempted hijacking. The flydubai flight was over Jordan when it diverted to Saudi Arabia, transmitting three emergency signals, one of which indicated a possible unlawful interference. The plane dipped dramatically during the reported fight, descending about 16,000ft in just two minutes. Israeli officials scrambled fighter jets, fearful of a possible hijacking attempt on a plane containing dozens of Israelis, and the plane landed at Tabuk airport in north-western Saudi Arabia.

What legacy do we leave behind when we die? As Sam Neill taught me, it’s more about sweetness than ego

Occasionally, in our lives, there are markers that arrive with enough strength to hop us off the treadmill just long enough to remind ourselves that everyone’s race has a finish line, and none of us are getting out of this jolly for free. One of these blots is often when someone we know passes away. I always find the saddest part of a funeral the idea that the deceased will never hear the nice words being shared around the room in that moment. Our online world has enhanced this grieving process with posthumous accolades flowing from friends and strangers alike, creating yet more space for others to add comment as well. These modern outpourings help shape a fuller picture of the person we’ve just lost and what that person meant to others. The recent death of the New Zealand acting legend Sam Neill is one such marker for so many of us. It was in the outpouring of words for Sir Sam after his death that we got a better glimpse of the person behind the actor, and a wonderful mosaic of a life properly lived.

Zomi Frankcom did not deserve to die. Israel’s refusal to investigate her death and its failure to apologise is despicable

Zomi Frankcom did not deserve to die. She and her six colleagues were traveling in a clearly marked humanitarian convoy to distribute food to starving Palestinians on a route that had been communicated well in advance to the Israel Defense Forces (IDF). It bombed them deliberately and repeatedly. Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, announced the next day that the attack was a “mistake” and a few days later its two commanders were forced to retire, and three others were disciplined. An internal inquiry followed, but this week – well over two years later – the IDF announced that there would be no further investigation because there could be no suspicion that any crime had been committed: it was merely a mistake. This is a serious misunderstanding of the law of war.

The crime of manslaughter in Australian and English law reflects this grave level of criminality. In war law, under article 8 of the statute of the international criminal court (ICC) “intentionally launching an attack in the knowledge that such an attack will cause loss of life to civilians” and “directing attacks against personnel or vehicles involved in humanitarian assistance” are serious war crimes which may be committed by mistakes made through negligence or blind eyes turned to their foreseeable consequences. The IDF decision not to investigate Zomi’s killing on the grounds that it was merely a “mistake” is not a legitimate reason and the Israeli government’s refusal even now to apologise is despicable.

Friedrich Merz is now on borrowed time. But that’s not why the AfD’s triumph is seismic

As shock at the scale of the far right’s resounding state-election victory in Germany reverberated on Sunday, not everybody was unhappy. Seconds after the first exit polls from Saxony-Anhalt were revealed, Donald Trump posted the results on his Truth Social platform, seemingly delighted by the devastation of the centrist-conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) and the surge of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD). It was indeed a humiliation for the CDU chancellor, Friedrich Merz, whose party lost more than half of its seats in the state parliament, while the AfD increased its count from 23 to 39. This was the exact opposite of what Merz promised to deliver when campaigning for office. With good government under his guidance, he insisted, he would easily cut the AfD in half. The AfD’s co-leaders did not miss the opportunity to point out the historic upset in their victory speeches, with Alice Weidel even boasting the CDU would “never win an election again”.

Friedrich Merz is now on borrowed time. But that’s not why the AfD’s triumph is seismic

Leaving the AfD’s swagger aside, this is a political earthquake with consequences far beyond a little state in the centre of Germany. The shock waves are still coming. To begin with, it is unclear if (and for how long) Merz can hold his own coalition together and cling to the chancellorship. True, the losses in the state of Saxony-Anhalt are not directly his fault. But that is only because he is so unpopular that his own party did not want him to campaign. Merz’s face was not on any posters, and when he visited the state capital, Magdeburg, the public was carefully excluded. That says it all about his standing in his own party. Two more elections are coming up on 20 September, in Berlin and the Baltic coastal state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. On the current trajectory, the CDU is looking at two more debacles. Merz’s leadership has become a liability, and it will be contested sooner rather than later. For now, only the absence of a convincing alternative and the many constitutional hurdles against sudden leadership changes in Germany protect him.

Friedrich Merz is now on borrowed time. But that’s not why the AfD’s triumph is seismic

He is the public face of a crisis of confidence in Germany’s leadership, but he is not its sole cause. The seismic nature of this moment goes far beyond party tactics. Germany is entering a period of political upheaval in which the core values of the postwar republic are up for dispute. Most shockingly, this extends to the anti-fascist consensus of “never again”, established over decades in many heated debates on the Holocaust and the crimes of the Wehrmacht. The AfD has managed to attack the national consensus that facing up to the Nazi past is fundamental for democracy in Germany. The party’s message is the opposite: the culture of remembrance is an “identity disorder” holding Germany back. It’s a central tenet of the AfD’s platform that it can “heal” the country by relativising its guilt and focusing on German greatness instead. This is why Charlotte Knobloch, a 93-year-old Holocaust survivor and former chair of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, expressed “horror” about the results.

Knobloch said she “struggled, on days like these, to recognise my homeland”, adding: “In my worst nightmares, I could not have imagined that rightwing extremists win elections again in this manner.” She is right to be alarmed. The Saxony-Anhalt state chapter of the AfD is confirmed by domestic intelligence to be among the most radical nationally. Hardcore former neo-Nazis sit in influential positions. A distinctive trait of Germany’s far right compared with France or Italy is often overlooked. The AfD is markedly different from other rightwing populist parties in Europe: it is becoming ever-more radical the closer it gets to power. The leadership in Magdeburg employs several former members of prohibited neo-Nazi groups. These people might soon serve in high offices in the state, controlling the police, the domestic spy service (Verfassungsschutz), the judiciary and education. It’s a sign of the deterioration of political norms in my country that this shocking outlook hardly figured in the aftermath of the election. The German taboo about hard-right extremists in executive office is crumbling.

Friedrich Merz is now on borrowed time. But that’s not why the AfD’s triumph is seismic

The AfD slogans against the mainstream parties (“Altparteien”) have a distinctly Weimar vibe, echoing hateful propaganda against the despised “system” from a century ago. It is no coincidence that books on the end of the Weimar republic are bestsellers these days. The AfD is not a normal party. It must be understood as a (counter)revolutionary movement trying to change the system from within. Its leaders’ ambitions go beyond this or that policy change. Look at the crucial topic of migration: the number of asylum applications is rapidly falling (down by 48% in July 2026 compared with the same month last year), partly due to restrictive measures by Merz’s government. Still, the hard right is growing and radicalising at the same time. At the core is the idea of a German ethnostate with as few foreigners as possible. The party’s rallying cry of “remigration” targets not just “illegals” but all immigrants (and their descendants) with unwanted foreign backgrounds. The leadership have coined a term for what they do not want to become: they vow to avoid “Melonisierung” (Meloni-isation).

Giorgia Meloni, despite her neo-fascist roots, surprised many at home and abroad by moving towards the mainstream, by standing with Ukraine and supporting the eurozone, Nato and the principle of free movement within the EU. The AfD, by contrast, promises to leave the EU and eurozone and put an end to the Schengen agreement. It is fiercely pro-Russian and wants to cut any support for Ukraine (including sending refugees back). Fear of escalation with Russia played a big part in the election. The recent hybrid attacks on Leipzig airport and other infrastructure may have tipped the scales: Merz had pointed a finger at Russia and vowed to “make the perpetrators pay”. This turned out to be perfect fodder for the AfD’s campaign. Abandoning Ukraine, rapprochement with Russia, reopening the Nord Stream pipeline in the Baltic – all this was presented as a “policy of peace”. This is also an election win for Vladimir Putin. What’s next? Without an absolute majority, the AFD may depend on the cooperation of a tiny splinter party.

The leadership of the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which broke away from the hard-left Die Linke, may want to help. They represent a new brand of leftist nationalism which is fiercely anti-immigrant and pro-Russian – and in that sense compatible with the AfD. Still, forming a government in Magdeburg will not be plain sailing. And it is a long way from this point for the AfD to take Berlin. One glimmer of light is that civil society is mobilising, now the initial shock has worn off. We can expect big demonstrations in major cities. A silent anti-fascist majority is beginning to organise. But it will be hard to break the dark spell that this victory in a troubled state has cast over the political landscape in Germany. One thing is certain: the coming weeks will be a challenge to the political imagination, not just for Germans.
